lessons.title: Identity is not equality
lessons.summary: Predict how aliases and copies behave.
body: A variable names an object. Assignment binds another name; it does not copy the object. Mutating a shared list is visible through every alias.
Equality asks whether values compare equal. Identity asks whether two references point to the same object. Use `is` for sentinels such as None, and `==` for values.
A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares its nested objects. Choose a deep copy only when you actually need independent nested mutable state.
lessons.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)
print(a)
print(a is b)
lessons.challenge: Change the example so that appending to b[0] leaves a unchanged.
lessons.solution:
import copy
a = [[1], [2]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0].append(3)
print(a)
lessons.question: After a shallow copy of a nested list, which objects are independent?
options: Only the outer list
Every nested object
No objects
Only immutable elements
lessons.explanation: The new outer list stores references to the original nested objects.

lessons.title: Iterators remember their position
body: An iterable can provide an iterator. The iterator supplies values through next() and eventually raises StopIteration.
A generator suspends execution at yield and resumes with its local state intact. It is usually single-pass. Laziness saves storage, but it does not make a previously consumed generator restart.
Use a generator for streaming transforms, and materialize a list when consumers need repeated traversal.
lessons.code:
g = (x * x for x in range(3))
print(list(g))
print(list(g))
lessons.challenge: Write a generator function yielding the first n squares.
lessons.question: What does a second list(g) return after fully consuming a generator?
options: The same values
An empty list
A copy of the generator
A TypeError
lessons.explanation: The generator is exhausted; a new instance is needed to iterate again.

lessons.title: Concurrency needs suspension points
lessons.summary: Separate cooperative async tasks from CPU parallelism.
body: Calling an async function creates a coroutine. It runs when awaited or scheduled as a task.
An event loop can switch to other tasks when a coroutine suspends. Blocking calls inside a coroutine still block the loop.
asyncio is useful for overlapping waiting. CPU-bound work needs a suitable executor or process strategy; merely adding async does not parallelize it.
lessons.code:
import asyncio
async def work(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return n * 2
async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(work(2), work(3)))
asyncio.run(main())
lessons.challenge: Run three waiting tasks concurrently and print their results.
lessons.solution:
import asyncio
async def task(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return n
async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(*(task(n) for n in range(3))))
asyncio.run(main())
lessons.question: What happens when time.sleep() runs directly inside an asyncio coroutine?
options: The event loop is blocked
It becomes a background thread
All tasks become parallel
It returns a Future
lessons.explanation: A synchronous sleep blocks its thread, including the event loop on that thread.

lessons.title: Read shapes from the right
lessons.summary: Check broadcasting before writing vectorized code.
body: NumPy compares shapes from the trailing dimensions. A pair of dimensions is compatible when sizes match or one is 1. Missing leading dimensions behave as 1.
Broadcasting expresses repetition without manually building repeated arrays. It is about compatible shapes, not matching the number of elements.
Adding a (3, 1) column and a (1, 4) row produces a (3, 4) grid. State intended axes explicitly to avoid a computation that runs but means the wrong thing.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(3).reshape(3, 1)
b = np.arange(4).reshape(1, 4)
print((a + b).shape)
print(a + b)
lessons.challenge: Subtract each column mean from a 2D array without a Python loop.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 6.]])
print(x - x.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True))
lessons.question: What shape results from (3, 1) + (1, 4)?
options: An error
lessons.explanation: Each size-1 dimension expands to match its corresponding non-1 dimension.

lessons.title: A slice can share memory
body: Basic slicing generally returns a view. Mutating that view can mutate the source array.
Advanced indexing generally returns a copy. Do not infer ownership just from whether two arrays look different.
Use copy() to make independence explicit, and shares_memory() when investigating memory relationships.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)
lessons.challenge: Create an independent slice before changing its first element.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3].copy()
b[0] = 99
print(a)
lessons.question: What does basic NumPy slicing generally return?
options: A view
A deep copy
A Python list
A generator
lessons.explanation: The view can refer to the original storage.

lessons.title: Axis means the dimension you reduce
lessons.summary: Predict reductions and preserve useful dimensions.
body: For a 2D array, reducing axis 0 combines rows for each column. Reducing axis 1 combines columns for each row.
keepdims=True retains a size-1 dimension at the reduced axis. This often makes later broadcasting unambiguous.
Shapes are part of the contract of numerical code. Check them alongside values, especially when writing batch computations.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(x.sum(axis=0))
print(x.sum(axis=1))
lessons.challenge: Normalize each row by its row sum, preserving a dimension for broadcasting.
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print(x / x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
lessons.question: For a 2D array, axis=0 produces sums for each…
options: Column
Row
Individual cell
Diagonal
lessons.explanation: The row dimension is reduced, leaving one value per column.

lessons.title: Labels and positions are different
body: loc selects by labels. iloc selects by integer positions. An integer index label does not automatically mean a row position.
Label slices with loc include their end label when present; positional slices with iloc follow Python’s usual excluded-stop convention.
Assign through a single loc operation. Avoid relying on chained assignment behavior, which also interacts with pandas copy-on-write semantics.
lessons.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=[100, 200, 300])
print(s.loc[200])
print(s.iloc[1])
lessons.challenge: Select rows with score >= 2 and assign their flag to True using loc.
lessons.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"score": [1, 2, 3], "flag": [False]*3})
df.loc[df["score"] >= 2, "flag"] = True
print(df)
lessons.question: Which selector uses integer positions?
options: loc
iloc
Both always
Neither
lessons.explanation: iloc selects by position regardless of the labels in the index.

lessons.title: Validate the relationship before joining
body: A join can multiply rows when keys are duplicated on both sides. This is valid many-to-many behavior, but it may violate the relationship you intended.
merge(validate=...) checks an expected cardinality such as one_to_one or many_to_one. Use indicator=True to inspect matched and unmatched rows.
Check key uniqueness and null handling before interpreting aggregates after a join.
lessons.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1], "x": [2, 3]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1], "y": [4, 5]})
print(len(a.merge(b, on="id")))
lessons.challenge: Join repeated event IDs to unique account IDs with a many_to_one check.
lessons.solution:
import pandas as pd
events = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2]})
accounts = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["A", "B"]})
print(events.merge(accounts, on="id", validate="many_to_one"))
lessons.question: Two rows with key 1 on each side produce how many matching rows?
lessons.explanation: Each left matching row pairs with each right matching row.

lessons.title: Aggregation shrinks; transform aligns
lessons.summary: Use the right shape for grouped results.
body: groupby().agg() produces results per group. groupby().transform() returns a result aligned with the original rows.
Use transform when you want to attach a group statistic to every row, such as each item’s deviation from its group mean.
Before assigning a grouped result, ask whether you need one row per group or one value per original observation.
lessons.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["A", "A", "B"], "score": [1, 3, 9]})
df["centered"] = df["score"] - df.groupby("team")["score"].transform("mean")
print(df)
lessons.challenge: Add each team’s total to every original row.
lessons.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["A", "A", "B"], "score": [1, 3, 9]})
df["total"] = df.groupby("team")["score"].transform("sum")
print(df)
lessons.question: Which operation returns results aligned with the original rows?
options: agg
transform
drop_duplicates
A cross join
lessons.explanation: transform broadcasts a group result back to its original rows.

lessons.title: Fit preprocessing on training data
body: A scaler, imputer, or feature selector learns information when fitted. Fitting it before splitting allows evaluation data to influence the model-building process.
Place preprocessing and the estimator in a Pipeline. Cross-validation then fits the complete pipeline separately inside each training fold.
Even unsupervised preprocessing can leak information. Treat every learned transformation as part of the model.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
print(model)
lessons.challenge: Build a pipeline with a median imputer and logistic regression.
lessons.solution:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
print(make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), LogisticRegression()))
lessons.question: Where should preprocessing be fitted during cross-validation?
options: On the entire dataset
Inside each training fold
Only on the test set
It never needs fitting
lessons.explanation: The validation fold must not influence learned preprocessing.

lessons.title: Accuracy can hide the wrong failure
lessons.summary: Choose metrics that match the cost of mistakes.
body: With rare positives, predicting only the majority class can achieve high accuracy while finding none of the cases you care about.
Precision describes how many predicted positives are correct. Recall describes how many actual positives were found.
Select a threshold and metric using validation data, guided by the cost of false positives and false negatives. Keep the final test set for evaluation.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score
y = [1, 1, 0, 0]
p = [1, 0, 1, 0]
print(precision_score(y, p), recall_score(y, p))
lessons.challenge: Compute recall when one of three actual positives is found.
lessons.solution:
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score
print(recall_score([1, 1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0, 0]))
lessons.question: Which metric answers “How many actual positives did we find?”
options: Precision
Recall
Accuracy
Specificity
lessons.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by actual positives.

lessons.title: Choose splits that resemble deployment
body: Random splits assume examples can be mixed without violating the deployment setting. That fails for future prediction when later observations reveal information about earlier ones.
Use time-aware splits for temporal prediction, and group-aware splits when several rows come from the same person, device, or other entity.
Hyperparameters are chosen with validation or cross-validation. Repeatedly choosing them based on the test score turns the test set into training feedback.
lessons.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
import numpy as np
for train, test in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=3).split(np.arange(8)):
    print(train.tolist(), test.tolist())
lessons.challenge: Explain which splitter you would use for multiple records per patient.
lessons.solution:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
print(GroupKFold(n_splits=3))
lessons.question: What split is suitable when patient IDs repeat across rows?
options: A random row split
A group-aware split
Sort by label then split
Use every row in every fold
lessons.explanation: Keeping each patient within a single side avoids leakage between correlated records.

lessons.title: Gradients accumulate until cleared
lessons.summary: Understand each stage of a training step.
body: backward() accumulates gradients in leaf tensors that require them. It does not automatically clear previous gradients.
A common training step clears gradients, computes predictions and loss, runs backward(), then steps the optimizer.
Zeroing to None can avoid unnecessary writes and distinguish missing gradients from zero-valued gradients.
lessons.code:
import torch
x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
(x*x).backward()
print(x.grad.item())
(x*x).backward()
print(x.grad.item())
lessons.challenge: Clear x.grad before the second backward call.
lessons.solution:
import torch
x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
(x*x).backward()
x.grad = None
(x*x).backward()
print(x.grad.item())
lessons.question: Without clearing, what does a second backward call do to leaf gradients?
options: Replaces them
Accumulates them
Deletes them
Moves them to a GPU
lessons.explanation: backward adds the new contribution to existing gradients.

lessons.title: Evaluation mode and no-grad do different jobs
lessons.summary: Separate layer behavior from autograd tracking.
body: model.eval() changes modules such as dropout and batch normalization to evaluation behavior. It does not disable gradient recording.
no_grad() disables gradient recording in its scope. inference_mode() offers a stricter inference context with additional restrictions.
For typical inference, set evaluation mode and use an appropriate inference context. Return to train() before training again.
lessons.code:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Dropout(p=0.5)
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    print(model(torch.ones(4)))
lessons.challenge: Run a small linear layer with eval and inference_mode.
lessons.solution:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Linear(2, 1)
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    print(model(torch.ones(1, 2)))
lessons.question: Does model.eval() disable autograd?
options: Yes, for all tensors
No
Only on the CPU
Only for parameters
lessons.explanation: eval changes module behavior; autograd is controlled separately.

lessons.title: Treat tensor shapes as contracts
lessons.summary: Check batch and feature dimensions explicitly.
body: A linear layer transforms the last dimension. For input (batch, features), Linear(features, outputs) produces (batch, outputs).
Broadcasting can silently make a loss compare the wrong elements. Check predicted and target shapes before computing it.
Reshape may return a view or copy depending on layout. Do not assume reshaping guarantees independent storage.
lessons.code:
import torch
layer = torch.nn.Linear(3, 2)
x = torch.ones(4, 3)
print(layer(x).shape)
lessons.challenge: Create five examples with four features and a layer producing one output.
lessons.solution:
import torch
x = torch.ones(5, 4)
print(torch.nn.Linear(4, 1)(x).shape)
lessons.question: Linear(3, 2) applied to a (4, 3) tensor returns which shape?
lessons.explanation: The last feature dimension is transformed, preserving the batch dimension.

lessons.title: Lifetime owns cleanup
lessons.summary: Use destructors to make resource release dependable.
body: RAII ties resource lifetime to an object. Construction acquires or establishes ownership, and destruction releases it.
Stack unwinding destroys fully constructed local objects when an exception leaves their scope. Destructors should generally not throw.
Prefer unique_ptr for exclusive heap ownership, and use shared_ptr only when shared ownership is part of the design.
lessons.challenge: Own a dynamic integer with unique_ptr, then move ownership to another variable.
lessons.question: Which smart pointer models exclusive ownership?
options: shared_ptr
unique_ptr
weak_ptr
A raw pointer always
lessons.explanation: unique_ptr expresses one owner and transfers ownership through moves.

lessons.title: Moving permits resource transfer
lessons.summary: A cast does not itself move a resource.
body: std::move casts an expression to an rvalue reference. It enables overload resolution to select a move operation.
Whether resources actually move depends on the selected constructor or assignment operator. A const source may still lead to copying.
A moved-from standard library object is generally valid but has an unspecified value unless a stronger guarantee is documented. Do not assume a moved-from string is empty.
lessons.challenge: Move a vector into a second vector and print the second vector’s size.
lessons.question: What does std::move itself do?
options: Transfers bytes
Deletes the source
Casts to an rvalue reference
Allocates new memory
lessons.explanation: The selected move constructor or assignment performs any transfer.

reading.title: C++ copy construction · LearningLad
reading.note: Review copying before comparing it with moves.

reading.title: Smart pointers · Hayden Smith
reading.note: Study unique_ptr ownership before running this lesson’s transfer example. For the precise role of std::move, use the lesson and current references.

lessons.title: Thread safety requires a memory model
lessons.summary: Shared writes need a synchronization strategy.
body: A data race involves conflicting operations in different threads, at least one a write, without the required synchronization and with non-atomic access. In C++, a data race yields undefined behavior.
A mutex protects a compound invariant when every relevant access follows the same locking discipline. An atomic protects its own operations; it does not automatically protect a larger data structure.
Choose synchronization based on the invariant first. Avoid guessing that relaxed atomic ordering makes a compound protocol correct.
lessons.challenge: Use lock_guard to protect a counter increment.
lessons.question: What is the language-level consequence of a C++ data race?
options: Only a stale read
Undefined behavior
Automatic locking
A compiler warning always
lessons.explanation: The program no longer has defined behavior under the C++ memory model.

lessons.title: A query may execute later
lessons.summary: Understand deferred execution before mutating inputs.
body: Many LINQ operators return a deferred sequence. Enumeration executes the query, which can reflect the source state at enumeration time.
ToList() materializes results at that point. Use it when you need a snapshot or want to avoid repeating an expensive traversal.
Not every LINQ operation is deferred. Terminal operators such as Count() generally compute their result when called.
lessons.challenge: Materialize the query before adding another source element.
lessons.question: What typically turns a deferred LINQ query into a snapshot?
options: Where
Select
ToList
AsEnumerable
lessons.explanation: ToList enumerates immediately and stores the resulting elements.

lessons.title: A Task is a handle to completion
lessons.summary: Await asynchronous work without blocking the caller.
body: Task represents eventual completion, possibly with a result. await asynchronously waits and resumes when the task completes.
async does not automatically create a new thread. Asynchronous I/O can complete without dedicating a blocked thread to each operation.
Prefer async Task over async void except for event handlers. Task-returning methods allow callers to await completion and observe exceptions.
lessons.challenge: Await two tasks using Task.WhenAll.
lessons.question: Which return type usually lets callers observe asynchronous errors?
options: void
Task
int only
IEnumerable only
lessons.explanation: Callers can await a Task and receive exceptions from it.

lessons.title: Resource lifetime is explicit
body: Garbage collection reclaims managed memory. It does not guarantee timely release of an unmanaged resource such as a file handle.
A using statement or declaration disposes an IDisposable object when its scope ends, including exceptional exits.
Use await using for IAsyncDisposable resources whose cleanup is asynchronous.
lessons.challenge: Read two lines from a StringReader inside a using scope.
lessons.question: What does using guarantee for IDisposable?
options: Immediate garbage collection
Disposal at scope exit
A new thread
Immutable contents
lessons.explanation: The generated cleanup calls Dispose even when the scope exits through an exception.

lessons.title: Slices describe shared storage
lessons.summary: Track length, capacity, and the backing array.
body: A slice is a descriptor for an underlying array segment. Copying a slice value copies that descriptor, not the elements.
append may reuse capacity or allocate a new backing array. Aliasing behavior can therefore change after an append.
Use make and copy to create independent storage when that is part of your function’s contract.
lessons.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
 a := []int{1,2,3}; b := a[:2]
 b[0] = 9
 fmt.Println(a)
}
lessons.challenge: Copy a slice so that modifying the copy does not change the original.
lessons.question: What does assigning a Go slice value copy?
options: All elements
The slice descriptor
The entire backing array
Nothing at all
lessons.explanation: The new descriptor can refer to the same backing array.

lessons.title: An interface can hold a typed nil
lessons.summary: Separate interface emptiness from its dynamic value.
body: An interface value carries a dynamic type and a dynamic value. It equals nil only when both are absent.
An interface holding a nil pointer still has a dynamic type, so the interface itself is not nil.
This often appears when returning a typed nil pointer as an error. Return a literal nil when there is no error.
lessons.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
 var p *int = nil
 var x any = p
 fmt.Println(p == nil, x == nil)
}
lessons.challenge: Explain why the interface prints false when compared to nil.
lessons.question: Is an interface holding a typed nil pointer equal to nil?
options: Always
No
Only on 64-bit systems
Only before a type assertion
lessons.explanation: Its dynamic type is present even though the stored pointer is nil.

lessons.title: Channels coordinate progress
lessons.summary: Know which sends can block and who closes.
body: An unbuffered send requires a receiving operation to rendezvous. Buffered sends can proceed until the buffer is full.
Closing a channel signals that no more values will be sent. Receivers can drain buffered values, then observe the closed state.
The sending side generally owns closing. Sending to a closed channel panics; receiving from a closed, drained channel yields a zero value with ok=false.
lessons.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
 ch := make(chan int, 1)
 ch <- 7; close(ch)
 v, ok := <-ch; fmt.Println(v,ok)
 v, ok = <-ch; fmt.Println(v,ok)
}
lessons.challenge: Start a producer goroutine that sends three values, closes, and lets main range over them.
lessons.question: What happens on a send to a closed channel?
options: It returns false
It panics
It silently discards
It reopens the channel
lessons.explanation: Sending after closure is a programming error and panics.

lessons.title: A closure retains access to bindings
body: A closure retains access to the lexical environment in which a function was created. It captures bindings, not a frozen snapshot of every value.
An inner function can therefore observe a later update to a captured variable. Separate closure instances can retain independent environments.
Block-scoped let declarations make each for-loop iteration binding distinct in the common closure-over-loop pattern.
lessons.challenge: Create two counters and show that their states are independent.
lessons.question: What does a closure retain access to?
options: Only copied constants
Its lexical bindings
Only global variables
A new thread
lessons.explanation: Bindings in its lexical environment remain accessible.

lessons.title: Promise reactions run after synchronous code
body: Promise callbacks are scheduled as microtasks after the current synchronous work completes.
await suspends the async function while allowing its caller and other work to proceed. Awaiting an already resolved promise still resumes asynchronously.
For several independent operations, Promise.all waits for all results and rejects if an input rejects. It does not itself start a function that has not been called.
lessons.challenge: Await two resolved promises together and print the results.
lessons.solution:
const results = await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(2), Promise.resolve(3)]);
console.log(results);
lessons.question: What is the output order of the example?
options: A B C
B A C
A C B
C B A
lessons.explanation: The synchronous A and C execute before the promise reaction B.

lessons.title: Identity matters for reference values
lessons.summary: Separate coercion, value equality, and object identity.
body: === compares without type coercion. For objects, arrays, and functions, it compares identity rather than structural content.
Two array literals with the same elements are different objects. To compare contents, define the equality appropriate to your data.
Object.is differs from === for NaN and signed zero. Choose the comparison that matches the intended semantics.
lessons.challenge: Compare two short arrays element by element.
lessons.solution:
const a=[1,2], b=[1,2];
console.log(a.length === b.length && a.every((x,i) => x === b[i]));
lessons.question: Why is [1] === [1] false?
options: Arrays cannot be compared
Different object identities
1 is coerced to text
An exception is thrown
lessons.explanation: The two literals create distinct array objects.

lessons.title: Ownership makes lifetime visible
lessons.summary: Map C++ value semantics onto Rust moves.
body: Each value has an owner responsible for its lifetime. A non-Copy value such as String is typically moved when assigned to another binding.
After a move, the old binding cannot be used as if it still owned the value. clone() explicitly duplicates data when the type supports it.
This resembles exclusive ownership in C++, but Rust checks many invalid uses before execution. Small Copy values such as integers behave differently from String.
lessons.challenge: Keep first usable by cloning it into second, then print both.
lessons.question: After moving a String from first into second, can first still be used?
options: Yes, always
No, unless reinitialized appropriately
Only in debug builds
Only when the string is short
lessons.explanation: The first binding no longer owns the moved value.

lessons.title: Borrow access without taking ownership
lessons.summary: Learn shared and exclusive reference rules.
body: A shared reference borrows read access. A mutable reference borrows exclusive access to the value for its active lifetime.

At a given time, you can have multiple shared references or one mutable reference to the same value. The compiler tracks when borrows are actually used, so their active lifetimes may end before a block ends.
Think of &T as temporary access and &mut T as temporary exclusive access. Neither automatically transfers ownership.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that appends ! through a mutable String reference.
lessons.question: Which accesses can coexist to the same value during their active lifetimes?
options: Two mutable references
A mutable and shared reference
Several shared references
Any references with any writes
lessons.explanation: Shared references permit concurrent read access; a mutable reference requires exclusivity.

lessons.title: Make missing values and failures explicit
body: Option<T> represents a value that may be absent. Result<T, E> represents success or a failure value.
match handles variants explicitly and is checked for exhaustiveness. The ? operator propagates compatible errors from a Result-returning function.

Prefer an explicit failure contract over panicking with unwrap() when failure is expected input behavior. This connects naturally to Go’s returned errors, but Rust’s enums encode the alternatives in one type.
lessons.challenge: Parse a number in a function returning Result and propagate the parse error with ?.
lessons.question: Which type expresses success or a failure value?
options: Option<T>
Result<T, E>
&mut T
usize
lessons.explanation: Result has Ok and Err variants.

reading.title: Rust video course
reading.note: freeCodeCamp.org / Arfan Zubi (2023). Pair this chapter with current Rust documentation.

lessons.title: Expressions return values
lessons.summary: Begin with immutable bindings and inference.
body: An OCaml let binding gives a name to a value. A function definition uses the same expression-oriented style, and types are often inferred.
Function application uses spaces rather than a parenthesized argument list. A function of several arguments can be partially applied to produce another function.
Unlike a Python reassignment, a later let with the same name creates a new binding. Prefer immutable data transformations until mutation is a deliberate requirement.
lessons.challenge: Define a function multiplying two integers, then partially apply it to make a double function.
lessons.question: What is the result of partially applying add 2?
options: An error
A function waiting for the other argument
The integer 2
A mutable reference
lessons.explanation: A curried function can return another function after receiving one argument.

lessons.title: Describe alternatives with variants
lessons.summary: Replace fragile flags with explicit cases.
body: A variant type names the possible alternatives of a value. Each constructor can carry different data.
Pattern matching inspects the constructor and extracts its data. Exhaustiveness checking helps reveal missing cases.
Compared with a collection of booleans and optional fields, a variant can make invalid combinations impossible to represent. Rust enums share this useful idea.
lessons.code:
type shape = Circle of float | Rectangle of float * float
let area = function
 | Circle r -> Float.pi *. r *. r
 | Rectangle (w, h) -> w *. h
let () = Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (area (Rectangle (3., 4.)))
lessons.challenge: Add a Square constructor carrying a side length and handle it in area.
lessons.solution:
type shape = Circle of float | Rectangle of float * float | Square of float
let area = function
 | Circle r -> Float.pi *. r *. r
 | Rectangle (w,h) -> w *. h
 | Square s -> s *. s
let () = Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (area (Square 3.))
lessons.question: What useful property does an exhaustive match provide?
options: Every constructor has a handled case
Every function is tail-recursive
All values are mutable
No allocation occurs
lessons.explanation: Matching each possible alternative prevents an omitted constructor case.

lessons.title: Lists are built from head and tail
body: An OCaml list is either empty or a head element followed by another list. Pattern matching mirrors that recursive structure.
Tail recursion places the recursive call in the final return position. An accumulator can make a computation tail-recursive.
Prepending with :: is efficient. Repeatedly appending to the end can make a list-building algorithm unnecessarily expensive.
lessons.code:
let rec sum acc = function
 | [] -> acc
 | x :: xs -> sum (acc + x) xs
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (sum 0 [1; 2; 3])
lessons.challenge: Implement a tail-recursive list length with an accumulator.
lessons.question: Which expression constructs a list by prepending x to xs?
options: x + xs
x :: xs
xs(x)
x && xs
lessons.explanation: :: is the list constructor for a head and a tail.

lessons.title: Lean is also a programming language
lessons.summary: Start with typed functions before proofs.
body: Lean 4 supports functional programming as well as theorem proving. A definition uses a name, typed parameters, a result type, and an expression.
Natural numbers Nat are non-negative integers. A program can evaluate pure definitions with #eval.
Your OCaml and Rust work with typed functions transfers here. The later step is to express a claim about a function as a type and construct a term proving it.
lessons.code:
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n
#eval double 7
lessons.challenge: Define square on Nat and evaluate square 5.
lessons.solution:
def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
#eval square 5
lessons.question: What does #eval ask Lean to do?
options: Check a theorem without running anything
Evaluate an expression
Create an axiom
Import every Mathlib module
lessons.explanation: #eval computes an expression and displays its result.

lessons.title: A proof is a term of a proposition
body: A theorem states a proposition and supplies a term inhabiting that proposition. Lean checks the term against the claimed type.
For a hypothesis h : P, the term h itself proves P. Tactic mode lets you build proof terms through commands such as intro and exact.
A proof exercise must not count an accepted sorry as mastery: Lean can accept a placeholder with a warning. Completion should require a checked proof without placeholders or unapproved axioms.
lessons.code:
theorem identity (P : Prop) : P → P := by
  intro h
  exact h
lessons.challenge: Prove P → Q → P by introducing both assumptions and returning the proof of P.
lessons.solution:
theorem keep_left (P Q : Prop) : P → Q → P := by
  intro hp hq
  exact hp
lessons.question: Given h : P, which tactic can close a goal P?
options: exact h
intro P always
#eval P
sorry as a completed proof
lessons.explanation: h is already a term of the proposition required by the goal.

lessons.title: Definitional equality can close simple goals
lessons.summary: Know when rfl is enough and when a theorem is needed.
body: rfl closes a goal when both sides are definitionally equal after Lean’s reductions.
Not every mathematically true equality is definitional. Some require rewriting, simplification, or induction using established theorems.
When a tactic fails, inspect the goal and hypotheses before trying random commands. The proof-state panel is part of the learning experience.
lessons.code:
def increment (n : Nat) : Nat := n + 1
example : increment 2 = 3 := by
  rfl
lessons.challenge: Prove that evaluating your double function at 3 yields 6.
lessons.solution:
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n
example : double 3 = 6 := by
  rfl
lessons.question: When is rfl typically sufficient?
options: For all true equations
When both sides are definitionally equal
Only with Mathlib
Only for floating point values
lessons.explanation: Reflexivity works when reduction makes the sides the same.

lessons.title: A type parameter keeps relationships explicit
lessons.summary: Reuse one definition without erasing its types.
body: A generic definition names a type parameter instead of choosing one concrete type. The same parameter in several positions means those positions must agree for a particular call.
The body must work under the declared constraints. An unconstrained T cannot be compared or printed just because the eventual caller uses integers.
Returning Option<&T> lets this function borrow an element and represent an empty slice without copying it. The borrow still obeys the input's lifetime.
lessons.challenge: Write a generic second function that returns None when the slice has fewer than two elements.
lessons.question: Without a trait bound, what must the body of a generic function assume about T?
options: Only the operations permitted by its declared constraints
That T is an integer
That every T can be printed
That T has a default constructor
lessons.explanation: The compiler checks the generic definition under its declared constraints, rather than assuming the capabilities of a particular caller's type.

lessons.title: A trait bound states the required behavior
lessons.summary: Separate an interface from a particular representation.
body: A trait names behavior that implementing types provide. Implementing the trait for a type supplies those methods; it does not require that the type inherit a data layout.
A generic trait bound such as T: Weight allows the body to call the trait's methods. This is a useful bridge from C# interfaces and C++ constrained templates.
The function below borrows each parcel. Computing its weight does not consume the parcel, and different implementations can supply the same interface.
lessons.challenge: Implement Weight for a Crate whose weight includes both its contents and its packaging.
lessons.question: What does T: Weight allow the generic total function to do?
options: Read every private field of T
Call the behavior required by Weight
Treat T as a subclass of Parcel
Skip borrow checking
lessons.explanation: The bound supplies the trait contract; it does not expose an implementing type's fields or bypass ownership rules.

lessons.title: Iterator adapters wait for a consumer
lessons.summary: Choose borrowing, mutation, or ownership before chaining.
body: Iterator adapters such as map and filter build a lazy computation. A consumer such as collect or sum asks it to produce results.
For a Vec, iter borrows elements, iter_mut borrows them mutably, and into_iter takes ownership of the vector's elements. Choose that relationship before writing a pipeline.
Here copied turns borrowed integers into copied values. The original vector remains available because the pipeline began with iter.
lessons.challenge: Use iter_mut to double every element in place, then print the updated vector.
lessons.question: For a Vec<T>, which iterator takes ownership of its elements?
options: iter()
iter_mut()
into_iter()
All three always
lessons.explanation: Calling into_iter on the owned vector consumes it; iter and iter_mut borrow instead.

lessons.title: A lifetime annotation describes a borrow relationship
body: A lifetime parameter relates references in a signature. It tells the checker which input borrows constrain an output borrow; it does not keep an object alive for longer.
When either input might be returned, the caller must be able to use both inputs for the lifetime required by the returned reference. The annotation expresses that shared constraint.
Many simple signatures use lifetime elision. Adding annotations cannot make a reference to a local temporary safe to return.
lessons.challenge: Write a first_word function borrowing from one input. Let lifetime elision connect the result to that input.
lessons.question: Can a lifetime annotation extend the life of a local String so a reference to it can be returned?
options: Yes, if named 'a
Yes, if the result is a string slice
No; it describes constraints rather than extending storage
Yes, with any generic parameter
lessons.explanation: An annotation cannot prevent the local value from being dropped when its scope ends.

lessons.title: Move transfers data; join waits for work
body: A spawned thread can outlive the scope that started it. An ordinary spawned closure therefore needs captures that meet the thread API's lifetime and Send requirements.
A move closure takes ownership of captures such as this vector. That solves the capture's ownership problem, but does not wait for the thread to finish.
Joining waits for completion and returns a Result containing the thread's returned value or panic information. Here the main thread prints only after joining, making the output deterministic.
lessons.challenge: Move a vector to a worker that counts even values. Join it and print the count.
lessons.question: Which operation waits for the spawned thread's completion?
options: The move keyword
Creating a Vec
Calling join on its handle
Importing std::thread
lessons.explanation: move determines how captures enter the closure; join supplies the synchronization with completion.

lessons.title: Turn an expected behavior into a check
lessons.summary: Use assertions while keeping test scope honest.
body: An assertion checks a concrete behavior and panics when the expectation fails. Check boundary cases as well as an ordinary happy path.
Rust's unit-test harness normally discovers functions marked #[test] through cargo test or rustc --test. Running a main program alone does not run those test functions.

The mobile lab currently runs a single program. These examples put assertions in main so the current execution contract actually exercises them. Passing selected cases still does not prove the function correct for every input.
lessons.challenge: Write a slice total and check both an empty slice and a non-empty slice before printing success.
lessons.question: Does running a normal main program automatically execute every #[test] function?
options: Always
Only if main returns zero
No; the test harness must be used
Only for tests in the same file
lessons.explanation: The ordinary program entry point and Rust's test harness are separate execution paths.

lessons.title: Record update creates a new value
lessons.summary: Name fields while making changes explicit.
body: A record groups named fields with declared types. Fields are immutable unless their declaration explicitly marks them mutable.
The with syntax constructs a new record using existing fields as defaults. It does not mutate the original record.
This is a shallow update: if a field refers to mutable storage, that storage can still be shared. Here both the integer and string fields are immutable values.
lessons.challenge: Write extend that returns a session with five extra minutes, leaving the input value unchanged.
lessons.question: What does { original with minutes = 15 } do for this immutable record?
options: Mutate original
Create a new record with that field replaced
Deep-copy every reachable object
Convert it to a variant
lessons.explanation: Record update builds a new record; it does not promise a deep copy of any referenced mutable values.

lessons.title: A type variable connects a function's positions
body: A polymorphic function can be used with different concrete types at different calls. Repeating a type variable within one function type records a relationship between positions.
For apply_twice, the argument function must return the same type that it accepts, because its first result becomes its next input.
Type inference is static checking, not a request to treat values as dynamically typed. Some definitions, particularly those involving mutable state, face restrictions on generalization.
lessons.challenge: Write compose f g x = f (g x), then compose String.length with String.uppercase_ascii.
lessons.question: Which type fits apply_twice f x = f (f x)?
options: int -> string
Every argument has an unrelated type
lessons.explanation: The output of f is used as another input to f, so those two types must agree.

lessons.title: The accumulator carries the computation
lessons.summary: Trace a fold instead of guessing its order.
body: A fold combines each list element with an accumulator. fold_left passes the current accumulator first; fold_right passes the current element first.
For non-associative operations such as subtraction, direction and argument order change the result. Write out the nested calls when reasoning about them.
Building a list by prepending to a fold_left accumulator reverses the order. Use that deliberately rather than assuming every fold preserves order.
lessons.code:
let values = [1; 2; 3]
let left = List.fold_left ( - ) 0 values
let right = List.fold_right ( - ) values 0
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" left right
lessons.challenge: Implement reverse with List.fold_left and ::, then print the reversed values separated by commas.
lessons.question: Which calculation describes List.fold_left ( - ) 0 [1; 2; 3]?
lessons.explanation: fold_left threads the accumulator from the left, making each intermediate result the next first argument.

lessons.title: A signature can hide a representation
lessons.summary: Expose operations while keeping a type abstract.
body: A module groups types and values. A signature describes what clients may see and use.
Writing type t in a signature without revealing its definition makes the representation abstract outside that interface. Clients must use the exported constructors and operations.
The implementation below uses int, but a client cannot assume Counter.t is int. This lets the implementation change while preserving its public contract.
lessons.code:
module Counter : sig
  type t
  val zero : t
  val next : t -> t
  val value : t -> int
end = struct
  type t = int
  let zero = 0
  let next n = n + 1
  let value n = n
end
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (Counter.value (Counter.next Counter.zero))
lessons.challenge: Add a reset operation to the signature and implementation, then reset an incremented counter.
lessons.solution:
module Counter : sig
  type t
  val zero : t
  val next : t -> t
  val reset : t -> t
  val value : t -> int
end = struct
  type t = int
  let zero = 0
  let next n = n + 1
  let reset _ = zero
  let value n = n
end
let () =
  let count = Counter.next (Counter.next Counter.zero) in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (Counter.value (Counter.reset count))
lessons.question: Can a client pass the integer 3 directly to Counter.value through this abstract signature?
options: Yes, because the implementation uses int
No, because Counter.t is abstract to the client
Only when compiled
Only when 3 is positive
lessons.explanation: The exported signature hides the equality between Counter.t and int.

lessons.title: A functor takes a module as its input
body: An OCaml functor maps a module satisfying an input signature to a result module. This is different from a map operation on a collection.
Use a functor when several definitions should depend on the same supplied types or operations. The module signature specifies the required dependency.
Here two applications can provide different offsets while reusing the implementation. The returned modules have their own exported names.
lessons.code:
module type Offset = sig val amount : int end
module Shift (O : Offset) = struct
  let apply n = n + O.amount
end
module PlusFive = Shift (struct let amount = 5 end)
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (PlusFive.apply 7)
lessons.challenge: Apply Shift twice to produce PlusTwo and PlusTen, then apply both to 7.
lessons.solution:
module type Offset = sig val amount : int end
module Shift (O : Offset) = struct
  let apply n = n + O.amount
end
module PlusTwo = Shift (struct let amount = 2 end)
module PlusTen = Shift (struct let amount = 10 end)
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (PlusTwo.apply 7) (PlusTen.apply 7)
lessons.question: What is the input to Shift in this example?
options: A single integer argument
A list of integers
A module satisfying Offset
A string naming a file
lessons.explanation: Shift is a functor whose parameter is a module exposing amount : int.

lessons.title: Expected failures can travel as values
body: The result type distinguishes Ok carrying a success value from Error carrying a failure value. Pattern matching makes the two paths visible.
For an expected validation failure, returning a result lets a caller choose how to report or recover. Exceptions remain useful for other error-handling designs.
Result.map changes the successful value and preserves an Error. Result.bind is for a next operation that can itself return a result.
lessons.challenge: Double a valid parsed number using Result.map while preserving an invalid input's Error.
lessons.question: What does Result.map do when its input is Error message?
options: Run the mapping function on message
Preserve the Error without mapping the success value
Throw an exception automatically
Replace it with Ok 0
lessons.explanation: The mapping function applies only to the Ok branch.

lessons.title: Pattern matching follows the constructors
lessons.summary: Compute by handling every shape of an input.
body: An inductive type describes values through constructors. Nat has zero and successor cases; pattern matching gives the computation for each case.
The successor pattern n + 1 binds the predecessor n. It is a pattern for a natural number's constructor shape, not a general equation solver.
Recursive calls must satisfy Lean's termination requirements. Structural recursion on the predecessor is a natural starting point before proving properties about a recursive definition.
lessons.code:
def remaining : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => n
#eval remaining 4
lessons.challenge: Define twiceBySteps recursively: return 0 at zero and add 2 for each successor. Evaluate it at 3.
lessons.solution:
def twiceBySteps : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => 2 + twiceBySteps n
#eval twiceBySteps 3
lessons.question: In the successor pattern n + 1, what does n represent?
options: A proof of addition
The predecessor of the matched natural number
Any unrelated natural number
Only the constant zero
lessons.explanation: The branch receives the predecessor from the successor constructor.

lessons.title: Conjunction needs evidence for both sides
lessons.summary: Build and use a pair of proofs.
body: A proof of P ∧ Q contains evidence for P and evidence for Q. Given h : P ∧ Q, h.1 and h.2 select those two proofs.
To construct a conjunction, supply both components, for example ⟨hp, hq⟩. In tactic mode, constructor creates the corresponding subgoals.
A conjunction differs from a disjunction: proving P ∨ Q requires choosing and proving one side, while a conjunction needs both.
lessons.code:
theorem swapBoth (P Q : Prop) : P ∧ Q → Q ∧ P := by
  intro h
  exact ⟨h.2, h.1⟩
lessons.challenge: Prove P → Q → P ∧ Q by introducing both assumptions and constructing the conjunction.
lessons.solution:
theorem keepBoth (P Q : Prop) : P → Q → P ∧ Q := by
  intro hp hq
  exact ⟨hp, hq⟩
lessons.question: Given h : P ∧ Q, which term proves Q?
options: P itself
A proof of either side chosen at random
lessons.explanation: The second projection selects the proof of Q from the conjunction.

lessons.title: A universal proof can be applied
lessons.summary: Distinguish evidence for every input from one witness.
body: A proof of ∀ n, P n behaves like a function taking n and returning evidence for P n. Apply it to a particular argument to get the corresponding proof.
An existential proof, ∃ n, P n, instead packages one witness together with evidence that the witness satisfies P.
When introducing a universal variable, it is arbitrary: checking a few numerical examples does not establish the universally quantified proposition.
lessons.code:
theorem atFive (P : Nat → Prop) (hEvery : ∀ n, P n) : P 5 := by
  exact hEvery 5
lessons.challenge: From h : P 4, construct a proof that there exists a natural number satisfying P.
lessons.solution:
theorem hasWitness (P : Nat → Prop) (h : P 4) : ∃ n, P n := by
  exact ⟨4, h⟩
lessons.question: What must be supplied to construct a proof of ∃ n, P n?
options: A witness n and evidence for P n
Evidence only for ∀ n, False
The type Nat without a value
A list of tested values without proofs
lessons.explanation: The existential constructor packages a particular witness with the proof of its property.

lessons.title: An equality can change the current goal
lessons.summary: Choose the direction of a rewrite.
body: Given h : a = b, rw [h] rewrites matching occurrences of a to b. The reverse direction, rw [← h], uses b = a.
Inspect the goal before and after a rewrite. Rewriting uses an equality theorem; it does not assert that every mathematically equal expression is definitionally identical.
If the transformed sides coincide, reflexivity can close the goal. For larger expressions, more rewrites or simplification may still be needed.
lessons.code:
example (a b : Nat) (h : a = b) : a + 2 = b + 2 := by
  rw [h]
lessons.challenge: Use h : a = b in the reverse direction to prove b + 3 = a + 3.
lessons.solution:
example (a b : Nat) (h : a = b) : b + 3 = a + 3 := by
  rw [← h]
lessons.question: What is the direction of rw [← h] when h : a = b?
options: a to b
b to a
Both directions simultaneously
It changes h to False
lessons.explanation: The left arrow requests the symmetric direction of the supplied equality.

lessons.title: Induction mirrors a recursive definition
lessons.summary: Use a smaller case to prove the next case.
body: Induction on a natural number creates a zero case and a successor case. In the successor case, the induction hypothesis describes the proposition for the predecessor.
A recursive function's defining equations often determine the proof steps: unfold the current case, use the induction hypothesis, and simplify.
The induction hypothesis is a proof for the smaller case, not permission to assume the final theorem for every value. Check the exact hypothesis and remaining goal.
lessons.code:
def tally : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => tally n + 1
theorem tallySelf (n : Nat) : tally n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ n ih => simp [tally, ih]
#eval tally 4
lessons.challenge: Define zeros n as a list of n zeroes and prove that its length is n by induction.
lessons.solution:
def zeros : Nat → List Nat
  | 0 => []
  | n + 1 => 0 :: zeros n
theorem zerosLength (n : Nat) : (zeros n).length = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ n ih => simp [zeros, ih]
#eval (zeros 3).length
lessons.question: In the successor case of this induction, what does ih describe?
options: The proposition for the predecessor n
The final result without conditions
Only the zero case
A runtime test output
lessons.explanation: The induction principle supplies evidence for the smaller case, which is used to prove the successor case.

lessons.title: A structure groups named fields
lessons.summary: Build a value and project its components.
body: A structure groups fields under a named type. Lean generates a constructor and field projections; dot notation lets you access fields from a value.
Record update constructs a new structure value with selected fields replaced. The original immutable value remains available.
Fields can also include proof obligations, but plain Nat fields do not automatically enforce a relationship such as completed ≤ total. State and prove an invariant when your design requires it.
lessons.code:
structure Progress where
  completed : Nat
  total : Nat
def start : Progress := { completed := 2, total := 5 }
#eval start.completed
lessons.challenge: Define advance returning a new Progress with completed incremented. Check the old and new counts.
lessons.question: Does this Progress declaration by itself guarantee completed ≤ total?
options: Yes, because both fields are Nat
No; the relationship needs its own constraint or proof
Yes, because it is a structure
Only after #eval
lessons.explanation: The field types restrict each value individually but do not impose the relationship between the fields.

lessons.title: Compilation and linking solve different problems
lessons.summary: Source practice · Compilation and linking solve different problems
body: A translation unit is preprocessed and compiled; the linker resolves definitions across object files. Headers expose declarations. Build settings and the selected language standard are part of reproducibility. Defining ordinary non-inline functions in shared headers can violate the one-definition rule.
lessons.workedExample: Two files both include a header defining the same ordinary external function. Compilation may succeed but linking can fail with duplicate definitions.
lessons.challenge: Divide a greeting function between a header, an implementation, and a caller. Explain which file needs the definition.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Put its declaration in the header, its definition in one source file, and include the header at the call site. Link both source files' object files.
lessons.question: What does a declaration provide?
options: An interface a caller can compile against
A new process
A guarantee of an inline definition
lessons.explanation: Put its declaration in the header, its definition in one source file, and include the header at the call site. Link both source files' object files.

lessons.title: Initialization and qualifiers carry a contract
lessons.summary: Source practice · Initialization and qualifiers carry a contract
body: Types determine representation and allowed operations. A reference aliases an existing object; a pointer may be null or reseated. const constrains access through a particular expression. Brace initialization rejects certain narrowing conversions; automatic variables of fundamental type still need deliberate initialization.
lessons.workedExample: int count; does not initialize an ordinary local count to zero. int count{} does.
lessons.challenge: Explain const int*, int* const, and why reading an uninitialized ordinary local int is invalid.
lessons.practiceAnswer: const int* prevents writes through that pointer; int* const prevents reseating the pointer. Reading an indeterminate ordinary local int does not produce a valid assumed zero.
lessons.question: Which declaration explicitly initializes a local int to zero?
options: int count;
extern int count;
int count{};
lessons.explanation: const int* prevents writes through that pointer; int* const prevents reseating the pointer. Reading an indeterminate ordinary local int does not produce a valid assumed zero.

lessons.title: Container choice changes invalidation
lessons.summary: Source practice · Container choice changes invalidation
body: vector stores contiguous elements; reallocation can invalidate pointers, references, and iterators to its elements. array has fixed size; string owns character storage. Iterators mark positions, and end marks a boundary rather than an element.
lessons.workedExample: Keeping a pointer into a vector and then growing it may leave the pointer dangling after reallocation.
lessons.challenge: Compare vector and list for indexed access and stable element references. Explain a safe way to revisit a vector element after growth.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use vector for efficient indexed access and locality. A list offers different reference stability but no constant-time indexed access. Keep an index and reacquire the vector element after mutation, provided the intended element's position remains valid.
lessons.question: Can vector reallocation invalidate element references?
options: Only if values are strings
Never
Yes
lessons.explanation: Use vector for efficient indexed access and locality. A list offers different reference stability but no constant-time indexed access. Keep an index and reacquire the vector element after mutation, provided the intended element's position remains valid.

lessons.title: Construction establishes a valid invariant
lessons.summary: Source practice · Construction establishes a valid invariant
body: A class should make invalid states difficult to create. Members initialize in declaration order, regardless of initializer-list order. Prefer member initializers for simple defaults and use constructors when validation or dependencies require work.
lessons.workedExample: A pointer member initialized from another member can be invalid if its dependency is declared later.
lessons.challenge: Design a range class requiring start <= end and explain where to reject invalid input.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Validate in the constructor or a factory before publishing the object. Declare dependent members after the members they depend on. Preserve the invariant in every mutating operation.
lessons.question: What determines member initialization order?
options: Alphabetical member names
Their declaration order
Initializer-list text order
lessons.explanation: Validate in the constructor or a factory before publishing the object. Declare dependent members after the members they depend on. Preserve the invariant in every mutating operation.

lessons.title: Streams report state as well as data
lessons.summary: Source practice · Streams report state as well as data
body: Stream extraction can fail without yielding a valid value. eof, fail, and bad represent different states. A robust loop checks the extraction operation. Formatting flags can persist, while width commonly applies to the next formatted insertion.
lessons.workedExample: while (input >> number) processes only successful reads. A loop based solely on !eof() can try to use an invalid final read.
lessons.challenge: Design a line-based numeric parser that rejects trailing non-space text.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Read a complete line, parse it with an istringstream, confirm extraction succeeded, then confirm only whitespace remains. Return an explicit failure rather than reusing an old value.
lessons.question: What should control a formatted read loop?
options: The success of extraction
Only !eof() before reading
The previous stored value
lessons.explanation: Read a complete line, parse it with an istringstream, confirm extraction succeeded, then confirm only whitespace remains. Return an explicit failure rather than reusing an old value.

lessons.title: Algorithms separate traversal from storage
lessons.summary: Source practice · Algorithms separate traversal from storage
body: Standard algorithms operate on iterator ranges with stated requirements. A half-open range excludes its end. erase-remove uses an algorithm to partition retained values and a container operation to change size. Comparators must satisfy their ordering contract.
lessons.workedExample: remove moves retained vector elements forward but leaves the vector's size unchanged until erase is called.
lessons.challenge: Describe how to remove all even integers and why a comparator using <= is unsuitable for ordinary sorting.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use erase with the range returned by remove_if, or a supported erase_if facility. A sort comparator needs strict ordering; <= reports an element less than itself.
lessons.question: Does std::remove shrink a vector?
options: Yes, immediately
Only when values are unique
No
lessons.explanation: Use erase with the range returned by remove_if, or a supported erase_if facility. A sort comparator needs strict ordering; <= reports an element less than itself.

lessons.title: Copy control defines a value's ownership
lessons.summary: Source practice · Copy control defines a value's ownership
body: Copying an owner needs a deliberate policy: independent ownership, shared ownership, or disallowed copying. The rule of zero uses members whose own types manage resources. A moved-from object's permitted use follows its type contract rather than a universal empty-state assumption.
lessons.workedExample: A class holding unique_ptr is noncopyable by default. A class holding vector normally obtains safe copy and move behavior from that member.
lessons.challenge: Design an owning buffer without manual new/delete and state its copy semantics.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Store a vector of bytes and rely on its value semantics. Copies own independent element storage; moves follow vector's contract. If copying must be forbidden, delete it explicitly.
lessons.question: What is the rule-of-zero preference?
options: Delegate lifetime to resource-managing members
Implement every special member manually
Allocate every member with new
lessons.explanation: Store a vector of bytes and rely on its value semantics. Copies own independent element storage; moves follow vector's contract. If copying must be forbidden, delete it explicitly.

lessons.title: Operator syntax should match the value model
lessons.summary: Source practice · Operator syntax should match the value model
body: Overloading changes behavior for permitted operators, not their precedence or operand count. Assignment and compound assignment should have coherent return and mutation contracts. Free functions permit symmetric conversions where a member-only operator may not.
lessons.workedExample: A += b changes a and normally returns a reference to it; a + b should normally produce a separate result.
lessons.challenge: Specify prefix and postfix increment for a small counter and explain their different return values.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Prefix increments and returns the updated object by reference. Postfix takes an unused int parameter, saves the old value, increments, and returns the saved value.
lessons.question: What does conventional postfix increment return?
options: The dummy int parameter
The previous value
Always a reference to the updated value
lessons.explanation: Prefix increments and returns the updated object by reference. Postfix takes an unused int parameter, saves the old value, increments, and returns the saved value.

lessons.title: Subscript, call, and arrow need explicit lifetimes
lessons.summary: Source practice · Subscript, call, and arrow need explicit lifetimes
body: operator[] models element access; operator() models calling an object; operator-> supports member access through a pointer-like interface. Accessors must state bounds, const behavior, and the lifetime of returned references. These operators cannot make destroyed storage valid.
lessons.workedExample: A subscript returning a reference into a temporary owner leaves a dangling reference after the temporary dies.
lessons.challenge: Design a callable multiplier and a checked two-element subscript interface. State how const access differs.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Store the multiplier factor and return factor*x from operator(). Check bounds for the custom subscript, return an element reference from a live owner, and provide const access that prevents writes.
lessons.question: What property must a returned element reference satisfy?
options: Its storage remains alive for its use
Its index is always zero
It is copied by every read
lessons.explanation: Store the multiplier factor and return factor*x from operator(). Check bounds for the custom subscript, return an element reference from a live owner, and provide const access that prevents writes.

lessons.title: Exception safety is an operation contract
lessons.summary: Source practice · Exception safety is an operation contract
body: Stack unwinding destroys completed automatic objects. Catch exceptions by const reference when appropriate. A basic guarantee preserves invariants; a strong guarantee leaves state unchanged on failure. Destructors should not let exceptions escape during unwinding.
lessons.workedExample: Updating two related fields and throwing between them can violate a class invariant even if no memory leaks.
lessons.challenge: Plan a strong-guarantee replacement operation and explain rethrowing from a catch block.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Prepare the new value without changing the old state, then commit with an appropriate nonthrowing operation. Use throw; to rethrow the current exception without slicing it.
lessons.question: What does the strong exception guarantee promise?
options: Failure leaves the operation's state unchanged
No operation can ever throw
Every exception terminates the program
lessons.explanation: Prepare the new value without changing the old state, then commit with an appropriate nonthrowing operation. Use throw; to rethrow the current exception without slicing it.

lessons.title: File operations need a format and failure policy
lessons.summary: Source practice · File operations need a format and failure policy
body: RAII closes streams, but opening, reading, writing, flushing, and finalizing can fail. Text and binary modes are not an application format. Serializing raw object bytes can embed pointers, padding, and machine-specific representation.
lessons.workedExample: Writing sizeof(object) bytes from a class with a string member does not serialize that string's text.
lessons.challenge: Specify a portable file record for a name and count, including version, encoding, lengths, and truncated-input behavior.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use an explicit format with a version, UTF-8 text, fixed-width integer encoding, defined byte order, and checked lengths. Reject incomplete records rather than treating them as valid defaults.
lessons.question: Does a binary-mode stream define a portable object format?
options: Yes if sizeof is known
No
Yes for every class
lessons.explanation: Use an explicit format with a version, UTF-8 text, fixed-width integer encoding, defined byte order, and checked lengths. Reject incomplete records rather than treating them as valid defaults.

lessons.title: Preprocessing performs token transformation
lessons.summary: Source practice · Preprocessing performs token transformation
body: Macros do not obey ordinary function evaluation or scope rules. A function-like macro may evaluate an argument more than once. Include guards prevent repeated header inclusion; conditional compilation selects source before compilation. Prefer typed functions and constexpr values where possible.
lessons.workedExample: A square macro expanding x*x can mis-handle a+b without parentheses and can evaluate side effects twice even with parentheses.
lessons.challenge: Replace a numeric square macro and describe a legitimate use for conditional compilation.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use a typed or constrained function for square. Conditional compilation can select a platform-specific declaration, with each selected path built and checked separately.
lessons.question: Why can a function-like macro be risky?
options: It may repeat argument evaluation
It automatically validates types
It executes only once at runtime
lessons.explanation: Use a typed or constrained function for square. Conditional compilation can select a platform-specific declaration, with each selected path built and checked separately.

lessons.title: Names and linkage organize a program
lessons.summary: Source practice · Names and linkage organize a program
body: Namespaces group names and avoid collisions. An unnamed namespace gives internal linkage within a translation unit. A namespace alias shortens a qualified name. A global using directive in a public header pollutes clients' lookup environment.
lessons.workedExample: Including a header with using namespace std changes unqualified lookup in the including file.
lessons.challenge: Organize a library namespace, a private source-file helper, and a public class split across header and implementation.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Put the public class in a named namespace, the private helper in an unnamed namespace in the source file, and include a guarded declaration header. Keep client lookup explicit.
lessons.question: Where is an unnamed namespace helper normally visible?
options: Only inside main
Within its translation unit
Across every linked library automatically
lessons.explanation: Put the public class in a named namespace, the private helper in an unnamed namespace in the source file, and include a guarded declaration header. Keep client lookup explicit.

lessons.title: Templates compile a family of typed operations
lessons.summary: Source practice · Templates compile a family of typed operations
body: A template's operations must be valid for each instantiated type. Type deduction and overload resolution select implementations under specific rules. Concepts describe requirements and can improve diagnostics. Template definitions normally need to be visible when instantiated.
lessons.workedExample: A template using + accepts types supporting the required addition; it does not imply every type has numeric meaning.
lessons.challenge: Design a reusable sum operation and state its requirement and identity value.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Require a compatible addition operation and a deliberate initial value. Decide whether heterogeneous elements or narrowing conversions are allowed; use a concept or explicit contract rather than assuming all types behave alike.
lessons.question: When must required template operations be valid?
options: For the chosen instantiation
Only when the template is first written
Never if auto is used
lessons.explanation: Require a compatible addition operation and a deliberate initial value. Decide whether heterogeneous elements or narrowing conversions are allowed; use a concept or explicit contract rather than assuming all types behave alike.

lessons.title: Dynamic dispatch needs a lifetime contract
lessons.summary: Source practice · Dynamic dispatch needs a lifetime contract
body: Virtual functions dispatch through a base interface. Deleting a derived object through a base pointer ordinarily requires a virtual base destructor. Copying a derived value into a base value slices away the derived part. Ownership and polymorphic behavior are separate choices.
lessons.workedExample: A vector of base objects cannot preserve every derived object's extra state merely because a method is virtual.
lessons.challenge: Choose a storage model for heterogeneous shapes and explain how destruction remains safe.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use owning smart pointers to a base with a suitable virtual destructor, or an explicit value-oriented alternative such as variant. Document whether copying is supported through cloning or disallowed.
lessons.question: What can copying a derived object into a base value cause?
options: Object slicing
Automatic deep cloning
A shared ownership cycle
lessons.explanation: Use owning smart pointers to a base with a suitable virtual destructor, or an explicit value-oriented alternative such as variant. Document whether copying is supported through cloning or disallowed.

lessons.title: Work scheduling needs shutdown and backpressure
lessons.summary: Source practice · Work scheduling needs shutdown and backpressure
body: A pool bounds active workers, but its queued work also needs bounds. Cancellation is cooperative unless the operation supports another mechanism. Shutdown must define how queued and running tasks finish, propagate failure, and release captured resources.
lessons.workedExample: A two-worker pool deadlocks if both workers block waiting for tasks queued behind them in the same pool.
lessons.challenge: Design shutdown for a bounded task pool and a policy for nested tasks.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Stop accepting work, choose drain or cancellation for queued tasks, signal workers, and join them. Avoid blocking workers on dependent work that requires exhausted workers; support a different scheduling strategy or nonblocking continuation.
lessons.question: Can a worker pool still deadlock?
options: Only if it has one worker
Yes
No, because workers are reused
lessons.explanation: Stop accepting work, choose drain or cancellation for queued tasks, signal workers, and join them. Avoid blocking workers on dependent work that requires exhausted workers; support a different scheduling strategy or nonblocking continuation.

lessons.title: TCP provides an ordered byte stream
lessons.summary: Source practice · TCP provides an ordered byte stream
body: TCP sequences bytes, acknowledges progress, retransmits when necessary, and controls flow and congestion. It does not preserve the boundaries of application writes. A received prefix is not automatically a complete application message.
lessons.workedExample: Two send calls of three bytes can arrive as one six-byte read or several shorter reads.
lessons.challenge: Design a length-prefixed protocol that handles partial headers and payloads safely.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Accumulate the fixed-size header, validate the length against a limit, then accumulate exactly that payload length. Handle EOF and errors without accepting truncated messages.
lessons.question: Does one TCP read necessarily match one sender write?
options: Yes
Only when writes are small
No
lessons.explanation: Accumulate the fixed-size header, validate the length against a limit, then accumulate exactly that payload length. Handle EOF and errors without accepting truncated messages.
