lessons.title: Cargo separates packages, crates, and targets
lessons.summary: Source practice · Cargo separates packages, crates, and targets
body: A package is a Cargo-managed project containing targets; a crate is a compilation unit. A lockfile records resolved dependency versions under the project's policy. Features select compile-time capabilities and should be checked in supported combinations.
lessons.workedExample: A package can expose a library target and a binary target that calls it. A single-file playground does not reproduce every package feature.
lessons.challenge: Plan a small library with a binary client and describe the commands to check, test, and build it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Keep reusable functions in the library and the entry point in the binary. Use cargo check, cargo test, and cargo build under a recorded toolchain and dependency policy. Multifile project work requires a project runner, not a single-file slot.
lessons.question: What is a Rust crate?
options: A compilation unit
Every function
A runtime thread
lessons.explanation: Keep reusable functions in the library and the entry point in the binary. Use cargo check, cargo test, and cargo build under a recorded toolchain and dependency policy. Multifile project work requires a project runner, not a single-file slot.

lessons.title: Mutability and shadowing are distinct
lessons.summary: Source practice · Mutability and shadowing are distinct
body: let introduces a binding; mut permits assignment through that binding. Shadowing introduces another binding and can change its type. const values require a type and a constant-compatible expression. A block is an expression whose final expression can supply its value.
lessons.workedExample: let input = "12"; let input = input.len(); shadows a string slice binding with a usize binding.
lessons.code: fn main() { let input = "12"; let input = input.len(); println!("{}", input); }
lessons.challenge: Explain the type and value after that shadowing, then contrast reassignment through mut.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The new input is a usize with value 2. Reassignment through a mutable binding must keep that binding's type; shadowing can introduce a different type.
lessons.question: Can shadowing change the binding's type?
options: Yes
No
Only inside unsafe
lessons.explanation: The new input is a usize with value 2. Reassignment through a mutable binding must keep that binding's type; shadowing can introduce a different type.

lessons.title: Numeric conversions need a range policy
lessons.summary: Source practice · Numeric conversions need a range policy
body: Integer width and signedness affect representation. as casts follow specified conversion behavior rather than universally checking for overflow. TryFrom expresses a fallible conversion. char is a Unicode scalar value, while a byte is an eight-bit value.
lessons.workedExample: Converting 300 to u8 with a narrowing as cast does not produce a checked success of 300.
lessons.code: fn main() { println!("{:?}", u8::try_from(300_i32)); println!("{:?}", u8::try_from(42_i32)); }
lessons.challenge: Choose a conversion from i32 input to u8 when out-of-range values should be rejected.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use u8::try_from(input) and handle the Result. Reject negative or greater-than-255 values explicitly; avoid a silent narrowing cast when validation is required.
lessons.question: Which conversion expresses possible failure?
options: TryFrom
An assumption that as always checks bounds
A type alias
lessons.explanation: Use u8::try_from(input) and handle the Result. Reject negative or greater-than-255 values explicitly; avoid a silent narrowing cast when validation is required.

lessons.title: Expression-oriented control flow returns values
lessons.summary: Source practice · Expression-oriented control flow returns values
body: if and match can produce values when their branches agree on type. for iterates through IntoIterator; loop can return through break with a value. A semicolon commonly changes a final expression into a statement whose contribution is unit.
lessons.workedExample: let n = if flag { 4 } else { 7 }; chooses an integer. Adding a semicolon inside one branch can break the expected type.
lessons.code: fn main() { let result = (1..8).find(|n| n % 2 == 0); println!("{:?}", result); }
lessons.challenge: Design a loop returning the first even value in a bounded sequence, with an explicit missing case.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use iterator find or a loop carrying an Option result. Ensure every exit has the intended return type; do not assume the sequence contains a match.
lessons.question: What must value-producing if branches ordinarily agree on?
options: The same number of statements
The same variable names
A compatible result type
lessons.explanation: Use iterator find or a loop carrying an Option result. Ensure every exit has the intended return type; do not assume the sequence contains a match.

lessons.title: Structs, methods, and enums model different contracts
lessons.summary: Source practice · Structs, methods, and enums model different contracts
body: Struct fields combine data; impl groups inherent methods; enum variants encode alternatives. A method receiver chooses borrowed, mutable, or owned access. Pattern matching destructures values and must respect moves and borrows.
lessons.workedExample: A status enum can distinguish Pending, Ready(value), and Failed(error) without independent flags that form invalid combinations.
lessons.challenge: Choose receivers for reading a length, appending text, and consuming a buffer into bytes.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use shared borrowing for observation, mutable borrowing for updates, and owned self when the operation consumes the buffer. Match enum cases exhaustively.
lessons.question: Which receiver permits an exclusive borrowed update?
options: A shared static string
&mut self
&self
lessons.explanation: Use shared borrowing for observation, mutable borrowing for updates, and owned self when the operation consumes the buffer. Match enum cases exhaustively.

lessons.title: Collections expose ownership and invalidation through borrows
lessons.summary: Source practice · Collections expose ownership and invalidation through borrows
body: Vec owns growable storage; String owns UTF-8 bytes; HashMap owns keys and values under its type parameters. References into mutable collections constrain later mutation. String byte offsets must lie on UTF-8 boundaries; integer indexing does not supply a universal character operation.
lessons.workedExample: The string é has two UTF-8 bytes. Slicing at byte 1 is not a valid boundary for that spelling.
lessons.code: fn main() { let text = "é"; println!("{} {}", text.len(), text.chars().count()); let values = vec![4, 5]; println!("{:?}", values.first()); }
lessons.challenge: Explain how to iterate Unicode scalar values and how to safely observe a vector's optional first value.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use chars() for scalar values, with grapheme handling delegated to an appropriate library when needed. Use first() to get an Option reference and avoid mutation that conflicts with the borrow.
lessons.question: Are arbitrary String byte indices always valid UTF-8 boundaries?
options: Yes
Only for immutable strings
No
lessons.explanation: Use chars() for scalar values, with grapheme handling delegated to an appropriate library when needed. Use first() to get an Option reference and avoid mutation that conflicts with the borrow.

lessons.title: Privacy expresses an interface rather than a file layout
lessons.summary: Source practice · Privacy expresses an interface rather than a file layout
body: Modules group names and control visibility. pub exposes an item subject to its surrounding visibility; use brings paths into scope; re-exporting can provide a stable public API. Files implement module organization but are not interchangeable with crates.
lessons.workedExample: A private helper remains inaccessible to an external caller even when its source file is present in the same package.
lessons.code:
mod parser { pub fn doubled(s: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> { let n = s.parse::<i32>()?; Ok(n * 2) } }
fn main() { println!("{:?}", parser::doubled("8")); }
lessons.challenge: Design a public parser interface with private implementation helpers.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Expose the parse operation and public result types from a documented module or re-export. Keep helper functions private and test their behavior through stable interfaces where practical.
lessons.question: Does a source file's presence automatically make its items public?
options: Only for functions
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Expose the parse operation and public result types from a documented module or re-export. Keep helper functions private and test their behavior through stable interfaces where practical.

lessons.title: Expected failure and broken invariants need different policies
lessons.summary: Source practice · Expected failure and broken invariants need different policies
body: Result and Option make ordinary outcomes explicit. ? propagates compatible failure. panic reports a failure outside the ordinary return contract, with unwind or abort behavior depending on configuration. unwrap is only justified under a known invariant or explicit failure policy.
lessons.workedExample: A malformed user number is expected input failure and should not crash a service merely because parse().unwrap() was convenient.
lessons.challenge: Design a parser returning a descriptive error and explain error conversion with From.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Return Result from the parser, propagate lower-level errors through ? with a compatible conversion or explicit mapping, and retain useful context. Avoid claiming every panic can be caught under abort settings.
lessons.question: What should represent expected parse failure?
options: A fabricated valid zero
A Result error
An unconditional panic
lessons.explanation: Return Result from the parser, propagate lower-level errors through ? with a compatible conversion or explicit mapping, and retain useful context. Avoid claiming every panic can be caught under abort settings.

lessons.title: Capture mode and call traits answer different questions
lessons.summary: Source practice · Capture mode and call traits answer different questions
body: A closure can borrow or own captured values. move changes capture ownership; it does not by itself make the closure callable only once. Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce describe how calling uses the environment, with FnOnce consuming it when necessary.
lessons.workedExample: A move closure owns a String but only reads it. It can be called repeatedly if its body does not consume that String.
lessons.code: fn main() { let text = String::from("owned"); let read = move || text.len(); println!("{} {}", read(), read()); }
lessons.challenge: Compare a move closure reading a captured string with one returning that owned string.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The reading closure can support repeated calls; returning the captured owned string consumes it and requires a once-call contract. Choose bounds according to the operation rather than the presence of move.
lessons.question: Does move automatically imply only one call?
options: Only for nonempty strings
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: The reading closure can support repeated calls; returning the captured owned string consumes it and requires a once-call contract. Choose bounds according to the operation rather than the presence of move.

lessons.title: Dispatch and storage are separate choices
lessons.summary: Source practice · Dispatch and storage are separate choices
body: A generic trait bound commonly enables monomorphized code; dyn Trait represents runtime dispatch under dyn-compatibility rules. A trait object can be borrowed or owned through a pointer such as Box. Dynamic dispatch does not automatically choose shared ownership.
lessons.workedExample: A borrowed &dyn Display and an owned Box<dyn Display> both dispatch dynamically but have different lifetime and ownership contracts.
lessons.code:
use std::fmt::Display;
fn main() { let values: Vec<Box<dyn Display>> = vec![Box::new(12), Box::new("text")]; for value in values { println!("{}", value); } }
lessons.challenge: Explain when a heterogeneous list might need trait objects rather than one generic element type.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Different concrete implementations can be stored through a common dyn-compatible interface. Choose owned or borrowed storage deliberately; a single generic T represents one concrete instantiation, not arbitrary unrelated values in one vector.
lessons.question: Does dyn Trait itself imply reference counting?
options: No
Yes
Only for Display
lessons.explanation: Different concrete implementations can be stored through a common dyn-compatible interface. Choose owned or borrowed storage deliberately; a single generic T represents one concrete instantiation, not arbitrary unrelated values in one vector.

lessons.title: An associated type belongs to an implementation relationship
lessons.summary: Source practice · An associated type belongs to an implementation relationship
body: A generic parameter lets an interface be instantiated with chosen types; an associated type names a type selected by an implementation. Iterator uses Item to specify what next yields. Operator traits and formatting traits define specific behavior contracts.
lessons.workedExample: One Iterator implementation names its Item, and next returns Option<Self::Item>.
lessons.challenge: Contrast a conversion-like generic trait with an iterator's associated Item and explain Debug versus Display.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Generic target types can express distinct conversion relationships; Item describes the output selected by that iterator implementation. Debug is diagnostic formatting, while Display is a user-facing format chosen by the type.
lessons.question: What does Iterator::Item describe?
options: Its current numeric position
Every possible error type
The implementation's yielded item type
lessons.explanation: Generic target types can express distinct conversion relationships; Item describes the output selected by that iterator implementation. Debug is diagnostic formatting, while Display is a user-facing format chosen by the type.

lessons.title: Smart pointers encode different sharing and mutation policies
lessons.summary: Source practice · Smart pointers encode different sharing and mutation policies
body: Box owns a heap value; Rc shares ownership within a single-threaded setting; Arc supports atomic reference counting across suitable thread boundaries. RefCell checks borrow rules at runtime. Weak references do not keep the target alive and can help avoid reference-counted ownership cycles.
lessons.workedExample: Two Rc owners strongly referring to each other can retain the cycle after external owners disappear.
lessons.code:
use std::rc::Rc;
fn main() { let strong = Rc::new(9); let weak = Rc::downgrade(&strong); println!("{}", weak.upgrade().is_some()); drop(strong); println!("{}", weak.upgrade().is_some()); }
lessons.challenge: Design parent-child links with ownership flowing from parent to child.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use strong ownership for children and weak observing links for parents under the intended model. Upgrade a Weak when needed and handle the target's absence. Shared ownership does not by itself permit arbitrary mutation.
lessons.question: Does a Weak reference keep its target alive?
options: Only when upgraded unsuccessfully
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Use strong ownership for children and weak observing links for parents under the intended model. Upgrade a Weak when needed and handle the target's absence. Shared ownership does not by itself permit arbitrary mutation.

lessons.title: Channels and locks support different coordination models
lessons.summary: Source practice · Channels and locks support different coordination models
body: A channel transfers messages; a mutex protects shared state. Send and Sync describe type-level cross-thread safety conditions. Joining establishes a thread completion boundary; a detached thread can outlive borrowed resources unless its API rules prevent it.
lessons.workedExample: A producer sends owned jobs to a worker and drops its sender when no more jobs remain. The receiver can detect disconnection after pending messages are consumed.
lessons.challenge: Plan shutdown for several producers and a worker, including blocking and failure behavior.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Close or drop all sender handles under the API contract, drain or cancel pending work by policy, and join the worker. Bound the queue where supported and report worker failure rather than waiting indefinitely without a contract.
lessons.question: What can an extra live sender prevent?
options: All message delivery
Integer addition
Receiver disconnection detection
lessons.explanation: Close or drop all sender handles under the API contract, drain or cancel pending work by policy, and join the worker. Bound the queue where supported and report worker failure rather than waiting indefinitely without a contract.

lessons.title: A Future progresses when driven by a runtime
lessons.summary: Source practice · A Future progresses when driven by a runtime
body: Calling an async function constructs a future; polling drives it toward completion. await can suspend the current task while another progresses. The runtime and libraries determine scheduling and I/O support. Blocking work inside a task can still block an executor thread.
lessons.workedExample: An async function with a blocking sleep stalls its executor thread instead of supplying asynchronous waiting.
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between constructing a future, awaiting it, and spawning it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Construction creates the computation; await drives or cooperates in driving it within another future; spawning schedules an independent task under a runtime's API and lifetime contract. A single-file runner may lack that runtime dependency.
lessons.question: Does writing async automatically make a blocking call nonblocking?
options: Only for short calls
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Construction creates the computation; await drives or cooperates in driving it within another future; spawning schedules an independent task under a runtime's API and lifetime contract. A single-file runner may lack that runtime dependency.

reading.title: The Rust Programming Language
reading.section: 17. Fundamentals of Asynchronous Programming: Async, Await, Futures, and Streams

lessons.title: A pattern states a structural case
lessons.summary: Source practice · A pattern states a structural case
body: Patterns can destructure structs, enums, and tuples, bind references, and apply guards. Exhaustive matching keeps alternatives explicit. A guard checks an additional condition; it does not necessarily provide full exhaustiveness for the variant alone.
lessons.workedExample: Matching Some(n) if n > 0 leaves nonpositive Some values to another arm.
lessons.code:
fn label(n: Option<i32>) -> &'static str { match n { None => "missing", Some(x) if x > 0 => "positive", Some(_) => "nonpositive" } }
fn main() { println!("{} {} {}", label(None), label(Some(3)), label(Some(0))); }
lessons.challenge: Design an exhaustive classification of Option<i32> into missing, positive, and nonpositive.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Handle None, a guarded Some for positive values, and a remaining Some arm. Keep bindings and borrow/move behavior consistent with how the input is used later.
lessons.question: Does a positive-only guard handle every Some value?
options: Yes
Only with i32
No
lessons.explanation: Handle None, a guarded Some for positive values, and a remaining Some arm. Keep bindings and borrow/move behavior consistent with how the input is used later.

reading.title: Rust complete course · Arfan Zubi / freeCodeCamp

lessons.title: Unsafe creates a proof obligation for the programmer
lessons.summary: Source practice · Unsafe creates a proof obligation for the programmer
body: unsafe enables specified operations while ordinary Rust rules still apply. Raw pointers, foreign interfaces, and low-level representation require valid lifetime, alignment, aliasing, and bounds. A safe wrapper must ensure every supported caller meets those preconditions.
lessons.workedExample: A raw pointer can be non-null while pointing to freed storage. Checking only non-null does not make dereferencing it valid.
lessons.challenge: List preconditions for turning a raw pointer and length into a slice.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The region must be valid for the whole access, correctly aligned, initialized as required, within supported size limits, and obey aliasing and lifetime rules. Encapsulate and document the argument rather than scattering unsafe blocks.
lessons.question: Does unsafe disable all Rust checks?
options: No
Yes
Only inside a function
lessons.explanation: The region must be valid for the whole access, correctly aligned, initialized as required, within supported size limits, and obey aliasing and lifetime rules. Encapsulate and document the argument rather than scattering unsafe blocks.

lessons.title: Macros transform syntax under a defined interface
lessons.summary: Source practice · Macros transform syntax under a defined interface
body: Declarative macros match token patterns and expand code. Procedural macros execute compile-time transformations through a separate crate setup. Attributes supply metadata or compile-time behavior; cfg selects code. A macro is useful when ordinary functions or generics cannot express the syntax contract.
lessons.workedExample: A repeated-expression macro should specify whether an input expression is evaluated once or several times.
lessons.code:
macro_rules! owned_values { ($($value:expr),* $(,)?) => { vec![$($value),*] }; }
fn main() { let values = owned_values![2, 4, 6,]; println!("{:?}", values); }
lessons.challenge: Design the contract of a small vector-building macro and name tests for it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Document accepted token forms, evaluation order/count, empty input, trailing separators, and result type. Compile examples and failure cases under the recorded toolchain; keep ordinary runtime behavior in functions when possible.
lessons.question: What should a macro contract include?
options: Accepted syntax and evaluation behavior
Only the macro's name
A promise of zero runtime work for every expansion
lessons.explanation: Document accepted token forms, evaluation order/count, empty input, trailing separators, and result type. Compile examples and failure cases under the recorded toolchain; keep ordinary runtime behavior in functions when possible.

lessons.title: Tests and documentation serve executable contracts
lessons.summary: Source practice · Tests and documentation serve executable contracts
body: Unit tests target modules; integration tests exercise public interfaces; documentation examples can be checked by the toolchain. should_panic describes a specific failure expectation, not general correctness. Benchmarks need a supported harness and a representative workload.
lessons.workedExample: A helper's unit test can pass while the binary wires its arguments incorrectly.
lessons.challenge: Plan unit, integration, and documentation checks for a parser package.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Check small parser cases and errors, exercise public entry points and binary behavior, and validate examples where supported. Record toolchain, features, and dependency versions. Keep performance comparison separate from ordinary correctness tests.
lessons.question: What do integration tests emphasize?
options: The public interfaces working together
Only private local variables
Only the fastest implementation
lessons.explanation: Check small parser cases and errors, exercise public entry points and binary behavior, and validate examples where supported. Record toolchain, features, and dependency versions. Keep performance comparison separate from ordinary correctness tests.

lessons.title: A command-line program has an input and output contract
lessons.summary: Source practice · A command-line program has an input and output contract
body: Arguments, environment, files, exit codes, stdout, and stderr are separate channels. A small reusable core makes the binary easier to test. Input encoding and error context matter; reading a whole file is not always appropriate for unbounded input.
lessons.workedExample: A search tool writes errors into stdout, corrupting a pipeline that expects only matching records.
lessons.challenge: Design a case-sensitive line search accepting a pattern and text input.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Validate arguments, separate a pure matching function, stream or bound input as appropriate, send records to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, and document exit codes and text encoding.
lessons.question: Where should diagnostics normally go in this contract?
options: Mixed into matching stdout records
Only into an unused local variable
stderr
lessons.explanation: Validate arguments, separate a pure matching function, stream or bound input as appropriate, send records to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, and document exit codes and text encoding.

lessons.title: Versioning includes editions and API contracts
lessons.summary: Source practice · Versioning includes editions and API contracts
body: Rust editions select language compatibility rules; they do not automatically update all dependencies. Semantic-version expectations, features, MSRV, and deprecations form a library compatibility policy. A type alias creates another name, while a newtype can create a distinct contract.
lessons.workedExample: Updating an edition in Cargo.toml does not establish that every dependency supports the project's minimum compiler.
lessons.code:
struct Meters(u32);
fn main() { let distance = Meters(12); println!("{}", distance.0); }
lessons.challenge: Plan a dependency upgrade and explain why a newtype can prevent accidental unit mixing.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Check supported toolchain and feature combinations, compile and test interfaces, and review changed APIs. Wrap a value in a distinct struct when type separation is required rather than only renaming it with an alias.
lessons.question: Does a type alias create a distinct new type?
options: Only for integers
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Check supported toolchain and feature combinations, compile and test interfaces, and review changed APIs. Wrap a value in a distinct struct when type separation is required rather than only renaming it with an alias.

reading.title: Rust complete course · Arfan Zubi / freeCodeCamp

lessons.title: Types can depend on values and live in universes
lessons.summary: Source practice · Types can depend on values and live in universes
body: Lean checks terms against types, and types themselves have sorts. Universe parameters express reusable definitions without one fixed universe level. Dependent function types can have a result type that refers to an input. A proposition's proof is checked as a term.
lessons.workedExample: A function returning a vector indexed by n has a result type mentioning the requested length.
lessons.code:
def keep {α : Type u} (x : α) : α := x
#eval keep (7 : Nat)
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between a constant result type and a result type depending on an argument.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An ordinary function can return the same type for every input; a dependent function can return a type that includes that input value. Universe levels classify types and must satisfy Lean's constraints.
lessons.question: What makes a function type dependent?
options: It requires floating-point arithmetic
Its result type can mention an input
It always uses mutable state
lessons.explanation: An ordinary function can return the same type for every input; a dependent function can return a type that includes that input value. Universe levels classify types and must satisfy Lean's constraints.

lessons.title: IO describes effects within an explicit interface
lessons.summary: Source practice · IO describes effects within an explicit interface
body: Pure definitions compute values; IO programs interact with the outside world. do notation organizes sequential effectful computations under a monadic interface. Lake manages projects and dependencies. A compiler check and a real process invocation test different behaviors.
lessons.workedExample: An IO program printing a message has an effect when run, unlike a pure String definition by itself.
lessons.challenge: Describe a Lean executable's main interface and how to test its output without assuming every #eval is an application entry point.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Define main with an appropriate IO result, build/run it using the project's toolchain, and assert the process output and exit behavior. #eval evaluates a command in the elaboration context; it is a different interface.
lessons.question: What does IO make explicit?
options: An automatic network sandbox
Effectful computation
A proof that no errors occur
lessons.explanation: Define main with an appropriate IO result, build/run it using the project's toolchain, and assert the process output and exit behavior. #eval evaluates a command in the elaboration context; it is a different interface.

lessons.title: Type classes resolve operations from types
lessons.summary: Source practice · Type classes resolve operations from types
body: A type class packages an interface and Lean can synthesize an instance when required. Numeric literals and overloaded operations use such interfaces. Instances should express coherent behavior and avoid accidental ambiguity or unexpected search costs.
lessons.workedExample: A custom display type needs an appropriate ToString instance for ordinary string conversion.
lessons.code:
structure Label where
  value : String
instance : ToString Label where
  toString x := x.value
#eval toString (Label.mk "tag")
lessons.challenge: Explain why an overloaded operation may fail even when a similarly named function exists.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Lean needs an instance satisfying the expected class for the chosen type. Define or import the intended instance, check type inference, and avoid adding unrelated instances merely to suppress an error.
lessons.question: What does instance synthesis search for?
options: An implementation of the required class
An arbitrary theorem with the same printed word
Only a global string name
lessons.explanation: Lean needs an instance satisfying the expected class for the chosen type. Define or import the intended instance, check type inference, and avoid adding unrelated instances merely to suppress an error.

lessons.title: Bind sequences computations with a context
lessons.summary: Source practice · Bind sequences computations with a context
body: A monad supplies return-like construction and bind-like sequencing under laws. Option stops on absence; Except propagates an error; IO sequences effects. do notation expresses such sequencing, but the chosen type determines what the sequencing means.
lessons.workedExample: An Option computation parsing two fields can stop at the first missing parse result.
lessons.code:
def combine (a b : Option Nat) : Option Nat := do
  let x ← a
  let y ← b
  pure (x + y)
#eval combine (some 2) (some 3)
#eval combine none (some 3)
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between mapping a pure function over Option and binding a function returning Option.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Map transforms the contained value while preserving the context; bind lets the function introduce another optional computation and avoids nesting Option layers. Handle absence according to the intended result type.
lessons.question: What does bind support here?
options: Automatically retrying every failure
Removing all contexts without checking them
Sequencing a function that returns an Option
lessons.explanation: Map transforms the contained value while preserving the context; bind lets the function introduce another optional computation and avoids nesting Option layers. Handle absence according to the intended result type.

lessons.title: Applicative and monadic structure have different dependencies
lessons.summary: Source practice · Applicative and monadic structure have different dependencies
body: Functor mapping transforms a result inside a context. Applicative combination applies contextual functions to contextual values. Monadic bind can choose the next computation from an earlier result. The laws let callers reason about composition without knowing every implementation detail.
lessons.workedExample: Combining two independent checks differs from choosing a second lookup key based on the first lookup's result.
lessons.challenge: Classify a dependent two-stage lookup and explain why merely combining fixed independent operations is different.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A second lookup chosen using the first result needs bind-like dependency. Independent contextual computations can often be combined applicatively. The context's own error or effect behavior still matters.
lessons.question: Which structure directly permits the next computation to depend on an earlier result?
options: Only a fixed literal
A string formatter
Monadic bind
lessons.explanation: A second lookup chosen using the first result needs bind-like dependency. Independent contextual computations can often be combined applicatively. The context's own error or effect behavior still matters.

lessons.title: Combining effects includes an ordering choice
lessons.summary: Source practice · Combining effects includes an ordering choice
body: Monad transformers add an effect layer to another computation. State, reader environments, and error propagation interact with the order of layers. A chosen stack needs a documented result and failure contract; similar type names do not guarantee identical semantics.
lessons.workedExample: A failing stateful computation can either discard or retain state changes depending on the arrangement and implementation.
lessons.challenge: Explain why state-plus-error code needs a failure-state policy before choosing a transformer order.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Decide whether changes before failure remain observable, then inspect the resulting type and run the stack's operations accordingly. Test one successful path and one failure after a state update.
lessons.question: Can transformer ordering affect observed failure behavior?
options: No
Only in the editor
Yes
lessons.explanation: Decide whether changes before failure remain observable, then inspect the resulting type and run the stack's operations accordingly. Test one successful path and one failure after a state update.

lessons.title: Indexed data can carry size and validity evidence
lessons.summary: Source practice · Indexed data can carry size and validity evidence
body: Dependent types can encode length or membership constraints. Fin n combines an index with evidence that it is within n. A checked runtime boundary can produce a value carrying evidence for later operations. Proof erasure and executable data have different roles.
lessons.workedExample: An API accepting Fin 3 cannot be called with an unchecked arbitrary Nat without constructing the required evidence.
lessons.code:
def second : Fin 3 := ⟨1, by decide⟩
#eval second.val
example : second.val < 3 := second.isLt
lessons.challenge: Plan a conversion from external Nat input to an index for a length-three container.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Check the bound at the input boundary and return an optional or error containing Fin 3 when valid. Use that validated index internally rather than repeating an unchecked access.
lessons.question: What extra contract does Fin n express?
options: The index is less than n
The index is a negative integer
The container is globally shared
lessons.explanation: Check the bound at the input boundary and return an optional or error containing Fin 3 when valid. Use that validated index internally rather than repeating an unchecked access.

lessons.title: Recursive definitions need a termination argument
lessons.summary: Source practice · Recursive definitions need a termination argument
body: Structural recursion follows an inductive input; more general recursion may need a decreasing measure or well-founded relation. A proof about recursion often follows the same cases. Fast execution and kernel reduction are related but distinct concerns.
lessons.workedExample: A recursive call on the tail of a list follows its structure, while a custom numeric search needs an argument that a measure decreases.
lessons.code:
def down : Nat → List Nat
  | 0 => []
  | n + 1 => (n + 1) :: down n
#eval down 3
lessons.challenge: Specify base case, recursive case, and measure for a countdown returning a list.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Stop at zero; for a successor, produce one element and recurse on the predecessor. The natural-number input decreases, and an induction proof can follow zero/successor cases.
lessons.question: What must a termination measure do at recursive calls?
options: Increase indefinitely
Remain unrelated to the arguments
Decrease under a well-founded relation
lessons.explanation: Stop at zero; for a successor, produce one element and recurse on the predecessor. The natural-number input decreases, and an induction proof can follow zero/successor cases.

lessons.title: Elaboration turns syntax into a checked term
lessons.summary: Source practice · Elaboration turns syntax into a checked term
body: Namespaces, sections, variables, imports, notation, and type inference organize Lean code. #check reports a type; #print inspects a declaration; errors and goals reveal missing constraints. A tactic script is accepted when it constructs an appropriate checked term.
lessons.workedExample: An unqualified theorem name can resolve differently after a namespace or import change.
lessons.challenge: Describe a debugging procedure for a theorem-name or type mismatch.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Inspect the expected goal and hypothesis types, qualify the declaration, use #check to confirm its signature, and apply arguments in the required order. Avoid replacing a missing argument with a proof placeholder.
lessons.question: What does #check primarily report?
options: The type of an expression
A runtime benchmark
A complete proof of any proposition
lessons.explanation: Inspect the expected goal and hypothesis types, qualify the declaration, use #check to confirm its signature, and apply arguments in the required order. Avoid replacing a missing argument with a proof placeholder.

lessons.title: Conversion focuses rewriting on a selected expression
lessons.summary: Source practice · Conversion focuses rewriting on a selected expression
body: conv mode navigates a goal or expression before applying transformations. It helps control which occurrence changes when ordinary rewriting is too broad. The transformed expression must still be justified by Lean's checking rules.
lessons.workedExample: An equality goal contains repeated terms but only one nested occurrence should be rewritten.
lessons.challenge: Explain why focused conversion can be preferable to a global rewrite and how to verify its effect.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Select the intended subexpression, apply a justified conversion, then inspect the resulting goal and close it with the remaining proof. Confirm the change did not target a different occurrence.
lessons.question: What is the purpose of conv focusing?
options: Select the expression occurrence being transformed
Disable proof checking
Change every hypothesis automatically
lessons.explanation: Select the intended subexpression, apply a justified conversion, then inspect the resulting goal and close it with the remaining proof. Confirm the change did not target a different occurrence.

lessons.title: Accepted terms can depend on explicit assumptions
lessons.summary: Source practice · Accepted terms can depend on explicit assumptions
body: Classical reasoning and axioms may support proofs while computational behavior depends on their role. Inspect theorem dependencies when assumptions matter. sorry supplies a placeholder rather than the intended proof and must not count as a completed learning exercise.
lessons.workedExample: A theorem can type-check while depending on sorryAx through a placeholder. That acceptance does not establish the authored proof.
lessons.challenge: Explain how to distinguish a checked proof exercise from one using a placeholder or undeclared assumption.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Reject placeholders in the learner's exercise contract, inspect warnings and declaration dependencies, and state allowed assumptions and imports. Type-check under the pinned toolchain and project environment.
lessons.question: Does an accepted sorry demonstrate completion of the intended proof?
options: No
Yes
Only when the theorem is short
lessons.explanation: Reject placeholders in the learner's exercise contract, inspect warnings and declaration dependencies, and state allowed assumptions and imports. Type-check under the pinned toolchain and project environment.

lessons.title: A set proof unfolds membership into a proposition
lessons.summary: Source practice · A set proof unfolds membership into a proposition
body: Set membership is a proposition. Inclusion is a function taking membership evidence in one set to evidence in another. Equality of sets is commonly proved extensionally. Function injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity have distinct quantifier contracts.
lessons.workedExample: To show A intersect B is contained in A, extract the left membership evidence from the conjunction.
lessons.challenge: Describe both directions needed to prove two sets equal extensionally.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Choose an arbitrary element and prove its membership equivalence. Provide a function from each side's membership evidence to the other side, using definitions and hypotheses explicitly.
lessons.question: What proves set inclusion?
options: A sample of matching elements
A function transforming membership evidence
Only equal printed names
lessons.explanation: Choose an arbitrary element and prove its membership equivalence. Provide a function from each side's membership evidence to the other side, using definitions and hypotheses explicitly.

lessons.title: Arithmetic formalization needs the right domain and lemmas
lessons.summary: Source practice · Arithmetic formalization needs the right domain and lemmas
body: Nat, Int, and other number types have different subtraction and divisibility behavior. A mathematical argument must be translated into exact hypotheses and available lemmas. Computation can discharge concrete cases, while symbolic claims require general proofs.
lessons.workedExample: Natural subtraction truncates at zero, so a familiar integer rearrangement may not hold unchanged for Nat.
lessons.code:
#eval (2 : Nat) - 5
#eval (2 : Int) - 5
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between 2-5 in Nat and Int, then plan a divisibility proof.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Nat subtraction gives 0; Int subtraction gives -3. For divisibility, introduce a witness or use an appropriate theorem under the exact numeric type and hypotheses. Inspect lemma types before rewriting.
lessons.question: Is natural subtraction identical to integer subtraction?
options: No
Yes
Only for unequal operands
lessons.explanation: Nat subtraction gives 0; Int subtraction gives -3. For divisibility, introduce a witness or use an appropriate theorem under the exact numeric type and hypotheses. Inspect lemma types before rewriting.

lessons.title: Algebraic structure supplies lawful operations
lessons.summary: Source practice · Algebraic structure supplies lawful operations
body: Structures and type classes package operations together with laws. Semigroup, monoid, group, ring, and field assumptions enable different conclusions. Do not assume commutativity or division laws from a weaker structure. A general theorem should require only the laws it uses.
lessons.workedExample: Associativity alone does not permit swapping two factors. A commutativity proof needs the corresponding law or stronger hypothesis.
lessons.challenge: Choose assumptions for proving that adding zero preserves a value and explain why cancellation may need more.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Require an additive identity law for the first claim. Cancellation depends on the relevant cancellative or group structure. Inspect the class assumptions rather than assuming all numeric-looking types are fields.
lessons.question: Does associativity alone imply commutativity?
options: No
Yes
Only for multiplication
lessons.explanation: Require an additive identity law for the first claim. Cancellation depends on the relevant cancellative or group structure. Inspect the class assumptions rather than assuming all numeric-looking types are fields.

lessons.title: Filters describe eventual behavior
lessons.summary: Source practice · Filters describe eventual behavior
body: A filter expresses which sets of points count as sufficiently large or near a situation. Limits become eventual-property statements through filters. At-top and neighborhood filters encode different notions of approach. Theorems require precise domain, codomain, and filter assumptions.
lessons.workedExample: A property holding for all natural numbers beyond some N is an eventual statement for the at-top filter.
lessons.challenge: Translate an eventual threshold property into ordinary quantified language.
lessons.practiceAnswer: There exists a threshold N such that for every n at least N the property holds. A limit additionally states that values eventually enter every required neighborhood of the target.
lessons.question: What does eventual mean for natural-number at-top behavior?
options: It holds for one arbitrarily chosen sample
It holds only at zero
The property holds beyond some threshold
lessons.explanation: There exists a threshold N such that for every n at least N the property holds. A limit additionally states that values eventually enter every required neighborhood of the target.

lessons.title: Topological claims use neighborhoods and structure
lessons.summary: Source practice · Topological claims use neighborhoods and structure
body: Continuity relates neighborhoods in domain and codomain; compactness, closure, and convergence have separate definitions. Metric-space intuitions require the appropriate structure. Formalization should state assumptions before selecting the theorem.
lessons.workedExample: A continuity argument about sums uses continuity of each component plus a theorem for the codomain's addition.
lessons.challenge: Outline a continuity proof by composition and identify what must be checked.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Confirm topological structures, domains, and hypotheses; prove the component functions continuous; then apply the appropriate composition theorem. A picture of the graph is intuition, not a checked proof.
lessons.question: What must precede applying a continuity theorem?
options: Renaming every variable
Matching its structures and hypotheses
A numerical plot only
lessons.explanation: Confirm topological structures, domains, and hypotheses; prove the component functions continuous; then apply the appropriate composition theorem. A picture of the graph is intuition, not a checked proof.

lessons.title: Derivative and integral theorems carry hypotheses
lessons.summary: Source practice · Derivative and integral theorems carry hypotheses
body: Differentiability, integrability, measure, domain, and regularity assumptions determine which calculus theorems apply. A formal proof cannot silently omit them. Mathlib is a project dependency; standalone Lean core does not provide every mathematical theorem used by these chapters.
lessons.workedExample: A symbolic derivative rule may require differentiability hypotheses at the point and a compatible normed field.
lessons.challenge: Plan a Mathlib-backed proof using a derivative rule.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Pin Lean and Mathlib together, inspect the exact theorem signature, discharge domain and differentiability requirements, then compose the rule. Validate in that project; do not advertise a core-only runner as equivalent.
lessons.question: Can every Mathlib calculus example run with only Lean core imports?
options: Only if it uses rfl
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Pin Lean and Mathlib together, inspect the exact theorem signature, discharge domain and differentiability requirements, then compose the rule. Validate in that project; do not advertise a core-only runner as equivalent.

lessons.title: Linear maps preserve operations over a chosen scalar structure
lessons.summary: Source practice · Linear maps preserve operations over a chosen scalar structure
body: A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication under specified module assumptions. Bases, dimension, matrices, and invertibility have different contracts. Coordinates depend on a basis; a matrix is not the abstract map itself.
lessons.workedExample: The same linear map has different matrix entries under different choices of basis.
lessons.challenge: State the two preservation laws of a linear map and explain what a basis contributes.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The map sends x+y to f(x)+f(y) and a scalar multiple a*x to a*f(x). A basis chooses coordinates and lets a compatible finite-dimensional map be represented by a matrix.
lessons.question: Does changing a basis necessarily change the abstract linear map?
options: No
Yes
Only if the matrix is square
lessons.explanation: The map sends x+y to f(x)+f(y) and a scalar multiple a*x to a*f(x). A basis chooses coordinates and lets a compatible finite-dimensional map be represented by a matrix.

lessons.title: Compile-time evaluation has a checked contract
lessons.summary: Source practice · Compile-time evaluation has a checked contract
body: constexpr permits appropriate constant evaluation and can also support runtime calls. A constant expression must satisfy language restrictions. const describes immutability through a contract; it does not by itself mean the initializer was evaluated at compile time.
lessons.workedExample: A constexpr square function can compute a compile-time array size from a constant argument and also square a runtime input.
lessons.challenge: Explain the difference between const, constexpr, and a runtime call to a constexpr function.
lessons.practiceAnswer: const constrains modification; constexpr requires suitable constant initialization where used for a variable and permits compile-time function evaluation. A constexpr function can still execute at runtime for a runtime argument.
lessons.question: Must every call to a constexpr function execute at compile time?
options: Yes
Only if it returns an int
No
lessons.explanation: const constrains modification; constexpr requires suitable constant initialization where used for a variable and permits compile-time function evaluation. A constexpr function can still execute at runtime for a runtime argument.

lessons.title: Allocation and construction are different phases
lessons.summary: Source practice · Allocation and construction are different phases
body: operator new obtains storage; a new-expression also constructs an object. A delete-expression destroys an object and invokes the appropriate deallocation. Custom allocation requires matching forms and failure behavior. Placement construction needs suitable storage and a valid lifetime protocol.
lessons.workedExample: An allocation succeeds but a constructor throws. The language's matching cleanup path must prevent losing that allocated storage.
lessons.challenge: Explain why custom allocation instrumentation must track allocation and construction separately.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Allocation counts storage acquisition, while construction counts successfully created objects. Handle constructor failure and matching delete forms; do not use a byte-copy operation as a substitute for constructing a nontrivial type.
lessons.question: Is operator new by itself the whole object-construction operation?
options: Yes
Only for classes with fields
No
lessons.explanation: Allocation counts storage acquisition, while construction counts successfully created objects. Handle constructor failure and matching delete forms; do not use a byte-copy operation as a substitute for constructing a nontrivial type.

lessons.title: Formatted streams carry state across operations
lessons.summary: Source practice · Formatted streams carry state across operations
body: Precision, fill characters, and format flags configure a stream. Width often affects only the next formatted operation. boolalpha changes boolean text formatting. A manipulator can configure or write through the stream and should return the stream to support chaining.
lessons.workedExample: After setting a fill character and width for one insertion, later fields may retain the fill character but need their own width setting.
lessons.challenge: Plan two aligned fields and explain what state a reusable formatting helper should preserve.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Set width for each field, choose precision and flags under a documented contract, and save/restore persistent stream state when the helper should not alter later output.
lessons.question: Does width normally remain active for every future insertion?
options: Yes
Only with boolalpha
No
lessons.explanation: Set width for each field, choose precision and flags under a documented contract, and save/restore persistent stream state when the helper should not alter later output.

lessons.title: Seeking changes an explicitly tracked position
lessons.summary: Source practice · Seeking changes an explicitly tracked position
body: Input and output positions can differ by stream type and mode. tellg/tellp report positions; seekg/seekp change them. A failed read can leave state that must be handled before another operation. Binary formats require defined record boundaries and representations.
lessons.workedExample: After reaching end-of-file, blindly seeking and reading without handling stream state may not behave as intended.
lessons.challenge: Describe a fixed-record reader that jumps to record k and rejects partial records.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Validate k and offset arithmetic, open under the format's mode, handle or clear the appropriate stream failure state, seek to the checked offset, and require exactly one complete record. Decode fields explicitly.
lessons.question: What must a random-access reader validate?
options: Only that k is positive
Offsets, stream state, and complete record length
Only the filename
lessons.explanation: Validate k and offset arithmetic, open under the format's mode, handle or clear the appropriate stream failure state, seek to the checked offset, and require exactly one complete record. Decode fields explicitly.

lessons.title: Finite mathematics still needs explicit combinatorial contracts
lessons.summary: Source practice · Finite mathematics still needs explicit combinatorial contracts
body: Finite sets, sequences, functions, and induction support counting and discrete arguments. A cardinality theorem depends on injectivity, disjointness, or another exact property. Examples can suggest a pattern but do not replace the universal argument.

lessons.title: Compilation, main, and the toolchain
body: Rust source is checked and compiled before it runs. A binary starts at fn main(); statements execute in order, and println! formats text followed by a newline. A compiler diagnostic describes a rejected program, while a runtime error happens after compilation.

Cargo manages a package: cargo new starts one, cargo check checks types without producing the final executable, cargo run builds and runs, and cargo test runs tests. A package can contain library and binary crates. This lesson is a single file so it can go straight into the Lab.

This guide targets Rust 1.99.0 with edition 2024. A compiler version and an edition are different: editions select compatibility rules inside Cargo.toml; upgrading rustc does not automatically change a crate’s edition. Run rustc --version and inspect edition before comparing examples.

lessons.question: What does cargo check primarily do?
options: Check compilation without building the final executable
Run the program’s main function
Change the package’s edition automatically

lessons.title: Bindings, mutability, and shadowing
body: A let binding is immutable unless written let mut. Mutability applies to that binding’s access to a value; it is not permission to ignore borrowing rules. Assigning to an immutable binding is rejected.
Shadowing creates a new binding with the same spelling. Its type can differ from the old one, which is useful when parsing text into a number. Assignment to a mut binding keeps the same type.

const declares a compile-time value with an explicit type; static declares storage with program lifetime. Prefer a constant for a reusable numerical parameter, and a local let for a value computed from input.
lessons.challenge: Shadow the text "20" with a parsed i32, then double a mutable total.
lessons.question: Which can change a name’s type?
options: A new shadowing let binding
Assignment to the same mut binding
Adding mut to an existing value at runtime

The parse produces a new i32 binding. += and *= update that binding without changing its type.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The parse produces a new i32 binding. += and *= update that binding without changing its type.

lessons.title: Numeric types and deliberate overflow
body: Rust distinguishes signed integers, unsigned integers, floating-point values, bool and char. usize is sized for the target’s pointer width and commonly indexes collections; it is not a portable substitute for a fixed-width serialized number.

Integer arithmetic can overflow. Ordinary arithmetic depends on overflow checking settings; do not make correctness depend on debug versus release behavior. checked_add returns Option, wrapping_add performs modular arithmetic, and saturating_add clamps at the boundary.

An as cast can truncate or reinterpret an integer conversion. TryFrom/TryInto report out-of-range conversions. State the valid range at an input boundary and use a checked conversion where loss would corrupt meaning.
lessons.challenge: Compare the same operations on 255u8 + 1 and explain the three outcomes.
lessons.question: Which operation reports overflow as a value?
options: checked_add
wrapping_add
An unchecked as cast

lessons.practiceAnswer: checked_add returns None when the result is outside u8. Wrapping reduces modulo 256; saturation keeps 255.

lessons.title: Tuples, arrays, and indexing
body: A tuple groups a fixed number of potentially different types; a tuple pattern extracts its fields. An array [T; N] stores N elements of one type, and its length is part of its type.
Indexing an array or slice panics if the index is outside its length. get returns Option instead, which makes an untrusted index an ordinary branch in the program.
A Vec can grow, but an array’s length is fixed. Choose an array for a fixed-size vector or protocol field; choose a tuple for a small heterogeneous result whose positions have clear meaning.

options: Use get and handle Option

Change the array’s length through indexing

lessons.practiceAnswer: The zero-based index 1 exists; 3 does not. get represents both possibilities in its return type.

lessons.title: Expressions, branches, and loops
body: An expression produces a value. if can produce a value when its branches agree on a type, and a block evaluates to its final expression without a semicolon. A trailing semicolon usually changes that result to unit ().
loop can return a value through break value. while repeats while a Boolean is true; for works through IntoIterator. A range a..b excludes b, while a..=b includes it.

Use labels to break or continue a particular enclosing loop. Prefer for over manual indexing when the program needs elements rather than index arithmetic; it also makes the iteration boundary visible.

lessons.practiceAnswer: The inclusive boundary adds the fifth value. The exclusive range stops before its upper bound.

lessons.title: Functions and explicit interfaces
body: Function parameters have explicit types, and -> names the return type. Returning the last expression is idiomatic; return is useful for an early exit. A block’s semicolon is therefore part of the function’s meaning.

Pass the smallest information a function needs. A pure calculation with inputs and an output is easier to test than a function that mutates hidden global state. Side effects still matter, but put them at a clear boundary.

Functions are items and can be called before their textual definition. A function pointer such as fn(i32) -> i32 describes a callable with a fixed signature; closures have additional captured state and distinct types.

options: Unit ()
The preceding expression’s unchanged value
An automatically inferred Result

lessons.title: Moves, Copy, and Clone
body: A value has an owner responsible for its lifetime. Moving an owned String transfers responsibility to the destination binding; the old binding can no longer be used. This prevents two independent owners from freeing the same buffer.

Copy types are implicitly duplicated on assignment, such as ordinary integer values. Clone requests an explicit duplication whose cost depends on the type: cloning a String copies its allocation, while cloning an Rc increments a count.

A function argument can take ownership, borrow, or borrow mutably. Read the signature to predict which caller values remain available afterward. A return value can transfer ownership back; you do not need a global owner.
lessons.challenge: Move a String into a function that returns its uppercase owned replacement.
lessons.question: After moving a String, what can you do with the old binding?
options: Use it only after assigning a new valid value
Continue using its former buffer
Assume it was implicitly deep-copied

lessons.practiceAnswer: The owner moved; backup is separately cloned. Reinitialization can give a moved binding a new value.

lessons.title: Shared and exclusive borrowing
body: A reference borrows a value without becoming its owner. &T permits shared access; &mut T permits exclusive access. While an exclusive borrow is in use, overlapping access to that location is restricted.

Non-lexical lifetimes allow many borrows to end after their last use, before the end of the block. The rule concerns actual loan usage, not merely the spelling of a scope. The compiler still rejects aliases used concurrently with an exclusive borrow.

For a read-only API, a borrowed slice or str is often more flexible than &Vec or &String. A mutable slice gives permission to update existing elements without exposing resizing or the whole container.

lessons.question: Why can the mutation follow the shared reference in the example?
options: The shared borrow’s last use has ended
String disables alias checks
Mutable references are always Copy

lessons.title: UTF-8, String, str, and characters
body: String owns a growable UTF-8 buffer; str is a dynamically sized text view commonly used behind &str. A char is a Unicode scalar value, not an arbitrary byte and not necessarily a user-perceived character.

len on String or str counts bytes. chars iterates scalar values; bytes iterates encoded bytes. Grapheme clusters can contain multiple scalars, so a cursor-oriented editor needs a Unicode segmentation policy beyond chars.

String slices require UTF-8 boundaries and a valid range. get on a range returns None when the range is invalid. Never use an arbitrary byte offset from untrusted input as though it were a character index.

options: Unicode scalar values
UTF-8 bytes
Grapheme clusters

lessons.title: Slices, split borrows, and windows
body: A slice is a view of contiguous elements with a runtime length. &[T] and &mut [T] borrow storage owned elsewhere; slicing does not copy the underlying values. Reallocation of an owner cannot happen while a slice into it is still used.

split_at_mut proves that two output slices are disjoint. It lets safe code mutate separate ranges without constructing overlapping mutable references. For fixed neighborhoods, windows returns overlapping shared views; chunks divides a slice into groups.

A view’s lifetime is tied to the source. A function cannot return a slice into a local vector that will be destroyed. Return the owned vector, borrow an input, or let the caller provide storage instead.

options: It safely produces two disjoint mutable slices
It copies all elements into new allocations
It extends storage to program lifetime

lessons.title: Structs, methods, and encapsulation
body: A struct names a product of fields. Associated functions belong to the type; methods take self, &self or &mut self to state ownership/access. Choose the receiver from the operation’s needs.

Private fields let a module maintain invariants. A public constructor can reject invalid data before a value is created; callers then use methods that preserve that condition. Public fields shift that responsibility to every caller.

Tuple structs provide a distinct type with positional fields, useful for newtypes such as UserId rather than interchangeable integers. Deriving Debug helps inspection; a derived trait is generated code with the trait’s own constraints.

options: No receiver for every operation
&mut self

lessons.title: Enums and exhaustive matching
body: An enum describes alternatives, and each variant may carry different data. A message is either one variant or another; unlike a struct of optional fields, the type can exclude combinations that make no sense.

match analyzes a value and must cover all cases. Adding a variant makes missing cases visible at compilation, unless a catch-all deliberately absorbs them. if let is concise for one interesting case; let else gives an early exit for a failed pattern.

Pattern matching can bind, borrow, destructure and guard values. A guard adds a runtime condition; it does not generally prove type-level exhaustiveness. Keep a catch-all when guarded alternatives leave possibilities.

It encodes which combinations are valid

lessons.title: Option and absence without sentinel values
body: Option<T> has Some(T) and None. It makes absence visible in the type instead of reserving an ordinary value such as -1 or an empty string. A caller must decide what absence means.

map transforms a present value; and_then chains a function that can itself return None. unwrap_or provides an eager fallback; unwrap_or_else computes a fallback only when needed. unwrap panics on None and needs a justified invariant.

Borrowing methods as_ref and as_mut let you inspect or modify the inside without moving it out of its owner. take replaces an Option with None and returns the old value, which is useful for transferring a resource exactly once.
lessons.challenge: Use take to consume a pending message once, then show it is absent.

options: A clone of the payload
A dangling reference
None

lessons.title: Result, ?, and error propagation
body: Result<T, E> represents success or a typed failure. Match when recovery is local; use ? when the caller should decide. ? returns early on Err and converts compatible error types through From.
map transforms success, map_err transforms failure, and and_then chains another fallible step. Give errors enough context to identify the boundary that failed without discarding the original cause.

Use Result for expected failures such as invalid input or missing files. panic expresses a failed invariant or unrecoverable policy, not an ordinary parser branch. A library should avoid surprising callers by panicking for routine input errors.

lessons.question: What does ? do to an Err in a Result-returning function?
options: Replace it with a default success
Return it early, converting the error when needed
Panic unconditionally

lessons.title: Vec growth, retention, and iteration
body: Vec<T> owns contiguous storage with a length and capacity. Length counts initialized elements; capacity describes allocated space. Pushing may reallocate, which explains why a live reference into a vector restricts mutation of its owner.
iter borrows elements, iter_mut borrows them exclusively, and into_iter consumes a vector. Choose the iteration mode deliberately; it determines what happens to the collection afterward.

retain removes elements failing a predicate, and drain transfers a range out while borrowing the vector. Reserve for a justified expected size; do not treat a guessed capacity as initialized storage or access beyond length.

options: into_iter
iter

lessons.title: HashMap entries and ordered alternatives
body: HashMap stores key/value associations with hash-based lookup. Keys need Eq and Hash with consistent behavior. Never assume iteration order; use BTreeMap or explicitly sort when deterministic order matters.
entry combines a lookup with conditional insertion. or_insert supplies a default and returns mutable access to the value, so a frequency counter avoids separate contains/get/insert branches.

Lookup can often borrow a compatible key representation, such as &str for a String key. Values and keys still have owners. Holding a mutable entry access restricts other overlapping access to that map.

options: HashMap
Every map has identical iteration order

lessons.title: Traits, defaults, and generic bounds
body: A trait specifies behavior that implementing types provide. A default method can compose required methods, allowing shared behavior without sharing a representation. A generic bound states the capabilities needed by a function.

impl Trait in an argument is a concise generic parameter; a named T is useful when several parameters must have the same type. Return-position impl Trait hides one concrete type chosen by the implementation; it does not mean any unrelated type can be returned per branch.

Trait implementations must satisfy coherence rules. You can implement your own trait for a foreign type or a foreign trait for an appropriate local type. A newtype gives a local wrapper when you need custom behavior around an external representation.

lessons.question: What does a generic trait bound specify?
options: The value’s exact runtime memory address
An automatic heap allocation
Capabilities the implementation may rely on

lessons.title: Lifetime relationships and elision
body: A lifetime annotation describes relationships between borrowed values; it does not lengthen storage duration. When a return reference might come from either input, the signature must express the shared usable lifetime.
Elision rules cover many common signatures, especially a single input reference or a method receiver. Explicit annotations are useful when those rules cannot identify the source of an output borrow.

A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter tied to the referent. An owned String field avoids that relationship at the cost of owning storage. Choose based on whether the value is a temporary view or independent data.

lessons.question: Do lifetime annotations keep an expired local alive?
options: No; they constrain valid borrow relationships
Yes, by extending the stack frame
Yes, by implicitly cloning it

lessons.title: Associated types, GATs, and iterator contracts
body: An associated type is selected by a trait implementation, rather than independently selected at each use. Iterator::Item is the element type chosen by that iterator. Bounds such as Iterator<Item = i32> constrain it.

A generic associated type can vary with parameters such as a borrow lifetime. This permits lending interfaces whose returned item borrows from the current receiver. Constraints such as where Self: 'a make the required lifetime relation explicit.

A trait generic parameter and an associated type solve different problems. A type can sometimes implement a generic trait for several argument types; each non-generic trait implementation chooses its associated type once.

lessons.title: Trait objects and dynamic dispatch
body: A dyn Trait value erases the concrete implementing type behind a pointer. Dynamic dispatch calls through trait metadata, letting a collection hold different concrete implementations of one contract.

Generic dispatch can specialize machine code for each concrete type. Dynamic dispatch trades that specialization for runtime heterogeneity and an indirect call. Box<dyn Trait> owns an erased value; &dyn Trait borrows one.

Only dyn-compatible traits can form trait objects. Generic methods and some uses of Self need special treatment, often a Self: Sized bound excluding those methods from the object interface. Check the trait contract before choosing an erased API.

lessons.question: Why use a trait object collection?
options: To hold different concrete implementations of one interface
To bypass the borrow checker
To make every trait automatically dyn-compatible

lessons.title: Const generics and fixed-size APIs
body: Const generics parameterize a type or function by compile-time values. [T; N] uses a length value in its type, so a function can preserve array length without accepting every input as a runtime slice.

Stable const-generic expressions have restrictions. A parameter N can appear as an array length, but arbitrary type-level arithmetic involving generic parameters is not generally available on stable Rust. Do not silently introduce nightly feature gates into a stable lesson.

Use a slice when runtime-sized inputs are natural and a const generic when size is a useful compile-time invariant. A fixed dimension is not automatically faster; measure the actual algorithm and generated code.

options: The element type and compile-time length
Only a runtime pointer
An arbitrary growable capacity

lessons.title: Closures and capture contracts
body: A closure combines behavior with captured environment. Capture mode follows how the body uses a value; move requests ownership of captures. move does not by itself imply the closure is callable only once.

FnOnce permits consuming captured state, FnMut permits mutating it, and Fn permits repeated calls through shared access. A closure can implement several of these traits; APIs should request the weakest contract their algorithm needs.
A closure returning a reference still has lifetime constraints. Capturing owned state is useful for a spawned task, but state must also meet that task’s thread/lifetime requirements.

options: Only a plain function pointer

lessons.title: Lazy iterators and fallible collection
body: Iterator adapters are lazy: map, filter and take describe work that a consumer drives. collect, fold, sum and for consume the sequence. Creating an adapter without consuming it does not perform all its transformations.
Collecting Iterator<Item = Result<T, E>> into Result<Vec<T>, E> stops at the first error. This composes parsing while preserving failure instead of silently throwing away bad records with filter_map.

Iterator chains can avoid intermediate collections, but order and side effects remain significant. Use clear loops when early control flow is clearer than a chain, and benchmark rather than assuming either style is faster.

options: Only when the compiler optimizes
As the iterator is consumed
Eagerly for every item when constructed

lessons.title: Box, recursive data, and dereferencing
body: Box<T> owns a heap allocation and releases it when dropped. Moving a Box moves the owning pointer rather than ordinarily relocating its allocated payload. Heap storage is useful for large or recursive values, but it does not remove type or lifetime checks.
A directly recursive enum has no finite size when a variant embeds the same enum without indirection. Box provides a fixed-size indirection so each node contains a pointer to the next node.

Deref lets pointer-like types expose borrowed access to a target. Implementing Deref is an API choice: use it for transparent pointer behavior, not as a substitute for every conversion or inheritance relationship.

lessons.question: Why does Box make a recursive enum representable?
options: It introduces fixed-size indirection
It makes the entire recursive value Copy
It disables destructor execution

A node stores a Box pointer rather than embedding an unbounded chain directly.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A node stores a Box pointer rather than embedding an unbounded chain directly.

lessons.title: Rc, Weak, and ownership cycles
body: Rc<T> shares ownership inside one thread. Cloning an Rc increments its strong count rather than deep-cloning T. The payload is dropped when no strong owners remain.
Weak<T> is a non-owning link that can be upgraded to Option<Rc<T>>. It may fail after the last strong owner disappears. Use weak parent/back links to avoid strong cycles in graphs.

Rust’s memory safety does not guarantee freedom from leaks: Rc cycles can keep resources alive forever. Draw the owning edges and explain which external owner releases the final strong reference; use Arc for corresponding cross-thread ownership.
lessons.challenge: Clone the strong owner, drop the original, then drop the clone and observe the weak link.
lessons.question: Can safe Rust leak through a strong Rc cycle?
options: No; all graphs are automatically collected
Only if every link is Weak
Yes; memory safety does not prevent ownership cycles
lessons.explanation: Weak does not keep the payload alive. The remaining clone does, until it too is dropped.

true

lessons.title: Cell and RefCell: controlled interior mutation
body: Interior mutability allows mutation through a shared reference using a type that enforces an appropriate policy. Cell moves/copies values without handing out ordinary references to its interior. RefCell tracks borrowing at runtime.

RefCell::borrow allows shared loans, and borrow_mut requests an exclusive one. Violations panic; try_borrow and try_borrow_mut report failure instead. Runtime checking replaces a particular static check, not the overall aliasing contract.

Rc<RefCell<T>> is a common single-threaded shared mutable model. It still needs a cycle policy. For threads, choose synchronized primitives such as Mutex; neither Rc nor RefCell is a general cross-thread replacement.

lessons.title: Drop, RAII, and resource boundaries
body: Drop runs cleanup when an owned value is destroyed. This is the basis of resource acquisition is initialization: an owner can manage a file, lock guard, buffer, or subscription. Cleanup should be tied to an explicit lifetime.

std::mem::drop consumes a value and ends ownership early. You do not call its Drop::drop method directly. Local owners are generally destroyed in reverse declaration order, while moving a value transfers the eventual cleanup responsibility.

Destructors are not guaranteed in all circumstances: process abort, intentional forget, leaks and cycles can prevent cleanup. A protocol requiring external confirmation cannot rely solely on Drop; expose an explicit close/commit operation when errors matter.
