lessons.title: Modules, visibility, and API boundaries
body: Modules organize names and privacy inside a crate. pub exposes an item to allowed external callers; pub(crate) limits it to the crate. use brings a path into scope, and pub use can present a chosen public facade.

crate starts at the current crate root, super refers to the parent module, and self refers to the current one. Separate files are a source organization convention; a module is not itself a separately linked package.
Design visibility from invariants: keep fields and implementation details private, expose operations that preserve valid states, and avoid unintentionally committing helper types to your public API.

lessons.title: Tests, assertions, and contracts
body: A test checks behavior against a contract. Unit tests can access private implementation details from their module; integration tests exercise the public crate API. Documentation tests keep examples connected to compiled behavior.

assert checks a condition; assert_eq and assert_ne compare values and report useful differences. Result-returning tests can use ?. A test expecting a panic should identify the intended failure rather than accepting any unrelated panic.

Test boundaries, invalid input and ownership consequences as well as happy paths. A passing test is evidence for those inputs, not proof of all possible behavior. Concurrency tests must avoid assuming a particular scheduler order.

lessons.title: Read and write interfaces with Result
body: The Read and Write traits abstract byte streams. A function using impl Read can accept a file, an in-memory cursor or another adapter. This keeps the algorithm testable without requiring the filesystem.

I/O can return partial work or errors. read_to_string and write_all handle their respective loops, while text decoding and size policy still matter. Never assume one read fills a buffer or one write consumes it all.

Separate parsing from resource acquisition. A bounded reader policy is needed for untrusted large input, and buffered I/O can reduce repeated system calls. Paths are platform values, not necessarily Unicode strings.

lessons.title: Threads, move, and scoped borrowing
body: std::thread::spawn creates concurrent execution. Its closure must satisfy Send and a static lifetime bound because it can outlive the caller’s local scope. move transfers captured ownership; join waits and reports a panic as an error.
Scoped threads may borrow local data because the scope ensures its threads finish before borrowed storage disappears. This avoids cloning an entire input merely to satisfy an unscoped lifetime bound.

Concurrency order is nondeterministic. Collect results through joins or channels before printing deterministic summaries, and make synchronization protect a real invariant rather than a hoped-for ordering.

lessons.title: Arc, Mutex, and lock guards
body: Arc shares ownership using atomic reference counting; it does not automatically make the payload’s operations synchronized. Mutex protects a value with exclusive access through a lock guard.

A guard releases its lock when dropped. Keep lock scopes short, avoid holding a synchronous lock across await, and adopt one lock ordering when several locks must be acquired. Poisoning reports a prior panic while locked, not necessarily irreparable corruption.

Send describes moving ownership between threads; Sync describes sharing references safely. These properties propagate through types subject to their fields and implementation contracts. Rc is not a substitute for Arc across threads.

lessons.title: Channels, closure, and backpressure
body: A channel transfers values from senders to a receiver. Ownership moves with each sent value. A receiver’s iterator ends after all senders are dropped and queued messages are consumed.

An unbounded queue can grow when producers outrun consumers. sync_channel supplies a capacity and blocks sending when full; capacity zero is a rendezvous. Define what should happen under overload rather than assuming unlimited buffering.

Keep sender lifetimes deliberate. An unnoticed sender clone can prevent receiver shutdown forever. When cancelling a pipeline, close channels or communicate shutdown so every worker has a way to stop and be joined.

lessons.title: Atomic operations and memory ordering
body: An atomic operation accesses one atomic location without a data race. Relaxed ordering guarantees atomicity for that location but does not publish arbitrary adjacent non-atomic data. A statistics counter may need only this guarantee.

Release/acquire ordering can establish visibility through a correctly designed synchronization relation. SeqCst additionally supplies a single order for those operations. Stronger ordering cannot repair a logically incorrect protocol or unsafe storage access.

Start with a lock unless a measured need justifies a lock-free protocol. Write the invariant and publication relation before choosing ordering; compare_exchange loops also need to handle contention and possible ABA-style state reuse.

lessons.title: Future, poll, wake, and await
body: Calling an async function creates a future; it does not complete the computation immediately. An executor polls futures. Ready carries a result; Pending means the future must arrange an appropriate wakeup when progress may be possible.

await suspends the current future until the awaited one is ready. It does not create an OS thread or guarantee parallel work. Blocking I/O inside async can stall an executor thread; use the runtime’s appropriate asynchronous or blocking boundary.

The demonstration polls an immediately ready future once, with a no-op waker. It is intentionally not a production executor: a genuinely pending future needs wakeup scheduling, cancellation and resource management. A runtime such as Tokio supplies those policies separately from the Rust language.

lessons.title: Pin, Unpin, and address-sensitive state
body:
Pin

restricts moving the pointee through its safe interface when the target is not Unpin. It does not pin every variable globally. Pointer ownership and the promise about the pointee’s address are distinct.

Some futures can hold references into their own state after polling, making movement unsafe. Box::pin owns pinned heap storage; pin! pins a local value within a controlled scope. Unpin types do not require that address guarantee.

Unsafe pin construction/projection requires a lasting invariant, including destruction and which fields are structurally pinned. Prefer safe constructors and a well-reviewed projection abstraction rather than assuming every field may be moved out.

lessons.title: Cancellation is dropping owned work
body: Dropping a future cancels further polling of that future and drops its owned state. It does not undo external effects already performed, and it may not stop a detached worker or remote request by itself.

Cancellation safety asks what remains true if suspension ends at any await point. Keep partial updates behind transactional boundaries, use explicit task ownership and join policies, and make resource guards release reliably when the future is dropped.

A future that returns Pending must arrange wakeup if it is intended to progress. This example intentionally remains pending and is then dropped; it demonstrates resource release rather than an executor or remote-job cancellation guarantee.

body: Stable Rust supports async methods in traits for static dispatch. The returned future is an opaque implementation type. The public trait contract must deliberately address Send and other requirements needed by consumers.

An async method does not automatically make a trait dyn-compatible. Erased APIs often return Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + appropriate bounds>> or use an adapter, with allocation and lifetime tradeoffs.

Do not assume every async result is safe to send between threads. Captured values and state held across await determine the future’s auto traits. Document the execution context and test the bounds required by your API.

lessons.title: macro_rules, repetition, and hygiene
body: A declarative macro matches token patterns and expands Rust syntax. Fragment kinds such as expr and ident constrain what a matcher accepts. Repetition can generate code for a variable number of inputs.

Macros are not ordinary functions: expansion happens before the resulting code is type checked. Keep a clear reason for syntax generation; a generic function is usually easier to debug when syntax itself need not change.

Hygiene controls name resolution, and exported helpers often need $crate to refer to their defining crate. Match delimiters and optional trailing separators intentionally, and make invalid invocations produce useful diagnostics.

lessons.title: Unsafe code and explicit safety invariants
body: unsafe permits specified operations such as dereferencing raw pointers; it does not disable the whole type system. A safe wrapper must establish every precondition of its unsafe implementation for every safe caller.

Raw pointers do not automatically carry ownership, validity, alignment or aliasing proof. Document where a pointer came from, which allocation is alive, what memory is initialized, and whether access conflicts with other references.

Keep unsafe blocks small and place a precise safety argument beside each one. A pointer that is non-null can still be dangling or misaligned. Passing tests is valuable evidence but cannot by itself establish soundness for all callers.

lessons.title: C ABI, extern blocks, and boundary ownership
body: FFI connects Rust with another language’s calling conventions and representations. extern "C" chooses a C ABI, not an ownership protocol. Check widths, layout, lifetimes, allocator ownership and error conventions on both sides.

Edition 2024 requires unsafe extern blocks; declarations inside describe functions the compiler cannot inspect. A foreign function can be marked safe only when all its uses meet a genuinely unconditional contract. Variadic interfaces add ABI-specific promotion requirements.

Do not unwind through an ABI boundary that forbids it. Use compatible unwind contracts where intended, or catch/translate failures. A Rust-facing safe wrapper should validate inputs and ensure foreign resources are released by the correct owner.

lessons.title: Representation, padding, and serialization
body: Rust’s default struct layout is not a stable serialization format. repr(C) follows a C-compatible field layout policy, while repr(transparent) supports a wrapper with the specified representation constraints.

Size includes padding and depends on the target and representation. Alignment requirements apply to references and raw accesses. Packed structs can create unaligned fields; taking an ordinary reference to such a field is not a safe way to access it.

Encode a network/file format explicitly with byte-order conversions and fixed-width fields. Do not transmute a struct into bytes and assume it is portable, fully initialized or free of sensitive padding.

lessons.title: MaybeUninit and initialization responsibility
body: MaybeUninit<T> can hold storage that is not yet a valid T. It is useful for low-level initialization and FFI out-parameters, but moving the wrapper does not prove the contents are initialized.

write initializes a value; assume_init is unsafe because the author must prove validity. An arbitrary bit pattern is not valid for every type. For example, references and many enums have representation constraints beyond byte count.

Cleanup is also your responsibility when partially initializing many elements. Track the initialized prefix and drop it on failure; prefer safe constructors such as Vec when they already express the operation. ManuallyDrop likewise changes cleanup obligations rather than making them disappear.

body: A const fn can be evaluated in a const context when its operations satisfy constant-evaluation rules. The same function can also run at runtime. const does not mean every call is automatically evaluated during compilation.

Compile-time evaluation has restrictions involving effects, allocations, traits and generic computations. These restrictions evolve; consult the target version rather than copying nightly syntax into a stable project.
Use constants for fixed tables or invariant parameters, and check edge cases such as overflow deliberately. A compile-time calculation still needs a meaningful mathematical/domain contract.

This is useful when an algorithm creates short-lived borrows and passes them to a callback. A callback tied to only one longer lifetime would not necessarily accept those temporary views.

Read the binder as a quantified contract. Lifetimes still describe borrow validity; they do not allocate, clone or extend the referent. Type variance then governs which lifetime substitutions are permitted inside a type.

lessons.title: A lending interface with a generic associated type
body: A generic associated type can express an output whose type depends on a borrow lifetime. A lending view trait can return a reference into self without pretending each output has a static lifetime.

The bound where Self: 'a states that Self is valid for the lifetime used by the associated output. The implementation chooses the output representation for that lifetime, and the method ties it to the receiver borrow.

lessons.title: Sized, ?Sized, and dynamically sized types
body: A generic type parameter is Sized by default. ?Sized relaxes that default, allowing a reference-based API to accept str, slices or trait objects in addition to sized values.

A dynamically sized type needs pointer metadata: a slice view carries its element count; a trait object carries metadata used for dynamic dispatch. This does not make an unsized value an ordinary stack-local value of known size.

Borrowing APIs can often be more general with T: ?Sized because the reference itself remains sized. Type aliases merely rename a type; a newtype introduces a distinct type and can enforce a separate interface.

Initialization policy is part of the API: who supplies configuration, what happens if initialization panics, and how repeated requests behave? Do not hide per-user state in a permanent global merely for convenience.
Long-lived caches can intentionally retain memory; distinguish that policy from abandoned ownership. Bound their contents or choose a scoped owner when the app/session should release them.

Matching a borrowed value often uses match ergonomics to infer reference bindings. Explicit ref, ref mut and reference patterns need particular care under edition 2024 rules. Prefer clear borrowed inputs and verify the resulting binding types.

@ binds a value while testing a subpattern. Or-patterns cover alternatives with compatible bindings, and guards add Boolean conditions. Exhaustiveness still needs an unguarded fallback for uncovered values.

body: From expresses an infallible conversion; implementing it also supplies Into through the standard blanket implementation. TryFrom/TryInto report a conversion that can fail, including range validation.

A custom newtype can require construction through a validated conversion rather than expose an unrestricted field. The error should identify the rejected condition and give callers an explicit recovery path.
as is useful for defined low-level conversions but is not a general validation boundary. Parsing textual input with FromStr and narrowing an already parsed integer with TryFrom are separate checks.

lessons.title: Panic strategy and failed invariants
body: panic reports a failure outside an ordinary Result path. Unwinding can run destructors while it walks the stack; a panic-abort build terminates without that unwinding. The selected build strategy matters to recovery and cleanup.

catch_unwind catches an unwinding panic with the required unwind-safety contract. It does not catch every abort or turn an arbitrary unsafe operation into defined behavior. Keep it at a deliberate boundary rather than replacing typed validation.

Custom panic hooks and error reporting may expose context. Avoid logging secrets, and distinguish a programmer invariant failure from expected input errors so callers can recover without interpreting text messages.

lessons.title: Newtypes, blanket impls, and coherence
body: A newtype has a distinct identity even if it wraps an existing representation. It can prevent confusing units and gives you a local type for trait implementations. A type alias does neither; it is another name for the same type.

Coherence prevents incompatible overlapping trait implementations. Blanket implementations can constrain which more-specific implementations are available. Before promising an extension point, examine the current and future implementation space.

Variance describes which subtype/lifetime substitutions a type allows. Shared references and mutable references differ in their treatment of the referent type, and UnsafeCell-based interior mutation affects variance. PhantomData can express ownership/variance relationships but does not allocate a value.

lessons.title: Rust 1.99: recovering NonNull-owned storage
body: A NonNull pointer proves that the address is not zero; it does not prove live storage, alignment, initialization or exclusive ownership. Converting an owner into a pointer transfers cleanup responsibility to your protocol.

Box::into_non_null and Box::from_non_null provide a NonNull ownership round trip. Recover the same allocation exactly once with matching type/allocator assumptions; do not also drop a second fabricated owner.

Vec::into_parts and Vec::from_parts likewise carry allocation metadata that must remain correct. These APIs are advanced ownership tools for a justified boundary, not a faster replacement for ordinary safe iteration.

lessons.title: Project: a tested text-search CLI
body: Build this after the ownership, Result, lifetime, iterator, module and testing lessons. Cargo turns one package into a reusable library crate and a small executable crate: src/lib.rs exports policy, while src/main.rs owns the operating-system boundary. The binary can use minigrep::Config without exposing private implementation details. No third-party crate or network fetch is required.

Config::parse accepts an iterator of owned UTF-8 arguments and returns either a fully valid configuration or a specific error. The process adapter uses args_os and fallible conversion so a non-UTF-8 argument becomes a usage error rather than an args() panic. The -- marker ends option interpretation, allowing a query beginning with a dash. Exactly two positional arguments are required; unknown flags and extra values are rejected. This version deliberately accepts UTF-8 file paths only; a production path interface could preserve OsString separately from the textual query.

search returns Vec<&str> borrowing the contents, not a set of copied lines. The explicit lifetime relates only the input text to the output, so a temporary query can disappear while the selected lines remain usable. The contents String in main therefore must stay alive until all selected lines are printed. Replacing the owned file buffer with a temporary inside search would make these references invalid and the borrow checker must reject that design.

The insensitive mode normalizes the query once, then normalizes each candidate line before testing contains. The output still borrows the original line, preserving its spelling. This is Unicode lowercase comparison, not locale-aware collation, normalization or full case folding: document that contract rather than claiming every human spelling is equivalent. lines() removes CRLF separators and omits the final empty line; an empty query selects every line actually yielded, while an empty file yields no lines.

The binary prints matches to stdout. Usage/argument errors go to stderr with status 2; file/UTF-8 decoding errors use status 1; a successful search with no matches uses status 0 in this teaching contract. Returning ExitCode lets ordinary Rust destructors run. Unlike process::exit in the middle of a function, the return does not skip cleanup of still-live local values. Broken-pipe handling and a streaming BufRead version are further design exercises, not established by these tests.

Run unit, integration and documentation tests. Five library tests isolate parsing, end-of-options, case behavior, CRLF/Unicode, and independent query/text lifetimes. Three integration tests spawn the actual compiled binary and check fixture output, usage failure and a missing file. The rustdoc example is also compiled and run. For the practice solution, add inversion without breaking search callers, then prove both library behavior and executable wiring. A passing quiz alone is not completion of these engineering exercises.

Add unit and executable tests before revealing the solution. Advanced: design a streaming implementation with numbered/context lines and explicit broken-pipe handling; explain why borrowing lines from a reused BufRead buffer cannot return the same Vec<&str> interface. The advanced design is an open extension, not part of the supplied answer.

lessons.title: Project: Cargo features, generated code and a workspace
body: Work through the basic Cargo, modules, cfg, constant and error lessons first. This complete workspace contains two packages: feature-engine owns an arithmetic policy, and feature-demo is a command-line client through a local path dependency. A package may contain several crates; workspace membership is a separate Cargo organization level. One virtual root manifest supplies resolver version 3 and shared edition, Rust-version, version and lint settings. Each member explicitly opts into inherited package/lint fields; declaring a workspace value alone does not apply it everywhere.

Run the default example and predict wrapping: 4 from the explicit u8 wrapping_add policy. Enable the demo checked feature to forward feature-engine/checked, rebuilding the dependency and returning checked: overflow. Cargo features select compiled capabilities and are unified for a given dependency in the relevant resolution context; they are not ordinary runtime booleans or an arbitrary mutually-exclusive choice system. Design library feature combinations to work together. Resolver 3 affects dependency resolution/MSRV behavior; it does not make every conflicting feature combination valid.

The engine build script runs on the build host before the target crate is compiled. It observes Cargo's CARGO_FEATURE_CHECKED variable, declares the custom engine_checked cfg name to the compiler, conditionally enables it, and writes mode.rs under OUT_DIR. include! reads that generated Rust source at compile time. Generated files belong in OUT_DIR, not src or the dependency registry. Cross compilation can run the script on one architecture while compiling its output for another: do not mistake a build-host probe for a target property.

cargo::rustc-check-cfg makes the custom cfg recognized; unexpected_cfgs=deny then catches spelling errors rather than silently selecting the wrong branch. cfg! expands to a boolean expression, so both branches of an ordinary if still need to type-check; #[cfg] removes a declaration/block from this compilation. The example uses #[cfg] for the arithmetic implementation and cfg! inside tests where both assertion branches are valid Rust. Shared unsafe_code=forbid rejects unsafe blocks, but does not prove the whole dependency graph or all logic correct.

The .cargo/config.toml verify alias runs workspace tests, including both packages and the library rustdoc example. A root cargo run without -p uses the configured default member; selecting -p feature-engine targets the library package instead. Test default and checked separately, and also --all-features so feature-unified builds cannot quietly escape testing. Profiles, target triples, build-script rerun inputs and environment overrides are independent configuration dimensions; this small project demonstrates the stated feature/build/lint contracts, not every Cargo setting.

For practice, make the CLI default to checked arithmetic while keeping the engine library's default policy unchanged. Add default=["checked"] only to demo/Cargo.toml. Then ordinary demo runs report overflow, --no-default-features on the selected demo opts back into wrapping, and direct engine tests still cover its wrapping default. Feature unification can enable checked when testing both members together; that is expected. A deployed project must commit and verify its lockfile and toolchain policy once external dependencies are introduced; this dependency-free project resolves offline.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: run the wrapping and checked commands, and explain where MODE is generated and who owns it. Intermediate: make only the demo default to checked; prove the ordinary command prints checked: overflow, --no-default-features restores wrapping: 4, and direct engine tests still pass without defaults. Advanced: introduce a second independent additive feature, test every supported combination, and deliberately misspell engine_checked to inspect the unexpected_cfgs diagnostic. Document host-versus-target behavior before proposing cross-compilation probes. The provided worked answer implements the intermediate requirement; the additional feature/probe design remains your extension.

options: In engine/Cargo.toml, enabling the feature for every library consumer.
In a runtime environment variable named CHECKED, which always changes compiled cfg blocks.
In workspace.package, because all arbitrary fields automatically propagate to members.
In demo/Cargo.toml as default = ["checked"], forwarding the existing engine feature.

Remember that --no-default-features disables defaults for the selected package; it cannot turn off a dependency feature another selected consumer has enabled. lessons.title: Project: a bounded HTTP server and owned thread pool
body: Build this after the I/O CLI, ownership, FnOnce, Send, channels, mutex, threads and Drop lessons. The six-file package separates transport/framing, response policy, worker ownership and process entry. It reworks the Rust Book final server as a bounded, dependency-free teaching project. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream, not HTTP request boundaries: one read may return part of a header or several messages. HTTP framing belongs above that stream. This project intentionally handles one small request per connection and announces Connection: close.

Read through the complete request header terminator, preserving bytes across reads. Enforce an 8,192-byte header limit before extending the buffer and compute one absolute read deadline with Instant. A client sending tiny chunks must not get a fresh whole-second budget after every read. Set each socket read timeout to the remaining budget. Incomplete EOF, expiry and oversized input return errors and close the connection in this version; they are not promised a formatted HTTP error response. The parser separately rejects unsupported framing, duplicate/missing Host, invalid UTF-8 and nonzero Content-Length.

reply builds status, CRLF-separated headers, the blank separator and body bytes. Content-Length counts bytes, not Unicode characters. The baseline supports GET / and a 404 route; other methods receive 405 with Allow: GET. A body or transfer encoding is outside this deliberately small subset. It is not a general HTTP parser, TLS server, persistent-connection implementation or replacement for a maintained protocol stack. Tests establish the stated subset, not arbitrary malformed-request robustness.

Pool uses sync_channel with a fixed queue capacity and try_send: a full queue rejects work immediately rather than creating unbounded retained closures or blocking the accept loop. serve closes a rejected connection when its dropped closure releases the moved TcpStream; it does not send 503. Workers share a Receiver through Arc<Mutex<_>>. Crucially, the receive guard is released in a separate expression before a job runs. Holding that guard around execution would serialize the workers even though several threads exist. The overlap regression requires two jobs to start before either is released.

Each job is FnOnce because it consumes its captured socket, Send because it crosses threads and static because the worker can outlive the submission stack. Static does not mean the allocation lives forever; it prevents borrowed stack data from escaping. A worker catches an unwinding job panic and accepts later jobs, but cannot recover a process abort or guarantee shared application state survived the panic. The queue and receiver hold no strong reference back to Pool. The self-owner regression also handles a job releasing the final Arc<Pool> without trying to join its own thread.

Shutdown first drops the final sender. The receiver can drain accepted jobs and then wakes with disconnection; Drop joins worker handles. Joining before closing the sender would deadlock idle receivers. Moving each JoinHandle out with drain avoids attempting to consume a borrowed handle. If destruction runs on a worker, all handles are detached after the sender closes. Joining even a peer could block the current callback from signaling that peer. Workers then drain/disconnect after their callbacks finish; this destructor does not synchronously wait for them. Outside the pool, destruction joins all workers. Generic jobs must eventually finish: this pool cannot preempt an infinite closure. The supplied network jobs have bounded reads and fixed responses with a socket write timeout.

The demonstration accepts exactly two connections before draining and joining, matching the Book shutdown progression. That limit counts accepted connections, including rejected jobs or malformed requests, rather than successful responses. It can wait indefinitely for the next client while accepting; that is listener waiting, not a worker leak. Ctrl-C is process termination and is not the graceful shutdown mechanism implemented here. A future cancellation-aware accept loop needs an explicit wakeup/shutdown design and a dependency/runtime policy.

Run the pure parser/pool tests, then actual loopback integration tests and the self-check executable. Tests cover concurrent overlap, a full queue, draining, panic recovery, final-owner release, status/length/framing, incomplete reads, maximum size and actual TCP responses. For the intermediate exercise, add HEAD while keeping the corresponding GET representation length and returning no body for success, 404 or recognizable HEAD validation errors. The answer replaces only http.rs and the integration tests; the pool and transport ownership remain unchanged. Further HTTP parsing, load tests, shutdown signaling and production async are separate projects.

Intermediate: implement HEAD for / and missing routes with the same status/Content-Length as GET and no response body, including recognizable HEAD validation errors; add actual TCP tests. Advanced: design cancellation that wakes an idle accept loop, explicit overload responses, absolute write deadlines and a framing/Unicode fuzz corpus. Explain why dropping a handle is different from cancelling or joining a worker. Those advanced extensions are not implemented by the provided HEAD answer.
lessons.question: Which ordering lets idle workers finish during pool destruction?
options: Drop JoinHandle values to forcibly cancel their worker threads.
Keep the receiver mutex locked while running jobs so shutdown can observe them.
Drop the final sender first, let receivers drain/disconnect, then join the worker handles.
Join every worker while keeping the sender alive.
lessons.explanation: The sender closes the channel when taken from its Option and dropped. Receivers first process accepted queued jobs and then return disconnection; join waits for those workers to finish. The receiver guard must be gone before each callback. The HEAD answer permits GET or HEAD and wraps the complete response builder, truncating transmitted bytes after the header separator for recognizable HEAD methods even when parsing returns an error response. Content-Length still describes the GET representation. The answer changes Allow to GET, HEAD, and its actual loopback tests compare GET and HEAD headers on /, /missing and three 400-error variants. The pool cannot cancel arbitrary blocking jobs and Ctrl-C is not the implemented orderly shutdown path.

lessons.title: Source project: environment configuration and precedence
body: This complete variant adapts the Rust Book environment-variable section and its configuration-precedence exercise. Start from the earlier CLI lesson, then create this independent five-file package. Config::parse still has its original case-sensitive default for library callers; parse_with_default injects a captured process policy. The library does not read ambient environment values itself. The executable snapshots IGNORE_CASE once and passes the resulting boolean into parsing, so the same inputs can be tested without global state.

The baseline follows the source presence policy: env::var("IGNORE_CASE").is_ok() enables insensitive search for any successfully decoded string. The strings 0 and false, and even an empty value, are still present values and therefore enable it. An absent variable disables it. var returns Result<String, VarError>; on Unix a present non-UTF-8 value yields NotUnicode and is_ok is false. That is distinct from var_os returning Some(OsString) for such a value. Predict this truth table before running the actual child-process cases.

Keep the original case-sensitive test while adding the insensitive test: one new feature must not silently erase the previous contract. The provided red step removes candidate normalization and fails the source-substring test; restoring it makes that same test pass. Searching rUsT matches both Rust: and Trust me., because contains matches substrings rather than whole words. Lowercase the query once and each candidate line before contains, but return the original borrowed line. Query normalization allocates a String, so contains borrows it; do not return a slice into the temporary lowercase candidate. Basic Unicode lowercase is not complete normalization, full case folding or locale-aware comparison. Existing lifetime, CRLF, empty-input, Unicode and rustdoc checks remain in this package.

An environment variable belongs to a process. A shell assignment for one command affects that child; a persistent shell variable can influence later commands. In Rust 2024, mutating process-global environment with set_var/remove_var is unsafe because other threads or libraries can read it. Reading a variable and setting a Command builder environment are different operations. These tests use Command::env_remove/env on individual child builders and an absolute Cargo-provided executable path; they never call unsafe global setters or print the rest of the host environment.

The source asks you to choose precedence when a flag and environment disagree. In the worked extension, first validate the environment snapshot as exactly 1, true, 0 or false, with missing meaning false. Empty, uppercase aliases, whitespace and other strings are errors. Non-Unicode is also an explicit error. Then apply flags in argument order: the last --ignore-case or --case-sensitive wins over that valid default. Invalid environment is rejected even if a flag could override it; that is a deliberate strict-validation policy, not the only possible interface design.

Write the precedence and invalid-value tests before changing the parser. The boolean policy function takes a Result value, making unit tests deterministic and parallel without modifying the process. Integration tests start the actual executable with absent, true, false, empty, invalid and Unix non-Unicode values. They check stdout/status/stderr as well as flag priority. Base and answer retain usage status 2, read failure status 1, borrowed output and the -- end-of-options behavior. Additional OS path/locale policies and shell portability are separate extensions.

Reject invalid/non-Unicode environment before applying flags, including when an override is present. Add pure policy and actual child-process tests without global environment mutation. Advanced: design a typed configuration layer for default/file/environment/CLI sources with provenance, and compare strict invalid-value rejection with override-first validation. That advanced layer is an open extension.

It removes the variable from the child environment.
It causes undefined behavior merely by reading the value.
It enables insensitive matching: 0 is a successfully decoded present string, not a parsed boolean.

lessons.title: CLI streams: redirection, diagnostics and fallible output
body: This independent five-file project adapts the Rust Book standard-error chapter. A command has separate stdout and stderr streams plus an exit status. Successful matching text belongs on stdout; usage, read and write diagnostics belong on stderr. Printing an error does not automatically make the status unsuccessful. This interface uses 2 for invalid arguments, 1 for read/write failure and 0 for a completed search, including no matches. Those are our documented policies rather than universal shell requirements.

The source demonstrates the bug by redirecting stdout while triggering an argument error. Reproduce it with the deliberate red step: change just the usage eprintln! to println!, then run usage_only_writes_stderr. The test checks exact stderr, empty stdout and status 2, so the incorrect implementation fails even though the message remains visible in an ordinary terminal. Restore eprintln! and run all tests. The same separation is checked for a missing input file.

Build first, then run the executable directly so Cargo diagnostics are not confused with program stderr. On a POSIX shell, target/debug/streamgrep > output.txt leaves output.txt empty and reports usage on stderr. With rust fixture.txt before the redirection, the file receives only rust is safe followed by a newline. Redirection opens or truncates its destination before the child starts, even if parsing later fails. Use a disposable output file and inspect the status immediately; a later command replaces the shell’s status value.

The integration test performs actual stdout-to-file redirection with Command and Stdio, without interpreting a shell string. It captures stderr separately, reads the file after the child exits and removes only its own temporary directory through an RAII guard. The success case must leave stderr empty; the error case must leave the redirected file empty. Separate captures do not establish any total ordering between stdout and stderr. Merging them is a caller decision and loses this channel distinction.

println! can panic when writing stdout fails. Here the library takes any Write, uses writeln! with ?, and explicitly flushes so buffered-output failure reaches the caller. Tests supply failing writers for both write and flush, preserving io::ErrorKind. The executable locks stdout once and returns ExitCode, allowing ordinary local destructors to run. It reads a UTF-8 file into memory, keeps the path as an OS string and requires only the query to decode as UTF-8. Streaming large files and allocation failures remain separate extensions.

The worked practice accepts BrokenPipe as success when a downstream consumer intentionally closes early, while preserving failure for other output errors. This is an explicit CLI policy. The library still reports BrokenPipe rather than hiding it from all callers. The answer checks its error-kind classifier. A real anonymous pipe test drops its reader before starting the executable: the base must return failure with a write diagnostic; the answer must succeed silently. This removes scheduling ambiguity about whether a reader closed before the write. Other unit tests inject write and flush failures. Partial output can already have escaped before a later write or flush fails, so Result does not make output atomic. Design an atomic file-output mode separately with its own replacement and durability contract.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: explain why an error printed with println! contaminates a redirected results file. Intermediate: implement the red/green stream tests before changing the output macro. Advanced: accept only BrokenPipe as successful early termination, keep other write/flush failures visible and explain partial-output limits; compare the replacement answer files.
lessons.question: A command redirects stdout to a file, then fails to parse its arguments. What should this interface do?
options: Return status 0 whenever eprintln! succeeds
Assume the two streams always preserve a shared ordering
Write the diagnostic to stderr, leave stdout empty and return status 2
Print the diagnostic to stdout because redirection preserves it
lessons.explanation: Stream routing and exit status are separate contracts. Results use stdout, diagnostics use stderr, and usage returns 2 in this project. Writer errors propagate; neither Result nor a status rolls back previously emitted output.

lessons.title: CLI iterators: ownership, laziness and precise captures
body: This separate project adapts the Rust Book I/O iterator refactor and both suggested search extensions. A borrowed slice of String values cannot give its elements away; cloning lets a returned Config own copies. An owning iterator can instead yield each owned value to the parser. This package consumes args_os directly, moves the query into a String with fallible conversion and moves the native path into PathBuf. It never collects the complete command line into a Vec or clones each input string. This does not promise that platform conversions allocate nothing.

The input iterator includes the executable name. Call next once to discard that item, then require a query and path with distinct errors. next needs mutable iterator state, hence mut args. The impl Iterator parameter accepts concrete iterator types without requiring boxed dynamic dispatch. Unlike the source’s minimal parser, this interface rejects extra arguments by reading one additional item; it does not consume an unbounded tail. A counted infinite-tail test proves exactly four items are visited. Arguments requiring flags need a different parser contract.

Replace the explicit result-pushing loop with lines, filter and collect. filter’s predicate receives a reference to each iterator item; method autoderef lets line.contains(query) express the condition directly. The base search still eagerly collects a Vec of borrowed original lines, so callers observe the same completed collection. Collection allocates space for references, not copies of the file text. The input must outlive those references. Tests preserve case-sensitive substring matching, CRLF line handling, no matches and empty input.

The generic search_lines adapter returns a lazy iterator. Building it does not visit any candidate. next advances only until the next match; dropping it after that prevents later visits. A Cell counter attached with inspect observes zero visits at construction and exactly two after the first match, with the third line untouched. Iterator adapters do not run themselves. collect, for, count and other consumers drive them. Loops and iterators can both be clear; concision alone proves neither speed nor parallel execution.

For the first worked extension, search returns the lazy adapter instead of a Vec. The executable’s for loop works for either return type; tests explicitly collect where comparing a vector is desired. The returned adapter borrows both query and file text while it exists, but each yielded item borrows only the text. Rust 2024 precise use captures make the two lifetime dependencies visible. A test collects within the query’s scope, then uses the output lines after the query has dropped while retaining the text owner.

The second worked extension returns a case-insensitive adapter. It owns one lowercased query String in a move closure and borrows the input text; use captures only the text lifetime, so the original query may drop before iteration begins. Each polled candidate still creates a lowercase String. Returned values preserve original spelling, and basic lowercase is not full Unicode case folding. The lazy answer avoids a result-vector allocation and can emit matches before scanning all candidate lines, but this CLI still reads the entire file first. No benchmark or streaming-file-memory claim follows from this refactor.

Intermediate: predict each counted next call, including the extra-argument check. Advanced: return lazy sensitive and insensitive adapters with correct query/text captures, preserve original output and demonstrate which owner can be dropped before iteration; compare the complete answer.

Every query String must live forever because the adapter used it
The Vec owns copies of all matching String values
No owner is needed because iterator adapters allocate automatically

lessons.title: Streaming files: line limits, read errors and early termination
body: Rust by Example contrasts reading a whole file into owned lines with a BufReader-backed line iterator. File::open can fail before an iterator exists, and each later line operation can fail independently. Its short demonstration uses map_while(Result::ok), which stops at the first error and does not report that error to its loop. That can be acceptable only when deliberately choosing a stop-and-ignore policy. This project instead propagates open, read, decoding, write and flush failures, so a damaged or unreadable input is not presented as an empty successful search.

BufReader owns the File and releases it when dropped. A generic BufRead library function can also accept in-memory cursors and controlled failure sources; the executable owns the concrete file and a 16 KiB read buffer. Borrowed fill_buf bytes are valid only until the next mutable reader operation. Copy the selected bytes into this line buffer, finish using the borrowed chunk, then consume exactly those bytes. The parser handles newlines split across buffers and validates UTF-8 only once a whole line has been assembled, so a multibyte scalar split between reads is not misdiagnosed.

Buffered line iteration alone does not bound a single enormous line. This implementation accepts a limit of 1 through 1 MiB and rejects a line before appending bytes beyond it. The limit counts encoded bytes including LF or CRLF delimiters, not Unicode characters. The executable chooses 8 KiB per line. Vec capacity can exceed logical length because of allocator growth, and a caller-supplied reader may have its own buffers; this is a bounded line-length contract, not an exact whole-process memory measurement. No complete input String or result Vec is created.

For line semantics, remove LF and then its optional preceding CR. A final standalone CR remains content. Emit the final unterminated line once; an empty file produces no lines, while explicit blank lines are real lines. Output preserves original spelling and uses one LF per match. Tests force one-byte input chunks, including split UTF-8, and check CRLF, blank input, final lines, invalid UTF-8 and exact byte-limit boundaries. Results are case-sensitive substring matches; Unicode normalization is a separate policy.

Processing can already have written matching lines when a later read fails. The Result then reports failure without rolling those bytes back. A custom BufRead returns one valid line and then an injected error; the test requires both the emitted prefix and the final error. Separate tests inject write and flush failures. The executable reports diagnostics on stderr and returns 1 for stream/open failures or 2 for invalid arguments, while a completed search returns 0. Atomic replacement of an output file would need a separate transactional design.

The worked extension adds an optional positive match limit. Once that many matches have been emitted, flush and return without polling another line. The answer test uses the one-line-then-error reader to prove the later error is never requested. This deliberately stops validation of the remaining input; it does not certify that unread suffix as valid. None preserves the original full-input behavior, and NonZeroUsize rules out the ambiguous zero-match request. Existing entry points and all base tests remain unchanged. Early termination may leave unread bytes buffered in the reader; callers decide whether to resume, discard or close it.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: distinguish opening a file from failing during iteration. Intermediate: enforce the byte limit without rejecting UTF-8 split across buffers, preserve CRLF/final-line semantics and test partial output on a later error. Advanced: stop after an optional positive match count, flush and prove no further read occurs; explain which unread-input guarantees this intentionally gives up.

Returns the same Err automatically from main

lessons.title: Staged file replacement: cleanup and publication boundaries
body: File::create and fs::write can truncate an existing destination before the new content is complete. For a trusted local Unix directory, this project instead prepares a sibling file, writes and synchronizes its content, closes it and renames its name over the destination. Putting the temporary file in the same directory avoids intentionally crossing mount points. Rename behavior and errors differ by platform and filesystem. This project explicitly requires Unix and is checked on macOS; it is not a portable transaction library or a hostile-directory security boundary.

OpenOptions with create_new reserves a previously absent staging name without the separate exists-then-create race. The process ID and relaxed atomic counter generate candidates, but reservation depends on create_new rather than unpredictability. AlreadyExists retries another candidate up to a fixed bound; other failures return immediately. New files request mode 0600. This deliberately replaces the destination with a newly owned file rather than preserving its permission bits, extended attributes, hard-link identity or open-handle identity. The parent directory must already exist and be trusted. This teaching API requires ASCII destination basenames and reserves .codetutor-stage- case-insensitively, rejecting them before creating anything. Parent directory paths may still contain Unicode. This explicit naming policy avoids case aliases on case-insensitive Mac filesystems without pretending to implement every filesystem’s Unicode equivalence rules. Otherwise a generated candidate could equal an absent destination and expose preparation bytes under its final name; the regression requires rejection before the writer runs.

The Stage guard owns both the file and its temporary pathname. On a preparation error or unwinding panic, Drop closes the file and then attempts to remove only that stage. Cleanup errors are ignored in Drop, so cleanup is best effort and leftover stages remain possible if removal fails. Aborting the process, forced termination, power loss and mem::forget do not run this normal cleanup path. Tests inject a write-then-error and an unwinding panic, requiring the old destination bytes and no stage residue on this local filesystem.

Write failures and file synchronization failures happen before publication. Rename failure also attempts stage cleanup; a test deliberately targets an existing directory and requires that directory to survive. After rename succeeds, clear the stage pathname so guard destruction cannot delete the published destination. Existing open descriptors may still refer to the earlier file object; replacing a directory entry does not rewrite all outstanding handles. Concurrent writers, parent-path symlink races, network-filesystem ambiguity and hostile directory replacement are outside this contract.

The worked extension requests parent-directory synchronization after rename. A failure at that point has different meaning: the new destination is already visible, and reporting an error cannot imply rollback. ReplaceError carries published alongside the original io::Error and exposes its source through the Error trait. An injected post-publication error proves the new bytes remain present while published is true. Callers must inspect that state before deciding whether a retry is safe. The base performs file sync and rename but omits the parent sync; the answer changes that one policy point.

File Drop ignores close errors; explicit sync_all reports a synchronization attempt, not a universal proof against power loss. This suite checks ordinary success, injected preparation/unwind/rename/post-publication failures, cleanup and actual executable output on this Mac. It does not inject device I/O failures or crash the OS, and it does not certify storage-device durability. Build a recovery/versioning protocol if that stronger requirement matters. Keep a disposable owned directory for practice: the command intentionally replaces its destination, so never experiment on an original personal book or real notes file. Even reporting success can fail while writing stdout after publication; the executable reports published=true rather than suggesting the destination stayed unchanged.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: explain why writing directly to an existing file can destroy the old content before success. Intermediate: add stage cleanup tests for an error and an unwinding panic, and preserve an existing directory on rename failure. Advanced: synchronize the parent directory after publication and ensure an error reports that publication already happened; compare the answer and list its durability/security limits.

options: Every Result::Err automatically rolls back file changes
The temporary guard should delete the destination to undo the rename
A successful file sync guarantees every storage device survives power loss
The new destination was published; an error does not imply the old bytes were restored
lessons.explanation: Rename is the publication boundary in this scoped local-filesystem protocol. Pre-publication and post-publication failures have different observable effects. Cleanup and sync calls provide bounded contracts, not universal crash durability or hostile-path safety.

lessons.title: HTTP source project: HTML files and slow-request comparison
body: This independent eight-file project extends the earlier bounded server with the Rust Book HTML and slow-request variants. Its base already includes the previous HEAD answer. The root and /sleep routes select a small original HTML page; every other path gets a fixed HTML 404 page. Response Content-Length counts UTF-8 bytes, including the multibyte seedling character. HEAD preserves the corresponding representation headers while suppressing its body, including error responses. This remains a small HTTP/1.1 teaching subset, not a general protocol implementation.

The base uses include_str! for its two project-owned HTML files. The compiler embeds their UTF-8 text, so edits require rebuilding and serving does not reopen them. The files live in assets and are part of the displayed complete project. The worked extension instead opens those fixed names under the Cargo manifest directory at request time. That is a deliberate trusted local deployment path, not a portable installed-resource locator. Never construct a filesystem pathname from the incoming request target; /../private receives the known 404 page.

Runtime HTML loading in the answer reads at most 65,537 bytes, rejects a page exceeding 65,536 and validates UTF-8 before constructing a response. A missing, oversized, unreadable or invalid page produces a generic 500 response rather than exposing host paths or partial source. Tests exercise the exact cap, one-byte overflow, invalid UTF-8 and an absent page. The file is locally owned through the read call and closes on return. There is no request-body support, recursive directory serving, templating, TLS or arbitrary user file access.

The valid /sleep route blocks its worker for 200 milliseconds to model a slow callback. Invalid framing, missing Host and unsupported methods are rejected before invoking that slow hook. A blocked worker cannot service another queued callback; another available worker can. Tests replace the delay with a channel gate so they observe the causal scheduling order rather than comparing noisy wall-clock timings. The one-worker case must leave fast work queued while the gate is held; the two-worker case must finish fast work before releasing it.

The comparison uses actual pool callbacks and the same validated reply path. Separate loopback TCP tests check HTML GET, HEAD and 404 bytes. This is not an end-to-end network throughput benchmark. The test gate has a finite fallback wait and a guard declared after the pool, so error unwinding releases the slow callback before pool destruction joins. Existing bounded queue, panic and worker-triggered teardown regressions remain in the copied pool. A queue-full rejection closes the connection; the example does not promise fair scheduling or unlimited slow-client capacity. The slow callback sends its gate result and response validity back to the test thread, which checks both after joining. Assertions inside a panic-catching worker cannot certify a test; an expired fallback also must not masquerade as an explicit release. Two deliberate outcome corruptions are required to fail the comparison before the restored tests pass.

Run the finite self-check first. The manual --requests 2 mode still accepts exactly two connections on loopback and then drains; it can wait indefinitely if a client never connects. A browser may open more connections than expected, so use deliberate clients for the comparison. Header reads retain the existing absolute deadline and byte cap. Writes use the earlier per-operation timeout, not a complete absolute response-write budget. Explicit accept-loop cancellation, production async I/O, full HTTP parsing and sustained network stress remain separate work. Compare compile-time and runtime resource failure modes before choosing a deployment design.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: match Content-Type and UTF-8 byte length to the actual HTML body and explain HEAD. Intermediate: prove a fast callback queues behind a slow callback with one worker but completes before its release with two. Advanced: replace compile-time HTML with capped, fallible runtime file loading, return generic500 errors, preserve HEAD semantics and explain deployment/teardown limits; compare the complete answer.
lessons.question: What does the two-worker gate test establish?
options: The server has unlimited capacity for slow clients
HTML file reads are always faster than include_str!
A per-write timeout is an absolute full-response deadline
A second worker can finish fast work while the slow callback is still blocked
lessons.explanation: The gate observes ordering directly, not a throughput ratio. Bounded workers/queues still impose capacity limits. Compile-time resources and runtime file reads have different failure and deployment contracts.

lessons.title: Owned servers: stop tokens, draining and absolute write budgets
body: This twelve-file project adds an owned server controller to the previous embedded-HTML server. A blocking accept loop can wait forever with no client, so the listener is nonblocking and checks a per-run stop flag between accepts. WouldBlock waits briefly rather than spinning; Interrupted retries, and other accept errors return. The five-millisecond polling interval is not a real-time guarantee. Stop asks acceptance to end, then drains accepted jobs and joins before finish returns. No dummy connection is needed to wake an idle listener.

The accept closure captures Arc<State>, never the Server controller itself. Server owns one optional JoinHandle. finish consumes the controller, signals stop and takes the handle before joining, leaving Drop no second handle to join. Drop provides a stop-and-join fallback and cannot report errors; call finish when an accept error or thread panic must be observed. Weak-reference tests require the controller to disappear and show that an explicitly retained StopToken keeps only run state alive. Once the token drops, the final state owner disappears too.

Every start creates fresh state. Cloning StopToken lets another thread request stopping that one run without owning the controller. An old token cannot cancel a replacement server; the integration test keeps the old token and calls stop after starting a fresh listener, then requires the new server to answer. The stop flag uses release/acquire ordering; the accepted counter is independent atomic telemetry, not a publication lock. This is cooperative cancellation: a request already racing through acceptance can still be dispatched and must be drained.

The bounded pool limits active and queued callbacks. Before dispatch, set each accepted socket back to blocking mode explicitly instead of assuming the listener’s nonblocking flag is or is not inherited. In-flight header reads, simulated slow callbacks and writes finish under their own policies; stop does not forcibly interrupt them. Draining a full queue may take several per-request budgets. The stalled-header test waits until a real connection is accepted, keeps the peer open and requires teardown to finish through the header deadline rather than peer closure. This is a scoped regression, not a hard scheduler-latency bound. In this implementation the listener itself remains bound during draining; ending the accept loop is distinct from closing the listening socket and releasing all connections. The pool closes its final job sender before joining: workers consume queued messages and then observe disconnection. Reversing that ownership order can leave joined workers waiting forever for a sender that is still alive.

The old per-operation write timeout could restart its allowance on every partial write. The new helper measures elapsed time from one write start, computes only the remaining total allowance, applies it to TcpStream, handles partial progress and retries Interrupted without resetting the clock. Zero progress is WriteZero; timeout configuration and I/O errors propagate. After the last byte it checks for late completion too. This budget covers response writing, excluding header parsing and the slow callback. The public helper accepts TcpStream; its small private writer abstraction exists for deterministic tests. OS timeout errors are platform-dependent: Unix commonly reports WouldBlock where Windows may report TimedOut. Preserve that error rather than assuming every exhausted socket timeout has one portable ErrorKind.

Fake elapsed time and one-byte writes make deadline tests repeatable: remaining allowances shrink from ten to six to two milliseconds, then the next write is refused. Other tests cover an interrupted call, failed timeout configuration, zero progress and a successful write reported too late. A timeout error can follow bytes already sent and cannot roll them back. Separate loopback tests and the actual controller self-check exercise the real socket adapter. A real-socket fixture now fills a nonblocking send path until WouldBlock, then keeps the peer open and unread while passing a 16 MiB synthetic payload through this same helper with a 50 ms allowance. Prefill is capped at 64 MiB and one second; failure to observe backpressure is inconclusive and fails the fixture. It requires a timeout-like error within a broad two-second local regression bound, not exact real-time scheduling. This tests the writer directly, not a full HTTP response or sustained pressure campaign. Successful prefill writes while the peer never reads also demonstrate that accepted bytes are not proof of application consumption.

The base statistics count accepted, dispatched and queue-rejected connections. They do not mean every response succeeded or carried status200. The answer adds atomic counters for handler Results, reads them only after pool draining, and keeps per-job state ownership scoped to each callback. An HTTP400 response can be a successful transport operation; EOF before a complete header is an I/O failure. The answer test proves that distinction. Panics caught by the pool are not counted as returned Results; add a separate completion guard if a production accounting contract must classify those too.

Use the finite self-check before manual serving. The --serve-for-five mode accepts on loopback7878 for five seconds and then drains, so total process time may exceed five seconds. Constructor failure on invalid pool configuration must release its listener; a test rebinds that exact unused address. Failed OS thread creation, arbitrary blocking filesystem operations, process termination, full HTTP parsing, TLS, fairness and sustained pressure are not certified by this suite. Embedded pages avoid runtime asset-file reads in this variant. Explain stop request, draining, joining and actual resource release as separate events before writing the worked counters.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: distinguish asking an accept loop to stop from draining queued requests and joining workers. Intermediate: prevent a thread closure retaining its controller, take the join handle once, and prove an old token cannot stop a new run. Advanced: enforce one total response-write budget across partial/Interrupted writes and add per-run I/O outcome counters that do not confuse HTTP400 with transport failure; compare the answer and state the remaining stress/accounting limits.
lessons.question: A stop token from a previous run is called after starting a fresh server. What prevents it cancelling the new run?
options: Joining a thread automatically rewrites all old tokens
A weak reference alone interrupts every blocking socket operation
Each start creates separate Arc-owned state; a token identifies only its own run
One global atomic flag can safely identify every server run
lessons.explanation: Ownership and cancellation identity are separate contracts. The controller owns its join handle; tokens own only per-run state. Stop ends acceptance cooperatively, then jobs drain within their own I/O policies. Neither HTTP status nor a cancellation request proves resource teardown is complete.

lessons.title: Core, alloc and std: an owned fixed-capacity queue
body: This four-file Cargo library separates three environments. core supplies language-independent primitives and iterator traits. alloc supplies heap-backed Vec, String and collections when a final program provides allocation. std adds hosted services such as files, threads and printing. With the std feature disabled, the crate-root no_std attribute changes the automatic prelude to core and stops automatically linking std. It does not ban explicit std imports or std-dependent dependencies; inspect the entire dependency and feature graph.

The manifest makes std the default and lets std enable alloc. These features are additive: enabling another dependency feature can enable more functionality. The library explicitly imports extern crate alloc only behind its alloc feature. Its Ring core uses an inline array of Option<T>, never Vec, and has no Clone or Copy bound on T. The const-block array initializer constructs a separate None for each slot. This deliberately safe representation pays for Option tags and padding rather than hiding uninitialized storage behind unsafe code.

The invariant is 0 <= len <= N; logical offsets below len identify occupied slots beginning at head, while other slots are empty. Full push returns Err(value), preserving ownership for the caller. pop takes one Option before advancing head and decreasing len. A capacity-zero ring is simultaneously empty and full: push returns its value and pop returns None before any indexing. physical avoids adding head and offset when that sum would wrap usize.

Borrowed iteration yields references tied to the ring. The compile-fail doctest demonstrates why retaining a reference prevents mutable push. ExactSizeIterator reports the remaining logical elements, and FusedIterator promises exhaustion stays exhausted. Owned iteration moves values out using pop. Dropping a partially consumed iterator drops its remaining array slots automatically; dropping already returned values remains the caller’s responsibility. clear advances queue state before running each user destructor. A panic-abort build cannot promise destructor cleanup on abort.

The tests compare 1,000 deterministic operations against an independent VecDeque model at capacities zero, one, three and eight. A non-Clone Probe records destruction through Rc<Cell<usize>>: full rejection, returned ownership, clear and partial iteration must each destroy every value exactly once. These are scoped ownership regression tests. They do not measure heap usage or certify all possible user destructors, panic paths or target hardware.

Inline queue storage does not make the whole program heapless: T may contain a String, and a caller may put the ring inside a Box. Large capacities can exhaust stack or static-memory budgets. The optional into_vec consumes the ring and moves each element into alloc::vec::Vec. An alloc-only embedded final executable still needs an appropriate allocator; a library build does not provide one or exercise out-of-memory behavior.

Run host tests with default features, no default features and alloc alone. Integration tests still use the host std test harness even when the library is no_std. Then build the library with no default features for thumbv7em-none-eabihf using the pinned Rust 1.99 target component. The negative mutation deliberately removes no_std and must fail because that target has no std. This cross-compiles a library; it neither links firmware nor supplies startup, a panic handler, a linker script or device support, and it has not run on an embedded board.

The worked answer adds DoubleEndedIterator to both borrowed and owning iterators. Borrowed front and back indices share one half-open range so mixed calls cannot yield an item twice. Owning next_back removes the last logical slot and decreases len; next continues removing the front. Tests alternate both directions across a wrapped ring and retain end values while dropping the rest. This is original reinforcement of a bounded no_std/prelude topic, not exhaustive coverage of the Reference or Embedded Rust Book.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: explain core versus alloc versus std and trace full/empty ownership at capacity zero. Intermediate: implement and test a wrapped FIFO without unsafe or a Clone bound. Advanced: add DoubleEndedIterator for borrowed and owning iteration, prove front/back calls never cross, and verify drop ownership after partial consumption. Cross-compile the library and explain which final firmware responsibilities remain.

options: Yes: host integration tests execute the target hardware
No: allocation features and final executable startup, panic and device requirements must be checked separately
Yes: no_std forbids every heap allocation and every std dependency

lessons.title: Real C buffers: safe wrappers and matching destruction
body: This nine-file project compiles an original C library and links it into a Rust package. The C header defines an opaque buffer, a size_t bookkeeping structure and status-returning constructor. build.rs invokes a native C11 compiler and archiver, puts objects and the static archive under Cargo OUT_DIR, then emits rustc-link-search and rustc-link-lib. Changed C/header files and CC/AR selections trigger rebuilds. CC and AR name executables, not shell command strings. This deliberately small build supports matching host/target Apple Darwin and Linux GNU builds; only the Mac host has been tested. Cross compilation needs a target compiler, sysroot and archiver rather than assuming the host cc is suitable.

The unsafe extern C declarations must match buffer.h exactly. On these supported targets, Rust usize matches C size_t and u8 matches uint8_t; c_int matches C int. Context uses repr(C), while the buffer is opaque and its private non-null handle is never interpreted as a Rust structure. The compiler cannot verify a foreign declaration or the implementation behind it. Every unsafe call states its pointer, initialization, aliasing and lifetime assumptions. extern C alone supplies none of those ownership guarantees.

The constructor borrows input only for its synchronous call and copies bytes into malloc storage. ASCII lowercase becomes uppercase; embedded NUL and non-ASCII bytes remain binary data. The byte 0xff deliberately represents a late input error. The C implementation may already have allocated and written a prefix when it sees that byte, so it frees the partial buffer before returning an error. Every failure sets the output pointer to NULL. Allocation failure paths are implemented but have not been forced with allocator fault injection.

C retains a pointer to the Context bookkeeping until release. Buffer therefore carries PhantomData of an exclusive context borrow, preventing safe Rust from moving, inspecting or dropping that Context while a handle exists. The marker is not runtime storage and does not keep an external object alive automatically; the public API must tie its lifetime to the actual borrow. The handle has no Clone or raw ownership escape. A thread marker deliberately prevents Send and Sync because this teaching foreign contract is confined to its creating thread.

Buffer.as_bytes returns a slice borrowed from the live owner. C promises its data pointer is initialized and readable for the reported length, and never mutates it while Rust reads. For length zero, C permits NULL data, so the wrapper returns an empty Rust slice before calling from_raw_parts. For positive lengths it relies on the reviewed C contract; a bounds check after arbitrary C corruption cannot repair memory safety. Drop calls teacher_release once, pairing C malloc with C free. Constructing a Rust Vec from this allocation would choose the wrong ownership protocol even if one host happens to use related allocators.

The tests check copied input, binary/empty buffers, late-error cleanup, 1,000 success/error cycles and a Rust panic after the C call has returned. Three compile-fail doctests reject a context that dies before its buffer, a slice that outlives its buffer and a handle sent to another thread. The unwind test stays entirely on the Rust side; it does not unwind through C. Panic-abort termination cannot promise RAII cleanup. Context counters count handles, not allocation bytes, and wrap as unsigned size_t counters eventually do; they are test observations, not a memory profiler.

A separate integration test compiles and runs the C contract harness with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. It checks NULL/empty/invalid arguments and 2,001 balanced handles. This instruments the standalone C executable, not the Rust/C binary, and is not a LeakSanitizer or whole-app heap measurement. Both debug and release Cargo suites run it. The release profile retains symbols for boundary inspection; an initial default stripping attempt exposed a local rust-objcopy/libLLVM lookup warning, so this teaching profile explicitly disables stripping. Sanitizer-capable native compiler tools remain required.

The answer adds append_upper: first obtain the foreign owner, then copy its completed bytes onto an existing Vec, then let RAII release the C handle. An invalid-byte or C allocation error returns before touching the caller’s output. Rust allocation abort, process termination and arbitrary foreign violations are outside that Result contract. The answer tests preserved prefix output on failure, successful binary append, empty append and balanced C ownership. This is original reinforcement for selected safe-interface/destructor/build-script concepts; Snappy bindings, callbacks, async foreign lifetimes, unwind ABIs and platform-wide FFI coverage remain separate work.
lessons.challenge: Beginner: trace which allocator creates and frees every buffer. Intermediate: keep C’s retained bookkeeping pointer valid and its copied bytes borrowed from a unique owner. Advanced: implement append_upper so foreign errors preserve existing output, then verify cleanup, lifetime rejections and the standalone C sanitizer harness. Explain why arbitrary foreign contract violations and allocation abort cannot be repaired by returning Result.
lessons.question: Why must this wrapper call teacher_release instead of taking ownership with Vec::from_raw_parts?
options: repr(C) automatically frees all pointed-to allocations
The allocation and destructor follow the C library’s ownership contract; Rust must use its matching release function
extern C automatically makes malloc storage a Rust Vec
A non-null pointer proves allocator identity and slice lifetime
lessons.explanation: ABI, layout, lifetime and allocator ownership are distinct obligations. The opaque handle owns C storage, and Drop calls the matching foreign destructor exactly once.
