lessons.title: A derive macro written by hand with proc_macro, no syn or quote
body: A derive macro is a function the compiler calls at build time. It receives the tokens of the item you attached it to, here a struct, as a proc_macro::TokenStream, and returns a TokenStream of new items that the compiler adds next to the original. The macro never sees types or names resolved, only tokens: identifiers, punctuation, literals and delimited groups (parentheses, brackets, braces). Real projects almost always use the syn crate to parse those tokens and quote to build the output. This lesson deliberately uses only the proc_macro crate that ships with the compiler, so you can see what syn does for you and why it exists.

The parser is a small state machine over a Peekable iterator of TokenTree values. It skips outer attributes (a # punct followed by a bracket group) and a pub or pub(...) visibility, expects the ident struct and a name, rejects a leading < as an unsupported generic struct, and requires a brace-delimited group for named fields. Inside the group each field is attributes, visibility, a name, a colon and a type that runs to the next comma. The catch is that < and > are ordinary punctuation, not groups, so HashMap<String, u8> contains a comma that must not end the field. The code counts angle-bracket depth and ignores the > in a -> arrow so that fn pointer types survive. That hand-counted depth is a shortcut with a known limit: exotic types need a real parser, and the code says so.

The output is generated as a string and parsed back into tokens with str::parse::<TokenStream>(). It adds an inherent impl with a FIELDS constant and a describe function, so the demo crate needs no runtime support library. Errors matter as much as the happy path. Unsupported input returns compile_error!("...") so the user sees an ordinary compiler diagnostic instead of a panic message from inside the macro. The proc_macro API only works while the compiler is expanding a macro, so parse_struct cannot be unit tested in the macro crate itself. The tests live in the consumer crate, which also exercises the macro exactly as a user would, and the validation mutates the demo to a generic struct and an enum and requires the right diagnostic.

Check that unsupported input produces compile_error!, that commas inside angle brackets and the arrow in fn types do not split fields, that every parse step handles the end of the stream, that the macro crate has proc-macro = true and exports only macros, and that tests exercise the macro from a consumer crate.
lessons.challenge: Support a helper attribute #[describe(skip)] on a field: declare it with attributes(describe) on the derive, detect it while skipping field attributes, and leave the field out of FIELDS and describe(). Add a Vec<u8> cache field to Trade marked skip, and a test that proves it is absent.
lessons.question: What does a derive macro receive and what does it return?
options: The fully type-checked syntax tree of the struct, with all field types resolved, and it returns a replacement tree for the struct
A plain string containing the struct's source text, and it returns a string that replaces the struct definition in the program
Nothing: a derive macro only reads the struct and reports errors, so it cannot add any new items to the program
A TokenStream of the item it is attached to, and a TokenStream of new items (here an impl block) that the compiler adds alongside the original
lessons.explanation: Procedural macros work on tokens before type checking. A derive adds items next to the annotated one; only attribute and function-like macros can replace their input.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does the field parser count angle brackets?
options: The parser sorts the fields alphabetically, and tracking angle-bracket depth is needed to keep that order stable
< and > are plain punctuation in a TokenStream, not groups, so a comma inside HashMap<String, u8> must not end the field
Rust forbids commas inside field types, so the parser must find and reject them before the compiler sees the struct
The compiler requires generic brackets to be balanced, so the macro validates them on its behalf before expanding
extraQuizzes.explanation: Parentheses, brackets and braces arrive as nested groups, but angle brackets do not, so the macro has to track nesting depth itself.

extraQuizzes.question: How should a macro report invalid input?
options: Panic with a generic message, because rustc turns every proc-macro panic into a clean diagnostic that is located precisely
Silently generate no code and let the later compiler passes complain about the missing impl
Print a warning to stderr and return the input unchanged so the build continues without any error
Emit compile_error!("...") so the user gets a normal compiler diagnostic pointing at the derive
extraQuizzes.explanation: A panic inside a macro produces an unhelpful "proc-macro panicked" error. compile_error! turns the problem into a clean diagnostic.

extraQuizzes.question: Why can parse_struct not be unit tested inside the macro crate?
options: The test harness replaces proc_macro with a stub, so parse_struct would run but always return an empty token stream
The proc_macro API is only usable while the compiler is expanding a macro, so tests exercise the macro through a consumer crate
Proc-macro crates cannot contain ordinary functions, so parse_struct can only exist as an exported macro entry point
Tests are disabled for crates with proc-macro = true, so cargo test skips the macro crate entirely and cannot run them
extraQuizzes.explanation: Outside an expansion the types panic. Crates like proc_macro2 exist partly to make token handling testable.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does the demo crate depend on the macro crate with a path dependency?
options: A proc-macro crate cannot be compiled on its own, so Cargo requires a consumer crate to build it as a dependency
The compiler requires macro definitions to sit in the same source file as their first use, so the demo must contain them
The macro crate has proc-macro = true and exports only macros, so any code that uses them lives in a separate crate
Path dependencies compile faster than registry dependencies, and the macro crate is small enough to benefit from that
extraQuizzes.explanation: A proc-macro crate is compiled as a compiler plugin for the host. It cannot also export ordinary items, so consumers depend on it.

lessons.title: Attribute macros and precise span diagnostics: a hand-written #[retry]
body: An attribute macro receives two token streams: the arguments inside the attribute (times = 3) and the item it decorates, and it returns the tokens that replace that item. That power to rewrite code is what lets #[retry(times = 3)] turn an ordinary function returning Result into one that runs its body up to three times. The expansion keeps the function signature (every token before the body, so generics, qualifiers and the return type are preserved), and replaces the body with a counter and a loop around a closure that holds the original body. Returns and the ? operator in the original body keep working because they now return from the closure.

The interesting engineering is in the diagnostics. A macro that fails with a panic or a call-site compile_error! leaves the user hunting for the problem. Every proc_macro token carries a Span, the source location it came from, and rustc reports an error at the span of the tokens in the error expansion. spanned_error builds compile_error!("message"); with set_span(span) on each token, using the offending token's own span: the literal 0 for "times must be at least 1", the identifier count for an unknown option, the struct keyword when the attribute is on something that is not a function. The compiler then underlines exactly that token in the user's source. On error the macro also re-emits the original item, so rustc does not pile a "function not found" error on top of the real one.

Test the failure paths like features. The validation mutates the demo to times = 0, to an unknown option, and to an attribute on a struct, and asserts each message; for the first it also asserts that the compiler prints the line #[retry(times = 0)], which proves the error is anchored in the user's code and not at the macro definition. Know the limits too: the closure borrows or moves the arguments, so the function parameters must be reusable across attempts (Copy values or references), and a where clause before the body is not handled. The macro says so instead of silently miscompiling.

Parse attribute arguments strictly, attach spans to errors, keep the original item when erroring, preserve the signature, and test each rejected input; document the shortcuts (reusable arguments, no where clause) so users are not surprised.
lessons.challenge: Make the argument list optional: a bare #[retry] should mean three attempts. Change parse_times for an empty attribute, add a function using the bare form that always fails, and a test that it runs exactly three attempts and returns the last error.
lessons.question: Why does the macro build compile_error! with the offending token's span instead of Span::call_site()?
options: Span::call_site() is rejected in attribute macros, so the macro must borrow another token's span to compile at all
The span selects which crate the error is attributed to, so the diagnostic lands in the macro crate instead of the user's

extraQuizzes.question: Why does the macro re-emit the original item when it reports an error?
options: Without it the function would vanish and rustc would add misleading "cannot find function" errors on top of the real diagnostic
To make the function run twice, once with the original body and once with the retry loop wrapped around it
Because compile_error! can only be attached to an existing item, so the macro needs the original function to hang it on
To satisfy the borrow checker, which would otherwise report that the function's parameters are never used
extraQuizzes.explanation: An attribute macro replaces its item. Returning only an error would delete the item; returning both keeps later compilation stages quiet.

extraQuizzes.question: How do `return` and `?` in the original body still work after expansion?
options: They are not allowed in functions marked #[retry], and the macro rejects such bodies with a compile error
They return from the outer function, so the retry loop is skipped entirely and the first error is returned directly
The body is wrapped in a closure with the declared return type, so they return from the closure and the retry loop sees the Result
They are rewritten by the macro into continue statements, so every early return simply starts the next attempt
extraQuizzes.explanation: The closure boundary gives the body its own return target, which is exactly the value the loop inspects.

extraQuizzes.question: What limitation does the closure approach impose on the function's parameters?
options: There is no limitation, because the macro clones every argument automatically before each new attempt
They must be usable repeatedly across attempts, such as Copy values or references, because the closure is called more than once
They must all be integer types, because the macro copies each argument into a counter that tracks the attempts
They must all be mutable references, because the closure needs to modify them between one attempt and the next
extraQuizzes.explanation: If the body moves a parameter out, the closure becomes FnOnce and cannot be called again, which rustc reports as a normal type error.

extraQuizzes.question: Why do the checks assert that stderr contains #[retry(times = 0)]?
options: It shows the macro crate was rebuilt, since the compiler prints source lines only after recompiling a dependency
It confirms the error was reported at the macro definition, because rustc quotes the line of the code that raised it
rustc prints the source line of the error's span, so seeing it proves the diagnostic is anchored in the user's code
It proves the macro compiled faster, because rustc prints the source line only for expansions that were cached
extraQuizzes.explanation: A call-site or definition-site error would show a different line. The snippet is evidence that spans were attached correctly.

lessons.title: Send and Sync: what the compiler proves about threads
body: Send and Sync are marker traits with no methods; they record facts about thread safety, and the compiler derives them automatically from a type's fields (they are auto traits). T: Send means ownership of a T may be moved to another thread. T: Sync means a shared reference &T may be used from another thread, which is exactly the statement &T: Send. Most types are both: integers, String, Vec<T> of such types. The interesting types are the exceptions. Rc<T> uses non-atomic reference counts, so it is neither Send nor Sync, and moving a clone to another thread would race on the count. Cell<T> and RefCell<T> allow mutation through a shared reference without synchronisation, so they are Send (move the whole thing) but not Sync. MutexGuard is not Send because some operating systems require a lock to be released by the thread that took it.

Composition rules explain the rest. A struct is Send if all its fields are Send, and a raw pointer is neither Send nor Sync, so any struct holding one opts out automatically. Mutex<T> is Sync whenever T is Send, even if T is not Sync: the lock guarantees exclusive access, which is why Mutex<Cell<i32>> can be shared between threads while Cell<i32> alone cannot. Arc<T> is Send and Sync only if T is both, since cloning an Arc lets two threads hold &T. Rust checks these facts at compile time: thread::spawn requires its closure to be Send and 'static (it may outlive the caller), so capturing an Rc is rejected with error E0277, not detected at run time.

When you build a type around raw pointers you decide the facts yourself with unsafe impl Send for Handle {}. That line is a promise, so it needs a comment proving it: here only the Owner creates handles, the pointee lives on the heap, and the thread that uses the handle has exclusive access. Edition 2021 adds a trap: closures capture disjoint fields, so move || unsafe { *handle.0 += 1 } captures only the raw pointer field, which is not Send, rather than the whole Handle. Writing let h = handle; inside the closure forces the whole wrapper to be captured. The program asserts the positive facts at compile time with empty generic functions such as assert_send::<T>(); the negative facts were checked against the compiler and are listed in the text.

Check Send and Sync as properties of the whole type, treat unsafe impl as a proof obligation with a written justification, use Mutex or atomics to share mutable data, and remember the disjoint-capture rule when moving wrapper types into closures.
lessons.challenge: Four scoped threads each push their id into a shared Vec<u32>. A RefCell<Vec<u32>> does not compile because RefCell is not Sync (E0277). Fix it with a Mutex, join all threads, sort the result and assert it is [0, 1, 2, 3]. Explain which marker trait the RefCell version violates.
lessons.question: What does the bound T: Send promise?
options: T can be copied bitwise with a memcpy between threads
T has no destructor, so no thread has to clean it up
Ownership of a T may be moved to another thread safely
A shared reference to T may be used from several threads at once
lessons.explanation: Send is about transferring ownership across threads. The shared-reference statement is Sync. Neither says anything about Copy or destructors.

T is protected by a mutex so only one thread can use it at a time
&T is Send: a shared reference to a T may be used from another thread

extraQuizzes.question: Why is Cell<i32> Send but not Sync?
options: Moving the whole Cell to one other thread is fine, but two threads holding &Cell could both mutate it without synchronisation
Cell uses atomic operations internally, so sharing it is safe but moving it to another thread is not
Cell<i32> is neither Send nor Sync, because any interior mutability makes a type unusable across threads
Because i32 is not Sync, so every container of an i32 is also excluded from being shared between threads
extraQuizzes.explanation: Exclusive ownership on one thread is safe. Shared access from two threads would be a data race, because Cell has no locking.

extraQuizzes.question: Why can Mutex<Cell<i32>> be shared between threads even though Cell<i32> cannot?
options: Mutex<T> is Sync when T is Send, because the lock ensures only one thread touches the T at a time
Mutex makes Cell atomic, so each read and write of the integer becomes a single indivisible instruction
Mutex<T> is Sync for every T, whatever T is, because the lock hides T's thread-safety properties
The compiler skips the Sync check for Mutex because it is part of the standard library prelude
extraQuizzes.explanation: The requirement is on T: Send, not T: Sync, since access is serialised by the lock.

extraQuizzes.question: In edition 2021, why might move || unsafe { *handle.0 += 1 } fail to compile even though Handle is Send?
options: unsafe blocks cannot appear inside closures that are passed to thread::spawn, so the closure is rejected outright
Handle must also implement Sync for a move closure to capture it, even though only one thread will use it
move closures cannot capture structs by value, only individual integers, so the whole handle is never moved
Closures capture disjoint fields, so it captures only the raw pointer handle.0, which is not Send; let h = handle captures the whole wrapper
extraQuizzes.explanation: Precise captures are a 2021 feature. Mentioning the whole variable, as in let h = handle, makes the closure capture the wrapper.

lessons.title: Variance and PhantomData: typed IDs and lifetime subtyping
body: Variance describes how subtyping of a type parameter carries over to the generic type. In Rust the only subtyping is between lifetimes: a longer lifetime 'static is a subtype of a shorter 'a, because a reference valid for longer can be used where a shorter one is needed. A type is covariant in a parameter if that direction is preserved, contravariant if reversed, and invariant if neither is allowed. &'a T is covariant in 'a and in T, which is why a &'static str can be passed where &'a str is expected. A function that takes an argument is contravariant in it: an fn(&str) that accepts any lifetime can be used where an fn(&'static str) is expected, but not the other way round.

&mut T is invariant in T, and the reason is soundness. If &mut &'static str could be treated as &mut &'a str, a function could write a short-lived reference through it into a place that the caller still believes holds a 'static one, leaving a dangling pointer. The compiler rejects that with E0597 (the value does not live long enough). Cell<T> and RefCell<T> are invariant for the same reason: they allow writes through a shared handle. Variance is usually invisible, and it only surfaces as puzzling lifetime errors, but when you design generic types with markers you choose it.

PhantomData<T> is a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler to treat a struct as if it contained a T without storing one. The choice of the marker type sets the properties. PhantomData<fn() -> T> says "I only produce T", is covariant in T and is Send and Sync regardless of T, which is what a typed ID wants: Id<Order> and Id<Trade> are distinct types that cost 4 bytes each and cannot be mixed up at call sites. PhantomData<T> instead claims ownership of a T, which affects drop checking and makes the struct Send only if T is. One more gotcha, verified against the compiler: #[derive(Clone, Copy)] on Id<T> adds T: Clone and T: Copy bounds even though no T is stored, so Id<Order> would stop being Copy when Order is not; implement Clone and Copy by hand.

Pick the PhantomData marker deliberately (fn() -> T for typed IDs), implement Copy and Clone manually for marker-parameterised types, and remember &mut T is invariant, which is why it cannot be shortened like a shared reference.
lessons.challenge: Create Registry<T> that stores names and hands out Id<T> values: insert(&mut self, name) -> Id<T> and get(&self, id: Id<T>) -> &str. Show that an Id<Order> from a Registry<Order> is a different type from an Id<Trade>, so passing it to a Registry<Trade> is a compile error (describe the error in a comment), and that Id<T> stays Copy.
lessons.question: Why can a &'static str be passed where a &'a str is expected, but a &mut &'static str cannot be used as a &mut &'a str?
options: Lifetimes only matter for owned types such as String, so a &str is never checked and both uses are accepted
Both are allowed, and the compiler only warns about the &mut case because the slot could briefly hold a shorter-lived reference
Shared references are covariant (a longer lifetime can stand in for a shorter one); &mut T is invariant, because it could store a short-lived value in a 'static slot
Shared references are invariant and mutable references are covariant, so the shorter lifetime may always replace the longer one in a &mut
lessons.explanation: Covariance is safe for read-only access. With a mutable reference the callee could store a shorter-lived reference into the caller's longer-lived slot, so the compiler requires an exact match.

lessons.title: Unsafe Rust: aliasing, provenance and writing a sound split_at_mut
body: Unsafe Rust does not switch off the rules; it lets you promise the compiler you uphold them. The central rule is aliasing: a live &mut T must be the only way to reach that data, and shared &T references must not coexist with mutation. Creating two overlapping &mut references is undefined behaviour even if you never use one of them, because the compiler optimises on the promise of exclusivity. Raw pointers (*const T, *mut T) carry no such promise, which is why they exist for building safe abstractions, but dereferencing one is unsafe because you must prove it is valid: non-null, aligned, pointing into a live allocation, and not violating aliasing for any references you create from it.

The classic proof is slice::split_at_mut, which hands out two disjoint mutable halves of one slice. Safe code cannot express it because the borrow checker sees two &mut borrows of the same slice. The implementation takes the base pointer once, builds one slice over [0, mid) and another over [mid, len) with from_raw_parts_mut, and the safety comment gives the argument: the ranges do not overlap, they stay within the original allocation, and the original &mut borrow is held for the returned lifetime, so no other access exists. Another sharp edge is repr(packed) structs: a field may be misaligned, and taking a reference to it is rejected with E0793. Use std::ptr::addr_of!(p.value) to get a raw pointer without creating a reference, then read_unaligned.

Provenance is the second idea. A pointer is not just an address: it also carries the right to access the allocation it came from. Converting a pointer to an integer and back with as casts blurs that right, and compilers and tools such as Miri model it carefully. The stable strict provenance APIs keep the right attached: addr() reads the address, map_addr(|a| ...) changes the address while preserving provenance. The program uses them to tag the low bits of an 8-aligned pointer (free because alignment guarantees zeros there), reads the tag, restores the clean pointer and frees the box. Run unsafe code under Miri in CI; it detects aliasing and provenance violations that tests do not.

Write a safety comment for every unsafe block that states why each requirement holds, prefer a safe abstraction around a small unsafe core, never create overlapping &mut references, use addr_of! for packed fields, keep provenance with map_addr instead of integer round trips, and run tests under Miri.
lessons.challenge: Implement pair_mut<T>(items: &mut [T], i: usize, j: usize) -> Option<(&mut T, &mut T)> that returns mutable references to two different elements, or None when i == j or either index is out of range. Do it with safe code only, using split_at_mut, and test swapping two elements through the references.
lessons.question: Why is it undefined behaviour to create two overlapping &mut references to the same data, even if you never use one of them?
options: Because &mut references are slower than raw pointers, and the compiler forbids the slower option in unsafe code
It is only a problem if both references are written through, since unused references make no claims
A &mut asserts exclusive access, and the compiler optimises on that promise; two live ones violate the aliasing rules by existing
The borrow checker rejects it at run time with a panic, so the program stops before any data can be corrupted
lessons.explanation: Aliasing rules are about what the references claim, not what they are used for. The compiler may reorder or cache reads and writes assuming exclusivity.

options: Because raw pointers are always valid, so converting a slice into pointers and back cannot break any rule
Because unsafe turns off the aliasing rules inside the block, so overlapping ranges would also have been fine
Because from_raw_parts_mut checks for overlap at run time and panics if the two ranges ever intersect

extraQuizzes.question: Why use ptr::addr_of!(p.value) on a repr(packed) struct instead of &p.value?

Packed structs cannot have u32 fields, so the example only compiles because addr_of! hides the field type

extraQuizzes.question: What does map_addr preserve that casting a pointer to usize and back does not?

The numeric value of the address, which an integer round trip would change by moving it to a new allocation
The alignment of the pointee, which a cast through usize would otherwise reset to one byte

extraQuizzes.question: Why is tagging the low three bits of a Box<u64> pointer legitimate?

Because Box is not a real pointer but an integer handle, so changing its low bits has no effect

lessons.title: A typed bump arena: stable references and wholesale deallocation
body: An arena (or bump allocator) trades individual deallocation for speed and simplicity. Allocation is just a push onto storage you already own, and everything is released together when the arena is dropped. That is exactly the lifetime of many compiler passes, request handlers and graph builders: build a lot of small interlinked objects, use them, then discard them all at once. The payoff in Rust is that objects allocated from the same arena can hold plain references to each other (&'a Node<'a>) with no Rc, no Box and no ownership puzzles, because they all share the arena's lifetime.

The trick is that alloc takes &self yet hands out &mut T. A normal Vec cannot do this: pushing may reallocate and move every element, which the borrow checker correctly forbids while references exist. The arena avoids reallocation instead of preventing the borrow. Elements live in chunks, each a Vec with a fixed capacity; when the last chunk is full a new, larger one is started and the old one is never touched again, so no element ever moves. A RefCell around the chunk list gives the interior mutability for alloc(&self), and one small unsafe block turns the pointer to the fresh element into a reference. The safety comment is the proof: stable addresses, unique elements so no aliasing, and the arena outliving the borrow.

Know the costs. Memory is not reclaimed until the arena is dropped, so a long-lived arena fed by a long-running loop is a leak by design. Values with destructors are dropped only when the arena drops, in an unspecified order that must not matter. The arena is not Sync, because RefCell is not, so each thread needs its own. Resetting needs &mut self (clear), and that requirement is the proof that no reference into the arena is still alive; the borrow checker enforces it. The demo links nodes into a list with Cell<Option<&'a Node<'a>>>, allocates a thousand more to force several chunks, and shows the early references still work.

Ensure no element ever moves after a reference is handed out, justify the unsafe block in a comment, document that memory is freed only on drop or clear, reset through &mut self, and keep the arena confined to one thread.
lessons.challenge: Add Arena::clear(&mut self), which drops every value but keeps the largest chunk's capacity for reuse. Explain in a comment why it must take &mut self, and show that after clearing you can allocate again and that all earlier values were dropped exactly once.
lessons.question: Why can Arena::alloc take &self and still return a &mut T that stays valid while more values are allocated?
options: Because RefCell makes any reference it hands out safe, since it re-checks every borrow at run time and panics on a conflict
Because the Vec reallocates in place without moving elements, so earlier addresses are preserved across pushes
Because the compiler proves it without unsafe, since lifetimes tied to &self already forbid aliasing
Each call returns a distinct element in a chunk that is never resized or moved, so the references never alias and their addresses stay stable
lessons.explanation: Safety comes from the chunk design: a full chunk is left untouched and a new one started. RefCell only supplies the interior mutability for the chunk list; the unsafe block depends on the no-move invariant.

extraQuizzes.question: Why must a chunk never be pushed to once it is full?
options: It would change the drop order, which must stay identical to the allocation order for the values
Pushing past capacity would reallocate and move its elements, leaving previously returned references dangling
It would make the arena slower, because each push into a full chunk copies the chunk's elements twice
Vec cannot hold more than its initial capacity, so pushing past it returns an error that the arena ignores
extraQuizzes.explanation: The no-reallocation rule is the invariant behind the unsafe block, so alloc starts a new chunk exactly when len equals capacity.

extraQuizzes.question: What do you give up by using an arena?
options: Memory safety, because values allocated in an arena are not checked by the borrow checker
Individual deallocation: memory is released only when the arena is dropped or cleared
The ability to hold references to the allocated values, since the arena's contents move whenever it grows
The ability to drop values, since an arena never runs destructors for anything that it holds
extraQuizzes.explanation: A bump arena has no free list per object. Its simplicity and speed come from freeing everything together.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does clear take &mut self?
options: Because RefCell cannot be borrowed otherwise, so clearing needs the exclusive borrow to release its flag
To make clear faster, since exclusive access lets the compiler skip the destructors of the stored values
Because clear needs to allocate a fresh chunk, which requires exclusive access to the arena's list
Exclusive access proves that no reference into the arena is still alive, so dropping the values cannot create dangling references
extraQuizzes.explanation: The borrow checker turns "no outstanding references" into a compile-time fact. alloc(&self) hands out borrows of self, which would conflict with a &mut self call.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is Arena<T> not Sync?
options: Because unsafe code is never Sync, so the unsafe block inside alloc removes the marker automatically
Because it implements Drop, and a type with a destructor can never be shared between threads
It uses RefCell for interior mutability, which is not thread safe, so each thread should use its own arena
Because chunks are Vec values, and Vec<T> is not Sync, so any struct containing one cannot be shared
extraQuizzes.explanation: RefCell checks borrows at run time without synchronisation, so sharing &Arena across threads would race on the borrow flag.

lessons.title: Generational slab: O(1) handles that cannot dangle
body: Many systems keep large collections of objects that refer to each other and come and go: resting orders in a book, sessions, entities in a simulation. References are awkward (lifetimes, self-referential structures) and Rc<RefCell<..>> is heavy. The alternative is an index into a Vec. A slab stores values in a Vec of slots and hands out small Copy keys; insertion and removal are O(1) because freed slots are threaded into a free list and reused. Keys have no lifetime, no borrow, and can be stored, copied, sent between threads and serialised.

Plain indices have one nasty flaw, the ABA problem. Insert A at slot 0, remove it, insert B which reuses slot 0, and a stale index that was meant for A now silently reaches B: a use-after-free expressed in safe code. The fix is a generation counter. Every slot has one, a key carries the generation it was created with, and removing a value increments the slot's generation. A lookup compares generations and returns None for a stale key. The free list is intrusive: freed entries store next_free pointers, so no extra allocation is needed to track free space.

There are edge cases worth stating. A u32 generation can wrap after about four billion removals of the same slot, after which a very old key could match again, so the slab retires an exhausted slot instead of recycling it (checked_add), trading a few bytes for correctness. get returns Option because a key can be stale; there is no panic path in normal use. The demo compares the slab with a HashMap model over 5,000 random inserts, removals and lookups, including operations with stale keys, and checks that every stale key is rejected and len always matches.

Use generations to defeat ABA, thread the free list through the slots, make every lookup fallible, retire slots whose generation is exhausted, and test against a simple map model with deliberately stale keys.
lessons.challenge: Add iter(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Key, &T)> yielding every live entry with its key, and check that the number of items equals len(), that each yielded key resolves through get to the same value, and that removed entries do not appear.
lessons.question: What problem does the generation counter solve?
options: It makes insertion faster, because a fresh generation lets the slab skip searching for a free slot in the Vec
It lets two keys share a slot safely, because each generation reserves its own copy of the value
It stores the number of values in the slab, so len() can be answered without walking the entries
The ABA problem: after a slot is freed and reused, a stale key would otherwise reach the new, unrelated value
lessons.explanation: Without generations an index is only a position. The generation turns it into an identity for one particular occupant of the slot.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does get return Option<&T> instead of &T?
options: To allow returning mutable references, which a plain &T return type would not be able to express
Because Option is cheaper than a reference, so returning it avoids a bounds check on every lookup
A key may be stale or foreign, so lookup can legitimately fail and the caller must handle it
Because slots can be empty only before the first insert, so get must report that one early case
extraQuizzes.explanation: Removal invalidates keys without notifying their holders. A fallible lookup makes that visible instead of causing a panic or a wrong answer.

extraQuizzes.question: How does the slab find a free slot in O(1)?
options: It scans the Vec from the start for an empty entry, which is fast because freed slots are usually early
It sorts the entries by generation after every removal, so the lowest generation is always reused next
It allocates a new Vec each time and moves the live entries into it, leaving the old slots behind
Freed entries form an intrusive linked list through their next_free fields, headed by free_head
extraQuizzes.explanation: Threading the list through the free slots needs no additional storage and makes both insert and remove constant time.

extraQuizzes.question: What happens when a slot's generation reaches u32::MAX?
options: The slot is retired and never reused, so a very old key can never match a recycled slot after the counter would have wrapped
The generation wraps to zero and reuse continues, which is safe because wrapped generations are compared by identity
The slab panics immediately, since a generation counter that overflows is treated as a corrupted slab
The slab stops accepting inserts entirely, because one exhausted slot makes every other key ambiguous
extraQuizzes.explanation: checked_add detects exhaustion. Retiring costs one slot of memory and removes any chance of a false match.

extraQuizzes.question: Why are slab keys better than references for objects that refer to each other?
options: References cannot be stored in a Vec, so a slab must hand out keys even for objects that never refer to others
Keys make cloning the object free, because a key copies the pointed-to value only when it is first read
Keys guarantee the object is never removed, so every lookup with a valid key is certain to succeed
Keys are small Copy values with no lifetime, so they avoid borrow conflicts, cycles of ownership and dangling pointers
extraQuizzes.explanation: A key is only a name for a slot. The slab remains the single owner, and a stale name is detected rather than followed.

lessons.title: Trait objects: fat pointers, vtables and dyn compatibility
body: A trait object, written dyn Trait behind a pointer, lets one collection hold values of different concrete types and call their methods through a shared interface. The price is a different pointer layout. A normal reference &T is one machine word, the address of the value. A reference to a trait object &dyn Trait is a fat pointer of two words: a data pointer to the value, and a pointer to a vtable for the pair (concrete type, trait). Box<dyn Trait>, Rc<dyn Trait> and *const dyn Trait have the same shape, and so do slices and &str, whose second word is a length. The program prints these sizes to make the layout concrete.

The vtable is a static table the compiler generates for each concrete type used as a given trait object. It holds the type's drop glue, its size and alignment, and one function pointer per method. A method call on a trait object loads the function pointer from the vtable and calls it indirectly, which blocks inlining; generic code with a T: Trait bound is instead monomorphised, one copy per type, with direct calls the optimizer can inline. Prefer generics on hot paths and trait objects where you need heterogeneity or want to limit code size. size_of_val and align_of_val read the concrete size from the vtable, which is how a Vec<Box<dyn Pricer>> can hold a zero-sized, an 8-byte and a 24-byte implementation side by side.

Not every trait can be made into an object. A trait is dyn compatible only if the compiler can build a vtable for it: methods cannot return Self or take generic type parameters (the concrete type is unknown, so the size or the set of instantiations is unknown), and the trait cannot require Self: Sized. dyn Clone fails with E0038, because clone returns Self. Two escape hatches matter. Adding where Self: Sized to a generic method exempts that method from the rules; it still exists for concrete types, and calling it through a trait object is rejected ("the g method cannot be invoked on a trait object"). And since Rust 1.86 trait upcasting is stable: with trait Pricer: Named, a &dyn Pricer coerces to &dyn Named.

Know the two-word layout, the vtable contents and the cost of an indirect call, choose generics for hot paths, check dyn compatibility (no Self returns, no generic methods without where Self: Sized), and use boxed_clone-style methods when you need cloning of boxed trait objects.
lessons.challenge: Make Box<dyn Pricer> cloneable. Add fn boxed_clone(&self) -> Box<dyn Pricer> to the trait, implement it for each type, and write impl Clone for Box<dyn Pricer> using it. Clone a Vec<Box<dyn Pricer>>, change the original, and show the clone is unaffected.
lessons.question: Why is &dyn Trait twice the size of &T on a 64-bit machine?
options: It carries the full type name as a string, which the runtime uses to find the right method each call
Because trait objects are always heap allocated, so the extra word is the allocation's size
It is a fat pointer: one word for the data pointer and one for the pointer to the vtable
It stores the value inline next to the pointer, so the second word holds the first bytes of the data
lessons.explanation: The reference must find both the value and the methods for its unknown concrete type. The vtable pointer is what makes dynamic dispatch possible.

extraQuizzes.question: What does a vtable contain?
options: The values of all the type's fields, copied once so that every method call can read them directly
The source code of the methods, which the runtime interprets when a call goes through the trait object
A list of every type that implements the trait, searched at each call to find the matching method
The concrete type's drop glue, size and alignment, and one function pointer per trait method
extraQuizzes.explanation: The size and alignment are why size_of_val and Box deallocation work on a trait object, and the method pointers are what calls go through.

extraQuizzes.question: Why can a trait with fn duplicate(&self) -> Self not be used as dyn Trait?
options: Because trait objects have no methods of their own, so any trait that returns Self is rejected by the parser
The concrete type is unknown behind the trait object, so the size of the returned value is unknown (the trait is not dyn compatible, E0038)
Because methods cannot return values from a trait object, since the vtable has no slot for return types
Because Self is a keyword reserved for structs, so a trait that mentions it can only describe struct types
extraQuizzes.explanation: Returning Self by value needs a known size at the call site. A boxed_clone method returning Box<dyn Trait> sidesteps it.

extraQuizzes.question: What does `where Self: Sized` on a generic method do?
options: It makes the method static, so it must be called as Trait::method with no receiver at all
Exempts that method from dyn compatibility: it exists for concrete types but cannot be called through a trait object
It makes the method callable on trait objects, by giving the vtable a special entry for generic calls
It forces the trait to be implemented only by structs, which rules out enums and primitive types
extraQuizzes.explanation: A generic method would need one vtable entry per instantiation, which is impossible. The bound opts it out and the compiler rejects trait-object calls to it.

extraQuizzes.question: When is generic (static) dispatch usually preferable to dyn dispatch?
options: In hot paths, where monomorphisation allows inlining and direct calls instead of an indirect call through a vtable
When the collection must hold different concrete types, because a generic can store only one type
When code size must be minimised, since a generic function has only one copy for all of its types
Never: dyn dispatch is always faster, because the vtable lookup is cached by the CPU on every call
extraQuizzes.explanation: Heterogeneous collections and smaller binaries favour trait objects. Tight loops favour generics.

lessons.title: Cow, Borrow and AsRef: designing APIs that avoid needless allocation
body: Cow<'a, B>, "clone on write", is an enum with two states: Borrowed(&'a B) and Owned(B::Owned). It lets a function return its input untouched when nothing needs changing and allocate a new value only when it must. normalize_symbol trims and upper-cases tickers: most inputs from a clean feed are already "AAPL", and for them the function returns Cow::Borrowed(input) with zero allocation; only " aapl " or "msft" produce an owned String. The caller treats both uniformly through Deref to str, and can call into_owned() or to_mut() when it needs ownership. to_mut clones a borrowed value on the first call and returns a mutable reference to the owned copy; later calls are free.

AsRef and Borrow look similar and are not interchangeable. AsRef<T> is a cheap reference-to-reference conversion with no extra promises: fn count_upper<S: AsRef<str>>(s: S) accepts String, &str and Box<str> alike, and sum_all<T: AsRef<[i64]>> accepts Vec<i64>, arrays and slices. Borrow<T> makes a stronger contract: the borrowed form must behave identically for Eq, Ord and Hash. That contract is what lets HashMap<String, V>::get accept a &str: get<Q>(&self, k: &Q) where String: Borrow<Q>, Q: Hash + Eq. The program verifies that a String and its &str hash to the same value. A wrapper that compares case-insensitively must not implement Borrow<str>, because lookups would find the wrong buckets; it can implement AsRef<str> safely.

A short guide to parameter types. To only read text, take &str, or impl AsRef<str> when callers hold varied owned types and you want to spare them conversions. To keep the value, take impl Into<String> so the caller can pass an owned String without a copy or a &str that will be allocated. To return something that is often unchanged, return Cow. Using Cow in a hot parsing or normalisation path removes an allocation per record without complicating callers, which is the point of the lesson.

Return Cow when the common case needs no change, accept AsRef for read-only generic inputs, accept Into<String> when you will own the data, and implement Borrow only when Eq, Ord and Hash really agree with the owned form.
lessons.challenge: Write normalize_all(symbols: &[&str]) -> (Vec<Cow<str>>, usize) returning the normalised tickers and how many needed allocation, and join_ids<I, S>(ids: I) -> String for any IntoIterator whose items are AsRef<str>, joined with commas. Check that a clean feed performs zero allocations and that join_ids accepts a Vec<String>, an array of &str and a slice.
lessons.question: What does returning Cow<'_, str> let normalize do?
options: Always allocate a new String, so the caller owns the result and never has to track the input's lifetime
Mutate the input string in place, avoiding both the allocation and the copy for every kind of edit
Avoid ever returning an owned value, which is why the function can promise it never allocates
Return the borrowed input unchanged when no edit is needed, and allocate an owned String only when it had to modify the text
lessons.explanation: Cow is "borrowed or owned". For already-clean data the function costs no allocation, and callers use the result through Deref either way.

extraQuizzes.question: What does Borrow promise that AsRef does not?
options: That the borrowed form is always shorter, so a lookup compares fewer bytes than the owned type
That the type is Copy, so the borrowed and owned forms can be compared without taking any reference
Equality, ordering and hashing of the borrowed form agree with the owned type, which HashMap lookups rely on
That the conversion never allocates, which AsRef is allowed to do when it builds a temporary
extraQuizzes.explanation: AsRef is just a cheap reference conversion. Borrow adds a semantic contract so a key can be looked up by its borrowed form.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does HashMap<String, V>::get("AAPL") compile with a &str argument?
options: Because HashMap stores &str internally, so a String key is only a convenient way to build one
Because get is defined only for str keys, and String is treated as a str by deref coercion
String implements Borrow<str>, and get accepts any Q where K: Borrow<Q> and Q: Hash + Eq
Because &str is automatically converted to String first, which costs one allocation for each lookup
extraQuizzes.explanation: The generic bound lets the lookup use the borrowed form without allocating a temporary String.

extraQuizzes.question: What does Cow::to_mut do to a Borrowed value?
options: It mutates the original borrowed data in place, so the source string changes for every other reader too
It panics because borrowed data is read-only, so callers must check is_owned() before every call
It always clones, even for owned values, so repeated calls keep allocating a fresh copy each time
It clones the data into an owned value on the first call and returns a mutable reference to it; later calls are free
extraQuizzes.explanation: This is the "clone on write" behaviour: pay for the allocation only when you actually modify.

extraQuizzes.question: Which parameter type fits a function that will store the string it receives?
options: impl AsRef<str>, because it accepts every string type and the function can keep the borrowed value
&str, which always allocates inside the function when it keeps the text, so callers lose nothing
&mut String, so the function can take the caller's buffer and keep it without asking for ownership
impl Into<String>, so the caller can hand over an owned String without copying, or a &str that is allocated once
extraQuizzes.explanation: If you need ownership, asking for it in the signature lets callers avoid a redundant copy. AsRef is for read-only use.

lessons.title: Writing iterator adapters: size_hint, DoubleEnded, ExactSize and extension traits
body: Iterator is the most reusable trait in the standard library, and writing your own adapter shows how the pieces fit. An adapter is a struct that wraps another iterator and implements Iterator itself, doing its work lazily inside next. Pairwise yields each consecutive pair of items, which is exactly what you need to turn a price series into changes: [100, 101, 99, 105] becomes (100, 101), (101, 99), (99, 105). It stores the wrapped iterator and the previous item (cloned, so the item type must be Clone), and it never collects anything, so it works on unbounded sources like (0..) and processes one element at a time.

The required method is next; the optional methods are where quality lives. size_hint returns (lower, upper) bounds on the remaining item count. collect and Vec::from_iter use it to preallocate, and a correct, exact hint makes ExactSizeIterator::len available. Pairwise has a subtle hint: before the first call it has not read the first item, so n inner items yield n - 1 pairs; after priming, each remaining inner item produces one pair. The code tracks a primed flag and adjusts both bounds with saturating subtraction, so an empty iterator gives (0, Some(0)) and an infinite one gives (0, None) or a huge lower bound without underflow. Implementing DoubleEndedIterator (next_back) adds .rev() and lets ends be consumed from both sides, which the Doubled adapter does by forwarding to the inner iterator. Not every iterator can promise an exact length: the compiler rejects .len() on a doubled RangeInclusive<i64>, because ranges over 64-bit integers are not ExactSizeIterator (their length might not fit in usize), so the demo uses a Vec iterator where it needs len().

To make adapters read fluently, add an extension trait with a blanket implementation: trait IterExt: Iterator + Sized { fn pairwise(self) -> Pairwise<Self> where Self::Item: Clone } and impl<I: Iterator> IterExt for I {}. Now any iterator has .pairwise(), and it chains with map, filter and the rest. A wrong size_hint is a logic bug, not memory unsafety in safe code, but callers and std rely on it for performance, and the unsafe TrustedLen marker is reserved for the standard library, so test your hints against the real counts.

Keep adapters lazy, implement size_hint correctly (use saturating arithmetic), add DoubleEndedIterator and ExactSizeIterator when they are truthful, expose the adapter through an extension trait, and test against the real item counts.
lessons.challenge: Write a Dedup adapter that skips consecutive duplicate items (for example 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1 gives 1, 2, 3, 1) for Item: PartialEq + Clone, with an honest size_hint (lower bound 0 or 1, upper bound from the inner iterator) and a dedup() extension method. Check it against Vec::dedup on random vectors.
lessons.question: Why does collect() benefit from a correct size_hint, and what does an exact hint enable?
options: It makes next() run in parallel, using the bounds to split the iterator across the available threads
It sorts the items before collecting, because the bounds tell the collector the order of the elements
It allows the iterator to be cloned cheaply, since the bounds record where to restart from
It preallocates capacity from the lower bound, and an exact hint lets ExactSizeIterator::len report the remaining count
lessons.explanation: size_hint is advice for consumers. Preallocation avoids repeated growth, and equal bounds mean the length is known without consuming the iterator.

Expected output:

pairs: [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]
size_hint before the first item: (3, Some(3)), len = 3
size_hint after one item: (2, Some(2)), len = 2
empty: (0, Some(0)), single: (0, Some(0))
infinite source stays lazy: [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]

doubled len = 3, reversed = [6, 4, 2]
from both ends: Some(2) Some(10) 3

extraQuizzes.question: Why does Pairwise::size_hint subtract one before the first item is read?
options: Nothing has been read yet, so n inner items will make only n - 1 pairs; once primed, each remaining item makes exactly one pair
Because pairs are always one fewer than the iterator length, so the same subtraction applies at every step
Because the first item is discarded when the adapter is created, so it never takes part in a pair
Because size_hint counts bytes rather than items, and a pair needs one byte fewer than its source
extraQuizzes.explanation: The adapter's state changes the arithmetic. Tracking primed lets both bounds stay correct at every step.

extraQuizzes.question: Why add an extension trait with a blanket impl for every Iterator?
options: It is required to implement Iterator, because every adapter must expose its own constructor method
It makes the adapter faster, since the blanket impl lets the compiler skip bounds checks entirely
It lets the adapter mutate the source iterator after it has been consumed by a for loop
It gives every iterator the new method so adapters chain fluently, like iter.pairwise().map(..)
extraQuizzes.explanation: impl<I: Iterator> IterExt for I {} attaches the method everywhere without modifying std types.

extraQuizzes.question: What does implementing DoubleEndedIterator add?
options: Parallel iteration, because both ends can be consumed by different threads without locking
Random access by index, so the iterator can be read at any position without consuming items
Cloning of the iterator, which the second end needs to remember where the first one stopped
next_back, which enables .rev() and consuming the iterator from both ends
extraQuizzes.explanation: Adapters that can preserve order from the back, such as Doubled, forward the call to the inner iterator.

extraQuizzes.question: What is the consequence of a wrong size_hint in safe code?
options: Undefined behaviour in safe code, because the standard library trusts the hint when it allocates the buffer
A compile error, since the trait checks that the lower bound never exceeds the real item count
The iterator stops being lazy, because collecting must now read every item before it can continue
A logic error with poor performance or surprising len() results, but not undefined behaviour; unsafe code must not trust it
extraQuizzes.explanation: The hint is advisory. Only the unsafe TrustedLen trait, reserved for the standard library, promises exactness.

lessons.title: Error design without dependencies: typed enums, source chains and boundaries
body: Good error handling is part of an API. A library should expose a typed error enum so callers can match on the failure and decide what to do. OrderError has one variant per way an order line can be wrong, and each variant carries the data that explains it: the offending text, the field name, or the underlying ParseIntError. To work with ?, `std::error::Error`, and error reporting, implement Display for a one-line description of this error alone, and Error with a source() method that returns the underlying cause when there is one. This is what the thiserror crate generates; writing it by hand once shows how little magic it contains.

Chains compose across layers. LineError wraps an OrderError with the line number, and its source() returns the OrderError, whose source() returns the ParseIntError. A reporter walks the chain with a loop over source() and prints "line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `abc` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string". The rule that makes this work: an error's Display should describe only itself, not repeat its source, because the reporter prints the cause separately and duplicated text becomes noise. Use map_err to attach context at the layer that knows it (the line number lives in load, not in parse_order) and ? to propagate unchanged.

Choose the type for the boundary. Libraries return concrete enums, and mark public enums #[non_exhaustive] so that adding a variant later is not a breaking change, since downstream matches must include a wildcard arm. Applications often return Box<dyn Error> at the top level, where the only goal is to report and exit; ? converts any error into it through From, and downcast_ref::<LineError>() recovers the concrete type when the program does need to inspect one. Avoid stringly-typed errors (Err(String)): they lose the structure, the source chain and the ability to match.

Give each failure its own variant with data, implement Display (this error only) and source (the cause), add context with map_err where it is known, return typed errors from libraries and Box<dyn Error> at application edges, and mark growing public enums #[non_exhaustive].
lessons.challenge: Change load to collect every bad line instead of stopping at the first: return Result<Vec<Order>, Vec<LineError>>. Print how many lines failed and the full chain of the first failure, and show that a file of only valid lines still returns Ok.
lessons.question: Why does OrderError::BadQuantity implement source() and keep its Display short?
options: So reporters can walk the chain to the root cause without the outer message repeating it
Because Display cannot contain data, so the details of the failure must live in the source instead
Because source() replaces Display, so the error's own message is never printed when a cause exists
To make the error Copy, since a short Display message lets the compiler duplicate the value cheaply
lessons.explanation: Display describes this error alone; source() exposes the underlying cause. A reporter joins them, so repeating the cause in Display would print it twice.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
parsed 2 orders, notional cents = 3951250
missing price: line 1 <- caused by: missing field `price`
bad side: line 1 <- caused by: unknown side `HOLD` (expected BUY or SELL)
bad quantity: line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `abc` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string
bad price: line 1 <- caused by: bad price `142.1`: expected exactly two decimals
through Box<dyn Error>: line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `-1` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string
downcast recovered the line number: 2
source chain depth for a bad quantity: 1
a missing field has no source: true

Display describes this error alone; source() exposes the underlying cause. A reporter joins them, so repeating the cause in Display would print it twice.

extraQuizzes.question: When should a function return Box<dyn Error> instead of a typed enum?
options: Always, because enums are slower than trait objects when the compiler has to match on their variants
Never: Box<dyn Error> is deprecated, and every function should return its own typed enum instead
Only in code that uses threads, since trait objects are the only error type that is safe to send
At application edges where the caller only reports the failure; libraries return typed errors so callers can match and react
extraQuizzes.explanation: Typed errors give callers structure to act on. Boxing is convenient at the top of a program, where errors are logged and the process exits.

extraQuizzes.question: What does #[non_exhaustive] on a public enum accomplish?
options: It removes the Debug implementation, because extensible enums cannot be printed without a wildcard arm
Downstream crates must include a wildcard arm when matching it, so adding a variant later is not a breaking change
It prevents the enum from being matched at all outside its own crate, so callers use methods instead
It makes every variant optional, so a value can be built without choosing any variant at all
extraQuizzes.explanation: The attribute affects other crates, so the library keeps the freedom to grow the enum.

extraQuizzes.question: What does ? do with a LineError in a function returning Result<_, Box<dyn Error>>?
options: It prints the error and continues, so the function keeps running after the failing line is reported
It unwraps the error and panics, because Box<dyn Error> cannot carry a LineError through a return
It discards the source chain, so only the outermost message survives the conversion into the box
It converts the error into the box with From and returns early; downcast_ref can later recover the LineError
extraQuizzes.explanation: Any type implementing Error converts into Box<dyn Error>. The source chain stays attached to the boxed value.

extraQuizzes.question: Where should the line number be attached to an OrderError?
options: In load, which knows the line, using map_err; parse_order only knows about one line of text
Inside every variant of OrderError, so each parse failure records the line it came from itself
In main, by parsing the error message string to find the number that the lower layer mentioned
It cannot be attached, because an error value is immutable once the lower layer has created it
extraQuizzes.explanation: Context should be added by the layer that has it. Wrapping in LineError keeps the lower layer reusable.

lessons.title: Panics, unwinding and ABI boundaries: catch_unwind, poisoning and C-unwind
body: A panic is Rust's response to a bug or an impossible state. With the default panic strategy (unwind) it runs destructors for every value on the way up the stack, then either ends the thread or is caught. With panic = "abort" it terminates the process immediately and no destructors run. Unwinding is what makes RAII cleanup work during a panic: the Guard in the program prints "cleanup" while the stack unwinds. std::panic::catch_unwind stops an unwind at a chosen point and returns Result<T, Box<dyn Any + Send>>; the payload is a &str for panic!("literal") and a String for a formatted message, so downcast_ref recovers the text. Catching panics is for isolation boundaries such as a worker thread pool or a plugin call, not for ordinary error handling, which belongs to Result.

Two things guard against observing half-finished state. A closure that captures &mut data is not UnwindSafe, because after a caught panic the data might violate its invariants; AssertUnwindSafe is the explicit statement that you have considered it. And Mutex poisoning applies this idea to locks: if a thread panics while holding the guard, the mutex is marked poisoned, lock() returns Err(PoisonError), and you decide whether the data is still usable; into_inner on the error gives the guard back. Thread::join similarly returns Err when the thread panicked. All of these assume the unwind strategy; under panic = "abort" there is nothing to catch.

The ABI boundary is the sharp edge. Unwinding out of a function declared extern "C" is not allowed to continue into a caller that cannot handle it, and since Rust 1.81 the runtime aborts the process instead: running the check for this lesson on 1.99, a panic in a plain extern "C" fn printed "before" and then killed the process with SIGABRT. If the caller can unwind (Rust code calling through the C ABI, or C++ built with exceptions that you control), declare extern "C-unwind" so the panic may propagate, and catch it on the other side. Never let a panic cross into C code that does not expect it.

Use Result for expected failures and panics for bugs, catch panics only at isolation boundaries, wrap captured state in AssertUnwindSafe consciously, handle poisoned locks on purpose, and declare "C-unwind" (never plain "C") on functions that may panic across an ABI boundary.

lessons.title: IEEE 754 floating point: what f64 really stores
body: An f64 is a 64-bit pattern: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits. For normal numbers the value is (-1)^sign * 1.fraction * 2^(exponent - 1023), where the leading 1 is implicit. to_bits exposes the pattern, so 1.0 has exponent field 1023 and an all-zero fraction. Because the fraction has finite length, only numbers of the form m * 2^k are exact. 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are not, so each is stored as the nearest representable neighbour, and arithmetic on those neighbours then rounds again.

That is why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false: the rounded sum lands one unit in the last place (ulp) away from the rounded literal 0.3. The gap between adjacent doubles grows with magnitude. Near 1.0 it is f64::EPSILON, about 2.2e-16, but near 1e16 neighbours are 2 apart, so adding 1.0 is absorbed and 1e16 + 1.0 == 1e16 is true. Subtracting nearly equal numbers causes catastrophic cancellation: (1 + x) - 1 for x = 1e-15 should be x, yet the leading digits cancel and what remains is mostly the rounding error of 1 + x, giving a relative error above 10 percent.

Equality on computed floats is therefore the wrong question. Compare with a tolerance scaled to the magnitude of the operands, or avoid floats for exact quantities and use integers. Subnormal numbers fill the gap below f64::MIN_POSITIVE with reduced precision, which keeps tiny results from flushing to zero but can be slow on some CPUs. Summing many values accumulates rounding error, so summation order and compensated algorithms matter; the next lessons return to that.

Check which quantity is exact (prices, quantities and counts should be integers), compare floats with a relative tolerance and never with ==, watch for absorption when mixing very large and very small magnitudes, and avoid subtracting nearly equal values when a rearranged formula exists.

Floating-point addition is only inexact in debug builds, so the same comparison is true in a release build
The literal 0.3 is stored as an integer, so comparing it with the float sum always converts and then fails
lessons.explanation: The behaviour comes from IEEE 754 binary representation, which Rust follows in every build mode. The values are doubles, == compares their bit-level values (with NaN and zero special cases), and no string comparison is involved.

lessons.title: NaN, signed zero and total ordering of floats
body: Floating point reserves a family of bit patterns for NaN (not a number), produced by operations such as 0.0 / 0.0 or inf - inf. NaN is unordered: it is not equal to anything, including itself, and partial_cmp against any number returns None. That is why f64 implements PartialOrd and PartialEq but not Ord or Eq, and why a Vec<f64> has no sort() method and a BTreeMap<f64, _> does not compile. The language is protecting you from containers whose invariants would break when a NaN arrives.

There are also two zeros. 0.0 == -0.0 is true under ==, yet they have different bits and 1.0 / -0.0 is negative infinity. f64::total_cmp implements the IEEE totalOrder predicate, a genuine total order on all bit patterns: negative NaN, negative infinity, finite negatives, -0.0, +0.0, finite positives, positive infinity, positive NaN. Use sort_by(f64::total_cmp) to sort safely. The common alternative, sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()), panics the first time it compares a NaN.

To use floats as keys, wrap them in a newtype whose Eq, Ord and Hash are all built from the same notion of identity. Here equality is total_cmp == Equal, which holds exactly when the bit patterns are equal, so hashing to_bits is consistent with it, as the Hash contract requires. min and max follow a different rule: f64::max returns the non-NaN operand, so NaN can silently vanish from a running maximum. In trading code the best defence is to reject NaN at the boundary where data enters, and to use integer ticks for prices so the question rarely arises.
Check that no NaN can reach a sort, key or comparison unexpectedly, choose total_cmp when you need an order, keep Eq/Ord/Hash consistent in a key wrapper, and remember that max and min ignore NaN.

Floating-point values cannot be compared at all, so == and < are rejected by the compiler for f64
lessons.explanation: Ord requires every pair of values to be comparable and consistent. NaN breaks that. f64 comparisons work, but only as a partial order.

lessons.title: Fixed-point money: exact integer arithmetic with checked operations
body: Money and prices are decimal quantities with a natural smallest unit, so store them as integers of that unit. Here a Money(i64) counts units of 1/10,000 (a scale of four decimal places). Integer addition and subtraction are exact, so ten additions of 0.1000 equal 1.0000 exactly, which f64 cannot promise. The type is a newtype: it prevents mixing raw integers and amounts, lets you implement Display once, and gives one place to put overflow policy.

Parsing must be explicit, not "parse an f64 and multiply by 10,000". The f64 parse has already rounded the decimal, so a price such as 1.0005 may arrive as 1.00049999..., and a later round turns the wrong way. The parser here splits at the decimal point, validates digits, rejects more than four decimals instead of silently rounding, pads the fraction to four digits and combines the parts with checked_mul and checked_add so a huge input becomes an Overflow error instead of wrapping.

Multiplication and scaling are where bugs hide. price * quantity can overflow i64 for large positions, so use checked_mul and surface None. Scaling by a ratio (price * numerator / denominator) can overflow in the intermediate product even when the final answer fits, so the code widens to i128, divides, rounds half away from zero on the magnitude and only then narrows with try_from. Display formats the integer part and a four-digit zero-padded fraction from unsigned_abs, which also handles i64::MIN without overflow.

Check that amounts are integers of a documented unit, parsing rejects excess precision rather than rounding silently, every arithmetic operation that can overflow is checked, and any division states its rounding rule.

f64 cannot represent any decimal fraction at all, so every money amount in f64 is already wrong
Rust forbids floating point for currency, and the compiler rejects f64 in money types
lessons.explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, and errors accumulate. Fixed-point integers make the unit explicit and arithmetic exact. Speed is not the reason, f64 can represent some fractions exactly, and Rust has no such rule.

lessons.title: Rounding modes and tick sizes for prices
body: Exchanges list prices on a grid: the tick size is the smallest allowed price increment, so every order price must be an integer multiple of it. Converting a computed value onto the grid is integer division with a rounding rule. The rule is a business decision: a buy limit must never be rounded up past the trader's limit, so buys floor to the tick; a sell limit must never be rounded below, so sells ceil. Round-to-nearest is for display and marks, not for protecting a limit.

Integer division in Rust truncates toward zero and % takes the dividend's sign, which makes floor logic wrong for negative numerators. div_euclid and rem_euclid give the floor quotient and a non-negative remainder when the divisor is positive, so q + 1 is the ceiling whenever the remainder is non-zero. From that, five modes follow: Floor, Ceil, TowardZero (truncate), HalfUp (ties go toward positive infinity) and HalfEven (ties go to the even neighbour). A tie means the remainder is exactly half of the divisor.

Why bother with half-even? Rounding ties always up adds a small upward bias to a long sum. The program rounds half-units 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5: the exact sum is 8, half-up gives 10 and half-even gives 8, because the ties split evenly up and down. Whenever many rounded values are added, bias accumulates linearly while the unbiased error grows more slowly. Decide the mode once, in one function, and test it on negative values and exact ties.
Check that every price sent to a venue is a multiple of the tick, buys floor and sells ceil, ties are handled by a documented mode, and negative numerators are tested.

Check over a range of limits that a buy never exceeds the limit, a sell is never below it, both results are multiples of the tick and quantizing twice changes nothing.

100.30, because ticks of 0.05 round to the nearest 0.10 before an order is sent
100.35, which floors the limit so the buyer never pays more than the stated limit
lessons.explanation: Buy limits are ceilings on what the trader will pay. Rounding up would exceed it. Venues reject prices off the tick grid rather than rounding them, and 0.05 ticks do not round to 0.10.

lessons.title: Streaming mean and variance with Welford's algorithm
body: A stream of prices or returns is too long to store, so mean and variance must be updated one observation at a time. The textbook shortcut keeps a running sum and a running sum of squares and computes variance as (sum of squares - sum^2 / n) / (n - 1). It is algebraically right and numerically dangerous: when the mean is large and the spread small, both terms are huge and nearly equal, and subtracting them is catastrophic cancellation. With values near 1e9 and a true variance of 30, the squares are near 1e18, where adjacent doubles are 128 apart, so the answer is mostly rounding error.

Welford's algorithm tracks the count n, the mean and m2, the sum of squared deviations from the current mean. For each x it computes delta = x - mean, updates mean += delta / n, then m2 += delta * (x - mean), using the old and the new mean. Nothing large is ever subtracted from something nearly equal, so accuracy holds even at 1e9. The sample variance is m2 / (n - 1), known as Bessel's correction: the mean is estimated from the same data, so dividing by n would underestimate the population variance. After a single observation the sample variance is undefined, so the method returns None.

Two partial results can be combined exactly with Chan's formula: n = na + nb, mean = mean_a + delta * nb / n and m2 = m2a + m2b + delta^2 * na * nb / n, where delta = mean_b - mean_a. That makes the statistic parallel and distributable: compute one Welford per chunk or per thread, then merge. The program checks that merging two halves matches a single pass to within 1e-9.

Check that no large nearly equal quantities are subtracted, that n - 1 is used for samples and undefined cases return None, and that partial accumulators are merged with the exact formula rather than averaged.
lessons.challenge: Write streaming_zscores(values) that returns, for each value, its z-score against the Welford statistics of all earlier values (None for the first two points, or when the earlier variance is zero). Print the z-score of the last point of [10, 11, 9, 10, 30].
lessons.question: Why is the sum-of-squares variance formula unreliable for prices near 1e9 with a spread of a few units?
options: It subtracts two huge nearly equal numbers, so catastrophic cancellation leaves mostly rounding error
Squaring a price always overflows f64, so the sum of squares becomes infinity for large inputs
The formula is wrong for any data with a non-zero mean, so it only works for centred data
f64 cannot store numbers above 1e8, so squares of prices near 1e9 are rounded to the nearest 1e8
lessons.explanation: The formula is algebraically valid, and f64 reaches about 1.8e308. The problem is precision: near 1e18 adjacent doubles differ by 128, which swamps a true difference of 90.

The mean was estimated from the same data, so dividing by n would underestimate the population variance

extraQuizzes.question: What should variance() return after exactly one observation?
options: 0.0, because one observation has no spread around its own mean
NaN, because dividing by n - 1 = 0 gives an undefined result

extraQuizzes.question: In the streaming z-score solution, why is the new point scored before it is pushed?

To avoid dividing by zero on the first value, where the standard deviation is undefined
Because Welford cannot be queried after a push, only before the first value arrives
Including the point in its own history would shrink its z-score and hide outliers
extraQuizzes.explanation: An outlier changes the mean and spread when it is included, making it look less extreme. Scoring against prior history gives the signal a trader would have had.

lessons.title: Rolling windows and exponential moving averages in O(1) per update
body: A rolling statistic summarises the last w observations. Recomputing it from scratch costs O(w) per tick; maintaining running totals costs O(1). Keep the window in a VecDeque, which supports push_back and pop_front in constant time, plus the running sum and sum of squares. On each new value, if the window is full, pop the oldest and subtract it, then add the new one. The mean is sum / w and the sample variance is (w * sum_sq - sum^2) / (w * (w - 1)).

Floating-point running sums drift: every subtract-and-add leaves a rounding residue that accumulates, and the squared form suffers cancellation. When inputs are integer ticks, avoid the problem entirely by accumulating in i128. The totals are then exact, adding and removing a value restores the state bit for bit, and only the final division becomes floating point. The program checks every window against a brute-force recomputation. Warm-up semantics matter too: until the window holds w values the statistic is not defined, so the methods return None instead of a misleading partial answer.

An exponential moving average (EMA) needs no window at all: ema = alpha * x + (1 - alpha) * previous, with alpha = 2 / (span + 1), so the weight of an observation k steps old is alpha * (1 - alpha)^k. The first value seeds the average. Choosing alpha through a half-life h instead, alpha = 1 - 0.5^(1/h), makes the memory interpretable: an observation loses half its weight every h steps. Rolling windows forget abruptly, an observation counting fully until it falls off the end, while EMAs forget smoothly, which is why they produce fewer jumps.
Check that the window length and warm-up rule are explicit, that integer inputs use exact integer accumulators, that updates are O(1), and that alpha is derived from a stated span or half-life.
lessons.challenge: Add Ema::with_half_life(h) using alpha = 1 - 0.5^(1/h). Show that the weight of an observation h steps old, (1 - alpha)^h, equals 0.5 for h = 1, 5 and 20, and that a constant series keeps the EMA at that constant.
lessons.question: Why does the rolling statistic accumulate integer ticks in i128 instead of using f64 running sums?
options: Integer totals are exact, so adding and later removing a value restores the state exactly with no rounding drift
i128 arithmetic is faster than f64 on current CPUs, so the running sums cost fewer cycles
f64 cannot represent prices above 1000, so larger ticks would lose their low digits
It lets the window length change at run time without recomputing any of the stored totals
lessons.explanation: Each f64 add/subtract rounds, and the residues accumulate over millions of updates. Integers carry exact totals; only the final division is floating point. Speed and range are not the reason.
