lessons.title: Reproducible Monte Carlo with a seeded xorshift generator
body: Monte Carlo estimates a quantity by averaging random samples. Two properties matter more than raw speed: reproducibility and a known error. A reproducible run uses an explicit seed so the same inputs produce the same stream, which lets you rerun a failing test, compare two code versions and audit a result. Operating-system randomness gives none of that. Here the generator is xorshift64*, a few shifts, xors and a multiply on a u64 state. It is fast and statistically adequate for simulation, it must start from a non-zero state, and it is not cryptographically secure: its outputs let an observer predict the rest.

To turn 64 random bits into a uniform f64 in [0, 1), keep the top 53 bits (next_u64() >> 11) and divide by 2^53. An f64 has a 53-bit significand, so every such value is exactly representable and the result can never equal 1.0. The program estimates pi by sampling points in the unit square and counting how many fall inside the quarter circle: pi is about 4 times the hit fraction. With p the hit probability and N samples, the standard error is 4 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / N).

That formula is the heart of the method. Error shrinks as 1 / sqrt(N), so 100 times more samples buy only 10 times more accuracy; a 2.5 sigma interval around the estimate is a statement about the estimator, not a guarantee about one run. Always report the estimate with its standard error. For independent streams in parallel work, derive each stream's seed from a master seed and an index with a mixing function such as splitmix64, rather than seeding with consecutive integers, which produce correlated starts.
Check that every random source takes an explicit seed, state is never zero, floats are built from the top 53 bits, results carry a standard error, and parallel streams have mixed independent seeds.
lessons.challenge: Estimate the integral of sin(x) from 0 to pi (exact value 2) by averaging pi * sin(x) over uniform x in [0, pi), with 200,000 samples. Report the estimate and its standard error computed from the sample standard deviation, and check it lies within 4 standard errors of 2.
lessons.question: Why does a Monte Carlo run take an explicit seed instead of using system randomness?
options: Seeds make the estimate more accurate, because the generator is tuned to the chosen value
Rust forbids system randomness in tests, so every simulation must supply its own seed
The same seed reproduces the same stream, so a result can be rerun, compared across code versions and audited
System randomness is slower than xorshift, so seeded generators are used purely for speed
lessons.explanation: Reproducibility is about debugging and auditing. Accuracy comes from the number of samples, not the seed.

Because it cannot produce 64-bit values, so keys built from it would be too short
Its output is predictable from a few values and its state can be recovered; zero is also a fixed point

Because xorshift refuses odd seeds, so only even numbers such as 2, 4 and 6 would work
Because it makes each stream faster, since mixed seeds avoid the first few warm-up steps
Consecutive small seeds can produce correlated early outputs, while mixing spreads the states apart
extraQuizzes.explanation: Mixing functions like splitmix64 turn nearby inputs into unrelated-looking states, which keeps parallel streams statistically independent in practice.

lessons.title: Linear algebra from scratch: matrices, pivoting and least squares
body: Quant code constantly solves linear systems: portfolio weights, regressions, covariance transforms. A small Matrix type with a flat row-major Vec<f64> is enough to see how it works. Element (r, c) lives at index r * cols + c, so rows are contiguous in memory and Index<(usize, usize)> gives natural m[(r, c)] syntax. Operations whose shapes may not agree, like multiplication, return Option so the caller handles a shape mismatch as ordinary input rather than a panic; panics are for logic bugs.

Gaussian elimination solves A x = b by turning A into an upper-triangular matrix with row operations and back-substituting. Without care it divides by zero or by a tiny pivot and amplifies rounding error. Partial pivoting fixes this: at each column swap in the row at or below the diagonal with the largest absolute entry. A matrix like [[0, 1], [1, 0]] is perfectly solvable but has a zero on its diagonal, so it only works with pivoting. If the best pivot is smaller than a tolerance, the matrix is treated as singular and solve returns None.

Least squares fits y = a + b x to points by minimising squared residuals. The normal equations (X^T X) beta = X^T y reduce the fit to a square system the solver can handle. They are easy to write and numerically weaker, because forming X^T X squares the condition number, so production code uses QR or SVD factorisations from a library such as nalgebra (a later lesson). With four points exactly on y = 1 + 2x the fit recovers coefficients 1 and 2, a handy test because the answer is known.

Check the shape rules (return Option on mismatch), pivot on the largest entry, choose and document a singularity tolerance, test against systems with known answers, and prefer QR or SVD over normal equations for ill-conditioned data.
lessons.challenge: Write determinant(a: &Matrix) -> Option<f64> using the same elimination with partial pivoting: multiply the pivots and flip the sign for each row swap. Return None for a non-square matrix. Check that the 3 by 3 system matrix from the lesson has determinant -1 and that swapping two rows flips the sign.
lessons.question: Why does solve() choose the pivot with the largest absolute value in the column?
options: It is required for the matrix to be square, so non-square inputs are rejected here
It avoids dividing by zero or a tiny number, which would amplify rounding error
It makes the matrix symmetric, which is required before elimination can start
It reduces the number of row operations to zero by finding the identity matrix first
lessons.explanation: Partial pivoting bounds the multipliers by one in magnitude, which keeps error growth in check. [[0, 1], [1, 0]] is solvable only because rows are swapped.

It flips the sign of the accumulated product for each swap, since a row swap negates the determinant
It ignores them, because swapping two rows never changes the value of the determinant
It squares the product of the pivots, because each swap doubles the sign
extraQuizzes.explanation: The determinant is the product of the pivots times (-1) raised to the number of swaps.

lessons.title: Time series with integer timestamps: bucketing, gaps and OHLCV bars
body: Market data arrives as irregular ticks, but models and charts want regular bars. A timestamp should be an integer count of nanoseconds since an epoch (an i64 covers about 292 years either side), because integers are exact, ordered and hashable, while f64 seconds lose sub-microsecond resolution at modern epoch values. A bar interval is also an integer, and the bucket a tick belongs to is start = ts.div_euclid(interval) * interval. Use div_euclid, not /, so timestamps before the epoch floor to the earlier bucket instead of truncating toward zero into the wrong one.

An OHLCV bar summarises the ticks in one bucket: open is the first price, high and low the extremes, close the last price and volume the total quantity. The resampler walks sorted ticks once, extending the current bar while the bucket is unchanged and starting a new one otherwise. Input order is a precondition, not a hope: silently resampling unsorted ticks would scatter them across buckets, so the function validates the order and returns an error instead.

Quiet intervals leave gaps. Downstream code with fixed-length windows needs every interval present, so the resampler forward-fills: for each missing bucket it emits a bar whose open, high, low and close all equal the previous close and whose volume and tick count are zero. The zero volume marks the bar as synthetic. Be careful when later merging bars into coarser ones: a forward-filled bar carries a price from earlier time, so high and low should be taken only from bars that actually traded.

Check that timestamps and intervals are integers, bucketing uses div_euclid, unsorted input is rejected, gaps are filled with explicit zero-volume bars, and synthetic bars are not allowed to influence highs and lows.
lessons.challenge: Add VWAP to each bar without floating point. Keep an i128 notional (price * qty summed) per bar and compute vwap(bar) -> Option<i64> as notional / volume rounded half away from zero, returning None for synthetic bars with zero volume. Check the bar from ticks (10000 x 10) and (10020 x 20) has VWAP 10013 (10013.33 rounded).
lessons.question: Why does the bucket calculation use ts.div_euclid(interval) instead of ts / interval?
options: div_euclid rounds to the nearest bucket, which centres each bar on its interval
/ truncates toward zero, which puts a pre-epoch timestamp such as -0.5 s in the wrong bucket; div_euclid floors
div_euclid is faster for positive timestamps, since it avoids a separate remainder step
/ panics when the timestamp is negative, so negative times could not be bucketed at all
lessons.explanation: With a positive divisor, div_euclid is the floor quotient for every sign. Truncation puts -0.5 s into bucket 0 instead of bucket -1.

lessons.title: A zero-copy CSV parser with Cow and precise errors
body: Parsing is a classic place to save allocations. A naive CSV parser turns every field into a String, so reading a million rows makes millions of small heap allocations. A zero-copy parser returns &str slices that point into the original input, so the only per-row cost is the Vec of field handles. The price is a lifetime: every field borrows from the text, so the text must outlive the parsed records. In the signature fn parse_line(line: &str, ..) -> Result<Vec<Cow<'_, str>>, CsvError> the elided lifetime ties each returned field to the input line.

Quoted fields complicate this. A field such as "split, adjusted" contains a comma, but its bytes still appear contiguously in the input, so the content between the quotes can be borrowed unchanged. Only a field with an escaped quote ("" standing for ") cannot be borrowed, because the unescaped text does not exist contiguously in the input. std::borrow::Cow models exactly that: Cow::Borrowed(&str) in the common case and Cow::Owned(String) when unescaping had to build a new string, with the same API for the caller.

Slicing by byte offsets is safe here because the delimiters are ASCII. In UTF-8 an ASCII byte never occurs inside a multi-byte character, so the positions of commas and quotes are always valid character boundaries, and &line[start..j] cannot panic. Errors carry location: unterminated quote, stray quote with line and column, and a wrong field count against the header. A known limit: quoted fields spanning several lines are not supported, which is acceptable for line-oriented market data exports and should be stated in the docs.

Check that returned fields are tied to the input lifetime, that allocation happens only where unescaping requires it, that slicing only happens at ASCII delimiters, and that every error carries a line number.
lessons.challenge: Make parsing lazy: write struct Records<'a> implementing Iterator<Item = Result<Vec<Cow<'a, str>>, CsvError>> that parses one line per next() call and checks the field count against the first record, so a large file never has to be collected. Print the first two data rows of a small input and stop after the first error.
lessons.question: Why can most fields be returned as borrowed &str instead of owned String values?
options: Because &str is always cheaper than String to compare, even when the bytes are identical
Because the parser converts the input to static memory, which lives for the whole program
Because the compiler removes the allocations automatically when it sees a String that is only read
Their bytes appear contiguously in the input, so a slice into the input is enough and no copy is needed
lessons.explanation: A borrowed slice is valid as long as the input stays alive. Only fields whose text must be rewritten (unescaped quotes) need new storage.

extraQuizzes.question: When does the parser have to return Cow::Owned?
options: When a quoted field contains an escaped quote "", because the unescaped text does not exist contiguously in the input
For every quoted field, because the quotes must be stripped before the text can be used
For every field longer than 8 bytes, since longer text cannot be borrowed from the line
For fields that contain a comma, because the comma would otherwise split the borrowed slice
extraQuizzes.explanation: Quoted fields without escapes are borrowed from between the quotes, even when they contain commas. Only unescaping builds a new string.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is slicing the line at the byte positions of commas and quotes safe in UTF-8 text?
options: Because the parser validates each character first, which makes every offset a safe boundary
ASCII bytes never appear inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, so those positions are always character boundaries
Because Rust strings are always ASCII, so every byte offset is a character boundary
Because slicing never panics in Rust, even when an offset falls inside a multi-byte character
extraQuizzes.explanation: In UTF-8 every byte of a multi-byte character has the high bit set, so an ASCII delimiter byte is always a full character on its own.

extraQuizzes.question: What constraint does returning Cow<'_, str> fields place on the caller?
options: The input must be a String, not a &str, because only an owned input can be borrowed from
The input text must outlive the parsed records, because borrowed fields point into it
The records must be consumed before the function returns, since they borrow its stack frame
The caller must clone every field before using it, because the borrowed fields are write-only
extraQuizzes.explanation: The elided lifetime in the signature ties the output to the input. Dropping the text while records exist would be rejected by the compiler.

extraQuizzes.question: What is the advantage of the lazy Records iterator over collecting every record?
options: It avoids reading the input at all, because the iterator only looks at the first line
It guarantees that no field is allocated, because iterators never create owned strings
It keeps one parsed line in memory at a time and can stop at the first error, so file size does not set memory use
It makes parsing run on several threads at once, one for each line of the input file
extraQuizzes.explanation: Iterators produce items on demand. The parsing work per line is the same, but peak memory and time to the first record are much smaller for large files.

lessons.title: Numerical Rust with ndarray and nalgebra: broadcasting, covariance, eigenvalues and least squares
body: Two crates dominate numerical Rust. ndarray provides n-dimensional arrays in the spirit of NumPy: Array1 and Array2 types, slicing with s![..] that returns views into the same memory instead of copies, element-wise operators, broadcasting, axis reductions such as mean_axis, and dot for matrix products. nalgebra provides linear-algebra types and decompositions: statically sized small matrices for geometry and dynamically sized DMatrix and DVector for data work, with QR, SVD, Cholesky and symmetric eigen decompositions. They overlap in places, but the working rule is simple: reach for ndarray to shape and reduce data, and for nalgebra when you need a decomposition. This project pins ndarray 0.17.2 and nalgebra 0.35.0 and ships its Cargo.lock; the first build needs network access.

The program computes a sample covariance matrix. mean_axis(Axis(0)) averages down the rows, giving one mean per column. data - &means broadcasts that length-2 row vector across every row, subtracting each column's mean without writing a loop; broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions, so a shape that does not line up is a panic or a compile-time-known error, never silent nonsense. centered.t().dot(&centered) / (n - 1) is then the covariance matrix, here [[2.5, 1.5], [1.5, 1.5]]. The matrix is handed to nalgebra's SymmetricEigen, whose eigenvalues, 0.4189 and 3.5811, are the variances along the principal axes (the basis of PCA). They sum to 4.0, the trace, which equals the total variance 2.5 + 1.5.

Least squares is solved with an SVD. QR::solve in nalgebra requires a square system and panics on this 4 by 2 problem, which is why the code uses svd(true, true).solve(&y, eps): the SVD handles rectangular and rank-deficient systems and treats singular values below eps as zero. Compared with the normal equations from the earlier hand-written lesson, a factorisation never forms X^T X, so it does not square the condition number. The fit recovers intercept 1 and slope 2 for four points lying exactly on y = 1 + 2x, a test whose answer is known in advance.

Check shape and broadcasting rules before trusting a result, remember that slices are views tied to the owner, round or compare floating output with a tolerance, prefer a factorisation over normal equations, and pin versions with a lock file because numerical crates change their APIs between releases.
lessons.challenge: Add correlation(cov: &Array2<f64>) -> Array2<f64> that divides cov[i][j] by sqrt(cov[i][i] * cov[j][j]), and print the correlation matrix rounded to four decimals. Explain why the diagonal is exactly 1 and what 0.7746 says about the two variables.
lessons.question: What is the practical difference between ndarray and nalgebra in this project?
options: ndarray gives n-dimensional arrays with views, broadcasting and reductions; nalgebra gives linear-algebra types and decompositions
ndarray only supports integer elements and nalgebra only supports f32, so the choice is made by element type alone, with no overlap
They are interchangeable and expose the same decompositions, so either crate can run the least-squares fit
nalgebra is only for strings and ndarray is only for images, so each belongs to a different domain
lessons.explanation: The crates have different centres of gravity. ndarray mirrors NumPy-style array manipulation, while nalgebra focuses on matrix algebra and factorisations. Both support floating-point and other numeric types, and each can do a little of the other's job.

extraQuizzes.question: What does data - &means do when data is 5 by 2 and means has length 2?
options: It fails to compile because the shapes differ, so a row vector can never meet a matrix
It subtracts the means from the first two rows only, leaving the other rows unchanged
It broadcasts the row vector across every row, subtracting each column's mean
It subtracts the mean of the whole matrix from every element, giving one scalar mean
extraQuizzes.explanation: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions, so the length-2 vector matches the 2 columns and is applied to each of the 5 rows.

extraQuizzes.question: What is data.slice(s![.., 0])?
options: A compile-time constant computed from the array's shape, with no access to the data
A view of the first column that borrows data and copies nothing
A new owned Vec that holds a copy of the column's elements, allocated on the heap
A raw pointer that must be freed manually once the view is no longer needed
extraQuizzes.explanation: ndarray slices are ArrayView values tied to the owner's lifetime, so they are cheap but cannot outlive the array.

extraQuizzes.question: Why solve least squares with an SVD or QR factorisation instead of the normal equations?
options: SVD is always faster than any other method, so it is the default choice for every size
A factorisation avoids needing any data in memory, so it can solve the system symbolically
The factorisation avoids forming X^T X, which squares the condition number and loses accuracy on ill-conditioned data
The normal equations are not mathematically valid for a rectangular matrix, so they give wrong answers
extraQuizzes.explanation: The normal equations are valid and are often fast, but numerically weaker. SVD is generally more expensive than normal equations in exchange for robustness.

extraQuizzes.question: What do the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix describe, and what do they sum to?
options: The residuals of the least-squares fit, summing to zero for a model with an intercept
The number of observations that fall along each principal axis, summing to n
The variances along the principal axes, summing to the trace, which is the total variance
The means of each column, summing to the grand mean of all observations in the matrix
extraQuizzes.explanation: For a symmetric covariance matrix the eigenvalues are variances along orthogonal directions. Their sum equals the trace: 3.5811 + 0.4189 = 4.0 = 2.5 + 1.5.

lessons.title: Serde data model: a market-data record with a custom price format
body: serde separates what your data is from how it is written. Types implement Serialize and Deserialize, usually through #[derive], and a format crate such as serde_json supplies a Serializer and Deserializer. The traits describe the serde data model: integers, strings, sequences, maps, structs and enums. Because the model sits in the middle, the same Quote struct can become JSON, a binary format or a database row without format-specific code in the type. This project pins serde 1.0.229 and serde_json 1.0.154 and ships its Cargo.lock; the first build needs network access.

Attributes shape the wire format without hand-writing code. rename_all = "lowercase" makes the enum value Side::Buy appear as "buy" and rejects "Buy". deny_unknown_fields makes deserialization fail when the input has a field the struct does not declare, which catches typos and version drift instead of silently ignoring data. default and skip_serializing_if on an Option field let a missing key become None and omit None from output. These are decisions about a public contract, so they deserve tests.

Prices need special care. JSON numbers are usually parsed as f64 by consumers, so a decimal price loses exactness on the way through. Price therefore implements the traits by hand: serialize writes an exact decimal string such as "189.4900" through collect_str, and deserialize reads a String and parses it with the same strict parser used elsewhere, converting a parse error into a serde error with Error::custom. Excess precision such as "1.23456" is rejected rather than rounded. Reading into String instead of &str works with every deserializer, whereas a borrowed &str only works when the input can be borrowed without unescaping.

Check that the wire format is deliberate (strings or integer ticks for money), unknown fields and wrong cases are rejected where the contract demands, optional fields are omitted when absent, parse errors surface as errors rather than rounded values, and round-trip tests cover each custom impl.
lessons.challenge: Add an internally tagged enum Event with variants Trade { symbol, price, qty } and Heartbeat { ts_ns } using #[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]. Print each event as JSON, parse it back and assert equality.
lessons.question: Why does Price implement Serialize and Deserialize by hand instead of deriving them over its i64?
options: To control the wire format: an exact decimal string such as "189.4900", validated on input, instead of the raw tick count
Because derive cannot handle i64 fields, so any newtype around an integer needs hand-written code
Because serde requires hand-written impls for every newtype, whatever type it wraps inside
Because serde_json cannot serialize integers, so ticks must be converted to strings first
lessons.explanation: A derive on Price(i64) would write the raw tick count, which couples the contract to an internal scale. A hand-written impl lets the format be exact, readable and validated.

extraQuizzes.question: What does #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] do?
options: Deserialization fails when the input contains a field the struct does not declare, catching typos and version drift
It deletes unknown fields from the input file, so a later save writes the cleaned version
It stores unknown fields in a hidden map so they can be written back unchanged on output
It makes serialization skip fields that are None, so the output stays free of null values
extraQuizzes.explanation: By default serde ignores extra keys. The attribute turns them into errors, which is stricter and often safer for configuration and protocol messages.

extraQuizzes.question: What do default and skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none" do for the venue field?
options: They serialize None as the string "None", which keeps the key present in every record
They convert venue into a number, with None mapped to zero in the JSON
A missing key becomes None on input, and a None value is omitted from the output
They make venue mandatory on input and output, so a missing key is reported as an error
extraQuizzes.explanation: default supplies a value when the key is absent and skip_serializing_if suppresses the key when the predicate is true, so the optional field round-trips cleanly.

extraQuizzes.question: Why are JSON numbers risky for money amounts?
options: JSON numbers are always integers, so a decimal price is silently truncated when written
Many consumers parse JSON numbers as f64, so decimal values can lose exactness; strings or integer ticks stay exact
JSON cannot contain numbers with decimals, so every price needs to be written as an integer
serde_json refuses to write numbers above 100, so larger prices must be stored as text
extraQuizzes.explanation: The JSON grammar allows decimals, but the receiver decides how to parse them. A string with fixed decimals is unambiguous.

extraQuizzes.question: Why does Deserialize for Price read a String instead of a &str?
options: Because the Deserialize trait forbids borrowed data, so every field must be an owned type
A borrowed &str works only when the input can lend the text without unescaping; String works with every deserializer
Because &str cannot hold digits, so a numeric text must be copied into an owned String first
Because String is faster to parse than a &str, since parse can reuse the allocation
extraQuizzes.explanation: Zero-copy deserialization is possible with the right lifetime bounds, but it only works when the input is available unchanged. Owned data is the portable default.

lessons.title: Benchmarking honestly: warm-up, black_box and medians
body: A benchmark answers one question: how long does this exact work take on this machine under these conditions? Rust compiles with an optimizer that is very good at noticing that a result is never used, or that an input is a constant, and then deleting or pre-computing the work. A loop that merely calls a pure function and discards the answer can time as zero nanoseconds. std::hint::black_box is the standard tool: it returns its argument unchanged but asks the compiler to treat the value as if it came from and went to somewhere unknown. Wrap both the input that would otherwise be a visible constant and the result that would otherwise be unused. The documentation calls it best effort, so a surprisingly fast number is a reason to inspect the machine code, not a reason to celebrate.

A trustworthy harness has three parts. Warm-up runs execute the work before recording so caches, branch predictors, lazily initialised statics and page tables are in their steady state. Repeated samples are each timed with Instant, a monotonic clock that is safe for measuring durations, whereas SystemTime can jump when the operating system adjusts the wall clock. Finally the samples are summarised with robust statistics. A median ignores the occasional sample inflated by a context switch or a page fault, while a mean lets one bad run distort the answer. Reporting the minimum and maximum next to the median shows how noisy the machine was.

Build mode matters as much as method. A plain cargo run builds without optimization, so iterator chains are not inlined, bounds checks are not hoisted and costs that disappear in release builds dominate the profile. Measure with cargo run --release (or the bench profile) and remember that the numbers describe one CPU, one compiler version and one load level. The program below keeps its printed output deterministic by timing internally but printing only the checksum of the work and the ordering facts it asserts, so it can be a reliable example while the real timings stay on your machine.

Check what you measured: use the result (accumulate a checksum and print it), keep inputs behind black_box, record several samples after warm-up, compare release builds only, and treat any difference under the observed min-to-max spread as noise.
lessons.challenge: Write checksum_of_runs(runs, f) that returns the wrapping sum of f() over that many calls, passing each result through black_box. Use it to show that doubling the number of runs doubles the checksum of sum_squares(1_000).
lessons.question: Why do benchmark inputs and results go through std::hint::black_box?
options: It hides the data flow from the optimizer so the work cannot be folded into a constant or removed as unused
It moves the computation onto a separate thread so timing is not disturbed by the work itself
It forces the function to be inlined into the timing loop so call overhead is not measured
It pins the CPU to a fixed clock frequency for the duration of the run, so timings repeat
lessons.explanation: black_box returns its argument unchanged, but the compiler must assume the value may be observed or produced elsewhere. Without it a pure computation on constants can be evaluated at compile time or deleted. It does not spawn threads, force inlining or touch CPU frequency, and its effect is best effort rather than a hard guarantee.

Expected output:
one run = 333383335000
checksum over 3 warm-up + 11 timed runs = 4667366690000
min <= median <= max: true

extraQuizzes.question: Why report the median of the samples instead of the mean?
options: A few samples disturbed by scheduling or page faults inflate the mean but barely move the median
The median is guaranteed to equal the minimum, so it reports the best case the machine could achieve
Integer nanosecond counts cannot be averaged, because the sum of the samples would overflow
The median removes the need for warm-up runs, because cold-start samples fall away automatically
extraQuizzes.explanation: Noise on a general-purpose machine is mostly one-sided: interruptions only add time. The median is robust to a minority of such outliers. It is not equal to the minimum, integers average fine, and warm-up serves a different purpose.

extraQuizzes.question: Why can timing a plain cargo run (debug) build mislead a performance decision?
options: Debug builds run on a different instruction set, so their timings cannot be compared with release ones
Debug builds skip most optimizations, so inlining, bounds-check removal and vectorization that drive release speed are absent
Debug builds cannot call Instant::now, so timing code has to be compiled out of unoptimized binaries
Debug builds always run slower by the same constant factor, so relative comparisons stay valid
extraQuizzes.explanation: Optimization changes relative costs, not just absolute speed: abstractions that are free in release can be expensive in debug. The slowdown is not a constant factor and the clock and CPU are the same.

extraQuizzes.question: Which clock should a benchmark use to measure elapsed time?
options: A counter incremented once for each loop iteration of the work
The date printed by the shell before and after the run
std::time::Instant, because it is monotonic and cannot jump backwards
std::time::SystemTime, because it is the most precise wall clock
extraQuizzes.explanation: Instant is designed for measuring durations. SystemTime follows the adjustable wall clock and can move backwards or jump, which would corrupt a measurement.

extraQuizzes.question: What is the purpose of the warm-up runs before the timed samples?
options: To bring caches, branch predictors and lazily initialised state to steady state before recording
To make the compiler re-optimize the function with profile data gathered from the first runs
To discard the checksum produced by the first runs so it cannot leak into the final result
To increase the resolution of Instant::now, which improves as the clock is read repeatedly
extraQuizzes.explanation: The first executions pay one-off costs such as cold caches and page faults. Rust is compiled ahead of time, so there is no runtime re-optimization, and warm-up does not change clock resolution.

lessons.title: Memory layout: array of structs versus struct of arrays
body: A struct is laid out in memory as its fields plus padding so that every field sits at an address that satisfies its alignment, and the struct is rounded up to a multiple of its largest alignment. A record with an i64, a u32 and a u8 holds 13 bytes of data but occupies 16, because 8-byte alignment forces three padding bytes. size_of and align_of report this, and the default Rust representation is allowed to reorder fields to shrink padding, which is why #[repr(C)] exists: it fixes declaration order and C-style padding when layout must be stable, for example across FFI or when reading a wire format.

A Vec of such records is an array of structs (AoS). Reading one record touches its fields together, which is ideal when an operation uses most of the record. A struct of arrays (SoA) stores each field in its own Vec instead. A loop that needs only price and quantity then streams through two dense arrays and never loads the side byte or the padding. CPUs fetch memory in cache lines, commonly 64 bytes on x86_64 and 128 bytes on Apple silicon (sysctl hw.cachelinesize reports 128 here), so the number of lines a loop touches is a good first estimate of its memory cost. The program computes that estimate for 1,000 rows both ways using a 64-byte line; the ratio between layouts, not the absolute count, is the point.

Neither layout is universally better. AoS wins when code handles a whole record at a time, such as matching one order, because one or two cache lines hold everything. SoA wins for scans over one or two fields of many records, such as computing notional across a day of ticks, and it also lends itself to vectorization because consecutive elements of one field are adjacent. Converting between the two is cheap, so measure the real access pattern in release mode before restructuring a hot type.

Check the access pattern before the layout: count how many fields each hot loop reads, print size_of for the record, and remember that the default representation is unspecified, so never rely on a particular padding unless the type is repr(C).
lessons.challenge: Add a venue: u8 field to TickRow. Predict, then print, the new size_of the row, its padding, and the bytes per row that a column layout stores. Explain why the row did not grow.
lessons.question: A loop sums price * qty over a million ticks and never reads the side field. Why can a struct-of-arrays layout touch fewer cache lines than an array of structs?
options: Struct-of-arrays removes every bounds check from the loop, which is where an AoS loop loses time
An array of structs cannot be iterated sequentially, so its loop jumps between unrelated cache lines
The loop reads only the price and qty arrays, so unused side bytes and padding never occupy cache lines
Struct-of-arrays values are kept in CPU registers instead of memory, so no cache lines are used
lessons.explanation: Cache lines are loaded whole. In AoS each 16-byte row drags the unused side byte and padding through the cache along with the useful fields. SoA keeps the hot fields dense. Bounds checks and sequential iteration are unrelated, and columns still live in memory.

extraQuizzes.question: What is size_of for a struct with an i64, a u32 and a u8 under the default representation?
options: 13 bytes: the exact sum of the field sizes, with no padding added
12 bytes: the u8 shares the slot of the u32, so only 12 are needed
24 bytes: each field takes its own 8-byte slot in the struct
16 bytes: 13 bytes of data rounded up to the 8-byte alignment
extraQuizzes.explanation: The size must be a multiple of the struct alignment, which is that of i64. 13 rounds up to 16. Fields can share space, but the total is still padded to the alignment.

extraQuizzes.question: When does an array of structs beat a struct of arrays?
options: Never, because struct-of-arrays is always faster, whatever the access pattern of the program
Only when records are larger than a memory page, since smaller records always favour columns
When an operation reads or writes most fields of one record together, so a record fits in one or two cache lines
When a loop reads a single field from every record, because the other fields then stay out of the cache
extraQuizzes.explanation: Handling a whole record at a time (for example matching one order) wants its fields adjacent. Single-field scans are the SoA case, and there is no universal winner.

extraQuizzes.question: What does #[repr(C)] guarantee that the default Rust layout does not?
options: Fields are reordered to minimise the struct size, which the default layout never does
The struct is allocated on the heap, so its address stays stable for foreign code
Fields stay in declaration order with C padding rules, so the layout is stable for FFI and wire formats
Fields are packed with no padding at all, so the struct is always as small as its data
extraQuizzes.explanation: repr(C) fixes order and padding, which is what an external consumer needs. The default representation may reorder fields and makes no promise. repr(C) does not pack or move anything to the heap.

lessons.title: Cache-aware loops: loop order and tiling for matrix multiply
body: Matrix multiply does the same arithmetic however you order the loops, yet the order decides how memory is read. A matrix stored row-major in a flat Vec has element (row, col) at row * n + col. The textbook i-j-k loop walks b down a column, jumping n elements (n * 8 bytes for i64) between reads, so almost every read lands on a different cache line and most of each line is wasted. Swapping to i-k-j keeps a[i][k] in a register and makes the inner loop sweep b and c along rows with stride one, so every byte of every loaded line is used. Nothing about the answer changes, only the traffic to memory.

Tiling (blocking) goes one step further. For matrices too large to stay in cache, even row sweeps evict data before it is reused. A tiled algorithm cuts each dimension into blocks and finishes all the work that touches a small block of a, b and c before moving on, so those blocks are reused while still cache resident. Three tile-by-tile blocks of i64 with tile = 32 occupy 3 * 32 * 32 * 8 = 24,576 bytes, a size that can sit in a typical 32 KiB L1 data cache. The last block along each edge may be short when the tile does not divide n, which the code handles with min(n).

With integers all three orders give identical results because addition is associative, as long as nothing overflows. With f64 the sums are grouped differently, so results can differ in the last bits, and a test that compares floating-point outputs needs a tolerance rather than equality. Production code usually calls a tuned BLAS-style kernel, but writing the loops once teaches you to read a hot loop by asking what addresses it touches, in what order, and how many times each is reused.

Check stride before cleverness: the innermost loop should move through memory contiguously, tile edges must be clipped, and compare against a simple reference implementation on awkward sizes such as n = 10 with tile = 4.
lessons.challenge: Write transpose(b, n) and matmul_bt(a, bt, n) that multiplies using a transposed copy of b so the inner k loop reads both operands along rows. Check it equals the naive result on a 5 by 5 example.
lessons.question: Why is the i-k-j loop order usually faster than i-j-k for row-major matrices?
options: It performs fewer multiplications than i-j-k, since the middle loop skips zero entries
It removes the bounds checks from the indexing, because the inner index is always in range
It is the only order that produces the correct product, because the others reorder the sums
Its inner loop walks b and c along rows with stride one, so each loaded cache line is fully used
lessons.explanation: All orders do the same n cubed multiply-adds and all are correct. The difference is access pattern: i-j-k jumps n elements through b on every step, wasting most of each cache line, while i-k-j reads contiguous memory.

extraQuizzes.question: What does tiling add on top of a good loop order?
options: It reduces the number of multiply-add operations, because blocks of zeros are skipped entirely
It makes floating-point results exact, since each small block accumulates without rounding
It lets the code skip rows that are zero, because a tile can be checked for zeros first
It reuses a small block of each matrix while it is still in cache, cutting trips to slower memory
extraQuizzes.explanation: Tiling does not change the operation count or the exactness of arithmetic; it reorders the work so data is reused before eviction.

extraQuizzes.question: The naive, ikj and tiled versions produce identical i64 results. Why?
options: Tiling changes rounding but only in the last digit, which the equality check tolerates
They only agree when the tile size divides n, because ragged tiles change the sums
They only agree in release builds, because debug builds skip the tiled loop order
Integer addition is associative, so regrouping the sums cannot change the result when nothing overflows
extraQuizzes.explanation: Exact integer arithmetic is order independent (without overflow). The tile does not need to divide n because the edges are clipped with min(n), and build mode does not change semantics.

extraQuizzes.question: If the same loops used f64, which statement is true?
options: Tiling always makes the answer more accurate, because it adds smaller numbers together first
f64 matrices cannot be tiled, because a tile must hold whole integer values
Different loop orders can differ in the last bits because floating-point addition is not associative
All orders are always bit-identical, since floating-point addition gives the same result in any order
extraQuizzes.explanation: Regrouping floating-point sums changes intermediate rounding, so compare with a tolerance. Accuracy may go up or down and tiling works for any element type.

extraQuizzes.question: For n = 10 and tile = 4, how many blocks does (0..n).step_by(tile) visit along one dimension?
options: 4, because 10 / 4 rounds up and adds one
10, one block for each element
3: blocks of 4, 4 and a clipped block of 2
2, because 10 / 4 rounds down to two blocks
extraQuizzes.explanation: step_by(4) yields starts 0, 4 and 8. The last block covers only indices 8 and 9, which is why the inner ranges use min(n).

lessons.title: SIMD on aarch64: NEON intrinsics with a portable fallback
body: SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) executes one operation on several lanes at once. On Apple silicon and other aarch64 CPUs the baseline vector unit is NEON with 128-bit registers, so one instruction can multiply four i32 lanes. Rust exposes the instructions as intrinsics in std::arch::aarch64, for example vld1q_s32 to load four i32 values, vmlaq_s32 to multiply and accumulate lanes, and vaddvq_s32 to add the lanes together. Because intrinsics belong to one architecture, the code is wrapped in #[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")] and a portable function with the same name is compiled everywhere else, so the crate builds and behaves the same on every target.

Intrinsics that dereference pointers are unsafe and the safety comment is a real proof obligation. Here the loop runs len / 4 times and each vld1q_s32 reads four elements starting at index i * 4, so the last load ends at 4 * (len / 4), which never passes the end of either slice. The remaining len % 4 elements, the tail, are handled with ordinary safe indexing. Always test the SIMD path against the scalar reference on lengths that are not multiples of the lane count, including zero and lengths below one vector.

NEON is part of the aarch64 baseline, so no detection is needed for it. Optional extensions are different: x86_64 code that uses AVX2 must check is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") at runtime and call a function marked #[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] only when the check passes, and aarch64 has the matching is_aarch64_feature_detected! macro for extensions such as dot-product instructions. Calling an instruction the CPU lacks is undefined behaviour, not a catchable panic. Many simple loops over slices are auto-vectorized by LLVM in release builds, so reach for intrinsics only after measuring that the compiler did not.
Check four things: a scalar reference exists and is compared in tests, loads stay in bounds, the tail is processed, and any optional CPU feature is detected at runtime before it is used.
lessons.challenge: Write sum_fast(values: &[i32]) -> i32 using vld1q_s32, vaddq_s32 and vaddvq_s32 on aarch64, with a portable fallback on other targets and a scalar tail. Check it against iter().sum() for several lengths.
lessons.question: Why is the NEON code guarded by #[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")] with a portable function for other targets?
options: The cfg attribute makes the intrinsics safe to call, so no unsafe block is needed on aarch64
The scalar version is needed to detect integer overflow, which the NEON version cannot report
The intrinsics exist only for that architecture, so without a portable fallback the crate would not compile elsewhere
NEON intrinsics are always slower than scalar code, so the cfg gate keeps them off other targets
lessons.explanation: std::arch is organised per architecture. Items for aarch64 are absent on x86_64, so a cfg gate plus a fallback keeps one code base portable. The cfg attribute changes what is compiled, not safety, and speed is the reason to use intrinsics in the first place.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is the pointer arithmetic in the NEON loop sound?
options: The loop runs len / 4 times, so every four-element load ends within both slices, and the tail uses safe indexing
Raw pointer arithmetic is always in bounds, so the loop needs no length reasoning of its own
NEON loads ignore bounds and wrap around, so an out-of-range load just reads the first lane again
unsafe turns off the borrow checker, so any pointer offset in the block is acceptable
extraQuizzes.explanation: Soundness comes from the arithmetic proof stated in the safety comment. Raw pointers are not checked and unsafe does not make an out-of-range read valid.

extraQuizzes.question: How should code use an instruction-set extension that only some CPUs of an architecture support, such as AVX2 on x86_64?
options: Detect it at run time with is_x86_feature_detected! and call a #[target_feature] function only when true
Compile for it and rely on catch_unwind to recover if the CPU lacks the instruction
Check cfg!(debug_assertions) before calling, because release builds select the right instructions
Call it unconditionally; unsupported instructions simply return zero without any error
extraQuizzes.explanation: Executing an unsupported instruction is undefined behaviour or a hardware trap, not a recoverable panic. Runtime detection gates the call.

extraQuizzes.question: Why might a plain iterator loop match the intrinsic version in release builds?
options: Scalar code never uses vector registers, so only intrinsics can make use of the vector unit
LLVM can auto-vectorize simple counted loops over slices, so intrinsics matter mainly where it does not
Iterators always emit SIMD instructions at run time, whatever the optimization level
Auto-vectorization works at opt-level 0 too, so debug builds are vectorized like release ones
extraQuizzes.explanation: Auto-vectorization is a compile-time optimization that needs optimization enabled and a vectorizable loop shape. Measure before hand-writing intrinsics.

extraQuizzes.question: With 4 lanes per vector and a slice of 19 elements, how many elements does the scalar tail process?
options: 4, because the tail is one vector
0, because NEON handles any length
19, because the tail does everything
3, because 19 = 4 * 4 + 3
extraQuizzes.explanation: len / 4 gives 4 full vectors covering 16 elements; the remaining 19 % 4 = 3 elements are summed with ordinary code.

lessons.title: Data parallelism with scoped threads and ordered reduction
body: std::thread::spawn requires a closure that is 'static, which forces Arc and cloning for data that already lives on your stack. std::thread::scope removes that requirement. Inside scope(|s| ...) every thread started with s.spawn is guaranteed to be joined before scope returns, so the compiler allows those threads to borrow local variables: the borrow cannot outlive the data because the scope cannot end first. This turns "split a slice among workers" into ordinary borrowing, with no reference counting and no unsafe.

Splitting is done with slice methods. chunks(n) yields shared sub-slices, so several threads can read different regions, and chunks_mut(n) yields non-overlapping &mut sub-slices, so each thread gets exclusive access to its own region and no lock is needed. The borrow checker accepts this because the pieces are disjoint by construction. The chunk length is len.div_ceil(parts), clamped to at least one so an empty or tiny slice does not ask for chunks of size zero, which panics.

Parallel code must also be reproducible. Each thread returns a partial result through its join handle, and the caller combines the partials in chunk order, not in the order threads happen to finish. For integers the order does not matter, but floating-point addition is not associative, so a fixed combination order makes the answer identical from run to run for a given number of parts. If one thread panics and its handle was not joined by you, scope panics after all threads finish, so failure is never silently lost.

Check that the work per chunk outweighs thread start-up and join cost, that chunk size is never zero, that partial results are combined in a fixed order, and that a thread panic is handled on purpose rather than ignored.
lessons.challenge: Write parallel_max(data: &[i64], parts: usize) -> Option<i64> using scoped threads that returns the largest element, or None for an empty slice. Compare it with iter().max() for several part counts.
lessons.question: Why can threads started inside std::thread::scope borrow local variables without Arc?
options: Borrow checking is switched off inside scoped threads, so the programmer must guarantee safety
Scoped threads run on the calling thread, never in parallel, so no sharing actually occurs
The scope joins every spawned thread before it returns, so a borrow cannot outlive the data it points to
Scoped threads copy the borrowed data into their own stacks, so the original can be dropped early
lessons.explanation: thread::spawn needs a 'static closure because the thread may outlive the caller. scope bounds the threads' lifetime by the scope itself, which lets the compiler accept shorter borrows. The borrow checker still runs and the threads do run concurrently.

extraQuizzes.question: Why combine partial sums in chunk order instead of in the order threads finish?
options: Integer sums need a fixed order but floats do not, because floats are always rounded the same way
Combining in completion order is impossible with join handles, because they hide the thread's finish time
f64 addition is not associative, so a fixed order gives reproducible sums while completion order varies run to run
Threads always finish in chunk order, so there is no difference between the two approaches
extraQuizzes.explanation: Different groupings of f64 additions can round differently, and the scheduler decides who finishes first. Joining handles in the order they were created fixes the grouping.

extraQuizzes.question: What does chunks_mut allow that makes lock-free parallel mutation possible?
options: It yields non-overlapping mutable sub-slices, so each thread has exclusive access to its own region
It wraps every element in a Mutex automatically, so each thread locks the elements it touches
It copies the data and merges the copies afterwards, so each thread works on a private copy
It disables the aliasing rules for the slice, so overlapping writes are allowed between threads
extraQuizzes.explanation: Disjoint &mut regions satisfy the aliasing rules by construction, so no synchronisation is required for the mutation itself.

extraQuizzes.question: What happens if a scoped thread panics and you never joined its handle?
options: The process aborts immediately without joining the other threads, so their work is lost
The panic is silently discarded, because the handle was never joined to receive it
All other scoped threads are killed instantly, and the scope returns without waiting
scope waits for all threads and then panics, so the failure is not silently lost
extraQuizzes.explanation: The scope joins automatically on exit and propagates a panic from any thread whose handle was not joined manually.

extraQuizzes.question: When is splitting work across threads a bad idea?
options: When the threads only borrow data, because borrowed data cannot be processed in parallel
When the work per chunk is small compared with the cost of starting and joining threads
When the element type is Copy, because copying the elements into each thread costs too much
When the program is built in release mode, since optimized code is already fast enough
extraQuizzes.explanation: Thread creation costs microseconds. Tiny chunks lose to a single-threaded loop. Copy types, release builds and borrowing are not reasons to avoid parallelism.

lessons.title: False sharing and cache-line padding
body: Cores do not share individual variables; they share cache lines, blocks of 64 or 128 bytes that the coherence protocol moves between cores. When one core writes to a line, copies in other cores are invalidated. Two threads that write two different variables stored in the same line therefore take turns owning that line even though they never touch each other's data. This is false sharing: the program is correct, but a counter per thread can run several times slower than it should because the line ping-pongs between cores.

The cure is layout. Give each independently written value its own line by padding and aligning it. #[repr(align(128))] on a wrapper struct raises the alignment to 128 and, because size must be a multiple of alignment, rounds its size up to 128, so consecutive array elements start on different lines. This machine reports a 128-byte line (sysctl hw.cachelinesize), and well-known libraries such as crossbeam pad to 128 bytes on aarch64 and x86_64, so 128 is a safe default; padding to 64 on hardware with 128-byte lines would leave neighbours sharing.

The lesson avoids printing times, which vary, and instead proves the layout: size_of and align_of of the wrapper, and the byte distance between adjacent elements. Two threads then increment their own AtomicU64 with Relaxed ordering. Relaxed is enough for an independent counter because only the atomicity of each increment matters, not ordering relative to other memory. Padding spends memory to buy speed, so apply it only to hot, per-thread, frequently written data.

Check that the hot fields are written by different threads, that padding matches the target's line size, and that you confirmed the slowdown with a release-mode measurement before spending the memory.
lessons.challenge: Predict and then print size_of and align_of for Padded<u8> and Padded<[u8; 129]> when Padded is #[repr(align(128))]. Explain why the second is larger.
lessons.question: What is false sharing?
options: Two threads write the same variable without synchronization, so the updates overwrite each other
A thread reads stale data because a memory fence is missing, so it sees an old value
Two Arc handles point to the same allocation, so cloning them contends on one counter
Threads write different variables that live in the same cache line, so the line bounces between cores
lessons.explanation: False sharing is a performance problem caused by the coherence protocol working on whole lines. The data accessed is distinct, so it is neither a data race nor a visibility bug.

extraQuizzes.question: What does #[repr(align(128))] do to a wrapper around an AtomicU64?
options: It shrinks the AtomicU64 to fit a smaller line, so more counters share each cache line
It makes the atomic operations stronger than SeqCst, so the increments are ordered globally
It allocates the value on the heap, so each counter lives in its own separate allocation
It raises the alignment to 128 and rounds the size up to 128, so adjacent array elements start on separate lines
extraQuizzes.explanation: Alignment dictates both the start address and, through the size-multiple rule, the size. It does not change the atomic operation semantics or allocation strategy.

extraQuizzes.question: Is false sharing a correctness bug?
options: No, the counts stay correct; only performance suffers from cache-coherence traffic
Yes, it loses increments, because both threads overwrite the shared line with stale values
Yes, it is a data race under the Rust memory model, because two threads touch one line
Only when Relaxed ordering is used, since stronger orderings keep the counts correct
extraQuizzes.explanation: Each thread updates its own atomic, so there is no race and no lost update. The cost is invalidation traffic between cores.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is Ordering::Relaxed enough for the independent per-thread counters?
options: Only the atomicity of each increment matters; no other memory access depends on ordering relative to the counter
Relaxed makes the increment non-atomic but faster, which is acceptable for a simple counter
Relaxed guarantees the threads run in lockstep, so the counts always end up equal
Relaxed is required whenever threads are scoped, since scoped threads reject stronger orderings
extraQuizzes.explanation: Relaxed still makes each read-modify-write atomic, and joining the scope synchronises the final read. Stronger orderings only matter when other data must be published with the counter.

extraQuizzes.question: Why should padding size follow the target hardware instead of always being 64?
options: Line size is the same on every CPU, so only the compiler version decides the right padding
Alignment above 64 is rejected by rustc, so 64 is the largest padding that can be written
Some CPUs, including Apple silicon, use 128-byte lines, so 64-byte padding could still leave neighbours sharing a line
Padding to 64 always wastes memory on every target, so smaller padding is better on all CPUs
extraQuizzes.explanation: Cache line size is a hardware property. Padding to the largest relevant line size avoids sharing at the cost of memory, which is why libraries use 128 on several architectures.

lessons.title: Memory ordering in practice: publishing data with Release and Acquire
body: Atomic operations take an Ordering argument because compilers and CPUs reorder memory accesses. Relaxed guarantees only that the operation itself is atomic and that each atomic has a single modification order; it promises nothing about other memory. That is exactly right for an independent counter, and exactly wrong for handing data from one thread to another. For a handoff you pair a Release store with an Acquire load of the same atomic: when the load observes the stored value, everything the writer did before the Release store is visible to the reader after the Acquire load. The pair forms a one-way bridge, called synchronizes-with.

The example publishes the number 42. The writer stores the data with Relaxed and then sets a ready flag with Release. The reader spins on the flag with Acquire and then reads the data with Relaxed. Because the flag load that sees true synchronizes with the flag store, the earlier data store must be visible, so the reader always sees 42. Change the flag store or load to Relaxed and the Rust memory model permits the reader to see true and still read the old zero. On a strongly ordered x86 machine you might never observe it; on weakly ordered aarch64 hardware, or after a compiler reordering, you can. Tests that pass on one machine do not prove an ordering is sufficient.

Read-modify-write operations such as fetch_add are always atomic; their ordering argument controls only the publication behaviour around them. compare_exchange_weak lets you build operations the library lacks. It may fail spuriously, so it sits in a loop that reloads the current value and retries, and the weak form can be cheaper than compare_exchange on some architectures. SeqCst is the strongest ordering and adds a single total order over all SeqCst operations. It is needed in patterns where two threads each write their own flag and then read the other's, because Acquire and Release alone do not forbid both threads reading the old values. Default to the weakest ordering you can justify in a comment and promote only with a reason.

Check every atomic for the claim it needs: independent counter (Relaxed), publication (Release store, Acquire load), read-modify-write retry loop (reload on failure), or a global order across several atomics (SeqCst), and never trust a passing run on one CPU as proof.
lessons.challenge: Publish a two-field message (price and qty) safely: the writer stores both fields Relaxed and then stores sequence number 1 with Release; the reader waits for sequence == 1 with Acquire and then reads both fields. Run it repeatedly and assert the reader never sees a partial message.
lessons.question: What does pairing a Release store with an Acquire load of the same atomic guarantee?
options: The two threads run in lockstep, one instruction at a time, with the store always before the load
Only the atomic variable itself is ordered; other memory accesses remain completely unordered
Every atomic operation in the program becomes sequentially consistent, whatever ordering it requested
If the load sees the stored value, everything the writer did before the store is visible to the reader after the load
lessons.explanation: Release/Acquire creates a synchronizes-with edge for that atomic, publishing earlier writes. It does not force lockstep execution, it is not limited to the one variable, and it does not change the ordering of unrelated atomics.

extraQuizzes.question: If the flag store were Relaxed instead of Release, what could go wrong in the example?
options: The data store would become non-atomic, since it was only atomic because of the Release flag
The reader could see ready == true yet still read the old data, because nothing orders the data store before the flag
The program would no longer compile, because Relaxed cannot be used to store a boolean flag
The flag would never become true, since a Relaxed store is not visible to other threads
extraQuizzes.explanation: Relaxed provides atomicity only. The memory model permits the data store to be observed after the flag, and weakly ordered CPUs or compiler reordering can expose it. Compilation and atomicity are unaffected.

extraQuizzes.question: For which job is Ordering::Relaxed correct?
options: Implementing a lock that protects other variables, since a Relaxed swap acquires the lock
Establishing one global order across several atomics, because Relaxed operations are ordered together
An independent counter or statistic where only the atomicity of each update matters and no other data is published through it
Publishing a buffer to another thread, because a counter ordering covers the buffer's contents too
extraQuizzes.explanation: Relaxed has no synchronising effect on other memory. Publication, locks and cross-atomic ordering need Acquire/Release or SeqCst.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is compare_exchange_weak normally used inside a retry loop?
options: It may fail spuriously on some architectures, so a loop reloads and retries; the weak form can be cheaper
It never fails, so the loop only handles integer overflow and the weak name is historical
It is the only compare-and-swap Rust provides, so every update loop has to use it
It automatically upgrades the ordering to SeqCst when the exchange fails, which makes retries safe
extraQuizzes.explanation: Spurious failure is allowed for the weak form. A retry loop is already needed for real contention, so the weak form costs nothing extra there.

extraQuizzes.question: When is SeqCst genuinely needed over Acquire and Release?
options: When several atomics must be seen in one global order, such as two threads each writing a flag then reading the other
Whenever threads share any atomic variable, since Acquire and Release never give consistent results
For every simple counter, because Relaxed increments can lose updates under contention
Only on x86_64 targets, because other architectures order every atomic operation globally
extraQuizzes.explanation: Release/Acquire does not forbid both threads reading the old value in the write-then-read-other pattern. SeqCst adds the single total order that does. Counters and ordinary handoffs do not need it.

lessons.title: A bounded lock-free single-producer single-consumer queue
body: A single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer is the workhorse of low-latency pipelines because exactly one thread writes and exactly one reads, so no locks or compare-and-swap loops are needed. The buffer has a power-of-two capacity. Two monotonically increasing counters, head (next slot to pop) and tail (next slot to push), are reduced to a slot with counter & (capacity - 1). The queue is empty when head == tail and full when tail.wrapping_sub(head) == capacity, so all slots can be used and wrap-around of the usize counters stays correct.

The unsafe core is small. Slots are UnsafeCell<MaybeUninit<T>>, since a slot is uninitialised until pushed. The producer reads head with Acquire to know space is free, writes the value into the slot at tail, then stores tail + 1 with Release. The consumer reads tail with Acquire, reads the value out of the slot at head, then stores head + 1 with Release. The Release/Acquire pairs give two guarantees: the consumer that sees the new tail also sees the written element, and the producer that sees the new head knows the slot has been fully read and may be reused.

Soundness depends on the API, not on the internals alone. channel() returns a Producer and a Consumer that are not Clone and whose methods take &mut self, so at most one thread can push and one can pop at a time. A shared Arc owns the buffer, and Shared implements Sync with a comment explaining the invariant. MaybeUninit never drops its contents, so Drop for Shared must drop exactly the elements between head and tail that were pushed but not popped, or values leak.

Check the invariants: one producer and one consumer by construction, Release on publishing an index and Acquire on reading the other side's index, only the initialised range is dropped, capacity is a power of two, and a single-threaded reference model agrees with the queue on full, empty and wrap-around.
lessons.challenge: Before trusting the unsafe queue, write the safe single-threaded reference model: RingModel<T> over Vec<Option<T>> with push -> Result<(), T> and pop -> Option<T>. Use it to check FIFO order, full, empty and wrap-around with capacity 4, the same behaviour the concurrent queue must have.
lessons.question: Why does the producer publish the new tail with Release and the consumer read it with Acquire?
options: So a consumer that observes the new tail also observes the element the producer wrote into the slot before publishing it
Release makes the usize store atomic, whereas a Relaxed store of a usize could be torn on aarch64
It stops the producer from overwriting slots the consumer has not read, by blocking until they are read
aarch64 cannot load a usize without Acquire, so every load of an index needs the ordering
lessons.explanation: The pair publishes the slot contents. Atomicity of a usize store holds for any ordering, and preventing overwrite is the job of the head counter (read by the producer with Acquire), not of the tail publication.

extraQuizzes.question: Why is `unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for Shared<T>` justified?
options: Sync only matters for types stored in an Arc, which is not the case for this shared buffer here
MaybeUninit prevents any data race on its contents, so the buffer is safe to share by itself
channel() gives out one Producer and one Consumer, neither Clone, so each slot has one writer and one reader
UnsafeCell is always Sync, so the impl is only a formality that documents an existing guarantee
extraQuizzes.explanation: UnsafeCell is not Sync; the impl is a promise by the author. It holds only because the public API enforces a single producer and single consumer with a correct handoff protocol.

extraQuizzes.question: How does the queue distinguish full from empty using monotonic counters?
options: It stores a separate length that both threads update, so full and empty are read directly
It always leaves one slot unused, so the indices are equal only when the queue is empty
It compares each slot with zero, because an empty slot always holds the value zero
tail - head == capacity means full and head == tail means empty, using wrapping arithmetic
extraQuizzes.explanation: Because the counters only grow, their difference is the number of queued items, so no slot has to be sacrificed and no shared length field is needed.

extraQuizzes.question: What must Drop for Shared do, and why?
options: Free the buffer manually with dealloc, because Box cannot release memory that holds MaybeUninit
Drop the elements between head and tail that were pushed but never popped, because MaybeUninit never drops its contents
Nothing, because MaybeUninit drops its value automatically when the buffer itself is dropped
Drop every slot, including uninitialised ones, so no value is leaked whatever the queue holds
extraQuizzes.explanation: MaybeUninit<T> has no drop glue, so leftover elements would leak. Dropping uninitialised slots would be undefined behaviour. The Box frees the buffer memory itself.

extraQuizzes.question: Why do push and pop take &mut self?
options: It is required by Arc, because Arc can only hand out mutable access to exclusive owners
It enforces one active producer and one active consumer; two threads pushing through shared references could race
It lets the compiler skip bounds checks, because exclusive access proves the index is in range
It makes the atomics unnecessary, since exclusive access already orders the two threads
extraQuizzes.explanation: The exclusive borrow is part of the safety argument for the unsafe code. The atomics are still required for the cross-thread handoff.

lessons.title: Zero-allocation hot paths: reuse buffers and prove it with a counting allocator
body: Calling the allocator is not free. It may take a lock, walk free lists, touch cold memory and, for large requests, ask the operating system for pages; the time varies from call to call, which is poison for a latency-sensitive loop. Low-latency systems therefore allocate everything they need up front, and the steady-state path allocates nothing. In Rust the usual sources of hidden allocation are String and Vec growth, collect into a new Vec, format!, to_string, clone of owned data and boxing. Each of them has an allocation-free form: borrow slices with &str, write into a buffer you own, or reuse a collection with clear().

Vec::clear and String::clear drop the elements and set the length to zero but keep the capacity, so a buffer that was grown once is reused for free afterwards. with_capacity (and reserve) pays the growth cost at start-up instead of inside the loop. Parsing is a good example: split_ascii_whitespace and parse::<u32> work on borrowed text and do not allocate, whereas collecting words into Vec<String> allocates the vector and one string per word. Formatting into a reused String with the fmt::Write trait avoids format!'s fresh allocation per message.

Do not guess; count. A global allocator is a type that implements GlobalAlloc and is registered with #[global_allocator]. The wrapper below forwards every call to System and increments an atomic counter in alloc and realloc, so allocations_during(work) reports how many times the closure called into the allocator. The trait is unsafe to implement because the compiler cannot check the contract (valid pointers, matching layouts), and delegating to System preserves it. Keep printing outside the measured closure, since the first use of stdout can allocate its buffer and would distort the count.
Check a hot loop with a counter, not with intuition: pre-size buffers, reuse them with clear(), prefer borrowed slices over owned strings, and assert that steady-state allocations are exactly zero.
lessons.challenge: A function collects every price into a new Vec<i64> each frame. Show with the counting allocator that growing a Vec from empty allocates repeatedly, that with_capacity allocates once, and that reusing one Vec with clear() across 100 frames allocates zero times after the first frame.
lessons.question: Why does clearing a reused Vec or String help a hot path?
options: clear() is the only operation that can allocate without taking the allocator's lock
clear() drops the elements but keeps the allocation, so later pushes reuse existing capacity without calling the allocator
clear() returns the memory to the allocator, which makes later allocations cheaper because the free list is warm
clear() converts the Vec into a stack array, so later pushes no longer touch the heap
lessons.explanation: Capacity is separate from length. clear() sets length to zero and drops elements while the heap block stays owned by the Vec. That is why a buffer sized once can serve every later frame without touching the allocator.
