extraQuizzes.question: Why is the result of a closed-form probability compared with enumeration?
options: Closed forms are never exact, so they are only used to approximate the enumerated count
Rust requires every formula to be enumerated, otherwise the compiler rejects the probability
Two independent routes agreeing is strong evidence against a counting mistake, the usual error in these problems
Enumeration is always faster than a formula, so it is used to produce the final answer
extraQuizzes.explanation: Counting arguments are easy to get subtly wrong. A brute-force check over a small sample space catches it.

lessons.title: Your first OCaml program
body: An OCaml source file is a sequence of definitions. The line `let () = print_endline "Hello, OCaml"` defines a value whose pattern is `()`, the single value of type `unit`, so evaluating the right-hand side runs the print as a side effect when the program starts.

You can try expressions interactively in `ocaml` (or `utop`) and you can compile a file with `ocamlfind ocamlopt main.ml -o main`. The toplevel prints each result with its type, such as `- : int = 4`; a compiled program prints only what you tell it to print.

Check that the file compiles before you reason about its output. Type errors are reported at compile time, with a line and column, and OCaml refuses to produce a program until every expression has a consistent type.
lessons.code:
let () = print_endline "Hello, OCaml"
let () = print_endline ("2 + 2 = " ^ string_of_int (2 + 2))
lessons.challenge: Add a third line that prints your own greeting followed by the length of that greeting, using String.length.
lessons.question: What does `let () = print_endline "x"` define?
options: A unit-valued binding that runs the print when the module is evaluated
A function named print that you can call later
A constant string named x
lessons.explanation: The pattern () matches the unit value, so the definition exists only to evaluate its right-hand side for its effect.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
Hello, OCaml
2 + 2 = 4

The pattern () matches the unit value, so the definition exists only to evaluate its right-hand side for its effect.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The pattern () matches the unit value, so the definition exists only to evaluate its right-hand side for its effect.

lessons.title: Names are immutable: let and shadowing
body: `let x = 5` gives the name `x` to a value. It does not create a variable that can be assigned later. Reusing the same name with `let x = x + 1` creates a new, different binding that hides the old one from then on; the old value is unchanged.
`let ... in ...` limits a binding to one expression. In `let y = 2 in y * y` the name `y` exists only to the right of `in`, which keeps helper values from leaking into the rest of the file.
When a result surprises you, ask which binding a name refers to at that point. Shadowing is legal and common, but a closure created earlier still sees the value that was in scope when it was written.
lessons.code:
let x = 5
let add_x n = n + x
let x = 100
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" x (add_x 1)
let area = let side = 4 in side * side
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" area
lessons.solution:
let base = 10
let scale n = n * base
let base = 1000
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" base (scale 2)
lessons.challenge: Define `base = 10`, a function `scale n = n * base`, then shadow `base` with 1000 and print `scale 2`. Predict the number before you run it.
lessons.question: After `let x = 5`, `let f n = n + x`, `let x = 100`, what is `f 1`?
options: 101, because x was reassigned
A type error, because x is defined twice
6, because f captured the first x
lessons.explanation: Shadowing adds a new binding; it never mutates the earlier one, so closures keep the value they captured.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
100 6
16

Shadowing adds a new binding; it never mutates the earlier one, so closures keep the value they captured.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Shadowing adds a new binding; it never mutates the earlier one, so closures keep the value they captured.

lessons.title: Basic types and separate operators
body: The core types are `int`, `float`, `bool`, `char`, `string` and `unit`. OCaml never converts between them silently: `1 + 2.0` is a type error. Convert explicitly with `float_of_int`, `int_of_float` and `string_of_int`.

Arithmetic operators are typed. `+ - * /` work on `int`, while `+. -. *. /.` work on `float`. Strings join with `^`. Integer division truncates toward zero and `mod` gives the remainder, so `7 / 2` is `3` and `(-7) mod 2` is `-1`.
Comparisons such as `=` and `<` are polymorphic structural comparisons and require both sides to have the same type. Use `==` only when you really mean physical identity, which is rare.
lessons.challenge: Compute the average of the integers 3, 4 and 8 as a float printed with two decimals, converting before dividing.
lessons.question: Why does `1 + 2.5` fail to compile?
options: Floats cannot be added to anything
`+` works on int only and OCaml does not convert automatically; use `+.` with floats
OCaml needs a semicolon between the operands
lessons.explanation: Operators are typed per number kind, and implicit conversion would hide precision loss, so the compiler asks you to be explicit.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
3 1 -1
3.50
abcd
true false

Operators are typed per number kind, and implicit conversion would hide precision loss, so the compiler asks you to be explicit.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Operators are typed per number kind, and implicit conversion would hide precision loss, so the compiler asks you to be explicit.

lessons.title: Functions: definition, application and fun
body: A function is a value. `let square x = x * x` is shorthand for `let square = fun x -> x * x`. You apply it by writing the argument after the name with no parentheses: `square 5`. Parentheses only group, as in `square (2 + 3)`.

Application binds tighter than any operator, so `square 2 + 3` means `(square 2) + 3`. A function with several parameters is written `let add x y = x + y` and called `add 1 2`; the next stage explains why that is really a chain of one-argument functions.
Functions that do not have a name are written with `fun`. They are used as arguments, for example `List.map (fun n -> n * 2) [1; 2; 3]`. Prefer a named function when the body is longer than one line.
lessons.solution:
let cube x = x * x * x
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (cube 3) (cube (1 + 1))
lessons.challenge: Write `cube` and print `cube 3`, then print `cube (1 + 1)` to see how parentheses change the argument.
lessons.question: How does OCaml read `square 2 + 3`?
options: As `square (2 + 3)`
As a syntax error without parentheses
As `(square 2) + 3`, because application binds tighter than `+`
lessons.explanation: Function application is the tightest-binding construct, so only explicit parentheses extend the argument.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
25 7 3
2 4 6 

Function application is the tightest-binding construct, so only explicit parentheses extend the argument.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Function application is the tightest-binding construct, so only explicit parentheses extend the argument.

lessons.title: if as an expression and Printf formats
body: `if` is an expression: both branches must have the same type and the whole `if` has that type. There is no statement form, so `let sign = if n < 0 then "negative" else "non-negative"` is the normal way to choose a value.

`Printf.printf` takes a format string whose conversions are checked against the arguments at compile time. `%d` is an int, `%s` a string, `%f` a float, `%c` a char and `%b` a bool; writing `%d` for a string is a type error, not a runtime crash.
An `if` without `else` must produce `unit`. When you see a type error about `unit`, check that you did not leave out the `else` branch of an expression that should return a value.
lessons.challenge: Write `fizz n` that returns "fizz" when n is divisible by 3 and the number as a string otherwise, then print it for 1 to 6 on one line.
lessons.question: What must be true of the two branches of `if c then a else b`?
options: They must both be unit
Only the then-branch is type checked
`a` and `b` must have the same type, which is the type of the whole expression
lessons.explanation: An if expression produces one value, so the compiler needs a single type for it regardless of which branch runs.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
-2 is negative
0 is zero
5 is positive
ocaml has 5 chars, ratio 0.5

An if expression produces one value, so the compiler needs a single type for it regardless of which branch runs.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An if expression produces one value, so the compiler needs a single type for it regardless of which branch runs.

lessons.title: Tuples and immutable lists
body: A tuple groups a fixed number of values that may have different types: `(1, "one", true)` has type `int * string * bool`. A list holds any number of values of one type: `[1; 2; 3]` has type `int list`. Elements of a list are separated by semicolons, not commas, because `[1, 2, 3]` is a list holding one three-element tuple.

A list is either empty, written `[]`, or a head joined to a tail with `::`. So `[1; 2; 3]` is `1 :: 2 :: 3 :: []`. Building a longer list with `::` shares the old list as its tail instead of copying it, which is why prepending is cheap and appending with `@` walks the whole left list.

Lists are immutable. A function such as `List.map` returns a new list and leaves the argument alone. When a list result looks wrong, check whether you used `,` where you meant `;`, since the type checker will accept it and give you a list of tuples.
lessons.challenge: Build the list `[10; 20; 30]` using only `::` and `[]`, then print its length and the doubled elements using List.map.
lessons.question: What is the type of `[1, 2, 3]`?
options: int list, the same as [1; 2; 3]
A syntax error because commas are not allowed
(int * int * int) list, a list holding one triple
lessons.explanation: Commas build tuples and semicolons separate list elements, so the comma form has exactly one element.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1 one
3 4
1
1 2 3 4 

Commas build tuples and semicolons separate list elements, so the comma form has exactly one element.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Commas build tuples and semicolons separate list elements, so the comma form has exactly one element.

lessons.title: Pattern matching on lists
body: `match e with` compares the value of `e` with patterns from top to bottom and evaluates the arm of the first one that fits. A pattern can name pieces of the value: `x :: rest` binds the head to `x` and the tail to `rest`, and `[]` matches only the empty list.

Because a list is either empty or a head with a tail, two patterns cover every list. The compiler checks this and warns when a case is missing, which turns forgotten cases into compile-time feedback instead of runtime surprises. Treat the non-exhaustive-match warning as an error in your own projects.

Match arms are tried in order, so put specific patterns before general ones. The wildcard `_` matches anything without binding it. A pattern that can never be reached triggers an unused-case warning, which usually means two arms overlap.
lessons.code:
let rec sum = function
  | [] -> 0
  | x :: rest -> x + sum rest

let describe = function
  | [] -> "empty"
  | [_] -> "one element"
  | _ :: _ :: _ -> "several"

let () =
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (sum [1; 2; 3; 4]);
  List.iter (fun l -> print_endline (describe l)) [[]; [7]; [7; 8]]
lessons.solution:
let rec last = function
  | [] -> -1
  | [x] -> x
  | _ :: rest -> last rest

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (last [4; 5; 6])
lessons.challenge: Write `last` that returns the last element of an int list or -1 for the empty list, using pattern matching, and print `last [4; 5; 6]`.
lessons.question: Why does a missing `[]` case in a list match matter at compile time?
options: It only fails when the program is optimised
The compiler reports the non-exhaustive match so the uncovered case is found before running
It silently returns 0 for the empty list
lessons.explanation: Exhaustiveness checking is a static analysis over the patterns, so every value shape must be covered by some arm.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
10
empty
one element
several

Exhaustiveness checking is a static analysis over the patterns, so every value shape must be covered by some arm.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Exhaustiveness checking is a static analysis over the patterns, so every value shape must be covered by some arm.

lessons.title: option: absence in the type
body: OCaml has no null. A value that might be missing has type `'a option`, which is either `None` or `Some v`. Because the possibility is in the type, the compiler forces every caller to decide what to do when the value is absent.

Pattern match on an option to handle both cases. The standard library offers `Option.map`, `Option.value ~default` and `Option.bind` for the common shapes, so you rarely need to write the match by hand for simple defaults.

Prefer options for ordinary, expected absence such as a lookup that finds nothing. Use `result` when the caller needs to know why it failed, and an exception only for truly exceptional conditions. The functions `List.find_opt` and `List.assoc_opt` return options for exactly this reason.
lessons.challenge: Write `safe_div a b` returning `None` when b is zero and `Some (a / b)` otherwise, and print both cases with `show`.
lessons.question: What does representing absence with `option` buy you over a null value?
options: It lets you ignore the missing case at runtime
The type shows the value may be missing, so the compiler forces callers to handle None
Option values are faster to compare than integers
lessons.explanation: The possibility of absence is part of the type, so unhandled cases are compile-time errors rather than runtime null failures.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
some 4
none
0
20

The possibility of absence is part of the type, so unhandled cases are compile-time errors rather than runtime null failures.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The possibility of absence is part of the type, so unhandled cases are compile-time errors rather than runtime null failures.

lessons.title: Variants model alternatives
body: A variant type lists the ways a value can be built, each with a constructor that may carry data: `type shape = Circle of float | Rect of float * float | Point`. A value of that type is exactly one of those cases, and matching on it is how you take it apart.

Because the cases are closed and known, the compiler can tell you when you forgot one after adding a constructor. This is the main reason to model states and message kinds as variants instead of integers or strings: adding a case turns every incomplete match into a warning at once.

Constructors start with a capital letter and are not functions in the usual sense, although `Circle 2.0` looks like an application. Use `List.map (fun r -> Circle r)` when you need a function. Keep payloads small and named by type so the match arms stay readable.
lessons.code:
type shape = Circle of float | Rect of float * float | Point

let area = function
  | Circle r -> 3.0 *. r *. r
  | Rect (w, h) -> w *. h
  | Point -> 0.0

let () =
  List.iter (fun s -> Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (area s))
    [Circle 2.0; Rect (2.0, 3.5); Point]
lessons.solution:
type shape = Circle of float | Rect of float * float | Square of float | Point

let area = function
  | Circle r -> 3.0 *. r *. r
  | Rect (w, h) -> w *. h
  | Square s -> s *. s
  | Point -> 0.0

let () = Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (area (Square 3.0))
lessons.challenge: Add a `Square of float` case to the type and extend `area`. Notice which compiler message tells you where the match is now incomplete.
lessons.question: What happens to existing matches when you add a constructor to a variant?
options: The compiler warns about each match that no longer covers every case
Nothing, because unmatched cases fall through
They raise Not_found at runtime only
lessons.explanation: Variants are closed sums, so exhaustiveness checking can find every place that needs a new arm.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
12.0
7.0
0.0

Variants are closed sums, so exhaustiveness checking can find every place that needs a new arm.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Variants are closed sums, so exhaustiveness checking can find every place that needs a new arm.

lessons.title: Records and functional update
body: A record groups named fields: `type user = { name : string; age : int }`. Build one with `{ name = "Ada"; age = 36 }` and read a field with `u.age`. Names make records clearer than tuples once there are more than two or three components.

Records are immutable by default. To change one field you create a new record with `{ u with age = u.age + 1 }`, which copies the other fields. Mark a field `mutable` only when you truly need in-place state; most programs do not.

Field names belong to the nearest type definition in scope, so two records with the same field name can confuse inference. Annotate the type of a function parameter, or qualify the first field, when the compiler picks the wrong record.
lessons.challenge: Add an `email : string` field and write `with_email u e` that returns a copy of the user with that email, leaving the original unchanged.
lessons.question: What does `{ u with age = 40 }` do?
options: It is a syntax error unless age is mutable
It builds a new record that copies u and replaces age, leaving u unchanged
It assigns 40 to u.age in place
lessons.explanation: Functional update is how immutable records change: you build a new value that shares the untouched fields.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
Ada is 36
Ada is 37

Functional update is how immutable records change: you build a new value that shares the untouched fields.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Functional update is how immutable records change: you build a new value that shares the untouched fields.

lessons.title: Guards, or-patterns and as-patterns
body: A guard adds a boolean condition to an arm: `| x when x < 0 -> ...`. The arm only applies when the pattern fits and the condition is true. Guards are opaque to the exhaustiveness checker, so a match that ends on a guarded arm still needs an unguarded fallback.

An or-pattern combines alternatives that bind the same names: `| Sat | Sun -> "weekend"`. An as-pattern names the whole value while also taking it apart: `| (x :: _) as whole -> ...`. These two tools remove duplicated arms and repeated reconstruction.

When a match grows long, ask whether the cases really belong to one function. Prefer more specific types over deep nesting, and keep guards simple, because the compiler cannot prove anything about them.
lessons.solution:
let bucket n =
  match n with
  | n when n < 10 -> "small"
  | n when n < 100 -> "medium"
  | _ -> "large"

let () = List.iter (fun n -> print_endline (bucket n)) [5; 50; 500]
lessons.challenge: Write `bucket n` that returns "small" for 0 to 9, "medium" for 10 to 99 and "large" otherwise, using guards, and print it for 5, 50 and 500.
lessons.question: Why should a match with guards still end with an unguarded arm?
options: Guards are evaluated after all other arms
An unguarded arm makes the guards faster
The compiler cannot prove a guard is always true, so it needs an unguarded case to be exhaustive
lessons.explanation: Exhaustiveness is checked on patterns alone; a guard may be false for any value, so only an unguarded arm guarantees coverage.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
weekday
weekend
zero
negative
even
odd
9 9 8 

Exhaustiveness is checked on patterns alone; a guard may be false for any value, so only an unguarded arm guarantees coverage.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Exhaustiveness is checked on patterns alone; a guard may be false for any value, so only an unguarded arm guarantees coverage.

lessons.title: Recursion with let rec
body: A function that calls itself must be declared with `let rec`. Without `rec`, the name on the right-hand side refers to an earlier binding, which is usually a compile error. Mutually recursive functions are declared together with `let rec f ... and g ...`.

Structure the recursion like the data. For a list, handle the empty list as the base case and make the recursive call on the tail, so the argument gets smaller each time. That shape is why recursion over lists, trees and variants is the default style in OCaml.

When a recursive function does not stop, check that every recursive call moves toward a base case. A stack overflow on a big input is a different problem, addressed by tail recursion in the next lesson.
lessons.solution:
let rec power b e = if e = 0 then 1 else b * power b (e - 1)
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (power 2 10)
lessons.challenge: Write `power b e` for non-negative e using recursion on e, and print `power 2 10`.
lessons.question: What does `let rec` do that `let` does not?
options: It brings the function name into scope inside its own body so it can call itself
It makes the function run faster
It allows the function to return several values
lessons.explanation: In a plain let, the right-hand side cannot see the name being defined; rec makes the binding visible there.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
120 3
true false

In a plain let, the right-hand side cannot see the name being defined; rec makes the binding visible there.
lessons.practiceAnswer: In a plain let, the right-hand side cannot see the name being defined; rec makes the binding visible there.

lessons.title: Tail calls and accumulators
body: A call is a tail call when its result is returned directly with nothing left to do. The native compiler turns self tail calls into jumps, so a tail-recursive function uses constant stack space. `1 + length rest` is not a tail call because the addition happens after the call returns.

To make a function tail recursive, carry the partial answer in an accumulator parameter and return it in the base case. Often this means a small inner helper, `let rec go acc = ...`, with the public function supplying the starting accumulator.

Check this when the input can be large. OCaml 5 grows the stack dynamically, so deep non-tail recursion rarely overflows now, but it still allocates stack memory in proportion to the depth, and an accumulator version stays flat.
lessons.solution:
let count_if p xs =
  let rec go acc = function
    | [] -> acc
    | x :: rest -> go (if p x then acc + 1 else acc) rest
  in
  go 0 xs

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (count_if (fun n -> n mod 2 = 0) (List.init 10 (fun i -> i + 1)))
lessons.challenge: Write a tail-recursive `count_if p xs` that counts the elements satisfying p, and print how many of 1 to 10 are even.
lessons.question: Why is `x + sum rest` not a tail call?
options: The addition runs after the recursive call returns, so the frame must stay alive
Because it uses the + operator
Because sum is defined with let rec
lessons.explanation: A tail call is the last action of the function; here the add still has to happen afterwards.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
499999500000
3 2 1 

A tail call is the last action of the function; here the add still has to happen afterwards.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A tail call is the last action of the function; here the add still has to happen afterwards.

lessons.title: Currying and partial application
body: Every OCaml function takes exactly one argument. `let add x y = x + y` has type `int -> int -> int`, which means `int -> (int -> int)`: applying it to one argument returns a function that waits for the second. This is currying.

Because of this, you can apply a function to fewer arguments than it lists and get a new function back. `let add5 = add 5` is a partial application, and `List.map (add 5) xs` reads naturally. Put the argument most likely to be fixed first.

Contrast this with a tuple parameter, `let add (x, y) = ...`, which takes one value and cannot be partially applied. Prefer the curried form for library-style functions and use tuples when the pair really is one value.
lessons.challenge: Define `greet greeting name` returning a string, make `hello = greet "Hello"` by partial application, and print `hello "Ada"`.
lessons.question: What is the type of `let add x y = x + y`?
options: int -> int
int -> int -> int, a function returning a function
(int * int) -> int
lessons.explanation: The arrow is right-associative, so the type reads int -> (int -> int): one argument at a time.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
6 5
2 4 6 
9

The arrow is right-associative, so the type reads int -> (int -> int): one argument at a time.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The arrow is right-associative, so the type reads int -> (int -> int): one argument at a time.

lessons.title: Higher-order functions and closures
body: A higher-order function takes or returns functions. `List.map`, `List.filter` and `List.fold_left` abstract common loops, so you write what to do with one element and let the library handle the traversal.

A closure is a function together with the bindings it refers to. `let make_counter_step n = fun x -> x + n` returns a function that remembers `n`. Because bindings are immutable, a closure over an ordinary value is easy to reason about.

Choose the specific combinator that matches your intent. `List.iter` is for effects, `List.map` is for building a new list, and `List.exists` or `List.for_all` answer yes or no without building anything.
lessons.challenge: Use List.filter and List.map to square the odd numbers from 1 to 9 and print them on one line.
lessons.question: What does a closure carry with it?
options: A copy of the whole program state
Only the argument types
The bindings of the names its body uses, as they were when it was created

lessons.title: Folds, pipelines and composition
body: `List.fold_left f init xs` combines the elements with `f`, threading an accumulator from left to right. Most list summaries, such as sums, maximums, grouping and even `map`, can be written as one fold.

The pipe operator `|>` passes a value into a function so that a chain reads in the order it runs: `xs |> List.filter p |> List.map f`. It is plain function application written backwards, not special syntax, which means you can define similar operators yourself.

Name the accumulator and keep the combining function pure. If you find yourself mutating a ref inside the fold, step back and ask whether another combinator, or a record accumulator, expresses the same thing.
lessons.solution:
let product = List.fold_left ( * ) 1
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (product [1; 2; 3; 4; 5])
lessons.challenge: Use List.fold_left to compute the product of the list [1; 2; 3; 4; 5] and print it.
lessons.question: What does `x |> f` mean?
options: Run f and x in parallel
Compose f with itself
Apply f to x, so pipelines read left to right
lessons.explanation: |> is defined as a function that takes a value and a function and applies the function to the value.

lessons.title: Type inference and when to annotate
body: OCaml infers the type of every expression without annotations. It collects constraints from how values are used: `let f x = x + 1` forces `x : int` because `+` only works on integers, so the type of `f` is `int -> int`. Inference is complete for the core language, which is why OCaml code looks so light.

You can still annotate, and often should. A signature such as `let f (x : int) : int = x + 1` documents intent, and in a module interface a `val` line is the contract. Annotations also help error messages: when inference blames the wrong line, adding one on a parameter moves the report to where you made the mistake.

Read type errors from the first expected-versus-found mismatch. The compiler reports where its constraints first conflict, not necessarily where your reasoning went wrong. Use `ocamlfind ocamlopt -i file.ml` or `ocaml-print-intf` to see the inferred interface.
lessons.challenge: Write `twice g x = g (g x)` without annotations, then use it on an int function and on a string function, and print both results.
lessons.question: Why is `let f x = x + 1` inferred as `int -> int`?
options: OCaml defaults every unannotated parameter to int
The literal 1 forces the result to be a float
The + operator only accepts ints, so using x with it constrains x to int
lessons.explanation: Inference unifies the types required by each use of a value; + requires int operands and returns int.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
42
1 x
n=7

Inference unifies the types required by each use of a value; + requires int operands and returns int.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Inference unifies the types required by each use of a value; + requires int operands and returns int.

lessons.title: Parametric polymorphism
body: A type variable such as `'a` stands for any type, and every occurrence of the same variable in a type means the same type. `let id x = x : 'a -> 'a` works for every type, and `let swap (a, b) = (b, a) : 'a * 'b -> 'b * 'a` relates its positions without knowing what they hold.

The type tells you what a function can do. A function of type `'a -> 'a` cannot inspect its argument, so it can only return it. A function `'a list -> int` can only use the list's shape, such as its length. This is the idea behind parametricity: more general types leave less room for surprising behaviour.

Polymorphic functions are instantiated freshly at every use, so one definition serves `int list` and `string list` alike. Be careful with comparison: `compare : 'a -> 'a -> int` is polymorphic but works structurally, so it raises on functional values.
lessons.solution:
let rec last_or default = function
  | [] -> default
  | [x] -> x
  | _ :: rest -> last_or default rest

let () =
  Printf.printf "%d %s\n" (last_or 0 [1; 2; 3]) (last_or "none" [])
lessons.challenge: Write a polymorphic `last_or default xs` that returns the last element or the default, and print it for an int list and a string list.
lessons.question: What can a function of type `'a -> 'a` do with its argument?
options: Only return it, because it knows nothing about what 'a is
Print it and return it
Compare it with zero
lessons.explanation: A universally quantified type variable gives the function no operations on the value, so the only total behaviour is the identity.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
one 1
3 s
1
2
0 none

A universally quantified type variable gives the function no operations on the value, so the only total behaviour is the identity.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A universally quantified type variable gives the function no operations on the value, so the only total behaviour is the identity.

lessons.title: Parameterised and recursive types
body: A type definition can take type parameters and refer to itself. `type 'a tree = Leaf | Node of 'a tree * 'a * 'a tree` describes binary trees whose elements may have any type, and `int tree` and `string tree` are different instances of one definition.

Functions over such types follow the type's shape. A function on `'a tree` handles `Leaf` and `Node` and recurses on both subtrees. Because the type is defined once with a parameter, you write each operation once instead of once per element type.

Use a type alias, `type point = float * float`, for readability only: aliases are interchangeable with the original type. Use a variant or a record when you want a distinct type that the checker will not confuse with its representation.
lessons.solution:
type 'a tree = Leaf | Node of 'a tree * 'a * 'a tree

let rec insert x = function
  | Leaf -> Node (Leaf, x, Leaf)
  | Node (l, v, r) as t ->
    if x < v then Node (insert x l, v, r)
    else if x > v then Node (l, v, insert x r)
    else t

let rec height = function
  | Leaf -> 0
  | Node (l, _, r) -> 1 + max (height l) (height r)

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) Leaf [5; 2; 8; 1] in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (height t)
lessons.challenge: Write `height : 'a tree -> int` returning the number of levels (Leaf is 0), and print the height of the tree built from [5; 2; 8; 1].
lessons.question: What does the parameter in `type 'a tree` allow?
options: One definition describes trees of any element type, such as int tree and string tree
Trees whose elements can have different types in the same tree
Trees that can change their element type at runtime
lessons.explanation: The parameter is instantiated once per use of the type, so all elements of a given tree share that instance.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

ab

The parameter is instantiated once per use of the type, so all elements of a given tree share that instance.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The parameter is instantiated once per use of the type, so all elements of a given tree share that instance.

lessons.title: The value restriction and weak types
body: Only syntactic values are generalised. `let id = fun x -> x` is polymorphic, but `let r = ref []` is not: its type is the weak type `'_weak1 list ref`, a placeholder that becomes fixed by the first use. If it were fully polymorphic you could store an int and read back a string.

This is why partial application can surprise you. `let f = List.map (fun x -> x)` applies a function, so the result is weakly typed, while `let f l = List.map (fun x -> x) l` is a function value and stays polymorphic. Eta-expanding, meaning adding the explicit parameter, usually fixes the problem.

A weak type that survives to the end of a compilation unit is a compile error. The usual repairs are to eta-expand, to annotate the binding with the type you intend, or to move the mutable cell inside a function.
lessons.challenge: Explain by experiment: define `let cell = ref None`, assign `Some 1` to it, then print whether it holds a value. Which use fixed its type?
lessons.question: Why is `let r = ref []` not generalised to `'a list ref`?
options: Applying ref is not a syntactic value, and a polymorphic mutable cell would be unsound
Because lists cannot be polymorphic
Because ref is a keyword
lessons.explanation: A polymorphic mutable cell could hold an int in one use and be read as a string in another, so the type stays weak.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
3
a
b
1 x

A polymorphic mutable cell could hold an int in one use and be read as a string in another, so the type stays weak.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A polymorphic mutable cell could hold an int in one use and be read as a string in another, so the type stays weak.

lessons.title: Structural equality, physical equality and compare
body: `=` and `<>` compare structurally: two values are equal when their contents are equal, however they were built. `==` and `!=` compare physical identity, asking whether two names refer to the very same block. Use `=` unless you are deliberately testing sharing.

`compare` returns a negative, zero or positive int and is the function to pass to sorting. The polymorphic versions work on most data, but they raise `Invalid_argument` on functional values and may not terminate on cyclic structures. For custom types, define a monomorphic comparison instead.
Floating point adds a trap: `nan = nan` is false while `compare nan nan` is 0, so sorting floats with `<` and with `compare` can behave differently. When you need a total order, use `Float.compare`.
lessons.challenge: Sort the strings ["pear"; "fig"; "apple"] by length, breaking ties alphabetically, using List.sort with a custom comparison, and print them.
lessons.question: What is the difference between `a = b` and `a == b`?
options: = works only on integers
= compares contents structurally; == tests whether both names are the same block in memory
== is the faster spelling of =
lessons.explanation: Structural equality walks the values while physical equality checks identity, so equal-looking separate values differ under ==.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
true false
true true
-1 1
false 0
1 2 3 
compare: functional value

Structural equality walks the values while physical equality checks identity, so equal-looking separate values differ under ==.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Structural equality walks the values while physical equality checks identity, so equal-looking separate values differ under ==.

lessons.title: result: errors that explain themselves
body: `('a, 'e) result` is `Ok of 'a | Error of 'e`. Unlike `option`, the error side carries information, so a parser can say which character was wrong and a validator can say which rule failed. The type forces callers to look at both outcomes.

Choose the error type deliberately. A string is quick for scripts, but a variant such as `Empty | Too_long of int | Bad_char of char` lets callers match on the reason and lets the compiler check that every case is handled. The standard library gives `Result.map`, `Result.bind` and `Result.value`.

Return `result` when failure is an expected part of the function's job, such as parsing user input. Do not wrap a programming error such as an impossible state in `Error`; that is what assertions and exceptions are for.
lessons.code:
type error = Empty | Too_long of int | Bad_char of char

let validate name =
  if name = "" then Error Empty
  else if String.length name > 8 then Error (Too_long (String.length name))
  else match String.to_seq name |> Seq.find (fun c -> not (Char.lowercase_ascii c >= 'a' && Char.lowercase_ascii c <= 'z')) with
    | Some c -> Error (Bad_char c)
    | None -> Ok name

let show = function
  | Ok n -> "ok " ^ n
  | Error Empty -> "empty"
  | Error (Too_long n) -> Printf.sprintf "too long (%d)" n
  | Error (Bad_char c) -> Printf.sprintf "bad char %c" c

let () = List.iter (fun n -> print_endline (show (validate n))) ["ada"; ""; "abcdefghij"; "a1"]
lessons.solution:
let parse_age s =
  match int_of_string_opt s with
  | None -> Error ("not a number: " ^ s)
  | Some n when n < 0 || n > 150 -> Error ("out of range: " ^ string_of_int n)
  | Some n -> Ok n

let show = function Ok n -> "ok " ^ string_of_int n | Error m -> m
let () = List.iter (fun s -> print_endline (show (parse_age s))) ["42"; "abc"; "200"]
lessons.challenge: Write `parse_age s` returning `Ok n` for an integer between 0 and 150 and a descriptive `Error` string otherwise, using `int_of_string_opt`. Print results for "42", "abc" and "200".
lessons.question: When is `result` a better return type than `option`?
options: When you want the function to raise an exception
When the caller needs to know why the operation failed
When the operation can never fail
lessons.explanation: Option records only absence; result carries an error value that callers can match on and report.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
ok ada
empty
too long (10)
bad char 1

Option records only absence; result carries an error value that callers can match on and report.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Option records only absence; result carries an error value that callers can match on and report.

lessons.title: Exceptions: raise, try and custom exceptions
body: An exception is raised with `raise` and caught with `try ... with`. Standard library functions use them for conditions such as `Not_found`, `Invalid_argument` and `Failure`. Exceptions are values of the extensible type `exn`, and you declare your own with `exception Parse_error of string`.

A `try` handler is an ordinary pattern match on `exn`, so you catch exactly the cases you handle and let the rest propagate. Catching everything with `_` hides bugs, including `Stack_overflow` and `Out_of_memory`; prefer naming the exceptions you expect.

Exceptions are cheap in OCaml, which is why `List.assoc` raises `Not_found` rather than returning an option. Prefer the `_opt` variants when absence is normal, and keep a `try` body as small as possible so you do not catch an exception from the wrong call.
lessons.challenge: Declare `exception Negative of int`, write `sqrt_int n` that raises it for negative input, and catch it to print a message.
lessons.question: Why is `try ... with _ -> ...` usually a mistake?
options: It also swallows unexpected exceptions, hiding bugs
It is a syntax error
It makes the body run twice
lessons.explanation: A catch-all handler cannot tell an expected failure from a bug, so unrelated errors vanish silently.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
7
not a digit: x
no key
div by zero
12
-1

A catch-all handler cannot tell an expected failure from a bug, so unrelated errors vanish silently.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A catch-all handler cannot tell an expected failure from a bug, so unrelated errors vanish silently.

lessons.title: Cleanup that survives failure: Fun.protect
body: When code acquires something, such as a file or a lock, it must release it on every path, including when an exception escapes. `Fun.protect ~finally f` runs `f ()` and always runs `finally ()` afterwards, then re-raises any exception from `f`.

Write acquire-use-release as a higher-order function, `with_resource name f`, so callers cannot forget the cleanup. The standard library does this for files: `In_channel.with_open_text` closes the channel for you.
If `finally` itself raises, you get `Fun.Finally_raised`, which signals a bug in the cleanup. Keep `finally` small and total, and never use it to hide the original failure.
lessons.challenge: Use Fun.protect to run a computation that raises `Not_found` and prove the cleanup ran by printing "cleaned" from the `finally` before the exception is caught.
lessons.question: What does `Fun.protect ~finally f` guarantee?
options: finally runs only if f succeeds
Exceptions from f are discarded
finally runs whether f returns or raises, and an exception from f is re-raised afterwards
lessons.explanation: It wraps f so the cleanup is unconditional, while still letting the original exception reach the caller.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
42
boom
open a;close a;open b;close b;

It wraps f so the cleanup is unconditional, while still letting the original exception reach the caller.
lessons.practiceAnswer: It wraps f so the cleanup is unconditional, while still letting the original exception reach the caller.

lessons.title: Binding operators: let* over result and option
body: Chaining several fallible steps with nested matches buries the logic. A binding operator such as `let*` lets you write the happy path in sequence: `let* a = step1 x in let* b = step2 a in Ok (a + b)`, with the first `Error` ending the computation.

You define the operator yourself: `let ( let* ) = Result.bind`. This is ordinary function definition with a special name, and OCaml translates `let*` into a call to it. `let+` plays the same role for `map`, and `and*` combines independent steps.

Keep each operator tied to one monad in a small local module so that the code reads cleanly. Do not mix option and result operators in one scope, since the type checker will report a confusing mismatch.
lessons.solution:
let ( let+ ) r f = Result.map f r
let parse s = match int_of_string_opt s with Some n -> Ok n | None -> Error "bad"
let doubled = let+ n = parse "21" in n * 2
let () = match doubled with Ok n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n | Error m -> print_endline m
lessons.challenge: Define `let ( let+ ) r f = Result.map f r` and use it to double the parsed integer of "21", printing the result.
lessons.question: What does `let* x = e in body` translate to?
options: An assignment to a mutable variable
A call to the user-defined ( let* ) operator with e and a function taking x
A built-in try-with block
lessons.explanation: Binding operators are ordinary functions; the syntax rewrites let* into an application of the operator.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
5
bad int: x
not positive: -1

Binding operators are ordinary functions; the syntax rewrites let* into an application of the operator.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Binding operators are ordinary functions; the syntax rewrites let* into an application of the operator.

lessons.title: Working with lists of results
body: Often you validate many items. There are two useful behaviours: stop at the first error, or collect every error. Folding with `Result.bind` gives the first, and partitioning the results gives the second.

To stop early, fold the list and carry `Ok acc` forward; the first `Error` short-circuits the rest because `Result.bind` does not call its function on an error. To report everything, map each item to a result, then split with `List.partition_map` so users see all the problems at once.
Pick the behaviour the caller needs. Short-circuiting is right for pipelines that cannot continue. Collecting is right for user-facing validation where fixing one error at a time is annoying.
lessons.challenge: Use List.partition_map to split ["4"; "x"; "6"] into parsed numbers and bad strings, and print the sum of the numbers and the count of bad strings.
lessons.question: Which approach reports every invalid item instead of only the first?
options: Fold with Result.bind
Wrap the whole list in a single try-with
Map each item to a result and partition the Ok and Error values
lessons.explanation: Result.bind stops at the first error; partitioning inspects all results so none is lost.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
3 items
first error: b
2 ok, errors: b,d

Result.bind stops at the first error; partitioning inspects all results so none is lost.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Result.bind stops at the first error; partitioning inspects all results so none is lost.

lessons.title: The List module in practice
body: `List` is the workhorse of everyday OCaml. Learn the families: transform (`map`, `mapi`, `filter_map`, `concat_map`), summarise (`fold_left`, `exists`, `for_all`, `length`), search (`find_opt`, `assoc_opt`, `mem`), reorder (`sort`, `rev`, `sort_uniq`) and split or join (`partition`, `combine`, `split`, `flatten`).

Pick the function that states your intent. `filter_map` replaces a filter followed by a map when the mapping can fail, and `concat_map` replaces map followed by flatten. A clear combinator is easier to read and to optimise than a hand-written recursion.

Remember cost. `List.nth` and `@` walk the list, so using them in a loop makes it quadratic. If you index often, convert to an array once. Many `List` functions are not tail-recursive on very long lists in older compilers, so check the manual if you process millions of elements.
lessons.solution:
let () =
  let words = ["a"; "tree"; "is"; "green"] in
  let lens = List.filter_map (fun w -> let n = String.length w in if n > 3 then Some n else None) words in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (List.fold_left ( + ) 0 lens)
lessons.challenge: Given words, use List.filter_map to keep the lengths of words longer than 3 characters, then print their sum.
lessons.question: Which function replaces a filter followed by a map when the mapping can fail?
options: List.partition
List.filter_map
List.concat
lessons.explanation: filter_map applies a function returning an option and keeps only the Some results, doing both steps in one pass.

lessons.title: Arrays, strings and bytes
body: An `array` has a fixed length, constant-time indexing and in-place update with `a.(i) <- v`. Create one with `Array.make`, `Array.init` or a literal `[| 1; 2; 3 |]`. Index out of range raises `Invalid_argument`, which the compiler cannot catch in advance.

`string` is immutable text. Operations like `String.sub`, `String.split_on_char` and `String.concat` return new strings. When you need to build or change text efficiently, use `Bytes` (mutable) or `Buffer` (growable), and convert at the end with `Bytes.to_string` or `Buffer.contents`.

Prefer `Buffer` for appending in a loop, because repeated `^` copies the whole string every time and becomes quadratic. Treat strings as byte sequences, so `String.length` counts bytes, not Unicode characters.
lessons.challenge: Reverse the string "stressed" by copying its characters into Bytes in reverse order, then print the result.
lessons.question: Why use Buffer instead of repeated `^` when building a long string in a loop?
options: Each ^ copies the whole string, so a loop becomes quadratic; Buffer appends in amortised constant time
Because ^ only works for two characters
Because Buffer sorts the characters
lessons.explanation: Strings are immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new copy; a Buffer grows in place and copies once at the end.
lessons.workedExample:

130
1,2,3,
a-b-c

OCAML

Strings are immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new copy; a Buffer grows in place and copies once at the end.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Strings are immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new copy; a Buffer grows in place and copies once at the end.

lessons.title: Hashtbl for mutable lookup tables
body: `Hashtbl` is a mutable hash table: `Hashtbl.create 16`, `add`/`replace`, `find_opt`, `mem` and `remove`. Lookup and update are on average constant time, which is what you want for counting, caching and memoisation.

Know the difference between `add` and `replace`. `add` hides an older binding for the same key but keeps it underneath, so `find_all` returns every binding, while `replace` overwrites. Most code wants `replace`, and `find_opt` instead of the exception-raising `find`.

Iteration order is unspecified, so sort the keys before printing. The default `Hashtbl.hash` is structural and only looks at a bounded amount of a value; for keys with custom equality, use the functor `Hashtbl.Make` with your own `equal` and `hash`.
lessons.solution:
let memo = Hashtbl.create 64

let rec fib n =
  if n < 2 then n
  else match Hashtbl.find_opt memo n with
    | Some v -> v
    | None -> let v = fib (n - 1) + fib (n - 2) in Hashtbl.replace memo n v; v

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (fib 40)
lessons.challenge: Memoise a slow Fibonacci with a Hashtbl and print fib 40.
lessons.question: Why sort the keys before printing a Hashtbl's contents?
options: Sorting is required by Hashtbl.fold
Iteration order is unspecified, so output would otherwise vary
Hashtbl stores keys in sorted order already
lessons.explanation: Hash tables do not guarantee any traversal order, so deterministic output needs an explicit sort.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
a=3 b=2 c=1 
true false
2

Hash tables do not guarantee any traversal order, so deterministic output needs an explicit sort.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Hash tables do not guarantee any traversal order, so deterministic output needs an explicit sort.

lessons.title: Persistent Map and Set
body: `Map.Make` and `Set.Make` are functors: you give them a module with a type `t` and a `compare` function, and you get a persistent (immutable) balanced tree. `module IntMap = Map.Make (Int)` yields maps with int keys.

Operations return new maps and leave the old one intact, so you can keep previous versions cheaply. Lookup, insert and remove are logarithmic. Iteration with `fold` or `bindings` is in sorted key order, which makes the output deterministic.

Use `Map` when you need ordered keys, sharing or immutability, and `Hashtbl` when you want mutable constant-time updates. A common mistake is expecting a `Map` operation to modify its argument; remember to bind the result.
lessons.challenge: Build a Map from string to int counting how many times each letter appears in "banana" (use SMap.update) and print it in key order.
lessons.question: What happens to the original map after `SMap.add "c" 3 m1`?
options: It gains the new binding in place
It is deleted
It is unchanged; add returns a new map that shares structure with it
lessons.explanation: Map is a persistent data structure, so every update produces a new value while old versions stay valid.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

2 3
none

1 2 3 9 

Map is a persistent data structure, so every update produces a new value while old versions stay valid.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Map is a persistent data structure, so every update produces a new value while old versions stay valid.

lessons.title: Seq: lazy sequences
body: A `Seq.t` is a lazy, possibly infinite sequence: a function that produces the next element only when asked. This lets you describe `naturals`, `primes` or a file's lines without building a whole list in memory.

Combinators such as `Seq.map`, `Seq.filter`, `Seq.take` and `Seq.fold_left` mirror the `List` functions but compute on demand. Nothing runs until a consumer like `fold_left`, `iter` or `List.of_seq` forces it, so you must bound an infinite sequence with `take` before collecting it.

Sequences are ephemeral by default: an effectful source may produce different results if you traverse it twice. Use `Seq.memoize` when you need to traverse a costly sequence more than once, and prefer a list when the data is small and reused.
lessons.challenge: Use Seq.unfold to produce the first 8 powers of two and print them.
lessons.question: When does a Seq pipeline actually compute elements?
options: When a consumer such as fold_left, iter or List.of_seq demands them
As soon as each combinator is applied
At program start
lessons.explanation: Seq values are functions producing the next element on demand, so combinators only build the plan.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
0 4 16 36 64 
5050
0
3

Seq values are functions producing the next element on demand, so combinators only build the plan.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Seq values are functions producing the next element on demand, so combinators only build the plan.

lessons.title: Formatting text: sprintf, Format and custom printers
body: `Printf.sprintf` returns a string instead of printing, so it is the standard way to build messages. The format string is typed, which is why `sprintf "%d" "x"` is a compile error. Padding and precision work as in C: `%5d`, `%-5s`, `%05.1f`.

The `Format` module adds pretty-printing: boxes, break hints and automatic line breaking at a margin. A printer for your type has the shape `Format.formatter -> t -> unit`, and you use it with `%a`, such as `Format.asprintf "%a" pp_point p`.

Write a `pp` function for every public type. Doing so gives toplevel printers, test failure messages and logging a single readable place, and later lessons on `ppx_deriving`/`ppx_jane` generate this boilerplate for you.

options: t -> string, used with %s
unit -> t
Format.formatter -> t -> unit, used with %a

lessons.title: References, sequencing and loops
body: A `ref` is a mutable cell: `let n = ref 0` creates it, `!n` reads it and `n := !n + 1` updates it. A ref is an ordinary record with one mutable field, so it is a value you can pass around, and the name itself is still immutable.

Sequence effects with `;`, which evaluates the left side, discards its `unit` result and continues. `for i = 1 to n do ... done` and `while cond do ... done` are the imperative loops. They have type `unit`, so they are used for their effects.

Reach for loops and refs when an algorithm is naturally imperative, such as filling an array, and keep the mutable state local to a function so that callers see a pure interface. A forgotten `;` or a missing `!` is the classic beginner error, and the type checker usually catches it.
lessons.challenge: Write `factorial_loop n` using a for loop and a ref, and print `factorial_loop 6`.
lessons.question: What is `r := !r + 1` doing?
options: Reading the cell with !, adding one and storing the result back with :=
Declaring a new variable r
Comparing r with r plus one
lessons.explanation: ! dereferences a ref and := assigns to it; the name r keeps pointing at the same mutable cell.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

111
1 2

! dereferences a ref and := assigns to it; the name r keeps pointing at the same mutable cell.
lessons.practiceAnswer: ! dereferences a ref and := assigns to it; the name r keeps pointing at the same mutable cell.

lessons.title: Mutable record fields and encapsulated state
body: A record field marked `mutable` can be assigned with `r.field <- v`. This is useful for counters, buffers and caches that really change over time, such as `type counter = { mutable count : int }`.

Encapsulate state behind functions. A closure over a ref gives you a private counter with no global variable, and a module with an abstract type hides the mutable record so that only your operations can change it. Callers then cannot break an invariant by writing to a field directly.

Keep mutation out of the data you share widely. Two names for the same mutable record see each other's changes, which is called aliasing, and it is the usual source of bugs when you copy a record by sharing it.
lessons.challenge: Add a `withdraw` that refuses to take the balance below zero by returning false, and print the balance after trying to withdraw 20 from 15.
lessons.question: After `let alias = a`, what does updating `alias.balance` do to `a`?
options: a sees the change, because both names refer to the same mutable record
a is unaffected because alias is a copy
It raises an exception
lessons.explanation: Binding a record to a second name copies the pointer, not the contents, so mutations are visible through both.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

15 115
1 2 1

Binding a record to a second name copies the pointer, not the contents, so mutations are visible through both.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Binding a record to a second name copies the pointer, not the contents, so mutations are visible through both.

lessons.title: In-place algorithms on arrays
body: Some algorithms are clearest and fastest in place. Insertion sort, binary search and swapping elements all rely on constant-time array indexing. Write the algorithm as a function that takes the array, mutates it, and returns `unit`.

State the invariant before writing the loop. For insertion sort: before step `i`, the prefix `a.(0..i-1)` is sorted. Writing the invariant in a comment makes off-by-one mistakes visible. Use `Array.copy` when you want to keep the original.

Check bounds explicitly. Array access is bounds-checked by default, so an off-by-one raises `Invalid_argument "index out of bounds"` rather than corrupting memory; compiling with `-unsafe` removes the check and should only be used on code you have proven.
lessons.challenge: Write `reverse_in_place a` using swap and a loop over the first half, and print the reversed array [|1;2;3;4|].
lessons.question: Why state a loop invariant before writing an in-place algorithm?
options: It makes the loop run faster
It tells you exactly what is true at each iteration, which exposes off-by-one errors
The compiler requires it
lessons.explanation: An invariant is the claim your loop maintains; checking it at the start, in the body and at the end is how you prove the algorithm correct.

An invariant is the claim your loop maintains; checking it at the start, in the body and at the end is how you prove the algorithm correct.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An invariant is the claim your loop maintains; checking it at the start, in the body and at the end is how you prove the algorithm correct.

lessons.title: Lazy values and memoised computation
body: `lazy e` delays evaluating `e` until it is forced with `Lazy.force`. The result is computed once and cached, so a second force returns the stored value without running the code again. This is the standard way to defer an expensive initialisation.

Laziness interacts with effects. A `lazy` body that prints runs its effects at force time, once. Forcing a lazy value from inside its own computation raises `Lazy.Undefined`, and a lazy value that raised an exception re-raises the same exception on each force.
Use `lazy` for optional expensive data and for knot-tying definitions. Do not use it to hide control flow that matters; an explicit function call is clearer when the computation should run each time.
lessons.solution:
let v = lazy (print_endline "init"; 10)
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (Lazy.force v) (Lazy.force v)
lessons.challenge: Create a lazy value whose evaluation prints "init" and returns 10, force it twice, and observe that "init" prints once.
lessons.question: How many times does the body of a `lazy` expression run when forced repeatedly?
options: Every time it is forced
Never, until the program ends
Once; the result is cached for later forces
lessons.explanation: A lazy value memoises its result after the first successful force.

computing

lessons.title: Persistent versus mutable data structures
body: A persistent structure keeps old versions valid after an update; a mutable one changes in place. Immutable lists and `Map` are persistent, while `Hashtbl`, `Array` and `Queue` are mutable. The trade-off is sharing and safety against raw speed and memory.

A functional queue shows the idea: keep a front list and a reversed back list. Push onto the back in constant time, and when the front is empty reverse the back once. Operations are amortised constant time, and every old queue remains usable.

Pick persistent when you need undo, backtracking or safe concurrent reads, and mutable when you profile a hot loop that needs it. A good design exposes a persistent interface and hides local mutation inside.
lessons.challenge: Write `size q` for the persistent queue as the sum of the two list lengths, and print the size after three pushes.
lessons.question: What is the main benefit of a persistent queue over Queue.t?
options: Old versions remain valid after pushing or popping, which suits undo and backtracking
It is always faster
It uses no memory
lessons.explanation: Updates return new values and never overwrite the old structure, so earlier states can still be used.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1
2
again 1
1 1

Updates return new values and never overwrite the old structure, so earlier states can still be used.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Updates return new values and never overwrite the old structure, so earlier states can still be used.

lessons.title: Evaluation order: what is and is not specified
body: OCaml does not specify the order in which the arguments of a function, the fields of a record or the elements of a tuple are evaluated. The native compiler happens to go right to left, but you must not depend on it. With pure expressions it makes no difference; with effects it changes the answer.

Order is specified in a few places: `let x = a in b` evaluates `a` first, `a; b` evaluates `a` then `b`, and `&&` and `||` evaluate left to right and stop as soon as the result is known. Use these to sequence effects deliberately.

When two arguments have effects, bind them with `let` in the order you want before the call. The same rule applies to reading input, taking from a queue and incrementing a counter inside an argument list.
lessons.code:
let counter = ref 0
let next () = incr counter; !counter

let () =
  let a = next () in
  let b = next () in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" a b;
  let log = Buffer.create 8 in
  let check name v = Buffer.add_string log name; v in
  let r = check "a" false && check "b" true in
  let s = check "c" true || check "d" false in
  Printf.printf "%b %b %s\n" r s (Buffer.contents log)
lessons.challenge: Read two values from a queue holding 10 and 20 into `x` then `y` using `let`, and print `x - y` so the answer does not depend on argument evaluation order.
lessons.question: Which construct guarantees left-to-right evaluation?
options: Writing the fields of a record in a literal
Binding with let ... in, or sequencing with ;
Passing arguments to a function
lessons.explanation: The language specifies the order of let-bindings and sequences, but leaves argument and field order unspecified.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1 2
false true ac

The language specifies the order of let-bindings and sequences, but leaves argument and field order unspecified.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The language specifies the order of let-bindings and sequences, but leaves argument and field order unspecified.
