lessons.title: Structures and signatures
body: A module is a named bundle of types, values and other modules. `module Stack = struct ... end` creates a structure, and `Stack.push` reaches inside it. Every `.ml` file is itself a module named after the file, so the language of modules is how large programs are organised.

A signature is the type of a module: the list of names and types it promises to expose. `module type STACK = sig type 'a t val empty : 'a t val push : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t end` describes an interface, and `module S : STACK = struct ... end` checks that the structure provides at least those items.
Think of the signature as the contract and the structure as one implementation of it. Anything not listed in the signature is invisible to users, which is the mechanism for hiding helper functions.
lessons.code:
module type STACK = sig
  type 'a t
  val empty : 'a t
  val push : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val pop : 'a t -> ('a * 'a t) option
  val size : 'a t -> int
end

module ListStack : STACK = struct
  type 'a t = 'a list
  let empty = []
  let push x s = x :: s
  let pop = function [] -> None | x :: rest -> Some (x, rest)
  let helper_not_exported = 42
  let size = List.length
end

let () =
  let s = ListStack.(push 2 (push 1 empty)) in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (ListStack.size s);
  match ListStack.pop s with Some (x, _) -> Printf.printf "%d\n" x | None -> ()
lessons.solution:
module type STACK = sig
  type 'a t
  val empty : 'a t
  val push : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val peek : 'a t -> 'a option
end

module ListStack : STACK = struct
  type 'a t = 'a list
  let empty = []
  let push x s = x :: s
  let peek = function [] -> None | x :: _ -> Some x
end

let () = match ListStack.(peek (push 7 empty)) with Some x -> Printf.printf "%d\n" x | None -> ()
lessons.challenge: Add a `peek : 'a t -> 'a option` to both the signature and the structure, and print the peek of a stack holding 7.
lessons.question: What does a signature control?
options: How fast the module runs
Which file the module is stored in
Which names and types of a module are visible to users
lessons.explanation: A signature lists what a module exposes; anything omitted is hidden from outside code.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
2
2

A signature lists what a module exposes; anything omitted is hidden from outside code.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A signature lists what a module exposes; anything omitted is hidden from outside code.

lessons.title: Abstract types protect invariants
body: Leaving a type's definition out of a signature makes it abstract: users can name `t` but cannot see that it is an `int` or a record. They can only create and inspect values through the functions you export, so you control every way a value can come into being.

That is how you maintain an invariant such as 'a percentage is between 0 and 100'. The constructor `of_int` returns an option and rejects bad input, and since nobody else can build a `t`, every `t` in the program has passed the check.

The compiler enforces the boundary. Trying to add an abstract `Percent.t` to an int is a type error, which protects you from mixing units. Expose a `to_int` or a printer when users need to see the value.
lessons.code:
module Percent : sig
  type t
  val of_int : int -> t option
  val to_int : t -> int
  val add : t -> t -> t
end = struct
  type t = int
  let of_int n = if n >= 0 && n <= 100 then Some n else None
  let to_int n = n
  let add a b = min 100 (a + b)
end

let () =
  match Percent.of_int 70, Percent.of_int 50, Percent.of_int 101 with
  | Some a, Some b, None ->
    Printf.printf "%d\n" (Percent.to_int (Percent.add a b))
  | _ -> print_endline "unexpected"
lessons.solution:
module Even : sig
  type t
  val of_int : int -> t option
  val to_int : t -> int
end = struct
  type t = int
  let of_int n = if n mod 2 = 0 then Some n else None
  let to_int n = n
end

let () =
  (match Even.of_int 8 with Some e -> Printf.printf "%d\n" (Even.to_int e) | None -> ());
  Printf.printf "%b\n" (Even.of_int 7 <> None)
lessons.challenge: Define a module `Even` with an abstract type that only holds even integers: `of_int` returns None for odd input. Print `Even.to_int` for 8 and whether 7 is accepted.
lessons.question: Why does hiding a type's representation help maintain an invariant?
options: It lets users modify the value directly
Only the module's own functions can create values, so every value has passed its checks
It makes the type smaller in memory
lessons.explanation: With the representation hidden, outside code cannot construct or alter a value except through the validated interface.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
100

With the representation hidden, outside code cannot construct or alter a value except through the validated interface.
lessons.practiceAnswer: With the representation hidden, outside code cannot construct or alter a value except through the validated interface.

lessons.title: open, include and local modules
body: `open M` brings every name of `M` into scope for the rest of the file, which can shadow your own names and make the origin of an identifier unclear. Prefer the local forms `M.(expr)` and `let open M in expr`, which limit the scope to the expression.

`include M` copies the contents of `M` into the current structure, so you can extend a module: `include List` followed by new functions yields a module that has everything from `List` plus your additions. In a signature, `include S` repeats the items of `S`.

A module can also be defined locally with `let module M = ... in`. Use these tools sparingly. The more names a reader must remember, the harder code review becomes, so keep `open` out of widely used files except for well-known, deliberately designed modules.
lessons.code:
module Ext = struct
  include List
  let sum = fold_left ( + ) 0
end

module Shapes = struct
  let pi = 3.0
  let area r = pi *. r *. r
end

let () =
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (Ext.length [1; 2; 3]) (Ext.sum [1; 2; 3]);
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" Shapes.(area 2.0);
  let open Shapes in
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (pi *. 2.0);
  let module Local = struct let greeting = "hi" end in
  print_endline Local.greeting
lessons.solution:
module Loud = struct
  include String
  let exclaim s = s ^ "!"
end

let () = print_endline (Loud.exclaim (Loud.uppercase_ascii "ok"))
lessons.challenge: Extend String with an `exclaim s = s ^ "!"` using include, and print `Loud.exclaim (Loud.uppercase_ascii "ok")`.
lessons.question: Why prefer `M.(expr)` over a file-level `open M`?
options: It is required by the compiler
It runs faster
It limits the scope of M's names to one expression so identifiers stay traceable
lessons.explanation: A global open can silently shadow names and hide where an identifier came from; local opens keep the effect small.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
3 6
12.0
6.0
hi

A global open can silently shadow names and hide where an identifier came from; local opens keep the effect small.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A global open can silently shadow names and hide where an identifier came from; local opens keep the effect small.

lessons.title: Functors: modules parameterised by modules
body: A functor is a function from modules to modules. `module Make (Ord : sig type t val compare : t -> t -> int end) = struct ... end` builds a new module for any ordered type. The standard library uses this for `Map.Make`, `Set.Make` and `Hashtbl.Make`.

The parameter has a signature, which states exactly what the functor needs from its argument. The functor body can then use `Ord.compare` without knowing the concrete type, and the result is a fresh module for each application.

Use a functor when an algorithm should be written once but depends on a type together with operations on it, such as ordering, hashing or printing. If you only need one function, pass the function instead of building a module.
lessons.code:
module type ORDERED = sig
  type t
  val compare : t -> t -> int
end

module MakeSorter (O : ORDERED) = struct
  let max_of = function
    | [] -> None
    | x :: rest -> Some (List.fold_left (fun m y -> if O.compare y m > 0 then y else m) x rest)
  let sort l = List.sort O.compare l
end

module IntSorter = MakeSorter (Int)
module ByLength = MakeSorter (struct type t = string let compare a b = compare (String.length a) (String.length b) end)

let () =
  List.iter (Printf.printf "%d ") (IntSorter.sort [3; 1; 2]);
  print_newline ();
  (match ByLength.max_of ["aa"; "bbbb"; "c"] with Some s -> print_endline s | None -> ());
  List.iter print_endline (ByLength.sort ["ccc"; "a"; "bb"])
lessons.solution:
module Counter (K : sig type t val compare : t -> t -> int end) = struct
  let count l =
    let sorted = List.sort K.compare l in
    List.fold_left (fun acc x ->
      match acc with
      | (y, n) :: rest when K.compare x y = 0 -> (y, n + 1) :: rest
      | _ -> (x, 1) :: acc) [] sorted
    |> List.rev
end

module IntCounter = Counter (Int)

let () = List.iter (fun (k, n) -> Printf.printf "%d:%d " k n) (IntCounter.count [2; 1; 2]); print_newline ()
lessons.challenge: Write a functor `Counter (K : sig type t val compare : t -> t -> int end)` exposing `count : K.t list -> (K.t * int) list` with sorted keys, and apply it to Int to print the counts of [2; 1; 2].
lessons.question: What does a functor take and return?
options: It takes a type and returns a value
It takes a module and returns a module
It takes a value and returns a type
lessons.explanation: Functors operate at the module level, mapping one structure to another according to the parameter's signature.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1 2 3 
bbbb
a
bb
ccc

Functors operate at the module level, mapping one structure to another according to the parameter's signature.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Functors operate at the module level, mapping one structure to another according to the parameter's signature.

lessons.title: Sharing constraints with with type
body: A functor's result signature often hides the type that it was parameterised over. If `MakeSet (E : ELEMENT) : SET`, the result's `elt` is abstract, so you cannot add an int to it even when `E.t` is `int`. A sharing constraint `with type elt = E.t` re-exposes the equality.

Write `module Make (E : ELEMENT) : SET with type elt = E.t = struct ... end`. The result stays abstract in the representation of the set but is no longer abstract in its element type, so users can pass ordinary values.
You will see `with type` constantly in library signatures. If the compiler says two types are different when you know they must be the same, look for a missing sharing constraint in a functor result.
lessons.code:
module type ELEMENT = sig type t val compare : t -> t -> int end

module type SET = sig
  type elt
  type t
  val empty : t
  val add : elt -> t -> t
  val mem : elt -> t -> bool
end

module Make (E : ELEMENT) : SET with type elt = E.t = struct
  type elt = E.t
  type t = elt list
  let empty = []
  let mem x s = List.exists (fun y -> E.compare x y = 0) s
  let add x s = if mem x s then s else x :: s
end

module IntSet = Make (Int)

let () =
  let s = IntSet.(add 3 (add 3 (add 4 empty))) in
  Printf.printf "%b %b\n" (IntSet.mem 3 s) (IntSet.mem 9 s)
lessons.solution:
module type ELEMENT = sig type t val compare : t -> t -> int end
module type SET = sig type elt type t val empty : t val add : elt -> t -> t val mem : elt -> t -> bool end

module Make (E : ELEMENT) : SET with type elt = E.t = struct
  type elt = E.t
  type t = elt list
  let empty = []
  let mem x s = List.exists (fun y -> E.compare x y = 0) s
  let add x s = if mem x s then s else x :: s
end

module IntSet = Make (Int)
let () = Printf.printf "%b\n" IntSet.(mem 4 (add 4 empty))
lessons.challenge: Remove the `with type elt = E.t` constraint and read the compiler error from `IntSet.add 3`. Then restore it and print whether IntSet.mem 4 holds for a set containing 4.
lessons.question: What does `SET with type elt = E.t` change?
options: It makes the set mutable
It makes the result's elt type equal to E.t instead of abstract, so callers can use ordinary values
It renames the module
lessons.explanation: A sharing constraint tells the type checker that two otherwise abstract types are the same type.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
true false

A sharing constraint tells the type checker that two otherwise abstract types are the same type.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A sharing constraint tells the type checker that two otherwise abstract types are the same type.

lessons.title: First-class modules
body: A module is not a value, but you can pack one into a value with `(module M : S)` and unpack it with `(module X : S)` in a function parameter or a `let module` binding. This lets you choose an implementation at runtime and store modules in lists or records.

The type of a packed module is `(module S)`. When a function takes a packed module and uses its types, the unpacking pattern gives the module a name, so later annotations like `(x : M.t)` can refer to it. That is the idiom for runtime-selected plug-ins.
Use first-class modules for dynamic choice, such as selecting a backend from configuration. If the choice is known at compile time, an ordinary functor is simpler and leaves more to the type checker.
lessons.code:
module type SHOWABLE = sig type t val default : t val show : t -> string end

module I = struct type t = int let default = 7 let show = string_of_int end
module B = struct type t = bool let default = true let show = string_of_bool end

let describe (module M : SHOWABLE) = M.show M.default
let describe_with (module M : SHOWABLE) (x : M.t) = M.show x

let all : (string * (module SHOWABLE)) list = [("int", (module I)); ("bool", (module B))]

let () =
  List.iter (fun (name, m) -> Printf.printf "%s=%s\n" name (describe m)) all;
  print_endline (describe_with (module I) 41)
lessons.solution:
module type SHOWABLE = sig type t val default : t val show : t -> string end
module I = struct type t = int let default = 7 let show = string_of_int end
module S = struct type t = string let default = "x" let show s = s end
let describe (module M : SHOWABLE) = M.show M.default
let all : (string * (module SHOWABLE)) list = [("int", (module I)); ("string", (module S))]
let () = List.iter (fun (n, m) -> Printf.printf "%s=%s\n" n (describe m)) all
lessons.challenge: Add a module `S` (type t = string, default "x") to the list under the name "string" and print every entry again.
lessons.question: When should you prefer a functor to a first-class module?
options: When the implementation is known at compile time and you want the type checker to do more of the work
When you need to pick an implementation from user input
When you want to store modules in a list
lessons.explanation: Functors are resolved statically and keep more type information; first-class modules are for genuinely dynamic choices.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
int=7
bool=true
41

Functors are resolved statically and keep more type information; first-class modules are for genuinely dynamic choices.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Functors are resolved statically and keep more type information; first-class modules are for genuinely dynamic choices.

lessons.title: Labelled and optional arguments
body: A labelled argument is written `~name` in a definition and at the call site: `let area ~width ~height = width * height` is called as `area ~height:2 ~width:5`. Labels make long parameter lists readable and let callers pass arguments in any order.

An optional argument has a default: `let greet ?(greeting = "Hello") name = ...`. Callers may omit it, or supply it with `~greeting:"Hi"`. Inside the function it is a plain value when you give a default, or an `option` when you write `?greeting` without one.

An optional argument needs a following positional argument so the compiler knows the call is complete. Put it before a required, unlabelled parameter. Excess optional arguments are a common source of confusing warnings, so use them for genuine options and not for every flag.
lessons.challenge: Write `repeat ?(sep = " ") ~times s` that joins `times` copies of `s` with the separator, and print `repeat ~times:3 "ab"` with default and `"-"` separators.
lessons.question: Why must an optional argument be followed by a positional argument?
options: Optional arguments only work on the last parameter
It improves performance
Otherwise the compiler cannot tell whether the call is finished and the default should apply
lessons.explanation: A function whose last parameter is optional could always accept more arguments, so the application would never be considered complete.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
10
Hello, Ada
Hi, Ada
x
pre-x
30

A function whose last parameter is optional could always accept more arguments, so the application would never be considered complete.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A function whose last parameter is optional could always accept more arguments, so the application would never be considered complete.

lessons.title: Polymorphic variants
body: A polymorphic variant is written with a backtick: `` `Red `` or `` `Rgb of int * int * int ``. It needs no type declaration, and the inferred type lists the tags, such as `[> `Red | `Green ]`. The `>` means 'at least these', so the value can be used wherever more tags are allowed.

Matching infers a closed upper bound `[< `Red | `Green ]`, 'at most these'. This makes it easy to share cases between types: a function handling `` [`Red | `Green] `` can be applied to a value known to be only `` `Red ``. Ordinary variants cannot overlap like this.

The price is weaker error messages and a risk of typos creating new tags silently. Use polymorphic variants for open-ended event types and for composing subsets of cases, and ordinary variants when you want the strictest checking.
lessons.solution:
type shape = [ `Circle of float | `Square of float ]

let area : shape -> float = function
  | `Circle r -> 3.0 *. r *. r
  | `Square s -> s *. s

let () = Printf.printf "%.1f %.1f\n" (area (`Square 3.0)) (area (`Circle 1.0))

options: A value that can only be Red or Green
A function from Red to Green
A value that has at least the tags Red and Green and may have more
lessons.explanation: The > bound is open, so extra tags are allowed; < would close the type to at most the listed tags.

lessons.title: Phantom types for compile-time tags
body: A phantom type parameter appears in a type's definition but not in its representation. `type 'unit_ length = Length of float` is just a float at runtime, but `meters length` and `feet length` are different types, so you cannot add them by mistake.

Keep the tag types abstract or empty and hide the constructor behind a signature, so only your conversion functions create values. The compiler then rejects mixing units, or using an unvalidated string where a validated one is required, without any runtime cost.

Phantom types model a state machine too: a `closed handle` has no `read`, and `close` returns `closed handle`. This turns whole classes of misuse into type errors, as long as the abstraction boundary stays sealed.
lessons.code:
module Length : sig
  type 'u t
  type meters
  type feet
  val meters : float -> meters t
  val feet : float -> feet t
  val add : 'u t -> 'u t -> 'u t
  val to_meters : feet t -> meters t
  val value : 'u t -> float
end = struct
  type 'u t = float
  type meters
  type feet
  let meters x = x
  let feet x = x
  let add = ( +. )
  let to_meters f = f *. 0.5
  let value x = x
end

let () =
  let a = Length.meters 3.0 and b = Length.meters 4.0 in
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (Length.value (Length.add a b));
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (Length.value (Length.to_meters (Length.feet 10.0)))

lessons.title: GADTs: types that depend on the constructor
body: A generalised algebraic data type lets each constructor choose its own result type. `type _ expr = Int : int -> int expr | Bool : bool -> bool expr | Add : int expr * int expr -> int expr | If : bool expr * 'a expr * 'a expr -> 'a expr` encodes the typing rules of a small language in OCaml's types.

An evaluator `eval : type a. a expr -> a` then returns an `int` for integer expressions and a `bool` for boolean ones, with no tags to check at runtime. Ill-typed expressions such as `Add (Bool true, Int 1)` are rejected when you write them, not when you run them.

Two details matter. A function that matches on a GADT usually needs an explicit polymorphic annotation, `type a. a expr -> a`, because the result type varies by case. And pattern matching refines types per branch, so the compiler can prove that some cases are impossible.
lessons.code:
type _ expr =
  | Int : int -> int expr
  | Bool : bool -> bool expr
  | Add : int expr * int expr -> int expr
  | Less : int expr * int expr -> bool expr
  | If : bool expr * 'a expr * 'a expr -> 'a expr

let rec eval : type a. a expr -> a = function
  | Int n -> n
  | Bool b -> b
  | Add (a, b) -> eval a + eval b
  | Less (a, b) -> eval a < eval b
  | If (c, t, e) -> if eval c then eval t else eval e

let () =
  let e = If (Less (Int 2, Add (Int 1, Int 3)), Int 10, Int 20) in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (eval e);
  Printf.printf "%b\n" (eval (Less (Int 5, Int 1)))
lessons.solution:
type _ expr =
  | Bool : bool -> bool expr
  | Not : bool expr -> bool expr

let rec eval : type a. a expr -> a = function
  | Bool b -> b
  | Not e -> not (eval e)

let () = Printf.printf "%b\n" (eval (Not (Bool false)))
lessons.challenge: Add a `Not : bool expr -> bool expr` constructor and extend `eval`, then print `eval (Not (Bool false))`.

options: That Add may take expressions of any type
The constructor builds an int expr and requires int expr arguments, so ill-typed terms cannot be built
That Add is evaluated lazily
lessons.explanation: Each constructor fixes its own result index, so the type checker enforces the object language's typing rules.

lessons.title: Existential types: hiding a type behind a value
body: Sometimes you want a list of things that can each be printed, but of different types. An existential packs a value together with the operations to use it and hides the value's type: `type showable = Show : 'a * ('a -> string) -> showable`. The `'a` appears on the right of the arrow only, so it is existentially quantified.

Consumers can unpack with a match and use the operations, but cannot learn what the hidden type is. This is the type-theory form of an object: data plus methods with a private representation, available without classes.

The type variable cannot escape the match. Returning the hidden value from the function is a type error, which is exactly the guarantee you wanted. If you need to return something, return the result of the packed operation.
lessons.code:
type showable = Show : 'a * ('a -> string) -> showable

let render (Show (v, f)) = f v

let items =
  [ Show (42, string_of_int)
  ; Show ("hi", fun s -> "\"" ^ s ^ "\"")
  ; Show ([1; 2; 3], fun l -> String.concat "+" (List.map string_of_int l))
  ; Show (true, string_of_bool) ]

let () = List.iter (fun x -> print_endline (render x)) items
lessons.solution:
type showable = Show : 'a * ('a -> string) -> showable
let render (Show (v, f)) = f v
let items = [ Show (1, string_of_int); Show ((1.5, 2.5), fun (a, b) -> Printf.sprintf "(%.1f,%.1f)" a b) ]

options: Because the value is garbage collected after the match
Its type is hidden and local to the match, so letting it escape would break type safety

lessons.explanation: The compiler gives the hidden type a fresh name valid only inside the match; it cannot appear in the result type.

lessons.title: Objects and classes: the O in OCaml
body: OCaml has structural objects. An immediate object, `object method area = 12 end`, has the type `< area : int >`, and any object with at least that method can be used where the type is expected. This is subtyping by structure, with no class needed.

Classes add constructors, inheritance and instance variables. `class counter = object val mutable n = 0 method incr = n <- n + 1 method get = n end` defines a type and a constructor, and `new counter` builds a fresh object. Instance variables are private; only methods can reach them.

Most OCaml code uses modules and records instead, and objects appear in GUI bindings and where open recursion is valuable. Reach for them when you need structural subtyping or inheritance with late binding, and use explicit upcasts, `(o :> shape)`, when a more specific object is passed as a more general one.
lessons.code:
class counter =
  object
    val mutable n = 0
    method incr = n <- n + 1
    method get = n
  end

class type shape = object method area : float end

class square side = object method area = side *. side end
class circle r = object method area = 3.0 *. r *. r end

let total (shapes : shape list) = List.fold_left (fun acc s -> acc +. s#area) 0.0 shapes

let () =
  let c = new counter in
  c#incr; c#incr;
  Printf.printf "%d\n" c#get;
  let o = object method area = 12.0 end in
  Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (total [ (new square 2.0 :> shape); (new circle 1.0 :> shape); (o :> shape) ])
lessons.solution:
class type shape = object method area : float end
class square side = object method area = side *. side end
class rect w h = object method area = w *. h end

let total (shapes : shape list) = List.fold_left (fun acc s -> acc +. s#area) 0.0 shapes
let () = Printf.printf "%.1f\n" (total [ (new square 2.0 :> shape); (new rect 2.0 5.0 :> shape) ])

By matching their class names
By structure: an object with at least the needed methods can be used, via an explicit upcast where required

lessons.title: Your first Dune project: a library and an executable
body: Dune is the standard build system for OCaml. A project is a directory with a `dune-project` file naming the Dune language version, and one or more `dune` files that declare what to build. `dune build` compiles everything, `dune exec bin/main.exe` runs a program, and `dune clean` removes the `_build` directory.

Split code into a library and an executable. A `(library (name greeter))` stanza turns every module in its directory into part of the library `Greeter`, and an `(executable (name main) (libraries greeter))` stanza links against it. Dune works out the dependency order itself, so you never list source files by hand.

Everything Dune generates lives in `_build`, which you do not edit or commit. When a build fails, read the first error: Dune prints the file, line and the compiler message, and re-running `dune build` only recompiles what changed.
lessons.challenge: Open src/greeter.ml and make `greet name` return "Hello, <name>!". Then run `dune exec --root . bin/main.exe` and confirm it prints the greeting for "world".
lessons.question: What does the `(libraries greeter)` field in an executable's dune file do?
options: It installs a package called greeter from opam
It copies greeter.ml into the executable's directory
It links the executable against the library named greeter defined elsewhere in the project
lessons.explanation: A library stanza defines a named unit of code; listing it in libraries lets another stanza use its modules.
lessons.workedExample: A library stanza defines a named unit of code; listing it in libraries lets another stanza use its modules.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A library stanza defines a named unit of code; listing it in libraries lets another stanza use its modules.

lessons.title: Expect tests: tests that show their output
body: An expect test prints values and records the output next to the code. With `ppx_expect` you write `let%expect_test "name" = print_endline (f x); [%expect {| result |}]`, and `dune test` fails if the real output differs. The expected text is part of the source, so a reviewer sees behaviour and test together.

When output legitimately changes, run `dune promote` and Dune rewrites the expected blocks to match; you then review the diff in version control. That workflow makes exploratory testing cheap, which is why Jane Street uses it widely, but the promotion step is a review step, not a rubber stamp.

Enable the tests by adding `(inline_tests)` and `(preprocess (pps ppx_expect))` to a library stanza. Keep tests deterministic: avoid timestamps, hash-table iteration order and absolute paths in the printed output.
lessons.challenge: The tests in test/slug_tests.ml fail because `Slug.slugify` returns its input unchanged. Implement it so it lowercases letters and digits, turns every run of other characters into one hyphen, and never starts or ends with a hyphen.
lessons.question: What does `dune promote` do after an expect test fails?
options: It re-runs the tests with a longer timeout
It rewrites the expected blocks in the source to match the actual output, which you then review
It deletes the failing tests
lessons.explanation: Expect tests store output in the source, so promotion updates those blocks; the human step is reviewing the resulting diff.
lessons.workedExample: Expect tests store output in the source, so promotion updates those blocks; the human step is reviewing the resulting diff.

lessons.title: Unit tests with Alcotest and a test stanza
body: Alcotest is a small, readable unit-test framework. A test is a function returning `unit` that calls `Alcotest.check` with a *testable* (a printer plus an equality), a message, the expected value and the actual value. Tests are grouped into named suites and run by `Alcotest.run`.

In Dune a separate executable is declared with `(test (name test_rpn) (libraries rpn alcotest))`. `dune test` builds and runs it, and a non-zero exit fails the build, which is what you want in continuous integration. The library under test stays free of test dependencies.

Write the failure cases as carefully as the success cases. For a calculator that means empty input, a missing operand and unknown tokens. Return a typed error variant from the library so that tests assert on a case rather than on message text.
lessons.challenge: src/rpn.ml defines the error type but `eval` always fails. Implement a reverse-polish calculator over `+`, `-` and `*` that returns `Ok n` for a valid expression, and the matching `Error` for empty input, stack underflow, a bad token, or leftover operands.
lessons.question: Why define a typed error variant rather than returning error strings?
options: Strings cannot be compared in tests
Variants make the code run faster
Tests and callers can match on the case, and the compiler checks every case is handled
lessons.explanation: A variant is part of the API: it is stable, exhaustive-checked and independent of message wording.
lessons.workedExample: A variant is part of the API: it is stable, exhaustive-checked and independent of message wording.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A variant is part of the API: it is stable, exhaustive-checked and independent of message wording.

type error =
  | Empty
  | Stack_underflow
  | Bad_token of string
  | Leftover of int

let string_of_error = function
  | Empty -> "empty"
  | Stack_underflow -> "stack underflow"
  | Bad_token t -> "bad token " ^ t
  | Leftover n -> Printf.sprintf "%d values left" n

let eval input : (int, error) result =
  let apply op stack =
    match stack with
    | b :: a :: rest -> Ok (op a b :: rest)
    | _ -> Error Stack_underflow
  in
  let step stack tok =
    Result.bind stack (fun stack ->
        match tok with
        | "+" -> apply ( + ) stack
        | "-" -> apply ( - ) stack
        | "*" -> apply ( * ) stack
        | t -> (
            match int_of_string_opt t with
            | Some n -> Ok (n :: stack)
            | None -> Error (Bad_token t)))
  in
  let tokens =
    String.split_on_char ' ' input |> List.filter (fun t -> t <> "")
  in
  if tokens = [] then Error Empty
  else
    match List.fold_left step (Ok []) tokens with
    | Ok [ n ] -> Ok n
    | Ok stack -> Error (Leftover (List.length stack))
    | Error e -> Error e

lessons.title: Formatting, documentation and opam packaging
body: `ocamlformat` gives a whole team one layout, so reviews are about behaviour and not about spacing. A `.ocamlformat` file in the project root pins the formatter's version and options, and `dune build @fmt` reports every file that would change; `dune fmt` (or `dune promote`) rewrites them. Pin the version, because different versions format differently.

`odoc` turns documentation comments written as `(** ... *)` into HTML. A library with a `public_name` belongs to a package, and `dune build @doc` builds the pages under `_build/default/_doc/_html`. Document the interface (`.mli`) rather than the implementation, and give each public value one sentence about what it returns.

Opam is the package manager, and Dune can generate the package description from the project. With `(generate_opam_files true)` and a `(package ...)` stanza in `dune-project`, `dune build` writes `tidy.opam` for you, so the dependency list lives in one place. Edit `dune-project`, never the generated `.opam` file.

lessons.question: Why pin a version in `.ocamlformat`?

Without a pin, ocamlformat refuses to run on comments
Different ocamlformat versions format differently, so a pin keeps everyone's output identical

lessons.title: Core idioms: Or_error, labelled iteration and Map
body: Jane Street's `Base` and `Core` replace parts of the standard library with a consistent, labelled, monomorphic style. `open Core` shadows `List`, `String`, `Map` and others, so higher-order functions take their function as a labelled `~f` argument: `List.map xs ~f:square`. The labels let you pipe with `|>` and partially apply without caring about argument order.

Polymorphic comparison is deliberately hidden. `=` works on `int` only, and `String.equal`, `Int.compare` and friends are explicit. Containers take the comparison in as a first-class module: `Map.of_alist_reduce (module String) pairs ~f:( + )` states the key type once, which is the idiom that replaces functor application at the call site.

`Or_error.t` is `('a, Error.t) result`, where `Error.t` is a lazily built message that can carry s-expressions and context. Build errors with `Or_error.errorf`, combine a list with `Or_error.all`, and sequence steps with the `Or_error.Let_syntax` operators (`let%map`, `let%bind`). It is the default error type in Jane Street code because callers rarely need to match on the reason.

options: It uses the polymorphic compare function
It converts every key to an int first
The first-class module argument supplies the comparison for the key type
lessons.explanation: Core containers take a first-class module carrying compare (and sexp) for the key type instead of relying on polymorphic comparison.

open Core

let parse_entry s : (string * int) Or_error.t =
  match String.lsplit2 s ~on:'=' with
  | None -> Or_error.errorf "missing '=' in %S" s
  | Some (name, value) -> (
      match Int.of_string value with
      | n -> Ok (name, n)
      | exception _ -> Or_error.errorf "bad number %S in %S" value s)

let totals entries : (string * int) list Or_error.t =
  let open Or_error.Let_syntax in
  let%map pairs = Or_error.all (List.map entries ~f:parse_entry) in
  Map.of_alist_reduce (module String) pairs ~f:( + ) |> Map.to_alist

lessons.title: ppx_jane derivers: sexp, compare, equal, hash
body: A PPX is a compile-time rewriter. Writing `type t = { major : int; minor : int; patch : int } [@@deriving sexp, compare, equal, hash]` asks the `ppx_jane` bundle to generate `sexp_of_t`, `t_of_sexp`, `compare`, `equal` and `hash_fold_t`/`hash` from the type definition. You write the type once, and the boilerplate can never drift out of date.

Derived functions compose. Because every field type has its own derived functions, a record of records gets structural versions of all of them, and `[%sexp (x : t)]` converts a value to an s-expression inline. S-expressions are Jane Street's universal text format for config files, debug output and expect tests.

`Comparable.Make (T)` then adds `<`, `>`, `max`, `min`, `ascending` and friends on top of a `compare` and `sexp_of_t`, so you get readable operators without shadowing polymorphic comparison. Derive only what you use: each deriver adds code and compile time.

open Core

module T = struct
  type t = { major : int; minor : int; patch : int }
  [@@deriving sexp, compare, equal, hash]
end

include T
include Comparable.Make (T)

let of_string s : t Or_error.t =
  let part p = Option.try_with (fun () -> Int.of_string p) in
  match List.map (String.split s ~on:'.') ~f:part with
  | [ Some major; Some minor; Some patch ]
    when Int.(major >= 0 && minor >= 0 && patch >= 0) ->
      Ok { major; minor; patch }
  | _ -> Or_error.errorf "not a version: %S" s

let bump_minor t = { t with minor = t.minor + 1; patch = 0 }
let to_string t = sprintf "%d.%d.%d" t.major t.minor t.patch

lessons.title: Command-line tools with Core.Command
body: `Command` builds command-line programs from typed parameters. A flag such as `flag "-n" (optional_with_default 3 int) ~doc:"N ..."` knows its type, its default and its help text, and `anon ("TEXT" %: string)` declares a positional argument. open Core

let top ~n text : (string * int) list =
  String.split_on_chars text ~on:[ ' '; '\n'; '\t' ]

lessons.title: Async: concurrency with deferreds
body: Jane Street's Async library runs many tasks on one thread by never blocking. An `'a Deferred.t` is a value that will be available later. `let%bind x = e in body` waits for `e` and then runs `body`, and `let%map x = e in v` transforms the eventual result. The scheduler runs other ready tasks while something waits, so one slow timer does not stop the rest.

Sequencing and concurrency are different choices. Chaining `let%bind a = f () in let%bind b = g () in ...` runs `g` only after `f` finishes. To run tasks at the same time, start them all first and then wait: `Deferred.all [ f (); g (); h () ]` returns the results in input order, whatever order they complete in.

Async is cooperative. A long computation without a `bind` blocks every other task, because nothing can preempt it. Use it for IO-bound work such as sockets and timers, and use domains (a later lesson) for CPU-bound parallelism. `Command.async` runs your deferred until it finishes and then exits.

The order of the input list, regardless of which deferred completes first
The order the deferreds complete
lessons.explanation: Deferred.all waits for every deferred and builds the result list positionally, so concurrency does not reorder it.

lessons.title: Domains: true parallelism in OCaml 5
body: Before OCaml 5 a single runtime lock meant only one thread could run OCaml code at a time. A *domain* is a unit of real parallelism: `Domain.spawn f` starts `f` on another core, and `Domain.join d` waits for it and returns its result (re-raising its exception). Each domain has its own minor heap, so allocation does not contend.

Divide work so domains share nothing mutable. Splitting an array into disjoint ranges, letting each domain return a partial sum, and combining the results on the main domain needs no locks at all. Spawning is not free, so create about `Domain.recommended_domain_count ()` domains at most and give each a substantial chunk.

Check the edges. An empty array, fewer elements than domains and a length that does not divide evenly are where chunking code breaks. Write the range arithmetic carefully with `min n (d * size)` so the last chunk is short rather than out of bounds.

projectSolutionFiles.content:
let sum ~domains a =
  if domains < 1 then invalid_arg "Psum.sum: domains must be at least 1";
  let n = Array.length a in
  let chunk lo hi =
    let total = ref 0 in
    for i = lo to hi - 1 do
      total := !total + a.(i)
    done;
    !total
  in
  if n = 0 then 0
  else
    let size = (n + domains - 1) / domains in
    List.init domains (fun d ->
        let lo = min n (d * size) and hi = min n ((d + 1) * size) in
        Domain.spawn (fun () -> chunk lo hi))
    |> List.map Domain.join
    |> List.fold_left ( + ) 0

lessons.title: Data races, Atomic and Mutex
body: When two domains touch the same mutable location and at least one writes, you have a data race. OCaml 5 has a memory model that keeps races from corrupting memory, but the result is still wrong: `n := !n + 1` is a read, an add and a write, so two domains can both read 5 and both write 6, and one increment is lost.

`Atomic.t` makes single operations indivisible. `Atomic.incr`, `Atomic.fetch_and_add` and `Atomic.compare_and_set` are executed without interruption, so a shared counter built from them never loses an update. Writing `Atomic.set c (Atomic.get c + 1)` is *not* atomic overall, because another domain can run between the get and the set.

For updates that involve several fields or a data structure, use a lock: `Mutex.protect m (fun () -> ...)` runs the function with the mutex held and releases it even on an exception. Prefer atomics for one counter or flag, and a mutex around code that must see a consistent whole.

lessons.question: Why is `Atomic.set c (Atomic.get c + 1)` still racy?
options: Atomic.set is not allowed after Atomic.get
Atomic values can only be read
The get and the set are two separate atomic steps, so another domain can update the counter in between
lessons.explanation: Atomicity applies to each operation individually; a read-modify-write needs one operation such as fetch_and_add or a compare_and_set loop.

lessons.practiceAnswer: Atomicity applies to each operation individually; a read-modify-write needs one operation such as fetch_and_add or a compare_and_set loop.

lessons.title: Effect handlers: generators and one-shot continuations
body: An effect lets code ask its context to do something without knowing how. You declare one with `type _ Effect.t += Yield : int -> unit Effect.t`, and code performs it with `Effect.perform (Yield 3)`. A *handler* installed further up the stack decides what happens: it receives the request together with a continuation `k` that represents the rest of the suspended computation.

A continuation is *one-shot*: you must resume it exactly once, with `continue k v` to carry on or `discontinue k exn` to raise an exception at the suspension point. Resuming twice raises `Continuation_already_resumed`, and never resuming it leaks the suspended stack along with any resources it holds. When you stop early, `discontinue` is how the producer's `Fun.protect ~finally` and other cleanup run.

This is the mechanism behind schedulers, async IO libraries and generators. Handlers are written with `Effect.Deep.match_with`: `retc` handles a normal return, `exnc` handles an exception, and `effc` picks the effects you intercept (returning `None` forwards the rest to outer handlers). Keep handlers small and cancellation explicit.

lessons.title: The garbage collector and the minor heap
body: OCaml allocates almost everything on a small, fast *minor heap* by bumping a pointer. When it fills, a minor collection copies the few live values to the *major heap* and discards the rest in one step. Most values die young, so allocation is cheap and short-lived garbage costs almost nothing.

Objects larger than 256 words, such as a big array, skip the minor heap and are allocated directly in the major heap. The major heap is collected incrementally and concurrently with the program, and `Gc.stat` and `Gc.quick_stat` report how many collections have run and how many words are live.

Reduce pressure by avoiding needless intermediate lists, not by calling `Gc.full_major` in a loop. Tune only after measuring: `OCAMLRUNPARAM=s=4M` enlarges the minor heap, and `Gc.set` changes it at runtime. The default settings are good for most programs.

Short-lived values are never allocated

lessons.title: Tail-modulo-cons: stack-safe list building
body: `let rec map f = function [] -> [] | x :: xs -> f x :: map f xs` is not tail recursive, because the cons happens after the recursive call returns. The usual fix reverses an accumulator, which allocates the list twice and reads awkwardly.

Marking the function `let[@tail_mod_cons] rec map ...` asks the compiler to rewrite the recursion so the constructor is allocated first with a hole, and the recursive call then fills the hole. The code stays in direct style, runs in constant stack space and is checked: the compiler reports an error if the call is not in a position it can transform.

It works when the recursive call is the last argument of a constructor, as in `y :: map f xs`. Use it for your own list-producing functions; the standard library already applies it to functions such as `List.map` in recent releases.
lessons.code:
let[@tail_mod_cons] rec map f = function
  | [] -> []
  | x :: xs ->
    let y = f x in
    y :: map f xs

let[@tail_mod_cons] rec filter p = function
  | [] -> []
  | x :: xs -> if p x then x :: filter p xs else filter p xs

let () =
  let big = List.init 1_000_000 Fun.id in
  let doubled = map (fun n -> n * 2) big in
  let evens = filter (fun n -> n mod 4 = 0) doubled in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (List.length doubled) (List.length evens);
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (List.fold_left ( + ) 0 doubled)
lessons.solution:
let[@tail_mod_cons] rec append_all xs ys =
  match xs with
  | [] -> ys
  | x :: rest -> x :: append_all rest ys

let () =
  let a = List.init 500_000 Fun.id in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (List.length (append_all a a))

lessons.title: Bigarray and float arrays for numeric data
body: An ordinary `float array` already stores unboxed doubles, and `Float.Array` is a specialised version with no boxing even when the compiler cannot see the element type. For large numeric data you want contiguous, predictably laid-out memory, and `Bigarray` provides that.

A `Bigarray.Array1` has an element kind such as `float64` and a layout such as `c_layout`. Its storage lives outside the OCaml heap, so the collector never scans it, and it can be shared with C code or memory-mapped from a file. Index it with `a.{i}`, and `Array1.sub` gives a view of a range that shares storage rather than copying.

Use these when profiling shows boxing or GC scanning dominates, or when you exchange buffers with native libraries. Keep ordinary arrays and lists for everything else, because bounds checks and layout tags make Bigarray code more verbose.

lessons.title: Measure before optimising: allocation counters
body: Performance work starts with a measurement, not a guess. Timers are noisy, so for allocation-heavy code compare *counts*: `Gc.minor_words ()` before and after a function gives the words it allocated, and the count is the same on every run for deterministic code.

Common causes of surprising cost are quadratic appends (`acc @ [x]` in a loop), repeated string concatenation, polymorphic comparison on large values, and intermediate lists. A counter shows the shape of the problem, such as one algorithm allocating a hundred times more than another, long before you reach for a profiler.
When counts are not enough, use `perf` with `perf report` on a native build, or a benchmarking library. Always keep a test that checks the result is unchanged, so a faster version is not a wrong one.

options: Counts are deterministic for deterministic code, while timings vary between runs and machines

lessons.title: Calling C: external declarations and stubs
body: An `external sum_ints : int array -> int = "ml_sum_ints"` declaration says that the function is implemented in C under that symbol. Dune compiles and links the C file when the library has `(foreign_stubs (language c) (names fastsum_stubs))`. The attribute `[@@noalloc]` promises that the stub never allocates or raises, which lets the compiler call it with less overhead.

C sees OCaml values through the `value` type. An `int` is stored tagged (`Val_long(n)` and `Long_val(v)` convert), and an array is a block whose elements are read with `Field(v, i)` and whose length is `Wosize_val(v)`. These macros come from `<caml/mlvalues.h>`, and getting a conversion wrong silently produces garbage rather than a type error.

If a stub allocates or calls back into OCaml, the collector may move values, so you must register roots with `CAMLparam`/`CAMLlocal` and return with `CAMLreturn`. Immediate integers need no protection, which is why this lesson's stubs are simple. Prefer `ctypes` for bindings that are not performance-critical, and keep stubs small and tested.

lessons.title: Writing a PPX with ppxlib
body: A PPX is an OCaml program that receives the parsed syntax tree of your file, rewrites it, and hands the result back to the compiler. `ppxlib` provides the shared driver and a stable copy of the AST types, so one rewriter works across compiler versions. Extension points such as `[%shout "hello"]` are the simplest hook: the tree contains an `Pexp_extension` node and your rewriter replaces it.

You declare an extension with `Extension.V3.declare name context pattern expander`. The *pattern* (from `Ast_pattern`) describes the payload you accept, here a single string literal, and the *expander* receives the extracted string and returns a new expression built with `Ast_builder.Default`. Registering it with `Driver.register_transformation` makes it run when a project lists the rewriter in `(preprocess (pps ppx_shout))`.

Compile-time code is part of your trust boundary: it runs on every build. Keep rewriters small and deterministic, reject payloads you do not understand with a located error rather than a crash, and test them with expect tests that show the generated output.

lessons.title: Capstone 1: a parser and interpreter
body: An interpreter has three parts: a lexer that turns text into tokens, a parser that turns tokens into a syntax tree, and an evaluator that gives the tree a meaning. Variants model the tokens and the tree, pattern matching walks them, and `result` carries errors with no exceptions, so each stage is a small total function you can test alone.

A recursive-descent parser has one function per precedence level. `expr` handles `+` and `-`, `term` handles `*` and `/`, `unary` handles prefix `-`, and `atom` handles numbers and parentheses. Each level calls the next-tighter one for its operands and then loops while it sees its own operators, which makes the operators left-associative: `2-3-4` is `(2-3)-4`.

Each parsing function takes the remaining tokens and returns the tree together with what is left over. Threading the remainder explicitly keeps the parser pure and makes error cases easy to test: unexpected end, a missing closing parenthesis and trailing input are all `Error` values. Binding operators (`let*`) keep the success path readable.
lessons.challenge: src/calc.ml provides the tokenizer, the AST and `eval`. Implement `parse : token list -> (expr, string) result` with the four precedence levels above, so that `calc "1+2*3"` is `Ok 7`, `calc "2-3-4"` is `Ok (-5)`, `calc "--4"` is `Ok 4`, and malformed input such as "1+", "(1" or "1 2" is an `Error`.
lessons.question: Why does looping on `+`/`-` inside `expr` make `2-3-4` equal `(2-3)-4`?
options: Because the tokenizer reorders the numbers
Each new operand is combined with the tree built so far, so operators group from the left
Because subtraction is commutative
lessons.explanation: The loop folds left: after parsing 2-3 it makes that the left operand for the next minus, giving left associativity.

type token = TNum of int | TOp of char | TLParen | TRParen
type expr = Num of int | Neg of expr | Bin of char * expr * expr

let tokenize s =
  let n = String.length s in
  let is_digit c = c >= '0' && c <= '9' in
  let rec go i acc =
    if i >= n then Ok (List.rev acc)
    else
      match s.[i] with
      | ' ' -> go (i + 1) acc
      | '0' .. '9' ->
          let j = ref i in
          while !j < n && is_digit s.[!j] do
            incr j
          done;
          go !j (TNum (int_of_string (String.sub s i (!j - i))) :: acc)
      | ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/') as c -> go (i + 1) (TOp c :: acc)
      | '(' -> go (i + 1) (TLParen :: acc)
      | ')' -> go (i + 1) (TRParen :: acc)
      | c -> Error (Printf.sprintf "unexpected character %C" c)
  in
  go 0 []

let parse tokens : (expr, string) result =
  let ( let* ) = Result.bind in
  let rec expr ts =
    let* lhs, ts = term ts in
    loop_expr lhs ts
  and loop_expr lhs = function
    | TOp (('+' | '-') as op) :: ts ->
        let* rhs, ts = term ts in
        loop_expr (Bin (op, lhs, rhs)) ts
    | ts -> Ok (lhs, ts)
  and term ts =
    let* lhs, ts = unary ts in
    loop_term lhs ts
  and loop_term lhs = function
    | TOp (('*' | '/') as op) :: ts ->
        let* rhs, ts = unary ts in
        loop_term (Bin (op, lhs, rhs)) ts
    | ts -> Ok (lhs, ts)
  and unary = function
    | TOp '-' :: ts ->
        let* e, ts = unary ts in
        Ok (Neg e, ts)
    | ts -> atom ts
  and atom = function
    | TNum n :: ts -> Ok (Num n, ts)
    | TLParen :: ts -> (
        let* e, ts = expr ts in
        match ts with
        | TRParen :: ts -> Ok (e, ts)
        | _ -> Error "expected )")
    | _ -> Error "expected a number or ("
  in
  let* e, rest = expr tokens in
  if rest = [] then Ok e else Error "unexpected trailing input"

let rec eval = function
  | Num n -> Ok n
  | Neg e -> Result.map (fun n -> -n) (eval e)
  | Bin (op, a, b) ->
      Result.bind (eval a) (fun x ->
          Result.bind (eval b) (fun y ->
              match op with
              | '+' -> Ok (x + y)
              | '-' -> Ok (x - y)
              | '*' -> Ok (x * y)
              | '/' -> if y = 0 then Error "division by zero" else Ok (x / y)
              | _ -> Error "bad operator"))

let calc s =
  Result.bind (tokenize s) (fun tokens -> Result.bind (parse tokens) eval)

lessons.title: Capstone 2: a persistent priority queue
body: A leftist heap is a persistent priority queue. It is a binary tree where every node is no larger than its children (the heap property) and the *rank*, the length of the right spine, of the left child is at least that of the right child. That second rule keeps the right spine short, which is what makes `merge` logarithmic.

Everything is built on `merge`. To merge two heaps, compare their roots, keep the smaller root, and recursively merge the *right* subtree of that heap with the other heap; then swap children if needed so the rank rule holds. `insert` merges a one-node heap in, and `delete_min` merges the root's two children. One recursive function gives the whole API.

Because nodes are immutable and shared, an old heap remains valid after any operation, which is persistence. The `Make` functor takes the element ordering as a module argument, the same shape as `Map.Make`, so the heap works for ints, strings or your own record type without polymorphic comparison.
lessons.challenge: In src/leftist.ml, `merge` returns its first argument, so inserting loses elements. Implement it: if either heap is empty return the other; otherwise keep the smaller root `x`, merge the right subtree with the other heap, and rebuild the node with `make` (which restores the rank rule).
lessons.question: Why is an old leftist heap still valid after `delete_min`?
options: Operations build new nodes and share the unchanged subtrees, so the original structure is never mutated
delete_min copies the whole heap first
The old heap is deleted but its elements remain in a hidden array
lessons.explanation: Persistent structures never overwrite nodes; updates allocate new nodes along the changed path and reuse everything else.
lessons.workedExample: Persistent structures never overwrite nodes; updates allocate new nodes along the changed path and reuse everything else.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Persistent structures never overwrite nodes; updates allocate new nodes along the changed path and reuse everything else.

(library
 (name leftist))

module type ORDERED = sig
  type t

  val compare : t -> t -> int
end

module Make (O : ORDERED) = struct
  type elt = O.t
  type t = E | T of int * elt * t * t (* rank, root, left, right *)

  let empty = E
  let is_empty = function E -> true | T _ -> false
  let rank = function E -> 0 | T (r, _, _, _) -> r

  (* Build a node, putting the higher-rank child on the left. *)
  let make x a b =
    if rank a >= rank b then T (rank b + 1, x, a, b)
    else T (rank a + 1, x, b, a)

  (* TODO: merge two heaps. If either is empty return the other. Otherwise the
     smaller root stays on top: merge its right subtree with the other heap
     and rebuild with [make]. *)
  let merge h1 (_ : t) = h1

  let insert x h = merge (T (1, x, E, E)) h
  let find_min = function E -> None | T (_, x, _, _) -> Some x
  let delete_min = function E -> None | T (_, _, a, b) -> Some (merge a b)
  let of_list l = List.fold_left (fun h x -> insert x h) empty l

  let to_sorted_list h =
    let rec go acc h =
      match (find_min h, delete_min h) with
      | Some x, Some rest -> go (x :: acc) rest
      | _ -> List.rev acc
    in
    go [] h
end

module type ORDERED = sig
  type t

  val compare : t -> t -> int
end

module Make (O : ORDERED) = struct
  type elt = O.t
  type t = E | T of int * elt * t * t (* rank, root, left, right *)

  let empty = E
  let is_empty = function E -> true | T _ -> false
  let rank = function E -> 0 | T (r, _, _, _) -> r

  (* Build a node, putting the higher-rank child on the left. *)
  let make x a b =
    if rank a >= rank b then T (rank b + 1, x, a, b)
    else T (rank a + 1, x, b, a)

  let rec merge h1 h2 =
    match (h1, h2) with
    | E, h | h, E -> h
    | T (_, x, a1, b1), T (_, y, a2, b2) ->
        if O.compare x y <= 0 then make x a1 (merge b1 h2)
        else make y a2 (merge h1 b2)

  let insert x h = merge (T (1, x, E, E)) h
  let find_min = function E -> None | T (_, x, _, _) -> Some x
  let delete_min = function E -> None | T (_, _, a, b) -> Some (merge a b)
  let of_list l = List.fold_left (fun h x -> insert x h) empty l

  let to_sorted_list h =
    let rec go acc h =
      match (find_min h, delete_min h) with
      | Some x, Some rest -> go (x :: acc) rest
      | _ -> List.rev acc
    in
    go [] h
end

lessons.title: Capstone 3: a typed printf with GADTs
body: A format description can compute the type of the function that uses it. With `type ('a, 'r) fmt = Lit : string -> ('r, 'r) fmt | Int : (int -> 'r, 'r) fmt | Str : (string -> 'r, 'r) fmt | Cat : ('a, 'b) fmt * ('b, 'r) fmt -> ('a, 'r) fmt`, the format `Cat (Lit "x=", Int)` has type `(int -> 'r, 'r) fmt`: printing with it needs exactly one `int`. Passing a string, or too few arguments, is a compile-time type error.

`'a` is the type of the printing function and `'r` is what it finally returns. A literal consumes nothing, so its two parameters are equal. `Int` consumes one int, so `'a` is `int -> 'r`. `Cat (f1, f2)` chains: `f1` turns `'a` into an intermediate `'b`, and `f2` turns that `'b` into `'r`, so the arguments of `f1` come before those of `f2`.

The interpreter is written in continuation-passing style, `kprintf : type a r. (string -> r) -> (a, r) fmt -> string -> a`, because each constructor changes the result type, which needs the explicit polymorphic annotation. `Lit` appends its text and calls the continuation. `Int` returns a function that waits for the int. `Cat` runs `f1` with a continuation that runs `f2`. This is the same idea as the standard library's `Printf`, in thirty lines.
lessons.challenge: In src/fmt.ml, `kprintf` only raises. Implement the four cases: `Lit s` calls `k (acc ^ s)`; `Int` and `Str` return a function that appends the converted argument and calls `k`; `Cat (f1, f2)` runs `f1` with a continuation that runs `f2` with the original `k`. `sprintf` is already `kprintf Fun.id f ""`.
lessons.question: What does the type of `Cat (Lit "x=", Int)` tell you at compile time?
options: That printing with it needs exactly one int argument, so a wrong argument is a type error
That it prints the letter x
That the format is checked only when it runs
lessons.explanation: The GADT indexes the format by the function type it requires, so the type checker rejects mismatched arguments.

type ('a, 'r) fmt =
  | Lit : string -> ('r, 'r) fmt
  | Int : (int -> 'r, 'r) fmt
  | Str : (string -> 'r, 'r) fmt
  | Cat : ('a, 'b) fmt * ('b, 'r) fmt -> ('a, 'r) fmt

let rec kprintf : type a r. (string -> r) -> (a, r) fmt -> string -> a =
 fun k fmt acc ->
  match fmt with
  | Lit s -> k (acc ^ s)
  | Int -> fun n -> k (acc ^ string_of_int n)
  | Str -> fun s -> k (acc ^ s)
  | Cat (f1, f2) -> kprintf (fun acc' -> kprintf k f2 acc') f1 acc

lessons.title: Capstone 4: a parallel pipeline that survives failure
body: This capstone combines domains, ownership and error handling. The pipeline splits the input lines into contiguous chunks, gives each chunk to its own domain, lets each domain count words into a *private* hash table, and merges the tables on the main domain. Nothing mutable is shared while the workers run, so there is no lock and no race.

Failure is the hard part. If one worker raises, `Domain.join` re-raises that exception in the caller. If you join the domains one at a time and let the first exception escape, the remaining domains are never joined: they keep running in the background and their resources leak. The correct shape is to join *every* domain, capture each outcome as a `result`, and only then re-raise the first error.

Make cleanup observable. Each worker increments an `Atomic` counter in a `Fun.protect ~finally`, so a test can assert that all workers finished even though one failed. The same discipline applies to Async and effect-based code: every spawned unit of work is either awaited or cancelled, and the error path is tested as carefully as the success path.
lessons.challenge: src/pipeline.ml defines `default_process` and the `finished` counter, but `count` returns an empty list. Implement `count ~workers ?process lines`: chunk the lines, run one domain per chunk, count words into a private Hashtbl (incrementing `finished` in a `Fun.protect ~finally`), join every domain capturing `Ok`/`Error`, re-raise the first error after all are joined, and otherwise merge the tables into a list of (word, count) sorted by word. Reject `workers < 1` with `Invalid_argument`, and if spawning fails part-way, join the domains that already started before re-raising.
lessons.question: Why join every domain before re-raising a worker's exception?
options: Otherwise the remaining domains are left running and unjoined, leaking work and resources on the error path
Domain.join never raises, so there is nothing to handle
Joining twice makes the result faster
lessons.explanation: Structured concurrency means every spawned task is awaited; capturing outcomes first lets the caller clean up everything before reporting the failure.

(* Number of workers that have finished, whether they succeeded or raised. *)
let finished = Atomic.make 0

let default_process line =
  String.split_on_char ' ' line |> List.filter (fun w -> w <> "")

let bump table word by =
  Hashtbl.replace table word
    (by + Option.value (Hashtbl.find_opt table word) ~default:0)

let count ~workers ?(process = default_process) lines :
    (string * int) list =
  if workers < 1 then invalid_arg "Pipeline.count: workers must be at least 1";
  let lines = Array.of_list lines in
  let n = Array.length lines in
  let size = max 1 ((n + workers - 1) / workers) in
  let work d () =
    Fun.protect
      ~finally:(fun () -> Atomic.incr finished)
      (fun () ->
        let table = Hashtbl.create 64 in
        for i = min n (d * size) to min n ((d + 1) * size) - 1 do
          List.iter (fun w -> bump table w 1) (process lines.(i))
        done;
        table)
  in
  (* If a spawn fails partway, join what already started before re-raising. *)
  let started = ref [] in
  (try
     for d = 0 to workers - 1 do
       started := Domain.spawn (work d) :: !started
     done
   with e ->
     List.iter (fun d -> try ignore (Domain.join d) with _ -> ()) !started;
     raise e);
  let domains = List.rev !started in
  (* Join every domain before reporting any failure. *)
  let outcomes =
    List.map (fun d -> try Ok (Domain.join d) with e -> Error e) domains
  in
  (match
     List.find_map (function Error e -> Some e | Ok _ -> None) outcomes
   with
  | Some e -> raise e
  | None -> ());
  let total = Hashtbl.create 64 in
  List.iter
    (function
      | Ok table -> Hashtbl.iter (fun w c -> bump total w c) table
      | Error _ -> ())
    outcomes;
  Hashtbl.fold (fun w c acc -> (w, c) :: acc) total [] |> List.sort compare

lessons.title: Debugging with printing, assertions and backtraces
body: The first debugging tool is a print. `Printf.printf` writes to standard output and `Printf.eprintf` writes to standard error, which keeps diagnostics out of a program's real output. Printing a value needs a conversion for its type, so you often write a small `string_of_...` function for a type you are inspecting.

`assert e` checks a condition that must always hold. If it is false the program raises `Assert_failure` carrying the file, line and column, so an assertion documents an assumption and stops the program at the first moment it is violated instead of letting a wrong value travel. Use assertions for programmer errors, not for input that a user might get wrong.

Exceptions can be turned into text with `Printexc.to_string`, and `Printexc.record_backtrace true` makes uncaught failures report the call stack. Debug by shrinking: find the smallest input that fails, print the intermediate values around the first wrong one, then replace the print with a test so the bug stays fixed.

eprintf is faster than printf
printf cannot print integers

lessons.title: Patterns on tuples, records and nested values
body: A pattern can mirror the shape of any value, so you can match several things at once. Matching a pair, `match (a, b) with | (0, 0) -> ...`, lets one function look at two inputs together, and it is the standard way to handle every combination of two variants.

Record patterns name the fields they care about and use `_` for the rest: `{ name = "square"; _ }` tests one field, and `{ sides = a :: b :: _; name }` both tests a list inside the record and binds names. A `let` can destructure too, so `let (a, (b, c)) = (1, (2, 3))` and `let { x; y } = p` bind several names without a `match`.

An or-pattern may bind variables only if every alternative binds the same names with the same types. Order the arms from most specific to most general, and let the compiler's exhaustiveness and unused-case warnings tell you whether an earlier arm already covers a later one.

lessons.title: Type synonyms and association lists
body: A type synonym gives a new name to an existing type: `type name = string` and `type directory = (name * age) list`. The synonym is only documentation. The compiler treats `name` and `string` as the same type, so a function that wants an `age` accepts any `int`, and a synonym will never catch you mixing two quantities that happen to share a representation.

An association list is a list of key-value pairs, `(string * int) list`, with `List.assoc_opt` to look up a key and `List.remove_assoc` to drop one. Lookup walks the list, so it is linear, which makes association lists a good fit for small tables and a poor one for large ones, where `Hashtbl` or `Map` belong.

Because lists are immutable, 'updating' a pair means building a new list, usually by putting the new binding at the front after removing the old one. When you need real distinction between two quantities, define an abstract type or a one-constructor variant instead of a synonym.
lessons.solution:
type directory = (string * int) list

let invert (d : directory) = List.map (fun (k, v) -> (v, k)) d

let () =
  let d = [ ("ada", 36); ("alan", 41) ] in
  match List.assoc_opt 41 (invert d) with Some n -> print_endline n | None -> print_endline "none"
lessons.challenge: Write `invert d` that swaps the key and value of every pair in an association list, and print the name looked up for the age 41 in the inverted directory.
lessons.question: What does a type synonym like `type age = int` add to type checking?
options: Nothing: age and int are the same type, so it only documents intent
A distinct type that rejects plain ints
A runtime check that the value is non-negative
lessons.explanation: Synonyms are transparent to the type checker; use an abstract or variant type for real distinction.

unknown

Synonyms are transparent to the type checker; use an abstract or variant type for real distinction.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Synonyms are transparent to the type checker; use an abstract or variant type for real distinction.

lessons.title: Recursive variants: expressions as trees
body: A variant whose constructors mention the type itself describes a tree. `type expr = Const of int | Add of expr * expr | Mul of expr * expr | Neg of expr` is the syntax tree of arithmetic: a leaf is a constant, and every other constructor holds smaller expressions. The shape of the type is the shape of the data.

A function over the tree has one arm per constructor, and recursive constructors turn into recursive calls on the sub-expressions. `eval` computes a meaning, `to_string` computes a display, and `simplify` rewrites the tree. The type checker's exhaustiveness check tells you when you have forgotten a constructor in any of them.

Rewrites such as 'adding zero changes nothing' are written as extra arms placed before the general case. Test a rewriting function against the evaluator: a correct simplification never changes `eval`, which is a property you can check on many generated trees.
lessons.code:
type expr =
  | Const of int
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Mul of expr * expr
  | Neg of expr

let rec eval = function
  | Const n -> n
  | Add (a, b) -> eval a + eval b
  | Mul (a, b) -> eval a * eval b
  | Neg e -> - eval e

let rec to_string = function
  | Const n -> string_of_int n
  | Add (a, b) -> "(" ^ to_string a ^ " + " ^ to_string b ^ ")"
  | Mul (a, b) -> "(" ^ to_string a ^ " * " ^ to_string b ^ ")"
  | Neg e -> "-" ^ to_string e

let rec simplify = function
  | Add (Const 0, e) | Add (e, Const 0) -> simplify e
  | Mul (Const 1, e) | Mul (e, Const 1) -> simplify e
  | Mul (Const 0, _) | Mul (_, Const 0) -> Const 0
  | Add (a, b) -> Add (simplify a, simplify b)
  | Mul (a, b) -> Mul (simplify a, simplify b)
  | Neg (Neg e) -> simplify e
  | Neg e -> Neg (simplify e)
  | Const _ as c -> c

let () =
  let e = Add (Const 2, Mul (Const 3, Const 4)) in
  Printf.printf "%d %s\n" (eval e) (to_string e);
  let messy = Add (Const 0, Mul (Const 1, Neg (Neg (Const 5)))) in
  Printf.printf "%s -> %s\n" (to_string messy) (to_string (simplify messy));
  Printf.printf "%b\n" (eval messy = eval (simplify messy))
lessons.solution:
type expr = Const of int | Add of expr * expr | Sub of expr * expr

let rec eval = function
  | Const n -> n
  | Add (a, b) -> eval a + eval b
  | Sub (a, b) -> eval a - eval b

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (eval (Sub (Const 10, Const 4)))
lessons.challenge: Define a smaller expression type with `Const`, `Add` and `Sub`, write `eval` for it, and print the value of `Sub (Const 10, Const 4)`.

options: Because OCaml requires recursion for every function
Because constructors are evaluated in reverse order
Each constructor gets an arm, and recursive constructors become recursive calls on their parts
lessons.explanation: Structural recursion follows the type's definition, which also guarantees it terminates on finite trees.

lessons.title: Natural numbers as a variant
body: Numbers themselves can be defined with a variant: `type nat = Z | S of nat`. `Z` is zero and `S n` is the successor of `n`, so three is `S (S (S Z))`. The type has exactly the values 0, 1, 2, ... and nothing else, so negative numbers cannot be written at all.

Arithmetic is structural recursion on the first argument. Adding is 'peel one `S` from the left and put it on the result': `add Z b = b` and `add (S a) b = S (add a b)`. Multiplication is repeated addition, and comparison walks both numbers down together until one runs out.

Nobody uses unary numbers for speed. The value of the exercise is seeing that recursive definitions follow the shape of the data, and that properties like 'adding zero on the left does nothing' fall out of the definition itself, which is the idea behind proofs by induction.
lessons.challenge: Write `pow a b` (a to the power b) using `mul`, with `pow _ Z = S Z`, and print `to_int (pow (of_int 2) (of_int 5))`.
lessons.question: On which argument does `add` recurse, and why does that terminate?
options: On the second, which grows each call
On neither; add is not recursive
On the first, which loses one S each call until it reaches Z
lessons.explanation: Each recursive call is on a strictly smaller natural number, and naturals are finite, so the recursion must reach Z.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
7 12
true false
3

Each recursive call is on a strictly smaller natural number, and naturals are finite, so the recursion must reach Z.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each recursive call is on a strictly smaller natural number, and naturals are finite, so the recursion must reach Z.

lessons.title: Designing exceptions: context, matching and re-raising
body: Define an exception for each failure a caller might want to tell apart, and carry the data they need: `exception Invalid_config of string`. Use the standard ones where they fit: `Invalid_argument` for a bad argument, `Failure` for a general failure, `Not_found` for a missing key.

`match f () with v -> ... | exception e -> ...` handles both outcomes in one place and keeps the success path out of the `try` body, so you cannot accidentally catch an exception raised by code that runs on success. To add context, catch, wrap and raise again with a message that says where the problem happened.

Document which exceptions a function can raise, and prefer `result` for failures callers are expected to handle routinely. When you re-raise an exception you caught, use `raise e` for a new context or `Printexc.raise_with_backtrace e bt` to keep the original call stack.
lessons.solution:
let first_positive xs = List.find (fun n -> n > 0) xs

let show xs =
  match first_positive xs with
  | n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n
  | exception Not_found -> print_endline "none"

let () = show [ -1; 0 ]; show [ -1; 5 ]
lessons.challenge: Write `first_positive xs` that raises `Not_found` when the list has no positive number, and use `match ... with exception Not_found` to print "none" for [-1; 0] and the value for [-1; 5].
lessons.question: What is the advantage of `match f () with v -> ... | exception e -> ...` over `try`?
options: The success path stays outside the handler, so exceptions raised by it are not caught by mistake
It runs faster than try
It catches every exception automatically
lessons.explanation: Only the scrutinee is protected, so the handler covers exactly the call you meant to guard.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
8080
not a number: x
server: out of range: 99999
not an int

Only the scrutinee is protected, so the handler covers exactly the call you meant to guard.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Only the scrutinee is protected, so the handler covers exactly the call you meant to guard.

lessons.title: Writing map and filter yourself, and going beyond lists
body: `map` applies a function to every element and keeps the structure; `filter` keeps the elements a predicate accepts. Writing them yourself shows that each is a recursion on the list with one arm for the empty list and one for a head and tail. A tail-recursive `map` accumulates in reverse and reverses once at the end.

The idea of 'apply a function to the contents and keep the shape' is not special to lists. `Option.map` transforms a value that might be missing, and a `map_tree` transforms every label of a tree while leaving its shape alone. Any container can have a `map`, and the result type is always the same container with new contents.

A well-behaved map changes values but never the shape, so `List.length (map f l) = List.length l`. If your own `map` for a type breaks that, it is probably also doing a filter. Keep the two ideas separate: map changes what is inside, filter changes how much there is.
lessons.solution:
let rec filter_map f = function
  | [] -> []
  | x :: xs -> (match f x with Some y -> y :: filter_map f xs | None -> filter_map f xs)

let () = List.iter (Printf.printf "%d ") (filter_map int_of_string_opt [ "1"; "x"; "3" ]); print_newline ()
lessons.challenge: Write `filter_map f xs` that maps with a function returning an option and keeps only the Some results, and print it for parsing ["1"; "x"; "3"] with int_of_string_opt.
lessons.question: What should `map` never change about a container?
options: Its shape: only the values inside are transformed
The type of its elements
Nothing; map may reorder the elements
lessons.explanation: Map is shape-preserving by definition; removing elements is filter's job.

1000000

Map is shape-preserving by definition; removing elements is filter's job.

lessons.title: Laws of map, filter and fold, checked by random testing
body: Higher-order functions obey laws you can rely on when refactoring. Mapping twice equals mapping once with the composition: `map f (map g l) = map (f % g) l`. Mapping the identity changes nothing. Two filters can be applied in either order. A fold with the list constructor rebuilds the list.

A law is a universally quantified equation, so a few examples never prove it. You can gain real confidence by generating many random inputs from a fixed seed and checking the equation on each. A counterexample is a bug in the law or in the code, and the seed makes any failure reproducible.

Proof is stronger than testing, and the next stages show how structural induction proves these laws for all lists. Until then, treat a passing property test as evidence rather than certainty, and keep the seed in the test so that anyone can rerun the same cases.
lessons.challenge: State and check the law `List.rev (List.rev l) = l` and the law `List.length (l @ m) = List.length l + List.length m` using the same random generator, printing both results.
lessons.question: Why use a fixed random seed when checking a law?
options: A fixed seed makes the law true
Random can only be used once per program
A failing case can be reproduced exactly by rerunning the test
lessons.explanation: A deterministic sequence of inputs turns a flaky-looking failure into one you can debug.
lessons.workedExample:

map id: true
filters commute: true

A deterministic sequence of inputs turns a flaky-looking failure into one you can debug.
