lessons.title: Compilation units and interfaces: hiding a representation with an .mli
body: Every `.ml` file is a *compilation unit*: a module named after the file, compiled separately and linked with the others. A file `bounded_stack.ml` defines the module `Bounded_stack`, and another file reaches it as `Bounded_stack.push`. Dune works out the order in which the units must be compiled, so you never write that order down.

A unit may have an interface file, `bounded_stack.mli`, which is the signature of the module. Without it, everything in the `.ml` is public, including the layout of its types. With it, only what the `.mli` lists is visible, and a type declared there as plain `type t` is abstract: other units can pass values of type `t` around but cannot look inside, build one by hand, or depend on how it is stored. That is the compile-time enforcement of a representation invariant.

In the toplevel the same ideas apply: `#use "file.ml"` loads a file as if typed in, while `#load` and `#require` bring in compiled units and libraries, and modules defined in the toplevel have no `.mli`, so nothing is hidden there. Keep the `.mli` small and documented, because it is the contract other code is allowed to depend on.
lessons.challenge: The starter's src/bounded_stack.mli exposes the record type, so leak/leak.ml compiles by reading `items` directly. Rewrite the .mli so `t` is abstract and each function carries a documentation comment. The leak must stop compiling while the app keeps building.
lessons.question: What does declaring `type t` without a definition in an .mli do?
options: It deletes the type from the compiled library
It makes the type mutable
It makes t abstract: other units can use values of type t but cannot see or construct its representation
lessons.explanation: The signature hides the definition, so the only way to build or inspect a t is through the functions the interface exports.
lessons.workedExample: The signature hides the definition, so the only way to build or inspect a t is through the functions the interface exports.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The signature hides the definition, so the only way to build or inspect a t is through the functions the interface exports.

lessons.title: Specifications, contracts and representation invariants
body: A specification says what a function promises, not how it works. A good one names the preconditions the caller must meet (`requires`), what the function returns, and which exceptions it raises. Writing it as a documentation comment before the code forces you to decide the edge cases first, and the comment becomes the contract that tests and proofs check against.

A module has a specification too. Its abstract type has an *abstraction function* that says which mathematical value a concrete representation stands for, and a *representation invariant* that says which concrete values are legitimate. A `rep_ok` function that asserts the invariant and returns its argument can be called at every boundary where a value is built, which turns a silent corruption into an immediate failure.

Check preconditions at the edge of the system and raise `Invalid_argument` with a message naming the function. Inside the module trust the invariant, and keep it cheap enough that you can leave the checks on while testing. A specification that nobody can test is a wish, so for every sentence in the comment ask what input would show it false.
lessons.challenge: Write a specification comment and an implementation for `clamp lo hi x` that requires `lo <= hi` and returns `x` limited to that range. Raise `Invalid_argument` when the precondition fails, and print `clamp 0 10 15`, `clamp 0 10 (-3)` and the caught error for `clamp 5 1 0`.
lessons.question: What does a representation invariant describe?
options: How fast the operations on the type run
The names of the functions the module exports
Which concrete values of an abstract type are legitimate
lessons.explanation: The invariant is the set of concrete values that actually stand for something, which is what every operation may assume and must preserve.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
2 full
Counter.create: limit must be positive
0 3 4

The invariant is the set of concrete values that actually stand for something, which is what every operation may assume and must preserve.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The invariant is the set of concrete values that actually stand for something, which is what every operation may assume and must preserve.

lessons.title: Black-box and glass-box testing
body: Black-box tests are derived from the specification alone, as if the code were hidden. Split the inputs into equivalence classes the specification treats alike, then test one value from each class and the boundaries between classes. For a triangle classifier those classes are equilateral, isosceles, scalene and invalid, and the boundaries are the degenerate triangle whose two shorter sides only just reach the third.

Glass-box tests are derived from the code. Read the implementation, list its branches, and add tests until every branch has run. Black-box tests find behaviour the code does not implement; glass-box tests find code the black-box tests never reach. You need both, and tracing which branch ran gives a simple measure of how much of the code a test suite exercises.

Coverage numbers prove less than they seem to: executing a branch is not the same as checking its result. Keep every test deterministic, give each a clear name, and when you find a bug add the smallest input that shows it to the suite before you fix it, so the bug cannot return unnoticed.
lessons.solution:
let grade score = if score < 50 then "fail" else if score < 80 then "pass" else "distinction"

let () =
  let cases = [ (49, "fail"); (50, "pass"); (79, "pass"); (80, "distinction") ] in
  print_endline (if List.for_all (fun (s, want) -> grade s = want) cases then "ok" else "bug")
lessons.challenge: Write `grade score` returning "fail" below 50, "pass" from 50 to 79 and "distinction" from 80 up. List the boundary scores 49, 50, 79 and 80 as tests and print "ok" if all four give the expected grade.
lessons.question: Where do black-box tests come from?
options: From whatever inputs happen to pass
From the specification alone, using equivalence classes and boundaries
From reading every branch of the implementation
lessons.explanation: They treat the code as hidden, so the only guide to what is correct is what the specification promises.

with only three tests: 2 of 5

They treat the code as hidden, so the only guide to what is correct is what the specification promises.

lessons.title: Randomized testing and shrinking
body: Hand-written tests cover the cases you thought of. A randomized test states a *property*, a claim that should hold for every input, and checks it on many generated inputs. The generator must produce the inputs the code can see, and the property must be a statement about the output rather than a copy of the implementation, such as 'sorting does not change the length'.

A random counterexample is usually big and noisy. *Shrinking* repeatedly tries simpler candidates, such as the same list with an element removed or all values set to zero, and keeps any candidate that still fails. When no simpler candidate fails you have a minimal counterexample, which names the bug far more clearly than the random list that first revealed it.

Seed the generator so a failure can be replayed exactly. Real libraries such as QCheck do all of this with more generators and smarter shrinkers, but the mechanism is what you build here: generate, check, and shrink greedily while the property still fails.
lessons.challenge: Test the property "reversing twice returns the original list" with `check`, then test the false property "reversing returns the original list" and print the length of the shrunk counterexample.
lessons.question: Why does shrinking help after a property fails?
options: It makes the test run faster
It finds a minimal failing input, which points at the bug more clearly than a large random one
It proves the property is true for all other inputs
lessons.explanation: Greedily simplifying a failing input removes everything irrelevant to the failure, leaving the smallest case that still shows it.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
good sort: no counterexample
bad sort counterexample: [0; 0]

Greedily simplifying a failing input removes everything irrelevant to the failure, leaving the smallest case that still shows it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Greedily simplifying a failing input removes everything irrelevant to the failure, leaving the smallest case that still shows it.

lessons.title: Equational reasoning and induction on lists
body: A proof about a recursive function follows the function. To show `length (a @ b) = length a + length b` for all lists, induct on `a`. In the base case `a = []`, both sides reduce to `length b`. In the inductive case `a = x :: a'`, assume the claim for `a'`, then `length ((x :: a') @ b) = 1 + length (a' @ b) = 1 + length a' + length b = length (x :: a') + length b`. Each step unfolds a definition or uses the hypothesis, which is what *equational reasoning* means.

Some claims need a stronger statement before induction works. To show the tail-recursive `sum_tr` equals `sum`, prove the more general fact `go acc l = acc + sum l` for every accumulator, because the plain claim gives no useful hypothesis for the recursive call. Choosing the right generalisation is the central skill, and it is the same idea as choosing the right accumulator when you write the function.

You can check a claim on every small input long before you prove it, and the checks find false claims quickly. Here all 121 lists of length up to four over {0, 1, 2} are enumerated, so a counterexample of that size would be found. A bounded check is evidence and not a proof, which is the reason the induction argument matters, and a *false* claim such as `rev (a @ b) = rev a @ rev b` is rejected at once by a counterexample.
lessons.solution:
let rec all n = if n = 0 then [ [] ] else List.concat_map (fun l -> List.map (fun x -> x :: l) [ 0; 1; 2 ]) (all (n - 1))
let universe = List.concat_map all [ 0; 1; 2; 3; 4 ]
let rec rev = function [] -> [] | x :: xs -> rev xs @ [ x ]

let () =
  Printf.printf "%b %b\n"
    (List.for_all (fun l -> List.length (rev l) = List.length l) universe)
    (List.for_all (fun l -> rev (rev l) = l) universe)
lessons.challenge: State and check, over the same universe, that `List.length (rev l) = List.length l` and that `rev (rev l) = l`, printing both results.
lessons.question: Why is the claim "sum_tr agrees with sum" proved through a generalised statement about `go acc l`?
options: Because induction only works on trees
The plain claim gives no useful hypothesis for the recursive call, which carries a different accumulator
Because accumulators are not allowed in proofs
lessons.explanation: Induction needs the hypothesis to cover the recursive call, and that call has a new accumulator, so the statement must quantify over every accumulator.

Induction needs the hypothesis to cover the recursive call, and that call has a new accumulator, so the statement must quantify over every accumulator.

lessons.title: Structural induction on trees and naturals
body: Structural induction works for any recursive type, with one case per constructor. For a tree, the base case is `Leaf`, and the inductive case assumes the claim for both subtrees and proves it for `Node (l, v, r)`. For a natural number defined by `Z | S of nat` it is the familiar induction on `n`: prove it for `Z`, and prove it for `S n` assuming it for `n`. The proof has exactly the shape of the recursion.

Typical facts are 'mirroring twice is the identity', 'mirroring preserves size', and 'the in-order list of a mirrored tree is the reverse of the original'. Each follows by unfolding the definitions of `mirror`, `size` and `to_list` and applying the hypothesis to the two subtrees, with a small lemma such as `rev (a @ b) = rev b @ rev a` doing the combining.

Again, enumerate before you prove. Every tree of height at most three with leaf-values 0 and 1 is generated here, 723 trees, and each claim is checked on all of them. The false claim 'mirroring changes nothing' is refuted by the first lopsided tree, and a refuted claim never needs a proof.
lessons.challenge: Define `height` for the tree type and check over all trees of height at most three that `height (mirror t) = height t`, printing the result.
lessons.question: What are the cases of structural induction on `type tree = Leaf | Node of tree * int * tree`?
options: A base case for Leaf, and an inductive case for Node that assumes the claim for both subtrees
Only the Node case, since Leaf has no data
One case for each integer stored in the tree
lessons.explanation: There is one case per constructor, and a recursive constructor gets an induction hypothesis for each recursive field.

lessons.title: A hash table from scratch
body: A hash table stores each key in a bucket chosen by a hash function. Looking a key up means hashing it, picking the bucket and searching the few entries there, which is constant time when buckets stay short. This version keeps an array of association lists (separate chaining), so a collision just means two entries share a bucket.

The *load factor* is the number of entries divided by the number of buckets. When it exceeds a threshold the table doubles its bucket array and re-inserts everything, which keeps buckets short. Because every doubling touches all entries but happens after the number of entries has doubled, the cost per insertion is constant on average (amortised).

State the representation invariant and check it: every entry lives in the bucket its key hashes to, the stored size equals the number of entries, and no key appears twice. The mutable table is easy to corrupt with a missed update, so a `rep_ok` function that verifies these facts is cheap insurance in tests.

Doubling makes hash collisions impossible
Because the array is copied without looking at entries
lessons.explanation: The expensive resizes are rare enough that their total cost, spread over all insertions, is a constant per insertion.

lessons.title: Amortised analysis with a two-list queue
body: A single operation can be slow while a long sequence of them is cheap. The two-list queue pushes onto a back list in constant time and pops from a front list; when the front is empty it reverses the back, which costs the length of the back. One pop can cost a lot, but each element is moved from back to front at most once in its lifetime.

The *banker's method* makes this precise: charge each push a few units, spend one to pay for the push and save the rest to pay in advance for the single reversal move that element will need later. The total cost of any sequence of n operations is then at most a constant times n, so the *amortised* cost per operation is constant. The code counts real units so you can watch the bound hold.

Amortised bounds assume each version of the structure is used once. If you keep an old version and pop from it repeatedly, every pop pays the full reversal again, and the bound collapses. Persistent data structures need laziness to restore amortisation, which is why the next lessons on streams and memoisation matter.
lessons.challenge: Run 10 pushes followed by 10 pops with the counting queue and print the total cost, which should be 30 (10 pushes, 10 pops and 10 moved elements).
lessons.question: What does the amortised bound assume about how the queue is used?
options: Each version is used once; reusing an old version repeats the expensive reversal
That the queue never holds more than ten elements
That pops always happen before pushes
lessons.explanation: The saved credit from each push is spent exactly once, so reusing a version lets the same credit be spent again and the accounting fails.

lessons.title: Red-black trees: balance by colour
body: A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are coloured so the tree stays roughly balanced. Two invariants do the work: no red node has a red child, and every path from the root to a leaf passes through the same number of black nodes. Together they bound the height by about twice the logarithm of the size, so lookup and insertion are logarithmic even for sorted input.

Okasaki's insertion is short. Insert as in an ordinary tree, colouring the new node red, then rebalance on the way back up. Whenever a black node has a red child with a red child (four possible shapes), one `balance` rewrite turns that shape into a red parent with two black children. The root is finally made black, which restores the invariant.

The four shapes share one result, which an or-pattern expresses directly. Because the invariants are easy to state, write a checker for them and run it after every insertion in a test: a missed shape in `balance` shows up as a violated invariant long before it shows up as a slow tree.
lessons.code:
type color = R | B
type 'a t = E | T of color * 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let balance = function
  | B, T (R, T (R, a, x, b), y, c), z, d
  | B, T (R, a, x, T (R, b, y, c)), z, d
  | B, a, x, T (R, T (R, b, y, c), z, d)
  | B, a, x, T (R, b, y, T (R, c, z, d)) ->
      T (R, T (B, a, x, b), y, T (B, c, z, d))
  | color, a, x, b -> T (color, a, x, b)

let insert x s =
  let rec ins = function
    | E -> T (R, E, x, E)
    | T (color, a, y, b) as t ->
        if x < y then balance (color, ins a, y, b)
        else if x > y then balance (color, a, y, ins b)
        else t
  in
  match ins s with T (_, a, y, b) -> T (B, a, y, b) | E -> assert false

let rec size = function E -> 0 | T (_, a, _, b) -> size a + 1 + size b
let rec height = function E -> 0 | T (_, a, _, b) -> 1 + max (height a) (height b)
let rec to_list = function E -> [] | T (_, a, x, b) -> to_list a @ [ x ] @ to_list b

(* Black height of a tree, or None if the invariants are violated. *)
let rec black_height = function
  | E -> Some 1
  | T (color, a, _, b) -> (
      let bad_red = function T (R, _, _, _) -> color = R | _ -> false in
      if bad_red a || bad_red b then None
      else
        match (black_height a, black_height b) with
        | Some x, Some y when x = y -> Some (if color = B then x + 1 else x)
        | _ -> None)

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E (List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1)) in
  Printf.printf "size %d\n" (size t);
  Printf.printf "sorted: %b\n" (to_list t = List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1));
  Printf.printf "invariants hold: %b\n" (black_height t <> None);
  Printf.printf "height at most 20 for 1000 sorted keys: %b\n" (height t <= 20)

type 'a t = E | T of color * 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let balance = function
  | B, T (R, T (R, a, x, b), y, c), z, d
  | B, T (R, a, x, T (R, b, y, c)), z, d
  | B, a, x, T (R, T (R, b, y, c), z, d)
  | B, a, x, T (R, b, y, T (R, c, z, d)) ->
      T (R, T (B, a, x, b), y, T (B, c, z, d))
  | color, a, x, b -> T (color, a, x, b)

let insert x s =
  let rec ins = function
    | E -> T (R, E, x, E)
    | T (color, a, y, b) as t ->
        if x < y then balance (color, ins a, y, b)
        else if x > y then balance (color, a, y, ins b)
        else t
  in
  match ins s with T (_, a, y, b) -> T (B, a, y, b) | E -> assert false

let rec mem x = function
  | E -> false
  | T (_, a, y, b) -> if x < y then mem x a else if x > y then mem x b else true

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E (List.init 1000 (fun i -> i + 1)) in
  Printf.printf "%b %b\n" (mem 500 t) (mem 1001 t)

lessons.title: Lazy streams and the sieve of Eratosthenes
body: A stream is a list whose tail is computed on demand, so it can be infinite. `type 'a stream = Cons of 'a * 'a stream Lazy.t` pairs a head with a lazy tail. Nothing past the head exists until someone forces it, and forcing happens at most once because `Lazy` caches the result.

Streams make some algorithms read like their mathematical definitions. The sieve of Eratosthenes is 'take the first number, keep only the numbers not divisible by it, and sieve the rest', and Fibonacci numbers are 'two numbers and then the stream that follows'. You take as many elements as you need with a `take` function and leave the infinite remainder unevaluated.

The standard library provides the same idea as `Seq`, whose tails are functions rather than cached lazy values, so a `Seq` recomputes work each time it is traversed. Prefer `Seq` for one-pass pipelines and a memoising stream when the same elements are demanded many times, and remember that a stream holding onto its head keeps every forced element alive.

lessons.question: Why does forcing a lazy value twice evaluate its body only once?
options: Because lazy values cannot be forced twice
Lazy caches the result of the first force
Because the second force raises an exception
lessons.explanation: A lazy value stores its result after the first evaluation, which is what makes streams safe to share.

lessons.title: Memoisation and dynamic programming
body: Memoisation remembers the result of a function for each argument it has seen, so repeated calls become lookups. The naive Fibonacci recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times; with a table the number of real computations is linear. This works whenever the function is *pure*, because returning a stored answer is indistinguishable from recomputing it.

A recursive function cannot be memoised by wrapping it from outside, because its recursive calls still go to the unmemoised version. Write it in *open recursion* style, taking `self` as a parameter for its recursive calls, and tie the knot with a `memo_rec` that supplies a table-checking `self`. The same trick turns a clear recursive definition into dynamic programming without rewriting it as loops.

Dynamic programming is memoisation of overlapping subproblems. Edit distance between two strings is the classic example: the distance of two prefixes depends only on the distances of shorter prefixes, so a table indexed by the two lengths holds all the work. Count how many table entries are computed to see the saving.
lessons.challenge: Use `memo_rec` to count the number of ways to climb 30 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time (ways n = ways (n-1) + ways (n-2), with ways 0 = ways 1 = 1) and print it.
lessons.question: Why must a recursive function be written in open-recursion style to be memoised?
options: Because Hashtbl cannot store recursive values
Because open recursion makes the function faster by itself
Its recursive calls must go through the memoising wrapper, which a plain recursive reference would bypass
lessons.explanation: Passing self lets the memoising wrapper intercept every recursive call, so each distinct argument is computed once.

lessons.title: Persistent arrays as balanced trees
body: An ordinary array is mutable: updating it destroys the old version. A persistent array keeps every version usable. The simplest design stores the elements at the leaves of a balanced binary tree; reading index i walks down choosing left or right by comparing i with the midpoint, and writing index i rebuilds only the path from the root to that leaf while sharing every other subtree.

Both operations take time logarithmic in the length, not constant, and an update allocates a handful of nodes instead of copying the whole array. This is the price of persistence: you pay a log factor to keep old versions, in exchange for undo, backtracking and safe sharing between threads with no locks.

You can observe the sharing directly. After setting one element, the subtree that did not contain it is the very same block in memory, which physical equality `==` confirms. Use persistent arrays when you need history; if you only ever use the newest version, a plain mutable array is simpler and faster.
lessons.challenge: Write `to_list a` that returns the elements of a persistent array in order, and print it for the array of squares of 0 to 5 after setting index 2 to 0.
lessons.question: What does an update of a persistent tree-array allocate?
options: A complete copy of the array
Nothing, because it mutates in place
New nodes only along the path to the changed leaf; every other subtree is shared
lessons.explanation: Path copying rebuilds just the ancestors of the changed leaf, so the old and new versions share everything else.

lessons.title: 2-3 trees: balance without colours
body: A 2-3 tree is a search tree whose nodes hold one key and two children (a 2-node) or two keys and three children (a 3-node), with every leaf at the same depth. Because the leaves are all at the same depth, the tree is perfectly balanced, and lookup follows one path of logarithmic length.

Insertion goes down to a leaf and comes back up. A 2-node that receives a key becomes a 3-node, and a 3-node that receives a key *splits* into a 2-node on each side and pushes the middle key up to its parent. A split that reaches the root creates a new root, which is the only way the tree grows taller, so all leaves stay at the same depth.

The recursive insert returns either `Fit` (the subtree absorbed the key) or `Split (left, middle, right)` (the parent must absorb a middle key). Red-black trees encode balanced trees with colours: the *left-leaning* variant encodes 2-3 trees exactly, while the four-case version in the previous lesson corresponds to 2-3-4 trees, whose full nodes hold three keys, which is why it needs four rewrite shapes. The idea of splitting a full node and pushing the middle key up is the same in both. The checker below verifies equal leaf depth and sorted order.
lessons.code:
type 'a t = E | N2 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t | N3 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t * 'a * 'a t
type 'a ins = Fit of 'a t | Split of 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let rec ins x = function
  | E -> Split (E, x, E)
  | N2 (l, y, r) as t ->
      if x = y then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N2 (l', y, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (a, z, b, y, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N2 (l, y, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (l, y, a, z, b)))
  | N3 (l, y, m, w, r) as t ->
      if x = y || x = w then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N3 (l', y, m, w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (a, z, b), y, N2 (m, w, r)))
      else if x < w then (
        match ins x m with
        | Fit m' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m', w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, a), z, N2 (b, w, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m, w, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, m), w, N2 (a, z, b)))

let insert x t = match ins x t with Fit t' -> t' | Split (a, z, b) -> N2 (a, z, b)

let rec to_list = function
  | E -> []
  | N2 (l, x, r) -> to_list l @ [ x ] @ to_list r
  | N3 (l, x, m, y, r) -> to_list l @ [ x ] @ to_list m @ [ y ] @ to_list r

(* Depth of all leaves, or None if they are not all at the same depth. *)
let rec depth = function
  | E -> Some 0
  | N2 (l, _, r) -> (match (depth l, depth r) with Some a, Some b when a = b -> Some (a + 1) | _ -> None)
  | N3 (l, _, m, _, r) ->
      (match (depth l, depth m, depth r) with Some a, Some b, Some c when a = b && b = c -> Some (a + 1) | _ -> None)

let () =
  (* 997 is prime, so multiplying by 389 mod 997 visits 500 distinct keys in a scrambled order *)
  let keys = List.init 500 (fun i -> (i * 389 + 1) mod 997) in
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E keys in
  Printf.printf "sorted: %b\n" (to_list t = List.sort_uniq compare keys);
  Printf.printf "all leaves at the same depth: %b\n" (depth t <> None);
  Printf.printf "keys: %d\n" (List.length (to_list t));
  Printf.printf "height at most 9: %b\n" (match depth t with Some d -> d <= 9 | None -> false)

type 'a t = E | N2 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t | N3 of 'a t * 'a * 'a t * 'a * 'a t
type 'a ins = Fit of 'a t | Split of 'a t * 'a * 'a t

let rec ins x = function
  | E -> Split (E, x, E)
  | N2 (l, y, r) as t ->
      if x = y then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N2 (l', y, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (a, z, b, y, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N2 (l, y, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Fit (N3 (l, y, a, z, b)))
  | N3 (l, y, m, w, r) as t ->
      if x = y || x = w then Fit t
      else if x < y then (
        match ins x l with
        | Fit l' -> Fit (N3 (l', y, m, w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (a, z, b), y, N2 (m, w, r)))
      else if x < w then (
        match ins x m with
        | Fit m' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m', w, r))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, a), z, N2 (b, w, r)))
      else (
        match ins x r with
        | Fit r' -> Fit (N3 (l, y, m, w, r'))
        | Split (a, z, b) -> Split (N2 (l, y, m), w, N2 (a, z, b)))

let insert x t = match ins x t with Fit t' -> t' | Split (a, z, b) -> N2 (a, z, b)

let rec depth = function
  | E -> 0
  | N2 (l, _, _) -> 1 + depth l
  | N3 (l, _, _, _, _) -> 1 + depth l

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (depth (List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) E [ 1; 2; 3; 4; 5; 6; 7 ]))

lessons.title: The substitution model: small-step and big-step evaluation
body: The substitution model says what a program means by rewriting it. To evaluate `let x = v in e` once `v` is a value, replace every free occurrence of `x` in `e` by `v` and carry on. A *small-step* semantics does one rewrite at a time, `e -> e'`, until a value remains. A *big-step* semantics jumps straight to the answer, `e ==> v`. Both define the same results, and a small-step trace is a useful picture of what the program does.

Substitution must respect scope. A binding `let x = ...` inside the expression shadows the outer `x`, so the substitution function stops replacing under a binder for the same name. Because only closed values are substituted here, variable capture cannot happen; in a language with functions, substituting open terms needs renaming to avoid it, which is what makes the environment model attractive.

An expression that is not a value and cannot step is *stuck*, for example adding an integer to a boolean. Stuck terms are exactly the ones a type checker should reject, which is the connection to the next lessons: a type system promises that well-typed programs never get stuck.
lessons.code:
type op = Add | Mul | Le

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Binop of op * expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

let is_value = function Int _ | Bool _ -> true | _ -> false

(* subst e v x is e with the value v substituted for the free variable x *)
let rec subst e v x =
  match e with
  | Var y -> if x = y then v else e
  | Int _ | Bool _ -> e
  | Binop (o, a, b) -> Binop (o, subst a v x, subst b v x)
  | If (c, t, f) -> If (subst c v x, subst t v x, subst f v x)
  | Let (y, e1, e2) ->
      let e1' = subst e1 v x in
      if x = y then Let (y, e1', e2) else Let (y, e1', subst e2 v x)

let rec step = function
  | Binop (Add, Int a, Int b) -> Int (a + b)
  | Binop (Mul, Int a, Int b) -> Int (a * b)
  | Binop (Le, Int a, Int b) -> Bool (a <= b)
  | Binop (o, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> Binop (o, e1, step e2)
  | Binop (o, e1, e2) -> Binop (o, step e1, e2)
  | If (Bool true, t, _) -> t
  | If (Bool false, _, f) -> f
  | If (c, t, f) -> If (step c, t, f)
  | Let (x, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> subst e2 e1 x
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> Let (x, step e1, e2)
  | Int _ | Bool _ | Var _ -> failwith "stuck"

let rec eval_small e = if is_value e then e else eval_small (step e)
let rec steps e n = if is_value e then n else steps (step e) (n + 1)

let rec eval_big = function
  | (Int _ | Bool _) as v -> v
  | Var x -> failwith ("unbound " ^ x)
  | Binop (o, a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_big a in
      let y = eval_big b in
      match (o, x, y) with
      | Add, Int x, Int y -> Int (x + y)
      | Mul, Int x, Int y -> Int (x * y)
      | Le, Int x, Int y -> Bool (x <= y)
      | _ -> failwith "stuck")
  | If (c, t, f) -> (
      match eval_big c with Bool true -> eval_big t | Bool false -> eval_big f | _ -> failwith "stuck")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_big (subst e2 (eval_big e1) x)

let show = function Int n -> string_of_int n | Bool b -> string_of_bool b | _ -> "<expr>"

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("x", Int 5,
         Let ("y", Binop (Mul, Var "x", Int 2),
              If (Binop (Le, Var "y", Int 10), Binop (Add, Var "y", Int 1), Int 0)))
  in
  Printf.printf "%s %s\n" (show (eval_small prog)) (show (eval_big prog));
  Printf.printf "%d steps\n" (steps prog 0);
  let shadow = Let ("x", Int 1, Let ("x", Int 2, Var "x")) in
  Printf.printf "shadowing: %s %s\n" (show (eval_small shadow)) (show (eval_big shadow));
  try ignore (eval_small (Binop (Add, Int 1, Bool true))) with Failure m -> print_endline m
lessons.solution:
type expr = Int of int | Var of string | Neg of expr | Let of string * expr * expr

let is_value = function Int _ -> true | _ -> false

let rec subst e v x =
  match e with
  | Var y -> if x = y then v else e
  | Int _ -> e
  | Neg a -> Neg (subst a v x)
  | Let (y, e1, e2) ->
      let e1' = subst e1 v x in
      if x = y then Let (y, e1', e2) else Let (y, e1', subst e2 v x)

let rec step = function
  | Neg (Int n) -> Int (-n)
  | Neg e -> Neg (step e)
  | Let (x, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> subst e2 e1 x
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> Let (x, step e1, e2)
  | Int _ | Var _ -> failwith "stuck"

let rec eval_small e = if is_value e then e else eval_small (step e)

let rec eval_big = function
  | Int n -> n
  | Var x -> failwith ("unbound " ^ x)
  | Neg e -> - eval_big e
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_big (subst e2 (Int (eval_big e1)) x)

let () =
  let p = Let ("x", Int 4, Neg (Var "x")) in
  (match eval_small p with Int n -> Printf.printf "%d %d\n" n (eval_big p) | _ -> ())

lessons.title: The environment model, closures and lexical scope
body: Substituting into a program is conceptually clean but inefficient, since each binding rewrites the whole body. The environment model keeps the body as it is and carries a table from names to values. Looking a variable up consults the table, and `let x = e1 in e2` evaluates `e2` in the table extended with `x`.

Functions make the choice of table matter. A *closure* pairs a function with the environment where it was defined, and calling it evaluates the body in that environment extended with the argument. This gives *lexical scope*: free names refer to the bindings visible where the function was written. If a function instead used the environment at the call site (*dynamic scope*), a later rebinding of `x` would change what an old function means.

The program below defines `f` using `x = 1`, rebinds `x` to 10, then calls `f 2`. Lexical scope gives `3` because the closure remembers `x = 1`; dynamic scope gives `12`. Almost every modern language, OCaml included, is lexically scoped, because it makes a function's behaviour depend only on its own text and its definition site.
lessons.code:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | Closure of string * expr * (string * value) list

let show = function VInt n -> string_of_int n | Closure _ -> "<closure>"

let rec eval_lex env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_lex env a in
      let y = eval_lex env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_lex ((x, eval_lex env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, env)
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval_lex env f with
      | Closure (x, body, closure_env) -> eval_lex ((x, eval_lex env arg) :: closure_env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

(* Dynamic scope: a function does not remember where it was defined. *)
let rec eval_dyn env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_dyn env a in
      let y = eval_dyn env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_dyn ((x, eval_dyn env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, [])
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval_dyn env f with
      | Closure (x, body, _) -> eval_dyn ((x, eval_dyn env arg) :: env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("x", Int 1,
         Let ("f", Fun ("y", Add (Var "x", Var "y")),
              Let ("x", Int 10, App (Var "f", Int 2))))
  in
  Printf.printf "lexical: %s\n" (show (eval_lex [] prog));
  Printf.printf "dynamic: %s\n" (show (eval_dyn [] prog));
  Printf.printf "a function value: %s\n" (show (eval_lex [] (Fun ("z", Var "z"))));
  try ignore (eval_lex [] (Var "missing")) with Not_found -> print_endline "unbound variable"
lessons.solution:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | Closure of string * expr * (string * value) list

let rec eval env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval env a in
      let y = eval env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval ((x, eval env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, env)
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval env f with
      | Closure (x, body, closure_env) -> eval ((x, eval env arg) :: closure_env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("add", Fun ("a", Fun ("b", Add (Var "a", Var "b"))), App (App (Var "add", Int 3), Int 4))
  in
  match eval [] prog with VInt n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n | Closure _ -> print_endline "closure"

lessons.title: A static type checker
body: A type checker predicts, without running the program, what kind of value each expression will produce. For a small language with integers and booleans, `typeof env e` returns the type of `e` in the typing environment `env`, or an error explaining the problem. `Add` needs two integers and gives an integer, `Le` compares integers and gives a boolean, and `If` needs a boolean condition and two branches of the same type.

The environment maps each variable to its type, extended at every `let`. An unbound variable is a type error. The result type is `(ty, string) result`, and `let*` threads the first error out, so the checker reads as the typing rules do: check the parts, then combine their types.

The point is *safety*: a well-typed program never gets stuck. Adding an integer to a boolean would stick the evaluator from the substitution lesson, and the checker rejects it first with a message. Type checking is conservative: it rejects some programs that would have run fine, and the art of a type system is rejecting as few useful programs as possible.
lessons.code:
type ty = TInt | TBool

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Le of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

let show_ty = function TInt -> "int" | TBool -> "bool"
let ( let* ) = Result.bind

let rec typeof env = function
  | Int _ -> Ok TInt
  | Bool _ -> Ok TBool
  | Var x -> (match List.assoc_opt x env with Some t -> Ok t | None -> Error ("unbound variable " ^ x))
  | Add (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect env a TInt in
      let* () = expect env b TInt in
      Ok TInt
  | Le (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect env a TInt in
      let* () = expect env b TInt in
      Ok TBool
  | If (c, t, f) ->
      let* () = expect env c TBool in
      let* tt = typeof env t in
      let* tf = typeof env f in
      if tt = tf then Ok tt else Error "branches differ"
  | Let (x, e1, e2) ->
      let* t1 = typeof env e1 in
      typeof ((x, t1) :: env) e2

and expect env e t =
  let* t' = typeof env e in
  if t' = t then Ok () else Error (Printf.sprintf "expected %s but got %s" (show_ty t) (show_ty t'))

let report e = print_endline (match typeof [] e with Ok t -> show_ty t | Error m -> "error: " ^ m)

let () =
  report (Add (Int 1, Int 2));
  report (If (Le (Int 1, Int 2), Int 3, Int 4));
  report (Let ("x", Bool true, If (Var "x", Int 1, Int 2)));
  report (Add (Int 1, Bool true));
  report (If (Int 1, Int 2, Int 3));
  report (If (Bool true, Int 1, Bool false));
  report (Var "z")
lessons.solution:
type ty = TInt | TBool
type expr = Int of int | Le of expr * expr | Not of expr

let show_ty = function TInt -> "int" | TBool -> "bool"
let ( let* ) = Result.bind

let rec typeof = function
  | Int _ -> Ok TInt
  | Le (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect a TInt in
      let* () = expect b TInt in
      Ok TBool
  | Not e ->
      let* () = expect e TBool in
      Ok TBool

and expect e t =
  let* t' = typeof e in
  if t' = t then Ok () else Error (Printf.sprintf "expected %s but got %s" (show_ty t) (show_ty t'))

let report e = print_endline (match typeof e with Ok t -> show_ty t | Error m -> "error: " ^ m)

let () =
  report (Not (Le (Int 1, Int 2)));
  report (Not (Int 3))

lessons.question: What guarantee does a sound type system give about a well-typed program?
options: It has no logic errors
It never gets stuck: evaluation either finishes with a value or keeps making progress
It always terminates quickly
lessons.explanation: Soundness means progress and preservation: a well-typed term either is a value or can step, and stepping keeps its type.

lessons.title: Type inference by unification
body: A checker needs annotations; an inferencer discovers the types. It gives every unknown a fresh *type variable*, walks the expression generating constraints, and solves them by *unification*. Applying a function `f : a` to an argument of type `b` with result type `c` demands that `a` equal `b -> c`. Unification makes two types equal by binding type variables, or fails with a mismatch.

Unifying a variable with a type must pass the *occurs check*: a variable cannot be bound to a type that contains it, since that would be an infinite type. This is why `fun x -> x x` is rejected: `x` would need the type `a` with `a = a -> b`. The substitution built up during inference is applied at the end, and leftover variables are printed as `'a`, `'b` and so on, which are exactly the polymorphic types of OCaml.

This is the heart of Hindley-Milner inference, the system behind OCaml, with let-polymorphism omitted here for brevity. Note how the printer names variables in the order they appear and sequences its work with `let`, since the order of evaluation of arguments is unspecified and would otherwise change the names.
lessons.code:
type ty = TInt | TBool | TVar of int | TFun of ty * ty

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr
  | Add of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr

exception Type_error of string

let counter = ref 0
let subst : (int * ty) list ref = ref []
let fresh () = incr counter; TVar !counter

let rec resolve t =
  match t with
  | TVar n -> (match List.assoc_opt n !subst with Some t' -> resolve t' | None -> t)
  | TFun (a, b) -> TFun (resolve a, resolve b)
  | TInt | TBool -> t

let rec occurs n t =
  match resolve t with
  | TVar m -> n = m
  | TFun (a, b) -> occurs n a || occurs n b
  | TInt | TBool -> false

let rec unify a b =
  match (resolve a, resolve b) with
  | TInt, TInt | TBool, TBool -> ()
  | TVar n, TVar m when n = m -> ()
  | TVar n, t | t, TVar n ->
      if occurs n t then raise (Type_error "occurs check: infinite type") else subst := (n, t) :: !subst
  | TFun (a1, b1), TFun (a2, b2) -> unify a1 a2; unify b1 b2
  | _ -> raise (Type_error "type mismatch")

let rec infer env = function
  | Int _ -> TInt
  | Bool _ -> TBool
  | Var x -> (match List.assoc_opt x env with Some t -> t | None -> raise (Type_error ("unbound variable " ^ x)))
  | Fun (x, body) ->
      let a = fresh () in
      let r = infer ((x, a) :: env) body in
      TFun (a, r)
  | App (f, arg) ->
      let tf = infer env f in
      let ta = infer env arg in
      let r = fresh () in
      unify tf (TFun (ta, r));
      r
  | Add (a, b) -> unify (infer env a) TInt; unify (infer env b) TInt; TInt
  | If (c, t, e) ->
      unify (infer env c) TBool;
      let tt = infer env t in
      let te = infer env e in
      unify tt te;
      tt

let show t =
  let names = ref [] in
  let name n =
    match List.assoc_opt n !names with
    | Some s -> s
    | None ->
        let s = "'" ^ String.make 1 (Char.chr (97 + List.length !names)) in
        names := (n, s) :: !names;
        s
  in
  let rec go t =
    match resolve t with
    | TInt -> "int"
    | TBool -> "bool"
    | TVar n -> name n
    | TFun (a, b) ->
        let left = match resolve a with TFun _ -> "(" ^ go a ^ ")" | _ -> go a in
        let right = go b in
        left ^ " -> " ^ right
  in
  go t

let typeof e =
  counter := 0;
  subst := [];
  match infer [] e with t -> show t | exception Type_error m -> "error: " ^ m

let () =
  List.iter (fun e -> print_endline (typeof e))
    [ Fun ("x", Add (Var "x", Int 1));
      Fun ("x", Var "x");
      Fun ("f", Fun ("x", App (Var "f", App (Var "f", Var "x"))));
      Fun ("x", App (Var "x", Var "x"));
      If (Bool true, Int 1, Bool false);
      App (Int 1, Int 2) ]
lessons.solution:
type ty = TInt | TBool | TVar of int | TFun of ty * ty
type expr = Var of string | Fun of string * expr | App of expr * expr

exception Type_error of string

let counter = ref 0
let subst : (int * ty) list ref = ref []
let fresh () = incr counter; TVar !counter

let rec resolve t =
  match t with
  | TVar n -> (match List.assoc_opt n !subst with Some t' -> resolve t' | None -> t)
  | TFun (a, b) -> TFun (resolve a, resolve b)
  | TInt | TBool -> t

let rec occurs n t =
  match resolve t with
  | TVar m -> n = m
  | TFun (a, b) -> occurs n a || occurs n b
  | TInt | TBool -> false

let rec unify a b =
  match (resolve a, resolve b) with
  | TInt, TInt | TBool, TBool -> ()
  | TVar n, TVar m when n = m -> ()
  | TVar n, t | t, TVar n ->
      if occurs n t then raise (Type_error "occurs check") else subst := (n, t) :: !subst
  | TFun (a1, b1), TFun (a2, b2) -> unify a1 a2; unify b1 b2
  | _ -> raise (Type_error "mismatch")

let rec infer env = function
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Fun (x, body) ->
      let a = fresh () in
      let r = infer ((x, a) :: env) body in
      TFun (a, r)
  | App (f, arg) ->
      let tf = infer env f in
      let ta = infer env arg in
      let r = fresh () in
      unify tf (TFun (ta, r));
      r

let show t =
  let names = ref [] in
  let name n =
    match List.assoc_opt n !names with
    | Some s -> s
    | None ->
        let s = "'" ^ String.make 1 (Char.chr (97 + List.length !names)) in
        names := (n, s) :: !names;
        s
  in
  let rec go t =
    match resolve t with
    | TInt -> "int"
    | TBool -> "bool"
    | TVar n -> name n
    | TFun (a, b) ->
        let left = match resolve a with TFun _ -> "(" ^ go a ^ ")" | _ -> go a in
        let right = go b in
        left ^ " -> " ^ right
  in
  go t

let () =
  let compose = Fun ("f", Fun ("g", Fun ("x", App (Var "f", App (Var "g", Var "x"))))) in
  print_endline (show (infer [] compose))

lessons.title: The Curry-Howard correspondence: programs as proofs
body: A type can be read as a proposition and a program of that type as a proof of it. A function type `A -> B` is the implication 'if A then B', a pair `A * B` is 'A and B', and `(A, B) Either.t` is 'A or B'. A *total* function of type `A -> B` turns any evidence for A into evidence for B, which is exactly what a proof of an implication does.

So `compose : (a -> b) -> (b -> c) -> (a -> c)` is the transitivity of implication, and `and_comm : a * b -> b * a` proves that 'and' is commutative. The empty type `type void = |` has no values, so it plays the role of falsehood, and `a -> void` is 'not a'. From `a` you can prove 'not not a' by applying the continuation to it, but you cannot prove 'not not a implies a' in general: that classical principle has no program.

OCaml is not sound as a logic. Non-termination (`let rec loop () = loop ()`), exceptions and `Obj.magic` all inhabit any type, so a type-correct program is evidence only when it is total and pure. The correspondence is nevertheless the foundation of proof assistants such as Lean and Coq, where the type system is restricted until programs really are proofs.

lessons.title: Big-O notation measured by counting
body: Big-O describes how the cost of an algorithm grows with the size n of its input, ignoring constant factors. Linear search is O(n), binary search is O(log n), insertion sort is O(n squared), and merge sort is O(n log n). The notation answers one question: if I double the input, what happens to the work?

You can see the growth rate by counting a basic operation instead of measuring time. Count the comparisons in each algorithm at sizes n and 2n. A linear algorithm doubles its count, a logarithmic one adds a constant, a quadratic one quadruples, and an n log n algorithm slightly more than doubles. Counts are exact and repeatable, where timings depend on the machine and the load.

Big-O is an upper bound on growth, not a prediction of speed. An O(n squared) algorithm with a tiny constant can beat an O(n log n) one for small inputs, and the worst case may be rare. Use the notation to choose the right algorithm family, then measure to decide among the contenders.

It increases by a constant amount
It roughly quadruples

lessons.title: Promises from scratch: state, callbacks and bind
body: Concurrency means a program can make progress on several tasks whose results arrive at unpredictable times, even on one thread. A *promise* is a placeholder for a result that is not ready yet. It is in one of three states: pending, resolved with a value, or rejected with an exception. Once it leaves pending it never changes again, and that single-assignment rule is what makes promises easy to reason about.

Code that depends on a result registers a *callback* with the promise. If the promise is already complete the callback runs at once; otherwise it is stored and run, in registration order, when the promise completes. `bind p f` is the central operation: it returns a new promise that completes when `f` has run on the value of `p` and the promise `f` returned has also completed. A rejection skips `f` and rejects the new promise, so errors propagate like exceptions do.

This is the design of Lwt and Async, and of promises in other languages. Their `let%bind` and `let*` are just `bind` written as syntax. Building one yourself shows there is no magic: a mutable state field, a list of callbacks, and the rule that completing a promise runs every stored callback exactly once.
lessons.challenge: Write `all ps` that takes a list of promises and returns a promise of the list of their values (in order), using `bind` and `return`, then resolve the three promises in reverse order and print the combined result, which still comes back in input order.
lessons.question: What does `bind p f` return when `p` is rejected?
options: A promise resolved with a default value
A pending promise that never completes
A promise rejected with the same exception, without calling f
lessons.explanation: Rejection propagates down the chain, which is how a failure anywhere in a sequence of asynchronous steps reaches the code that handles it.

lessons.title: Callbacks and a simulated event loop
body: An event loop is the scheduler behind asynchronous programs. It keeps a queue of actions tagged with the time they become ready, repeatedly takes the earliest one, advances the clock to its time and runs it. While a task waits for the clock, the loop runs others, which is how one thread keeps many tasks moving. This version uses a virtual clock so the output is exact.

A *callback* is the continuation of a waiting task: instead of blocking, `fetch name k` schedules a completion and `k` is called with the result later. Chaining three fetches by nesting callbacks runs them one after another, and the total time is the sum of the delays. Starting all three at once and counting completions runs them concurrently, and the total time is the longest delay.

Nested callbacks drift to the right and tangle error handling, which is the reason for promises and `let*`. The mechanism underneath does not change: a queue ordered by time, ties broken first-come first-served, and a rule that handlers run to completion without being interrupted, so no handler ever sees another in the middle of its work.

The one with the shorter name
Both run at once in parallel

lessons.title: Monads and their three laws
body: A monad is a type constructor `'a t` with two operations: `return : 'a -> 'a t`, which wraps a plain value, and `bind : 'a t -> ('a -> 'b t) -> 'b t`, which feeds the contents of a computation into the next step. `option` (computations that may fail), `list` (computations with many results), `result`, promises, and a *writer* that collects a log are all monads. The common shape is why one piece of syntax, `let*`, works for all of them.

To count as a monad the operations must obey three laws. *Left identity*: `bind (return a) f = f a`. *Right identity*: `bind m return = m`. *Associativity*: `bind (bind m f) g = bind m (fun x -> bind (f x) g)`. They say that `return` does nothing and that chaining does not depend on how you group the steps, which is exactly what you need to refactor a chain of steps safely.

Laws can be tested like any property: pick sample values and functions, and compare both sides with structural equality. A function that merely has the right type is not enough. The deliberately broken list monad below keeps only the first result and so violates right identity, which is why `let*` code built on it would silently lose answers.
lessons.code:
module type MONAD = sig
  type 'a t

  val return : 'a -> 'a t
  val bind : 'a t -> ('a -> 'b t) -> 'b t
end

module Option_m : MONAD with type 'a t = 'a option = struct
  type 'a t = 'a option

  let return x = Some x
  let bind m f = match m with None -> None | Some x -> f x
end

module List_m : MONAD with type 'a t = 'a list = struct
  type 'a t = 'a list

  let return x = [ x ]
  let bind m f = List.concat_map f m
end

module Writer : MONAD with type 'a t = 'a * string list = struct
  type 'a t = 'a * string list

  let return x = (x, [])

  let bind (x, log) f =
    let y, log' = f x in
    (y, log @ log')
end

(* Not a monad: it keeps only the first result. *)
module Broken_list : MONAD with type 'a t = 'a list = struct
  type 'a t = 'a list

  let return x = [ x ]
  let bind m f = match List.concat_map f m with [] -> [] | x :: _ -> [ x ]
end

module Laws (M : MONAD) = struct
  let left_identity a f = M.bind (M.return a) f = f a
  let right_identity m = M.bind m M.return = m
  let associativity m f g = M.bind (M.bind m f) g = M.bind m (fun x -> M.bind (f x) g)
end

let check_option () =
  let module L = Laws (Option_m) in
  let f x = if x > 0 then Some (x - 1) else None and g x = Some (x * 2) in
  let ms = [ None; Some 0; Some 5 ] in
  ( List.for_all (fun a -> L.left_identity a f) [ 0; 3 ],
    List.for_all L.right_identity ms,
    List.for_all (fun m -> L.associativity m f g) ms )

let check_list () =
  let module L = Laws (List_m) in
  let f x = [ x; x + 1 ] and g x = [ x * 10 ] in
  let ms = [ []; [ 1 ]; [ 1; 2; 3 ] ] in
  ( List.for_all (fun a -> L.left_identity a f) [ 0; 3 ],
    List.for_all L.right_identity ms,
    List.for_all (fun m -> L.associativity m f g) ms )

let check_writer () =
  let module L = Laws (Writer) in
  let f x = (x + 1, [ "inc" ]) and g x = (x * 2, [ "double" ]) in
  let ms = [ (1, []); (5, [ "start" ]) ] in
  ( List.for_all (fun a -> L.left_identity a f) [ 0; 3 ],
    List.for_all L.right_identity ms,
    List.for_all (fun m -> L.associativity m f g) ms )

let show (a, b, c) = Printf.sprintf "%b %b %b" a b c

let () =
  Printf.printf "option laws: %s\n" (show (check_option ()));
  Printf.printf "list laws: %s\n" (show (check_list ()));
  Printf.printf "writer laws: %s\n" (show (check_writer ()));
  let module B = Laws (Broken_list) in
  Printf.printf "broken list monad, right identity: %b\n" (List.for_all B.right_identity [ []; [ 1 ]; [ 1; 2; 3 ] ]);
  let ( let* ) = Option_m.bind in
  let safe_div a b = if b = 0 then None else Some (a / b) in
  let result = let* x = safe_div 100 5 in let* y = safe_div x 2 in Some (x + y) in
  Printf.printf "let* over option: %s\n" (match result with Some n -> string_of_int n | None -> "none")
lessons.solution:
module Result_m = struct
  let return x = Ok x
  let bind m f = match m with Error e -> Error e | Ok x -> f x
end

let ( let* ) = Result_m.bind
let parse s = match int_of_string_opt s with Some n -> Ok n | None -> Error ("not a number: " ^ s)
let halve n = if n mod 2 = 0 then Ok (n / 2) else Error "odd"

let run s =
  let* n = parse s in
  let* h = halve n in
  Result_m.return (h + 1)

let show = function Ok n -> string_of_int n | Error e -> e

let () =
  print_endline (show (run "12"));
  print_endline (show (run "x"))
lessons.challenge: Write a `Result_m` monad over `('a, string) result`, make a tiny `parse` and `halve` pair of steps, and use `let*` to chain them, printing the result for "12" and for "x".
lessons.question: What do the monad laws guarantee?
options: That every computation terminates
That bind runs its argument twice
That return does nothing and that chaining steps does not depend on how they are grouped
lessons.explanation: Left and right identity say return is neutral, and associativity says a chain can be regrouped without changing its meaning.

Expected output:
option laws: true true true
list laws: true true true
writer laws: true true true
broken list monad, right identity: false
let* over option: 30

Left and right identity say return is neutral, and associativity says a chain can be regrouped without changing its meaning.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Left and right identity say return is neutral, and associativity says a chain can be regrouped without changing its meaning.

lessons.title: Lexical conventions, literals and operator precedence
body: The lexer turns characters into tokens before anything else happens. Integers may contain underscores for readability (`1_000_000`) and be written in hexadecimal (`0xFF`), octal (`0o17`) or binary (`0b1010`). A character literal can be an escape such as `'\n'`, a decimal code `'\065'` or a hexadecimal one `'\x41'`. A string may contain escapes, may continue over a line with a trailing backslash, and may be written in the quoted form `{|...|}` or `{id|...|id}` in which nothing is an escape.

Comments nest: `(* a (* b *) c *)` is one comment, so you can comment out code that already contains comments. Operators are ordinary identifiers made of symbol characters, and their *first* characters decide precedence and associativity: names starting with `+` or `-` are additive and left-associative, `*`, `/` and `%` multiplicative, and `**` right-associative. You may define your own, such as `let ( +++ ) a b = a * 10 + b`.

Function application binds tighter than any operator, so `f x + g y` is `(f x) + (g y)`, and the prefix `-` binds tighter than `*`. `@@` and `|>` are ordinary operators that follow the leading-character rule: `@@` starts with `@`, so it is right-associative and binds more loosely than `+` but more tightly than the comparisons (`f @@ x = y` is `(f @@ x) = y`), while `|>` starts with `|` and sits at the comparison level, grouping from the left. That is why `print_endline @@ string_of_int 3` needs no parentheses. When you are unsure how an expression groups, add parentheses: they cost nothing.
lessons.solution:
let ( **> ) a b = a - b

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (1 **> 2 **> 3)
lessons.challenge: Define a right-associative operator `**>` such that `1 **> 2 **> 3` means `1 **> (2 **> 3)` using the rule that names starting with `**` are right-associative, with `a **> b = a - b`, and print the result.
lessons.question: What decides the precedence and associativity of a user-defined operator?
options: Its first characters: for example names starting with + or - are additive and left-associative
The order in which operators are defined
The length of the operator name
lessons.explanation: The language fixes a table by leading characters, so any operator that starts with them inherits that behaviour.

lessons.title: Names, namespaces and scope
body: OCaml keeps several namespaces apart, so one spelling can mean different things in different positions: values, type constructors, data constructors, record labels, modules, module types and classes each have their own. `type t = A | B`, `let t = 5`, `module T = struct ... end` and `type r = { t : int }` can all coexist, and the context says which `t` or `T` you mean.

Within one namespace a later definition shadows an earlier one. Constructors are shadowed too: after `type u = A of int`, the name `A` refers to `u` unless a type annotation such as `(A : t)` says otherwise, because OCaml uses the expected type to disambiguate. `type nonrec t = t list` says the right-hand `t` is the *previous* definition, and a qualified name such as `Stdlib.List.length` reaches a module that your own `List` has hidden.

Scope is lexical and nested. `let module M = ... in`, `let open M in` and `M.(expr)` limit a name's reach to one expression. Use shadowing deliberately and sparingly: it is safe for a value you transform step by step, and a trap when it hides a module from the standard library that other code expects.
lessons.solution:
module Option = struct let get = 0 end

let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" Option.get (Stdlib.Option.get (Some 7))
lessons.challenge: Define a module `Option` of your own with a value `get = 0`, then print both `Option.get` and `Stdlib.Option.get (Some 7)` to show how the qualified name reaches the standard one.

options: It makes the earlier type shadow the later one everywhere
It tells the compiler to pick the constructor of type t instead of the most recent A
It converts A to a string
lessons.explanation: OCaml uses the expected type to disambiguate constructors and labels, so the annotation selects the right one.

OCaml uses the expected type to disambiguate constructors and labels, so the annotation selects the right one.

lessons.title: Polymorphism and its limitations
body: Inference is fully automatic for the basic language, but some polymorphism cannot be inferred. A recursive function is monomorphic inside its own body, which breaks *polymorphic recursion*, where the recursive call is at a different type: for `type 'a nested = Flat of 'a | Nested of 'a list nested` the call inside `depth` has type `'a list nested`. You must write the explicit polymorphic annotation `let rec depth : 'a. 'a nested -> int = ...` to tell the checker that the function is polymorphic within its own definition.

A function argument is also monomorphic: `fun f -> (f 1, f "s")` does not type-check because `f` has one type. The way to pass something polymorphic as an argument is *higher-rank polymorphism* through a record with a polymorphic field, `type id = { f : 'a. 'a -> 'a }`, or an object method. Locally abstract types, `fun (type a) (x : a) -> ...`, introduce a type name that the checker treats as abstract inside the body and that you can use in annotations.

These are exactly the places where you add annotations. The compiler error messages point at the recursive call or the argument, and the cure is an explicit `'a.` or a record. If you find yourself needing them often, consider whether a module or functor expresses the same idea more simply.
lessons.solution:
type 'a nested = Flat of 'a | Nested of 'a list nested

(* The recursive call is at type 'a list nested, so depth must be polymorphic
   inside its own body; only the explicit 'a. annotation allows that. *)
let rec depth : 'a. 'a nested -> int = function
  | Flat _ -> 0
  | Nested n -> 1 + depth n

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (depth (Nested (Nested (Nested (Flat [ [ [ 1 ] ] ])))))
lessons.challenge: Explain in a comment why `depth` needs the explicit `'a.` annotation, then build a value nested three levels deep with `Nested` and print its depth.
lessons.question: Why does a polymorphically recursive function need an explicit `'a.` annotation?
options: Because recursion is not allowed on variants
Because the compiler cannot print polymorphic types
Inference treats a function as monomorphic inside its own body, so a call at a different type is rejected without the annotation
lessons.explanation: The annotation states the function is polymorphic within its own definition, which inference alone cannot discover.

Expected output:

1 s
a,b

The annotation states the function is polymorphic within its own definition, which inference alone cannot discover.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The annotation states the function is polymorphic within its own definition, which inference alone cannot discover.

lessons.title: Recursive values, recursive modules and mutually recursive types
body: `let rec` is not only for functions. A *value* may be defined in terms of itself if the right-hand side is a constructor application, a record, a lazy value or a function: `let rec ones = 1 :: ones` builds a cyclic list in which the tail points back to the head. The compiler accepts only definitions whose recursion is guarded by such a constructor; something like `let rec evens = 0 :: List.map succ evens` is rejected because the recursive use sits inside a function call.

Types can be mutually recursive with `and`: an expression type that holds statements and a statement type that holds expressions must be defined together. Modules can too, with `module rec A : SIG = ... and B : SIG = ...`; every recursive module needs a full signature so the checker can see through the cycle. Use this sparingly, since it hides the dependency order that normally keeps programs easy to read.

Cyclic data is easy to create and dangerous to traverse: a naive `List.length ones` never terminates, and structural equality or printing of a cycle can loop forever. Always bound the traversal, as `take` does below.
lessons.challenge: Define a cyclic list `let rec cycle = 1 :: 2 :: 3 :: cycle` and print its first seven elements with a bounded `take`.
lessons.question: Why must every recursive module have a full signature?
options: So the modules can be compiled in any order at runtime
Because recursive modules cannot contain functions
The checker needs to see the interface of each module to type the references across the cycle
lessons.explanation: Without declared signatures the modules would depend on each other's inferred types, which does not terminate, so the interfaces break the cycle.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1,1,1,1,1
true
4
true true false

Without declared signatures the modules would depend on each other's inferred types, which does not terminate, so the interfaces break the cycle.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Without declared signatures the modules would depend on each other's inferred types, which does not terminate, so the interfaces break the cycle.

lessons.title: Private types, extensible variants and inline records
body: A *private* type abbreviation, `type t = private float`, can be read as a float (`(m :> float)`) but cannot be created except through the module's own functions. It is a lightweight abstract type: users keep the convenience of the representation while you keep control over how values are made, which is useful for validated numbers such as lengths that must not be negative.

An *extensible variant* type, declared `type event = ..`, has no fixed list of cases; any module can add constructors with `type event += Click of int`. Exceptions are the best-known example: `exn` is an extensible type. A match must end with a catch-all `_` case because new constructors may appear later, which makes extensible types the right tool for plug-in style events and the wrong one when you want exhaustiveness checking.

*Inline records* give a constructor named fields, `Circle of { radius : float }`, without a separate record type. The record is not a first-class value and cannot escape the pattern that binds it, which avoids an allocation and keeps the fields close to the constructor that owns them. Choose them when a constructor has several fields that are easy to confuse positionally.
lessons.code:
module Meters : sig
  type t = private float

  val of_float : float -> t
  val to_float : t -> float
end = struct
  type t = float

  let of_float x = if x < 0. then invalid_arg "negative length" else x
  let to_float x = x
end

type event = ..
type event += Click of int | Key of char

let describe = function
  | Click n -> Printf.sprintf "click %d" n
  | Key c -> Printf.sprintf "key %c" c
  | _ -> "unknown event"

type event += Scroll

type shape = Circle of { radius : float } | Rect of { w : float; h : float }

let area = function
  | Circle { radius } -> 3. *. radius *. radius
  | Rect { w; h } -> w *. h

let () =
  let m = Meters.of_float 2.5 in
  Printf.printf "%.1f %.1f\n" (m :> float) (Meters.to_float m);
  (try ignore (Meters.of_float (-1.)) with Invalid_argument msg -> print_endline msg);
  List.iter (fun e -> print_endline (describe e)) [ Click 3; Key 'x'; Scroll ];
  Printf.printf "%.1f %.1f\n" (area (Circle { radius = 2. })) (area (Rect { w = 2.; h = 4.5 }))
lessons.challenge: Add a `Triangle of { base : float; height : float }` inline-record constructor with area half the base times the height, and print its area for base 4 and height 3.
lessons.question: Why must a match on an extensible variant end with a catch-all case?
options: Because extensible variants have only one constructor
Because the match would be too slow
Other modules can add constructors later, so the compiler can never know every case
lessons.explanation: The set of constructors is open, so exhaustiveness cannot be checked and a wildcard handles whatever is added.

lessons.title: Attributes and extension points
body: An *attribute*, written `[@name payload]` on an expression or `[@@name]` on a declaration, attaches information to the syntax tree. The compiler understands a few: `[@inline]` asks for a function to be inlined, `[@tailcall]` makes the compiler warn if a call is not a tail call, `[@deprecated "message"]` makes uses of a definition produce an alert, `[@@unboxed]` removes the box around a single-constructor type, and `[@warning "-8"]` changes warnings for a region.

Unknown attributes are ignored by the compiler and left for PPX rewriters to read, which is how `[@@deriving show]` works. An *extension point*, `[%name payload]`, is different: it marks a place where a rewriter must produce code, and the compiler rejects an extension node that no rewriter has handled. Attributes annotate code; extension points ask for code.

Because `[@@unboxed]` changes the runtime representation, `Id 5` is stored as the integer 5 itself. You can observe that with `Obj.is_int`, a function meant for debugging and not for production code. Use attributes for performance tuning only after measuring, since the compiler already inlines small functions without being asked.
lessons.challenge: Mark a recursive `count_down` function with `[@tailcall]` on its recursive call and a `[@inline]` helper, and print `count_down 100000`.
lessons.question: What is the difference between `[@name]` and `[%name]`?
options: An attribute annotates existing code, while an extension point marks a place a rewriter must replace with code
They are two spellings of the same thing
Attributes run at runtime and extension points at compile time
lessons.explanation: Attributes are metadata the compiler may ignore; extension nodes must be expanded by a rewriter or compilation fails.

Expected output:
36 10
true
false
9
9

Attributes are metadata the compiler may ignore; extension nodes must be expanded by a rewriter or compilation fails.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Attributes are metadata the compiler may ignore; extension nodes must be expanded by a rewriter or compilation fails.

lessons.title: The module system in depth: substitution, aliases and functor styles
body: A signature constraint `S with type t = int` makes the abstract type equal to `int`, and keeps `t` in the signature. *Destructive substitution*, `S with type t := int`, goes further and removes `t` from the signature, replacing every use by `int`. It is the neat way to specialise a generic signature without leaving a redundant type behind.

A *module alias*, `module M = List`, makes `M` another name for the same module, with no copy and no new types. A functor can be *applicative* (`module F (X : S) = ...`), where applying it twice to the same argument yields compatible types, or *generative* (`module G () = ...`), where each application creates fresh abstract types. Generativity is what you want when each application should own distinct state or types, such as a unique-identifier generator.

`module type of M` gives the signature of an existing module, and `include` copies a module's contents into another, so a wrapper module can extend a library module by including it and adding functions. These tools together let you reshape module interfaces after the fact, which is how large libraries expose a small public API over a big implementation.
lessons.code:
module type S = sig
  type t

  val x : t
  val show : t -> string
end

module type S_int = S with type t := int

module A : S_int = struct
  let x = 5
  let show = string_of_int
end

module L = List

module Fresh () : sig
  type id

  val next : unit -> id
  val to_int : id -> int
end = struct
  type id = int

  let counter = ref 0
  let next () = incr counter; !counter
  let to_int i = i
end

module Ids1 = Fresh ()
module Ids2 = Fresh ()

module Extended_list = struct
  include List

  let second = function _ :: x :: _ -> Some x | _ -> None
end

let () =
  Printf.printf "%s %d\n" (A.show A.x) (A.x + 1);
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (L.length [ 1; 2; 3 ]);
  let a = Ids1.next () in
  let b = Ids1.next () in
  let c = Ids2.next () in
  Printf.printf "%d %d %d\n" (Ids1.to_int a) (Ids1.to_int b) (Ids2.to_int c);
  Printf.printf "%s\n" (match Extended_list.second [ 10; 20; 30 ] with Some n -> string_of_int n | None -> "none")
lessons.solution:
module Fresh () : sig
  type id

  val next : unit -> id
  val to_int : id -> int
end = struct
  type id = int

  let counter = ref 0
  let next () = incr counter; !counter
  let to_int i = i
end

module Ids1 = Fresh ()
module Ids3 = Fresh ()

let () =
  ignore (Ids1.next ());
  ignore (Ids1.next ());
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (Ids3.to_int (Ids3.next ()))

options: With = keeps t in the signature as an equation; with := removes t and replaces its uses by int
They are identical
The first applies to values and the second to types
lessons.explanation: Destructive substitution deletes the abstract type from the signature, leaving a smaller interface.

3

lessons.title: Classes, inheritance and virtual methods
body: A class describes objects with state (`val`) and behaviour (`method`). `inherit parent` reuses the parent's fields and methods, `object (self) ... end` gives the object a name for calling its own methods with `self#m`, and `inherit parent as super` lets an override call `super#m`. A *virtual* class declares methods without implementing them (`method virtual area : float`) and cannot be instantiated, so it works as an abstract base whose subclasses must fill the gaps.

An `initializer` block runs when an object is created, after the fields are set. Objects are mutable by default through `val mutable`, but an *immutable* style works too: the functional update `{< x = x + d >}` returns a copy of the object with some fields changed. Classes can be polymorphic, `class ['a] stack`, and a *class type* lists the methods an object must have without any implementation.

Method calls are resolved at runtime through the object, which is *open recursion*: a method in a parent calling `self#area` uses the subclass's `area`. That flexibility is what objects offer beyond modules and records, and its price is weaker static guarantees and harder reasoning. Most OCaml code reaches for modules first and keeps classes for open-ended extension.
lessons.code:
class virtual shape name =
  object (self)
    method virtual area : float
    method describe = Printf.sprintf "%s with area %.1f" name self#area
  end

class circle r = object inherit shape "circle" method area = 3.0 *. r *. r end
class square s = object inherit shape "square" method area = s *. s end

class big_circle r =
  object
    inherit circle r as super
    method! area = super#area *. 2.0
  end

class greeter name =
  object
    initializer print_endline ("created " ^ name)
    method hi = "hi " ^ name
  end

class point x =
  object
    val x = x
    method get = x
    method move d = {< x = x + d >}
  end

class ['a] stack =
  object
    val items : 'a list = []
    method push (v : 'a) = {< items = v :: items >}
    method top = match items with [] -> None | v :: _ -> Some v
  end

class type printable = object method describe : string end

let () =
  let shapes : printable list = [ (new circle 1.0 :> printable); (new square 2.0 :> printable); (new big_circle 1.0 :> printable) ] in
  List.iter (fun s -> print_endline s#describe) shapes;
  let g = new greeter "ada" in
  print_endline g#hi;
  let p = new point 1 in
  let q = p#move 5 in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" p#get q#get;
  let s = (new stack)#push 1 in
  let s = s#push 2 in
  Printf.printf "%s\n" (match s#top with Some n -> string_of_int n | None -> "empty")
lessons.solution:
class virtual shape name =
  object (self)
    method virtual area : float
    method describe = Printf.sprintf "%s with area %.1f" name self#area
  end

class triangle base height =
  object
    inherit shape "triangle"
    method area = base *. height /. 2.0
  end

let () = print_endline (new triangle 4.0 3.0)#describe

options: Its fields are always immutable
It declares at least one method without implementing it, so it cannot be instantiated directly
It runs its methods on another thread
lessons.explanation: A virtual class is an abstract base: subclasses must supply the missing methods before objects can be created.
