lessons.title: A tour of the standard library
body: The standard library is a set of modules named for the types they serve, all opened by default through `Stdlib`: `Int`, `Float`, `Char`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Option`, `Result`, `Either`, `Fun`, `Lazy`, `Seq`, `List`, `Array`, `Stack`, `Queue`, `Hashtbl`, `Map`, `Set`, `Buffer`, `Format`, `Scanf`, `Filename`, `Digest`, `In_channel` and `Out_channel`. Learning the library is largely learning which module holds the function you need, so the module name is the first place to look.

The conventions repeat across modules: a type `t`, `create`/`of_...` constructors, `to_string`, `compare`, `equal`, and `_opt` variants that return an option instead of raising. A module with `compare` and `t` can be passed to `Map.Make` or `Set.Make`, which is why `Int`, `String` and `Float` all provide them. Functions that may fail come in pairs, such as `List.find` and `List.find_opt`.

The tour below touches many modules with deterministic output. Reading the documentation for a module you rarely use is cheap compared with rewriting what it already does, and the OCaml manual lists every module with its types and functions.
lessons.challenge: Use `Scanf.sscanf` to parse the string "7,4" with the format "%d,%d" and print the sum, then print `Filename.remove_extension "report.pdf"`.
lessons.question: Why do many standard modules provide both `find` and `find_opt` style functions?
options: They search in different directions
One is for lists and the other for arrays
One raises an exception when nothing matches and the other returns an option, so callers can choose how to handle absence
lessons.explanation: The _opt variants make absence part of the return type, which is usually safer than catching an exception.

lessons.title: How values are laid out in memory
body: Every OCaml value is one machine word. An *immediate* value, such as an `int`, a `char`, a `bool`, `()`, `[]`, `None` or a constant constructor, is stored directly with its lowest bit set, so it needs no allocation. Anything else is a pointer to a *block* in the heap, which begins with a header recording the block's size in words and a *tag* byte, followed by the fields.

The tag tells the runtime and the garbage collector what the block holds. Constructors with arguments are numbered in order of declaration starting at 0, separately from the constant constructors, so `type c = A | B of int | C of int * int` stores `A` as an immediate, `B 1` as a one-field block with tag 0, and `C (1, 2)` as a two-field block with tag 1. Tuples, records, `Some x` and list cells are blocks with tag 0, floats and strings have special tags, and a float array is stored unboxed.

The `Obj` module can look at this layout, which is the way to see it for yourself, but it bypasses the type system and its functions can crash a program if misused. Use it for exploration and never for application logic. Knowing the layout explains costs such as why a list of floats allocates a box per element while a `float array` does not.
lessons.challenge: Print the description of the record `{ x = 1; y = 2 }` and of `Some (Some 1)` with `describe`, and say in a comment what the tags tell you.
lessons.question: How is the constant constructor `A` of `type c = A | B of int` stored?
options: As a block with tag 0 and size 0
As a pointer to a shared static string
As an immediate integer, with no heap block
lessons.explanation: Constant constructors carry no data, so the runtime represents them as small tagged integers in the word itself.

lessons.title: JSON with Yojson: parsing, validating and printing
body: JSON is the common format for configuration and web APIs, and Yojson is the usual OCaml library for it. `Yojson.Safe.from_string` parses text into a variant tree: `` `Assoc `` for objects, `` `List `` for arrays, `` `String ``, `` `Int ``, `` `Float ``, `` `Bool `` and `` `Null ``. Malformed text raises `Yojson.Json_error`, so a parser for untrusted input must catch it.

The `Yojson.Safe.Util` module reads values out of the tree: `member "port" json` returns the field, or `` `Null `` when it is missing, and `to_int`, `to_string` and `to_list` convert a value or raise `Type_error` when it has the wrong shape. Wrapping the whole conversion in one `try` turns every kind of bad input into a single `Error` message, which is the right boundary between untrusted text and your own typed record.

Printing goes the other way: build the variant tree from your record and call `Yojson.Safe.to_string`. Keep the conversion in both directions next to the type and test the round trip. For large schemas, `ppx_deriving_yojson` generates both functions from the type, in the same way `ppx_jane` derives s-expressions.
lessons.challenge: Implement `Appconfig.parse` so it turns a JSON object with `name` (string), `port` (int) and `tags` (list of strings) into the record, and returns `Error` with a message for invalid JSON or a missing or wrongly typed field. `to_json` is already written.
lessons.question: What does `Yojson.Safe.Util.member "port" json` return when the field is missing?
options: `Null, which a later to_int then rejects with a Type_error
It raises Not_found immediately
It returns the integer 0
lessons.explanation: member is total, so absence shows up as Null, and the failure appears when the conversion function cannot accept it.

lessons.title: Lexer and parser generators: ocamllex and Menhir
body: Writing a lexer and parser by hand, as in the interpreter capstone, is fine for small languages and tedious for large ones. `ocamllex` generates a lexer from a `.mll` file of regular expressions and actions, and Menhir generates an LR parser from a `.mly` grammar. Dune runs both with the stanzas `(ocamllex lexer)` and `(menhir (modules parser))`, so the generated OCaml never needs to be checked in.

In the grammar, `%token` declares the tokens the lexer produces, each production names its parts and returns an abstract-syntax value, and `%start` names the entry point with its result type. A grammar like `expr: expr PLUS expr | expr STAR expr | ...` is *ambiguous*: `1 + 2 * 3` can be grouped two ways. Menhir reports the shift/reduce conflicts and picks one arbitrarily, which gives wrong answers, so you resolve them with precedence declarations: `%left PLUS MINUS` binds more loosely than the later `%left STAR`, and `%nonassoc UMINUS` with `%prec UMINUS` handles unary minus.

Treat conflict warnings as bugs in the grammar, not noise. Each declaration line adds a precedence level, later lines bind tighter, and `%left` makes an operator group from the left, so `2-3-4` means `(2-3)-4`. Test the parser on the examples that expose associativity and precedence, because a grammar can accept every string and still build the wrong tree.
lessons.challenge: src/parser.mly declares precedence only for unary minus, so binary operators group the wrong way. Add `%left PLUS MINUS` and then `%left STAR` above the existing `%nonassoc UMINUS` so that `1+2*3` is 7, `2-3-4` is -5 and `-(2+3)*2` is -10.
lessons.question: What do the `%left` lines in a Menhir grammar do?
options: They tell the lexer which characters to skip
They make the parser reject left recursion
They resolve shift/reduce conflicts by giving operators a precedence (later lines bind tighter) and left associativity
lessons.explanation: Without them, the ambiguous grammar leaves the parser to choose a grouping arbitrarily; the declarations state which one is intended.
lessons.workedExample: Without them, the ambiguous grammar leaves the parser to choose a grouping arbitrarily; the declarations state which one is intended.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Without them, the ambiguous grammar leaves the parser to choose a grouping arbitrarily; the declarations state which one is intended.

lessons.title: The compiler front end: parsetree, typedtree and compiler-libs
body: The compiler is a pipeline. The *front end* turns text into a typed tree: the lexer and parser produce a `Parsetree`, which is plain syntax with no meaning attached; type checking then produces a `Typedtree` in which every name is resolved and every expression is annotated with its type. The *back end* turns that tree into lower-level forms and finally into machine code, which the next lesson examines.

You can look at each stage with a flag. `-dparsetree` prints the parsetree (`Pstr_value`, `Ppat_var`, `Pexp_apply` and so on), `-dtypedtree` prints the typedtree (`Tstr_value`, `Texp_apply`), and `-dsource` prints the program again from the parsetree, which is the quickest way to see how the parser grouped an expression or what a PPX produced. A type error is raised between those two stages, so a file with an error shows a parsetree but no typedtree.

The compiler's own libraries are available as `compiler-libs.common`. Calling `Parse.implementation (Lexing.from_string source)` gives you the parsetree of a string, which is the foundation of PPX rewriters, linters and code-analysis tools. The AST types change between compiler versions, so a tool built on them is tied to one release unless it goes through `ppxlib`, which provides a stable copy.
lessons.challenge: First fix example/hello.ml so it compiles (`x * 2.0` mixes int and float arithmetic). Then implement `Count.count_lets` in src/count.ml: parse a string with `Parse.implementation` and return how many top-level items are value bindings (`Pstr_value`).
lessons.question: Why does a file with a type error show a parsetree but no typedtree?
options: The typedtree is only printed for files with no comments
-dparsetree prints errors instead of the tree
Parsing succeeds because the syntax is valid; type checking, which builds the typedtree, then fails
lessons.explanation: The stages run in order, so an error in type checking happens after the parsetree exists and before the typedtree can be completed.
lessons.workedExample: The stages run in order, so an error in type checking happens after the parsetree exists and before the typedtree can be completed.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The stages run in order, so an error in type checking happens after the parsetree exists and before the typedtree can be completed.

lessons.title: The compiler back end: bytecode, native code and runtime parameters
body: After type checking, the compiler lowers the typedtree to *lambda*, a small untyped intermediate language in which pattern matches are already compiled to tests. From lambda, `ocamlc` produces portable *bytecode* that the `ocamlrun` interpreter executes, while `ocamlopt` goes on to produce native machine code (`-S` keeps the assembly). Both read the same source, and for a correct program they give the same output; native code is faster, bytecode is more portable and easier to debug.

`-dlambda` prints the lambda form, where a call in tail position is marked `tailcall`. Tail calls matter because the compiler turns a self tail call into a jump, so a tail-recursive loop uses constant stack space. The attribute `[@tailcall]` on a call asks the compiler to check this: with `-w +51` the compiler warns, and with `-warn-error +51` refuses to build, if the call is not actually a tail call. That makes the guarantee a compile-time check instead of a hope.

The runtime is configured without recompiling, through the `OCAMLRUNPARAM` environment variable. The setting `v=0x400` prints garbage-collection statistics when the program exits, `b` turns on backtraces, and `s` sets the minor heap size. Use these to see what the collector is doing before you decide whether any tuning is needed.
lessons.challenge: example/loop.ml marks a non-tail call with `[@tailcall]`, so the compiler rejects it under `-w +51 -warn-error +51`. Rewrite `sum` with an accumulator so the recursive call really is a tail call, keeping `Loop.sum 1_000_000 = 500000500000`.
lessons.question: What does `[@tailcall]` with warning 51 enabled guarantee?
options: That the marked call is in tail position, or compilation fails
That the function will be inlined
That the function runs on a second thread
lessons.explanation: The attribute states an expectation and the warning checks it, so a refactoring that breaks tail-recursion is caught at compile time.
lessons.workedExample: The attribute states an expectation and the warning checks it, so a refactoring that breaks tail-recursion is caught at compile time.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The attribute states an expectation and the warning checks it, so a refactoring that breaks tail-recursion is caught at compile time.

lessons.title: The unix library: files, directories and descriptor safety
body: The `unix` library exposes operating-system calls: `Unix.stat` returns a file's size and kind, `Unix.opendir` and `Unix.readdir` list a directory, and `Unix.openfile`, `Unix.read` and `Unix.write` work on raw file descriptors. Failures raise `Unix.Unix_error (code, function, argument)`, where the code is a constructor such as `ENOENT` for a missing file, so a caller can match on the reason instead of parsing a message.

A file descriptor is a scarce resource. Each process has a limit, often only a few hundred on a desktop system, and a descriptor that is opened and never closed stays open until the program ends. A function that forgets to close on an error path may pass every normal test and then fail in production with `Too many open files`. The fix is the pattern from the exceptions lesson: acquire, then `Fun.protect ~finally:(fun () -> Unix.close fd)`.

`Unix.read` may return fewer bytes than requested and `Unix.write` may write fewer than given, so copy loops must handle partial transfers, and end-of-file is a zero-byte read. Test for leaks directly by counting the open descriptors (`/dev/fd` on macOS and Linux) before and after many calls, both on success and on failure: a leak then fails the test immediately, without waiting to hit the system limit.
lessons.challenge: Implement `file_size`, `list_dir` (sorted, without `.` and `..`) and `copy_file` in src/fileops.ml with the `Unix` module. `copy_file` must close both descriptors even when copying fails, and must handle partial reads and writes. The test counts the open descriptors in /dev/fd before and after hundreds of failing and successful calls, so any leak is detected whatever the system limit is.
lessons.question: Why is `Fun.protect ~finally` used around opening and copying a file?
options: It closes the descriptor on every path, including errors, so repeated failures cannot exhaust the process's descriptor limit
It makes reads faster
It converts Unix_error into Failure
lessons.explanation: The finalizer runs whether the body returns or raises, so cleanup does not depend on the happy path.
lessons.workedExample: The finalizer runs whether the body returns or raises, so cleanup does not depend on the happy path.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The finalizer runs whether the body returns or raises, so cleanup does not depend on the happy path.

projectSolutionFiles.content:
let file_size path = (Unix.stat path).Unix.st_size

let list_dir dir =
  let handle = Unix.opendir dir in
  Fun.protect
    ~finally:(fun () -> Unix.closedir handle)
    (fun () ->
      let rec go acc =
        match Unix.readdir handle with
        | name -> go (if name = "." || name = ".." then acc else name :: acc)
        | exception End_of_file -> List.sort compare acc
      in
      go [])

let copy_file src dst =
  let ifd = Unix.openfile src [ Unix.O_RDONLY ] 0 in
  Fun.protect
    ~finally:(fun () -> Unix.close ifd)
    (fun () ->
      let ofd = Unix.openfile dst [ Unix.O_WRONLY; Unix.O_CREAT; Unix.O_TRUNC ] 0o644 in
      Fun.protect
        ~finally:(fun () -> Unix.close ofd)
        (fun () ->
          let buf = Bytes.create 4096 in
          let rec copy () =
            let n = Unix.read ifd buf 0 4096 in
            if n > 0 then begin
              let written = ref 0 in
              while !written < n do
                written := !written + Unix.write ofd buf !written (n - !written)
              done;
              copy ()
            end
          in
          copy ()))

lessons.title: The str library: regular expressions
body: The `str` library provides simple regular expressions for text processing. `Str.regexp "[0-9]+"` compiles a pattern, `Str.search_forward re s pos` finds the next match at or after `pos` and returns its position (raising `Not_found` when there is none), and `Str.matched_string s` returns the text of the last match. `Str.split` cuts a string on a separator pattern and `Str.global_replace` substitutes every match.

Its syntax is older and smaller than the Perl-style syntax of most languages: the special characters `+`, `?`, `*`, `[...]` and `^` work as usual, but grouping and alternation are written with backslashes, `\(` `\)` and `\|`, and there are no lookaheads or non-greedy operators. The library is also not thread-safe, because the last match is global state. For anything heavier, libraries such as `re` or `ocaml-re` are the usual choice.

A search loop needs care about where to resume. After a match, continue from the end of the match, `p + String.length m`, or an empty match would loop forever. Collect results in an accumulator and reverse at the end, and test with strings that contain no match, adjacent matches and leading or trailing separators, because those are the cases that expose off-by-one errors.
lessons.challenge: Implement `numbers` (every run of digits in a string, as ints, in order), `words` (split on runs of spaces, tabs and newlines, dropping empty pieces) and `squeeze` (collapse runs of blanks to a single space and trim) in src/textutil.ml using `Str`.
lessons.question: Why must a regexp search loop resume from the end of the previous match?
options: Because search_forward resets the string
Otherwise the same match, or an empty one, would be found again and the loop would never advance
Str only allows one match per string
lessons.explanation: The next search must start after the text already consumed, or the loop repeats the same position.
lessons.workedExample: The next search must start after the text already consumed, or the loop repeats the same position.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The next search must start after the text already consumed, or the loop repeats the same position.

projectSolutionFiles.content:
let numbers s =
  let re = Str.regexp "[0-9]+" in
  let rec go pos acc =
    match Str.search_forward re s pos with
    | start ->
        let m = Str.matched_string s in
        go (start + String.length m) (int_of_string m :: acc)
    | exception Not_found -> List.rev acc
  in
  go 0 []

let words s = Str.split (Str.regexp "[ \t\n]+") s
let squeeze s = String.trim (Str.global_replace (Str.regexp "[ \t]+") " " s)

lessons.title: The threads library: a blocking queue with Mutex and Condition
body: The `threads.posix` library gives OCaml system threads. `Thread.create f x` starts a thread, `Thread.join` waits for it, and `Thread.delay` sleeps. In OCaml 5 threads run inside a domain and share one runtime lock, so they interleave rather than run in parallel; they are the tool for overlapping *waiting* (input, timers, locks), while domains are the tool for parallel computation.

Shared state needs a `Mutex`. `Mutex.protect m f` locks, runs `f`, and always unlocks. To *wait* for a condition, such as 'the queue is not empty', use a `Condition`: `Condition.wait c m` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and re-acquires the mutex when another thread calls `Condition.signal c`. Always wait in a `while` loop that rechecks the condition, because a thread can wake when the condition is no longer true.

A bounded blocking queue uses two conditions, `not_empty` for consumers and `not_full` for producers. `pop` waits while the queue is empty, takes an item and signals `not_full`; `push` waits while the queue is at capacity, adds an item and signals `not_empty`. The tests start a consumer on an empty queue and a producer on a full one and check that each really blocks, which is the property a plain `Queue` does not have.
lessons.challenge: In src/bq.ml, `pop` raises on an empty queue and `push` ignores the capacity. Make both block: guard the queue with a mutex, add `not_empty` and `not_full` conditions, wait in `while` loops, and signal after every change.
lessons.question: Why wait on a Condition inside a `while` loop and not an `if`?
options: A while loop makes the wait shorter
Condition.wait returns immediately unless it is in a loop
A thread can wake up when the condition is no longer true, so it must recheck before proceeding
lessons.explanation: Another thread may have consumed the item between the signal and the wakeup, so the predicate has to be tested again after every wake.
lessons.workedExample: Another thread may have consumed the item between the signal and the wakeup, so the predicate has to be tested again after every wake.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Another thread may have consumed the item between the signal and the wakeup, so the predicate has to be tested again after every wake.

(* TODO: a bounded BLOCKING queue. Protect the queue with a mutex and use two
   conditions: pop waits while the queue is empty, push waits while it is at

let create capacity = { items = Queue.create (); capacity }
let push q x = Queue.add x q.items
let pop q = match Queue.take_opt q.items with Some x -> x | None -> failwith "empty"

lessons.title: Dynlink: loading plug-ins at run time
body: A program normally contains every module it will ever run. The `dynlink` library lets a native program load compiled code *while it is running*: `Dynlink.loadfile "plugin.cmxs"` links a shared object (`.cmxs`) built with `ocamlopt -shared`, runs its top-level code, and adds its modules to the program. The host and the plug-in must agree on the interfaces they share, which the loader checks with module checksums.

The usual design is a small *registry* library that both sides link. The host loads whatever plug-in the user names; each plug-in's top-level code calls `Registry.register name f`, and the host then finds the new entries in the registry. Because the plug-in only depends on the registry's interface, new behaviour is added without recompiling or even restarting the host. Dune builds the shared object for a library with the target `plugins/double.cmxs`.

Loading code is a trust decision: a plug-in runs with the full privileges of the host, so load only code you control. Handle `Dynlink.Error` and report it, since a missing file, a wrong compiler version or an interface mismatch are all normal failure modes.

lessons.title: Runtime events: tracing the garbage collector from inside the program
body: OCaml 5's runtime can record what it is doing, such as the start and end of each garbage-collection phase, into a ring buffer with very low overhead. The `Runtime_events` library starts that recording and reads it back: `Runtime_events.start ()` begins tracing, `create_cursor None` opens a cursor on this process's own buffer, and `read_poll cursor callbacks None` calls your callbacks for each event that has been written since the last poll.

Callbacks are built with `Runtime_events.Callbacks.create`, with an optional function for each kind of event: `~runtime_begin` and `~runtime_end` for runtime phases, `~runtime_counter` for counters, and `~lifecycle` for domain events. A callback receives the domain id, a timestamp and the phase, so it can both count events and time them. External tools such as `olly` read the same buffer from outside a running program, with no change to its code.

Tracing answers questions that guessing cannot: how many collections did this function cause, and how long did the pauses last? Because the buffer is a fixed-size ring, a program that produces events faster than they are read overwrites the oldest ones, so poll often enough and treat a count as a lower bound.
lessons.challenge: `Tracing.count_gc_events` returns 0 without tracing anything. Implement it: start the runtime events, create a cursor on this process, register a `runtime_begin` callback that counts phases, force a full major collection with `Gc.full_major ()`, poll the cursor once, free it and return the count.
lessons.question: Why is the number of events a lower bound rather than an exact count?
options: The events live in a fixed-size ring buffer, so a slow reader can miss events that were overwritten
Events are only recorded for the main domain
The runtime records every other event to save time
lessons.explanation: A ring buffer favours recent events; if the writer laps the reader, the oldest unread events are lost.
lessons.workedExample: A ring buffer favours recent events; if the writer laps the reader, the oldest unread events are lost.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A ring buffer favours recent events; if the writer laps the reader, the oldest unread events are lost.

lessons.title: The toplevel as a script runner, ocamldep and ocamldoc
body: The `ocaml` command is not only an interactive prompt. Given a file, it reads the file as a script and runs it, evaluating each top-level phrase in order, so `ocaml script.ml` is a quick way to try an idea without a build. Inside a script, directives start with `#`: `#use "file.ml"` loads another source file as if it had been typed in (the path is resolved relative to the script's own directory), and `#load` and `#require` bring in compiled units and libraries. A type error in a script stops it with a non-zero exit code, exactly as a compiler would.

`ocamldep` reads source files and prints the modules each one refers to. `ocamldep -modules a.ml` lists the dependencies of one file, and `ocamldep -sort a.ml b.ml` orders files so that every file comes after the ones it depends on, which is the order in which they must be compiled and linked. Build systems such as Dune run this for you, but the tool is useful when you debug a dependency cycle or write a Makefile by hand.

`ocamldoc` generates HTML documentation from the special comments `(** ... *)`. It is the older tool: new projects normally use `odoc` through `dune build @doc`, as in the packaging lesson, because `odoc` understands modern language features and cross-package links. Knowing both is useful when you meet an older code base that still builds its documentation with `ocamldoc`.

The compiled bytecode of both files
The files reordered so each one comes after the files it depends on

lessons.title: Debugging and profiling: backtraces, ocamldebug and ocamlprof
body: When an exception escapes, the most useful fact is where it was raised. OCaml can record a *backtrace*, the chain of calls that led to the raise, but only while recording is on: set the environment variable `OCAMLRUNPARAM=b` or call `Printexc.record_backtrace true` early in the program. Then `Printexc.get_backtrace ()` returns the trace as a string with a file and line for each frame. If recording is off, the trace is simply empty, which is the bug in the starter.

Source locations also depend on how the code was compiled. For *bytecode*, `ocamlc` must be given `-g`: without it every frame reads `Called from unknown location`, which this project checks. The compiler's help lists `-g` as the way to record debugging information, and you should pass it in any build you intend to debug. On the 5.5.1 native compiler used for this guide, the same example printed locations even without `-g`, so treat `-g` as required for bytecode and as the safe spelling for native code rather than relying on that behaviour.

Two classic tools complement backtraces. `ocamldebug` is a time-travel debugger for bytecode: you set breakpoints, step, inspect values and go backwards, which works because bytecode execution can be replayed from checkpoints. For native programs you use the system debugger, `gdb` on Linux or `lldb` on macOS. Both are interactive, so they are learnt by using them; this project checks the non-interactive part. `ocamlcp` builds bytecode that counts how often each part of the code runs, and after one run `ocamlprof` prints the source annotated with the counts.

The bytecode was compiled without -g, so it carries no source locations

lessons.title: Merlin: how editors understand OCaml
body: Editor support for OCaml, such as error squiggles, type-on-hover and jump-to-definition, comes from Merlin. `ocamlmerlin` is a small server that holds a parsed and typed view of a file and answers queries about it. An editor plug-in sends a query, with the buffer on standard input, and receives JSON, so any editor can use it by speaking the same protocol.

You can speak the protocol yourself. `ocamlmerlin single errors -filename example/bad.ml < example/bad.ml` type-checks the buffer and reports each error with its position and message; an empty list means the file is fine. `type-enclosing -position 1:4` asks for the type at a position, which is what powers hover. Merlin reads the project's build settings from a configuration, which Dune generates for you with `dune ocaml merlin dump-config`, so the editor sees the same libraries and flags as the build.

Together with `dune` (build), `opam` (packages), `ocamlformat` (layout), `odoc` (documentation) and `utop` (a better toplevel), Merlin makes up the *OCaml Platform* that the Real World OCaml chapter describes. When your editor shows no information, run Merlin by hand: an error here usually points to a missing library in the build file or a file that Dune does not know about.

It links the Merlin library into the editor and calls it directly

lessons.title: Build variants: flambda, fuzzing and ThreadSanitizer
body: An OCaml compiler can be built in several variants, chosen when the compiler is installed and visible in `ocamlopt -config`. *Flambda* is an optimising middle end: with it, `-O2` and `-O3` enable aggressive inlining and specialisation, and attributes such as `[@inline always]`, `[@inlined always]`, `[@specialise]` and `[@unrolled n]` become instructions the compiler follows. Without flambda the same flags and attributes are accepted and the classic inliner is used, so portable code can carry them safely. Flambda changes speed, never meaning.

*Fuzzing* with `afl-fuzz` feeds a program thousands of mutated inputs and watches which code paths they reach. A program built with `-afl-instrument` reports its coverage to the fuzzer, which steers the inputs toward new paths and records the ones that crash it. It finds parser and decoder bugs that hand-written tests miss. *ThreadSanitizer* (TSan) is a runtime that detects data races in OCaml 5 programs that use domains or threads: it reports the two conflicting accesses with their stacks, at the cost of a large slowdown.

These variants are installed as separate opam switches, for example with the `ocaml-option-flambda`, `ocaml-option-afl` and `ocaml-option-tsan` packages, and the build you are using tells you what it has. The switch used to validate this guide reports `flambda: false`, `afl_instrument: false` and `tsan: false`, so this lesson describes the variants and exercises only what behaves identically everywhere: the attributes, and the `Sys` functions that report the runtime in use.

(* 1. last_two: the final two elements of a list, if there are at least two. *)
let rec last_two = function [] | [ _ ] -> None | [ a; b ] -> Some (a, b) | _ :: rest -> last_two rest

(* 2. compress: remove adjacent duplicates. *)
let rec compress = function a :: (b :: _ as rest) -> if a = b then compress rest else a :: compress rest | l -> l

(* 3. run-length encoding as (count, element) pairs. *)
let encode l =
  let rec go acc = function
    | [] -> List.rev acc
    | x :: rest -> (
        match acc with
        | (n, y) :: acc' when y = x -> go ((n + 1, y) :: acc') rest
        | _ -> go ((1, x) :: acc) rest)
  in
  go [] l

(* 4. a student record and its average, as an option for the empty case. *)
type student = { name : string; marks : int list }

let average s =
  match s.marks with [] -> None | ms -> Some (float_of_int (List.fold_left ( + ) 0 ms) /. float_of_int (List.length ms))

let area = function Circle r -> 3.0 *. r *. r | Rect (w, h) -> w *. h | Square s -> s *. s

body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Modules" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check what the signature hides: a client must not be able to build a queue or look inside a set except through the exported functions.
lessons.code:
module type QUEUE = sig
  type 'a t

  val empty : 'a t
  val enqueue : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val dequeue : 'a t -> ('a * 'a t) option
  val size : 'a t -> int
end

module TwoListQueue : QUEUE = struct
  type 'a t = { front : 'a list; back : 'a list }

  let empty = { front = []; back = [] }
  let enqueue x q = { q with back = x :: q.back }

  let dequeue q =
    match q.front with
    | x :: front -> Some (x, { q with front })
    | [] -> (
        match List.rev q.back with [] -> None | x :: front -> Some (x, { front; back = [] }))

  let size q = List.length q.front + List.length q.back
end

(* A functor taking any ordered type and returning a sorted-unique set. *)
module type ORDERED = sig
  type t

  val compare : t -> t -> int
end

module MakeSortedSet (O : ORDERED) = struct
  type elt = O.t
  type t = elt list

  let empty = []

  let rec add x = function
    | [] -> [ x ]
    | y :: rest as l ->
        let c = O.compare x y in
        if c = 0 then l else if c < 0 then x :: l else y :: add x rest

  let to_list s = s
end

module IntSet = MakeSortedSet (Int)
module StringSet = MakeSortedSet (String)

let () =
  let q = TwoListQueue.(empty |> enqueue 1 |> enqueue 2 |> enqueue 3) in
  (match TwoListQueue.dequeue q with
   | Some (x, rest) -> Printf.printf "%d %d\n" x (TwoListQueue.size rest)
   | None -> print_endline "empty");
  print_endline (String.concat "," (List.map string_of_int (IntSet.to_list (List.fold_left (fun s x -> IntSet.add x s) IntSet.empty [ 3; 1; 2; 3; 1 ]))));
  print_endline (String.concat "," (StringSet.to_list (List.fold_left (fun s x -> StringSet.add x s) StringSet.empty [ "pear"; "apple"; "pear" ])))

module type QUEUE = sig
  type 'a t

  val empty : 'a t
  val enqueue : 'a -> 'a t -> 'a t
  val peek : 'a t -> 'a option
end

module Q : QUEUE = struct
  type 'a t = { front : 'a list; back : 'a list }

  let empty = { front = []; back = [] }
  let enqueue x q = { q with back = x :: q.back }

  let peek q =
    match q.front with x :: _ -> Some x | [] -> (match List.rev q.back with x :: _ -> Some x | [] -> None)
end

let () = match Q.(empty |> enqueue 7 |> enqueue 8 |> peek) with Some n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n | None -> print_endline "empty"

body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Data structures" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Check the invariant after every operation: a binary search tree stays ordered, and the two-stack queue pops in first-in first-out order.
lessons.solution:
type tree = Leaf | Node of tree * int * tree

let rec insert x = function
  | Leaf -> Node (Leaf, x, Leaf)
  | Node (l, v, r) as t -> if x < v then Node (insert x l, v, r) else if x > v then Node (l, v, insert x r) else t

let rec delete_min = function Leaf -> Leaf | Node (Leaf, _, r) -> r | Node (l, v, r) -> Node (delete_min l, v, r)
let rec inorder = function Leaf -> [] | Node (l, v, r) -> inorder l @ [ v ] @ inorder r

let () =
  let t = List.fold_left (fun t x -> insert x t) Leaf [ 5; 3; 8; 1 ] in
  print_endline (String.concat "," (List.map string_of_int (inorder (delete_min t))))

lessons.title: Practice: extending a small interpreter
body: This is a set of original exercises for the "Interpreters" chapter of the CS 3110 textbook. They practise the same skills as that chapter without reproducing its exercises. Each exercise has a specification, and the program below contains one worked answer for each, with its output printed so you can check your own version against it.

Work in this order: read the specification, write your own solution without looking, run it on the examples, then compare with the worked answer. If they disagree, find the smallest input where they differ, because that input usually exposes a misread specification or a missing case.
Check evaluation order: the right side of a short-circuit operator must not run when the left side decides the answer, and unbound names must fail cleanly.
lessons.code:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Le of expr * expr
  | Not of expr
  | And of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | VBool of bool

let rec eval env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Bool b -> VBool b
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (match (eval env a, eval env b) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Le (a, b) -> (match (eval env a, eval env b) with VInt x, VInt y -> VBool (x <= y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Not e -> (match eval env e with VBool b -> VBool (not b) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | And (a, b) -> (
      (* short-circuit: the right side is not evaluated when the left is false *)
      match eval env a with VBool false -> VBool false | VBool true -> eval env b | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | If (c, t, e) -> (match eval env c with VBool true -> eval env t | VBool false -> eval env e | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval ((x, eval env e1) :: env) e2

let show = function VInt n -> string_of_int n | VBool b -> string_of_bool b

let () =
  let run e = try show (eval [] e) with Failure m -> m | Not_found -> "unbound" in
  print_endline (run (Let ("x", Int 5, If (Le (Var "x", Int 10), Add (Var "x", Int 1), Int 0))));
  print_endline (run (Not (Le (Int 3, Int 2))));
  print_endline (run (And (Bool false, Var "never_evaluated")));
  print_endline (run (And (Bool true, Bool true)));
  print_endline (run (Add (Int 1, Bool true)));
  print_endline (run (Var "y"))
lessons.solution:
type expr = Bool of bool | Var of string | Or of expr * expr
type value = VBool of bool

let rec eval env = function
  | Bool b -> VBool b
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Or (a, b) -> (
      match eval env a with
      | VBool true -> VBool true
      | VBool false -> eval env b)

let () = match eval [] (Or (Bool true, Var "unused")) with VBool b -> Printf.printf "%b\n" b
lessons.challenge: Write a tiny evaluator for booleans and variables with an `Or` constructor that short-circuits, and print the value of `Or (Bool true, Var "unused")`.
lessons.question: Why must `And` evaluate its right operand only after checking the left?
options: To make evaluation parallel
To short-circuit: if the left side is false the right side must not run, which matters for errors and effects
Because the right side is always a variable
lessons.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation is part of the meaning of and/or, so the interpreter has to evaluate lazily on the right.

true
false
true
type error

lessons.title: Asking Lean questions: #eval, #check, #print
body: A Lean file is a list of commands that Lean reads from top to bottom. The three commands you will use every day are questions you put to the compiler. `#eval` asks "what value does this expression compute?", `#check` asks "what type does this expression have?", and `#print` asks "how was this name defined?". None of them change your program; they only report back, and the answer appears in your editor's info panel or in the terminal if you run `lean File.lean`.

Try arithmetic first. `#eval 2 + 3 * 4` prints `14` because multiplication binds tighter than addition, exactly as in school maths. Text works too: `"Lean" ++ " 4"` glues two strings together. Division of natural numbers throws away the remainder (`10 / 3` is `3`) and `%` gives the remainder (`10 % 3` is `1`). Every value in Lean has a type, and numbers written without a decimal point default to `Nat`, the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on.

`#check` is how you learn what something is without running it. `#check 2 + 3` answers `2 + 3 : Nat`, which you read as "the expression `2 + 3` has type `Nat`". Types are themselves things you can check: `#check Nat` answers `Nat : Type`, and `#check Type` answers `Type : Type 1`, a first hint that types live in a tower of universes. When you meet an unfamiliar function in a library, `#check` on its name is usually the fastest documentation.

`#print` shows a definition. `#print Nat` reveals that `Nat` is an inductive type with exactly two constructors, `Nat.zero` and `Nat.succ`: every natural number is either zero or the successor of a smaller one. You will lean on that fact when we write recursive functions. Comments help you leave notes for yourself: `--` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line, and `/- ... -/` wraps a comment that can span many lines.

What to check: if `#eval` prints something surprising, run `#check` on the same expression first, because the type usually explains it (for example `10 / 3` is `Nat` division, not a decimal). A common beginner mistake is forgetting that every command must start at the left margin; an indented `#eval` is treated as a continuation of the previous command and produces a confusing parse error.
lessons.code:
-- A line comment: Lean ignores everything after the two dashes.
/- A block comment
   can span several lines. -/
#eval 2 + 3 * 4
#eval "Lean" ++ " 4"
#eval 10 / 3
#eval 10 % 3
#check 2 + 3
#check "hi"
#check Nat
#check Type
#print Nat
lessons.solution:
-- Practise the three questions Lean can answer.
#eval (7 + 5) * 2
#eval "Hello" ++ " " ++ "World"
#check "Hello".length
#eval "Hello".length

lessons.title: Names, definitions and the basic types
body: `def` gives a name to a value. In `def answer : Nat := 42` the pieces are: the keyword `def`, the name `answer`, a colon followed by the type `Nat`, then `:=` and the value. The type annotation after the colon is usually optional because Lean can infer it, but writing it is good habit: it documents your intent, and when the value does not match you get an error pointing at the right place instead of a mysterious one three lines later.

Four types cover most beginner programs. `Nat` holds non-negative whole numbers, `Int` holds whole numbers that may be negative, `String` holds text in double quotes, and `Bool` holds `true` or `false`. There is also `Float` for decimals such as `0.5`. They do not mix automatically: Lean will not quietly add a `Nat` to a `String`, which is one of the main ways it prevents bugs.

The most famous trap is that `Nat` subtraction cannot go below zero. `3 - 5` evaluates to `0`, because there is no natural number smaller than zero, so Lean stops at the floor. If you want `-2` you must say you are working with integers, for example `(3 : Int) - 5`. The expression `(3 : Int)` is a type ascription: it tells Lean to read the literal `3` as an `Int`. Mixing `Nat` and `Int` works when you ascribe the target type, as in `(answer : Int) + temperature`, because Lean inserts a coercion that turns the `Nat` into an `Int`.

Booleans combine with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not). Comparisons such as `3 < 5` produce truth values that `#eval` can display, and `==` tests equality of two values. Strings have helper functions you call with a dot: `greeting.length` is the number of characters. The dot form is just a neater way to write `String.length greeting`; Lean finds the function by looking at the type of the thing to the left of the dot.

What to check: when a definition fails with `type mismatch`, read the two types in the message, the one Lean expected and the one you supplied, and fix whichever is wrong. A frequent mistake is writing `def x : Nat := -3`; negative literals need `Int`. Remember also that `Nat` subtraction silently truncates at zero rather than raising an error.
lessons.code:
def greeting : String := "Hello, Lean"
def answer : Nat := 42
def temperature : Int := -7
def isReady : Bool := true

#eval greeting
#eval greeting.length
#eval answer
#eval temperature
#eval isReady && !false
#eval 3 - 5
#eval (3 : Int) - 5
#eval (answer : Int) + temperature
#eval 3 < 5
#eval answer == 42
#check temperature
lessons.solution:
def price : Nat := 120
def discount : Nat := 150
def owed : Int := (price : Int) - (discount : Int)
def isFree : Bool := price <= discount

#eval owed
#eval isFree
#eval price - discount

lessons.title: Functions, application and currying
body: A function takes arguments and returns a result. You write `def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n * 2`: the parameter `n` has a type in parentheses, then a colon and the result type, then the body. To call it you put the arguments after the name separated by spaces, with no brackets and no commas: `double 21`. Parentheses are only for grouping, so `double (add 1 2)` means "first compute `add 1 2`, then double it".

Several parameters of the same type can share one annotation, as in `def add (a b : Nat) : Nat := a + b`. Underneath, Lean has only one-argument functions. `add` really has type `Nat → Nat → Nat`, which reads as `Nat → (Nat → Nat)`: give it a number and you get back another function that is waiting for the second number. This is called currying, and it means that `add 3` is a perfectly good value, a function that adds three. We use that to define `addThree : Nat → Nat := add 3`.

Functions are values, so you can write one without naming it by using `fun`. `fun x => x * x` is a nameless squaring function, and `(fun x => x * x) 9` applies it immediately. You will see anonymous functions constantly with list operations later. A shorthand for the common case is `(· * 2)`, where the centred dot marks the missing argument.

Deeply nested parentheses get hard to read, so Lean offers two small operators. `f <| x` means `f x` but lets you drop the closing bracket: `double <| add 1 2`. The pipeline `x |> f` reads left to right, so `add 1 2 |> double` first computes the sum, then doubles it. `#check add` shows `add (a b : Nat) : Nat`, and `#check add 2` shows `add 2 : Nat → Nat`, a partially applied function whose type tells you it still needs one `Nat`.

What to check: in `double add 1 2` Lean reads three arguments given to `double` and complains that `double` is applied to too many arguments, or that `add` is not a `Nat`. Whenever an argument is itself a call, put it in parentheses or use `<|`. If the error mentions a function type like `Nat → Nat` where you expected `Nat`, you probably forgot an argument.
lessons.code:
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n * 2
def add (a b : Nat) : Nat := a + b
def addThree : Nat → Nat := add 3

#eval double 21
#eval add 2 3
#eval addThree 10
#check add
#check add 2
#check fun (x : Nat) => x + 1
#eval (fun x => x * x) 9
#eval double (add 1 2)
#eval double <| add 1 2
#eval add 1 2 |> double
lessons.solution:
def area (w h : Nat) : Nat := w * h
def areaOfWidthFive : Nat → Nat := area 5
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n * 2

#eval area 3 4
#eval areaOfWidthFive 6
#check area 5
#eval double (area 2 3)

lessons.title: Local names, namespaces, sections and open
body: As soon as a definition does more than one step you want to name intermediate results. `let a2 := a * a` introduces a local name that lives only inside the rest of the expression, and each `let` goes on its own line, followed by the final expression. The type is inferred, but you may add one: `let a2 : Nat := a * a`. Local names make the code read like a recipe and avoid repeating long expressions.

`where` attaches helper definitions to the end of a function. In `def circleLike (r : Nat) : Nat := 3 * sq r` followed by `where sq (x : Nat) : Nat := x * x`, the helper `sq` is used in the body but declared afterwards, which keeps the main idea at the top. The helper is a real definition with the full name `circleLike.sq`, so you can test it with `#eval circleLike.sq 6` from outside.

Names are organised with namespaces. Everything declared between `namespace Shapes` and `end Shapes` gets the prefix `Shapes.`, so inside the block you write `square` but outside you write `Shapes.square`. This is how the library keeps `List.length` and `String.length` apart. If you grow tired of the prefix, `open Shapes` makes the names available unqualified for the rest of the file, and `open Shapes in` followed by a command limits that effect to one command.

A `section` is a scope that is not a namespace, mainly used for shared `variable` declarations. After `variable (taxPercent : Nat)`, every definition inside the section that mentions `taxPercent` automatically takes it as its first argument, so `withTax` has type `Nat → Nat → Nat`. When the section ends, the variable disappears. Sections and namespaces can be nested, and you can even give them names so mistakes in closing them are caught.

What to check: the name after `end` must match the `namespace` or `section` it closes, otherwise Lean reports an invalid `end`. If you see `unknown identifier 'square'` outside the namespace, either write `Shapes.square` or add `open Shapes`. Remember that a `variable` only becomes a parameter of definitions that actually use it; check the argument order with `#check`.
lessons.code:
def hypotenuseSq (a b : Nat) : Nat :=
  let a2 := a * a
  let b2 := b * b
  a2 + b2

def circleLike (r : Nat) : Nat := 3 * sq r
where
  sq (x : Nat) : Nat := x * x

namespace Shapes
def square (s : Nat) : Nat := s * s
def rect (w h : Nat) : Nat := w * h
end Shapes

section Pricing
variable (taxPercent : Nat)
def withTax (price : Nat) : Nat := price + price * taxPercent / 100
end Pricing

#eval hypotenuseSq 3 4
#eval circleLike 5
#eval circleLike.sq 6
#eval Shapes.square 4
open Shapes in
#eval rect 2 3
#check withTax
#eval withTax 10 200
lessons.solution:
namespace Temp
def toFahrenheit (c : Nat) : Nat := c * 9 / 5 + 32

def describe (c : Nat) : String :=
  let f := toFahrenheit c
  s!"{c}C is {f}F"
end Temp

open Temp in
#eval describe 100
#eval Temp.toFahrenheit 0

Outside the namespace, use `open Temp in` to print `describe 100` and print `Temp.toFahrenheit 0` with its full name.
lessons.question: After `variable (taxPercent : Nat)` in a section, what happens to a definition `withTax (price : Nat)` whose body uses `taxPercent`?
options: `taxPercent` becomes the last parameter, after price
`taxPercent` becomes its first parameter, so the type is `Nat → Nat → Nat`

lessons.title: Lists, pairs and looking things up safely
body: A `List α` is an ordered sequence of values that all have the same type `α`. You write one with square brackets: `[2, 3, 5, 7]` has type `List Nat`. The empty list is `[]`, and because it carries no values you often need a type annotation such as `([] : List Nat)` so Lean knows what the list would hold. Lists are the workhorse data structure of functional programming and the first example of a type that is built from another type.

Under the hood a list is either empty or a head element consed onto a tail, and `::` is the cons operator: `1 :: [2, 3]` is `[1, 2, 3]`. Adding to the front with `::` is cheap, while `++` appends two whole lists. The functions `length`, `reverse` and `sum` do what their names say. None of them modifies the original list; Lean values never change in place, they produce new values.

Getting a single element deserves care because the list might be too short. `xs.head?` returns an `Option`: `some 2` when there is a first element and `none` when the list is empty. The bracket forms follow the same idea: `xs[10]?` safely gives `none` for an index that is too large, whereas `xs[2]!` insists the index is valid and panics at run time (printing a message and a default value) if it is not. Prefer the question-mark forms in code you care about.

A pair groups two possibly different types: `(1, "one")` has type `Nat × String`, and you take it apart with `.fst` and `.snd`. Pairs make it easy to return two results from one function. Tuples with more components are nested pairs written the same way. You will see `Option` properly in the next stage; for now read `some x` as "there is a value x" and `none` as "there is nothing".

What to check: all elements of a list must share one type, so `[1, "two"]` is rejected with a type mismatch message. Another classic slip is writing `primes.length()` with brackets; in Lean the dot-call takes no empty parentheses, just `primes.length`. When unsure whether an index is safe, use `?` and handle the `none` case.
lessons.code:
def primes : List Nat := [2, 3, 5, 7]

#eval primes
#eval 1 :: primes
#eval primes ++ [11]
#eval primes.length
#eval primes.reverse
#eval primes.sum
#eval primes.head?
#eval ([] : List Nat).head?
#eval primes[2]!
#eval primes[10]?
#eval List.range 5
#check primes
#eval (1, "one").fst
#eval (1, "one").snd
#check (1, "one")
lessons.solution:
def evens : List Nat := [2, 4, 6]
def odds : List Nat := [1, 3, 5]
def both : List Nat := evens ++ odds

#eval both
#eval both.length
#eval both[7]?
#eval (evens.length, odds.sum)

lessons.title: Files, projects and reading error messages
body: A Lean source file ends in `.lean`. For experiments you can run `lean Hello.lean` directly: it checks the file, prints the output of every `#eval`, and reports errors. For anything bigger you create a project with Lake, Lean's build tool: `lake new hello` makes a folder holding `lakefile.toml` (the package description), `lean-toolchain` (the exact Lean version), `Main.lean` (the program entry point), and a library folder such as `Hello/` with `Hello.lean` and `Hello/Basic.lean`. `lake build` compiles it and `lake exe hello` runs it.

A runnable program defines `def main : IO Unit`, a value of type "input/output action returning nothing". Inside a `do` block each line is one step, so `IO.println "..."` prints a line. String interpolation `s!"2 + 2 = {2 + 2}"` splices computed values into text. In a scratch file you can test `main` with `#eval main`, which runs the action while the file is being checked.

Errors are the compiler talking to you, and they follow a pattern: a position (file, line, column), a severity (`error` or `warning`), and a message that often shows an expected type and an actual type. Read the first error first, since later ones are frequently fallout from it. The message `Type mismatch` followed by the term and its type tells you precisely which value did not fit. `Unknown identifier` means a name is misspelled or not in scope, perhaps because you forgot a namespace or `open`.

A neat tool for practising errors is `#guard_msgs`. Write a doc comment with the expected message immediately before `#guard_msgs in` and the command; Lean compares the real message with your text and complains only if they differ. That lets a lesson file contain a deliberate error and still compile, and in your own projects it turns messages into regression tests. The messages shown in the lesson below were produced by the compiler itself.

What to check: the position `file:line:column` points where Lean noticed the problem, which can be one token after the real cause, so look just before it too. Another common slip is mixed indentation in a `do` block, which produces a parse error about an unexpected token. If a project will not build, check that the version in `lean-toolchain` matches the Lean you installed.
lessons.code:
def main : IO Unit := do
  IO.println "Hello from main"
  IO.println s!"2 + 2 = {2 + 2}"

#eval main

/-- error: Type mismatch
  "text"
has type
  String
but is expected to have type
  Nat
-/
#guard_msgs in
def bad : Nat := "text"

/-- error: Unknown identifier `colour` -/
#guard_msgs in
#eval colour + 1
lessons.solution:
def main : IO Unit := do
  IO.println "Lean is fun"
  IO.println s!"6 * 7 = {6 * 7}"

#eval main

/-- error: Unknown identifier `undefinedName` -/
#guard_msgs in
#eval undefinedName
lessons.challenge: Write `def main : IO Unit` that prints two lines: "Lean is fun" and the interpolated text "6 * 7 = 42" where 42 is computed by `6 * 7` inside the string. Run it with `#eval main`. Then use `#guard_msgs` to capture the error Lean reports for `#eval undefinedName`; copy the expected text from the compiler diagnostics.
lessons.question: In what order should you usually read a list of several compiler errors?
options: Start with the first error, because later ones are often caused by it
Start with the last error, because it is the most recent
Start with the longest message, because it has the most detail
Ignore errors and fix warnings first
lessons.explanation: Lean continues after an error, so one wrong definition can trigger many later complaints; fixing the first often clears the rest. The output shows `Hello from main` and `2 + 2 = 4` from running `main`, while the two intentional errors are absorbed silently by `#guard_msgs`, proving the expected text matches the compiler exactly.

lessons.title: Structures: records with named fields
body: A `structure` bundles several named values into one new type. `structure Point where x : Nat  y : Nat` declares a type `Point` whose values carry an `x` and a `y`. Lean generates a constructor `Point.mk`, one accessor function per field (`Point.x` and `Point.y`), and everything else in this lesson is built on top of those. Reach for a structure whenever you catch yourself passing the same two or three loose values around together.

There are three ways to build a value. The braces form `{ x := 3, y := 4 }` names every field and so is the most readable. The anonymous constructor `⟨3, 4⟩` (typed with `\<` and `\>`) lists the fields in order and is handy for small structures. Calling `Point.mk 3 4` works too. In each case Lean needs to know the expected type, so you normally write the definition with a type annotation such as `def p1 : Point := ...`.

Fields are read with dot notation: `p1.x`. Because values are immutable, "changing" a field means making a modified copy, which Lean spells `{ p1 with y := 10 }`. The result is a new `Point` that agrees with `p1` everywhere except `y`, while `p1` itself is untouched. This `with` form scales nicely to records with a dozen fields where you only want to alter one.

You may give fields default values, as in `retries : Nat := 3`, so that callers only mention what differs from the norm: `{ name := "demo" }` fills in the rest. Functions that belong to a type are conventionally placed in its namespace, so `def Point.add (a b : Point) : Point := ...` lets you call `p1.add p2`. The line `deriving Repr` asks Lean to generate a printer so that `#eval` can show a value; we study deriving properly in stage 3.

What to check: if you forget a field in braces and it has no default, Lean tells you the field is missing; if you add one that does not exist, it says the structure has no such field. Another trap is trying to assign with `p1.x := 5`, which is not Lean syntax. Always produce a new value with `with`. And if `#eval` complains it cannot show your structure, you simply forgot `deriving Repr`.
lessons.code:
structure Point where
  x : Nat
  y : Nat
deriving Repr

structure Config where
  name : String
  verbose : Bool := false
  retries : Nat := 3
deriving Repr

def p1 : Point := { x := 3, y := 4 }
def p2 : Point := ⟨1, 2⟩
def p3 : Point := Point.mk 10 20

def Point.add (a b : Point) : Point := { x := a.x + b.x, y := a.y + b.y }

#eval p1
#eval p1.x + p1.y
#eval { p1 with y := 10 }
#eval p1.add p2
#eval p3
#check Point.mk
#check @Point.x
#eval ({ name := "demo" } : Config)
#eval ({ name := "demo", retries := 5 } : Config)
lessons.solution:
structure Rect where
  width : Nat
  height : Nat
deriving Repr

def Rect.area (r : Rect) : Nat := r.width * r.height

structure Player where
  name : String
  score : Nat := 0
deriving Repr

def r1 : Rect := { width := 4, height := 5 }

#eval r1
#eval r1.area
#eval { r1 with height := 8 }.area
#eval ({ name := "Ada" } : Player)
lessons.challenge: Define a structure `Rect` with `width` and `height` fields (both `Nat`) deriving `Repr`, and a function `Rect.area` that multiplies them. Create a rectangle 4 by 5, print it and its area, then use the `with` syntax to build a copy whose height is 8 and print that copy's area. Finally define a `Player` structure with a `name : String`, a `score : Nat := 0` default, and print `{ name := "Ada" }`.
lessons.question: How do you get a copy of `p1` with only `y` changed to 10?
options: `p1.y := 10`, which updates the field in place
`Point.y p1 10`, because the accessor also sets the field
`p1 + { y := 10 }`, because structures can be added
`{ p1 with y := 10 }`, which builds a new value and leaves `p1` unchanged
lessons.explanation: Lean values are immutable, so updating means creating a new structure with the `with` syntax. The output shows `{ x := 3, y := 10 }` for the update while `p1` itself still prints `{ x := 3, y := 4 }`, and `{ name := "demo" }` is displayed with the defaults `verbose := false` and `retries := 3` filled in.

lessons.title: Inductive types and pattern matching
body: A structure says "a value has all of these fields". An `inductive` type says "a value is exactly one of these alternatives". `inductive Color where | red | green | blue` creates a type with three constructors, and every `Color` is one of them. When the alternatives carry data you list the arguments: `| circle (r : Nat)` and `| rect (w h : Nat)` make a `Shape` that is either a circle with a radius or a rectangle with two sides. This is the functional version of an enum combined with a union.

You take such values apart with pattern matching. A function defined by cases lists one arm per constructor: `| .red => .green`. The leading dot is shorthand that lets Lean fill in the namespace from the expected type, so `.red` means `Color.red`. For the shape you bind the data in the pattern, `| .circle r => 3 * r * r`, and the name `r` is available on the right of the arrow. Lean checks that your arms are exhaustive, covering every constructor, and tells you which case is missing if you leave one out; that check is one of the best reasons to prefer inductive types.

You can match on numbers too. `match n with | 0 => "zero" | 1 => "one" | _ => "many"` uses literals, and `_` is the wildcard that matches anything. Patterns can be nested and can inspect several values at once, e.g. `match a, b with | 0, _ => ...`. Arms are tried in order, so put specific patterns before general ones; a later arm that can never be reached is reported as redundant.

Constructor names live in the type's namespace, which is why `Color.next` can be called as `Color.red.next`: Lean sees that `Color.red` has type `Color` and looks for `Color.next`. Functions written as `def Color.next : Color → Color` followed by arms are shorthand for a function that immediately matches on its argument, with no need to name it.

What to check: a missing arm produces an error that begins with `Missing cases` and lists the unhandled pattern, such as `Color.blue`. Fix it by adding the arm, or deliberately use `_` if you want a default. A subtle mistake is forgetting the leading dot, which makes Lean search for a plain `red` in scope and report an unknown identifier.
lessons.code:
inductive Color where
  | red
  | green
  | blue
deriving Repr

def Color.next : Color → Color
  | .red => .green
  | .green => .blue
  | .blue => .red

inductive Shape where
  | circle (r : Nat)
  | rect (w h : Nat)
deriving Repr

def Shape.area : Shape → Nat
  | .circle r => 3 * r * r
  | .rect w h => w * h

def describe (n : Nat) : String :=
  match n with
  | 0 => "zero"
  | 1 => "one"
  | _ => "many"

#eval Color.red.next
#eval Color.blue.next.next
#eval (Shape.circle 2).area
#eval (Shape.rect 3 4).area
#eval Shape.rect 3 4
#eval describe 0
#eval describe 1
#eval describe 99
lessons.solution:
inductive Coin where
  | heads
  | tails
deriving Repr

def Coin.flip : Coin → Coin
  | .heads => .tails
  | .tails => .heads

inductive Vehicle where
  | bike
  | car (seats : Nat)
  | bus (seats : Nat) (stops : Nat)

def Vehicle.capacity : Vehicle → Nat
  | .bike => 1
  | .car seats => seats
  | .bus seats _ => seats

#eval Coin.heads.flip
#eval Vehicle.bike.capacity
#eval (Vehicle.car 4).capacity
#eval (Vehicle.bus 40 12).capacity
lessons.challenge: Define `inductive Coin where | heads | tails` deriving `Repr`, and a function `Coin.flip` that swaps the two. Then define `inductive Vehicle` with constructors `bike`, `car (seats : Nat)` and `bus (seats : Nat) (stops : Nat)`, and a function `Vehicle.capacity` returning 1 for a bike, the seats for a car, and the seats for a bus. Print `Coin.heads.flip`, and the capacity of one vehicle of each kind.
lessons.question: What does Lean do if a `match` on `Color` omits the `.blue` arm?
options: It reports an error listing the missing case, because matches must cover every constructor
It silently returns a default value for blue
It compiles and crashes only when blue is encountered at run time
It treats blue as red
lessons.explanation: Lean's exhaustiveness check rejects incomplete matches at compile time, so no value can fall through unhandled. The output shows `Color.green` for `Color.red.next`, `Color.green` for two steps from blue, areas 12 and 12 for the circle of radius 2 and the 3 by 4 rectangle, and the words "zero", "one" and "many" for the three literal cases.

lessons.title: Option and Except: values that might be missing or fail
body: Some functions cannot always produce an answer: dividing by zero, looking up a missing key, parsing text that is not a number. Instead of returning a magic value like -1 or crashing, Lean programs return `Option α`, which is either `none` or `some x` holding a value of type `α`. `safeDiv 10 0 : Option Nat` is `none`, `safeDiv 10 2` is `some 5`. Because the type says the answer may be absent, the compiler forces every caller to deal with that case.

You consume an `Option` with `match`, or with helpers. `opt.getD 0` means "the value, or 0 if there is none". `opt.map f` applies `f` inside the `some` and leaves `none` alone, so `(safeDiv 10 2).map (· + 1)` is `some 6`. When you need a chain of steps that each may fail, `do` notation is the clearest tool: `let x ← safeDiv a b` unwraps a `some`, and if any step yields `none` the whole block immediately becomes `none`. This replaces a ladder of nested matches.

`none` does not say why something failed. `Except ε α` carries either `Except.error e` with an explanation of type `ε`, or `Except.ok a` with a result. A parser can return `Except String Nat` and say `"not a number: abc"` or `"too old"`. The same `do` notation works: the first `error` aborts the block and is passed to the caller untouched. Choose `Option` when absence is self-explanatory and `Except` when the caller benefits from a message.

Both types are ordinary inductive types, so the pattern matching from the last lesson applies. `s.toNat?` is a library function that returns `Option Nat` and is the standard way to parse a number; the question mark in a name is a convention meaning "may fail, returns Option". The related `!` suffix means "panics on failure" and `getD` supplies a default.

What to check: the arrow `←` is only legal inside a `do` block, and the block's return type must be the same kind of container (`Option` or `Except`). If you see an error about a failure to synthesize `Monad` or a type mismatch involving `Option`, check that you wrapped the final result with `pure` or `some`. Do not unwrap with `!` unless you can prove the value is present.
lessons.code:
def safeDiv (a b : Nat) : Option Nat :=
  if b == 0 then none else some (a / b)

def addDivs (a b c : Nat) : Option Nat := do
  let x ← safeDiv a b
  let y ← safeDiv a c
  pure (x + y)

def parseAge (s : String) : Except String Nat :=
  match s.toNat? with
  | none => .error s!"not a number: {s}"
  | some n => if n > 150 then .error "too old" else .ok n

def ageNextYear (s : String) : Except String Nat := do
  let age ← parseAge s
  pure (age + 1)

#eval safeDiv 10 2
#eval safeDiv 10 0
#eval (safeDiv 10 0).getD 0
#eval (safeDiv 10 2).map (· + 1)
#eval addDivs 100 5 10
#eval addDivs 100 5 0
#eval parseAge "42"
#eval parseAge "abc"
#eval parseAge "200"
#eval ageNextYear "41"
#eval ageNextYear "x"
lessons.solution:
def safeSub (a b : Nat) : Option Nat :=
  if b > a then none else some (a - b)

def twoSteps (a b c : Nat) : Option Nat := do
  let first ← safeSub a b
  safeSub first c

#eval twoSteps 10 3 2
#eval twoSteps 10 3 20
#eval (safeSub 5 9).getD 0
lessons.challenge: Write `def safeSub (a b : Nat) : Option Nat` that returns `none` when `b > a` and `some (a - b)` otherwise. Then write `def twoSteps (a b c : Nat) : Option Nat` using `do` that computes `safeSub a b` and then subtracts `c` from that result with `safeSub`. Print `twoSteps 10 3 2`, `twoSteps 10 3 20` and `(safeSub 5 9).getD 0`.
lessons.question: What does a `do` block over `Option` return if one of its `←` steps produces `none`?
options: `none` for the whole block, skipping the remaining steps
It raises a run-time exception
It continues with the default value 0
It returns `some` of the previous step's value

The output shows `some 30` for `addDivs 100 5 10` (20 + 10) but `none` for `addDivs 100 5 0`, and `Except.error "not a number: abc"` versus `Except.ok 42` shows how Except keeps the failure reason.

lessons.title: Polymorphism and implicit arguments
body: A polymorphic definition works for many types at once. `List` is the model example: the same type constructor gives `List Nat`, `List String` and so on. You can write your own the same way. `structure Pair (α β : Type) where first : α  second : β` takes two type parameters, so `Pair Nat String` is a different type from `Pair String Nat`. The Greek letters are just conventional names for type variables; any identifier works.

A polymorphic function receives the types as arguments too. `def myId {α : Type} (a : α) : α := a` has a first parameter `α` whose braces mean "implicit": Lean works it out from the other arguments, so you write `myId 5` and `myId "x"`, not `myId Nat 5`. Braces are for things that can be inferred, parentheses are for things you must supply. `#check @myId` with an at-sign turns every implicit argument explicit and shows the full type `{α : Type} → α → α`.

Occasionally inference cannot decide, for example with `myId` applied to a numeric literal that could have several types. You can then give the implicit argument by name, `myId (α := String) "x"`, or annotate the expression `(5 : Int)`. Type parameters are not limited to `Type`; there are bigger universes written `Type u`, and library code uses `{α : Type u}` so that definitions also apply to types that themselves contain types. In everyday programs plain `Type` is enough.

Polymorphic functions can only use what all types share, which is why they are so predictable. `firstOr (xs : List α) (d : α) : α` can only return an element of the list or the default you passed in, because it knows nothing else about `α`. If you need more, such as comparing or printing, you add a requirement written in square brackets, which is the subject of stage 3.

What to check: the error `don't know how to synthesize implicit argument` means Lean could not infer a type, so add an annotation or a named argument. If you accidentally write a type parameter in parentheses, callers will have to pass the type by hand. And in a `structure` or `inductive` with parameters, remember the parameters appear in the type: write `Pair α β` in signatures, never just `Pair`.
lessons.code:
def myId {α : Type} (a : α) : α := a

structure Pair (α β : Type) where
  first : α
  second : β
deriving Repr

def Pair.swap {α β : Type} (p : Pair α β) : Pair β α :=
  { first := p.second, second := p.first }

def firstOr {α : Type} (xs : List α) (d : α) : α :=
  match xs with
  | [] => d

lessons.title: Recursion on data and why Lean checks termination
body: Lean has no `for` loops over mutable counters in pure code; repetition is expressed with recursion: a function defined in terms of itself on a smaller input. The shape mirrors the data. For `Nat` there are two cases, `0` and `n + 1`, so `sumTo` has two arms: `sumTo 0 = 0` and `sumTo (n + 1) = (n + 1) + sumTo n`. The recursive call is on `n`, which is strictly smaller than `n + 1`, so the computation must end.

This matters because every Lean function must terminate; otherwise one could 'prove' false statements with an endless loop. Lean therefore accepts only recursion it can show to shrink, most simply structural recursion, where the recursive call is on a piece of the argument obtained by pattern matching. The same pattern works for lists (`| [] => 0 | _ :: xs => 1 + length' xs`) and for your own inductive types such as a binary tree whose recursive calls are on the left and right subtrees.

A tree makes the idea concrete: `inductive Tree (α : Type) | leaf | node (left : Tree α) (value : α) (right : Tree α)`. Counting nodes calls itself on both children, and the two calls together still follow the structure of the data. Doubly recursive functions like `fib n + fib (n+1)` are fine for structural recursion but slow for large inputs because they recompute subresults; an accumulator version with a helper `go` runs in linear time.

When the argument does not shrink structurally, you can still convince Lean by naming a measure with `termination_by` and, if needed, proving the decrease. `def countdown (n : Nat) : List Nat := if h : n = 0 then [] else n :: countdown (n - 1)` with `termination_by n` and `decreasing_by omega` shows that `n - 1 < n` when `n ≠ 0`. You rarely need this at first, but you should recognise the message `fail to show termination` when it appears.

What to check: the error `fail to show termination` usually means the recursive call is not on a smaller piece, for instance `f n = f n` or a call on `n + 1`. Check that every recursive call is on a pattern variable from the match. Use `#eval` on a small input first and be careful with huge ones such as `fib 40`, which takes noticeable time with the doubly recursive definition.
lessons.code:
def sumTo : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => (n + 1) + sumTo n

def myLength {α : Type} : List α → Nat
  | [] => 0
  | _ :: xs => 1 + myLength xs

inductive Tree (α : Type) where
  | leaf
  | node (left : Tree α) (value : α) (right : Tree α)

def Tree.size {α : Type} : Tree α → Nat
  | .leaf => 0
  | .node l _ r => l.size + 1 + r.size

def fib : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => fib n + fib (n + 1)

def fibFast (n : Nat) : Nat := go n 0 1
where
  go : Nat → Nat → Nat → Nat
    | 0, a, _ => a
    | k + 1, a, b => go k b (a + b)

def countdown (n : Nat) : List Nat :=
  if h : n = 0 then [] else n :: countdown (n - 1)
termination_by n
decreasing_by omega

example : sumTo 3 = 6 := rfl

#eval sumTo 10
#eval myLength ["a", "b", "c"]
#eval (Tree.node (.node .leaf 1 .leaf) 2 .leaf).size
#eval fib 15
#eval fibFast 15
#eval fibFast 90
#eval countdown 5

  | leaf
  | node (left : Tree α) (value : α) (right : Tree α)

lessons.title: Working with collections: map, filter, foldl and Array
body: Instead of writing a recursive function for every task, Lean's List type ships with higher-order helpers that take a function as an argument. `xs.map f` makes a new list by applying `f` to each element, `xs.filter p` keeps the elements for which the test `p` returns `true`, and `xs.foldl f init` walks left to right combining elements into one result. With the shorthand `(· * 2)` or `fun x => ...` these often fit on a single line: `nums.map (· * 2)` doubles everything, `nums.filter (· % 2 == 0)` keeps even numbers, and `nums.foldl (· + ·) 0` adds them up.

Folds are worth understanding properly. `foldl f init [a, b, c]` computes `f (f (f init a) b) c`, starting on the left; `foldr` starts at the right and rebuilds the list structure, which is why `foldr (· :: ·) []` returns the list unchanged. The starting value is both the answer for an empty list and the type of the accumulator, so a fold can turn a list of numbers into a string or a pair, not just a number.

More helpers you will meet constantly: `take n` and `drop n` cut a list, `zip` pairs elements with those of another list and stops at the shorter one, `any` and `all` ask yes/no questions about the whole list, `find?` returns the first element passing a test as an `Option`, and `filterMap` combines a map with dropping the `none` results. These are all ordinary library functions; `#check @List.map` shows their types, which is the best way to remember what order the arguments come in.

An `Array` is the contiguous, growable cousin of `List`, written with a hash and brackets: `#[1, 2, 3]`. Reading by index is fast, `push` adds to the end, `size` is the length, and `map`, `filter` and `foldl` work almost identically. Use `List` when you build things by consing and pattern matching, and `Array` when you index or append a lot. `toArray` and `toList` convert between them. The library also offers `Array.qsort` for sorting with a comparison function.

What to check: with `foldl`, the function receives the accumulator first and the element second, so subtracting gives different answers from `foldr`. If `xs.filter (· > 2)` is rejected, remember `filter` wants a `Bool`-valued function, and `>` on numbers is converted automatically only when it is decidable. When indexing an array, `arr[i]!` panics out of range, so prefer `arr[i]?` for untrusted indices.

#eval nums.take 2

#eval nums.zip ["a", "b", "c"]
#eval nums.any (· > 5)
#eval nums.all (· > 1)
#eval nums.find? (· > 3)
