lessons.title: Axioms, #print axioms and classical reasoning
body: Lean's logic rests on a tiny set of assumptions beyond type theory itself: `propext` (propositions that are logically equivalent are equal), `Quot.sound` (related elements of a quotient become equal), and `Classical.choice` (a nonempty type has an element, with no recipe for finding it). The command `#print axioms thm` lists exactly which of them a proof relies on, following every lemma it used. It is how you audit a result.

Run the code and read the list. `two_plus_two` is proved by computation and depends on nothing. `le_or_gt` splits on `a ≤ b`; because `Nat` order is decidable, `by_cases` uses the decision procedure and the proof is axiom-free. `my_em` uses `Classical.em` and picks up all three axioms, since the classical machinery is built from them. `add_zero_left`, proved by `omega`, reports `[propext, Quot.sound]`: automation reasons by rewriting equivalent propositions and so touches `propext` even when the mathematics is constructive. That is harmless, but it is a reminder not to expect `omega` and `simp` proofs to be axiom-free.

Classical reasoning is where *non-computable content* appears. `pickBig` selects a witness using `Classical.choose`. Leaving off `noncomputable` yields `failed to compile definition, consider marking it as 'noncomputable' because it depends on 'Classical.choose'`. The theorem `pickBig_spec` about it uses only `[Classical.choice]`. There is no contradiction: theorems about existence are fine, but a program cannot return an element that it has no way to find.

The constructive alternative is the `Decidable` class. For decidable propositions Lean can compute which side holds, so `if n < 10 then ... else ...` runs, and `decide (3 ∣ 12)` evaluates to `true`. Double negation elimination shows the divide in the exercise: `dne_dec` for a decidable `p` is axiom-free, whereas `dne_classical` for arbitrary `p` needs `Classical.byContradiction`. Meanwhile `¬¬(p ∨ ¬p)` can be proved constructively for every `p`, which is a good sign that excluded middle is 'irrefutable but not provable' without the axiom.

Check: `#print axioms` lists what a theorem depends on, classical axioms enter through `Classical.em`, `by_contra` on arbitrary propositions and `Classical.choose`, and any definition built from `Classical.choose` must be `noncomputable`.
lessons.code:
-- 1. Pure computation: no axioms at all.
theorem two_plus_two : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
#print axioms two_plus_two

-- 2. A constructive proof about a decidable proposition: still no axioms.
theorem le_or_gt (a b : Nat) : a ≤ b ∨ b < a := by
  by_cases h : a ≤ b
  · exact Or.inl h
  · exact Or.inr (Nat.lt_of_not_le h)
#print axioms le_or_gt

-- 3. Excluded middle for an *arbitrary* proposition is where classical logic enters.
theorem my_em (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p := Classical.em p
#print axioms my_em

-- 4. Double negation elimination is equivalent to excluded middle.
theorem dne (p : Prop) (h : ¬¬p) : p := by
  by_cases hp : p
  · exact hp
  · exact absurd hp h
#print axioms dne

-- 5. `propext` shows up when a proof rewrites one proposition into another that is merely
--    equivalent, which `simp` and `omega` do routinely.
theorem add_zero_left (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by omega
#print axioms add_zero_left

-- 6. A *definition* that picks an element from `∃` cannot compute, so Lean makes you say so.
noncomputable def pickBig (h : ∃ n : Nat, n > 3) : Nat := Classical.choose h

theorem pickBig_spec (h : ∃ n : Nat, n > 3) : pickBig h > 3 := Classical.choose_spec h
#print axioms pickBig_spec

-- 7. Decidable instances give constructive case splits that actually compute.
def isSmall (n : Nat) : Bool := if n < 10 then true else false
#eval isSmall 3
#eval isSmall 30
#eval (decide (7 < 5), decide (3 ∣ 12))
lessons.solution:
-- Constructive: never needs excluded middle, even for arbitrary propositions.
theorem nn_em (p : Prop) : ¬¬(p ∨ ¬p) :=
  fun h => h (Or.inr (fun hp => h (Or.inl hp)))
#print axioms nn_em

theorem contra (p q : Prop) (hpq : p → q) (hnq : ¬q) : ¬p :=
  fun hp => hnq (hpq hp)
#print axioms contra

-- Double-negation elimination is fine when `p` is decidable; the instance replaces the axiom.
theorem dne_dec (p : Prop) [Decidable p] (h : ¬¬p) : p :=
  Decidable.byContradiction h
#print axioms dne_dec

-- The same statement for an arbitrary `p` needs the classical axiom.
theorem dne_classical (p : Prop) (h : ¬¬p) : p :=
  Classical.byContradiction h
#print axioms dne_classical
lessons.challenge: Prove `¬¬(p ∨ ¬p)` and the contrapositive `(p → q) → ¬q → ¬p` for arbitrary propositions without any axioms, prove double-negation elimination for a decidable `p` with `Decidable.byContradiction`, and print the axioms of each.
lessons.question: Why does a theorem proved with `Classical.em` report `Classical.choice` among its axioms?
options: Because `Classical.em` is declared with the `noncomputable` keyword and Lean lists it
Because `#print axioms` always lists all three axioms regardless of the proof
Excluded middle for arbitrary propositions is derived from choice (via `propext` and `Quot.sound` too), so they are all listed
Because every proof by contradiction secretly runs code

lessons.title: funext, propext and quotients
body: Function extensionality, `funext`, says two functions that agree at every input are equal. In many systems it must be assumed; in Lean it is a *theorem* derived from the quotient axiom, and `#print axioms funext` reports `[Quot.sound]`. In practice it turns the proof of `(fun n => n + n) = (fun n => 2 * n)` into a proof about one arbitrary `n`: `funext fun n => by omega`. `propext` does the same for propositions: logically equivalent statements are equal, so you may rewrite one into the other inside any context.

A *quotient* builds a new type by identifying elements. Start with a type and a setoid, which is an equivalence relation. Integers can be modelled as differences of naturals: the pair `(a, b)` stands for `a - b`, and `(a, b) ~ (c, d)` when `a + d = c + b`. So `(5, 2)` and `(7, 4)` both represent `3`. The `Setoid` instance packages the relation together with a proof that it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; here `omega` supplies the transitivity.

You can't pattern match on a quotient, because that would distinguish representatives. Instead, `Quotient.lift f h` defines a function out of the quotient from a function `f` on representatives plus a proof `h` that `f` gives the same answer on related inputs. Both `MyInt.neg` and `MyInt.toInt` do this; the obligation is stated as `p ≈ q`, which unfolds to our relation, so we restate it with `have h : p.1 + q.2 = q.1 + p.2 := h` and let `omega` finish. Lean refuses the definition if you cannot prove the function respects the relation, which is exactly the safeguard you want.

Equality of quotient elements comes from `Quotient.sound`: `MyInt.mk 5 2 = MyInt.mk 7 4` follows from the arithmetic fact `5 + 4 = 7 + 2`. The theorems `three_eq` and `MyInt.neg_neg` then list `[propext, Quot.sound]` under `#print axioms`, which is the price of using quotients. To prove a statement about every element of the quotient, use `Quotient.ind` (the `induction x using Quotient.ind` line), which reduces to the claim for an arbitrary pair; for `neg_neg`, the pair swaps twice and `rfl` closes it.

Check: use `Quotient.lift` only with a proof that the function respects the relation, use `Quotient.sound` to equate related representatives, and expect `Quot.sound` in the axiom list of anything built on quotients.
lessons.code:
-- funext: two functions that agree everywhere are equal. It is a theorem, derived from Quot.sound.
#check @funext
#print axioms funext

theorem double_eq_shift : (fun n : Nat => n + n) = (fun n => 2 * n) :=
  funext fun n => by omega

-- propext: logically equivalent propositions are equal.
#check @propext
#print axioms propext

-- Quotients: build a new type by forgetting differences.
-- Integers as differences a - b of naturals; (a, b) and (c, d) name the same integer
-- exactly when a + d = c + b.
def sameInt (p q : Nat × Nat) : Prop := p.1 + q.2 = q.1 + p.2

instance intSetoid : Setoid (Nat × Nat) where
  r := sameInt
  iseqv := {
    refl := fun _ => rfl
    symm := fun h => h.symm
    trans := fun {p q r} h1 h2 => by unfold sameInt at *; omega
  }

def MyInt := Quotient intSetoid

def MyInt.mk (a b : Nat) : MyInt := Quotient.mk intSetoid (a, b)

/-- Lifting a function out of a quotient obliges us to prove it respects the relation. -/
def MyInt.neg : MyInt → MyInt :=
  Quotient.lift (fun p => MyInt.mk p.2 p.1) (by
    intro p q h
    have h : p.1 + q.2 = q.1 + p.2 := h
    apply Quotient.sound
    show p.2 + q.1 = q.2 + p.1
    omega)

def MyInt.toInt : MyInt → Int :=
  Quotient.lift (fun p => (p.1 : Int) - p.2) (by
    intro p q h
    have h : p.1 + q.2 = q.1 + p.2 := h
    show (p.1 : Int) - p.2 = q.1 - q.2
    omega)

#eval (MyInt.mk 5 2).toInt
#eval (MyInt.mk 7 4).toInt
#eval (MyInt.mk 2 5).neg.toInt

-- Different representatives, equal values: this is what Quotient.sound provides.
theorem three_eq : MyInt.mk 5 2 = MyInt.mk 7 4 := Quotient.sound (show 5 + 4 = 7 + 2 from rfl)

theorem MyInt.neg_neg (x : MyInt) : x.neg.neg = x := by
  induction x using Quotient.ind with
  | _ p => rfl

#print axioms three_eq
#print axioms MyInt.neg_neg
lessons.solution:
instance paritySetoid : Setoid Nat where
  r a b := a % 2 = b % 2
  iseqv := ⟨fun _ => rfl, fun h => h.symm, fun h1 h2 => h1.trans h2⟩

def Parity := Quotient paritySetoid

def Parity.mk (n : Nat) : Parity := Quotient.mk paritySetoid n

def Parity.isEven : Parity → Bool :=
  Quotient.lift (fun n => n % 2 == 0) (by
    intro a b h
    have h : a % 2 = b % 2 := h
    simp [h])

#eval (Parity.mk 10).isEven
#eval (Parity.mk 7).isEven

theorem parity_3_7 : Parity.mk 3 = Parity.mk 7 := Quotient.sound (show 3 % 2 = 7 % 2 from rfl)

theorem parity_isEven_respects : (Parity.mk 3).isEven = (Parity.mk 7).isEven := by
  rw [parity_3_7]

#print axioms parity_3_7

options: That `f` is injective on representatives
That the relation is decidable
That every element of the quotient has a unique representative

lessons.title: Declaring axioms, and what to do instead
body: The `axiom` command adds a constant to the environment with a type and no definition. Lean accepts it on trust: `axiom Oracle : Nat → Bool` and `axiom oracle_zero : Oracle 0 = true` let you prove theorems that mention them. This is how Lean's own `propext` is introduced, and it is the way a library can postulate a fact it cannot prove. It is also the one feature that can invalidate everything else, so you should know what it does.

An axiom spreads through dependency. `oracle_zero_or_one` is a one-line theorem, but `#print axioms` shows `[Oracle, oracle_zero]`, so the claim is only as sound as those postulates. Theorems that do not mention them, like `plain_fact`, stay clean. And since an axiom has no value, any def that calls it cannot be compiled: `useOracle` must be `noncomputable`, otherwise Lean says `Oracle not supported by code generator; consider marking definition as noncomputable`.

The danger is inconsistency. After `axiom inconsistent : False`, the theorem `1 = 2` is proved by `inconsistent.elim`, and so is every proposition, as the `anything` theorem shows. Nothing in the proof warns you except the axiom list. The same applies to the placeholder `sorry`: it is not an axiom declaration, but it elaborates to the compiler-generated `sorryAx`, which shows in `#print axioms` and in the warning `declaration uses sorry`. Even a theorem that failed to elaborate may be recorded with `sorryAx`; in the experiment for this lesson, a broken proof reported `depends on axioms: [sorryAx]`. So `sorryAx` in an axiom list means 'an unproved gap', never 'finished'.

The better habit is to turn assumptions into hypotheses. `plus_two_even (seed : Nat) (h : seed % 2 = 0)` states its requirement, and its axiom list contains only the standard ones. A structure like `EvenSeed` bundles the assumption so many theorems can share it, and users must supply a real value with a real proof. Use axioms for foundational extensions you accept deliberately (as Lean itself does) and audit with `#print axioms`; in an application, prefer explicit hypotheses.

Check: an `axiom` is trusted without proof and infects every theorem that depends on it, so audit with `#print axioms`, treat `sorryAx` as an unproved gap, and prefer explicit hypotheses or structures over new axioms.
lessons.code:
-- An axiom is a declaration with a type but no proof or value. Lean takes it on trust.
axiom Oracle : Nat → Bool
axiom oracle_zero : Oracle 0 = true

#check @Oracle
#check @oracle_zero

-- A theorem that uses the axiom inherits it; #print axioms shows the dependency.
theorem oracle_zero_or_one : Oracle 0 = true ∨ Oracle 1 = true :=
  Or.inl oracle_zero
#print axioms oracle_zero_or_one

-- A theorem that does not touch it is unaffected.
theorem plain_fact : 3 * 4 = 12 := rfl
#print axioms plain_fact

-- Axioms have no computational content, so any definition that calls one must be
-- `noncomputable`; leaving that off gives: `Oracle` not supported by code generator.
noncomputable def useOracle (n : Nat) : Bool := !Oracle n

-- The danger: one inconsistent axiom proves everything, and nothing warns you except the
-- axiom list. Never do this outside a demonstration.
axiom inconsistent : False

theorem one_eq_two : 1 = 2 := inconsistent.elim
#print axioms one_eq_two

theorem anything (p : Prop) : p := inconsistent.elim
#print axioms anything

-- Lean's own foundation adds only three axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).
-- Here is the one for choice; it is an axiom, so it lists itself:
#check @Classical.choice
#print axioms Classical.choice
lessons.solution:
-- Version 1: an axiom. Every later theorem silently inherits it.
axiom Seed : Nat
axiom seed_even : Seed % 2 = 0

theorem seed_plus_two_even : (Seed + 2) % 2 = 0 := by
  have h := seed_even
  omega
#print axioms seed_plus_two_even

-- Version 2: the assumption becomes an explicit hypothesis. The theorem is honest about what it
-- needs, and `#print axioms` stays clean.
theorem plus_two_even (seed : Nat) (h : seed % 2 = 0) : (seed + 2) % 2 = 0 := by
  omega
#print axioms plus_two_even

-- Version 3: package the assumption as a structure, so many theorems can share it.
structure EvenSeed where
  value : Nat
  even : value % 2 = 0

theorem EvenSeed.plus_two_even (s : EvenSeed) : (s.value + 2) % 2 = 0 := by
  have := s.even
  omega
#print axioms EvenSeed.plus_two_even

lessons.question: What does `#print axioms t` showing `sorryAx` tell you?
options: The theorem is correct but was compiled in a different universe
The theorem was proved by `decide` and is therefore computed
The proof depends on a gap that was never filled in: a `sorry` or an elaboration error
The theorem used classical logic through `Classical.choice`

lessons.title: Mathlib: the library and how to search it
body: Everything so far used only what ships with Lean itself. Mathlib is a separate, enormous library of formalised mathematics: ordered fields, groups, topology, number theory and the tactics that go with them. A file opts in with a single line, `import Mathlib`, which pulls in the whole library. That makes the first compile of a session slow but spares you from guessing which module holds a lemma.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Lemma names follow a convention that you can often guess. A name lists the pieces of the statement in order, joined with underscores: `add_comm` is commutativity of addition, `mul_pos` says a product is positive, `sq_nonneg` says a square is nonnegative. Lemmas about one type live in its namespace, so `Nat.succ_le_of_lt` and `Nat.Prime.two_le` are reached through the type or through dot notation on a hypothesis, as in `hp.two_le`. `open Nat in` shortens names for one command, and a plain `open Nat` does it for the rest of the section.

When you do not know the name, ask the library. `exact?` searches for a single lemma that closes the goal, `apply?` finds lemmas whose conclusion matches, and `rw?` lists rewrites. Each prints a "Try this" suggestion; treat it as a hint, replace the search call with the suggested proof, and keep the file free of search tactics. `#check @name` shows a statement with every implicit argument visible, which is the quickest way to learn how to call a lemma.

Check: a finished file should contain no `exact?`, because the search is slow and its answer may change when Mathlib is updated. Common mistake: using `#check name` on a lemma with implicit arguments and being surprised by the output; write `#check @name` to see the whole signature.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- Names describe the statement: `add_comm`, `mul_pos`, `Nat.succ_le_of_lt`, ...
#check @add_comm
#check @mul_pos
#check @Nat.succ_le_of_lt
#check @sq_nonneg

-- `open ... in` shortens names for one command only.
open Nat in
#check @succ_le_of_lt

-- When you do not know the lemma name, ask the library.
example (a b : ℕ) (h : a ≤ b) : a < b + 1 := by exact?

-- Once the search has found a name, write the short proof instead.
example (a b : ℕ) (h : a ≤ b) : a < b + 1 := Nat.lt_succ_of_le h

-- `rw?` lists rewrites that apply to the goal.
example (a b : ℕ) : a + b = b + a := by rw [Nat.add_comm]

theorem sum_sq_nonneg (a b : ℝ) : 0 ≤ (a + b) ^ 2 := sq_nonneg _

#check sum_sq_nonneg
#eval Nat.choose 5 2
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

-- Challenge: prove three small facts by finding library lemmas, not by `simp`.
-- 1. a product of two positive reals is positive
theorem pos_product (x y : ℝ) (hx : 0 < x) (hy : 0 < y) : 0 < x * y := mul_pos hx hy

-- 2. every prime is at least two
theorem prime_ge_two (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) : 2 ≤ p := hp.two_le

-- 3. a sum of two squares is never negative (the search tactic found `add_nonneg`)
theorem sum_of_squares (a b : ℝ) : 0 ≤ a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 := add_nonneg (sq_nonneg a) (sq_nonneg b)

#check pos_product
#check prime_ge_two
#check sum_of_squares
#eval Nat.gcd 12 18

options: The search tactic is not allowed to run under `import Mathlib`
A named lemma proves a stronger statement than the search result
The search is slow and its answer can change with the Mathlib version, while the named lemma is a stable, fast proof
`exact?` is only legal inside `example` blocks, never in theorems
lessons.explanation: `exact?` prints a "Try this" line containing a concrete proof term. Writing that term directly gives a proof that checks quickly and does not depend on the search succeeding again. The output of the `#check` lines shows the statements the names refer to.

lessons.title: Mathlib automation: ring, linarith, norm_num and friends
body: Mathlib ships tactics that settle whole families of goals, so you rarely do routine algebra by hand. `ring` proves any identity that holds in a commutative ring, treating variables as unknowns and normalising both sides. `norm_num` evaluates numerals, including powers, fractions and divisibility facts such as primality of a small number.

Inequalities have their own tools. `linarith` multiplies your hypotheses by constants and adds them to find a contradiction, so it needs the goal and hypotheses to be linear. `nlinarith` first multiplies pairs of hypotheses and hint terms together and then calls the linear engine; the trick is to supply the product you believe is needed, such as `sq_nonneg (a - b)` for the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means. `positivity` works structurally: it proves `0 < e` or `0 ≤ e` by showing every piece of `e` is positive or nonnegative.

Division needs one more step. `field_simp` multiplies out denominators when it can prove they are nonzero (from hypotheses like `hx : x ≠ 0`), and usually leaves a polynomial goal for `ring`. Recent Mathlib versions can close the goal inside `field_simp` itself, so if `ring` afterwards reports no goals, delete it. `gcongr` handles goals of the form "same expression with a bigger part", reducing `x ^ 2 + 3 ≤ y ^ 2 + 3` to `x ≤ y`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: pick the tactic by the shape of the goal, not by trial. Common mistake: expecting `linarith` to prove a nonlinear fact such as `2 * a * b ≤ a ^ 2 + b ^ 2` with no hint; add the right square with `nlinarith [sq_nonneg (a - b)]`.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- `ring` proves identities in commutative (semi)rings.
theorem diff_squares (a b : ℤ) : (a + b) * (a - b) = a ^ 2 - b ^ 2 := by ring

-- `linarith` combines linear hypotheses.
theorem bound_y (x y : ℝ) (h1 : x + y ≤ 10) (h2 : 3 ≤ x) : y ≤ 7 := by linarith

-- `nlinarith` also multiplies hypotheses together; give it the product you need as a hint.
theorem am_gm (a b : ℝ) : 2 * a * b ≤ a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 := by nlinarith [sq_nonneg (a - b)]

-- `norm_num` evaluates numerals.
theorem big_numeral : (2 : ℚ) ^ 10 - 24 = 1000 := by norm_num

-- `positivity` proves `0 < e` or `0 ≤ e` by looking at the shape of `e`.
theorem pos_expr (x y : ℝ) : 0 < x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 + 1 := by positivity

-- `field_simp` clears denominators once it knows they are nonzero.
theorem half_plus_half (x : ℝ) (hx : x ≠ 0) : 1 / x + 1 / x = 2 / x := by
  field_simp
  ring

-- `gcongr` reduces `f a ≤ f b` to `a ≤ b` for monotone shapes.
theorem mono_expr (x y : ℕ) (h : x ≤ y) : x ^ 2 + 3 ≤ y ^ 2 + 3 := by gcongr

#check @am_gm
#eval (2 : ℚ) ^ 10 - 24
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

-- Challenge: choose the right tactic for each statement.
theorem cube_expand (a b : ℤ) : (a + b) ^ 3 = a ^ 3 + 3 * a ^ 2 * b + 3 * a * b ^ 2 + b ^ 3 := by ring

theorem three_vars (x y z : ℝ) (h1 : x < y) (h2 : y < z) : x < z + 1 := by linarith

theorem shifted_squares (x : ℝ) : 4 * x ≤ x ^ 2 + 4 := by nlinarith [sq_nonneg (x - 2)]

theorem arithmetic_fact : (7 : ℕ) * 8 + 2 ^ 5 = 88 := by norm_num

theorem always_pos (a b : ℝ) : 0 < (a - b) ^ 2 + 1 := by positivity

theorem scaled (a b c : ℝ) (h : a ≤ b) (hc : 0 ≤ c) : a * c + 1 ≤ b * c + 1 := by gcongr

#check @cube_expand
#eval (7 : ℕ) * 8 + 2 ^ 5

lessons.question: Which tactic call proves `2 * a * b ≤ a ^ 2 + b ^ 2` for real numbers?
options: `linarith` with no hints
`ring`
`norm_num`
`nlinarith [sq_nonneg (a - b)]`

lessons.title: Sets and functions in Mathlib
body: In Mathlib a set is not a collection built from scratch: `Set α` is the type of predicates on `α`, and `x ∈ s` just means `s x`. Set-builder notation `{n | Even n}` defines a set by its predicate. Because membership unfolds to the predicate, proving `4 ∈ evens` can start with `show Even 4`.

Subset and equality proofs follow patterns you already know. To show `s ⊆ t`, `intro x hx` and prove `x ∈ t`. To show two sets equal, use `ext x` and then prove the iff. Intersection membership is a pair, so `hx.1` and `hx.2` pick out the two parts, and union membership is an `Or`, handled with `rintro (h | h)`.

Images and preimages connect sets across a function. `f '' s` is the image: `y ∈ f '' s` unfolds to `∃ x, x ∈ s ∧ f x = y`, so `rintro y ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩` takes it apart and `⟨x, h hx, rfl⟩` builds one. The preimage `f ⁻¹' u` is easier: `x ∈ f ⁻¹' u` is `f x ∈ u`, and many preimage equalities hold by `rfl`.

Two function properties come up constantly. `Injective f` says `f a = f b → a = b`; `Surjective f` says every `y` equals some `f x`. Both are definitions, so `intro` unfolds them. The `open Set Function` line lets you write `Injective` without the `Function.` prefix. Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: after `ext`, the goal is an iff about one arbitrary element. Common mistake: forgetting that an image membership is an existential, so `exact hx` fails; destructure it with `rintro ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩`.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

open Set Function

-- A `Set α` is a predicate on `α`; `x ∈ s` unfolds to `s x`.
def evens : Set ℕ := {n | Even n}

theorem four_mem : 4 ∈ evens := by
  show Even 4
  decide

-- Subset proofs introduce a point, then use the hypothesis.
theorem inter_sub_left (s t : Set ℕ) : s ∩ t ⊆ s := by
  intro x hx
  exact hx.1

-- Images and preimages.
theorem image_mono_demo (f : ℕ → ℕ) (s t : Set ℕ) (h : s ⊆ t) : f '' s ⊆ f '' t := by
  rintro y ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  exact ⟨x, h hx, rfl⟩

theorem preimage_inter (f : ℕ → ℕ) (u v : Set ℕ) : f ⁻¹' (u ∩ v) = f ⁻¹' u ∩ f ⁻¹' v := by
  ext x
  rfl

-- Injective: different inputs give different outputs.
theorem double_injective : Injective (fun n : ℕ => 2 * n) := by
  intro a b h
  simp only at h
  omega

-- Surjective: every output is hit.
theorem succ_int_surjective : Surjective (fun z : ℤ => z + 1) := by
  intro y
  exact ⟨y - 1, by ring⟩

#check @Set.image_mono
#check @Function.Injective.comp
#eval (List.range 10).filter (fun n => n % 2 == 0)
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

open Set Function

-- Challenge: composition and set algebra.
theorem union_comm_demo (s t : Set ℕ) : s ∪ t = t ∪ s := by
  ext x
  constructor
  · rintro (h | h)
    · exact Or.inr h
    · exact Or.inl h
  · rintro (h | h)
    · exact Or.inr h
    · exact Or.inl h

theorem comp_injective (f g : ℕ → ℕ) (hf : Injective f) (hg : Injective g) : Injective (g ∘ f) := by
  intro a b h
  exact hf (hg h)

theorem image_union_demo (f : ℕ → ℕ) (s t : Set ℕ) : f '' (s ∪ t) = f '' s ∪ f '' t := by
  ext y
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨x, hx | hx, rfl⟩
    · exact Or.inl ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
    · exact Or.inr ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  · rintro (⟨x, hx, rfl⟩ | ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩)
    · exact ⟨x, Or.inl hx, rfl⟩
    · exact ⟨x, Or.inr hx, rfl⟩

#check @comp_injective
#eval ((List.range 5).map (fun n => n * n))

lessons.title: Orders and lattices
body: Ordering is a type class. Any type with a `PartialOrder` instance gets `≤`, `<`, and the lemmas `le_refl`, `le_trans` and `le_antisymm`. Because the lemmas are stated for the class, one proof works for natural numbers, reals, sets and many other types. A `Monotone` function is one that preserves the order.

A lattice adds two operations. `a ⊔ b` is the least upper bound (join) and `a ⊓ b` is the greatest lower bound (meet). Their defining properties are the lemmas `le_sup_left`, `sup_le`, `inf_le_left` and `le_inf`. The same symbols mean different things on different types: on `ℕ` they are `max` and `min`, and on `Set α` they are union and intersection, which is why `s ⊔ t = s ∪ t` holds by `rfl`.

This is the benefit of Mathlib's hierarchy. A lemma such as `sup_comm` is proved once for all semilattices, then reused for sets, numbers and ideals. When a statement mentions `⊔`, search for `sup_` lemmas; when it mentions `⊓`, search for `inf_`. Lemmas like `sup_eq_right : a ⊔ b = b ↔ a ≤ b` turn an order fact into an equation.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.
Check: the symbols `⊔` and `⊓` are typed `\sqcup` and `\sqcap`, not `\cup` and `\cap`. Common mistake: assuming `⊔` on numbers is addition; it is `max`, and `#eval (3 : ℕ) ⊔ 8` prints `8`.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- Orders are type classes: `≤` works on any type with a `PartialOrder` instance.
theorem le_antisymm_demo (a b : ℕ) (h1 : a ≤ b) (h2 : b ≤ a) : a = b := le_antisymm h1 h2

-- Lattices add `⊔` (join / least upper bound) and `⊓` (meet / greatest lower bound).
theorem sup_comm_demo (a b : ℕ) : a ⊔ b = b ⊔ a := sup_comm a b

theorem inf_le_left_demo (a b : ℕ) : a ⊓ b ≤ a := inf_le_left

-- On sets, `⊔` is union and `⊓` is intersection, so lattice lemmas apply to them.
theorem set_sup_demo (s t : Set ℕ) : s ⊔ t = s ∪ t := rfl

-- On `ℕ` with `≤`, join is `max` and meet is `min`.
theorem nat_sup_is_max (a b : ℕ) : a ⊔ b = max a b := rfl

-- A monotone function preserves `≤`.
theorem monotone_double : Monotone (fun n : ℕ => 2 * n) := by
  intro a b h
  simp only
  omega

#eval (3 : ℕ) ⊔ 8
#eval (3 : ℕ) ⊓ 8
#check @le_sup_left
#check @sup_le
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

-- Challenge: use only order and lattice lemmas.
theorem sup_absorb (a b : ℕ) (h : a ≤ b) : a ⊔ b = b := sup_eq_right.mpr h

theorem inf_absorb (a b : ℕ) (h : a ≤ b) : a ⊓ b = a := inf_eq_left.mpr h

theorem sup_three (a b c : ℕ) : a ≤ a ⊔ b ⊔ c :=
  le_trans le_sup_left le_sup_left

theorem monotone_add_const (k : ℕ) : Monotone (fun n : ℕ => n + k) := by
  intro a b h
  simp only
  omega

#eval (10 : ℕ) ⊔ 4 ⊓ 6
#check @sup_absorb
lessons.challenge: Prove that `a ⊔ b = b` when `a ≤ b`, the matching fact for `⊓`, that `a ≤ a ⊔ b ⊔ c`, and that adding a constant is monotone.
lessons.question: What does `(3 : ℕ) ⊔ 8` evaluate to?
lessons.explanation: On natural numbers the join is the maximum, so the result is 8. `⊔` is not addition and not multiplication. The two `#eval` lines print 8 for the join and 3 for the meet.

lessons.title: Number theory: divisibility, primes and gcd
body: Divisibility `a ∣ b` is defined as `∃ c, b = a * c`, typed `\|`, which is not the ordinary vertical bar. To prove it, supply the witness: `⟨12, by norm_num⟩` shows `12 ∣ 144`. Library lemmas such as `dvd_trans`, `dvd_add` and `dvd_mul_right` cover the routine closure properties, so you seldom unfold the definition.

`Nat.Prime p` states that `p` is at least two and its only divisors are one and itself. For specific small numbers, `norm_num` proves primality, and `#eval Nat.Prime 97` decides it by computation. The key structural fact is Euclid's lemma: `Nat.Prime.dvd_mul` says a prime dividing a product divides one factor, and `Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow` extends that to powers. Mathlib also proves `Nat.exists_infinite_primes`: for every `n` there is a prime at least `n`.

`Nat.gcd` and `Nat.lcm` compute and have a rich lemma set: `Nat.gcd_dvd_left`, `Nat.gcd_self`, and `Nat.Coprime a b` (which means the gcd is one). Coprimality is the working form of "no common factor", and proofs about it often use `Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.
Check: `a ∣ b` is a statement, not a number, so it is proved, not evaluated. Common mistake: typing the ASCII bar `|`, which Lean reads as something else; use `\|`.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- Divisibility: `a ∣ b` means `∃ c, b = a * c`.
theorem dvd_demo (a b c : ℕ) (hab : a ∣ b) (hbc : b ∣ c) : a ∣ c := dvd_trans hab hbc

theorem dvd_sum_demo (a b c : ℕ) (hab : a ∣ b) (hac : a ∣ c) : a ∣ b + c := dvd_add hab hac

-- Primes: `Nat.Prime p` means `p ≥ 2` and the only divisors are 1 and p.
theorem seven_prime : Nat.Prime 7 := by norm_num

theorem prime_dvd_mul_demo (p a b : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (h : p ∣ a * b) : p ∣ a ∨ p ∣ b :=
  (Nat.Prime.dvd_mul hp).mp h

-- gcd: `Nat.gcd` computes, and the library supplies its laws.
theorem gcd_dvd_demo (a b : ℕ) : Nat.gcd a b ∣ a := Nat.gcd_dvd_left a b

theorem coprime_demo : Nat.Coprime 8 15 := by norm_num

-- Euclid: there is always a prime above any bound.
theorem exists_big_prime (n : ℕ) : ∃ p, n ≤ p ∧ p.Prime := Nat.exists_infinite_primes n

#eval Nat.gcd 12 18
#eval Nat.lcm 4 6
#eval (List.range 30).filter Nat.Prime
#check @Nat.Prime.two_le

import Mathlib

-- Challenge: three number-theory facts.

theorem twelve_dvd : 12 ∣ 144 := ⟨12, by norm_num⟩

-- 2. a prime that divides a square divides the base
theorem prime_dvd_sq (p n : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) (h : p ∣ n ^ 2) : p ∣ n :=
  hp.dvd_of_dvd_pow h

-- 3. gcd with itself
theorem gcd_self_demo (n : ℕ) : Nat.gcd n n = n := Nat.gcd_self n

#eval Nat.gcd 84 36
#eval Nat.Prime 97
#check @Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow

lessons.title: Modular arithmetic with ZMod and Nat.ModEq
body: Modular arithmetic has two styles in Mathlib. `a ≡ b [MOD n]` is the relation `Nat.ModEq n a b`, for natural numbers that stay natural. `ZMod n` is a ring of residues: a type whose elements are the classes mod `n`, with ordinary `+` and `*`. The second style is usually easier, because ring tactics and `decide` apply.

For a small modulus, `decide` can check statements about every residue because `ZMod n` is a finite type with decidable equality. The theorem `∀ x : ZMod 4, x ^ 2 = 0 ∨ x ^ 2 = 1` is a four-case check that `decide` settles, and it proves that no square is congruent to two or three modulo four. Larger moduli may need `decide +kernel` or a smarter argument.

Casts connect the worlds. `((n : ℕ) : ZMod m) = 0 ↔ m ∣ n` is `ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff`, so a divisibility claim becomes a ring equation. Mathlib also proves Fermat's little theorem as `ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one`; its hypothesis `[Fact p.Prime]` is how Lean passes "p is prime" as a type class instance.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.
Check: in `ZMod 7`, the numeral `3 + 5` is computed mod 7 and prints `1`. Common mistake: writing `(3 + 5 : ZMod 7)` and expecting `8`; the numeral lives in the quotient ring, so it equals 1.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- `ZMod n` is the integers mod n; for small n, `decide` can check every case.
theorem zmod_arith : (3 : ZMod 7) + 5 = 1 := by decide

theorem zmod_mul : (4 : ZMod 9) * 7 = 1 := by decide

-- Every square mod 4 is 0 or 1: check all four residues.
theorem sq_mod_four : ∀ x : ZMod 4, x ^ 2 = 0 ∨ x ^ 2 = 1 := by decide

-- `Int.emod_emod_of_dvd` and friends are the Nat/Int versions; `Nat.ModEq` is the congruence relation.
theorem modeq_demo : 17 ≡ 2 [MOD 5] := by decide

theorem modeq_add (a b c d n : ℕ) (h1 : a ≡ b [MOD n]) (h2 : c ≡ d [MOD n]) :
    a + c ≡ b + d [MOD n] := h1.add h2

-- Casting links the two worlds: `(n : ZMod m) = 0` iff `m ∣ n`.
theorem cast_zero_iff (m n : ℕ) : (n : ZMod m) = 0 ↔ m ∣ n := ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff n m

-- Fermat's little theorem in `ZMod p`.
theorem fermat_demo (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (a : ZMod p) (ha : a ≠ 0) : a ^ (p - 1) = 1 :=
  ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one ha

#eval (3 : ZMod 7) + 5
#eval (4 : ZMod 9) * 7
#eval 17 % 5

import Mathlib

-- Challenge: residues and congruences.
theorem cube_mod_nine : ∀ x : ZMod 9, x ^ 3 = 0 ∨ x ^ 3 = 1 ∨ x ^ 3 = 8 := by decide

theorem pow_mod_demo : (2 : ZMod 11) ^ 10 = 1 := by decide

theorem modeq_mul (a b c d n : ℕ) (h1 : a ≡ b [MOD n]) (h2 : c ≡ d [MOD n]) :
    a * c ≡ b * d [MOD n] := h1.mul h2

#eval (2 : ZMod 11) ^ 10
#eval (List.range 9).map (fun x => ((x : ZMod 9) ^ 3).val)

lessons.question: Why is `(3 : ZMod 7) + 5 = 1` true?
options: `ZMod 7` rounds every sum down to its nearest prime
The numerals 3 and 5 are different types so `+` truncates
Lean rewrites 8 as 1 only because `decide` is unsound
Arithmetic in `ZMod 7` wraps around: 3 + 5 = 8, and 8 leaves remainder 1 on division by 7

lessons.title: Algebra: groups, rings, subgroups and homomorphisms
body: Algebraic structures in Mathlib are type classes. Write `{G : Type*} [Group G]` and every element of `G` has `*`, `1` and `⁻¹` with the group laws available as lemmas: `mul_assoc`, `one_mul`, `inv_mul_cancel`. Theorems proved this way apply to every group, from permutations to matrices, without being restated.

Rings and fields follow the same pattern with `[CommRing R]` and `[Field K]`. The tactics you met earlier are class-aware: `ring` works in any commutative ring, and `group` normalises expressions in a group. Division in a field is total in Lean, so facts like `mul_inv_cancel₀` carry the hypothesis `x ≠ 0` explicitly. A subscript zero in a lemma name often signals a "with zero" version that needs this hypothesis.

Substructures and maps are bundled records. A subgroup is a structure with a `carrier` set and proofs that it contains the identity and is closed under the operation and inverses; for additive groups these are `zero_mem'`, `add_mem'` and `neg_mem'`. A homomorphism `G →* H` bundles a function with its multiplicativity proof, and lemmas such as `map_one` and `map_mul` apply to it by the coercion.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: bundled morphisms are used like functions (`f 1`), and the laws are separate lemmas (`map_one f`). Common mistake: trying to apply a plain function to the group laws; the homomorphism type `→*` is what carries the proof.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

-- A group is a class: any type with `Group G` gets multiplication, inverse, and the laws.
theorem inv_mul_cancel_demo {G : Type*} [Group G] (a : G) : a⁻¹ * a = 1 := inv_mul_cancel a

-- Uniqueness of inverses, proved from the axioms.
theorem inv_unique_demo {G : Type*} [Group G] (a b : G) (h : a * b = 1) : b = a⁻¹ := by
  calc b = a⁻¹ * (a * b) := by group
    _ = a⁻¹ := by rw [h, mul_one]

-- Rings and fields: `ring` and `field_simp` work in any commutative ring / field.
theorem binomial_ring {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (a b : R) :
    (a + b) ^ 2 = a ^ 2 + 2 * a * b + b ^ 2 := by ring

theorem field_demo {K : Type*} [Field K] (x : K) (hx : x ≠ 0) : x * x⁻¹ = 1 := mul_inv_cancel₀ hx

-- A subgroup is a bundled structure; membership is a proposition about elements.
def evenSubgroup : AddSubgroup ℤ where
  carrier := {n | Even n}
  add_mem' := by
    intro a b ha hb
    exact Even.add ha hb
  zero_mem' := Even.zero
  neg_mem' := by
    intro a ha
    exact Even.neg ha

theorem four_in_even : (4 : ℤ) ∈ evenSubgroup := by
  show Even (4 : ℤ)
  decide

-- A homomorphism is a function plus a proof that it respects multiplication.
def doubleHom : ℤ →+ ℤ := AddMonoidHom.mk' (fun n => 2 * n) (by intro a b; ring)

theorem doubleHom_apply (n : ℤ) : doubleHom n = 2 * n := rfl

theorem hom_zero {G H : Type*} [Group G] [Group H] (f : G →* H) : f 1 = 1 := map_one f

#eval doubleHom 21
#check @map_mul
#check Subgroup

import Mathlib

-- Challenge: group facts from the axioms, plus one subgroup and one homomorphism.
theorem mul_left_cancel_demo {G : Type*} [Group G] (a b c : G) (h : a * b = a * c) : b = c := by
  have := congrArg (fun x => a⁻¹ * x) h
  simpa using this

theorem inv_mul_demo {G : Type*} [Group G] (a b : G) : (a * b)⁻¹ = b⁻¹ * a⁻¹ := mul_inv_rev a b

-- the multiples of 3 form an additive subgroup
def threeMultiples : AddSubgroup ℤ where
  carrier := {n | 3 ∣ n}
  add_mem' := by
    intro a b ha hb
    exact dvd_add ha hb
  zero_mem' := dvd_zero 3
  neg_mem' := by
    intro a ha
    exact (dvd_neg).mpr ha

theorem nine_in : (9 : ℤ) ∈ threeMultiples := by
  show (3 : ℤ) ∣ 9
  norm_num

-- squaring is a homomorphism on a commutative monoid
def sqHom : ℤ →* ℤ where
  toFun n := n ^ 2
  map_one' := by norm_num
  map_mul' := by intro a b; ring

#eval sqHom 12
#check @sqHom

lessons.title: Linear algebra: modules, linear maps and matrices
body: Mathlib treats a vector space as a module over a field: write `[Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V]`. Scalar multiplication is `c • v`, and the module axioms are lemmas such as `smul_add` and `add_smul`. Assuming only the class means the statement covers every vector space, not just coordinate ones.

A linear map is the bundled type `V →ₗ[K] W`. It carries a function plus proofs of additivity (`map_add`) and compatibility with scalars (`map_smul`). Once bundled it behaves like a function: `f (u + v)` rewrites using `map_add f u v`. To build one, supply `toFun`, `map_add'` and `map_smul'`; for concrete cases like swapping coordinates, all proofs close by `rfl`.

Matrices are functions from two index types, `Matrix m n α`. For small concrete sizes use `Fin 2` and the literal syntax `!![1, 2; 3, 4]`. Computation works: `#eval A * B` multiplies, and `A.det` gives the determinant for square matrices. Proving concrete facts can use `decide +kernel`, `simp` with `Matrix.det_fin_two`, or the general lemmas such as `Matrix.transpose_mul` and `Matrix.det_one`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.
Check: matrix products `*` are noncommutative, and `transpose_mul` reverses the order. Common mistake: writing `(M * N)ᵀ = Mᵀ * Nᵀ`; it is `Nᵀ * Mᵀ`.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

open Matrix

-- A vector space is a module over a field. Typeclass assumptions say so.
theorem smul_add_demo {K V : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] (c : K) (u v : V) :
    c • (u + v) = c • u + c • v := smul_add c u v

-- Linear maps are bundled: `V →ₗ[K] W` is a function with proofs of additivity and homogeneity.
theorem map_add_demo {K V W : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] [AddCommGroup W]
    [Module K W] (f : V →ₗ[K] W) (u v : V) : f (u + v) = f u + f v := map_add f u v

theorem map_smul_demo {K V W : Type*} [Field K] [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] [AddCommGroup W]
    [Module K W] (f : V →ₗ[K] W) (c : K) (v : V) : f (c • v) = c • f v := map_smul f c v

-- Matrices are functions from index types; `!![...]` writes small literals.
def A : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ := !![1, 2; 3, 4]
def B : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ := !![0, 1; 1, 0]

theorem A_mul_B : A * B = !![2, 1; 4, 3] := by
  decide +kernel

theorem det_A : A.det = -2 := by
  simp [A, Matrix.det_fin_two]

theorem transpose_mul_demo {n : Type*} [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] (M N : Matrix n n ℤ) :
    (M * N)ᵀ = Nᵀ * Mᵀ := Matrix.transpose_mul M N

#eval A * B
#eval A.det
#eval A.transpose

import Mathlib

open Matrix

-- Challenge: a linear map built by hand, and a matrix identity.
def swapMap : (ℤ × ℤ) →ₗ[ℤ] (ℤ × ℤ) where
  toFun p := (p.2, p.1)
  map_add' := by intro p q; rfl
  map_smul' := by intro c p; rfl

theorem swap_twice (p : ℤ × ℤ) : swapMap (swapMap p) = p := rfl

def I2 : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ := 1

theorem one_mul_demo (M : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ) : I2 * M = M := by
  simp [I2]

theorem det_one_demo : (1 : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ).det = 1 := Matrix.det_one

#eval swapMap (3, 8)
#eval (!![2, 0; 0, 3] : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ).det

lessons.title: Analysis: limits, continuity and derivatives
body: The epsilon-delta idea survives in Lean exactly as you would write it on paper. A sequence term tends to a limit when for every positive epsilon there is an index beyond which the terms stay within epsilon. The proof begins with `intro ε hε`, chooses `N` using the Archimedean property (`exists_nat_gt`), and finishes with algebra from `linarith` or `positivity`.

Mathlib packages convergence uniformly with filters. `Tendsto u atTop (𝓝 a)` says the sequence `u` tends to `a`: `atTop` is the filter of "large indices" and `𝓝 a` is the filter of neighbourhoods of `a` (open the `Topology` namespace to type `𝓝`). One definition covers sequences, function limits and limits at infinity, and lemmas such as `Tendsto.add` combine limits without any epsilons.

Continuity and differentiation have automation as well. `fun_prop` proves continuity of expressions built from known continuous pieces, such as polynomials. For derivatives, `HasDerivAt f f' x` is the proof-carrying statement, `deriv f x` is the number, and `HasDerivAt.deriv` converts between them. Library lemmas such as `hasDerivAt_pow` give derivatives of basic functions, which you assemble with `.add` and `.const_mul`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: `deriv f x` is junk (zero) when `f` is not differentiable at `x`, so derivative facts need a `HasDerivAt` or `DifferentiableAt` hypothesis first. Common mistake: proving `deriv f x = c` by `simp` for a function you have not shown differentiable.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

open Filter Topology

-- Epsilon-delta, written out by hand: a sequence that converges to 0.
theorem inv_succ_tendsto : ∀ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n ≥ N, |1 / ((n : ℝ) + 1)| < ε := by
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := exists_nat_gt (1 / ε)
  refine ⟨N, fun n hn => ?_⟩
  have hn' : (N : ℝ) ≤ n := by exact_mod_cast hn
  have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < (n : ℝ) + 1 := by positivity
  rw [abs_of_pos (by positivity)]
  rw [div_lt_iff₀ hpos]
  have h1 : 1 / ε < (n : ℝ) + 1 := by linarith
  rw [div_lt_iff₀ hε] at h1
  linarith

-- The same fact in Mathlib's language: a limit along the filter `atTop`.
theorem tendsto_inv_demo : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => 1 / ((n : ℝ) + 1)) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
  tendsto_one_div_add_atTop_nhds_zero_nat

-- Continuity and derivatives of simple functions come as ready-made lemmas.
theorem cont_demo : Continuous (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2 + 3 * x) := by fun_prop

theorem deriv_demo (x : ℝ) : deriv (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2) x = 2 * x := by
  simp

theorem hasDeriv_demo (x : ℝ) : HasDerivAt (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 3) (3 * x ^ 2) x := by
  simpa using hasDerivAt_pow 3 x

#eval (1 : ℚ) / (9 + 1)
#check @Metric.tendsto_atTop
#check @Continuous.add
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

open Filter Topology

-- Challenge: limits and derivatives.
theorem const_tendsto (c : ℝ) : Tendsto (fun _ : ℕ => c) atTop (𝓝 c) := tendsto_const_nhds

theorem add_tendsto (u v : ℕ → ℝ) (a b : ℝ) (hu : Tendsto u atTop (𝓝 a))
    (hv : Tendsto v atTop (𝓝 b)) : Tendsto (fun n => u n + v n) atTop (𝓝 (a + b)) :=
  hu.add hv

theorem cont_poly : Continuous (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 3 - 2 * x + 1) := by fun_prop

theorem deriv_sq_plus (x : ℝ) : deriv (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2 + 5 * x) x = 2 * x + 5 := by
  have h : HasDerivAt (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2 + 5 * x) (2 * x + 5) x := by
    have h1 : HasDerivAt (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2) (2 * x) x := by
      simpa using hasDerivAt_pow 2 x
    have h2 : HasDerivAt (fun x : ℝ => 5 * x) 5 x := by
      simpa using (hasDerivAt_id x).const_mul 5
    exact h1.add h2
  exact h.deriv

#eval (2 : ℚ) * 3 + 5
#check @HasDerivAt.deriv

`u` is continuous at `a`

lessons.title: Topology: open sets, continuity and compactness
body: A topological space in Mathlib is a type with a `TopologicalSpace` instance, which supplies the predicate `IsOpen`. The axioms are available as lemmas: finite intersections of open sets are open (`IsOpen.inter`), arbitrary unions are open (`isOpen_iUnion`), and the whole space and empty set are open. Closed sets are defined through complements and have dual lemmas.

Continuity is defined by preimages: `Continuous f` means the preimage of every open set is open. That is why `hu.preimage hf` shows `f ⁻¹' u` is open, and `hg.comp hf` shows a composition is continuous. On the real line the topology comes from the metric, so intervals such as `Ioo 0 1` are open (`isOpen_Ioo`) and the tactic `fun_prop` proves continuity of ordinary expressions.

Compactness is the finite-subcover property, available as `IsCompact`. The two facts to remember are that closed bounded intervals are compact (`isCompact_Icc`) and that continuous images of compact sets are compact (`IsCompact.image`). Together they give the extreme value theorem: a continuous function on `Icc 0 1` attains a minimum, as stated by `IsCompact.exists_isMinOn`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: a statement about a continuous function on a compact set usually follows from one library lemma. Common mistake: using `Continuous` where only `ContinuousOn` is available; `hf.continuousOn` converts the first into the second.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

open Set Topology

-- Open sets: `IsOpen s` is part of the `TopologicalSpace` structure.
theorem open_inter_demo {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] (s t : Set X)
    (hs : IsOpen s) (ht : IsOpen t) : IsOpen (s ∩ t) := hs.inter ht

theorem open_union_demo {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] (s t : Set X)
    (hs : IsOpen s) (ht : IsOpen t) : IsOpen (s ∪ t) := hs.union ht

-- Real intervals are open.
theorem ioo_open : IsOpen (Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) := isOpen_Ioo

-- Continuity means preimages of open sets are open.
theorem continuous_preimage {X Y : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    (f : X → Y) (hf : Continuous f) (u : Set Y) (hu : IsOpen u) : IsOpen (f ⁻¹' u) :=
  hu.preimage hf

theorem comp_continuous {X Y Z : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
    [TopologicalSpace Z] (f : X → Y) (g : Y → Z) (hf : Continuous f) (hg : Continuous g) :
    Continuous (g ∘ f) := hg.comp hf

-- Compactness: closed intervals in `ℝ` are compact, and continuous images of compact sets are compact.
theorem icc_compact : IsCompact (Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) := isCompact_Icc

theorem image_compact (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Continuous f) : IsCompact (f '' Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :=
  isCompact_Icc.image hf

-- The extreme value theorem, as a library lemma.
theorem extreme_value (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : Continuous f) : ∃ x ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, ∀ y ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, f x ≤ f y :=
  isCompact_Icc.exists_isMinOn (nonempty_Icc.mpr zero_le_one) hf.continuousOn

#check @IsCompact.exists_isMinOn
#eval (List.range 4).map (fun n => n * 2)

import Mathlib

open Set Topology

-- Challenge: closed sets and continuity.
theorem closed_inter_demo {X : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] (s t : Set X)
    (hs : IsClosed s) (ht : IsClosed t) : IsClosed (s ∩ t) := hs.inter ht

theorem preimage_closed {X Y : Type*} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y] (f : X → Y)
    (hf : Continuous f) (c : Set Y) (hc : IsClosed c) : IsClosed (f ⁻¹' c) := hc.preimage hf

theorem sq_continuous : Continuous (fun x : ℝ => x ^ 2) := by fun_prop

lessons.title: Discrete mathematics: Finset, sums and counting
body: Finite collections in Mathlib are `Finset`s. `Finset.range n` is `{0, ..., n - 1}` and the big-operator notation `∑ i ∈ range n, f i` sums over it. The key rewriting lemma is `Finset.sum_range_succ`, which peels off the last term: `∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), f i = ∑ i ∈ range n, f i + f n`.

That lemma turns every formula about sums into an induction. For Gauss's formula, state it as `2 * ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), i = n * (n + 1)` to avoid natural-number division. The `zero` case is `simp`; in the `succ` case rewrite with `sum_range_succ`, then the induction hypothesis, and close with `ring`. The sum of the first `n` odd numbers equals `n ^ 2` by the same recipe.

Counting uses binomial coefficients `Nat.choose n k`, with Pascal's rule `Nat.choose_succ_succ`. Small values are decided by `decide`, and `#eval Nat.choose 10 3` prints 120. The pigeonhole principle is a library lemma: `Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt` says that a function from a larger finite type to a smaller one sends two different elements to the same place. You supply the function and a proof that the cardinalities compare the right way, which `simp` settles for `Fin 5` and `Fin 4`.
Mathlib code needs a Mathlib-enabled Lake project or the web editor at live.lean-lang.org; the in-app runner checks single files without Mathlib, so treat these listings as study text there.

Check: formulas with division are easier as multiplied identities in `ℕ`. Common mistake: stating Gauss's formula with `/ 2` in the naturals; truncated division makes the induction step awkward, so multiply both sides instead.
lessons.code:
import Mathlib

open Finset

-- `Finset.range n` is {0, ..., n-1}; `∑ i ∈ range n, f i` is a finite sum.
theorem sum_range_four : ∑ i ∈ range 4, i = 6 := by decide

-- Induction on finite sums: Gauss's formula, doubled to avoid division.
theorem gauss (n : ℕ) : 2 * ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), i = n * (n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    rw [sum_range_succ, mul_add, ih]
    ring

-- Sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2.
theorem sum_odd (n : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ range n, (2 * i + 1) = n ^ 2 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    rw [sum_range_succ, ih]
    ring

-- Binomial coefficients: Pascal's rule is a library lemma.
theorem pascal (n k : ℕ) : Nat.choose (n + 1) (k + 1) = Nat.choose n k + Nat.choose n (k + 1) :=
  Nat.choose_succ_succ n k

theorem choose_five_two : Nat.choose 5 2 = 10 := by decide

-- Pigeonhole: more pigeons than holes forces a shared hole.
theorem pigeonhole_demo (f : Fin 5 → Fin 4) : ∃ a b, a ≠ b ∧ f a = f b :=
  Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt f (by simp)

#eval ∑ i ∈ range 11, i
#eval Nat.choose 10 3
#eval (range 5).card
#eval Nat.factorial 6
lessons.solution:
import Mathlib

open Finset

-- Challenge: sum of squares, and a counting fact.
theorem sum_squares (n : ℕ) : 6 * ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), i ^ 2 = n * (n + 1) * (2 * n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    rw [sum_range_succ, mul_add, ih]
    ring

theorem sum_two_pow (n : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ range n, 2 ^ i = 2 ^ n - 1 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    rw [sum_range_succ, ih]
    have : 1 ≤ 2 ^ k := Nat.one_le_two_pow
    omega

theorem subsets_of_four : (powerset (range 4)).card = 16 := by decide

#eval ∑ i ∈ range 6, i ^ 2
#eval (powerset (range 4)).card

lessons.title: Notation, infix operators and the syntax command
body: Metaprogramming starts with a simple observation: everything you type is first parsed into a tree of syntax, and only then given meaning. Lean lets you extend that parser from inside an ordinary file. The gentlest extensions are `infixl`, `infixr`, `infix` and `notation`. Each one introduces a new piece of surface syntax and says which existing function it stands for, so `infixl:65 " ⊞ " => V2.add` means "a left-associative operator at precedence 65 whose meaning is `V2.add`".

The number is a binding power. Higher numbers bind tighter, so `∙` at 70 groups before `⊞` at 65, just as `*` groups before `+`. The three infix forms differ only in associativity: `infixl` groups to the left, `infixr` to the right, and plain `infix` refuses to chain at all, so `a ∙ b ∙ c` is a parse error. `notation` is the general form: it takes any mixfix shape, such as the bracket pair `⟪a, b⟫`, and names the arguments you want to use in the result.

Under the hood these are abbreviations for two separate declarations. `syntax` teaches the parser a new shape and gives it a name; a rule such as `macro_rules` then says what that shape means by rewriting it into other syntax. Writing them apart, as in `syntax "twice! " term : term` followed by `macro_rules | `(twice! $e) => `($e + $e)`, makes the split visible: the parser only recognises, the rule only translates. `syntax:max` gives a form maximal precedence, which is why `abs! (-5 : Int) + 1` reads as `(abs! (-5)) + 1`.

Good notation is cheap to add and expensive to read later, so use it for operators a reader would already recognise. Remember that the quotation marks around the symbol include the spaces you write: `" ⊞ "` tells the pretty printer to print spaces around it. Mathlib adds thousands of such notations, which is why reading its source requires knowing that every symbol is just a registered syntax rule.

Check: if a new notation fails with an unexpected-token error, look at its precedence and at spacing in the quoted symbol. A common mistake is to forget that `infix` is non-associative, so chains of the operator need parentheses or a switch to `infixl` or `infixr`.
lessons.code:
import Lean

structure V2 where
  x : Int
  y : Int
deriving Repr

def V2.add (a b : V2) : V2 := ⟨a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y⟩
def V2.dot (a b : V2) : Int := a.x * b.x + a.y * b.y

-- infixl: left-associative binary operator, precedence 65 (same level as +)
infixl:65 " ⊞ " => V2.add
-- infix: non-associative, so a ∙ b ∙ c is a parse error
infix:70 " ∙ " => V2.dot
-- notation: arbitrary mixfix shape, here a pair-bracket around two arguments
notation "⟪" a ", " b "⟫" => V2.mk a b

#eval (⟪1, 2⟫ ⊞ ⟪10, 20⟫ ⊞ ⟪100, 200⟫)
#eval ⟪1, 2⟫ ∙ ⟪3, 4⟫ + 1

-- `syntax` only teaches the PARSER; the meaning comes from a separate rule.
syntax "twice! " term : term
macro_rules
  | `(twice! $e) => `($e + $e)

#eval twice! 21

-- A leading-precedence example: `abs!` binds tighter than `+`.
syntax:max "abs! " term:max : term
macro_rules
  | `(abs! $e) => `(Int.natAbs $e)

#eval abs! (-5 : Int) + 1
#check (⟪1, 2⟫ : V2)
lessons.solution:
import Lean

structure V2 where
  x : Int
  y : Int
deriving Repr

def V2.smul (k : Int) (v : V2) : V2 := ⟨k * v.x, k * v.y⟩
def V2.norm1 (v : V2) : Nat := v.x.natAbs + v.y.natAbs

-- right-associative, tighter than ⊞-style addition: 2 ⬝ 3 ⬝ v = 2 ⬝ (3 ⬝ v)
infixr:75 " ⬝ " => V2.smul
notation "‖" v "‖₁" => V2.norm1 v
syntax "flip! " term : term
macro_rules
  | `(flip! $v) => `(V2.mk (V2.y $v) (V2.x $v))

def v : V2 := ⟨3, -4⟩
#eval 2 ⬝ 3 ⬝ v
#eval ‖v‖₁
#eval flip! v

lessons.title: Macros, quotations and hygiene
body: A macro is a function from syntax to syntax. Lean calls it after parsing and before elaboration, and it never looks at types, only at the shape of the tree. The one-line form `macro "square! " e:term : term => `($e * $e)` declares the syntax and the expansion together. The backtick-parenthesis form `` `( ... ) `` is a quotation: it builds new syntax, and `$e` splices the matched piece back in. Because `$e` is inserted as one unit, `square! (3 + 1)` becomes `(3 + 1) * (3 + 1)` and not `3 + 1 * 3 + 1`.

Splicing raises a question: what if the macro introduces a variable of its own? In `dup_in`, the expansion contains `let tmp := ...; $body`. If the user also has something called `tmp`, a naive text substitution would let the macro's binder capture the user's name. Lean prevents this with hygiene. Every identifier written inside a quotation is tagged with the scope of its macro expansion, so the macro's `tmp` and the user's `tmp` are different names even though they print alike. The output of `dup_in 1 in tmp` is the global `100`, not the let-bound `2`.

`set_option hygiene false in` turns this off for one declaration, and the leaky version shows what hygiene was protecting you from: the user's `tmp` is now captured by the macro's binder. Unhygienic macros are occasionally needed, for example when a macro must introduce a name the user can refer to, but they are the main source of surprising bugs and should be the exception.

A single syntax can have several rules, which Lean tries in order. The `sum!` example uses the repetition `term,*`, which matches zero or more comma-separated terms, and defines the empty case, the one-element case, and a recursive case that peels off the head. This is how macros do loops: recursion on the syntax, ending when the pattern for the empty list matches.

Check: when a macro does something surprising, print its expansion with `set_option pp.macroStack true` or by writing the quotation by hand. A common mistake is generating a new identifier from a string without `mkIdent`, which produces a name that hygiene will rename or that other code cannot see.
lessons.code:
import Lean

-- `macro` = `syntax` + `macro_rules` in one line. The right side builds NEW syntax
-- inside a quotation `( ... )`, and `$name` splices the matched pieces back in.
macro "square! " e:term : term => `($e * $e)
#eval square! (3 + 1)      -- the argument stays one unit: (3 + 1) * (3 + 1)

-- A macro that introduces its own binder `tmp`.
macro "dup_in " e:term " in " body:term : term => `(let tmp := $e + $e; $body)

def tmp : Nat := 100
-- Hygiene: the `tmp` written in the macro is renamed internally,
-- so the user's `tmp` below still means the global 100, not the let-bound 2.
#eval dup_in 1 in tmp

-- Switching hygiene off lets the macro's `tmp` capture the user's `tmp` (usually a bug).
set_option hygiene false in
macro "dup_in_leaky " e:term " in " body:term : term => `(let tmp := $e + $e; $body)
#eval dup_in_leaky 1 in tmp

-- Several rules: Lean tries them in order and picks the first pattern that matches.
syntax "sum! " term,* : term
macro_rules
  | `(sum!) => `(0)
  | `(sum! $x) => `($x)
  | `(sum! $x, $xs,*) => `($x + sum! $xs,*)

#eval sum! 1, 2, 3, 4
#eval sum!
#check sum! 1, 2

import Lean

-- The macro introduces a local named `m`; hygiene keeps it apart from the user's `m`.
macro "max3! " a:term ", " b:term ", " c:term : term =>
  `(let m := max $a $b; max m $c)

def m : Nat := 50
#eval max3! 1, 2, m
#eval max3! 7, 9, m
#eval max3! 70, 9, m

-- Count the elements of a literal list at macro time with a recursive rule.
syntax "count! " term,* : term
macro_rules
  | `(count!) => `(0)
  | `(count! $_) => `(1)
  | `(count! $_, $xs,*) => `(1 + count! $xs,*)
#eval count! "a", "b", "c"

Then define a `count!` syntax that counts the elements of a literal comma-separated list using recursive macro rules.

lessons.title: Building a small language with declare_syntax_cat
body: So far the new syntax has lived inside the existing `term` category. For a domain-specific language you often want a separate grammar that is not Lean at all, with its own operators and precedence, embedded into Lean through a single doorway. `declare_syntax_cat ex` creates such a category. You then add productions with `syntax`, each ending in `: ex`, and finally one production into `term` that introduces the island, here `[ex| ... ]`.

Precedence works the same way as for infix operators, but you now write it by hand on each production. `syntax:60 ex:60 " + " ex:61 : ex` says: this production sits at level 60, its left operand may be at level 60 or higher, and its right operand must be at level 61 or higher. That asymmetry is what makes the operator left-associative, so `10 - 3 - 2` groups as `(10 - 3) - 2`. Multiplication at level 70 binds tighter, so `1 + 2 * 3` groups as `1 + (2 * 3)`.

The grammar only recognises text. Meaning comes from `macro_rules`, one rule per production, translating each form into a constructor of an ordinary inductive type. Notice that the rules call the doorway again on the sub-expressions, `[ex| $a]` and `[ex| $b]`. The macro expander keeps rewriting until no `[ex| ...]` remains, which is how the recursion over the tree is expressed.

The result is a real value you can evaluate or prove things about. The `prog` example parses `2 + x * (y + 3)`, builds an `Ex` tree, and evaluates it under an environment. Because the DSL compiles to plain data, you keep the whole proof toolbox: you can state and prove a theorem about the evaluator for every program the DSL can express.

Check: an ambiguous or missing parenthesis rule makes the parser stop with an unexpected-token error, so always add the `"(" ex ")"` production. A common mistake is forgetting the doorway recursion in the translation rules, which leaves a literal `[ex| ...]` inside the output.
lessons.code:
import Lean
open Lean

-- Target of the DSL: an ordinary inductive type.
inductive Ex where
  | num (n : Nat)
  | var (name : String)
  | add (a b : Ex)
  | mul (a b : Ex)
deriving Repr

def Ex.eval (env : String → Nat) : Ex → Nat
  | .num n => n
  | .var s => env s
  | .add a b => a.eval env + b.eval env
  | .mul a b => a.eval env * b.eval env

-- 1. A new syntax CATEGORY: a grammar island that is not `term`.
declare_syntax_cat ex
-- 2. Productions of that category. The numbers are binding powers:
--    `+` at 60, `*` at 70, so * binds tighter; left operand allows the same level,
--    right operand needs a higher level, giving left associativity.
syntax num : ex
syntax ident : ex
syntax:60 ex:60 " + " ex:61 : ex
syntax:70 ex:70 " * " ex:71 : ex
syntax "(" ex ")" : ex
-- 3. The doorway from ordinary Lean terms into the category.
syntax "[ex| " ex " ]" : term

-- 4. Translation rules, one per production. They call back into the doorway recursively.
macro_rules
  | `([ex| $n:num]) => `(Ex.num $n)
  | `([ex| $x:ident]) => `(Ex.var $(Syntax.mkStrLit x.getId.toString))
  | `([ex| $a + $b]) => `(Ex.add [ex| $a] [ex| $b])
  | `([ex| $a * $b]) => `(Ex.mul [ex| $a] [ex| $b])
  | `([ex| ($a)]) => `([ex| $a])

def prog : Ex := [ex| 2 + x * (y + 3)]
#eval prog
#eval prog.eval fun s => if s == "x" then 10 else 1
-- precedence check: this must group as 1 + (2 * 3)
#eval [ex| 1 + 2 * 3]
lessons.solution:
import Lean
open Lean

inductive Ex where
  | num (n : Nat)
  | add (a b : Ex)
  | sub (a b : Ex)
  | mul (a b : Ex)
deriving Repr

def Ex.eval : Ex → Nat
  | .num n => n
  | .add a b => a.eval + b.eval
  | .sub a b => a.eval - b.eval
  | .mul a b => a.eval * b.eval

declare_syntax_cat arith
syntax num : arith
syntax:60 arith:60 " + " arith:61 : arith
syntax:60 arith:60 " - " arith:61 : arith
syntax:70 arith:70 " * " arith:71 : arith
syntax "(" arith ")" : arith
syntax "[arith| " arith " ]" : term

macro_rules
  | `([arith| $n:num]) => `(Ex.num $n)
  | `([arith| $a + $b]) => `(Ex.add [arith| $a] [arith| $b])
  | `([arith| $a - $b]) => `(Ex.sub [arith| $a] [arith| $b])
  | `([arith| $a * $b]) => `(Ex.mul [arith| $a] [arith| $b])
  | `([arith| ($a)]) => `([arith| $a])

-- left associativity of `-`: (10 - 3) - 2 = 5, not 10 - (3 - 2) = 9
#eval [arith| 10 - 3 - 2].eval
#eval [arith| 2 * (3 + 4) - 4].eval
#eval [arith| 1 - 2 + 5]
lessons.challenge: Create a second DSL category `arith` with numbers, `+`, `-`, `*` and parentheses, translated into an `Ex` type with an `add`, `sub`, `mul` and `num` constructor. Make `-` left-associative, evaluate `10 - 3 - 2` and `2 * (3 + 4) - 4`, and print the tree for `1 - 2 + 5`.
lessons.question: What makes a binary operator left-associative in `syntax:60 ex:60 " + " ex:61 : ex`?
options: Precedence 60 is smaller than the default
The left operand may be at the operator's own level but the right operand must be strictly higher
The word `ex` appears twice
The operator is written between two terms
lessons.explanation: Left associativity comes from allowing the left operand at the operator's own level while requiring a strictly higher level on the right. The output shows the tree for `2 + x * (y + 3)`, the value `42` under the environment x = 10, y = 1, and `1 + 2 * 3` grouped as `Ex.add (Ex.num 1) (Ex.mul ...)`, which proves that `*` binds tighter.

lessons.title: Syntax trees, macros and elaborators
body: Lean processes source in phases. First the parser turns text into a `Syntax` tree. Then macros may rewrite that tree into other syntax. Finally the elaborator turns syntax into a typed term (`Expr`), solving implicit arguments and unifying types on the way. Metaprogramming is writing your own code for one of these phases, so the first skill is knowing which phase a problem belongs to.

`Syntax` is a plain tree. Each node has a kind (its production name), a list of children, and the leaves are atoms such as keywords and identifiers. The `#syntax_shape` command prints the kind and children of the term you give it, which is a good way to learn what the parser produced. An `elab ... : command` receives that syntax and runs in the command monad, so it can log messages and inspect anything it likes.

A macro has type `Syntax → MacroM Syntax`. It sees only tokens, which is why it can be cheap and simple, and why it cannot answer questions about types. The `def_answer` macro builds a new declaration name with `mkIdent`, which is the standard way to construct a fresh identifier from a string. An elaborator has type `Syntax → TermElabM Expr`. It runs inside the elaborator, so it can elaborate subterms, ask `inferType` what they are, and unify.

The `type_string%` example shows the difference. It elaborates its argument and returns the type as a string, something a macro cannot do because the type does not exist until elaboration. The reverse composition also works: `show_type%` is a macro that expands to a use of the elaborator `type_string%`, because macro expansion happens first and the elaborator then handles the result.

Check: choose the weakest tool that works. If you only rearrange syntax, write a macro; if you need types, instances or the environment, write an elaborator. A common mistake is writing an elaborator when a macro would do, which makes the code harder to read and slower to run.
lessons.code:
import Lean
open Lean Elab Command Term Meta

-- Syntax is a plain tree: nodes with a KIND and children, atoms (keywords), identifiers.
-- A command elaborator receives the user's syntax and can inspect it as data.
elab "#syntax_shape " t:term : command => do
  let stx : Syntax := t.raw                     -- TSyntax `term  ->  Syntax
  logInfo m!"kind = {stx.getKind}, children = {stx.getNumArgs}"
  logInfo m!"child kinds = {stx.getArgs.toList.map (·.getKind)}"

#syntax_shape 1 + f x

-- MACRO: a function Syntax -> MacroM Syntax. It never looks at types.
-- Building a NEW identifier from a string is the classic unhygienic step: use mkIdent.
macro "def_answer " n:ident : command =>
  `(def $(mkIdent (n.getId.appendAfter "_answer")) : Nat := 42)
def_answer life
#eval life_answer

-- ELAB: a function Syntax -> TermElabM Expr. It runs after parsing, inside the elaborator,
-- so it may elaborate subterms, ask for their TYPES, unify, and read the environment.
elab "type_string% " t:term : term => do
  let e ← elabTerm t none
  let ty ← inferType e
  return mkStrLit (toString (← ppExpr ty))

#eval type_string% (3 : Int)
#eval type_string% [some (1 : Nat), none]
#eval type_string% fun (n : Nat) => n = n

-- The same job as a macro is impossible: a macro sees only the tokens, not the type.
-- (Macros may still call `elab`-defined syntax, since expansion happens first.)
macro "show_type% " t:term : term => `(type_string% $t)
#eval show_type% "hello"
lessons.solution:
import Lean
open Lean Elab Term Meta

-- Needs types, so it must be an elab: count the arrows (head Pi binders) of a term's type.
elab "arity% " t:term : term => do
  let e ← elabTerm t none
  let ty ← inferType e
  return mkNatLit ty.getNumHeadForalls

#eval arity% Nat.add
#eval arity% (fun (a b c : Nat) => a + b + c)
#eval arity% (5 : Nat)
#eval arity% List.map (α := Nat) (β := Nat)

-- Needs no types, so a macro is the right (cheaper) tool: swap two arguments of a function.
macro "flip% " f:term : term => `(fun a b => $f b a)
#eval (flip% Nat.sub) 3 10
lessons.challenge: Write an elaborator `arity% e` that returns the number of arguments in the type of `e` (count the leading arrows), and test it on `Nat.add`, a three-argument lambda, and a plain number. Then write a macro `flip% f` that swaps the arguments of a binary function and test it on `Nat.sub`. Explain in a comment why one needs `elab` and the other only `macro`.
lessons.question: Why can `arity%` not be written as a macro?
options: The parser rejects the word arity
The number of arrows is a property of the term's type, which only exists once the elaborator has typed the term
Macros are not allowed to return numbers
Macros cannot use quotations

lessons.title: Expr: the anatomy of a term
body: Every theorem, definition and proof in Lean is ultimately an `Expr`, the data structure the kernel checks. It is a small inductive type with only a handful of constructors: constants (`.const`), applications (`.app`), lambdas (`.lam`), dependent function types (`.forallE`), local variables (`.fvar`), bound variables (`.bvar`), metavariables (`.mvar`) and literals. Learning to read and build `Expr` values is the foundation for every tactic.

Application is binary, so `Nat.add 1 2` is `app (app (const Nat.add) 1) 2`. The helpers `mkApp2` and `getAppFn` / `getAppArgs` hide that nesting. A constant is a name plus universe levels, here none. Literals are stored specially: `mkNatLit 1` is the raw numeral and is not the same Expr as the elaborated `OfNat` form you get from the parser, a distinction that matters when matching terms.

Binders use de Bruijn indices. In `fun x => x` the body is `.bvar 0`, meaning "the nearest enclosing binder". In `fun x y => x` the body is `.bvar 1`, because the inner binder `y` is skipped. Counting indices by hand is error-prone, so tactics normally open a binder with a free variable (`withLocalDeclD`), build the body using that variable, and call `mkLambdaFVars` to close it again. The solution to the exercise builds the same function both ways and shows they are structurally equal.

A metavariable is a typed hole that unification may fill in later; `mkFreshExprMVar` creates one. `instantiate1` replaces `bvar 0` in a body with a value, which is how a binder is opened. `inferType` computes the type of any closed term, and `whnf` reduces it just enough to expose its head. Most of what a tactic does is some combination of building, inspecting and comparing these values.

Check: if a term you built is rejected, print it with `logInfo` and look for a loose bound variable (a `bvar` that escaped its binder) or a missing universe level. A common mistake is mixing up `bvar` and `fvar`, since the first is an index into enclosing binders and the second is a name in the local context.
lessons.code:
import Lean
open Lean Meta

-- Expr is the kernel's term language. We build terms by hand, with no parser involved.
-- A constant: the NAME of a declaration (plus universe levels, none here).
def natT : Expr := .const ``Nat []

-- Application is binary: `Nat.add 1 2` is app (app (const Nat.add) 1) 2.
def oneAddTwo : Expr := mkApp2 (.const ``Nat.add []) (mkNatLit 1) (mkNatLit 2)

-- Lambdas use de Bruijn indices: `.bvar 0` means "the nearest enclosing binder".
-- fun (x : Nat) => x
def idNat : Expr := .lam `x natT (.bvar 0) .default
-- fun (x y : Nat) => x   (bvar 1 skips the inner binder `y`)
def constNat : Expr := .lam `x natT (.lam `y natT (.bvar 1) .default) .default

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  logInfo m!"{oneAddTwo} : {← inferType oneAddTwo}"
  logInfo m!"{idNat} : {← inferType idNat}"
  logInfo m!"{constNat} : {← inferType constNat}"
  -- taking an application apart
  logInfo m!"head = {oneAddTwo.getAppFn}, args = {oneAddTwo.getAppArgs}"
  logInfo m!"is app: {oneAddTwo.isApp}, is lambda: {idNat.isLambda}, ctor: {idNat.ctorName}"
  -- instantiating the body of a binder with a value replaces bvar 0
  let body := idNat.bindingBody!
  logInfo m!"bvar 0 := 7 gives {body.instantiate1 (mkNatLit 7)}"
  -- a metavariable: a typed hole that unification may fill in later
  let hole ← mkFreshExprMVar (some natT)
  logInfo m!"hole is mvar: {hole.isMVar}, its type: {← inferType hole}"
  -- the same term read back as a real Lean value
  let v ← unsafe evalExpr Nat natT oneAddTwo
  logInfo m!"evaluates to {v}"
lessons.solution:
import Lean
open Lean Meta

def natT : Expr := .const ``Nat []
def succ2Raw : Expr :=
  .lam `n natT (mkApp (.const ``Nat.succ []) (mkApp (.const ``Nat.succ []) (.bvar 0))) .default

-- Same function, built with a local hypothesis instead of counting de Bruijn indices.
def succ2Fvar : MetaM Expr :=
  withLocalDeclD `n natT fun n => do
    let body := mkApp (.const ``Nat.succ []) (mkApp (.const ``Nat.succ []) n)
    mkLambdaFVars #[n] body   -- abstracts the free variable back into bvar 0

#eval show MetaM Unit from do
  let viaFvar ← succ2Fvar
  logInfo m!"raw   : {succ2Raw}"
  logInfo m!"fvar  : {viaFvar}"
  logInfo m!"structurally equal: {succ2Raw == viaFvar}"
  logInfo m!"type: {← inferType viaFvar}"
  let applied := mkApp viaFvar (mkNatLit 5)
  logInfo m!"applied: {applied}, reduced: {← whnf applied}"

options: A free variable from the local context
The type natT

The inner variable y, since it was bound last

The output prints the hand-built terms and their types, shows `bvar 0 := 7` instantiating the identity body to `7`, and confirms that the lambda built with de Bruijn indices equals the one built with a local variable.
