lessons.title: Skip rejected elements
body: continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Put the rejection condition before any state update that should apply only to accepted elements.
For input [-1, 0, 2], the worked computation produces [0, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting rejected elements violates the filter predicate.

continue skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and proceeds to the next item. It does not terminate traversal. Placing a rejection guard near the top of the loop lets later statements describe the accepted path without extra nesting.

Decide which bookkeeping applies to rejected items. In this task, rejected_count changes before continue; appending to accepted happens only afterward. If continue is removed, the invalid item still reaches the accepted update even though its rejection was recorded.

Zero belongs to the accepted domain because the rule excludes negative values, not falsy values. Keep input order and duplicates unless the contract explicitly requests sorting or deduplication. A filter changes membership; it does not silently change other properties.

Transfer walkthrough: The negative values increment the rejection count and skip append. Zero remains present. Without continue, rejected values would appear in the accepted output despite being counted as rejected.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [-1, 0, 2]
result = []
for x in data:
    if x < 0:
        continue
    result.append(x)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Understand loop else
body: A loop else runs when the loop finishes without break, including an empty traversal. It can express failure of an early-exit search.
For input [1, 7], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An unconditional final assignment overwrites the successful search.

A loop's else block runs when the loop finishes without break. For a for loop, that means normal exhaustion, including an iterable that was empty from the start. The else block belongs to the loop's completion condition, not to the nearest if statement.

A search can use break to represent the early success path and else to represent failure after all candidates. Returning from a containing function or propagating an exception does not cause the loop's else to execute. The rule is about normal completion, not whether the loop body ever ran.

In a compact example indentation makes the control structure visible. Trace an empty input, an early match and a final-position match before editing it. Replacing break with pass allows exhaustion and the else block can overwrite a previously stored success.
Transfer walkthrough: A match sets found and breaks, skipping else. A nonmatch search and an empty iterable reach normal exhaustion and assign absent. Pass does not bypass the else block.

lessons.title: Short circuit unsafe operations
body: and evaluates its right operand only when its left operand is truthy. A denominator guard prevents division by zero before comparison.
For input 0, the worked computation produces false. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing the guard evaluates unsafe division first.

and evaluates its right operand only when the left operand is truthy. or evaluates its right operand only when the left operand is falsy. This allows a cheap validity guard to protect a later operation that would otherwise be invalid.

Place a nonzero-denominator check before division. Reversing the two operands defeats the guard because the dangerous operation is attempted first. Replacing and with or also changes which path is evaluated and can both misclassify valid inputs and attempt division by zero.

and and or return operands, not necessarily Boolean objects. This example uses comparison results on both sides, so its result is Boolean. When the contract demands a Boolean but operands are arbitrary values, make that conversion explicit. Short circuiting specifies evaluation order; it does not validate an entire input schema.
Transfer walkthrough: For [6,2], the guard succeeds and the ratio is three. For [6,0], the guard is false and division is skipped. For [0,3], division is valid but the final comparison is false.

lessons.title: Enumerate index and value
body: enumerate supplies a counter alongside each value. Its start argument controls the labels without changing the input collection.
For input ['a', 'b'], the worked computation produces [[1, "a"], [2, "b"]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A zero-based label is wrong when the output contract is one-based.

enumerate pairs a running position with each value from an iterable. Its start parameter selects the first reported number. This avoids managing a separate counter and makes the relationship between a row and its position explicit.

A reported offset does not change the underlying iterable's indexing. Starting labels at ten produces ten and eleven; it does not read elements ten and eleven from the input. Repeated values must still receive separate positions, so looking up each value with list.index is not a substitute.

Choose a zero-based position for internal indexing and an explicit offset for user-facing line numbers or external record identifiers. Keep the contract clear about which one is being returned. Empty input produces no pairs regardless of the starting offset.
Transfer walkthrough: The starting offset labels the first traversed element, not a position to skip to. Each following element increments the number once, including repeated labels.
lessons.code:
import json

data = ['a', 'b']
result = [[i,x] for i,x in enumerate(data,start=1)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Zip and length contracts
body: zip stops at the shortest input by default. Use strict=True when unequal lengths indicate invalid paired records.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [[1, 3], [2, 4]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Silently truncating pairs discards unpaired data.

zip pairs corresponding items from its input iterables. By default it stops when the shortest input is exhausted, so extra items in a longer input are silently unused. That is useful for some tasks but dangerous when every field must align.

strict=True raises ValueError when the iterables do not end together. The check happens while consuming the zip iterator; merely constructing it does not establish equal lengths. Materializing all pairs inside the try block ensures the complete alignment check runs here.

Equal lengths do not prove semantic alignment. If two arrays have been sorted independently, their rows may still be paired incorrectly. The strict check catches a structural mismatch, while a real data pipeline also needs stable keys, ordering contracts or validated joins. The transfer problem deliberately checks only complete positional pairing.
Transfer walkthrough: The equal-length lists produce two ordered pairs. Either longer side violates the one-to-one contract. Default zip would silently drop an unmatched key or value.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
try:
    result = [list(p) for p in zip(*data,strict=True)]
except ValueError:
    result = None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))
lessons.solution:

data = [[1, 2], [3]]
try:
    result = [list(p) for p in zip(*data,strict=True)]
except ValueError:

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Normalize Unicode intentionally
body: Visually similar text may use different code-point sequences. NFC normalization combines canonical equivalents before equality comparison.
For input ['é', 'é'], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Raw code-point equality can disagree with canonical equivalence.

Unicode allows some visually similar text to have different code-point sequences. NFC normalization composes canonical equivalents where possible. It is useful when a contract intentionally treats canonically equivalent spellings as the same text.

Compatibility normalization is a broader policy. NFKC can fold a fullwidth Latin letter into an ordinary Latin letter, while NFC retains that distinction. Normalization is also different from case folding, accent removal and grapheme segmentation. Do not treat these transformations as interchangeable cleaning operations.

The transfer exercise exposes the normalized text and its code-point count. It includes both decomposed accents and a compatibility distinction, so an implementation using the wrong normalization form cannot pass by handling only common accented text. Normalization alone is not a defense against all visually confusable identifiers.
Transfer walkthrough: The decomposed accent composes to one code point, matching precomposed é. Fullwidth A remains distinct because canonical normalization does not apply its compatibility mapping.
lessons.code:
import json
import unicodedata
data = ['é', 'é']
result = unicodedata.normalize('NFC',data[0]) == unicodedata.normalize('NFC',data[1])
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Separate bytes from text
body: Encoding turns text into bytes using an explicit codec. UTF-8 uses a variable number of bytes per code point, so byte length and string length differ.
For input 'cat', the worked computation produces 3. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting characters is not a UTF-8 payload byte count.

Text and encoded bytes are separate representations. str holds Unicode code points; bytes holds integers from zero to 255. Encoding chooses how to represent text as bytes, and decoding interprets bytes using a specified encoding.

Choose UTF-8 because the input contract says UTF-8, not because a byte sequence looks readable. Strict decoding rejects an invalid sequence. Using errors='replace' keeps processing but inserts replacement characters, so it is a data-loss policy that must be deliberate and visible.

The transfer input is a list of byte integers so it can be written as portable input data. bytes(data) constructs the byte sequence; decode then interprets it. An empty byte sequence decodes to empty text. Invalid UTF-8 is reported separately from that successful empty value.

Transfer walkthrough: The two-byte suffix represents é, and the four-byte fixture represents a single brain code point. Byte 255 is not a valid standalone UTF-8 sequence and follows the explicit error path.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 'cat'
result = len(data.encode('utf-8'))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Slice with a step
body: A slice selects a subsequence without mutating the original list. A negative step walks backward, while the stop remains exclusive.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [3, 2, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing the input in place changes shared state.

A slice describes positions rather than element values. Its start is included, its stop is excluded, and its step controls both spacing and direction. A negative step walks toward lower positions. A zero step raises ValueError; it does not describe an empty slice.

Omitted bounds are represented by None in a slice expression built from variables. For a negative step, leaving stop omitted is different from explicitly writing -1: an explicit negative index is interpreted relative to the sequence, while the omitted bound permits traversal past index zero. This explains why items[::-1] is the usual reversal spelling.

Slices clamp out-of-range endpoints and preserve sequence shape; element indexing instead raises for a nonexistent position. For lists, the result is a new outer list that still refers to the selected objects. Inspect both values and length in the transfer task, including reverse and empty cases.
Transfer walkthrough: The first slice visits positions one and three. The omitted-bound negative-step slice reverses the list. Empty and clamped-outside inputs produce empty lists with count zero.

import json

data = [1, 2, 3]
result = data[::-1]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Copy nested mutable structures
body: A shallow copy duplicates the outer list while nested mutable objects stay shared. deepcopy is appropriate when independent nested state is the required contract.
For input [[1], [2]], the worked computation produces [[1], [2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Copying only the outer container still shares inner lists.

An outer list contains references to its elements. Repeating a list of one mutable row repeats the reference; it does not construct independent rows. A shallow outer copy also preserves references to the same nested objects. The resulting rows can look independent until a mutation exposes their shared identity.

Create a fresh inner list on each comprehension iteration when constructing independent rows. Use deepcopy when copying an existing nested object graph actually requires that policy. Deep copying is not a universal reset: it preserves internal graph relationships with memoization and user-defined types can customize copying.

A useful regression mutates one chosen row and checks every other row, not just the selected cell. Include at least two rows, since a single-row example cannot distinguish an independent construction from repeated aliases. This is the bounded ownership concept adapted from the supplied book's nested-list section.

Transfer walkthrough: Each row is a separately constructed list. Updating row zero cannot change row one. The one-row case is valid but the two- and three-row cases are required to expose the shared-row alternative.
lessons.code:
import json
import copy
data = [[1], [2]]
other = copy.deepcopy(data)
other[0].append(9)
result = data
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Count with dictionaries
body: Dictionary lookup associates a hashable key with a value. get supplies the initial count only when the key is absent, then repeated keys increment it.
For input ['a', 'b', 'a'], the worked computation produces {"a": 2, "b": 1}. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Overwriting with one loses occurrence counts.

A dictionary associates each hashable key with a value. A frequency table uses the observed item as the key and a count as the value. get(key, 0) supplies a starting count for a missing key; adding one and assigning back records the current occurrence.

Missing and present-with-zero are different states in many dictionaries, but this frequency contract deliberately treats both as the same starting count. Do not generalize that policy to every configuration or data-cleaning task. An empty string can be a legitimate key and should not be rejected by an unrelated truthiness test.

Dictionary insertion order is deterministic for a given traversal, but an output sorted by key is a separate requirement. The transfer problem explicitly sorts the report without changing the counting rule. Duplicates must increase counts; replacing the stored value with one loses that information.
Transfer walkthrough: The traversal counts b twice and a once. Sorting the keys produces a before b in the report. Empty input gives no entries and an empty-string key remains valid.
lessons.code:
import json

data = ['a', 'b', 'a']
counts = {}
for x in data:
    counts[x] = counts.get(x,0)+1
result = counts
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.title: Transfer: a deterministic frequency report
exercises.prompt:
data is a list of strings, including possible empty strings and duplicates. Return [key, occurrence_count] pairs sorted by key.
Check all these cases:
Input ['b', 'a', 'b'] → [["a", 1], ["b", 2]]
Input [] → []
Input ['', ''] → [["", 2]]
Input ['0', 'False', '0'] → [["0", 2], ["False", 1]]

data = ['b', 'a', 'b']
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.
result = None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
exercises.solution:
import json

data = ['b', 'a', 'b']
counts = {}
for key in data:
    counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1
result = [[key, counts[key]] for key in sorted(counts)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: Use the whole string as the dictionary key.
Increment the stored count for every occurrence.
Sort keys only when constructing the final report.

lessons.title: Deduplicate with sets
body: A set represents distinct hashable values and supports membership. Sort the distinct values when a deterministic output order is part of the contract.
For input [3, 1, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A sorted list alone retains duplicates.

A set stores distinct hashable values. Membership answers whether a value is present, while set difference asks which values occur in one set but not the other. Neither operation preserves occurrence counts.

If incoming values contain duplicates, constructing a set intentionally removes those duplicates. Subtract the known set to find previously unseen values. Union instead combines both sides and would reintroduce known values into a new-only report.

Set iteration order is not an output-order contract. Sort comparable values when a deterministic report is required. If original first-seen order or multiplicity matters, use a different representation rather than relying on whichever order a set happens to display.
Transfer walkthrough: The repeated c contributes one distinct new name. Known b is excluded. Union would incorrectly include a and b, violating the new-only condition.

lessons.title: Stable sorting and keys
body: Python sorting is stable: equal keys preserve their input order. A key function controls ordering without changing the records themselves.

For input [['b', 2], ['a', 1], ['c', 1]], the worked computation produces [["a", 1], ["c", 1], ["b", 2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Sorting on the wrong field changes the intended ranking.

sorted returns a new list. list.sort changes its target list in place and returns None. Assigning the return value of list.sort to a variable therefore does not produce the sorted list. Select the API from the ownership and return-value contract.

Python sorting is stable: records with equal keys retain their input order, including when reverse=True selects descending key order. Adding an identifier as a secondary key is a different ordering policy. It can make a result look deterministic while violating the required tie order.

Use equal-key records in an intentionally non-secondary-key order to test stability. Also verify whether the original list should remain unchanged. The transfer receipt reports the ranked list and an explicit unchanged-input check; it does not infer independence of the nested record objects.
Transfer walkthrough: The highest score moves to the front, while the equal-score a and b records keep their arrival order. A descending secondary ID key would incorrectly reverse that pair.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [['b', 2], ['a', 1], ['c', 1]]
result = sorted(data,key=lambda row:row[1])
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Comprehensions combine map and filter
body: A comprehension first selects each input satisfying its condition, then computes an output expression. Filtering and transforming are separate parts of the contract.
For input [-2, 0, 3], the worked computation produces [0, 9]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Squaring rejected negative values includes records meant to be removed.

A comprehension combines traversal, selection and transformation into an expression. The for clause produces candidates, the if clause decides which candidates survive, and the leading expression constructs each retained result. Reading those responsibilities separately makes the compact syntax easier to trace.

Filtering even integers is a numeric predicate, not a positive-value test. Negative even values and zero satisfy the evenness rule. Duplicates and traversal order remain unless another operation explicitly changes them.

Prefer an ordinary loop when branching or side effects make the comprehension difficult to explain. A shorter expression is not automatically clearer. The transfer task is intentionally a simple pure transformation, so a comprehension expresses its contract without hidden updates.
Transfer walkthrough: Minus two, zero and two survive the evenness predicate and are doubled. The positive-only alternative discards a valid negative and zero while admitting positive odd values.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [-2, 0, 3]
result = [x*x for x in data if x >= 0]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Queues need efficient end operations
body: deque supports appending at one end and removing from the other without shifting every remaining element. FIFO removes the oldest item.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Popping from the insertion end implements a stack instead.

A FIFO queue removes the oldest pending item. Appending on the right and removing with popleft on the left implements that order. Removing with pop from the right instead gives stack behavior. The same container can support different policies; the operation pair defines which one is being used.

Removing index zero from a list also gives FIFO order, but it shifts remaining references. deque supports efficient operations at both ends. This is an algorithmic data-structure distinction, not a measured throughput claim for every workload or a guarantee about a compound multi-step threaded operation.

Source correction: the supplied first edition describes append followed by pop(0) as LIFO in its queue discussion. The actual operation sequence is FIFO. The original exercise below checks this observable ordering using fresh work IDs rather than reproducing the book's example. Bounded deque eviction and thread coordination have separate contracts.

Transfer walkthrough: Appending arrivals a, b and c and removing from the left processes a then b. Removing from the right would process c then b. The empty and one-job fixtures protect the removal boundary.

lessons.title: Maintain a min heap
body: A min heap exposes the smallest value at its root. heapify establishes the invariant; heap order does not mean every array position is globally sorted.
For input [4, 1, 3], the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reading the first unsorted input element is not a minimum operation.

A min heap maintains a partial ordering that puts a smallest item at the root. It does not store every item in globally sorted order. heapify establishes the heap invariant, and heappop both removes the root and restores the invariant for the remaining items.

Copy input values when the caller's list must remain unchanged. Calling heappop repeatedly on the copy yields values in ascending order, including duplicates. Indexing the internal heap array or removing arbitrary positions is not a substitute for the heap operations.

State how many results are requested and what happens when fewer items exist. The transfer task returns at most k items, so k=0 and an empty input are legitimate boundaries. It uses a trusted small fixture rather than claiming any measured performance advantage.
Transfer walkthrough: Heapifying makes one a root minimum and each pop restores the invariant. Two equal minima are both retained. Bounding the count avoids popping from an exhausted heap.

import json
import heapq
data = [4, 1, 3]
items = list(data)
heapq.heapify(items)
result = heapq.heappop(items) if items else None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Binary search needs sorted data
body: bisect_left returns the first insertion position preserving sorted order. Check both the bound and equality when using that position for membership.
For input [[1, 3, 5], 3], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An insertion position can exist even when the target is absent.

Binary search relies on sorted input. bisect_left returns the first insertion position that keeps ascending order, putting an equal value at or after that boundary. An insertion position can be valid even when the searched value does not exist.

For membership or a first equal index, check both that the position is in bounds and that the value there equals the target. With duplicates, bisect_left identifies the first equal position while bisect_right identifies the position after the equal run. They are not interchangeable.

Do not silently sort an input when the required output is an index into its existing order. Sortedness is an explicit precondition in this exercise. Binary search locates a position efficiently; inserting into a Python list can still shift later elements, so search and insertion have different costs.

Transfer walkthrough: Three's equal run starts at index one. The right boundary would land after both equal entries and fail the first-equal contract. Interior and end absence cases must both return None.

result = i < len(items) and items[i] == target

lessons.title: Equality and hashing agree
body: Equal immutable tuples must have equal hashes. Hash equality alone cannot prove value equality because hash functions may collide.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [true, true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Identity is not a substitute for structural value equality.

Hash-based containers use both hashes and equality. Equal hashable values must have equal hashes, but unequal values can share a hash. A hash is a lookup aid, not a unique identity or proof of equality.

Some values of different numeric types compare equal. In Python, True, 1 and 1.0 are equal as mapping keys and occupy one entry. Text '1' is a different key. Converting keys to text would change those equivalence rules and can both split equal numeric keys and merge unequal text/numeric keys.

A mutable object's changing equality-relevant state makes hashing difficult; a key must remain usable throughout its lifetime in the container. The transfer lab uses immutable JSON scalar keys and observes key equivalence only. It does not prescribe a hash implementation for arbitrary user-defined mutable classes.

Transfer walkthrough: True, one and one-point-zero represent one native mapping key. Zero and False also share a key, while text '1' and numeric one remain separate. Stringification violates both kinds of distinction.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [1, 2]
a = tuple(data)
b = tuple(list(data))
result = [a==b,hash(a)==hash(b)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Prefix sums avoid repeated work
body: A prefix sum records the total through each position. One traversal maintains a running total rather than recomputing every prefix from scratch.
For input [2, 3, 4], the worked computation produces [2, 5, 9]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Emitting the unaccumulated values does not produce prefix totals.

A prefix-sum table stores a total for each prefix. Including an initial zero makes prefix[k] the sum of the first k items. This aligns positions with half-open intervals and handles empty prefixes naturally.

The sum over values[start:stop] is prefix[stop] minus prefix[start]. Subtracting removes the contribution before start. An empty interval has equal prefix positions and therefore sum zero, even when earlier values are nonzero.

Building the table takes one traversal and retains one more total than the number of items. Each later valid range query needs two table reads and a subtraction. This is an operation-count argument for repeated queries, not a measured timing result or a reason to allocate a table for every one-off sum.

Transfer walkthrough: The first range includes minus one and four, totaling three. Prefix[3] is five and prefix[1] is two, so their difference is three. The empty-interval fixture checks exact cancellation.
lessons.code:
import json
import itertools
data = [2, 3, 4]
result = list(itertools.accumulate(data))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Return values explicitly
body: A function call evaluates its body and returns a value to its caller. Falling off the end returns None; printing a value is a separate side effect.
For input 4, the worked computation produces 8. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Computing a value without returning it loses the function result.

Calling a function evaluates its arguments, binds the parameter names and executes the function body. return sends a value back to the caller and stops that call. Falling off the end returns None. Printing a value has a visible side effect but does not send that value back as the function's result.

Design a function from its input and output contract. State how the empty case is represented before using operations such as min or max, which require at least one item. A caller should not need to read console output to recover the answer.

A result can contain several related values. The transfer function returns a two-element list when observations exist and None when no range can be computed. This makes absence distinct from a legitimate zero-width range such as [2,2].

lessons.title: Avoid mutable default state
body: Default argument objects are created at function definition. Use None and allocate inside the call when each invocation needs an independent list.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [[1], [2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A shared default list carries values from earlier calls.

Default argument expressions run when the function definition executes, not anew on each call. A list in that position can therefore accumulate state across calls. An immutable None default lets the function decide to allocate fresh storage during each call that omitted a container.

Fresh storage should not erase an explicitly supplied container. Testing items is None preserves a caller's intentionally empty list, while if not items can replace that legitimate list. Distinguish the default-storage policy from a policy that always copies arguments.

The transfer fixture observes independent default calls and deliberate sharing in the same program. It checks both contents and whether the explicit container is returned as the same object. Different references and equal contents answer different questions.

Transfer walkthrough: The default calls allocate separately. The explicit list receives both values and remains identical to the returned container. A mutable default joins the first two calls unexpectedly.

    if items is None:

    items.append(x)
    return items

b = collect(data[1])
result = [a,b]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Keyword-only API boundaries
body: A parameter after * must be passed by name. This prevents ambiguous positional configuration and produces TypeError for a positional call.
For input [2, 3], the worked computation produces "keyword required". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing * permits a call the public contract rejects.

A parameter after a bare * is keyword-only. Calling the function must spell that parameter's name. This makes configuration such as a discount, encoding or timeout visible at the call site instead of depending on a reader remembering positional order.

A default controls whether an argument may be omitted; keyword-only controls how a supplied argument is passed. These are separate API choices. Removing * silently expands the accepted calling forms even if valid keyword calls still compute the same values.

An API contract includes rejected calls as well as successful ones. The transfer exercise runs a correct keyword call and observes that the corresponding positional call raises TypeError. Comparing only the arithmetic result of the valid call would miss the signature regression.

Transfer walkthrough: The arithmetic result is eight. Supplying the discount positionally must raise TypeError, yielding False in the receipt. Removing the star preserves eight but incorrectly changes the second field.

lessons.title: Positional-only parameters
body: A slash marks parameters that callers must supply positionally. This lets implementations rename internal parameter names without supporting those names as public keywords.
For input 3, the worked computation produces "positional required". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing the slash changes which keyword calls are accepted.

A slash marks earlier parameters as positional-only. Their internal names are not accepted as keywords for those parameters. This lets an API rename an internal parameter without promising that name as part of the keyword interface.

A useful consequence appears with **metadata: a keyword whose spelling matches a positional-only parameter can still belong to the metadata dictionary. Without the slash, that keyword would try to bind the same ordinary parameter a second time and raise TypeError.

Do not add positional-only markers indiscriminately. They make sense when names are incidental or when a separate keyword namespace is intentional. The transfer task makes that namespace distinction observable instead of treating the slash as syntax to memorize.

Transfer walkthrough: Seven binds the positional-only parameter, while 'note' is stored under the metadata key value. An ordinary value parameter would instead receive both a positional and keyword argument.

lessons.title: Unpack argument sequences
body: The * operator expands an iterable into positional arguments. It does not wrap the whole sequence as one argument.
For input [2, 3], the worked computation produces 5. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Passing the list as one argument violates a two-argument signature.

*values expands an iterable into positional arguments at a call site. **options expands a mapping into keyword arguments. Passing values without the star sends the whole iterable as one argument rather than supplying its members separately.

Unpacking still obeys the function's signature. Too many values, a missing required parameter, duplicate bindings or an unexpected keyword can raise TypeError. It is not an escape from input validation, and arbitrary external dictionaries should not be blindly forwarded to unrelated APIs.

The transfer fixture combines exactly two positional numbers with one named scale. The shape of the argument list and the name of the option are explicit preconditions. This makes the distinction between packaging data and calling an API concrete.
Transfer walkthrough: One and two bind a and b; scale=3 binds the keyword-only parameter, giving nine. Passing the list as one argument leaves b missing.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [2, 3]
def add_pair(a,b):
    return a+b
result = add_pair(*data)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Closures capture bindings
body: Closures look up captured names when called. A default parameter can snapshot the current loop value when constructing independent callbacks.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Late binding makes every callback observe the final loop value.

A nested function can refer to names from an enclosing scope. The reference is a binding to look up when the function is called, not automatically a snapshot of the value when the function was created. A loop commonly reuses the same target name for every iteration.

A default parameter expression is evaluated when each function is defined. Binding value=value in a generated callback therefore stores that iteration's object as a default. It snapshots a reference, not a deep copy; mutable objects can still be shared deliberately or accidentally.

Call generated callbacks after the construction loop has finished to expose late binding. Calling each callback immediately inside the loop can hide the defect because the loop variable still has that iteration's value. Distinct inputs are necessary to make the difference observable.
Transfer walkthrough: The three callbacks retain defaults one, two and three and later add ten. Without the default binding, all three look up the final loop value three.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [1, 2, 3]
callbacks = [lambda x=x:x for x in data]
result = [f() for f in callbacks]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Update enclosing state with nonlocal
body: A nested function needs nonlocal to rebind a variable in its enclosing function. The closure can then maintain state across calls.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [1, 2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Creating a local counter disconnects updates from the enclosing state.

Assigning to a name inside a function normally makes it local to that function. nonlocal declares that rebinding should instead affect an existing binding in a containing function scope. It does not select a module global, and that enclosing binding must already exist.

A closure can use this rule to retain a small private counter across calls. The outer call creates the initial state once; each inner call updates the same enclosing binding. Reinitializing a local variable inside the inner call would erase the previous updates.

Stateful functions need sequence-based tests. A single increment can agree with an incorrect implementation that resets before every call. The transfer fixture applies a positive, negative and later positive adjustment to verify cumulative state rather than independent calculations.
Transfer walkthrough: Starting at ten gives eleven, then nine, then twelve. Resetting current to initial inside each step would produce independent results instead of a cumulative sequence.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 3
def counter():
    n = 0
    def step():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return step
f = counter()
result = [f() for _ in range(data)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Recursion needs a base case
body: A recursive function solves a smaller subproblem and stops at a base case. For factorial on nonnegative integers, zero maps to one.
For input 0, the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A zero base result makes every positive factorial zero.

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller subproblem. Correctness needs a domain, a base result and a rule that moves every recursive path toward that base. For factorial on nonnegative integers, the base value is one because it is the multiplicative identity.

Rejecting a negative input prevents a recursion that moves farther from zero forever. A base case that returns zero makes every positive factorial zero. A mathematically correct recurrence also has practical recursion-depth limits; an iterative implementation is usually better for very large counts in Python.

Test the base itself, the first recursive step, a larger valid input and an invalid input. These distinguish a correct base identity, a correct recurrence and an explicit domain policy. The small fixture does not claim arbitrary-depth safety.

Transfer walkthrough: Zero returns one directly; five multiplies down to that identity. The negative case is rejected before any recursion. Returning zero at the base collapses every nonnegative factorial.

lessons.title: Separate import from script entry
body: A module is executed during its first import. The __main__ guard protects script-only behavior so importing definitions does not invoke the entry point.
For input '__main__', the worked computation produces ["run"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Running the entry point unconditionally causes import-time side effects.

Import executes a module's top-level definitions and statements. A main guard does not prevent all import-time execution; it prevents only the guarded script entry from running during an ordinary import. Definitions and lightweight initialization still happen.

Place reusable functions outside the guard and script-only calls inside it. The imported module can then supply functions without printing a command's result, reading stdin or starting owned work merely because another module needs its definitions.

The transfer program writes a temporary trusted module, imports it through Python's loader, and launches that file as a real child script. It observes quiet import, usable definitions and script output separately. The temporary directory and finite child timeout bound this authored check; it is not a learner-code execution sandbox.

Transfer walkthrough: The imported definition doubles three without printing. The child runs the same file with __name__ equal to __main__ and emits entry. An unconditional guard makes the import noisy even though the function still works.
lessons.code:
import json

data = '__main__'
namespace = {'__name__':data,'calls':[]}
exec("if __name__ == '__main__':\n    calls.append('run')",namespace)
result = namespace['calls']
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import contextlib, importlib.util, io, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
data = 3
source = "def double(value):\n    return value * 2\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    print('entry')\n"

lessons.title: Bind configuration with partial
body: partial pre-binds some function arguments while leaving others for later calls. Bind keyword configuration explicitly when it should not consume a data argument.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 9. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the bound exponent changes the operation.

partial creates a callable with selected arguments already supplied. It is useful for separating configuration from the data that arrives later. The resulting object still calls the original function and does not cache its results.

Prebound keyword arguments are defaults for that callable's future calls, not an immutable configuration seal. A later supplied keyword can override a prebound keyword. Mutable argument objects are stored by reference, so their ownership must still be considered.

Bind configuration by name when that improves the API's readability. The transfer fixture retains the value parameter for later calls and binds factor and offset explicitly. Test a zero factor or an empty sequence so omitted work and intentional zero behavior stay distinct.

lessons.title: Inspect modules without wildcard imports
body: import_module loads a module by name and returns the module object. Access a known public attribute explicitly; do not execute arbitrary untrusted module names.
For input 1.5, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Looking up a nonexistent attribute fails even when the module import succeeds.

import_module loads a named module and returns its module object. getattr can then retrieve a specific attribute. Both names are part of the lookup contract; a module existing does not imply every requested attribute exists or is safe to call.

Importing can execute code, so dynamic import is not a harmless string lookup for untrusted input. A small allowlist is appropriate for this authored dispatch example. It supports only the math module and two named functions, rejecting other choices before loading them.

Discovery and execution should remain separate in larger plugin systems. Validate the selected callable's interface and ownership before invoking it. This transfer task deliberately avoids third-party plugins, package installation or a general-purpose dynamic execution feature.

Transfer walkthrough: Floor maps 2.7 to two; ceil maps minus 1.2 to minus one. Unapproved module or operation names take the explicit unsupported path. Always choosing floor would silently violate the approved ceil request.
lessons.code:
import json
import importlib
data = 1.5
module = importlib.import_module('math')
result = getattr(module,'isfinite')(data)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

Common mistake: Using zero for parse failure confuses invalid text with an actual zero.

An exception handler should describe a failure the function knows how to interpret. A parser may translate malformed integer text into a missing result, but that does not mean it should hide every TypeError, missing variable or unrelated bug from a larger block.

Keep the try body small. The code inside else runs only after the try body succeeds and is not protected by the preceding handlers. This can prevent a later calculation's failure from being mistaken for an input-parsing failure.

The transfer task separates the parser's policy from a caller observing a wrong-type error. Valid zero must remain successful, invalid text becomes None, and None supplied as the wrong input type propagates TypeError to the outer observer. A broad first handler would erase that distinction.
Transfer walkthrough: Valid '0' returns zero. Malformed text returns None through the declared parser policy. None is an unsupported argument type and reaches the separate outer TypeError path.

lessons.title: Preserve an error cause
body: raise NewError from original attaches the causal exception explicitly. Callers can inspect the stable outer error without losing low-level context.
For input 'x', the worked computation produces "ValueError". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Suppressing the cause erases diagnostic context.

An API can translate a low-level failure into a stable domain-facing error while retaining the original cause. raise NewError(...) from error sets an explicit cause that callers and tracebacks can inspect.

from None suppresses display of the implicit context; it does not mean the original failure never happened. Use suppression only as a deliberate presentation decision. Replacing an explicit cause with suppression can remove information that an API or debugging workflow expects.

Test a successful path as well as the translated failure. For a failure, inspect the outer error type, the explicit cause type and the stable message separately. Matching a message alone can miss lost causal structure.
Transfer walkthrough: The outer RuntimeError provides a stable domain message while its cause retains ValueError. Suppression leaves the outer message intact but changes the explicit cause to None.

lessons.title: Cleanup runs on exceptional exits
body: finally executes when control leaves a try block, including after an exception. It is the place for unconditional cleanup rather than success-only bookkeeping.
For input True, the worked computation produces ["error", "close"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Cleanup placed only on the successful path misses failures.

finally runs as control leaves a try statement, whether by normal completion, return or an exception. It is a place to release owned resources and record unconditional cleanup. It does not imply that the protected operation succeeded.

A return from finally can replace an earlier return or suppress an exception. Cleanup code that reports success or supplies a new return value therefore risks disguising the original outcome. Keep teardown separate from the operation's result whenever possible.

Observe both the operation's status and its cleanup events. A test that only sees a finalizer event can miss a swallowed failure; a test that only sees a result can miss skipped teardown. The transfer fixture checks the success and exceptional paths together.

Transfer walkthrough: Both paths record close. The failure still reaches the caller and becomes error; the successful result stays ok. A return in finally would replace both outcomes and remove the cleanup event.
lessons.code:
import json

data = True
events = []
try:
    if data:
        raise ValueError('stop')
except ValueError:
    events.append('error')
finally:
    events.append('close')
result = events
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json

data = True
events = []
def work(fail):
    try:
        events.append('work')
        if fail:
            raise ValueError('bad')
        return 'ok'
    finally:
        events.append('close')
try:
    status = work(data)
except ValueError:
    status = 'error'
result = [status, events]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: A context manager scopes a resource
body: The with statement enters a resource scope and exits it even when the body raises. A contextmanager generator should place its teardown in finally.
For input True, the worked computation produces ["open", "close"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Skipping the finalizer leaves ownership work unfinished.

A context manager defines an acquisition/exit boundary. A generator-based contextmanager should put release logic in finally so exceptions thrown into the generator at its yield still trigger teardown.

ExitStack can own a variable number of acquired contexts. Each successful entry is registered immediately, and exit unwinds them in reverse order. If acquiring a later resource fails, earlier successfully acquired resources are still released.

Do not assume that a cleanup event proves every surrounding operation completed. The fixture distinguishes normal completion, an error before the second acquisition and an error inside both scopes. Its explicit event order checks partial ownership and reverse teardown without using sleeps.

Transfer walkthrough: Normal and body-error paths close inner before outer. The earlier acquisition error closes only outer, then records handled. The event order makes both the ownership boundary and the exceptional outcome observable.

lessons.title: Use path APIs for paths
body: Path joins components according to filesystem path rules. Its name property returns the final component without assuming a fixed slash-delimited prefix length.
For input 'logs/run.txt', the worked computation produces "run.txt". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning the parent directory is not the final filename.

A path has structured components. Its name is the final component, suffix is its final extension and stem is the name without that final suffix. A multi-extension filename such as archive.tar.gz therefore has suffix .gz and stem archive.tar.

PurePosixPath performs lexical POSIX path operations without opening a file or asking the filesystem whether a target exists. It is useful when that syntax is part of the input contract, including on a host with other path conventions.

Lexical inspection is not a security containment check. Parent components, symlinks, filesystem permissions and actual resolved locations require their own policies. The transfer task reports components only and does not claim that a filename is safe to open in a protected directory.

Transfer walkthrough: run.csv has the expected CSV suffix. archive.tar.gz keeps .tar in its stem because only the final suffix is removed. The hidden filename and empty lexical path expose naive split assumptions.

lessons.title: Close text files deterministically
body: Open text with an explicit encoding and close it using with. A temporary directory isolates this trusted local example and is removed on exit.
For input 'café', the worked computation produces "caf\u00e9". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A write of the wrong text can still exit successfully.

Opening a file in text mode introduces an encoding boundary between strings and stored bytes. Specify UTF-8 when it is the file contract instead of depending on a machine's locale. A context manager closes the stream when the write scope exits, including on exceptions.

Closing the stream and deleting a temporary workspace are separate ownership steps. The inner with closes the file; the TemporaryDirectory context removes the directory later. Test cleanup after leaving the outer scope, not while it still legitimately owns the files.

Non-ASCII and empty fixtures matter. ASCII-only text can accidentally pass with several incompatible encodings. Byte count and code-point count need not agree. This bounded temporary-file exercise makes the chosen encoding and the final cleanup status visible without retaining personal data.

Transfer walkthrough: café contains four code points but five UTF-8 bytes. The workspace is gone before the final existence check. A locale-like single-byte encoding cannot satisfy the accented and brain-character fixtures.
lessons.code:
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
data = 'café'
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory)/"sample.txt"
    with path.open("w",encoding="utf-8") as stream:
        stream.write(data)
    result = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: JSON preserves supported structures
body: JSON encodes portable data structures, not arbitrary Python object identity. Round-trip a record using its explicit schema and validate required keys at the boundary.
For input {'x': [1, 2]}, the worked computation produces {"x": [1, 2]}. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Stringifying a record loses its structured JSON representation.

Successful JSON parsing proves that text was decoded into supported values, not that those values satisfy an application's schema. A record still needs required-field, type and domain checks before business logic relies on it.

In Python, bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is true. If a count must be an actual integer rather than a Boolean flag, use a policy that explicitly excludes booleans. Shape and exact field policy also matter: a list is not the required object and an extra field is not automatically harmless.

This exercise names a deliberately strict two-field schema. It does not claim to reject duplicate textual keys before decoding; the standard decoder normally retains the last one. If duplicate detection or nonstandard numeric constants matter at a boundary, configure and test those policies separately.

Transfer walkthrough: The complete nonnegative integer record is accepted. The Boolean, list, missing field, malformed text and negative count all take the explicit invalid path. The mutation admits a Boolean count incorrectly.

lessons.title: CSV fields can contain delimiters
body: A CSV parser handles quoting and escaped delimiters. Splitting on commas manually is not equivalent when fields contain commas inside quotes.
For input 'a,"b,c"', the worked computation produces ["a", "b,c"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Manual comma splitting breaks quoted records.

CSV records are not simply lines split on commas. A quoted field can contain a comma, a newline or an escaped quote. The parser has to track quoting state across those characters rather than treating each as an unconditional separator.

Use a text stream and let csv.reader interpret records. When opening real files for this API, newline='' leaves newline handling to the CSV module. The transfer example uses StringIO with the same explicit newline policy and small in-memory text.

Parsing CSV supplies rows of text fields; it does not infer an application schema or make a spreadsheet formula safe to open. Numeric conversion, row-width validation and exported-formula policies are separate requirements. This fixture focuses on preserving field boundaries exactly.
Transfer walkthrough: The comma inside b,c stays in one field. The multiline note stays in one record. The escaped quote becomes a single quote character rather than a field separator.

import json

lessons.title: Time zones are part of timestamps
body: An aware datetime identifies an instant using its offset. Converting to UTC adjusts clock time while preserving that instant; replacing tzinfo alone does not.

For input '2026-01-01T12:00:00+02:00', the worked computation produces "2026-01-01T10:00:00+00:00". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Relabelling a timezone does not convert the instant.

An aware timestamp includes an offset that relates its wall-clock reading to an instant. A naive timestamp lacks that information. Interpreting a naive value requires a policy; silently assuming a local timezone makes behavior machine-dependent.

astimezone converts the displayed clock and offset while preserving the instant. replace(tzinfo=...) merely attaches a different timezone object without adjusting the clock. The two operations can look similar in code and represent different moments in time.

Test a conversion that crosses a date boundary in each direction, plus an explicit naive-input policy. This small fixture uses fixed offsets only. It does not validate named-zone daylight-saving transitions, ambiguous local times or a timezone database version.

Transfer walkthrough: The +02:00 early-morning value moves back into the previous UTC date. The -03:00 late-night value moves into the next UTC date. A naive string is not assigned an invented instant.
lessons.code:
import json
from datetime import datetime,timezone
data = '2026-01-01T12:00:00+02:00'
dt = datetime.fromisoformat(data)
result = dt.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Parse CLI types at the boundary
body: argparse converts option text according to its type specification. The result namespace should contain domain values before application logic starts.
For input '3', the worked computation produces 3. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Omitting the type leaves the value as text.

A command line arrives as text tokens. argparse can convert an option with type=int and report a conversion failure. Conversion and business validation are separate: an integer parser can accept a negative number that a nonnegative count contract rejects.

Use a supplied argument list in a unit-sized example so it does not consume the validator's own process arguments. exit_on_error=False lets the particular invalid-integer option path here raise ArgumentError for explicit observation. Other command-line failures still need their own exit/error policy and tests.

Test a positive count, valid zero, malformed integer text and a negative integer. These four cases distinguish token parsing from the nonnegative domain rule. Zero must not be rejected merely because it is falsy.
Transfer walkthrough: Three and zero parse and satisfy the domain. The malformed token fails conversion, while minus two parses successfully and fails only the range check.
lessons.code:
import json
import argparse
data = '3'
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--count",type=int)
result = parser.parse_args(["--count",data]).count
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Handle related failures with except star
body: ExceptionGroup preserves multiple failures. except* handles matching leaves while allowing other kinds to be handled independently.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces 2. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting only one leaf loses concurrent failure information.

ExceptionGroup can carry several failures without collapsing them into one string. except* selects matching leaves and handles the matching subgroup. Nonmatching failures remain available for propagation rather than disappearing because one category was handled.

An except* clause and an ordinary except cannot appear on the same try statement. A nested outer try can observe the remaining group after the inner except* has handled selected failures. This fixture deliberately uses a flat group so its counts are unambiguous.

Test all-matching, mixed, no-matching and no-error cases. Catching Exception with except* instead of the intended ValueError can wrongly label TypeError failures as handled values. That is a semantic error even if the program no longer raises.

Transfer walkthrough: Two ValueErrors are handled first; the TypeError remains in a separate propagated group. A broad matching clause would count all three as values and lose the remaining-type observation.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [1, 2]
try:
    raise ExceptionGroup("batch",[ValueError(str(x)) for x in data])
except* ValueError as group:
    result = len(group.exceptions)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Dataclasses describe values
body: A dataclass generates initialization and value equality from annotated fields. frozen=True rejects field rebinding; it does not recursively freeze mutable members.
For input 2, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A mutable dataclass permits an assignment the frozen contract rejects.

A dataclass turns annotated class attributes into fields and generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from them. Use it when an object is mainly a named bundle of values. The generated code is ordinary Python; reading the field list tells you exactly what initialization and equality consider.

frozen=True makes field assignment raise FrozenInstanceError after construction. That protects the binding between the instance and each field object. It does not copy or freeze those objects. A list stored in a frozen field can still be appended to, and every holder of that list observes the change.

dataclasses.replace builds a new instance from an existing one plus changed fields. It is the normal way to 'update' a frozen value. The copy is shallow: unchanged fields refer to the same objects as before. If a field must be independently mutable, copy it explicitly or store an immutable type such as a tuple.

The transfer task observes all three facts together: rebinding is rejected, a mutable member can still change, and replace() shares that member. Treat frozen as a guard against accidental rebinding, not as a deep-immutability guarantee.

Transfer walkthrough: Rebinding rate fails, so c.rate stays 2 and d.rate becomes 3. The append succeeds because frozen does not freeze the list, and replace() shares that same list with the new instance.

lessons.title: Keep mutable instance state per instance
body: Assign mutable fields on self during initialization. A class attribute is shared by instances and is appropriate only when the data is intentionally shared.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [[3], []]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A class-level list joins state from unrelated objects.

Attribute lookup on an instance first checks the instance's own namespace, then its class. A list assigned in the class body therefore lives on the class and is found by every instance that has no attribute of that name. Calling append on it mutates the single shared list.

Assignment behaves differently from mutation. self.items = self.items + [x] creates a new list and binds it on the instance, shadowing the class attribute for that instance only. This explains why some 'shared state' bugs appear only with in-place operations such as append, extend or +=.

Dataclasses refuse a bare mutable default such as items: list = [] because it would be shared. field(default_factory=list) calls the factory once per instance during __init__. Use class attributes for genuinely shared constants or registries, and per-instance initialization for per-object state.
The transfer contrasts both designs with the same operations. Only by checking the untouched second instance can you see whether state leaked between instances.

Transfer walkthrough: Shared.add mutates the class list, so s2 sees [3, 4]. Owned instances each receive a new list, so o2 stays empty. Replacing append with rebinding shadows the class attribute on s1 and hides the shared-state effect.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 3
class Bag:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []
a,b = Bag(),Bag()
a.items.append(data)
result = [a.items,b.items]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Validate updates through properties
body: A property can enforce an invariant on assignment while exposing ordinary attribute syntax. Store the backing value separately to avoid recursive setter calls.
For input 4, the worked computation produces 4. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Bypassing validation accepts a negative value outside the domain.

A property is a class attribute that routes reading, assignment and deletion through functions. Callers keep writing obj.value and obj.value = x, while the class enforces an invariant. The backing value needs a different name, conventionally _value, or the setter would call itself recursively.

An invariant is only as strong as its weakest entry point. If __init__ assigns self._value directly, construction bypasses the setter and an invalid object can exist from the start. Assign through the property in __init__ so creation and later updates share one validation rule.

Raise a specific exception such as ValueError for an invalid value and leave the previous state unchanged. Callers can then decide whether to report, skip or stop. A property cannot stop code that deliberately writes _value; the underscore is a convention communicating that the name is internal.
The transfer constructs several objects, counts rejections and keeps accepted values. Inclusive bounds are tested at both edges because off-by-one comparisons are a common validation defect.
Transfer walkthrough: 0, 50 and 100 lie within the inclusive range. -1 and 101 raise ValueError and are counted. Writing _value in __init__ would accept every value silently.

lessons.title: Compose objects with explicit dependencies
body: Composition delegates one responsibility to an injected collaborator. Supplying the dependency explicitly makes behavior easy to replace in tests without inheritance.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ignoring the collaborator breaks the configured behavior.

Inheritance says an object is a specialized kind of its base class and reuses its methods. Composition says an object has collaborators and delegates part of its work to them. When behavior varies independently, such as where output goes or how time is read, composition keeps each concern replaceable.

Pass collaborators into the constructor rather than creating them inside methods. A reporter that receives a clock function and an output list can be tested with a deterministic fake clock and an in-memory sink. The same class runs in production with time.time and a file or logger, with no subclass needed.

Explicit dependencies also make ownership visible. The caller that created a collaborator decides its lifetime; the composed object uses it. This matters later for files, network sessions and model handles, where the owner must close them.
In the transfer, a counter-based clock makes timestamps predictable. Ordering is part of the contract: messages are recorded in the order reported.
Transfer walkthrough: The first report reads tick 100 and the second 101, appended in order. Inserting at the front would reverse the record while still looking plausible for a single message.

lessons.title: Define value equality intentionally
body: Dataclass equality compares the declared fields for matching dataclass types. Identity asks a separate question about whether references denote the same object.
For input 2, the worked computation produces [true, false]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Two separately created equal values do not have to share identity.

Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes, because sets and dict keys first use the hash to find candidates and then __eq__ to confirm. If a class defines __eq__ without __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None so instances cannot be used as keys with an inconsistent hash.

A plain @dataclass generates __eq__ and therefore becomes unhashable. @dataclass(frozen=True) generates both __eq__ and a field-based __hash__, which is safe because the fields cannot be rebound. Use frozen value objects as dictionary keys and set members.

Generated dataclass equality only compares instances of exactly the same class; comparing different dataclass types returns NotImplemented, and Python falls back to identity, giving False. Identity (is) remains a separate question about whether two names refer to one object.
The transfer checks hashability, set deduplication through value equality and cross-type comparison. eq=False would restore identity hashing and stop deduplication.

Transfer walkthrough: Loose is unhashable. The two Key(2) values are equal with equal hashes, so the set keeps one, giving [1, 2]. Key and Loose are different classes, so equality is False. With eq=False the set would keep both Key(2) objects.

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
data = 2
@dataclass
class Token:
    value: int
a,b = Token(data),Token(data)
result = [a==b,a is b]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Order domain records explicitly
body: Order records using the business key rather than incidental field order. A tuple key makes primary and secondary ordering criteria explicit.

For input [['b', 1], ['a', 2], ['c', 1]], the worked computation produces [["b", 1], ["c", 1], ["a", 2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing tuple-key components changes the primary criterion.

sorted and list.sort compare keys, not the records themselves, when you pass key=. The key function runs once per element. A tuple key compares field by field, so (primary, secondary) expresses a complete ordering rule in one place.

To sort one numeric field descending and another ascending, negate the numeric field in the key: (-score, name). Using reverse=True would reverse both fields. For non-numeric descending fields, use Python's guaranteed stability: sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary key with reverse=True.

Stability means records with equal keys keep their existing relative order. It makes multi-pass sorting correct, and it means the input order matters when keys tie. State whether ties are broken by a field or by arrival order, and test a tie.
The transfer ranks scores high to low and breaks ties alphabetically. Its fixtures include a tie and a negative score.
Transfer walkthrough: c has the highest score. a and b tie at 2, and the ascending name rule puts a first. Without negation, the lowest scores would come first.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [['b', 1], ['a', 2], ['c', 1]]
result = sorted(data,key=lambda x:(x[1],x[0]))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Slots restrict instance attributes
body: Declaring slots reserves a fixed set of instance attribute names when no dictionary is inherited. It can reduce per-instance overhead but does not freeze allowed fields.
For input 3, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing slots allows accidental new attribute names.

__slots__ declares a fixed set of attribute names and replaces the per-instance __dict__ with compact storage. Assigning a name that is not declared raises AttributeError. It can save memory when you create many small objects and catches attribute-name typos.

The restriction holds only if every class in the hierarchy cooperates. A subclass that does not define __slots__ gets a __dict__ again, so arbitrary attributes become allowed on subclass instances. A subclass that declares its own __slots__ adds names while keeping the restriction.

Slots are not immutability: declared attributes can still be reassigned. They also interact with features that expect __dict__, such as some pickling and dynamic attribute patterns, and weak references need '__weakref__' in the slots. Measure memory before adopting slots for performance.
The transfer checks three classes built from the same slotted base and shows which instances accept an extra attribute.
Transfer walkthrough: Base and Tight reject the undeclared attribute; Loose accepts it because it has a __dict__. Replacing Tight's slots with pass gives it a __dict__ too.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 3
class Row:
    __slots__ = ("x",)
r = Row()
r.x = data
try:
    r.extra = 1
    result = False
except AttributeError:
    result = True
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Descriptors participate in lookup
body: A descriptor implements attribute access through __get__. It receives the instance and owner, allowing reusable field policies independent of one class property.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning an unscaled stored value ignores the descriptor contract.

A descriptor is an object stored on a class that defines __get__, and optionally __set__ or __delete__. Attribute access on instances calls those methods. Properties, methods and classmethod are all built from this mechanism, so understanding it explains how much of Python's object model works.

One descriptor instance is shared by every instance of the owning class. It must not store per-instance values on itself. Store them on the instance under a private name. __set_name__(owner, name) runs when the class is created and tells the descriptor which attribute name it was assigned to, so each field gets its own private storage name.

A data descriptor (defining __set__) takes priority over the instance dictionary, so validation in __set__ runs for every assignment, including those in __init__. __get__ receives obj=None when accessed on the class; returning the descriptor itself then supports introspection.
The transfer reuses one Positive descriptor for two fields. A storage-name bug would make both fields share one value, which a test with different field values exposes.

Transfer walkthrough: qty and price are stored separately as _qty and _price, giving 2 * 5 = 10. A zero quantity raises ValueError in __set__. A fixed storage name makes both fields share one slot, so the product would be price squared.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 3
class Doubled:
    def __get__(self,obj,owner):
        return obj.raw*2
class Record:
    value = Doubled()
r = Record()
r.raw = data
result = r.value
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Implement the iterator protocol
body: An iterator supplies __next__ and returns itself from __iter__. StopIteration signals exhaustion; a fresh iterable traversal needs a fresh iterator when replay is required.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [[1, 2], []]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Restarting position during iteration repeats earlier items.

An iterable can produce iterators: its __iter__ returns a new iterator each time. An iterator yields items through __next__, raises StopIteration when exhausted and returns itself from __iter__. A list is iterable; iter(list) is an iterator.

Because an iterator returns itself from __iter__, looping over it twice continues from where it stopped, and an exhausted iterator yields nothing. A container class that wants repeated traversal should return a fresh iterator from __iter__, often iter(self._items) or a generator.

This distinction matters for data pipelines: passing an iterator to two consumers splits the items between them, and checking emptiness by consuming loses data. Choose whether a function accepts any iterable and calls iter() once, or requires a re-iterable collection, and document the choice.
The transfer partially consumes one iterator and then traverses the container twice. The container's traversals stay complete while the separate iterator continues from its own position.
