lessons.title: Abstract classes prevent incomplete instances
body: An abstract base class can require a method before instantiation. An abstract method specifies a contract but does not automatically validate a concrete implementation.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing the abstract marker permits incomplete construction.

Inheriting from ABC and marking methods with @abstractmethod records them in the class's __abstractmethods__ set. Instantiating any class whose set is non-empty raises TypeError. This turns 'forgot to implement save' into an immediate, clear failure at construction.

A subclass becomes concrete only when it overrides every abstract method. Implementing some of them leaves the subclass abstract, and its __abstractmethods__ names what is missing. Misspelling a method name has the same effect, which makes the check useful against typos too.

The check covers names, not behavior. It does not verify signatures, return types or semantics. Pair an abstract interface with tests that exercise a concrete implementation, and keep the interface small enough that every method is genuinely required.
The transfer defines a storage interface, a partial implementation and a complete in-memory implementation, then exercises the complete one.
Transfer walkthrough: Partial is abstract with save missing. Memory overrides both and returns 1 for key a. Misspelling save as store would leave Memory abstract and make its construction fail.

lessons.title: Context exit controls suppression
body: __exit__ receives exception details. Returning false propagates the exception after cleanup; returning true deliberately suppresses it.
For input 1, the worked computation produces "propagated". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Accidentally returning true hides a failure from the caller.

A with statement calls __enter__ before its block and __exit__ afterwards, whether the block finished normally or raised. __exit__ receives the exception type, value and traceback, or three Nones. Cleanup placed there always runs.

A true return value from __exit__ suppresses the exception; a false value lets it propagate after cleanup. Returning True unconditionally swallows every error, including programming mistakes. Suppress only the specific exception types you can justify, by testing exc_type.

contextlib.suppress(KeyError) packages this exact pattern. Prefer it in ordinary code, and keep the suppressed region small so unrelated errors are not hidden. A custom manager is appropriate when cleanup or recording must accompany the decision.
The transfer records enter and exit events and checks three paths: no error, an allowed error that is suppressed, and an unrelated error that must still propagate.

Transfer walkthrough: With no error both events are recorded and nothing propagates. KeyError is suppressed. ValueError is not a KeyError, so __exit__ returns False and it propagates after cleanup. Returning True always would hide the ValueError.

lessons.title: Implicit special methods use the type
body: An implicit special operation such as len(obj) resolves its special method on the type. An ordinary explicit attribute lookup on that instance can observe a different attribute.
For input [], the worked computation produces [0, 99]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing an instance attribute named __len__ does not redefine the implicit len protocol.

Special methods connect an object's type to language operations. Implement __len__ on the class so len(instance) has a defined meaning. Normally call the public operation, not a special method directly, because Python can apply additional protocol rules around that operation.

Implicit special-method lookup differs from ordinary instance attribute lookup. Assigning a new instance.__len__ attribute can change an explicit instance.__len__() call while len(instance) still uses the type's implementation. The worked example intentionally contrasts those two lookups; it is a diagnostic demonstration, not a recommended monkey-patching API.

The length protocol also checks its result. A negative length is invalid, and a string is not an integer length. Do not infer these checks from a method merely existing. The transfer exercise observes valid lengths and the actual exception categories for invalid return values.

The supplied book introduces the benefit of familiar built-in operations. The current Python reference supplies the more precise type-lookup rule used here. This lesson does not benchmark CPython's internal length fields or certify every interpreter's implementation strategy.

Transfer walkthrough: Zero and three are valid lengths. A negative return raises ValueError, and a string raises TypeError. Applying abs would hide the negative-result violation rather than faithfully observing it.

lessons.title: A small sequence can support familiar operations
body: A read-only sequence can supply __len__ and __getitem__, delegating indexing and slicing to its owned tuple. Iteration and membership can fall back to the sequence protocol without a custom __iter__.
For input [[2, 5, 9], 5], the worked computation produces [3, [2, 5, 9], [9, 5, 2], true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the returned element changes iteration, membership and slicing together; syntax support is a behavioral contract.

A small read-only sequence can compose an owned tuple and delegate indexed lookup to it. Integers, negative indices and slice objects then retain the tuple's bounds behavior. The class needs to state what a slice returns; here it returns the backing tuple's selected values rather than inventing a new domain object.

When __iter__ is absent, Python can iterate through integer __getitem__ requests beginning at zero until IndexError. Membership can use that iteration fallback, while reversed can use length and indexed access. Supporting familiar operations is a set of behavioral promises, not simply having methods with particular names.

A read-only element API does not establish deep immutability of arbitrary nested objects or a security boundary around attributes. This lesson stores integer values in a tuple and intentionally omits __setitem__. Assignment through obj[index] therefore raises TypeError. A mutable sequence or shuffle operation would need additional behavior.

The original source demonstrates interoperability with a card collection. This original measurement-window exercise checks negative indexing, iteration, membership, slicing, sorting and reverse traversal with small integer data. It does not claim implementation of every collections.abc.Sequence method.

Transfer walkthrough: The original order is 3,1,2, so reverse traversal yields 2,1,3 while sorted returns 1,2,3. Last is two. Item assignment is rejected because no writable-element protocol is defined.

lessons.title: Separate diagnostic representation from display text
body: repr(obj) should give an unambiguous diagnostic representation. str(obj) supplies user-facing text, and an empty-format f-string uses that display representation.
For input 'x', the worked computation produces ["Label('x')", "x", "x"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Dropping repr conversion for text fields removes quoting and escape information needed to distinguish their contents.

Diagnostic and user-facing text have different jobs. repr should make the object's relevant state unambiguous, including whether a field contains quotes or newlines. str can choose a readable display value. If __str__ is absent, the default display behavior can fall back to __repr__.

The !r conversion inside an f-string asks for the field's representation. It preserves quoting and escape distinctions that inserting a raw string would lose. A useful representation can resemble construction syntax, but do not assume that evaluating arbitrary representation text is a safe or complete serialization format.

Containers such as lists use their elements' representations in their own repr output. This makes a good __repr__ useful when inspecting a collection of domain objects, even if direct printing of one object uses its simpler __str__.

The fixture includes an embedded newline and empty text. These values can appear deceptively similar in casual output, but their diagnostic representations need to remain distinct. The task supplies complete object definitions and compares actual strings, not screenshots of a console.

Transfer walkthrough: The standalone representation and the list's element representation retain the same quoted text. The display string remains x. Removing !r loses the quoted-field distinction and mishandles embedded newlines.

lessons.title: Define truth from the domain contract
body: A custom __bool__ returns a Boolean describing the domain. Numeric zero can be false while negative nonzero values remain true; positivity and truth are different predicates.
For input 0, the worked computation produces false. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using greater-than-zero misclassifies a valid negative nonzero amount as false.

bool(obj) first uses __bool__ when the type supplies it. Otherwise a defined __len__ can provide truth through zero versus nonzero length. With neither method, ordinary user-defined instances are truthy by default.

A custom __bool__ must return a Boolean. Returning a truthy list or integer is not accepted merely because an if statement could test that value by itself. Implement a predicate or explicitly convert the intended domain expression when writing a valid class.

Choose the predicate from the domain rather than an incidental sign or storage detail. A numeric delta with negative magnitude is still nonzero, so amount > 0 would implement positivity instead of numeric truth. In another domain, truth might mean a validated signal exists; that policy should be documented.

The transfer task intentionally supplies valid and invalid raw method returns and observes the actual protocol boundary. It does not silently repair the invalid return by coercion, because that would hide the behavior being taught.

Transfer walkthrough: True and False pass through the protocol. Returning integer one or an empty list raises TypeError. Coercing inside the method changes the observation and hides those invalid raw returns.

lessons.title: Return NotImplemented to permit operator fallback
body: An unsupported binary operation can return NotImplemented so Python can try the other operand’s reflected operation. This differs from raising TypeError immediately, and from returning a fabricated result.
For input [3, -2], the worked computation produces [1, 3, -2, 3, 13, true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Raising before dispatch fallback prevents a compatible right operand from handling the operation.

A binary special method must decide which operand types it supports. Return NotImplemented for an unsupported combination when Python should try the remaining dispatch rules. The singleton is not the exception class NotImplementedError and is not a fabricated successful answer.

A compatible right operand can supply a reflected operation such as __radd__. Raising TypeError immediately from the left method can prevent that fallback. Once both sides decline the operation, Python reports the unsupported pair as TypeError.

Nonmutating arithmetic normally returns a new result object and leaves both operands' observed values intact. This is a stated policy here, not a claim that every Python operator on every type is immutable. Augmented assignment has additional semantics and separate tests.

The original book's early arithmetic example leaves reflected multiplication for a later chapter. This original transfer exercise adds both multiplication directions explicitly and checks equality of their values while retaining the operand. Subclass dispatch priority and the full numeric tower remain beyond this bounded lab.

Transfer walkthrough: Three scaled by two gives six regardless of operand order, and the original still stores three. A reflected method that adds instead of multiplying violates only one direction, so both directions must be tested.

lessons.title: Use abs with a domain magnitude
body: A numeric-like object can implement __abs__ to return its magnitude. For a pair of orthogonal components, hypot computes Euclidean magnitude; truth can then explicitly use whether that magnitude is nonzero.
For input [3, 4], the worked computation produces [5.0, true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Adding signed components is not a magnitude and can cancel nonzero components incorrectly.

abs is another public operation that a domain object can implement through a special method. For orthogonal components x and y, the Euclidean magnitude is hypot(x,y), not their signed sum. Changing a component's sign does not change that magnitude.

Using math.hypot states the intended magnitude directly and avoids manually expanding this calculation into an unexamined square/sum/square-root sequence. That API choice does not establish acceptable error for every application or every scale; numerical stability receives its own later stage.

Clipping a two-component measurement to a maximum magnitude scales both components by the same factor. Preserve its direction when nonzero. A zero measurement needs an explicit branch to avoid division by zero; a zero cap turns any nonzero measurement into zero.

The transfer fixture reports the original magnitude, scaled components and factor. It checks a measurement already inside the cap, one that needs clipping, the zero measurement and a zero cap. These cases reveal reversed-ratio and missing-zero-guard errors.

Transfer walkthrough: The 3/4 components have magnitude five. A cap of 2.5 gives factor one half and components 1.5/2. A zero measurement keeps factor one; a zero cap scales a nonzero measurement to zero.

import json
import math
data = [[3, 4], 10]
class Components:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y
    def __abs__(self):

value = Components(*coordinates)
magnitude = abs(value)
factor = 1.0 if magnitude == 0 or magnitude <= cap else cap / magnitude
result = [magnitude, [value.x * factor, value.y * factor], factor]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Generators defer work
body: Calling a generator function creates an iterator without running its body. Each next resumes until a yield; unrequested elements are not computed yet.
For input [2, 3], the worked computation produces [4, [2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Materializing the generator eagerly performs all work.

A generator function returns a generator object without executing its body. Each next() call runs the body until the following yield, hands back that value and suspends with all local variables preserved. Values are produced on demand rather than all at once.

Laziness makes infinite sources practical: a generator can loop forever, and a consumer such as itertools.islice(source, n) pulls exactly the number of items it needs. Generator expressions chain onto generators without materialising intermediate lists, so a filter-and-take pipeline only does the work its output requires.

Laziness also moves when work and errors happen. Side effects inside the generator occur during consumption, not at creation. A pipeline that is never consumed does no work, and an exception in a source appears where a consumer advances it. Count or log work at the source when you need to verify the amount of computation.
The transfer filters even numbers from an infinite counter and takes the first few. It records how many source values were produced, which shows that the pipeline stops at the last needed item.

Transfer walkthrough: Taking three evens produces 0, 2 and 4 after five source values. A zero limit never starts the pipeline. Selecting odd values instead would change both the output and the work count.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [2, 3]
seen = []
def squares():
    for x in data:
        seen.append(x)
        yield x*x
g = squares()
first = next(g,None)
result = [first,seen]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

seen = []

first = next(g,None)

exercises.prompt:
data is a non-negative limit. numbers() yields 0, 1, 2, ... forever and records each produced value in work. Take limit even values through a generator expression and islice. Return [taken_values, len(work)].
Check all these cases:
Input 3 → [[0, 2, 4], 5]
Input 0 → [[], 0]

data = 3
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.

exercises.solution:
import json
from itertools import islice
data = 3
work = []
def numbers():
    n = 0
    while True:
        work.append(n)
        yield n
        n += 1
evens = (x for x in numbers() if x % 2 == 0)
result = [list(islice(evens, data)), len(work)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: islice stops pulling once it has the requested count.
The filter pulls source values until one passes.
A limit of zero pulls nothing at all.
exercises.explanation: Taking three evens produces 0, 2 and 4 after five source values. A zero limit never starts the pipeline. Selecting odd values instead would change both the output and the work count.

lessons.title: Send values into a suspended generator
body: send resumes a generator and makes the supplied value the result of its suspended yield expression. Prime a new generator before sending a non-None value.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Calling next instead of send supplies None to the yield expression.

yield is an expression. value = yield out hands out to the caller and suspends; when the caller resumes with gen.send(x), the suspended yield evaluates to x. next(gen) is equivalent to gen.send(None).

A new generator has not reached any yield, so there is nowhere to deliver a value. Sending a non-None value first raises TypeError. Prime it with next(gen), which runs to the first yield and returns its output. Some code wraps priming in a helper so callers cannot forget it.

A generator that both receives and yields can keep running state, such as a running mean, without a class. Each send updates state and returns the new summary. Classes or explicit objects are usually clearer for complex protocols; use send for small, well-documented state machines.
The transfer primes an averager, sends several values and collects each returned running mean. The first output, from priming, is None because no value has arrived yet.
Transfer walkthrough: Priming returns None. Sending 10, 20 and 30 gives running means 10, 15 and 20. Dividing the latest value instead of the total gives a plausible but wrong summary.

import json

data = 3
def receiver():
    value = yield
    yield value*2
g = receiver()
next(g)
result = g.send(data)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:
data is a list of numbers. averager() yields the current mean (None before any value). Prime it, send every value and return [primed_output] + [each send result].
Check all these cases:
Input [10, 20, 30] → [null, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0]
Input [] → [null]
Input [-4, 4] → [null, -4.0, 0.0]

data = [10, 20, 30]
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
exercises.solution:
import json

data = [10, 20, 30]
def averager():
    total, count, average = 0, 0, None
    while True:
        value = yield average
        total += value
        count += 1
        average = total / count
g = averager()
primed = next(g)
result = [primed] + [g.send(x) for x in data]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: next(g) runs to the first yield and returns None.
Each send makes the suspended yield evaluate to the sent value.
Keep total and count across iterations.
exercises.explanation: Priming returns None. Sending 10, 20 and 30 gives running means 10, 15 and 20. Dividing the latest value instead of the total gives a plausible but wrong summary.

lessons.title: Close suspended generators
body: A generator can hold resources across suspension. close raises GeneratorExit at the suspended yield so finally can release those resources before object collection.
For input 1, the worked computation produces ["closed"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Leaving a suspended generator open delays its finally cleanup.

A generator suspended inside try/finally or with holds that cleanup until it either finishes or is closed. close() raises GeneratorExit at the suspended yield so the finally block runs. Closing a finished generator does nothing.

Breaking out of a for loop does not close the generator. If another name still refers to it, cleanup waits until garbage collection, which on other interpreters or with reference cycles may be much later. Files, sockets or locks held by a generator can therefore stay open after the loop.

contextlib.closing(gen) calls gen.close() when its with block exits, making cleanup deterministic even after break or an exception. A generator should not yield inside finally in response to GeneratorExit; that raises RuntimeError.
The transfer stops early on a negative value and records the order of events. Closing happens at the end of the with block, after the loop's own follow-up step.

Transfer walkthrough: With an early break, close runs at the end of the with block, after 'after-loop'. When the input is exhausted, the generator finishes on its own, so close comes first. Without closing(), the broken-off generator would stay suspended.
lessons.code:
import json

data = 1
events = []
def source():
    try:
        yield data
    finally:
        events.append("closed")
g = source()
next(g)
g.close()
result = list(events)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.title: Transfer: deterministic cleanup after break
exercises.prompt:
data is a list of numbers. rows() records 'open', yields values and records 'close' in finally. Inside with closing(rows()), take values until a negative appears, then record 'after-loop'. Return [taken, events].
Check all these cases:
Input [1, -1, 2] → [[1], ["open", "after-loop", "close"]]
Input [] → [[], ["open", "close", "after-loop"]]
Input [3] → [[3], ["open", "close", "after-loop"]]
exercises.starter:
import json
from contextlib import closing, nullcontext
data = [1, -1, 2]
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.
result = None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
exercises.solution:
import json
from contextlib import closing, nullcontext
data = [1, -1, 2]
events = []
def rows():
    events.append('open')
    try:
        for x in data:
            yield x
    finally:
        events.append('close')
taken = []
with closing(rows()) as source:
    for x in source:
        if x < 0:
            break
        taken.append(x)
    events.append('after-loop')
result = [taken, events]

lessons.title: Delegate iteration with yield from
body: yield from delegates iteration to a subiterator. It yields the contained values rather than yielding the subiterator object as one value.
For input [[1, 2], [3]], the worked computation produces [1, 2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Yielding the list itself adds a nesting level.

yield from sub delegates to a subiterator: every value it produces passes straight to the caller, and send() and throw() are forwarded too. It replaces a hand-written for loop and handles those forwarding details correctly.

A generator's return value travels in StopIteration.value. The expression yield from sub evaluates to that value, so an outer generator can collect results from its delegates, such as how many items each chunk produced, while still streaming the items themselves.

A plain for loop over a generator discards its return value. When you need the final result of a whole generator outside, catch StopIteration from next() or use yield from inside another generator. Keep returned values small summaries; the stream is the main output.
The transfer streams items from several groups and collects each group's returned size, including an empty group.
Transfer walkthrough: The items stream as 1, 2, 3 while the sizes 2, 0 and 1 come back through the delegation. Without chunk's return, every collected size would be None.

import json

data = [[1, 2], [3]]
def flattened():
    for group in data:
        yield from group
result = list(flattened())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Preserve decorator metadata
body: A decorator replaces a function with another callable. functools.wraps copies identifying metadata and records the wrapped function for introspection.
For input 2, the worked computation produces [5, "square"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A bare wrapper hides the original name and signature metadata.

A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a replacement. A parameterized decorator such as @retry(3) is a function that returns the actual decorator, so there are three layers: the configuration, the decorator and the wrapper.

Without functools.wraps the wrapper's __name__, __doc__ and module replace the original's, which confuses logs, debuggers and documentation tools. wraps copies them and records the original as __wrapped__, which inspect and tests can use to reach the undecorated function.

A retry decorator must decide which exceptions are retryable, how many attempts to make and what happens when attempts run out. Retrying every exception hides bugs; re-raising the last error on exhaustion preserves the failure. Real network retries also need delays and idempotent operations.
The transfer counts calls to a function that fails a set number of times, checks the attempt on which it succeeded and verifies the preserved metadata.

Transfer walkthrough: One failure then success returns on attempt 2 after two calls. Three failures with three attempts exhaust the retries and re-raise. An off-by-one range drops the last attempt and silently returns None.

lessons.title: Cache only compatible computations
body: lru_cache memoizes results for hashable argument combinations. It is suitable when reusing a prior result preserves semantics; impure computations need an invalidation policy.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A cache size of zero disables reuse.

lru_cache stores results keyed by the call's arguments. A repeated call with equal, hashable arguments returns the stored result without running the function. Unhashable arguments such as lists raise TypeError, because they cannot be dictionary keys.

With maxsize set, the cache keeps at most that many entries and evicts the least recently used one when full. A hit refreshes an entry's recency. cache_info() reports hits, misses, maxsize and current size, which lets tests confirm caching behavior instead of guessing.

Caching is only correct for functions whose result depends solely on their arguments and that have no needed side effects. Reading files, the clock or mutable globals breaks that assumption; call cache_clear() when the underlying data changes. Cached return values are shared, so do not mutate a returned list.
The transfer traces an LRU cache of size two over a call sequence where a hit protects an entry from eviction.
Transfer walkthrough: 1 and 2 miss, 1 hits, 3 misses and evicts 2, and the final 1 hits: 2 hits, 3 misses, size 2. A one-entry cache would turn every alternating call into a miss.
lessons.code:
import json
import functools
data = 3
calls = []
@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=8)
def f(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x*x
f(data)
f(data)
result = len(calls)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Structural patterns extract data
body: match selects a structural pattern and binds names inside that pattern. A wildcard handles unsupported shapes without assuming every mapping has the same keys.
For input {'kind': 'point', 'x': 4}, the worked computation produces 4. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A literal key mismatch prevents the intended record pattern from matching.

match compares a subject against case patterns from top to bottom and runs the first that matches. Sequence patterns such as ['move', x, y] check length and items; mapping patterns such as {'quit': True} check that keys exist with matching values, ignoring extra keys.

Class patterns such as int(x) check the type and bind the value. A guard, if condition, adds a test that runs after binding; if it fails, matching continues with later cases. Order matters: put specific cases before general fallbacks such as ['move', *_].

Strings are deliberately not treated as sequences by sequence patterns, so 'say hi' does not match ['say', text]. The wildcard _ matches anything and binds nothing. A final case _ makes unsupported shapes explicit instead of leaving a silent fall-through.
The transfer dispatches command-like data with type checks, a guard for non-negative coordinates, a mapping pattern and a string that must not be mistaken for a sequence.

Transfer walkthrough: The negative move fails the guard and falls to 'bad move'. quit False does not match {'quit': True}. The bare string 'say hi' is not a sequence subject, so it is unknown. Removing the guard would accept negative coordinates.

exercises.solution:
import json

data = [['move', 1, 2], ['move', -1, 0], ['say', 'hi'], {'quit': True}, ['jump']]
def handle(command):
    match command:
        case ['move', int(x), int(y)] if x >= 0 and y >= 0:
            return f'move {x},{y}'
        case ['move', *_]:
            return 'bad move'
        case ['say', str(text)]:
            return 'say ' + text
        case {'quit': True}:
            return 'quit'
        case _:
            return 'unknown'
result = [handle(c) for c in data]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Annotations do not enforce values
body: Type annotations document contracts and support static checking. Ordinary Python calls do not automatically reject a runtime value that violates an annotation.
For input 'text', the worked computation produces "text". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Assuming annotations perform runtime validation produces false confidence.

Annotations are metadata. The interpreter stores them but does not check calls against them: a function annotated value: int happily receives a string. Static checkers such as mypy or pyright use annotations before the program runs.

When untrusted data enters at a boundary, such as a request, file or configuration, validate it explicitly at runtime. typing.get_type_hints(fn) resolves a function's annotations into objects your validation code can read. Validation libraries build on the same idea.

Decide precise rules. bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True; an exact type check rejects it. By the numeric-tower convention, a float parameter usually accepts int too. Write these choices down and test them, because the annotation alone does not express them.
The transfer validates keyword arguments against resolved hints and then calls the function unchecked once to show that annotations alone enforce nothing.

Transfer walkthrough: 2 * 1.5 is 3.0. True is rejected by the exact int check, and 'x' is not numeric. The direct call returns 'abab' because nothing enforced the annotation. isinstance would let True through as an int.

def identity(x:int)->int:

result = identity(data)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Protocols describe supported operations
body: A runtime-checkable Protocol can check the presence of required attributes. This shallow structural check does not validate full signatures, types or semantic behavior.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An object without the required operation does not satisfy the runtime shape check.

A Protocol describes the members an object must have, without requiring inheritance. A static checker verifies that a passed object structurally matches, including method signatures. This is the typed form of duck typing.

@runtime_checkable lets isinstance(obj, Proto) run at runtime, but it only checks that the named members exist. It does not check that they are callable with the right signature, their types or behavior. An object with close = 3 passes an isinstance check for a protocol requiring close().

Use runtime protocol checks for coarse routing, then handle failures when actually calling. For trustworthy guarantees, rely on static checking plus tests. Runtime protocol checks are also slower than ordinary isinstance against a concrete class.
The transfer routes three objects through a runtime protocol check: a real implementation, an attribute that is not callable and an object lacking the member.
Transfer walkthrough: File closes. Liar passes the shallow check but fails when called. Nothing lacks the member and is skipped. Checking the wrong attribute name would skip everything.

lessons.title: Metaclasses govern class creation
body: A metaclass customizes how class objects are constructed. Use this mechanism sparingly when class-level behavior cannot be expressed with a simpler decorator or hook.
For input 1, the worked computation produces "demo". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the metaclass policy changes every class created through it.

A metaclass controls how class objects are created, but most class-creation needs are simpler. __init_subclass__ runs on the parent whenever a subclass is defined, and receives keyword arguments written in the class statement, such as class CSV(Plugin, name='csv').

This is enough for plugin registries, enforcing required class attributes or validating subclass configuration. It composes with inheritance and avoids metaclass conflicts when a class has bases with different metaclasses. Call super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs) so cooperative hooks keep working.

Registries are shared mutable state. Decide what a duplicate name means, here a ValueError, and how tests reset the registry. Because registration happens at class definition, importing a module has side effects, which is worth documenting.
The transfer defines subclasses dynamically with type(name, bases, namespace, **kwargs), which passes the keywords on to __init_subclass__, and checks duplicate rejection.
Transfer walkthrough: csv and json register; the second csv raises ValueError. Replacing the dictionary instead of inserting would forget earlier plugins and let the duplicate through.

lessons.title: Weak references do not own objects
body: weakref.ref observes an object without keeping it alive. When the last strong reference is removed, the weak reference becomes empty on this reference-counted interpreter.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Keeping a hidden strong alias prevents the observed object from being released.

A normal dictionary holds strong references, so a cache built on dict keeps every value alive for as long as the cache exists. That is a common source of unbounded memory growth in long-running services and notebooks.

WeakValueDictionary holds weak references to its values. When the last strong reference elsewhere disappears, the entry is removed automatically. The cache can then share an object while someone uses it, without becoming its owner.

On CPython, objects without reference cycles are freed as soon as their reference count drops to zero, so entries vanish immediately. Other interpreters, free-threaded builds or objects in cycles may delay collection until the garbage collector runs; tests that observe removal should state that dependency. Some built-in types, such as int and list, cannot be weakly referenced.
The transfer creates objects, keeps strong references to only some of them and observes which cache entries survive after the temporary references go away.
Transfer walkthrough: a and c stay alive through held; b loses its last strong reference when the loop variable is rebound, so its entry disappears. A plain dict would keep all three.

import weakref
data = 1
class Item:
    pass
item = Item()
watch = weakref.ref(item)
del item
result = watch() is None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import weakref
data = [['a', True], ['b', False], ['c', True]]
class Model:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
held = []
model = None
for name, keep in data:
    model = Model(name)
    cache[name] = model
    if keep:
        held.append(model)
model = None
result = sorted(cache.keys())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

assert condition, message raises AssertionError when the condition is false. It states something you believe must already be true, which makes it a natural way to express test expectations and internal invariants.

Running Python with -O removes assert statements entirely. Never use assert to validate user input, permissions or file contents: that validation would vanish in optimized mode. Raise ValueError, PermissionError or a domain exception for conditions that real inputs can trigger.

Exact equality is the wrong expectation for most floating-point results. 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point. Compare with math.isclose and state both the relative tolerance and an absolute tolerance, because a purely relative tolerance cannot accept any value near zero.
The transfer compares computed and expected floats with explicit tolerances, including a value that differs from zero by less than the absolute tolerance.

import json
import math
data = [[0.30000000000000004, 0.3], [1.0, 1.1], [0.0, 1e-13]]

lessons.title: Run actual unit assertions
body: unittest records assertion failures as test outcomes. Inspect wasSuccessful rather than assuming that construction of a TestCase means the test passed.
For input [2, 2], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A test that compares a value with itself cannot reject a wrong expected value.
A test method stops at its first failing assertion. When one test loops over a table of cases, the first failure hides every later failure, and the report does not say which input broke.

with self.subTest(value=value) runs each iteration as a sub-test. A failure is recorded with its parameters and the loop continues, so the report lists every failing case. The method still counts as one test run, but its failures list one entry per failing sub-test.

Run tests through a TestResult or a runner and inspect wasSuccessful, failures and errors. failures are assertion mismatches, errors are unexpected exceptions; distinguishing them helps separate wrong answers from crashes.
The transfer runs a table of doubling cases with two wrong expectations, so the report must contain both failures rather than stopping at the first.
Transfer walkthrough: Cases 2 and 3 have wrong expectations, so two sub-test failures are recorded in one run. Removing subTest would report only the first.

import json
import unittest
data = [2, 2]
class Contract(unittest.TestCase):
    def runTest(self):
        self.assertEqual(data[0],data[1])
report = unittest.TestResult()
Contract().run(report)
result = report.wasSuccessful()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Mock a dependency boundary
body: A mock can substitute a controlled result for an external dependency. Assert how it was called as well as what its caller returns; avoid mocking the behavior under test.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [7, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Passing the wrong argument still produces the configured mock result.
Mock the boundary your code talks to, such as an HTTP client or database, not the logic you are testing. A mock lets a test choose what the boundary returns and then check how the code used it.

side_effect controls each call. An iterable returns its items in turn, and an exception instance in that iterable is raised instead of returned. This reproduces sequences such as success, connection failure, success without a real network.

Check calls as well as results. call_count and call_args_list show whether the code retried, used the right arguments and did not make extra calls. A test that only checks the final return value cannot detect a function that silently calls the service twice.
The transfer feeds a fallback function a sequence containing a connection failure and verifies both the outcomes and the exact calls made.

Transfer walkthrough: The second call raises, so the fallback returns cached:k1. Exactly three calls were made with keys k0, k1 and k2. Returning None on failure would pass a test that only checks the successful calls.

lessons.title: Test multiple boundary cases
body: A compact case table makes input/result relationships explicit. Include boundary and negative cases rather than testing only one convenient positive example.
For input [0, 1], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: all and any express different acceptance rules.
Boundary-value testing checks inputs at, just below and just above each threshold, because off-by-one mistakes appear exactly there. A table of cases makes those choices visible and easy to review.

bisect(breakpoints, x) returns the insertion point to the right of equal values, so a score equal to a breakpoint moves into the higher band. bisect_left inserts to the left and keeps equal values in the lower band. The choice is a policy: is 60 a pass or a fail?

A lookup table driven by sorted breakpoints replaces long if/elif chains. It keeps the thresholds as data, and the same boundary cases test every band. The breakpoints must be sorted, or bisect gives meaningless answers.
The transfer grades scores at both sides of every breakpoint, including the lowest and highest values.
Transfer walkthrough: 59 is F and 60 is D; 89 is B and 90 is A. bisect_left would move every exact breakpoint down one band.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Read pyproject metadata
body: pyproject.toml stores build and project metadata in explicit tables. Use a TOML parser and read the intended table rather than relying on line positions.
For input '[project]\nname="sample"\nversion="1.0"', the worked computation produces "sample". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reading a different metadata key returns a different contract value.

pyproject.toml is the standard place for a Python project's metadata. The [project] table holds name, version, requires-python and dependencies; [project.optional-dependencies] holds extras such as a torch group. tomllib parses it into ordinary dictionaries and lists.

A dependency string can carry a version specifier and an environment marker after a semicolon, such as "pandas>=2.3; python_version >= '3.13'". Tools that report the requirement itself should separate the marker rather than treat the whole string as a package name.

Report missing required fields explicitly instead of failing later with a KeyError deep inside a build script. Use .get with defaults for optional tables, so a project without extras is valid. tomllib reads only; writing TOML needs a separate library.
The transfer validates the required keys, strips environment markers from dependencies and lists extras across complete, incomplete and minimal files.

Transfer walkthrough: The complete file has no missing keys, two dependencies once the marker is removed, one torch extra and a Python floor. A file without [project] lacks both required keys. Keeping markers would misreport the pandas requirement.

lessons.title: Record interpreter compatibility
body: An environment receipt must include the actual running interpreter. A major/minor compatibility check differs from claiming the newest release is installed.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A hard-coded incompatible major version misrepresents the environment.
sys.version_info is a tuple-like value such as (3, 13, 14, 'final', 0). Tuples compare item by item, so sys.version_info >= (3, 13) is the correct way to check the running interpreter.

Version strings must not be compared as text. String comparison is character by character, so '3.9' > '3.13' is True because '9' sorts after '1'. Parse each dotted part into an integer tuple before comparing.

Real package versions also have pre-releases, post-releases and local labels, such as 2.0.0rc1. Installers use the packaging library's Version class to order them correctly; the integer parser here is only valid for plain dotted releases. Record the actual running versions in receipts rather than assuming the newest release is installed.
The transfer checks plain versions against a 3.13 floor, including a case where text comparison gives the wrong answer.
Transfer walkthrough: 3.9 is below 3.13 numerically, while 3.13.14 and 4.0 meet the floor. Comparing strings would accept 3.9.

lessons.title: Isolate tests with temporary directories
body: TemporaryDirectory creates a unique scope and removes it on exit. Assert the cleanup after leaving the context so teardown failures are observable.
For input 3, the worked computation produces false. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning while still inside the resource scope does not establish cleanup.

A test that writes files should own a private directory. TemporaryDirectory creates a unique one and removes it with its contents when the with block exits, so tests do not interfere with each other or leave files behind.

Writing a file in place can leave a truncated file if the process stops halfway. A safer pattern writes to a temporary file in the same directory, then calls os.replace(tmp, target). The replacement is atomic on the same filesystem: readers see either the old or the new complete file.

Copying instead of replacing leaves the temporary file behind and loses atomicity. Test both the final content and the directory listing, so leftovers are caught. After the with block, check that the directory itself is gone.
The transfer writes several versions atomically into an isolated directory and inspects the content, the leftover files and the cleanup.
Transfer walkthrough: The last version b wins, only state.txt remains, and the directory is gone afterwards. Copying would leave state.txt.tmp behind.

    (path/"value").write_text(str(data))
result = path.exists()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import os, shutil, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
data = ['a', 'b']
def atomic_write(path, text):
    tmp = path.with_name(path.name + '.tmp')
    tmp.write_text(text, encoding='utf-8')
    os.replace(tmp, path)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    target = Path(directory) / 'state.txt'
    for text in data:
        atomic_write(target, text)
    final = target.read_text(encoding='utf-8') if data else None
    names = sorted(p.name for p in Path(directory).iterdir())
result = [final, names, Path(directory).exists()]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

A log call passes two filters. The logger's level decides whether a record is created at all. Each handler then applies its own level before emitting. A record reaches output only if it passes both.

This split lets one logger send everything at INFO to a file while a console handler shows only WARNING and above. It also explains a common surprise: lowering a handler's level shows nothing new if the logger's level still discards those records.

Pass arguments separately, as logger.info('loaded %s', name), rather than formatting first. Formatting then happens only for records that are emitted, and handlers receive the template and arguments. Avoid logging secrets; levels do not redact.
The transfer captures emitted records with a small handler and varies the logger and handler levels independently.

Transfer walkthrough: Logger DEBUG with handler WARNING emits only warning and error. Logger INFO with handler DEBUG emits info and above, with the argument merged. Dropping the handler level would let every logger-accepted record through.

lessons.title: Use profiler evidence
body: cProfile records actual calls made during a scoped workload. A call count establishes that workload only; timing and speed claims require representative measurements.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 3. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Skipping a workload call changes the observed count.

A profiler records how many times each function ran and how long it took during one workload. Call counts are deterministic for a given input, which makes them good evidence of algorithmic cost, independent of machine speed.

Naive recursive Fibonacci calls itself about 1.6 times more for each increase in n, giving exponential growth: computing fib(10) takes 177 calls. Memoizing with functools.cache stores each result, so each n is computed once and fib(10) needs 11 underlying calls.

Timings vary between runs and machines and require repeated measurement with representative inputs. Report the workload with any profiling claim. Profile before optimizing, because the slowest part of a program is often not where you expect.
The transfer profiles both implementations on the same input and reports their results and call counts.
Transfer walkthrough: Both return 55, but the naive version makes 177 calls and the memoized one 11. Removing the cache makes memo exponential too.
lessons.code:
import json
import cProfile
data = 3
profiler = cProfile.Profile()
def work():
    return 1
profiler.enable()
for _ in range(data):
    work()
profiler.disable()
result = sum(row.callcount for row in profiler.getstats() if getattr(row.code,"co_name",None)=="work")
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Bound retained diagnostic history
body: Retain only the history needed by the feature. A bounded deque evicts the oldest records while keeping newest records in arrival order.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An unbounded list retains records beyond the stated limit.
deque(maxlen=n) keeps at most n items. Appending to a full deque discards the item at the opposite end automatically, so it holds the most recent n values in arrival order with constant-time appends.

That makes it the standard structure for sliding windows: moving averages, recent-error buffers and rate monitors. Diagnostic history in a long-running process must be bounded; an unbounded list grows forever and is a memory leak in practice.

While the window is filling, it contains fewer than n items. Divide by len(window), not n, or early averages are too small. Decide whether partial windows should produce output at all, and test that start-up behavior.
The transfer computes a moving average over a stream, including the warm-up values and a window of size one.
Transfer walkthrough: Averages are 2, then (2+4)/2, (4+6)/2 and (6+8)/2. An unbounded deque would compute running averages of all values instead.
lessons.code:
import json
from collections import deque
data = [1, 2, 3]
history = deque(maxlen=2)
for x in data:
    history.append(x)
result = list(history)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

data is [window, values]. Keep the most recent window values in a deque(maxlen=window) and append the average of the current window after each value. Return the averages.
Check all these cases:
Input [2, [2, 4, 6, 8]] → [2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]
Input [3, []] → []
Input [1, [5, -5]] → [5.0, -5.0]
exercises.starter:
import json
from collections import deque
data = [2, [2, 4, 6, 8]]
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
exercises.solution:
import json
from collections import deque
data = [2, [2, 4, 6, 8]]
window, values = data
recent = deque(maxlen=window)
averages = []
for x in values:
    recent.append(x)
    averages.append(sum(recent) / len(recent))
result = averages
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: maxlen discards the oldest value automatically.
Divide by the current length during warm-up.
A window of one returns each value itself.
exercises.explanation: Averages are 2, then (2+4)/2, (4+6)/2 and (6+8)/2. An unbounded deque would compute running averages of all values instead.

lessons.title: Check a transformation property
body: A property-based check describes a relationship across inputs. Reversing twice should recover the original sequence; generated inputs complement rather than replace domain examples.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A single reversal does not satisfy the round-trip property.

A property-based check states a relationship that should hold for every input, such as decode(encode(x)) == x, then tests it on many generated inputs. It finds cases that hand-picked examples miss, such as runs of three equal characters.

Use a dedicated random.Random(seed) instance for generation. A fixed seed makes the generated inputs reproducible, so a failing case can be re-run exactly. Using the global random functions couples tests to each other's random state.
Report the failing inputs, not just a count, and add the smallest one as an explicit regression example. Libraries such as Hypothesis automate generation and shrinking; the idea is the same.
The transfer generates short strings from a seeded generator and checks that run-length encoding round-trips. A plausible bug that miscounts longer runs is caught by the generated cases.

Transfer walkthrough: The correct encoder round-trips every generated string. A version that sets the count to 2 still encodes 'aab' correctly but fails on generated runs of three, which hand-picked examples might miss.

lessons.title: Await coroutine results
body: Calling an async function creates a coroutine. await runs it within an event-loop task and obtains the result after any suspension.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning the original input ignores the coroutine transformation.

Calling an async function does not run it. It returns a coroutine object, which runs only when awaited or wrapped in a task. A coroutine that is never awaited does nothing, and Python warns when one is garbage-collected unawaited.

await runs one coroutine to completion before the next line continues, so awaiting in a loop is sequential even inside async code. Concurrency comes from scheduling several awaitables together, for example with asyncio.gather, so that while one waits, another runs.

Concurrency here means interleaving at await points on one thread. It overlaps waiting such as network or disk I/O; it does not make CPU-bound Python code faster. A coroutine that never awaits anything blocks every other task until it finishes.
The transfer logs start and end events for the same steps run sequentially and then concurrently, and inspects an unawaited call.

Transfer walkthrough: Sequentially, each step starts and ends before the next. Under gather, both start before either ends because each yields at sleep(0). Without that await there is no switch point, and the concurrent log looks sequential.
lessons.code:
import json
import asyncio
data = 3
async def double(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return x*2
result = asyncio.run(double(data))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:
data is a list of names. step(name, log) logs name:start, awaits sleep(0) and logs name:end. Run the steps sequentially, then concurrently with gather, then create (and close) one unawaited coroutine. Return [sequential_log, concurrent_log, unawaited_type_name].

Input [] → [[], [], "coroutine"]
Input ['x'] → [["x:start", "x:end"], ["x:start", "x:end"], "coroutine"]

exercises.solution:
import json
import asyncio
data = ['a', 'b']
async def step(name, log):
    log.append(name + ':start')
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    log.append(name + ':end')
    return name
async def main():
    sequential, concurrent = [], []
    for name in data:
        await step(name, sequential)
    await asyncio.gather(*(step(name, concurrent) for name in data))
    pending = step('x', [])
    kind = type(pending).__name__
    pending.close()
    return [sequential, concurrent, kind]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

gather lets each step run until its first await, then switches.
Close the unawaited coroutine to avoid a warning.
exercises.explanation: Sequentially, each step starts and ends before the next. Under gather, both start before either ends because each yields at sleep(0). Without that await there is no switch point, and the concurrent log looks sequential.

lessons.title: Gather preserves input ordering
body: gather schedules awaitables concurrently but returns results in the order the awaitables were supplied. Completion order is a separate scheduling detail.
For input [3, 1, 2], the worked computation produces [3, 1, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Sorting returned values destroys the requested input order.

asyncio.gather returns results in the order the awaitables were passed, regardless of which finished first. That makes it easy to pair results with inputs. as_completed instead yields awaitables in completion order, for handling results as soon as each is ready.

By default, the first exception raised by any awaitable propagates out of gather, and you lose the other results. With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are placed in the result list at their positions, so the caller can report each failure alongside the successes.

With return_exceptions=True you must check each result's type; otherwise errors pass silently as values. In new code, TaskGroup is often preferable, because it cancels siblings when one fails; gather fits when partial results are wanted.
The transfer runs jobs that take different numbers of scheduler turns, one of which fails, and compares gather's positional results with as_completed's completion order.

Transfer walkthrough: gather keeps slow, bad and fast in input order, with bad recorded as an error value. as_completed reports bad (zero turns), then fast, then slow. Without return_exceptions the ValueError propagates and no results are returned.

    return await asyncio.gather(*(value(x) for x in data))

import json
import asyncio
data = [['slow', 3], ['bad', -1], ['fast', 1]]
async def job(name, turns):
    for _ in range(turns):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
    if turns < 0:
        raise ValueError(name)
    return name
async def main():
    gathered = await asyncio.gather(*(job(n, t) for n, t in data), return_exceptions=True)
    labels = [g if isinstance(g, str) else 'error:' + str(g) for g in gathered]
    finished = []
    for next_done in asyncio.as_completed([job(n, max(t, 0)) for n, t in data]):
        finished.append(await next_done)
    return [labels, finished]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: TaskGroup owns child tasks
body: A TaskGroup waits for its children before its context exits. Keep child handles when their results are needed and read results only after successful group completion.
For input [1, 3], the worked computation produces [2, 6]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Creating tasks without recording their handles loses the intended result inventory.

A TaskGroup owns every task created through it. Leaving the async with block waits for all of them, so no child can outlive the scope that started it. This is structured concurrency: task lifetimes follow the code's block structure.

If any child raises, the group cancels the remaining children, waits for them to finish their cleanup and then raises an ExceptionGroup containing the failures. Children see CancelledError and should clean up and re-raise it.

except* ValueError handles the matching exceptions inside an ExceptionGroup, and other types continue to propagate. A failure therefore cannot leave orphaned background work running, which is the main difference from creating tasks individually.
The transfer runs children that finish, fail or are still waiting, and records which ones completed and which were cancelled.

Transfer walkthrough: c completes immediately, a fails after one turn and the group cancels b. Only a's ValueError is reported. Inverting the failure condition changes which children fail and which are cancelled.

import asyncio
data = [1, 3]
async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        tasks = [group.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0,result=x*2)) for x in data]
    return [task.result() for task in tasks]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import asyncio
data = [['a', 1, True], ['b', 5, False], ['c', 0, False]]
async def main():
    events = []
    async def child(name, turns, fail):
        try:
            for _ in range(turns):
                await asyncio.sleep(0)
            if fail:
                raise ValueError(name)
            events.append(name + ':done')
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            events.append(name + ':cancelled')
            raise
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
            for name, turns, fail in data:
                group.create_task(child(name, turns, fail))
        outcome = 'ok'
    except* ValueError as errors:
        outcome = sorted(str(e) for e in errors.exceptions)
    return [outcome, sorted(events)]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Cancellation must run cleanup
body: Cancelling a suspended task raises CancelledError in that task. Await its completion and allow finally to release owned resources before considering teardown finished.
For input 1, the worked computation produces ["closed"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning without the finalizer event loses evidence of cleanup.
task.cancel() asks a task to stop by raising CancelledError at its current await. The task can clean up in except or finally blocks, and the caller should await it to know the cleanup has finished.

After cleanup, re-raise CancelledError. Returning normally instead swallows the cancellation: the task then reports as successfully finished, task.cancelled() is False, and structures such as TaskGroup and timeouts that rely on cancellation can misbehave.
Suppress cancellation only in rare, deliberate cases, and document them. Use finally for cleanup that must happen on every path, so success, errors and cancellation all release the same resources.
The transfer cancels two workers, one that re-raises and one that swallows the cancellation, and reports how each task appears to its owner.
Transfer walkthrough: The re-raising worker reports cancelled with no value. The swallowing worker cleans up too but reports a normal result, hiding the cancellation from its owner.
lessons.code:
import json

exercises.solution:
import json
import asyncio
data = [False, True]
async def main():
    events = []
    async def worker(swallow):
        try:
            await asyncio.Event().wait()
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            events.append('cleanup')
            if not swallow:
                raise
            return 'swallowed'
    report = []
    for swallow in data:
        task = asyncio.create_task(worker(swallow))
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        task.cancel()
        try:
            value = await task
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            value = None
        report.append([task.cancelled(), value])
    return [report, events]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Timeouts bound an await scope
body: asyncio.timeout cancels the current task when its deadline expires and translates that cancellation into TimeoutError outside the context. Cleanup still belongs in finally.
For input 1, the worked computation produces "timeout". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Suppressing a timeout and reporting success misstates completion.

async with asyncio.timeout(seconds) cancels the work inside it when the deadline passes and converts that cancellation into TimeoutError at the block's exit. Code that completes without suspending past the deadline is unaffected.

Where the timeout scope sits decides what a slow operation affects. A timeout around a whole loop aborts the remaining items; a timeout around each item records the slow one and continues with the rest. Choose deliberately and test with a hanging input.
Report a timeout as a timeout. Converting it into a normal-looking value hides that the result is missing. Cleanup belongs in finally inside the timed work, because cancellation runs it.
The transfer applies a zero-second deadline to each item; one item waits forever and must be reported without stopping the batch.
Transfer walkthrough: a and b complete; slow times out and is recorded, and b still runs. Recording a normal result on timeout would hide the missing data.

    except TimeoutError:

import asyncio
data = ['a', 'slow', 'b']

lessons.title: Join thread-pool work
body: A ThreadPoolExecutor context waits for owned work during shutdown. map returns results in input order; threads overlap waiting but do not guarantee CPU parallel speedups.
For input [1, 3], the worked computation produces [2, 6]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ignoring the transformation changes every nonzero result.

Executor.submit schedules one call and returns a Future. as_completed(futures) yields futures as they finish, in an order you cannot predict. Keep a dictionary from each future to its input so every result can be attributed correctly.

future.result() returns the value or re-raises the worker's exception. Handle errors per future, so one bad input is reported without losing the others. Sort or key the collected results when the output must be deterministic.

The with block shuts the pool down and waits for submitted work, so threads are not leaked. Threads overlap I/O waits; because of the GIL, CPU-bound pure-Python work generally needs processes, not threads, for parallel speedup on standard builds.
The transfer parses inputs concurrently, separates successes from failures and returns them in a deterministic order.
Transfer walkthrough: '1' and '3' parse and 'x' fails; each is attributed through the dict. Using a fixed input instead would overwrite results under one key.
lessons.code:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
data = [1, 3]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    result = list(pool.map(lambda x:x*2,data))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Protect a compound state update
body: A lock defines a critical section around a shared read-modify-write operation. The invariant is the protected update, independent of incidental interpreter scheduling.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces 6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Assigning instead of accumulating loses contributions.

A race happens when two threads read shared state, decide, and write back, and their steps interleave. Checking a balance and then withdrawing is a check-then-act sequence: two threads can both see enough money and both withdraw.

Hold one lock around the entire sequence, the check and the update together. Protecting only the write still lets two threads pass the check with the same old value. The lock defines what must happen atomically; the GIL does not provide that guarantee for compound operations.

With a lock, the result is independent of thread scheduling: the invariant (no overdraft) holds and the number of accepted withdrawals is determined by the inputs alone. Use with lock: so the lock is released even if the block raises.
The transfer runs concurrent withdrawals against one balance and checks that the invariant and the accepted count are deterministic.
Transfer walkthrough: Ten covers three withdrawals of three, leaving one; the remaining two attempts are rejected. Checking only for a non-negative balance would allow the account to go negative.
lessons.code:
import json
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
data = [1, 2, 3]
lock = threading.Lock()
state = [0]
def update(x):
    with lock:
        state[0] += x
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    list(pool.map(update,data))
result = state[0]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
data = [10, 3, 5]
balance, amount, attempts = data
lock = threading.Lock()
state = {'balance': balance, 'accepted': 0}
def withdraw(_):
    with lock:
        if state['balance'] >= amount:
            state['balance'] -= amount
            state['accepted'] += 1
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    list(pool.map(withdraw, range(attempts)))
result = [state['balance'], state['accepted']]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

A balance of 1 cannot cover a withdrawal of 3.

lessons.title: Queues express backpressure
body: A bounded queue rejects an immediate put when capacity is exhausted. Real producers can block or await capacity rather than allowing memory use to grow without a bound.
For input 3, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An unbounded queue accepts work beyond the intended capacity.

A bounded queue between a producer and a consumer applies backpressure: when the queue is full, await queue.put() suspends the producer until the consumer removes an item. Memory use stays bounded however fast the producer is.

maxsize=0, the default, means unbounded, not zero capacity. An unbounded queue lets a fast producer buffer everything, which hides the slowdown until memory runs out. Pick an explicit capacity and test that it holds.

The consumer needs a clear stop signal. A sentinel value such as None placed after the last item, or Queue.shutdown in newer Python versions, lets it exit without being cancelled while items remain. Make sure every item is processed before shutdown.
The transfer runs a producer and consumer with a small capacity, checks that every item was processed in order and that the queue never exceeded its bound.
Transfer walkthrough: All four items are processed in order and the queue never holds more than two. An unbounded queue lets the producer buffer everything at once, exceeding the intended capacity.
lessons.code:
import json
import queue
data = 3
q = queue.Queue(maxsize=1)
q.put_nowait(data)
try:
    q.put_nowait(data)
    result = False
except queue.Full:
    result = True
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

data is [capacity, items]. A producer puts each item into asyncio.Queue(maxsize=capacity), tracking the peak qsize, then puts a None sentinel. A consumer multiplies items by 10 until it sees None. Return [consumed, peak_within_capacity].
Check all these cases:
Input [2, [1, 2, 3, 4]] → [[10, 20, 30, 40], true]
Input [1, []] → [[], true]
Input [3, [5]] → [[50], true]
exercises.starter:
import json
import asyncio
data = [2, [1, 2, 3, 4]]
# Write the computation for the stated input contract.
result = None
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
exercises.solution:
import json
import asyncio
data = [2, [1, 2, 3, 4]]
async def main():
    q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=data[0])
    peak, consumed = 0, []
    async def producer():
        nonlocal peak
        for item in data[1]:
            await q.put(item)
            peak = max(peak, q.qsize())
        await q.put(None)
    async def consumer():
        while (item := await q.get()) is not None:
            consumed.append(item * 10)
            await asyncio.sleep(0)
    await asyncio.gather(producer(), consumer())
    return [consumed, peak <= data[0]]
result = asyncio.run(main())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: put suspends while the queue is full.
The sentinel tells the consumer to stop after the last item.
A default Queue() is unbounded.
exercises.explanation: All four items are processed in order and the queue never holds more than two. An unbounded queue lets the producer buffer everything at once, exceeding the intended capacity.

lessons.title: Own subprocess completion
body: subprocess.run waits for its child, captures bounded lesson output, and reports the exit status. A timeout and scoped cleanup are required for less predictable workloads.
For input 0, the worked computation produces 0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An explicit wrong exit code is a failure even with no stderr.

subprocess.run starts a child process, waits for it and returns a CompletedProcess. Pass the command as a list of arguments; it is then executed without a shell, so spaces and special characters in arguments cannot be interpreted as shell syntax.

By default a non-zero exit status is just a value in returncode, which is easy to ignore. check=True turns it into CalledProcessError, so failures cannot pass unnoticed. capture_output=True with text=True collects stdout and stderr as strings.

A child can hang. timeout=seconds kills the child when the limit expires and raises TimeoutExpired, so the parent does not wait forever. Distinguish success, failure exit and timeout in the result, because they need different handling.
The transfer runs a successful command, a failing exit and a hanging child, each with check=True and a short timeout.

Transfer walkthrough: The first child prints hi, the second exits with 3, and the third is killed after one second. Without check=True the failing exit would be reported as a success with empty output.
lessons.code:
import json
import subprocess,sys
data = 0
child = subprocess.run([sys.executable,"-c","import sys;sys.exit(int(sys.argv[1]))",str(data)],capture_output=True,text=True,timeout=5)
result = child.returncode
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Retrieve worker failures
body: Calling result on a completed future re-raises the worker exception. A submitted task is not a successful operation until its result or failure has been observed.
For input 1, the worked computation produces "failed". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Swallowing worker failure and reporting success changes the outcome.

Executor.map returns results in input order through an iterator. If a call raised, its exception is re-raised when iteration reaches that position, after the earlier results have already been delivered.

Code that collects results inside the loop therefore holds a partial result when the exception arrives. Decide whether partial output is acceptable, must be discarded or must be reported with the failure position, and test that path.

When failures should be handled per item, submit futures individually or wrap the function to return an error value. Never discard the iterator without consuming it: an unobserved exception is a failure nobody sees.
The transfer maps a function that fails on one input and reports how many results were collected before the failure.
Transfer walkthrough: 1 and 0.5 arrive before the zero raises, so two results are collected. Filtering zeros out would hide the failure and report a complete run.
lessons.code:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
data = 1
def work():
    raise ValueError(str(data))
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as pool:
    task = pool.submit(work)
    try:
        task.result()
    except ValueError:
        result = "failed"
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
data = [1, 2, 0, 4]
def invert(x):
    return 1 / x
collected = []
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    try:
        for value in pool.map(invert, data):
            collected.append(value)
        status = 'complete'
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        status = 'failed-after-' + str(len(collected))
result = [collected, status]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

Record how many results arrived before the failure.
