lessons.title: Events coordinate ownership
body: An Event signals a condition without sharing a mutable payload. Test its state explicitly; a signal and a completed computation are separate concepts.
For input True, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Setting an event unconditionally reports a condition that has not occurred.

An Event is a flag threads can wait on. set() wakes every waiter; wait() blocks until the flag is set. wait(timeout) returns True if the flag was set and False if the timeout expired first, so the return value tells you which happened.
Ignoring that return value is a common bug: code continues as if the condition were met after a timeout. Check it and handle the timeout path explicitly.

Always join threads you start, with a timeout, and check is_alive() afterwards. A thread that is still alive after join(timeout) is leaked work that keeps running. An Event signals a condition; results still travel through a separate, owned channel.
The transfer starts a waiting thread, signals or does not signal it, and records what the waiter observed and whether the thread finished.

Transfer walkthrough: When the event is set, the waiter sees True; without it, the short timeout gives False. Both threads are joined. Clearing instead of setting makes the waiter time out and see False.

lessons.title: Dot products combine aligned components
body: A dot product sums pairwise products of equal-length vectors. It measures alignment and underlies linear models; strict pairing rejects a malformed dimensional contract.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces 11. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Adding components instead of multiplying changes the dot product.

The dot product a·b sums the products of aligned components. Geometrically it equals |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Dividing by both lengths gives cosine similarity, which compares direction while ignoring magnitude: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular and -1 for opposite.

math.sumprod(a, b) computes the dot product with extended precision, and math.hypot(*a) computes the Euclidean length. Using the library functions states the intent and avoids writing the accumulation by hand.

Two edge cases need a policy. Vectors of different lengths have no defined dot product; report that explicitly rather than letting zip truncate silently. A zero vector has no direction, so its cosine similarity is undefined; returning None is clearer than dividing by zero or inventing 0.
Embedding search, recommendation and many similarity features use exactly this computation. The transfer covers perpendicular, parallel, opposite, zero and mismatched-length inputs.

Transfer walkthrough: Perpendicular vectors give 0, parallel ones 1 and opposite ones -1. [3,4]·[4,3] = 24 and both lengths are 5, so the similarity is 0.96. Dividing by the sum of lengths would break the [-1, 1] range.

lessons.title: Euclidean norms measure magnitude
body: The L2 norm is the square root of the sum of squared components. It is nonnegative and vanishes only for the zero vector.
For input [3, 4], the worked computation produces 5.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: The sum of components is not a Euclidean norm.

A norm measures a vector's size. The L1 norm sums absolute values, the L2 (Euclidean) norm is the square root of the sum of squares, and the L-infinity norm is the largest absolute component. All three are zero only for the zero vector.

They measure different things. L1 grows with every component, L2 is the ordinary geometric length, and L-infinity reports the worst single component. In machine learning, L1 and L2 penalties regularize model weights, and L-infinity bounds appear in robustness constraints.

Dividing a vector by its L2 norm gives a unit vector with the same direction. The zero vector cannot be normalized; return None or raise rather than dividing by zero. Taking absolute values matters for L-infinity: max(data) on [3, -4] returns 3, but the largest magnitude is 4.
The transfer computes all three norms and the unit vector, including the empty and zero-heavy cases.
Transfer walkthrough: [3, -4] has L1 7, L2 5 and L-infinity 4, and its unit vector is [0.6, -0.8]. Using max(data) would report 3 because it ignores the negative component's magnitude.

lessons.title: Population and sample variance differ
body: The sample variance divides squared deviations by n-1 when estimating population variance from independent observations. The population formula uses n.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using population variance underestimates this sample-variance contract.

Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. statistics.pvariance divides by n and describes the data as a complete population. statistics.variance divides by n - 1 and estimates the variance of the population a sample was drawn from.

The n - 1 correction exists because deviations are measured from the sample's own mean, which is closer to the data than the true mean. Dividing by n would underestimate the spread on average. With a single observation there is no spread to estimate, so variance raises StatisticsError; pvariance of one value is 0.

Pick the formula from the question being asked, then document it. Libraries differ in their defaults: NumPy's var uses n unless ddof=1, while pandas' var uses n - 1. Mixing them silently produces different numbers from the same data.
The transfer computes both quantities for several samples, including one observation and an empty list.

Transfer walkthrough: For the eight-value sample the squared deviations sum to 32, giving 32/8 = 4 and 32/7 ≈ 4.571. One observation has population variance 0 and no sample estimate. Using pvariance for both would understate the sample estimate.

lessons.title: Bayes updates a prior with evidence
body: Posterior probability is likelihood times prior divided by total evidence probability. Include false positives from the alternative class in the denominator.
For input [0.5, 0.8, 0.2], the worked computation produces 0.8. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ignoring false positives makes the posterior unjustifiably large.

Bayes' rule computes P(condition | positive) = P(positive | condition) P(condition) / P(positive). The denominator counts every way to test positive: true positives from the condition plus false positives from everyone else.

When a condition is rare, false positives from the large unaffected group can outnumber true positives. With a 1% prior, 90% sensitivity and a 10% false-positive rate, one positive test only raises the probability to 1/12. Ignoring the base rate is one of the most common reasoning errors with classifiers.

A second independent positive test uses the first posterior as its new prior. fractions.Fraction keeps these updates exact, so you can see the true values without rounding error. Real tests are often not independent, so repeated updating needs that assumption stated.
The transfer applies zero, one and two positive results and reports the exact posterior and a rounded decimal.

Transfer walkthrough: One positive raises 1/100 to 1/12; a second raises it to 9/20. Dropping the (1 - posterior) weighting treats every case as possibly a false positive and gives the wrong denominator.
lessons.code:
import json

data = [0.5, 0.8, 0.2]
prior,sensitivity,false_positive = data
a = prior*sensitivity
result = a/(a+(1-prior)*false_positive)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
from fractions import Fraction
data = ['1/100', '9/10', '1/10', 1]
prior, sensitivity, false_positive, positives = (Fraction(x) for x in data)
posterior = prior
for _ in range(int(positives)):
    hit = posterior * sensitivity
    posterior = hit / (hit + (1 - posterior) * false_positive)
result = [str(posterior), round(float(posterior), 6)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

    hit = posterior * sensitivity
    posterior = hit / (hit + (1 - posterior) * false_positive)
result = [str(posterior), round(float(posterior), 6)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Expected values weight outcomes
body: An expectation sums each outcome times its probability. Probabilities must describe a normalized distribution; an unweighted average is a different quantity.
For input [[0, 10], [0.9, 0.1]], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ignoring probabilities gives the wrong expected outcome.

The expected value of a discrete random variable is the probability-weighted average of its outcomes. statistics.fmean(values, weights=probabilities) computes it directly. Its variance is E[X²] - (E[X])², the expected squared value minus the squared mean.

A probability vector must have non-negative entries summing to one. Validate that before computing anything; an unnormalized vector produces a weighted average that is not an expectation of any distribution. Compare the sum with math.isclose, because float sums rarely equal 1 exactly.

Expectation and variance answer different questions. A lottery paying 10 with probability 0.1 has expected value 1, the same as a certain payment of 1, but its variance is 9 rather than 0. Risk, uncertainty estimates and loss functions depend on that difference.
The transfer validates a distribution and returns its mean and variance, rejecting probabilities that do not sum to one.

Transfer walkthrough: The mean is 1 and E[X²] is 10, so the variance is 9. Probabilities summing to 1.5 are rejected. Subtracting the mean instead of its square happens to give 10 - 1 = 9 in the first case too, which is why the certain outcome matters: it exposes 25 - 5 = 20 versus the correct 0.

data = [[0, 10], [0.9, 0.1]]
values,probabilities = data
result = sum(v*p for v,p in zip(values,probabilities,strict=True))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Check a derivative numerically
body: A central difference estimates a derivative from symmetric perturbations. Choose a step that balances truncation and roundoff error; this is a check rather than a symbolic proof.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 6.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A one-sided difference with a large step has different error behavior.

A numerical derivative approximates f'(x) from function values. The forward difference (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h has an error proportional to h. The central difference (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / (2h) cancels the first error term, so its error is proportional to h², which is usually far smaller for the same h.

Making h smaller is not always better. Below a point, subtracting two nearly equal floats loses significant digits, and rounding error grows like ε/h, where ε is about 2.2e-16 (see math.ulp). Values of h around 1e-4 to 1e-5 are a common compromise for double precision central differences.

Gradient checks compare an analytic or automatic derivative against a central difference at a few points, with a relative tolerance. They catch sign errors and missing terms in hand-written backward passes. They are a test, not a training method: they cost two function evaluations per input dimension.
The transfer compares both estimates with the exact derivative of sin, cos(x), and confirms the central difference is closer.
Transfer walkthrough: At x = 1 the central estimate matches cos(1) ≈ 0.540302 to six places and beats the forward estimate. Dividing by h instead of 2h doubles the estimate.

import json

data = 3
h = 1e-4
f = lambda x:x*x
result = (f(data+h)-f(data-h))/(2*h)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Move against the gradient
body: Gradient descent subtracts a positive learning rate times the gradient. On a quadratic with a suitable small step this moves toward its minimum.
For input [3, 0.1], the worked computation produces 2.4. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Adding the gradient moves uphill on this quadratic.

Gradient descent repeatedly moves against the gradient: x ← x - η f'(x), where η is the learning rate. For f(x) = (x - 3)², f'(x) = 2(x - 3), so each step multiplies the distance to the minimum by (1 - 2η).

That factor explains the learning-rate behaviour. With 0 < η < 1 the distance shrinks and the iteration converges. With η = 0.5 it lands on the minimum in one step. With η > 1 the factor's magnitude exceeds one, so each step overshoots further and the iteration diverges.

A practical loop needs a stopping rule and a step limit. Stop when the gradient is small enough, cap the number of steps so a divergent run cannot loop forever, and report whether the target was reached rather than returning the last value as if it were a solution.
The transfer runs the update with a convergent rate, a divergent rate and a start at the minimum, reporting the final point, the steps taken and whether it converged.

Transfer walkthrough: At rate 0.25 the error halves each step until the gradient is tiny. At 1.1 the error grows by a factor of 1.2 with alternating sign. Starting at 3 stops immediately. Adding the gradient climbs away from the minimum.

data = [3, 0.1]
x,rate = data
result = x-rate*2*x
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Normalize exponentials stably
body: Subtract the largest logit before exponentiation. This preserves softmax probabilities while reducing overflow risk; the normalized probabilities sum to one.
For input [1000, 1000], the worked computation produces [0.5, 0.5]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Exponentiating very large raw logits can overflow.
Softmax turns scores into probabilities: exp(x_i) / Σ exp(x_j). math.exp overflows for arguments above about 709, raising OverflowError, so scores like 1000 cannot be exponentiated directly.

Subtracting the maximum score m first leaves softmax unchanged, because the factor exp(-m) cancels in the ratio, and makes every exponent at most zero. The same trick gives the log-sum-exp: log Σ exp(x_j) = m + log Σ exp(x_j - m).

Log-softmax, x_i - logsumexp(x), is what classification losses actually use. It avoids computing a probability and then taking its log, which loses precision for small probabilities. Libraries implement these fused, stable forms; understand them so you can recognise when a hand-written version will overflow or underflow.
The transfer computes a stable log-sum-exp and log-softmax and compares them with the naive formula, which overflows on large scores.

Transfer walkthrough: Two equal scores of 1000 give log-sum-exp 1000 + log 2 and log-probabilities of -log 2, while the naive formula overflows. Forgetting to add m back leaves the result off by exactly the maximum score.

result = [x/sum(weights) for x in weights]

exercises.solution:
import json
import math
data = [1000, 1000]
def logsumexp(xs):
    m = max(xs)
    return m + math.log(sum(math.exp(x - m) for x in xs))
lse = logsumexp(data)
log_probs = [x - lse for x in data]
try:
    naive = round(math.log(sum(math.exp(x) for x in data)), 6)
except OverflowError:
    naive = 'overflow'
result = [round(lse, 6), [round(v, 6) for v in log_probs], naive]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Cross entropy penalizes confident mistakes
body: For a one-hot target, cross entropy is the negative log probability assigned to the correct class. Probabilities must be positive; logits require a stable log-softmax implementation.
For input 1.0, the worked computation produces 0.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Negating a probability is not the negative logarithm loss.

For one example with a correct class t, cross-entropy is -log p_t, the negative log probability the model gave to the right answer. A confident correct prediction costs almost nothing; a confident wrong one costs a lot, growing without bound as p_t approaches zero.

Models output logits, unnormalized scores. Computing softmax and then the log can underflow to log(0). The stable form is logsumexp(z) - z_t, which equals -log softmax(z)_t exactly and never takes the log of a tiny number.

Training minimizes the mean loss over a batch. Report both the mean and the per-example losses when debugging: one extremely wrong example can dominate the mean. An empty batch has no defined mean and should be reported, not divided by zero.
The transfer computes per-example and mean cross-entropy from logits, including a uniform prediction over three classes, whose loss is log 3.
Transfer walkthrough: The confident correct example costs 0.127 and the confident wrong one 2.127, for a mean of 1.127. Reversing the subtraction makes every loss negative.

exercises.solution:
import json
import math
data = [[[2, 0], 0], [[0, 2], 0]]
def nll(logits, target):
    m = max(logits)
    lse = m + math.log(sum(math.exp(z - m) for z in logits))
    return lse - logits[target]
losses = [nll(logits, target) for logits, target in data]
result = [round(sum(losses) / len(losses), 6) if losses else None, [round(l, 6) for l in losses]]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Entropy measures distribution uncertainty
body: Discrete entropy sums -p log p and treats zero-probability terms as zero by continuity. A concentrated distribution has lower entropy than a uniform one.
For input [1, 0], the worked computation produces 0.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Taking log zero is undefined without the zero-probability convention.
Entropy H(p) = -Σ p_i log2 p_i measures the uncertainty of a distribution in bits. A fair coin has 1 bit; a certain outcome has 0. Terms with p_i = 0 contribute nothing, by the limit p log p → 0.

KL divergence D(p‖q) = Σ p_i log2(p_i / q_i) measures the extra bits needed when outcomes from p are encoded using a code built for q. It is zero when p = q, is never negative and is not symmetric: D(p‖q) and D(q‖p) generally differ.

If q assigns zero probability to an outcome that p allows, the divergence is infinite: q declares impossible something that happens. Handle this explicitly. Cross-entropy, the usual classification loss, equals H(p) + D(p‖q), so minimizing it over q minimizes the divergence.
The transfer computes entropy and KL divergence, including a case where q gives zero probability to a possible outcome.

Transfer walkthrough: A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy and zero divergence from itself. A certain outcome has 0 bits but is 1 bit away from a fair coin. Reversing the roles gives an infinite divergence. Weighting by q computes the other direction.

lessons.title: Sample size affects uncertainty
body: For independent observations with fixed sample standard deviation, the standard error of the mean scales as one over the square root of sample size.
For input [4, 16], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Dividing by sample size instead of its square root shrinks uncertainty too fast.
The standard error of a sample mean is s / sqrt(n), where s is the sample standard deviation. Quadrupling the sample size halves the uncertainty, which is why estimates improve slowly with more data.

A normal-approximation 95% interval is mean ± z·SE, with z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975) ≈ 1.96. For small samples, a Student t critical value is the correct choice and is wider (about 3.18 for n = 4); the standard library has no t distribution, so this lab uses z only as a stated approximation.

Rearranging the half-width formula plans data collection: to get a half-width of at most w, you need n ≥ (z·s / w)². Round up, because a fractional observation is impossible. Remember the interval describes uncertainty in the mean, not the spread of individual values.
The transfer computes a normal-approximation interval and the sample size needed for a target precision.

Transfer walkthrough: For 10, 12, 14, 16 the mean is 13 and s ≈ 2.582, so SE ≈ 1.291 and the interval is about 13 ± 2.53; a half-width of 1 needs 26 observations. Dividing by n instead of sqrt(n) makes the interval far too narrow.

import json
import math, statistics
data = [[10, 12, 14, 16], 1.0]
sample, half_width = data
mean = statistics.fmean(sample)
s = statistics.stdev(sample)
se = s / math.sqrt(len(sample))

needed = math.ceil((z * s / half_width) ** 2)
result = [interval, needed]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Read array shapes
body: shape describes the length of each axis; size counts all elements. Record both before choosing a reshape or reduction so axis semantics stay explicit.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [[2, 2], 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting only rows is not the total element count.

An ndarray is a grid of values of one dtype. ndim is the number of axes, shape gives the length along each axis and size is their product, the total number of elements. A table of 3 rows and 2 features has shape (3, 2); a batch of 1 image with 2 rows and 1 column has shape (1, 2, 1).

Every row along an axis must have the same length. Since NumPy 1.24, np.asarray of ragged nested lists with a numeric dtype raises ValueError instead of quietly creating an array of Python list objects. That error is useful: it reports malformed input at the boundary.

Asking for dtype=object accepts ragged input, but it produces a 1-D array of list objects that loses vectorized arithmetic. Use it deliberately, not as a way to silence the error. An empty list becomes shape (0,), a valid one-dimensional array with no elements.
The transfer describes several inputs, including a ragged one that must be reported rather than converted.
Transfer walkthrough: Three rows of two give shape (3, 2) and size 6. The ragged input is rejected. dtype=object would accept it as a 1-D array of lists, hiding the malformed rows.

lessons.title: Choose numeric dtypes
body: An explicit floating dtype preserves fractional values during array construction. Integer conversion truncates fractional parts and can change a model input contract.
For input [1.5, 2.5], the worked computation produces [1.5, 2.5]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An integer dtype silently discards these fractions.
An array's dtype fixes how every element is stored. Converting float to integer with astype truncates toward zero: 1.7 becomes 1 and -1.7 becomes -1. It does not round, and it does not warn.

np.rint and np.round round to the nearest integer and send exact halves to the nearest even number, so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. This half-to-even rule avoids systematic upward bias when many values are rounded. Python's built-in round uses the same rule.

Lower precision changes values. float32 has about seven significant decimal digits, so float(np.float32(0.1)) is not equal to the float64 value 0.1. Models are often trained in float32 to save memory; compare with tolerances and never assume a cast round-trips exactly.
The transfer contrasts truncation, half-to-even rounding and single precision on the same inputs.

Transfer walkthrough: 1.7 and -1.7 truncate to 1 and -1 but round to 2 and -2; 2.5 rounds to 2 and 3.5 to 4. Flooring would give -2 for -1.7 and 3 for 3.5. The float32 value of 0.1 differs from the float64 one.

lessons.title: Broadcast along compatible trailing axes
body: Broadcasting compares dimensions from the right; each paired size must match or be one. A row vector can be applied to each matrix row without explicitly copying it.
For input [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [10, 20]], the worked computation produces [[11, 22], [13, 24]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using only the first offset applies a scalar instead of the row offsets.

Broadcasting compares shapes from the last axis backwards. Two dimensions are compatible when they are equal or one of them is 1; a missing leading dimension counts as 1. The smaller array is then treated as repeated along those axes without copying data.

A (rows, features) matrix minus a (features,) vector of column means subtracts each column's mean from that column. This is how feature standardization, z = (x - mean) / std, is written without loops. np.broadcast_shapes reports the result shape or raises if the shapes are incompatible.

Guard against a zero standard deviation: a constant column has no spread, and dividing by zero produces NaN or infinity. Replacing zero with one leaves that column at zero after centring. Shapes like (4, 1) and (3, 1) are incompatible and raise ValueError, which is better than silently aligning the wrong axis.
The transfer standardizes columns, reports the broadcast shape and confirms that a mismatched row count is rejected.

Transfer walkthrough: Column one has mean 2 and std 1, giving -1 and 1; column two is constant and becomes 0. Row counts 2 and 3 cannot broadcast, but a one-row matrix stretches against two rows, so that case reports 'broadcast'. Using row means would centre each row instead of each feature.

mean = x.mean(axis=0)

lessons.title: Basic slicing usually shares storage
body: A basic NumPy slice is normally a view. Mutating it can update the parent array; use copy when independent storage is the required contract.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 0, 0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An independent copy does not propagate writes back to its parent.

A basic slice such as a[1:3] creates a view: a new array object describing part of the same memory. Writing through the view changes the original array. view.base points at the array that owns the memory.

Views make slicing cheap, even for huge arrays, but they cause surprising bugs when a function modifies a slice it received. If independent data is required, call .copy() explicitly. np.shares_memory(a, b) checks whether two arrays overlap.

Augmented assignments such as window *= 10 operate in place on the view. Plain assignment, window = window * 10, creates a new array and leaves the original untouched. Code review should check which one is intended whenever a slice is modified.
The transfer modifies a view and a copy of the same region and observes the effect on the original.
Transfer walkthrough: The view's change appears in a, while the copy's change does not. Fancy indexing with a list would create a copy and leave a unchanged.

view[:] = 0

lessons.title: Advanced indexing creates a copy
body: Integer-array indexing selects values into a new array. Mutating that result does not update the original array; indexed assignment is a separate operation.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Replacing advanced indexing with a slice changes ownership.

Indexing with an integer array selects elements into a new array, a copy. Assigning through an index array, a[idx] = values, writes to the original. These are different operations with the same bracket syntax.

With repeated indices, a[idx] += 1 does not accumulate. It reads all selected values, adds one, then writes them back, so an index that appears twice is incremented once. This is a classic bug when counting or scattering gradients.

np.add.at(a, idx, 1) performs an unbuffered addition, applying every occurrence. For counting non-negative integers, np.bincount(idx, minlength=k) is simpler and faster. Choose the operation from the required semantics and test it with duplicates.
The transfer counts occurrences three ways, showing which ones handle repeated indices correctly.
Transfer walkthrough: Index 2 appears twice: buffered assignment records 1, while add.at and bincount record 2. Replacing add.at with buffered assignment loses the duplicates.

lessons.title: Boolean masks select records
body: A Boolean mask selects positions where the predicate is true. Parenthesize elementwise comparisons when combining them, and avoid Python scalar and/or on arrays.
For input [-1, 0, 2], the worked computation produces [2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Including zero changes a strictly-positive filter.
A comparison such as a > 0 produces a Boolean array of the same shape. Indexing with it, a[mask], selects the elements where the mask is True, returning a 1-D copy.

Combine masks with the elementwise operators &, | and ~, and parenthesize each comparison: (a >= 0) & (a <= 10). Python's and, or and not ask for a single truth value, which is ambiguous for a multi-element array and raises ValueError. The & operator binds more tightly than comparisons, which is why the parentheses are required.

np.where(mask, a, fallback) keeps the shape and replaces unselected positions, which suits feature pipelines that must preserve row alignment. mask.sum() counts selected elements because True counts as 1.
The transfer filters a range, replaces out-of-range values and demonstrates why Python's and fails on arrays.
Transfer walkthrough: 5 and 10 are inside the inclusive range; -1 and 12 are replaced by -1. Python's and fails for several elements but works for one. Using | would accept every value.

lessons.title: Reduction axes describe what disappears
body: Summing along axis zero collapses rows and retains one value per column. Summing along axis one instead produces one value per row.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [4, 6]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the reduction axis changes the meaning and often the output shape.

A reduction along an axis removes that axis. For a (samples, features) matrix, axis=0 reduces over samples and leaves one value per feature; axis=1 reduces over features and leaves one value per sample. axis=None reduces everything to a scalar.

argmax follows the same rule. argmax(axis=1) gives, for each sample, the index of its largest feature, which is exactly how predicted classes are read from a matrix of class scores. Using the wrong axis returns plausible integers of the wrong meaning and length.
Name axes in comments or variable names, such as per_feature_mean, and check result shapes in tests. Reductions return NumPy scalars; convert with float() or int() at JSON or API boundaries.
The transfer computes per-feature means, per-sample sums, per-sample argmax and the grand total.
Transfer walkthrough: Feature means are 2 and 3; sample sums are 6 and 4; the first sample's largest feature is index 1. argmax over axis 0 would return one index per feature instead.

lessons.title: Keep dimensions for later broadcasting
body: keepdims retains reduced axes with length one. This makes the result broadcast back against the original array without accidentally aligning with another axis.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [[3], [7]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Dropping the axis changes a two-dimensional shape contract.

keepdims=True keeps a reduced axis with length 1. Summing a (rows, cols) array over axis 1 with keepdims gives shape (rows, 1) instead of (rows,). The kept axis lines the result up with the axis it came from.

That matters for broadcasting. x / x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) divides each row by its own total. Without keepdims, the (rows,) result aligns with the last axis, columns, so a square matrix is silently divided by the wrong totals and a non-square one raises an error.
Row normalization appears in softmax, probability tables and attention weights. Check that each normalized row sums to one, and handle all-zero rows, whose total of zero cannot be divided by.
The transfer normalizes rows and reports the shape of the totals, the normalized values and the row sums.

Transfer walkthrough: The totals have shape (2, 1), so each row is divided by its own sum. Without keepdims the totals have shape (2,), which only happens to give the same numbers here because both rows sum to 4.

lessons.title: Write ufunc results into explicit output
body: A ufunc out parameter writes into supplied compatible storage. Choose a dtype that can represent the result and reason about aliasing before reusing buffers.
For input [1, 3], the worked computation produces [3, 5]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Multiplying instead of adding changes the transformation.

Universal functions such as np.add and np.divide accept out= to write into an existing array, avoiding a new allocation in tight loops. The output must be able to hold the result type under the same_kind casting rule.

Dividing integers produces floats, so writing the result into an integer array would discard fractions. NumPy refuses and raises a UFuncTypeError, a subclass of TypeError. That is a feature: the alternative is silent truncation.

where= computes only at positions where a condition holds, such as non-zero denominators. Positions where it is false are left untouched, so out must be initialized; with np.empty they would contain arbitrary memory. Safe division is therefore np.divide(a, b, out=np.zeros(...), where=b != 0).
The transfer writes a float result into a buffer, shows that an integer output is rejected and divides safely around zeros.

Transfer walkthrough: Halving writes fractions into the float buffer, while the integer output is rejected. Safe division gives 1 where a is non-zero and keeps 0 elsewhere. Initializing out with ones would leave 1 at the masked zero positions.

a = np.asarray(data,dtype=float)
out = np.empty_like(a)
np.add(a,2,out=out)
result = out.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Own a random generator
body: default_rng constructs an independent random generator. A fixed seed reproduces this generator sequence in the pinned environment, without establishing cross-version or GPU reproducibility.
For input 7, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Advancing only one generator breaks sequence agreement.

np.random.default_rng(seed) creates a Generator with its own state. The same seed reproduces the same sequence in the same NumPy version, which makes data splits and initialization repeatable. Avoid the legacy global np.random functions, whose shared state couples unrelated code.

Each draw advances the generator. Two calls on one generator give different results; recreating a generator from the same seed restarts the sequence. Pass a Generator into functions instead of reseeding inside them.

Parallel workers need independent streams. Generator.spawn(n) creates child generators whose streams are statistically independent, which is safer than seeding workers with seed, seed + 1 and so on. Reproducibility is guaranteed within a NumPy version, not across versions.
The transfer reproduces a permutation from a seed and checks that spawned child streams differ.

Transfer walkthrough: A fresh generator reproduces the permutation, which always contains 0 to 4, and the two spawned children produce different streams. Drawing again from the same parent continues the sequence, so the permutations generally differ.

b = np.random.default_rng(data)
result = bool(np.array_equal(a.integers(0,100000,size=8),b.integers(0,100000,size=8)))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Check nonfinite numeric values
body: isfinite rejects both infinities and NaNs. A missingness check alone does not reject every nonfinite value, so choose a predicate that matches the data contract.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [true, true, false]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Checking only for NaN admits infinite values.

Floating-point data can contain NaN (not a number) and positive or negative infinity. np.isnan detects only NaN; np.isfinite is False for NaN and both infinities. Choose the predicate that matches the data contract; a NaN check alone lets infinities through.

NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, so x == np.nan is always False. Test with np.isnan. A single NaN or infinity makes an ordinary mean NaN or infinite, and one bad sensor reading can corrupt a whole feature.

Count and report non-finite values before deciding a policy: drop, impute or reject the record. Strict JSON cannot represent NaN or infinity, so they must be handled before data leaves a numeric pipeline. Textual 'nan' and 'inf' can be parsed by NumPy with dtype=float.
The transfer parses text values, counts non-finite and NaN entries and averages only the finite ones.
Transfer walkthrough: Two values are non-finite, one of them NaN, and the finite values 1 and 3 average to 2. Filtering only NaN would leave infinity in the mean.

lessons.title: Reshaping preserves element count
body: reshape changes dimensions while preserving the number of elements. A -1 dimension can be inferred when the remaining sizes divide the element count.
For input [1, 2, 3, 4], the worked computation produces [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the column count changes the resulting shape.

reshape changes how a fixed sequence of elements is grouped into axes; it never reorders the underlying sequence. The default order='C' reads and writes the last axis fastest (row-major). order='F' reads the first axis fastest (column-major).

Transposing is different from reshaping. a.T swaps axes, so flattening a.T walks the original columns, which equals flattening a in Fortran order. Confusing reshape with transpose is a common bug when converting (batch, channels) to (channels, batch): the shape looks right while the values are scrambled.

A -1 dimension is inferred from the element count. If the requested sizes cannot divide the count, reshape raises ValueError instead of padding or truncating. Check shapes and a few values whenever a reshape crosses a semantic boundary such as images, sequences or channels.
The transfer flattens a small matrix in C order, in Fortran order and through its transpose, and confirms that an impossible shape is rejected.

Transfer walkthrough: Row-major order gives 0 through 5; column-major gives 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5, the same as flattening the transpose. Six elements cannot form four rows. Dropping order='F' would make the second result row-major.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Strides describe memory steps
body: Array strides give byte increments along axes. A reversed view has a negative stride and can share storage without being C-contiguous.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [-8, true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Taking an unreversed copy changes the stride direction.

strides gives the number of bytes to step in memory to move one position along each axis. A C-contiguous (rows, cols) int64 array has strides (cols*8, 8): moving across a row steps 8 bytes, moving down a column steps a whole row.

Transposing does not move data. a.T is a view with the shape and strides swapped, so it shares memory and is usually not C-contiguous. Many operations accept such views, but some libraries, file writers and GPU transfers require contiguous memory.

np.ascontiguousarray returns a C-contiguous array, copying only when necessary. When the input already is contiguous it may return the same memory, so do not rely on it to produce an independent copy; use .copy() for that. Axes of length one do not affect contiguity.
The transfer inspects strides, contiguity and memory sharing for an array, its transpose and a contiguous version.

Transfer walkthrough: A (2, 3) int64 array has strides 24 and 8; its transpose swaps them and is not C-contiguous, so ascontiguousarray copies it into new memory with strides 16 and 8. A (1, 4) array's transpose has a length-one axis and is already contiguous, so no copy is made and the memory is shared. Skipping the call would leave the non-contiguous view.

result = [int(b.strides[0]),bool(np.shares_memory(a,b))]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Matrix multiplication differs from elementwise multiplication
body: The @ operator contracts the inner matrix dimension. Elementwise multiplication pairs corresponding entries and follows broadcasting rules rather than matrix-product rules.
For input [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[1, 0], [0, 1]]], the worked computation produces [[1, 2], [3, 4]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using * instead of @ computes a different operation.

x @ W multiplies matrices: an (n, k) batch of inputs times a (k, m) weight matrix gives an (n, m) batch of outputs. The inner dimension k must match and is summed over. This is the core operation of a linear layer.

The * operator multiplies elementwise, pairing entries at the same positions and broadcasting shapes. It is a different operation that happens to agree with @ only in special cases such as 1 × 1 matrices. Mixing them up is a frequent bug when porting formulas.
Order matters: x @ W and W @ x are generally different, and one of them may not even be defined. Write the expected shapes beside matrix code and assert them in tests.
The transfer applies a weight matrix to a batch, reports the output shape and contrasts it with elementwise multiplication where the shapes allow it.

Transfer walkthrough: Each input row is combined with the weight columns: [1, 1] becomes [1, 2]. Summing a row against the single weight column gives 3, 7 and 11. Reversing the operand order computes a different product, or fails.

lessons.title: Name contractions with einsum
body: einsum can express index contractions explicitly. Repeated labels identify a contracted axis; output labels identify axes preserved in the result.
For input [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [10, 20]], the worked computation produces [50, 110]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Keeping the contracted label requests a different shape.

einsum writes a computation as index labels. 'ij,ij->i' multiplies matching entries and sums over j, keeping i: one dot product per row. Labels missing from the output are summed; labels present are kept.

'ik,jk->ij' computes every pair of row dot products, the Gram matrix A Aᵀ, which underlies kernels and attention scores. 'ii->' sums the diagonal, the trace. One notation covers many contractions without temporary transposes.

Verify an einsum against an explicit expression such as a @ a.T with np.allclose in tests; a mistyped label silently computes a different contraction. For performance-critical code, compare with the equivalent matmul, which is often faster.
The transfer computes row-wise dot products, a Gram matrix and its trace, and checks the Gram matrix against matmul.

Transfer walkthrough: Row dots against the identity pick out 1 and 4. The Gram matrix of [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is [[5, 11], [11, 25]], with trace 30. Keeping j instead of i gives column sums, which coincide for the identity but not in general.

import numpy as np
data = [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [10, 20]]
a,b = map(np.asarray,data)
result = np.einsum("ij,j->i",a,b).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Solve systems without explicitly inverting
body: linalg.solve computes a solution for a square nonsingular system. Check residuals and conditioning; a successful solve alone does not establish numerical reliability.
For input [[[2, 0], [0, 4]], [4, 8]], the worked computation produces [2, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Multiplying the coefficient matrix by the target does not solve the system.
np.linalg.solve(A, b) finds x with A x = b for a square matrix. Solving directly is faster and more accurate than computing inv(A) @ b. Check the residual ‖A x - b‖ to confirm the solution.

A singular matrix, one whose rows are linearly dependent, has no unique solution, and solve raises LinAlgError. Do not swap in least squares to make the error disappear unless a least-squares answer is what the problem actually requires; it returns a number for an ill-posed question.

The condition number, np.linalg.cond(A), estimates how much errors in b are amplified in x. A value near 1 is benign; a large value means small input noise can change the answer substantially even when the residual looks fine.
The transfer solves well-conditioned, singular and diagonal systems, reporting the solution, the residual check and the condition number.

Transfer walkthrough: The symmetric system gives x = [0.8, 1.4] with condition number about 2.618. The second matrix's rows are multiples, so it is singular. Substituting least squares would return a number for the singular system and hide the problem.

lessons.title: Least squares handles overdetermined systems
body: lstsq minimizes squared residuals rather than requiring an exact square system. The returned coefficient vector must be interpreted alongside rank and singular values.
For input [[[1], [2], [3]], [2, 4, 6]], the worked computation produces [2.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Replacing the fit with a zero coefficient vector ignores the data.

Least squares finds coefficients minimizing the sum of squared residuals when there are more equations than unknowns. To fit y = m x + c, build a design matrix with an x column and a column of ones; the ones column estimates the intercept.

Leaving out the ones column forces the line through the origin. The fit still runs and returns a coefficient, but it answers a different question and usually has a larger error. This is one of the most common silent modelling mistakes.

lstsq also returns the rank of the design matrix. If all x values are equal, the x column is a multiple of the ones column, the rank drops, and the slope is not identifiable: many lines fit equally well. Check rank before interpreting coefficients.
The transfer fits lines with an intercept, reports the rank and the residual sum of squares, including a degenerate design.

Transfer walkthrough: The points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5) lie exactly on y = 2x + 1. The noisy points give slope 0.6 and intercept 0.1 with residual 0.2. With every x equal to 1 the rank is 1, so lstsq returns the minimum-norm split m = c = 1 of the mean 2, not a meaningful slope. Dropping the ones column forces the line through the origin: slope 2.6 with residual 1.2 for the first data set.

import json
import numpy as np
data = [[0, 1, 2], [1, 3, 5]]
x, y = (np.asarray(v, dtype=float) for v in data)
design = np.column_stack([x, np.ones_like(x)])
coef, _, rank, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y, rcond=None)
fitted = design @ coef
result = [np.round(coef, 6).tolist(), int(rank), round(float(np.sum((y - fitted) ** 2)), 6)]

exercises.explanation: The points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5) lie exactly on y = 2x + 1. The noisy points give slope 0.6 and intercept 0.1 with residual 0.2. With every x equal to 1 the rank is 1, so lstsq returns the minimum-norm split m = c = 1 of the mean 2, not a meaningful slope. Dropping the ones column forces the line through the origin: slope 2.6 with residual 1.2 for the first data set.

lessons.title: Singular values reveal numerical rank
body: SVD factors a matrix into orthogonal directions and nonnegative singular values. Numerical rank uses a tolerance; exact symbolic rank and floating rank are different claims.
For input [[1, 2], [2, 4]], the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting every dimension as independent ignores rank deficiency.
The singular value decomposition writes A = U Σ Vᵀ, with orthonormal U and V and non-negative singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … on Σ's diagonal. Each σ measures how strongly A stretches one direction.

Numerical rank counts singular values above a tolerance. A matrix whose rows are exactly proportional has a zero singular value and rank one; a nearly proportional one has a tiny but non-zero value, so its numerical rank depends on the tolerance chosen.

Keeping only the largest k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation, and its error in the spectral norm is exactly σ_{k+1} (the Eckart–Young theorem). This is the basis of PCA, compression and many recommender models.
The transfer computes singular values and rank and checks that the rank-one approximation error equals the second singular value.

Transfer walkthrough: diag(3, 1) has singular values 3 and 1, and keeping only the first leaves an error of exactly 1 = σ₂. The proportional rows of [[1, 2], [2, 4]] give σ₂ = 0, rank 1 and an exact rank-one approximation. Forgetting the σ₁ scale leaves a large error that no longer matches σ₂.

import json
import numpy as np
data = [[3, 0], [0, 1]]
a = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
u, s, vt = np.linalg.svd(a, full_matrices=False)

lessons.title: FFT coefficients have a frequency interpretation
body: The FFT transforms a sequence into complex frequency coefficients. A constant signal has only a DC component under this unnormalized forward convention.
For input [1, 1, 1, 1], the worked computation produces [4, 0, 0, 0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning input magnitudes instead of spectral magnitudes changes domains.

The discrete Fourier transform expresses a sampled signal as a sum of frequencies. For real input, np.fft.rfft returns n // 2 + 1 complex coefficients, from zero frequency up to the Nyquist frequency, half the sampling rate.

np.fft.rfftfreq(n, d=1/rate) labels those coefficients in hertz. Without d it reports cycles per sample instead, a correct but differently scaled axis that is easy to misread. The magnitude of each coefficient measures how much of that frequency is present.

Coefficient 0 is the DC component: with NumPy's unnormalized forward convention, it equals the sum of the signal, so dividing by n gives the mean. Skip it when looking for the dominant oscillation. A frequency that falls between bins spreads into neighbouring bins (leakage); the fixtures use whole-bin frequencies.
The transfer samples a sine wave plus an offset and recovers its frequency in hertz and its mean.
Transfer walkthrough: A 5 Hz sine sampled at 64 Hz peaks at 5 Hz, and the DC term divided by n recovers the 0.5 offset. Without d, the peak would be reported as 5/64 cycles per sample.

lessons.title: Integer dtypes have finite ranges
body: A fixed-width NumPy integer wraps according to its dtype arithmetic. Promote before an operation if the mathematical result must fit; promotion afterward cannot recover overflowed bits.
For input [100, -100], the worked computation produces [200, -200]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Casting only after multiplication preserves an already-overflowed value.

Fixed-width integer arrays wrap around on overflow. uint8 holds 0 to 255, so 200 + 100 becomes 44 (300 - 256). Array arithmetic does this silently, without an exception, which is a classic image-processing bug when brightening pixels.

Widen first, compute, then clip and narrow: convert to int16, add, clip to [0, 255] and convert back to uint8. Clipping after the overflow has already happened is too late, because the wrapped values look valid.

Reductions are vulnerable too. Pass dtype=np.int64 to sum when totals can exceed the input type's range, and record the dtype used. The same reasoning applies to int32 indices on large datasets and to low-precision floats in mixed-precision training.
The transfer brightens uint8 pixel values with and without widening and computes a safe total.

Transfer walkthrough: 200 + 100 wraps to 44 and 255 + 100 to 99, while the widened version saturates at 255. Clipping after uint8 addition is too late, because the wrapped values are already within range.
lessons.code:
import json

import numpy as np
data = [100, -100]
a = np.asarray(data,dtype=np.int8)
result = (a.astype(np.int64)*2).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Keep missingness separate from values
body: A masked array excludes masked positions from reductions. Filling a masked value with zero before taking a mean changes the effective denominator.
For input [[2, 100, 4], [False, True, False]], the worked computation produces 3.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Including masked zeros biases the mean.
Legacy data often marks missing values with a sentinel such as -999. Treating it as a real number corrupts statistics: one -999 drags the mean of 2 and 4 to -331.

np.ma.masked_equal(values, -999) builds a masked array in which those positions are excluded from reductions. count() reports the valid entries and mean() averages only them. filled(0) produces an ordinary array with a chosen replacement, for libraries that do not understand masks.

Filling before reducing changes the result: averaging after filling with zero divides by the full length and biases the mean. Decide the missing-value policy explicitly, and handle the case where every value is masked, which has no mean.
The transfer masks a sentinel, compares the clean and naive means and produces a filled array.
Transfer walkthrough: Masking -999 leaves 2 and 4 with mean 3, while the naive mean is -331. Masking zero instead would leave the sentinel in the statistics.
lessons.code:
import json

import numpy as np
data = [[2, 100, 4], [False, True, False]]
values,mask = data
a = np.ma.array(values,mask=mask)
result = float(a.mean())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Memory maps still own resources
body: memmap exposes file-backed array storage. Flush changes, release mappings before scope cleanup, and avoid assuming that memory mapping bounds every downstream allocation.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [1.0, 2.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Writing a different value is still a successful file operation.

np.memmap maps a binary file into memory as an array. Pages are loaded on demand, so a file larger than memory can be processed in chunks. The file has no header: dtype and shape must be known, or recorded separately, to read it back.

Open with mode='w+' to create and write, call flush() to push changes to disk, and release the mapping before deleting or replacing the file. Reopening with mode='r' makes the array read-only, so an accidental write raises ValueError instead of altering the data.
Process a large map in fixed-size chunks and keep only small results. Holding slices of the map keeps it open. Note that an empty file cannot be mapped; handle zero-length data separately.
The transfer writes values to a memory-mapped file, reopens it read-only, sums it in chunks and checks the file size and write protection.
Transfer walkthrough: Five values in chunks of two sum to 3, 7 and 5, the file holds 5 × 8 bytes and the read-only map rejects the write. Stopping the range early drops the final partial chunk.

    mapped[:] = data

import json
import numpy as np
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
data = [[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2]
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / 'values.f64'
    values, chunk = data
    writer = np.memmap(path, dtype='float64', mode='w+', shape=(len(values),))
    writer[:] = values
    writer.flush()
    del writer
    reader = np.memmap(path, dtype='float64', mode='r')
    sums = [float(reader[i:i + chunk].sum()) for i in range(0, len(reader), chunk)]
    try:
        reader[0] = 1
        writable = True
    except ValueError:
        writable = False
    size = path.stat().st_size
    del reader
result = [sums, writable, size]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Series indexing has labels
body: loc selects labels while iloc selects integer positions. Integer-looking labels do not make these two interfaces interchangeable.
For input [3, 4], the worked computation produces 4. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Position zero is not necessarily the requested label.

A Series pairs values with index labels. .loc selects by label and .iloc by integer position. With an integer index such as [30, 10, 20], s.loc[10] means the label 10, the second element, while s.iloc[0] means the first position.

Slices follow different rules. A label slice s.loc[30:10] includes both endpoints, because labels need not be consecutive integers and 'up to but excluding' a label is rarely what you mean. A position slice s.iloc[0:1] excludes its end, like ordinary Python slicing.

Plain s[...] can mean either labels or positions depending on the index type, and pandas has been tightening that behaviour. Write .loc or .iloc explicitly in data code, especially after filtering or sorting, when labels no longer match positions.
The transfer contrasts label and position access on an unsorted integer index.
Transfer walkthrough: Label 10 is the second value, while position 0 is the first. The label slice from 30 to 10 includes both labels, but the position slice 0:1 contains one element.

lessons.title: Select DataFrame columns by name
body: A DataFrame stores named columns with potentially different dtypes. A list of column names preserves two-dimensional structure even when selecting one column.
For input {'x': [1, 2], 'y': [3, 4]}, the worked computation produces [2, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Selecting a scalar column name returns a Series with different shape.

frame['x'] returns a Series, one column without its two-dimensional structure. frame[['x']] returns a DataFrame with a single column. Code that later expects .columns or two dimensions needs the list form.

Each column has its own dtype. frame.dtypes lists them, and select_dtypes('number') picks numeric columns, which is how preprocessing code separates numeric features from text. Boolean columns are not included in 'number'.

Text columns in pandas 2.3 default to object dtype unless the string dtype is requested. Check dtypes after loading data instead of assuming them, because a single malformed value can turn a numeric column into object.
The transfer selects columns both ways and identifies numeric features in mixed tables.
Transfer walkthrough: x and y are numeric while name is text. The Boolean flag is excluded from numeric features. Selecting only integers would drop the float column y.

lessons.title: Arithmetic aligns labels
body: pandas arithmetic aligns by index labels rather than row position. Specify a fill policy deliberately when one side lacks a label.
For input [[1, 2], [10, 20]], the worked computation produces [21, 12]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Combining values positionally pairs different records.
Arithmetic between Series aligns on index labels. The result's index is the union of both indexes, and a label present on only one side produces NaN, because there is nothing to combine it with.

left.add(right, fill_value=0) treats a missing label on one side as 0 before adding, so one-sided entries keep their value. Whether 0 is right is a domain decision: it suits counts, not temperatures or prices.

Alignment is usually what you want, but it surprises code ported from NumPy, where position decides pairing. After a merge or filter, check the index before combining Series, and count NaNs created by misalignment.
The transfer adds two partly overlapping Series with and without a fill value.
Transfer walkthrough: Only b exists on both sides, giving 12; a and c are NaN in plain addition and keep their own values with fill_value=0. A fill of 1 would inflate one-sided entries.

lessons.title: Missingness needs an explicit policy
body: fillna replaces missing entries using a chosen value. Filling with zero is a domain decision and must not silently substitute for a training-only imputation strategy.
For input [1, None, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 0, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Dropping missing rows changes row count and alignment.

fillna replaces missing values with a chosen value. Filling with the column mean is common, but the mean must come from the training data. Computing it over training and test data together leaks information about the test set into the model.

Treat imputation as a fitted step: learn the fill value on the training split, then apply that same value to validation, test and production data. This is the same discipline scikit-learn pipelines enforce with SimpleImputer.

Count missing values before and after, and keep a record of which rows were imputed, because missingness itself can be informative. Do not fill with zero by default; zero is a real value with meaning.
The transfer fits a mean on training data, applies it to test data and reports how many values were filled.
Transfer walkthrough: The training mean of 1 and 3 is 2, which fills the test gap. Including the test value 10 would shift the fill to about 4.67, leaking test information.

lessons.title: Nullable integers preserve absent values
body: The Int64 extension dtype supports integer values with a missing sentinel. Fill or explicitly serialize missing entries before converting them into ordinary Python integers.
For input [1, None], the worked computation produces ["Int64", 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using zero as the missing count understates absent records.

A NumPy-backed int64 column cannot hold a missing value, so pandas converts integers with None to float64 and uses NaN. That changes the dtype and can lose precision: float64 represents integers exactly only up to 2**53.
The nullable Int64 extension dtype stores integers plus a separate mask of missing positions, shown as <NA>. Values stay exact integers, and reductions such as sum skip missing entries by default.

Converting an Int64 column with missing values to plain int64 raises, because there is no integer to put in the missing slot. Decide the policy explicitly: fill, drop or keep the nullable type through to the output.
The transfer compares default and nullable construction, including a large integer that float64 cannot represent exactly.
Transfer walkthrough: Missing values make the default column float, while Int64 keeps exact integers. 2**53 + 1 survives in Int64 but would round to 2**53 as a float.

lessons.title: Vectorized strings need missing policies
body: The str accessor performs string operations elementwise. Set na explicitly when a Boolean predicate must have a definite result for missing text.
For input ['cat', None, 'dog'], the worked computation produces [true, false, false]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Treating missing text as a match changes filter membership.
The .str accessor applies string methods elementwise. Chaining str.strip().str.lower() normalizes whitespace and case before comparisons, so ' Cat ' and 'cat' are treated alike.

With the dedicated 'string' dtype, missing values are <NA>, and string methods return <NA> for them. A Boolean predicate such as str.contains then needs na=False (or True) to produce a definite result usable as a filter.

str.contains treats its pattern as a regular expression by default. Pass regex=False for literal text, so characters such as '.' or '+' are not interpreted. Note that substring matching also hits words like 'concat'; use a word-boundary pattern when that matters.
The transfer normalizes text, matches a literal substring and counts missing entries.
Transfer walkthrough: ' Cat ' normalizes to 'cat' and matches; 'concat' also matches as a substring; the missing value stays missing. Without lowercasing, 'Cat' and 'CATS' would not match.

import pandas as pd
data = ['cat', None, 'dog']
result = pd.Series(data,dtype="string").str.contains("cat",regex=False,na=False).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Categories define a finite vocabulary
body: Categorical codes refer to a declared category order and use -1 for missing or unknown values. The codes are not ordinal measurements unless the domain says so.
For input ['high', 'low', 'other'], the worked computation produces [1, 0, -1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reordering the vocabulary changes the numeric codes.

A categorical stores each value as an integer code into a fixed list of categories. Values outside the declared categories become missing, with code -1. This is a quick way to detect unexpected labels in a supposedly closed vocabulary.

ordered=True makes the category list an order. Sorting then follows that order rather than alphabetical order, and comparisons such as s >= 'medium' become valid. Unordered categoricals reject such comparisons.

Codes are storage, not measurements. Feeding codes 0, 1, 2 to a model implies equal spacing and an order; that is only reasonable for genuinely ordinal data. For nominal labels, use one-hot encoding instead.
The transfer encodes ordered levels, detects an unknown label, sorts by level and compares against a threshold.

Transfer walkthrough: The codes follow the declared order, 'huge' is missing, sorting uses low < medium < high and the threshold comparison marks high and medium. An unordered categorical would reject the comparison.

lessons.title: Validate join cardinality
body: A many-to-one merge requires unique keys on the right. Validate that assumption so duplicate lookup rows do not silently multiply training examples.
For input [1], the worked computation produces "rejected". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A many-to-many allowance accepts unintended row expansion.

A left join keeps every row of the left table and attaches matching columns from the right. With a many-to-one relationship, such as orders to customers, the row count must not change. If the right side has duplicate keys, rows multiply and totals silently inflate.

validate='many_to_one' makes pandas check that the right keys are unique and raise MergeError otherwise. indicator=True adds a _merge column saying whether each row matched ('both') or not ('left_only'), so unmatched keys can be counted and investigated.
Choose the join type from the requirement. An inner join drops unmatched rows, which may silently remove data you meant to keep. Assert the row count after joins in pipelines.
The transfer joins orders to customers, preserves the row count and reports unmatched customers.
Transfer walkthrough: All four orders survive, customer 4 is unmatched and reported, and the region list keeps positions. An inner join would drop the unmatched order and hide it.
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [1]
left = pd.DataFrame({"id":data})
right = pd.DataFrame({"id":[1,1],"value":[2,3]})
try:
    left.merge(right,on="id",validate="many_to_one")
    result = "accepted"
except pd.errors.MergeError:
    result = "rejected"
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

body: A Boolean row mask has one entry per row. Construct it from the intended column and retain only rows satisfying the stated predicate.
For input [0, 1, 2], the worked computation produces [2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An inclusive threshold admits the boundary row.

Filter rows with a Boolean Series built from column conditions. isin tests membership in a list, and between(low, high) tests a range, inclusive at both ends by default. Combine conditions with & and |, parenthesizing each one.

Being explicit about inclusivity avoids boundary errors. between(0, 20) keeps exactly 0 and 20; inclusive='neither' excludes both, and 'left' or 'right' exclude one. Write the requirement down and test the boundaries.

Use .loc[mask, column] to select filtered rows and a column in one step. This avoids chained indexing such as frame[mask][column], which is less clear and was a source of copy warnings before copy-on-write.
The transfer filters by city membership and an inclusive temperature range, with values exactly on the boundaries.
Transfer walkthrough: Rome at exactly 20 and Oslo at exactly 0 are kept; Oslo at -5 and Lima are excluded. Excluding both bounds would drop the two boundary rows.

import json

import pandas as pd
data = [0, 1, 2]
frame = pd.DataFrame({"x":data})
result = frame.loc[frame.x>1,"x"].tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Choose a duplicate policy
body: drop_duplicates can retain the first or last observation for a key. Specify the policy explicitly when ingestion order encodes which observation is authoritative.
For input [[1, 10], [1, 20]], the worked computation produces [[1, 20]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Keeping the first record discards the newer replacement.

drop_duplicates(subset, keep='last') keeps the last row for each key in the current row order. If records arrive out of order, 'last' means 'arrived last', not 'most recent'. Sort by the key and timestamp first so that position reflects time.

duplicated(subset, keep=False) marks every row whose key appears more than once. Reporting those keys shows how often conflicting records occur, which is useful data-quality evidence before choosing a policy.
Write the policy down: latest by event time, first seen, or reject conflicting records. Each one yields a different training set. Ties in timestamp need a further rule.
The transfer keeps the latest value per ID when records arrive out of order and reports the IDs with conflicts.
Transfer walkthrough: After sorting, ID 1's latest record is 'new' at ts 5, and ID 1 is reported as a conflict. Without sorting, the arrival-order last row 'old' would win.
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [[1, 10], [1, 20]]
frame = pd.DataFrame(data,columns=["id","value"])
result = frame.drop_duplicates("id",keep="last").values.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:
data is a list of [id, ts, value] rows in arrival order. Keep the record with the largest ts per id. Return [[id, value] pairs sorted by id, sorted ids that had duplicates].
Check all these cases:
Input [[1, 5, 'new'], [1, 2, 'old'], [2, 1, 'x']] → [[[1, "new"], [2, "x"]], [1]]
Input [] → [[], []]
Input [[3, 1, 'a']] → [[[3, "a"]], []]

exercises.solution:
import json
import pandas as pd
data = [[1, 5, 'new'], [1, 2, 'old'], [2, 1, 'x']]
frame = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=['id', 'ts', 'value'])
latest = frame.sort_values(['id', 'ts']).drop_duplicates('id', keep='last')
conflicts = sorted(frame.loc[frame.duplicated('id', keep=False), 'id'].unique().tolist())
result = [[list(pair) for pair in zip(latest['id'].tolist(), latest['value'].tolist())], conflicts]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

duplicated(keep=False) flags every member of a duplicate group.
exercises.explanation: After sorting, ID 1's latest record is 'new' at ts 5, and ID 1 is reported as a conflict. Without sorting, the arrival-order last row 'old' would win.

lessons.title: Round-trip tabular data with a schema
body: CSV does not carry a complete dtype schema. This numeric example excludes the index explicitly so reading it does not create an unintended extra feature column.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces ["x"]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Writing the index adds a new column on import.
CSV stores text without types. read_csv infers types, and inference can change data: ZIP codes such as 02139 become the integer 2139, losing the leading zero, and dates stay as text strings.

Pass dtype={'zip': 'string'} for identifiers that look numeric but are labels, and parse_dates=['day'] for date columns. Declaring the schema at read time keeps it consistent across files and machines.

Write index=False unless the index carries meaning, or the next read will add an unnamed column. For data that must preserve dtypes exactly between pandas runs, prefer a typed format such as Parquet, and keep CSV for interchange.
The transfer writes identifiers and dates to CSV and reads them back naively and with an explicit schema.
Transfer walkthrough: The naive read turns 02139 into 2139 and keeps dates as text. Declaring the schema preserves the ZIP codes and parses the dates. Declaring zip as int64 reproduces the loss.
lessons.code:
import json
import io
import pandas as pd
data = [1, 2]
frame = pd.DataFrame({"x":data})
stream = io.StringIO()
frame.to_csv(stream,index=False)
stream.seek(0)
result = list(pd.read_csv(stream).columns)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Aggregation reduces each group
body: groupby aggregation produces one output per group. Specify key sorting when deterministic output order matters and distinguish missing group keys from missing values.
For input [['b', 3], ['a', 1], ['a', 2]], the worked computation produces [3, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Counting rows is different from summing their values.

groupby splits rows by key, applies an aggregation to each group and combines one row per group. Named aggregation, agg(n=('score', 'size'), mean=('score', 'mean')), produces clearly named output columns in a single pass.

By default, rows whose group key is missing are dropped from groupby results. A summary built that way silently omits those rows. dropna=False keeps a separate group for the missing key, so totals still add up to the input.
size counts rows, including those with missing values in the aggregated column; count counts only non-missing values. Choose deliberately, and pass sort=True when output order must be deterministic.
The transfer summarizes scores per team, including a row without a team.
Transfer walkthrough: Team a has two scores averaging 3 with best 5, b has one, and the row without a team forms its own group. With dropna=True that row would vanish from the summary.

lessons.title: Transform preserves row alignment
body: A group transform broadcasts a group-level calculation back to each original row. It differs from aggregation, whose output has one row per group.
For input [['a', 1], ['a', 3], ['b', 8]], the worked computation produces [2, 2, 8]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An aggregate loses the original row-level shape.

groupby(...).transform(f) computes a group-level statistic and broadcasts it back to every row of that group. The result has the same length and index as the input, so it can be assigned as a new column.

This is how group-relative features are built: value minus the group mean, value divided by the group total, or a rank within the group. Aggregation would instead return one row per group, which cannot be assigned back without a merge.

Group statistics used as model features must also follow the train/test discipline: compute them from training data, or in a way that does not peek at the target or the future. Within one table, transform keeps rows aligned automatically.
The transfer centres each value on its group mean and computes each value's share of its group total.
Transfer walkthrough: Group a's values 1 and 3 centre to -1 and 1 with shares 0.25 and 0.75; b's single value is its whole group. Dividing by the grand total would mix groups together.
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [['a', 1], ['a', 3], ['b', 8]]
frame = pd.DataFrame(data,columns=["group","value"])
result = frame.groupby("group").value.transform("mean").tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import pandas as pd
data = [['a', 1], ['b', 4], ['a', 3]]
frame = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=['group', 'value'])
grouped = frame.groupby('group')['value']
