lessons.title: Pivot requires a unique cell mapping
body: pivot maps index/column pairs to cells and requires uniqueness. pivot_table can aggregate duplicates, but doing so changes the operation and should be deliberate.
For input [['a', 'x', 1], ['a', 'x', 2]], the worked computation produces "duplicate". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Silently averaging duplicate cells conceals a violated uniqueness contract.

pivot requires exactly one value per (row, column) cell and raises on duplicates. pivot_table aggregates duplicates with aggfunc, which changes the meaning of the table: a cell becomes a mean, sum or count over several records.
Pair a mean table with a count table (aggfunc='size') so readers can see how many records each cell summarizes. A mean of one record and a mean of a thousand look identical otherwise.
fill_value replaces empty cells, which have no records at all. Filling with 0 is right for counts and often misleading for means; document the choice, or leave such cells missing.
The transfer builds mean and count pivot tables from records with a duplicate cell.
Transfer walkthrough: Cell (a, x) averages 1 and 3 to 2 from two records; (b, y) has one record. Summing instead would report 4 for (a, x).
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [['a', 'x', 1], ['a', 'x', 2]]
frame = pd.DataFrame(data,columns=["row","column","value"])
try:
    frame.pivot(index="row",columns="column",values="value")
    result = "unique"
except ValueError:
    result = "duplicate"
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Reshape wide tables to long records
body: melt turns measured columns into variable/value rows while retaining identifier columns. State the identifier columns so they are not accidentally treated as measurements.
For input {'id': [1, 2], 'a': [3, 4], 'b': [5, 6]}, the worked computation produces 4. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Melting the identifier adds records with the wrong meaning.

melt turns a wide table, one column per measurement, into a long table with one row per (identifier, measurement) pair. id_vars lists the identifier columns to keep; var_name and value_name name the new columns.

Long form suits grouping, plotting and storing sparse measurements. pivot reverses it when each (identifier, variable) pair is unique. Checking that pivoting a melted table reproduces the original is a cheap test that no identifier was accidentally melted or lost.

After pivot, the column index carries a name (here 'metric'), and the identifier is in the index. reset_index and clearing columns.name restore the original layout for comparison. DataFrame.equals compares values, labels and dtypes.
The transfer melts a wide table, counts the long rows and confirms a lossless round trip.
Transfer walkthrough: Two rows with two measurements give four long rows, and pivoting back reproduces the table. Melting without id_vars turns id into a measurement and the pivot back fails.

lessons.title: MultiIndex keys identify hierarchical records
body: A MultiIndex represents compound labels. Select a complete key when the contract requests one record; selecting only one level returns a larger substructure.
For input [3, 7], the worked computation produces 7. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Swapping key components addresses a different record or fails.

A MultiIndex labels each row with a tuple such as (store, day). Selecting a complete key returns one value. s.xs('a', level='store') returns every row for store a, dropping that level, and s.xs(1, level='day') returns every store on day 1.
groupby(level='store') aggregates across the other levels, for example total sales per store over all days. Naming levels makes code readable and robust to level order.

Sort a MultiIndex with sort_index before slicing; many selections are faster and some partial slices require a sorted index. When a hierarchy gets complicated, plain columns plus groupby are often clearer.
The transfer selects by each level and aggregates by store.
Transfer walkthrough: Store a sold 10 and 7 on its two days; day 1 had sales of 10 and 5; store totals are 17 and 5. Grouping by day would total per day instead.

lessons.title: Rolling windows encode local history
body: A trailing rolling mean uses the current and preceding values. min_periods defines when there is enough history to emit a value; centered windows can leak future information.
For input [2, 4, 8], the worked computation produces [2, 3, 6]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A one-element window does not smooth over two observations.

rolling(2) uses the last two rows, whatever their timestamps. With irregular timestamps, a time-based window such as rolling('2D') uses all observations in the preceding two days, (t - 2 days, t], which is usually what 'recent history' means.

A rolling statistic at time t includes the value at t. Used as a feature to predict that same value, it leaks the target. shift(1) moves each statistic one step later, so the feature at t uses only earlier observations.

The first rows have no history; decide how to represent that (missing, a default or dropping the rows) and keep it consistent between training and serving. min_periods controls how much history is required before a value is emitted.
The transfer computes a time-based rolling sum and a past-only rolling mean feature on irregular timestamps.

Transfer walkthrough: The Jan 5 value has no neighbour within two days, so its time-window sum is just 4, while a two-row window would include Jan 2. Without the shift, the feature for each row would include that row's own value.

lessons.title: Resampling groups by time bins
body: Resample aggregates records into explicit time intervals. The bin frequency, timezone and boundary labels are part of the analytical contract.
For input [1, 2, 3, 4], the worked computation produces [3, 7]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An hourly frequency is not a daily aggregation.

resample('D') groups timestamps into calendar days. A calendar day depends on the time zone: 02:00 UTC on 1 January is still 31 December in New York. Daily totals computed in UTC and in local time can differ.

Store timestamps in UTC with an explicit zone, and convert with tz_convert to the zone whose days the business question uses, such as a store's local trading day. Naive timestamps without a zone leave that choice implicit and error-prone.

Bin edges and labels are part of the definition: resample bins are closed on the left and labelled by their start by default. Daylight-saving transitions make some local days 23 or 25 hours long. State the zone and binning in reports.
The transfer aggregates the same UTC events by UTC day and by New York day.

lessons.title: As-of joins need a time direction
body: merge_asof matches nearby ordered keys. A backward match uses only an observation at or before the query, while a forward match can select future information.
For input [2, 8], the worked computation produces [1, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Forward matching can leak future observations into historical features.

merge_asof matches each left row to the nearest right row by an ordered key, typically time. direction='backward' uses the latest right observation at or before the left time, which is the only choice that avoids using future information.

A backward match can be arbitrarily old. tolerance limits how stale a match may be; beyond it the result is missing. Without a tolerance, a trade could be joined to a price from hours earlier and look perfectly valid.
Both inputs must be sorted by the key, and the key dtypes must match. Use by= to match within groups such as ticker symbols. Report how many rows went unmatched instead of filling them silently.
The transfer matches trades to the latest quote no more than three time units earlier.
Transfer walkthrough: Trade 9's latest quote is at 5, four units earlier, which exceeds the tolerance. A larger tolerance would attach that stale price.
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [2, 8]
left = pd.DataFrame({"t":data})
right = pd.DataFrame({"t":[0,10],"x":[1,9]})
result = pd.merge_asof(left,right,on="t",direction="backward").x.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Version copy semantics explicitly
body: In pandas 2.3, enabling copy-on-write makes a derived Series write independent of its parent DataFrame. Pin this option rather than assuming behavior from another pandas release.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [1, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Disabling copy-on-write can let the view mutation update the parent.

Under Copy-on-Write, any DataFrame or Series derived from another behaves as an independent copy. Modifying a filtered subset never changes the parent; pandas copies lazily, only when one side is written.

This removes the old ambiguity of chained assignment, where frame[mask]['col'] = value sometimes worked and sometimes silently did nothing. To change the original frame, assign through it directly: frame.loc[mask, 'col'] = value.
Copy-on-Write is optional in pandas 2.3 and becomes the default in pandas 3.0. Pin the option in code that depends on it, and test that modifications land in the frame you intend.
The transfer modifies a filtered subset and the parent frame, and checks which changes are visible where.
Transfer walkthrough: The subset's change stays in the subset, and the parent's .loc assignment changes only the parent. Writing to the subset instead would leave the parent untouched.
lessons.code:
import json

import pandas as pd
data = [1, 2]
with pd.option_context("mode.copy_on_write",True):
    frame = pd.DataFrame({"x":data})
    view = frame["x"]
    view.iloc[0] = 99
    result = frame.x.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Sparse values retain an implicit fill
body: A sparse array stores entries different from its fill value. The fill value is part of the representation contract; sparse storage is beneficial only for suitable data distributions.
For input [0, 0, 2], the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A different implicit fill changes the number of stored entries.

A SparseArray stores only the entries that differ from its fill_value, plus their positions. For mostly-zero data with fill_value=0, that saves memory in proportion to the density, the fraction of stored entries.

The default fill value for floats is NaN, not 0. A float array of zeros with the default fill stores every zero explicitly and saves nothing. Choose the fill value to match the data's most common value.

Sparse storage helps only when density is low; many operations convert back to dense, which can use more memory than the original. to_dense() must reproduce the original values exactly, which is a simple correctness check.
The transfer compares stored-entry counts for zero and default fill values and verifies the dense round trip.
Transfer walkthrough: With fill 0 only the 5 is stored, density 0.25; with the default NaN fill all four values are stored. A fill of 5 would store the three zeros instead.

lessons.title: Combine chunk-level sufficient statistics
body: A total can be computed by summing chunk totals. Combining means requires weighting by chunk counts; simply averaging chunk means fails when sizes differ.
For input [[1, 3], [8]], the worked computation produces 4.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Averaging chunk means without counts biases the overall mean.

read_csv(..., chunksize=n) returns an iterator of DataFrames, so a file larger than memory can be processed piece by piece. Only statistics that can be combined across chunks give correct overall results.

Counts, sums and sums of squares combine by addition. From them, the mean is sum / count and the population variance is E[x²] - mean². Averaging per-chunk means is wrong when chunks have different sizes, which the last chunk usually does.

The sum-of-squares formula can lose precision when values are large relative to their spread. Welford's algorithm, or combining per-chunk means and variances with counts, is more stable; use it for production data. Compare against a full computation on a sample in tests.
The transfer streams a CSV in chunks, combines sufficient statistics and checks them against the full computation.
Transfer walkthrough: The five values sum to 20 with squares summing to 130, so the mean is 4 and the variance 26 - 16 = 10, matching pandas. Adding chunk means instead of sums gives a wrong total.

total = sum(sum(chunk) for chunk in data)
count = sum(len(chunk) for chunk in data)
result = total/count

import json
import pandas as pd
import io
data = [[1, 2, 3, 4, 10], 2]
stream = io.StringIO('value\n' + '\n'.join(str(v) for v in data[0]))
count = total = squares = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(stream, chunksize=data[1]):
    values = chunk['value']
    count += len(values)

lessons.title: Keep holdout records disjoint
body: A holdout set must contain records excluded from training. Fix random_state for reproducible examples, and choose a split policy that matches how predictions will be used.
For input 8, the worked computation produces 0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reusing training indices as test indices invalidates holdout evaluation.

A holdout set estimates performance on data the model never saw, so its records must be disjoint from training. train_test_split shuffles and splits indices or arrays; random_state makes the split reproducible.

With imbalanced classes, a purely random split can put few or no minority examples in a small test set, making metrics unstable or undefined. stratify=y keeps the class proportions in both parts as closely as the sizes allow.

Disjoint rows are not always enough. Duplicated records, several rows per customer or time ordering can still leak information; those need group-aware or time-aware splits, covered next. Record the split seed and sizes with every result.
The transfer makes a stratified split of an imbalanced label vector and checks sizes, minority count and overlap.

Transfer walkthrough: Sixteen labels with a 25% positive rate give a test set of four containing exactly one positive, and no shared indices. Without stratification, the number of positives in a small test set depends on chance.
lessons.code:

train,test = train_test_split(indices,test_size=0.25,random_state=7)
result = len(set(train)&set(test))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Validate using future observations
body: TimeSeriesSplit places validation observations after their training history. Shuffle-based splits can be inappropriate when future data would not exist at prediction time.
For input 9, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing chronological indices exposes later observations to earlier tests.
For time-ordered data, validation must come after training, as it will in production. TimeSeriesSplit produces expanding training windows, each followed by a later test window, and never shuffles.

Features computed from recent history, such as rolling means or lagged targets, can still connect the end of training to the start of the test window. gap=k drops k samples between them so that no test example's features overlap the training period.

Each fold's test window has the same size, n_samples // (n_splits + 1) by default. Report per-fold results, because performance often drifts over time, and the last fold is the most realistic estimate of the next period.
The transfer lists the last training index and the test window of each fold, with and without a gap.
Transfer walkthrough: With ten samples and two splits, test windows are 4–6 and 7–9; a gap of one ends training at 2 and 5 instead of 3 and 6.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
data = 9
splits = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=2).split(np.arange(data))
result = all(max(train)<min(test) for train,test in splits)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Separate related entities across folds
body: GroupKFold keeps records with the same group in one side of each split. Entity leakage can remain even when individual row indices are disjoint.
For input 4, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Checking row separation alone does not establish entity separation.

Several rows often belong to one entity: scans of the same patient, sessions of the same user, photos of the same object. If an entity appears in both training and test folds, the model can memorize it, and the score overstates performance on new entities.
GroupKFold assigns whole groups to folds, so no group is split. Plain KFold splits rows and can cut a group in half, especially when rows of a group are adjacent or shuffled.
Use the entity that will be new in production as the group: if the model will see new patients, group by patient. Combine with stratification (StratifiedGroupKFold) when classes are also imbalanced.
The transfer counts folds in which some group appears on both sides, for KFold and for GroupKFold.

Transfer walkthrough: KFold cuts patient p2 across the halves, so both folds leak; interleaved rows leak too. GroupKFold never splits a group. When groups happen to align with the KFold halves, neither leaks.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
data = 4
groups = np.repeat(np.arange(data),2)
splits = GroupKFold(n_splits=2).split(np.zeros((len(groups),1)),groups=groups)
result = all(set(groups[a]).isdisjoint(groups[b]) for a,b in splits)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Fit preprocessing on training data
body: Learn preprocessing statistics from training records only. Apply the fitted transformation to validation records without allowing those records to influence the fitted state.
For input [[0, 2], [100]], the worked computation produces [1.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Fitting on held-out values leaks their distribution into preprocessing.

fit learns statistics from data; transform applies them. A StandardScaler learns mean_ and scale_ during fit and then maps x to (x - mean_) / scale_. Fitting on training data only and transforming test data with those statistics mirrors deployment, where future data is unknown.

Fitting on all data before splitting leaks test information into training: the test set influenced the centring and scaling, so evaluation is optimistic. With small datasets or outliers in the test set, the effect can be large.

A feature with zero variance in training gets scale_ = 1, so transformed values are just centred differences. Test values can legitimately fall far outside the training range; standardized values beyond ±3 are a useful drift signal.
The transfer fits a scaler on training data and transforms a test point, comparing with a leaked fit.

Transfer walkthrough: The training mean 1 and scale 1 map the test value 100 to 99, which correctly flags it as far outside training. Fitting on all three values would shrink that signal and leak the test point.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
data = [[0, 2], [100]]
train,test = data
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(np.asarray(train).reshape(-1,1))
result = scaler.mean_.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Accuracy can hide minority failures
body: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions. A majority-class predictor can score highly on an imbalanced dataset while detecting none of the minority cases.
For input [0, 0, 0, 1], the worked computation produces 0.75. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Balanced accuracy and ordinary accuracy answer different questions.
Accuracy counts correct predictions over all examples. When 80% of labels are negative, predicting negative for everything scores 80% accuracy while never finding a positive.

Balanced accuracy averages recall over classes. The all-negative predictor gets recall 1 on negatives and 0 on positives, so its balanced accuracy is 0.5, the same as random guessing. Two models with identical accuracy can differ substantially in balanced accuracy.
Always compare a model with the majority-class baseline, and report per-class metrics for imbalanced problems. Choose the headline metric from the cost of each error type, not from habit.
The transfer compares a majority-class predictor and a model that finds some positives, using both metrics.
Transfer walkthrough: Both the baseline and the model have accuracy 0.8, but the model finds one of two positives, giving balanced accuracy (0.875 + 0.5) / 2 = 0.6875 against the baseline's 0.5.

lessons.title: Precision and recall use different denominators
body: Precision asks what fraction of predicted positives are correct. Recall asks what fraction of actual positives are found; choose zero-division handling explicitly.
For input [[1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0]], the worked computation produces [1.0, 0.5]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Swapping precision and recall reverses their interpretation.
Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are correct; recall is the fraction of actual positives that are found. F1 is their harmonic mean, which is low whenever either one is low.

F-beta weights recall beta times as much as precision. beta = 2 suits problems where missing a positive is worse than a false alarm, such as screening; beta = 0.5 suits problems where false alarms are costly.

With no predicted positives, precision is undefined; zero_division=0 records it as 0 instead of warning. Report precision and recall alongside any F score, because the same F1 can come from very different trade-offs.
The transfer computes precision, recall, F1 and F2 for a classifier that misses most positives.

Transfer walkthrough: One of two predicted positives is correct (precision 0.5) and one of three actual positives is found (recall 1/3). F1 is 0.4 and F2, which weights the weak recall more, is lower at about 0.357.

lessons.title: Regression metrics express error costs
body: MAE averages absolute errors, while MSE squares errors and therefore gives larger deviations more weight. Compare values only with their units and decision context.
For input [[0, 0], [1, 3]], the worked computation produces [2.0, 5.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Squared error is not interchangeable with absolute error.
Mean absolute error averages |y - ŷ|; mean squared error averages (y - ŷ)². Squaring makes large errors dominate, so MSE is far more sensitive to outliers than MAE.

The best constant prediction differs between them: the median minimizes MAE and the mean minimizes MSE. A dataset with one extreme value shows the gap clearly, and explains why a model trained on MSE chases outliers.

Pick the loss that matches the cost of errors in the application, report it in the target's units (RMSE or MAE) and compare models against a constant baseline. Never compare MSE values across differently scaled targets.
The transfer evaluates constant median and mean predictions under both losses on data with an outlier.

Transfer walkthrough: With the outlier, the median gives MAE 25 against 36.75 for the mean, while the mean gives MSE about 1801 against about 2378 for the median. Each loss prefers its own optimal constant.

lessons.title: AUC measures ranking across thresholds
body: ROC AUC measures how scores rank positive examples relative to negatives. Supply continuous scores and both classes; it does not choose a production threshold or prove calibration.
For input [[0, 0, 1, 1], [0.1, 0.2, 0.8, 0.9]], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing score order reverses the ranking quality.

ROC AUC equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive example receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one, counting ties as half. It measures ranking quality across all thresholds.

Because it depends only on the order of scores, any strictly increasing transformation, such as exp or a logistic squashing, leaves AUC unchanged. AUC therefore says nothing about whether scores are calibrated probabilities.

AUC is undefined when only one class is present, and a high AUC can coexist with poor performance at the operating threshold you actually use. Pair it with threshold-specific metrics and calibration checks.
The transfer computes AUC with scikit-learn, by counting correctly ordered pairs, and after a monotonic transformation.
Transfer walkthrough: Three of four positive/negative pairs are ordered correctly, so AUC is 0.75 by both methods and after exp. Counting ties as correct would turn the tied case's 0.5 into 1.

lessons.title: Thresholds implement decision policy
body: A probability threshold converts scores into actions. Choose it using validation data and the cost of errors, then evaluate the fixed policy on untouched test data.
For input [[0.2, 0.5, 0.8], 0.5], the worked computation produces [0, 1, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing >= to > changes decisions exactly at the threshold.
A classifier's scores become decisions only through a threshold. 0.5 is a convention, not an optimum. The right threshold depends on what false positives and false negatives cost in the application.

Given costs, compute the total cost at each candidate threshold on validation data and choose the cheapest. When missing a positive costs ten times a false alarm, the best threshold is usually much lower than 0.5.

Choose the threshold on validation data and then measure it once on test data; tuning on the test set makes the reported cost optimistic. scikit-learn's TunedThresholdClassifierCV automates the cross-validated version.
The transfer searches a small grid of thresholds for the lowest total cost under two cost settings.
Transfer walkthrough: With costly misses, threshold 0.3 catches both positives at the price of two false alarms, costing 2 against 11 at 0.5. With equal costs, 0.7 is cheapest.

import json
import numpy as np

data = [[0.2, 0.5, 0.8], 0.5]
scores,threshold = data
result = (np.asarray(scores)>=threshold).astype(int).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:
data is [labels, scores, cost_fp, cost_fn]. For thresholds 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9, compute total cost. Return [cheapest threshold (smallest on ties), its cost, the cost at 0.5].

Input [[0, 0, 1, 1, 0], [0.2, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8, 0.6], 1, 1] → [0.7, 1, 2]

exercises.solution:
import json
import numpy as np
data = [[0, 0, 1, 1, 0], [0.2, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8, 0.6], 1, 10]
labels, scores, cost_fp, cost_fn = data
labels, scores = np.asarray(labels), np.asarray(scores)
costs = {}
for t in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
    pred = scores >= t
    costs[t] = int(cost_fp * np.sum(pred & (labels == 0)) + cost_fn * np.sum(~pred & (labels == 1)))
best = min(costs, key=lambda t: (costs[t], t))
result = [best, costs[best], costs[0.5]]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Inspect the confusion matrix
body: With explicit binary label order, confusion-matrix rows are actual classes and columns are predicted classes. Read false positives and false negatives from their correct cells.
For input [[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1, 1]], the worked computation produces [[1, 1], [0, 2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Transposing the matrix interchanges the error types.

For binary labels ordered [0, 1], confusion_matrix rows are actual classes and columns predicted ones, so ravel() returns tn, fp, fn, tp. Passing labels= fixes that order even when one class is absent from a batch.
normalize='true' divides each row by its total, turning counts into per-class rates: the diagonal holds specificity and recall. A row with no examples has no rates; scikit-learn reports zeros there.

Reading the raw counts beside the rates prevents misinterpretation: a rate of 1.0 from two examples is weak evidence. Put labels in a fixed order in every report so that columns mean the same thing across runs.
The transfer unpacks the four counts and computes row-normalized rates.

Transfer walkthrough: One negative is correct and one is a false positive; two of three positives are found. Each row of rates sums to one. Reversing the label order would unpack the counts as tp, fn, fp, tn.

lessons.title: Compare with a simple baseline
body: A DummyClassifier exposes performance achievable without feature learning. Evaluate a candidate against an appropriate baseline before interpreting model complexity as progress.
For input [0, 0, 1], the worked computation produces [0, 0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Predicting the minority instead of the majority violates this baseline strategy.
A DummyClassifier predicts without using features: the most frequent class, a stratified random guess or a constant. Its cross-validated score is the bar any real model must clear.

Evaluate the baseline with exactly the same splits and metric as the model. A model scoring 0.9 accuracy is unimpressive if predicting the majority class also scores 0.9. A model that does not beat the baseline has learned nothing useful from its features.
Report the baseline next to every result. For regression, DummyRegressor(strategy='mean') gives an R² of about zero, which is the corresponding reference point.
The transfer cross-validates a majority baseline and a logistic regression on informative and uninformative features.

Transfer walkthrough: On the separable data, each stratified training fold holds two of one class and one of the other, so the majority baseline predicts the class that is the minority in its test fold and scores 1/3, while logistic regression scores 1.0. With alternating labels the feature carries no usable signal and the model only ties the baseline. A constant-1 baseline would score differently, which is why the baseline strategy must be stated.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
data = [0, 0, 1]
model = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(np.zeros((len(data),1)),data)
result = model.predict([[0],[0]]).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Standardize with fitted statistics
body: StandardScaler stores training means and scales. Its transform centers data using the fitted mean; centering can be disabled when sparse storage or a model contract requires it.
For input [1, 3], the worked computation produces [-1, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Disabling centering leaves an offset in these dense features.

StandardScaler centres each column on its training mean and divides by its training standard deviation. Models that use distances or gradient-based optimization, such as k-nearest neighbours, SVMs and regularized linear models, are sensitive to feature scale; tree models are not.

with_mean=False skips centring and only divides by the standard deviation. It is required for sparse input, where subtracting a mean would fill every zero, but it changes the transformed values, so it must be a deliberate choice.

A column with zero variance is left with scale 1, so it becomes all zeros after centring rather than dividing by zero. inverse_transform maps scaled values back to original units, which is how predictions or cluster centres are reported to people.
The transfer scales a matrix with a constant column and checks the inverse round trip.

Transfer walkthrough: Column one has mean 2 and standard deviation 1, giving -1 and 1; the constant column becomes zeros with scale 1. The inverse recovers the input. Skipping centring would only divide, leaving 1 and 3 unchanged.

lessons.title: Impute with a fitted policy
body: SimpleImputer learns a replacement from training observations. Median and mean are different policies, especially with outliers; missingness itself can also carry predictive information.
For input [1, 2, 100, None], the worked computation produces [1, 2, 100, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An outlier pulls the mean away from the median.
SimpleImputer learns a replacement value per column during fit, such as the median, and uses it during transform. The median is robust to outliers; the mean of [1, 2, 100] is pulled to about 34.

add_indicator=True appends a 0/1 column marking which values were missing, so a model can learn whether missingness itself is informative. By default the indicator is only added for columns that had missing values during fit.
Fit the imputer on training data only and apply it unchanged to new data, ideally inside a Pipeline so cross-validation refits it per fold. Inspect statistics_ to see the learned replacements.
The transfer imputes test values with training medians and shows when the missing-value indicator appears.

Transfer walkthrough: The training median 2 fills the missing test value and the indicator marks it. A training column without gaps gets no indicator. The mean would be pulled to about 34.3 by the outlier.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
data = [1, 2, 100, None]
a = np.array([np.nan if x is None else x for x in data]).reshape(-1,1)
result = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(a).ravel().tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

data is [train, test] value lists with None for missing. Fit SimpleImputer(strategy='median', add_indicator=True) on train. Return [learned median, transformed test rows].
Check all these cases:
Input [[1, 2, 100, None], [None, 5]] → [2.0, [[2.0, 1.0], [5.0, 0.0]]]
Input [[1, 3], [None]] → [2.0, [[2.0]]]
Input [[None, 4, 6, 8], [7]] → [6.0, [[7.0, 0.0]]]
exercises.starter:
import json

exercises.solution:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
data = [[1, 2, 100, None], [None, 5]]
def column(values):
    return np.array([np.nan if v is None else v for v in values], dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
train, test = (column(v) for v in data)
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='median', add_indicator=True).fit(train)
result = [float(imputer.statistics_[0]), imputer.transform(test).tolist()]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))
hints: The median ignores the outlier 100.
The indicator marks imputed positions with 1.
Without training gaps, no indicator column is added.
exercises.explanation: The training median 2 fills the missing test value and the indicator marks it. A training column without gaps gets no indicator. The mean would be pulled to about 34.3 by the outlier.

lessons.title: Define an unknown-category policy
body: OneHotEncoder learns categories from training values. With handle_unknown=ignore, a new category transforms to zeros rather than changing feature width or crashing inference.
For input 'a', the worked computation produces [[1, 0]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Rejecting unseen categories makes the documented inference request fail.
OneHotEncoder learns the categories seen during fit and creates one 0/1 column for each. get_feature_names_out reports names such as color_blue, which keep model inputs traceable.

A category that never appeared in training must be handled at prediction time. The default handle_unknown='error' raises ValueError, which is safe but can break a production service. handle_unknown='ignore' encodes it as all zeros, an explicit 'none of the known categories' representation.

Whichever policy you choose, monitor how often unknown categories occur: a rising rate signals drift. Rare categories can be grouped with min_frequency so the encoder does not create columns for one-off values.
The transfer encodes known and unknown colours under both policies.
Transfer walkthrough: Blue encodes as [1, 0] and the unseen green as all zeros, while the strict encoder rejects green. Without the ignore policy, the first encoder would raise too.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
data = 'a'
encoder = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore",sparse_output=False).fit([["a"],["b"]])
result = encoder.transform([[data]]).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:

exercises.solution:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
data = [['red', 'blue', 'red'], ['blue', 'green']]
encoder = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False).fit(np.array(data[0]).reshape(-1, 1))
strict = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False).fit(np.array(data[0]).reshape(-1, 1))
try:
    strict.transform(np.array(data[1]).reshape(-1, 1))
    strict_result = 'ok'
except ValueError:
    strict_result = 'unknown-rejected'
result = [encoder.get_feature_names_out(['color']).tolist(), encoder.transform(np.array(data[1]).reshape(-1, 1)).tolist(), strict_result]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

An ignored unknown becomes all zeros.
The default policy raises ValueError for unknowns.

lessons.title: Transform feature groups separately
body: ColumnTransformer applies different preprocessing to named groups of columns and combines their outputs. Declare the remainder policy to avoid silently dropping intended features.
For input [[1, 10], [3, 20]], the worked computation produces [2, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Dropping a required remainder column changes the output feature count.
Real tables mix numeric and categorical columns that need different preprocessing. ColumnTransformer applies each transformer to its own named columns and concatenates the outputs.
get_feature_names_out prefixes each output with its transformer's name, such as num__age and cat__city_a, so model coefficients and importances can be traced back to inputs.

Columns not listed are dropped by default (remainder='drop'); pass remainder='passthrough' only when unlisted columns are genuinely ready to use. Put the ColumnTransformer inside a Pipeline with the model so every step is fitted on training folds only.
The transfer scales a numeric column and one-hot encodes a categorical column from a DataFrame.
Transfer walkthrough: Ages 20 and 40 scale to -1 and 1, followed by one-hot city columns. Passing age through unscaled would leave 20 and 40 in the first column.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
data = [[1, 10], [3, 20]]
a = np.asarray(data,dtype=float)
transform = ColumnTransformer([("scale",StandardScaler(),[0])],remainder="passthrough")
result = list(transform.fit_transform(a).shape)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Fit preprocessing and model as one pipeline
body: A Pipeline refits preprocessing inside each training split and applies the same fitted transformation at prediction time. This prevents a common preprocessing leakage path.
For input [-2, 2], the worked computation produces [0, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Training with a constant target cannot learn the intended decision boundary.

A Pipeline chains preprocessing and a final estimator into one object. Fitting it fits each step in order on the same training data; predicting applies the fitted steps in order. Inside cross-validation, every fold refits the whole chain on that fold's training part, which prevents preprocessing leakage.

cross_val_score clones the estimator for each fold. The object you passed in is not fitted afterwards. Call fit separately to obtain the final model, typically on all training data once evaluation is done.
named_steps gives access to fitted steps, for example to read the learned scaler mean or the model coefficients. Step names default to the lower-cased class names when you use make_pipeline.
The transfer cross-validates a pipeline, then fits it and inspects the learned scaler mean and predictions at the extremes.

Transfer walkthrough: Two folds give two scores; the final fit learns the mean of all x values and predicts the classes at both extremes. Skipping the explicit fit leaves the scaler unfitted, so reading mean_ fails.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
data = [-2, 2]
x = np.array([[-3],[-2],[-1],[1],[2],[3]])
y = np.array([0,0,0,1,1,1])
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),LogisticRegression(random_state=7)).fit(x,y)
result = model.predict(np.asarray(data).reshape(-1,1)).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
data = [[-3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3], [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]]
x = np.asarray(data[0], dtype=float).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.asarray(data[1])
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(model, x, y, cv=2)
model.fit(x, y)
result = [len(scores), round(float(model.named_steps['standardscaler'].mean_[0]), 6), model.predict([[min(data[0])], [max(data[0])]]).tolist()]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Fit a linear relationship
body: LinearRegression minimizes squared residuals with an intercept by default. Check coefficient, residual and validation behavior rather than assuming a line is suitable for every dataset.
For input [0, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 7]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Disabling the intercept cannot represent this shifted line.

LinearRegression finds coefficients and an intercept minimizing squared error. coef_ is the change in prediction per unit change of each feature, and intercept_ is the prediction when all features are zero.
score returns R², the fraction of target variance explained relative to predicting the mean. R² of 1 is a perfect fit; 0 is no better than the mean; on new data it can be negative.

fit_intercept=False forces predictions through the origin. Only use it when theory demands a zero intercept; otherwise the slope absorbs the missing offset and the fit degrades. Evaluate R² on held-out data, not just the training set.
The transfer fits lines with and without an intercept and compares their training R².
Transfer walkthrough: y = 2x + 1 fits exactly with an intercept. Through the origin, the best slope is 2.6 and R² drops to 0.85. When the data truly passes through zero, both fits agree.

lessons.title: Regularization trades fit against coefficient size
body: Ridge adds an L2 penalty to the squared-error objective. With the same centered data, a larger positive alpha shrinks this coefficient toward zero.
For input [-2, -1, 1, 2], the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Comparing the coefficient in the opposite direction reverses the shrinkage claim.

Ridge regression minimizes squared error plus alpha times the sum of squared coefficients. Larger alpha shrinks coefficients toward zero, trading a little bias for lower variance and more stable estimates with correlated features.

For one centred feature, the ridge slope is Σxy / (Σx² + alpha): as alpha grows, the slope shrinks smoothly toward zero but never exactly reaches it. Tracing coefficients over a range of alphas, the regularization path, shows this monotone shrinkage.

The intercept is not penalized, so heavy regularization pulls predictions toward the mean of y rather than toward zero. Penalties depend on feature scale, so standardize features before comparing alphas or coefficients.
The transfer computes slopes for increasing alpha and checks shrinkage and the intercept.
Transfer walkthrough: For x = -2, -1, 1, 2, Σx² = 10, so the slopes are 20/10, 20/11, 20/20 and 20/1010, and the intercept stays at the mean of y, 5. Without the +5 offset the intercept would be 0.

b = Ridge(alpha=100).fit(x,y).coef_[0]
result = bool(abs(b)<abs(a))

lessons.title: L1 penalties can zero coefficients
body: Lasso uses an L1 penalty that can set coefficients exactly to zero. Scaling and alpha affect the solution; sparse coefficients alone do not establish causal relevance.
For input [0, 1, 2], the worked computation produces [0.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing regularization changes this intentionally zeroed coefficient.

Lasso penalizes the sum of absolute coefficients. Unlike the squared ridge penalty, the absolute value has a corner at zero, so for a sufficiently large alpha, coefficients of weakly useful features become exactly zero. This performs feature selection as part of fitting.

Ridge shrinks coefficients but leaves them non-zero, so every feature keeps some influence. With many irrelevant features, Lasso produces a sparse, interpretable model; with groups of correlated useful features, it tends to pick one arbitrarily, where Elastic Net is often steadier.
Lasso also shrinks the coefficients it keeps, so the surviving coefficient is slightly smaller than the true effect. Choose alpha by cross-validation (LassoCV) and standardize features first.
The transfer fits Lasso and Ridge to data where only one of three features matters.

Transfer walkthrough: For every seed, Lasso sets both irrelevant coefficients exactly to zero and keeps x0 at about 2.9, slightly below the true 3 because the penalty also shrinks it. Ridge leaves all three non-zero. A tiny alpha would keep every coefficient non-zero as well.

result = model.coef_.tolist()

lessons.title: Neighbors depend on representation
body: A nearest-neighbor classifier predicts from nearby training points under its chosen metric. Feature scaling, k and distance weighting are modeling choices.
For input [1, 9], the worked computation produces [0, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using the opposite training label changes the nearest-neighbor prediction.

k-nearest neighbours predicts from the closest training points under a distance metric. With Euclidean distance, a feature measured in tens of thousands, such as income, outweighs one measured in tens, such as age, regardless of which matters more.

Standardizing features puts them on comparable scales, so each contributes according to its spread rather than its units. The same query can then have a different nearest neighbour and a different predicted class.

k, the distance metric and the feature scaling are all modelling choices; tune them with cross-validation inside a pipeline. kNN stores the training set, so prediction cost and memory grow with data size.
The transfer classifies a query with and without standardization where the two disagree.

Transfer walkthrough: Unscaled, the query is 100 income units from the second point versus 900 from the first, so income decides. After standardization, the age difference outweighs the income difference and the first point is nearer.

lessons.title: Separate classes with a margin
body: A linear SVC learns a separating hyperplane using support-vector constraints and regularization. Kernel and C choices change the inductive bias and require validation.
For input [-2, 2], the worked computation produces [0, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Swapping labels reverses this learned classifier.

A linear support vector classifier finds the separating boundary with the widest margin. Only the points nearest the boundary, the support vectors, determine it; moving other points slightly does not change the model.

C controls the penalty for margin violations. Large C insists on classifying training points correctly, giving a narrow margin decided by a few support vectors. Small C allows violations, widening the margin and making many points support vectors.

decision_function returns the signed distance-like score; its sign is the predicted side. With separable one-dimensional data, the boundary lies midway between the closest points of each class. Scale features first, as with any distance-based method.
The transfer fits a hard-margin linear SVC and inspects its support vectors and decision signs near the boundary.

Transfer walkthrough: The closest points of each class, -1 and 2, are the only support vectors, so the boundary sits at 0.5: both -0.1 and 0.1 fall on the negative side. With symmetric data the boundary is at 0, and with -4 and 1 it is at -1.5. A tiny C makes every point a support vector.

import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
data = [-2, 2]
model = SVC(kernel="linear",C=1).fit([[-2],[-1],[1],[2]],[0,0,1,1])
result = model.predict(np.asarray(data).reshape(-1,1)).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Trees partition feature space
body: A decision tree recursively partitions observations using feature thresholds. Limit complexity and validate; a perfect training fit can still generalize poorly.
For input [0, 3], the worked computation produces [0, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A tree fitted to reversed labels learns a different target.

A decision tree splits the feature space with threshold rules until its leaves are pure or a limit is reached. With no limit, it can isolate every training point, including mislabelled ones, and reach perfect training accuracy.

Perfect training accuracy is not evidence of a good model. Leaves built around noisy points give wrong predictions in their neighbourhoods on new data. Limiting max_depth or min_samples_leaf forces the tree to capture broad structure instead.

get_depth reports how deep the fitted tree grew. Compare training and held-out scores: a large gap signals overfitting. Ensembles such as random forests and boosting reduce the variance of individual deep trees.
The transfer fits a deep tree and a stump to labels with two noisy points and compares their held-out accuracy.

Transfer walkthrough: The unlimited tree grows to depth 3 to isolate the two noisy labels at 3 and 4, reaching perfect training accuracy, but misclassifies 3.2 and 4.2 for a test accuracy of 0.5; the stump scores 0.75. On clean data both trees agree. Capping the deep tree at depth 1 turns it into the stump.

result = model.predict(np.asarray(data).reshape(-1,1)).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Bagged trees average unstable learners
body: A random forest combines trees trained with randomized samples and feature choices. Set random_state for this reproducible example and evaluate rather than assuming ensembling guarantees improvement.
For input [0, 3], the worked computation produces [0, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the target labels changes ensemble predictions.
A random forest trains many trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets and averages their predicted probabilities. Averaging reduces the variance of individual deep trees.

Each tree leaves out about a third of the rows. The out-of-bag (OOB) score evaluates every row using only trees that did not see it, giving a built-in validation estimate without a separate holdout when oob_score=True.

Randomness makes results depend on random_state. Fixing it makes runs reproducible: two forests with the same data and seed produce identical probabilities. Changing n_estimators changes the model, so record it with every result.
The transfer fits two identically seeded forests, inspects the tree count, predictions at both ends and the OOB score.

Transfer walkthrough: Identically seeded forests produce identical probabilities, there are 25 trees, the extremes are classified correctly and the OOB estimate is high on this separable data. Changing the tree count changes the model.

lessons.title: Boosting fits corrections sequentially
body: Gradient boosting adds learners that reduce the remaining loss. Learning rate and number/depth of learners jointly control capacity and must be selected using validation.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing training targets reverses the learned response.

Gradient boosting starts from a constant prediction and adds small trees one at a time, each fitted to the current residuals. The learning rate scales each tree's contribution, so many small steps approach the target gradually.

staged_predict yields the predictions after each stage, which shows how the training error falls as trees are added. On a step function with depth-one trees and learning rate 0.5, each stage halves the remaining residual, so the mean squared error falls by a factor of four per stage.

A lower learning rate needs more trees for the same fit but usually generalizes better; n_estimators and learning_rate must be tuned together, typically with early stopping on validation data. Watching only training error hides overfitting.
The transfer tracks staged training error for a boosted model on a step function.
Transfer walkthrough: After one stage the residual is 2.5, MSE 6.25; after three it is 0.625, MSE about 0.39. A learning rate of 0.1 shrinks the residual far more slowly.

lessons.title: Stratify classification folds
body: StratifiedKFold preserves class proportions as closely as possible in each fold. It addresses class balance, while group and time constraints still need their own split policies.
For input 4, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A test fold is not necessarily all one class.

KFold without shuffling takes consecutive blocks of rows. If the data is sorted by label, as exported tables often are, a test fold can contain only one class, and its accuracy or AUC is misleading or undefined.

StratifiedKFold assigns rows so that each fold's class proportions match the whole dataset as closely as possible. For classification, scikit-learn's cross_val_score uses stratified folds by default when given an integer cv.

Stratification balances labels, nothing more. Grouped or time-ordered data still needs GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold or TimeSeriesSplit. Shuffle with a fixed random_state when row order carries no meaning.
The transfer counts positives in each test fold for KFold and StratifiedKFold on sorted labels.

Transfer walkthrough: With six negatives then two positives, KFold puts both positives in the second fold, while stratification places one in each. Replacing the stratified splitter with KFold reproduces the imbalance.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
data = 4
y = np.array([0,1]*data)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=2,shuffle=True,random_state=7)
result = all(len(set(y[test]))==2 for _,test in cv.split(np.zeros((len(y),1)),y))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Search inside a pipeline
body: GridSearchCV evaluates candidate parameter settings using training folds. Double-underscore names address nested estimator parameters without fitting preprocessing on held-out folds.
For input 12, the worked computation produces 0.01. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reporting an unsearched parameter is not the chosen best candidate.

GridSearchCV evaluates each parameter combination with cross-validation and records the mean scores in cv_results_. rank_test_score orders candidates, with 1 for the best. Nested parameter names use step__parameter, such as logisticregression__C.
With refit=True (the default), the best combination is refitted on all the data passed to fit, available as best_estimator_. predict and score on the search object use that refitted model.

best_score_ is the cross-validated score of the winner, chosen because it was highest, so it is optimistic. Report performance on a separate test set or with nested cross-validation. Keep grids small and meaningful; huge grids also overfit the validation folds.
The transfer searches regularization strengths for a logistic regression and inspects the ranking.

Transfer walkthrough: Only a quarter of the labels are positive. With C = 0.001 the penalty flattens the slope so the model mostly predicts the majority class, ranking last; C = 1 ranks first and is refitted as best_estimator_. Dropping a candidate changes the ranking list itself.

lessons.title: Separate tuning from performance estimation
body: Nested CV evaluates the entire inner model-selection process using outer held-out folds. The inner best score is optimistically selected and is not a substitute for outer evaluation.
For input 18, the worked computation produces 3. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning only one inner score does not provide one estimate per outer fold.

Nested cross-validation puts a whole model-selection procedure, such as a GridSearchCV, inside an outer cross-validation loop. Each outer fold runs its own inner search on its training part and is then scored on its held-out part.

The outer score estimates how well the procedure, search included, generalizes. It is the honest number to report when hyperparameters were tuned. The inner best scores are biased upward by selection.

Different outer folds may select different hyperparameters. That variation is informative: it shows how stable the choice is. return_estimator=True keeps the fitted inner searches so you can inspect each choice.
The transfer runs a tree-depth search inside stratified outer folds and reports the per-fold choices and the outer mean.

Transfer walkthrough: The periodic target cannot be captured by a shallow tree on x, so each outer fold picks a different depth and the honest outer mean stays near chance. That instability is exactly what nested CV reveals and an inner best score would hide. Two outer folds would change both the count and the choices.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV,cross_val_score,StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
data = 18
x = np.arange(data).reshape(-1,1)
y = (x.ravel()>data/2).astype(int)
inner = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=7),{"max_depth":[1,2]},cv=2)
scores = cross_val_score(inner,x,y,cv=StratifiedKFold(3,shuffle=True,random_state=7))
result = len(scores)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Compare fit and validation as data grows
body: Learning curves evaluate performance at multiple training sizes. Inspect both training and validation behavior when diagnosing high variance, underfitting or data limitations.
For input 18, the worked computation produces [2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Collapsing all sizes into one value removes the curve dimension.

A learning curve plots training and validation scores as the training set grows. It separates two failure modes: high bias, where both scores are low and close, and high variance, where training is high but validation lags behind.

If validation keeps improving with more data, collecting data will help. If the curves have converged at a poor score, a more expressive model or better features are needed instead. An unconstrained decision tree typically shows perfect training scores at every size.

Shuffle with a fixed random_state when the data is ordered, otherwise early training subsets are unrepresentative. The returned arrays have one row per training size and one column per CV fold; average across columns.
The transfer computes learning curves for an unconstrained tree on a periodic target.

Transfer walkthrough: Each fold trains on two thirds of the data, so the sizes are half of that and all of it. The unconstrained tree scores 1.0 on its training data at both sizes, while validation is lower: a variance gap. Changing the fractions changes the absolute sizes.

lessons.title: Evaluate probability quality
body: Brier score averages squared probability errors for binary outcomes. It measures probability quality, which differs from threshold accuracy and ranking metrics.
For input [[0, 1], [0.2, 0.8]], the worked computation produces 0.04. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Thresholding scores first discards probability information.
Two models can make identical class decisions at a 0.5 threshold yet give very different probabilities. Accuracy cannot tell them apart; proper scoring rules such as the Brier score and log loss can.

The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome. Log loss is the mean negative log probability of the true outcome, and it punishes confident mistakes very heavily: predicting 0.01 for an event that happens costs about 4.6.

When probabilities feed decisions, such as expected cost, risk scores or ranking by likelihood, evaluate them with these metrics and inspect calibration curves. CalibratedClassifierCV can recalibrate a model's scores on validation data.
The transfer compares an overconfident and a hedged model that make the same decisions.

Transfer walkthrough: Both models predict [1, 0, 0, 1], so accuracy cannot separate them. The confident model's two 0.99-wrong answers give Brier 0.49 and log loss 2.31, while the hedged model scores 0.225 and 0.64. When the confident model is right, as in the other cases, it scores better.

lessons.title: Remove constant features within training
body: VarianceThreshold removes features whose fitted variance fails its threshold. Put data-dependent feature selection inside the validation pipeline to avoid leakage.
For input [[1, 0], [1, 2]], the worked computation produces [[0], [2]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Passing all original features ignores the selection contract.
VarianceThreshold removes features whose training variance does not exceed a threshold. The default of 0 drops only constant columns, which carry no information for any model.

For a binary feature that is 1 with frequency p, the variance is p(1 - p). A threshold of 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16 removes features where one value occurs in more than 80% of rows, a common way to drop near-constant indicator columns.
The selector is fitted, so put it inside a Pipeline to compute variances on training folds only. get_support shows which columns survived, and variances_ records the values the decision was based on.
The transfer applies an 80% threshold to binary features and reports kept columns and variances.

Transfer walkthrough: The constant column has variance 0 and the 5-of-6 column 0.139, both at or below 0.16, so only the balanced column is kept. A zero threshold would keep the near-constant column too.

lessons.title: PCA projects onto learned directions
body: PCA learns orthogonal directions of variance from training data. Choose components using validation and domain goals; explained variance is not prediction performance.
For input [[1, 2], [2, 3], [4, 1]], the worked computation produces [3, 1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Retaining both coordinates violates a one-component output contract.
PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance in centred data. explained_variance_ratio_ gives the fraction of total variance captured by each component, in decreasing order.
Passing a float such as n_components=0.95 keeps the smallest number of components that together explain at least 95% of the variance. That turns an arbitrary choice into a stated criterion.

inverse_transform maps the reduced representation back to the original space; the mean squared difference from the input is the information lost. PCA is sensitive to feature scale, so standardize first when features have different units, and fit it on training data only.
The transfer fits PCA to nearly collinear points, chooses components by variance and measures reconstruction error.

Transfer walkthrough: The nearly collinear points put 99.9% of the variance on one component, so one component is kept with a tiny reconstruction error. Symmetric points need both components. Asking for 99.99% would keep both and reconstruct exactly.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
data = [[1, 1], [2, 2.1], [3, 2.9], [4, 4]]

lessons.title: Cluster labels have no intrinsic class meaning
body: KMeans cluster numbers are arbitrary identifiers. Evaluate co-membership or an appropriate clustering metric instead of comparing numeric labels as if they were supervised classes.
For input [0, 0.1, 10, 10.1], the worked computation produces [true, false]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Treating separated points as the same cluster changes the partition.

Cluster numbers are arbitrary names. KMeans may call the same group 0 in one run and 1 in another, so comparing labels directly with reference classes, as in accuracy, can report 0% for a perfect clustering.

adjusted_rand_score compares two partitions by asking which pairs of points are grouped together. It is invariant to renaming clusters: 1.0 means identical partitions, about 0 means chance agreement and negative values mean worse than chance.

Without reference labels, use internal measures such as the silhouette score, and check stability across seeds. Fix random_state and n_init for reproducibility, and remember that KMeans assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size.
The transfer clusters one-dimensional points and evaluates the result with ARI and with permutation-aware accuracy.

Transfer walkthrough: KMeans recovers the two groups perfectly; ARI is 1 whichever way the clusters are named, and best-naming accuracy is 1. When the reference labels cut across the natural groups, ARI is negative. Comparing with a constant labelling instead gives 0.

lessons.title: Density clustering can reject noise
body: DBSCAN groups dense neighborhoods and labels unassigned observations as -1. eps depends on feature scale, and the number of discovered clusters is not fixed in advance.
For input [0, 0.1, 10], the worked computation produces [0, 0, -1]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An overly large radius joins isolated noise with the dense group.

DBSCAN groups points that have at least min_samples neighbours within distance eps, called core points, plus points reachable from them. Points in no dense region are labelled -1, noise. The number of clusters is not fixed in advance.

eps is a distance in the units of the features. The same eps can merge everything on one scale and isolate every point on another. Standardizing features first makes eps comparable across features, but it still has to be tuned for the data.
core_sample_indices_ lists the core points; border points belong to a cluster without being core. A k-distance plot (distance to the k-th neighbour, sorted) is a common way to pick eps.
The transfer clusters the same points before and after standardization with a fixed eps.

Transfer walkthrough: Raw points 0 and 0.3, and 5 and 5.2, are within 0.5 of each other, forming two clusters with 20 as noise. For 0, 3, 6, 100, raw spacing exceeds eps so everything is noise, but after standardization the first three are close and form a cluster. A larger raw eps merges the first two groups.

lessons.title: Separate novelty from training anomalies
body: An anomaly detector assigns unusualness according to its learned distribution. Keep the scoring convention explicit; a negative decision function marks outliers for this IsolationForest.
For input 100, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing the sign condition interchanges outlier and inlier decisions.

Outlier detection looks for unusual points within the training data itself; novelty detection trains on clean data and asks whether new observations differ from it. The two tasks need different usage.

LocalOutlierFactor compares each point's local density with its neighbours'. With novelty=False (the default), it only labels the training set via fit_predict. With novelty=True, it exposes predict, decision_function and score_samples for new data, returning 1 for inliers and -1 for novelties.

Calling predict on a model fitted with novelty=False is an error, which prevents silently scoring new data with the wrong procedure. Scale features first, and validate thresholds on held-out normal and abnormal examples where available.
The transfer fits on evenly spaced normal points and classifies new queries inside and outside that range.
Transfer walkthrough: 0.5 sits inside the training range and is an inlier; 5 and -3 are far outside. With novelty=False the model cannot score new points at all.
lessons.code:

result = bool(model.decision_function([[data]])[0]<0)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Interpret models using held-out perturbations
body: Permutation importance measures score changes after shuffling a feature. Correlated features and the evaluation distribution affect interpretation; importance is neither intrinsic nor causal.
For input 12, the worked computation produces 0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ranking the constant feature first contradicts this fitted model sensitivity.
Permutation importance shuffles one feature's values and measures how much the model's score drops. A large drop means the model relies on that feature; no drop means it does not.
Compute it on held-out data. On training data, an overfitted model can appear to rely on features that do not help it generalize. n_repeats averages several shuffles and gives a spread to report.
Correlated features share importance: shuffling one leaves the other to carry the signal, so both can look unimportant. Importance describes the model, not causal effects in the world.
The transfer fits a linear model where only one feature matters and measures importance on a held-out split.

Transfer walkthrough: Shuffling the signal destroys the R² on held-out rows, so its importance is large; shuffling the noise changes almost nothing. If the target depended on the noise column instead, the ranking would flip.
lessons.code:
import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
data = 12
x = np.column_stack([np.arange(data),np.zeros(data)])
y = x[:,0]*2
model = LinearRegression().fit(x,y)
importance = permutation_importance(model,x,y,n_repeats=3,random_state=7)
result = int(np.argmax(importance.importances_mean))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Tensor dimensions are model contracts
body: A tensor shape records each axis length. Establish batch and feature meanings before choosing a layer, broadcast or loss; equal element counts do not imply interchangeable semantics.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [2, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Flattening erases the original axis contract.
Models expect a leading batch axis. A single image with shape (channels, height, width) becomes a batch of one with unsqueeze(0), shape (1, C, H, W). squeeze(0) removes a length-one axis again.

Flattening for a fully connected layer must keep the batch axis: x.flatten(start_dim=1) turns (N, C, H, W) into (N, C·H·W). flatten() with no arguments collapses everything into one long vector and mixes samples together, a bug that can still run if the sizes happen to line up later.
Write expected shapes in comments or assertions at each stage of a model. Shape mistakes are the most common deep-learning bug, and they are cheap to catch before training starts.
The transfer adds a batch axis, flattens per sample and removes the batch axis again.
Transfer walkthrough: A (3, 4, 4) image becomes a batch of one and flattens to (1, 48). Flattening everything would lose the batch axis and give (48,).
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
a = torch.tensor(data)
result = list(a.shape)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Choose floating tensors for fractional computation
body: An explicit floating dtype retains fractional inputs. Integer tensors cannot represent fractional model features and cannot require ordinary floating gradients.
For input [1.5, 2.5], the worked computation produces [1.5, 2.5]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Integer construction truncates fractional values.

torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]) is int64. Adding a Python float promotes the result to the default float dtype, float32. True division with / always produces a float result, even between integers; floor division // keeps integers.

Promotion follows categories: an integer tensor combined with a floating value becomes floating. A zero-dimensional tensor or Python scalar does not raise a tensor's precision within the same category, so a float32 tensor plus a 0-dim float64 tensor stays float32.
Explicit dtypes avoid surprises: create features as float32, targets for classification as int64, and check dtypes at model boundaries. Integer tensors cannot require gradients.
The transfer inspects promoted dtypes for several operations on an integer tensor.

Transfer walkthrough: The integers are int64; adding 0.5 or dividing with / gives float32, while // keeps integers and floors toward negative infinity, so -3 // 2 is -2. The 0-dim float64 tensor does not upgrade the float32 tensor. True division in place of // would return fractional values.

torch.set_num_threads(1)

result = torch.tensor(data,dtype=torch.float32).tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Broadcast tensor features deliberately
body: Tensor broadcasting aligns trailing axes. Verify both input shapes and the resulting shape; a valid broadcast can still express the wrong model operation.
For input [[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [10, 20]], the worked computation produces [[11, 22], [13, 24]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A scalar offset is not a per-feature row vector.

Broadcasting stretches length-one axes. That is convenient, and dangerous when shapes are slightly wrong: predictions of shape (N, 1) minus targets of shape (N,) broadcast to an (N, N) matrix of every pairwise difference.

The resulting mean squared error is a valid number with the wrong meaning, so training runs and quietly learns the wrong objective. Many loss functions warn about mismatched shapes; hand-written losses do not.
Squeeze or reshape so both sides have the same shape before combining them, and assert shapes inside loss functions. Checking the shape of an intermediate result is the fastest way to find the bug.
The transfer computes a loss with and without the shape fix and reports the broadcast shape.

Transfer walkthrough: Two predictions and two targets give a 2 × 2 difference matrix with mean squared value 1.5, while the matched loss is 0.5. Perfect predictions still show a non-zero broadcast loss.

lessons.title: Tensor views can share storage
body: A slice normally shares tensor storage with its parent. clone creates an independent copy; detach changes gradient tracking while still sharing storage unless cloned.
For input [1, 2, 3], the worked computation produces [1, 0, 0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Cloning the slice prevents mutation from updating the parent.
Slicing, transposing and view create tensors that share storage with their source. Writing through any of them changes the others. clone() creates independent storage.

view requires a memory layout compatible with the new shape and raises RuntimeError otherwise, for example on a transposed tensor. reshape returns a view when possible and silently copies when not, so whether it shares memory depends on the input.

In-place operations, whose names end with an underscore such as add_ and fill_, modify shared storage directly. When an independent snapshot is needed, as for a saved target or a logged value, clone it first.
The transfer contrasts view and reshape on a transposed tensor and shows aliasing through in-place operations.

Transfer walkthrough: view fails on the transposed tensor, while reshape copies it. The clone is independent, but adding 1 through the row view changes a. Without clone, the fill would also overwrite a's first row.
