lessons.title: Autograd accumulates derivatives on leaves
body: With requires_grad, PyTorch records differentiable operations and backward propagates derivatives. A leaf tensor receives its gradient; the computed value is not itself the gradient.
For input 3, the worked computation produces 6.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: The derivative of x squared is twice x, not x.
Tensors created by you with requires_grad=True are leaves. Operations on them build a graph, and backward() computes gradients of a scalar with respect to the leaves, storing them in .grad.

Intermediate (non-leaf) tensors do not keep .grad by default, to save memory; their .grad is None after backward. Call retain_grad() on an intermediate before backward when you need to inspect it, for example while debugging vanishing gradients.
backward needs a scalar output, so reduce with sum or mean first. Check gradients against a hand-derived formula on small inputs: for loss = Σ 3x², the gradient is 6x.
The transfer computes gradients for a vector input and inspects an intermediate's gradient.

lessons.title: Backward adds to existing gradients
body: Repeated backward calls add contributions to a leaf gradient. Clear gradients at the intended optimizer-step boundary; otherwise earlier batches remain in the accumulation.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 7.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Zeroing between contributions changes an intentional accumulated sum.
backward adds new gradients to whatever is already in .grad. PyTorch does this deliberately so gradients can be accumulated across several backward calls.

In an ordinary training loop, that means each step must clear gradients with optimizer.zero_grad() before backward. Forgetting it makes every update use the sum of all past gradients, so steps grow and training diverges or oscillates.

The bug is invisible for the first step, which starts from empty gradients, and only appears from the second step on. Tests should therefore run at least two steps and compare with the expected trajectory.
The transfer runs a few SGD steps on (x - 3)² with and without clearing gradients.

Transfer walkthrough: With clearing, each step uses only the current gradient; without it, the second update adds the stale first gradient and moves to 1.68 instead of 1.08, and after three steps the drift reaches 3.024 against 1.464. The first step is identical either way, hiding the bug.

import json
import torch
data = 1
def run(clear):
    x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.0))

lessons.title: Detach cuts the differentiation graph
body: detach returns a tensor without the prior autograd history. Use it for explicitly nondifferentiable boundaries; converting data to detach can unintentionally block intended learning.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 4.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Leaving the branch attached adds its derivative to the gradient.
detach() returns a tensor with the same values but no connection to the computation graph. Gradients do not flow through it, so it acts as a constant during backward.

This is how fixed targets work: in bootstrapped value learning or self-distillation, the target is computed from the model but treated as constant, so the model moves its prediction toward the target instead of also moving the target toward the prediction.

Detaching changes the gradient, not the forward value. Compare gradients with and without detach on a small example to confirm that the intended path is cut. Detached tensors still share storage; clone if you will modify them.
The transfer computes the gradient of a squared error with a detached and a live target that both depend on the same parameter.
Transfer walkthrough: At w = 2 the difference is 1. Through the prediction alone the gradient is 2·1·2 = 4; letting the target move too gives 2·1·1 = 2.

lessons.title: Register trainable parameters on modules
body: nn.Parameter assigned as a module attribute is discovered by parameters and state_dict. A plain tensor attribute is not automatically an optimizable registered parameter.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An unregistered tensor is absent from the module parameter inventory.

A module tracks three kinds of state. nn.Parameter attributes are trainable and appear in parameters(). Buffers registered with register_buffer are saved in state_dict and moved with the module but not trained, like BatchNorm's running statistics. Plain tensor attributes are neither saved nor moved.

Submodules must also be registered. Modules held in nn.ModuleList or nn.ModuleDict are found; modules held in an ordinary Python list are invisible to parameters(), state_dict() and .to(device), so their weights are never trained or saved.

Check registration by listing state_dict keys and counting parameters. That catches the plain-list bug, which otherwise shows up only as a model that does not learn or a checkpoint that does not restore.
The transfer builds a module with each kind of attribute and lists what is saved and trained.

Transfer walkthrough: state_dict holds the parameter, the buffer and the ModuleList layer's weight and bias, but not the plain tensor or the plain-list layer. A plain list in place of the ModuleList would drop that layer too.

import json
import torch
data = 3
class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.ones(data))
        self.register_buffer('scale', torch.ones(1))

lessons.title: Cross entropy expects logits
body: CrossEntropyLoss applies the stable log-softmax calculation internally. Supply raw class logits and integer target indices rather than applying softmax first.
For input [2.0, 0.0], the worked computation produces 0.126928011. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Softmaxing twice changes the optimized loss.
F.cross_entropy applies log_softmax internally and then the negative log likelihood of the target class. Its input must be raw logits, one row per example, with integer class targets.

Passing probabilities, softmax already applied, makes the loss apply softmax twice. Probabilities lie in [0, 1], so the second softmax is nearly uniform: the loss stays high, gradients become small and the model learns slowly or not at all.

Verify a loss with a manual computation on a tiny batch: -log_softmax(logits)[target], averaged. If a model's predicted probabilities are needed, compute softmax separately for reporting, not for the loss.
The transfer compares the correct loss, a double-softmax loss and a manual computation.

Transfer walkthrough: Logits [2, 0] give loss 0.127, matching the manual log_softmax. Feeding the probabilities [0.88, 0.12] through softmax again flattens them, so the loss rises to 0.383 even though the prediction is confident and correct. A very confident logit vector suffers most.

lessons.title: An optimizer applies a parameter update
body: After backward, an SGD step subtracts learning rate times the accumulated gradient. zero_grad controls the next accumulation cycle; step does not infer the loss by itself.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 1.6. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An ascent update moves the parameter in the opposite direction.

optimizer.step() reads each parameter's .grad and applies the update rule. For plain SGD, x ← x - lr · grad. With weight_decay = λ, PyTorch's SGD adds λx to the gradient first, which shrinks weights toward zero, equivalent to an L2 penalty of (λ/2)x².

Reproducing one update by hand is a strong check that you understand an optimizer's settings. Momentum, Nesterov and decoupled weight decay (AdamW) each change the rule; read the documented algorithm rather than assuming.
step changes parameters in place and does not clear gradients. The order zero_grad, forward, backward, step is the standard loop.
The transfer applies one SGD step to x² with and without weight decay and compares with a manual calculation.
Transfer walkthrough: Without decay, x = 2 moves to 1.6; with decay 0.5 the effective gradient is 5 and x moves to 1.5, matching the manual rule. Ignoring the decay setting breaks the second case.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 2
x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(data)))
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=0.1)
(x*x).backward()
optimizer.step()
result = float(x.detach())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: DataLoader batches dataset records
body: A DataLoader combines dataset samples into batches. drop_last discards an incomplete final batch; keep it false when every record must contribute to this evaluation.
For input 5, the worked computation produces [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Discarding the final partial batch loses observations.

A DataLoader groups dataset samples into batches. With shuffle=True it draws a new order each epoch; passing a torch.Generator seeded with a fixed value makes that order reproducible, independent of other random code.

Within an epoch, every sample appears exactly once. drop_last=True discards a final batch smaller than batch_size, which keeps batch statistics uniform but skips data each epoch; with few samples it can skip most of them.
num_workers > 0 loads batches in separate processes that need their own seeding and cleanup. Start with num_workers=0 for correctness, then measure before adding workers.
The transfer checks reproducible shuffling, sample coverage and the batch counts with and without drop_last.

Transfer walkthrough: The same seed gives the same order and all five samples appear; dropping the short last batch leaves two batches instead of three. With batch_size larger than the dataset, drop_last leaves no batches at all.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 5
dataset = torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(torch.arange(data))
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset,batch_size=2,drop_last=False,num_workers=0)
result = [batch[0].tolist() for batch in loader]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import torch
data = [5, 2]
n, batch = data
dataset = torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(torch.arange(n))
def epoch(seed, drop):

lessons.title: Reset gradients at the step boundary
body: zero_grad(set_to_none=True) removes previous gradient buffers. Accumulate intentionally within a step and reset before the next independent step.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 3.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Skipping the reset carries the previous derivative into the next step.
When a batch is too large for memory, split it into microbatches, call backward on each and step once. Because backward adds gradients, the step then uses their sum.

Divide each microbatch loss by the number of microbatches per step so that the summed gradient equals the gradient of the average loss. Call zero_grad after each step, not after each backward, or the accumulation is lost.

Leftover microbatches at the end of an epoch leave gradients in .grad without a step. Either step on them or clear them, and make the choice explicit. zero_grad(set_to_none=True) frees the memory and makes stale use visible as None.
The transfer accumulates gradients across microbatches and checks the step count, the result and the leftover state.

Transfer walkthrough: Targets 1 and 3 give scaled gradients -1 and -3, one step of size 0.4. With one target per step the updates follow ordinary SGD. The leftover third target in the last case leaves .grad set. Without clearing, later steps would reuse old gradients.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 2
x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(data)))
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=0.1)
(x*x).backward()
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
(x*3).backward()
result = float(x.grad)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.prompt:
data is [targets, microbatches_per_step]. Starting at x = 0, backpropagate (x - target)² / every for each target and step SGD (lr 0.1) after every `every` targets, then clear with set_to_none. Return [steps taken, x rounded to 4 places, whether .grad is None at the end].
Check all these cases:
Input [[1, 3], 2] → [1, 0.4, true]
Input [[2, 2, 2], 1] → [3, 0.976, true]
Input [[1, 3, 5], 2] → [1, 0.4, false]

exercises.solution:
import json
import torch
data = [[1, 3], 2]
x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.0))
opt = torch.optim.SGD([x], lr=0.1)
targets, every = data
steps = 0
for i, target in enumerate(targets, 1):
    ((x - target) ** 2 / every).backward()
    if i % every == 0:
        opt.step()
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        steps += 1
result = [steps, round(float(x.detach()), 4), x.grad is None]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Evaluation mode changes module behavior
body: eval switches modules such as Dropout and BatchNorm to evaluation behavior. It does not disable gradient recording; use a separate grad-mode context for inference.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [1, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Leaving dropout in training mode changes this deterministic evaluation.

In training mode, Dropout zeroes each element with probability p and multiplies the survivors by 1/(1 - p). This 'inverted' scaling keeps the expected value of each activation unchanged, so no adjustment is needed at evaluation time.

In evaluation mode, set with model.eval(), Dropout passes its input through unchanged. Forgetting eval() before validation or inference leaves random zeroing on, producing noisy, worse and non-reproducible predictions.
eval() and train() switch the mode of every submodule, including BatchNorm. They do not affect gradient tracking; that is torch.no_grad's job.
The transfer measures the survivor scale and mean of dropout in training mode and its output in evaluation mode.

Transfer walkthrough: With p = 0.5 survivors become 2 and the mean stays about 1; in eval mode the ones pass through unchanged. Leaving the layer in training mode would still zero and rescale inputs at evaluation time.

lessons.title: Disable gradient recording explicitly
body: no_grad prevents recording operations performed inside its scope. It is separate from eval, which changes layer behavior but can still produce differentiable outputs.
For input 2, the worked computation produces false. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An enabled grad context retains a graph when inference should not.

model.eval() changes layer behaviour, such as dropout and batch normalization, but operations still record gradients. Outputs of a model in eval mode still have requires_grad=True if its parameters do.

torch.no_grad() stops recording operations, saving memory and time during validation. torch.inference_mode() goes further: tensors created inside are marked as inference tensors and cannot later be used in autograd, which enables extra optimizations.

Use eval() together with no_grad or inference_mode for evaluation. Use inference_mode only when the outputs will never be needed for backward; no_grad is the safer default for code that may later mix with training.
The transfer evaluates one model under each setting and inspects the outputs' gradient flags.
Transfer walkthrough: Only the context managers stop gradient recording; eval alone leaves requires_grad True. inference_mode additionally marks its output as an inference tensor.

lessons.title: Seed the relevant random generators
body: manual_seed sets PyTorch random-generator state. Reproducibility also depends on data order, kernels, devices, package versions and other random libraries.
For input 7, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Drawing twice without reseeding advances the sequence.

torch.manual_seed sets the global generator. Any code that draws random numbers in between, such as a data augmentation, dropout layer or library call, consumes from the same stream and changes every later draw.

A torch.Generator object owns its own state. Passing generator=g to random functions and DataLoaders isolates that stream: its results depend only on its own seed and draws, not on unrelated code elsewhere.

Full reproducibility also needs fixed data order, deterministic algorithms where available (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms), the same library versions and hardware. Record seeds, and test that a rerun reproduces the same results.
The transfer shows a global draw shifted by unrelated consumption and a local generator unaffected by it.

Transfer walkthrough: The unrelated draws shift the global sequence, so the later pair differs, while a dedicated generator with the same seed reproduces the original pair. Removing the unrelated draws makes the global pair match again.

lessons.title: Restore model state explicitly
body: state_dict contains registered parameters and buffers. Save a state snapshot and load it into a compatible model; a Python object alias is not an immutable checkpoint.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 2.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: An in-memory state dictionary without cloned values can track later mutations.

model.state_dict() returns a dictionary of references to the live parameter and buffer tensors, not copies. If training continues, the dictionary's tensors change too, so a 'snapshot' kept in memory is not a snapshot at all.

torch.save serializes the values at the moment it is called. A checkpoint written to a file or buffer is therefore fixed, while an in-memory state_dict must be deep-copied (clone each tensor) to preserve a moment in training.

Load checkpoints with torch.load(..., weights_only=True) when they contain only tensors and plain containers; it refuses arbitrary pickled objects. Save the optimizer and scheduler state as well when training must resume.
The transfer keeps an in-memory state_dict and a serialized one, then updates the model and compares.
Transfer walkthrough: The in-memory alias shows the updated weight 3, while the serialized checkpoint keeps 2. Saving after the update would capture 3 instead.

with torch.no_grad():
    model.weight.add_(1)
model.load_state_dict(state)
result = float(model.weight.detach().item())

lessons.title: Resume optimizer state as well as weights
body: Stateful optimizers retain moments or momentum buffers beyond model parameters. A resumable checkpoint must include optimizer state and the training position.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 1. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A new optimizer without restored state has no momentum history.

Optimizers such as SGD with momentum and Adam keep internal state, like momentum buffers and running averages, separate from the model weights. A run resumed with fresh optimizer state takes different steps than an uninterrupted run.

Save optimizer.state_dict() with the model in each checkpoint and load it into an optimizer constructed with the same parameters and hyperparameters. Then an interrupted and resumed run follows the same trajectory as one that never stopped.

Test resumption directly: train k steps straight through, and separately train with a save/restore in the middle, then compare the final parameters. The same applies to schedulers, random states and data-loader position.
The transfer compares a continuous run with one that rebuilds its momentum optimizer midway, with and without restored state.

Transfer walkthrough: Restoring the momentum buffer makes the resumed run end at exactly the same point as the uninterrupted one, 0.124 from a start of 2. A fresh optimizer forgets the accumulated velocity and ends far away, at 0.736.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 2
x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(data)))
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=0.1,momentum=0.9)
(x*x).backward()
optimizer.step()
state = optimizer.state_dict()
other = torch.optim.SGD([x],lr=0.1,momentum=0.9)
other.load_state_dict(state)
result = len(other.state)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import torch
data = 2
def train(steps, resume_at=None):
    x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(float(data)))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD([x], lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
    for i in range(steps):
        if i == resume_at:
            state = opt.state_dict()
            opt = torch.optim.SGD([x], lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
            opt.load_state_dict(state)
        opt.zero_grad()
        (x * x).backward()
        opt.step()
    return round(float(x.detach()), 5)
result = [train(3), train(3, resume_at=2)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Clip gradients before the update
body: clip_grad_norm_ rescales gradients whose combined norm exceeds a threshold. It modifies gradients, not parameter values, and must occur before optimizer.step.
For input 2, the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Skipping clipping leaves this intentionally large gradient unchanged.

clip_grad_norm_(parameters, max_norm) computes the total norm of all the given gradients together, as if they were one long vector. If it exceeds max_norm, every gradient is scaled by the same factor, preserving the overall direction.
It returns the norm before clipping, which is worth logging: frequent clipping or exploding norms are early signs of instability. Clipping happens after backward and before the optimizer step.
Clipping each parameter separately is a different operation: it changes the relative size of different parameters' updates. Pass all model parameters in one call to get the documented behaviour.
The transfer clips gradients spread over two parameters and checks the total norm and the scaled values.
Transfer walkthrough: The combined gradient [3, 0, 4] has norm 5 and is scaled to [0.6, 0, 0.8]. A norm already below 1 is left alone. Clipping only a would leave b's gradient at 4.

lessons.title: Scale accumulated microbatch losses
body: To match the mean loss over equal-sized microbatches, divide each microbatch contribution by their count. Unequal batch sizes require weighting by observation count instead.
For input 0, the worked computation produces -4.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Adding unscaled batch losses multiplies the effective gradient.

Accumulating gradients over microbatches reproduces the full-batch gradient only if each microbatch's loss is weighted correctly. The full-batch mean loss is the sum of per-sample losses divided by the total sample count.

Averaging per-microbatch means and dividing by the number of microbatches weights every microbatch equally. When microbatches have different sizes, typically the last one, samples in the small microbatch count more than they should.
Sum the per-sample losses in each microbatch and divide by the total number of samples in the step. Verify by comparing the accumulated gradient with a single backward over the concatenated batch.
The transfer compares accumulated and full-batch gradients for uneven microbatches.
Transfer walkthrough: Targets 1, 3 and 5 have mean 3, so both gradients are -6. Averaging microbatch means would give (-4 - 10) / 2 = -7, over-weighting the single-sample microbatch.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 0
x = torch.tensor(float(data),requires_grad=True)
for target in [1.0,3.0]:
    ((x-target)**2/2).backward()
result = float(x.grad)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Track the schedule alongside optimizer state
body: A learning-rate scheduler changes optimizer settings over steps. Record its state and step timing when resuming; scheduler stepping is not itself a parameter update.
For input 1, the worked computation produces 0.05. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Omitting the scheduler step keeps the previous learning rate.

A learning-rate scheduler changes the optimizer's learning rate as training progresses. LambdaLR multiplies the base rate by a function of the step count; min(1, (step + 1) / k) is a linear warmup over k steps.
Call scheduler.step() after optimizer.step(). The rate used for each update is the one in effect before scheduler.step() advances it; logging it at that point shows exactly what was applied.
A scheduler has state, notably last_epoch, the number of steps taken. Save it in checkpoints and load it with load_state_dict when resuming, or the warmup restarts from the beginning.
The transfer records warmup learning rates and restores the scheduler's step count into a new scheduler.

Transfer walkthrough: Warmup takes the rate from a third of 0.1 to the full 0.1 by the third step. The restored scheduler continues from step 4. A factor of step/3 would start training with a zero learning rate.

import json
import torch
data = 4
x = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0))
opt = torch.optim.SGD([x], lr=0.1)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(opt, lambda step: min(1.0, (step + 1) / 3))
rates = []
for _ in range(data):
    rates.append(round(opt.param_groups[0]['lr'], 6))
    opt.step()
    sched.step()
resumed = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(torch.optim.SGD([x], lr=0.1), lambda step: min(1.0, (step + 1) / 3))
resumed.load_state_dict(sched.state_dict())
result = [rates, resumed.last_epoch]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Overfit a tiny batch as a diagnostic
body: A small deterministic training problem checks that gradients, loss and optimizer updates connect correctly. Falling training loss on this batch is a diagnostic, not evidence of generalization.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A zero learning rate prevents fitting this nonzero target.
Before training a real model, check that the loop can drive the loss to almost zero on a tiny, exactly learnable dataset. If it cannot, the bug is in the loop, not in the data or the model capacity.

Common loop bugs, such as a missing optimizer.step(), a missing zero_grad, a detached loss or a wrong sign, all show up here: the loss stays high, oscillates or the learned parameters are wrong. Checking the learned parameters, not just the loss, confirms the loop learned the intended function.
Keep the smoke test deterministic with a fixed seed and few steps so it runs in tests. It cannot detect generalization problems; it only proves the plumbing works.
The transfer fits y = slope·x + bias with a linear layer and checks the learned parameters and loss.
Transfer walkthrough: A working loop recovers the slope and bias and drives the loss to almost zero. Without optimizer.step(), the parameters keep their random initial values and the loss stays high.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = 1
torch.manual_seed(7)
x = torch.tensor([[0.0],[1.0],[2.0]])
y = 2*x+1
model = torch.nn.Linear(1,1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(),lr=0.1)
for _ in range(200):
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss = ((model(x)-y)**2).mean()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
result = bool(((model(x)-y)**2).mean().item()<0.001)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Batch normalization owns running statistics
body: BatchNorm updates running estimates during training and uses them in evaluation. Registered buffers must be checkpointed along with trainable parameters.
For input [2, 4], the worked computation produces [3.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Evaluation mode does not update running training means.

In training mode, BatchNorm normalizes each batch with that batch's mean and (biased) variance, and updates running estimates: running = (1 - momentum) · running + momentum · batch_statistic, where the running variance uses the unbiased batch variance.

In evaluation mode, it normalizes with the running estimates instead, so outputs no longer depend on the other samples in the batch. Forgetting eval() makes predictions depend on batch composition and keeps updating the running statistics during inference.

Running statistics start at mean 0 and variance 1 and take many batches to converge with the default momentum of 0.1. They are buffers, saved in state_dict; checkpoint and restore them with the weights.
The transfer applies one training batch, inspects the running statistics and compares training and evaluation outputs.

Transfer walkthrough: The batch [2, 4] has mean 3 and unbiased variance 2, so the running estimates move to 0.3 and 1.1. Training mode normalizes with the batch's own statistics, giving -1 and 1; eval mode uses the barely-updated running statistics, giving 1.62 and 3.53. Staying in training mode would keep normalizing per batch.

layer.train()
layer(torch.tensor(data,dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1,1))
result = layer.running_mean.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Convolution output depends on geometry
body: Convolution output length depends on input length, kernel size, stride, dilation and padding. Specify channels and spatial axes before constructing the layer.
For input 4, the worked computation produces [1, 2, 4, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Removing padding shrinks the spatial output.

For input size n, kernel k, stride s and padding p (dilation 1), a convolution's output size is floor((n + 2p - k) / s) + 1. Padding of (k - 1) / 2 with stride 1 keeps the size; stride 2 roughly halves it.

A Conv2d layer with C_in input channels, C_out output channels and a k × k kernel has C_out · C_in · k · k weights plus C_out biases. The count does not depend on image size, which is why convolutions are far smaller than fully connected layers on images.

Compute expected shapes before building a network, then assert them against a dummy forward pass. A mismatch usually shows up only at the first fully connected layer, far from the convolution that caused it.
The transfer compares the formula with an actual layer and counts a layer's parameters.
Transfer walkthrough: A 3 × 3 kernel with padding 1 keeps 32; stride 2 halves it to 16. Conv2d(3, 8, 3) has 8·3·9 + 8 = 224 parameters. Ignoring padding would predict 30.

lessons.title: Pooling reduces spatial resolution
body: Max pooling selects the largest value in each local window. It changes resolution and can lose spatial detail; average pooling encodes a different aggregation.
For input [1, 2, 3, 4], the worked computation produces [4.0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A mean is not the maximum of a pooling region.
Pooling summarizes local windows. Max pooling keeps the strongest response in each window; average pooling keeps the mean. Both reduce resolution and make features less sensitive to small shifts.

Adaptive pooling takes the desired output size instead of a window size, computing whatever windows are needed. adaptive_avg_pool2d(x, 1) is global average pooling: one number per channel, so a classifier head works for any input resolution.
Pooling discards spatial detail. Tasks that need precise locations, such as segmentation or detection, often use strided convolutions or keep higher-resolution paths instead.
The transfer applies max, average and global average pooling to a 4 × 4 map.

Transfer walkthrough: On the values 0–15, the top-left window [0, 1, 4, 5] gives max 5 and mean 2.5, and the global mean is 7.5. A single bright pixel dominates max pooling but is diluted by averaging.

lessons.title: Transform inputs and labels consistently
body: A horizontal image flip reverses the final spatial axis. Apply compatible transforms to spatial labels and restrict augmentation to the appropriate training scope.
For input [[1, 2], [3, 4]], the worked computation produces [[2, 1], [4, 3]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Flipping the vertical axis creates a different spatial transform.

A horizontal flip reverses the width axis of an image: img.flip(-1). For classification, the label is unchanged. For tasks whose labels describe positions, such as bounding boxes, keypoints or segmentation masks, the labels must be flipped too.

A box [x0, y0, x1, y1] in an image of width W becomes [W - x1, y0, W - x0, y1] after a horizontal flip; the left and right edges swap and mirror. Forgetting this trains the model on boxes that no longer cover the object.

Some augmentations are invalid for some data: flipping text or medical images with meaningful left–right orientation can change the label itself. Test augmentations by drawing transformed samples and checking that labels still match.
The transfer flips a small image and its bounding box.

Transfer walkthrough: The box covering the first column moves to the last column, [2, 0, 3, 2]. A box spanning the full width, or one centred, maps to itself. Leaving the box unchanged mislabels the flipped image.

lessons.title: Embeddings index learned rows
body: An embedding maps integer token IDs to learned vectors. Padding indices and vocabulary boundaries are explicit data contracts, not arbitrary floating features.
For input [0, 2], the worked computation produces [[0, 1], [4, 5]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Shifting token IDs changes which learned vectors are selected.
An embedding layer is a learnable table: token id i selects row i. Only rows that appear in a batch receive gradient, and a row used twice gets the sum of both contributions.
padding_idx marks the id used for padding. Its row is initialized to zeros and never receives gradient, so padding positions do not learn and contribute a zero vector.
An id outside [0, num_embeddings) raises an error rather than wrapping around. Build vocabularies with explicit padding and unknown ids, and check id ranges at the boundary where text is converted.
The transfer looks up ids including padding, inspects gradients per row and tries an out-of-range id.

lessons.title: RNN layouts distinguish batch and sequence
body: With batch_first=True, recurrent input is batch by sequence by feature. Hidden state still has layers by batch by hidden width, which is a separate layout.
For input 5, the worked computation produces [2, 5, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning hidden-state shape in place of sequence-output shape changes the contract.

With batch_first=True, recurrent layers take input of shape (batch, steps, features) and return output of shape (batch, steps, hidden): one hidden vector per step. The default batch_first=False expects (steps, batch, features), a frequent source of silent bugs.
The second return value, h_n, has shape (layers × directions, batch, hidden) regardless of batch_first. For a single-layer, unidirectional RNN, h_n[0] equals the output at the last step.
With padded variable-length sequences, the 'last step' of a short sequence is padding. Use pack_padded_sequence, or gather the output at each sequence's true length, rather than taking output[:, -1].
The transfer checks output and hidden shapes and the relationship between them.

Transfer walkthrough: Two sequences of five steps give output (2, 5, 4) and hidden (1, 2, 4), and the last output equals the hidden state. Comparing with the first step fails whenever there is more than one step.

lessons.title: LSTM carries hidden and cell state
body: An LSTM returns sequence outputs plus hidden and cell states. Preserve both states when carrying context; batch and layer dimensions must match the next invocation.
For input 5, the worked computation produces [[1, 2, 4], [1, 2, 4]]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Flattening hidden and cell states loses their separate shapes.

An LSTM keeps two states, the hidden state h and the cell state c, and returns both as (h_n, c_n). Passing them as the initial state of the next call continues the sequence exactly where the previous call stopped.

Processing a long sequence in chunks, as in truncated backpropagation through time or streaming inference, therefore gives the same outputs as one long pass, provided the state is carried. Starting a chunk from zeros forgets all previous context.

When training on chunks, detach the carried state between chunks so gradients do not flow into earlier chunks, and reset it at sequence boundaries. Batched states must line up with the same sequences in every chunk.
The transfer compares a full pass with a chunked pass that carries the state and one that resets it.
Transfer walkthrough: Carrying the state reproduces the full pass exactly; starting the second half from zeros does not. Dropping the carried state makes the chunked result diverge too.

import json
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
data = [1, 2, 3, 4]

lessons.title: Causal attention excludes future tokens
body: A causal attention mask restricts each position to its own and earlier keys. Without the mask, a token can read future information during autoregressive training.
For input [2, 4], the worked computation produces [2, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Unmasked attention averages values from future positions in this example.
Attention mixes value vectors with weights softmax(QKᵀ/√d). A causal mask restricts position i to keys 0..i, so a language model cannot read future tokens while predicting the next one.

is_causal=True applies exactly that mask. The equivalent explicit attn_mask is a lower-triangular Boolean matrix where True means 'may attend'. Using an upper-triangular mask by mistake lets every position see only the future.
With all-zero queries and keys, the weights are uniform over the allowed keys, so causal outputs are running means of the values. That makes a handy hand-checkable test of masking code.
The transfer compares is_causal, an explicit mask and unmasked attention.

Transfer walkthrough: Position 0 sees only 2, position 1 averages 2 and 4, and position 2 averages all three; unmasked attention gives the overall mean everywhere. An upper-triangular mask would let each position see only itself and the future.

lessons.title: Attention heads preserve a model-width contract
body: MultiheadAttention splits a model width across compatible heads and combines their results. Batch-first layout changes how the first two input axes are interpreted.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [2, 3, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Flattening the attended output discards batch and token axes.

Multi-head attention splits the model width embed_dim into num_heads heads of size embed_dim / num_heads, attends separately in each and concatenates the results. The width must be divisible by the number of heads.
key_padding_mask has shape (batch, keys); True marks padded keys that must receive zero attention weight. Without it, padding tokens dilute every real token's representation.
The returned weights are averaged over heads by default, shape (batch, queries, keys). Checking that weights on padded keys are zero is a quick test that masking works.
The transfer constructs attention layers with valid and invalid widths and checks padded-key weights.

lessons.title: Exclude padded tokens from loss
body: ignore_index excludes specified target entries from cross entropy. The mask belongs to target positions; confusing a real class with padding changes which examples train the model.
For input 0, the worked computation produces 0.6931471806. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Treating the padding marker as a class is invalid.
Sequence batches pad short sequences to a common length. Targets at padded positions are set to an ignore value, conventionally -100, and cross_entropy(..., ignore_index=-100) excludes them.

With the default reduction='mean', the loss is averaged over the non-ignored tokens only. A hand-written masked mean that divides by all positions, padding included, underestimates the loss and changes as padding changes.

Compute per-token losses with reduction='none' when you need to inspect them, mask out padding and average over the valid count. Report the number of valid tokens with the loss, because batches with more padding contribute fewer real tokens.
The transfer computes a padded-batch loss with ignore_index and checks it against a manual masked mean.

Transfer walkthrough: Two confident correct tokens each cost 0.127 and the padded position is ignored, so both computations give 0.127. Averaging over every position would include the padding's 0.693 and report 0.316.

lessons.title: Reserve an out-of-vocabulary token
body: A fixed vocabulary maps known tokens to stable IDs and unknown tokens to an explicit fallback. Fit vocabulary on training data rather than changing it during inference.
For input ['cat', 'bird'], the worked computation produces [1, 0]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using a real token ID for unknown text conflates distinct cases.

A vocabulary maps tokens to ids. Build it from training data only, reserving fixed ids for padding and unknown tokens, for example <pad> = 0 and <unk> = 1. Sorting tokens before assigning ids makes the mapping deterministic.

A minimum count drops rare tokens, which the model cannot learn well anyway, and maps them to <unk>, as it will map genuinely new words at prediction time. Test-time tokens never add vocabulary entries.

pad_sequence stacks variable-length id tensors into a rectangular batch, filling with the padding id. Pair it with a mask or ignore_index so padding does not affect the model or the loss. Save the vocabulary with the model; ids are meaningless without it.
The transfer builds a vocabulary with a minimum count and pads a batch of encoded sentences.
Transfer walkthrough: cat and dog appear twice and get ids 2 and 3; eel appears once and becomes <unk>. The shorter sentence is padded with 0. A minimum count of 1 would give eel its own id.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import torch
from collections import Counter
from torch.nn.utils.rnn import pad_sequence
data = [['cat', 'dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'eel'], [['cat', 'eel'], ['dog']]]
train, batch = data
counts = Counter(train)
vocab = {'<pad>': 0, '<unk>': 1}

result = [sorted(vocab, key=vocab.get), padded.tolist()]

lessons.title: Transformer blocks retain token structure
body: TransformerEncoderLayer combines attention, normalization and a feed-forward sublayer while preserving model width. Its shape contract does not establish useful learned language behavior.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [2, 3, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning a flattened tensor hides the token structure.
A transformer encoder layer applies self-attention and a feed-forward network with residual connections and normalization, keeping the shape (batch, tokens, d_model).

src_key_padding_mask marks padded tokens (True = padding). Real tokens then cannot attend to them, so their outputs are independent of whatever values sit in the padded positions. Without the mask, changing padding content changes every token's output.

This independence is a strong test of masking code: perturb the padding and assert the real tokens' outputs are unchanged. Run the check in eval mode with dropout off, so the outputs are deterministic.
The transfer changes the padded token's content and compares real-token outputs with and without the mask.
Transfer walkthrough: With the mask, setting the padded token to 100 leaves the real tokens' outputs unchanged; without it, they change. Dropping the mask on the perturbed pass breaks the equality.

result = list(output.shape)

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
data = 3
torch.manual_seed(0)
layer = torch.nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model=4, nhead=2, dim_feedforward=8, batch_first=True, dropout=0.0)

lessons.title: Score recommendations with latent factors
body: A latent-factor recommender scores an item using alignment between user and item vectors. Ranking quality, missing-not-at-random feedback and cold-start behavior require separate evaluation.
For input [[1, 0], [[2, 3], [4, 1]]], the worked computation produces [2, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A componentwise sum does not express user-item compatibility.
A latent-factor recommender scores every item as the dot product of a user vector with item vectors. torch.topk returns the k highest scores and their indices, the recommendation list.

Items the user has already interacted with usually should not be recommended again. Setting their scores to negative infinity before topk removes them from consideration without changing the other scores.
Evaluate recommendations with ranking metrics such as recall@k on held-out interactions, and compare against a popularity baseline. Ties and cold-start users with no history need explicit policies.
The transfer scores items for a user, masks seen items and takes the top k.
Transfer walkthrough: Item 1 has the highest score but was seen, so the recommendations are items 3 and 0. Without the mask, item 1 would top the list.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)

lessons.title: Pairwise losses express relative preferences
body: A hinge ranking loss penalizes a positive score that fails to exceed a negative score by the required margin. This differs from predicting an absolute calibrated probability.
For input [3, 1], the worked computation produces 0.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reversing positive and negative scores penalizes the wrong ordering.
Pairwise ranking losses compare a preferred item's score with a non-preferred one's. The hinge max(0, margin - (pos - neg)) is zero once the positive leads by the margin and grows linearly otherwise.

nn.MarginRankingLoss(margin)(x1, x2, y) computes max(0, -y · (x1 - x2) + margin); y = 1 means x1 should rank higher. Passing y = -1 by mistake reverses the preference and trains the model to rank items backwards.

Only pairs that violate the margin produce gradients, so training focuses on hard pairs. Count violations to see how many pairs still contribute, and sample negatives carefully: very easy negatives teach nothing.
The transfer compares a manual hinge with the library loss and counts margin violations.

Transfer walkthrough: The first pair meets the margin; the second leads by only 0.1 and the third ties, costing 0.9 and 1 for a mean of 0.633. A target of -1 would reward ranking negatives above positives.

lessons.title: Forecasts may use only available history
body: A trailing moving average can form a simple forecasting baseline. Fix the horizon and use only observations that exist at forecast time before evaluating on later targets.
For input [[1, 3, 9, 20], 2], the worked computation produces 2.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A leading window uses information outside the declared history endpoint.

To forecast with a model, turn a series into supervised examples: each input holds the previous w values and the target is the next value. series.unfold(0, w + 1, 1) produces all sliding windows of length w + 1 at once.
The first w columns are the inputs and the last column is the target. Taking any window that includes the target among its inputs leaks the answer and gives meaninglessly perfect validation scores.
Always compare against a naive baseline, such as predicting the last observed value. Split windows by time, never randomly, so validation windows come after training ones.
The transfer builds windows, extracts targets and scores the naive last-value forecast.

Transfer walkthrough: From 1, 2, 4, 7 with window 2, the inputs [1, 2] and [2, 4] predict 4 and 7; repeating the last value errs by 2 and 3. Shifting the inputs to include the target would leak it and make the naive error zero.

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
data = [[1, 2, 4, 7], 2]
series = torch.tensor(data[0], dtype=torch.float32)
w = data[1]
windows = series.unfold(0, w + 1, 1)
inputs, targets = windows[:, :w], windows[:, w]
naive = inputs[:, -1]
result = [inputs.tolist(), targets.tolist(), round(float((naive - targets).abs().mean()), 4)]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Reconstruction losses compare input and output
body: An autoencoder compresses and reconstructs data. Reconstruction error must compare the decoder output with the intended target; low training error alone does not establish anomaly-detection quality.
For input [[1, 2], [0, 2]], the worked computation produces 0.5. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Comparing a reconstruction with itself always reports zero error.

An autoencoder is trained to reproduce its input; the reconstruction error measures how well it does. F.mse_loss averages squared errors over every element by default, and reduction='sum' adds them instead, which scales with batch and feature size.
For anomaly detection, compute the error per sample by averaging over the feature dimension only. Samples the model reconstructs poorly, unlike its training data, get high scores.

Choose the threshold on validation data of known-normal examples, for example a high percentile of their errors, and report it with the data it came from. Averaging over the wrong dimension produces per-feature scores that cannot flag samples.
The transfer computes batch losses and per-sample errors and finds the worst-reconstructed sample.

Transfer walkthrough: The second sample's squared errors 9 and 16 average to 12.5, making it the anomaly; over the batch, the mean is 6.25 and the sum 25. Averaging over samples would produce per-feature numbers instead.

import json
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
data = [[[1, 2], [0, 0]], [[1, 2], [3, 4]]]
target, predicted = (torch.tensor(v, dtype=torch.float32) for v in data)
per_sample = ((target - predicted) ** 2).mean(dim=1)
result = [round(float(F.mse_loss(predicted, target)), 4), round(float(F.mse_loss(predicted, target, reduction='sum')), 4), [round(v, 4) for v in per_sample.tolist()], int(per_sample.argmax())]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Variational objectives regularize latent distributions
body: For a diagonal Gaussian posterior, KL to a unit Gaussian uses mean and log variance. Combine it with a correctly scaled reconstruction term; this formula is not a full trained VAE.
For input [[0], [0]], the worked computation produces 0.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Omitting the exponential variance term changes the KL objective.
A variational autoencoder's encoder outputs a mean and log-variance for each latent dimension. Its KL term to a standard normal prior has the closed form -½ Σ (1 + log σ² - μ² - σ²).

torch.distributions provides Normal and kl_divergence, which compute the same quantity and serve as a check on hand-written formulas. Normal takes a standard deviation, σ = exp(½ log σ²); passing exp(log σ²), the variance, is a classic bug.

The KL term is zero exactly when the posterior equals the prior (μ = 0, σ = 1) and grows as the encoder moves away from it. It is balanced against the reconstruction loss; weighting it differently, as in β-VAEs, changes that trade-off.
The transfer compares the closed form with torch.distributions for several posteriors.

Transfer walkthrough: A posterior equal to the prior has zero KL; a mean of 1 adds 0.5. With log-variance log 2 the second dimension adds about 0.153, so the total is 0.653. Passing the variance as scale breaks the agreement whenever log-variance is non-zero.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [[0], [0]]
mean,logvar = map(lambda x:torch.tensor(x,dtype=torch.float32),data)
result = float(-0.5*torch.sum(1+logvar-mean.square()-logvar.exp()))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import json
import torch
from torch.distributions import Normal, kl_divergence
data = [[0], [0]]
mean, logvar = (torch.tensor(v, dtype=torch.float32) for v in data)
closed = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mean ** 2 - logvar.exp())

library = kl_divergence(q, p).sum()
result = [round(float(closed), 4), round(float(library), 4)]

lessons.title: Diffusion mixes signal with scheduled noise
body: A forward diffusion step weights clean signal and noise using a cumulative variance schedule. State whether alpha denotes a per-step or cumulative quantity to avoid a mismatched process.
For input [2, 0, 0.25], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Using alpha rather than its square root changes signal variance.

The forward diffusion process mixes a clean sample with Gaussian noise: x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 - ᾱ_t) · ε, where ᾱ_t falls from 1 towards 0 as t increases. The weights keep the variance of x_t at one for unit-variance data.
Diffusion models are commonly trained to predict ε from x_t. Given the true or predicted noise, the clean sample is recovered by inverting the mixture: x₀ = (x_t - √(1 - ᾱ_t) · ε) / √ᾱ_t.

Getting the square roots wrong, for example subtracting ε without its weight, produces samples that look plausible but are systematically biased. Check inversion on known noise before trusting a sampler.
The transfer noises a sample and recovers it from the known noise.

Transfer walkthrough: With ᾱ = 0.25, x₀ = 2 contributes 0.5·2 = 1 and noise 1 contributes √0.75 ≈ 0.866; subtracting the weighted noise and dividing by 0.5 recovers 2 and 0. Subtracting unweighted noise gives a biased reconstruction.

import json

torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [2, 0, 0.25]
clean,noise,alpha = data
result = (alpha**0.5)*clean+((1-alpha)**0.5)*noise
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Normalize vectors before cosine similarity
body: Cosine similarity compares directions after dividing by vector norms. Decide how to handle zero vectors and avoid treating a raw dot product as scale invariant.
For input [[2, 0], [3, 0]], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A raw dot product changes when an embedding is rescaled.

Contrastive learning trains two encoders so that matching pairs, such as two views of one image or an image and its caption, have similar embeddings while other pairs do not. F.normalize(x, dim=1) scales each embedding to unit length, so dot products become cosine similarities.

The InfoNCE loss treats each row of the similarity matrix as a classification over all candidates in the batch, with the matching item on the diagonal as the correct class: cross_entropy(sim / τ, arange(n)). A small temperature τ sharpens the softmax.
Without normalization, embedding length dominates the similarity and the model can lower the loss by inflating norms instead of aligning directions. Larger batches supply more negatives per example.
The transfer normalizes two sets of embeddings, builds the similarity matrix and computes InfoNCE.

Transfer walkthrough: After normalization, matching directions have similarity 1 and the diagonal wins with almost zero loss; swapped pairs put the positives at similarity 0 and cost about 10. Without normalization the similarities reflect the lengths 2 and 3 instead of directions.

lessons.title: Bootstrap only nonterminal transitions
body: A one-step value-learning target combines reward with discounted next-state value. Terminal transitions exclude that bootstrap term; environment termination and truncation need an explicit policy.
For input [1, 0.9, 10, True], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Bootstrapping a terminal transition adds value beyond the episode endpoint.
A one-step value target is r + γ · V(s'), the reward plus the discounted value of the next state. When the episode ended at this transition, there is no next state, so the target is just r.
In batched code the 'done' flags form a mask: target = r + γ · V(s') · (1 - done). Forgetting the mask bootstraps from states after the episode ended, which inflates values near terminal states.

Next-state values usually come from a target network or are detached, so the target is treated as a constant during the update. Distinguish true termination from time-limit truncation, which should still bootstrap.
The transfer computes batched targets with and without terminal transitions.
Transfer walkthrough: The first transition gets 1 + 0.9·10 = 10, the terminal one just its reward 0, and the third 2 + 0.9·3 = 4.7. Without the mask, the terminal transition would wrongly add 4.5.
lessons.code:

print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Causal estimates require assumptions
body: Inverse-propensity weighting can rebalance observed treatment assignment under overlap and no-unmeasured-confounding assumptions. Numerical weighting does not verify those causal assumptions.
For input [[0, 10], [0.25, 0.5]], the worked computation produces 3.3333333333333335. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Ignoring treatment probability changes the weighted estimate.

In observational data, treatment is not randomized: if healthier patients were more likely to be treated, the naive difference in outcomes mixes the treatment effect with that selection. Inverse-propensity weighting reweights each unit by 1 / P(its treatment), creating a pseudo-population where treatment is independent of the measured confounders.

The normalized (Hájek) estimator divides the weighted outcome sum by the sum of weights within each group, which is more stable than dividing by n. Clipping propensities to, say, [0.05, 0.95] stops a few units with extreme weights from dominating, at the cost of some bias.

IPW relies on assumptions that data cannot verify alone: no unmeasured confounding, overlap (every unit could receive either treatment) and a correct propensity model. State them alongside any estimate.
The transfer computes weighted treated and control means and their difference, compared with the naive mean.

Transfer walkthrough: The treated unit with propensity 0.2 gets weight 5 against 1.25 for the other, pulling the treated mean from the naive 4 down to 3.4. The 0.01 propensity is clipped to 0.05, capping its weight at 20.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [[0, 10], [0.25, 0.5]]
values,propensities = data
weights = [1/p for p in propensities]
result = sum(v*w for v,w in zip(values,weights))/sum(weights)
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

import torch
data = [[5, 3, 4, 2], [1, 1, 0, 0], [0.8, 0.2, 0.5, 0.5]]

lessons.title: Inspect error rates across groups
body: A single aggregate metric can hide different outcomes across groups. Report group sample counts and uncertainty alongside rates, and distinguish fairness criteria before choosing interventions.
For input [[1, 1], [0, 0]], the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Averaging all records hides the requested between-group gap.

An overall metric can hide large differences between groups, such as regions, devices or demographic groups. Report per-group metrics with their sample counts, because a rate computed from a handful of examples is uncertain.
torch.bincount(group) counts samples per group, and bincount(group, weights=correct) sums correct predictions per group. Their ratio is the per-group accuracy, computed without a Python loop.

The largest gap between groups is one simple summary; which disparity matters depends on the application and its harms. Overall accuracy is a sample-weighted average and is dominated by the largest groups.
The transfer computes counts, per-group accuracies, the gap and the overall accuracy.

Transfer walkthrough: Group 0 is fully correct over 4 samples and group 1 half correct over 2, a gap of 0.5, while overall accuracy is 5/6. Counting samples instead of correct predictions would make every group look perfect.
lessons.code:
import json

import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [[1, 1], [0, 0]]
a,b = data
result = abs(sum(a)/len(a)-sum(b)/len(b))
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Separate device availability from model logic
body: This CPU lab moves data explicitly to cpu and checks the resulting device. CUDA/MPS availability, kernel behavior and real accelerator performance require checks on that hardware.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces "cpu". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Claiming CUDA from a CPU tensor misreports the tested environment.

Choose the device once, for example cuda when available and cpu otherwise, and move both the model and every input batch to it. Operations between tensors on different devices raise errors, so the decision must be shared, not repeated ad hoc.

tensor.to(device) returns the same tensor object when it is already on that device with the requested dtype, and a copy otherwise. Code that mutates the result in place can therefore unexpectedly change the original on CPU-only machines.

This lab runs on CPU and verifies the device bookkeeping only. GPU and Apple MPS behaviour, kernel availability and performance require their own hardware validation, which this guide labels separately.
The transfer resolves a device, moves a tensor and a model, and checks that they agree.
Transfer walkthrough: On this CPU host both the tensor and the model are on cpu, and to() returns the original tensor object. clone() would always copy, so identity no longer holds.

lessons.title: Autocast chooses eligible operation dtypes
body: CPU autocast can run eligible operations in bfloat16 while other operations retain their own policy. Mixed precision requires accuracy validation and is not a blanket cast of every tensor.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces "torch.bfloat16". Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Disabling autocast leaves this linear result in float32.

torch.autocast(device_type='cpu', dtype=torch.bfloat16) runs eligible operations, such as linear layers and matrix multiplications, in bfloat16, a listed set of numerically sensitive operations runs in float32, and everything else simply follows its inputs' dtype. On CPU, softmax is not on the float32 list, so the softmax of a bfloat16 output stays bfloat16. The policy is per operation, not per tensor.

bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range but only about three significant decimal digits. Outputs are close to, not equal to, full precision, so compare them with a tolerance and keep losses and accumulations in float32.
Outside the autocast region, the same layer computes in float32 again. Measure accuracy and speed on the target hardware before adopting mixed precision; benefits on CPU vary with the processor.
The transfer runs a linear layer and a softmax under CPU autocast and compares with full precision.

Transfer walkthrough: The linear output is bfloat16 under autocast, the softmax inherits that dtype, and the same layer outside the region computes in float32. The two outputs agree within 0.05. Disabling autocast leaves everything in float32.

lessons.title: NumPy bridges can share memory
body: torch.from_numpy shares supported CPU array storage. clone breaks that sharing; write policies and object lifetimes must be explicit when crossing the library boundary.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [9, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Cloning the bridge prevents writes from reaching the original array.

torch.from_numpy(a) wraps a NumPy array's memory without copying, and tensor.numpy() does the same in the other direction for CPU tensors. Changing one changes the other. The dtype is preserved, so float64 arrays become float64 tensors.
torch.tensor(a) always copies. Use it when the tensor must be independent of later changes to the array, for example when an input buffer is reused for the next batch.
Most models use float32; a float64 tensor from NumPy will either be rejected by a float32 layer or silently slow computation. Convert explicitly with .float() at the boundary.
The transfer modifies a NumPy array after creating shared and copied tensors.
Transfer walkthrough: The shared tensor and the NumPy view both show 99, while the copy keeps 1. The dtype stays float64. Using from_numpy for the copy would share the change too.

import json

import torch

torch.set_num_threads(1)

a = np.asarray(data,dtype=np.float32)
b = torch.from_numpy(a)
b[0] = 9
result = a.tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Contiguity is a layout property
body: Transposing a dense tensor changes strides and often makes it noncontiguous. contiguous materializes the requested layout when needed; view and reshape have different copying constraints.
For input 1, the worked computation produces true. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A transpose without materialization need not be contiguous.

A tensor is contiguous when its elements are laid out in row-major order without gaps. Transposes and some slices are views with other strides and are not contiguous; view() and some kernels and exporters require contiguous input.

contiguous() returns the tensor itself when it already is contiguous, and otherwise copies into new row-major memory. Comparing data_ptr() shows whether a copy happened. Axes of length one do not affect contiguity, so a transposed (1, n) tensor is still contiguous.
Each copy costs memory bandwidth. Call contiguous() where it is required, not reflexively everywhere, and measure when performance matters.
The transfer inspects contiguity and copying for a tensor and its transpose.

Transfer walkthrough: The 2 × 3 transpose is not contiguous, so contiguous() copies it into new memory, after which view works. The transpose of a single row is already contiguous and is returned as is. clone() keeps the transposed strides, so view would still fail.

result = bool(a.contiguous().is_contiguous())
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Load owned weights with explicit placement
body: For an owned in-memory state dictionary, weights_only=True limits the deserialization surface and map_location selects CPU placement. Still accept artifacts only from trusted provenance.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [1, 2]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Returning a modified tensor changes the recovered checkpoint values.

torch.save uses Python's pickle format, and loading a pickle can execute arbitrary code. torch.load(..., weights_only=True), the default since PyTorch 2.6, restricts unpickling to tensors, primitive types and a small allowlist of containers.

A checkpoint containing other objects, such as datetime values or custom classes, is rejected with an UnpicklingError. Store such metadata as plain strings or numbers, or in a separate JSON file, so checkpoints stay loadable in the safe mode.
map_location='cpu' loads tensors onto the CPU regardless of the device they were saved from. Verify a checkpoint's integrity (for example, a recorded SHA-256 digest) before loading it at all.
The transfer saves a tensor-only checkpoint and one with an extra object, then loads both with weights_only=True.
Transfer walkthrough: The tensor-only checkpoint loads and the one with a date object is rejected. Disabling weights_only would load both, including whatever code a malicious pickle carried.

import json
import io
import torch
import numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(1)
data = [1, 2]
stream = io.BytesIO()
torch.save({"weight":torch.tensor(data)},stream)
stream.seek(0)
state = torch.load(stream,weights_only=True,map_location="cpu")
result = state["weight"].tolist()
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

exercises.solution:
import json
import torch
import datetime, io, pickle
data = [1, 2]
def roundtrip(obj):
    stream = io.BytesIO()
    torch.save(obj, stream)
    stream.seek(0)
    try:
        torch.load(stream, weights_only=True, map_location='cpu')
        return 'loaded'
    except pickle.UnpicklingError:
        return 'rejected'
result = [roundtrip({'w': torch.tensor(data)}), roundtrip({'w': torch.tensor(data), 'when': datetime.date(2026, 1, 1)})]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

Tensors and plain containers are allowed.
Arbitrary Python objects are rejected.

lessons.title: Quantization trades representation for error
body: Quantizing a scaled value rounds it onto a finite grid. Measure reconstruction error against an explicit tolerance; this scalar lab does not establish hardware integer-inference speed.
For input 1.1, the worked computation produces 1.0. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Omitting the scale on reconstruction changes the numeric units.
Quantization stores values as small integers: q = clamp(round(x / scale) + zero_point, qmin, qmax). For qint8, q lies in [-128, 127]. Dequantizing gives (q - zero_point) · scale.

Values inside the representable range have rounding error of at most scale / 2. Values outside it saturate at qmin or qmax, and their error can be huge. Choosing scale is a trade-off: smaller scales are more precise but cover a narrower range.

Calibrate scale and zero point on representative data, and measure the end-to-end accuracy of the quantized model, not just per-tensor error. Outliers, as in the transfer, are the usual cause of poor quantized accuracy.
The transfer quantizes values including an outlier and reports integer codes, reconstructions and the maximum error.

Transfer walkthrough: 1.1 / 0.25 rounds to code 4 (1.0, error 0.1) and -0.3 to -1, but 100 needs code 400 and saturates at 127, reconstructing as 31.75 with an error of 68.25. Values on the grid reconstruct exactly. A non-zero zero point shifts every code and changes which values saturate.

lessons.title: Compilation needs semantic equivalence checks
body: torch.compile can transform execution while preserving intended outputs. The eager backend here checks the API contract only; it does not validate Inductor code generation or a speedup.
For input [2, 3], the worked computation produces [5, 10]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: A changed function is not equivalent to the original computation.

torch.compile captures a function or module and runs an optimized version. The goal is identical results with better speed, but capture can change numerics slightly or fail on unsupported Python features.

Treat compilation like any refactor: compare compiled and eager outputs on representative inputs, including edge cases such as zeros and branches, with an appropriate tolerance. backend='eager' exercises the capture machinery without a compiler toolchain, which makes it suitable for a fast correctness check.
Speed claims need measurements on the target hardware after warm-up, because the first call includes compilation time. Record the backend and versions with any result.
The transfer compiles a piecewise function and compares it with eager execution.
Transfer walkthrough: 2 maps to 5, -3 to 4 and 0 to 1, and the compiled function matches eager execution. Dropping the negation changes the non-positive branch.

lessons.title: Export captures a bounded graph contract
body: torch.export captures a graph with input constraints. This example uses fixed batch shape; dynamic shapes, target runtimes and operator support need additional validation.
For input [1, 2], the worked computation produces [2, 4]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Changing the model changes the exported program behavior.
torch.export captures a model as a graph with explicit input constraints. By default, input shapes are specialized to the example: an export traced with batch size 2 rejects a batch of 3.

Declaring a dimension dynamic, dynamic_shapes={'x': {0: torch.export.Dim('batch')}}, makes the graph accept any batch size the model's operations allow. The constraint is recorded in the exported program, which documents its contract.

Deployment code should test the exported program with the shapes it will actually see, including batch sizes other than the example. Exported graphs also fix control flow; data-dependent Python branches need special handling.
The transfer exports a model with static and dynamic batch dimensions and runs both on a different batch size.

Transfer walkthrough: The dynamic export handles three rows, while the static one accepts only the example's batch size of two. Removing the dynamic declaration makes the 'dynamic' export reject three rows too.

import torch

torch.set_num_threads(1)

import json
import torch
data = [[1, 1, 1], [2, 2, 2], [0, 0, 1]]
class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) * 2
example = torch.ones(2, 3)
batch = torch.export.Dim('batch')
dynamic = torch.export.export(Model(), (example,), dynamic_shapes={'x': {0: batch}})
static = torch.export.export(Model(), (example,))
x = torch.tensor(data, dtype=torch.float32)
try:
    static.module()(x)
    static_result = 'accepted'
except Exception:
    static_result = 'rejected'
result = [dynamic.module()(x).ravel().tolist(), static_result]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True, allow_nan=False))

lessons.title: Partition work by rank explicitly
body: This CPU simulation assigns each record to exactly one rank using strided indices. It checks partition logic only; real DDP communication, failure handling and accelerator execution remain separate labs.
For input [7, 3], the worked computation produces [[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], true]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Giving every rank all records duplicates the workload.

In data-parallel training, each process (rank) must see a different part of the dataset every epoch. DistributedSampler assigns indices by striding: rank r takes indices r, r + world, r + 2·world and so on.

Every rank must take the same number of steps, or collective operations deadlock. With drop_last=False the sampler pads by repeating indices from the start so the total divides evenly; with drop_last=True it drops the remainder instead. Either way, some samples are repeated or skipped each epoch, which matters for exact evaluation.

Call sampler.set_epoch(epoch) when shuffling so each epoch uses a different permutation. Passing num_replicas and rank explicitly, as here, lets the partitioning be tested without starting a process group.
The transfer partitions a dataset across ranks with padding and checks coverage.

Transfer walkthrough: Seven samples over three ranks become nine indices: 0 and 1 are repeated so each rank takes three steps, and every sample is covered. drop_last would give two each and skip one sample.

flat = [x for shard in shards for x in shard]
result = [sorted(flat),len(flat)==len(set(flat))]
print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True))

lessons.title: Choose data worker counts deliberately
body: DataLoader num_workers=0 loads samples in the current process. Extra workers introduce process ownership, initialization and teardown obligations that require separate lifecycle tests.
For input 3, the worked computation produces [0, 3]. Trace the intermediate values in the code and check the contract again with the other supplied cases.
Common mistake: Reporting extra workers misrepresents this in-process baseline.

With num_workers=0, the DataLoader calls the dataset's __getitem__ in the main process. With num_workers > 0, separate worker processes load batches in parallel; each worker has its own copy of the dataset and its own random state.

torch.utils.data.get_worker_info() returns None in the main process and a description (id, num_workers, seed) inside a worker. Datasets use it to split work, such as streaming shards, or to seed per-worker randomness.

Workers add process start-up time, memory and shutdown responsibilities, and on macOS and Windows they are spawned, which requires picklable datasets defined in importable modules. Start with num_workers=0 for correctness, then measure before adding workers.
The transfer records, for each sample, whether it was loaded in the main process.
