lessons.question: Does trivially copyable imply a portable network encoding?
options: Yes, all such types use network byte order
Only when sizeof is four
No; representation and platform details still vary
lessons.explanation: Object-copy guarantees are different from a specified external data format.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Both objects already exist, have the same trivially copyable type, and do not overlap. This local copy still does not define an external serialization format.

lessons.title: ADL finds operations associated with an argument type

This pattern is useful for symmetric operators whose operands include the domain type. It does not mean every arbitrary unqualified name is searched everywhere.
Understand ordinary lookup, ADL, and overload resolution as separate steps. Unexpected implicit conversions or generic overloads can still make an API confusing.

lessons.title: A clone operation needs a deep-copy ownership policy
body: A polymorphic clone returns an independently owned object while preserving the relevant dynamic type. It must define how owned resources and shared dependencies are copied.

Returning unique_ptr<Base> makes release ownership explicit when the base has a virtual destructor. Copying a raw pointer field alone may accidentally share mutable state or double-delete an allocation.
Test that modifying the clone leaves the original independent where that is the contract. A shared cache or external service may intentionally remain shared and needs separate documentation.

options: That every dependency must be shared
Ownership, dynamic type, and copying policy for contained resources
Only the method name

lessons.title: Queued commands must survive or reject target loss
body: A command stores an action for later execution. Captured inputs and target references need a lifetime policy because execution can occur after the original scope has ended.
A weak_ptr target can let a command reject work when its target is gone. lock obtains temporary strong ownership only when the object is still alive; it does not synchronize mutable object data.
Retries and undo need additional semantics. Repeating an external side effect is not automatically safe merely because an action fits inside a callable wrapper.

options: No
Always
Only for std::function

Composition keeps the legacy object behind a narrow wrapper without requiring the client to inherit from its concrete type. The adapter must translate failure and ownership behavior too.
Do not silently retain a borrowed legacy object beyond its lifetime. Store ownership or a reference according to the intended relationship and state which party must outlive the wrapper.

lessons.title: Default arguments follow the static declaration
body: Default arguments are supplied at the call site according to the visible declaration. A virtual override can change the called function without changing the default argument selected through a base interface.
This combination can surprise callers: the dynamic function body may receive a default from the static base type. Avoid giving overrides inconsistent defaults when that ambiguity is not intentional.
Prefer one nonvirtual front door with a stable default that delegates to a virtual implementation, or require an explicit argument at the polymorphic boundary.

The visible Base declaration

lessons.title: Virtual dispatch selects by dynamic type at a measurable cost
body: A call to a virtual function through a reference or pointer selects the final overrider for the dynamic type of the object. Common implementations store a hidden pointer in each polymorphic object to a per-class table of function addresses.

The hidden pointer usually enlarges every object, and the call is indirect. The larger cost is often lost inlining: unless the compiler can prove the dynamic type, it cannot see the target body. A qualified call such as obj.Base::f() names a function directly and bypasses dispatch.

Calling through an object by value slices the derived part and calls the base version. Measure before replacing virtual calls for speed; final classes, sealed hierarchies, std::variant, or templates trade openness for static knowledge.

lessons.practiceAnswer: Copying into a Shape parameter creates a Shape object, so its dynamic type is Shape and dispatch selects Shape::name.

lessons.title: Virtual inheritance shares one base subobject
body: With ordinary multiple inheritance, a class reaching the same base through two paths contains two separate base subobjects. Unqualified access to a member of that base is then ambiguous.

Declaring the inheritance virtual makes all virtual paths share one subobject. The most derived class constructs that shared base before any non-virtual base, and an intermediate class's initializer for it is ignored when it is not the most derived class.

Virtual bases add indirection to locate the shared subobject and complicate construction. Prefer composition or interfaces without data; use virtual inheritance deliberately when one shared base state is actually required.

lessons.title: Member order, padding, and empty members decide object size
body: Each member must sit at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment, so the compiler inserts padding between members and at the end. The size of a class is a multiple of its strictest member alignment so that arrays keep every element aligned. Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment often removes padding.

Every complete object has a nonzero size, so an empty member still occupies at least one byte plus padding. An empty base can occupy no storage (the empty base optimization). C++20 [[no_unique_address]] allows an empty member to overlap other members in the same way, which suits stateless allocators, comparators, and policies.

Exact numbers are an ABI property; the values shown are those of common LP64 ABIs such as arm64 and x86-64. Two subobjects of the same empty type still need distinct addresses. Do not serialize raw layout or depend on sizes without static_assert.

The compiler adds a hidden pointer to every struct
Padding aligns int b to 4 bytes and rounds the size to a multiple of its alignment
lessons.explanation: char a at 0, three bytes of padding, int b at 4, char c at 8, then tail padding to 12.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Eight bytes of double, four of int, and two chars total fourteen; the size rounds up to the 8-byte alignment of double.

lessons.title: override and final turn silent mismatches into errors
body: A function overrides a base virtual only if its name, parameter types, cv-qualifiers, and ref-qualifier match. A small mismatch, such as long instead of int or a missing const, declares a new function that hides the base version instead.

override asks the compiler to verify that the function really overrides something. final on a virtual function forbids further overriding, and final on a class forbids deriving from it; both also tell the optimizer the dynamic target is known.

Use override on every overriding declaration so interface changes break the build rather than behavior. Apply final where extension is genuinely not intended; it is a design commitment that later subclasses cannot undo.

lessons.title: Pimpl hides a representation behind one owning pointer
body: The pointer-to-implementation idiom moves private data into a separately defined Impl struct and keeps only a pointer to it in the public class. Clients include a header that never changes when Impl changes, which reduces rebuilds and keeps the class layout stable.

std::unique_ptr<Impl> needs the complete Impl type wherever its deleter is instantiated. Declare the destructor and move operations in the class and define them, even as = default, after Impl is complete in the implementation file. Copying must be written explicitly if it is wanted.
The cost is one allocation per object and an extra indirection on every access. A moved-from object holds a null pointer, so member functions must document whether they may be called on it.

lessons.title: Declaring a destructor suppresses the implicit move
body: The compiler implicitly declares a move constructor and move assignment only if the class declares no copy constructor, copy assignment, move operation of the other kind, or destructor. Declaring any of them, even as = default, suppresses the implicit moves.

Without a move constructor, an rvalue argument binds to the const copy constructor instead, so std::move quietly copies. Declaring a move constructor or move assignment, in turn, defines the implicit copy operations as deleted.
An empty destructor added for logging or as a breakpoint can therefore turn moves into copies throughout a program. Either follow the rule of zero, or explicitly default all the operations you want.

lessons.practiceAnswer: With no user-declared special member, Holder gets an implicit move constructor that moves its Probe member.

lessons.title: explicit restricts conversions to deliberate contexts
body: A constructor callable with one argument is also an implicit conversion unless it is marked explicit. Implicit conversions let unrelated values flow into function parameters and comparisons without a visible cast.

explicit constructors still work in direct initialization such as Meters{1.5} and static_cast. An explicit operator bool can still be used where the language performs a contextual conversion: if and while conditions, the operands of !, && and the logical-or operator, and the conditional operator's first operand.

Make single-argument constructors and conversion operators explicit by default. Allow implicit conversions only when the source and target represent the same abstract value, as with a string literal to a string type.
lessons.challenge: Test the closed handle in a conditional expression as well.
lessons.question: Which statement compiles with these types?
options: bool b = open;
twice(1.5);
if (open) {}

lessons.title: Inline static data members are defined in the class
body: A static data member belongs to the class, not to any object, so there is exactly one copy shared by all instances and it does not contribute to sizeof.

Before C++17, a non-const static data member declared in the class also needed one out-of-class definition in exactly one translation unit. Since C++17, inline static allows the in-class declaration to be the definition, and constexpr static data members are implicitly inline.

A shared mutable counter is global state: unsynchronized access from several threads is a data race, and tests can interfere through it. Static initialization order across translation units remains a separate hazard.

lessons.title: User-defined literals attach units to constants
body: A literal operator such as operator""_km lets a numeric or string literal carry a suffix that produces a domain type. Integer literals select a parameter of type unsigned long long, floating literals select long double, and string literals select a pointer plus a length.

The suffix applies to the literal token only. In -5_m, the minus sign is a unary operator applied to the result, so the domain type needs its own operator-. Literal operators can be constexpr, making unit-safe constants available at compile time.

Suffixes that do not begin with an underscore are reserved for the standard library, such as the s suffix for std::string and the chrono suffixes. Keep user literal operators in a namespace and bring them in with a using-directive where they are needed.

The underscore marks the operator as constexpr

lessons.practiceAnswer: The floating literal uses the long double operator and the integer literal uses the unsigned long long operator.

lessons.title: Virtual calls in constructors use the class under construction
body: While a base-class constructor or destructor runs, the object's dynamic type is that base class. Virtual calls made from it, directly or indirectly, dispatch to the version for the class whose constructor or destructor is running, not to a more derived override.

This is deliberate: the derived members are not yet constructed, or are already destroyed, so a derived override could read invalid state. typeid and dynamic_cast follow the same rule during construction and destruction.

Calling a pure virtual function this way is undefined behavior and commonly aborts. Pass needed information to the base constructor as arguments, or use a factory that completes initialization after construction.

options: Base::kind, because the dynamic type is Base while Base is being constructed
Derived::kind, because the object is a Derived
It is always undefined behavior
lessons.explanation: Dispatch during construction uses the class whose constructor is executing.
lessons.practiceAnswer: After construction completes, the dynamic type is Derived, so dispatch through a base reference still reaches Derived::kind.

lessons.title: A non-virtual interface keeps policy in the base
body: In the non-virtual interface idiom, the public functions are non-virtual and call private or protected virtual hooks. The base class owns the contract: argument checks, logging, locking, and postconditions run on every call no matter which derived class supplies the hook.
A derived class may override a private virtual function; access control governs who can call a name, not who can override it. Clients cannot bypass the wrapper by calling the hook directly.

The idiom adds a layer of indirection and works best when the wrapper has real policy to enforce. Keep the hooks narrow and document which preconditions the base already established before calling them.

Yes; access controls calling a name, not overriding it
No; private virtual functions cannot be overridden

lessons.practiceAnswer: The policy lives in one non-virtual function, so every encoder picks up the new framing without changing derived classes.

lessons.title: Access control is per class, and friendship is granted explicitly
body: private and protected restrict which code may name a member. The check is per class, not per object: a member function of Account may read the private balance of any Account, which is how copy constructors and comparison functions work.

A friend declaration grants one function or class access to the private members of the declaring class. Friendship is not inherited, not transitive, and not reciprocal. Protected members of a base may be accessed by a derived class only through objects of that derived type.
Access control is a compile-time aid for keeping invariants, not a security boundary. Every friend widens the set of code that must preserve the invariants, so grant it narrowly.

lessons.practiceAnswer: richer_than still reads other.balance_ legally; only the compared values changed.

lessons.title: Deduction guides select a class-template specialization
body: Class-template argument deduction can infer template arguments from an initializer. Deduction guides add declarations describing that inference; they do not execute a constructor body themselves.
The deduced specialization must still be constructible from the supplied arguments. A guide can intentionally deduce an owned string instead of a borrowed character pointer.
Review ownership and initializer_list interactions when adding guides. Convenient deduction should not silently change which object owns external storage.
lessons.challenge: Construct the second box from an explicit std::string while retaining the same owned type.
lessons.question: Does a deduction guide itself allocate or execute a constructor body?
options: Always
Only when the guide returns string
No; it participates in selecting template arguments
lessons.explanation: Construction occurs after the specialization has been deduced.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The constructor-based deduction now supplies Box<string> directly. The guide handled the character-pointer spelling in the original.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '1 1\n'

lessons.title: initializer_list is a view of a backing array
body: initializer_list provides read-only access to a compiler-created backing array under its lifetime rules. Copying the initializer_list wrapper does not copy the elements into independent owned storage.

A local initializer_list initialized by a braced list can keep its backing array live for that local use. Returning a wrapper for a new local backing array does not make that array survive the return.
Use an owning container for a returned sequence. Const elements also constrain attempts to move resources out of initializer-list construction.
lessons.challenge: Make the copied range an owning vector instead of another list view.
lessons.question: Does copying an initializer_list wrapper copy its backing elements?
options: Only when the list has three elements
No
Always
lessons.explanation: The wrapper refers to the backing array and does not become its own independent container.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The vector constructs its own elements from the live initializer list. It remains an owner independently of the wrapper lifetime.

lessons.title: Type traits select an implementation through tag dispatch
body: A type trait is a compile-time query or transformation over types. iterator_traits exposes an iterator category tag, and passing an object of that tag type to an overloaded helper lets ordinary overload resolution choose an implementation before the program runs.

The iterator tags form an inheritance chain: random_access derives from bidirectional, which derives from forward, which derives from input. A helper overload taking a base tag therefore accepts every stronger category, and an exact-match overload for a stronger tag wins when it exists.

Tag dispatch selects code, it does not check semantics. A user iterator that advertises random_access_iterator_tag without constant-time jumps silently receives the wrong algorithm; the tag is a promise the type author must keep.
lessons.challenge: Add a dedicated bidirectional overload that returns 3 and observe which helper the list iterator now selects.
lessons.question: Why does a list iterator reach the input_iterator_tag overload when only random-access and input overloads exist?
options: Overload resolution picks the last declared overload
list iterators report input_iterator_tag
bidirectional_iterator_tag derives (through forward) from input_iterator_tag, so the base conversion is viable
lessons.explanation: Tag types are ordinary classes. A derived-to-base conversion makes the input overload viable, while the random-access overload is not.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The list tag is bidirectional_iterator_tag. An exact match now exists, so the derived-to-base conversion to input_iterator_tag is no longer the best candidate. The vector call still matches random access exactly.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '1 2\n'

lessons.title: if constexpr discards the branch a type cannot use
body: if constexpr evaluates its condition as a constant expression. Inside a template, the branch not taken is a discarded statement and is not instantiated for that specialization, so it may contain operations the current type does not support.

This replaces many tag-dispatch and enable_if patterns with straight-line code. Each branch may return a different type when the function uses deduced return type, because only the selected return statements participate in deduction.

Outside a template the discarded branch is still fully checked, and even inside a template it must be syntactically valid and not ill-formed for every possible type. A plain if with a constant condition instantiates both branches.
lessons.challenge: Describe a long value instead of the int.
lessons.question: For describe("hi"), why is value * 2 not an error?
options: if constexpr converts errors into runtime exceptions
The integral branch is a discarded statement and is not instantiated for T = const char[3]
Arrays support multiplication by an integer
lessons.explanation: Inside a template, a discarded constexpr branch is not instantiated for that specialization.
lessons.practiceAnswer: long is integral, so the first branch is instantiated for T=long. The character-array call still instantiates only the else branch, where value*2 would be ill-formed.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: 'int:42 text:hi\n'

lessons.title: Non-type template parameters can deduce their type
body: A non-type template parameter is a compile-time value that becomes part of the type. Since C++17, template<auto N> deduces the parameter type from the argument, so Constant<5> and Constant<'x'> are both valid and carry different value types.

C++20 widened the permitted parameter types: floating-point values and structural class types (all bases and members public and themselves structural) can be template arguments. Two arguments name the same specialization only when their values are template-argument-equivalent.

Each distinct value creates a distinct type, which can multiply instantiations and code size. Pointer arguments must refer to objects with static storage duration; a string literal itself cannot be a template argument.
lessons.challenge: Use a constant expression rather than a literal for the first argument.
lessons.question: Are Constant<5> and Constant<5u> the same type?
options: Yes, because the values are equal
Only on platforms where int and unsigned have the same width
No; the deduced parameter types differ (int versus unsigned)
lessons.explanation: With auto, the argument type is part of the template argument, so equal numeric values of different types name different specializations.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Any converted constant expression of a permitted type works. The argument is evaluated during translation and its int type is deduced.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '5 x 1\n'

lessons.title: Template template parameters accept a template, not a type
body: A template template parameter lets a class template receive another template, such as std::vector, and apply it to types of its own choosing. Bag<std::vector> passes the template; Bag<std::vector<int>> would pass a type and does not match.

The parameter declares the shape it expects. Standard containers have a defaulted allocator parameter, so a portable declaration either lists both parameters or uses a variadic pack. C++17 relaxed matching lets a parameter with fewer parameters accept a template with defaulted extras, but older compilers needed a flag.
Do not use this feature when a type parameter would do. Accepting a fully formed container type is usually simpler and lets callers supply allocators and comparators directly.
lessons.challenge: Store the items in a std::list instead.
lessons.question: Which argument matches template<template<class, class> class Container>?
options: std::vector<int>
std::vector<int>::iterator
std::vector
lessons.explanation: A template template parameter requires a template name, not a specialization or another type.
lessons.practiceAnswer: std::list also takes an element type and an allocator, so it matches the declared template shape. Bag uses only push_back, size and back, which list supports.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '2 4\n'

lessons.title: Variable templates name a family of constants
body: A variable template declares a variable parameterized by types or values, such as pi<T> or is_small<T>. Each specialization is a separate variable, typically constexpr, and the standard _v traits are variable templates over the class-template traits.
Variable templates can be partially and explicitly specialized, which makes recursive compile-time definitions such as pointer depth concise. They are instantiated only when used.

A non-const variable template creates one mutable global per type, with the usual initialization-order and data-race concerns. Converting a long double initializer to int truncates; the template does not choose a safe rounding policy.
lessons.challenge: Test char instead of long.
lessons.question: What does pi<int> evaluate to?
options: 4, because the conversion rounds to nearest
It does not compile for integral types
3, because the long double value is converted to int by truncation
lessons.explanation: T(value) performs a functional cast; floating-to-integral conversion truncates toward zero.
lessons.practiceAnswer: sizeof(char) is 1 by definition, so is_small<char> is true. sizeof(short) is at least 2 bytes and is 2 on this target.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '3 10\n'

lessons.title: Names from a dependent base need this-> or qualification
body: Templates are checked in two phases. Non-dependent names are looked up when the template is defined; dependent names are resolved at instantiation. A base class that depends on a template parameter is not searched by unqualified lookup at definition time, because its members are unknown until instantiation.

Writing this->size() or Base<T>::size() makes the name dependent, deferring lookup to the instantiated base. Without it, unqualified lookup may silently find an unrelated global function or fail with an undeclared-identifier error.

Argument-dependent lookup at the point of instantiation can still find functions declared after the template, but only through associated namespaces of class-type arguments. Fundamental types have none, so a later overload for int is not found.
lessons.challenge: Remove this-> and observe which size the template binds.
lessons.question: Why is the base member found only with this->?
options: this-> makes the name dependent, so lookup happens in the instantiated base
this-> forces virtual dispatch
Unqualified lookup searches dependent bases only in C++20
lessons.explanation: Unqualified lookup does not search a dependent base class at the template definition.
lessons.practiceAnswer: size() is now a non-dependent name. Lookup at the definition finds the global size and ignores the dependent base, so report returns 99.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '3\n'

lessons.title: T&& is a forwarding reference only when T is deduced
body: In a function template, a parameter of the form T&& where T is deduced from the call is a forwarding reference. An lvalue argument deduces T as an lvalue reference and reference collapsing yields T&; an rvalue deduces a non-reference T.

In a member of a class template, T is already fixed by the class, so void take(T&&) is an ordinary rvalue reference parameter and rejects lvalues. const T&& and std::vector<T>&& are not forwarding references either.

A greedy forwarding overload often beats an overload taking const X& for non-const lvalues, because it deduces an exact match. Constrain forwarding constructors or overloads rather than assuming the const reference version is preferred.
lessons.challenge: Pass n as an xvalue.
lessons.question: Can Box<int>::take accept an int lvalue?
options: Yes; every T&& is a forwarding reference
Yes, but only for const lvalues
No; T is fixed by the class, so T&& is an ordinary rvalue reference
lessons.explanation: Forwarding reference deduction requires T to be a template parameter of the function being called.
lessons.practiceAnswer: std::move produces an xvalue, so deduction yields a non-reference T and the trait reports an rvalue.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: 'lvalue rvalue\n'

lessons.title: Subsumption picks the more constrained overload
body: When two constrained candidates are otherwise equally good, the one whose constraints subsume the other wins. Constraints are normalized into conjunctions and disjunctions of atomic constraints, and subsumption compares those atoms.

Whole is defined as Number<T> && is_integral_v<T>, so it contains Number as a conjunct and is more constrained. For an int argument both pick overloads are viable and the Whole overload is chosen; for a double only Number is satisfied.

Atomic constraints are identical only if they come from the same expression in the source, normally via the same concept. Repeating std::is_integral_v<T> textually in two requires-clauses does not create subsumption and yields an ambiguity.
lessons.challenge: Pass a floating literal in the second call.
lessons.question: Why is pick(7) not ambiguous?
options: The later declaration always wins
Integral types always prefer the overload declared with auto
Whole subsumes Number because Whole is defined as a conjunction containing Number
lessons.explanation: Normalized constraints compare atomic constraints that come from the same concept definition.
lessons.practiceAnswer: double satisfies Number but not Whole, so only the first overload is viable.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: 'number whole\n'

lessons.title: index_sequence turns a pack of indices into code
body: std::integer_sequence<T, I...> carries a compile-time pack of integers in its type. make_index_sequence<N> produces indices 0..N-1 and index_sequence_for<Ts...> produces one index per type.

A helper deduces the pack from the sequence argument and expands an expression such as std::get<I>(t) for each index. In C++14 a braced array initializer sequences the expansions left to right; C++17 fold expressions express the same idea more directly.
The sequence object is empty; all the information lives in its type. Large N creates large instantiations and slow builds, and negative lengths are rejected.
lessons.challenge: Sum a two-element tuple instead.
lessons.question: Where are the indices stored in std::index_sequence<0, 1, 2>?
options: In three int data members
In the type itself; the object carries no data
In a heap-allocated array
lessons.explanation: integer_sequence is an empty class whose template arguments encode the values.
lessons.practiceAnswer: index_sequence_for<int, int> is index_sequence<0, 1>, so two get expansions are generated.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '6 4\n'

lessons.title: A typelist is a pack you can query and transform
body: A typelist is an empty class template holding a pack of types. Metafunctions are partial specializations that pattern-match the pack and expose a result as a static value or nested type alias.
Fold expressions make queries such as Contains a single line. Transformations such as front, push or map produce a new TypeList type instead of mutating anything.

Every intermediate list is a distinct instantiation. Applying a metafunction to a list shape it does not handle, such as Front of an empty list, produces an incomplete-type error rather than a clear message unless you add a static_assert.
lessons.challenge: Ask whether double is in the list.
lessons.question: What does (std::is_same_v<T, U> || ...) yield for an empty TypeList<>?
options: false, the identity of a unary || fold
true
It fails to compile
lessons.explanation: A unary fold over an empty pack is permitted for &&, || and the comma operator.
lessons.practiceAnswer: double is the third element, so one is_same_v term is true and the disjunction is true.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '3 10\n'

lessons.title: C++20 constant evaluation can allocate transiently
body: Since C++20, constant evaluation may call new and delete, and std::vector and std::string have constexpr members. A constexpr function can build a vector, compute with it and return a scalar result during translation.

The allocation must be released before the constant evaluation ends. A transient vector that is destroyed inside the function is fine; a constexpr variable whose value still owns heap memory is ill-formed.

The same function remains callable at runtime with dynamic allocation. Compilers bound constant-evaluation steps, so very large compile-time computations can fail with a limit rather than a logic error.
lessons.challenge: Compute the sum for five squares and update the assertion.
lessons.question: Can a constexpr std::vector<int> variable keep its heap elements after constant evaluation?
options: Yes, but only for fewer than 16 elements
No; every allocation must be deallocated within the same constant evaluation
Yes, the compiler stores them in read-only data
lessons.explanation: C++20 permits transient constexpr allocation only.
lessons.practiceAnswer: 1+4+9+16+25 is 55. The vector is created and destroyed inside one constant evaluation.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '30\n'

lessons.title: Choose a sequence by operations and invalidation
body: vector, deque, list, and forward_list have different storage and iterator contracts. Contiguity favors vector for many traversals; node-based storage can support other stability requirements but incurs indirection and allocation.
Choose the container from required operations and measured workload, not a slogan about insertion complexity. Finding the insertion position can dominate the advertised insertion cost.
Do not transfer one container invalidation rule to another. Review the exact operation, including end iterators and allocator conditions.
lessons.challenge: Remove both endpoints and inspect the remaining endpoints.
lessons.question: Why can insertion cost alone mislead container selection?
options: Node allocation is always free
Locating the position and cache behavior also matter
All containers have identical layout
lessons.explanation: The whole workload includes search, allocation, locality, and iterator requirements.
lessons.practiceAnswer: After removing 1 and 4, the deque contains 2 and 3. The precondition for both pop operations is nonempty input.

lessons.title: Lookup containers have different ordering contracts
body: map maintains key ordering according to its comparator, while unordered_map partitions keys using hash and equality. Iteration order in an unordered container is not a portable sorted order.
operator[] can insert a missing key and value-initialize its mapped value. Use find when lookup must not mutate the container; try_emplace separates conditional insertion from later access.
Equivalent keys must satisfy the comparator or hash/equality requirements. A poor or inconsistent policy can break correctness or expected performance.
lessons.challenge: Use operator[] for the missing key and observe insertion.
lessons.question: Can map::operator[] insert a missing key?
options: Only if the mapped value is a pointer
Yes
No, it is always read-only
lessons.explanation: The operation supplies a mapped object for a missing key.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The missing mapped int is value-initialized to zero and the map grows. A lookup that must not insert should use find.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '1 1\n'

lessons.title: Comparators must establish a strict weak ordering
body: Sorting and ordered containers require a comparator with semantic ordering properties. less(a,a) must be false, and the induced ordering and equivalence must satisfy their transitivity requirements.
Using <= instead of < violates irreflexivity. A comparator depending on mutable external state can invalidate the data structure ordering after insertion.
Test equal elements, distinct equivalence classes, and boundary values. Floating NaNs require a deliberate policy instead of assuming ordinary numeric comparison orders every input.
lessons.challenge: Sort ascending using a strict comparator.
lessons.question: Why is a <= b unsuitable as the sorting comparator?
options: It reports true when comparing an element with itself
It sorts too slowly
It only supports unsigned values
lessons.explanation: A strict weak ordering must be irreflexive.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Strict greater-than and strict less-than each define an ordering on these integers. Replacing them with a non-strict comparison would violate the comparator contract.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '4 3 1 '

lessons.title: Algorithms need specific traversal capabilities
body: An iterator category describes supported traversal operations and semantic guarantees. A forward iterator supports multipass traversal; a random-access iterator supports efficient jumps and differences under its contract.
Do not apply random-access assumptions to a list iterator or assume an input iterator can be traversed twice. Concept checks in newer standards make some constraints clearer.
Iterator and sentinel validity depends on the underlying range. A valid iterator type does not guarantee that a particular iterator value is still usable.
lessons.challenge: Advance one position and read the middle element.
lessons.question: Can a list iterator generally use it + 2?
options: No; it is not a random-access iterator
Yes, for every iterator
Only when the list has even size
lessons.explanation: Use operations supported by the iterator category and remain within valid bounds.
lessons.practiceAnswer: advance works with this bidirectional iterator by stepping. It does not make list traversal constant-time random access.

lessons.title: Separate logical removal from container erasure
body: remove_if moves retained values toward the front and returns the new logical end. It does not shrink the container. The tail still contains objects with unspecified values under the algorithm contract.
The erase-remove idiom erases that tail from a sequence container. C++20 erase_if packages common container-specific removal patterns.
After erasure, observe the container invalidation rules. Do not continue with a saved invalid iterator just because the removal algorithm returned successfully.
lessons.challenge: Retain only the even numbers.
lessons.question: Does remove_if itself shrink a vector?
options: Yes
Only if every value is removed
No; erase must remove the logical tail
lessons.explanation: Algorithms operate on iterator ranges without necessarily controlling container size.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The predicate marks elements to remove, not elements to retain. Erasing the returned tail changes vector size.

lessons.title: Ranges compose lazy traversal operations
body: A view can describe a computation over a range without materializing a new container. filter chooses elements and transform computes values as they are traversed.
Laziness changes when work and side effects happen. A pipeline may depend on live source storage and captured state; constructing the pipeline does not generally perform every transformation.
Understand ownership of each adapted range and callable. Prefer pure transformations for predictable repeated traversal and check whether a view is single-pass or multipass.

lessons.question: When does this transform compute values?
options: As the view is traversed
Always when the pipeline is declared
Only when the vector is destroyed
lessons.explanation: This view pipeline describes deferred traversal work.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The filter controls which source values reach transform. No output vector is required to traverse this pipeline.

lessons.title: Borrowing requirements are separate from iterator types
body: A range algorithm may return an iterator whose usefulness depends on the range lifetime. borrowed_range identifies ranges whose iterators can remain usable independently of the range wrapper lifetime under its requirements.
Borrowed status does not keep underlying storage alive. A span wrapper may be temporary while its backing array remains live; an owning temporary vector destroys its elements when it dies.
Store the owner when a returned position must remain usable. Recognize dangling result types instead of forcing a cast around a lifetime error.
lessons.challenge: Inspect an lvalue vector range, whose lifetime remains the caller responsibility.
lessons.question: Does borrowed_range extend the backing storage lifetime?
options: Yes, through reference counting
Only for spans
No
lessons.explanation: The concept describes iterator validity relative to a range wrapper, not automatic ownership.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An lvalue range expression can meet borrowed_range while the program still has to keep the referenced vector alive.

lessons.title: A memory resource must outlive its allocations
body: Polymorphic allocators delegate allocation through a memory_resource interface. PMR lets runtime-selected resource policies serve containers without changing their element type.

A monotonic_buffer_resource releases its accumulated storage together rather than reclaiming each individual deallocation. Its upstream resource can allocate if the supplied buffer is insufficient unless that fallback is deliberately disabled.
Destroy resource-using objects before the resource. Resetting a resource while its containers still use the storage invalidates those objects; stack placement alone does not prove lifetime order.
lessons.challenge: Store two integers and report the container size.
lessons.question: What must outlive a PMR container that uses its storage?
options: Only the allocator variable name
Nothing, because PMR copies the arena
The supplying memory resource
lessons.explanation: Allocator indirection does not transfer ownership of the resource.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The vector is declared after the arena, so it is destroyed first. null_memory_resource makes exhaustion throw rather than silently allocate from a heap resource.

lessons.title: Span adds extent without ownership
body: span<T> pairs access to contiguous elements with an extent. It can use a static or dynamic extent but does not allocate or own the elements.
A span can be a safer interface than unrelated pointer and length parameters, yet operator[] still requires a valid index. The backing storage must stay live and suitably stable.
Use const element access when mutation is not intended. Constness of the span wrapper itself differs from constness of the elements it views.

lessons.question: Does a span own the elements it references?
options: No
Yes, it frees them at destruction
Only for static extent
lessons.explanation: Extent information and ownership are separate responsibilities.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The final array element becomes 7 while a[1] remains 2. subspan changes the viewed range and does not change the original span extent.

lessons.title: Reduction order affects admissible operations
body: accumulate evaluates a left fold in its specified order. reduce permits regrouping and reordering under its contract, which supports parallel implementations but changes what results can be assumed.
Integer addition within range works well for this demonstration. Floating addition and non-associative operations require more careful expectations.
Do not assume a parallel execution policy creates threads or speeds up every workload. Backend support, input size, synchronization, and exceptions affect the behavior.

options: Yes, subject to its requirements
No, both specify the same left-to-right fold
Only for strings
lessons.explanation: Algorithms with different evaluation-order contracts can yield different floating results.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The initial value participates in both accumulator type and result. A wider accumulator can avoid overflow for a bounded input range, but is not an unlimited integer.

lessons.title: Equivalent keys control duplicate retention
body: set keeps one element per comparator-equivalence class; multiset can retain multiple equivalent elements. Equivalence is defined by the ordering relation, not necessarily operator==.

For hashed containers, equality and hashing must agree so equivalent keys produce the required compatible hash values. Modifying an indexed key through an unsupported route can break lookup invariants.
Choose a container from duplicate and ordering requirements. Do not discard records silently when their business identity is finer than the selected key.
lessons.challenge: Insert a third equivalent value into each container.
lessons.question: What is the exact stdout of the displayed base program?
options: The program is ill-formed in its stated standard.

lessons.title: std::function erases a copyable callable
body: std::function<R(Args...)> stores any copy-constructible callable whose call signature fits, then calls it through an indirect, type-erased path. The wrapper owns its target: copying the wrapper copies the stored callable, including a lambda's captured state.

Implementations keep small targets in an internal buffer and allocate larger ones on the heap; the buffer size is not specified, so do not design around it. Calling through the wrapper usually prevents inlining. Calling an empty wrapper throws std::bad_function_call.

Because the target must be copy-constructible, a lambda that captures a unique_ptr cannot be stored. Prefer a template parameter or a function reference when the callable does not need to be stored, and std::move_only_function (C++23) where it is available for move-only targets.

lessons.practiceAnswer: g is now a std::reference_wrapper to f, so it forwards each call to f's target. The counter is shared: f() yields 3, then both g() calls advance the same state to 4 and 5.

lessons.title: sync_with_stdio and tie trade ordering for speed
body: By default the standard C++ streams are synchronized with C stdio, so printf and std::cout output interleave in program order. std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false) removes that guarantee and lets the streams buffer independently; it returns the previous setting.

lessons.title: Custom hashes must agree with equality

body: std::shared_mutex has two modes. std::shared_lock acquires shared ownership, and any number of threads may hold it together; std::unique_lock acquires exclusive ownership and excludes all readers and writers.

There is no upgrade from shared to exclusive. Locking the same shared_mutex again from a thread that already owns it, in either mode, is undefined and in practice deadlocks. For short critical sections a plain std::mutex is often faster.
lessons.challenge: Have every reader look up a key that was never set.
lessons.question: A thread holds a shared_lock and then constructs a unique_lock on the same shared_mutex. What happens?
options: The shared lock is upgraded atomically
unique_lock throws std::system_error immediately
Undefined behavior; in practice it deadlocks waiting for itself
lessons.explanation: shared_mutex has no upgrade operation, and acquiring it again while already owning it is a precondition violation.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each of the four readers finds no entry and contributes -1. The shared locks still allow the lookups to run together.

lessons.title: call_once runs an initializer exactly once
body: std::call_once(flag, f) runs f on the first call for a given std::once_flag. Concurrent callers wait until that call completes, and its effects happen before every caller returns.

If f exits with an exception, the flag stays unset, the exception propagates, and a later call tries again. A function-local static is initialized with the same guarantee and is often simpler for a lazily created singleton.
Do not replace call_once with double-checked locking on a plain bool: the unlocked read races with the locked write. Calling call_once recursively on the same flag from inside f deadlocks.

lessons.question: What happens if the callable passed to call_once throws?
options: The flag is marked done and the exception is swallowed
std::terminate is called
The exception propagates and a later call_once on that flag runs a callable again
lessons.explanation: Only a normal return completes the once_flag. An exceptional exit leaves it ready for another attempt.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Without the once_flag every thread runs init, and the atomic counter records all four calls.

lessons.title: thread_local gives each thread its own object
body: A variable declared thread_local has thread storage duration: every thread that uses it gets a separate instance, constructed on first use in that thread (or at thread start) and destroyed when that thread exits.

thread_local suits per-thread caches, counters and random engines because no synchronization is needed for each thread's own instance. A static local declared thread_local is initialized once per thread.

thread_local does not prevent a data race if a pointer to the object escapes to another thread, and that pointer dangles once the owning thread exits. Thread pools reuse threads, so state can leak between tasks, and a coroutine resumed on another thread sees that thread's instance.

Yes; thread_local only changes initialization
Only if the variable is not atomic
lessons.explanation: The name refers to a different object in each thread. A race needs two threads to access the same memory location.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The main thread has its own calls instance, untouched by the workers, so work(2) returns 2 and main's instance then holds 2.

lessons.title: Relaxed, sequentially consistent and fence orderings
body: memory_order_relaxed guarantees atomicity and a single modification order for that one variable, but no ordering with other memory. It is enough for a statistics counter that is read after join, because join itself synchronizes.

memory_order_seq_cst, the default, adds a single total order over all seq_cst operations, which rules out outcomes such as both threads reading 0 in a store-buffering test. A release fence before a relaxed store, paired with an acquire fence after a relaxed load that reads that store, synchronizes like a release store and acquire load.
A relaxed flag does not publish other data: reading the payload afterwards is a data race. A fence orders nothing by itself; it needs an atomic operation that observes the other thread's write.
lessons.challenge: Replace both fences with a release store and an acquire load.
lessons.question: Which order is sufficient for a hit counter that is only read after all threads are joined?
options: memory_order_relaxed
memory_order_acquire on every increment
memory_order_seq_cst is required for any counter
lessons.explanation: fetch_add is atomic in every order, and join provides the synchronization for the final read.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The acquire load that reads the release store synchronizes with it, giving the same happens-before edge as the fence pair.

lessons.title: False sharing costs time, not correctness
body: Caches move memory in lines. When two threads write different variables that share one line, each write invalidates the other core's copy, and the line bounces between cores. The program stays correct but can slow down sharply.

Aligning each hot per-thread object to std::hardware_destructive_interference_size puts it on its own line. Apple clang 21 with libc++ provides the constant; on this arm64 Mac it is 256, while the constructive size is 64, so the lesson checks only a portable lower bound.

The constant is a compile-time estimate and can differ from the real line size of the machine running the binary. Measure before and after padding: padding increases memory use and can reduce cache locality.
lessons.challenge: Check the distance between the two counters instead of the type size.
lessons.question: Two threads update adjacent atomics on the same cache line. What changes compared with padded atomics?
options: The counts become nondeterministic
It is a data race
Only performance; the results are identical
lessons.explanation: Each atomic is a separate memory location, so there is no race. Sharing a line only adds coherence traffic.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Array elements are sizeof apart, and alignas rounds sizeof up to the alignment, so neighbouring counters are at least one interference size apart.

lessons.title: A single-producer single-consumer ring needs only two atomics
body: In an SPSC ring only the producer writes tail and only the consumer writes head. The producer writes a slot and then publishes it with a release store of tail; the consumer's acquire load of tail makes the slot contents visible. The consumer releases head to hand the slot back.
One slot stays empty so that head == tail means empty and next(tail) == head means full; capacity is N - 1. Each side may read its own index relaxed because no other thread writes it.
The design relies on exactly one producer and one consumer. A second producer races on the slot and tail. Spinning on a full or empty ring burns a core; add backoff or a wait strategy for real use.
lessons.challenge: Transfer the values 1 to 1000.
lessons.question: Why may push load tail_ with memory_order_relaxed?
options: The consumer never reads tail_
Only the producer writes tail_, so it always reads its own latest value
Relaxed loads are always sufficient for indices
lessons.explanation: A thread observes its own writes in program order. The cross-thread edges come from release stores paired with acquire loads.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Both loop bounds change together. The ring keeps at most seven values in flight, and every pushed value is popped exactly once.

lessons.title: compare_exchange loops and the ABA problem
body: compare_exchange_strong(expected, desired) atomically replaces the value with desired if it equals expected and returns true; otherwise it returns false and writes the current value into expected. compare_exchange_weak may also fail spuriously even when the values match.

Use weak inside a retry loop, where a spurious failure just causes another iteration and can be cheaper on load-linked/store-conditional hardware such as ARM. Use strong when a single attempt decides what to do next.

CAS compares values, not history. In a pointer-based lock-free stack, a node can be popped, freed and reallocated at the same address between a thread's read and its CAS, so the CAS succeeds on stale assumptions. Tagged counters, hazard pointers, epoch reclamation or a mutex avoid this ABA problem.
lessons.challenge: Start with the expected value that x actually holds.
lessons.question: What does a failed compare_exchange do to its expected argument?
options: Sets it to desired
Overwrites it with the value currently stored
Leaves it unchanged
lessons.explanation: Updating expected lets a retry loop recompute desired from the latest value without a separate load.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The comparison now succeeds, so x becomes 9 and expected keeps the 5 it already held.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '0 5 5 99\n'

lessons.title: atomic_flag builds a spinlock, which rarely beats a mutex
body: std::atomic_flag is the one atomic type guaranteed to be lock-free. test_and_set with acquire ordering takes the lock and clear with release ordering releases it, so writes inside one critical section happen before the next. Since C++20 a default-constructed flag is clear and test() reads it without writing.

Spinning on test() (test-and-test-and-set) before retrying test_and_set keeps the cache line shared while waiting. A class with lock and unlock satisfies BasicLockable, so std::lock_guard and std::scoped_lock work with it.

A spinning thread wastes CPU while the owner is descheduled and can suffer priority inversion. Prefer std::mutex unless the critical section is tiny, threads are not oversubscribed, and measurement shows a benefit.

lessons.question: Why does lock use memory_order_acquire on test_and_set?
options: Because test_and_set requires acquire
To make the spin loop faster
So writes made by the previous holder before its release clear are visible inside the critical section
lessons.explanation: A lock must create a happens-before edge from unlock to the next lock. Relaxed ordering would leave the protected data racing.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each thread still performs 10000 protected increments, so two threads total 20000.

lessons.title: async launch policies and the blocking future
body: std::launch::async runs the task as if on a new thread. std::launch::deferred runs it lazily on the thread that first calls get or wait. The default policy, async | deferred, lets the implementation choose.

A deferred task never runs if no one waits for it, and wait_for on it returns future_status::deferred immediately, so a polling loop with the default policy may never finish. The future returned by std::async is special: its destructor blocks until an async task completes.
Discarding the result of std::async therefore makes the call synchronous, and a future destroyed at the end of a scope waits there. Use std::launch::async explicitly when concurrency is required.
lessons.challenge: Report the deferred status before running the lazy task.
lessons.question: What does std::async(std::launch::async, f); do when its result is discarded?
options: It blocks until f finishes, because the temporary future's destructor waits
It runs f in the background and returns immediately
It never runs f
lessons.explanation: Futures created by std::async with the async policy join their task in the destructor of the last shared-state owner.
lessons.practiceAnswer: wait_for on a deferred task does not start it; it reports deferred. get then runs it on the main thread.

lessons.title: packaged_task and promise are the write side of a future
body: A std::promise<T> is the producer end of a shared state: set_value or set_exception stores the result, and the future obtained from get_future reads it. A std::packaged_task<R(Args...)> wraps a callable and stores its return value or exception in its shared state when invoked.

Both are move-only and are often moved into a thread. future::get waits, returns the value or rethrows the exception, and can be called only once; afterwards valid() is false. std::shared_future allows several readers.
Destroying a promise or packaged_task without providing a result stores a future_error with broken_promise. Setting a value twice throws future_error with promise_already_satisfied.

lessons.question: What does future::get report if the promise was destroyed without a value?
options: It throws std::future_error with code broken_promise
It returns a value-initialized T
It blocks forever
lessons.explanation: The promise destructor stores broken_promise in an unsatisfied shared state so waiters are released.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The worker invokes the packaged task with 6 and 7, and the sum becomes the shared-state value read by get.

lessons.title: An awaiter controls suspension with three functions
body: co_await expr obtains an awaiter and calls await_ready. If it returns false, the coroutine suspends and await_suspend receives its handle; when the coroutine is resumed, await_resume supplies the value of the co_await expression.

await_suspend may return void (stay suspended), bool (false resumes immediately) or another coroutine handle to resume next (symmetric transfer). Storing the handle somewhere is how a scheduler, timer or I/O completion resumes the coroutine later.

Once the handle is published another thread may resume or destroy the frame, so do not touch awaiter or frame state after publishing it. Resuming a finished coroutine or a destroyed frame is undefined, and reference parameters may dangle across a suspension.
lessons.challenge: Make the awaiter ready so the coroutine never suspends, and guard the resume.
lessons.question: What does await_suspend returning false mean?
options: Do not suspend; resume the current coroutine immediately
Destroy the coroutine frame
Suspend and never resume
lessons.explanation: The bool form lets an awaiter decide at the last moment that the result is already available.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A ready awaiter skips await_suspend, so the handle is never stored and the body runs to final suspension before run returns.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: 'start suspended resumed 7 done=1\n'

lessons.title: A declaration is not a missing definition
body: Separate translation units can share declarations through headers. A declaration tells the compiler about an entity; a definition supplies the entity subject to linkage and one-definition rules.
Header guards or pragma once prevent repeated inclusion within a translation unit. They do not generally permit multiple non-inline external definitions across a linked program.

Put a non-inline function definition in one implementation file and share its declaration, or use an appropriately inline definition. Templates and inline entities have their own cross-translation-unit requirements.

lessons.question: Do header guards alone solve duplicate external definitions across translation units?
options: Only when the header extension is hpp
No
Yes
lessons.explanation: Guards affect preprocessing within each translation unit, while the ODR governs the linked program.
lessons.practiceAnswer: inline permits specified repeated definitions across translation units, provided the ODR requirements such as corresponding definitions are satisfied. It does not require machine-code inlining.

lessons.title: Measure the intended workload and verify the result
body: Algorithmic complexity models growth; measurement captures a particular implementation, machine, and workload. Both matter when choosing a data structure or optimization.

lessons.title: Sender/receiver operations own completion and cancellation state
body: Execution facilities compose asynchronous operations around an explicit completion protocol. A sender description, a connected operation state, and actual starting/completion are distinct concepts.

The operation state and resources borrowed by callbacks must live until the completion protocol permits release. Cancellation is a request with specified observation behavior, not proof that every operation has already stopped.

Route value, error, and stopped completions through one run identity and finalize exactly once. Request cancellation through the documented stop channel and defer resource release until the operation can no longer access them.

lessons.title: Inspect object bytes without breaking the aliasing rule
body: The aliasing rule in the core language lists the glvalue types through which an object may be accessed: its own type (with cv and signedness variations), char, unsigned char, and std::byte, among a few others. Reading a float through an unsigned integer lvalue is not on that list, so the access has undefined behavior even when the sizes match.

Copy the object representation instead. std::memcpy into a separate integer object is well defined for trivially copyable types and compilers usually lower a small fixed-size copy to a single register move. C++20 adds std::bit_cast for the same conversion as a constant-expressible value operation.

Optimizers use the rule to assume that stores through an int pointer cannot modify a float object, so a type-punned read can observe a stale value or be reordered. -fno-strict-aliasing disables that assumption on clang and GCC but does not make the program portable; fix the access instead of relying on a flag.

It only fails on big-endian machines
It accesses a float through an unrelated glvalue type, which the aliasing rule makes undefined
lessons.explanation: Matching sizes do not create a permitted access type. Copy the representation with memcpy or std::bit_cast.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The sign bit is set, the biased exponent is 128 and the fraction is zero, giving 0xc0000000 in IEEE 754 binary32. memcpy copies the representation without accessing the float through an unrelated type.

lessons.title: Optimizers may assume signed overflow never happens
body: When a signed arithmetic result is not representable, behavior is undefined. Compilers therefore treat expressions such as x + 1 > x as always true for int x and can delete overflow checks written after the arithmetic.

Check the operands before computing: for y > 0 the sum overflows exactly when x > max - y, and for y < 0 exactly when x < min - y. Those subtractions cannot overflow under their guards. Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N, and compiler builtins such as __builtin_add_overflow are another option on clang and GCC.

-fwrapv makes signed overflow wrap on clang and GCC, but it is a dialect flag, not standard C++. UBSan (-fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow) reports overflow at run time on exercised paths; it cannot prove that untested inputs are safe.
lessons.challenge: Extend the check to negative y and test INT_MIN + (-1).
lessons.question: Why may a compiler fold x + 1 < x to false for int x?
options: Signed overflow is undefined, so it may assume x + 1 does not wrap
Because int arithmetic saturates
Because the comparison is evaluated at compile time only
lessons.explanation: Assuming no undefined behavior, x + 1 is mathematically larger than x, so the comparison is false on every valid execution.
lessons.practiceAnswer: For negative y, min - y is representable and the sum underflows exactly when x is below it. No operation in the check itself can overflow.

lessons.title: Reading an indeterminate value is not a random number

lessons.title: Sanitizers turn silent undefined behavior into reports
body: AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) detects out-of-bounds and use-after-free accesses on heap, stack and globals. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (-fsanitize=undefined) checks operations such as signed overflow, invalid shifts and misaligned pointers. A clean sanitizer run only covers the executed paths and inputs. Sanitizers change memory layout and timing, so they complement tests, fuzzing and code review rather than proving absence of undefined behavior.

lessons.title: Removed C++98 facilities and their replacements

The replacements are not just renames. unique_ptr transfers ownership only by explicit move, so it cannot be silently emptied by copying the way auto_ptr was. std::shuffle takes a uniform random bit generator, which makes the randomness source and seed explicit.

lessons.title: Recognize C++17 to C++23 deprecations and their replacements

lessons.title: Named requirements carry semantic obligations
body: The library specifies named requirements such as Hash, Allocator and LegacyIterator. A type passed where a requirement is expected must provide the listed expressions and also satisfy semantic rules that the compiler cannot check.

For Hash, equal keys under the container equality predicate must produce equal hash values; the reverse is not required. C++20 concepts express the syntactic part of some requirements, for example std::forward_iterator, while named requirements still state the semantic part in prose.

A hash that ignores a field used by equality is valid but may collide heavily. A hash that uses a field equality ignores breaks the requirement and can put equal keys in different buckets, so lookups and duplicate detection fail.

h(a) == h(b)

lessons.practiceAnswer: The duplicate {1, 2} compares equal and hashes equally, so it is stored once. {2, 1} and {3, 4} are distinct keys.

lessons.title: Allocator propagation traits decide where storage lives after assignment
body: std::allocator_traits exposes propagate_on_container_copy_assignment, propagate_on_container_move_assignment and propagate_on_container_swap, plus is_always_equal. Containers consult them to decide whether the destination adopts the source allocator during assignment and swap.

std::allocator moves with the container and is always equal. std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator propagates on none of these operations, so a pmr container keeps its own memory resource; copy construction uses select_on_container_copy_construction, which yields the default resource for pmr.

When move assignment does not propagate and the allocators compare unequal, the container cannot steal the source buffer; it moves elements one by one into its own storage. Swapping containers with unequal, non-propagating allocators has undefined behavior.
lessons.challenge: Inspect the copy-assignment propagation trait of std::allocator instead.
lessons.question: Move assignment between pmr vectors with different resources: what happens?
options: The source buffer is always stolen

lessons.title: noexcept is a queryable contract that terminates when violated
body: A noexcept specification may be conditional: noexcept(expr) takes a constant boolean. The noexcept operator asks, without evaluating its operand, whether an expression is declared not to throw. Together they let a template promise exactly what its operations promise.

Containers use this information. vector reallocation calls std::move_if_noexcept, so a type whose move constructor may throw and that can be copied is copied during growth to keep the strong exception guarantee.
If an exception leaves a noexcept function, std::terminate is called and stack unwinding may not happen. Mark functions noexcept when failure is impossible or fatal, not to make code look faster.
lessons.challenge: Declare both Throwing move operations noexcept and predict the result.
lessons.question: What happens if an exception escapes a noexcept function?
options: It is undefined behavior that usually continues
std::terminate is called, possibly without unwinding the stack
The exception is converted to std::bad_exception and rethrown
lessons.explanation: The noexcept boundary is enforced at run time by termination; whether the stack is unwound first is implementation-defined.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The conditional specification is computed from both traits, so it becomes true only when both move operations are noexcept.

lessons.title: Function-local statics avoid initialization order dependencies
body: Variables with static storage duration are first zero- or constant-initialized; dynamic initialization follows. Within one translation unit, ordered dynamic initialization follows declaration order, but across translation units the order is unspecified, so one global constructor may read another global before it is initialized.

A function-local static is initialized the first time control passes through its declaration, and since C++11 that initialization is thread-safe. Returning it by reference from an accessor turns an ordering problem into an on-demand initialization. C++20 constinit requires constant initialization and rejects a dynamic initializer.

Destruction happens in reverse order of completed construction, so a static destroyed early can still be used by a later destructor. Long-lived registries are sometimes intentionally leaked; document that choice instead of relying on accidental order.
lessons.challenge: Add a third registrar object and predict the count.
lessons.question: Why does the accessor avoid the static initialization order problem?
options: Function-local statics are initialized before main in declaration order
The linker sorts globals by dependency
Its local static is initialized the first time control passes through the declaration
lessons.explanation: Initialization on first use guarantees the counter exists before any caller reads it, regardless of translation-unit order.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each global constructor calls the accessor, which initializes the local static on first use, so no constructor reads an uninitialized counter.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '2\n'

lessons.title: Inline namespaces version an ABI without changing spelling
body: Members of an inline namespace are also members of the enclosing namespace for lookup and specialization. lib::version names lib::v2::version when v2 is inline, so client source does not mention the version.

The inline namespace name is part of mangled symbols. If a library changes a type layout and moves it to a new inline namespace, objects compiled against different versions fail to link instead of silently mixing incompatible layouts. libc++ places std entities in std::__1 for this reason.

Only one version should be inline for a given name, or unqualified references become ambiguous. Inline namespaces do not fix ODR violations within one build; they make mismatches between separately built components visible.
lessons.challenge: Call the current version through its explicit name.
lessons.question: Why do inline namespaces help ABI versioning?
options: They let two layouts share one symbol safely
The version name is part of mangled symbols, so mismatched builds fail to link
They make every function inline
lessons.explanation: Mangling includes the inline namespace, so lib::v2::version and lib::v1::version are different link-time names.
lessons.practiceAnswer: lib::version and lib::v2::version name the same function. Qualifying with v1 selects the old version deliberately.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '2 1\n'

lessons.title: Select code with feature-test macros, not compiler names
body: Each library facility has a __cpp_lib_* macro defined in <version> and in its own header, and language features have __cpp_* macros predefined by the compiler. The values are dates, so a newer revision of a feature has a larger number. __has_include, standardized in C++17, checks whether a header can be included.

__cplusplus states the selected language mode, but a library can lag behind the compiler, and individual features are adopted separately. Testing the specific macro keeps a fallback correct across compilers and standard libraries.

A macro check only tells you what the implementation claims. Keep the fallback compiled and tested on at least one configuration, and avoid using __has_include alone as proof that the facility inside the header is enabled in the current mode.
lessons.challenge: Test for std::expected the same way while compiling as C++17.
lessons.question: Why test __cpp_lib_optional rather than only __cplusplus?
options: __cplusplus is not defined in C++17
Feature-test macros are evaluated at run time
A standard library can lack a facility even when the compiler accepts the language mode
lessons.explanation: Language mode and library support evolve separately; the facility macro reports the specific library feature.
lessons.practiceAnswer: std::expected is a C++23 facility, so its macro is not defined in C++17 mode and the fallback branch runs.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: 'optional 1\n'

lessons.title: Build a checked command-line integer parser
body: The CLI accepts separate base-10 integer arguments and prints their checked sum. A token must be consumed completely; whitespace and a plus sign are intentionally not accepted by the single-token grammar.

Both successful conversion and a stopping pointer at the end
A nonempty input alone

lessons.title: Design a checked value library
body: Amount stores signed 64-bit cents as a domain value. Its explicit constructor prevents accidental mixing with unrelated scalar quantities. It is a teaching money-like value, without currency conversion or financial rounding policy.

The rule-of-zero representation delegates ordinary copy and move behavior to its integer member. Addition checks the range before changing state and supplies a nonmutating operator+ through a value copy.
Boundary checks verify the strong failure behavior: a rejected operation leaves the original Amount unchanged. Signed overflow is never used as a test oracle.
The answer implements subtraction directly rather than negating the right operand, because negating the minimum signed integer would itself overflow.

options: Negate every right operand first
Check bounds before committing the new representation
Perform signed overflow and inspect the result
lessons.explanation: Check subtraction bounds before evaluating a-b. Commit the new representation only after the check succeeds, preserving value semantics and the strong failure guarantee.

lessons.title: Own a bounded generic container and its allocator
body: Ring allocates storage for a fixed maximum number of elements through a caller-provided memory_resource. Only occupied positions contain live T objects. The resource must outlive the ring.

Copying and moving the container are deliberately disabled; element moves and destructors must be nonthrowing. A full insertion rejects without consuming the supplied argument, while a successful construction commits the new size.
The test uses move-only owners, wraparound, rejection, empty and zero-capacity paths, and a counting upstream resource. Remaining elements are destroyed before storage deallocation.

This is not a standard-container implementation: it has no iterators, general allocator propagation, concurrent access, or support for throwing element moves. The answer adds a const non-owning front view whose lifetime is bounded by the next invalidating operation.
lessons.challenge: Add const T* front() const. Return nullptr when empty, preserve ownership, and verify that the view identifies the first element after wraparound.
lessons.question: What must outlive the allocator-backed Ring?
options: The memory_resource supplying its storage
Only the last popped element
No external object because PMR owns the resource
lessons.explanation: Return a pointer only to an actually constructed front element. The caller must not retain it across pop, destruction, or later slot reuse. The resource owns allocation policy while the ring owns element lifetimes.

lessons.title: Drain a bounded concurrent pipeline safely
body: The queue owns bounded pending integers and protects its closed state and contents with one mutex. pop waits on a state predicate; close wakes all consumers and allows queued items to drain.

Pipeline owns two workers and closes the queue before joining them. Its constructor also closes and joins partially created workers if thread construction fails, avoiding a teardown wait on an open empty queue.
finish is idempotent and rejects later submissions. Workers borrow the externally owned Pipeline only until finish joins them. Concurrent calls to finish are not supported.

Tests cover saturation without consumers, FIFO drain after close, empty waiter wakeup, repeated finish, idle destruction, and repeated parallel totals. No user callback runs on a worker, so final-owner destruction on that worker is deliberately outside this project interface.
lessons.challenge: Add a synchronized pending() snapshot to Queue. Test full, partially drained, and closed/drained states without using the snapshot as a check-then-act synchronization substitute.
lessons.question: What is the pipeline teardown order?
options: Close and notify the queue, then join workers before releasing state
Destroy the queue before joining
Detach all workers and release state immediately
lessons.explanation: Read size under the same mutex used for modifications. The snapshot is immediately stale when other threads can modify the queue; use try_push/pop themselves to perform atomic decisions.

lessons.title: Give each coroutine frame exactly one owner
body: Generator owns a suspended coroutine frame through a move-only wrapper. Its promise counts live frames, stores the current yielded int, and preserves exceptions for the next caller observation.
initial_suspend and final_suspend leave destruction to the wrapper. next refuses to resume a completed or moved-from handle, and value requires a current yield.

Early abandonment, full iteration, exception propagation, move construction, and move assignment all release frames through the same ownership path. The counters are scoped regression evidence, not a universal heap proof.

This generator is synchronous and confined to one thread. It does not implement asynchronous callback cancellation, scheduler integration, or shared concurrent resume; those require a more elaborate lifetime protocol.
lessons.challenge: Add range(first,last) with a half-open interval. Empty and reversed intervals must yield nothing; abandoning a range early must still destroy its frame.
lessons.question: Who destroys this generator frame after early abandonment?
options: The single owning Generator wrapper
Every copied coroutine_handle automatically
The caller of value()
lessons.explanation: The frame owns its by-value bounds, so it borrows no caller locals. The loop stops before incrementing past last-1, and the wrapper releases the frame on every exit path.
