lessons.title: Traverse memory in the order it is laid out
body: Caches move memory in fixed-size lines, commonly 64 bytes on x86-64; Apple silicon reports 128-byte lines. Accessing consecutive addresses reuses each fetched line and lets the hardware prefetcher stream ahead, while large strides tend to waste most of each line.

A two-dimensional grid stored row-major in one vector places each row contiguously. Iterating rows in the outer loop and columns in the inner loop walks memory sequentially; swapping the loops produces a stride of one full row per access.

Locality effects depend on data size relative to each cache level, the hardware, and what else runs. Small grids that fit in L1 show little difference. Measure with representative sizes and hardware counters before restructuring code.
lessons.challenge: Swap the loops so the traversal is column by column, and predict the result.
lessons.question: Why is row-by-row traversal of a row-major grid usually faster for large grids?
options: Consecutive accesses share cache lines and suit hardware prefetching
Because the compiler skips bounds checks only in row order
Because column order changes the arithmetic result
lessons.explanation: Both orders compute the same value; row order touches memory sequentially and uses each fetched line fully.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The sum is unchanged, but each inner step now jumps cols * sizeof(int) bytes. For grids larger than cache this tends to touch a new line on most accesses.

lessons.title: Structure of arrays streams only the fields a loop uses
body: An array of structures stores each record contiguously, which suits code that reads whole records. A structure of arrays stores each field in its own contiguous array, so a loop over one field reads only that field's bytes and is easier for the compiler to vectorize.

Padding also counts: a record of three doubles and an int occupies 32 bytes on LP64 targets, so a loop summing x reads 32 bytes per element in AoS form but 8 bytes in SoA form. Field order changes padding and therefore memory traffic.

SoA makes record insertion and whole-record access touch several arrays and keeps parallel arrays in sync by convention. Choose the layout from the dominant access pattern and measure; hybrid layouts (arrays of small field blocks) are common.
lessons.challenge: Sum the id column instead of x.
lessons.question: A hot loop reads only x from a million particles. Which layout moves fewer bytes through the cache?
options: SoA: about 8 bytes per particle instead of whole 32-byte records
AoS, because records are contiguous
They move the same bytes because sizeof is identical
lessons.explanation: In AoS form each fetched line also carries y, z, id and padding that the loop never uses.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The id array is contiguous on its own, so this loop reads only four-byte ids. The AoS record size is unaffected.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '32 6\n'

lessons.title: [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] are layout hints, not guarantees
body: Modern CPUs predict branch directions and speculatively execute ahead; a misprediction discards that work and typically costs on the order of tens of cycles. Branches that follow a pattern are cheap, while data-dependent branches on random input are expensive.

C++20 [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] attach to a statement or label and hint which path is more frequent, mostly influencing code layout and block ordering. They do not change program semantics or teach the hardware predictor anything at run time.

Wrong hints can make code slower, and profile-guided optimization usually does better than hand annotations. Measure with hardware counters (branch-misses with perf on Linux, CPU counters in Instruments on macOS) and keep hints on genuinely rare paths such as error handling.
lessons.challenge: Return zero for negative values instead of -1.
lessons.question: What does [[unlikely]] change about program semantics?
options: It removes the branch when the condition is false
Nothing; it is an optimization hint
It makes the branch evaluate lazily
lessons.explanation: Likelihood attributes affect optimization only. Correct programs behave the same with or without them.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The attribute only hints at frequency; the result changes because the returned value changed. 0 + 1 + 0 + 2 is 3.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '2\n'

lessons.title: final lets the compiler devirtualize calls
body: A virtual call normally loads the vtable pointer and calls through it, which blocks inlining. If the static type of the object expression is a class marked final, or the function is marked final, no further override can exist and the compiler may call the known function directly and inline it.

Devirtualization also happens when the dynamic type is visible, for example a local object, and link-time optimization can prove that a hierarchy is closed. Alternatives for hot paths include CRTP static polymorphism and std::variant with std::visit.

final is a design commitment: it forbids future derivation or overriding. The optimization is permitted, not guaranteed; check the generated assembly or optimization remarks before relying on it, and measure whether the call was hot.
lessons.challenge: Measure a side of five through the same final type.
lessons.question: Why may a call through const Square& be devirtualized when Square is final?
options: Virtual calls through references are never dynamic
No class can derive from Square, so the dynamic target of area is known
final makes area a static function
lessons.explanation: Without further derivation, the static type determines the final overrider.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The parameter type is const Square&. Because Square is final, Square::area is the only possible target and the call may be made directly.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '16\n'

lessons.title: Short strings fit inline: observing libc++ small-string storage
body: std::string implementations commonly keep short strings inside the object itself, avoiding a heap allocation. The standard does not require this or fix the inline capacity. libc++ on 64-bit targets uses a 24-byte string with 22 inline characters; libstdc++ uses a 32-byte string with 15.

capacity() reveals the policy: a default or short libc++ string reports 22. Once the content exceeds the inline buffer, the string allocates and capacity grows. Moving a long string transfers its heap buffer; moving a short string copies its inline characters.

The output of this example is libc++-specific; libstdc++ prints different numbers. Do not hard-code inline capacities in production logic, and remember that string_view or pointers into a short string refer to the string object itself, not to a stable heap block.
lessons.challenge: Assign exactly 22 characters to the short string and predict its capacity on libc++.
lessons.question: On libc++ with 64-bit pointers, how many characters fit in std::string without allocating?
options: 15 on every implementation
0, because std::string always allocates
lessons.explanation: libc++ uses 23 inline bytes including the terminator; libstdc++ uses 15 characters. The standard leaves this unspecified.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Twenty-two characters plus the terminator still fit in the inline buffer, so libc++ reports the same capacity and no allocation is needed.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '24 22 1\n'

requirements.support: Expected output is libc++-specific (Apple clang); libstdc++ reports a 32-byte string with 15 inline characters.

lessons.title: A monotonic buffer resource turns allocations into pointer bumps
body: std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource hands out memory by advancing a position in a buffer and never reuses freed memory. Allocation is a few instructions and deallocate does nothing; everything is released at once when the resource is destroyed or release() is called.

Pass a stack or preallocated buffer and an upstream resource. With std::pmr::null_memory_resource() as upstream, running out of the buffer throws std::bad_alloc instead of silently reaching the heap, which makes an allocation budget testable. pmr containers propagate the resource to nested pmr elements through uses-allocator construction.

Memory freed by growing containers is not reused, so repeated vector growth wastes old blocks; reserve up front. The resource is not thread-safe, and every object using it must be destroyed before the buffer goes out of scope.
lessons.challenge: Try to reserve 300 ints, more than the 1024-byte buffer, and report the failure.
lessons.question: What does deallocate do on a monotonic_buffer_resource?
options: It forwards the block to the upstream resource
Nothing; memory is reclaimed only by release() or destruction
It returns the block for reuse by the next allocation
lessons.explanation: Monotonic means the allocation position only moves forward; individual frees are ignored.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Twelve hundred bytes do not fit and the null upstream refuses, so bad_alloc is thrown. The following pushes still fit in the remaining buffer.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '28\n'

lessons.title: A benchmark must keep its work observable
body: Optimizers remove computations whose results are unused, hoist loop-invariant work, and fold constants. A timed loop that produces nothing observable may measure an empty loop. Feed inputs the compiler cannot predict and consume results, for example by accumulating a checksum that is printed or checked.

Use std::chrono::steady_clock, which never goes backwards; system_clock can jump when the wall clock is adjusted. Run warmup iterations to fault in pages and warm caches and predictors, repeat many samples, and report a median or distribution rather than one number.

Record compiler flags, hardware, CPU frequency behavior and input sizes. Timing values are not deterministic, so tests should check correctness and keep timing output out of compared stdout. Libraries such as Google Benchmark provide DoNotOptimize and statistics; still verify the result being timed.
lessons.challenge: Run five repetitions instead of three.
lessons.question: Why accumulate and print a checksum of the measured work?
options: So the optimizer cannot delete the computation as dead code
Because printing makes the loop run faster
Because steady_clock requires output
lessons.explanation: Only observable behavior must be preserved. An unused result lets the compiler remove the timed work.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each pass adds 2997 (142 full cycles of 0..6 plus 0..5), so five passes give 14985. steady_clock is monotonic, so the elapsed duration is never negative.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '8991 1\n'

lessons.title: Branchless selection trades a branch for data dependencies
body: A comparison yields a bool that converts to 0 or 1. Adding it counts matches without a conditional jump, and negating it gives an all-zero or all-ones mask for selecting a value with &. The work is the same for every input, so there is nothing to mispredict.

Compilers often emit conditional-select instructions (csel on arm64, cmov on x86-64) for simple ternaries already, so hand-written masks may not change the generated code. Inspect the assembly before and after.

Branchless code always computes both sides and lengthens the dependency chain. When the branch is predictable, a branch is often faster. Keep the readable version unless measurement on representative data shows a win.
lessons.challenge: Count and sum the non-negative values instead.
lessons.question: When does branchless code tend to win?
options: When the branch is almost always taken
When the branch depends on unpredictable data
Always, because branches are slow
lessons.explanation: A predictable branch costs little; branchless code pays for both sides on every element.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Zero now passes the test, so the count rises to four while the sum is unchanged. Both occurrences of the comparison are replaced.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '3 20\n'

lessons.title: Power-of-two masks and bit counts replace division and loops
body: For unsigned x and a power of two n, x % n equals x & (n - 1), because n - 1 masks the low bits. Ring buffers choose power-of-two capacities so index wrapping is a single AND. C++20 <bit> provides std::has_single_bit, std::bit_ceil, std::popcount, std::countr_zero and related functions.

These functions usually compile to single instructions where the target has them, such as a count-trailing-zeros instruction, and to short sequences otherwise. Compilers already rewrite unsigned % by a constant power of two, so the mask matters most when n is a runtime value.

The identity fails for signed negative operands: -3 % 8 is -3 in C++, while -3 & 7 is 5. Keep indices unsigned, assert the power-of-two precondition, and prefer the <bit> functions to hand-written loops.
lessons.challenge: Use a capacity of eight and predict every value.
lessons.question: For unsigned x, why does x & (n - 1) equal x % n only when n is a power of two?
options: Because & rounds toward zero
It holds for every n greater than one
Only then is n - 1 a mask of the low log2(n) bits
lessons.explanation: For n = 6, n - 1 is 0b101, which does not select a contiguous low bit range.
lessons.practiceAnswer: 45 is 0b101101; masking with 7 keeps 0b101. The popcount literal is unchanged, and eight has three trailing zero bits.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '13 13 5 4\n'

lessons.title: Memory-order cost differs between x86 and ARM
body: x86-64 has a strong (TSO) memory model: ordinary loads already behave like acquire and ordinary stores like release, so acquire and release atomics compile to plain moves; only sequentially consistent stores need an extra fence or exchange. ARMv8 is weaker and uses dedicated instructions such as LDAR or LDAPR for acquire and STLR for release.

Relaxed operations are still atomic and are the right choice for counters whose final total is read after a synchronizing operation. Release and acquire pair to publish ordinary data: everything sequenced before the release store is visible after an acquire load that reads it.

Code missing an acquire often appears to work on x86 because the hardware already orders it, then fails on ARM machines including Apple silicon. Reason from the C++ memory model, test on weakly ordered hardware, and use ThreadSanitizer; do not infer correctness from one architecture.
lessons.challenge: Count two thousand events before publishing.
lessons.question: Why can a missing acquire go unnoticed on x86 but fail on ARM?
options: ARM does not support atomics
x86 compilers ignore memory orders
x86 hardware already orders ordinary loads like acquire, while ARM may reorder them
lessons.explanation: The language bug exists on both; only the hardware reordering that exposes it differs.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The relaxed increments are sequenced before the release store, so the acquire load that sees true also guarantees every increment and the payload are visible.

lessons.title: Keep hot fields together and move cold data out of line
body: A hot path that touches only a few fields should not drag rarely used data through the cache. Hot/cold splitting keeps frequently accessed fields in a compact record and moves cold fields, such as descriptions and audit data, behind a pointer or into a parallel structure.

The same idea applies to code: marking error handling as cold or moving it into a separate non-inlined function keeps the hot instruction stream compact. Clang and GCC accept [[gnu::cold]] and [[gnu::noinline]] as extensions for that purpose.

Splitting adds an indirection and an allocation when cold data is needed, and it can complicate ownership. Measure the record size with sizeof, count how many hot records fit in a cache line on the target, and confirm the win on the real access pattern.
lessons.challenge: Store the cold data inline instead of behind a pointer.
lessons.question: Why move rarely used fields behind a pointer?
options: It removes the need to allocate cold data
It makes the cold fields faster to read
More hot records fit per cache line, at the cost of an indirection for cold access
lessons.explanation: The hot loop reads fewer bytes per record; cold access pays one extra load.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The inline Cold block adds a 24-byte libc++ string and 64 audit bytes, so the record grows from 32 to 112 bytes on LP64 libc++ and no longer fits a 64-byte line.

lessons.title: Count allocations by replacing global operator new
body: A program may replace the global operator new and operator delete. A replacement that increments a counter and forwards to malloc makes allocation counts observable in tests, which is more stable than timing for catching regressions such as a missing reserve.

vector growth multiplies capacity, so n push_back calls perform about log n allocations; libc++ and libstdc++ double from one. reserve(n) allocates once and later insertions within capacity never allocate.

Define the sized and unsized delete forms as well, since compilers call sized delete by default in C++14 and later. The counter is global and not thread-safe here; use an atomic for multithreaded tests, and remember that the standard library or the runtime may allocate on its own before main.
lessons.challenge: Reserve only fifty elements before the hundred insertions.
lessons.question: Why is reserve(100) followed by 100 push_back calls exactly one allocation?
options: reserve is only a hint that may be ignored
The reserved capacity covers every insertion, so no reallocation occurs
push_back always allocates one node per element
lessons.explanation: reserve guarantees capacity of at least n; insertions that do not exceed capacity do not reallocate.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Capacity 50 covers the first fifty insertions; the fifty-first grows to 100 (double the capacity), which holds the rest. Growth without reserve passes 1, 2, 4, ..., 128: eight allocations.
lessons.workedExample: Expected stdout: '8 1\n'

lessons.title: Your first program and the dotnet toolchain
body: C# is a statically typed language: the compiler checks every name, type and call before the program runs. The .NET SDK provides the compiler, the runtime and the dotnet command. A compile-time error means no program was produced; a runtime exception happens later, while a successfully compiled program executes.

Since .NET 10 you can run a single file directly: save hello.cs and run dotnet run hello.cs. Larger programs use a project: dotnet new console -o Hello creates Hello.csproj plus Program.cs, and dotnet run builds and runs it. dotnet build compiles without running, which is the quickest way to check your code. A file-based app can later become a project with dotnet project convert hello.cs.

The example uses top-level statements: the statements at the top of one file become the body of the program's entry point. The compiler generates the Main method for you. Only one file in a program may contain top-level statements. Older code shows the explicit static void Main(string[] args) form inside a class; both compile to the same kind of entry point.

Console.WriteLine writes text followed by a newline; Console.Write omits the newline. Statements end with a semicolon, and braces group statements into blocks. Identifiers are case-sensitive: console and Console are different names. // starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.

Check that you can explain three outcomes: the compiler rejected the code, the program threw an exception while running, or it ran and printed something unexpected. Each needs a different fix, and reading the exact diagnostic code (for example CS0103, a name that does not exist) is the first step.
lessons.solution:
Console.WriteLine("Ada");
Console.WriteLine(12 * 12);
lessons.challenge: Write a program that prints your name on one line and then the result of 12 * 12 on the next line.
lessons.question: What does dotnet build do that dotnet run also does, but without the final step?
options: Publishes a self-contained installer
Compiles the project and reports diagnostics without executing it
Executes the program without compiling it
lessons.explanation: run = build + execute. Use build when you only need the compiler's verdict.

lessons.practiceAnswer:

6 * 7 = 42

Worked answer for: Write a program that prints your name on one line and then the result of 12 * 12 on the next line.
Its output:

lessons.title: Variables and built-in types
body: A variable is a named storage location with a fixed type. int count = 3; declares an int and initializes it. var count = 3; asks the compiler to infer the type from the initializer; the variable is still statically an int and cannot later hold a string. Use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side and spell the type out when it is not.

The everyday numeric types are int (32-bit signed), long (64-bit), double (64-bit binary floating point) and decimal (128-bit base-10, used for money because 0.1 is exact). bool holds true or false, char holds one UTF-16 code unit such as 'A', and string holds immutable text. Literal suffixes choose a type: 10L is long, 1.5 is double, 1.5m is decimal, 1.5f is float.

C# never implicitly narrows. Assigning a long to an int or a double to an int needs an explicit cast such as (int)3.9, which truncates toward zero to 3. Widening conversions, such as int to long or int to double, are implicit because they cannot lose the magnitude.

Integer arithmetic silently wraps on overflow by default: int.MaxValue + 1 becomes int.MinValue. Wrap the expression in checked(...) or enable the CheckForOverflowUnderflow project option to throw OverflowException instead. Floating-point arithmetic does not throw; it produces infinity or NaN.

const declares a compile-time constant, such as const int Days = 7;. A local variable must be definitely assigned before it is read; the compiler rejects reads of a variable that might be unassigned (CS0165). Before relying on a number, check its type, its range and whether overflow should wrap or throw.
lessons.challenge: Store a price of 19.99 as a decimal and a quantity of 3 as an int, then print the total price and the total as an int after an explicit cast.
lessons.question: Why is decimal preferred over double for currency amounts?
options: It can store larger exponents than double
It stores base-10 fractions such as 0.1 exactly
It is faster than double on every CPU
lessons.explanation: double is binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. decimal uses base 10, so typical money values are exact.

lessons.title: Operators, precedence and evaluation
body: Arithmetic operators follow the operand types. 7 / 2 divides two ints and truncates toward zero to 3; 7 / 2.0 promotes to double and gives 3.5. % is the remainder and keeps the sign of the left operand, so -7 % 3 is -1. Promote deliberately rather than hoping the result type is what you meant.

Precedence decides grouping: *, / and % bind tighter than + and -, which bind tighter than comparisons, which bind tighter than &&, then ||. Use parentheses whenever a reader might hesitate. && and || short-circuit: the right side is evaluated only if needed, so s != null && s.Length > 0 is safe.

Increment and decrement have prefix and postfix forms. i++ yields the old value then increments; ++i increments then yields the new value. Compound assignments such as total += x read, combine and write back. Avoid using the same variable twice in one expression with side effects; it compiles, but readers struggle.

The conditional operator condition ? a : b chooses one of two expressions and evaluates only the chosen one. The null-coalescing operator a ?? b yields a unless it is null, and x ??= y assigns only when x is null. These are expressions, so they can appear inside other expressions.

Operands are evaluated left to right, then operators apply by precedence and associativity. When an expression mixes side effects (method calls, ++), check the evaluation order explicitly; when it mixes types, check which conversion C# applies before the operator runs.
lessons.challenge: Given int a = 17 and int b = 5, print the quotient, the remainder, and the exact quotient as a double rounded to 2 decimals.
lessons.question: What does 7 / 2 evaluate to in C#?
options: 4, because integer division rounds to nearest
3, because both operands are int
3.5, because division always produces a double
lessons.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero. Make one operand a double (7 / 2.0) to get 3.5.

lessons.title: Strings, interpolation and formatting
body: A string is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units. Methods such as ToUpper, Replace and Trim return new strings and never modify the original. Because of immutability, building a long string by repeated += in a loop copies repeatedly; System.Text.StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer instead.

Interpolated strings start with $ and embed expressions in braces: $"{name} is {age}". A format specifier follows a colon ({price:F2} for two decimals, {n:N0} for digit grouping, {x:X} for hex) and an alignment follows a comma ({word,-8} pads to 8 characters, left-aligned). Formatting uses the current culture unless you pass CultureInfo.InvariantCulture; the guide's checks run with invariant culture.

Escape sequences such as \n and \t work in regular literals. A verbatim literal @"C:\temp" treats backslashes literally. Raw string literals use three or more double quotes and can span lines without escaping quotes; the indentation of the closing quotes is removed from every line. Combine $ with a raw literal for templated text such as JSON.

Length counts UTF-16 code units, not user-perceived characters: an emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane uses two. Index with s[0] for a char, and use ranges such as s[1..4] (start inclusive, end exclusive) or s[^3..] for the last three characters.

Compare strings deliberately. == compares content ordinally for strings. For user-facing or case-insensitive comparisons pass a StringComparison, for example string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase). Check culture, case and length semantics whenever text crosses a boundary such as a file, a URL or a user.

options: Converts s in place
Throws unless s is mutable
Nothing; it returns a new upper-case string
lessons.explanation: Strings are immutable. Assign the result (s = s.ToUpper()) if you want the variable to refer to the new value.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
body: if (condition) { ... } else if (...) { ... } else { ... } runs the first branch whose condition is true. The condition must be a bool; C# does not treat 0 or null as false, so if (count) is a compile error. Always use braces for multi-line branches.

A switch statement selects a section by matching a value against case labels; each section ends with break, return, throw or goto case because C# forbids silent fall-through between non-empty sections. Several labels may share one section. Later stages replace many switch statements with switch expressions and patterns.

while (condition) checks before each iteration and may run zero times. do { ... } while (condition); checks after, so the body runs at least once. for (init; condition; step) packages a counter loop. foreach (var item in collection) visits each element of anything enumerable without manual indexing.

break leaves the innermost loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration of the innermost loop. To leave nested loops in C# 14, extract a method and return, or use a flag. C# 15 adds labeled break/continue, covered in the final stage.

A foreach loop variable is read-only, and the collection must not be modified while it is being enumerated (a List throws InvalidOperationException). Before writing a loop, check the termination condition, whether the body may run zero times and whether anything mutates the collection being walked.

options: while
foreach over an empty array
do ... while
lessons.explanation: do ... while tests its condition after the body, so the first iteration always runs.

lessons.title: Methods, parameters and overloading
body: A method packages a computation behind a name, parameters and a return type: static int Square(int x) => x * x; The => form is an expression body; a block body uses braces and return. A method returning void produces no value. In a file with top-level statements, methods declared at the bottom are local functions of the entry point.

Arguments are passed by value by default. For a value type such as int the method receives a copy, so assigning to the parameter does not affect the caller. ref passes the variable itself (the caller must initialize it), out requires the method to assign it before returning (the caller need not initialize it), and in passes a read-only reference, useful for large structs.

Optional parameters supply defaults (int retries = 3) and must come after required ones. Named arguments (Connect(host: "db", retries: 5)) document intent and allow skipping optional parameters. params int[] values accepts any number of trailing arguments; since C# 13 params also works with spans and other collection types.

Overloading lets several methods share a name if their parameter lists differ. The compiler picks the best match at compile time from the static argument types, preferring exact matches and then the most specific implicit conversion. Ambiguous calls are compile errors. A different return type alone does not create a distinct overload. Overloading applies to methods of a type; local functions cannot be overloaded, so a second local Describe is rejected with CS0128. Put overloads in a class, as the example does.

Static local functions (static int Helper(...)) cannot capture surrounding variables, which makes their inputs explicit. Before calling a method, check whether each argument is copied or passed by reference, and whether out results are valid only when a Try-style method returns true.

Read its incoming value first
Nothing; out parameters are optional

lessons.title: Reading input safely
body: Console.ReadLine() returns the next line of standard input without its newline, or null when input has ended. Its return type is string?, so with nullable reference types enabled the compiler warns if you use the result as if it were never null. Handling the null case is part of a correct program, not boilerplate.

Convert text to numbers with int.TryParse(text, out int value), which returns false instead of throwing on bad input. int.Parse throws FormatException for malformed text and OverflowException for out-of-range values; reserve it for input you have already validated. Parsing honours culture, so pass CultureInfo.InvariantCulture for machine-readable data like 3.14.

A typical input loop reads until null: while (Console.ReadLine() is string line) { ... }. The is string line pattern both checks for null and declares a non-null variable. Trim whitespace with line.Trim() and skip empty lines explicitly. The example is shown with the input lines 4, x, an empty line and 10, followed by end of input.

Command-line arguments arrive in args, which top-level statements expose as a string[]. Environment variables come from Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable, which also returns string?. Exit codes are set by returning an int from top-level statements or by Environment.ExitCode.
Treat all input as untrusted: check for end of input, empty lines, bad numbers and out-of-range values, and report problems on Console.Error so they do not mix with normal output.

null
An empty string
lessons.explanation: End of input is null; an empty line is the empty string. Code that confuses the two either loops forever or crashes.

lessons.title: Value types and reference types
body: Every C# type is either a value type or a reference type. Structs (including int, double, bool, DateTime) and enums are value types: a variable of a value type directly contains the value, and assignment copies it. Classes, arrays, strings, delegates and records declared with record class are reference types: a variable holds a reference to an object on the managed heap, and assignment copies the reference, not the object.

After var b = a; with a struct, a and b are independent: changing b.X leaves a.X alone. With a class, both variables refer to the same object, so a change through one name is visible through the other. This aliasing is the single most important thing to predict when reading C#.

Passing an argument copies the variable's contents too. A method that receives a class reference can mutate the shared object, but assigning a new object to its parameter only changes the method's local copy of the reference. To replace the caller's variable itself, the parameter must be ref.

Value types are not always on the stack: a struct field inside a class lives inside that object on the heap, and an array of structs stores the structs inline. Think in terms of copy semantics, not storage location. Small, immutable structs (marked readonly struct) are cheap to copy and avoid accidental mutation of a copy.

A classic bug is mutating a copy: list[0].X = 5 on a List<MutablePoint> struct is a compile error (CS1612) because the indexer returns a copy. Before mutating, check whether the expression gives you the original storage or a copy, and prefer immutable structs so the question rarely matters.

lessons.question: After var b = a; where a is a class instance, what does changing b.Name do?
options: Changes the object that a also refers to
Changes only b's private copy
Is rejected because a and b alias
lessons.explanation: Class assignment copies the reference, so both variables name the same object.

lessons.title: Nullable value types and nullable reference types
body: Value types cannot normally be null. int? (short for Nullable<int>) adds a null state: HasValue tells you whether a value is present and Value reads it, throwing InvalidOperationException if absent. GetValueOrDefault() and ?? supply fallbacks without throwing. Arithmetic on int? lifts: null + 1 is null.

Reference types could always be null, which caused NullReferenceException. With nullable reference types enabled (the default in new projects via <Nullable>enable</Nullable>), string means 'should never be null' and string? means 'may be null'. This is a compile-time annotation: the runtime type is the same, and the compiler produces warnings, not runtime checks.

The compiler tracks null-state through your code. After if (name is null) return; it knows name is not null. Dereferencing a maybe-null value produces warning CS8602; assigning a maybe-null value to a non-nullable variable produces CS8600. This guide's checks treat warnings as errors, which is a good habit for real projects too.

The null-forgiving operator name! tells the compiler 'trust me, this is not null' and suppresses the warning. It changes nothing at runtime, so a wrong ! still crashes. Prefer a check, a pattern such as is { } value, or ?. and ??: name?.Length ?? 0 yields 0 when name is null.

Public methods should still validate arguments at runtime, because callers may have nullable warnings disabled: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(arg). When you see ?, check whether the code handles the null path; when you see !, check what proves the value is present.

lessons.question: What does the null-forgiving operator x! do at runtime?
options: Throws ArgumentNullException if x is null
Converts null to a default value
Nothing; it only silences the compiler's nullable warning
lessons.explanation: Nullable reference types are compile-time analysis. ! removes a warning but adds no check.

lessons.title: Equality, identity and boxing
body: C# has two questions that look similar: are these the same object (identity), and do these represent the same value (equality)? ReferenceEquals(a, b) answers identity. a.Equals(b) and == answer equality, but what 'equal' means depends on the type.

For classes, the default Equals and == compare references. Records (stage 4) and most BCL types such as string override equality to compare contents, so two separately created strings 'abc' are ==. Structs get a default Equals that compares fields, but it can be slow (it may use reflection), so performance-sensitive structs implement IEquatable<T>.

If you override Equals, you must also override GetHashCode so equal objects produce equal hash codes; otherwise dictionaries and hash sets lose your objects. HashCode.Combine(a, b) builds a good hash. Implement == and != too, or users get reference comparison through the operator but value comparison through Equals.

Boxing happens when a value type is converted to object or to an interface it implements: the runtime allocates a heap object containing a copy. Unboxing ((int)obj) copies it back out and requires the exact type. Comparing two boxed values with == on object compares references, so (object)5 == (object)5 is false while Equals is true.

Boxing costs an allocation and the boxed copy does not track later changes to the original. Before comparing, check which equality a type defines and whether a value type is being boxed by an object or non-generic API; generics (stage 7) usually avoid boxing.
lessons.challenge: Make class Ticket value-equal by id: override Equals, GetHashCode, == and !=, then show that two tickets with id 7 are equal and that a HashSet<Ticket> holds only one of them.
lessons.question: Why must an override of Equals be accompanied by GetHashCode?
options: The compiler cannot generate Equals without it
GetHashCode decides reference identity
Hash-based collections assume equal objects have equal hash codes
lessons.explanation: Dictionary and HashSet look in the bucket chosen by GetHashCode before calling Equals; mismatched hashes hide equal keys.

lessons.title: Arrays, indices and ranges
body: An array is a fixed-length, zero-indexed block of elements of one type: int[] scores = new int[3]; creates three zeros, because new arrays hold each element type's default value (0, false, null). A collection expression int[] primes = [2, 3, 5]; creates and fills one. Arrays are reference types, so assigning an array variable aliases it.

Indexing checks bounds at runtime: scores[3] on a three-element array throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Length gives the element count. ^1 is an index from the end, so primes[^1] is the last element. A range a[1..3] creates a new array containing indices 1 and 2; the end is exclusive.

Multidimensional arrays int[,] grid = new int[2, 3]; are rectangular and indexed grid[row, col], with GetLength(0) and GetLength(1) for sizes. Jagged arrays int[][] are arrays of arrays whose rows may differ in length; each row must be created separately.

Array.Sort, Array.Reverse, Array.IndexOf and Array.Fill work in place. Array.Copy and CopyTo duplicate elements; Clone() makes a shallow copy (the elements of a reference-type array still alias the same objects). Use List<T> (stage 6) when the size changes.

A range on an array copies, while a range on a span (stage 10) is a view without copying. Before slicing, check whether you need an independent copy or a view of the same memory, and remember that an out-of-range index is a runtime failure, not a compile error.
lessons.challenge: Given int[] values = [3, 8, 1, 9, 4], print the last two elements using a range from the end, then rotate the array left by one in place and print it.
lessons.question: What does primes[1..4] produce for an int[] in C#?
options: Elements at indices 1 through 4 inclusive
A new array with the elements at indices 1, 2 and 3
A view sharing the original array's storage
lessons.explanation: Range ends are exclusive, and slicing an array allocates a copy; use AsSpan() for a non-copying view.

lessons.title: Enums and flags
body: An enum gives names to a set of integral constants: enum Status { Pending, Active, Closed }. By default the underlying type is int and members count up from 0. Enums make code self-documenting and let the compiler reject passing an arbitrary string where a status is expected.

An enum value is just its underlying number, so any int can be cast to the enum even if no member has that value: (Status)42 is legal. Validate input with Enum.IsDefined or Enum.TryParse(text, ignoreCase: true, out Status s) and handle unknown values in switches with a default arm.

ToString() returns the member name, which is convenient for logging but couples output to identifiers; renaming a member changes the text. Enum.GetValues<Status>() enumerates the members in numeric order.

A [Flags] enum uses powers of two so members can be combined with |: Permissions.Read | Permissions.Write. Test a flag with (value & Permissions.Write) != 0 or HasFlag. Include a None = 0 member and never use 0 for a real flag, because x & 0 is always 0.

When adding a member later, check every switch over the enum; the compiler only warns about missing cases in switch expressions without a discard arm. Treat enums read from files or networks as untrusted numbers until validated.
lessons.challenge: Define [Flags] enum Days with Monday..Sunday as powers of two, plus Weekend = Saturday | Sunday. Print whether Weekend includes Sunday and print Weekend itself.
lessons.question: Is (Status)42 legal when Status has only members 0, 1 and 2?
options: Yes; enums accept any value of the underlying type
No; it is a compile-time error
It throws InvalidCastException at runtime
lessons.explanation: Enums are named integers. Validate with Enum.IsDefined or TryParse and keep a default arm in switches.

lessons.title: Classes, constructors and static members
body: A class is a blueprint for objects: it declares fields (stored data), methods (behaviour) and constructors (initialization). new Account("Ada") allocates an object on the heap, runs the matching constructor and returns a reference. Members are private by default; mark the members other code needs as public.

A constructor has the class's name and no return type. Constructors can chain with : this(...) to avoid duplicating setup. If a class declares no constructor, the compiler supplies a public parameterless one; once you declare any constructor, that default disappears. Object initializers (new Account("Ada") { Limit = 50 }) set accessible properties after the constructor runs.

Primary constructors (C# 12) put parameters on the type declaration: class Account(string owner). The parameters are in scope throughout the class body. If a member uses one, the compiler captures it in a hidden field; it is not a property and stays mutable inside the class. Assign it to a readonly field or property when you want an explicit, immutable member.

static members belong to the type, not to an instance: Account.Count is shared by all accounts. A static constructor runs once before the type is first used. A static class contains only static members and cannot be instantiated; it is the home for helpers and, as you will see later, extension members.

this refers to the current instance and disambiguates a field from a parameter of the same name. Before adding state, check whether it belongs to each object (instance) or to the type (static), and whether a constructor leaves every field in a valid state.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite a Temperature class with a primary constructor (double celsius), a readonly Celsius property initialized from it, a computed Fahrenheit property and a static FromFahrenheit factory. Print 100 C in F and 212 F in C.
lessons.question: What happens to the compiler-supplied parameterless constructor once a class declares its own constructor?
options: It becomes private
It is no longer generated
It is still generated alongside yours
lessons.explanation: The implicit default constructor exists only when you declare none, so new Account() stops compiling once you add Account(string).

lessons.title: Properties, init, required and the field keyword
body: A property looks like a field to callers but runs accessor code. public string Name { get; set; } is an auto-property: the compiler creates a hidden backing field. Expression-bodied properties such as public bool IsEmpty => Count == 0; compute a value on each read. Prefer properties over public fields so you can add validation later without changing callers.

Accessors can have different accessibility (public int Count { get; private set; }). An init accessor allows assignment only during object creation, including object initializers and with expressions, then makes the property read-only. A required property must be set by every object initializer; forgetting it is error CS9035.

C# 14 adds the field keyword for field-backed properties: inside an accessor, field refers to the compiler-generated backing field. set => field = value ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value)); validates without declaring a separate private field. You may give a body to one accessor and leave the other as get;.

Because field is now a keyword inside accessors, an existing member actually named field must be written this.field or @field there. That is the C# 14 source-breaking risk to check when upgrading older code.

Property getters should be cheap and side-effect free; callers assume reading twice gives the same answer. Check that setters keep the object valid, that init/required express the construction contract, and that expensive work lives in a method whose name says so.

options: A new local variable created for each call
The compiler-generated backing field of that property
Any field named field declared in the class
lessons.explanation: field lets you add logic to an auto-property without declaring the backing field yourself.

lessons.title: Encapsulation, access modifiers and immutability
body: Access modifiers decide who can use a member. public: anyone. private: only the containing type (the default for members). protected: the type and its derived types. internal: any code in the same assembly (the default for top-level types). protected internal and private protected combine these. file (C# 11) limits a type to its source file.

Encapsulation means callers can change an object only through members that keep its invariants. A BankAccount with a public Balance setter cannot guarantee the balance never goes negative; one with a private setter and a Withdraw method that checks the amount can.

readonly fields can be assigned only in their declaration or a constructor. const values are compile-time constants baked into callers, so changing a public const requires recompiling every consumer; prefer static readonly for values that might change between versions.

Exposing a mutable collection breaks encapsulation even when the property is get-only: callers can still add or remove items. Return IReadOnlyList<T> (or a copy) and keep the List<T> private. Note that a read-only view is not a frozen copy; it reflects later internal changes.

Immutability makes objects easier to share across threads and to reason about. Before adding a setter or a public field, check which invariant could be broken through it and whether a method with validation, init or a new object would serve better.

options: Nothing; get-only makes the list immutable
Only read items, because the setter is missing
Add and remove items through the returned list
lessons.explanation: get-only stops callers replacing the reference, not mutating the object it refers to.

lessons.title: Inheritance, virtual dispatch and abstract classes
body: A derived class inherits the members of its base class: class Circle : Shape. C# supports single class inheritance (one base class) and multiple interface implementation. Constructors are not inherited; a derived constructor chains to a base constructor with : base(...), and the base part is initialized first.

A virtual member can be replaced with override in a derived class. Calls through a base-typed reference dispatch to the most derived override at runtime: Shape s = new Circle(1); s.Area() runs Circle.Area. That runtime choice is polymorphism. base.Describe() calls the base implementation from inside an override.

An abstract class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract members with no body that every concrete derived class must override. Use it when derived types share state or implementation. sealed on a class prevents further derivation; on an override it stops deeper overrides.

Declaring a member with the same name but without override hides the base member (the compiler warns CS0114 or CS0108; use new to say it is deliberate). Hidden members are chosen by the static type of the reference, not the runtime type, which surprises readers. Prefer override.

Calling a virtual method from a base constructor runs the derived override before the derived constructor has initialized its fields. Before designing a hierarchy, check whether composition or an interface would be simpler, and mark classes sealed unless they are designed for inheritance.

options: Whichever was declared last in the file
Circle.Area, chosen at runtime
Shape.Area, because s is declared as Shape
lessons.explanation: virtual/override dispatches on the runtime type; only hiding with new uses the static type.

lessons.title: Interfaces and type tests
body: An interface is a contract: a set of members that implementing types promise to provide. interface IShape { double Area(); } and class Circle : IShape. A type can implement many interfaces, which is how C# expresses 'can do' capabilities such as IComparable<T>, IDisposable and IEnumerable<T> without a shared base class.

Code written against an interface works with any implementation: a method taking IShape accepts circles, squares and test doubles. Depending on small interfaces rather than concrete classes makes code easier to test and change. Structs can implement interfaces too, but converting a struct to an interface type boxes it.

Explicit implementation (double IShape.Area() => ...) makes a member callable only through the interface, which resolves name clashes between two interfaces. Default interface methods (C# 8) give an interface member a body that implementers may override; use them to evolve published interfaces without breaking implementers. Static abstract members are covered with generic math in stage 7.

is tests a runtime type and can declare a variable (if (shape is Circle c)); as returns null instead of throwing when the cast fails; a direct cast (Circle)shape throws InvalidCastException. Prefer pattern-based is checks, and prefer virtual or interface members over long chains of type tests.

Before adding an interface, check that there are (or will be) multiple implementations or a testing seam; an interface for a single class adds indirection without benefit. Keep interfaces small and named for a capability.

lessons.title: Object members and operator overloading
body: Every type derives from object, which supplies ToString, Equals, GetHashCode and GetType. Override ToString to produce readable output for logs and debugging; interpolation and Console.WriteLine call it automatically.

A type can define operators as public static methods: public static Vector operator +(Vector a, Vector b). Overload operators only when the meaning is obvious (numbers, vectors, money). Some operators come in required pairs: == with !=, < with >, <= with >=.

Conversion operators define casts. An implicit conversion should never lose information or throw; an explicit one is for conversions that can. A Celsius to double conversion can be explicit to make the unit change visible at call sites.

C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment operators. Before C# 14, a += b always meant a = a + b, creating a new object. Now a class can declare an instance public void operator +=(Vector other) that mutates in place, which avoids allocations for large mutable types. Types without it keep the old behaviour.

Operators must not surprise readers: + should not have side effects, and an in-place += must leave the object consistent with what + would produce. Check that equality operators agree with Equals and that conversions say clearly whether they can lose data.

options: Make + and += have unrelated meanings legally required
Allow += on types that have no + operator only at runtime
Update the existing object in place instead of creating a new one
lessons.explanation: User-defined compound assignment lets mutable types avoid allocating a new result for every +=.

lessons.title: Records: value equality and non-destructive mutation
body: A record is a type designed to hold data. record Person(string Name, int Age); is a positional record: the compiler generates a constructor, init-only properties, value-based Equals/GetHashCode/==, a readable ToString and a Deconstruct method. record alone means record class, a reference type; record struct is a value type.

Two records are equal when they have the same runtime type and equal property values, even if they are distinct objects. This makes records natural for messages, DTOs, keys and results. Equality is shallow: a property holding a List<T> compares the list references, not the items.

Records are immutable by default (positional properties are init). The with expression creates a copy with some properties changed: older = person with { Age = person.Age + 1 };. The original is untouched. with also works on structs and anonymous types.

Records can declare extra members, override ToString, and inherit from other records (not from classes). A readonly record struct gives a small immutable value type with generated equality and no heap allocation. Positional record struct properties are mutable unless the struct is marked readonly.

Use a class when identity matters (two customers with the same name are still two customers) and a record when the data is the identity. Check collection-valued properties: either use an immutable collection or remember that equality and with copy only the reference.
lessons.challenge: Declare record Order(int Id, decimal Total, string Status). Create one, then use with to produce a shipped copy, and print both plus whether they are equal.
lessons.question: Two separately constructed record Person(string Name) objects with the same Name compare with ==. What is the result?
options: A compile error; records cannot use ==
true, because records compare property values
false, because they are different objects
lessons.explanation: Records generate value-based equality; ReferenceEquals would still be false.

lessons.title: Tuples and deconstruction
body: A tuple groups a few values without declaring a type: (string Name, int Score) best = ("Ada", 97);. Tuples are value types (System.ValueTuple), so assignment copies them. Element names are compile-time conveniences; the underlying fields are Item1, Item2.
Methods can return several values as a tuple: static (int Min, int Max) Range(int[] xs). That is often clearer than out parameters. When a grouping gets a name and behaviour, promote it to a record.

Deconstruction unpacks a tuple or any type with a Deconstruct method into variables: var (min, max) = Range(data);. Use _ to discard elements you do not need. Deconstruction also enables swapping without a temporary: (a, b) = (b, a);.
Tuples support == and != element by element, and they make convenient composite keys for dictionaries and switch expressions ((x, y) switch { (0, 0) => ... }).

Tuple element names do not participate in type identity: (int A, int B) and (int X, int Y) convert to each other silently. Check that positional order, not just names, matches when passing tuples between methods.
lessons.challenge: Write a method Stats(int[] xs) returning (int Count, double Mean) and deconstruct the result for [2, 4, 9], printing the mean with one decimal.
lessons.question: What does (a, b) = (b, a); do?
options: Sets both to b
Creates a new tuple but leaves a and b unchanged
Swaps a and b
lessons.explanation: The right-hand tuple is built first from the old values, then deconstructed into a and b.

lessons.title: Switch expressions and patterns
body: Pattern matching tests a value's shape and extracts parts of it. Patterns appear after is and in switch expressions: shape switch { Circle c => ..., Rect { Width: 0 } => ..., _ => ... }. A switch expression yields a value; arms are tried top to bottom and the first match wins.

Common patterns: type patterns (Circle c), constant patterns (0, null, "admin"), relational patterns (< 0, >= 90), logical combinators (and, or, not), property patterns ({ Status: "open", Total: > 100 }), positional patterns for deconstructable types (Point(0, var y)) and the discard _.

var patterns always match and capture the value. Parenthesized and nested patterns compose: { Address.City: "Paris" } uses an extended property pattern. is not null is the idiomatic null check because it cannot be changed by an overloaded ==.

The compiler checks switch expressions for exhaustiveness and warns (CS8509) when some input could match no arm; at runtime such an input throws SwitchExpressionException. It also rejects arms that can never be reached because an earlier arm subsumes them (CS8510).
Order arms from most to least specific and avoid _ when you want the compiler to tell you about a new case. Check for null explicitly: a type pattern never matches null.
lessons.challenge: Write a switch expression that classifies a (int Hour, bool Weekend) tuple as "sleep" (hour < 7), "brunch" (weekend and 7-11), "work" (weekday 9-16) or "free".
lessons.question: What happens at runtime when no arm of a switch expression matches?
options: The expression returns default
The first arm is used
A SwitchExpressionException is thrown
lessons.explanation: The compiler warns about non-exhaustive switches (CS8509); add arms or a discard to handle every input.

lessons.title: List patterns and slices
body: List patterns (C# 11) match sequences by element: [1, 2, 3] matches exactly that array, [first, ..] captures the first element of a non-empty list, [.., last] the last, and [_, _] any two-element list. They work on arrays, lists, spans and any type with an indexer and a Length or Count.

The slice pattern .. matches zero or more elements and can capture them with a var pattern: [var head, .. var tail] binds tail to the remaining elements (a new array for arrays, a slice for spans). Only one slice pattern is allowed per list pattern.
Elements are patterns themselves, so you can nest: [> 0, .., < 0] matches lists that start positive and end negative, and [string cmd, .. var rest] is a neat way to parse command-line style input.

List patterns combine well with recursion for teaching: Sum([]) = 0, Sum([var x, .. var rest]) = x + Sum(rest). Be aware that capturing the slice of an array allocates each time, so production code over large arrays should use spans or indexes.
Check the empty case first and remember the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis for list patterns is limited; keep a discard arm for inputs you did not anticipate.
lessons.challenge: Write IsPalindrome(char[] cs) using list patterns recursively: empty and single-element arrays are palindromes; otherwise compare first and last and recurse on the middle.
lessons.question: In [var first, .. var rest] applied to an int[], what is rest?
options: The second element only
A live view that changes with the original array
A new array holding every element after the first
lessons.explanation: Slices of arrays are copies; use spans if you need a non-allocating view.

lessons.title: Throwing and catching exceptions
body: An exception reports that an operation could not do what its name promises. throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(count)) stops the current method; the runtime unwinds the call stack looking for a matching catch block. If none is found, the process terminates with the exception's message and stack trace.

try { ... } catch (FormatException e) { ... } handles one exception type and its subclasses. Catch blocks are checked in order, so put specific types before general ones (the compiler rejects an unreachable catch, CS0160). Catch only what you can handle meaningfully; catching Exception everywhere hides bugs.

finally runs whether the try block completes, returns or throws, which makes it the place for cleanup. The using statement (stage 10) is a try/finally that calls Dispose. A return inside try still runs finally before the method returns.

Every exception carries Message, StackTrace and optionally InnerException. Wrapping a low-level exception (throw new ConfigException("bad config", e)) adds context while preserving the cause. Exceptions are expensive compared with normal returns, so do not use them for expected control flow such as parsing user input in a loop.

Common built-in types and their meaning: ArgumentException/ArgumentNullException/ArgumentOutOfRangeException (caller passed bad input), InvalidOperationException (object is in the wrong state), NotSupportedException, KeyNotFoundException, IOException. Check that the type you throw tells the caller what they did wrong.
lessons.challenge: Write ReadSetting(Dictionary<string,string> settings, string key) that throws KeyNotFoundException with a helpful message if the key is missing. Call it for an existing and a missing key, catching and printing the message.
lessons.question: When does a finally block run?
options: Only when no exception occurred
After the try (and any matching catch) whether it returned, threw or completed
Only when an exception was caught
lessons.explanation: finally exists for cleanup that must happen on every exit path.

lessons.title: Exception filters, rethrow and custom exceptions
body: An exception filter adds a condition to a catch: catch (HttpRequestException e) when (e.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound). If the condition is false, the catch is skipped and the search continues, and the stack is not unwound yet, so debuggers and crash dumps still see the original failure point.

Inside a catch, throw; rethrows the current exception and preserves its original stack trace. throw e; resets the stack trace to the current line, destroying the most useful diagnostic information; analyzers flag it (CA2200). To add context, throw a new exception with the original as InnerException.

Define a custom exception when callers need to catch a specific failure: derive from Exception (or a more specific base), name it with the Exception suffix, and provide the standard constructors (none, message, message plus inner exception). Add properties for data callers need, such as the invalid key.

AggregateException collects several exceptions, typically from parallel or task code; Flatten() and InnerExceptions let you inspect them. ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(e).Throw() rethrows an exception captured earlier, possibly on another thread, while preserving its trace; await does this for you.
Never swallow exceptions silently with an empty catch. Check that each catch either recovers, translates with the inner exception attached, or logs and rethrows with throw;.
lessons.challenge: Write a Retry(Func<int> action, int attempts) helper that retries only when the exception is a TimeoutException (use a filter) and rethrows anything else unchanged. Demonstrate it with an action that times out twice and then returns 7.
lessons.question: Why is throw; preferred over throw e; inside a catch block?
options: throw e; does not compile in C#
throw; also runs the finally block twice
throw; keeps the original stack trace
lessons.explanation: throw e; restarts the stack trace at the rethrow line, hiding where the failure began.

lessons.title: Guard clauses, the Try pattern and result values
body: Validate arguments at the top of public methods so bad input fails fast with a precise message. The throw helpers make guards one line: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(name), ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(name), ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegative(count) and ThrowIfGreaterThan(value, max). They capture the argument's name automatically via CallerArgumentExpression.

For failures that are expected and frequent, such as parsing user input or looking up an optional key, the Try pattern avoids exceptions: bool TryParse(string s, out T result). Annotate the out parameter with [NotNullWhen(true)] so nullable analysis knows the result is non-null when the method returns true.

A result type makes failure part of the return value: a record that holds either a value or an error. Callers must inspect it before using the value, which suits validation pipelines. C# 14 has no built-in union type, so a small record hierarchy or a Result<T> record is common; C# 15 unions (final stage) express this directly.

Choose deliberately. Exceptions: a bug or an unexpected environment problem the immediate caller cannot fix. Try pattern: a cheap yes/no with one result. Result value: several possible failure reasons the caller should handle and report.
Check that guards run before any state changes, so a rejected call leaves the object unchanged, and that the Try pattern never throws for ordinary bad input.
lessons.challenge: Write TryDivide(int a, int b, out int quotient) that returns false (instead of throwing) when b is 0, and use it for 9/3 and 1/0.
lessons.question: When is the Try pattern a better fit than throwing an exception?
options: When failure is an expected, frequent outcome such as invalid user input
When the failure indicates a programming bug
Whenever the method is public
lessons.explanation: Exceptions are for unexpected failures; Try methods make the common failure path cheap and explicit.

lessons.title: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
body: List<T> is a growable array: Add appends in amortized O(1), indexing is O(1), and Insert/RemoveAt in the middle shift elements in O(n). Count is the number of elements, Capacity the allocated size; when it fills, the list allocates a larger array and copies. Pass an initial capacity when you know the size.

Dictionary<TKey, TValue> maps keys to values with average O(1) lookup using the key's GetHashCode and Equals. The indexer dict[key] throws KeyNotFoundException for a missing key; TryGetValue returns false instead. Assigning through the indexer adds or overwrites, while Add throws on a duplicate key.

Keys must not change in ways that affect their hash while stored; a mutated key becomes unreachable. Strings and records make good keys. Supply a comparer for alternative equality, such as new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).

CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(dict, key, out bool existed) returns a reference to the value slot so counting with structs avoids a second lookup; for most code dict[key] = dict.GetValueOrDefault(key) + 1 is clear enough. Dictionary enumeration order is not guaranteed; sort keys when output order matters.
Before choosing, check the operations you perform most often: indexed access and appends suit List; lookups by key suit Dictionary. Check missing-key behaviour on every read.

lessons.question: What does dict[key] do when the key is absent and you are reading?
options: Throws KeyNotFoundException
Returns default(TValue)
Adds the key with a default value
lessons.explanation: Reading through the indexer requires the key; use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault for optional keys.

lessons.title: Sets, queues, stacks and priority queues
body: HashSet<T> stores unique elements with O(1) average Add, Remove and Contains; Add returns false for a duplicate. Set operations (UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, IsSubsetOf) modify the set in place. SortedSet<T> keeps elements ordered at O(log n) per operation.

Queue<T> is first-in first-out: Enqueue, Dequeue, Peek. Stack<T> is last-in first-out: Push, Pop, Peek. Both throw InvalidOperationException when empty; TryDequeue and TryPop avoid that. A queue drives breadth-first search; a stack drives depth-first search and undo histories.

PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> dequeues the element with the smallest priority first (a min-heap). Enqueue and dequeue are O(log n). Elements with equal priority come out in no guaranteed order, so add a tie-breaker to the priority (for example a tuple of priority and sequence number) when stability matters.
LinkedList<T> offers O(1) insertion and removal at a known node but poor cache behaviour; it is rarely the fastest choice in practice. Measure before reaching for it.
Check empty-collection behaviour before every Dequeue, Pop or Peek, and check whether ties in a priority queue need a deterministic order.
lessons.challenge: Use a Queue to do a breadth-first search on the graph a->[b,c], b->[d], c->[d,e], d->[], e->[] starting at a, printing nodes in visit order without repeats.
lessons.question: Which item does PriorityQueue<TElement, int> dequeue first?
options: The element with the largest priority value
The element with the smallest priority value
The element enqueued first
lessons.explanation: It is a min-heap; ties are not ordered, so add a sequence number to the priority for stability.

lessons.title: Collection expressions, immutable and frozen collections
body: Collection expressions (C# 12) create collections with one syntax for many target types: int[] a = [1, 2];, List<int> l = [1, 2];, Span<int> s = [1, 2];, ImmutableArray<int> im = [1, 2];. The spread element ..other inlines another sequence: [0, ..a, 9]. The target type decides what is built, so the same expression can produce an array or a list.

Immutable collections (System.Collections.Immutable) never change after creation; operations such as Add return a new collection that shares structure with the old one. They are safe to share between threads and to hand out from APIs without defensive copies. Use builders (ImmutableList.CreateBuilder<T>()) when producing many items.

Frozen collections (FrozenDictionary, FrozenSet, .NET 8+) are read-only and optimized for lookup speed at the cost of slower creation. Create them once with ToFrozenDictionary() for configuration or lookup tables read many times.

Read-only interfaces (IReadOnlyList<T>, IReadOnlyDictionary<K,V>) describe what a caller may do, not whether the data can change; the producer may still mutate the underlying list. Immutable and frozen types guarantee the data cannot change.

Choose by the guarantee you need: a read-only view for encapsulation, an immutable collection for safe sharing with occasional updates, a frozen collection for build-once/read-many lookup. Check that 'immutable' items do not themselves contain mutable objects.

lessons.question: What does ImmutableList<T>.Add return?
options: The same list instance with the element appended
A new list containing the extra element; the original is unchanged
void, after mutating the list
lessons.explanation: Immutable collections return new versions that share structure with the old one.

lessons.title: IEnumerable, enumerators and modification during iteration
body: foreach works with anything that has a GetEnumerator() method; normally that means implementing IEnumerable<T>. The enumerator exposes Current and MoveNext(). foreach calls MoveNext until it returns false, and disposes the enumerator at the end.

IEnumerable<T> is the most general sequence contract: it promises only forward iteration. ICollection<T> adds Count, Add and Remove; IList<T> adds indexing. Accept the most general interface your method needs (often IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyList<T>) and return the most specific useful type.

Changing a List<T> or Dictionary while enumerating it invalidates the enumerator: the next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException ('Collection was modified'). To remove items, iterate over a copy, iterate backwards with an index, or use RemoveAll(predicate). Dictionary does allow Remove during enumeration since .NET Core 3.0, but not additions.
Some enumerables are single-use or lazy (a LINQ query, a file reader); enumerating twice may repeat expensive work or produce different results. Stage 9 covers this in depth.
Before mutating inside a loop, check whether you are enumerating the same collection. Prefer RemoveAll, building a new collection, or an index-based loop that accounts for shifting indices.

lessons.question: What happens if you Add to a List<T> while a foreach over the same list is running?
options: The loop restarts from the beginning
The next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException
The new item is silently skipped
lessons.explanation: List enumerators check a version counter; any structural change invalidates them.

lessons.title: Generic types and methods
body: Generics let you write a type or method once and use it with many types while keeping static type checking. List<int> and List<string> are constructed from the generic definition List<T>; T is a type parameter. Without generics you would use object and lose type safety, pay for boxing and need casts.

A generic method declares its own type parameters: static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>. The compiler usually infers the type argument from the arguments, so Max(3, 7) means Max<int>(3, 7). Inference uses only arguments, not the return type.

In .NET, generics are reified: the runtime knows List<int> and List<string> are different types, and value-type instantiations get specialized machine code with no boxing. typeof(T) and default(T) work at runtime. default(T) is 0 for numbers, null for reference types and a zeroed struct otherwise.
Static fields in a generic type exist once per closed type: Counter<int>.Count and Counter<string>.Count are separate. This is useful for per-type caches.
Prefer generics whenever the algorithm does not care about the element type. Check that default(T) is a meaningful value for your algorithm, especially when T may be a non-nullable value type.

lessons.question: Does List<int> box its integers?
options: Yes; generics always store object references
Only when the list grows beyond its capacity
No; .NET generates specialized code for value-type instantiations
lessons.explanation: Reified generics keep List<int> storing raw ints, unlike the old non-generic ArrayList.

lessons.title: Constraints
body: A constraint restricts which types may be used for a type parameter and, in exchange, lets the generic code use their members. where T : IComparable<T> allows a.CompareTo(b). Without constraints, only members of object are available on a T.

The common constraints: class (reference type), class? (nullable reference type allowed), struct (non-nullable value type), notnull, unmanaged (a value type with no references, usable with pointers and spans of bytes), new() (has a public parameterless constructor), a base class, one or more interfaces, and another type parameter (where TDerived : TBase).

where T : allows ref struct (C# 13) lets a generic method accept ref struct types such as Span<T>; the compiler then forbids operations that would box or store T on the heap. The BCL uses it for APIs like IEnumerable-style helpers over spans.

Constraints are checked at compile time where the generic is used: Max(new object(), new object()) is rejected because object does not implement IComparable<object> (CS0311). Nothing is checked at runtime, so constraints cost nothing.

Add the weakest constraints that let the code compile, and prefer interface constraints to base-class constraints. Check that a new() constraint really is needed; a factory delegate is often more flexible.

lessons.question: Why does a generic method need where T : IComparable<T> before calling a.CompareTo(b)?
options: Because CompareTo is checked at runtime
Because value types cannot implement interfaces otherwise
Without the constraint the compiler only knows T has object's members
lessons.explanation: Constraints are the compiler's evidence about what T can do; they cost nothing at runtime.

lessons.title: Covariance and contravariance
body: Variance answers: if Cat derives from Animal, can a Thing<Cat> be used where a Thing<Animal> is expected? For most generic types the answer is no; List<Cat> is not a List<Animal>, because you could then add a Dog to a list of cats.

An interface or delegate type parameter marked out is covariant: it only produces values. IEnumerable<out T> lets IEnumerable<Cat> convert to IEnumerable<Animal>, which is safe because you can only read animals out of it. Func<out TResult> is covariant in its result.

A type parameter marked in is contravariant: it only consumes values. IComparer<in T> and Action<in T> let an Action<Animal> be used where an Action<Cat> is needed: something that can handle any animal can certainly handle a cat.

Variance only applies to interfaces and delegates, only to reference-type arguments (an IEnumerable<int> is not an IEnumerable<object>), and the compiler enforces that out parameters appear only in output positions (CS1961). Arrays are covariant for historical reasons, which is unsafe: storing the wrong type throws ArrayTypeMismatchException at runtime.
When an assignment between generic types fails to compile, check whether the type parameter is only read (could be out) or only written (could be in); if it is both, invariance is protecting you.

lessons.title: Static abstract members and generic math
body: Interfaces can declare static abstract members (C# 11), which implementing types must provide as static members. Generic code constrained to such an interface can call them through the type parameter: T.Zero, T.Parse(text, null), or operators like a + b. This makes 'factory' and 'operator' contracts possible without instances.

.NET uses this for generic math. INumber<T> and its smaller pieces (IAdditionOperators<TSelf, TOther, TResult>, IAdditiveIdentity<TSelf, TResult>, IComparisonOperators, IParsable<TSelf>) are implemented by all built-in numeric types. One Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T>) where T : INumber<T> works for int, double, decimal and BigInteger.

Your own types can participate: a Money or Vector struct implementing IAdditionOperators<Money, Money, Money> and IAdditiveIdentity<Money, Money> works with any algorithm written against those interfaces. Constrain to the smallest interface the algorithm needs.

The TSelf pattern (where TSelf : IThing<TSelf>) lets the interface refer to the implementing type. Static virtual members (with a default body) are also allowed. C# 15 adds non-virtual static interface members, covered in the final stage.

Generic math code is compiled per value type, so it runs as fast as hand-written code. Check overflow behaviour: T.CreateChecked(x) throws when a value does not fit, CreateSaturating clamps and CreateTruncating wraps.

lessons.question: What lets generic code write T.AdditiveIdentity or a + b for a type parameter T?
options: Marking the method unsafe
Constraining T to interfaces with static abstract members
Casting T to dynamic
lessons.explanation: Static abstract interface members expose operators and static factories to generic code at compile time.
