lessons.title: Delegates, Func and Action
body: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method: a value you can store, pass and invoke. Func<int, int> square = x => x * x; holds a function from int to int. Func<..., TResult> returns a value; Action<...> returns void; Predicate<T> is Func<T, bool> with an older name. Custom delegate types (delegate bool Validator(string s);) add a meaningful name.

A delegate can refer to a static method, an instance method (it then also holds the target object) or a lambda. Passing behaviour as a parameter is how List.Sort(comparison), LINQ's Where(predicate) and callbacks work.

Delegates are multicast: += combines several methods into an invocation list called in order. For a Func, only the last return value is kept, so multicast is mainly useful for Action and events. -= removes the last matching entry and can leave the variable null once nothing remains, so its type should be nullable (Action?). Invoking a null delegate throws NullReferenceException; use handler?.Invoke(...).

Method group conversion lets you pass a method name directly: numbers.Select(int.Parse) or Run(Log). Since C# 10, lambdas and method groups have a 'natural type', so var twice = Twice; infers Func<int, int>. That inference needs exactly one candidate: var parse = int.Parse; is rejected (CS8917) because int.Parse has several overloads, although passing it where a Func<string, int> is expected works.
Delegates hold strong references to their targets. Before storing a delegate in a long-lived place (a static field, a cache, an event on a long-lived object), check what object it keeps alive.
lessons.challenge: Write Compose(Func<int,int> f, Func<int,int> g) that returns a function computing g(f(x)). Compose add-one with double and print the result for 3, then compose them in the other order.
lessons.question: What does a multicast Func<int> return when invoked?
options: The sum of all results
The return value of the last method in its invocation list
An array of every method's result
lessons.explanation: All methods run in order, but only the final result is returned; multicast suits Action and events.

lessons.title: Lambdas, closures and captured variables
body: A lambda can use variables from its enclosing scope; the lambda plus those variables is a closure. C# captures variables, not values: the compiler moves captured locals into a hidden class instance shared by the method and the lambda. A later change to the variable is visible to the lambda, and the lambda can change it too.

foreach gives each iteration a fresh loop variable, so lambdas created in a foreach capture different variables. A for loop has one counter variable for the whole loop: every lambda captures the same i and sees its final value. Copy it into a local inside the body (int copy = i;) to capture per-iteration values.

Capturing allocates the closure object and keeps captured variables (and anything they reference) alive as long as the delegate lives. A static lambda (static x => x * 2) cannot capture, which the compiler enforces (CS8820); use it on hot paths to guarantee no hidden allocation and pass state explicitly instead.

Lambdas can declare parameter types, attributes and a return type (int (string s) => s.Length), use discards ((_, _) => 0), and have default parameter values (C# 12). C# 14 allows modifiers like out, ref, in and scoped on implicitly typed lambda parameters: TryParse<int> p = (text, out result) => int.TryParse(text, out result);.
Check what each lambda captures, whether it captures a shared loop counter, and whether storing the delegate extends the lifetime of large objects.
lessons.challenge: Write MakeAccumulator(int start) returning a Func<int,int> that adds its argument to a running total captured in a closure. Show that two accumulators keep independent totals.

options: 0, 1 and 2
A compile error because i is out of scope
3, 3 and 3
lessons.explanation: A for loop has one i shared by every closure; foreach creates a fresh variable per iteration.

lessons.title: Events and the event pattern
body: An event is a delegate field wrapped so that outside code can only subscribe (+=) and unsubscribe (-=); only the declaring class can raise it or reset it. public event EventHandler<OrderPlaced>? Placed; declares one. This prevents subscribers from clearing each other's handlers or raising the event themselves.

The .NET event pattern uses EventHandler<TEventArgs>, a delegate taking (object? sender, TEventArgs e). Event data can be any type; a record is a neat choice. Raise with Placed?.Invoke(this, data); which copies the delegate reference first, so a concurrent unsubscribe cannot cause a null reference between the check and the call.

Handlers run synchronously, in subscription order, on the thread that raises the event. If a handler throws, later handlers do not run and the exception propagates to the raiser. Long work in a handler delays the publisher.

Custom add/remove accessors let a type control storage, for example to forward subscriptions to an inner object. C# 14 allows partial events: one declaration defines the event and another, often generated, implements its accessors.

Check that every subscription has a matching unsubscription when the subscriber's lifetime is shorter than the publisher's, and that handlers do not assume they run in a particular order unless the publisher documents it.
lessons.challenge: Add a Thermostat class with an event EventHandler<double>? TooHot raised when Set(double celsius) exceeds 30. Subscribe a handler that prints the reading, then set 25 and 31.
lessons.question: What can code outside the declaring class do with a public event?
options: Raise it by invoking it directly
Assign null to clear every handler
Only subscribe with += and unsubscribe with -=
lessons.explanation: The event keyword restricts outside access to add and remove; raising and resetting stay private.

lessons.title: Event subscriptions and object lifetime
body: A publisher's event holds a delegate, and the delegate holds a strong reference to the subscriber object whose method it calls. If a long-lived publisher (a static event, an application-wide service, a timer) keeps that subscription, the subscriber can never be garbage collected, even after everything else has forgotten it. This is the most common managed-memory leak in C# programs.

The example shows it deterministically. A Window subscribes to a long-lived Clock and is then dropped. A WeakReference observes whether the window object is still alive after a full, blocking garbage collection. While subscribed, it survives; after unsubscribing, it is collected.

The window is created inside a separate non-inlined method so no local variable in the caller keeps it reachable; debug builds otherwise extend local lifetimes to the end of a method. GC.Collect() and GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers() are used only to make the demonstration observable; production code should not call them.

Fixes, in order of preference: unsubscribe when the subscriber's lifetime ends, usually in Dispose (stage 10) so a using guarantees it; return an IDisposable subscription token from the publisher so callers cannot forget the matching -=; or use a weak-event pattern for frameworks where explicit unsubscription is impractical. Unsubscribing requires the same delegate instance, so store a lambda in a field if you need to remove it later.
When a subscriber lives shorter than its publisher, check where its subscription ends. Static events deserve special suspicion because their publisher lives for the whole process.

lessons.question: Why can a subscriber stay in memory after the rest of the program drops it?
options: The publisher's event delegate still references the subscriber
Events pin objects so the GC cannot move them
The finalizer queue keeps all subscribers
lessons.explanation: Delegates hold their target strongly, so a longer-lived publisher keeps subscribers reachable until they unsubscribe.

lessons.title: Iterators with yield
body: An iterator method returns IEnumerable<T> (or IEnumerator<T>) and uses yield return to produce elements one at a time. The compiler turns the method into a state machine. Nothing in the body runs when you call the method; it runs piece by piece as the caller enumerates, pausing at each yield return and resuming on the next MoveNext.

yield break ends the sequence. Iterators can be infinite (while (true) yield return next;) because the caller decides how many elements to take. finally blocks in an iterator run when enumeration completes or when the foreach loop exits early and disposes the enumerator.

Because execution is deferred, argument validation inside an iterator also happens late: ReadLines(null) does not throw until the first MoveNext. The standard fix is a non-iterator public method that validates and then returns a call to a private (or local) iterator function.
Iterators cannot have ref, out or in parameters, and cannot yield inside a catch block. Since C# 13 they may contain ref struct locals and unsafe blocks as long as they do not cross a yield.
Check whether the caller may stop early (put cleanup in finally), whether validation should be eager, and whether enumerating twice re-runs side effects.

lessons.question: When does the body of an iterator method start running?
options: Only after the whole sequence has been requested
On the first MoveNext call of an enumerator, not when the method is called
Immediately when the method is called
lessons.explanation: Iterators are lazy state machines; that is why validation inside them is deferred too.

lessons.title: LINQ and deferred execution
body: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) is a set of extension methods on IEnumerable<T> in System.Linq: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy and many more. Most return a new lazy sequence that remembers the source and the operation. No elements are processed until something enumerates the query: a foreach, ToList(), Count(), First() and so on.

Deferred execution means the query sees the source as it is at enumeration time, not at definition time. Add an item to the list after building the query and the query includes it. Captured variables are also read at enumeration time.

Each enumeration re-runs the whole pipeline. Enumerating a query twice (for example Count() then foreach) does the work twice and repeats side effects in lambdas; with a source that reads a file or a network stream it may even return different data. Materialize once with ToList() or ToArray() when you need several passes or a stable snapshot.

Operators differ: streaming operators (Where, Select, Take) process one element at a time; buffering operators (OrderBy, GroupBy, Reverse) must read the whole input before producing the first result; immediate operators (Count, Sum, ToList, First) run the query at once.

Analyzers warn about possible multiple enumeration of an IEnumerable<T> parameter. Check where each query is enumerated and how many times, and decide deliberately between a lazy view and a materialized snapshot.

options: Never; Count reads a stored length
Twice: each enumeration re-runs the pipeline
Once, because LINQ caches results
lessons.explanation: Queries are recipes, not results. Materialize with ToList when you need several passes.

lessons.title: Filtering, projection, ordering, grouping and joins
body: Where filters, Select projects each element (optionally with its index), and SelectMany flattens a sequence of sequences. OrderBy/OrderByDescending sort by a key, ThenBy adds tie-breakers; LINQ sorting is stable. Order() and OrderDescending() (.NET 7) sort by the elements themselves.

GroupBy(key) produces IGrouping<TKey, TElement> objects, each with a Key and its elements. ToDictionary and ToLookup build indexes; ToDictionary throws on duplicate keys while ToLookup allows several values per key.

Join(inner, outerKey, innerKey, result) is an inner join that matches elements with equal keys using hashing. GroupJoin gives each outer element its group of matches. .NET 10 adds LeftJoin and RightJoin, so an outer join no longer needs the GroupJoin + SelectMany + DefaultIfEmpty pattern; unmatched elements get null/default for the other side.

Query syntax (from c in customers where c.Active orderby c.Name select c.Name) compiles to the same method calls. It reads well for joins and let clauses; method syntax covers every operator. Mix them freely.
Check sort keys for ties, choose ToLookup when keys repeat, and in outer joins check how the code handles the missing side.

lessons.title: Aggregation and the newer LINQ operators
body: Aggregates reduce a sequence to one value: Count, Sum, Average, Min, Max and the general Aggregate(seed, (acc, x) => ...). Min/Max/Average on an empty sequence of non-nullable numbers throw InvalidOperationException; check Any() first, or use DefaultIfEmpty or a nullable projection.

Element operators pick one item: First/Last/Single throw when nothing (or, for Single, more than one item) matches; the OrDefault variants return default, and since .NET 6 accept the default value to use. MaxBy/MinBy return the element with the largest or smallest key rather than the key itself.

Set-like and shaping operators: Distinct, DistinctBy(key), Union, Intersect, Except (with ...By variants), Chunk(size) for batches, Zip for pairing sequences, Take/Skip and their While forms, plus Take(range) such as Take(^3..).

Newer operators replace common GroupBy patterns: CountBy(key) and AggregateBy(key, seed, func) (.NET 9) return key/value pairs without building groups, and Index() (.NET 9) pairs each element with its position. They are cheaper and clearer for frequency counts and per-key totals.
Before calling an aggregate, check what happens on an empty input and whether duplicates should count. Prefer Any() to Count() > 0, which may enumerate everything.

lessons.title: IQueryable and expression trees
body: LINQ has two worlds. IEnumerable<T> operators take delegates and run your lambdas in memory. IQueryable<T> operators take Expression<Func<...>>: the compiler turns the lambda into a data structure describing the code, so a provider such as Entity Framework Core can translate it to SQL or another query language.

The same lambda text can become either a delegate or an expression tree depending on the target type. Func<int, bool> f = x => x > 2; compiles to code; Expression<Func<int, bool>> e = x => x > 2; compiles to a tree with a Parameter, a Constant and a GreaterThan node that you can inspect, rewrite or compile with e.Compile().

Providers can only translate what they understand. Calling your own C# method inside a query is fine in memory but a database provider throws at runtime because it cannot turn the method into SQL. Expression lambdas also cannot contain statement bodies, assignments or some newer syntax.

Switching from IQueryable to IEnumerable with AsEnumerable() moves the rest of the query into memory: filtering after that point downloads every row first. Keep filters and projections on the queryable side when a database is involved.
Check the static type of a query variable: IQueryable<T> means the predicate becomes data for a provider, IEnumerable<T> means it runs as your code, possibly after fetching everything.

A compiled delegate identical to Func<int, bool>

lessons.explanation: Expression trees are data a provider can inspect and translate; Compile() turns them into a delegate.

lessons.title: The managed heap and garbage collection
body: Objects of reference types are allocated on the managed heap. You never free them; the garbage collector (GC) periodically finds objects that are no longer reachable from roots (static fields, local variables of running methods, CPU registers, GC handles) and reclaims their memory. Reachability, not scope or reference counting, decides lifetime, so cycles of objects that reference each other are still collected.

The heap is generational. New objects start in generation 0, which is collected often and cheaply because most objects die young. Survivors are promoted to generation 1 and then 2. Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the large object heap, collected with generation 2. GC.GetGeneration(obj) shows where an object currently lives.

Collections compact memory by moving surviving objects, which is why ordinary code cannot hold raw addresses of managed objects without pinning them (fixed, stage 13). Allocation itself is cheap (a pointer bump); the cost comes from collections, which scale with surviving objects and generation-2 activity.

Memory problems in managed code are usually unintended reachability (a static cache, an event subscription, a captured closure) or excessive allocation in hot paths. Tools: dotnet-counters for live GC statistics, dotnet-gcdump and dotnet-trace for heap and allocation analysis. GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() measures allocations in a test.
Do not call GC.Collect() in production code to fix memory issues; find what keeps objects reachable instead. Check long-lived roots first: statics, singletons, caches and events.

lessons.question: Two objects reference only each other and nothing else references them. What does the .NET GC do?
options: Keeps both forever because their reference counts are non-zero
Collects only the newer one
Collects both, because neither is reachable from a root
lessons.explanation: The GC traces reachability from roots; it does not use reference counts, so cycles are not leaks.

lessons.title: IDisposable and using
body: The GC manages memory, not other resources. File handles, sockets, database connections, locks and native memory must be released deterministically, as soon as you are done, rather than whenever a collection happens. Types owning such resources implement IDisposable with a single Dispose() method.

using (var file = File.OpenRead(path)) { ... } calls Dispose when the block exits, normally or by exception; it is a try/finally. The using declaration using var file = File.OpenRead(path); disposes at the end of the enclosing scope. Multiple using declarations dispose in reverse order of declaration, so later resources (which may depend on earlier ones) are released first.

Ownership decides who disposes. The code that creates a disposable usually owns it; when you pass it to another object, document whether ownership transfers (for example new StreamReader(stream, leaveOpen: true) leaves the stream for the caller). A class that owns disposable fields should itself implement IDisposable and dispose them.

Dispose should be idempotent (safe to call twice) and, after disposal, other members should throw ObjectDisposedException (ObjectDisposedException.ThrowIf(disposed, this)). Asynchronous cleanup uses IAsyncDisposable and await using, covered in stage 11.

Check every new of a disposable type: who owns it, where it is disposed, and what happens if an exception occurs between creation and the using. Analyzer CA2000 flags objects not disposed on all paths.

lessons.question: In what order are using var a and then using var b disposed at the end of a method?
options: b first, then a
a first, then b
In whatever order the GC finalizes them
lessons.explanation: using declarations unwind in reverse order, like nested using blocks, so dependents are released before what they depend on.

lessons.title: Finalizers, SafeHandle and the dispose pattern
body: A finalizer (~Resource() { ... }) runs on a GC thread some time after an object becomes unreachable, if ever before process exit. It is a last-chance safety net for unmanaged resources when callers forget to dispose, not a substitute for Dispose. Finalizable objects survive at least one extra collection and slow the GC, so most classes should not have one.

Instead of writing finalizers, wrap native handles in a SafeHandle subclass (such as SafeFileHandle). SafeHandle has a reliable finalizer, protects against handle recycling races and makes your class's Dispose simply call handle.Dispose(). Classes that only hold managed disposables never need a finalizer.

The full dispose pattern for unsealed classes uses protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing). Dispose() calls Dispose(true) and then GC.SuppressFinalize(this); a finalizer, if present, calls Dispose(false). When disposing is false you must not touch other managed objects, because they may already have been finalized. Derived classes override Dispose(bool) and call base.Dispose(disposing).

GC.SuppressFinalize(this) tells the runtime the finalizer no longer needs to run, removing the extra cost once cleanup has happened deterministically. Seal classes when you can; a sealed class can use a simple Dispose() without the virtual pattern.
Check whether a type truly owns an unmanaged resource. If not, do not add a finalizer; if so, prefer SafeHandle, and make sure finalizer code touches only that resource.
lessons.challenge: Write a sealed class Pinned holding a GCHandle that pins a byte[] in its constructor and frees it in Dispose, with a finalizer fallback (the GC never frees a pinned handle, so a forgotten Dispose would leak the array) and GC.SuppressFinalize in Dispose. Print IsAllocated before and after a using block.
lessons.question: Why should a finalizer not use other managed objects referenced by fields?
options: They may already have been finalized or collected in the same cycle
Finalizers run before constructors
Managed objects are always null during finalization
lessons.explanation: Finalization order is undefined; only touch the unmanaged resource the object owns. Prefer SafeHandle.

lessons.title: Span<T>, Memory<T> and ref structs
body: Span<T> is a view over a contiguous region of memory: part of an array, a stackalloc buffer or native memory. Slicing a span (span[2..5] or Slice) creates another view without copying. ReadOnlySpan<T> is the read-only version; string.AsSpan() gives a ReadOnlySpan<char> so you can parse substrings without allocating new strings.

Span is a ref struct: it may live only on the stack. It cannot be a field of a class, be boxed, be captured by a lambda or (until C# 13's relaxations) live across an await or yield. These rules let the compiler guarantee a span never outlives the memory it points to. stackalloc int[16] assigned to a Span<int> is safe without unsafe.

Memory<T> and ReadOnlyMemory<T> are the heap-friendly counterparts: ordinary structs you can store in fields and pass to async methods, then call .Span when you need to process the data synchronously.

C# 14 adds implicit span conversions: arrays convert to Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T>, Span<T> to ReadOnlySpan<T>, and string to ReadOnlySpan<char>, and these conversions now take part in extension method lookup and generic inference. An extension method defined on ReadOnlySpan<T> can be called directly on an array, which previously required AsSpan(). One consequence: overload resolution may now prefer span-based overloads such as MemoryExtensions.Contains over LINQ's Enumerable.Contains.

Use spans in parsing, formatting and buffer code where allocation matters. Check that a span never escapes the lifetime of its memory (the compiler enforces most of this) and that a stackalloc size is small and bounded, because a large stack allocation can overflow the stack.
lessons.challenge: Write CountWords(ReadOnlySpan<char> text) that counts space-separated words without allocating (no Split, no Substring). Call it with "  the quick  brown fox ".
lessons.question: Why can't a Span<T> be stored in a field of a class?
options: It is a ref struct that must stay on the stack so it cannot outlive its memory
Spans are too large for class fields
Classes cannot have struct fields
lessons.explanation: The ref struct rules let the compiler prove a span never refers to memory that is gone; use Memory<T> for storage.

lessons.title: Pooling and reducing allocations
body: In hot paths, allocation pressure becomes GC time. The first fixes are simple: reuse a StringBuilder, presize lists and dictionaries, avoid LINQ in tight loops, avoid boxing (generic APIs instead of object), and use spans to slice instead of Substring/ToArray.

ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(minimumLength) lends an array that may be longer than requested; Return(array) gives it back for reuse. Always track the length you actually use, never use an array after returning it, and return it in a finally so exceptions do not leak pool arrays. Pass clearArray: true when the buffer held sensitive data.

ObjectPool<T> (Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool) pools larger reusable objects; string.Create(length, state, (span, state) => ...) builds a string by writing into its final buffer once. stackalloc with a size threshold and a pool fallback is a common pattern: small buffers on the stack, large ones rented.

Measure before and after. GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() in a test, BenchmarkDotNet's [MemoryDiagnoser] for micro-benchmarks, and dotnet-counters in production show whether a change actually reduced allocation. Readability costs are real; optimize the paths the measurements point at.

Pools turn memory bugs into data bugs: a returned array still in use gets overwritten by the next renter. Check every Rent has exactly one Return on every path and that nothing keeps the array afterwards.
lessons.challenge: Write ReverseWords(string text) that rents a char[] from ArrayPool, writes the words in reverse order separated by single spaces, builds the result with new string(buffer, 0, length) and returns the array in a finally block. Test with "one two three".
lessons.question: What must you track when renting from ArrayPool<T>.Shared?
options: The length you actually use, since the rented array may be longer
Nothing; Rent returns exactly the requested length
The pool index, to pass back to Return
lessons.explanation: Rent returns at least the requested size. Use your own length, return the array exactly once and never touch it afterwards.

lessons.title: Tasks, async and await
body: A Task represents an operation that will complete in the future; Task<T> also carries a result. Asynchronous APIs (File.ReadAllTextAsync, HttpClient.GetStringAsync, Task.Delay) return tasks immediately and complete them when the I/O or timer finishes, without blocking a thread while waiting.

An async method can use await task, which pauses the method until the task completes, then resumes with its result (or rethrows its exception). While paused, the thread is free to do other work. The method itself returns a Task/Task<T> to its caller as soon as it first awaits something incomplete. Top-level statements may use await directly.

Awaiting one task after another runs them sequentially. To run independent operations concurrently, start them all first (store the tasks) and then await them, for example with Task.WhenAll. Starting a task and awaiting it on the next line gives no concurrency.

Task.Run(() => Work()) queues CPU-bound work to the thread pool and returns a task for it. Use it to keep a UI thread responsive or to parallelize CPU work; do not wrap I/O-bound async APIs in Task.Run, which just wastes a thread. Async is about not blocking threads during waits, not automatically about parallelism.

Name async methods with an Async suffix and return Task, not void. Check every task you create is awaited (or deliberately observed): an unawaited task's exception is silently lost and analyzers warn with CS4014.
lessons.challenge: Write SquareLaterAsync(int n) that awaits Task.Yield() and returns n * n. Start three calls for 2, 3 and 4 before awaiting any, then await all and print the sum.
lessons.question: Two async calls are awaited one after the other: var x = await A(); var y = await B();. When does B start?
options: At the same time as A
Before A, because awaits are reordered
Only after A has completed
lessons.explanation: Start both tasks first and then await them (for example with Task.WhenAll) to overlap the waits.

lessons.title: How await works: continuations, contexts and pitfalls
body: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. At each await, if the task has already completed the method simply continues synchronously; otherwise it registers the rest of the method as a continuation and returns. When the task completes, the continuation runs, possibly on a different thread.

Where the continuation runs depends on the captured context. In UI frameworks a SynchronizationContext brings it back to the UI thread; in ASP.NET Core and console apps there is no such context, so it runs on a thread-pool thread. Library code that does not need the original context can use await task.ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid the cost and avoid deadlocks when a caller blocks.

Blocking on async code (task.Result, task.Wait(), GetAwaiter().GetResult()) is called sync-over-async. On a single-threaded context it can deadlock: the blocked thread waits for a continuation that needs that same thread. Elsewhere it wastes a thread and can starve the pool. Make the call chain async all the way up instead.

async void methods cannot be awaited and their exceptions are raised on the captured context, typically crashing the process. Use them only for event handlers. An exception in an async Task method is stored in the task and rethrown at await, which is where you catch it.

Code before the first incomplete await runs synchronously on the caller's thread, including argument validation. Check that expensive synchronous work is not hiding before the first await, and that .Result/.Wait() never appear in code that could run on a context-bound thread.
lessons.challenge: Write an async method ValidateAndDelayAsync(int ms) that must throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException immediately (at the call, not at await) for negative input. Use a non-async wrapper with a local async function and show the exception is thrown before any await.
lessons.question: Why is calling .Result on a task from a UI thread risky?
options: Result cancels the task
The continuation may need the blocked UI thread, causing a deadlock
Result always returns null for incomplete tasks
lessons.explanation: Sync-over-async blocks the thread the async continuation is waiting to run on; go async all the way.

lessons.title: Cancellation tokens and timeouts
body: Cancellation in .NET is cooperative. A CancellationTokenSource (CTS) creates a CancellationToken; the caller passes the token down, and code that does the work checks it (token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()) or passes it on to APIs that accept one (Task.Delay(ms, token), ReadAsync(buffer, token)). Calling cts.Cancel() only signals; nothing is aborted forcibly.

Cancelled work ends by throwing OperationCanceledException (or the derived TaskCanceledException), and the task's status becomes Canceled. Catch it where cancellation is an expected outcome, and check that the exception's token is yours if you need to distinguish your own cancellation from an inner timeout.

cts.CancelAfter(timeout) or new CancellationTokenSource(timeout) gives a timeout. CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b) cancels when either source does, which combines a caller's token with a local timeout. A CTS owns a timer and registrations, so dispose it (using var cts = ...).

token.Register(callback) runs code on cancellation and returns a registration you should dispose when the operation finishes, otherwise the callback, and anything it captures, stays alive as long as the token's source. When bridging callbacks to tasks with TaskCompletionSource, use the Try... methods so a result and a cancellation racing each other complete the task exactly once, and create it with RunContinuationsAsynchronously so awaiting code does not run inline inside the completing callback.

Accept a CancellationToken cancellationToken = default as the last parameter of public async methods and pass it to everything you call. Check that every registration is disposed, every CTS is disposed, and that cancellation leaves shared state consistent.
lessons.challenge: Write ProcessAsync(int[] items, CancellationToken token) that adds items one at a time with await Task.Yield() between them and returns the partial sum when cancelled after the third item (catch the cancellation inside and return what was summed). Cancel from inside a progress callback.
lessons.question: What does calling CancellationTokenSource.Cancel() do to running work?
options: It aborts the threads running the work
It immediately completes all related tasks as Canceled
It signals the token; the work must observe it and stop itself
lessons.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: code checks the token or passes it to APIs that do.

lessons.title: WhenAll, WhenAny, WhenEach and timeouts
body: Task.WhenAll(tasks) completes when every task has completed. If any failed, awaiting it rethrows the first exception, but the returned task's Exception property is an AggregateException holding all of them; inspect it when you need every failure. If any was cancelled and none failed, it ends cancelled.

Task.WhenAny(tasks) completes when the first task does and returns that task (it never throws itself); await the returned task to get its result or exception. It is the building block for 'first response wins' and for racing work against a timeout. The losing tasks keep running unless you cancel them.
Task.WhenEach(tasks) (.NET 9) is an IAsyncEnumerable<Task<T>> that yields tasks in completion order, replacing the old loop of WhenAny plus Remove, which was O(n²).

task.WaitAsync(timeout) or WaitAsync(token) (.NET 6) stops waiting after a timeout by throwing TimeoutException, but it does not cancel the underlying operation. Pass a cancellation token to the operation itself when you want it to stop.

Throttle large fan-outs: starting ten thousand HTTP requests at once can exhaust sockets. Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism or a SemaphoreSlim bounds concurrency. Check what happens to the tasks that lose a race or exceed a timeout.
lessons.challenge: Write FirstSuccessfulAsync(IEnumerable<Task<int>> tasks) that returns the result of the first task to succeed, ignoring failures, and throws InvalidOperationException if all fail. Use Task.WhenEach.
lessons.question: What does await Task.WhenAll(a, b) throw when both a and b fail?
options: Nothing; WhenAll swallows failures
The first exception; the task's Exception property holds both
An AggregateException directly
lessons.explanation: await unwraps to the first inner exception. Inspect the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions for all failures.

lessons.title: Async streams, await using and ValueTask
body: An async iterator returns IAsyncEnumerable<T> and can both await and yield return. Consumers use await foreach. It suits paged APIs, reading lines from a network stream, or any sequence whose elements arrive over time. System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable (.NET 10) provides LINQ operators such as Where, Select and ToListAsync for async streams.

Pass cancellation to async streams with WithCancellation(token); inside the iterator, a parameter marked [EnumeratorCancellation] receives it. Breaking out of await foreach disposes the enumerator, which runs the iterator's finally blocks.

IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync() releases resources whose cleanup needs I/O, such as flushing a network stream. await using var x = ...; calls it at the end of the scope. A class holding async disposables implements IAsyncDisposable (and usually IDisposable too).

ValueTask<T> avoids allocating a Task when a method usually completes synchronously, for example a cache hit. The rules are strict: await a ValueTask exactly once, never await it concurrently, and never call .Result before it completes. If you need any of that, convert with .AsTask(). When in doubt, return Task<T>.
Check that async streams honour cancellation, that resources acquired inside them are released in finally, and that every ValueTask is consumed exactly once.
lessons.challenge: Write an async iterator NumbersAsync(int count) and consume it with await foreach, summing only the even numbers. Then compute the same total with System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable (.NET 10): filter with Where, materialize with ToListAsync and Sum the list.
lessons.question: Which rule applies to a ValueTask<T> but not to a Task<T>?
options: It cannot carry a result
It always allocates on the heap
It must be awaited at most once
lessons.explanation: A ValueTask may wrap a pooled object reused after completion; await it once or convert with AsTask().

lessons.title: Threads, the thread pool and data races
body: A thread is an independent path of execution. new Thread(Work).Start() creates a dedicated OS thread, which is expensive; most code instead queues work to the shared thread pool via Task.Run, ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem, async continuations or Parallel. The pool grows and shrinks its threads to balance throughput.

When threads share mutable data without coordination you get a data race. count++ is a read, an add and a write; two threads can read the same old value and both write old+1, losing an update. The result varies from run to run, which makes races hard to reproduce and test.

Interlocked provides atomic operations on single variables: Increment, Add, Exchange and CompareExchange (compare-and-swap). They are the cheapest correct fix for counters and flags. For anything involving more than one variable, use a lock (next lesson) or an immutable snapshot swapped in with Interlocked.Exchange.

Compilers and CPUs may reorder memory operations as long as single-threaded behaviour is preserved, so one thread may observe another's writes in a surprising order. Locks and Interlocked operations include the necessary memory barriers; Volatile.Read/Volatile.Write give ordering for single fields. Avoid writing lock-free code beyond simple counters unless you have studied the .NET memory model.

The safest shared state is no shared state: give each thread its own data and combine results at the end, or communicate through channels. Before sharing a variable between threads, check every read and write path for atomicity and visibility.
lessons.challenge: Start 8 tasks that each add the numbers 1..1000 to a shared long total using Interlocked.Add, wait for all of them and print the total.
lessons.question: Why can count++ from several threads lose updates?
options: Because ints are 64-bit on modern CPUs
Because the GC moves count between threads
It is a separate read, add and write that other threads can interleave with
lessons.explanation: Use Interlocked.Increment or a lock so the read-modify-write is atomic.

lessons.title: Locks, System.Threading.Lock and deadlocks
body: A lock lets only one thread at a time run a critical section. lock (gate) { ... } acquires the lock, runs the block and releases it even if an exception is thrown. Every access to the protected state, reads included, must hold the same lock, or the protection is incomplete.

C# 13/.NET 9 introduced System.Threading.Lock, a dedicated lock type. When the lock statement's expression is a Lock, the compiler uses its faster EnterScope() API instead of Monitor. Use a private readonly Lock gate = new(); field; never lock on this, a Type or a string, which outside code could also lock.

Keep critical sections short and never await inside a lock (the compiler forbids it, CS1996) because the continuation may resume on another thread. For async code use SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) with await WaitAsync() and release in finally.

A deadlock happens when two threads each hold a lock the other needs. The standard prevention is a global lock order: always acquire locks in the same order (for example by account id). Monitor.TryEnter and SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync(timeout) let you give up instead of waiting forever.

ReaderWriterLockSlim allows many readers or one writer, worthwhile only for read-heavy, long critical sections. Check that each piece of shared state has exactly one guarding lock, that the lock is private, and that nested acquisitions follow one order.
lessons.challenge: Write a thread-safe BoundedLog class using a Lock that keeps only the last 3 messages added. Add 10 messages from parallel loop iterations, then print how many are kept.
lessons.question: What is the standard way to prevent deadlocks when a method must take two locks?
options: Always acquire the locks in one global order
Lock on this instead of a private field
Use await inside the lock
lessons.explanation: If every thread acquires locks in the same order, no cycle of waiting can form.

lessons.title: Concurrent collections and channels
body: ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>, ConcurrentQueue<T>, ConcurrentStack<T> and ConcurrentBag<T> are safe to use from many threads without external locks. Use their atomic compound operations: GetOrAdd, AddOrUpdate, TryRemove, TryDequeue. Note that the factory passed to GetOrAdd may run more than once under contention, even though only one value is stored.

System.Threading.Channels is the modern producer/consumer pipe. Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity) gives a writer and a reader; await writer.WriteAsync(item) waits when the channel is full, so a fast producer is slowed to the consumer's pace. That waiting is backpressure, and it keeps memory bounded. Unbounded channels never wait and can grow without limit.

Consumers use await foreach (var item in reader.ReadAllAsync(token)). The producer calls writer.Complete() when done, which ends the consumers' loops once the remaining items are drained. Complete(exception) propagates a failure to readers.

BoundedChannelOptions chooses what happens when full: Wait (backpressure, the default), DropOldest, DropNewest or DropWrite. SingleReader/SingleWriter hints enable faster implementations. Multiple consumers reading the same channel share the work; each item goes to exactly one reader.
Check that every channel is completed exactly once (or consumers wait forever), that cancellation stops both sides, and that bounded capacity matches how much memory you can afford.
lessons.challenge: Build a two-stage pipeline: stage one writes the numbers 1..5 to a bounded channel of capacity 1; stage two reads them, squares them and writes to a second channel; the main code reads the second channel and prints the squares. Complete each channel when its writer finishes.
lessons.question: What does await writer.WriteAsync(item) do on a full bounded channel with FullMode.Wait?
options: Throws ChannelClosedException
Drops the oldest item silently
Waits until a reader makes room
lessons.explanation: Waiting writers are backpressure: the producer runs no faster than the consumer, keeping memory bounded.

lessons.title: Data parallelism with Parallel and PLINQ
body: Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach split CPU-bound loops across thread-pool threads; Parallel.ForEachAsync does the same for async bodies. They block until all iterations finish and aggregate exceptions into an AggregateException. ParallelOptions sets MaxDegreeOfParallelism and a cancellation token.

PLINQ adds .AsParallel() to a LINQ query to run operators on several threads. Results are unordered by default; .AsOrdered() preserves source order at some cost. WithDegreeOfParallelism and WithCancellation control execution. Side effects inside PLINQ lambdas are races unless protected.

Parallelism helps only when each item does enough CPU work to outweigh scheduling overhead and when the work is independent. Small loops, I/O-bound work and loops dominated by a shared lock often get slower. Measure with realistic data.

Use the thread-local overloads (Parallel.For(from, to, localInit, body, localFinally)) to accumulate per-thread results and combine them once, avoiding contention on a shared total. For floating-point sums, the combination order changes, so parallel results may differ in the last digits from a sequential sum.
Check iterations are independent, that shared results are combined safely, and that ordering requirements are explicit (AsOrdered, or sort afterwards).
lessons.challenge: Use PLINQ to find the five largest numbers below 100000 whose digit sum is 30, printing them in descending order.
lessons.question: By default, in what order does a PLINQ query produce results?
options: Always the source order
Always ascending by value
Unspecified; use AsOrdered or sort to impose an order
lessons.explanation: PLINQ partitions the input across threads; ordering costs extra and must be requested.

lessons.title: Extension methods and C# 14 extension members
body: Extension methods add methods to existing types without modifying them. The classic form is a static method in a static class whose first parameter has this: public static bool IsBlank(this string? s). Callers write name.IsBlank() once the namespace is imported. LINQ is built this way. Extensions cannot access private members and lose to an instance method with the same signature.

C# 14 adds extension blocks, a new syntax that also supports extension properties, static extension members and operators. Inside a static class, extension(string? text) { public bool IsBlank => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text); } declares an extension property used as name.IsBlank. The parameter in parentheses is the receiver.

A block with only a receiver type and no name, extension(Temperature) { public static Temperature Freezing => ... }, declares static extension members called as if they were static members of the type: Temperature.Freezing. Static extension operators are allowed too, so you can define + for a type you do not own.

Extension blocks may be generic, extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source), with constraints. The new syntax is source- and binary-compatible with classic extension methods: both can coexist and callers cannot tell them apart. C# 15 adds extension indexers (final stage).

Extensions are resolved statically from the variable's compile-time type and the imported namespaces. Check for ambiguity when two imported namespaces define the same extension, and prefer instance members when you own the type.

options: Static extension members called like Temperature.Member
Instance extension methods with an implicit this

lessons.title: Null-conditional assignment, nameof and partial members
body: C# 14 allows ?. and ?[] on the left of assignments: customer?.Order = GetOrder(); assigns only when customer is not null, and the right-hand side is not evaluated at all when it is null. Compound assignments such as counter?.Value += 1 work too; ++ and -- do not (CS1059). Using ?. on an expression also tells nullable analysis that it might be null, so a later plain dereference of the same expression warns.

nameof now accepts unbound generic types: nameof(List<>) is "List" and nameof(Dictionary<,>) is "Dictionary". Previously you had to write a closed type such as List<int> purely to satisfy the compiler.

Partial members let one part of a type declare a member and another part implement it, which is how source generators fill in code. C# 13 added partial properties and indexers; C# 14 adds partial instance constructors and partial events. Each needs exactly one defining declaration and one implementing declaration; only the implementing constructor may have a this()/base() initializer, and the implementing event must declare add and remove.

Other C# 14 refinements covered elsewhere in this guide: the field keyword (stage 3), implicit span conversions (stage 10), modifiers on simple lambda parameters (stage 8) and user-defined compound assignment (stage 3). File-based apps gained #:package, #:sdk and #:property directives so a single .cs file can reference NuGet packages.
When adopting ?.=, check that skipping the right-hand side is intended: side effects there (logging, increments) no longer happen when the target is null.

lessons.question: In customer?.Order = Compute();, when is Compute() called?
options: Never; the statement is a compile error
Only when customer is not null
Always, before the null check
lessons.explanation: Null-conditional assignment evaluates the right side only after the receiver passes the null check.

lessons.title: Attributes and reflection
body: Attributes attach metadata to code: [Obsolete("use V2")], [Flags], [JsonPropertyName("id")]. They do nothing by themselves; the compiler, the runtime, frameworks or your own code read them. Define your own by deriving from Attribute and restrict where it may appear with [AttributeUsage].

Reflection inspects types at runtime: typeof(T) or obj.GetType() returns a Type, from which you can list properties, methods and attributes, read and write values, and invoke members. Serializers, test runners, dependency-injection containers and ORMs rely on it.

Reflection is slow compared with direct calls, bypasses compile-time checking and breaks when code is trimmed or compiled ahead of time (Native AOT), because the trimmer cannot see which members are used. Mark APIs that need it with [DynamicallyAccessedMembers], or prefer source generators, which produce ordinary code at compile time.

Generic attributes (C# 11) take type arguments: [Validator<EmailRule>]. Caller-information attributes ([CallerMemberName], [CallerArgumentExpression]) let the compiler pass names and source text into parameters, which is how ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull reports parameter names.
Use reflection at boundaries (startup, configuration, tooling), cache what you discover, and check whether the app will be trimmed or AOT-compiled before depending on it.

lessons.question: Why is heavy reflection a problem for Native AOT and trimmed apps?
options: The trimmer cannot see members used only via reflection and may remove them
Reflection is unavailable on 64-bit platforms
Attributes are stripped by the C# compiler
lessons.explanation: Annotate with DynamicallyAccessedMembers or replace reflection with source-generated code.

lessons.title: ref locals, ref structs, scoped and unsafe code
body: ref can do more than pass parameters. A ref local aliases another variable (ref int slot = ref array[2];), and a method can return by reference (ref int Find(...)) so callers update storage in place, avoiding copies of large structs. ref readonly returns allow aliasing without mutation. A struct method cannot return a reference to its own fields (CS8170) because this may be a temporary copy; classes can, since their fields live in the heap object.

ref struct types (like Span<T>) may live only on the stack. Since C# 11 a ref struct can hold ref fields, which is how Span<T> itself is written. The compiler tracks 'escape scope' to stop a reference to a local from leaking out of the method. The scoped modifier promises a parameter or local will not escape, which lets the compiler accept more code safely.

Unsafe code (unsafe blocks, enabled with AllowUnsafeBlocks) uses raw pointers: int*, &x, *p, pointer arithmetic, stackalloc to a pointer, sizeof, and fixed to pin a managed object so the GC cannot move it while you hold its address. Function pointers (delegate*<int, int>) call methods without delegate allocation, mainly for interop.

Unsafe code disables the safety guarantees: an out-of-bounds pointer write silently corrupts memory. Most performance needs are met with spans and ref locals instead. Interop with native libraries uses [LibraryImport] (source-generated marshalling) rather than hand-written pointers where possible.

C# 15 begins redefining unsafe so that only memory-accessing operations require unsafe (final stage). Today, check every unsafe block for bounds, pinning duration and aliasing, and keep it as small as possible.

lessons.question: What does the fixed statement do in unsafe code?
options: Makes a variable immutable
Allocates memory outside the GC heap
Pins a managed object so the GC cannot move it while its address is used
lessons.explanation: The GC compacts the heap; pinning keeps addresses valid for the duration of the fixed block only.

lessons.title: Source generators and compile-time code
body: A source generator is a compiler plug-in that inspects your code during compilation and adds new C# source files to it. Generated code is ordinary code: it is type-checked, debuggable and AOT-friendly, which makes generators the modern replacement for many uses of reflection.

The BCL ships several. [GeneratedRegex("pattern")] on a partial method or (since C# 13) a partial property produces an optimized regular-expression implementation at build time. System.Text.Json source generation (JsonSerializerContext) produces serializers without reflection. [LibraryImport] generates P/Invoke marshalling, and logging's [LoggerMessage] generates allocation-free log methods.

The pattern is always the same: you write a partial declaration plus an attribute, and the generator writes the other half. That is why partial methods, properties, constructors and events keep expanding in recent C# versions. Writing your own generator means an IIncrementalGenerator in a separate analyzer project targeting .NET Standard 2.0, referenced with OutputItemType="Analyzer".

Generated files can be inspected: set EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles to true in the project, or open the Analyzers node in an IDE. Generators must be incremental and deterministic so builds stay fast and reproducible.
Prefer a built-in generator when one exists (regex, JSON, logging, interop). Check that the generated code is what you expect and that the generator is pinned to a version, like any other dependency.
lessons.challenge: Use [GeneratedRegex] to write a partial method Hex() matching a # followed by exactly six hex digits (ignore case), and print which of #A1B2C3, #12345, abc123 match.
lessons.question: What does a source generator add to a compilation?
options: Reflection calls executed at startup
New C# source code that is compiled with your project
IL patched into the binary after compilation
lessons.explanation: Generators emit ordinary source during the build, so the result is type-checked and works with trimming and AOT.

lessons.title: Projects, solutions, packages and analyzers
body: A .csproj file is an MSBuild project. SDK-style projects (<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">) include every .cs file under their folder automatically, so the file mostly holds properties: TargetFramework (for example net10.0), OutputType (Exe or a library by default), Nullable, ImplicitUsings, LangVersion and TreatWarningsAsErrors. Directory.Build.props in a parent folder applies shared properties to every project beneath it.

A solution groups projects. The .NET 10 SDK creates the XML-based .slnx format by default (dotnet new sln), which is far easier to read and merge than the old .sln. dotnet sln add, dotnet add reference and dotnet add package edit these files for you. global.json pins the SDK version for a repository and, in .NET 10, selects the test runner.

NuGet packages are referenced with <PackageReference Include="Name" />. Central Package Management puts every version in one Directory.Packages.props (ManagePackageVersionsCentrally), so all projects agree. Commit a lock file (RestorePackagesWithLockFile) or at least pin exact versions, and audit dependencies with dotnet list package --vulnerable; NuGet audit warnings are on by default.

Analyzers run during compilation. The .NET SDK includes code-quality rules (CA*) and style rules (IDE*); AnalysisLevel such as latest-recommended chooses how many are enabled, and .editorconfig adjusts individual rule severities. Treating warnings as errors in CI keeps nullable and analyzer findings from accumulating.

dotnet publish -c Release produces a deployable app. Options include framework-dependent versus self-contained output, a single-file bundle, trimming (PublishTrimmed) and Native AOT (PublishAot), which compiles ahead of time for fast startup and small memory use but forbids unconstrained reflection and runtime code generation. Check those constraints before choosing AOT.

lessons.question: What does Central Package Management change about PackageReference items?
options: Versions move to Directory.Packages.props and references omit them
Packages are downloaded once per machine instead of per project
Analyzers become disabled
lessons.explanation: One file owns every version, preventing projects in a repository from drifting apart.

lessons.title: Project: a tested text-search CLI
body: This project is a small solution with three projects: a TextSearch class library holding the logic, a TextSearch.Cli console app that handles arguments, files and exit codes, and a TextSearch.Tests xUnit v3 project. Keeping logic in a library makes it testable without starting processes or touching the file system.

Searcher.Search reads from any TextReader, so tests pass a StringReader and the CLI passes a file. It validates eagerly and then returns a local iterator, combining stage 9's lazy evaluation with immediate argument checks; the ReadsLazily test proves only one line is read when the caller takes one match.

The CLI uses a list pattern (args is not [var query, var path]) to validate arguments, writes errors to standard error and returns distinct exit codes (1 for usage, 2 for a missing file) so scripts can react. using var reader disposes the file even if enumeration throws.

Repository-level files carry shared settings: global.json pins SDK 10.0.402 and opts into Microsoft.Testing.Platform for dotnet test; Directory.Build.props enables nullable, warnings as errors and recommended analyzers for every project; Directory.Packages.props pins xUnit v3 centrally; TextSearch.slnx lists the projects.

Run dotnet test from the solution folder, then dotnet run --project src/TextSearch.Cli -- fox poem.txt. The guide's validator also injects a bug (case-insensitive matching in the base version) and confirms the tests fail, showing they actually guard the behaviour.

Practice: add an ignoreCase option to Search (default false so existing callers keep their behaviour), accept -i/--ignore-case as the first CLI argument, and add tests for both modes. The answer replaces Searcher.cs and Program.cs and adds IgnoreCaseTests.cs.

options: Because iterators cannot accept parameters
To read the whole file into memory first
So invalid arguments throw at the call instead of on first enumeration
lessons.explanation: Iterator bodies are deferred; splitting validation from iteration makes failures immediate while keeping lazy reading.

lessons.title: Project: a bounded async pipeline with cancellation
body: This project builds a reusable producer/worker pipeline on System.Threading.Channels. BoundedPipeline.RunAsync writes items into a bounded channel, starts a fixed number of workers that read and process them, and returns the sum of their results. It combines stages 11 and 12: bounded capacity for backpressure, cooperative cancellation and Task.WhenAll for completion.

The tests check behaviour rather than implementation: every result is summed, no more than workers items run at once, the producer stops early when the channel is full (backpressure), cancellation surfaces as OperationCanceledException, and bad arguments fail before any work starts.

Concurrency tests need care to stay deterministic. The backpressure test blocks the worker on a TaskCompletionSource and asserts a range rather than an exact count; the concurrency test records the peak with Interlocked.CompareExchange. TestContext.Current.CancellationToken (xUnit v3) cancels tests that hang when the run is aborted.

The base version has a lifetime flaw: if one worker throws, the other workers and the producer keep waiting for items or space, so RunAsync can hang and work outlives the failed call. The validator also injects a different bug (ignoring the capacity) to show the backpressure test catches it.

Practice: make a worker failure cancel the whole run. Own a linked CancellationTokenSource for the duration of RunAsync, cancel it when a worker fails, wait for every task to finish, and rethrow the original exception rather than a sibling's cancellation. Any task that exits by exception, including a worker whose own timeout cancels it and a source that throws mid-iteration, must cancel the run. The answer's new tests prove no worker is still running when RunAsync completes and that neither case hangs.
This ownership rule (work started by a call finishes, or is cancelled, before the call returns) is what prevents leaked tasks, captured state and unobserved exceptions in long-running services.
lessons.challenge: Make a worker failure cancel the whole run, wait for every task and rethrow the original exception; prove no worker outlives RunAsync.
lessons.question: In the base pipeline, what can happen when one worker throws?
options: The channel automatically cancels every other worker
The exception is swallowed and the sum is returned
Other workers and the producer keep waiting, so the call can hang and work outlives it
lessons.explanation: Nothing links the failure to the others. Owning a linked CancellationTokenSource lets the failure stop all work before the call returns.

lessons.title: Capstone: a generic statistics library and CLI
body: The capstone combines generic math (stage 7), spans (stage 10), LINQ (stage 9), input validation (stages 1 and 5) and testing. Stats provides Mean, Variance, Median and Histogram for any numeric type: the input type T is constrained to INumber<T> and the result type TResult to IFloatingPoint<TResult>, so integer inputs can produce fractional means.

Algorithms take ReadOnlySpan<T> so callers can pass arrays, slices or collection expressions without copying. Median copies once into an array to sort, leaving the caller's data untouched, which the API contract promises. Histogram uses .NET 9's CountBy and returns pairs sorted by value.

The CLI reads one number per line from standard input using invariant culture (so 3.5 parses the same everywhere), reports the first bad line with its line number on standard error and exits with code 1. Formatting uses FormattableString.Invariant for the same reason.

Tests use [Theory] with [InlineData] to cover odd and even counts in one method, and check the population variance against a known textbook data set (mean 5, variance 4). The validator injects an off-by-one bug into Median to show the theory catches it.
Run dotnet test, then dotnet run --project src/Statistics.Cli < data.txt (the validator pipes data.txt to standard input).

Practice: add Percentiles.Percentile<T, TResult>(values, p) using linear interpolation between closest ranks (p from 0 to 100), with validation, tests that the 50th percentile equals the median, and a p90 line in the CLI output.

lessons.question: Why does Stats use two type parameters, T : INumber<T> and TResult : IFloatingPoint<TResult>?
options: Because INumber<T> cannot be used with spans
To make the methods run in parallel
So integer inputs can produce fractional results such as a mean of 2.5
lessons.explanation: Averaging ints in int arithmetic would truncate; converting into a floating-point TResult keeps precision while still accepting any numeric input.

lessons.title: Union types
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

A union type holds a value that is exactly one of several case types: public union Pet(Cat, Dog, Bird);. Each case type converts implicitly to the union, so Pet pet = new Dog("Rex"); just works. Case types can be classes, records, structs or built-in types such as int.

The compiler knows the complete list of cases, so a switch over a union is exhaustive when it handles every case type: no discard arm is needed, and leaving a case out produces warning CS8509 (an error when warnings are errors). Adding a case later makes every incomplete switch light up, which is the main safety benefit.

Before C# 15 the same idea needed a closed class hierarchy you maintained by convention, a OneOf-style library, or the Result<T> record from stage 5. Unions express 'one of these' directly, including for types you do not own and value types, without a shared base class.

The runtime support types (UnionAttribute, IUnion) arrived in .NET 11 Preview 5, and Microsoft notes that some parts of the specification are still being implemented. Use unions for closed sets of alternatives such as results, messages and parse outcomes, and check new releases for additions to the feature.

lessons.question: What happens when a switch over a union omits one of its case types?
options: The compiler warns that the switch is not exhaustive (CS8509)
The missing case silently matches the first arm
The union removes that case type
lessons.explanation: The compiler knows every case of a union, so incomplete switches are reported; with warnings as errors they fail the build.

lessons.title: Closed class hierarchies
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

The closed modifier on a class (C# 15) means it can be derived from only inside its own assembly. Because the compiler then knows every direct descendant, a switch that handles each one is exhaustive without a discard arm, just as with unions.

A closed class is implicitly abstract and cannot also be sealed, static or explicitly abstract. It suits state machines and domain alternatives that share data or behaviour through the base class, for example closed record GateState with Open and Closed records.
Closure is not transitive: a non-closed descendant can still be extended in other assemblies. Mark intermediate classes closed too if you want exhaustiveness further down the hierarchy.

Choose between the two C# 15 tools by shape: a union when the alternatives are unrelated existing types, a closed hierarchy when the alternatives are your own types that share a base. Check that adding a new descendant is meant to break incomplete switches, because that is exactly what it will do.
lessons.challenge: Model an expression tree with closed record Expr and descendants Num(double), Add(Expr, Expr), Mul(Expr, Expr). Write Eval with an exhaustive switch and evaluate (2 + 3) * 4.
lessons.question: Why does a switch over a closed class need no discard arm when it handles every direct descendant?
options: Only the declaring assembly can add descendants, so the compiler knows them all
Closed classes are sealed, so only the base type can appear
The runtime throws for unknown types anyway
lessons.explanation: closed fixes the set of direct descendants at compile time, enabling exhaustiveness checks.

lessons.title: Collection expression arguments and extension indexers
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

Collection expressions (stage 6) could not pass constructor arguments, so specifying a capacity or a comparer meant falling back to new. C# 15 allows a with(...) element first: List<string> names = [with(capacity: 32), ..source]; or HashSet<string> set = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "a", "A"];. The arguments go to the collection's constructor or factory method.

This matters for correctness, not just speed: a dictionary or set built with the wrong comparer behaves differently. Dictionary<string, int> d = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), ...] keeps the concise syntax while stating the equality rule.

C# 15 also allows indexers in extension blocks (stage 13): extension(IEnumerable<int> sequence) { public int this[int index] => sequence.ElementAt(index); } lets callers write numbers[2] on a type that has no indexer. An extension block that declares an indexer must name its receiver.

Extension indexers are resolved statically like other extensions, and an instance indexer on the type always wins: an extension indexer on string is never chosen for text[1], because string already has one. Check the cost hidden behind the brackets: indexing an IEnumerable<T> by position is O(n), unlike an array or list.
lessons.solution:
SortedSet<string> fruit = [with(Comparer<string>.Create((a, b) => string.CompareOrdinal(b, a))), "apple", "cherry", "banana"];
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", fruit));
lessons.challenge: Create a SortedSet<string> with a descending comparer using a collection expression argument, add apple, cherry and banana, and print the set in order.
lessons.question: In HashSet<string> s = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "a", "A"];, what does with(...) do?
options: Applies the comparer only when printing
Passes the comparer to the HashSet constructor before the elements are added
Adds the comparer as an element
lessons.explanation: with(...) must come first and supplies constructor or factory arguments, so the set holds one element.

lessons.title: Labeled break and continue
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

Stage 1 noted that break and continue affect only the innermost loop, so leaving nested loops needed a flag, a goto or an extracted method. C# 15 lets them name a label on an enclosing loop or switch: continue outer; starts the next iteration of the loop labelled outer, and break outer; leaves it.

Put the label directly on the loop statement it names (outer: for (...)). Without a label, break and continue keep their old meaning. The IDE0410 style rule suggests labeled jumps where code uses the flag or goto workarounds.
Labeled jumps help in searches over grids or nested collections and in parsers that skip ahead. Very deep nesting is still a sign that extracting a method with return might read better.
Check that the label names the loop you mean; continue outer re-evaluates the outer loop's condition and increment, which is easy to forget when the outer loop also maintains state.
lessons.challenge: Given lines of comma-separated numbers, sum each line but skip the whole line (continue to the next line) as soon as a non-number appears, using a labeled continue. Lines: "1,2,3", "4,x,5", "6".
lessons.question: What does continue outer; do inside a nested loop in C# 15?
options: Restarts the inner loop from its first element
Jumps to the statement after the outer loop
Starts the next iteration of the loop labelled outer
lessons.explanation: A labeled continue targets the named enclosing loop; break outer would leave it instead.

lessons.title: The memory-safety redesign (preview)
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA. This lesson goes further: it needs LangVersion set to preview even on the .NET 11 SDK, so treat it as a look at where the language is heading.

C# 15 begins a multi-release effort to tie unsafe to operations that actually access unmanaged memory, rather than to the mere presence of pointer types. With the preview language version, declaring a pointer, taking an address with &, fixed, converting stackalloc to a pointer and sizeof on unmanaged types no longer require an unsafe context.

Dereferencing still does: *p, p->member, p[i] and function-pointer calls need unsafe. The new unsafe(expression) form creates an unsafe context for one expression, useful in field initializers, constructor initializers and catch filters where an unsafe block cannot appear.

Opting into the updated rules (the updated-memory-safety-rules feature) also makes unsafe on a member mean 'requires unsafe': the obligation passes to callers, who must call it from an unsafe context. A safe contextual keyword marks extern members and certain fields as safe. The compiler records the choice with MemorySafetyRulesAttribute.

The goal is that reviewers can find every memory-accessing operation by searching for unsafe. Until the feature ships in a released language version, keep production code on stage 13's rules and check the C# 15/16 notes for the final design.

lessons.question: Under the C# 15 preview rules, which operation still requires an unsafe context?

Declaring a variable of type int*
Taking an address with &
lessons.explanation: The redesign keeps unsafe for operations that access memory; creating pointers and pinning are relaxed.

lessons.title: Your first Go program and the go command
body: A Go program is a set of packages compiled into one executable. Execution starts in package main at func main(); when main returns the process exits, even if other work is still running. The go command is the single front door: go run compiles to a temporary binary and runs it, go build leaves a binary behind, and go vet looks for suspicious code that still compiles.

Every source file begins with a package clause, then imports, then declarations. Imports name packages by path, so "fmt" is the formatted-I/O package from the standard library. Exported names start with an upper-case letter, which is why you call fmt.Println and not fmt.println.

Go compiles quickly and refuses to build code that imports a package it does not use or declares a local variable it never reads. These rules feel strict at first; they keep programs free of dead dependencies and half-finished edits. Treat a compiler error as precise feedback: it names the file, line and column.
lessons.challenge: Print two lines: the word Go, then the result of 8 * 8.
lessons.question: What does fmt.Println put between its operands?
options: Nothing; operands are concatenated
A comma and a space
A single space, followed by a newline at the end
lessons.explanation: Println always separates operands with spaces and appends a newline. That is why "Go:" and 42 appear as "Go: 42".
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
Go: 42

Println always separates operands with spaces and appends a newline. That is why "Go:" and 42 appear as "Go: 42".
lessons.practiceAnswer: Println always separates operands with spaces and appends a newline. That is why "Go:" and 42 appear as "Go: 42".

lessons.title: Modules, go.mod, and building a binary
body: A module is a tree of packages with a go.mod file at its root. go mod init example.com/hello writes a go.mod naming the module path and a go directive such as go 1.27. The go line is the language version the module is written for. It enables features of that release and tells newer toolchains which semantics to use.

Inside a module, go run . builds the package in the current directory and runs it; go build produces an executable named after the directory; go install places it in GOBIN. A toolchain line in go.mod, or the GOTOOLCHAIN environment variable, can ask the go command to download and use a specific release, which is how this guide pins go1.27.2.

Programs read their command-line arguments through os.Args, where os.Args[0] is the program name. Exit codes come from os.Exit; returning from main exits with status 0. Deferred functions do not run when os.Exit is called, so do cleanup before exiting.
lessons.challenge: Print the number of arguments, then print "none" if there are no arguments and "some" otherwise.
lessons.question: What does the go directive in go.mod control?
options: The Go language version and semantics the module is written for
The exact compiler binary that must be installed
The version of every dependency
lessons.explanation: go 1.27 selects language features and defaults (such as per-iteration loop variables from 1.22). Dependencies are recorded on require lines, and the toolchain line or GOTOOLCHAIN selects a compiler.

lessons.title: Printing with fmt: Print, Printf and verbs
body: fmt offers three families: Print/Println/Printf write to standard output, Sprint/Sprintln/Sprintf return a string, and Fprint/Fprintln/Fprintf write to any io.Writer such as os.Stderr. Printf takes a format string whose verbs describe how each argument is shown.

Common verbs: %v prints a value in its default format, %+v adds struct field names, %#v prints Go syntax, %T prints the type, %d an integer, %s a string, %q a quoted string, %x hexadecimal, %f a float and %t a boolean. Width and precision sit between % and the verb: %5d pads to five columns and %.2f rounds to two decimal places.

Printf does not add a newline; put \n in the format. go vet checks that verbs match their arguments, so a %d given a string is reported before the program ever runs. Use %% for a literal percent sign.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name, score := "Ada", 93.456
	fmt.Printf("%s scored %.1f%%\n", name, score)
	fmt.Printf("%q has type %T\n", name, name)
	fmt.Printf("[%5d] [%-5d]\n", 42, 42)
}
lessons.challenge: Use Sprintf to build the string "07:05" from hours 7 and minutes 5, then print it.
lessons.question: Which verb prints a value together with its Go type name?
options: %#v prints only the type
%T prints the type; combine it with %v for the value
%v prints both automatically
lessons.explanation: %T formats the dynamic type of its operand. %#v prints a Go-syntax representation of the value, which often includes the type for composite literals but is not the type name alone.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

"Ada" has type string
[   42] [42   ]

%T formats the dynamic type of its operand. %#v prints a Go-syntax representation of the value, which often includes the type for composite literals but is not the type name alone.
lessons.practiceAnswer: %T formats the dynamic type of its operand. %#v prints a Go-syntax representation of the value, which often includes the type for composite literals but is not the type name alone.

lessons.title: gofmt, comments, and the shape of Go source
body: gofmt prints Go source in one canonical layout: tabs for indentation, aligned comments and a fixed brace style. Teams do not argue about formatting because the tool decides. Run go fmt ./... or let your editor format on save; every example in this guide is checked to be unchanged by gofmt.

The opening brace of a block must be on the same line as its statement. Go inserts semicolons automatically at the end of a line that ends with an identifier, literal, closing bracket or certain keywords, so moving a brace onto the next line changes the meaning and fails to compile.

Line comments start with //; block comments use /* */. A comment directly above a declaration is its doc comment and should begin with the declared name, for example // Area returns.... go doc and pkg.go.dev render those comments as documentation.
lessons.challenge: Add a documented function Perimeter(w, h int) int and print the perimeter of a 3 by 4 rectangle.
lessons.question: Why does putting a function's opening brace on the next line fail to compile?
options: Go forbids blank lines inside declarations
Automatic semicolon insertion ends the declaration at the line break
gofmt rejects the file before compilation
lessons.explanation: The lexer inserts a semicolon after the closing parenthesis, so the brace starts a separate statement. gofmt is a formatter, not part of the compiler.

The lexer inserts a semicolon after the closing parenthesis, so the brace starts a separate statement. gofmt is a formatter, not part of the compiler.
