lessons.title: Reading the standard library with go doc
body: The standard library is documented in the source and readable offline: go doc strings.Cut prints one function, go doc -all strings prints a whole package, and go doc -src shows the implementation. Go 1.27 adds go doc package@version for modules and go doc -ex for running examples.

Learn a package by its types and the verbs on them. For strings, start with Contains, Index, Cut, Fields, Split, Join, Repeat, ToUpper and the strings.Builder type. Most functions accept and return plain values, so you can predict them from their signature.

strings.Cut(s, sep) splits around the first separator and reports whether it was found; Go 1.27 adds strings.CutLast for the last separator. Prefer Cut over Index plus slicing because the found flag makes the not-found case explicit.

options: It panics with an index error
The whole input, an empty string, and false
Two empty strings and false
lessons.explanation: Cut returns before=s, after="" and found=false, so code can test found instead of comparing indices against -1.

lessons.title: Reading standard input line by line
body: Interactive and pipeline programs read standard input. bufio.Scanner wraps os.Stdin and splits it into lines by default: call Scan in a loop, read the current line with Text, and check Err after the loop. Scan returns false at end of input or on an error.

Scanner has a maximum token size (64 KiB by default). A longer line makes Scan stop with bufio.ErrTooLong, so always check Err; use Scanner.Buffer to raise the limit or bufio.Reader for unbounded lines.
Write results to os.Stdout and diagnostics to os.Stderr so pipelines can separate them. fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, ...) writes a diagnostic without mixing it into the data stream.
lessons.challenge: Read lines and print only the non-empty ones, each prefixed with its line number starting at 1.
lessons.question: Why check scanner.Err() after the Scan loop?
options: Err resets the scanner for the next file
Scan panics on errors, and Err recovers it
Scan returns false for both end of input and failures such as a too-long line
lessons.explanation: A false Scan is ambiguous. Err returns nil at a clean end of input and the error otherwise, for example bufio.ErrTooLong.

lessons.title: Variables, short declarations and zero values
body: var name Type declares a variable and sets it to the zero value of its type: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions and interfaces. There is no uninitialised memory in Go; every variable always holds a valid value of its type.

Inside a function, x := expr declares and initialises in one step, inferring the type from the expression. := needs at least one new variable on its left. In a new scope it creates a new variable even if an outer one has the same name; this is called shadowing and is a common source of bugs with err.

Declarations can be grouped in var ( ... ) blocks, and several variables can be declared at once: a, b := 1, 2. Swapping is a single statement, a, b = b, a, because all right-hand values are evaluated before any assignment happens.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int
	var label string
	var ready bool
	fmt.Printf("%d %q %t\n", count, label, ready)
	a, b := 1, 2
	a, b = b, a
	fmt.Println(a, b)
}
lessons.challenge: Declare x := 1, then in an inner block write x := 2 and print it; print x again after the block. Predict both lines first.
lessons.question: What value does a newly declared var m map[string]int hold?
options: An empty, ready-to-use map
Uninitialised memory until make is called
nil: reads work and return zero, but writes panic
lessons.explanation: The zero value of a map is nil. Looking up a key in a nil map returns the zero value, but assigning to one panics, so maps are made with make or a literal before writing.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

lessons.title: Constants, untyped constants and iota
body: A constant is a compile-time value: const Pi = 3.14159. Constants can be typed (const Max int = 10) or untyped. An untyped constant has arbitrary precision and takes a type only when it is used, so const Big = 1 << 100 is legal as long as it is never stored in a type too small for it.

Inside a const block, iota counts from 0 and increases by one per line. An omitted expression repeats the previous one, so a block of enumerated values needs iota only on its first line. Expressions such as 1 << iota build bit flags.

Go has no enum keyword. The idiom is a named integer type with iota constants and a String method for printing. A named type stops values of one enumeration from being mixed with plain integers by accident.
lessons.challenge: Define byte-size constants KB, MB and GB with iota so that KB = 1 << 10, then print MB.
lessons.question: Why does const huge = 1 << 100 compile even though no integer type can hold it?
options: Constants are always float64
Untyped constants have arbitrary precision until converted to a type
The compiler silently wraps it to zero
lessons.explanation: Untyped constant arithmetic is exact. It only fails if the value is used where it must fit a concrete type, such as assigning huge to an int.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

Untyped constant arithmetic is exact. It only fails if the value is used where it must fit a concrete type, such as assigning huge to an int.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Untyped constant arithmetic is exact. It only fails if the value is used where it must fit a concrete type, such as assigning huge to an int.

lessons.title: Integers, floats, overflow and explicit conversion
body: Go has sized integers (int8 to int64, uint8 to uint64), int and uint (64 bits on current 64-bit platforms), uintptr, float32/float64 and complex64/complex128. byte is an alias for uint8 and rune is an alias for int32.

Go never converts between numeric types implicitly. Adding an int and a float64 is a compile error until you write float64(n). Converting a float to an integer truncates toward zero; converting to a smaller integer type keeps the low bits.

Integer arithmetic wraps on overflow with no error: an int8 holding 127 plus one becomes -128. Integer division truncates toward zero, and % keeps the sign of the dividend. Dividing an integer by a constant zero is a compile error; dividing by a variable that is zero panics at run time. Floating-point division by zero gives ±Inf or NaN.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var small int8 = 127
	small++
	fmt.Println(small)
	n, f := 7, 2.5
	fmt.Println(float64(n) * f)
	neg := -3.9
	fmt.Println(-7/2, -7%2, int(neg))
	var big int32 = 300
	fmt.Println(uint8(big))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	sum := 3 + 4 + 4
	avg := float64(sum) / 3
	fmt.Printf("%.2f\n", avg)
}

lessons.question: What happens when int and float64 values are added directly?
options: The int is promoted to float64
The float is truncated to int
A compile error; one operand must be converted explicitly

lessons.title: Strings, bytes, runes and UTF-8
body: A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes, conventionally UTF-8. len(s) counts bytes, not characters, and s[i] is a byte. Indexing never decodes text; "é" occupies two bytes.

A rune is a Unicode code point (an int32). Ranging over a string with for i, r := range s decodes UTF-8 and yields the byte offset and rune of each character. Invalid bytes decode as the replacement character U+FFFD. utf8.RuneCountInString counts code points.

Converting a string to []byte or []rune copies it. Building strings by repeated + allocates a new string each time; use strings.Builder for loops. Raw string literals in backquotes keep backslashes and newlines literally, which suits regular expressions and multi-line text.
lessons.challenge: Reverse the string "Go→é" by runes (not bytes) and print it.
lessons.question: What does len("é") return?
options: 1, because it counts characters
4, because runes are int32
2, because len counts the UTF-8 bytes
lessons.explanation: Strings are byte sequences. "é" (U+00E9) is encoded in UTF-8 as two bytes, 0xC3 0xA9.

lessons.title: Operators, precedence and bit manipulation
body: Go has five precedence levels for binary operators: * / % << >> & &^ bind tightest, then + - | ^, then comparisons, then &&, then ||. The levels are fewer than in C, so a<<1 + 1 groups as (a<<1) + 1.
Increment and decrement are statements, not expressions: i++ is allowed on its own line, but x := i++ is a syntax error. Assignment is also a statement, so it cannot appear inside a condition.

Bitwise operators work on integers: & and, | or, ^ xor (and unary ^ for bitwise not), &^ and-not (bit clear), << and >> shifts. && and || short-circuit, which makes guards such as p != nil && p.ok safe.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := 3
	fmt.Println(a<<1 + 1)
	flags := 0b1011
	fmt.Printf("%04b %04b %04b\n", flags&0b0110, flags&^0b0011, ^flags&0xf)
	fmt.Println(1 < 2 && 2 < 3 || false)
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	bits := uint8(0b1010_0101)
	bits = bits&^1 | 1<<1
	fmt.Printf("%08b\n", bits)
}
lessons.challenge: Given bits := uint8(0b1010_0101), print it with bit 0 cleared and bit 1 set, in %08b form.
lessons.question: How does a<<1 + 1 group in Go?
options: It is a compile error without parentheses
(a<<1) + 1, because shifts bind tighter than addition
a << (1 + 1), as in C
lessons.explanation: << shares the multiplication precedence level, which is above +. gofmt even removes the spaces around << to show the grouping.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
7
0010 1000 0100
true

<< shares the multiplication precedence level, which is above +. gofmt even removes the spaces around << to show the grouping.
lessons.practiceAnswer: << shares the multiplication precedence level, which is above +. gofmt even removes the spaces around << to show the grouping.

lessons.title: Defined types, aliases and underlying types
body: type Celsius float64 defines a new named type whose underlying type is float64. Celsius and float64 are different types: mixing them needs a conversion, and Celsius can have its own methods. This is how Go expresses units and domain meanings in the type system.

type Name = string is an alias: another name for exactly the same type. Aliases exist mainly for gradual refactoring across packages, and since Go 1.24 they can have type parameters. byte and rune are predeclared aliases.

Conversion between a defined type and its underlying type is always allowed, and so is conversion between two defined types that share an underlying type. Untyped constants convert implicitly, so var c Celsius = 100 compiles without a cast.
lessons.challenge: Define type Meters float64 and type Feet float64 and write a function converting Feet to Meters (1 ft = 0.3048 m); print the result for 10 feet.
lessons.question: What is the difference between type A B and type A = B?
options: The first defines a distinct type; the second is an alias for the same type
They are identical spellings
The first is an alias; the second copies B's methods into a new type
lessons.explanation: A type definition creates a new, distinct named type with no methods of its own yet. An alias is just another name, so values flow between A and B freely.

A type definition creates a new, distinct named type with no methods of its own yet. An alias is just another name, so values flow between A and B freely.

lessons.title: if with init statements and the single for loop
body: if needs no parentheses but always needs braces. An if can start with a short statement: if v, ok := m[k]; ok { ... }. Variables declared there are scoped to the if and its else branches, which keeps temporary values out of the surrounding function.
for is Go's only loop. It has three forms: the C-style for i := 0; i < n; i++, the condition-only for cond (a while loop), and the infinite for { } that ends with break or return.
Since Go 1.22 you can range over an integer: for i := range 5 runs i = 0..4. Use it when you only need a count; it removes off-by-one mistakes in the condition.
lessons.challenge: Count the Collatz steps for 6 (halve when even, 3n+1 when odd) until it reaches 1; print the count.
lessons.question: Where is a variable declared in if v := f(); v > 0 { } visible?
options: Only inside the if block
In the condition, the if block and any else blocks
For the rest of the function
lessons.explanation: The init statement opens an implicit scope covering the whole if/else chain and ending after it.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

1

The init statement opens an implicit scope covering the whole if/else chain and ending after it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The init statement opens an implicit scope covering the whole if/else chain and ending after it.

lessons.title: switch: no fallthrough by default, tagless switch
body: A switch compares a value against cases from top to bottom and runs the first match. Unlike C, a case ends without break; the explicit fallthrough keyword continues into the next case body without testing it. A case may list several values: case "sat", "sun":.
A switch with no tag is a cleaner if/else-if chain: each case is a boolean expression. Like if, switch accepts an init statement before the tag.
break inside a switch leaves the switch, not an enclosing loop. To leave a loop from inside a switch, label the loop and use break Label.
lessons.challenge: Write a tagless switch that prints "fizzbuzz", "fizz", "buzz" or the number for 1 to 15, all on one line separated by spaces.
lessons.question: What does break do inside a switch that is inside a for loop?
options: It is a compile error
It leaves only the switch; use a labelled break to leave the loop
It leaves the loop
lessons.explanation: break targets the innermost for, switch or select. A label names the outer statement explicitly.

break targets the innermost for, switch or select. A label names the outer statement explicitly.

lessons.title: Labels, break, continue and goto
body: A label names a statement: outer: for .... break outer leaves that loop and continue outer starts its next iteration. Labels are the clear way to exit nested loops, for example after finding a match in a grid.
goto jumps to a label in the same function. It cannot jump over variable declarations or into a block. It is legal but rare; generated code and a few error-cleanup paths use it.
Unused labels are compile errors, like unused variables. A labelled continue is usually clearer than a flag variable checked after the inner loop.
lessons.challenge: Print every pair (i, j) with 0 <= i, j < 3 except that when j == i you skip the rest of that row with continue outer.
lessons.question: Which statement starts the next iteration of an enclosing loop labelled outer?
options: continue outer
break outer
goto outer
lessons.explanation: continue with a label applies to that labelled for statement. break outer would leave it, and goto outer would restart the loop from its initialisation.

lessons.title: Functions, multiple results and named results
body: A function declares typed parameters and results: func divmod(a, b int) (int, int). Consecutive parameters of one type can share it. Arguments are passed by value: the function receives copies, so to let it change the caller's variable you pass a pointer.
Returning several values is idiomatic, especially (result, error) and (value, ok). The blank identifier _ discards a result you do not need. Every result must be received or explicitly discarded.

Results can be named. Named results start as zero values and a bare return returns their current values. Use them for short functions or for documentation; in long functions bare returns hide what is being returned.
lessons.challenge: Write func parsePair(s string) (string, string, bool) that splits "k=v" on the first "=" and reports whether it succeeded; print the results for "a=b" and "ab".
lessons.question: What does a bare return do in a function with named results?
options: Returns zero values regardless of assignments
Is only allowed in functions with no results
Returns the current values of the named result variables
lessons.explanation: Named results are ordinary local variables initialised to zero. A bare return returns whatever they hold at that moment, including changes made by deferred functions.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

Named results are ordinary local variables initialised to zero. A bare return returns whatever they hold at that moment, including changes made by deferred functions.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Named results are ordinary local variables initialised to zero. A bare return returns whatever they hold at that moment, including changes made by deferred functions.

lessons.title: Variadic functions and functions as values
body: A final parameter ...T accepts any number of T values and receives them as a []T. A caller can pass an existing slice with s..., which passes the slice itself without copying, so the function can see and modify the caller's elements.

Functions are values with types such as func(int) int. They can be stored in variables, maps and struct fields, passed as arguments and returned. The zero value of a function type is nil, and calling a nil function panics.
Function values compare only to nil. Passing behaviour as a function is often simpler than defining a one-method interface, and the sort and slices packages accept comparison functions this way.
lessons.challenge: Build a map from operator strings "+", "-", "*" to func(int, int) int and print the result of each on 6 and 3, in that order.
lessons.question: What does a variadic function receive when called as f(s...)?
options: The caller's slice itself, sharing its backing array
A fresh copy of the slice
Each element as a separate parameter
lessons.explanation: s... passes the slice header unchanged, so writes to elements are visible to the caller. Calling f(a, b) instead builds a new slice.

s... passes the slice header unchanged, so writes to elements are visible to the caller. Calling f(a, b) instead builds a new slice.
lessons.practiceAnswer: s... passes the slice header unchanged, so writes to elements are visible to the caller. Calling f(a, b) instead builds a new slice.

lessons.title: Closures and per-iteration loop variables
body: A function literal can refer to variables of the enclosing function; it captures the variables themselves, not copies of their values. A counter generator returns a closure that keeps its own count alive after the outer function returns. The captured variable then lives on the heap.

Before Go 1.22, a for loop had one variable shared by all iterations, so closures created in the loop all saw its final value. Since Go 1.22, in modules whose go line is 1.22 or later, each iteration of a 3-clause or range loop gets a fresh variable. This guide targets go 1.27, so each closure sees its own iteration value.
Closures make small strategies and callbacks easy, but capturing a variable that another goroutine also writes is a data race. Pass values as arguments when in doubt.
lessons.challenge: Write func adder(start int) func(int) int that returns a closure accumulating a running total; print the results of adding 5, then 10, to adder(1).
lessons.question: With go 1.27 in go.mod, what do closures created in for i := range 3 capture?
options: A copy of i taken when the closure is called
A distinct i for each iteration, so they see 0, 1 and 2
One shared i, so they all see 3
lessons.explanation: Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration for modules declaring go 1.22 or later. The closures capture variables, but each iteration has its own.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
3
0 1 2 

Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration for modules declaring go 1.22 or later. The closures capture variables, but each iteration has its own.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration for modules declaring go 1.22 or later. The closures capture variables, but each iteration has its own.

lessons.title: defer: cleanup that runs on every return path
body: defer schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns, whether by return, reaching the end, or a panic. Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order, which matches acquiring resources in order and releasing them in reverse.

The arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when the defer statement runs, not when the call happens. defer fmt.Println(i) prints the value i had at that moment. A deferred closure that reads i instead sees its final value.

The common pattern is acquire, check the error, then defer the release: f, err := os.Open(p); if err != nil { return err }; defer f.Close(). A defer inside a loop does not run until the function returns, so a loop that opens many files should call a helper function per item.
lessons.challenge: Write func trace(name string) func() that prints "enter name" and returns a function printing "exit name"; use it as defer trace("work")() and print "working" in between.
lessons.question: When are the arguments of a deferred function call evaluated?
options: When the defer statement executes
When the surrounding function returns
Lazily, the first time the call reads them
lessons.explanation: defer evaluates the function value and its arguments immediately and saves them; only the call is postponed.

Expected output:

argument evaluated early: 1

defer evaluates the function value and its arguments immediately and saves them; only the call is postponed.

lessons.title: Arrays are values with a fixed length
body: An array type includes its length: [3]int and [4]int are different types. Arrays are values, so assigning or passing one copies every element. That makes small arrays useful as map keys and as fixed-size records, but it surprises programmers coming from C, where arrays decay to pointers.

Array literals can let the compiler count: [...]string{"a", "b"} has type [2]string. Indexed literals such as [5]int{2: 7} set selected positions and leave the rest zero. Indexing out of range with a constant index is a compile error; with a variable index it panics at run time.

Arrays of comparable elements can be compared with ==. In practice most Go code uses slices, which are views onto arrays; arrays appear in hashes ([32]byte), coordinates and buffers sized at compile time.
lessons.challenge: Use a [2]int{x, y} array as a map key to count how many times each grid point appears in the list (1,2), (3,4), (1,2); print the count for (1,2).
lessons.question: What happens when an array is passed to a function?
options: A slice view is created automatically
The whole array is copied
A pointer to the first element is passed
lessons.explanation: Arrays are values. To share one, pass a pointer (*[3]int) or a slice of it (a[:]).
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
[1 2 3] [100 2 3]
[0 0 7 0 9] 5

Arrays are values. To share one, pass a pointer (*[3]int) or a slice of it (a[:]).

lessons.title: Slices: length, capacity and shared backing arrays
body: A slice is a small header: a pointer into a backing array, a length and a capacity. s[lo:hi] makes a new header over the same array, with length hi-lo and capacity reaching to the end of the array. Writing through one slice is visible through every slice that shares the array.

append(s, x) writes into the existing array when len < cap and returns a header with a larger length. When capacity runs out it allocates a bigger array, copies the elements and returns a header pointing there. Always assign the result: s = append(s, x).

Because append may or may not reallocate, two slices that once shared memory may silently stop sharing. A full slice expression s[lo:hi:max] limits the capacity, forcing the next append on the sub-slice to copy instead of overwriting the parent's later elements.
A nil slice has length and capacity zero, and works with len, append and range. make([]T, n, c) allocates a slice with length n and capacity c.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	base := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
	head := base[:2]
	fmt.Println(len(head), cap(head))
	head = append(head, 99)
	fmt.Println(base)
	safe := base[:2:2]
	safe = append(safe, -1)
	fmt.Println(base, safe)
	var empty []int
	fmt.Println(empty == nil, len(empty), append(empty, 7))
}
lessons.challenge: Write func remove(s []int, i int) []int that deletes element i without changing order, then show that the caller's original slice was modified by printing it.
lessons.question: After t := s[:2]; t = append(t, 9), when is s[2] overwritten?
options: When cap(t) > 2, because append writes into the shared array
Never; append always copies
Only if s is a nil slice
lessons.explanation: With spare capacity, append places the new element in the backing array that s also uses. A full slice expression s[:2:2] prevents this.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

[1 2 99 4 5]

With spare capacity, append places the new element in the backing array that s also uses. A full slice expression s[:2:2] prevents this.
lessons.practiceAnswer: With spare capacity, append places the new element in the backing array that s also uses. A full slice expression s[:2:2] prevents this.

lessons.title: The slices package: sort, search, insert, compact
body: The generic slices package (Go 1.21+) replaces many hand-written loops: slices.Sort, SortFunc, SortStableFunc, BinarySearch, Contains, Index, IndexFunc, Insert, Delete, Compact, Reverse, Max, Min, Equal and Clone.

Comparison functions return a negative, zero or positive int; cmp.Compare and cmp.Or help compose multi-key orderings. SortFunc is not stable; use SortStableFunc when equal elements must keep their order.

Delete, Insert and Compact return the new slice and may reuse the old backing array. Since Go 1.22 the removed tail elements are zeroed, so pointers left behind do not keep objects alive. As with append, use the returned slice.
lessons.challenge: Sort people by name length, then alphabetically for equal lengths, using cmp.Or; print the names for "bob", "al", "eve", "zo".
lessons.question: Why use SortStableFunc rather than SortFunc?
options: It keeps equal elements in their original relative order
It is always faster
It sorts in descending order
lessons.explanation: SortFunc may reorder elements that compare equal. Stability matters when sorting by a secondary key after an earlier sort.

Expected output:

SortFunc may reorder elements that compare equal. Stability matters when sorting by a secondary key after an earlier sort.

lessons.title: Maps: lookup, comma-ok, deletion and iteration order
body: map[K]V stores key/value pairs; K must be comparable. m[k] returns the zero value for a missing key, so use the comma-ok form v, ok := m[k] to tell "missing" from "present with zero value". delete(m, k) removes a key and is a no-op if it is absent.

Iteration order over a map is unspecified and deliberately varies between runs. If output must be deterministic, collect the keys, sort them (slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) does both since Go 1.23) and range over the sorted keys.

Maps are reference-like: assigning a map copies the header, so both names see the same entries. Writing to a nil map panics. Maps are not safe for concurrent writes; the runtime detects many such races and crashes with "concurrent map writes".
lessons.challenge: Count word frequencies in "the cat and the hat and the bat" and print each word with its count in alphabetical order.
lessons.question: How should you print a map's entries in a stable order?
options: Collect and sort the keys, then range over the sorted keys
Range over the map; insertion order is preserved
Call maps.Clone first to fix the order
lessons.explanation: Map iteration order is unspecified and randomised. fmt prints maps with sorted keys, but range does not.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

ada 36
cy 41

Map iteration order is unspecified and randomised. fmt prints maps with sorted keys, but range does not.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Map iteration order is unspecified and randomised. fmt prints maps with sorted keys, but range does not.

lessons.title: Structs, field tags and embedding
body: A struct groups named fields: type Point struct { X, Y int }. Composite literals can name fields (Point{X: 1}) or list them positionally; naming fields keeps code working when fields are added. Structs of comparable fields can be compared with ==.

Embedding a type in a struct (a field with no name) promotes the embedded type's fields and methods to the outer struct. This is composition, not inheritance: the outer value contains the inner one, and methods still receive the inner value as their receiver. An outer field or method with the same name shadows the promoted one.

Field tags are string metadata read by reflection, for example `json:"name,omitempty"`. They do not change the language semantics; packages such as encoding/json interpret them. Anonymous structs are useful for one-off groupings and table-driven tests.
lessons.challenge: Define type Animal struct{ Name string } with method Hello() string returning "I am "+Name, and type Dog struct{ Animal; Breed string }; print Hello for a Dog named Rex.
lessons.question: When Dog embeds Animal and you call d.Hello(), what is the receiver?
options: The whole Dog value
A new Animal copied from Dog's fields
The embedded Animal value inside d
lessons.explanation: Promotion rewrites d.Hello() to d.Animal.Hello(). The method has no knowledge of the outer Dog, which is why embedding is not virtual dispatch.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

Promotion rewrites d.Hello() to d.Animal.Hello(). The method has no knowledge of the outer Dog, which is why embedding is not virtual dispatch.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Promotion rewrites d.Hello() to d.Animal.Hello(). The method has no knowledge of the outer Dog, which is why embedding is not virtual dispatch.

lessons.title: Pointers, new, new(expr) and addressability
body: &x takes the address of a variable and *p reads or writes through a pointer. Go has no pointer arithmetic outside package unsafe. Taking the address of a local variable is safe: if the pointer outlives the function, the compiler moves the variable to the heap (escape analysis).

new(T) allocates a zero T and returns *T. Since Go 1.26, new also accepts an expression: new(42) or new(time.Now()) allocates a variable initialised to that value. This removes small helper functions written only to get a pointer to a constant, common with optional fields.

Composite literals are addressable through &: &Point{1, 2} is idiomatic. Map elements are not addressable (&m[k] is a compile error) because a map may move its entries as it grows. The field selector p.X automatically dereferences a pointer to a struct.
lessons.challenge: Write func swap(a, b *int) and use it to swap two variables holding 1 and 2; print them.
lessons.question: Why is &m["k"] a compile error?
options: The & operator only applies to struct fields
Map elements are not addressable because the map may relocate them
Strings cannot be map keys
lessons.explanation: Growing a map rehashes and moves entries, so a pointer to an element could dangle. Store pointers as values (map[string]*T) if you need shared mutable elements.

lessons.title: Go 1.27 struct literals with promoted field keys
body: Before Go 1.27, a struct literal could only name the struct's own top-level fields. To set a field promoted from an embedded struct, you had to spell the nesting: Named{Point: Point{X: 1}}.

Go 1.27 lets a key be any valid field selector for the struct type, so Named{X: 1, Name: "a"} sets the promoted X directly. The embedded struct is still a real field; the literal is shorthand for initialising inside it.

This only works when the selector is unambiguous and does not pass through an embedded pointer, which could be nil. Older modules with a go line below 1.27 reject the shorter form, so the go directive matters for which literals compile.
lessons.challenge: Embed type Meta struct{ ID int } in type Doc struct{ Meta; Title string } and build a Doc with ID 7 and title "go" using the 1.27 promoted-key form; print it with %+v.
lessons.question: What does Named{X: 3} mean under Go 1.27 when Named embeds Point?
options: It declares a new field X on Named
It is still a compile error
It initialises the promoted field Named.Point.X
lessons.explanation: The 1.27 rule allows any valid field selector as a key. X selects the promoted field inside the embedded Point.

lessons.title: Built-ins: len, cap, copy, clear, min and max
body: copy(dst, src) copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements and returns that count; it handles overlapping slices correctly. It also copies bytes from a string into a []byte.
clear (Go 1.21) deletes every entry from a map, or sets every element of a slice to its zero value without changing its length. Clearing is how to reuse a map without reallocating.
min and max (Go 1.21) are built-ins for any ordered type and take one or more arguments. For floats, if any argument is NaN the result is NaN. They work with constants at compile time too.
lessons.challenge: Shift the elements of []int{1, 2, 3, 4} one place left in place with copy, then set the last element to 0; print the slice.
lessons.question: What does clear(s) do to a slice s?
options: Frees the backing array
Zeroes every element; the length is unchanged
Sets the length to zero
lessons.explanation: clear on a slice zeroes elements up to len(s). For a map, clear removes all entries. Use s = s[:0] to reset a slice's length.

lessons.title: Methods, value receivers and pointer receivers
body: A method is a function with a receiver: func (c Counter) Value() int. Methods can be declared on any defined type in the same package, not only structs. The receiver is an ordinary parameter, so a value receiver works on a copy and a pointer receiver can modify the caller's value.

Use a pointer receiver when the method mutates the receiver, when the value is large, or when it contains something that must not be copied, such as a sync.Mutex. Be consistent: if some methods need pointers, give all methods of the type pointer receivers.

Calls are convenient in both directions. If v is addressable, v.Inc() on a pointer method is shorthand for (&v).Inc(). If p is a pointer, p.Value() on a value method is shorthand for (*p).Value(). The shorthand does not apply to values that are not addressable, such as map elements or return values.
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

type Stack []int

func (s *Stack) Push(v int) { *s = append(*s, v) }

func (s *Stack) Pop() int {
	old := *s
	v := old[len(old)-1]
	*s = old[:len(old)-1]
	return v
}

func main() {
	var s Stack
	s.Push(1)
	s.Push(2)
	s.Push(3)
	fmt.Println(s.Pop(), s)
}
lessons.challenge: Define type Stack []int with pointer-receiver methods Push(int) and Pop() int; push 1, 2, 3, pop once and print the popped value and the remaining stack.
lessons.question: Why did BrokenInc not change c?
options: Methods cannot modify struct fields
The compiler optimised the call away
A value receiver increments a copy of c
lessons.explanation: The receiver is a parameter passed by value. Only a pointer receiver can change the caller's Counter.

The receiver is a parameter passed by value. Only a pointer receiver can change the caller's Counter.

lessons.title: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly
body: An interface type lists method signatures. Any type whose method set includes those methods satisfies the interface; there is no implements keyword. This lets you define small interfaces where they are used, and lets existing types satisfy interfaces written later.
An interface value holds two things: a dynamic type and a value of that type. Calling a method dispatches to the dynamic type's implementation. The zero interface value has neither and is nil.

Method sets decide satisfaction. The method set of T contains its value-receiver methods; the method set of *T contains both value- and pointer-receiver methods. So if Write has a pointer receiver, *Buffer satisfies io.Writer but Buffer does not. A compile-time assertion var _ io.Writer = (*Buffer)(nil) documents and checks this.

Both Buffer and *Buffer

lessons.title: nil interfaces versus interfaces holding nil pointers
body: An interface is nil only when both its dynamic type and value are absent. Storing a nil *MyError in an error variable gives a non-nil interface whose dynamic type is *MyError and whose value is nil.

The classic bug is a function returning a concrete pointer type through an error result: var e *MyError; return e. The caller's err != nil is true even though nothing failed. Return a literal nil for "no error", and declare the result as error rather than *MyError.
A method with a pointer receiver can be called on a nil pointer, and can even handle it deliberately. That is why the runtime cannot simply treat "interface holding nil" as nil.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite a function find(ok bool) error so it returns &MyError{} when ok is false and a true nil interface otherwise; print find(true) == nil and find(false) == nil.
lessons.question: Why is bad() != nil even though e was nil?
options: nil pointers are converted to empty structs
Comparison with nil always fails for errors
The interface has a dynamic type (*MyError) even though its value is nil
lessons.explanation: An interface compares equal to nil only if it has no dynamic type. Return untyped nil to signal "no error".
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
false true
*main.MyError

An interface compares equal to nil only if it has no dynamic type. Return untyped nil to signal "no error".
lessons.practiceAnswer: An interface compares equal to nil only if it has no dynamic type. Return untyped nil to signal "no error".

lessons.title: Type assertions and type switches
body: x.(T) asserts that interface value x holds a T. With one result it panics if wrong; with two, v, ok := x.(T), it reports success instead. If T is an interface type, the assertion checks whether the dynamic type implements T, which is how optional capabilities (such as io.WriterTo) are discovered.

A type switch, switch v := x.(type), branches on the dynamic type. In each case v has that case's type; in a case listing several types, or in default, v keeps the interface type. case nil matches a nil interface.

Prefer methods and small interfaces to large type switches: a type switch must be edited for each new type, while an interface lets new types plug in. Type switches are right for closed sets of message or AST node types.
lessons.challenge: Write func sum(xs []any) float64 that adds int and float64 elements and ignores everything else; print sum([]any{1, 2.5, "x", 3}).
lessons.question: What does v, ok := x.(T) do when x does not hold a T?
options: Panics with a type assertion error
Converts x to T if possible
Sets ok to false and v to T's zero value, without panicking
lessons.explanation: The comma-ok form makes the assertion non-panicking. The single-result form panics on failure.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
nil
int+1=42
text go
other float64
0 false

The comma-ok form makes the assertion non-panicking. The single-result form panics on failure.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The comma-ok form makes the assertion non-panicking. The single-result form panics on failure.

lessons.title: Small interfaces, embedding and any
body: The standard library favours one-method interfaces: io.Reader, io.Writer, fmt.Stringer, error. Larger interfaces are built by embedding: io.ReadWriter embeds Reader and Writer. A small interface is easy to satisfy and easy to fake in tests.

any is an alias for interface{}, the interface with no methods, satisfied by every type. Accepting any discards static typing, so use it only when values really can be of any type, such as formatting and encoding. Generics are usually a better fit for containers.

Define interfaces in the package that consumes them, sized to what that code needs. Returning concrete types and accepting interfaces keeps APIs flexible: callers can pass anything with the needed methods.
lessons.challenge: Write a type countingWriter that wraps an io.Writer, counts bytes written, and forwards them; write "hello" and " go" through it to os.Stdout and then print the count on its own line.
lessons.question: Where should a Go interface usually be declared?
options: In a shared interfaces package for the whole program
In the package that uses it, with only the methods it needs
Next to every type that implements it
lessons.explanation: Implicit satisfaction lets consumers declare the minimal interface they depend on without the implementer importing it.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
SMALL INTERFACES COMPOSE <nil>

Implicit satisfaction lets consumers declare the minimal interface they depend on without the implementer importing it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Implicit satisfaction lets consumers declare the minimal interface they depend on without the implementer importing it.

lessons.title: Stringer, error and custom formatting
body: If a type has a String() string method, fmt uses it for %v and %s. If it has Error() string, fmt uses that, and error takes priority over String. Defining String on a value receiver means both values and pointers print nicely.
Calling fmt.Sprint(s) inside s.String() on the same type recurses forever. Convert to an underlying type without the method first, for example fmt.Sprint(int(d)).
For full control implement fmt.Formatter, or fmt.GoStringer for %#v. Most code only needs String. go vet warns when a String method has the wrong signature, because fmt would silently ignore it.
lessons.challenge: Give type Celsius float64 a String method that prints one decimal and a °C suffix; print Celsius(21.55).
lessons.question: Why convert to int(d) inside Weekday.String before formatting?
options: Formatting d itself would call String again and recurse forever
%d does not accept named types
String methods must return only constants
lessons.explanation: fmt checks for a String method on the operand. The underlying int has none, so the conversion breaks the recursion.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
Monday Weekday(9)
Sunday 0 Monday

fmt checks for a String method on the operand. The underlying int has none, so the conversion breaks the recursion.
lessons.practiceAnswer: fmt checks for a String method on the operand. The underlying int has none, so the conversion breaks the recursion.

lessons.title: Equality, comparability and interface comparison panics
body: Booleans, numbers, strings, pointers, channels and interfaces are comparable, and so are structs and arrays whose elements are comparable. Slices, maps and functions are not comparable except with nil; use slices.Equal and maps.Equal for contents.

Two interface values are equal if their dynamic types are identical and their values are equal. If the dynamic type is not comparable, for example a slice, the comparison compiles but panics at run time. The same applies to using such an interface as a map key.
Pointers are equal when they point to the same variable. Two distinct zero-size variables may or may not have equal addresses, so do not rely on pointer identity for empty structs.
lessons.challenge: Show that two struct values type key struct{ a string; b int } with equal fields are == and can be used as the same map key; print the map length after inserting key{"x", 1} twice.
lessons.question: What happens when two any values holding slices are compared with ==?
options: It is always a compile error
It compiles but panics at run time
It compares the slice contents
lessons.explanation: Interface comparison is checked dynamically. The static type any is comparable, but the dynamic type []int is not, so the runtime panics.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
true
true
recovered: runtime error: comparing uncomparable type []int

Interface comparison is checked dynamically. The static type any is comparable, but the dynamic type []int is not, so the runtime panics.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Interface comparison is checked dynamically. The static type any is comparable, but the dynamic type []int is not, so the runtime panics.

lessons.title: Errors are values: return, check, add context
body: error is a predeclared interface with one method, Error() string. Functions that can fail return an error as their last result, and callers check it immediately: if err != nil { return ..., err }. Errors are ordinary values, so they can be stored, compared, wrapped and inspected.

errors.New and fmt.Errorf create errors. Messages are lower-case, without trailing punctuation, because they are often joined into chains such as "load config: open app.toml: no such file or directory".
Handle each error once: either deal with it (retry, use a default, report it) or return it with added context. Logging an error and also returning it produces duplicate reports further up the stack.
lessons.challenge: Write func safeDiv(a, b int) (int, error) that returns an error "division by zero" for b == 0; print the results of safeDiv(7, 2) and safeDiv(1, 0).
lessons.question: What is the idiomatic way to handle an error you cannot resolve locally?
options: Log it and return it so nothing is missed
Panic so the caller notices
Return it with added context, without also logging it
lessons.explanation: Each error should be handled once. Adding context while returning builds a readable chain for whoever finally handles it.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
age 36
error: age cannot be negative
error: parse age "old": strconv.Atoi: parsing "old": invalid syntax

Each error should be handled once. Adding context while returning builds a readable chain for whoever finally handles it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Each error should be handled once. Adding context while returning builds a readable chain for whoever finally handles it.

lessons.title: Wrapping with %w, errors.Is, errors.As and errors.AsType
body: fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error: the new error's message includes the old one, and errors.Unwrap returns the original. %v includes the message but breaks the chain, which is right when you deliberately hide an implementation detail.

errors.Is(err, target) walks the chain looking for an error equal to target, for sentinels such as io.EOF or fs.ErrNotExist. errors.As(err, &target) walks the chain looking for an error assignable to target's type and stores it, for typed errors such as *fs.PathError.

Go 1.26 adds the generic errors.AsType[E](err) (E, bool), which returns the matching error directly instead of needing a pointer variable, and is checked at compile time. Prefer it in new code that targets 1.26 or later.
Never compare wrapped errors with ==; use errors.Is. go vet reports %w used with a non-error operand, and Go 1.27's vet also reports %w given a pointer to an error.
lessons.challenge: Wrap io.EOF twice with different context using %w and print whether errors.Is still finds io.EOF, then print the full message.
lessons.question: What is the difference between wrapping with %w and formatting with %v?
options: %v wraps and %w discards the original
%w keeps the original error inspectable through Is/As; %v keeps only its text
They are identical; %w is just a newer spelling
lessons.explanation: %w records the operand as the wrapped error returned by Unwrap. %v formats it into a string, so callers can no longer match it.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
true
open /definitely/missing.toml
true false

%w records the operand as the wrapped error returned by Unwrap. %v formats it into a string, so callers can no longer match it.
lessons.practiceAnswer: %w records the operand as the wrapped error returned by Unwrap. %v formats it into a string, so callers can no longer match it.

lessons.title: Designing errors: sentinels, types and opaque errors
body: A sentinel error is a package-level variable, such as var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found"). Callers test it with errors.Is. Sentinels are part of your API: once exported, callers depend on them.

An error type carries structured data: type ValidationError struct{ Field string }. Callers extract it with errors.As or errors.AsType. Give error types pointer receivers consistently so a single dynamic type is matched.

An error type can customise matching by implementing Is(target error) bool or As(target any) bool, for example to say that every ValidationError counts as ErrInvalid. Expose as little as callers need; opaque errors that are only printed are the easiest to evolve.
lessons.challenge: Define var ErrNotFound and func find(id int) error that returns ErrNotFound wrapped as "user 7: not found" for id 7 and nil otherwise; print errors.Is(find(7), ErrNotFound) and find(1).
lessons.question: When should an error be a struct type rather than a sentinel?
options: When callers need structured details such as the failing field
Always; sentinels are deprecated
Only when the error is never wrapped
lessons.explanation: Sentinels answer "which error?". Types answer "what are the details?" and are matched with errors.As or AsType.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
validate user: invalid field name
true
field: name

Sentinels answer "which error?". Types answer "what are the details?" and are matched with errors.As or AsType.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Sentinels answer "which error?". Types answer "what are the details?" and are matched with errors.As or AsType.

lessons.title: Combining errors with errors.Join and multiple %w
body: errors.Join(errs...) returns one error that wraps several. Its message puts each on its own line, and errors.Is and errors.As search all of them. nil inputs are skipped, and Join of only nils returns nil.
fmt.Errorf can also wrap more than one error with several %w verbs. Such errors implement Unwrap() []error rather than Unwrap() error, so errors.Unwrap returns nil for them; use Is and As instead.
Join suits validation that reports every problem, and cleanup where both the operation and Close failed: err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()).
lessons.challenge: Combine two errors with a single fmt.Errorf using two %w verbs and print whether errors.Is finds each of them.
lessons.question: What does errors.Join(nil, nil) return?
options: An empty non-nil error
It panics on nil inputs
nil
lessons.explanation: Join discards nil errors and returns nil if none remain, so it is safe to accumulate optional failures.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
name required
email required
true true

Join discards nil errors and returns nil if none remain, so it is safe to accumulate optional failures.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Join discards nil errors and returns nil if none remain, so it is safe to accumulate optional failures.

lessons.title: panic, recover and when not to use them
body: panic stops normal execution of the current goroutine and starts running its deferred calls. If nothing recovers, the program prints the panic value and a stack trace and exits with status 2. Run-time errors such as an out-of-range index or a nil map write are panics.

recover() inside a deferred function stops the panic and returns its value; anywhere else it returns nil. A recover only catches panics in its own goroutine. Use it at boundaries, such as a server that converts a handler panic into a 500 response, and convert the panic to an error.

Use panic for programmer errors and impossible states, not for expected failures like a missing file. Since Go 1.21, panic(nil) becomes a *runtime.PanicNilError, so recover() == nil reliably means "no panic".
lessons.challenge: Write func mustPositive(n int) int that panics with "negative" for n < 0, and func try(n int) (result string) that recovers and returns "caught: negative"; print try(-1) and try(3).
lessons.question: Why could the deferred function change err in safeIndex?
options: Panics always return the zero value with an error
err is a named result, and deferred functions run before the caller receives the results
recover returns the error to the caller automatically
lessons.explanation: Deferred closures can assign to named results after a panic or return. That is how recovery is converted into an ordinary error.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
2 <nil>
recovered: runtime error: index out of range [5] with length 2
true

Deferred closures can assign to named results after a panic or return. That is how recovery is converted into an ordinary error.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Deferred closures can assign to named results after a panic or return. That is how recovery is converted into an ordinary error.

lessons.title: Cleanup errors, defer ordering and Close
body: Close on a file being written can fail: data may be flushed only when it is closed. defer f.Close() discards that error. For writers, capture it with a named result: defer func() { err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()) }().
Deferred calls run in reverse order, so acquiring A then B and deferring both releases B before A. A deferred method value such as defer w.Flush() evaluates the receiver w immediately.

Readers can usually ignore Close errors, but writers, network transactions and database commits should not. os.CreateTemp, then write, sync, close and rename is the safe way to replace a file: a failure at any step leaves the old file in place.
lessons.challenge: Write a value to a temporary file with os.CreateTemp, return any Close error with errors.Join, read it back, remove the file and print the contents.
lessons.question: Why can defer f.Close() be wrong for a file you are writing?
options: Deferred Close runs before the writes finish
It discards the Close error, which may report data that failed to flush
Close cannot be deferred for writable files
lessons.explanation: Write errors can surface at Close. Capture the error into a named result so the caller learns the write failed.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
working
close b
close a
result: close b failed

Write errors can surface at Close. Capture the error into a named result so the caller learns the write failed.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Write errors can surface at Close. Capture the error into a named result so the caller learns the write failed.

lessons.title: Packages, exported names and initialisation order
body: A package is a directory of .go files sharing one package clause. Its import path is the module path plus the directory, so example.com/shop/price lives in shop/price. Identifiers starting with an upper-case letter are exported to other packages; everything else is private to the package, across all of its files.

Package initialisation runs once, before main: package-level variables are initialised in dependency order, then each file's init functions run. Imported packages initialise before the packages that import them. Keep init small; hidden work there makes programs hard to test.

A package should be named for what it provides (price, not utils), and its exported names should read well with the package qualifier: price.Format, not price.FormatPrice. Package main is special: it builds a command rather than a library.
This lesson is a two-package module. Run it as shown, then do the practice by changing only the price package.
lessons.challenge: Make price.Format handle negative amounts so that Format(-250) returns "-2.50 EUR".
lessons.question: In what order do package-level variables, init functions and main run?
options: init functions in alphabetical order of package name
Imported packages first; within a package, variables then init functions; main last
main first, then init functions lazily
lessons.explanation: Initialisation follows the import graph. Each package finishes initialising its variables and running its inits before packages that import it start.

Initialisation follows the import graph. Each package finishes initialising its variables and running its inits before packages that import it start.

lessons.title: The go and toolchain lines, GOTOOLCHAIN and versions
body: The go line in go.mod is a minimum: the module needs at least that language version, and the go command refuses to build it with an older toolchain unless it can switch. Since Go 1.21 the go command can download a newer toolchain automatically when go.mod demands one.

The optional toolchain line names a preferred toolchain for work inside this module, for example toolchain go1.27.2. GOTOOLCHAIN overrides the choice: local uses the installed toolchain, go1.27.2 forces a release, and go1.27.2+auto allows upgrades.

runtime.Version reports the toolchain that built the binary, and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo reports the module path, main version and dependency versions embedded at build time. go version -m binary prints the same information for an existing executable.
lessons.challenge: Print the main module path and the number of dependency modules reported by debug.ReadBuildInfo.
lessons.question: What does go 1.27 in go.mod mean?
options: The module only builds with exactly Go 1.27.0
Dependencies must be at version 1.27
The module requires at least Go 1.27 language semantics and toolchain
lessons.explanation: Since Go 1.21 the go line is a mandatory minimum. Newer toolchains build it with 1.27 semantics; older ones must switch or fail.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
true
true guide.example/lesson true

Since Go 1.21 the go line is a mandatory minimum. Newer toolchains build it with 1.27 semantics; older ones must switch or fail.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Since Go 1.21 the go line is a mandatory minimum. Newer toolchains build it with 1.27 semantics; older ones must switch or fail.

lessons.title: Requirements, go.sum, replace and minimal version selection
body: require lines name the minimum version of each dependency. When several modules require different versions, the go command uses minimal version selection: it picks the highest of the stated minimums, never a newer release nobody asked for. Builds are therefore reproducible without a lock file.

go.sum records cryptographic hashes of every module version used, checked against the public checksum database on first download. Commit go.sum with go.mod. go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0 changes a requirement, go mod tidy adds missing and removes unused requirements, and go list -m all prints the selected build list.

A replace directive substitutes a different source, such as a local directory, for a module version. It applies only when building this main module, which makes it right for local development and offline examples like this one, and wrong for libraries others depend on.
Go 1.27 makes go mod tidy merge duplicate require blocks for modules with go 1.27 or later.
lessons.challenge: Add func Shout(name string) string to the greet module returning the upper-case greeting followed by "!", and print greet.Shout("modules").
lessons.question: Which version does minimal version selection choose when A needs lib v1.2.0 and B needs lib v1.3.0?
options: The newest published version of lib
v1.2.0, the lowest requested
v1.3.0, the highest of the stated minimums
lessons.explanation: Each requirement is a minimum. MVS selects the smallest version that satisfies all of them, which is the maximum of the minimums.

lessons.title: Multi-module workspaces with go.work
body: A workspace lets you edit several modules together without replace directives. go work init ./app ./lib writes a go.work file with use lines; inside the workspace, imports of example.com/lib resolve to the local directory.

go.work is a developer convenience and is usually not committed for libraries. GOWORK=off disables it, which is how CI checks that each module builds on its own. Commands such as go work sync push the workspace's selected versions back into each module's go.mod.
Workspaces suit a service and a library changing in the same pull request, or trying a fix to a dependency before it is released.

lessons.title: internal packages and enforced boundaries
body: A package whose path contains an internal element can be imported only by code rooted at the parent of that internal directory. example.com/shop/internal/db can be used by example.com/shop/... but not by other modules or sibling trees. The go command enforces it.
Use internal for implementation packages you want to share across your own packages without making them public API. It is the main tool for keeping a module's exported surface small.

vendor directories are a different mechanism: go mod vendor copies dependencies into vendor/ so builds need no network. Since Go 1.14 the go command uses vendor automatically when vendor/modules.txt matches go.mod.

go tool lists available tools, and go install tool installs them into GOBIN. Because tools are module requirements, go.sum verifies them and minimal version selection applies to their dependencies too.

A tool version pinned and verified with the module's other requirements

lessons.title: Semantic versions, major-version paths and retract
body: Module versions are semantic: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Within a major version, newer releases must stay compatible. A v2 or later release must change the module path, for example example.com/lib/v2, so v1 and v2 can be imported side by side and old code keeps compiling.
Pre-release versions such as v1.3.0-rc.1 sort before v1.3.0, and pseudo-versions like v0.0.0-20261016120000-abcdef123456 identify untagged commits. v0 makes no compatibility promise.

A retract directive in a later release marks bad versions: go get and go list -m -u avoid them and explain why, but existing builds that require them still work. Retraction is how a maintainer withdraws a broken or accidentally published tag.

So incompatible major versions are distinct import paths that can coexist
The proxy rejects tags above v1 otherwise
lessons.explanation: Semantic import versioning: an incompatible API gets a new import path, so existing importers of v1 are never broken by v2.

lessons.title: go test and table-driven tests
body: Tests live in files ending _test.go next to the code. A test is func TestXxx(t *testing.T). t.Errorf records a failure and continues; t.Fatalf records it and stops this test. go test ./... builds and runs every package's tests; -run takes a regular expression to select tests and -v prints each one.
A table-driven test lists cases as a slice of structs and loops over them. Adding a case is one line, and failure messages print the input, the result and the expectation: Reverse(%q) = %q, want %q.

Tests in package x see its unexported names. Tests in package x_test (an external test package in the same directory) see only the exported API, which checks it the way callers will use it. Both kinds can live side by side.
This project starts with a byte-based Reverse that breaks multi-byte characters. One check adds a failing case on purpose to show what a failure looks like; the answer fixes the function.

lessons.explanation: Fatalf calls FailNow, which ends the current test function via runtime.Goexit. Other tests still run.

lessons.title: Subtests, helpers, cleanup, temp dirs and parallel tests
body: t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T)) runs a named subtest. Each table case becomes its own entry, can be selected with -run TestParse/empty, and a Fatal in one case does not stop the others.

t.Helper() marks a function as a test helper, so failure locations point at the caller rather than the helper. t.Cleanup registers teardown that runs after the test and its subtests, in last-in, first-out order. t.TempDir returns a directory removed automatically, and t.Context returns a context cancelled just before cleanup runs (Go 1.24).

t.Parallel() lets a test run alongside other parallel tests. Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration has its own variable, so parallel subtests in a loop no longer need the old tc := tc copy. t.Setenv and t.Chdir change process-wide state and therefore cannot be combined with Parallel.

lessons.title: Benchmarks with b.Loop and allocation reports
body: A benchmark is func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B). Since Go 1.24, write the measured code inside for b.Loop() { ... }. Loop resets the timer the first time it is called, stops it at the end, and keeps the loop body's results alive so the compiler cannot optimise the work away.

Run benchmarks with go test -run=^$ -bench=. so ordinary tests are skipped. -benchmem or b.ReportAllocs adds bytes and allocations per operation, often the most useful number. -count=10 repeats runs so a tool such as benchstat can compare before and after.

Benchmarks measure one machine at one moment. Compare variants on the same machine, look at allocations as well as time, and treat small differences as noise unless benchstat shows them as significant.

lessons.question: What does for b.Loop() do that the older for range b.N did not?
options: It times only the loop and keeps the body's results alive against dead-code elimination
It runs the benchmark in parallel automatically
It fixes the iteration count at one million
lessons.explanation: Loop resets and stops the timer itself and prevents the compiler from discarding results computed in the body, two classic benchmark mistakes.

lessons.title: Native fuzzing with seed corpora
body: A fuzz test is func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). f.Add supplies seed inputs; f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, in string) { ... }) is the target. Plain go test runs only the seeds, so fuzz tests also act as regression tests.

go test -fuzz=FuzzXxx generates new inputs, guided by coverage, until it finds a failure or -fuzztime ends. A failing input is written to testdata/fuzz/FuzzXxx/ and replayed by every later go test run, so commit those files.

Fuzz targets should check properties rather than exact outputs: reversing twice gives the input back, the output is valid UTF-8, parsing what you formatted round-trips. Inputs that are invalid by design should be skipped with t.Skip or rejected with an error, not crash.

Runs it on the seed corpus and saved failing inputs only
Fuzzes for a default of ten seconds

lessons.title: Coverage profiles and what they do not prove
body: go test -cover reports the percentage of statements executed by the tests. -coverprofile=c.out writes per-block data, go tool cover -func=c.out lists coverage by function and go tool cover -html=c.out shows uncovered lines in a browser. -covermode=atomic is needed for accurate counts with concurrent tests.
Since Go 1.20, go build -cover produces an instrumented binary that writes coverage data to GOCOVERDIR, so integration tests that run the real program can contribute coverage too.

Coverage shows what was executed, not what was checked. A test that calls every function without asserting anything reaches 100%. Use coverage to find untested branches, especially error paths, then write tests that check the behaviour there.

lessons.title: Deterministic concurrent tests with testing/synctest
body: testing/synctest (stable since Go 1.25) runs a test function in an isolated bubble. Goroutines started inside belong to the bubble, and time inside it is fake: it starts at midnight UTC on 1 January 2000 and advances only when every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked.

synctest.Wait blocks until every other goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked, which gives a precise point to check state without sleeping. Code that waits for a timeout of one hour therefore finishes instantly and deterministically.

Go 1.27 adds synctest.Sleep, which advances the fake clock and then waits for the bubble to settle. Durably blocked means blocked on something inside the bubble, such as a channel created there, a timer or a sync.WaitGroup; blocking on real I/O or an outside mutex is not durable.
lessons.challenge: Add a synctest test in which a goroutine refreshes the cache every 30 seconds; advance 65 seconds with synctest.Sleep and check the stored time is 00:01:00.
lessons.question: When does fake time advance inside a synctest bubble?
options: Only when every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked
At real wall-clock speed
Each time the test calls t.Log
lessons.explanation: The clock jumps to the next timer only when nothing in the bubble can make progress, which makes timing-dependent tests deterministic.

lessons.title: Type parameters and generic functions
body: A generic function declares type parameters in square brackets: func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U. Each type parameter has a constraint, an interface describing what the function may do with values of that type. any allows only operations every type supports: assignment, passing, and comparison with nil for some kinds.

Callers can write type arguments explicitly, Map[int, string](xs, f), but usually the compiler infers them from the ordinary arguments. Inference works from function arguments and, for untyped constants, picks the default type.

Generics remove duplicated code for containers and algorithms that are the same for every type. They do not replace interfaces: if a function only calls methods, an interface parameter is simpler. Reach for type parameters when you need to keep the concrete type, such as returning []T rather than []any.
lessons.challenge: Write func Reduce[T, A any](xs []T, init A, f func(A, T) A) A and use it to sum []int{1, 2, 3} and to join []string{"a", "b"} into "ab".

options: When the function works with slices
When the function only calls methods and does not need the concrete type back
Never; generics are always faster
lessons.explanation: Interfaces give dynamic dispatch with simple signatures. Type parameters help when the type must be preserved in results or containers.

lessons.title: Constraints, type sets, ~ and cmp.Ordered
body: A constraint is an interface, and an interface defines a type set. Besides methods, a constraint can list types: interface{ int | int64 | float64 } permits exactly those types, and operators such as + and < are allowed only if every type in the set supports them.

~T means "any type whose underlying type is T". interface{ ~int } accepts int and also type Celsius int. Without the tilde, defined types built on int are excluded, which is rarely what you want for numeric helpers.

The standard library provides cmp.Ordered (types supporting < <= > >=) and comparable (types supporting == and !=). Interfaces containing type elements can only be used as constraints, never as ordinary variable types.

Every integer type of any size

lessons.title: comparable, map keys and strict comparability
body: A type parameter used as a map key or compared with == needs the comparable constraint. func Index[T comparable](xs []T, v T) int works for strings, numbers, pointers, structs of comparable fields, and so on.

Since Go 1.20, interface types such as any also satisfy comparable, even though comparing two interface values can panic if their dynamic types are not comparable. Only strictly comparable types guarantee == never panics.
Generic sets and deduplication are typical uses: type Set[T comparable] map[T]struct{}. The empty struct value takes no space, so the map stores only keys.

Yes, and comparison can never panic

lessons.title: Type inference, including Go 1.27's assignment inference

func Scale[S ~[]E, E Number](s S, k E) S returns the caller's own slice type, not plain []E. That matters when the caller has methods on a named slice type.

Go 1.21 allowed inference when a generic function is assigned to a variable of a function type. Go 1.27 generalises this to every context where a generic function is assigned or converted to a matching function type, such as struct fields and return values. You no longer need to write Double[int] when the target type already says int.

lessons.title: Generic types, methods on them and generic aliases

Instantiating a generic type with type arguments makes an ordinary type: Stack[int] and Stack[string] are distinct. The zero value works if the struct is designed for it, which is the usual Go goal.
Since Go 1.24 type aliases can be generic: type Set[T comparable] = map[T]struct{}. That helps move generic types between packages without breaking callers.

lessons.title: Go 1.27 generic methods
body: Go 1.27 lets a method declare its own type parameters in addition to the receiver's: func (l List[T]) Map[U any](f func(T) U) List[U]. Before 1.27 such helpers had to be package-level functions, Map(l, f), because methods could not introduce new types.

Type arguments are inferred at the call as for functions, or can be given explicitly: l.Map[string](f). Non-generic types can have generic methods too, for example func (r Reader) Decode[T any]() (T, error).

A generic method does not belong to any interface's method set, because an interface cannot list a method whose type depends on a parameter chosen per call. So generic methods are for convenience on concrete types, not for satisfying interfaces. Older modules need go 1.27 in go.mod to use them.
lessons.challenge: Add a generic method Fold[A any](init A, f func(A, T) A) A to List[T] and use it to sum the lengths of List[string]{items: []string{"a", "bb", "ccc"}}.
lessons.question: Can a generic method be used to satisfy an interface?
options: No; generic methods are not part of any interface's method set
Yes, if the interface lists the same name
Yes, but only with explicit type arguments
lessons.explanation: An interface method has one fixed signature, while a generic method has a family of signatures chosen per call.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
[2 6] [GO GOPHER]
true <nil>

An interface method has one fixed signature, while a generic method has a family of signatures chosen per call.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An interface method has one fixed signature, while a generic method has a family of signatures chosen per call.

lessons.title: Generics: limits, costs and design trade-offs
body: Type parameters cannot be used in a type switch directly; switch any(v).(type) converts to an interface first. You cannot declare a type parameter on an embedded field or use one as an embedded type. Before 1.27, methods could not have their own type parameters.

The compiler shares code between instantiations whose types have the same memory shape (GC shape stenciling), passing a dictionary for the specific types. Generic code is usually as fast as hand-written code, but calling methods through a type parameter can cost an indirect call similar to an interface call.

Start with concrete code; introduce type parameters when a second or third type needs the same logic. Constraints should be as loose as possible: any, then comparable, then cmp.Ordered, then custom sets.
lessons.challenge: Write func Zero[T any]() T and print Zero[int](), Zero[string]() quoted with %q, and whether Zero[*int]() is nil.
lessons.question: How do you branch on the concrete type of a type parameter value v?
options: switch v.(type) works directly
Use reflect only; type switches are impossible
Convert it to an interface: switch any(v).(type)
lessons.explanation: Type switches apply to interface values. Converting with any(v) gives an interface holding the concrete type argument.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
int 7
string "go"
[]uint8

Type switches apply to interface values. Converting with any(v) gives an interface holding the concrete type argument.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Type switches apply to interface values. Converting with any(v) gives an interface holding the concrete type argument.

lessons.title: Range-over-func iterators: iter.Seq and iter.Seq2
body: Since Go 1.23, for range accepts functions. An iter.Seq[V] is func(yield func(V) bool), and iter.Seq2[K, V] is func(yield func(K, V) bool). The loop body becomes the yield function; the iterator calls it once per element.

yield returns false when the loop stops early with break or return. The iterator must then stop and must not call yield again, otherwise the program panics. Write iterators as: for ... { if !yield(v) { return } }.

Iterators are lazy: nothing happens until a loop or a consumer such as slices.Collect pulls values. They let collections expose traversal without allocating a slice, and let infinite sequences, such as Fibonacci numbers, be consumed in bounded amounts.
lessons.challenge: Write func Countdown(n int) iter.Seq[int] yielding n down to 1, and print the values from Countdown(3) on one line.
lessons.question: What must an iterator do when yield returns false?
options: Stop immediately and never call yield again
Restart from the first element
Keep yielding but the loop ignores the values
lessons.explanation: false means the loop body executed break or return. Calling yield after that panics at run time.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13 
1 go
2 iter

false means the loop body executed break or return. Calling yield after that panics at run time.
lessons.practiceAnswer: false means the loop body executed break or return. Calling yield after that panics at run time.

lessons.title: Pull iterators with iter.Pull and cleanup
body: A push iterator calls your code. Sometimes you need to pull values one at a time, for example to merge two sorted sequences. iter.Pull(seq) returns next() (V, bool) and stop(). Each next call resumes the iterator until it yields one value.
Always call stop when you finish early, usually with defer stop(). stop ends the iterator and lets its deferred cleanup run. Forgetting it leaks the iterator's state.

Iterators may also need to release resources, such as files, when the consumer breaks early. Put the cleanup in a defer inside the iterator function: it runs whether the loop finishes, breaks, or the pull iterator is stopped.
lessons.challenge: Write an iterator that prints "open" when started, yields 1, 2, 3, and prints "closed" in a defer; consume it with a loop that breaks after the first value and show that "closed" is printed.
lessons.question: Why defer stop() after iter.Pull?
options: So the iterator ends and runs its cleanup even if you stop pulling early
next panics unless stop is deferred
stop rewinds the iterator for reuse
lessons.explanation: A pulled iterator is suspended mid-loop. stop resumes it with yield returning false so its deferred cleanup runs.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
[1 2 3 4 9 10]

A pulled iterator is suspended mid-loop. stop resumes it with yield returning false so its deferred cleanup runs.
lessons.practiceAnswer: A pulled iterator is suspended mid-loop. stop resumes it with yield returning false so its deferred cleanup runs.

lessons.title: Iterator helpers in slices, maps and strings
body: slices.All, slices.Values and slices.Backward produce iterators over a slice; slices.Collect, slices.AppendSeq and slices.Sorted consume them. maps.Keys, maps.Values and maps.All iterate a map; maps.Collect builds one from an iter.Seq2.

Since Go 1.24 strings and bytes offer iterator versions of splitting: strings.Lines, strings.SplitSeq, strings.FieldsSeq and strings.FieldsFuncSeq. They avoid allocating the whole []string when you only scan.

Chaining is explicit and still lazy: slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) collects only once. There is no built-in Map or Filter over iterators in the standard library; writing them is a few lines with iter.Seq.
lessons.challenge: Write a generic Filter[V any](seq iter.Seq[V], keep func(V) bool) iter.Seq[V] and use it with slices.Values and slices.Collect to keep the even numbers of []int{1, 2, 3, 4}.

options: "one", "two" and a final empty string
"one\n" and "two\n", keeping each newline
"one" and "two" without newlines
lessons.explanation: Lines yields each line including its terminating newline, so rejoining them reproduces the input exactly.
