lessons.title: Designing collection APIs with iterators
body: A collection type exposes traversal by returning an iterator from a method: func (t *Tree[T]) All() iter.Seq[T]. Callers loop with for v := range t.All() and can stop early without the type allocating a slice.

Recursive structures fit naturally: an in-order traversal yields left, node, right, and propagates a false yield upward so the whole walk stops. Return false from your helper when yield does, and check it at every level.

Document whether an iterator can be used more than once and whether the collection may change during iteration. Single-use iterators, such as those reading a stream, should say so in their doc comment.
lessons.challenge: Add a method Backward() iter.Seq[T] to Tree that yields values in descending order, and print all values of the tree above in that order.
lessons.question: Why does walk return a bool?
options: To report whether the tree is empty
Because iter.Seq requires helpers to return bool
To stop the whole recursive traversal once yield returns false
lessons.explanation: After the consumer breaks, every level must stop. The && chain short-circuits as soon as any call reports false.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
1 2 5 

After the consumer breaks, every level must stop. The && chain short-circuits as soon as any call reports false.
lessons.practiceAnswer: After the consumer breaks, every level must stop. The && chain short-circuits as soon as any call reports false.

lessons.title: io.Reader and io.Writer composition
body: io.Reader has one method, Read(p []byte) (n int, err error). It fills up to len(p) bytes and returns how many; it may return fewer than requested without error, and io.EOF signals the end. Always process the n bytes before looking at err, because a reader may return data and io.EOF together.

Small adapters combine readers and writers: io.MultiReader concatenates, io.TeeReader copies what it reads to a writer, io.LimitReader caps how much can be read, io.MultiWriter duplicates writes, and io.Pipe connects a writer goroutine to a reader. io.Copy moves data between them with a reusable buffer.

Accepting io.Reader instead of a filename makes code testable: tests pass strings.NewReader, production passes a file or network connection. io.ReadAll is fine for small inputs; for large or untrusted input, wrap with io.LimitReader first.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	r := io.MultiReader(strings.NewReader("hello, "), strings.NewReader("readers\n"))
	var seen strings.Builder
	tee := io.TeeReader(r, &seen)
	n, err := io.Copy(os.Stdout, io.LimitReader(tee, 100))
	fmt.Println(n, err, seen.Len())
	capped, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(strings.NewReader("0123456789"), 4))
	fmt.Println(string(capped))
}
lessons.challenge: Use io.Pipe: a goroutine writes "from a pipe" to the writer and closes it, while main reads everything with io.ReadAll and prints it.
lessons.question: A Read call returns n > 0 and io.EOF together. What should the caller do?
options: Call Read again to get the bytes without the error
Use the n bytes first, then stop because of EOF
Discard the bytes because an error occurred
lessons.explanation: The io.Reader contract allows data and EOF in the same call. Processing p[:n] before checking err is the safe pattern.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
hello, readers
15 <nil> 15
0123

The io.Reader contract allows data and EOF in the same call. Processing p[:n] before checking err is the safe pattern.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The io.Reader contract allows data and EOF in the same call. Processing p[:n] before checking err is the safe pattern.

lessons.title: Buffered I/O: bufio.Reader, Writer and Scanner splitters
body: Small reads and writes on files or sockets are expensive system calls. bufio.Reader and bufio.Writer batch them with an in-memory buffer. A bufio.Writer must be flushed: until Flush is called the bytes may sit in memory, and an error from a failed write appears at Flush.

bufio.Scanner splits input into tokens with a SplitFunc: ScanLines (default), ScanWords, ScanRunes or ScanBytes. Custom split functions parse other formats. For lines longer than the buffer, call Buffer to raise the limit, or use Reader.ReadString.
bufio.Reader offers ReadString('\n'), ReadRune and Peek. ReadString returns the data read before an error, so the last line without a trailing newline comes back together with io.EOF.
lessons.challenge:
Read "a
b
last" with bufio.Reader.ReadString('
') in a loop, printing each line with %q and stopping after the line returned together with io.EOF.
lessons.question: Why did "buffered line" print after "unbuffered first"?
options: bufio.Writer held it in memory until Flush
fmt.Fprintln writes asynchronously
Standard output reorders writes
lessons.explanation: The buffered bytes reached os.Stdout only when Flush ran. Forgetting Flush loses output entirely.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
words: 5 <nil>
unbuffered first
buffered line

The buffered bytes reached os.Stdout only when Flush ran. Forgetting Flush loses output entirely.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The buffered bytes reached os.Stdout only when Flush ran. Forgetting Flush loses output entirely.

lessons.title: Files, directories and traversal-safe os.Root
body: os.ReadFile and os.WriteFile handle whole small files. os.Open returns a read-only *os.File; os.Create truncates or creates for writing; os.OpenFile takes flags such as os.O_APPEND|os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY and permissions such as 0o644. os.MkdirAll, os.ReadDir and os.RemoveAll work on directories.

Joining an untrusted name onto a directory, filepath.Join(dir, name), is unsafe: "../secret" or a symlink can escape. Go 1.24 added os.Root: os.OpenRoot(dir) returns a handle whose Open, Create, ReadFile, WriteFile, Mkdir and Remove methods refuse any path, including symlinks, that resolves outside the root.
Use os.Root whenever paths come from users, archives or network requests. root.FS() adapts it to fs.FS. Close the root when done.
lessons.challenge: Inside an os.Root, create a subdirectory "logs" with root.Mkdir, write "logs/a.txt", then try root.Create("logs/../../x") and print whether it failed.
lessons.question: Why use os.Root instead of filepath.Join for user-supplied names?
options: Root is faster for every file operation
filepath.Join cannot handle subdirectories
Root rejects paths and symlinks that escape the directory
lessons.explanation: Join only cleans the string; it does not stop ".." or symlinks pointing elsewhere. Root checks every resolved component.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
inside <nil>
true
1 notes.txt

Join only cleans the string; it does not stop ".." or symlinks pointing elsewhere. Root checks every resolved component.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Join only cleans the string; it does not stop ".." or symlinks pointing elsewhere. Root checks every resolved component.

lessons.title: path/filepath, io/fs and embedded files
body: path/filepath handles operating-system paths: Join, Base, Dir, Ext, Rel, Clean and WalkDir. The plain path package is for slash-separated paths such as URLs and fs.FS names, which always use / on every OS.

io/fs defines a read-only file-system interface. fs.WalkDir, fs.ReadFile, fs.Glob and fs.Sub work on any fs.FS: os.DirFS, an os.Root, a zip archive, testing/fstest.MapFS, or files embedded in the binary.

//go:embed patterns before a variable of type string, []byte or embed.FS include files at build time. Embedded files ship inside the executable, so templates and static assets need no deployment step. fstest.MapFS is the in-memory fs.FS for tests.
lessons.challenge: Use fs.Sub to view the "docs" directory of a MapFS as its own file system and read "a.md" from it with fs.ReadFile.
lessons.question: Which separator do fs.FS paths use on Windows?
options: Whatever os.PathSeparator is
Always forward slashes
Backslashes, like filepath
lessons.explanation: fs.FS names are slash-separated and unrooted on every platform; filepath converts to OS form only at the edges.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
a/c.txt .gz
[docs/a.md docs/b.md]
file docs/a.md
file docs/b.md
file docs/img/x.png

fs.FS names are slash-separated and unrooted on every platform; filepath converts to OS form only at the edges.
lessons.practiceAnswer: fs.FS names are slash-separated and unrooted on every platform; filepath converts to OS form only at the edges.

lessons.title: strconv, strings, bytes and unicode
body: strconv converts between strings and numbers with explicit errors: Atoi, ParseInt(s, base, bits), ParseFloat, ParseBool, and the reverse Itoa, FormatInt and FormatFloat. Quote and Unquote handle Go-syntax string literals. Errors are *strconv.NumError values with Func, Num and Err fields.

strings and bytes mirror each other: Contains, HasPrefix, TrimSpace, TrimFunc, Fields, Split, Replace, EqualFold (case-insensitive comparison), Map and Title-free casing with ToUpper and ToLower. strings.NewReplacer performs many replacements in one pass.

unicode classifies runes: IsLetter, IsDigit, IsSpace, IsUpper. Go 1.27 updates the tables to Unicode 17. Case conversion is per rune and does not handle every language's rules; golang.org/x/text covers those.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"unicode"
)

func main() {
	n, err := strconv.ParseInt("ff", 16, 64)
	fmt.Println(n, err)
	_, err = strconv.Atoi("12x")
	var ne *strconv.NumError
	fmt.Println(errors.As(err, &ne), ne.Func, ne.Err)
	fmt.Println(strconv.FormatFloat(3.14159, 'f', 2, 64), strconv.Quote("tab\t"))
	r := strings.NewReplacer("&", "&", "<", "<")
	fmt.Println(r.Replace("a<b & c"))
	fmt.Println(strings.EqualFold("Go", "GO"), strings.IndexFunc("ab1", unicode.IsDigit))
}

lessons.question: What does strconv.ParseInt("300", 10, 8) return?
options: 44, the low 8 bits, and nil
127 and a range error, because 300 does not fit in 8 bits
300 and nil; bitSize is only a hint
lessons.explanation: bitSize limits the accepted range. Out-of-range input returns the nearest limit with ErrRange.

Expected output:

true Atoi invalid syntax
3.14 "tab\t"
a<b & c

lessons.title: time: durations, monotonic clocks, layouts and zones
body: time.Duration is an int64 count of nanoseconds with constants such as time.Second; multiply a duration by an integer constant (3*time.Second), but convert a variable: time.Duration(n)*time.Second.

time.Now() includes a monotonic clock reading, so time.Since(start) measures elapsed time correctly even if the wall clock is changed. The monotonic reading is dropped by operations such as t.Round(0), Truncate and serialisation; compare times with Before, After and Equal, not ==.

Formatting uses a reference time, Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006, written in the desired layout: t.Format("2006-01-02 15:04"). time.RFC3339 and time.DateOnly are predefined layouts. time.LoadLocation reads zone data; time.Parse defaults to UTC.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	d := 90 * time.Minute
	fmt.Println(d, d.Hours())
	t := time.Date(2026, time.October, 16, 21, 5, 0, 0, time.UTC)
	fmt.Println(t.Format("Mon 2 Jan 2006 15:04"), t.Format(time.DateOnly))
	later := t.Add(36 * time.Hour)
	fmt.Println(later.Weekday(), later.Sub(t), later.After(t))
	parsed, err := time.Parse(time.RFC3339, "2026-08-12T10:00:00+02:00")
	fmt.Println(parsed.UTC(), err)
	n := 3
	fmt.Println(time.Duration(n) * time.Second)
}
lessons.challenge: Compute how many whole days lie between 2026-01-01 and 2026-10-16 (UTC) and print them.
lessons.question: Why should elapsed time be measured with time.Since rather than subtracting wall-clock readings you saved as strings?
options: Strings lose time zones
time.Since rounds to milliseconds
Since uses the monotonic clock, which is immune to wall-clock changes
lessons.explanation: The monotonic reading inside time.Now values only moves forward. Serialised times keep only the wall clock.

Expected output:

Sunday 36h0m0s true

The monotonic reading inside time.Now values only moves forward. Serialised times keep only the wall clock.

lessons.title: Sorting, searching and ordering with cmp
body: slices.Sort and slices.SortFunc are the modern way to sort; the older sort package with sort.Slice and sort.Interface still works and is widely used. Sorting is in place and not stable unless you pick the stable variant.

slices.BinarySearch and sort.Search find positions in sorted data in O(log n). sort.Search(n, f) returns the smallest index for which f is true, assuming f is false then true: a general tool for monotone predicates, not just equality.

Ordering functions must be consistent: if a < b and b < c then a < c. An inconsistent comparator, such as one that compares floats containing NaN with <, can produce unsorted output. cmp.Compare treats NaN as less than every other value, which gives a total order.
lessons.challenge: Use sort.Search to find the smallest integer n in [0, 100) such that n*n >= 50, and print it.
lessons.question: What does sort.Search(n, f) require of f?
options: f must return true exactly once
f must compare against a target value with ==
f must be false for a prefix of indices and true for the rest
lessons.explanation: Search is a binary search over a monotone predicate and returns the first index where it becomes true, or n if never.
lessons.workedExample:

[NaN 1 2 3]

[Al bo cy] true

lessons.title: encoding/json: struct tags, decoding and streaming
body: json.Marshal turns Go values into JSON: exported struct fields become object members named by their `json:"name"` tag. Options in the tag include omitempty (skip zero values like 0, "", nil) and, since Go 1.24, omitzero (skip values whose IsZero or zero value is zero, useful for time.Time and structs). Unexported fields are ignored.

json.Unmarshal decodes into a pointer. Unknown members are ignored by default; a json.Decoder with DisallowUnknownFields rejects them. Numbers decode into float64 when the target is any; use json.Number or concrete types to avoid precision loss.
json.NewDecoder(r) and json.NewEncoder(w) stream values from and to readers and writers, which avoids holding a whole document in memory. Encoder.SetIndent pretty-prints.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

type User struct {
	Name   string   `json:"name"`
	Email  string   `json:"email,omitempty"`
	Tags   []string `json:"tags"`
	secret string
}

func main() {
	out, _ := json.Marshal(User{Name: "Ada", secret: "x"})
	fmt.Println(string(out))
	var u User
	err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"name":"Bo","tags":["go"],"extra":1}`), &u)
	fmt.Println(u.Name, u.Tags, err)
	dec := json.NewDecoder(strings.NewReader(`{"name":"Cy","age":3}`))
	dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
	fmt.Println(dec.Decode(&u))
	enc := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout)
	enc.Encode(map[string]int{"b": 2, "a": 1})
}

lessons.question: Why did Tags marshal as null in the first line?
options: Slices are never encoded
A nil slice encodes as null in encoding/json v1
Tags lacked omitempty
lessons.explanation: v1 distinguishes nil slices (null) from empty slices ([]). json/v2 encodes nil slices as [] by default.
lessons.practiceAnswer: v1 distinguishes nil slices (null) from empty slices ([]). json/v2 encodes nil slices as [] by default.

lessons.title: Go 1.27 encoding/json/v2 and jsontext
body: Go 1.27 adds encoding/json/v2, a revised API with stricter, more consistent defaults, and encoding/json/jsontext for low-level tokens. encoding/json v1 now runs on the v2 implementation while keeping its old behaviour.

Notable v2 defaults: nil slices and maps encode as [] and {}, member names match case-sensitively, duplicate names are rejected, and invalid UTF-8 is an error. Behaviour is adjusted with options passed to Marshal and Unmarshal, such as json.Deterministic(true), json.RejectUnknownMembers(true) or json.OmitZeroStructFields(true).

jsontext.Value is a raw JSON value with methods for formatting and canonicalising, and jsontext.Encoder and Decoder stream tokens. MarshalWrite and UnmarshalRead read and write io streams directly. Prefer v2 for new code that targets 1.27; migrate v1 code by checking the documented behaviour differences.
lessons.challenge: Marshal map[string]int{"z": 1, "a": 2} with json/v2 and json.Deterministic(true), then reformat the bytes with jsontext.Value.Indent using "  " and print them.
lessons.question: How does json/v2 encode a nil []string by default?
options: As null, like v1
It omits the member
As an empty array []
lessons.explanation: v2 treats nil and empty slices alike by default. The FormatNilSliceAsNull option restores v1-style null.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
{"name":"api","hosts":[]} <nil>
"" <nil>
true
{"b":2,"a":[1,2]}

v2 treats nil and empty slices alike by default. The FormatNilSliceAsNull option restores v1-style null.

lessons.title: Structured logging with log/slog
body: log/slog (Go 1.21) writes structured records: a time, a level, a message and key-value attributes. slog.Info("saved", "user", id, "bytes", n) produces machine-readable output that log systems can filter by field.

A Logger sends records to a Handler. slog.NewTextHandler writes key=value text and slog.NewJSONHandler writes JSON objects; HandlerOptions sets the minimum level, adds source locations, or rewrites attributes with ReplaceAttr (for example to drop the time in tests). logger.With adds attributes to every record and WithGroup nests them.

slog.SetDefault installs a logger used by the top-level functions and by the older log package. Use typed attributes such as slog.Int and slog.Any in hot paths to avoid allocation, and implement slog.LogValuer to control how a type is logged, such as redacting secrets.
lessons.challenge: Log one Info record with a JSON handler (time removed) containing user="ada" and attempts=3, and print it.
lessons.question: How do you stop a secret type from appearing in logs?
options: Implement slog.LogValuer to return a redacted value
Mark the field unexported
Log it at Debug level only
lessons.explanation: Handlers resolve LogValuer before formatting, so the redacted value is all any handler sees.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
level=DEBUG msg=starting port=8080
level=INFO msg=auth request=42 token=REDACTED
level=WARN msg=slow request=42 db.ms=250

Handlers resolve LogValuer before formatting, so the redacted value is all any handler sees.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Handlers resolve LogValuer before formatting, so the redacted value is all any handler sees.

lessons.title: Command-line flags with the flag package
body: flag defines typed options: n := flag.Int("n", 10, "number of lines"). After flag.Parse(), *n holds the value and flag.Args() returns the remaining positional arguments. flag.StringVar and friends bind to existing variables, and flag.Func or a type implementing flag.Value supports custom parsing.
Flags may be written -n=5, -n 5 or --n 5. Boolean flags need -v=false to turn off. -h or -help prints usage generated from the descriptions; set flag.Usage to customise it.

For testable programs use a flag.FlagSet created with flag.ContinueOnError and parse an explicit []string, instead of the global flag set and os.Args. FlagSet.Parse then returns an error instead of exiting.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"strings"
)

func parse(args []string) (int, bool, []string, error) {
	fs := flag.NewFlagSet("demo", flag.ContinueOnError)
	fs.SetOutput(io.Discard)
	n := fs.Int("n", 10, "number of lines")
	verbose := fs.Bool("v", false, "verbose output")
	err := fs.Parse(args)
	return *n, *verbose, fs.Args(), err
}

func main() {
	fmt.Println(parse([]string{"-n=3", "-v", "a.txt", "b.txt"}))
	fmt.Println(parse(nil))
	_, _, _, err := parse([]string{"-n", "many"})
	fmt.Println(strings.Contains(err.Error(), "invalid value"))
}

lessons.title: The Go 1.27 uuid package
body: Go 1.27 adds package uuid to the standard library. uuid.UUID is a [16]byte array type, so UUIDs are comparable with == and usable as map keys. uuid.New returns a random version 4 UUID; uuid.NewV7 returns a version 7 UUID whose leading bits are a timestamp, so values sort roughly by creation time, which suits database keys.

uuid.Parse and uuid.MustParse read the standard 36-character hyphenated text form; String writes it. UUID implements encoding.TextMarshaler, so it works with JSON and other text encodings. Compare orders two UUIDs bytewise.
Random UUIDs are unpredictable but not secret tokens; use crypto/rand for credentials. Nil() is the all-zero UUID and Max() the all-ones value.

lessons.question: Why might you prefer uuid.NewV7 over uuid.New for database primary keys?
options: V7 is cryptographically stronger
V4 cannot be stored in a [16]byte
V7 values start with a timestamp, so new keys sort near each other
lessons.explanation: Time-ordered keys keep B-tree inserts local. V4 values are uniformly random, which scatters inserts.

lessons.title: math, math/big and math/rand/v2
body: math provides float functions (Sqrt, Floor, Inf, NaN, IsNaN) and integer limits (math.MaxInt64). math/bits does bit counting and overflow-checked arithmetic. Floating-point variables are not exact: x+y with x=0.1, y=0.2 differs from 0.3, so compare with a tolerance. Constant expressions are evaluated exactly at compile time, which is why the constant 0.1+0.2 == 0.3 is true.

math/big gives arbitrary-precision Int, Rat and Float. Methods set a receiver and return it, so z := new(big.Int).Mul(x, y) avoids allocations in loops. Go 1.27 adds Int.Divide with explicit rounding modes (Trunc, Floor, Round, Ceil).

math/rand/v2 (Go 1.22) has rand.IntN, rand.N for any integer type or duration, and seedable sources such as rand.NewPCG for reproducible simulations. Go 1.27 adds the generic Rand.N method. These are not suitable for secrets; use crypto/rand for keys and tokens.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"math/big"
	"math/rand/v2"
)

func main() {
	const exact = 0.1+0.2 == 0.3
	x, y := 0.1, 0.2
	fmt.Println(exact, x+y == 0.3, math.Abs(x+y-0.3) < 1e-9)
	f := new(big.Int)
	f.MulRange(1, 25)
	fmt.Println(f)
	q, r := new(big.Int).Divide(big.NewInt(-7), big.NewInt(2), new(big.Int), big.Floor)
	fmt.Println(q, r)
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
	a := rng.IntN(100)
	rng2 := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))
	fmt.Println(a == rng2.IntN(100), rand.N(int64(10)) < 10)
}

lessons.title: Goroutines and the Go scheduler
body: go f(x) starts a goroutine: a function running concurrently with the caller. Goroutines are cheap, starting with a few kilobytes of stack that grows as needed, so programs can run hundreds of thousands. The runtime multiplexes them onto operating-system threads with an M:N scheduler: G (goroutines) run on M (threads) holding P (processors, GOMAXPROCS of them).

The arguments of go f(x) are evaluated immediately in the calling goroutine; f runs later. When main returns the program exits, killing every other goroutine, so main must wait for work it started. sync.WaitGroup and channels are the usual ways to wait.

Goroutine execution order is not specified. Output from several goroutines interleaves differently between runs unless you synchronise. The scheduler is preemptive (since Go 1.14), so a tight loop cannot starve the others forever.
lessons.challenge: Start three goroutines that each compute the sum of a third of 1..300 into their own slot of a [3]int, wait for them, and print the total.
lessons.question: Why is writing results[i] from separate goroutines safe here?
options: Slices are protected by an internal lock
Goroutines run one after another in order
Each goroutine writes a different element, and Wait orders those writes before the read
lessons.explanation: Distinct elements are distinct memory locations, so there is no data race. wg.Wait synchronises with each Done, making the writes visible to main.

lessons.title: Unbuffered and buffered channels
body: A channel carries values of one type between goroutines: ch := make(chan int). A send ch <- v and a receive v := <-ch on an unbuffered channel wait for each other: the send completes only when a receiver takes the value, so it also synchronises the two goroutines.

make(chan int, 3) creates a buffered channel. Sends succeed without a receiver until the buffer is full; receives succeed until it is empty. len(ch) and cap(ch) report the queue length and capacity, but checking len before acting is racy.

Use unbuffered channels for hand-offs and synchronisation, small buffers to absorb bursts, and never a buffer size chosen to "avoid deadlock": if correctness depends on the buffer size, the design has a bug. Channel direction types, chan<- int (send-only) and <-chan int (receive-only), document intent in signatures.
lessons.challenge: Write a ping-pong: two goroutines pass an int back and forth on two unbuffered channels, each adding 1, until it reaches 6; print each value as it is received by main's side.
lessons.question: When does a send on an unbuffered channel complete?
options: Immediately; the value is queued
When the channel is closed
When another goroutine receives the value
lessons.explanation: An unbuffered channel has no storage, so sender and receiver must meet. That rendezvous is also a synchronisation point.

lessons.title: Closing channels, comma-ok receives and ownership
body: close(ch) records that no more values will be sent. Receivers then drain the remaining buffered values and afterwards receive the zero value immediately. v, ok := <-ch reports ok=false once the channel is closed and empty, and for v := range ch stops at that point.

Only the sender should close, and only once. Sending on a closed channel panics, and so does closing it twice. With several senders, close after all of them are done, typically from a goroutine that waits on a WaitGroup.

Closing is a broadcast: every receiver sees it, which makes a closed chan struct{} a cheap "done" signal. You do not have to close a channel for garbage collection; close it to tell receivers to stop.
lessons.challenge: Use a closed chan struct{} named done to stop three waiting goroutines at once; each prints nothing but signals a WaitGroup when it sees done closed. Print "all stopped" after waiting.
lessons.question: Who should close a channel with several senders?
options: The receiver, once it has seen enough values
A coordinator that closes it after every sender has finished
Each sender, after its last send
lessons.explanation: Closing twice or sending after close panics. Waiting for all senders, then closing once, avoids both.

lessons.title: select, timeouts and non-blocking operations
body: select waits on several channel operations and runs the first that can proceed; if several are ready it picks one at random, which prevents starvation. A default case makes the select non-blocking: it runs immediately when no other case is ready.

time.After(d) returns a channel that receives after d, so case <-time.After(time.Second): implements a timeout. In a loop, prefer one time.Timer or a context deadline over creating a new After channel per iteration. Since Go 1.23 unreferenced timers are collected even if not stopped.
A select with no cases, select {}, blocks forever. Each case expression is evaluated once on entry, including the right-hand side of sends.

options: All of them in order
One chosen uniformly at random
The first one in source order
lessons.explanation: Random choice stops one busy channel from starving the others. Code must not rely on case order.

lessons.title: nil channels to disable select cases
body: Sending to or receiving from a nil channel blocks forever. Inside select, a case on a nil channel is never ready, so setting a channel variable to nil switches that case off.
This is how to merge two inputs that close at different times: when one input is closed, set its variable to nil and keep selecting on the other until both are nil.
Closing a nil channel panics. A nil channel is the zero value of a channel type, so an uninitialised struct field of channel type blocks every operation; make channels in constructors.

lessons.title: Pipelines of stages connected by channels
body: A pipeline is a chain of stages, each a goroutine that receives from an inbound channel, processes values and sends them outbound. Each stage owns and closes its output channel, so the end of input propagates down the chain.
Stages that may be abandoned must be cancellable. If the consumer stops early, upstream stages blocked on sends leak. Pass a done channel or context.Context and select on it alongside every send.
Return receive-only channels from stage constructors (func square(in <-chan int) <-chan int). The types then prevent callers from sending into or closing a stage's output.

options: Select makes sends faster
Channels cannot be closed otherwise
So the stage can exit instead of blocking forever if the consumer stops early

lessons.title: Fan-out, fan-in and preserving order
body: Fan-out starts several goroutines reading from one channel, spreading work across CPUs. Fan-in merges several channels into one, usually with a WaitGroup that closes the merged output after every input is drained.
Fan-out loses ordering: results arrive in completion order. When order matters, send results with their index and place them into a pre-sized slice, or sort afterwards.

Fan-out helps CPU-bound work up to GOMAXPROCS goroutines and I/O-bound work further, until an external limit such as a connection pool is reached. Measure; more goroutines than useful parallelism only adds scheduling cost.

options: Use a buffered channel the size of the input
Start the workers in order
Send each result with its index and store it at that position

lessons.title: Bounded concurrency: worker pools and semaphores
body: Starting one goroutine per item is fine for small inputs but unbounded for large ones: it can exhaust memory, file descriptors or a remote service. Bound concurrency with a fixed pool of workers reading from a jobs channel, or with a semaphore.
A buffered channel is a counting semaphore: sem := make(chan struct{}, n); acquire with sem <- struct{}{} before work and release with <-sem after. At most n holders exist at once.

Collect errors as well as results. Common patterns are a result struct carrying an error, or the first-error-cancels-the-rest pattern of errgroup (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup), which combines a WaitGroup, a context and an error.
lessons.challenge: Build a pool of 3 workers that read words from a jobs channel and send their lengths on a results channel; process "go", "gopher", "channel", "x" and print the total length.
lessons.question: How does a buffered channel of capacity n act as a semaphore?
options: It makes the channel n times faster
Each worker sends to acquire and receives to release, so at most n hold a slot
The buffer stores the results of n workers
lessons.explanation: A send blocks when the buffer is full, which happens exactly when n slots are held.

lessons.title: Goroutine leaks and the Go 1.27 goroutineleak profile
body: A goroutine leaks when it can never finish, usually because it is blocked forever on a channel nobody will use again, such as a send after the receiver returned early. Leaked goroutines keep their stacks and everything they reference alive.

Prevent leaks by giving every goroutine an exit path: buffered result channels sized to the number of senders, done channels or contexts on every blocking operation, and an owner that waits for goroutines it started.

Go 1.27 adds a goroutineleak profile to runtime/pprof (and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof). Collecting it runs a garbage collection that finds goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives no running goroutine can reach, and reports their stacks. It finds leaks that can be proven; a goroutine blocked on a reachable channel is not reported even if it will never be woken.
lessons.challenge: Fix firstOf so no goroutine leaks: give the channel enough buffer for every sender, then show that the goroutineleak profile reports total 0.
lessons.question: Why did two goroutines leak in the original firstOf?
options: They sent on an unbuffered channel after its only receiver had returned
time.Sleep never returns inside goroutines
pprof itself starts two goroutines

lessons.title: sync.Mutex and RWMutex: protecting shared state
body: A sync.Mutex makes a critical section exclusive: Lock, change shared state, Unlock. Pair them with defer mu.Unlock() right after Lock so every return path releases the lock. The zero Mutex is unlocked and ready to use.

Keep the mutex next to the data it protects, usually as an unexported struct field, and give the type pointer receivers: copying a struct copies its mutex, which breaks the protection. go vet's copylocks check reports such copies.

sync.RWMutex allows many concurrent readers or one writer. It helps only when reads dominate and the critical sections are long enough to matter; otherwise a plain Mutex is simpler and often faster. Go mutexes are not re-entrant: locking twice in the same goroutine deadlocks.
lessons.challenge: Write a Cache type with an RWMutex-protected map, using RLock in Get and Lock in Set; set "go" to 1 from ten goroutines and print Get("go").
lessons.question: Why must a struct containing a sync.Mutex have pointer receivers?
options: Value receivers cannot call Lock
A value receiver copies the struct and its mutex, so methods lock different mutexes
Mutexes cannot be struct fields otherwise
lessons.explanation: Each copy has its own lock state. go vet copylocks flags copies of values containing locks.

lessons.title: sync.WaitGroup and WaitGroup.Go
body: A WaitGroup waits for a collection of goroutines. The classic pattern is wg.Add(1) before go, defer wg.Done() inside, and wg.Wait() in the owner. Add must happen before Wait could return, which is why it is called in the starting goroutine rather than inside the new one.

Go 1.25 added wg.Go(f): it calls Add(1), starts f in a goroutine and calls Done when f returns. It removes the most common WaitGroup mistakes, forgetting Done or calling Add inside the goroutine. Go 1.27 renames the go fix modernizer that rewrites old patterns to waitgroupgo.
The return of each function started by Go synchronises before Wait returns, so results written by the goroutines are visible after Wait. f must not panic; recover inside f if it can.
lessons.challenge: Use wg.Go to compute the lengths of four words concurrently into a slice, then print the slice and its sum.
lessons.question: Why must wg.Add(1) run before the go statement rather than inside the goroutine?
options: Add panics when called from a new goroutine
The goroutine cannot access wg
Otherwise Wait might run while the counter is still zero and return too early
lessons.explanation: If the goroutine has not started yet, its Add has not happened and Wait sees zero. wg.Go performs Add before starting the goroutine.

lessons.title: sync.Once, OnceFunc, OnceValue and lazy initialisation
body: sync.Once runs a function exactly once, however many goroutines call Do, and every caller returns only after it has finished. It is the safe way to initialise something lazily, such as a configuration or a compiled regular expression.

Go 1.21 added helpers: sync.OnceFunc(f) returns a function that runs f once, sync.OnceValue(f) caches one result, and sync.OnceValues(f) caches a (value, error) pair. If f panics, every call re-panics with the same value.
Prefer package-level variable initialisation when the value is always needed; use Once when initialisation is expensive or may not be needed at all.

The next call retries the function
The panic is swallowed and zero is returned
lessons.explanation: The Once helpers remember the panic and re-raise it, so a failed initialisation is never silently retried or ignored.

lessons.title: sync.Cond for waiting on state changes
body: A sync.Cond lets goroutines wait until some condition on shared state holds. Each Cond is tied to a Locker. Waiters hold the lock, check the condition in a for loop and call Wait, which atomically unlocks, sleeps and relocks when woken.
Signal wakes one waiter and Broadcast wakes all. Always re-check the condition after Wait returns: another goroutine may have changed the state first, and spurious wake-ups are allowed.

Channels usually express the same thing more simply. Cond is useful when many goroutines wait for a condition on data already protected by a mutex, such as a bounded queue with "not empty" and "not full" states.

The condition may be false again by the time the waiter relocks

lessons.title: Typed atomics: atomic.Int64, Bool and Pointer
body: sync/atomic performs indivisible operations on single words. The typed values added in Go 1.19, atomic.Int32, Int64, Uint64, Bool and Pointer[T], cannot be accessed non-atomically by mistake and are correctly aligned automatically. Go 1.27's go fix atomictypes modernizer rewrites older atomic.AddInt64(&x, 1) code to them.

Load, Store, Add, Swap and CompareAndSwap are sequentially consistent in Go: all goroutines observe atomic operations in a single order, and an atomic write synchronises with the atomic read that observes it.

Atomics suit counters, flags and publishing an immutable snapshot through atomic.Pointer. When an update touches several values together, use a mutex; combining several atomics does not make the group atomic.

lessons.title: sync.Map and sync.Pool: specialised tools
body: sync.Map is a concurrent map optimised for two cases: keys written once and read many times, and goroutines working on disjoint keys. For most code a plain map with a Mutex is clearer and type-safe. Its methods include Load, Store, LoadOrStore, CompareAndSwap, Delete and Range.

sync.Pool caches temporary objects to reduce allocation, for example buffers reused across requests. The pool may drop items at any garbage collection, so it is a cache, not a free list with guaranteed reuse. Reset objects before putting them back, and do not store objects that hold onto large memory.
Both are tools for measured hot spots. Benchmark first; a Pool adds complexity and can retain memory you expected to be freed.

lessons.title: Finding data races with the race detector
body: A data race is two goroutines accessing the same variable concurrently, at least one writing, without synchronisation. Racy Go programs have undefined results: torn values, lost updates and, for maps and interfaces, crashes.

Build or test with -race (go test -race ./..., go run -race .) and the runtime instruments every memory access. When two unsynchronised accesses happen, it prints WARNING: DATA RACE with both stacks and makes the test fail. It finds races that actually occur during the run, so run it on tests that exercise concurrency.
The detector costs roughly 5–10x CPU and memory, so use it in CI and staging rather than production. It needs cgo on most platforms; this project runs it on macOS.

lessons.explanation: The detector is dynamic: it reports races it observes. Code paths not exercised by the run are not checked.

lessons.title: The Go memory model: happens-before
body: The memory model defines when a write in one goroutine is guaranteed to be seen by a read in another. Within one goroutine, actions happen in program order. Across goroutines, only synchronisation creates ordering: a send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes, closing a channel happens before a receive that observes the close, and Unlock happens before the next Lock returns.

If a write happens before a read and no other write intervenes, the read sees that write. Without such an edge there is no guarantee at all. A loop that spins on a plain bool set by another goroutine may never see the change, because the compiler may hoist the read out of the loop.

Programs free of data races behave as if goroutines were interleaved in some sequential order (DRF-SC). Make that your rule: every shared variable is protected by a channel, a lock or an atomic, and then you can reason sequentially.
lessons.challenge: Publish a slice of three numbers from a goroutine to main using an unbuffered channel of struct{} as the only synchronisation, and print the sum in main.
lessons.question: Why is reading message after <-done guaranteed to see the write?
options: The write precedes close in its goroutine, and close happens before the receive that observes it
Strings are always shared atomically
Goroutines run before main resumes
lessons.explanation: Program order plus the close/receive synchronisation edge give a happens-before chain from the write to the read.
lessons.workedExample:

written before close

Program order plus the close/receive synchronisation edge give a happens-before chain from the write to the read.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Program order plus the close/receive synchronisation edge give a happens-before chain from the write to the read.

lessons.title: What racy programs may do, and why atomics fix it
body: In Go a data race on a single-word variable can produce any value previously written, or cause a crash for multi-word values such as interfaces, slices and strings, whose parts can be torn. Unlike C, Go limits the damage, but a racy program is still wrong.

Double-checked locking with a plain flag is broken: another goroutine can see the flag set before the data it guards. Use sync.Once, a mutex, or publish through an atomic.Pointer so the pointer and the data it points to are ordered.

A store to an atomic and a load observing it create a happens-before edge, just like a channel. That is why atomic.Pointer can safely publish an immutable configuration that readers then use without locks.
lessons.challenge: Replace a racy "initialised bool plus value" lazy initialiser with sync.OnceValue so ten goroutines all read the same computed value 42; print it.
lessons.question: Why is publishing a struct through atomic.Pointer safe for lock-free readers?
options: atomic.Pointer copies the struct for each reader
Pointers can never be torn
The Store happens before any Load that observes it, so the struct's fields are visible
lessons.explanation: Atomic operations synchronise. Writes to the fields before Store are ordered before reads after the matching Load, provided the struct is not modified afterwards.

lessons.title: context: cancellation and deadlines
body: context.Context carries cancellation, deadlines and request-scoped values across API boundaries. By convention it is the first parameter, named ctx. context.Background() is the root; WithCancel, WithTimeout and WithDeadline derive children that are cancelled when their parent is, or when their own cancel function or deadline fires.

Always call the cancel function, usually with defer cancel(), even if the context times out by itself; it releases the timer and the parent's reference. go vet's lostcancel check reports cancel functions that are dropped.

Code that blocks should select on <-ctx.Done() and return ctx.Err(), which is context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded. Standard library functions that take a context, such as http.NewRequestWithContext and net.Dialer.DialContext, stop their work when it is cancelled.
lessons.challenge: Write func firstResult(ctx context.Context, delays []time.Duration) int that starts one goroutine per delay, returns the index of the first to finish, and cancels the others; make sure the losers exit by checking ctx.Done(). Print the result for delays 30ms, 1ms, 50ms.
lessons.question: Why call cancel even after a WithTimeout context has expired?
options: It releases resources such as the timer and the parent's reference to the child
Otherwise ctx.Err stays nil
Expired contexts restart without it
lessons.explanation: Cancel is idempotent and cheap. Not calling it keeps the child registered with its parent until the parent ends.

lessons.title: Causes, AfterFunc, WithoutCancel and values
body: WithCancelCause and WithTimeoutCause (Go 1.20, 1.21) record why a context ended: cancel(errQuotaExceeded) makes context.Cause(ctx) return that error while ctx.Err() still returns context.Canceled. Causes make logs explain cancellations.

context.AfterFunc(ctx, f) runs f in its own goroutine after ctx is done and returns a stop function that unregisters it. It connects contexts to APIs that do not accept one, such as closing a connection or waking a sync.Cond.

context.WithoutCancel(ctx) keeps values but drops cancellation, for work that must finish after a request ends, such as an audit write. context.WithValue carries request-scoped data like trace IDs. Use an unexported key type to avoid collisions, and never pass optional parameters through values.

lessons.question: What does context.WithoutCancel(ctx) keep and drop?
options: It copies everything but makes cancel a no-op for the parent
It keeps ctx's values and drops its cancellation and deadline
It keeps cancellation and drops values

lessons.title: Timers, tickers and the Go 1.23 timer semantics
body: time.NewTimer(d) delivers one value on its channel C after d; time.NewTicker(d) delivers repeatedly. Stop prevents future deliveries and Reset reschedules.

Go 1.23 changed timers for modules declaring go 1.23 or later: timer channels are unbuffered (synchronous), so after Stop or Reset returns no stale value from the old setting will be received, and timers and tickers that are no longer referenced are garbage collected even if never stopped. The old "drain the channel after Stop" idiom is no longer needed. Go 1.27 removes the asynctimerchan setting that restored the old behaviour.
Use time.AfterFunc to run a function after a delay in its own goroutine. For deadlines on a whole operation, a context is usually better than hand-managed timers.
lessons.challenge: Implement a debounce: events arrive on a channel at 1ms intervals five times; reset a single timer of 100ms on each event and print "flushed 5" when it finally fires.
lessons.question: With go 1.23 or later in go.mod, what can you rely on after t.Stop() returns?
options: t.C is closed
You must drain t.C manually before Reset
No stale value from before the Stop will be received from t.C
lessons.explanation: Timer channels became synchronous in Go 1.23, which removed the need for the drain idiom for modules declaring 1.23+.

lessons.title: Stack, heap and escape analysis
body: Go decides where each variable lives. If the compiler can prove a variable is not referenced after its function returns, it stays on the goroutine's stack and costs nothing to free. Otherwise it "escapes" to the heap and the garbage collector must reclaim it later.

Common causes of escape: returning a pointer to a local, storing a pointer in a heap object or global, converting a value to an interface that is retained, closures that outlive their function, and slices whose size is not known at compile time. go build -gcflags=-m prints the decisions; repeat -m for more detail.

Escape is not wrong; it is how Go makes pointers safe. Look at it only for hot paths, after a profile shows allocation cost. Returning a value instead of a pointer, or letting callers pass a buffer, often removes allocations.

lessons.title: The garbage collector, GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT and Green Tea
body: Go's garbage collector is concurrent and non-moving: it marks reachable objects while the program runs and sweeps the rest, with short stop-the-world pauses. Go 1.26 made the Green Tea collector the default; it scans memory span by span for better locality, reducing GC CPU cost by 10–40% in many programs.

GOGC (default 100) sets how much the heap may grow over the live heap before the next collection: 100 means the heap can double. Lower values use less memory and more CPU; GOGC=off disables collection. debug.SetGCPercent changes it at run time and returns the old value.

GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19) sets a soft memory limit for the whole runtime, such as GOMEMLIMIT=512MiB. The GC works harder as the limit approaches, which suits containers with fixed memory. runtime.ReadMemStats and runtime/metrics report heap size and GC counts.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"runtime/debug"
)

var keep [][]byte

func main() {
	old := debug.SetGCPercent(50)
	fmt.Println("previous GOGC:", old)
	debug.SetGCPercent(old)
	limit := debug.SetMemoryLimit(-1)
	fmt.Println("default limit is effectively unlimited:", limit > 1<<60)
	var before, after runtime.MemStats
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&before)
	for range 1000 {
		keep = append(keep, make([]byte, 1024))
	}
	keep = nil
	runtime.GC()
	runtime.ReadMemStats(&after)
	fmt.Println("collections ran:", after.NumGC > before.NumGC)
	fmt.Println("allocated at least 1 MB:", after.TotalAlloc-before.TotalAlloc >= 1000*1024)
}

lessons.question: What does GOGC=100 mean?
options: The heap may grow to about twice the live heap before the next collection
The GC runs every 100 milliseconds
The program may use at most 100 MB
lessons.explanation: GOGC is a growth percentage relative to the live heap after the last cycle. GOMEMLIMIT is the absolute limit.

lessons.title: GOMAXPROCS and container-aware scheduling
body: GOMAXPROCS is the number of Ps, so the maximum number of goroutines executing Go code at the same instant. Goroutines blocked in system calls do not count. runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0) reads it without changing it, and runtime.NumCPU reports logical CPUs.

Since Go 1.25, on Linux the default respects the cgroup CPU limit of a container: a pod limited to 2 CPUs on a 64-core machine gets GOMAXPROCS=2, and the runtime updates it if the limit changes. Before 1.25 it used the host CPU count, which caused heavy throttling.
Setting the GOMAXPROCS environment variable, or calling runtime.GOMAXPROCS with a positive value, disables the automatic adjustment. runtime.SetDefaultGOMAXPROCS (1.25) restores it.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
)

func main() {
	procs := runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)
	fmt.Println(procs >= 1, procs <= runtime.NumCPU())
	old := runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1)
	fmt.Println(runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0))
	runtime.GOMAXPROCS(old)
	runtime.SetDefaultGOMAXPROCS()
	fmt.Println(runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0) == procs)
}

lessons.title: Profiling CPU and memory with pprof
body: Profiles show where a program spends time or allocates memory. go test -cpuprofile=cpu.out and -memprofile=mem.out profile tests and benchmarks; a running service exposes /debug/pprof/ by importing net/http/pprof; runtime/pprof writes profiles from any program.

go tool pprof reads them: -top lists the heaviest functions, -list=Func annotates source lines, and -http=:8080 opens a web UI with flame graphs. For memory, -sample_index=alloc_space shows total bytes allocated and inuse_space shows live bytes at the moment of the profile.

Profile first, then optimise the largest cost. Allocation profiles are often more revealing than CPU profiles, because allocation also costs GC time later. Setting -memprofilerate=1 records every allocation, which is exact but slow, so use it only in focused tests like this one.

lessons.explanation: alloc_space accumulates every allocation; inuse_space shows only what was still live when the profile was written.

lessons.title: Execution traces, regions and the flight recorder
body: An execution trace records scheduler events, goroutine creation and blocking, system calls, GC phases and user annotations with nanosecond timestamps. trace.Start(w) and trace.Stop() capture one, go test -trace=trace.out does so for tests, and go tool trace trace.out opens a timeline viewer. Since Go 1.27 the viewer listens only on localhost by default.

Annotate with trace.NewTask, trace.WithRegion and trace.Log so the viewer groups work by request. Traces explain latency that profiles average away, such as a goroutine waiting for a lock or a GC pause in the middle of a request.

Go 1.25 added trace.FlightRecorder: it keeps the last few seconds of trace data in a ring buffer with low overhead. When something unusual happens, such as a slow request, call WriteTo to save just that recent window. This makes tracing practical in production.

It records traces only for the race detector
It keeps a cheap rolling window so you can save a trace of what just happened

lessons.title: Benchmarking method: variance, benchstat and fair comparisons
body: One benchmark run is an anecdote. Run each variant several times with -count=10, on a quiet machine, and compare the distributions. benchstat (golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat) reports means, variation and whether a difference is statistically significant.

Guard against measuring the wrong thing: keep setup outside the b.Loop body, make inputs realistic in size, avoid benchmarks whose result the compiler can discard (b.Loop helps), and check allocations as well as time.

testing.AllocsPerRun and the allocs/op column are stable across machines, which makes them good regression tests. Wall-clock numbers vary with CPU, frequency scaling and other processes, so they belong in reports rather than pass/fail tests.

lessons.title: Profile-guided optimisation
body: Profile-guided optimisation (PGO, Go 1.21) feeds a CPU profile from representative runs back into the compiler, which then inlines and devirtualises hot calls more aggressively. Typical gains are 2–14% CPU.

Put the profile in the main package directory as default.pgo and go build uses it automatically (-pgo=auto is the default). -pgo=off disables it and -pgo=path selects another file. The binary records the setting, visible with go version -m.

Profiles from production are best; profiles from benchmarks work if they exercise the same hot paths. Commit default.pgo and refresh it periodically. Builds stay reproducible because the profile is a normal input.

lessons.title: Reducing allocations: preallocation, reuse and value types
body: The cheapest allocation is the one you avoid. Preallocate slices and maps when the final size is known (make([]T, 0, n), make(map[K]V, n)), append into caller-provided buffers (the AppendX convention used by strconv and time), and return small structs by value.

Converting between string and []byte copies, except in cases the compiler optimises, such as map lookups m[string(b)] and comparisons. Interfaces holding non-pointer values usually allocate when the value escapes. strings.Builder avoids the copy in its String method.
Reuse long-lived buffers with sync.Pool only after measuring. Clarity first: most code is not hot, and the allocator got about 30% faster for small objects in Go 1.27.

lessons.title: weak pointers, unique handles and runtime.AddCleanup
body: Go 1.24 added package weak: weak.Make(p) returns a weak.Pointer that does not keep its target alive, and Value() returns nil once the target has been collected. Weak pointers build caches that never prevent memory from being freed.

Package unique (Go 1.23) interns values: unique.Make(v) returns a Handle[T], and two handles are equal exactly when their values are equal. Comparing handles is a pointer comparison, and identical strings share one copy, which saves memory for repetitive data such as host names.

runtime.AddCleanup (Go 1.24) runs a function after an object becomes unreachable, replacing most uses of runtime.SetFinalizer. Cleanups receive a separate argument, not the object itself, so they cannot resurrect it; they run on a runtime goroutine at an unspecified time and are not guaranteed to run before exit. Use them as a safety net, never as the main way to release resources: call Close explicitly.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"time"
	"unique"
	"weak"
)

type blob struct{ data [1 << 16]byte }

func main() {
	a := unique.Make("example.com")
	b := unique.Make("example." + "com")
	fmt.Println(a == b, a.Value())
	obj := &blob{}
	w := weak.Make(obj)
	done := make(chan string, 1)
	runtime.AddCleanup(obj, func(name string) { done <- name + " cleaned" }, "blob")
	fmt.Println(w.Value() == obj)
	obj = nil
	runtime.GC()
	fmt.Println(w.Value() == nil)
	select {
	case msg := <-done:
		fmt.Println(msg)
	case <-time.After(5 * time.Second):
		fmt.Println("cleanup not run yet")
	}
}

lessons.title: TCP servers and clients with package net
body: net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") opens a listener on a free port; ln.Addr() reports which. Accept returns a net.Conn for each client, and a server usually handles each connection in its own goroutine. net.Dial connects a client. A net.Conn is an io.Reader and io.Writer, so bufio, io.Copy and fmt work on it.

TCP is a byte stream, not a sequence of messages. One Write may arrive as several Reads or be merged with the next, so protocols need framing: newline-terminated lines, length prefixes, or a format such as HTTP.

Set deadlines with SetDeadline, SetReadDeadline and SetWriteDeadline; a blocked Read then fails with an error satisfying os.ErrDeadlineExceeded. Close the listener to stop Accept, and close each connection when its handler returns.

lessons.title: http.ServeMux routing patterns: methods and wildcards
body: Since Go 1.22, http.ServeMux patterns can include a method and wildcards: "GET /items/{id}" matches only GET (and HEAD) requests, and r.PathValue("id") returns the segment. "{path...}" matches the rest of the path, and "{$}" anchors a pattern to the exact path, so "/{$}" matches only the root.

When two patterns match, the more specific one wins, and registering two patterns that conflict without either being more specific panics. A path that matches a pattern with a different method gets 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header, not 404.
Handlers implement ServeHTTP(w, r); http.HandlerFunc adapts a function. Write headers before the body: the first Write sends status 200 if WriteHeader was not called.

options: 404 Not Found
It runs the GET handler

lessons.title: HTTP clients: timeouts, contexts and closing bodies
body: http.Get uses http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout: a server that never answers blocks forever. Create an http.Client with Timeout for a whole-request limit, or attach a context with http.NewRequestWithContext for per-call deadlines and cancellation.

Always close resp.Body, usually with defer resp.Body.Close() right after checking err. A non-2xx status is not an error: check resp.StatusCode yourself. Limit how much you read from untrusted servers with io.LimitReader.

Reuse one Client (and its Transport) across requests; it pools connections and is safe for concurrent use. Since Go 1.27 the HTTP/1 client drains a closed body automatically so the connection can be reused.
lessons.challenge: Instead of Client.Timeout, use a context with a 30ms deadline and http.NewRequestWithContext for the slow request; print whether errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded).
lessons.question: Is a 404 response an error from client.Get?
options: No; err is nil and you must check resp.StatusCode
Yes, every non-2xx status returns an error
Only 5xx statuses are errors
lessons.explanation: The client returns an error only when it could not get a response at all. Status codes are application-level results.
lessons.workedExample:

The client returns an error only when it could not get a response at all. Status codes are application-level results.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The client returns an error only when it could not get a response at all. Status codes are application-level results.

lessons.title: Middleware: wrapping handlers for logging, limits and recovery
body: Middleware is a function from http.Handler to http.Handler. It can act before and after calling next.ServeHTTP: logging, authentication, adding headers, measuring latency or recovering from panics. Chain middlewares by nesting them.

To observe the status code, wrap the ResponseWriter in a struct that records WriteHeader. http.ResponseController (Go 1.20) reaches optional features such as Flush and per-request deadlines through such wrappers if they implement Unwrap.

http.MaxBytesReader limits request bodies, protecting servers from huge uploads. http.TimeoutHandler bounds handler time. Go 1.25 added http.CrossOriginProtection, which rejects unsafe cross-origin browser requests using Fetch metadata headers, a modern defence against CSRF.
lessons.challenge: Write a recoverPanic middleware that turns a handler panic into a 500 response with body "internal error", and show it with a handler that panics.
lessons.question: How does middleware observe the status code a handler writes?
options: By reading r.Response after next returns
ServeMux stores it in the request context
By wrapping the ResponseWriter and recording WriteHeader calls
lessons.explanation: The status goes to the ResponseWriter. A wrapper that embeds it and overrides WriteHeader sees the value as it passes through.

lessons.title: Server timeouts and graceful shutdown
body: An http.Server should set timeouts: ReadHeaderTimeout protects against slow clients that never finish headers, ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout bound whole requests, and IdleTimeout closes idle keep-alive connections. The zero values mean no limits.

srv.Shutdown(ctx) stops accepting new connections, closes idle ones and waits for active requests to finish, or for ctx to expire. ListenAndServe and Serve then return http.ErrServerClosed, which is the expected result and not a failure.

Typical main: start Serve in a goroutine, wait for SIGINT or SIGTERM with signal.NotifyContext, call Shutdown with a deadline, then exit. RegisterOnShutdown and BaseContext help close long-lived connections such as WebSockets.
lessons.challenge: Show what happens when Shutdown's context expires first: give it a 10ms deadline while the handler sleeps 200ms, and print whether the error is context.DeadlineExceeded.
lessons.question: What does srv.Serve return after a successful Shutdown?
options: context.Canceled
http.ErrServerClosed, which signals a normal stop
nil
lessons.explanation: Serve always returns a non-nil error. ErrServerClosed distinguishes a requested shutdown from a real failure.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
shutdown: <nil>
finished in-flight request
true

Serve always returns a non-nil error. ErrServerClosed distinguishes a requested shutdown from a real failure.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Serve always returns a non-nil error. ErrServerClosed distinguishes a requested shutdown from a real failure.

lessons.title: TLS clients and servers with crypto/tls
body: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. srv.ListenAndServeTLS(certFile, keyFile) serves it; a tls.Config controls versions, cipher suites and certificates. Go's defaults are secure: TLS 1.2 minimum for clients and servers, modern cipher suites, and certificate verification on by default.

Never set InsecureSkipVerify in production; it disables server authentication. For tests, httptest.NewTLSServer creates a server with a self-signed certificate, and srv.Client() returns a client that trusts exactly that certificate.

Go 1.24 enabled the hybrid post-quantum key exchange X25519MLKEM768 by default. Go 1.27 adds ML-DSA signature support in crypto/tls and crypto/x509, an MLKEM1024 key exchange, and the crypto/mldsa package.
lessons.challenge: Configure a test server with MaxVersion TLS 1.2 by setting srv.TLS before StartTLS (use httptest.NewUnstartedServer), and print the negotiated version name.
lessons.question: Why does http.Get fail against httptest.NewTLSServer?
options: The default client verifies certificates and does not trust the test server's self-signed one
TLS is disabled in the default client
Test servers only speak HTTP/2
lessons.explanation: srv.Client() is configured with the test certificate. The default client uses the system roots, which correctly reject it.
lessons.workedExample:

lessons.title: A JSON API handler: decode, validate, respond
body: A robust JSON endpoint limits the body size, decodes into a struct with unknown fields rejected, validates the values, and responds with a consistent JSON error shape and the right status: 400 for malformed input, 422 for semantically invalid input, 201 for creation.

Set Content-Type: application/json before writing the body. Encode responses with json.NewEncoder(w).Encode; if encoding fails after headers were sent, all you can do is log, so encode simple, known-good types.
Keep handlers thin: parse and validate HTTP input, call ordinary functions that hold the logic, and map their errors to statuses. Those functions are then testable without HTTP.
lessons.challenge: Extend the handler so a title longer than 20 characters is rejected with 422 and "title too long"; test it with a 25-character title.
lessons.question: Which status suits a well-formed JSON body whose title is empty?
options: 500 Internal Server Error
422 Unprocessable Entity
400 Bad Request
lessons.explanation: 400 means the request could not be parsed. 422 means it parsed but failed validation, which helps clients fix the right thing.
lessons.practiceAnswer: 400 means the request could not be parsed. 422 means it parsed but failed validation, which helps clients fix the right thing.

lessons.title: Running processes with os/exec
body: exec.Command(name, args...) prepares a process; arguments are passed directly, not through a shell, so there is no quoting or injection risk from spaces and metacharacters. Output runs it and returns stdout; CombinedOutput merges stderr. Run, Start and Wait give finer control, and StdinPipe/StdoutPipe connect streams.
exec.CommandContext kills the process when the context is cancelled or its deadline passes; Cmd.Cancel and WaitDelay customise how. A non-zero exit returns an *exec.ExitError carrying the exit code.

exec.LookPath finds programs on PATH and, since Go 1.19, refuses to run a program found in the current directory through a relative PATH entry, a common attack. Never build a command line by concatenating untrusted input into "sh -c".
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	out, err := exec.Command("echo", "hello", "from a child").Output()
	fmt.Printf("%q %v\n", out, err)
	err = exec.Command("sh", "-c", "exit 3").Run()
	var exitErr *exec.ExitError
	fmt.Println(errors.As(err, &exitErr), exitErr.ExitCode())
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 50*time.Millisecond)
	defer cancel()
	err = exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sleep", "5").Run()
	fmt.Println(strings.Contains(err.Error(), "killed"), ctx.Err())
}

options: Arguments go straight to the program, so no shell parses the untrusted text
rm refuses paths from Go programs
sh -c is not available on Unix
lessons.explanation: A shell interprets spaces, semicolons and $(…). Passing arguments directly keeps the path a single, literal argument.

lessons.title: Handling signals with os/signal
body: Programs receive signals such as SIGINT (Ctrl-C) and SIGTERM (container stop). signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) returns a context cancelled when one arrives, which plugs straight into graceful shutdown code.

signal.Notify(ch, sigs...) delivers signals to a channel instead; use a buffered channel so the runtime never drops a signal while you are busy. signal.Stop or the stop function from NotifyContext restores default behaviour, so a second Ctrl-C can kill a stuck program.
SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught. Signal handling is process-wide, so libraries should not install handlers; leave that to main.
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	ch := make(chan os.Signal, 2)
	signal.Notify(ch, syscall.SIGUSR2)
	defer signal.Stop(ch)
	syscall.Kill(os.Getpid(), syscall.SIGUSR2)
	<-ch
	syscall.Kill(os.Getpid(), syscall.SIGUSR2)
	<-ch
	select {
	case <-ch:
		fmt.Println("unexpected")
	case <-time.After(10 * time.Millisecond):
		fmt.Println(2)
	}
}
lessons.challenge: Use signal.Notify with a buffered channel to catch SIGUSR2 sent to yourself twice, and print the number of signals received.
lessons.question: Why must the channel passed to signal.Notify be buffered?
options: The runtime does not block when sending, so signals arriving while you are busy would be dropped
Unbuffered channels cannot carry os.Signal
Notify panics on unbuffered channels
lessons.explanation: Signal delivery uses a non-blocking send. A buffer gives the receiver time to catch up.
lessons.workedExample:

Signal delivery uses a non-blocking send. A buffer gives the receiver time to catch up.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Signal delivery uses a non-blocking send. A buffer gives the receiver time to catch up.

lessons.title: Reflection with reflect: types, values and struct tags
body: reflect.TypeOf(x) returns a reflect.Type describing x's dynamic type; reflect.ValueOf(x) returns a reflect.Value holding it. Kind() reports the basic category (Struct, Slice, Ptr…), NumField and Field walk struct fields, and Field(i).Tag.Get("json") reads tags. reflect.TypeFor[T]() (Go 1.22) gets a Type without a value.

To modify a value through reflection you need an addressable Value: reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem(). CanSet reports whether a field can be set; unexported fields cannot. Setting a value of the wrong type panics.

Reflection powers encoding/json, fmt and template packages, but it is slower, bypasses compile-time checking and panics on misuse. Prefer generics or interfaces in ordinary code; use reflection for generic infrastructure such as encoders and validators.

lessons.question: Why does reflect.ValueOf(u).Field(0).SetString("x") panic?
options: ValueOf(u) holds a copy, which is not addressable; use ValueOf(&u).Elem()
Strings cannot be set through reflection
Field(0) is unexported
lessons.explanation: Setting needs an addressable value that refers to the original variable. Passing a pointer and calling Elem provides one.
lessons.workedExample:

User struct

Setting needs an addressable value that refers to the original variable. Passing a pointer and calling Elem provides one.

lessons.title: unsafe.Pointer and its valid conversion patterns
body: Package unsafe steps outside Go's type safety. unsafe.Pointer can be converted to and from any pointer type and to uintptr. The unsafe package documents six valid patterns, such as converting *T1 to *T2 when the memory layouts are compatible, and pointer arithmetic expressed in a single expression: unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + offset).

A uintptr is just an integer: the garbage collector does not treat it as a reference and may move or free the object it came from, so storing a uintptr and converting back later is invalid. unsafe.Add(p, n) (Go 1.17) performs the arithmetic safely without a uintptr round trip.

unsafe code is not portable across architectures or Go versions, and go vet's unsafeptr check flags suspicious conversions. Use it only for interoperability (cgo, syscalls) or measured performance work, and isolate it behind a safe API.
lessons.challenge: Read the second element of an [4]int32 array through unsafe.Add on a pointer to its first element, and print it.
lessons.question: Why is storing uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(p)) in a variable and converting it back later invalid?
options: uintptr is only 32 bits
The conversion is a compile error
The GC does not see a uintptr as a reference, so the object may be freed or moved
lessons.explanation: Only unsafe.Pointer values keep objects alive. A stored integer address can dangle, so conversions must stay within one expression.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

1024 4

Only unsafe.Pointer values keep objects alive. A stored integer address can dangle, so conversions must stay within one expression.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Only unsafe.Pointer values keep objects alive. A stored integer address can dangle, so conversions must stay within one expression.

lessons.title: unsafe.Slice, unsafe.String and zero-copy views
body: unsafe.Slice(ptr, len) builds a slice over existing memory, and unsafe.String(ptr, len) builds a string. unsafe.SliceData and unsafe.StringData return the pointer to the first element. Together they convert between []byte and string without copying.

A zero-copy string made from a []byte must never see the bytes change afterwards: strings are immutable, and the compiler and runtime rely on that (for example, map keys and interning). Converting a string to a []byte with unsafe and writing to it is undefined behaviour and may crash on read-only memory.

Most programs never need this. The compiler already avoids copies for common cases (map lookups, comparisons, range over []byte(s)), and strings.Builder hands its buffer to a string without a copy. Reserve unsafe conversions for profiled hot paths.
lessons.challenge: Write stringToBytes(s string) []byte using unsafe.Slice and unsafe.StringData, use it only to read, and print the sum of the bytes of "abc".
lessons.question: What must stay true after creating a string with unsafe.String over a []byte?
options: The string must be shorter than 64 bytes
The bytes must never be modified while the string is in use
The slice must be freed immediately
lessons.explanation: Go assumes strings are immutable. Mutating the shared bytes silently changes a "constant" string and breaks that assumption.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

Go assumes strings are immutable. Mutating the shared bytes silently changes a "constant" string and breaks that assumption.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Go assumes strings are immutable. Mutating the shared bytes silently changes a "constant" string and breaks that assumption.

lessons.title: Struct layout, alignment and padding
body: Each type has a size (unsafe.Sizeof) and an alignment (unsafe.Alignof). The compiler inserts padding so every field starts at a multiple of its alignment, and pads the end so arrays of the struct stay aligned. On 64-bit platforms int64, pointers and float64 align to 8 bytes.

Field order changes size: {a bool; b int64; c bool} takes 24 bytes, while {b int64; a bool; c bool} takes 16. In large slices of structs, ordering fields from largest to smallest alignment saves memory and cache space. The fieldalignment analyzer (in golang.org/x/tools) reports such savings.

64-bit atomic operations need 8-byte alignment; on 32-bit platforms a plain int64 field may not be aligned, which is one reason the typed atomic.Int64 exists: it guarantees alignment. A zero-size field at the end of a struct also gets padding so a pointer to it never points past the object.
lessons.challenge: Reorder the fields of struct{ a byte; b int32; c byte; d int64; e byte } to minimise its size; print the original and reordered sizes.
lessons.question: Why is struct{ a bool; b int64; c bool } 24 bytes on 64-bit platforms?
options: Padding aligns b to 8 bytes and rounds the total up to a multiple of 8
bool takes 8 bytes
Go adds a hidden 8-byte header to structs
lessons.explanation: a takes 1 byte plus 7 padding, b 8, c 1 plus 7 trailing padding: 24 in total.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
24 16
0 8 16
8 16 24 16

a takes 1 byte plus 7 padding, b 8, c 1 plus 7 trailing padding: 24 in total.
lessons.practiceAnswer: a takes 1 byte plus 7 padding, b 8, c 1 plus 7 trailing padding: 24 in total.

lessons.title: Calling C with cgo
body: A Go file that imports "C" is processed by cgo: the comment directly above the import is C source (preamble), and C.name refers to C functions, types and variables. C.CString copies a Go string into C memory that you must free with C.free; C.GoString copies back.

cgo calls cost more than Go calls (tens of nanoseconds), and C code is invisible to the race detector and GC. The pointer-passing rules forbid C from keeping Go pointers after a call returns; runtime.Pinner (Go 1.21) pins Go memory when C must hold a pointer temporarily.

cgo needs a C toolchain and disables simple cross-compilation; CGO_ENABLED=0 builds pure-Go binaries and makes import "C" files fail to build. Prefer pure-Go libraries unless you need an existing C library.
lessons.challenge: Add a C function that upper-cases a C string in place, call it on the C copy, and print the result with C.GoString.
lessons.question: Who frees memory returned by C.CString?
options: It is freed automatically when the C call returns
You must, with C.free, because it is allocated by C malloc
The Go garbage collector
lessons.explanation: CString copies into C heap memory that Go's GC does not manage. Pair it with defer C.free.

lessons.title: go vet, analyzers and the stdversion check
body: go vet runs analyzers that find likely bugs in code that compiles: Printf format mismatches, copied locks, unreachable code, malformed struct tags, lost context cancel functions, self-assignment and more. go test runs a subset of them automatically before tests.

Go 1.27 adds stdversion to the vet checks run by go test: it reports standard-library symbols newer than the go version in force for a file, from the go.mod go line or a //go:build constraint. Using strings.CutLast in a module declaring go 1.22 is reported because older toolchains would fail to build it.

Additional analyzers come from golang.org/x/tools and tools such as staticcheck. go vet -vettool=prog runs a custom analysis binary; analyzers are written with the golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis framework.

lessons.title: go fix and modernizers
body: Since Go 1.26 go fix runs modernizers: analyzers whose suggested fixes rewrite code to newer idioms. Examples include any (interface{} to any), rangeint (3-clause loops to range over int), minmax (if/else to min/max), newexpr (helper functions to new(expr)), errorsastype (errors.As to errors.AsType) and waitgroupgo (Add/Done to WaitGroup.Go, renamed in 1.27).

Go 1.27 adds atomictypes (sync/atomic functions to typed atomics), embedlit (shorter composite literals using promoted fields), slicesbackward and unsafefuncs. go fix -diff prints the patch without applying it and exits non-zero when there is something to change, which suits CI.

Each fix respects the go version declared for the file, so it never introduces a feature the module cannot use. //go:fix inline directives let library authors mark functions whose calls go fix should inline, which helps migrate users off deprecated APIs.

lessons.title: Reading Go source with go/parser, go/ast and go/token
body: The go/ packages expose the toolchain's view of source code. go/parser builds an abstract syntax tree, go/ast defines its node types and provides ast.Inspect to walk it, and go/token records positions in a FileSet so tools can report file:line:column.

go/types adds type checking, resolving every identifier to its object and type; golang.org/x/tools/go/packages loads whole modules with types. Linters, code generators, refactoring tools and gopls are built on these packages. Go 1.27 adds token.File.String and scanner.Scanner.End among other refinements.
go/format formats an AST or source the same way gofmt does, so generated code can be canonical.

A mapping from compact positions to file, line and column
The type of every expression

lessons.title: Code generation with go generate
body: //go:generate command args... comments mark commands that go generate runs, in the directory of the file. Typical generators are stringer (String methods for enumerations), protocol-buffer compilers and mock generators. Generated files are committed so ordinary builds do not need the generator.

go generate is never run by go build or go test. Generated files should start with a line matching ^// Code generated .* DO NOT EDIT\.$ so tools and reviewers know not to edit them; gofmt-ing the output keeps diffs clean.

A small generator can be a Go program in the same module run with go run, guarded by //go:build ignore so it is not part of the package build. Since Go 1.24, versioned generators can be declared as tool dependencies and run with go tool.

Automatically when go.mod changes
Only when you invoke go generate explicitly

body: GOOS and GOARCH select the target: GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build cross-compiles with no extra toolchain for pure-Go code. go tool dist list prints all supported targets.
