lessons.title: Debugging: stack traces, GOTRACEBACK, Delve and govulncheck
body: An unrecovered panic prints the panicking goroutine's stack; GOTRACEBACK=all prints every goroutine, and GOTRACEBACK=crash also dumps core. runtime/debug.Stack and runtime.Stack capture stacks programmatically, and since Go 1.27 tracebacks include runtime/pprof goroutine labels.

Delve (github.com/go-delve/delve, run as dlv debug or dlv test) is the standard Go debugger and understands goroutines, channels and interfaces. Build with -gcflags=all="-N -l" to disable optimisation and inlining when stepping through code. GODEBUG settings, such as gctrace=1, print runtime diagnostics.

govulncheck (golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck) checks dependencies against the Go vulnerability database and reports only vulnerabilities your code actually reaches. Run it in CI alongside go vet and the race detector.

lessons.title: Make the zero value useful
body: Idiomatic Go types work without a constructor: var buf bytes.Buffer, var mu sync.Mutex and var wg sync.WaitGroup are ready to use. Design your types the same way, so a zero struct is a valid, empty instance and users cannot forget to initialise it.

Techniques: lazily create maps on first write, treat nil slices as empty, use zero numbers as "use the default", and make methods on a nil pointer receiver behave sensibly when that is natural, as in a linked list where nil is the empty list.
When a zero value cannot be valid, for example a client that needs a URL, provide a New function and make the type's fields unexported so the invalid state cannot be built from outside the package.

lessons.title: Constructors, functional options and config structs
body: When a constructor has several optional settings, avoid long parameter lists. Two idioms are common: a Config struct passed by value whose zero fields mean defaults, and functional options, variadic func(*Server) values such as WithTimeout(5*time.Second).

Functional options keep the common call short (NewServer(addr)), let new options be added without breaking callers, and can validate as they apply. A Config struct is simpler, self-documenting, and easy to load from files; prefer it unless options need logic.
Either way, validate in the constructor and return an error rather than building an invalid object. Keep defaults in one place.

lessons.title: Accept interfaces, return concrete types
body: Functions should accept the smallest interface they need, such as io.Reader rather than *os.File, so callers can pass files, buffers, network connections or test doubles. They should return concrete types, so callers get every method and future additions do not break them.

Returning an interface hides capabilities and makes adding methods a breaking change for implementers. The exception is a constructor that genuinely chooses among implementations, or the error interface.
Test doubles follow naturally: a fake that implements the consumer's small interface replaces a database or HTTP client in tests, with no mocking framework.

lessons.title: Package and project layout
body: Start small: a single package at the module root is fine for a library, and a single main package for a command. Split packages when a part has a clear, independent purpose and a small API, not to mirror layers such as models/controllers/utils.

Conventions from the official module layout guide: commands under cmd/name/, private shared code under internal/, and packages named for what they provide. Avoid import cycles by keeping dependencies flowing one way, with lower-level packages unaware of higher-level ones.

Package names are short, lower-case and singular (http, json, user). Avoid stutter in exported names: user.New, not user.NewUser. Unit tests sit next to the code; larger test data goes in testdata/, which the go tool ignores.

lessons.title: Designing concurrent APIs
body: Prefer synchronous APIs: a function that does its work and returns lets callers add concurrency with go and a WaitGroup if they want it. An API that starts goroutines internally must say who stops them, usually by taking a context and providing Close or Stop, and must wait for them before returning from Close.
Make ownership clear. Whoever starts a goroutine is responsible for its exit. Channels in signatures should have directions, and the side that sends should be the side that closes.

Document whether a type is safe for concurrent use. Many standard types are not (maps, bytes.Buffer, strings.Builder); http.Client and *sql.DB are. Hide locks inside the type rather than asking callers to lock.

Only cancel the context and return immediately
Nothing; goroutines end when the type is garbage collected

lessons.title: Project: a tested word-count command
body: This project builds a small but complete command-line tool: a reusable wc package with a Count(io.Reader) function, and a cmd/wc command that handles flags, files, standard input, exit codes and error messages.

The command's logic lives in run(args, stdin, stdout, stderr) int, and main only calls os.Exit(run(...)). Tests can then call run with buffers and fake inputs, checking output and exit status without starting a process.

Count streams the input with bufio.Reader.ReadRune instead of reading it all, so memory stays constant for large files. Words are maximal runs of non-space runes, using unicode.IsSpace so tabs and Unicode spaces count as separators. Bytes are counted from the encoded size of each rune.
Error handling follows Unix conventions: a missing file prints wc: <error> to stderr and makes the final status 1, but the remaining files are still processed. Bad flags return status 2.
Tests cover edge cases: empty input, no trailing newline, multi-byte characters, mixed whitespace, and a read error injected with testing/iotest.ErrReader.
The practice adds a -w flag for words only. Make it mutually exclusive with -l: when both are given, print usage and exit 2.

lessons.title: Project: a bounded, cancellable concurrent fetcher
body: fetch.All downloads many URLs concurrently while respecting three contracts: at most limit requests are in flight, results come back in input order, and cancelling the context stops both new and in-flight requests.

A buffered channel is the semaphore. The loop acquires a slot before starting each goroutine, selecting on ctx.Done() so a cancelled context stops the loop instead of blocking. Each goroutine writes only its own results[i], which preserves order without a mutex, and wg.Wait orders those writes before the return.

Every request carries the context through http.NewRequestWithContext, so cancellation reaches the transport. Bodies are always closed, and reads are capped with io.LimitReader so a hostile server cannot exhaust memory.

Tests use a fake http.RoundTripper rather than the network. It records peak concurrency with atomics, simulates latency, returns a 404 for one path, and honours request cancellation. The tests run under the race detector.
The cancellation test uses a transport that would wait an hour; the context deadline must end the whole call within moments, with every result carrying context.DeadlineExceeded.
The practice adds per-request timeouts: each URL gets its own deadline derived from the parent context, so one slow server cannot use up the whole budget.

options: The semaphore serialises the writes

Goroutines finish in the order they start

lessons.title: Project: an in-memory JSON REST API
body: This project is a small task API: create a task, fetch it, and mark it done. It brings together ServeMux method and wildcard patterns, JSON decoding with limits and unknown-field rejection, consistent JSON errors, a mutex-protected store, and two levels of testing.

Handlers are methods on *Store, so they share state without globals. The store's lock covers only the map access, never the encoding of the response, which keeps critical sections short. IDs come from a counter incremented under the same lock, so concurrent creates never collide.

Status codes carry meaning: 201 with a Location header on create, 404 for unknown IDs, 400 for malformed input or a non-integer ID, 422 for a valid document that fails validation, and 405, produced by ServeMux itself, for unsupported methods.

The table-driven lifecycle test drives the handler directly with httptest.NewRecorder, step by step. The concurrency test uses Go 1.27's httptest.NewTestServer and twenty parallel POST requests under the race detector, then checks that IDs are unique.
The practice adds DELETE /tasks/{id} returning 204 No Content, then 404 for later reads.

lessons.title: Project: a generic LRU cache with iterators
body: An LRU cache keeps the most recently used entries and evicts the oldest when it is full. This implementation combines a map for O(1) lookup with container/list, a doubly linked list, for O(1) reordering: Get and Put move entries to the front and eviction removes from the back.

The cache is generic over a comparable key and any value, so Cache[string, []byte] and Cache[int, *User] share one implementation with full type safety. The list stores *entry values in its untyped Element.Value field, so methods type-assert them back; this is the one place where the type system cannot help.

All returns an iter.Seq2[K, V] that walks from most to least recent without changing the order, so callers can range over the cache, stop early, or collect it with maps.Collect. New panics on a non-positive capacity, a programmer error, rather than returning an error.
Tests check eviction order, updates of existing keys, early termination of the iterator, and the panic. A benchmark measures Put/Get cost with b.Loop.

The cache is documented as not safe for concurrent use; the practice adds a concurrent wrapper with a mutex and a race-tested test, which is the usual way to add locking without slowing single-goroutine users.

lessons.title: Project: a token-bucket rate limiter tested with synctest
body: A token bucket allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate: the bucket holds up to burst tokens, refills continuously at rate tokens per second, and each event spends one. Allow answers immediately; Wait blocks until a token is available or the context ends.

Refilling is computed lazily from elapsed time whenever the bucket is used, so no background goroutine is needed and an idle limiter costs nothing. A mutex protects the counters because many goroutines share one bucket.

Wait computes exactly how long until the next token and sleeps on a timer, re-checking afterwards because another goroutine may have taken the token first. It releases the lock before sleeping, so waiters do not block each other.

Timing code is notoriously flaky to test with real sleeps. These tests run inside synctest bubbles: the fake clock advances only when every goroutine is blocked, so "half a second" or "400 ms" are exact, instant and deterministic, even with five goroutines competing under the race detector.
The practice adds a Reserve-style method, Tokens() float64, reporting the current balance, and a test showing it rises fractionally over time.

lessons.title: Project: a zero-allocation log summariser
body: logstat.Scan streams key=value log lines and summarises them: counts per level and the slowest request time. It is designed for large inputs, so it works on the scanner's []byte buffer directly and avoids allocating per line.

Three techniques keep allocations near zero. bufio.Scanner.Bytes returns a view into its buffer instead of a new string. field uses bytes.Cut and bytes.CutPrefix, which return sub-slices rather than copies. And counting goes through bump: the compiler optimises a lookup written as m[string(b)] so it does not copy the bytes, but an assignment such as m[string(b)]++ must own its key and allocates on every line. bump looks up a *int and increments it, inserting a new string key only the first time a level is seen; flatten builds the public map once at the end.

atoi parses digits by hand to avoid strconv's string conversion; it is safe here because the format is known and it stops at the first non-digit. That trade-off, a small specialised parser in a measured hot path, is the kind profiles justify.

Tests turn performance into contracts: field must not allocate at all, and scanning 1000 lines must stay within an allocation budget of 10, independent of input size. Unlike timings, allocation counts are deterministic, so these are reliable regression tests.

The practice adds a per-message count while preserving the budget. The obvious s.Msgs[string(m)]++ would cost one allocation per line and fail the budget test; reuse bump so repeated messages are lookups only.

lessons.title: Reading the spec: notation, source text, identifiers and keywords
body: The Go specification is short enough to read in an evening and is the final authority on what a program means. Its grammar is written in Extended Backus-Naur Form: Production = name "=" Expression ".", with | for alternatives, () for grouping, [] for an optional part and {} for repetition. Reading one production, such as IdentifierList = identifier { "," identifier }, tells you exactly what the parser accepts.

Source code is Unicode text encoded in UTF-8, and the compiler does not normalise it: an accented letter written as one code point and as a letter plus combining mark are different identifiers. A byte order mark is ignored only at the very start of a file. The NUL character is not allowed.

An identifier is a letter followed by letters and digits, where letter means any Unicode letter or the underscore. So π and _tmp are valid names, while 2x is not. Exported identifiers start with an upper-case letter (Unicode class Lu); names in scripts without case, such as 名前, are therefore never exported.

Go has exactly 25 keywords: break, case, chan, const, continue, default, defer, else, fallthrough, for, func, go, goto, if, import, interface, map, package, range, return, select, struct, switch, type, var. Names such as int, len, true, nil, any and error are predeclared identifiers, not keywords, so they can be shadowed, which is legal and usually a mistake.

lessons.title: Integer, floating-point, imaginary and rune literals in full
body: Integer literals come in four bases: decimal 255, binary 0b1111_1111, octal 0o377 (or the legacy 0377), and hexadecimal 0xFF. Underscores may separate digits for readability, but only between digits or after the base prefix: 1_000_000 is valid, while _100 is an identifier and 100_ is an error. The 0b, 0o and underscore forms need go 1.13 or later.

Floating-point literals are decimal (1.5, .5, 1e9, 6.02e23) or hexadecimal with a mandatory p exponent: 0x1p-2 is 0.25. An imaginary literal is an integer or float followed by i, such as 2i or 1.5e3i, and denotes a complex constant.

The built-ins complex, real and imag build and take apart complex values; complex128 holds two float64s. math/cmplx provides Abs, Sqrt, Exp, Pow and friends. Rune literals can use escapes: '\n', '\x41', '\u00e9', '\U0001F600' and octal '\101'.

It is invalid; hex floats are not allowed
0.25, because p gives a power-of-two exponent
lessons.explanation: Hex floating-point literals scale the mantissa by 2 to the power after p: 1 × 2⁻² = 0.25.

lessons.title: Types, type identity, assignability and representability
body: Every named type is distinct from every other type, while two type literals are identical when they have the same structure: []int and []int are identical, and struct{ X int } in two packages is identical too, unless one of its fields is unexported. That is why the defined types Celsius and Fahrenheit never mix, but two anonymous struct types with the same fields do.

A value x is assignable to a variable of type T when the types are identical, when they share an underlying type and at least one is not a named type, when T is an interface that x implements, for bidirectional channels assigned to a directional channel of the same element type, when x is the predeclared nil and T is a pointer, function, slice, map, channel or interface, or when x is an untyped constant representable as T.

Representable means the constant fits: 1.0 is representable as an int, while 1.5 or 300 as a byte is not. bool is its own type: there is no implicit conversion between booleans and integers, which removes a whole class of C bugs.
lessons.challenge: Predict, then confirm by compiling, which of these is assignable to []int: a value of type IntSlice, a value of a type Ints that is defined as IntSlice, and nil. Print a line for each that compiles.
lessons.question: Why can an IntSlice value be passed to func sum(xs []int)?
options: Named slice types convert automatically to any slice type
Because IntSlice has no methods
They share an underlying type and []int is not a named type
lessons.explanation: Assignability allows identical underlying types when at least one side is unnamed. Two different named types, such as Celsius and Fahrenheit, need a conversion.

lessons.title: Blocks, scope, predeclared identifiers and uniqueness
body: Go has nested blocks: the universe block (predeclared identifiers), the package block (all files of the package), the file block (imports), and the blocks of functions, statements and clauses. Each if, for and switch is its own implicit block, and each case clause is another. A declaration is visible from its point of declaration to the end of the innermost enclosing block, except that package-level names are visible throughout the package, so order there does not matter.

Shadowing an outer name in an inner block is legal. The predeclared identifiers include the types bool, byte, comparable, complex64/128, error, float32/64, int and its sizes, rune, string, uint and its sizes, uintptr and any; the constants true, false and iota; the zero value nil; and the functions append, cap, clear, close, complex, copy, delete, imag, len, make, max, min, new, panic, print, println, real and recover.

Two identifiers are different if they are spelled differently, or if they appear in different packages and are not exported: the unexported name count in package a is unrelated to count in package b. A qualified identifier, pkg.Name, reaches an exported name through an import.
lessons.challenge: Show that the predeclared nil can be shadowed: declare nil := 0 inside a block and print nil+1, then show the real nil still works outside by comparing a nil slice.
lessons.question: Why can later() use early even though early is declared after it?
options: Package-level identifiers are scoped to the whole package block
The compiler reorders functions alphabetically
Only variables declared with var can be used before declaration
lessons.explanation: Order matters inside function bodies, but at package level every name is visible throughout; initialisation order is then computed from dependencies.

lessons.title: Operands, primary expressions, method values and method expressions
body: An expression computes a value from operands (literals, identifiers, qualified identifiers and parenthesised expressions) using primary expressions such as selectors x.f, index expressions a[i], slices a[i:j], type assertions x.(T) and calls f(x).

A method value t.M is a function value bound to the receiver: f := counter.Inc saves both the method and the receiver, which is evaluated and copied at that moment. For a value receiver, later changes to counter do not affect f; for a pointer receiver bound through &counter, they do.

A method expression T.M (or (*T).M) is an ordinary function whose first parameter is the receiver: Point.Dist has type func(Point, Point) float64. Method expressions turn methods into plain functions for tables and higher-order code.
lessons.challenge: Build a map[string]func(*Counter) from the method expressions (*Counter).Inc and a new (*Counter).Reset, apply "inc", "inc", "reset", "inc" to one counter, and print n.

options: Get caches its first result
inc changed a different counter
The method value c.Get copied the value receiver when it was created
lessons.explanation: inc was bound to &c, so it changes c. get was bound to a copy of c taken before the increments.

lessons.title: Converting slices to arrays and array pointers
body: Go 1.17 allowed converting a slice to an array pointer: (*[4]byte)(s) returns a pointer that shares s's backing array. Go 1.20 added direct conversion to an array value: [4]byte(s) copies the first four elements.
Both conversions panic at run time if len(s) is smaller than the array length. A nil slice converts to a nil array pointer, and to a zero-length array value without panicking.
These conversions are handy for fixed-size keys, hashes and headers: parsing a 16-byte UUID from a slice, or using the first bytes of a buffer as a map key.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := []byte{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
	p := (*[4]byte)(s)
	p[0] = 9
	fmt.Println(s[0], len(p))
	a := [4]byte(s)
	a[1] = 0
	fmt.Println(s[1], a)
	var empty []int
	fmt.Println((*[0]int)(empty) == nil, [0]int(empty))
	defer func() { fmt.Println("recovered:", recover()) }()
	_ = [8]byte(s)
}

lessons.question: What is the difference between (*[4]byte)(s) and [4]byte(s)?
options: The pointer shares s's memory; the array value is a copy
They are identical spellings
The pointer form copies, the array form shares
lessons.explanation: Array pointers alias the backing array, so writes are visible through s. Array values are independent copies.

lessons.title: Order of evaluation and statements
body: Within an expression, function calls, method calls, receive operations and binary logical operations are evaluated left to right. Other details are unspecified: in a := f() + g() the calls happen left to right, but in y[f()], ok = g(h(), i()+x[j()], <-c), k() the evaluation of the index expressions relative to x is not pinned down. Do not write code whose meaning depends on such details.

Assignment happens in two phases: first all index expressions and pointer indirections on the left and all expressions on the right are evaluated in the usual order, then the assignments are carried out left to right. That is why a, b = b, a swaps, and why i, x[i] = 1, 2 sets x[0] (with the old i) rather than x[1].

Function calls, method calls and receive operations can appear as statements (expression statements); most other expressions cannot, so len(s) on its own line is an error. An empty statement does nothing; it appears, for example, as the missing post statement in for i := 0; i < n; {.
lessons.challenge: Predict and print the result of xs[trace(0)], xs[trace(1)] = trace(10), trace(20) where trace prints its argument; show the order of the four calls and the final slice.
lessons.question: After i := 0; x := []int{0, 0}; i, x[i] = 1, 2, which element of x is 2?
options: Neither; the statement does not compile
x[0], because index expressions are evaluated before any assignment
x[1], because i is assigned first
lessons.explanation: Phase one evaluates x[i] with i == 0; phase two assigns i = 1 and x[0] = 2.
lessons.workedExample:

Phase one evaluates x[i] with i == 0; phase two assigns i = 1 and x[0] = 2.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Phase one evaluates x[i] with i == 0; phase two assigns i = 1 and x[0] = 2.

lessons.title: Terminating statements and missing returns
body: A function with results must end in a terminating statement, and the compiler decides this syntactically, not by data flow. Terminating statements include return and goto, a call to panic, a block ending in a terminating statement, an if with an else where both branches terminate, a for with no condition and no break referring to it, and switch or select statements whose every case (including a default for switch) terminates and that contain no break.

So a function ending in for { ... } with no break needs no return, and a switch with an exhaustive-looking set of cases still needs a default or a final return, because the compiler does not know the cases are exhaustive.
When the compiler reports "missing return", either add the return or restructure, for example by turning if/else chains into a final return or a panic("unreachable") for truly impossible states.
lessons.challenge: Write func classify(r rune) string with an if/else-if/else chain (letter, digit, other) that compiles without a trailing return, and print it for 'a', '7' and '!'.
lessons.question: Why does a switch without a default, whose cases all return, still cause "missing return"?
options: Switches can never terminate a function
Cases must use fallthrough to terminate
A switch is terminating only with a default case; the compiler does not prove exhaustiveness
lessons.explanation: The rule is syntactic. Without default, control may fall out of the switch, so a return must follow.
lessons.workedExample:

The rule is syntactic. Without default, control may fall out of the switch, so a return must follow.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The rule is syntactic. Without default, control may fall out of the switch, so a return must follow.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping built-ins, the spec's example package and system considerations
body: print and println are bootstrapping built-ins: they write to standard error, their output format is implementation-specific, and they may be removed. They exist for the runtime's own debugging. Use fmt in real programs.

The specification's example package is a concurrent prime sieve: a generator goroutine sends 2, 3, 4, ... on a channel, and each discovered prime adds a filter goroutine that removes its multiples. It demonstrates goroutines, directional channels and pipelines in a dozen lines.

System considerations covers package unsafe and the size and alignment guarantees: for example, a struct or array of size zero may share an address with another variable, and unsafe.Sizeof of a value of a given type is the same on every call. Program execution begins by initialising the main package and its imports, then calls main.main; when it returns, the program exits without waiting for other goroutines.
lessons.challenge: Change the sieve to stop cleanly: pass a done channel to generate and filter, close it after collecting the primes below 50, and print them.
lessons.question: Where does println write?
options: To standard output, like fmt.Println
Nowhere unless built with -debug
To standard error, in an implementation-defined format
lessons.explanation: The bootstrapping built-ins are for runtime development; fmt.Println is the stable, documented way to print.

The bootstrapping built-ins are for runtime development; fmt.Println is the stable, documented way to print.

lessons.title: The language-version appendix: features gated by the go line
body: The appendix lists what changed in each language version, so the compiler can reject newer features in modules that declare an older go line. Go 1.9 added type aliases; 1.13 the 0b/0o/underscore literals and signed shift counts; 1.14 duplicate methods from embedded interfaces; 1.17 slice-to-array-pointer conversion; 1.18 generics; 1.20 slice-to-array conversion and comparable for interfaces; 1.21 min, max, clear and better inference; 1.22 per-iteration loop variables and range over int; 1.23 range over functions; 1.24 generic type aliases; 1.26 new(expr); 1.27 generic methods and promoted-field literal keys.

A file can also select a version with a //go:build go1.N constraint, which only ever upgrades within the module's range. Library authors declare the oldest go version they support, test with it, and adopt newer features only when they raise it.
This project declares go 1.20 and uses min, which arrived in 1.21: the compiler refuses. Raising the go line to 1.21 fixes it.

options: The go line fixes the language version, and min was added in Go 1.21
The 1.27 toolchain removed min
min needs an import of math
lessons.explanation: Newer toolchains honour the declared language version, rejecting features from later versions so the module keeps building with the toolchains it claims to support.

lessons.title: Regular expressions with regexp and regexp/syntax
body: regexp implements RE2 syntax with a guarantee: matching runs in time linear in the input, because the engine never backtracks. The price is that backreferences and look-around are not supported. Compile once with regexp.MustCompile at package level, since compiling is far more expensive than matching, and reuse the *Regexp, which is safe for concurrent use.

The method names follow a pattern: Find, FindAll, with String for string input, Submatch for capture groups and Index for positions. Named groups (?P<year>\d{4}) or (?<year>\d{4}) are read with SubexpIndex. ReplaceAllString expands $1 or ${name}; ReplaceAllStringFunc calls a function per match.

regexp/syntax parses patterns into an abstract syntax tree and simplifies them. It is what regexp uses internally, and is useful for tools that analyse or rewrite patterns. Prefer strings functions for fixed substrings; regular expressions are for structure.
lessons.challenge: Extract every key=value pair from "a=1 bb=22 ccc=x" with one regexp and FindAllStringSubmatch, and print them as key:value.
lessons.question: Why does regexp reject the backreference \1?
options: RE2 guarantees linear-time matching, which backreferences would break
Backreferences need the Perl flag
Capture groups cannot be numbered in Go
lessons.explanation: Backreferences make matching NP-hard in general. Go trades that feature for predictable performance on untrusted input.

lessons.title: text/template and its parse tree
body: text/template renders text from data: {{.Name}} reads a field, {{range .Items}}...{{end}} loops, {{if}}/{{else}} branches, {{with}} rebinds the dot, and {{template "name" .}} includes another template. Pipelines pass values through functions: {{.Price | printf "%.2f"}}. A leading or trailing dash, {{- or -}}, trims surrounding whitespace.

Functions are added with Funcs before parsing. Option("missingkey=error") turns a missing map key into an error instead of printing <no value>. Templates are safe for concurrent execution once parsed.

text/template/parse exposes the parsed tree: tmpl.Tree.Root lists ActionNodes, TextNodes and others. Tools use it to inspect which fields a template reads. Never use text/template for HTML: it does no escaping.
lessons.challenge: Write a template that prints a comma-separated list of names using range with $index, printing no comma before the first item, for []string{"go", "rust", "lean"}.
lessons.question: Why must HTML output use html/template rather than text/template?
options: text/template cannot produce angle brackets
html/template is faster
text/template performs no escaping, so user data could inject markup or script
lessons.explanation: html/template understands HTML, CSS, JavaScript and URL contexts and escapes each correctly. text/template prints values verbatim.

lessons.title: Contextual escaping with html/template and package html
body: html/template has the same API as text/template but escapes every value according to where it appears: element text, attribute values, URLs, JavaScript and CSS each get their own escaping. A value placed in an href that starts with javascript: is replaced with #ZgotmplZ, a harmless marker.
To include trusted markup on purpose, wrap it in template.HTML (or template.URL, template.JS). Those types bypass escaping, so use them only for content you produced, never for user input.
Package html provides the low-level EscapeString and UnescapeString for the five characters < > & ' ". Use them for plain text outside templates.
lessons.challenge: Render a link whose URL comes from data as /search?q={{.}} with the value "go & rust" and show that the query is URL-escaped.
lessons.question: What does html/template do with a value "javascript:alert(1)" in an href?
options: Replaces it with #ZgotmplZ because the URL scheme is unsafe
Escapes the colon and keeps the link
Leaves it unchanged inside quotes
lessons.explanation: The URL context filter only allows safe schemes such as http, https and mailto. Anything else becomes an inert placeholder.

lessons.title: Aligned columns, tokenising text and UTF-16
body: text/tabwriter aligns tab-separated cells into columns: create it with minimum width, tab width, padding and pad character, write lines with \t between cells, then Flush. AlignRight and Debug flags adjust the layout. go doc and gofmt use it for alignment.

text/scanner tokenises Go-like text (identifiers, numbers, strings, comments) from an io.Reader with positions, which suits small configuration languages and calculators. Mode selects which token kinds to recognise.

unicode/utf16 converts between runes and UTF-16 code units, which Windows APIs, JavaScript strings and some file formats use. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane become surrogate pairs: utf16.Encode([]rune("😀")) yields two units.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"
	"text/scanner"
	"text/tabwriter"
	"unicode/utf16"
)

func main() {
	w := tabwriter.NewWriter(os.Stdout, 0, 0, 2, ' ', 0)
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "name\tlang\tstars")
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "gopher\tgo\t5")
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "ferris\trust\t4")
	w.Flush()
	var s scanner.Scanner
	s.Init(strings.NewReader(`total = price * 1.2 // tax`))
	for tok := s.Scan(); tok != scanner.EOF; tok = s.Scan() {
		fmt.Print(scanner.TokenString(tok), " ")
	}
	fmt.Println()
	units := utf16.Encode([]rune("a😀"))
	fmt.Printf("%d %#04x %s\n", len(units), units[1], string(utf16.Decode(units)))
}

lessons.question: How many UTF-16 code units encode "😀"?
options: Four, the same as its UTF-8 length
Two, a surrogate pair, because it lies outside the Basic Multilingual Plane
One, because it is a single rune
lessons.explanation: UTF-16 represents code points above U+FFFF with a high and a low surrogate.

lessons.title: base64, base32, hex, ascii85, PEM and the encoding interfaces
body: encoding/base64 has StdEncoding, URLEncoding (with - and _ for URLs) and Raw variants without padding. encoding/base32 offers StdEncoding and HexEncoding. encoding/hex prints bytes as hex and Dump shows a hexdump. encoding/ascii85 is denser than base64 and used in PDF and PostScript.

encoding/pem wraps base64 data between -----BEGIN TYPE----- and -----END TYPE----- lines with optional headers, the format of certificates and keys. pem.Decode returns the first block and the remaining input.

Package encoding defines the interfaces that let types choose their own representation: TextMarshaler/TextUnmarshaler (used by JSON, XML and flag), BinaryMarshaler/BinaryUnmarshaler (used by gob), and since Go 1.24 TextAppender/BinaryAppender for allocation-free encoding.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding"
	"encoding/ascii85"
	"encoding/base32"
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/hex"
	"encoding/pem"
	"fmt"
	"net/netip"
)

func main() {
	data := []byte("go?>")
	fmt.Println(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(data), base64.URLEncoding.EncodeToString(data), base64.RawStdEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte("a")))
	fmt.Println(base32.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(data), hex.EncodeToString(data))
	dst := make([]byte, ascii85.MaxEncodedLen(len(data)))
	n := ascii85.Encode(dst, data)
	fmt.Println(string(dst[:n]))
	block := &pem.Block{Type: "NOTE", Headers: map[string]string{"Lang": "go"}, Bytes: data}
	text := pem.EncodeToMemory(block)
	back, rest := pem.Decode(text)
	fmt.Printf("%s%s %q %d\n", text, back.Type, back.Bytes, len(rest))
	var m encoding.TextMarshaler = netip.MustParseAddr("::ffff:10.0.0.1")
	out, _ := m.MarshalText()
	fmt.Println(string(out))
}

lessons.title: encoding/binary, checksums, maphash and math/bits
body: encoding/binary converts numbers to and from bytes in a chosen byte order: binary.BigEndian.PutUint32, binary.LittleEndian.Uint16, the Append variants added in Go 1.19, and Read/Write for fixed-size structs. Uvarint encodings store small numbers in fewer bytes, as protocol buffers do.

Package hash defines Hash, Hash32 and Hash64; hash/crc32 (with the IEEE and Castagnoli tables), hash/crc64 and hash/adler32 compute checksums that detect accidental corruption, not tampering. hash/maphash provides fast, randomly seeded hashing for hash tables; since Go 1.24 maphash.Comparable hashes any comparable value.
math/bits gives portable bit tricks that compile to single instructions: OnesCount, LeadingZeros, TrailingZeros, RotateLeft, Reverse and overflow-detecting Add64 and Mul64.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"hash"
	"hash/adler32"
	"hash/crc32"
	"hash/crc64"
	"hash/maphash"
	"math/bits"
)

func main() {
	buf := binary.BigEndian.AppendUint32(nil, 0xCAFEBABE)
	fmt.Printf("% x %#x\n", buf, binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(buf))
	v := binary.AppendUvarint(nil, 300)
	n, size := binary.Uvarint(v)
	fmt.Println(len(v), n, size)
	var h hash.Hash32 = crc32.NewIEEE()
	h.Write([]byte("hello"))
	fmt.Printf("%08x %08x\n", h.Sum32(), adler32.Checksum([]byte("hello")))
	fmt.Printf("%016x\n", crc64.Checksum([]byte("hello"), crc64.MakeTable(crc64.ISO)))
	seed := maphash.MakeSeed()
	fmt.Println(maphash.Comparable(seed, [2]int{1, 2}) == maphash.Comparable(seed, [2]int{1, 2}))
	hi, lo := bits.Mul64(1<<63, 4)
	fmt.Println(bits.OnesCount(255), bits.LeadingZeros64(1), hi, lo)
}

lessons.title: Reading and writing CSV with encoding/csv
body: csv.NewReader parses RFC 4180 CSV: quoted fields may contain commas, quotes ("") and newlines. Read returns one record; ReadAll returns them all. Set Comma for other separators such as tabs, Comment to skip lines, and FieldsPerRecord to enforce a fixed column count (0 means "same as the first record").
Errors are *csv.ParseError values with line and column. ReuseRecord avoids allocating a new slice per record when streaming large files.
csv.NewWriter quotes fields only when needed. Call Flush and then check Error, because writes are buffered.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/csv"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	in := "name,quote\nada,\"says \"\"hi\"\", ok\"\nbo,\"two\nlines\"\n"
	records, err := csv.NewReader(strings.NewReader(in)).ReadAll()
	fmt.Printf("%q %v\n", records[1:], err)
	bad := csv.NewReader(strings.NewReader("a,b\nc\n"))
	_, err = bad.ReadAll()
	var pe *csv.ParseError
	fmt.Println(errors.As(err, &pe), pe.Line)
	w := csv.NewWriter(os.Stdout)
	w.Write([]string{"plain", "with,comma", `with "quote"`})
	w.Flush()
	fmt.Println(w.Error())
}

lessons.title: XML with encoding/xml: struct tags and token streams
body: encoding/xml maps structs to elements using tags: `xml:"name"` for child elements, `xml:"id,attr"` for attributes, `xml:",chardata"` for text, `xml:",innerxml"` for raw content and `xml:"a>b"` for nested paths. XMLName records the element name.

xml.Unmarshal decodes a whole document; xml.NewDecoder(r).Token streams StartElement, EndElement and CharData tokens, which handles large documents and selective extraction. MarshalIndent pretty-prints.
The decoder does not resolve external entities or fetch DTDs, which avoids XXE attacks. Namespaces appear in Name.Space.

lessons.title: Go-native binary streams with encoding/gob
body: encoding/gob serialises Go values in a self-describing binary format designed for Go-to-Go communication, as used by net/rpc. The first value of each type sends a type description, so streams of many values are compact.

Fields are matched by name, not position: the receiver may have extra or missing fields, and integer sizes may differ, which allows gentle evolution of types. Interface values must have their concrete types registered with gob.Register.
Gob is not a cross-language format and is not hardened against hostile input of unbounded size; use JSON or protocol buffers for public APIs, and bound inputs from untrusted sources.
lessons.challenge: Encode three Point{X, Y int} values onto one gob stream with a single Encoder and decode them back in a loop until io.EOF; print them.
lessons.question: How does gob match struct fields between sender and receiver?
options: By field position
By struct type name, so types must be identical
By field name, so added or removed fields are tolerated
lessons.explanation: Name matching lets V1 decode into V2: Name transfers, Age is dropped and Email stays zero.

lessons.title: ASN.1 DER with encoding/asn1
body: ASN.1 with DER encoding is the binary format beneath X.509 certificates, PKCS keys and many telecom protocols. encoding/asn1 marshals Go structs to DER and back, using tags such as `asn1:"optional"`, `asn1:"explicit,tag:0"` and `asn1:"utf8"`.
DER is a tag-length-value encoding: an INTEGER 5 is 02 01 05, a SEQUENCE is 30 followed by its length and contents. ObjectIdentifier represents OIDs such as 1.2.840.113549 used to name algorithms.
Most code reaches ASN.1 through crypto/x509 rather than directly. golang.org/x/crypto/cryptobyte is a safer, more flexible parser for new protocol code.

options: An INTEGER (tag 02) of length 1 with value 5
A SEQUENCE of two elements
The string "5"
lessons.explanation: DER is tag, length, value. Tag 0x02 is INTEGER, and the single content byte is 5.

lessons.title: MIME types, multipart bodies, quoted-printable and mail messages
body: mime maps file extensions to types (mime.TypeByExtension(".json")), parses media-type headers with parameters (ParseMediaType) and encodes non-ASCII header words (mime.QEncoding). mime/quotedprintable encodes mostly-ASCII text for email bodies.

mime/multipart reads and writes multipart bodies, used by HTML form uploads and email attachments: a Writer creates parts with headers and a boundary, and a Reader iterates them with NextPart. http.Request.ParseMultipartForm builds on it.

net/mail parses RFC 5322 messages and addresses: mail.ReadMessage splits headers from the body, and mail.ParseAddress handles display names. Together these are what an email client needs below the network layer.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"mime"
	"mime/multipart"
	"mime/quotedprintable"
	"net/mail"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Println(mime.TypeByExtension(".json"))
	mt, params, _ := mime.ParseMediaType(`multipart/form-data; boundary=XYZ`)
	fmt.Println(mt, params["boundary"])
	fmt.Println(mime.QEncoding.Encode("utf-8", "Café"))
	var qp bytes.Buffer
	w := quotedprintable.NewWriter(&qp)
	w.Write([]byte("naïve = 1"))
	w.Close()
	fmt.Println(qp.String())
	var body bytes.Buffer
	mw := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
	mw.SetBoundary("XYZ")
	mw.WriteField("lang", "go")
	mw.Close()
	mr := multipart.NewReader(&body, "XYZ")
	part, _ := mr.NextPart()
	value, _ := io.ReadAll(part)
	fmt.Println(part.FormName(), string(value))
	msg, _ := mail.ReadMessage(strings.NewReader("From: Ada <ada@example.com>\r\nSubject: hi\r\n\r\nbody\r\n"))
	from, _ := mail.ParseAddress(msg.Header.Get("From"))
	rest, _ := io.ReadAll(msg.Body)
	fmt.Printf("%s %s %q\n", from.Name, msg.Header.Get("Subject"), rest)
}

lessons.title: index/suffixarray, container/heap and container/ring
body: index/suffixarray builds a suffix array over a byte slice once, then answers substring queries in O(log n) per lookup: Lookup returns every offset of a pattern and FindAllIndex accepts a regular expression. It suits read-mostly search over a large text.

container/heap turns any type implementing heap.Interface (sort.Interface plus Push and Pop) into a binary heap: heap.Init, heap.Push, heap.Pop and heap.Fix keep the minimum at index 0. It is how you build priority queues, Dijkstra's algorithm and schedulers.
container/ring is a circular doubly linked list: Next, Prev, Move, Link and Do. It fits fixed-size round-robin buffers, though a slice with a moving index is often simpler.

lessons.title: Cryptographic hashes: SHA-2, SHA-3 and the legacy MD5/SHA-1
body: A cryptographic hash maps any input to a fixed-size digest such that finding two inputs with the same digest, or an input for a given digest, is infeasible. crypto/sha256 and crypto/sha512 (SHA-2) and crypto/sha3 (SHA-3, plus the SHAKE extendable-output functions) are the current choices. Each offers a one-shot Sum function and a streaming hash.Hash from New.

crypto/md5 and crypto/sha1 are broken for collision resistance: attackers can craft two documents with the same digest. Keep them only for compatibility, such as legacy checksums or Git object names, never for signatures or integrity against attackers.

Package crypto names algorithms with crypto.Hash constants (crypto.SHA256, crypto.SHA3_256) and links them to implementations; Available reports whether an implementation is linked in. Signature APIs take these constants to say which hash was used.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto"
	"crypto/md5"
	"crypto/sha1"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"crypto/sha3"
	"crypto/sha512"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	data := []byte("abc")
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", sha256.Sum256(data))
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", sha512.Sum512_256(data))
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", sha3.Sum256(data))
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", sha3.SumSHAKE128(data, 8))
	fmt.Printf("%x %x\n", md5.Sum(data), sha1.Sum(data))
	h := crypto.SHA256.New()
	io.Copy(h, strings.NewReader("abc"))
	fmt.Println(h.Size(), fmt.Sprintf("%x", h.Sum(nil)) == fmt.Sprintf("%x", sha256.Sum256(data)), crypto.SHA3_256.Available())
}

lessons.title: HMAC, constant-time comparison, key derivation and secure randomness
body: crypto/hmac authenticates messages with a shared key: anyone without the key cannot produce a valid tag. Compare tags with hmac.Equal, which runs in constant time; a normal == leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing. crypto/subtle provides ConstantTimeCompare and related primitives for the same reason.

Key derivation turns secrets into keys. crypto/hkdf (Go 1.24) extracts and expands high-entropy secrets, such as a Diffie-Hellman result, into several independent keys with different info labels. crypto/pbkdf2 stretches low-entropy passwords with many iterations; for new password storage prefer a memory-hard function such as argon2 or bcrypt from golang.org/x/crypto.

crypto/rand is the only correct source of randomness for keys, nonces and tokens. rand.Read never fails on supported platforms since Go 1.24, and rand.Text returns a secure random string suitable for tokens.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/hkdf"
	"crypto/hmac"
	"crypto/pbkdf2"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"fmt"
)

func sign(key, msg []byte) []byte {
	m := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
	m.Write(msg)
	return m.Sum(nil)
}

func main() {
	key := []byte("shared secret")
	tag := sign(key, []byte("transfer 10"))
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", tag[:8])
	fmt.Println(hmac.Equal(tag, sign(key, []byte("transfer 10"))), hmac.Equal(tag, sign(key, []byte("transfer 99"))))
	fmt.Println(subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte("abc"), []byte("abd")))
	encKey, _ := hkdf.Key(sha256.New, []byte("dh-shared-secret"), []byte("salt"), "encryption", 32)
	macKey, _ := hkdf.Key(sha256.New, []byte("dh-shared-secret"), []byte("salt"), "authentication", 32)
	fmt.Println(len(encKey), string(encKey) != string(macKey))
	stretched, _ := pbkdf2.Key(sha256.New, "correct horse", []byte("salt"), 600_000, 32)
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", stretched[:8])
	token := rand.Text()
	fmt.Println(len(token))
}

bytes.Equal cannot compare 32-byte slices
hmac.Equal also checks the key

lessons.title: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, and why DES and RC4 are legacy
body: Use authenticated encryption (AEAD): it provides confidentiality and detects any modification. crypto/aes provides the AES block cipher and crypto/cipher wraps it in modes; cipher.NewGCM gives AES-GCM. Seal encrypts and appends a tag; Open verifies the tag before returning any plaintext and fails on any tampering.

A GCM nonce must never repeat for the same key, or security collapses. Generate random 12-byte nonces from crypto/rand, or use cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce (Go 1.24), which manages them for you. Additional data, such as a header, is authenticated but not encrypted.

crypto/des (including triple DES) and crypto/rc4 remain for interoperability with old systems only: DES keys are brute-forceable, 3DES has a 64-bit block that leaks over large data, and RC4 has statistical biases. Never choose them for new designs.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/aes"
	"crypto/cipher"
	"crypto/des"
	"crypto/rc4"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	key := make([]byte, 32)
	block, _ := aes.NewCipher(key)
	aead, _ := cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce(block)
	sealed := aead.Seal(nil, nil, []byte("secret message"), []byte("header"))
	fmt.Println(len(sealed), aead.Overhead())
	plain, err := aead.Open(nil, nil, sealed, []byte("header"))
	fmt.Println(string(plain), err)
	sealed[len(sealed)-1] ^= 1
	_, err = aead.Open(nil, nil, sealed, []byte("header"))
	fmt.Println(err)
	_, err = aead.Open(nil, nil, sealed, []byte("other header"))
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
	d, _ := des.NewTripleDESCipher(make([]byte, 24))
	r, _ := rc4.NewCipher([]byte("legacy"))
	fmt.Println(d.BlockSize(), r != nil)
}

lessons.title: Digital signatures: Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA-PSS and crypto.Signer
body: A signature proves that the holder of a private key approved a message, and anyone with the public key can check it. crypto/ed25519 is the simplest safe choice: fixed-size keys and signatures, deterministic, fast. crypto/ecdsa with P-256 is required by many standards; crypto/rsa with PSS padding (or PKCS #1 v1.5 for legacy) is ubiquitous. New RSA keys should be at least 2048 bits; since Go 1.24, keys smaller than 1024 bits are rejected by default (GODEBUG=rsa1024min=0 restores them for legacy tests).
All of them implement crypto.Signer: Public() and Sign(rand, digest, opts). Code that only needs to sign, such as TLS or a hardware key, depends on crypto.Signer rather than a concrete key type.

crypto/elliptic exposes the NIST curves' parameters; its low-level point arithmetic is deprecated in favour of crypto/ecdh and crypto/ecdsa. crypto/dsa is deprecated and insecure at its common sizes; it remains only to verify old signatures.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto"
	"crypto/dsa"
	"crypto/ecdsa"
	"crypto/ed25519"
	"crypto/elliptic"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/rsa"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
)

func check(s crypto.Signer, verify func([]byte, []byte) bool, digest []byte, opts crypto.SignerOpts) bool {
	sig, err := s.Sign(rand.Reader, digest, opts)
	return err == nil && verify(digest, sig)
}

func main() {
	msg := []byte("release v1.27")
	pub, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(nil)
	sig := ed25519.Sign(priv, msg)
	fmt.Println(len(sig), ed25519.Verify(pub, msg, sig), ed25519.Verify(pub, []byte("tampered"), sig))
	digest := sha256.Sum256(msg)
	ec, _ := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
	fmt.Println(check(ec, func(d, s []byte) bool { return ecdsa.VerifyASN1(&ec.PublicKey, d, s) }, digest[:], crypto.SHA256))
	rk, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
	pss := &rsa.PSSOptions{Hash: crypto.SHA256}
	fmt.Println(check(rk, func(d, s []byte) bool { return rsa.VerifyPSS(&rk.PublicKey, crypto.SHA256, d, s, pss) == nil }, digest[:], pss))
	_, err := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 512)
	fmt.Println(err != nil, elliptic.P256().Params().Name)
	var params dsa.Parameters
	fmt.Println(dsa.L1024N160 == 0, params.P == nil)
}

lessons.title: Key exchange: X25519 with crypto/ecdh and ML-KEM
body: Key exchange lets two parties agree a shared secret over an open channel. crypto/ecdh (Go 1.20) implements X25519 and the NIST curves: each side generates a key pair, sends its public key, and computes ECDH(own private, peer public), which yields the same secret on both sides.

Quantum computers would break elliptic-curve exchange, so crypto/mlkem (Go 1.24) provides ML-KEM, the NIST post-quantum key-encapsulation mechanism. The receiver publishes an encapsulation key; the sender calls Encapsulate to get a shared key plus a ciphertext; the receiver Decapsulates the ciphertext to recover the same key. TLS in Go combines both as the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 by default.

crypto/mlkem/mlkemtest exposes deterministic encapsulation from fixed randomness for known-answer tests; it must never be used in production. Always derive working keys from a shared secret with HKDF rather than using it directly.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"crypto/ecdh"
	"crypto/mlkem"
	"crypto/mlkem/mlkemtest"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	alice, _ := ecdh.X25519().GenerateKey(nil)
	bob, _ := ecdh.X25519().GenerateKey(nil)
	s1, _ := alice.ECDH(bob.PublicKey())
	s2, _ := bob.ECDH(alice.PublicKey())
	fmt.Println(len(s1), bytes.Equal(s1, s2))
	dk, _ := mlkem.GenerateKey768()
	ek := dk.EncapsulationKey()
	shared, ciphertext := ek.Encapsulate()
	recovered, err := dk.Decapsulate(ciphertext)
	fmt.Println(len(ek.Bytes()), len(ciphertext), bytes.Equal(shared, recovered), err)
	fixed := make([]byte, 32)
	k1, c1, _ := mlkemtest.Encapsulate768(ek, fixed)
	k2, c2, _ := mlkemtest.Encapsulate768(ek, fixed)
	fmt.Println(bytes.Equal(k1, k2) && bytes.Equal(c1, c2))
}

lessons.title: Post-quantum signatures, HPKE and FIPS 140-3 mode
body: Go 1.27 adds crypto/mldsa, the NIST ML-DSA post-quantum signature scheme (FIPS 204), with three parameter sets: MLDSA44, MLDSA65 and MLDSA87. Keys implement crypto.Signer; Options.Context separates signatures made for different purposes. Signatures are larger than Ed25519 (2420 bytes for ML-DSA-44).

crypto/hpke implements Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180): Seal encrypts to a recipient's public key by combining a KEM, a KDF and an AEAD; Open decrypts with the private key. With the MLKEM768X25519 KEM, the encryption is post-quantum hybrid. Encrypted Client Hello and MLS build on HPKE.

crypto/fips140 reports whether the program runs in FIPS 140-3 mode (GODEBUG=fips140=on), which restricts algorithms to approved ones. Version names the Go Cryptographic Module in use. Most programs never need it; regulated environments do.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/fips140"
	"crypto/hpke"
	"crypto/mldsa"
	"fmt"
)

func main() {
	sk, _ := mldsa.GenerateKey(mldsa.MLDSA44())
	opts := &mldsa.Options{Context: "release-signing"}
	sig, err := sk.Sign(nil, []byte("v1.27.2"), opts)
	fmt.Println(len(sig), err)
	fmt.Println(mldsa.Verify(sk.PublicKey(), []byte("v1.27.2"), sig, opts) == nil)
	fmt.Println(mldsa.Verify(sk.PublicKey(), []byte("v1.27.2"), sig, &mldsa.Options{Context: "other"}) != nil)
	kem := hpke.MLKEM768X25519()
	priv, _ := kem.GenerateKey()
	ct, _ := hpke.Seal(priv.PublicKey(), hpke.HKDFSHA256(), hpke.AES256GCM(), []byte("app info"), []byte("hello, future"))
	pt, err := hpke.Open(priv, hpke.HKDFSHA256(), hpke.AES256GCM(), []byte("app info"), ct)
	fmt.Println(string(pt), err)
	fmt.Println(fips140.Enabled())
}

lessons.title: Certificates with crypto/x509 and pkix names
body: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to a name, signed by an issuer. x509.CreateCertificate builds one from a template: subject (a pkix.Name with CommonName, Organization and so on), validity period, key usages, DNS names and the issuer. Encode it in PEM with pem.Encode for files.

x509.ParseCertificate decodes DER, and cert.Verify checks the signature chain up to roots in a CertPool, the validity period and the host name. Verification failures return typed errors such as x509.UnknownAuthorityError and x509.HostnameError.

crypto/x509/pkix holds the ASN.1 structures for names, extensions and revocation lists. Go 1.27 adds ML-DSA certificate support. For TLS, tls.Config consumes these certificates; for an internal CA, keep the root key offline.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/ed25519"
	"crypto/x509"
	"crypto/x509/pkix"
	"encoding/pem"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	pub, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(nil)
	now := time.Now()
	tmpl := &x509.Certificate{
		SerialNumber:          big.NewInt(1),
		Subject:               pkix.Name{CommonName: "guide root", Organization: []string{"Gophers"}},
		NotBefore:             now.Add(-time.Hour),
		NotAfter:              now.Add(time.Hour),
		IsCA:                  true,
		BasicConstraintsValid: true,
		KeyUsage:              x509.KeyUsageCertSign | x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature,
		DNSNames:              []string{"guide.test"},
	}
	der, err := x509.CreateCertificate(nil, tmpl, tmpl, pub, priv)
	fmt.Println(err)
	cert, _ := x509.ParseCertificate(der)
	fmt.Println(cert.Subject.String(), cert.SignatureAlgorithm)
	roots := x509.NewCertPool()
	roots.AddCert(cert)
	_, err = cert.Verify(x509.VerifyOptions{Roots: roots, DNSName: "guide.test"})
	fmt.Println(err)
	_, err = cert.Verify(x509.VerifyOptions{Roots: roots, DNSName: "evil.test"})
	var hostErr x509.HostnameError
	fmt.Println(errors.As(err, &hostErr))
	block := pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "CERTIFICATE", Bytes: der})
	fmt.Println(string(block[:27]))
}

	"errors"

)

func main() {
	pub, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(nil)
	tmpl := &x509.Certificate{SerialNumber: big.NewInt(1), Subject: pkix.Name{CommonName: "x"},
		NotBefore: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour), NotAfter: time.Now().Add(time.Hour)}

}

lessons.title: Deterministic cryptographic tests with testing/cryptotest
body: Cryptographic code is hard to test because keys and nonces are random. testing/cryptotest.SetGlobalRandom(t, seed) makes crypto/rand, and every implicit random source in the crypto packages, deterministic for the duration of one test. The same seed then produces the same keys and ciphertexts.

Because it changes process-wide state, it cannot be used with t.Parallel. The exact bytes produced for a seed are not a stable API across Go releases, so tests should compare two runs within the same test, or check properties, rather than hard-coding outputs.
This project tests a token-signing package: one test proves determinism under a fixed seed, another proves that different seeds give different keys, and the practice adds a tampering test.

lessons.title: Compression: flate, gzip, zlib, lzw and bzip2
body: compress/flate implements DEFLATE, the algorithm underneath compress/gzip (files with a header, name and CRC) and compress/zlib (a smaller header and Adler-32 checksum used by PNG and HTTP deflate). All of them are streams: wrap an io.Writer with NewWriter, write, then Close to flush the final block and checksum. Forgetting Close produces truncated output.

Compression levels trade speed for size: flate.BestSpeed, flate.BestCompression, flate.DefaultCompression and flate.HuffmanOnly. Go 1.27 made compress/flate faster. Readers verify checksums and report gzip.ErrChecksum on corruption.

compress/lzw implements the LZW codes used by GIF and TIFF. compress/bzip2 only decompresses: the standard library has no bzip2 writer. Always bound decompressed size from untrusted input with io.LimitReader, because a tiny archive can expand to gigabytes.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"compress/bzip2"
	"compress/flate"
	"compress/gzip"
	"compress/lzw"
	"compress/zlib"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	text := strings.Repeat("go gopher ", 100)
	var gz bytes.Buffer
	zw := gzip.NewWriter(&gz)
	zw.Name = "notes.txt"
	zw.Write([]byte(text))
	zw.Close()
	zr, _ := gzip.NewReader(&gz)
	back, _ := io.ReadAll(zr)
	fmt.Println(len(text), gz.Len() < 100, zr.Name, string(back) == text)
	var fast, best bytes.Buffer
	fw, _ := flate.NewWriter(&fast, flate.HuffmanOnly)
	fw.Write([]byte(text))
	fw.Close()
	bw, _ := flate.NewWriter(&best, flate.BestCompression)
	bw.Write([]byte(text))
	bw.Close()
	fmt.Println(best.Len() < fast.Len())
	var z bytes.Buffer
	w := zlib.NewWriter(&z)
	w.Write([]byte("zlib"))
	w.Close()
	fmt.Printf("% x\n", z.Bytes()[:2])
	var l bytes.Buffer
	lw := lzw.NewWriter(&l, lzw.LSB, 8)
	lw.Write([]byte("TOBEORNOTTOBEORTOBEORNOT"))
	lw.Close()
	lr := lzw.NewReader(&l, lzw.LSB, 8)
	plain, _ := io.ReadAll(lr)
	fmt.Println(string(plain))
	bz := []byte{0x42, 0x5a, 0x68, 0x39, 0x31, 0x41, 0x59, 0x26, 0x53, 0x59, 0xab, 0x6b, 0xa1, 0xf1, 0x00, 0x00, 0x02, 0xd9, 0x80, 0x00, 0x10, 0x40, 0x00, 0x10, 0x00, 0x12, 0x64, 0xc0, 0x10, 0x20, 0x00, 0x31, 0x00, 0xd3, 0x4d, 0x04, 0x00, 0x1e, 0xa3, 0xef, 0x4e, 0x51, 0xa2, 0x07, 0x8b, 0xb9, 0x22, 0x9c, 0x28, 0x48, 0x55, 0xb5, 0xd0, 0xf8, 0x80}
	unz, err := io.ReadAll(bzip2.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(bz)))
	fmt.Printf("%q %v\n", unz, err)
}

lessons.title: Archives: archive/tar and archive/zip
body: archive/tar writes a sequence of entries, each a tar.Header (name, mode, size, type) followed by its content; combine it with compress/gzip for .tar.gz. tar.Reader.Next walks the entries. archive/zip stores a central directory, so readers can jump to any file; zip.NewReader needs an io.ReaderAt and the total size.

Both formats can hold names such as ../../etc/passwd. When extracting, reject absolute paths and any name that escapes the destination: use filepath.IsLocal (Go 1.20) or open files through an os.Root. Since Go 1.20 the readers can also reject such names themselves, returning zip.ErrInsecurePath or tar.ErrInsecurePath, when GODEBUG=zipinsecurepath=0 or tarinsecurepath=0 is set.
zip.Writer.Create adds a deflated file; CreateHeader sets the method and timestamps. Both archive writers must be closed to write their trailers.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"archive/tar"
	"archive/zip"
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	var tb bytes.Buffer
	tw := tar.NewWriter(&tb)
	for name, body := range map[string]string{"a.txt": "alpha"} {
		tw.WriteHeader(&tar.Header{Name: name, Mode: 0o644, Size: int64(len(body))})
		tw.Write([]byte(body))
	}
	tw.Close()
	tr := tar.NewReader(&tb)
	hdr, _ := tr.Next()
	data, _ := io.ReadAll(tr)
	fmt.Println(hdr.Name, hdr.Size, string(data))
	var zb bytes.Buffer
	zw := zip.NewWriter(&zb)
	w, _ := zw.Create("docs/readme.md")
	w.Write([]byte("# zip"))
	zw.Close()
	zr, _ := zip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(zb.Bytes()), int64(zb.Len()))
	rc, _ := zr.File[0].Open()
	body, _ := io.ReadAll(rc)
	rc.Close()
	fmt.Println(zr.File[0].Name, zr.File[0].Method == zip.Deflate, string(body))
	for _, name := range []string{"docs/readme.md", "../escape", "/etc/passwd"} {
		fmt.Print(filepath.IsLocal(name), " ")
	}
	fmt.Println()
}

lessons.title: database/sql and writing a driver with database/sql/driver
body: database/sql is a driver-agnostic API over a connection pool: sql.Open(driverName, dsn) returns a *sql.DB that is safe for concurrent use and should live for the program's lifetime. QueryContext returns *sql.Rows to iterate with Next and Scan; always defer rows.Close() and check rows.Err(). QueryRowContext returns one row, and ErrNoRows reports none. ExecContext runs statements; BeginTx starts transactions.

Use placeholders (? or $1 depending on the driver) for every value, never string concatenation, so the driver passes data separately from SQL and injection is impossible. SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns and SetConnMaxLifetime tune the pool.

Drivers implement the small interfaces in database/sql/driver: Driver.Open returns a Conn, which prepares Stmts that return Rows. This lesson implements a toy in-memory driver to show what a real one (for PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite) provides. Go 1.27 adds sql.ConvertAssign and driver.RowsColumnScanner for drivers that scan columns themselves.

database/sql forbids string literals
The driver sends values separately from the SQL text, so they can never be parsed as SQL

lessons.title: Embedding files in the binary with embed
body: A //go:embed directive above a package-level variable copies files into the compiled binary at build time. A string or []byte variable takes exactly one file; an embed.FS variable takes many files and directories, matched by patterns such as static/* or templates.

embed.FS implements fs.FS, fs.ReadDirFS and fs.ReadFileFS, so it plugs into http.FileServerFS, template.ParseFS and fs.WalkDir. Paths are slash-separated and relative to the source file's directory; patterns cannot contain .. and files whose names start with . or _ are excluded unless the pattern names them or uses the all: prefix.

The package must import embed (a blank import is enough when only string or []byte variables are used). Embedded data is read-only and requires no deployment step, which makes single-binary tools and servers easy to ship.

lessons.title: Classic packages: log, io/ioutil, math/rand v1, os/user, time/tzdata and structs
body: The classic log package writes timestamped lines to standard error; log.New makes loggers with a prefix and flags such as log.Lshortfile, and Fatal/Panic variants exit or panic after logging. New services prefer log/slog, but log remains common in small tools.

io/ioutil is deprecated since Go 1.16: its functions moved to io and os (ioutil.ReadAll is io.ReadAll, ioutil.ReadFile is os.ReadFile). math/rand (v1) is kept for compatibility; since Go 1.20 its global functions are randomly seeded, and new code should use math/rand/v2.

os/user looks up the current user and groups. time/tzdata embeds the time-zone database into the binary (about 450 KB), so time.LoadLocation works on systems without zoneinfo, such as minimal containers; importing it for its side effect is enough. Package structs (Go 1.23) provides HostLayout, a marker field that requests the platform's C memory layout for a struct passed to foreign code.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"io/ioutil"
	"log"
	"math/rand"
	"os/user"
	"strings"
	"structs"
	"time"
	_ "time/tzdata"
	"unsafe"
)

type cPoint struct {
	_    structs.HostLayout
	X, Y int32
}

func main() {
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	l := log.New(&buf, "app: ", 0)
	l.Printf("started %d workers", 4)
	fmt.Print(buf.String())
	data, _ := ioutil.ReadAll(strings.NewReader("deprecated but working"))
	fmt.Println(string(data))
	r := rand.New(rand.NewSource(1))
	fmt.Println(r.Intn(100) == rand.New(rand.NewSource(1)).Intn(100))
	u, err := user.Current()
	fmt.Println(err == nil && u.Username != "")
	tokyo, err := time.LoadLocation("Asia/Tokyo")
	t := time.Date(2026, 10, 17, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC).In(tokyo)
	fmt.Println(t.Format("15:04 MST"), err)
	fmt.Println(unsafe.Sizeof(cPoint{}))
}

lessons.title: Exported metrics with expvar and logging to syslog
body: expvar publishes named variables (Int, Float, String, Map, Func) and serves them as JSON at /debug/vars when the package is imported by a program with an HTTP server. It is a dependency-free way to expose counters for monitoring; expvar.Handler returns the handler for custom muxes.

log/syslog writes to the system log daemon, locally through a Unix socket or remotely over UDP or TCP with syslog.Dial. Each message carries a priority, a facility and a tag. It is not available on Windows or Plan 9.

For new services, structured logs to standard output collected by the platform, and metrics through a client library, are usual. expvar and syslog remain useful for small daemons and legacy integration.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"expvar"
	"fmt"
	"log/syslog"
	"net"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
)

var requests = expvar.NewInt("requests")

func main() {
	requests.Add(3)
	expvar.NewMap("byStatus").Add("200", 2)
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	expvar.Handler().ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/debug/vars", nil))
	var vars map[string]any
	json.Unmarshal(rec.Body.Bytes(), &vars)
	fmt.Println(vars["requests"], vars["byStatus"])
	pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer pc.Close()
	w, err := syslog.Dial("udp", pc.LocalAddr().String(), syslog.LOG_WARNING|syslog.LOG_DAEMON, "guide")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	w.Warning("disk almost full")
	buf := make([]byte, 512)
	n, _, _ := pc.ReadFrom(buf)
	msg := string(buf[:n])
	fmt.Println(strings.HasPrefix(msg, "<28>"), strings.Contains(msg, "guide["), strings.HasSuffix(strings.TrimSpace(msg), "disk almost full"))
}

lessons.question: What does the <28> at the start of the syslog message encode?
options: The message length
The process ID
The priority: facility daemon (3) × 8 plus severity warning (4)
lessons.explanation: Syslog priority is facility*8 + severity. LOG_DAEMON is 3 and LOG_WARNING is 4, giving 28.

lessons.title: URLs with net/url and client cookies with net/http/cookiejar
body: url.Parse splits a URL into Scheme, User, Host, Path, RawQuery and Fragment, and decodes percent-escapes in the path. Query() parses the query into url.Values, a map[string][]string; Values.Encode sorts keys and escapes values. Build URLs by setting fields or using JoinPath (Go 1.19) rather than concatenating strings, which breaks on special characters.

url.QueryEscape escapes a value for a query string (spaces become +), while url.PathEscape escapes a path segment (spaces become %20). ResolveReference resolves relative links the way a browser does. Go 1.27 adds URL.Clone and Values.Clone for safe copies.

An http.Client ignores cookies unless it has a Jar. cookiejar.New returns an in-memory jar that stores Set-Cookie responses and sends matching cookies back, following domain and path rules; pass publicsuffix.List from golang.org/x/net to stop sites setting cookies for whole top-level domains.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/cookiejar"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"net/url"
)

func main() {
	u, _ := url.Parse("https://ada@example.com:8443/docs/go%20guide?lang=go&tag=a&tag=b#intro")
	fmt.Println(u.Scheme, u.User.Username(), u.Hostname(), u.Port(), u.Path, u.Fragment)
	q := u.Query()
	fmt.Println(q["tag"], q.Get("lang"))
	q.Set("page", "2 of 3")
	u.RawQuery = q.Encode()
	fmt.Println(u.RawQuery)
	base, _ := url.Parse("https://example.com/a/b/")
	ref, _ := url.Parse("../c?x=1")
	fmt.Println(base.ResolveReference(ref), base.JoinPath("x y"), url.PathEscape("x y"), url.QueryEscape("x y"))
	copyURL := u.Clone()
	copyURL.Host = "other.test"
	fmt.Println(u.Host != copyURL.Host)
	srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if c, err := r.Cookie("session"); err == nil {
			fmt.Fprint(w, "welcome back ", c.Value)
			return
		}
		http.SetCookie(w, &http.Cookie{Name: "session", Value: "s1", Path: "/"})
		fmt.Fprint(w, "new visitor")
	}))
	defer srv.Close()
	jar, _ := cookiejar.New(nil)
	client := &http.Client{Jar: jar}
	for range 2 {
		resp, _ := client.Get(srv.URL)
		body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
		resp.Body.Close()
		fmt.Println(string(body))
	}
}

lessons.title: Request tracing with httptrace and proxies with httputil
body: net/http/httptrace attaches hooks to a request's context: DNS start and done, connection acquisition (with GotConnInfo.Reused telling you whether keep-alive worked), TLS handshake, first response byte. It is the tool for explaining slow requests and confirming connection reuse.

net/http/httputil provides DumpRequest and DumpResponse for debugging wire formats, and ReverseProxy for forwarding requests to a backend. Configure the proxy with a Rewrite function (Go 1.20), which receives both the inbound and outbound request and is safer than the older Director because it handles hop-by-hop and forwarding headers correctly; SetXForwarded adds X-Forwarded-For and friends.
A reverse proxy should set timeouts on its Transport and limit request sizes, like any server. Never dump requests containing credentials into logs.

lessons.title: Live profiling endpoints with net/http/pprof
body: Importing net/http/pprof registers handlers under /debug/pprof/ on http.DefaultServeMux: an index, goroutine, heap, allocs, block, mutex and threadcreate profiles, a 30-second CPU profile at /debug/pprof/profile, an execution trace at /debug/pprof/trace, and, since Go 1.27, goroutineleak. go tool pprof http://host/debug/pprof/heap fetches and analyses one directly.

Expose these endpoints only on a private listener or behind authentication: they reveal internals and the CPU and trace endpoints are expensive. A common pattern is a second server on localhost:6060 that serves http.DefaultServeMux, while public traffic uses its own mux.
The handlers can also be mounted explicitly on any mux with pprof.Index, pprof.Profile, pprof.Symbol, pprof.Trace and pprof.Handler(name), which avoids relying on the default mux at all.
lessons.solution:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"net/http/pprof"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.Handle("/internal/heap", pprof.Handler("heap"))
	srv := httptest.NewServer(mux)
	defer srv.Close()
	resp, err := http.Get(srv.URL + "/internal/heap?debug=1")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	b, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	fmt.Println(strings.HasPrefix(string(b), "heap profile:"))
}

lessons.title: Line protocols with net/textproto and email with net/smtp
body: net/textproto implements the shared machinery of text protocols such as SMTP, HTTP/1 headers, NNTP and FTP: reading CRLF lines, multi-line responses with numeric codes (ReadResponse), MIME-style headers (ReadMIMEHeader) and dot-encoded bodies. CanonicalMIMEHeaderKey turns content-type into Content-Type.

net/smtp is a small SMTP client: Dial or NewClient, then Hello, Auth, Mail, Rcpt, Data and Quit, or the one-call SendMail. PlainAuth refuses to send credentials over an unencrypted connection except to localhost. The package is frozen; production mail usually goes through a provider's API or a maintained library.
This lesson runs a tiny fake SMTP server on a loopback listener, built with textproto, and sends a message to it with net/smtp, so the whole protocol exchange happens without the internet.

lessons.title: Remote procedure calls with net/rpc and net/rpc/jsonrpc
body: net/rpc exposes the exported methods of a registered value over a connection. Methods must have the form func (t *T) Method(args A, reply *R) error. The client calls client.Call("Service.Method", args, &reply), or Go for an asynchronous call that completes on a channel. The default codec is gob.

net/rpc/jsonrpc swaps in a JSON-RPC 1.0 codec, so non-Go clients can talk to the same server. Both packages are frozen: they work and are stable, but new systems usually choose gRPC or plain HTTP/JSON APIs with explicit schemas and versioning.
Errors returned by a method arrive at the client as rpc.ServerError strings; transport failures return rpc.ErrShutdown or the network error.

lessons.title: CGI and FastCGI with net/http/cgi and net/http/fcgi
body: CGI runs a program per request: the web server passes request data in environment variables and standard input, and the program writes headers, a blank line and the body to standard output. cgi.Handler runs such a program from a Go server; cgi.Serve and cgi.Request let a Go program be the CGI script.

FastCGI keeps the application running and multiplexes requests over a socket, avoiding process start-up per request. fcgi.Serve(listener, handler) turns any http.Handler into a FastCGI application behind servers such as nginx or Apache, and fcgi.ProcessEnv exposes the extra variables those servers pass.
Both exist mainly for integration with traditional hosting. A Go service normally serves HTTP directly behind a reverse proxy.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/cgi"
	"net/http/fcgi"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	dir, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "cgi")
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	script := filepath.Join(dir, "hello.sh")
	os.WriteFile(script, []byte("#!/bin/sh\nprintf 'Content-Type: text/plain\\r\\n\\r\\nmethod=%s query=%s\\n' \"$REQUEST_METHOD\" \"$QUERY_STRING\"\n"), 0o755)
	h := &cgi.Handler{Path: script}
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	h.ServeHTTP(rec, httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/cgi?lang=go", nil))
	fmt.Print(rec.Code, " ", rec.Header().Get("Content-Type"), " ", rec.Body.String())
	req, err := cgi.RequestFromMap(map[string]string{"REQUEST_METHOD": "POST", "SERVER_PROTOCOL": "HTTP/1.1", "REQUEST_URI": "/form?x=1"})
	fmt.Println(req.Method, req.URL.Query().Get("x"), err)
	ln, _ := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	ln.Close()
	err = fcgi.Serve(ln, http.NotFoundHandler())
	fmt.Println(err != nil, len(fcgi.ProcessEnv(httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/", nil))))
}

lessons.title: Type-checking source with go/types, go/importer, go/constant and go/printer
lessons.summary: 26 · Toolchain, binaries, runtime modes and images
body: go/types is the type checker used by gopls, vet and most analysers. types.Config.Check takes parsed files and an Importer for dependencies and fills a types.Info with the type of every expression (Types), the object each identifier refers to (Defs and Uses) and more. Type errors are returned rather than printed.

go/importer supplies importers: ForCompiler(fset, "source", nil) type-checks dependencies from source, while Default reads compiler export data. Constant expressions are evaluated exactly with go/constant values, so a checker knows that 1 << 62 fits in int64 and 1 << 64 does not.

go/printer prints an AST back as source, honouring comments and positions; go/format is the gofmt-styled wrapper. Together these packages let you build linters, code generators and refactoring tools that understand types, not just syntax.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"go/ast"
	"go/constant"
	"go/format"
	"go/importer"
	"go/parser"
	"go/printer"
	"go/token"
	"go/types"
)

const src = `package demo

import "strings"

const Big = 1 << 62

func Shout(s string) string { return strings.ToUpper(s) + "!" }

var n = len(Shout("go"))
`

func main() {
	fset := token.NewFileSet()
	file, err := parser.ParseFile(fset, "demo.go", src, parser.ParseComments)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	info := &types.Info{Types: map[ast.Expr]types.TypeAndValue{}, Defs: map[*ast.Ident]types.Object{}}
	conf := types.Config{Importer: importer.ForCompiler(fset, "source", nil)}
	pkg, err := conf.Check("demo", fset, []*ast.File{file}, info)
	fmt.Println(pkg.Path(), err)
	for _, name := range []string{"Big", "Shout", "n"} {
		fmt.Println(name, pkg.Scope().Lookup(name).Type())
	}
	big := pkg.Scope().Lookup("Big").(*types.Const).Val()
	v, exact := constant.Int64Val(big)
	fmt.Println(v, exact, constant.Compare(big, token.LSS, constant.MakeInt64(1<<63-1)))
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	printer.Fprint(&buf, fset, file.Decls[2])
	fmt.Println(buf.String())
	formatted, err := format.Source([]byte("package p\nfunc  f( ){ }"))
	fmt.Printf("%q %v\n", formatted, err)
}
