lessons.title: Building command lines with arrays
body: Arrays are the correct way to build a command whose arguments vary. Put the command and its arguments in an array, add options conditionally, and run it with "${cmd[@]}". Every element stays exactly one argument, whatever it contains.

The tempting alternative — building a string and running it unquoted, or with eval — breaks on spaces and quotes and invites code injection. BashFAQ 50, "I'm trying to put a command in a variable", exists because this mistake is so common.

Optional arguments: start with args=() and append with args+=(--verbose) inside an if. For printing the command for a log, use printf '%q ' "${cmd[@]}" so the logged line can be pasted back into a shell.

Filtering and de-duplicating: loop and append the elements you keep; use an associative array as a "seen" set to drop duplicates while keeping the original order. Sorting goes through an external sort with NUL delimiters and mapfile.
Functions can return arrays through a nameref (local -n) or by printing NUL-separated values that the caller reads with mapfile -d ''.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
show() { printf '<%s> ' "$@"; echo; }
verbose=1
pattern='two words'
args=(--count)
(( verbose )) && args+=(--verbose)
args+=(-- "$pattern" 'my file.txt')
show "${args[@]}"
printf '%q ' grep "${args[@]}"; echo
declare -A seen=()
unique=()
for item in b a b c a; do
    [[ -v seen[$item] ]] && continue
    seen[$item]=1
    unique+=("$item")
done
echo "unique in order: ${unique[*]}"
mapfile -d '' -t sorted < <(printf '%s\0' "${unique[@]}" | sort -rz)
echo "sorted desc: ${sorted[*]}"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # kept is filled through the nameref
only_long() {
    local -n _result=$1
    local min=$2 word
    shift 2
    _result=()
    for word in "$@"; do
        (( ${#word} >= min )) && _result+=("$word")
    done
    return 0
}
only_long kept 5 bash shell script cron awk pipeline
echo "${kept[*]}"

options: Store a string and run $cmd
Store a string and run eval "$cmd"
Store a string and run "$cmd"

lessons.title: Safe subscripts with array_expand_once (Bash 5.3)
body: Some builtins evaluate an array subscript a second time. With an attacker-controlled key such as $(command), test -v "m[$key]", printf -v "m[$key]", unset "m[$key]" and read into "m[$key]" can run the embedded command substitution: the first expansion produces the text, and the builtin then expands the subscript again.

Bash 5.3 adds shopt array_expand_once (replacing the older assoc_expand_once, which is now a deprecated synonym). When set, the shell expands subscripts only once in arithmetic evaluation and in builtins that assign or dereference array elements, so keys are treated purely as data.

Enable it at the top of any script that uses untrusted strings as array keys: shopt -s array_expand_once. The [[ -v m[$key] ]] keyword form is parsed by the shell itself and is already safe; the risk is in the builtins that receive the subscript as a string argument.

Defence in depth still applies: validate keys when you can, prefer keyword tests, and remember that indexed-array subscripts are arithmetic expressions, so arbitrary text should never be used as an indexed subscript at all.
The option is unknown to older Bash versions, so shopt -s array_expand_once fails there. That failure is a useful early signal that the script needs a newer shell.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A m
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the key must stay literal: it simulates hostile input
key='$(echo INJECTED >&2; echo k)'
m[$key]=1
shopt -s array_expand_once
test -v "m[$key]" && echo 'test -v treats the key as data'
printf -v "m[$key]" '%s' 2
echo "printf -v updated it to ${m[$key]}"
unset "m[$key]"
echo "entries left: ${#m[@]}"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
shopt -s array_expand_once
declare -A seen=()
while IFS= read -r key; do
    printf -v "seen[$key]" '%d' $(( ${seen[$key]:-0} + 1 ))
done <<'EOF'
a
$(id)
a
EOF
while IFS= read -r key; do
    printf '%q %s\n' "$key" "${seen[$key]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!seen[@]}" | sort)
lessons.challenge: With array_expand_once enabled, count occurrences of three untrusted keys read from a here-document — a, $(id), a — in an associative array using printf -v, then print each key with %q and its count in sorted order.
lessons.question: What problem does shopt -s array_expand_once address?
options: Builtins expanding an array subscript a second time, which can run code hidden in a key
Arrays being expanded twice by "${a[@]}"
Slow expansion of very large arrays
Associative arrays losing insertion order
lessons.explanation: With the option set, subscripts given to builtins like test -v, printf -v and unset are expanded only once.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:

entries left: 0

With the option set, subscripts given to builtins like test -v, printf -v and unset are expanded only once.
lessons.practiceAnswer: With the option set, subscripts given to builtins like test -v, printf -v and unset are expanded only once.

lessons.title: Defining and calling functions
body: A function is a named compound command: name() { commands; }. The function keyword (function name { ... }) is a Bash alternative; the name() form is portable. Define a function before the line that calls it runs — Bash executes top to bottom, so a common layout is all functions first, then main "$@" at the bottom.

Functions are called exactly like commands and receive their own positional parameters: inside, $1, $2, "$@" and $# refer to the function's arguments, while $0 is still the script name. FUNCNAME[0] is the current function's name.

The body can be any compound command. name() ( ... ) with parentheses runs the body in a subshell every time, which automatically isolates variable changes, cd and shell options — handy for helpers that must not leak state, at the cost of a fork.

A function's exit status is the status of its last command, or the value given to return N. return without a number keeps the last status. exit inside a function ends the whole script, not just the function, which is rarely what a library function should do.
Keep functions small and named for what they do. A good test is whether you can describe a function in one sentence that does not use "and".
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
max() {
    (( $# )) || return 1
    local best=$1 n
    for n in "$@"; do
        (( n > best )) && best=$n
    done
    echo "$best"
}
max 3 9 2
max
echo "status: $?"
lessons.challenge: Write a function max that prints the largest of any number of integer arguments, and returns status 1 with no output when called with no arguments. Test it with 3 9 2 and with no arguments, printing the status.
lessons.question: What does exit inside a function do?
options: Returns from the function only
Ends only the current loop
Nothing unless the function runs in background
Ends the entire script (or current shell)
lessons.explanation: exit terminates the shell process; use return to leave just the function.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
greet got 2 args: one two words
inside: /
outside: work changed=no
3 is odd
4 is even

exit terminates the shell process; use return to leave just the function.
lessons.practiceAnswer: exit terminates the shell process; use return to leave just the function.

lessons.title: local variables and dynamic scope
body: Variables are global by default, even when first assigned inside a function. Declare function variables with local (or declare inside a function, which is local by default) so a helper cannot overwrite the caller's variables.

Bash uses dynamic scoping: a local variable is visible to every function called from the function that declared it, for as long as that call is active. A callee that reads or assigns a name sees the nearest one on the call stack, not just globals. This is powerful and surprising; it is why library functions should use local generously and distinctive names.
declare -g inside a function creates or assigns a global even when a local of the same name exists further up the stack — the way to deliberately set global state, for example from an initializer.

local var=$(command) hides the command's failure: the status you get is local's own, which is always 0. Declare first and assign separately — local out; out=$(command) — when you need to check that the command succeeded. ShellCheck reports this as SC2155.
A local array is declared with local -a and a local map with local -A. local - (a single dash) makes shell option changes made with set local to the function, restoring them on return.
lessons.challenge: Write a function parse_kv that sets two variables, key and value, local to its caller's caller chain, by being called from a function report that declares them local; report should print "key=lang value=bash" and the globals must remain unset afterwards.
lessons.question: Why should you write `local out; out=$(cmd)` instead of `local out=$(cmd)`?
options: Command substitution is not allowed in functions
The combined form returns local's status and hides cmd's failure
The combined form makes out global
local cannot assign values
lessons.explanation: $? after local out=$(cmd) is the status of local itself, almost always 0.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
inside safe_bump: 101
global counter: 1
mode: global
caught the failure after capturing [partial]
inside: u
after: 

$? after local out=$(cmd) is the status of local itself, almost always 0.
lessons.practiceAnswer: $? after local out=$(cmd) is the status of local itself, almost always 0.

lessons.title: Returning results from functions
body: A function has three channels back to its caller: the exit status (0–255, meaning success or kind of failure), the text it writes to standard output, and variables it sets. Use each for what it is good at.

Status answers yes/no questions: is_valid "$x" && ... . Output is natural for producing a value: result=$(compute) captures it, but every $(...) forks a subshell, so the function cannot set variables or change directories for the caller, and trailing newlines are stripped.

For several values, or for speed inside loops, write into a variable named by the caller using a nameref, or into an agreed global such as REPLY. Bash itself uses REPLY for read without a name. Document whichever convention you choose.
Errors belong on standard error: echo "error: ..." >&2, followed by a non-zero return. Keeping diagnostics off stdout means $(...) captures only the real result.

Bash 5.3 adds ${ command; } and ${| command; } command substitutions that run in the current shell without forking; stage 9 covers them. They make output capture cheap and let the function set variables too.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
divide() {
    if (( $2 == 0 )); then
        echo 'divide: division by zero' >&2
        return 1
    fi
    echo $(( $1 / $2 ))
}
result=$(divide 10 2) && echo "10/2 = $result"
result=$(divide 1 0 2>&1) || echo "failed with: $result"
minmax() {
    local -n _lo=$1 _hi=$2
    shift 2
    _lo=$1 _hi=$1
    local n
    for n in "$@"; do
        (( n < _lo )) && _lo=$n
        (( n > _hi )) && _hi=$n
    done
    return 0
}
minmax lo hi 4 9 1 7
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # lo and hi are assigned through namerefs
echo "min=$lo max=$hi"

stderr is faster

lessons.practiceAnswer: Command substitution captures stdout only; mixing diagnostics into it corrupts the result.

lessons.title: Parsing options with getopts
body: getopts is the builtin option parser for short options. getopts 'vo:h' opt reads the next option into opt; a colon after a letter (o:) means it takes an argument, delivered in OPTARG. Loop with while getopts ...; do case $opt in ...; esac; done, then shift $((OPTIND - 1)) to leave only the operands.
It handles the conventional forms automatically: -v -o file, -vo file, -ofile and -- to end options. Bundled flags and attached arguments work without extra code.

Starting the option string with a colon selects silent error reporting: an unknown option sets opt to ? and OPTARG to the letter; a missing argument sets opt to : and OPTARG to the letter. Your case branches can then print helpful messages and exit with status 2, the conventional code for usage errors.

getopts does not understand long options like --output. Common approaches are a hand-written while/case loop over "$@" with shift, or the external GNU getopt (not available in the same form on macOS). Many scripts support both short options via getopts and a few long ones via a pre-pass.
When parsing inside a function, set local OPTIND so repeated calls start fresh; OPTIND is global state otherwise.
lessons.challenge: Write a function cli that accepts -n NUM (default 1) and -q, plus a --name=VALUE long option handled before getopts, and prints "n=NUM quiet=0|1 name=VALUE rest=...". Call it with --name=ada -q -n 3 file.txt.
lessons.question: What does a leading colon in the getopts option string do?
options: Allows long options
Ignores unknown options completely
Enables silent error reporting so your code handles unknown options and missing arguments
Makes every option take an argument
lessons.explanation: With a leading colon, getopts sets opt to ? or : and puts the offending letter in OPTARG instead of printing its own message.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
verbose=1 output=out.txt operands=a b
verbose=1 output=file.txt operands=-notanoption
unknown option -x
status 2
option -o needs an argument
status 2

With a leading colon, getopts sets opt to ? or : and puts the offending letter in OPTARG instead of printing its own message.
lessons.practiceAnswer: With a leading colon, getopts sets opt to ? or : and puts the offending letter in OPTARG instead of printing its own message.

lessons.title: Libraries, source -p and the main pattern
body: source file (or . file) reads and executes a file in the current shell, so its functions and variables become available. Large scripts split helpers into library files and source them at start-up. Extra arguments after the file name become its positional parameters while it runs.

Locate libraries relative to the script, not the current directory: dir=${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*} gives the directory of the file being executed, even when it is sourced. BASH_SOURCE is an array that mirrors FUNCNAME, recording which file each stack frame came from.

Bash 5.3 adds source -p PATH: the file is searched for in the colon-separated directories you give instead of in $PATH. This avoids both hard-coded absolute paths and accidental lookups in the user's PATH. Older versions reject the option.

Libraries should only define functions and constants. Guard against double inclusion with a variable such as [[ -v _UTIL_LOADED ]] && return; _UTIL_LOADED=1 — return at the top level of a sourced file stops sourcing it.

Put the program's logic in a main function and finish the file with main "$@". To make a file usable both as a program and as a library, run main only when executed directly: if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi. Use if rather than the shorter [[ ... ]] && main: when the file is sourced, the && form leaves status 1 as the file's last status, so `source tool.sh && next` would wrongly fail.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p lib
cat > lib/util.sh <<'EOF'
[[ -v _UTIL_LOADED ]] && return
_UTIL_LOADED=1
loads=$(( ${loads:-0} + 1 ))
shout() { echo "${1^^}!"; }
EOF
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/lib" util.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/lib" util.sh
shout hello
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # loads is set by the sourced library
echo "library body ran $loads time(s)"
cat > tool.sh <<'EOF'
main() { echo "main ran with: $*"; }
if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi
EOF
bash tool.sh a b
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source ./tool.sh && echo 'sourced: main not run'
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p lib
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the library text must keep $1 literal
echo 'square() { echo $(( $1 * $1 )); }' > lib/math.sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source -p "$PWD/missing:$PWD/lib" math.sh
square 12
lessons.challenge: Create lib/math.sh defining square() (prints n*n), then source it with source -p using a search path containing a nonexistent directory followed by lib, and print square 12.
lessons.question: What does Bash 5.3's source -p PATH change?
options: It requires the file to be executable
The file is searched in the given directories instead of $PATH
It sources the file in a subshell
It prints each line before running it
lessons.explanation: source -p takes an explicit colon-separated search path, avoiding dependence on the user's PATH.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
HELLO!
library body ran 1 time(s)
main ran with: a b
sourced: main not run

source -p takes an explicit colon-separated search path, avoiding dependence on the user's PATH.
lessons.practiceAnswer: source -p takes an explicit colon-separated search path, avoiding dependence on the user's PATH.

lessons.title: File descriptors and redirection
body: Every process starts with three open file descriptors: 0 standard input, 1 standard output and 2 standard error. Redirections rewire them before the command runs: > file truncates and writes stdout to file, >> appends, < file reads stdin from file, and 2> file sends stderr to file. N> and N< apply to any descriptor number.

2>&1 means "make descriptor 2 point where descriptor 1 points right now". Redirections are processed left to right, so order matters: cmd > out 2>&1 sends both streams to out, while cmd 2>&1 > out sends stderr to the original stdout (the terminal) and only stdout to out. &> file is Bash shorthand for > file 2>&1.
/dev/null discards output and supplies empty input. cmd > /dev/null 2>&1 silences a command completely — useful, but be careful not to hide errors you need to see.
set -o noclobber (set -C) makes > refuse to overwrite an existing file; >| overrides it deliberately. It protects against accidental truncation in interactive work and some scripts.

Redirections can appear on compound commands: { ...; } > file, a while loop's done < file, or a function definition, so a whole block shares one redirection — and the file is opened once instead of on every line.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
both() { echo out; echo err >&2; }
both > a.txt 2>&1
printf 'a.txt: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < a.txt)"
both 2>&1 > b.txt | sed 's/^/via pipe: /'
printf 'b.txt: %s\n' "$(cat b.txt)"
both &> c.txt; echo "c.txt has $(wc -l < c.txt | tr -d ' ') lines"
echo first > log.txt; echo second >> log.txt; cat log.txt
set -o noclobber
{ echo third > log.txt; } 2>/dev/null || echo 'noclobber refused to overwrite'
echo forced >| log.txt; cat log.txt
{ echo header; for i in 1 2; do echo "row $i"; done; } > table.txt
cat table.txt
lessons.challenge: Write a function run_quiet that runs its arguments as a command with stdout discarded but stderr kept, and prints "ok" or "failed (N)". Test it with ls . and with ls /nonexistent (whose error message you should redirect to /dev/null at the call site so only the status line prints).
lessons.question: Where does stderr go in `cmd 2>&1 > out`?
options: Into out together with stdout
To /dev/null
Nowhere; this is a syntax error
To the original stdout, because 2>&1 is applied before stdout is redirected
lessons.explanation: Redirections are applied left to right; 2>&1 copies the destination of fd 1 at that moment.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
a.txt: out err 
via pipe: err
b.txt: out
c.txt has 2 lines
first
second
noclobber refused to overwrite
forced
header
row 1
row 2

Redirections are applied left to right; 2>&1 copies the destination of fd 1 at that moment.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Redirections are applied left to right; 2>&1 copies the destination of fd 1 at that moment.

lessons.title: Here-documents and here-strings
body: A here-document feeds lines of the script itself to a command's standard input: cmd <<EOF ... EOF. The terminator must appear alone on its own line, exactly as written.

If the delimiter word is quoted (<<'EOF' or <<"EOF"), the body is completely literal. Unquoted, the body undergoes parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic expansion — useful for templates, dangerous when the body contains $ meant literally. Quote the delimiter by default and unquote it only when you want expansion.

<<-EOF strips leading tab characters (not spaces) from body lines and the terminator, which lets you indent here-documents inside functions — but only with real tabs, which many editors convert to spaces.
A here-string, cmd <<< "$text", feeds one string plus a trailing newline to stdin. It is the concise way to give a variable to read, a regex tool or bc without echo and a pipe.

Here-documents are a convenient way to write files from scripts: cat > config.ini <<'EOF'. For generated files containing user data, still prefer printf with explicit quoting so values cannot break the file's format.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
name=ada
cat <<EOF
Hello $name, today has $((24 * 60)) minutes.
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
Literal: $name and $((1 + 1)) stay as typed.
EOF
indented() {
	cat <<-EOF
		tabs removed for $name
	EOF
}
indented
read -r first rest <<< 'one two three'
echo "first=$first rest=$rest"
tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<< "here-string for $name"
lessons.challenge: Write a function make_config that writes a file app.ini from a here-document containing [server], host=HOST and port=PORT lines, with HOST and PORT taken from its two arguments. Call it with example.org 8443 and print the file.
lessons.question: What changes when a here-document delimiter is quoted, as in <<'EOF'?
options: The body is sent to stderr
The terminator may be indented
The body is taken literally, with no expansions
Leading tabs are removed
lessons.explanation: Quoting any part of the delimiter disables expansion inside the body.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
Hello ada, today has 1440 minutes.
Literal: $name and $((1 + 1)) stay as typed.
tabs removed for ada
first=one rest=two three
HERE-STRING FOR ADA

Quoting any part of the delimiter disables expansion inside the body.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Quoting any part of the delimiter disables expansion inside the body.

lessons.title: Managing descriptors with exec
body: exec without a command applies redirections to the current shell itself. exec > log.txt sends all further stdout of the script to log.txt; exec 2>&1 merges stderr into it. This is how scripts start logging everything from one point on.

Additional descriptors keep files open across many commands: exec 3< input.txt opens input for reading on fd 3, and read -r line <&3 (or read -u 3 line) reads the next line from it. Two files can then be read in parallel, line by line.

Bash can allocate a free descriptor for you: exec {fd}> file stores the number (10 or higher) in the variable fd. Use it as >&"$fd" and close it with exec {fd}>&-. This avoids clashes with descriptors used by other code.

Save and restore a stream by duplicating it first: exec {saved}>&1 > file ... exec >&"$saved" {saved}>&-. Closing descriptors you opened matters in long-running scripts: each open descriptor is a resource, and an unclosed write end can keep a reader waiting forever.

exec with a command replaces the shell process with that command — nothing after it runs. Wrapper scripts end with exec real-program "$@" so that signals and exit statuses go directly to the real program.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%s\n' a b c > left.txt
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 > right.txt
exec 3< left.txt 4< right.txt
while read -r l <&3 && read -r r <&4; do
    echo "$l$r"
done
exec 3<&- 4<&-
exec {log}> log.txt
echo "allocated fd >= 10: $(( log >= 10 ))"
echo 'to the log' >&"$log"
exec {log}>&-
exec {saved}>&1 > captured.txt
echo 'this line goes to captured.txt'
exec >&"$saved" {saved}>&-
echo "restored; captured: $(cat captured.txt), log: $(cat log.txt)"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {out}> notes.txt
for i in 1 2 3; do
    echo "note $i" >&"$out"
done
exec {out}>&-
cat notes.txt
lessons.challenge: Open notes.txt for writing on an automatically allocated descriptor, write three numbered lines to it in a loop through that descriptor, close it, and print the file.
lessons.question: What does `exec {fd}> file` do?
options: Opens file for writing on a free descriptor number stored in fd
Runs a program named fd
Writes the descriptor number into file
Closes descriptor fd
lessons.explanation: The {varname} form asks Bash to allocate a descriptor of 10 or above and record its number.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
a1
b2
c3
allocated fd >= 10: 1
restored; captured: this line goes to captured.txt, log: to the log

The {varname} form asks Bash to allocate a descriptor of 10 or above and record its number.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The {varname} form asks Bash to allocate a descriptor of 10 or above and record its number.

lessons.title: Reading input with read
body: read reads one line from standard input, splits it with IFS and assigns the fields to the named variables, the last variable receiving the remainder. With no name, the whole line goes into REPLY. It returns non-zero at end of file, which is what ends while read loops.

Always use -r. Without it, backslashes in the input are treated as escapes and line continuations, silently changing data. ShellCheck warns about read without -r (SC2162). Combine with IFS= to keep leading and trailing whitespace.

Other options: -p prompt prints a prompt to stderr (interactive input only), -s hides typed characters for passwords, -n N returns after N characters, -N N reads exactly N characters ignoring delimiters, -d c stops at character c instead of newline (-d '' means NUL), -t seconds times out (status above 128), -a name fills an array and -u fd reads from a descriptor.
-e uses Readline for line editing in interactive shells, and Bash 5.3 adds -E, which also enables Bash's own programmable completion while reading. Both only matter when input comes from a terminal.

A final line without a trailing newline makes read return failure even though it filled the variable. Process it with while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]. Timeouts with -t 0 test whether input is available without reading anything.
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
declare -A conf=()
while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
    [[ -z $line || $line == \#* ]] && continue
    conf[${line%%=*}]=${line#*=}
done <<'EOF'
# config
name=demo

port=8080
EOF
while IFS= read -r key; do
    echo "$key=${conf[$key]}"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!conf[@]}" | sort)
lessons.challenge: Read key=value lines from a here-document into an associative array, skipping blank lines and lines starting with #, then print the keys in sorted order with their values. Input: "# config", "name=demo", "", "port=8080".
lessons.question: Why should read almost always be used with -r?
options: -r preserves leading spaces
Without -r, backslashes in the input are interpreted and can alter the data
-r makes read faster
-r is required to read from files
lessons.explanation: -r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= is what preserves surrounding whitespace.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
with -r: path\to\file
without -r: pathtofile
[  spaced  ]
REPLY=into REPLY
first 3: ABC
up to ;: one
timed out (status >128)
processed: last line, no newline

-r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= is what preserves surrounding whitespace.
lessons.practiceAnswer: -r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= is what preserves surrounding whitespace.

lessons.title: NUL-safe file name handling
body: A Unix file name may contain any byte except / and NUL — including spaces, newlines, quotes, glob characters and leading dashes. Line-based processing (ls | while read, for f in $(find ...)) breaks on such names. The only delimiter that cannot occur in a path is the NUL byte.

Produce NUL-separated lists with find -print0, printf '%s\0', or git ls-files -z; consume them with read -r -d '' in a while loop, mapfile -d '', xargs -0 and sort -z. Bash variables cannot contain NUL, so NULs work only as separators between values.

Globs are already safe: for f in *.txt gives each name as one word, however strange. Prefer globs (with nullglob) when you only need names in one directory, and find -print0 when you need recursion or filters.
Leading dashes are the other trap: a file named -rf passed to rm becomes an option. Use -- to end options (rm -- "$f") or prefix relative names with ./ (rm ./*).
find -exec cmd {} + passes many names directly to the command with no parsing at all, and is often the simplest safe choice.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p tricky
touch 'tricky/plain.txt' 'tricky/with space.txt' $'tricky/new\nline.txt' 'tricky/-dash.txt'
printf 'naive line count: %s\n' "$(find tricky -type f | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
count=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    (( ++count ))
done < <(find tricky -type f -print0)
echo "NUL-safe count: $count"
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $# belongs to the inner shell
find tricky -type f -exec bash -c 'echo "-exec + passed $# names in one batch"' _ {} +
cd tricky || exit
for f in *; do printf '%q\n' "$f"; done
rm -- -dash.txt && echo 'removed -dash.txt safely'
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
mkdir -p logs/sub
printf 'hello' > 'logs/a b.log'
printf 'abc' > logs/sub/c.log
total=0
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    bytes=$(wc -c < "$f")
    total=$(( total + bytes ))
done < <(find logs -type f -name '*.log' -print0)
echo "total bytes: $total"
lessons.challenge: Count the total bytes of all .log files under a directory tree that contains a file named "a b.log" (5 bytes) and "c.log" (3 bytes), using find -print0 and a NUL-safe loop with wc -c reading each file via redirection.
lessons.question: Which character can never appear in a Unix path and so is a safe separator?
options: Colon
Tab
The NUL byte
Newline
lessons.explanation: Paths may contain every byte except NUL (and / separates components), so NUL-delimited lists are unambiguous.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
naive line count: 5
NUL-safe count: 4
-exec + passed 4 names in one batch
-dash.txt
$'new\nline.txt'
plain.txt
with\ space.txt
removed -dash.txt safely

Paths may contain every byte except NUL (and / separates components), so NUL-delimited lists are unambiguous.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Paths may contain every byte except NUL (and / separates components), so NUL-delimited lists are unambiguous.

lessons.title: Pipelines, PIPESTATUS and pipefail
body: cmd1 | cmd2 connects cmd1's stdout to cmd2's stdin; all parts start at the same time and run concurrently. |& also sends stderr through the pipe (shorthand for 2>&1 |).

By default a pipeline's exit status is that of its last command, so failing_command | sort succeeds. set -o pipefail makes the status the rightmost non-zero one, so a failure anywhere is reported. The PIPESTATUS array holds every part's status from the most recent pipeline; copy it immediately, since the next command replaces it.

pipefail has a famous false alarm: when a reader exits early (head -n 1, grep -q), the writer may be killed by SIGPIPE and report 141 (128+13). Under pipefail the pipeline then "fails" although nothing went wrong. Handle it by checking PIPESTATUS explicitly, or by avoiding early-exit readers when the writer's status matters.

Each part of a pipeline runs in a subshell, so variables assigned in a while loop at the end of a pipe are lost. shopt -s lastpipe runs the last part in the current shell when job control is off (always true in scripts), keeping those variables.
Prefer one tool over long chains where you can: grep pattern file | wc -l is grep -c pattern file, and cat file | cmd is cmd < file. Fewer processes are faster and have fewer failure points.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
false | true; echo "default status: $?"
false | true; echo "PIPESTATUS: ${PIPESTATUS[*]}"
set -o pipefail
false | true; echo "with pipefail: $?"
yes | head -n 1 > /dev/null; statuses=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")
echo "yes|head statuses: ${statuses[*]} (141 = SIGPIPE)"
set +o pipefail
total=0
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 | while read -r n; do total=$((total + n)); done
echo "without lastpipe: $total"
shopt -s lastpipe
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 | while read -r n; do total=$((total + n)); done
echo "with lastpipe: $total"
lessons.challenge: Write a function safe_first that prints the first line of a command's output (given as arguments) and returns the command's own status, ignoring SIGPIPE caused by head. Test with printf '%s\n' a b and with false.
lessons.question: Why can `yes | head -n 1` fail under pipefail?
options: yes is killed by SIGPIPE when head exits, giving status 141
head returns 1 after one line
pipefail forbids infinite producers
yes requires an argument
lessons.explanation: An early-exiting reader makes the writer die with SIGPIPE (128+13), which pipefail reports as failure.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
default status: 0
PIPESTATUS: 1 0
with pipefail: 1
yes|head statuses: 141 0 (141 = SIGPIPE)
without lastpipe: 0
with lastpipe: 6

An early-exiting reader makes the writer die with SIGPIPE (128+13), which pipefail reports as failure.
lessons.practiceAnswer: An early-exiting reader makes the writer die with SIGPIPE (128+13), which pipefail reports as failure.

lessons.title: Subshells versus the current shell
body: A subshell is a forked copy of the shell. It inherits all variables (exported or not), functions, options and open descriptors, but changes it makes — variables, cd, umask, traps, shell options — disappear when it exits. Parentheses ( ... ), $( ... ), each pipeline part (except the last with lastpipe), & background commands and <( ) all create subshells.

{ ...; } braces group commands in the current shell, so their changes persist. Choose parentheses when you want isolation — a temporary cd, a changed IFS or shell option — and braces when you want the effects.
$BASH_SUBSHELL counts nesting depth and $BASHPID gives the real process ID, while $$ always reports the main shell. These help when debugging where code actually runs.
exit inside a subshell only leaves the subshell. That is why `cmd || ( echo error; exit 1 )` does not stop the script; use braces: cmd || { echo error >&2; exit 1; }.
Forking costs time: thousands of $(...) in a loop are measurably slow. The next lesson shows how to avoid forks for capturing output.
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
in_dir() (
    cd "$1" || exit
    shift
    "$@"
)
in_dir / pwd
echo "caller still in: ${PWD##*/}"
lessons.challenge: Write a function in_dir that runs a command (its remaining arguments) inside the directory given as its first argument without changing the caller's directory, using a subshell body. Use it to print the base name of $PWD inside /tmp's parent (/) and show the caller's directory is unchanged.
lessons.question: Why does `cmd || ( echo failed; exit 1 )` not stop the script?
options: echo resets the status to 0
Subshells cannot run exit
exit only ends the subshell created by the parentheses
exit is ignored after ||
lessons.explanation: Use { echo failed; exit 1; } so exit runs in the current shell.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
subshell: x=inner pwd=/ depth=1
after ( ): x=outer pwd=work
after { }: x=braced
depth inside $(): 1
exit in ( ) only leaves the subshell
still running
exit in { } leaves the shell
fail_hard status: 1

Use { echo failed; exit 1; } so exit runs in the current shell.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Use { echo failed; exit 1; } so exit runs in the current shell.

lessons.title: Command substitution, including ${ cmd; } (Bash 5.3)
body: $(command) runs command in a subshell and replaces itself with the command's standard output, minus all trailing newlines. Quote it ("$(cmd)") to avoid word splitting and globbing. It nests cleanly: "$(dirname "$(pwd)")". The old backquote form `cmd` needs escaping to nest and should not be used in new code.
Because the trailing newlines are stripped, $(printf 'a\n\n') is just a. To keep them, append a sentinel character and remove it afterwards: out=$(cmd; printf x); out=${out%x}.

Bash 5.3 adds ${ command; }: the command runs in the current shell, without forking, and its output is captured the same way. Variable assignments and cd inside it persist, and it is much faster in loops. The space (or newline) after ${ and the final ; or newline before } are required.

${| command; } is a variant that captures nothing from stdout; instead its value is whatever the command assigns to REPLY. REPLY is local to the substitution, so the caller's REPLY is untouched. This lets functions return values with no subshell and no output parsing.

These forms are unknown to older shells — macOS /bin/bash 3.2 reports "bad substitution" — so use them only in scripts that require Bash 5.3. Within such scripts they are the preferred way to capture output from shell functions.
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
counter=0
next_id() {
    counter=$((counter + 1))
    REPLY="id-$counter"
}
ids=()
for _ in 1 2 3; do
    ids+=("${| next_id; }")
done
echo "${ids[*]}"
echo "counter=$counter"
lessons.challenge: Write a function next_id that increments a global counter and assigns "id-N" to REPLY. Generate three ids with ${| next_id; } into an array and print them, then print the counter (3) to show no subshell lost the increments.
lessons.question: What is the key difference between $(cmd) and ${ cmd; }?
options: ${ cmd; } captures stderr as well
${ cmd; } runs in the current shell, so no fork happens and side effects persist
${ cmd; } keeps trailing newlines
$(cmd) cannot capture functions
lessons.explanation: Both capture stdout and strip trailing newlines; the 5.3 form avoids the subshell.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
classic: work
stripped: [a]
kept 3 chars
same process: 1, count=1
shout=QUIET REPLY=untouched

Both capture stdout and strip trailing newlines; the 5.3 form avoids the subshell.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Both capture stdout and strip trailing newlines; the 5.3 form avoids the subshell.

lessons.title: Process substitution
body: <(command) runs command asynchronously and expands to a file name — such as /dev/fd/63 — from which its output can be read. >(command) gives a file name to write to, whose data becomes the command's input. They let programs that only accept file names work with command output.

Classic uses: diff <(sort a) <(sort b) compares sorted versions without temporary files; while read ... done < <(cmd) feeds a loop without a pipeline subshell; tee >(gzip > log.gz) >(wc -l > count) sends one stream to several consumers.

Process substitutions run in the background. Their exit status is not available as $? of the main command; since Bash 5.1 (and improved in 5.3), $! holds the PID of the last one, and wait "$!" collects its status.

Output written to >(...) may still be in flight when the main command returns, so a later command reading the result can race. Wait for it ($! and wait) or use a regular pipeline when ordering matters.
Process substitution is a Bash/ksh/zsh feature; it needs /dev/fd or named pipes and is not POSIX sh.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%s\n' pear apple fig > a.txt
printf '%s\n' fig pear apple kiwi > b.txt
diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt) && echo same || echo 'diff shows kiwi only in b'
echo "the substitution is a file name: $(echo <(true) | sed 's/[0-9]*$/N/')"
printf '%s\n' one two three | tee >(wc -l | tr -d ' ' > count.txt) > copy.txt
wait "$!"
echo "copied $(wc -l < copy.txt | tr -d ' ') lines, counted $(cat count.txt)"
max=0
while read -r n; do (( n > max )) && max=$n; done < <(printf '%s\n' 4 11 7)
echo "max kept after loop: $max"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
comm -12 <(printf '%s\n' red green blue | sort) <(printf '%s\n' blue yellow red | sort)
lessons.challenge: Use comm with two process substitutions to print the words present in both lists "red green blue" and "blue yellow red" (one per line, sorted).
lessons.question: What does <(cmd) expand to?
options: The PID of cmd
A file name, such as /dev/fd/63, connected to cmd's output
The output text of cmd
The exit status of cmd
lessons.explanation: Process substitution turns a command's output into a readable path for programs expecting files.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
2a3
> kiwi
diff shows kiwi only in b
the substitution is a file name: /dev/fd/N
copied 3 lines, counted 3
max kept after loop: 11

Process substitution turns a command's output into a readable path for programs expecting files.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Process substitution turns a command's output into a readable path for programs expecting files.

lessons.title: Background jobs, wait and wait -n
body: cmd & starts cmd in the background and continues immediately; $! holds its PID. wait with no arguments waits for all background children; wait PID waits for one and returns its exit status. A script that starts jobs should always wait for them, otherwise their failures go unnoticed and they may outlive the script.

wait -n waits for the next job to finish, whichever it is, and returns its status. With -p var (Bash 5.1+) it also stores the finished job's PID in var, so you can tell which task ended. This is the building block of a concurrency limiter: start jobs until N are running, then wait -n before starting the next.
Background jobs share the terminal's stdout and stderr, so their output interleaves unpredictably. Give each job its own output file, or collect and print results after waiting, when order matters.
Job control (fg, bg, %1, Ctrl-Z) is an interactive feature and is off in scripts. In scripts, think in terms of PIDs and wait.

Since Bash 5.3, wait -n can also report process substitutions and already-notified jobs, behaving more like plain wait. Write loops that track their own PIDs instead of assuming which job will finish first.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
task() { sleep "$1"; echo "task $2 done" > "out.$2"; return "$3"; }
task 1 a 0 &
pid_a=$!
task 0.1 b 4 &
wait -n -p finished
echo "first to finish exited $? (it was $([[ $finished == "$pid_a" ]] && echo a || echo b))"
wait "$pid_a"; echo "a exited $?"
cat out.a out.b
max_jobs=2 running=0 results=()
for n in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    if (( running >= max_jobs )); then wait -n; (( running-- )); fi
    { sleep 0.05; echo $(( n * n )) > "sq.$n"; } &
    (( ++running ))
done
wait
for n in 1 2 3 4 5; do results+=("$(< "sq.$n")"); done
echo "squares: ${results[*]}"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
pids=()
for status in 0 3 0; do
    ( sleep 0.05; exit "$status" ) &
    pids+=("$!")
done
failed=0
for pid in "${pids[@]}"; do
    wait "$pid" || (( ++failed ))
done
echo "failed: $failed"
lessons.challenge: Run three background tasks that exit with statuses 0, 3 and 0, wait for each by PID, and print how many failed (1).
lessons.question: What does `wait -n -p var` do?
options: Waits for all jobs and stores their count in var
Kills the newest job
Starts var as a new job
Waits for the next background job to finish and stores its PID in var
lessons.explanation: -n waits for any single job; -p records which PID finished, enabling concurrency-limited loops.

Expected output:

a exited 0
task a done
task b done
squares: 1 4 9 16 25

-n waits for any single job; -p records which PID finished, enabling concurrency-limited loops.
lessons.practiceAnswer: -n waits for any single job; -p records which PID finished, enabling concurrency-limited loops.

lessons.title: Coprocesses
body: coproc NAME { commands; } starts commands in the background with two-way pipes: NAME[0] is a descriptor for reading its output and NAME[1] for writing to its input, and NAME_PID holds its PID. It is how a script keeps a long-running helper (bc, a database client, a line-oriented server) open and talks to it repeatedly.

Write a request with printf ... >&"${NAME[1]}" and read the answer with read -r reply <&"${NAME[0]}". Make sure the helper does not buffer its output: many programs buffer when writing to a pipe, which deadlocks a request/response conversation. Line-oriented tools often have an option to flush, or use stdbuf where available.

When finished, close the write end — copy it to a plain variable and close that, in=${NAME[1]}; exec {in}>&- — so the helper sees end of input and exits, then wait "$NAME_PID". Name every coprocess; unnamed ones are called COPROC.
Since Bash 5.3 multiple coprocesses can be active at once by default (MULTIPLE_COPROCS). Each needs a distinct name.

Coprocesses are powerful but easy to deadlock. For one-shot work, a pipeline or process substitution is simpler; reach for coproc when the per-request cost of starting a process would otherwise dominate.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
coproc CALC { while read -r a b; do echo $(( a * b )); done; }
for pair in '6 7' '12 12' '3 1000'; do
    printf '%s\n' "$pair" >&"${CALC[1]}"
    read -r answer <&"${CALC[0]}"
    echo "$pair -> $answer"
done
in=${CALC[1]}
exec {in}>&-
wait "$CALC_PID"
echo "helper exited with $?"
lessons.challenge: Start a coprocess named UPPER that converts each input line to uppercase with a read loop (no external tools), send it the words alpha and beta, print each reply, then close it and wait for it.
lessons.question: Why can a request/response coprocess deadlock with an external program?
options: The program may buffer its output when writing to a pipe, so the reply never arrives
Coprocesses cannot read input
Bash closes the pipe after one line
read cannot use file descriptors
lessons.explanation: Block-buffered output waits for a full buffer; the script waits for a reply; neither progresses.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
6 7 -> 42
12 12 -> 144
3 1000 -> 3000
helper exited with 0

Block-buffered output waits for a full buffer; the script waits for a reply; neither progresses.
lessons.practiceAnswer: Block-buffered output waits for a full buffer; the script waits for a reply; neither progresses.

lessons.title: set -e, set -u and their real limits
body: set -e (errexit) exits the script when a command fails. set -u (nounset) treats expansion of an unset variable as an error. set -o pipefail makes pipelines report failures anywhere. Together, set -euo pipefail is often called "strict mode" and catches many mistakes early.

errexit is deliberately ignored in many contexts: the condition of if, while and until; any command in a && or || list except the last; commands negated with !; and — the big surprise — everything inside a function that is itself called from one of those contexts. `if myfunc; then` disables errexit for the whole body of myfunc.

Command substitution does not inherit errexit by default, and local x=$(cmd) hides the failure anyway. shopt -s inherit_errexit makes $(...) inherit set -e. Arithmetic (( expr )) returning 1 for a zero result also triggers errexit, a common source of mysterious exits with (( count++ )).

set -u fails on ${unset}, but ${var-default}, ${var:-default} and [[ -v var ]] are safe ways to test optional variables. "$@" with no arguments is fine with set -u since Bash 4.4; ${array[@]} of an empty array is too.

Strict mode is a safety net, not error handling. Check the commands whose failure you can anticipate explicitly (if ! cmd; then ...), give a useful message, and let errexit catch the rest. Some teams avoid set -e entirely for this reason; whichever you choose, know these rules.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
shopt -s inherit_errexit
step() { false; echo '  step continued after false'; }
if step; then echo '  if step: errexit was off inside the function'; fi
false || echo '  failure on the left of || is allowed'
count=0
(( count++ )) || true
echo "  count=$count (|| true kept (( )) from exiting)"
echo "  optional: ${MAYBE_UNSET:-default}"
[[ -v MAYBE_UNSET ]] || echo '  -v test is safe under set -u'
# shellcheck disable=SC2154  # deliberately unset to trigger nounset
( echo "  ${missing_var}" ) 2>/dev/null || echo "  set -u stopped the subshell with status $?"
step
echo 'never printed: plain step call exits the script'
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
require_file() {
    if [[ ! -f $1 ]]; then
        echo "error: missing $1" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}
touch present.txt
require_file present.txt && echo ok
if ! require_file absent.txt 2>/dev/null; then
    echo 'handled missing input'
    exit 3
fi
lessons.challenge: Write a script under set -euo pipefail with a function require_file that prints "error: missing NAME" to stderr and returns 1 when a file is absent. Call it for an existing file (print "ok") and then, explicitly handled with if !, for a missing one, printing "handled missing input" and exiting with status 3.
lessons.question: Why does `if myfunc; then` disable set -e inside myfunc?
options: if runs the function in a subshell
set -e only applies to external programs
errexit is ignored for every command executed as part of an if condition, including function bodies
Functions never honour set -e
lessons.explanation: Bash suppresses errexit throughout a condition context, so failures inside the function do not exit.

  failure on the left of || is allowed
  count=1 (|| true kept (( )) from exiting)

  set -u stopped the subshell with status 1

lessons.practiceAnswer: Bash suppresses errexit throughout a condition context, so failures inside the function do not exit.

lessons.title: trap: cleanup and signals
body: trap 'commands' SIGNAL... registers commands to run when the shell receives a signal or reaches a pseudo-signal. EXIT runs when the shell exits for any reason — normal end, exit, errexit or a fatal signal it handles — and is the right place for cleanup such as deleting temporary files.

INT (Ctrl-C) and TERM (the default of kill) are the signals scripts most often handle. A handler should clean up and then exit with the conventional status 128+N, or re-raise the signal (trap - INT; kill -INT $$) so the caller sees that the script was interrupted.

Use single quotes so the trap command is expanded when the trap runs, not when it is set: trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT uses the value of tmp at exit time. Calling a function from the trap keeps complex handlers readable.

trap -p lists traps as re-usable commands; Bash 5.3 adds trap -P to print only the action for each signal named. Also new in 5.3, BASH_TRAPSIG holds the number of the signal whose trap is running, so one handler can serve several signals.

Traps are reset in subshells (except that the EXIT trap of a subshell is its own), ignored signals stay ignored, and SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be trapped at all. A script cannot guarantee cleanup after kill -9; design so that leftover files are harmless.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shellcheck disable=SC2329  # both functions are invoked by traps
cleanup() { echo "cleanup: removing the work directory (status was $1)"; rm -rf -- "$work"; }
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'cleanup $?' EXIT
on_signal() { echo "handler: signal $BASH_TRAPSIG"; }
trap on_signal TERM INT
trap -P TERM
kill -TERM $$
kill -INT $$
touch "$work/data"
echo "work dir has: $(ls "$work")"
exit 7
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"; echo deleted' EXIT
trap 'echo terminating; exit 143' TERM
kill -TERM $$
echo 'not reached'
lessons.challenge: Write a script that creates a temporary file, installs an EXIT trap that deletes it and prints "deleted", handles TERM by printing "terminating" and exiting 143, then sends itself TERM. Show the trap order: terminating, then deleted.
lessons.question: Which trap runs on normal completion, explicit exit and errexit alike?
options: EXIT
ERR
TERM
RETURN
lessons.explanation: The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the shell exits, making it the place for cleanup.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
on_signal
handler: signal 15
handler: signal 2
work dir has: data
cleanup: removing the work directory (status was 7)

The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the shell exits, making it the place for cleanup.
lessons.practiceAnswer: The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the shell exits, making it the place for cleanup.

lessons.title: Temporary files and directories
body: Never create temporary files with predictable names like /tmp/myscript.$$: another user can pre-create or symlink that path, and two copies of the script collide. mktemp creates a uniquely named file with permissions 600 and prints its path; mktemp -d creates a private directory.

Pair every mktemp with an EXIT trap that removes it, set immediately after creation. If you create several temporary paths, make one temporary directory and put everything in it, so one rm -rf cleans up.

mktemp honours TMPDIR, so users and CI systems can redirect temporary storage. Pass a template when you want a recognizable name: mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/backup.XXXXXX" — the Xs are replaced by random characters. GNU and BSD mktemp differ in some options, so stick to plain mktemp, -d and a template ending in XXXXXX for portability.
umask controls the permissions of new files. umask 077 at the top of a script that handles secrets makes every file it creates private.
Guard destructive commands: rm -rf -- "${work:?}" fails safely if work is unexpectedly empty instead of operating on the wrong path, and the -- protects against names starting with a dash.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "${work:?}"' EXIT
file=$(mktemp "$work/report.XXXXXX")
echo "name pattern ok: $([[ ${file##*/} =~ ^report\.[A-Za-z0-9]{6}$ ]] && echo yes)"
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # ls -l is used only for its permission column
perm=$(ls -l "$file" | cut -c1-10)
echo "mktemp file permissions: $perm"
# shellcheck disable=SC2012
( umask 077; touch "$work/secret"; ls -l "$work/secret" | cut -c1-10 )
unset work_typo
if ! message=$( ( rm -rf -- "${work_typo:?refusing to delete an empty path}" ) 2>&1 ); then
    echo "guarded: ${message##*: }"
fi
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
with_temp_dir() {
    local dir status
    dir=$(mktemp -d)
    ( cd "$dir" && "$@" )
    status=$?
    rm -rf -- "$dir"
    [[ -d $dir ]] && echo 'leaked' || echo 'cleaned up'
    return "$status"
}
with_temp_dir touch x; echo "status $?"
with_temp_dir false; echo "status $?"
lessons.challenge: Write a function with_temp_dir that creates a temporary directory, runs the given command inside it in a subshell, and always removes the directory afterwards (even if the command fails), returning the command's status. Run it with touch x and with false, printing each status and whether the directory still exists.
lessons.question: Why is /tmp/script.$$ a poor temporary file name?
options: It is predictable, so another process can pre-create or symlink it
$$ is not allowed in paths
It is too long
/tmp is read-only for scripts
lessons.explanation: mktemp creates an unpredictable name atomically with safe permissions.

Expected output:

mktemp file permissions: -rw-------
-rw-------

mktemp creates an unpredictable name atomically with safe permissions.
lessons.practiceAnswer: mktemp creates an unpredictable name atomically with safe permissions.

lessons.title: ERR traps, stack traces and die
body: trap 'handler' ERR runs whenever a command fails under the same rules that errexit uses (so not in if conditions or && lists). Inside the handler, $? is the failing status, BASH_COMMAND the command text and LINENO or BASH_LINENO the line.

By default the ERR trap is not inherited by functions, command substitutions or subshells. set -o errtrace (set -E) makes it inherited, which you almost always want together with an ERR trap. set -o functrace (set -T) does the same for DEBUG and RETURN traps.
The caller builtin and the arrays FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE and BASH_LINENO describe the call stack. Walking them in the handler produces a stack trace: each frame's function, file and line.

A die function — print a message to stderr and exit non-zero — makes intentional failure explicit: [[ -r $config ]] || die "cannot read $config". Use exit codes consistently: 1 general failure, 2 usage error, and documented specific codes for distinct conditions.
Report errors where the user can act on them: say what failed, with which input, and what to do next. Messages like "error" alone waste the reader's time.
lessons.challenge: Write a die function that prints "fatal: MESSAGE" to stderr and exits with an optional status (default 1). Use it to reject a missing argument: call a main function with no arguments, which should print "usage: main NAME" via die with status 2. Print nothing to stdout.
lessons.question: Why combine an ERR trap with set -E (errtrace)?
options: ERR traps require it to be parsed
set -E disables errexit inside the trap
Without it, the ERR trap does not fire for failures inside functions and subshells
set -E makes the trap run twice
lessons.explanation: ERR traps are not inherited by functions, command substitutions and subshells unless errtrace is enabled.
lessons.workedExample:
Expected output:
starting

ERR traps are not inherited by functions, command substitutions and subshells unless errtrace is enabled.
lessons.practiceAnswer: ERR traps are not inherited by functions, command substitutions and subshells unless errtrace is enabled.

lessons.title: Idempotent, atomic and locked operations
body: An idempotent script can run twice and end in the same state: mkdir -p instead of mkdir, ln -sfn instead of ln -s, checks like [[ -e $target ]] || create. Idempotency makes reruns after a partial failure safe — the most common way scripts are recovered.

Writing a file in place risks leaving it half-written if the script is interrupted. Write to a temporary file in the same directory and mv it over the target: rename within one filesystem is atomic, so readers see either the old or the new file, never a mix.

Prevent two copies of a script from running at once with a lock. mkdir is atomic and portable: if mkdir "$lockdir" 2>/dev/null; then ... else exit; fi, with an EXIT trap that removes the directory. On Linux, flock on a file descriptor is an alternative, but it is not installed on macOS by default.

Guard paths used in destructive commands: ${dir:?} on empty values, -- before arguments, and never rm -rf "$dir/"* with an unchecked variable. A dry-run mode that prints actions instead of performing them (via a run function that echoes or executes) makes risky scripts reviewable.
Return clear statuses and print what changed. "created X", "X already present" output tells the operator exactly what the rerun did.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ensure_dir() {
    if [[ -d $1 ]]; then echo "exists: $1"; else mkdir -p -- "$1"; echo "created: $1"; fi
}
ensure_dir out; ensure_dir out
write_atomic() {
    local target=$1 tmp
    tmp=$(mktemp "${target%/*}/.${target##*/}.XXXXXX")
    cat > "$tmp"
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$target"
}
printf 'version=1\n' | write_atomic out/config
printf 'version=2\n' | write_atomic out/config
echo "config: $(cat out/config); leftovers: $(find out -name '.config.*' | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
lock=out/.lock
if mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null; then
    trap 'rmdir "$lock"' EXIT
    echo 'lock acquired'
    mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null || echo 'second instance would be refused'
fi
DRY_RUN=1
run() { if (( DRY_RUN )); then printf 'would run:'; printf ' %q' "$@"; echo; else "$@"; fi; }
run rm -rf -- 'out/old data'
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
append_once() {
    local line=$1 file=$2
    if [[ -f $file ]] && grep -Fxq -- "$line" "$file"; then
        echo present
    else
        printf '%s\n' "$line" >> "$file"
        echo added
    fi
}
append_once 'PATH=/opt/bin' profile.txt
append_once 'PATH=/opt/bin' profile.txt
append_once 'EDITOR=vi' profile.txt
cat profile.txt
lessons.challenge: Write a function append_once that adds a line to a file only if that exact line is not already present (use grep -Fxq), printing "added" or "present". Call it three times with the lines "PATH=/opt/bin", "PATH=/opt/bin", "EDITOR=vi" on profile.txt and print the file.
lessons.question: Why write to a temporary file and then mv it over the target?
options: It keeps a backup of the old version
A rename within one filesystem is atomic, so readers never see a half-written file
mv compresses the file
Temporary files are faster to write
lessons.explanation: Writing in place can be interrupted midway; rename replaces the file in a single step.

exists: out

second instance would be refused

lessons.title: eval, printf -v and generating shell code safely
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: eval concatenates its arguments and parses the result as shell code a second time. Anything inside a value — ;, $(...), quotes — becomes code. eval "echo $input" with input='x; rm -rf ~' runs the rm. Most uses of eval are attempts to do something Bash already supports safely.

Safer replacements: indirect expansion ${!name} or namerefs for dynamic variable names; printf -v "$name" '%s' "$value" to assign to a computed name; arrays for dynamic commands; declare -A for computed keys.

printf -v var fmt args formats directly into a variable, with no subshell and no word-splitting surprises — also the fastest way to build strings in loops. Validate the variable name first, because a name like a[$(cmd)] is itself code.

When code generation is truly needed — writing a script, an ssh remote command, a config read back by a shell — quote every value with printf %q or ${var@Q}. The result re-parses to exactly the original value.
declare -p var produces a re-loadable definition of a variable, including arrays and attributes; sourcing that output recreates it. This is a clean way to save shell state to a file.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
input='x; echo INJECTED'
eval "echo $input"
echo ---
printf -v greeting '%s, %s!' Hello 'world; echo nope'
echo "$greeting"
name=color
[[ $name =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$ ]] && printf -v "$name" '%s' blue
echo "color=${!name}"
remote="ls -- $(printf '%q' 'my dir; rm x')"
echo "safe remote command: $remote"
declare -A saved=([a]=1 [b]='two words')
declare -p saved > state.sh
unset saved
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source state.sh
echo "restored: ${saved[b]}"
lessons.challenge: Write a function set_var NAME VALUE that rejects invalid names with status 2 and otherwise assigns VALUE via printf -v. Call it with valid name x and value "a b", and with the name 'y[$(id)]', printing the outcome of each.
lessons.question: What is the safest way to assign to a variable whose name is computed?
options: declare $name=$value without validation
export $name
Validate the name, then use printf -v "$name" '%s' "$value"
eval "$name=$value"

Expected output:

INJECTED
---
Hello, world; echo nope!
color=blue
safe remote command: ls -- my\ dir\;\ rm\ x
restored: two words

lessons.title: Debugging: xtrace, PS4, BASH_XTRACEFD and DEBUG traps
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: set -x (xtrace) prints each command after expansion, prefixed by PS4, before running it — the fastest way to see what a script really does, including how quoting and expansions turned out. set +x turns it off; bash -x script.sh traces a whole run.

Customize PS4 to show where each line came from: PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '. Use single quotes so the variables expand each time a trace line is printed. The first character of PS4 is repeated to show nesting depth.

Trace output goes to stderr by default, mixing with real errors. BASH_XTRACEFD=N sends it to descriptor N instead: exec {trace}> trace.log; BASH_XTRACEFD=$trace. Then the trace can be inspected without disturbing normal output.

bash -n script checks syntax without running anything — useful in CI. trap '...' DEBUG runs before every simple command, with BASH_COMMAND holding the command about to run; it can implement step tracing or timing. caller prints the line and function of the current call site.
Debug systematically: reproduce with the smallest input, trace only the suspect section, print values with declare -p or printf '[%s]\n' to see boundaries, and run ShellCheck before guessing.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {trace}> trace.log
BASH_XTRACEFD=$trace
PS4='+ ${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}:${LINENO}: '
greet() { local who=${1^}; echo "hello $who"; }
set -x
greet 'ada lovelace'
set +x
exec {trace}>&-
echo '--- trace.log ---'
cat trace.log
where() { caller 0 | cut -d' ' -f1-2; }
where
steps=0
trap '(( ++steps ))' DEBUG
true; true; true
trap - DEBUG
echo "DEBUG trap saw $steps commands"
lessons.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
exec {fd}> loop.trace
BASH_XTRACEFD=$fd
PS4='+ line ${LINENO}: '
set -x
for n in 1 2 3; do
    doubled=$((n * 2))
done
set +x
exec {fd}>&-
echo "doubled=$doubled"
grep -c 'doubled=' loop.trace

options: The prompt for interactive input
The file descriptor that set -x trace output is written to
How many lines xtrace prints
Which functions are traced

lessons.title: Performance: builtins first, fewer forks
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: The main cost in shell scripts is starting processes. Each external command and each $(...) subshell is a fork (and usually an exec), costing on the order of a millisecond. A loop that calls sed, cut or $(...) per line over 100,000 lines spends minutes where builtins would take a second.

Prefer built-in features: parameter expansion instead of basename, dirname, cut and sed for single values; [[ =~ ]] instead of grep for one string; $(( )) instead of expr; printf -v or Bash 5.3's ${ ...; } instead of $(...) for capturing; read and mapfile instead of piping through head and tail.

For whole-file processing, the opposite holds: one awk, sed, sort or grep invocation over the file is far faster than a Bash read loop over every line. Move work into a single external process, not one process per line.

Measure rather than guess: time cmd reports elapsed and CPU time. EPOCHREALTIME gives microsecond wall-clock time, and Bash 5.3's BASH_MONOSECONDS reads the monotonic clock, which is immune to clock adjustments. Compare alternatives on realistic input sizes.
Optimize only hot paths. Clear code that runs once is better than clever code that saves a millisecond; a loop over a large dataset is where these techniques matter.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
now_us() { local t=${EPOCHREALTIME/./}; echo "$t"; }
n=300
path=/srv/app/releases/v1.2.3/bin/server
start=$(now_us)
for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do name=$(basename "$path"); done
forked=$(( $(now_us) - start ))
start=$(now_us)
for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do name=${path##*/}; done
builtin=$(( $(now_us) - start ))
echo "same result: $name"

lessons.title: Portability: POSIX sh, Bash versions and macOS
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: #!/bin/sh promises POSIX shell code. On Debian and Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash; on macOS it is Bash 3.2 in POSIX mode; on Alpine it is BusyBox ash. [[ ]], arrays, local (technically), ${var//a/b}, <( ), $'...', {1..5}, == in [ ] and function name { } are not POSIX. If you need these, use #!/usr/bin/env bash.

Bash itself differs by version. macOS ships 3.2 (2007) as /bin/bash for licensing reasons: no associative arrays, mapfile, ${var,,}, nameref, ;;& or |&. Check BASH_VERSINFO at the top when you rely on newer features and fail with a clear message rather than a confusing syntax error.

External tools differ too: GNU versus BSD sed -i, date, stat, readlink -f, grep -P, find options. Stick to POSIX options, detect the variant (sed --version succeeds only on GNU), or require GNU tools explicitly.

bash --posix or set -o posix makes Bash follow POSIX where they differ — useful for testing that a #!/bin/sh script really is portable, together with running it under dash. ShellCheck checks against the dialect named in the shebang or with -s sh.
Choose deliberately: for scripts run on machines you control, require Bash 5.x and use its features freely; for installers that must run anywhere, write POSIX sh and keep them small.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
require_bash() {
    local major=$1 minor=$2
    if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] > major || (BASH_VERSINFO[0] == major && BASH_VERSINFO[1] >= minor) )); then
        echo "Bash ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}.${BASH_VERSINFO[1]} satisfies >= $major.$minor"
    else
        echo "need Bash >= $major.$minor" >&2; return 1
    fi
}
require_bash 4 4
require_bash 99 0 2>&1 || true
cat > portable.sh <<'EOF'
set -- "two words" three
for arg do
    case $arg in
        *" "*) printf '%s has a space\n' "$arg" ;;
        *) printf '%s\n' "$arg" ;;
    esac
done
EOF
sh portable.sh
shellcheck -s sh portable.sh && echo 'ShellCheck: valid POSIX sh'
printf 'a=(1 2)\n[[ -n x ]]\n' > bashism.sh
shellcheck -s sh -f gcc bashism.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]*' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' '; echo

lessons.title: Static analysis with ShellCheck
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: ShellCheck reads scripts and reports likely bugs: unquoted expansions (SC2086), read without -r (SC2162), cd without error handling (SC2164), unused or unassigned variables (SC2034, SC2154), useless cat and many portability problems. Each warning has a wiki page explaining the reasoning, at shellcheck.net/wiki/SCxxxx.

It infers the dialect from the shebang; override with -s bash or -s sh. -x follows source statements, and a `# shellcheck source=path` directive tells it where a dynamically computed source path points.

When a warning is a deliberate choice, disable it narrowly: a `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` directive applies to the next command (or to the whole file when placed before the first command), and should carry a comment saying why. Never disable a check just to make output quiet.

A .shellcheckrc file in the project sets defaults such as enabled optional checks (enable=require-variable-braces) or external-sources=true. -S warning raises the minimum severity reported; -f gcc or -f json produce machine-readable output for editors and CI.
Make ShellCheck a gate in CI: every .sh file must pass. Every script in this guide does, except where a lesson deliberately shows a pitfall and declares the expected finding.

#!/usr/bin/env bash

for f in $files; do

done

cd /tmp
EOF

shellcheck -f gcc sample.sh | grep -o 'SC[0-9]*' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{ print "  " $2 " x" $1 }'
cat > fixed.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
shopt -s nullglob
for f in *.txt; do
    wc -l < "$f"
done
read -r name

EOF

lessons.title: Security: injection, PATH, privileges and secrets
lessons.summary: 11 · Mastery: debugging, performance, portability and security
body: Treat every external value — arguments, environment, file contents, file names, network data — as data, never as code. The main injection points are eval, sh -c/bash -c strings, ssh remote commands, arithmetic contexts and array subscripts, and unquoted expansions that glob.

To run a command string with user data, pass the data as arguments, not inside the string: bash -c 'grep -- "$1" "$2"' _ "$pattern" "$file". The _ fills $0; the values arrive as positional parameters and are never parsed as code.

Control the environment of privileged scripts: set PATH explicitly (PATH=/usr/bin:/bin), use absolute paths for critical tools, reset IFS, and do not trust inherited variables such as BASH_ENV, LD_PRELOAD or ENV. Bash ignores imported functions with unusual names and has been hardened since Shellshock (2014), but never source files writable by others.

Keep secrets out of command lines (visible in ps) and out of xtrace output. Read them from files with restrictive permissions or from stdin, pass them via environment variables or descriptors, and set +x around code that handles them. umask 077 protects files you create.

Validate early with allow-lists — explicit patterns like ^[a-z0-9-]+$ — rather than trying to block dangerous characters. Run with least privilege, and prefer failing closed: refuse input you do not understand.
lessons.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
user_input='x"; echo INJECTED; echo "'
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # $1 and $2 belong to the inner shell
bash -c 'printf "searching for [%s] in %s\n" "$1" "$2"' _ "$user_input" notes.txt
validate_slug() { [[ $1 =~ ^[a-z0-9-]+$ ]]; }
for slug in release-2026 '../etc' 'a b'; do
    if validate_slug "$slug"; then echo "accept: $slug"; else printf 'reject: %q\n' "$slug"; fi
done
mkdir -p evil
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho HIJACKED\n' > evil/ls; chmod +x evil/ls
PATH="$PWD/evil:$PATH" bash -c 'PATH=/usr/bin:/bin; ls -d / '
printf 's3cret\n' > token.txt; chmod 600 token.txt
IFS= read -r token < token.txt
echo "token length: ${#token} (value never printed or passed as an argument)"

lessons.title: Project: a tested command-line task manager
body: This project combines the earlier stages into one small but complete tool: todo.sh keeps a task list in a text file and supports add, list and complete subcommands, a -f FILE option, a TODO_FILE environment default and both -h and --help. Read the whole script before running it; every technique in it has its own earlier lesson.

Structure: strict mode at the top; usage and die helpers; one function per subcommand; a main function that parses options with getopts, then dispatches with case; and a final main "$@". Usage errors exit with status 2 and runtime errors with status 1, with every message on stderr.

Data safety: task text is written with printf '%s' so stars, dollar signs and backslashes are stored literally. Completing a task reads the file with mapfile, edits one array element and replaces the file via a mktemp file in the same directory followed by mv, so an interruption never leaves a half-written list. The temporary file starts as a cp -p copy, so the list keeps its permissions (a symlinked list is still replaced by a regular file — a documented limit). Task numbers are limited to nine digits, because longer values would wrap in 64-bit arithmetic and mark the wrong task.

Testing: tests/test_todo.sh runs the tool as a separate process in a fresh temporary directory, compares exact output and exit statuses with a tiny check helper from tests/lib.sh, and removes its directory in an EXIT trap. Tests cover the happy path, invalid numbers, a second completion, missing option arguments, unknown commands, the -f option, the environment default and leftover temporary files.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the tests, then predict the output of list after adding three tasks and completing the second. Intermediate: add an undo N subcommand that reopens a finished task and refuses an open one. Advanced: add a count subcommand printing "OPEN open of TOTAL", working even when the file does not exist, with tests for each behaviour. The worked answer implements both and adds four checks.

Validation in this guide also runs a mutation check: the completion line is deliberately broken and the suite must fail. A test suite that still passes after a real bug is introduced is not testing that behaviour.

mv is faster than redirection

Bash cannot write to an existing file

# shellcheck shell=bash
# Minimal assertion helpers; sourced by test files, no framework required.
passed=0
failed=0

check() {
    local name=$1 expected=$2 actual=$3
    if [[ $actual == "$expected" ]]; then
        passed=$((passed + 1))
    else
        failed=$((failed + 1))
        printf 'FAIL %s\n  expected: %q\n  actual:   %q\n' "$name" "$expected" "$actual"
    fi
}

finish() {
    echo "$passed passed, $failed failed"
    (( failed == 0 ))
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run from the project directory: bash tests/test_todo.sh
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # literal $HOME in task text is test data
set -uo pipefail
here=$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}/.." && pwd)
# shellcheck source=tests/lib.sh
source "$here/tests/lib.sh"
todo="$here/todo.sh"
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$work"' EXIT
cd "$work" || exit

bash "$todo" add 'buy milk'
bash "$todo" add 'literal *.txt and $HOME'
check 'list shows open tasks' $'1. buy milk\n2. literal *.txt and $HOME' "$(bash "$todo" list)"
chmod 644 todo.txt
bash "$todo" complete 1
# shellcheck disable=SC2012  # only the permission column is used
check 'permissions survive a rewrite' '-rw-r--r--' "$(ls -l todo.txt | cut -c1-10)"
check 'complete hides the task' '2. literal *.txt and $HOME' "$(bash "$todo" list)"
check 'file keeps finished task' '[x] buy milk' "$(head -n 1 todo.txt)"
bash "$todo" complete 1 2>/dev/null; check 'finishing twice fails' 1 "$?"
bash "$todo" complete 9 2>/dev/null; check 'unknown task fails' 1 "$?"
bash "$todo" complete 18446744073709551617 2>/dev/null; check 'oversized number is rejected, not wrapped' 2 "$?"
bash "$todo" complete x 2>/dev/null; check 'non-numeric task is a usage error' 2 "$?"
bash "$todo" 2>/dev/null; check 'no command is a usage error' 2 "$?"
bash "$todo" -f 2>/dev/null; check 'missing -f argument' 2 "$?"
bash "$todo" fly 2>/dev/null; check 'unknown command' 2 "$?"
bash "$todo" -f other.txt add 'separate list'
check '-f selects another file' '1. separate list' "$(bash "$todo" -f other.txt list)"
check 'TODO_FILE is honoured' '1. separate list' "$(TODO_FILE=other.txt bash "$todo" list)"
check '--help prints usage' 'usage: todo.sh [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS]' "$(bash "$todo" --help | head -n 1)"
check 'no temporary files left' '' "$(find . -name 'todo.txt.*')"
finish

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# todo.sh: a small task list kept in a plain text file.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    cat <<'TXT'
usage: todo.sh [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS]
commands:
  add TEXT...   append an open task
  list          show open tasks with their numbers
  complete N    mark task N as done
options:
  -f FILE       task file (default: $TODO_FILE, else ./todo.txt)
  -h, --help    show this help
TXT
}

die() {
    echo "todo: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

# Replace the file in one rename so an interruption never leaves half a list.
write_lines() {
    local file=$1 tmp
    shift
    tmp=$(mktemp "$file.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions (mktemp files are 0600).
    cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    printf '%s\n' "$@" > "$tmp"
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
}

cmd_add() {
    (( $# )) || die 'add needs task text' 2
    printf '[ ] %s\n' "$*" >> "$file"
}

cmd_list() {
    [[ -f $file ]] || return 0
    local n=0 line
    while IFS= read -r line; do
        n=$((n + 1))
        if [[ $line == '[ ] '* ]]; then
            printf '%d. %s\n' "$n" "${line#'[ ] '}"
        fi
    done < "$file"
}

cmd_complete() {
    # Nine digits at most: longer numbers would overflow 64-bit arithmetic and wrap.
    [[ ${1-} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$ ]] || die 'complete needs a task number' 2
    [[ -f $file ]] || die "no tasks in $file"
    local lines i=$(($1 - 1))
    mapfile -t lines < "$file"
    (( i < ${#lines[@]} )) || die "no task $1"
    [[ ${lines[i]} == '[ ] '* ]] || die "task $1 is already done"
    lines[i]="[x] ${lines[i]#'[ ] '}"
    write_lines "$file" "${lines[@]}"
}

main() {
    file=${TODO_FILE:-todo.txt}
    if [[ ${1-} == --help ]]; then
        usage
        return
    fi
    local OPTIND opt
    while getopts ':f:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            f) file=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            :) die "option -$OPTARG needs an argument" 2 ;;
            *) die "unknown option -$OPTARG" 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    if (( $# == 0 )); then
        usage >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    local command=$1
    shift
    case $command in
        add) cmd_add "$@" ;;
        list) cmd_list ;;
        complete) cmd_complete "$@" ;;
        *) die "unknown command: $command" 2 ;;
    esac
}

main "$@"

# todo.sh: a small task list kept in a plain text file.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    cat <<'TXT'
usage: todo.sh [-f FILE] COMMAND [ARGS]
commands:

die() {
    echo "todo: $1" >&2
