}

# Replace the file in one rename so an interruption never leaves half a list.
write_lines() {
    local file=$1 tmp
    shift
    tmp=$(mktemp "$file.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions (mktemp files are 0600).
    cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    printf '%s\n' "$@" > "$tmp"
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
}

cmd_add() {
    (( $# )) || die 'add needs task text' 2
    printf '[ ] %s\n' "$*" >> "$file"
}

    [[ -f $file ]] || return 0

        n=$((n + 1))
        if [[ $line == '[ ] '* ]]; then
            printf '%d. %s\n' "$n" "${line#'[ ] '}"
        fi
    done < "$file"
}

cmd_complete() {
    # Nine digits at most: longer numbers would overflow 64-bit arithmetic and wrap.
    [[ ${1-} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$ ]] || die 'complete needs a task number' 2
    [[ -f $file ]] || die "no tasks in $file"
    local lines i=$(($1 - 1))
    mapfile -t lines < "$file"
    (( i < ${#lines[@]} )) || die "no task $1"
    [[ ${lines[i]} == '[ ] '* ]] || die "task $1 is already done"
    lines[i]="[x] ${lines[i]#'[ ] '}"
    write_lines "$file" "${lines[@]}"
}

cmd_undo() {
    [[ ${1-} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$ ]] || die 'undo needs a task number' 2
    [[ -f $file ]] || die "no tasks in $file"
    local lines i=$(($1 - 1))
    mapfile -t lines < "$file"
    (( i < ${#lines[@]} )) || die "no task $1"
    [[ ${lines[i]} == '[x] '* ]] || die "task $1 is still open"
    lines[i]="[ ] ${lines[i]#'[x] '}"
    write_lines "$file" "${lines[@]}"
}

cmd_count() {
    local lines=() line open=0
    [[ -f $file ]] && mapfile -t lines < "$file"
    for line in "${lines[@]}"; do

main() {

        list) cmd_list ;;
        complete) cmd_complete "$@" ;;
        undo) cmd_undo "$@" ;;
        count) cmd_count ;;

lessons.title: Project: a streaming access-log analyzer
body: analyze.sh summarises web server logs in Common Log Format: total requests, malformed lines, bytes served, counts per status code and the busiest paths. It reads any number of files, or standard input when given no file or -, and streams line by line so input size is limited only by time.

Parsing uses one extended regular expression with capture groups and BASH_REMATCH instead of cut or awk per line, so no process is started per line. Malformed lines are counted and reported on stderr with their file name and line number; blank lines are ignored and a final line without a newline is still processed.

Counting uses associative arrays keyed by status and path. Log content is untrusted: keys are used only in assignments and ${...} expansions, never in eval, arithmetic subscripts or builtin arguments that re-expand them. A test feeds a path containing $(touch pwned) and checks that no file appears.

Reporting sorts keys explicitly because associative arrays have no order. Ranking pipes counts into sort and reads the full result with mapfile, then slices the first TOP entries in Bash. Using head here would let sort die from SIGPIPE, which pipefail and errexit would turn into a failed run.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the suite and explain each line of the expected report. Intermediate: add a -e option for monitoring that exits with status 3 when any 5xx response was seen, explaining the reason on stderr. Advanced: decide where the Bash loop stops being fast enough and compare with an awk version on a million generated lines. The worked answer implements -e with three new checks.
A mutation check reverses the ranking order; the suite must fail, showing that the report test pins the ordering, not just the counts.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# analyze.sh: summarise web server access logs in Common Log Format.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: analyze.sh [-n TOP] [FILE...]   (reads stdin when no FILE is given or FILE is -)'
}

die() {
    echo "analyze: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

# 203.0.113.9 - - [16/Oct/2026:10:00:00 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512
line_re='^[^ ]+ [^ ]+ [^ ]+ \[[^]]+\] "([A-Z]+) ([^ "]+)[^"]*" ([0-9]{3}) ([0-9]+|-)$'

declare -A by_status=() by_path=()
requests=0 malformed=0 bytes=0

# Log text is data: keys are only used in assignments and ${...}, never re-parsed.
analyze_stream() {
    local name=$1 line n=0 status path size
    while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
        n=$((n + 1))
        if [[ $line =~ $line_re ]]; then
            path=${BASH_REMATCH[2]} status=${BASH_REMATCH[3]} size=${BASH_REMATCH[4]}
            requests=$((requests + 1))
            by_status[$status]=$(( ${by_status[$status]:-0} + 1 ))
            by_path[$path]=$(( ${by_path[$path]:-0} + 1 ))
            [[ $size == - ]] || bytes=$((bytes + size))
        elif [[ -n $line ]]; then
            malformed=$((malformed + 1))
            echo "analyze: $name:$n: malformed line" >&2
        fi
    done
}

report() {
    local top=$1 code path ranked=() entry
    echo "requests: $requests"
    echo "malformed: $malformed"
    echo "bytes: $bytes"
    echo 'status:'
    if (( ${#by_status[@]} )); then
        while IFS= read -r code; do
            printf '  %s %d\n' "$code" "${by_status[$code]}"
        done < <(printf '%s\n' "${!by_status[@]}" | sort)
    fi
    echo "top $top paths:"
    if (( ${#by_path[@]} )); then
        # Sort everything, then slice in Bash: head would SIGPIPE sort under pipefail.
        mapfile -t ranked < <(for path in "${!by_path[@]}"; do
            printf '%d\t%s\n' "${by_path[$path]}" "$path"
        done | sort -t $'\t' -k1,1nr -k2,2)
        for entry in "${ranked[@]:0:top}"; do
            printf '  %d %s\n' "${entry%%$'\t'*}" "${entry#*$'\t'}"
        done
    fi
}

main() {
    local top=3 opt OPTIND file
    while getopts ':n:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            # Six digits at most keeps the later array slice far from integer overflow.
            n) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]{0,5}$ ]] || die '-n needs a number from 1 to 999999' 2
               top=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || set -- -
    for file in "$@"; do
        if [[ $file == - ]]; then
            analyze_stream stdin
        elif [[ -f $file && -r $file ]]; then
            # shellcheck disable=SC2094  # the name is only a label for messages
            analyze_stream "$file" < "$file"
        else
            die "cannot read $file"
        fi
    done
    report "$top"
}

main "$@"

}

finish() {

}

lessons.title: Project: an atomic, locked configuration updater
body: setconf.sh sets KEY=VALUE in a configuration file. It keeps comments, blank lines and ordering, appends new keys, reports added, updated or unchanged, supports a dry run and creates the file when it does not exist.

Safety is the theme. The key is validated against an allow-list pattern and values containing newlines are rejected, so input cannot add extra lines. The new content is rendered into a mktemp file in the same directory and moved over the original in one atomic rename.

The temporary file is created by copying the original with cp -p first, so the replacement keeps the original permissions — a config readable only by its group stays that way. A plain mktemp file would silently become mode 600; when the file is new, the script applies the normal umask-derived mode instead. Duplicate keys are all rewritten, and any differing copy counts as an update, so the tool never reports unchanged while a stale value remains.

Concurrency: a lock directory created with mkdir guarantees only one writer at a time; a second writer fails immediately with status 75 (EX_TEMPFAIL, "try again later"). An EXIT trap removes the temporary file and the lock in every outcome, and a test checks nothing is left behind.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the tests and explain why the special-character value is stored literally. Intermediate: add -d KEY to delete a key, reporting deleted or absent. Advanced: add a wait-with-timeout option for the lock and discuss stale locks after a crash. The worked answer implements -d with five new checks.
The mutation check removes the cp -p line; the permission test must fail, demonstrating that the test protects a real, easily broken property.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setconf.sh: set KEY=VALUE in a config file atomically, under a lock.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: setconf.sh [-n] [-f FILE] KEY VALUE   (-n: dry run; default FILE: app.conf)'
}

die() {
    echo "setconf: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

tmp='' lock=''
cleanup() {
    [[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -f -- "$tmp"
    [[ -n $lock ]] && rmdir -- "$lock"
    return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT

acquire_lock() {
    # mkdir is atomic: exactly one process can create the directory.
    if mkdir -- "$1.lock" 2>/dev/null; then
        lock=$1.lock
    else
        die "$1 is locked by another process" 75
    fi
}

# Print the new file contents and set result to added, updated or unchanged.
render() {
    local key=$1 value=$2 file=$3 line found=0 differs=0
    result=added
    if [[ -f $file ]]; then
        while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]; do
            if [[ $line == "$key="* ]]; then
                found=1
                # Every duplicate is rewritten, so any differing copy means the file changes.
                [[ ${line#*=} == "$value" ]] || differs=1
                printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "$value"
            else
                printf '%s\n' "$line"
            fi
        done < "$file"
    fi
    if (( found )); then
        if (( differs )); then result=updated; else result=unchanged; fi
    else
        printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "$value"
    fi
}

main() {
    local file=app.conf dry_run=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':nf:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            n) dry_run=1 ;;
            f) file=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# == 2 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
    local key=$1 value=$2
    [[ $key =~ ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*$ ]] || die "invalid key: $key" 2
    [[ $value != *$'\n'* ]] || die 'values cannot contain newlines' 2

    acquire_lock "$file"
    local dir=.
    [[ $file == */* ]] && dir=${file%/*}
    tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.setconf.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions.
    if [[ -f $file ]]; then
        cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    else
        # A new file gets the usual umask-based mode, not mktemp's private 0600.
        chmod "$(printf '%o' $(( 0666 & ~$(umask) )))" "$tmp"
    fi
    render "$key" "$value" "$file" > "$tmp"
    if (( dry_run )); then
        echo "would be $result: $key"
    elif [[ $result == unchanged ]]; then
        echo "unchanged: $key"
    else
        mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
        tmp=''
        echo "$result: $key"
    fi
}

main "$@"

    [[ $value != *$'\n'* ]] || die 'values cannot contain newlines' 2

    acquire_lock "$file"
    local dir=.
    [[ $file == */* ]] && dir=${file%/*}
    tmp=$(mktemp "$dir/.setconf.XXXXXX")
    # Copy first so the replacement keeps the original permissions.
    if [[ -f $file ]]; then
        cp -p -- "$file" "$tmp"
    else
        # A new file gets the usual umask-based mode, not mktemp's private 0600.
        chmod "$(printf '%o' $(( 0666 & ~$(umask) )))" "$tmp"
    fi
    if (( delete )); then
        render_delete "$key" "$file" > "$tmp"
    else
        render "$key" "$value" "$file" > "$tmp"
    fi
    if (( dry_run )); then
        echo "would be $result: $key"
    elif [[ $result == unchanged || $result == absent ]]; then
        echo "$result: $key"
    else
        mv -f -- "$tmp" "$file"
        tmp=''
        echo "$result: $key"
    fi
}

main "$@"

lessons.title: Project: a bounded parallel job runner
body: prun.sh runs a command once per input, with at most JOBS running at a time: printf '%s\n' a b c | prun.sh -j 2 -- gzip -k. Inputs arrive on stdin, one per line or NUL-separated with -0 so that any file name works.

Concurrency control uses wait -n -p: when JOBS are running, wait for any one to finish, record its status by input index through a PID-to-index associative array, and free the slot. This keeps the pool full without polling or sleeping.

Every job writes stdout and stderr to its own file in a private temporary directory. After all jobs finish, outputs are printed in input order, so the result is deterministic even though completion order is not. The directory is removed by an EXIT trap.

Failures are not hidden: each failed input is reported with printf %q and its status (127 for a missing command), a summary goes to stderr, and the runner exits 1 if any job failed. Arguments are passed as an array ("$@" followed by the input) — no eval, no sh -c string.

Tests use a helper job that records how many jobs are running at once, proving -j 1 is sequential, -j 2 never exceeds two and -j 3 really overlaps. Exercise levels — Beginner: run the tests. Intermediate: add -f (fail fast): once a failure has been observed — including failures among other jobs that have already ended when a slot is reaped — no new job starts, and skipped inputs are counted. Jobs already running are allowed to finish. Advanced: add per-job timeouts. The worked answer implements -f.
The mutation check lets one extra job start; the concurrency tests must fail.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# prun.sh: run COMMAND once per input with at most JOBS running at a time.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: prun.sh [-j JOBS] [-0] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]   (inputs on stdin, one per line or NUL-separated with -0)'
}

die() {
    echo "prun: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

out=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$out"' EXIT

# Wait for any one job, record its status by input index and free a slot.
collect() {
    local finished status=0
    wait -n -p finished || status=$?
    statuses[${index_of[$finished]}]=$status
    unset "index_of[$finished]"
    running=$((running - 1))
}

main() {
    local jobs=2 delimiter=$'\n' opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':j:0h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            j) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-j needs a positive number' 2
               jobs=$OPTARG ;;
            0) delimiter='' ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }

    local inputs=() statuses=() i running=0 ok=0 failed=0
    local -A index_of=()
    mapfile -t -d "$delimiter" inputs
    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        (( running < jobs )) || collect
        # Each job writes to its own file, so concurrent output never interleaves.
        "$@" "${inputs[i]}" > "$out/$i" 2>&1 &
        index_of[$!]=$i
        running=$((running + 1))
    done
    while (( running )); do collect; done

    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        cat -- "$out/$i"
        if (( statuses[i] == 0 )); then
            ok=$((ok + 1))
        else
            failed=$((failed + 1))
            printf 'prun: %q failed with status %d\n' "${inputs[i]}" "${statuses[i]}" >&2
        fi
    done
    echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed" >&2
    (( failed == 0 ))
}

main "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# prun.sh: run COMMAND once per input with at most JOBS running at a time.
set -euo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: prun.sh [-j JOBS] [-0] [-f] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]   (inputs on stdin, one per line or NUL-separated with -0; -f stops starting jobs after a failure)'
}

die() {
    echo "prun: $1" >&2
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

out=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$out"' EXIT

record() {
    statuses[${index_of[$1]}]=$2
    unset "index_of[$1]"
    running=$((running - 1))
    (( $2 == 0 )) || any_failed=1
}

# Wait for any one job, record its status by input index and free a slot.
collect() {
    local finished status=0 pid
    wait -n -p finished || status=$?
    record "$finished" "$status"
    # Fail fast must also see failures among other jobs that have already ended.
    if (( fail_fast )); then
        for pid in "${!index_of[@]}"; do
            kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null && continue
            status=0
            wait "$pid" || status=$?
            record "$pid" "$status"
        done
    fi
}

main() {
    local jobs=2 delimiter=$'\n' fail_fast=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':j:0fh' opt; do
        case $opt in
            j) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-j needs a positive number' 2
               jobs=$OPTARG ;;
            0) delimiter='' ;;
            f) fail_fast=1 ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }

    local inputs=() statuses=() i running=0 ok=0 failed=0 skipped=0 any_failed=0
    local -A index_of=()
    mapfile -t -d "$delimiter" inputs
    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        (( running < jobs )) || collect
        (( fail_fast && any_failed )) && break
        # Each job writes to its own file, so concurrent output never interleaves.
        "$@" "${inputs[i]}" > "$out/$i" 2>&1 &
        index_of[$!]=$i
        running=$((running + 1))
    done
    while (( running )); do collect; done

    for i in "${!inputs[@]}"; do
        if [[ ! -v statuses[i] ]]; then
            skipped=$((skipped + 1))
            continue
        fi
        cat -- "$out/$i"
        if (( statuses[i] == 0 )); then
            ok=$((ok + 1))
        else
            failed=$((failed + 1))
            printf 'prun: %q failed with status %d\n' "${inputs[i]}" "${statuses[i]}" >&2
        fi
    done
    if (( skipped )); then
        echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed, $skipped skipped" >&2
    else
        echo "prun: $ok ok, $failed failed" >&2
    fi
    (( failed == 0 ))
}

main "$@"

lessons.title: Capstone: a verified, rotating backup tool
body: The capstone brings everything together in backup.sh SOURCE DEST: it creates a timestamped tar.gz of a directory, verifies it can be read, keeps the newest KEEP archives, supports a dry run and refuses to run twice at once. Treat it as a reference for structuring production shell tools.

Robustness: set -eEuo pipefail with an ERR trap reports the failing command and line; an EXIT trap removes the temporary archive and lock in every outcome; destructive operations use -- and quoted, checked paths; exit statuses distinguish usage (2), failure (1) and a held lock (75). Diagnostics go to stderr while stdout carries only the archive path, so callers can capture it.

Atomicity: tar writes into a mktemp file in the destination directory, tar -tzf reads it back, and only then mv publishes it under its final name. A crash or failure never leaves a truncated archive with a real-looking name, and an existing archive is never overwritten.

Testability: BACKUP_NOW overrides the clock, so tests produce exact names. Rotation relies on timestamps that sort lexicographically — a deliberate naming choice that makes glob order chronological on any Bash (GLOBSORT=name would make it explicit on 5.3). The rotation glob spells out the stamp shape, so backing up data never deletes archives of a different source named data-old; a dry run counts the archive it would create, so it lists exactly what a real run deletes. Tests restore an archive and compare it with diff -r, exercise rotation, dry run, locking, invalid input and a real tar failure caught by the ERR trap.

Exercise levels — Beginner: run the suite and trace one backup through the code. Intermediate: write a cksum manifest beside each archive and remove it during rotation. Advanced: add -V DEST to verify every archive against its manifest, report ok/corrupt/unverified and exit 1 on corruption without triggering the ERR trap. The worked answer does both; note how calling verify as an if condition keeps the ERR trap for genuine errors.

The mutation check makes rotation keep one archive too many; the suite must fail. Going further: add compression choice, exclusion patterns via an array of --exclude arguments and remote copies with rsync, keeping each feature tested.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh: create a verified, timestamped tar.gz of a directory and keep the newest KEEP.
set -eEuo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: backup.sh [-n] [-k KEEP] SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR   (-n: dry run; KEEP defaults to 5)'
}

log() { echo "backup: $*" >&2; }

die() {
    log "$1"
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

on_error() {
    local status=$?
    log "failed (status $status) at line ${BASH_LINENO[0]}: $BASH_COMMAND"
    exit "$status"
}
trap on_error ERR

tmp='' lock=''
cleanup() {
    [[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -f -- "$tmp"
    [[ -n $lock ]] && rmdir -- "$lock"
    return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# Delete all but the newest KEEP archives; timestamped names sort chronologically.
# The glob matches only this source's stamp shape, so another source named "$base-x" is never touched.
rotate() {
    local dest=$1 base=$2 keep=$3 dry_run=$4 archives old
    shopt -s nullglob
    archives=("$dest/$base"-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]T[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9].tar.gz)
    shopt -u nullglob
    (( ${#archives[@]} > keep )) || return 0
    for old in "${archives[@]:0:${#archives[@]} - keep}"; do
        if (( dry_run )); then
            echo "would delete ${old##*/}"
        else
            rm -f -- "$old"
            log "deleted ${old##*/}"
        fi
    done
}

main() {
    local keep=5 dry_run=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':nk:h' opt; do
        case $opt in
            n) dry_run=1 ;;
            k) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-k needs a positive number' 2
               keep=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    (( $# == 2 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
    local source=${1%/} dest=${2%/}
    [[ -d $source ]] || die "source is not a directory: $source"
    [[ -d $dest ]] || die "destination is not a directory: $dest"

    local base stamp name parent
    base=${source##*/}
    parent=.
    [[ $source == */* ]] && parent=${source%/*}
    stamp=${BACKUP_NOW:-$(date +%Y%m%dT%H%M%S)}
    [[ $stamp =~ ^[0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6}$ ]] || die "bad timestamp: $stamp" 2
    name=$base-$stamp.tar.gz

    if (( dry_run )); then
        echo "would create $name"
        # The new archive would be one of the kept ones, so one fewer old archive survives.
        rotate "$dest" "$base" $((keep - 1)) 1
        return
    fi

    if mkdir -- "$dest/.backup.lock" 2>/dev/null; then
        lock=$dest/.backup.lock
    else
        die "another backup is running in $dest" 75
    fi
    [[ ! -e $dest/$name ]] || die "$name already exists"

    tmp=$(mktemp "$dest/.$name.XXXXXX")
    tar -czf "$tmp" -C "$parent" -- "$base"
    tar -tzf "$tmp" > /dev/null
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$dest/$name"
    tmp=''
    log "created $name"
    rotate "$dest" "$base" "$keep" 0
    echo "$dest/$name"
}

main "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh: create a verified, timestamped tar.gz of a directory and keep the newest KEEP.
set -eEuo pipefail

usage() {
    echo 'usage: backup.sh [-n] [-k KEEP] SOURCE_DIR DEST_DIR | -V DEST_DIR   (-n: dry run; KEEP defaults to 5; -V: verify checksums)'
}

log() { echo "backup: $*" >&2; }

die() {
    log "$1"
    exit "${2:-1}"
}

on_error() {
    local status=$?
    log "failed (status $status) at line ${BASH_LINENO[0]}: $BASH_COMMAND"
    exit "$status"
}
trap on_error ERR

tmp='' lock=''
cleanup() {
    [[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -f -- "$tmp"
    [[ -n $lock ]] && rmdir -- "$lock"
    return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# Delete all but the newest KEEP archives; timestamped names sort chronologically.
# The glob matches only this source's stamp shape, so another source named "$base-x" is never touched.
rotate() {
    local dest=$1 base=$2 keep=$3 dry_run=$4 archives old
    shopt -s nullglob
    archives=("$dest/$base"-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]T[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9].tar.gz)
    shopt -u nullglob
    (( ${#archives[@]} > keep )) || return 0
    for old in "${archives[@]:0:${#archives[@]} - keep}"; do
        if (( dry_run )); then
            echo "would delete ${old##*/}"
        else
            rm -f -- "$old" "$old.cksum"
            log "deleted ${old##*/}"
        fi
    done
}

# Compare every archive with its recorded checksum; fail if any differ.
verify() {
    local dest=$1 archive name corrupt=0
    shopt -s nullglob
    for archive in "$dest"/*.tar.gz; do
        name=${archive##*/}
        if [[ ! -f $archive.cksum ]]; then
            echo "unverified $name"
        elif [[ $(cksum < "$archive") == "$(< "$archive.cksum")" ]]; then
            echo "ok $name"
        else
            echo "corrupt $name"
            corrupt=1
        fi
    done
    shopt -u nullglob
    (( corrupt == 0 ))
}

main() {
    local keep=5 dry_run=0 verify_only=0 opt OPTIND
    while getopts ':nk:Vh' opt; do
        case $opt in
            n) dry_run=1 ;;
            V) verify_only=1 ;;
            k) [[ $OPTARG =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || die '-k needs a positive number' 2
               keep=$OPTARG ;;
            h) usage; return ;;
            *) usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift $((OPTIND - 1))
    if (( verify_only )); then
        (( $# == 1 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
        [[ -d $1 ]] || die "destination is not a directory: $1"
        # Calling verify as a condition keeps the ERR trap for real errors only.
        if ! verify "${1%/}"; then
            log 'verification failed'
            exit 1
        fi
        return
    fi
    (( $# == 2 )) || { usage >&2; exit 2; }
    local source=${1%/} dest=${2%/}
    [[ -d $source ]] || die "source is not a directory: $source"
    [[ -d $dest ]] || die "destination is not a directory: $dest"

    local base stamp name parent
    base=${source##*/}
    parent=.
    [[ $source == */* ]] && parent=${source%/*}
    stamp=${BACKUP_NOW:-$(date +%Y%m%dT%H%M%S)}
    [[ $stamp =~ ^[0-9]{8}T[0-9]{6}$ ]] || die "bad timestamp: $stamp" 2
    name=$base-$stamp.tar.gz

    if (( dry_run )); then
        echo "would create $name"
        # The new archive would be one of the kept ones, so one fewer old archive survives.
        rotate "$dest" "$base" $((keep - 1)) 1
        return
    fi

    if mkdir -- "$dest/.backup.lock" 2>/dev/null; then
        lock=$dest/.backup.lock
    else
        die "another backup is running in $dest" 75
    fi
    [[ ! -e $dest/$name ]] || die "$name already exists"

    tmp=$(mktemp "$dest/.$name.XXXXXX")
    tar -czf "$tmp" -C "$parent" -- "$base"
    tar -tzf "$tmp" > /dev/null
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$dest/$name"
    tmp=''
    cksum < "$dest/$name" > "$dest/$name.cksum"
    log "created $name"
    rotate "$dest" "$base" "$keep" 0
    echo "$dest/$name"
}

main "$@"

cards.prompt: What does Python assignment copy?
cards.answer: Assignment binds a name to an object. It does not copy the object.

cards.prompt: When can a shallow list copy still share mutations?
cards.answer: When a nested mutable object is shared between the original and the copy.

cards.prompt: What state does a generator retain between yields?
cards.answer: Its execution position and local variables.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between iterable and iterator?
cards.answer: An iterable can produce an iterator; an iterator tracks traversal and supplies the next value.

cards.prompt: Does calling an async function execute its body immediately?
cards.answer: No. It creates a coroutine, which must be awaited or scheduled.

cards.prompt: Why is blocking I/O inside an async coroutine a problem?
cards.answer: It blocks the event-loop thread and prevents other tasks on that loop from progressing.

cards.prompt: Which dimensions does broadcasting compare first?
cards.answer: The trailing dimensions, working toward the leading dimensions.

cards.prompt: When are two broadcast dimensions compatible?
cards.answer: When their sizes match, or one of the sizes is 1.

cards.prompt: How do you make an independent NumPy slice?
cards.answer: Call .copy() on the slice.

cards.prompt: Why can writing through a NumPy view change another array?
cards.answer: The arrays share underlying memory.

cards.prompt: Why use keepdims=True in a reduction?
cards.answer: It preserves reduced axes as size-1 dimensions for predictable broadcasting.

cards.prompt: What is reduced by axis=1 in a 2D array?
cards.answer: The column dimension, yielding a result for each row.

cards.prompt: How do loc and iloc differ?
cards.answer: loc uses labels; iloc uses integer positions.

cards.prompt: How should you update a filtered set of pandas rows?
cards.answer: Use a single df.loc[mask, column] assignment.

cards.prompt: What catches an unexpected many-to-many merge?
cards.answer: Use merge(validate=...) with the intended key relationship.

cards.prompt: Why might a join unexpectedly inflate an aggregate?
cards.answer: Duplicate keys can multiply rows during the join.

cards.prompt: When should you use groupby transform?
cards.answer: When the result should align with each original row.

cards.prompt: How does groupby agg change the result’s granularity?
cards.answer: It usually yields one summary row per group.

cards.prompt: Can fitting a scaler on all data cause leakage?
cards.answer: Yes. Validation or test statistics can influence preprocessing.

cards.prompt: What does a scikit-learn Pipeline help protect during cross-validation?
cards.answer: It fits preprocessing and the estimator together within each training fold.

cards.prompt: What is precision?
cards.answer: The fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive.

cards.prompt: Why can accuracy mislead on imbalanced data?
cards.answer: A majority-only predictor can score well while missing the rare class.

cards.prompt: When is a time-aware split useful?
cards.answer: When deployment predicts future observations from past observations.

cards.prompt: Why should the test set not choose hyperparameters?
cards.answer: Repeated tuning to its score makes it a source of training feedback.

cards.prompt: Does backward() clear old gradients?
cards.answer: No. Gradients accumulate until cleared.

cards.prompt: What is a conventional optimizer step order?
cards.answer: Clear gradients; compute predictions and loss; call backward(); call optimizer.step().

cards.prompt: What does model.eval() change?
cards.answer: The training/evaluation behavior of modules such as dropout and batch normalization.

cards.prompt: What does torch.no_grad() change?
cards.answer: It disables gradient recording in its scope.

cards.prompt: Which dimension does torch.nn.Linear transform?
cards.answer: The last dimension.

cards.prompt: Why check prediction and target shapes before a loss?
cards.answer: Broadcasting may otherwise compute a valid but unintended comparison.

cards.prompt: What does RAII connect?
cards.answer: Resource acquisition and release to object construction and destruction.

cards.prompt: When is shared_ptr appropriate?
cards.answer: When shared ownership is a real requirement, rather than just to avoid deciding who owns a resource.

cards.prompt: Does std::move itself transfer ownership?
cards.answer: No. It casts the expression; an appropriate move operation may then transfer resources.

cards.prompt: Can you assume a moved-from std::string is empty?
cards.answer: No. It remains valid, but its value is generally unspecified.

cards.prompt: What does a mutex protect when used consistently?
cards.answer: A critical section and the shared invariant that all accesses obey.

cards.prompt: Does one atomic variable make a whole data structure thread-safe?
cards.answer: No. Compound invariants need an appropriate synchronization protocol.

cards.prompt: When does a deferred LINQ query execute?
cards.answer: When it is enumerated.

cards.prompt: Why materialize a LINQ query with ToList()?
cards.answer: To take a result snapshot or avoid repeated enumeration.

cards.prompt: Does async always start a new thread in C#?
cards.answer: No. async changes how the method handles suspension and continuation.

cards.prompt: Why avoid async void outside event handlers?
cards.answer: Callers cannot await completion and handle its exceptions through a returned Task.

cards.prompt: How does disposal differ from garbage collection?
cards.answer: Disposal releases resources deterministically; garbage collection reclaims managed memory at an unspecified time.

cards.prompt: When is await using appropriate?
cards.answer: For an IAsyncDisposable resource that needs asynchronous cleanup.

cards.prompt: Can two Go slices share mutations?
cards.answer: Yes, when their descriptors reference overlapping backing-array storage.

cards.prompt: When can append change a slice’s backing array?
cards.answer: When existing capacity is insufficient and a new array is allocated.

cards.prompt: When is a Go interface value nil?
cards.answer: When it has neither a dynamic type nor a dynamic value.

cards.prompt: What should an error-returning function return on success?
cards.answer: A literal nil error, rather than a typed nil pointer wrapped in an interface.

cards.prompt: What happens on receiving from a closed and drained channel?
cards.answer: It returns the element type’s zero value with ok=false.

cards.prompt: Who should generally close a Go channel?
cards.answer: The sending side, once all sends are complete.

cards.prompt: Does a JavaScript closure capture a frozen snapshot of mutable variables?
cards.answer: No. It retains access to lexical bindings and can observe updates.

cards.prompt: Why can two calls to a counter factory create independent counters?
cards.answer: Each call creates a separate lexical environment.

cards.prompt: When do promise reactions run relative to the current synchronous code?
cards.answer: After it completes, through the microtask queue.

cards.prompt: What happens if one input of Promise.all rejects?
cards.answer: The returned promise rejects; this does not automatically cancel the other operations.

cards.prompt: What does === compare for objects?
cards.answer: Object identity, without structural comparison.

cards.prompt: How does Object.is handle NaN?
cards.answer: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true.

cards.prompt: What normally happens when assigning a Rust String to another binding?
cards.answer: Ownership moves to the new binding.

cards.prompt: How do you explicitly duplicate a Rust String?
cards.answer: Call .clone() when an independent copy is needed.

cards.prompt: Does borrowing normally transfer ownership?
cards.answer: No. A reference borrows access for a limited lifetime.

cards.prompt: What is the core shared-versus-mutable borrowing rule?
cards.answer: Multiple shared references or one exclusive mutable reference during active borrows, subject to Rust’s rules.

cards.prompt: How do Option and Result differ?
cards.answer: Option encodes presence or absence; Result encodes success or a failure value.

cards.prompt: What does ? do on a Result in a compatible Result-returning function?
cards.answer: It extracts an Ok value or returns early with a converted Err.

cards.prompt: How is function application written in OCaml?
cards.answer: By placing arguments after the function, separated by spaces.

cards.prompt: What does partial application produce?
cards.answer: A function with some arguments already supplied.

cards.prompt: What does a variant type describe?
cards.answer: A value drawn from explicitly named alternatives, whose constructors may carry data.

cards.prompt: Why prefer a variant over loosely related flags?
cards.answer: It can encode valid alternatives while excluding invalid combinations.

cards.prompt: What are the two structural cases of an OCaml list?
cards.answer: The empty list [], or a head and tail x :: xs.

cards.prompt: When is a recursive call in tail position?
cards.answer: When its result is returned directly with no further work after the call.

cards.prompt: What two roles does Lean 4 combine?
cards.answer: Functional programming and interactive theorem proving.

cards.prompt: What values inhabit Nat?
cards.answer: The non-negative integers, including zero.

cards.prompt: What does h : P mean when P is a proposition?
cards.answer: h is a proof term of P.

cards.prompt: Why must a learning app treat sorry differently from a completed proof?
cards.answer: sorry supplies a placeholder that can be accepted with a warning without constructing the intended proof.

cards.prompt: What kind of equality does rfl use?
cards.answer: Definitional equality after Lean’s reductions.

cards.prompt: Why is the current proof goal useful after a tactic error?
cards.answer: It shows exactly which proposition remains and which hypotheses are available.

cards.prompt: Why repeat the same type parameter in several positions?
cards.answer: It expresses a type relationship: those positions use the same chosen type in a particular call.

cards.prompt: Why return Option<&T> from a slice lookup?
cards.answer: It represents absence and borrows the element without requiring it to be copied.

cards.prompt: What does a trait bound give a generic function?
cards.answer: A declared set of capabilities that the function can rely on.

cards.prompt: Does implementing a Rust trait imply shared field layout?
cards.answer: No. Types can implement the same behavior with different representations.

cards.prompt: What makes an iterator adapter run its computation?
cards.answer: A consumer requests elements, for example through collect, sum, or a loop.

cards.prompt: How do Vec iter and into_iter differ?
cards.answer: iter borrows elements; into_iter on the owned vector consumes it and yields owned elements.

cards.prompt: What does a Rust lifetime annotation describe?
cards.answer: Relationships and validity constraints between borrowed references.

cards.prompt: Why can annotations not fix returning a reference to a local value?
cards.answer: The local value is dropped; annotations do not extend its storage lifetime.

cards.prompt: Does a move closure wait for its thread?
cards.answer: No. It determines capture ownership; join waits for completion.

cards.prompt: What does a thread JoinHandle's join return?
cards.answer: A Result with the returned value on success or panic information on failure.

cards.prompt: Why include boundary cases in tests?
cards.answer: They check behavior where ordinary inputs may miss bugs, such as empty collections or exact thresholds.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between passing tests and a general proof?
cards.answer: Tests check selected cases; a proof establishes a stated proposition under its definitions and assumptions.

cards.prompt: Are OCaml record fields mutable by default?
cards.answer: No. A field must explicitly be declared mutable.

cards.prompt: Does an OCaml record update deep-copy referenced storage?
cards.answer: No. It constructs a new record while retaining the other field values, which may refer to shared storage.

cards.prompt: What does a repeated OCaml type variable express?
cards.answer: The corresponding positions share the same chosen type within that use of the function.

cards.prompt: Why must f accept and return the same type in apply_twice?
cards.answer: The first result is passed to f again.

cards.prompt: Which argument receives the accumulator in fold_left's combining function?
cards.answer: The first argument.

cards.prompt: Why can fold_left and fold_right differ for subtraction?
cards.answer: Their nesting and argument order differ, and subtraction is not associative.

cards.prompt: What does an abstract type in a module signature hide?
cards.answer: Its concrete representation and any type equality that has not been exposed.

cards.prompt: How can clients create values of an abstract type?
cards.answer: Through operations exported by the signature, such as zero or a constructor function.

cards.prompt: What does an OCaml functor accept and return?
cards.answer: It accepts a module matching a signature and produces a module.

cards.prompt: Why use a module parameter rather than pass one value to every function?
cards.answer: It groups shared type/operation dependencies so several definitions can use the same contract.

cards.prompt: How do result's two constructors differ?
cards.answer: Ok carries a success value; Error carries a failure value.

cards.prompt: When use Result.bind rather than Result.map?
cards.answer: Use bind when the next successful step can itself return a result and fail.

cards.prompt: What cases are needed to pattern-match on Nat?
cards.answer: Zero and successor.

cards.prompt: Why is recursion on the predecessor a useful Lean starting point?
cards.answer: It follows the inductive structure and supplies a structurally smaller recursive argument.

cards.prompt: What evidence is needed to prove P ∧ Q?
cards.answer: A proof of P and a proof of Q.

cards.prompt: How does conjunction differ from disjunction when constructing evidence?
cards.answer: Conjunction needs both sides; disjunction needs a selected side and its proof.

cards.prompt: How do you use h : ∀ n, P n to prove P 5?
cards.answer: Apply h to 5.

cards.prompt: What does evidence for an existential proposition contain?
cards.answer: A witness and a proof that the witness satisfies the stated property.

cards.prompt: How do you request the reverse direction of a Lean rewrite?
cards.answer: Use rw [← h] for the equality h.

cards.prompt: How does rewriting differ from definitional equality?
cards.answer: Rewriting uses an equality proof; definitional equality comes from Lean's reductions.

cards.prompt: What two cases arise from induction on Nat?
cards.answer: Zero and successor, with an induction hypothesis for the predecessor in the successor case.

cards.prompt: Why can a recursive definition guide an induction proof?
cards.answer: Its cases identify how to reduce the expression and where the smaller-case hypothesis applies.

cards.prompt: What does Lean generate for a structure declaration?
cards.answer: A constructor, field projections, and supporting eliminators/theorems.

cards.prompt: How can a Lean structure express an invariant beyond field types?
cards.answer: Include a corresponding proof field or establish the invariant through separate definitions and theorems.

cards.prompt: What does a declaration provide?
cards.answer: An interface a caller can compile against A translation unit is preprocessed and compiled; the linker resolves definitions across object files. Headers expose declarations. Build settings and the selected language standard are part of reproducibility. Defining ordinary non-inline functions in shared headers can violate the one-definition rule.

cards.prompt: Divide a greeting function between a header, an implementation, and a caller. Explain which file needs the definition.
cards.answer: Put its declaration in the header, its definition in one source file, and include the header at the call site. Link both source files' object files.

cards.prompt: Which declaration explicitly initializes a local int to zero?
cards.answer: int count{}; Types determine representation and allowed operations. A reference aliases an existing object; a pointer may be null or reseated. const constrains access through a particular expression. Brace initialization rejects certain narrowing conversions; automatic variables of fundamental type still need deliberate initialization.

cards.prompt: Explain const int*, int* const, and why reading an uninitialized ordinary local int is invalid.
cards.answer: const int* prevents writes through that pointer; int* const prevents reseating the pointer. Reading an indeterminate ordinary local int does not produce a valid assumed zero.

cards.prompt: Can vector reallocation invalidate element references?
cards.answer: Yes vector stores contiguous elements; reallocation can invalidate pointers, references, and iterators to its elements. array has fixed size; string owns character storage. Iterators mark positions, and end marks a boundary rather than an element.

cards.prompt: Compare vector and list for indexed access and stable element references. Explain a safe way to revisit a vector element after growth.
cards.answer: Use vector for efficient indexed access and locality. A list offers different reference stability but no constant-time indexed access. Keep an index and reacquire the vector element after mutation, provided the intended element's position remains valid.

cards.prompt: What determines member initialization order?
cards.answer: Their declaration order A class should make invalid states difficult to create. Members initialize in declaration order, regardless of initializer-list order. Prefer member initializers for simple defaults and use constructors when validation or dependencies require work.

cards.prompt: Design a range class requiring start <= end and explain where to reject invalid input.
cards.answer: Validate in the constructor or a factory before publishing the object. Declare dependent members after the members they depend on. Preserve the invariant in every mutating operation.

cards.prompt: What should control a formatted read loop?
cards.answer: The success of extraction Stream extraction can fail without yielding a valid value. eof, fail, and bad represent different states. A robust loop checks the extraction operation. Formatting flags can persist, while width commonly applies to the next formatted insertion.

cards.prompt: Design a line-based numeric parser that rejects trailing non-space text.
cards.answer: Read a complete line, parse it with an istringstream, confirm extraction succeeded, then confirm only whitespace remains. Return an explicit failure rather than reusing an old value.

cards.prompt: Does std::remove shrink a vector?
cards.answer: No Standard algorithms operate on iterator ranges with stated requirements. A half-open range excludes its end. erase-remove uses an algorithm to partition retained values and a container operation to change size. Comparators must satisfy their ordering contract.

cards.prompt: Describe how to remove all even integers and why a comparator using <= is unsuitable for ordinary sorting.
cards.answer: Use erase with the range returned by remove_if, or a supported erase_if facility. A sort comparator needs strict ordering; <= reports an element less than itself.

cards.prompt: What is the rule-of-zero preference?
cards.answer: Delegate lifetime to resource-managing members Copying an owner needs a deliberate policy: independent ownership, shared ownership, or disallowed copying. The rule of zero uses members whose own types manage resources. A moved-from object's permitted use follows its type contract rather than a universal empty-state assumption.

cards.prompt: Design an owning buffer without manual new/delete and state its copy semantics.
cards.answer: Store a vector of bytes and rely on its value semantics. Copies own independent element storage; moves follow vector's contract. If copying must be forbidden, delete it explicitly.

cards.prompt: What does conventional postfix increment return?
cards.answer: The previous value Overloading changes behavior for permitted operators, not their precedence or operand count. Assignment and compound assignment should have coherent return and mutation contracts. Free functions permit symmetric conversions where a member-only operator may not.

cards.prompt: Specify prefix and postfix increment for a small counter and explain their different return values.
cards.answer: Prefix increments and returns the updated object by reference. Postfix takes an unused int parameter, saves the old value, increments, and returns the saved value.

cards.prompt: What property must a returned element reference satisfy?
cards.answer: Its storage remains alive for its use operator[] models element access; operator() models calling an object; operator-> supports member access through a pointer-like interface. Accessors must state bounds, const behavior, and the lifetime of returned references. These operators cannot make destroyed storage valid.

cards.prompt: Design a callable multiplier and a checked two-element subscript interface. State how const access differs.
cards.answer: Store the multiplier factor and return factor*x from operator(). Check bounds for the custom subscript, return an element reference from a live owner, and provide const access that prevents writes.

cards.prompt: What does the strong exception guarantee promise?
cards.answer: Failure leaves the operation's state unchanged Stack unwinding destroys completed automatic objects. Catch exceptions by const reference when appropriate. A basic guarantee preserves invariants; a strong guarantee leaves state unchanged on failure. Destructors should not let exceptions escape during unwinding.

cards.prompt: Plan a strong-guarantee replacement operation and explain rethrowing from a catch block.
cards.answer: Prepare the new value without changing the old state, then commit with an appropriate nonthrowing operation. Use throw; to rethrow the current exception without slicing it.

cards.prompt: Does a binary-mode stream define a portable object format?
cards.answer: No RAII closes streams, but opening, reading, writing, flushing, and finalizing can fail. Text and binary modes are not an application format. Serializing raw object bytes can embed pointers, padding, and machine-specific representation.

cards.prompt: Specify a portable file record for a name and count, including version, encoding, lengths, and truncated-input behavior.
cards.answer: Use an explicit format with a version, UTF-8 text, fixed-width integer encoding, defined byte order, and checked lengths. Reject incomplete records rather than treating them as valid defaults.

cards.prompt: Why can a function-like macro be risky?
cards.answer: It may repeat argument evaluation Macros do not obey ordinary function evaluation or scope rules. A function-like macro may evaluate an argument more than once. Include guards prevent repeated header inclusion; conditional compilation selects source before compilation. Prefer typed functions and constexpr values where possible.

cards.prompt: Replace a numeric square macro and describe a legitimate use for conditional compilation.
cards.answer: Use a typed or constrained function for square. Conditional compilation can select a platform-specific declaration, with each selected path built and checked separately.

cards.prompt: Where is an unnamed namespace helper normally visible?
cards.answer: Within its translation unit Namespaces group names and avoid collisions. An unnamed namespace gives internal linkage within a translation unit. A namespace alias shortens a qualified name. A global using directive in a public header pollutes clients' lookup environment.

cards.prompt: Organize a library namespace, a private source-file helper, and a public class split across header and implementation.
cards.answer: Put the public class in a named namespace, the private helper in an unnamed namespace in the source file, and include a guarded declaration header. Keep client lookup explicit.

cards.prompt: When must required template operations be valid?
cards.answer: For the chosen instantiation A template's operations must be valid for each instantiated type. Type deduction and overload resolution select implementations under specific rules. Concepts describe requirements and can improve diagnostics. Template definitions normally need to be visible when instantiated.

cards.prompt: Design a reusable sum operation and state its requirement and identity value.
cards.answer: Require a compatible addition operation and a deliberate initial value. Decide whether heterogeneous elements or narrowing conversions are allowed; use a concept or explicit contract rather than assuming all types behave alike.

cards.prompt: What can copying a derived object into a base value cause?
cards.answer: Object slicing Virtual functions dispatch through a base interface. Deleting a derived object through a base pointer ordinarily requires a virtual base destructor. Copying a derived value into a base value slices away the derived part. Ownership and polymorphic behavior are separate choices.

cards.prompt: Choose a storage model for heterogeneous shapes and explain how destruction remains safe.
cards.answer: Use owning smart pointers to a base with a suitable virtual destructor, or an explicit value-oriented alternative such as variant. Document whether copying is supported through cloning or disallowed.

cards.prompt: Can a worker pool still deadlock?
cards.answer: Yes A pool bounds active workers, but its queued work also needs bounds. Cancellation is cooperative unless the operation supports another mechanism. Shutdown must define how queued and running tasks finish, propagate failure, and release captured resources.

cards.prompt: Design shutdown for a bounded task pool and a policy for nested tasks.
cards.answer: Stop accepting work, choose drain or cancellation for queued tasks, signal workers, and join them. Avoid blocking workers on dependent work that requires exhausted workers; support a different scheduling strategy or nonblocking continuation.

cards.prompt: Does one TCP read necessarily match one sender write?
cards.answer: No TCP sequences bytes, acknowledges progress, retransmits when necessary, and controls flow and congestion. It does not preserve the boundaries of application writes. A received prefix is not automatically a complete application message.

cards.prompt: Design a length-prefixed protocol that handles partial headers and payloads safely.
cards.answer: Accumulate the fixed-size header, validate the length against a limit, then accumulate exactly that payload length. Handle EOF and errors without accepting truncated messages.

cards.prompt: What is a Rust crate?
cards.answer: A compilation unit A package is a Cargo-managed project containing targets; a crate is a compilation unit. A lockfile records resolved dependency versions under the project's policy. Features select compile-time capabilities and should be checked in supported combinations.

cards.prompt: Plan a small library with a binary client and describe the commands to check, test, and build it.
cards.answer: Keep reusable functions in the library and the entry point in the binary. Use cargo check, cargo test, and cargo build under a recorded toolchain and dependency policy. Multifile project work requires a project runner, not a single-file slot.

cards.prompt: Can shadowing change the binding's type?
cards.answer: Yes let introduces a binding; mut permits assignment through that binding. Shadowing introduces another binding and can change its type. const values require a type and a constant-compatible expression. A block is an expression whose final expression can supply its value.

cards.prompt: Explain the type and value after that shadowing, then contrast reassignment through mut.
cards.answer: The new input is a usize with value 2. Reassignment through a mutable binding must keep that binding's type; shadowing can introduce a different type.

cards.prompt: Which conversion expresses possible failure?
cards.answer: TryFrom Integer width and signedness affect representation. as casts follow specified conversion behavior rather than universally checking for overflow. TryFrom expresses a fallible conversion. char is a Unicode scalar value, while a byte is an eight-bit value.

cards.prompt: Choose a conversion from i32 input to u8 when out-of-range values should be rejected.
cards.answer: Use u8::try_from(input) and handle the Result. Reject negative or greater-than-255 values explicitly; avoid a silent narrowing cast when validation is required.

cards.prompt: What must value-producing if branches ordinarily agree on?
cards.answer: A compatible result type if and match can produce values when their branches agree on type. for iterates through IntoIterator; loop can return through break with a value. A semicolon commonly changes a final expression into a statement whose contribution is unit.

cards.prompt: Design a loop returning the first even value in a bounded sequence, with an explicit missing case.
cards.answer: Use iterator find or a loop carrying an Option result. Ensure every exit has the intended return type; do not assume the sequence contains a match.

cards.prompt: Which receiver permits an exclusive borrowed update?
cards.answer: &mut self Struct fields combine data; impl groups inherent methods; enum variants encode alternatives. A method receiver chooses borrowed, mutable, or owned access. Pattern matching destructures values and must respect moves and borrows.

cards.prompt: Choose receivers for reading a length, appending text, and consuming a buffer into bytes.
cards.answer: Use shared borrowing for observation, mutable borrowing for updates, and owned self when the operation consumes the buffer. Match enum cases exhaustively.

cards.prompt: Are arbitrary String byte indices always valid UTF-8 boundaries?
cards.answer: No Vec owns growable storage; String owns UTF-8 bytes; HashMap owns keys and values under its type parameters. References into mutable collections constrain later mutation. String byte offsets must lie on UTF-8 boundaries; integer indexing does not supply a universal character operation.

cards.prompt: Explain how to iterate Unicode scalar values and how to safely observe a vector's optional first value.
cards.answer: Use chars() for scalar values, with grapheme handling delegated to an appropriate library when needed. Use first() to get an Option reference and avoid mutation that conflicts with the borrow.

cards.prompt: Does a source file's presence automatically make its items public?
cards.answer: No Modules group names and control visibility. pub exposes an item subject to its surrounding visibility; use brings paths into scope; re-exporting can provide a stable public API. Files implement module organization but are not interchangeable with crates.

cards.prompt: Design a public parser interface with private implementation helpers.
cards.answer: Expose the parse operation and public result types from a documented module or re-export. Keep helper functions private and test their behavior through stable interfaces where practical.

cards.prompt: What should represent expected parse failure?
cards.answer: A Result error Result and Option make ordinary outcomes explicit. ? propagates compatible failure. panic reports a failure outside the ordinary return contract, with unwind or abort behavior depending on configuration. unwrap is only justified under a known invariant or explicit failure policy.

cards.prompt: Design a parser returning a descriptive error and explain error conversion with From.
cards.answer: Return Result from the parser, propagate lower-level errors through ? with a compatible conversion or explicit mapping, and retain useful context. Avoid claiming every panic can be caught under abort settings.

cards.prompt: Does move automatically imply only one call?
cards.answer: No A closure can borrow or own captured values. move changes capture ownership; it does not by itself make the closure callable only once. Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce describe how calling uses the environment, with FnOnce consuming it when necessary.

cards.prompt: Compare a move closure reading a captured string with one returning that owned string.
cards.answer: The reading closure can support repeated calls; returning the captured owned string consumes it and requires a once-call contract. Choose bounds according to the operation rather than the presence of move.

cards.prompt: Does dyn Trait itself imply reference counting?
cards.answer: No A generic trait bound commonly enables monomorphized code; dyn Trait represents runtime dispatch under dyn-compatibility rules. A trait object can be borrowed or owned through a pointer such as Box. Dynamic dispatch does not automatically choose shared ownership.

cards.prompt: Explain when a heterogeneous list might need trait objects rather than one generic element type.
cards.answer: Different concrete implementations can be stored through a common dyn-compatible interface. Choose owned or borrowed storage deliberately; a single generic T represents one concrete instantiation, not arbitrary unrelated values in one vector.

cards.prompt: What does Iterator::Item describe?
cards.answer: The implementation's yielded item type A generic parameter lets an interface be instantiated with chosen types; an associated type names a type selected by an implementation. Iterator uses Item to specify what next yields. Operator traits and formatting traits define specific behavior contracts.

cards.prompt: Contrast a conversion-like generic trait with an iterator's associated Item and explain Debug versus Display.
cards.answer: Generic target types can express distinct conversion relationships; Item describes the output selected by that iterator implementation. Debug is diagnostic formatting, while Display is a user-facing format chosen by the type.

cards.prompt: Does a Weak reference keep its target alive?
cards.answer: No Box owns a heap value; Rc shares ownership within a single-threaded setting; Arc supports atomic reference counting across suitable thread boundaries. RefCell checks borrow rules at runtime. Weak references do not keep the target alive and can help avoid reference-counted ownership cycles.

cards.prompt: Design parent-child links with ownership flowing from parent to child.
cards.answer: Use strong ownership for children and weak observing links for parents under the intended model. Upgrade a Weak when needed and handle the target's absence. Shared ownership does not by itself permit arbitrary mutation.

cards.prompt: What can an extra live sender prevent?
cards.answer: Receiver disconnection detection A channel transfers messages; a mutex protects shared state. Send and Sync describe type-level cross-thread safety conditions. Joining establishes a thread completion boundary; a detached thread can outlive borrowed resources unless its API rules prevent it.

cards.prompt: Plan shutdown for several producers and a worker, including blocking and failure behavior.
cards.answer: Close or drop all sender handles under the API contract, drain or cancel pending work by policy, and join the worker. Bound the queue where supported and report worker failure rather than waiting indefinitely without a contract.

cards.prompt: Does writing async automatically make a blocking call nonblocking?
cards.answer: No Calling an async function constructs a future; polling drives it toward completion. await can suspend the current task while another progresses. The runtime and libraries determine scheduling and I/O support. Blocking work inside a task can still block an executor thread.

cards.prompt: Explain the difference between constructing a future, awaiting it, and spawning it.
cards.answer: Construction creates the computation; await drives or cooperates in driving it within another future; spawning schedules an independent task under a runtime's API and lifetime contract. A single-file runner may lack that runtime dependency.

cards.prompt: Does a positive-only guard handle every Some value?
cards.answer: No Patterns can destructure structs, enums, and tuples, bind references, and apply guards. Exhaustive matching keeps alternatives explicit. A guard checks an additional condition; it does not necessarily provide full exhaustiveness for the variant alone.

cards.prompt: Design an exhaustive classification of Option<i32> into missing, positive, and nonpositive.
cards.answer: Handle None, a guarded Some for positive values, and a remaining Some arm. Keep bindings and borrow/move behavior consistent with how the input is used later.

cards.prompt: Does unsafe disable all Rust checks?
cards.answer: No unsafe enables specified operations while ordinary Rust rules still apply. Raw pointers, foreign interfaces, and low-level representation require valid lifetime, alignment, aliasing, and bounds. A safe wrapper must ensure every supported caller meets those preconditions.

cards.prompt: List preconditions for turning a raw pointer and length into a slice.
cards.answer: The region must be valid for the whole access, correctly aligned, initialized as required, within supported size limits, and obey aliasing and lifetime rules. Encapsulate and document the argument rather than scattering unsafe blocks.

cards.prompt: What should a macro contract include?
cards.answer: Accepted syntax and evaluation behavior Declarative macros match token patterns and expand code. Procedural macros execute compile-time transformations through a separate crate setup. Attributes supply metadata or compile-time behavior; cfg selects code. A macro is useful when ordinary functions or generics cannot express the syntax contract.

cards.prompt: Design the contract of a small vector-building macro and name tests for it.
cards.answer: Document accepted token forms, evaluation order/count, empty input, trailing separators, and result type. Compile examples and failure cases under the recorded toolchain; keep ordinary runtime behavior in functions when possible.

cards.prompt: What do integration tests emphasize?
cards.answer: The public interfaces working together Unit tests target modules; integration tests exercise public interfaces; documentation examples can be checked by the toolchain. should_panic describes a specific failure expectation, not general correctness. Benchmarks need a supported harness and a representative workload.

cards.prompt: Plan unit, integration, and documentation checks for a parser package.
cards.answer: Check small parser cases and errors, exercise public entry points and binary behavior, and validate examples where supported. Record toolchain, features, and dependency versions. Keep performance comparison separate from ordinary correctness tests.

cards.prompt: Where should diagnostics normally go in this contract?
cards.answer: stderr Arguments, environment, files, exit codes, stdout, and stderr are separate channels. A small reusable core makes the binary easier to test. Input encoding and error context matter; reading a whole file is not always appropriate for unbounded input.

cards.prompt: Design a case-sensitive line search accepting a pattern and text input.
cards.answer: Validate arguments, separate a pure matching function, stream or bound input as appropriate, send records to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, and document exit codes and text encoding.

cards.prompt: Does a type alias create a distinct new type?
cards.answer: No Rust editions select language compatibility rules; they do not automatically update all dependencies. Semantic-version expectations, features, MSRV, and deprecations form a library compatibility policy. A type alias creates another name, while a newtype can create a distinct contract.

cards.prompt: Plan a dependency upgrade and explain why a newtype can prevent accidental unit mixing.
cards.answer: Check supported toolchain and feature combinations, compile and test interfaces, and review changed APIs. Wrap a value in a distinct struct when type separation is required rather than only renaming it with an alias.

cards.prompt: What makes a function type dependent?
cards.answer: Its result type can mention an input Lean checks terms against types, and types themselves have sorts. Universe parameters express reusable definitions without one fixed universe level. Dependent function types can have a result type that refers to an input. A proposition's proof is checked as a term.

cards.prompt: Explain the difference between a constant result type and a result type depending on an argument.
cards.answer: An ordinary function can return the same type for every input; a dependent function can return a type that includes that input value. Universe levels classify types and must satisfy Lean's constraints.

cards.prompt: What does IO make explicit?
cards.answer: Effectful computation Pure definitions compute values; IO programs interact with the outside world. do notation organizes sequential effectful computations under a monadic interface. Lake manages projects and dependencies. A compiler check and a real process invocation test different behaviors.

cards.prompt: Describe a Lean executable's main interface and how to test its output without assuming every #eval is an application entry point.
cards.answer: Define main with an appropriate IO result, build/run it using the project's toolchain, and assert the process output and exit behavior. #eval evaluates a command in the elaboration context; it is a different interface.

cards.prompt: What does instance synthesis search for?
cards.answer: An implementation of the required class A type class packages an interface and Lean can synthesize an instance when required. Numeric literals and overloaded operations use such interfaces. Instances should express coherent behavior and avoid accidental ambiguity or unexpected search costs.

cards.prompt: Explain why an overloaded operation may fail even when a similarly named function exists.
cards.answer: Lean needs an instance satisfying the expected class for the chosen type. Define or import the intended instance, check type inference, and avoid adding unrelated instances merely to suppress an error.

cards.prompt: What does bind support here?
cards.answer: Sequencing a function that returns an Option A monad supplies return-like construction and bind-like sequencing under laws. Option stops on absence; Except propagates an error; IO sequences effects. do notation expresses such sequencing, but the chosen type determines what the sequencing means.

cards.prompt: Explain the difference between mapping a pure function over Option and binding a function returning Option.
cards.answer: Map transforms the contained value while preserving the context; bind lets the function introduce another optional computation and avoids nesting Option layers. Handle absence according to the intended result type.

cards.prompt: Which structure directly permits the next computation to depend on an earlier result?
cards.answer: Monadic bind Functor mapping transforms a result inside a context. Applicative combination applies contextual functions to contextual values. Monadic bind can choose the next computation from an earlier result. The laws let callers reason about composition without knowing every implementation detail.

cards.prompt: Classify a dependent two-stage lookup and explain why merely combining fixed independent operations is different.
cards.answer: A second lookup chosen using the first result needs bind-like dependency. Independent contextual computations can often be combined applicatively. The context's own error or effect behavior still matters.

cards.prompt: Can transformer ordering affect observed failure behavior?
cards.answer: Yes Monad transformers add an effect layer to another computation. State, reader environments, and error propagation interact with the order of layers. A chosen stack needs a documented result and failure contract; similar type names do not guarantee identical semantics.

cards.prompt: Explain why state-plus-error code needs a failure-state policy before choosing a transformer order.
cards.answer: Decide whether changes before failure remain observable, then inspect the resulting type and run the stack's operations accordingly. Test one successful path and one failure after a state update.

cards.prompt: What extra contract does Fin n express?
cards.answer: The index is less than n Dependent types can encode length or membership constraints. Fin n combines an index with evidence that it is within n. A checked runtime boundary can produce a value carrying evidence for later operations. Proof erasure and executable data have different roles.

cards.prompt: Plan a conversion from external Nat input to an index for a length-three container.
cards.answer: Check the bound at the input boundary and return an optional or error containing Fin 3 when valid. Use that validated index internally rather than repeating an unchecked access.

cards.prompt: What must a termination measure do at recursive calls?
cards.answer: Decrease under a well-founded relation Structural recursion follows an inductive input; more general recursion may need a decreasing measure or well-founded relation. A proof about recursion often follows the same cases. Fast execution and kernel reduction are related but distinct concerns.

cards.prompt: Specify base case, recursive case, and measure for a countdown returning a list.
cards.answer: Stop at zero; for a successor, produce one element and recurse on the predecessor. The natural-number input decreases, and an induction proof can follow zero/successor cases.

cards.prompt: What does #check primarily report?
cards.answer: The type of an expression Namespaces, sections, variables, imports, notation, and type inference organize Lean code. #check reports a type; #print inspects a declaration; errors and goals reveal missing constraints. A tactic script is accepted when it constructs an appropriate checked term.

cards.prompt: Describe a debugging procedure for a theorem-name or type mismatch.
cards.answer: Inspect the expected goal and hypothesis types, qualify the declaration, use #check to confirm its signature, and apply arguments in the required order. Avoid replacing a missing argument with a proof placeholder.

cards.prompt: What is the purpose of conv focusing?
cards.answer: Select the expression occurrence being transformed conv mode navigates a goal or expression before applying transformations. It helps control which occurrence changes when ordinary rewriting is too broad. The transformed expression must still be justified by Lean's checking rules.

cards.prompt: Explain why focused conversion can be preferable to a global rewrite and how to verify its effect.
cards.answer: Select the intended subexpression, apply a justified conversion, then inspect the resulting goal and close it with the remaining proof. Confirm the change did not target a different occurrence.

cards.prompt: Does an accepted sorry demonstrate completion of the intended proof?
cards.answer: No Classical reasoning and axioms may support proofs while computational behavior depends on their role. Inspect theorem dependencies when assumptions matter. sorry supplies a placeholder rather than the intended proof and must not count as a completed learning exercise.

cards.prompt: Explain how to distinguish a checked proof exercise from one using a placeholder or undeclared assumption.
cards.answer: Reject placeholders in the learner's exercise contract, inspect warnings and declaration dependencies, and state allowed assumptions and imports. Type-check under the pinned toolchain and project environment.

cards.prompt: What proves set inclusion?
cards.answer: A function transforming membership evidence Set membership is a proposition. Inclusion is a function taking membership evidence in one set to evidence in another. Equality of sets is commonly proved extensionally. Function injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity have distinct quantifier contracts.

cards.prompt: Describe both directions needed to prove two sets equal extensionally.
cards.answer: Choose an arbitrary element and prove its membership equivalence. Provide a function from each side's membership evidence to the other side, using definitions and hypotheses explicitly.

cards.prompt: Is natural subtraction identical to integer subtraction?
cards.answer: No Nat, Int, and other number types have different subtraction and divisibility behavior. A mathematical argument must be translated into exact hypotheses and available lemmas. Computation can discharge concrete cases, while symbolic claims require general proofs.

cards.prompt: Explain the difference between 2-5 in Nat and Int, then plan a divisibility proof.
cards.answer: Nat subtraction gives 0; Int subtraction gives -3. For divisibility, introduce a witness or use an appropriate theorem under the exact numeric type and hypotheses. Inspect lemma types before rewriting.

cards.prompt: Does associativity alone imply commutativity?
cards.answer: No Structures and type classes package operations together with laws. Semigroup, monoid, group, ring, and field assumptions enable different conclusions. Do not assume commutativity or division laws from a weaker structure. A general theorem should require only the laws it uses.

cards.prompt: Choose assumptions for proving that adding zero preserves a value and explain why cancellation may need more.
cards.answer: Require an additive identity law for the first claim. Cancellation depends on the relevant cancellative or group structure. Inspect the class assumptions rather than assuming all numeric-looking types are fields.

cards.prompt: What does eventual mean for natural-number at-top behavior?
cards.answer: The property holds beyond some threshold A filter expresses which sets of points count as sufficiently large or near a situation. Limits become eventual-property statements through filters. At-top and neighborhood filters encode different notions of approach. Theorems require precise domain, codomain, and filter assumptions.

cards.prompt: Translate an eventual threshold property into ordinary quantified language.
cards.answer: There exists a threshold N such that for every n at least N the property holds. A limit additionally states that values eventually enter every required neighborhood of the target.

cards.prompt: What must precede applying a continuity theorem?
cards.answer: Matching its structures and hypotheses Continuity relates neighborhoods in domain and codomain; compactness, closure, and convergence have separate definitions. Metric-space intuitions require the appropriate structure. Formalization should state assumptions before selecting the theorem.

cards.prompt: Outline a continuity proof by composition and identify what must be checked.
cards.answer: Confirm topological structures, domains, and hypotheses; prove the component functions continuous; then apply the appropriate composition theorem. A picture of the graph is intuition, not a checked proof.

cards.prompt: Can every Mathlib calculus example run with only Lean core imports?
cards.answer: No Differentiability, integrability, measure, domain, and regularity assumptions determine which calculus theorems apply. A formal proof cannot silently omit them. Mathlib is a project dependency; standalone Lean core does not provide every mathematical theorem used by these chapters.

cards.prompt: Plan a Mathlib-backed proof using a derivative rule.
cards.answer: Pin Lean and Mathlib together, inspect the exact theorem signature, discharge domain and differentiability requirements, then compose the rule. Validate in that project; do not advertise a core-only runner as equivalent.

cards.prompt: Does changing a basis necessarily change the abstract linear map?
cards.answer: No A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication under specified module assumptions. Bases, dimension, matrices, and invertibility have different contracts. Coordinates depend on a basis; a matrix is not the abstract map itself.

cards.prompt: State the two preservation laws of a linear map and explain what a basis contributes.
cards.answer: The map sends x+y to f(x)+f(y) and a scalar multiple a*x to a*f(x). A basis chooses coordinates and lets a compatible finite-dimensional map be represented by a matrix.

cards.prompt: Must every call to a constexpr function execute at compile time?
cards.answer: No constexpr permits appropriate constant evaluation and can also support runtime calls. A constant expression must satisfy language restrictions. const describes immutability through a contract; it does not by itself mean the initializer was evaluated at compile time.
