cards.prompt: Which statement is correct for Project: tiny vision training system?
cards.answer: Build a deterministic CPU image classifier with explicit input shapes, train/evaluation separation, loss diagnostics, a checkpoint and tests that reload and reproduce predictions.

cards.prompt: What mistake must you avoid in project: tiny vision training system?
cards.answer: Transposing image shape conventions can retain element count while breaking semantics.

cards.prompt: What output shape does a valid convolution produce?
cards.answer: (H - kh + 1) × (W - kw + 1) for an H × W input and kh × kw kernel.

cards.prompt: Which statement is correct for Project: masked attention text model?
cards.answer: Build a tiny attention text classifier with a fixed vocabulary, unknown/padding IDs, masking, trained weights and checkpoint tests. Explain the model limitations and avoid claims about large language models.

cards.prompt: What mistake must you avoid in project: masked attention text model?
cards.answer: Using a real token as the unknown ID conflates inputs.

cards.prompt: What does an attention mask mark?
cards.answer: Real tokens with 1 and padding with 0.

cards.prompt: Which statement is correct for Project: time-aware forecasting evaluation?
cards.answer: Build rolling-origin evaluation that uses only historical observations, compares a baseline and candidate, and tests future-perturbation invariance of earlier predictions.

cards.prompt: What mistake must you avoid in project: time-aware forecasting evaluation?
cards.answer: Selecting the target observation as an input leaks the future.

cards.prompt: What is the signature of look-ahead leakage in forecasting evaluation?
cards.answer: Implausibly small errors, especially a perfect last-value baseline.

cards.prompt: Which statement is correct for Project: train, serve and monitor?
cards.answer: Build a bounded local model service with schema validation, batch/online parity, health checks, artifact checksums, drift simulation and an operational rollback runbook.

cards.prompt: What mistake must you avoid in project: train, serve and monitor?
cards.answer: Treating absent artifact metadata as valid bypasses the release gate.

cards.prompt: Which HTTP-style status fits a well-formed request with the wrong fields?
cards.answer: 422 (unprocessable), distinct from 400 for malformed JSON.
Linking The linker combines object files and resolves external definitions. Compilation of one translation unit does not supply missing definitions.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in From source file to a running program.
cards.answer: Use the displayed command in a terminal with a C++ compiler. A missing compiler, a compile error, a linker error, and unexpected program output are different failures; diagnose the stage before changing code.
Initializes count to zero Empty braces value-initialize this scalar. Reading an uninitialized scalar is a separate and potentially invalid operation.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Initialization establishes a value.
cards.answer: Initialize every object deliberately. A default constructor may establish a class invariant; zero-filled bytes are not a universal substitute for construction.
Integer division happens before the cast The operand expression has already evaluated to the integer 3. Cast an operand before division.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Conversions can discard information.
cards.answer: Mixed signed/unsigned arithmetic follows the usual arithmetic conversions. Check representability before changing signedness or narrowing a value.
Unsigned arithmetic wraps; signed overflow is undefined The two arithmetic models have different contracts. Optimizers may assume signed overflow does not occur.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Integer arithmetic needs range arguments.
cards.answer: A test that happens to print a plausible number after signed overflow has not validated the program. Derive bounds and test values at the boundary.
No; intermediate rounding can change the result Machine arithmetic approximates real arithmetic. Intermediate rounding invalidates a general associativity assumption.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Floating-point answers depend on representation.
cards.answer: Check special values with facilities such as isfinite. Do not use exact equality as a general numerical accuracy test or assume every platform has the same floating representation.
Built-in && short-circuits after a false left operand Short-circuit evaluation gives the guard its safety. operator[] alone does not check the index.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Separate precedence from evaluation order.
cards.answer: Avoid depending on unsequenced side effects or an unspecified argument evaluation order. Extra parentheses can clarify grouping without establishing sequencing.
No; validate external values explicitly A cast is a conversion, not a parser with domain validation.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Use scoped enums for distinct domains.
cards.answer: An exhaustive switch communicates the intended state handling. Keep error states visible rather than treating every unknown integer as a valid enum.
char elements, which may be encoding units A string is a sequence of its character type. Unicode interpretation requires an encoding-aware layer.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Strings own characters.
cards.answer: Check encoding and boundary assumptions when processing external text. A byte position is not automatically a Unicode character boundary.
Zero reserve allocates storage without constructing elements or changing size.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Vectors manage contiguous sequences.
cards.answer: Growth can invalidate pointers, references, and iterators. Do not retain them across operations unless the precise invalidation rules permit it.
No; other valid mutable aliases may exist Const qualification governs access through the qualified path, not every alias to the object.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Scope, lifetime, and const answer different questions.
cards.answer: Avoid returning references to local automatic objects. The name may have gone out of scope because the object itself has already been destroyed.
n is 0 and failbit is set Failed numeric extraction stores zero and sets failbit. Streams do not throw unless exceptions() was configured.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Reading input means checking every extraction.
cards.answer: Never use a value before testing the stream. A range check such as value >= 0 is a separate decision from a successful parse, and trailing characters after a valid prefix need an explicit policy.
std::initializer_list<int> Copy-list-initialization with auto deduces an initializer_list. Only direct-list auto x{1} deduces int in C++17.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in auto deduces a type from its initializer.
cards.answer: auto does not mean dynamic typing, and it can hide a proxy type such as std::vector<bool>::reference. Spell the type when the exact representation is part of the reasoning.
All three elements are copied into the parameter std::array is a class type with value semantics; only built-in arrays decay to pointers.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in std::array keeps a fixed extent with value semantics.
cards.answer: Passing a large std::array by value copies every element. Use const std::array<T, N>& for read-only access, and remember that the extent is fixed at compile time.
No; the temporary string is destroyed and v dangles A view does not extend the lifetime of what it refers to. The temporary dies at the end of the full-expression.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in string_view borrows characters it does not own.
cards.answer: The owner must outlive every view. Binding a view to a temporary std::string or keeping a view across a modification that reallocates the string leaves it dangling.
x & (1 == 0) Equality has higher precedence than bitwise AND, so the comparison happens first.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Bitwise, compound, and increment operators.
cards.answer: Shifting by a negative count or by at least the width of the promoted type is undefined. == binds tighter than &, so x & 1 == 0 means x & (1 == 0); parenthesize mask tests.
0 Omitted aggregate members use their default member initializers.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Structs group named members.
cards.answer: Brace initialization rejects narrowing and extra initializers. Members are laid out in declaration order with possible padding, so do not assume sizeof equals the sum of member sizes.

Two translation units define the same non-inline function, violating the one-definition rule Include guards work per translation unit only. Each .cpp gets its own copy of the definition, and the linker sees two.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Headers declare; source files define.
cards.answer: A non-inline function or variable definition in a header included by two source files violates the one-definition rule and usually fails at link time. Put definitions in one .cpp, or mark them inline.
The digits 0 to 9 have consecutive values Only decimal digit contiguity is guaranteed; letter contiguity is an ASCII property and char signedness is implementation-defined.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Characters are small integers with escapes.
cards.answer: Letters are not guaranteed contiguous, and whether plain char is signed is implementation-defined. Use std::isdigit and friends with a value converted to unsigned char.
No; both are the type double An alias declaration introduces a name, not a new type.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Type aliases rename a type, they do not create one.
cards.answer: An alias does not prevent mixing units. If the argument order of meters and seconds matters, a distinct struct type is needed to make the compiler reject a swap.
A property preserved across iterations An invariant connects initialization, each iteration, and the postcondition.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Loops maintain an invariant.
cards.answer: An empty range executes the body zero times. Choose an initial accumulator that gives the correct empty result and avoid unsigned reverse-loop underflow.
No The parameter is a separate object initialized from the argument.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Functions separate a contract from its caller.
cards.answer: State preconditions and failure behavior. A function called twice should not secretly rely on a previous call unless shared state is part of its documented contract.
An existing int object The reference parameter aliases the argument. Its lifetime cannot exceed the referenced object lifetime.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Reference parameters make mutation visible.
cards.answer: Never retain a reference parameter beyond the referenced object lifetime. The type alone does not make an asynchronous capture safe.
No The parameter list must distinguish ordinary function overloads; the expected return type does not solve that conflict.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Overloads are selected from types and conversions.
cards.answer: Keep overload sets coherent. Use explicit conversions at important boundaries, and test integral, floating, const, and reference arguments that exercise different candidates.
A well-founded measure decreases on each recursive call A base case alone is insufficient if recursive calls do not move toward it.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Recursion needs a terminating measure.
cards.answer: Validate inputs before converting signed values to unsigned recursion parameters. For large inputs, choose an iterative or divide-and-conquer algorithm with explicit resource bounds.
No; it stores its own captured value mutable permits modifying the closure copy; it does not convert that copy into a reference.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Lambda captures carry ownership choices.
cards.answer: For stored or asynchronous callbacks, identify who owns every capture. Capturing this does not extend the pointed-to object lifetime safely.
No; lifetime, type, alignment, and bounds still matter A dangling or otherwise invalid pointer may remain non-null.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Pointers need validity and extent.
cards.answer: Prefer ownership types for owners and bounded interfaces for ranges. A raw pointer by itself does not convey how many elements are available or who releases storage.
2 C++ sequences use zero-based indexing; the one-past position is not an element.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Array extent is part of an interface.
cards.answer: Choose a clear invalid-index policy. Bounds checking does not solve dangling lifetime, and unsigned index arithmetic can overflow before an access occurs.
To observe it without slicing or copying the exception object Reference binding preserves dynamic type and avoids an unnecessary copy.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Failure belongs in the function contract.
cards.answer: Do not silently replace every failure with a plausible success value. Preserve diagnostics and define which state changes have happened when failure is reported.
No State flags and buffered characters are separate. Recovery must handle both.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Parsing must check the stream state.
cards.answer: clear resets state flags; it does not remove an offending token. Recovery must also consume or otherwise handle invalid input, with a bound on work.
Yes; the attribute only documents intent Fall-through is the default switch behavior. The attribute affects diagnostics only.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in switch dispatches on integral values.
cards.answer: A jump to a case label may not skip the initialization of a variable still in scope. Put such declarations inside braces. Strings cannot be switched on directly.
Only the innermost loop break transfers control to the end of the smallest enclosing loop or switch.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in do-while, break, continue, and nested exits.
cards.answer: To leave nested loops, use a flag tested by the outer condition, return from a helper function, or restructure. A loop that edits its own counter or relies on break to stop needs an argument that it terminates.
No; only captureless lambdas convert to function pointers A function pointer has no storage for captured state.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Function pointers select behavior at run time.
cards.answer: Calling a null function pointer is undefined. The pointer type must match exactly; casting to a different function type and calling through it is undefined.
Its first initialization The standard requires concurrent initialization to wait; subsequent accesses are not synchronized.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Static locals persist across calls.
cards.answer: Hidden state makes a function harder to test and reason about. Prefer passing state explicitly unless a lazily built, program-lifetime value is truly intended.
A null pointer The argument array is terminated by a null pointer after the last argument.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Command-line arguments are an array of C strings.
cards.answer: Validate every argument: count, flags, and numeric conversion. std::atoi returns 0 for garbage with no error indication, so prefer a checked conversion.
Handlers are tried in order and the base handler would match first Handler selection takes the first match, not the best match.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Catch handlers are tried in order.
cards.answer: A base handler placed first makes later derived handlers unreachable. catch (...) catches everything and belongs last; use throw; inside a handler to rethrow the original exception.
check() is not called at all The assert macro expands to a no-op expression when NDEBUG is defined.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in assert checks at run time; static_assert at compile time.
cards.answer: Because assert can disappear, never put required side effects inside it, and do not use it to validate untrusted input. Assertions document internal assumptions; input errors need real error handling.
No; only static-storage objects are destroyed std::exit performs static destruction and stream flushing, not stack unwinding.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in std::exit skips automatic destructors.
cards.answer: Prefer returning an error to main or throwing an exception that main handles. Reserve std::exit for situations where skipping local cleanup is acceptable.
An identical definition may appear in multiple translation units The guaranteed meaning concerns the one-definition rule; call expansion is not required.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in inline is about definitions, not speed.
cards.answer: All definitions of an inline entity must be token-for-token identical with the same meaning. Differing definitions in different translation units are an ODR violation that needs no diagnostic.
Fully constructed automatic objects whose scopes are exited Construction completion determines which automatic objects need destruction.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A destructor closes every normal ownership path.
cards.answer: Keep owning members in RAII types and prefer the rule of zero. A scope exit test should cover success, early return, and exception paths rather than only the happy path.
Its owning handle and deleter state as specified Exclusive ownership changes hands; two simultaneous owners are not created.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in unique_ptr transfers one owning handle.
cards.answer: A moved-from unique_ptr is empty. Check before dereferencing and never create a second owning smart pointer from the same raw address.
No; lock may acquire ownership if it is still alive A weak observer does not increment the strong owner count.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Break ownership cycles with observing handles.
cards.answer: Control-block thread safety does not make the pointed-to object thread-safe. Concurrent mutable access to that object needs its own synchronization.
Its vector member already owns and releases its storage Ownership is delegated to a value member with the needed special-member behavior.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Let member values implement copy ownership.
cards.answer: If a class directly owns a raw resource, review all special members together. A destructor alone can leave an accidental shallow copy and a double release.
No; it changes the expression category used in overload resolution The operation selected after the cast determines whether anything is moved.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in std::move requests a value category.
cards.answer: Do not assume every moved-from object is empty. Use its documented postconditions; standard-library objects are generally valid but unspecified unless a stronger guarantee is stated.
To preserve the argument category captured by deduction Forwarding conditionally casts according to T; moving casts unconditionally.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Forward only a deduced forwarding reference.
cards.answer: Perfect forwarding still has boundaries, including braced initializer lists and overload sets. A generic wrapper is responsible for exception, lifetime, and return-reference behavior as well as argument categories.
The operation leaves observable state unchanged when it fails Strong rollback behavior differs from the basic invariant-preservation guarantee.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Commit changes after fallible preparation.
cards.answer: Do not describe a whole operation as strongly exception-safe merely because it uses a temporary. External side effects, throwing swaps, and partially updated related objects can violate that claim.
The member declaration order in the class The language defines initialization order independently of initializer-list ordering.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Members are destroyed in reverse construction order.
cards.answer: Destructors should normally not throw. A second exception escaping during stack unwinding terminates the program; resource cleanup needs an explicit failure-reporting strategy when release can fail.
No A view stores access information, not ownership.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Views borrow rather than own.
cards.answer: Do not return a view into a local string or retain a view into a temporary. Also remember that a view is not required to be null-terminated.
The iterator returned by erase The returned iterator is the specified continuation point; invalidation rules apply to previously saved positions.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Mutation can invalidate a saved position.
cards.answer: Test empty input, consecutive removals, and removal of the final element. Never demonstrate a dangling iterator by running undefined behavior and treating the output as a stable answer.
'3 2\n' The stdout is '3 2\n'. Parentheses select the count/value constructor with size three; braces select the two-element initializer list.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Braces can select a different constructor.
cards.answer: Check size and values when migrating initialization syntax. Replacing every parenthesis with braces can silently change behavior even when the program compiles cleanly.
No; named return value optimization is a separate case Optional NRVO must be distinguished from specified prvalue construction.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A prvalue can construct the result directly.
cards.answer: Do not use log counts from one optimized build as a universal rule. Distinguish mandatory language behavior from optional optimizations and keep destructor accessibility requirements visible.
'borrow consume\n' The stdout is 'borrow consume\n'. The named receiver is an lvalue, while std::move supplies an rvalue receiver expression.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Member ref qualifiers distinguish borrowing from consumption.
cards.answer: Returning references from a temporary receiver can dangle. Use a value-returning rvalue overload when transferring a result out of a temporary is the intended contract.

The parentheses make it an expression, so decltype encodes its value category decltype(id) names the declared type of the entity; decltype((expr)) applies the expression rule, giving int& for the lvalue x.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in decltype exposes an expression value category.
cards.answer: Category is a property of an expression, not of a variable. A named variable declared as T&& is still an lvalue when it appears in an expression, and a string literal is an lvalue array. Reason from the expression form when predicting overload selection or lifetime rules.

No; extension does not pass through a function that returns a reference Only a reference bound directly to the temporary or its subobject extends lifetime. The returned reference is not such a binding.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Reference binding can extend a temporary only directly.
cards.answer: A getter returning const std::string& from a temporary object returns a reference into an object that dies at the semicolon. Prefer returning or storing values when a result must outlive the expression, and treat surprising compiled output as unverified rather than as evidence.
Both objects hold the same pointer and both delete it, which is undefined behavior The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer member. Two destructors then release one allocation.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Write all five operations for a raw owning resource.
cards.answer: Prefer the rule of zero by wrapping the resource in an existing owner such as std::vector or std::unique_ptr. Writing five members by hand is a maintenance boundary: a destructor plus implicit copying would make two objects delete the same pointer.
Any throwing copy happens while constructing the parameter, before the target changes The target is modified only by the nonthrowing swap. A failed copy leaves the target untouched.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Copy-and-swap commits assignment with a nonthrowing swap.
cards.answer: The idiom always builds a complete new representation, so it cannot reuse existing capacity and may cost more than a hand-written assignment. swap must not throw; if it could, the guarantee would be lost.
The program, with an explicit destructor call The array has no knowledge of the object built inside it. delete would try to free storage that was never allocated by operator new.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Placement new starts a lifetime the program must end.
cards.answer: Forgetting the destructor skips cleanup silently. Constructing into misaligned or undersized storage, or reading through a stale pointer after replacing an object with const or reference members, has undefined behavior. Prefer std::optional, std::variant, or a container unless you are implementing such a facility.
Undefined behavior: an array new-expression must be released with delete[] The delete form must match the new form. The single-object form does not know the element count or array layout.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Release each new-expression with its matching delete.
cards.answer: Every mismatch is undefined behavior even if a particular run seems fine. Prefer std::make_unique<T>(), std::make_unique<T[]>(n), or std::vector<T>, which pair allocation and release automatically.
The move constructor may throw and a copy constructor exists, so vector copies to keep the strong guarantee move_if_noexcept selects copying for a potentially throwing move when a copy is available.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Vector growth copies when moving might throw.
cards.answer: A forgotten noexcept can silently turn every reallocation into deep copies. Mark move operations noexcept only when they truly cannot throw; a lie would call std::terminate instead of reporting an error.

One block holding both the control block and the object Combining the allocations is the usual implementation and the standard recommends it. It also ties the storage lifetime to outstanding weak_ptrs.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in make_shared and enable_shared_from_this share one control block.
cards.answer: shared_from_this requires that a shared_ptr already owns the object. Since C++17 it throws std::bad_weak_ptr otherwise; before C++17 the behavior was undefined. Do not call it from the constructor, where no owner exists yet.
Assigning a new value or calling clear() Valid but unspecified means operations without preconditions work; reading a particular value does not.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Moved-from objects keep a documented minimal contract.
cards.answer: Using a moved-from object is not use-after-free. The real errors are calling an operation with an unmet precondition, such as dereferencing an empty unique_ptr or calling front() on a possibly empty container. Your own types should document what a moved-from object supports.

The temporary string is destroyed at the end of the full-expression and a view does not extend its lifetime Only references bound directly to a temporary extend it. string_view is a separate object holding a pointer and length.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Views and references must not outlive their temporaries.
cards.answer: Keep an owning object alive for at least as long as every view of it. String literals have static storage duration, so views of them are safe. Treat any view parameter as borrowed for the call only unless the interface states otherwise.
To preserve the positive-value invariant through the API Access control supports an invariant but does not itself provide synchronization.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Construct only valid domain values.
cards.answer: Check both creation and later mutation. A validating constructor does not protect a public field that callers can overwrite with an invalid value.
Changing p through the bound member names The reference qualification changes decomposition ownership and aliasing.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Aggregate values expose a simple representation.
cards.answer: Use an encapsulated class when initialization must enforce relationships among fields. Aggregate convenience does not justify exposing an invalid state.
Yes, because get is const-qualified The const member-function qualifier makes the implicit object parameter suitable for const objects.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Const member functions document access.
cards.answer: Return const access when callers should observe without mutation. A const method returning a mutable pointer to shared state needs particular ownership and synchronization scrutiny.
The derived portion of the object Object slicing creates a standalone Base value rather than retaining a Derived dynamic object.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Polymorphism requires preserving the dynamic object.
cards.answer: Use inheritance for an intentional substitutability contract. Prefer composition when code reuse alone is the goal, and avoid promising behavior a derived class cannot preserve.
To destroy the complete derived object through the owning base pointer The polymorphic release path must match the object actually allocated.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Deletion through an interface needs a release contract.
cards.answer: Use unique_ptr<Base> only when its deleter is correct for the actual dynamic object. An interface declaration is incomplete until construction and destruction responsibilities are clear.
No The grammar and precedence remain fixed; overloads change the function called.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Operators should preserve value expectations.
cards.answer: Check overflow, unit compatibility, and symmetry where they matter. An elegant spelling does not compensate for an undocumented domain error.
It returns nullptr The pointer and reference forms have different failure behavior.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Choose casts by the property being checked.
cards.answer: A cast does not create a new object lifetime, validate arbitrary bytes, or make modification of a truly const object legal. Prefer an interface that avoids repeated downcasts.
Concrete representation behind a selected operation contract The public operation set remains visible while concrete implementation types can vary.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Erase representation behind a chosen contract.
cards.answer: Compare inheritance, templates, variants, and type erasure by the extension boundary: whether new types or new operations are expected, and where dependencies should live.
The narrow behavior the algorithm actually needs A small contract reduces coupling and makes alternative implementations easier to reason about.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Inject the dependency that varies.
cards.answer: Keep the injected interface narrow. A mock that merely mirrors implementation details can hide a broken contract; test visible behavior and meaningful failure paths.
No; representation and platform details still vary Object-copy guarantees are different from a specified external data format.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Bytes are not a portable serialization format.
cards.answer: Avoid reading uninitialized padding or violating aliasing and lifetime rules through casts. A byte operation must satisfy the requirements of both the source and destination objects.
'1\n' The stdout is '1\n'. ADL finds the equality friend and both stored integers equal three.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in ADL finds operations associated with an argument type.
cards.answer: Understand ordinary lookup, ADL, and overload resolution as separate steps. Unexpected implicit conversions or generic overloads can still make an API confusing.
Ownership, dynamic type, and copying policy for contained resources Cloning is a resource and value-semantics contract, not just copying an address.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A clone operation needs a deep-copy ownership policy.
cards.answer: Test that modifying the clone leaves the original independent where that is the contract. A shared cache or external service may intentionally remain shared and needs separate documentation.
No Delayed invocation requires a deliberate ownership or availability check.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Queued commands must survive or reject target loss.
cards.answer: Retries and undo need additional semantics. Repeating an external side effect is not automatically safe merely because an action fits inside a callable wrapper.
The borrowed Legacy object Composition through a reference does not extend the target lifetime.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Adapt an old interface without hiding its dependency.
cards.answer: Do not silently retain a borrowed legacy object beyond its lifetime. Store ownership or a reference according to the intended relationship and state which party must outlive the wrapper.
The visible Base declaration Default-argument substitution is a call-site rule separate from virtual dispatch.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Default arguments follow the static declaration.
cards.answer: Prefer one nonvirtual front door with a stable default that delegates to a virtual implementation, or require an explicit argument at the polymorphic boundary.
Calls Shape::name directly, bypassing virtual dispatch A qualified-id suppresses the virtual call mechanism.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Virtual dispatch selects by dynamic type at a measurable cost.
cards.answer: Calling through an object by value slices the derived part and calls the base version. Measure before replacing virtual calls for speed; final classes, sealed hierarchies, std::variant, or templates trade openness for static knowledge.
Port contains two Device subobjects, so the name is ambiguous Name lookup finds id in two distinct base subobjects. Qualifying the path or using virtual inheritance resolves it.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Virtual inheritance shares one base subobject.
cards.answer: Virtual bases add indirection to locate the shared subobject and complicate construction. Prefer composition or interfaces without data; use virtual inheritance deliberately when one shared base state is actually required.
Padding aligns int b to 4 bytes and rounds the size to a multiple of its alignment char a at 0, three bytes of padding, int b at 4, char c at 8, then tail padding to 12.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Member order, padding, and empty members decide object size.
cards.answer: Exact numbers are an ABI property; the values shown are those of common LP64 ABIs such as arm64 and x86-64. Two subobjects of the same empty type still need distinct addresses. Do not serialize raw layout or depend on sizes without static_assert.
A compile error if the function does not override a base virtual function override is a checked assertion about overriding; it does not change which function a correct override calls.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in override and final turn silent mismatches into errors.
cards.answer: Use override on every overriding declaration so interface changes break the build rather than behavior. Apply final where extension is genuinely not intended; it is a design commitment that later subclasses cannot undo.

unique_ptr's default deleter needs the complete Impl type where it is instantiated Instantiating the deleter inside the class definition would apply sizeof and delete to an incomplete type and fail to compile.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Pimpl hides a representation behind one owning pointer.
cards.answer: The cost is one allocation per object and an extra indirection on every access. A moved-from object holds a null pointer, so member functions must document whether they may be called on it.
The user-declared destructor suppresses Holder's implicit move constructor, so the copy constructor is used The rvalue binds to const Holder& because no move constructor was declared.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Declaring a destructor suppresses the implicit move.
cards.answer: An empty destructor added for logging or as a breakpoint can therefore turn moves into copies throughout a program. Either follow the rule of zero, or explicitly default all the operations you want.
if (open) {} An if condition is a contextual conversion. Copy-initializing a bool and implicitly converting 1.5 to Meters are both blocked by explicit.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in explicit restricts conversions to deliberate contexts.
cards.answer: Make single-argument constructors and conversion operators explicit by default. Allow implicit conversions only when the source and target represent the same abstract value, as with a string literal to a string type.

The in-class declaration is a definition, so no separate out-of-class definition is needed inline applies the one-definition rule for inline entities to the variable, permitting a definition in a header.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Inline static data members are defined in the class.
cards.answer: A shared mutable counter is global state: unsynchronized access from several threads is a data race, and tests can interfere through it. Static initialization order across translation units remains a separate hazard.
Suffixes without an underscore are reserved for the standard library Programs that declare non-underscore suffixes use reserved names.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in User-defined literals attach units to constants.
cards.answer: Suffixes that do not begin with an underscore are reserved for the standard library, such as the s suffix for std::string and the chrono suffixes. Keep user literal operators in a namespace and bring them in with a using-directive where they are needed.
Base::kind, because the dynamic type is Base while Base is being constructed Dispatch during construction uses the class whose constructor is executing.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Virtual calls in constructors use the class under construction.
cards.answer: Calling a pure virtual function this way is undefined behavior and commonly aborts. Pass needed information to the base constructor as arguments, or use a factory that completes initialization after construction.
Yes; access controls calling a name, not overriding it Overriding is about matching signatures; access checks apply at the point of a call.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A non-virtual interface keeps policy in the base.
cards.answer: The idiom adds a layer of indirection and works best when the wrapper has real policy to enforce. Keep the hooks narrow and document which preconditions the base already established before calling them.
Yes; access is checked per class, not per object Member functions of a class can access private members of any object of that class.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Access control is per class, and friendship is granted explicitly.
cards.answer: Access control is a compile-time aid for keeping invariants, not a security boundary. Every friend widens the set of code that must preserve the invariants, so grant it narrowly.
No; semantic contracts still need reasoning and tests Type checking verifies permitted expressions, not every ordering or mathematical law.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Templates generate typed operations.
cards.answer: State the semantic requirements as well as the syntax. A comparison operator existing does not prove that it establishes the ordering an algorithm requires.
Usually no; use auto& when reference binding is intended Plain value deduction and reference deduction have different rules.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Deduction can copy or preserve a reference.
cards.answer: Choose value versus reference intentionally in range loops, structured bindings, and return types. An apparently harmless deduction change can alter ownership or mutation.
No; use overloads or another dispatch mechanism Class and function templates have different specialization facilities.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Specialization selects a distinct implementation.
cards.answer: Avoid using a specialization to violate the semantic promise of the generic interface. A selected implementation still owes the caller the documented contract.
No; its immediate-context boundaries matter Errors outside the relevant substitution context can remain hard compilation errors.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Substitution failure can remove an overload.
cards.answer: Understand where the constraint participates in substitution. A hard error deep inside an instantiated body is not automatically a substitution failure.
The number of elements in the parameter pack The pack length is a compile-time property.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A parameter pack represents a sequence of arguments.
cards.answer: Do not infer sequencing or ownership from pack syntax alone. Forwarding each argument and evaluating side effects require a deliberate contract.
It defines the empty-pack result and participates in the reduction The initial operand is part of both the expression type and its value semantics.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Folds make the reduction identity explicit.
cards.answer: An algebraic-looking fold still uses C++ operator semantics. Signed overflow, overloaded operators, and evaluation order must be considered for the chosen operation.
No; range correctness is a separate contract The type category is checked, but operand bounds still matter.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Constraints express the admissible interface.
cards.answer: Concept satisfaction checks syntax and specified compile-time predicates. It does not mechanically prove every semantic law such as equality preservation or strict weak ordering.
No; the call context and arguments matter constexpr makes eligible evaluation possible; a required constant-expression context demands it.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Constant evaluation is a usable execution mode.
cards.answer: Rules expand across standards. Label examples by the minimum standard they actually require and do not infer support from a compiler accepting a newer extension silently.
consteval consteval and constexpr express different requirements on eligible function calls.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Immediate functions require constant evaluation.
cards.answer: Keep diagnostics and valid input domains explicit. A compile-time result does not make later indexing or arithmetic automatically safe.
No; it constrains initialization, not later mutability Initialization timing and const qualification are independent properties.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Static initialization and constness are independent.
cards.answer: Initialization-order reasoning still needs dependency analysis. constinit does not synchronize later concurrent access or replace an atomic or mutex.
'2\n' The stdout is '2\n'. The nonempty vector starts with two; the dependent value_type resolves to int.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Dependent types need explicit parsing guidance.
cards.answer: Do not fix every template diagnostic by adding keywords blindly. Identify whether the name is a type, template, value, or overload set and which lookup phase applies.
'0 1\n' The stdout is '0 1\n'. int has no size member, while const vector<int> provides a size expression.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Detect an expression in a substitution context.
cards.answer: Prefer a named concept in C++20 when it better expresses the contract, while understanding detection traits when maintaining C++17 interfaces.
No The derived type is supplied as a template argument and selected statically.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Static polymorphism trades runtime openness for type coupling.
cards.answer: Use static polymorphism when compile-time composition fits the extension boundary. It does not replace a runtime plugin interface or automatically guarantee better measured performance.
No; an appropriate receiver must be supplied A member pointer identifies a member operation, not the lifetime of a target instance.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Invoke unifies callable and member-pointer forms.
cards.answer: Generic callable wrappers must preserve argument and return lifetimes. Returning a reference obtained through invoke does not extend the receiver lifetime.
No; it participates in selecting template arguments Construction occurs after the specialization has been deduced.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Deduction guides select a class-template specialization.
cards.answer: Review ownership and initializer_list interactions when adding guides. Convenient deduction should not silently change which object owns external storage.
No The wrapper refers to the backing array and does not become its own independent container.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in initializer_list is a view of a backing array.
cards.answer: Use an owning container for a returned sequence. Const elements also constrain attempts to move resources out of initializer-list construction.

bidirectional_iterator_tag derives (through forward) from input_iterator_tag, so the base conversion is viable Tag types are ordinary classes. A derived-to-base conversion makes the input overload viable, while the random-access overload is not.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Type traits select an implementation through tag dispatch.
cards.answer: Tag dispatch selects code, it does not check semantics. A user iterator that advertises random_access_iterator_tag without constant-time jumps silently receives the wrong algorithm; the tag is a promise the type author must keep.
The integral branch is a discarded statement and is not instantiated for T = const char[3] Inside a template, a discarded constexpr branch is not instantiated for that specialization.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in if constexpr discards the branch a type cannot use.
cards.answer: Outside a template the discarded branch is still fully checked, and even inside a template it must be syntactically valid and not ill-formed for every possible type. A plain if with a constant condition instantiates both branches.
No; the deduced parameter types differ (int versus unsigned) With auto, the argument type is part of the template argument, so equal numeric values of different types name different specializations.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Non-type template parameters can deduce their type.
cards.answer: Each distinct value creates a distinct type, which can multiply instantiations and code size. Pointer arguments must refer to objects with static storage duration; a string literal itself cannot be a template argument.
std::vector A template template parameter requires a template name, not a specialization or another type.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Template template parameters accept a template, not a type.
cards.answer: Do not use this feature when a type parameter would do. Accepting a fully formed container type is usually simpler and lets callers supply allocators and comparators directly.
3, because the long double value is converted to int by truncation T(value) performs a functional cast; floating-to-integral conversion truncates toward zero.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Variable templates name a family of constants.
cards.answer: A non-const variable template creates one mutable global per type, with the usual initialization-order and data-race concerns. Converting a long double initializer to int truncates; the template does not choose a safe rounding policy.
this-> makes the name dependent, so lookup happens in the instantiated base Unqualified lookup does not search a dependent base class at the template definition.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Names from a dependent base need this-> or qualification.
cards.answer: Argument-dependent lookup at the point of instantiation can still find functions declared after the template, but only through associated namespaces of class-type arguments. Fundamental types have none, so a later overload for int is not found.
No; T is fixed by the class, so T&& is an ordinary rvalue reference Forwarding reference deduction requires T to be a template parameter of the function being called.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in T&& is a forwarding reference only when T is deduced.
cards.answer: A greedy forwarding overload often beats an overload taking const X& for non-const lvalues, because it deduces an exact match. Constrain forwarding constructors or overloads rather than assuming the const reference version is preferred.
Whole subsumes Number because Whole is defined as a conjunction containing Number Normalized constraints compare atomic constraints that come from the same concept definition.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Subsumption picks the more constrained overload.
cards.answer: Atomic constraints are identical only if they come from the same expression in the source, normally via the same concept. Repeating std::is_integral_v<T> textually in two requires-clauses does not create subsumption and yields an ambiguity.
In the type itself; the object carries no data integer_sequence is an empty class whose template arguments encode the values.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in index_sequence turns a pack of indices into code.
cards.answer: The sequence object is empty; all the information lives in its type. Large N creates large instantiations and slow builds, and negative lengths are rejected.
false, the identity of a unary || fold A unary fold over an empty pack is permitted for &&, || and the comma operator.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A typelist is a pack you can query and transform.
cards.answer: Every intermediate list is a distinct instantiation. Applying a metafunction to a list shape it does not handle, such as Front of an empty list, produces an incomplete-type error rather than a clear message unless you add a static_assert.
No; every allocation must be deallocated within the same constant evaluation C++20 permits transient constexpr allocation only.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in C++20 constant evaluation can allocate transiently.
cards.answer: The same function remains callable at runtime with dynamic allocation. Compilers bound constant-evaluation steps, so very large compile-time computations can fail with a limit rather than a logic error.
Locating the position and cache behavior also matter The whole workload includes search, allocation, locality, and iterator requirements.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Choose a sequence by operations and invalidation.
cards.answer: Do not transfer one container invalidation rule to another. Review the exact operation, including end iterators and allocator conditions.
Yes The operation supplies a mapped object for a missing key.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Lookup containers have different ordering contracts.
cards.answer: Equivalent keys must satisfy the comparator or hash/equality requirements. A poor or inconsistent policy can break correctness or expected performance.
It reports true when comparing an element with itself A strict weak ordering must be irreflexive.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Comparators must establish a strict weak ordering.
cards.answer: Test equal elements, distinct equivalence classes, and boundary values. Floating NaNs require a deliberate policy instead of assuming ordinary numeric comparison orders every input.
No; it is not a random-access iterator Use operations supported by the iterator category and remain within valid bounds.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Algorithms need specific traversal capabilities.
cards.answer: Iterator and sentinel validity depends on the underlying range. A valid iterator type does not guarantee that a particular iterator value is still usable.
No; erase must remove the logical tail Algorithms operate on iterator ranges without necessarily controlling container size.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Separate logical removal from container erasure.
cards.answer: After erasure, observe the container invalidation rules. Do not continue with a saved invalid iterator just because the removal algorithm returned successfully.
As the view is traversed This view pipeline describes deferred traversal work.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Ranges compose lazy traversal operations.
cards.answer: Understand ownership of each adapted range and callable. Prefer pure transformations for predictable repeated traversal and check whether a view is single-pass or multipass.
No The concept describes iterator validity relative to a range wrapper, not automatic ownership.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Borrowing requirements are separate from iterator types.
cards.answer: Store the owner when a returned position must remain usable. Recognize dangling result types instead of forcing a cast around a lifetime error.
The supplying memory resource Allocator indirection does not transfer ownership of the resource.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A memory resource must outlive its allocations.
cards.answer: Destroy resource-using objects before the resource. Resetting a resource while its containers still use the storage invalidates those objects; stack placement alone does not prove lifetime order.
No Extent information and ownership are separate responsibilities.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Span adds extent without ownership.
cards.answer: Use const element access when mutation is not intended. Constness of the span wrapper itself differs from constness of the elements it views.
Yes, subject to its requirements Algorithms with different evaluation-order contracts can yield different floating results.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Reduction order affects admissible operations.
cards.answer: Do not assume a parallel execution policy creates threads or speeds up every workload. Backend support, input size, synchronization, and exceptions affect the behavior.
'1 2\n' The stdout is '1 2\n'. set retains one representative of key two, while multiset retains both equivalent occurrences.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Equivalent keys control duplicate retention.
cards.answer: Choose a container from duplicate and ordering requirements. Do not discard records silently when their business identity is finer than the selected key.
'7\n' The stdout is '7\n'. The default priority queue exposes its largest stored value, seven.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A priority queue exposes one selected extreme.
cards.answer: Do not assume stable order among equivalent priorities. Add an explicit sequence key if deterministic FIFO behavior for equal priorities is part of the requirement.
It stays valid and now refers to an element of a splice moves nodes, not values, so iterators follow their elements.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Node containers move elements without invalidating them.
cards.answer: Splicing a range between different lists is linear because the size must be recounted. Node containers trade locality and per-node allocation for this stability, so they are slower to traverse than vector.
Keys that compare equal must produce equal hash values Collisions are allowed; inconsistency with equality breaks lookup.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Hashed containers trade buckets for load factor.
cards.answer: Rehashing invalidates iterators but not references or pointers to elements. Never print or test unordered iteration order; it depends on the hash, the bucket count and the implementation.
std::less<> is transparent, which enables the template find overload The heterogeneous overloads exist only when the comparator declares is_transparent.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Transparent comparators avoid temporary keys.
cards.answer: The comparator must order the other type consistently with the key ordering. Transparent lookup does not apply to operator[] or insert, which still need a key_type.
It stays in b merge never replaces existing keys; it only transfers non-conflicting nodes.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Node handles move elements between associative containers.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Range algorithms accept a projection.

The required operations and associated types exist with the right forms Concepts check syntactic requirements; semantic requirements remain the author's responsibility.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A custom iterator must model the concept it claims.
cards.answer: Satisfying a concept checks syntax, not meaning. A forward iterator must be multipass: copies advance independently and equal iterators dereference to the same value. Breaking that law compiles but makes algorithms wrong.

Elements before position k are not greater than the element at k nth_element only guarantees the partition around the selected element.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Sort only as much as the question needs.
cards.answer: After nth_element, neither side is sorted. After partial_sort, the tail is in unspecified order. Read only the guarantees the algorithm makes.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Optional distinguishes absence from a value.
cards.answer: Optional describes absence but carries no error reason. Use a richer result representation when callers need to distinguish multiple failure cases.
A closed set of possible alternative types The listed alternatives are part of the variant type.

cards.answer: Choose variants when the type set is closed and new operations are common. An open plugin type set may call for a different extension boundary.
No; it checks the stored concrete type Type erasure preserves runtime type identity rather than enabling every conversion.

regex_match Search and whole-input matching answer different parsing questions.

cards.answer: For simple structured numeric input, a direct parser may offer clearer diagnostics and resource bounds. Escaping exists at both the C++ string and regular-expression layers.
Its error category A numeric value is meaningful only within its category contract.

println Formatting a string and writing output are separate operations.

'5 25\n' The stdout is '5 25\n'. Magnitude is sqrt(3*3+4*4)=5; norm is the squared magnitude 25.

C++26 reflection needs a versioned metaprogramming contract
Does member reflection automatically define a safe persistent schema?
cards.answer: No Use an explicit allowlist or opt-in metadata for serialized members, stable external field identifiers separate from source names, and a versioned decoding policy. Reject or deliberately migrate incompatible schema changes. Test that excluded fields never enter output and that old fixtures remain decodable.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in C++26 reflection needs a versioned metaprogramming contract.
cards.answer: This is reference-only practice. The local Apple Clang 21 check does not validate reflection support; compiler branches, feature macros, and required flags must be recorded before an executable example is marked verified.

cards.prompt:
Contracts express obligations with specified evaluation semantics
Should optional diagnostic evaluation replace validation of untrusted input?
cards.answer: No Validate and bound the external integer before calling the trusted helper. Document the helper precondition and the selected contract evaluation behavior. Ensure checked parsing remains effective independently of optional diagnostic checks, and test invalid external values without invoking undefined access.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Contracts express obligations with specified evaluation semantics.
cards.answer: This is reference-only practice. Do not silently substitute assert, exceptions, or a proposal-era syntax and call it a verified implementation of the adopted contract facility.

cards.prompt:
Sender/receiver operations own completion and cancellation state
Does requesting stop prove every asynchronous callback has already finished?
cards.answer: No Give one enclosing owner the connected operation state and its input buffer through terminal completion. Route value, error, and stopped completions through one run identity and finalize exactly once. Request cancellation through the documented stop channel and defer resource release until the operation can no longer access them.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Sender/receiver operations own completion and cancellation state.
cards.answer: This unit is reference-only. Check the adopted library specification, feature macros, scheduler backend, and actual toolchain before labelling a sender example runnable.

cards.prompt:
Fixed-capacity growth still constructs and destroys elements
Does inline container storage prevent element-owned allocations?
cards.answer: No Check the facility-specific full-capacity behavior without invoking an operation outside its preconditions. Track whether the incoming owner remains valid or was consumed according to that API. Verify destruction counts after successful insertion, removal, failed construction, and container teardown, including a zero-capacity case when supported.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Fixed-capacity growth still constructs and destroys elements.
cards.answer: This is reference-only C++26 practice. Do not claim that inline storage establishes universal allocation freedom or that a homegrown ring is a conforming implementation of the standard container.

cards.prompt:
Data parallelism needs a lane and remainder policy
Can a vectorized load read past the valid range just because unused lanes are ignored later?
cards.answer: No Compare with a scalar reference on empty input, shorter-than-one-group input, exact group multiples, and remainders. Process the tail using a specified masked or scalar path and obey load alignment requirements. Use exact comparison for bounded integer arithmetic or a justified error budget for floating results.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Data parallelism needs a lane and remainder policy.
cards.answer: This is reference-only practice. Record adopted API names and actual compiler/library/target support before presenting a runnable SIMD program; instruction-set marketing alone is not validation.
No Parentheses affect grouping while the token expansion can still duplicate an argument.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Macros transform tokens before type checking.
cards.answer: Do not run a repeated-side-effect macro as a portable prediction exercise. Some such expressions have undefined or version-sensitive behavior; reason about expansion and replace the unsafe interface.
No; it gives another spelling for the namespace Aliases name an existing namespace rather than duplicating its entities.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Qualification selects the intended declaration.
cards.answer: An anonymous namespace gives translation-unit-local entities under its rules. Namespaces alone do not define an ABI versioning or symbol-visibility policy.
No; the wrapper must manage that policy A manual union is not an automatically tagged variant.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A union needs an active-member lifetime policy.
cards.answer: Prefer variant when its closed-alternative semantics fit. A production manual union wrapper needs a tag, exception policy, and correct special members; the minimal demonstration intentionally manages one known transition only.
The resource allocation and release contract Ownership is correct only when release is appropriate for the acquired resource.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A unique owner can carry the correct release function.
cards.answer: The worked example counts one custom delete on scope exit. Such counts cover the exercised ownership paths; they are not a process-wide heap profile.
No Naming a receiver does not change the underlying value, reference, or lifetime contract.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Explicit object parameters name the receiver.
cards.answer: Use the receiver form intentionally and avoid returning a borrowed subobject from a temporary receiver. An explicit spelling makes the parameter visible; it does not remove lifetime reasoning.
No; it controls the resulting access category The later operation selected through that access determines whether copying or moving occurs.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in forward_like transfers cv and reference intent.
cards.answer: Check constness and lvalue/rvalue category separately. Making a member look consumable is appropriate only when its owner permits that consumption and the referenced storage remains live.
No The static declaration removes an implicit object parameter while retaining the explicit call arguments.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A stateless call operator can be static.
cards.answer: Use a stateful callable when the policy really depends on captured or stored configuration. Choosing static does not automatically produce a measurable performance improvement.
The operator implementation The language permits the interface shape while its implementation supplies the access policy.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A subscript operator can accept several indices.
cards.answer: Do not assume multidimensional syntax supplies automatic bounds checking. A library view and a user-defined operator each have their own access contract.
No Value conversion and reference binding to the original object have different aliasing semantics.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in auto(expression) makes a value conversion explicit.
cards.answer: Distinguish taking a value from retaining a reference. Both can be correct, but later mutation of the source makes their behavior visibly different.

It accesses a float through an unrelated glvalue type, which the aliasing rule makes undefined Matching sizes do not create a permitted access type. Copy the representation with memcpy or std::bit_cast.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Inspect object bytes without breaking the aliasing rule.
cards.answer: Optimizers use the rule to assume that stores through an int pointer cannot modify a float object, so a type-punned read can observe a stale value or be reordered. -fno-strict-aliasing disables that assumption on clang and GCC but does not make the program portable; fix the access instead of relying on a flag.
Signed overflow is undefined, so it may assume x + 1 does not wrap Assuming no undefined behavior, x + 1 is mathematically larger than x, so the comparison is false on every valid execution.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Optimizers may assume signed overflow never happens.
cards.answer: -fwrapv makes signed overflow wrap on clang and GCC, but it is a dialect flag, not standard C++. UBSan (-fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow) reports overflow at run time on exercised paths; it cannot prove that untested inputs are safe.
1, 0, 0, 0 Elements without an explicit initializer in aggregate initialization are value-initialized, which zeroes ints.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Reading an indeterminate value is not a random number.
cards.answer: Do not test for uninitialized reads by printing a value: a debug build may show zero by accident. Use compiler warnings such as -Wuninitialized, a sanitizer where available (MemorySanitizer is not supported on Apple platforms), or hardening options such as -ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero while still fixing the source.
AddressSanitizer ASan instruments memory accesses with shadow memory. TSan looks for races and -Wall cannot see run-time indices.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Sanitizers turn silent undefined behavior into reports.
cards.answer: A clean sanitizer run only covers the executed paths and inputs. Sanitizers change memory layout and timing, so they complement tests, fuzzing and code review rather than proving absence of undefined behavior.
std::shuffle with an explicit uniform random bit generator std::shuffle makes the generator explicit. A random comparator violates the strict weak ordering requirement of std::sort.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Removed C++98 facilities and their replacements.
cards.answer: Some standard libraries keep removed names behind opt-in compatibility macros. Do not depend on them in new code: migrate the code, compile with the target -std, and treat deprecation warnings as a migration list rather than noise.

Implicitly capturing this through [=] is deprecated; write [=, this] or [*this] The capture default still captures this by pointer, which looks like a copy but is not. C++20 deprecates that implicit form.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Recognize C++17 to C++23 deprecations and their replacements.
cards.answer: Deprecated features still compile, usually with a warning, and may be removed later. Fix them when you raise the language standard so the migration diff stays small and does not hide behavior changes.
h(a) == h(b) Equal keys must hash equally. Distinct keys may collide, which costs time but not correctness.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Named requirements carry semantic obligations.
cards.answer: A hash that ignores a field used by equality is valid but may collide heavily. A hash that uses a field equality ignores breaks the requirement and can put equal keys in different buckets, so lookups and duplicate detection fail.

Elements are moved individually into storage from the destination resource polymorphic_allocator does not propagate and unequal resources cannot free each other's memory, so the buffer cannot transfer.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Allocator propagation traits decide where storage lives after assignment.
cards.answer: When move assignment does not propagate and the allocators compare unequal, the container cannot steal the source buffer; it moves elements one by one into its own storage. Swapping containers with unequal, non-propagating allocators has undefined behavior.
std::terminate is called, possibly without unwinding the stack The noexcept boundary is enforced at run time by termination; whether the stack is unwound first is implementation-defined.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in noexcept is a queryable contract that terminates when violated.
cards.answer: If an exception leaves a noexcept function, std::terminate is called and stack unwinding may not happen. Mark functions noexcept when failure is impossible or fatal, not to make code look faster.

Its local static is initialized the first time control passes through the declaration Initialization on first use guarantees the counter exists before any caller reads it, regardless of translation-unit order.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Function-local statics avoid initialization order dependencies.
cards.answer: Destruction happens in reverse order of completed construction, so a static destroyed early can still be used by a later destructor. Long-lived registries are sometimes intentionally leaked; document that choice instead of relying on accidental order.
The version name is part of mangled symbols, so mismatched builds fail to link Mangling includes the inline namespace, so lib::v2::version and lib::v1::version are different link-time names.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Inline namespaces version an ABI without changing spelling.
cards.answer: Only one version should be inline for a given name, or unqualified references become ambiguous. Inline namespaces do not fix ODR violations within one build; they make mismatches between separately built components visible.
A standard library can lack a facility even when the compiler accepts the language mode Language mode and library support evolve separately; the facility macro reports the specific library feature.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Select code with feature-test macros, not compiler names.
cards.answer: A macro check only tells you what the implementation claims. Keep the fallback compiled and tested on at least one configuration, and avoid using __has_include alone as proof that the facility inside the header is enabled in the current mode.

cards.prompt:
Build a checked command-line integer parser
What establishes whole-token numeric parsing?
cards.answer: Both successful conversion and a stopping pointer at the end Scan bounded string_view tokens without retaining views beyond the input lifetime. Require full-token conversion and use checked_add for every accumulated value; the local total is discarded if an error occurs.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Build a checked command-line integer parser.
cards.answer: The answer adds a line parser whose separator grammar is ASCII spaces. Tabs and other whitespace remain invalid rather than being silently accepted.

cards.prompt:
Design a checked value library
How does Amount preserve its value on arithmetic overflow?
cards.answer: Check bounds before committing the new representation Check subtraction bounds before evaluating a-b. Commit the new representation only after the check succeeds, preserving value semantics and the strong failure guarantee.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Design a checked value library.
cards.answer: The answer implements subtraction directly rather than negating the right operand, because negating the minimum signed integer would itself overflow.

cards.prompt:
Own a bounded generic container and its allocator
What must outlive the allocator-backed Ring?
cards.answer: The memory_resource supplying its storage Return a pointer only to an actually constructed front element. The caller must not retain it across pop, destruction, or later slot reuse. The resource owns allocation policy while the ring owns element lifetimes.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Own a bounded generic container and its allocator.
cards.answer: This is not a standard-container implementation: it has no iterators, general allocator propagation, concurrent access, or support for throwing element moves. The answer adds a const non-owning front view whose lifetime is bounded by the next invalidating operation.

cards.prompt:
Drain a bounded concurrent pipeline safely
What is the pipeline teardown order?
cards.answer: Close and notify the queue, then join workers before releasing state Read size under the same mutex used for modifications. The snapshot is immediately stale when other threads can modify the queue; use try_push/pop themselves to perform atomic decisions.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Drain a bounded concurrent pipeline safely.
cards.answer: Tests cover saturation without consumers, FIFO drain after close, empty waiter wakeup, repeated finish, idle destruction, and repeated parallel totals. No user callback runs on a worker, so final-owner destruction on that worker is deliberately outside this project interface.

cards.prompt:
Give each coroutine frame exactly one owner
Who destroys this generator frame after early abandonment?
cards.answer: The single owning Generator wrapper The frame owns its by-value bounds, so it borrows no caller locals. The loop stops before incrementing past last-1, and the wrapper releases the frame on every exit path.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Give each coroutine frame exactly one owner.
cards.answer: This generator is synchronous and confined to one thread. It does not implement asynchronous callback cancellation, scheduler integration, or shared concurrent resume; those require a more elaborate lifetime protocol.

cards.prompt:
Refactor a tagged API into closed value alternatives
What changes when adding Triangle to this closed variant?
cards.answer: The alternative set changes and clients need recompilation Add the alternative to the closed variant and provide its area member. The generic visitor still calls the same operation; extending the type set changes the variant interface and requires recompilation.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Refactor a tagged API into closed value alternatives.
cards.answer: The answer adds an integer-area triangle and states that odd products truncate. This is a deliberate domain choice for the exercise, not exact real-valued geometry.
Consecutive accesses share cache lines and suit hardware prefetching Both orders compute the same value; row order touches memory sequentially and uses each fetched line fully.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Traverse memory in the order it is laid out.
cards.answer: Locality effects depend on data size relative to each cache level, the hardware, and what else runs. Small grids that fit in L1 show little difference. Measure with representative sizes and hardware counters before restructuring code.
SoA: about 8 bytes per particle instead of whole 32-byte records In AoS form each fetched line also carries y, z, id and padding that the loop never uses.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Structure of arrays streams only the fields a loop uses.
cards.answer: SoA makes record insertion and whole-record access touch several arrays and keeps parallel arrays in sync by convention. Choose the layout from the dominant access pattern and measure; hybrid layouts (arrays of small field blocks) are common.
Nothing; it is an optimization hint Likelihood attributes affect optimization only. Correct programs behave the same with or without them.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in [[likely]] and [[unlikely]] are layout hints, not guarantees.
cards.answer: Wrong hints can make code slower, and profile-guided optimization usually does better than hand annotations. Measure with hardware counters (branch-misses with perf on Linux, CPU counters in Instruments on macOS) and keep hints on genuinely rare paths such as error handling.
No class can derive from Square, so the dynamic target of area is known Without further derivation, the static type determines the final overrider.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in final lets the compiler devirtualize calls.
cards.answer: final is a design commitment: it forbids future derivation or overriding. The optimization is permitted, not guaranteed; check the generated assembly or optimization remarks before relying on it, and measure whether the call was hot.
22 libc++ uses 23 inline bytes including the terminator; libstdc++ uses 15 characters. The standard leaves this unspecified.
