cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Short strings fit inline: observing libc++ small-string storage.
cards.answer: The output of this example is libc++-specific; libstdc++ prints different numbers. Do not hard-code inline capacities in production logic, and remember that string_view or pointers into a short string refer to the string object itself, not to a stable heap block.
Nothing; memory is reclaimed only by release() or destruction Monotonic means the allocation position only moves forward; individual frees are ignored.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A monotonic buffer resource turns allocations into pointer bumps.
cards.answer: Memory freed by growing containers is not reused, so repeated vector growth wastes old blocks; reserve up front. The resource is not thread-safe, and every object using it must be destroyed before the buffer goes out of scope.
So the optimizer cannot delete the computation as dead code Only observable behavior must be preserved. An unused result lets the compiler remove the timed work.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in A benchmark must keep its work observable.
cards.answer: Record compiler flags, hardware, CPU frequency behavior and input sizes. Timing values are not deterministic, so tests should check correctness and keep timing output out of compared stdout. Libraries such as Google Benchmark provide DoNotOptimize and statistics; still verify the result being timed.
When the branch depends on unpredictable data A predictable branch costs little; branchless code pays for both sides on every element.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Branchless selection trades a branch for data dependencies.
cards.answer: Branchless code always computes both sides and lengthens the dependency chain. When the branch is predictable, a branch is often faster. Keep the readable version unless measurement on representative data shows a win.
Only then is n - 1 a mask of the low log2(n) bits For n = 6, n - 1 is 0b101, which does not select a contiguous low bit range.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Power-of-two masks and bit counts replace division and loops.
cards.answer: The identity fails for signed negative operands: -3 % 8 is -3 in C++, while -3 & 7 is 5. Keep indices unsigned, assert the power-of-two precondition, and prefer the <bit> functions to hand-written loops.
x86 hardware already orders ordinary loads like acquire, while ARM may reorder them The language bug exists on both; only the hardware reordering that exposes it differs.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Memory-order cost differs between x86 and ARM.
cards.answer: Code missing an acquire often appears to work on x86 because the hardware already orders it, then fails on ARM machines including Apple silicon. Reason from the C++ memory model, test on weakly ordered hardware, and use ThreadSanitizer; do not infer correctness from one architecture.
More hot records fit per cache line, at the cost of an indirection for cold access The hot loop reads fewer bytes per record; cold access pays one extra load.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Keep hot fields together and move cold data out of line.
cards.answer: Splitting adds an indirection and an allocation when cold data is needed, and it can complicate ownership. Measure the record size with sizeof, count how many hot records fit in a cache line on the target, and confirm the win on the real access pattern.
The reserved capacity covers every insertion, so no reallocation occurs reserve guarantees capacity of at least n; insertions that do not exceed capacity do not reallocate.

cards.prompt: Explain the safety boundary in Count allocations by replacing global operator new.
cards.answer: Define the sized and unsized delete forms as well, since compilers call sized delete by default in C++14 and later. The counter is global and not thread-safe here; use an atomic for multithreaded tests, and remember that the standard library or the runtime may allocate on its own before main.

cards.prompt: What does dotnet build do that dotnet run also does, but without the final step?
cards.answer: Compiles the project and reports diagnostics without executing it run = build + execute. Use build when you only need the compiler's verdict.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Your first program and the dotnet toolchain'?
cards.answer: Check that you can explain three outcomes: the compiler rejected the code, the program threw an exception while running, or it ran and printed something unexpected. Each needs a different fix, and reading the exact diagnostic code (for example CS0103, a name that does not exist) is the first step.

cards.prompt: Why is decimal preferred over double for currency amounts?
cards.answer: It stores base-10 fractions such as 0.1 exactly double is binary floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. decimal uses base 10, so typical money values are exact.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Variables and built-in types'?
cards.answer: const declares a compile-time constant, such as const int Days = 7;. A local variable must be definitely assigned before it is read; the compiler rejects reads of a variable that might be unassigned (CS0165). Before relying on a number, check its type, its range and whether overflow should wrap or throw.

cards.prompt: What does 7 / 2 evaluate to in C#?
cards.answer: 3, because both operands are int Integer division truncates toward zero. Make one operand a double (7 / 2.0) to get 3.5.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Operators, precedence and evaluation'?
cards.answer: Operands are evaluated left to right, then operators apply by precedence and associativity. When an expression mixes side effects (method calls, ++), check the evaluation order explicitly; when it mixes types, check which conversion C# applies before the operator runs.

cards.prompt: What does s.ToUpper() do to the string stored in s?
cards.answer: Nothing; it returns a new upper-case string Strings are immutable. Assign the result (s = s.ToUpper()) if you want the variable to refer to the new value.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Strings, interpolation and formatting'?
cards.answer: Compare strings deliberately. == compares content ordinally for strings. For user-facing or case-insensitive comparisons pass a StringComparison, for example string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase). Check culture, case and length semantics whenever text crosses a boundary such as a file, a URL or a user.

cards.prompt: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
cards.answer: do ... while do ... while tests its condition after the body, so the first iteration always runs.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Decisions and loops'?
cards.answer: A foreach loop variable is read-only, and the collection must not be modified while it is being enumerated (a List throws InvalidOperationException). Before writing a loop, check the termination condition, whether the body may run zero times and whether anything mutates the collection being walked.

cards.prompt: What must a method do with an out parameter before it returns normally?
cards.answer: Assign it on every normal return path The compiler enforces definite assignment of out parameters, which is why callers can use them without initializing first.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Methods, parameters and overloading'?
cards.answer: Static local functions (static int Helper(...)) cannot capture surrounding variables, which makes their inputs explicit. Before calling a method, check whether each argument is copied or passed by reference, and whether out results are valid only when a Try-style method returns true.

cards.prompt: What does Console.ReadLine() return when standard input has ended?
cards.answer: null End of input is null; an empty line is the empty string. Code that confuses the two either loops forever or crashes.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Reading input safely'?
cards.answer: Treat all input as untrusted: check for end of input, empty lines, bad numbers and out-of-range values, and report problems on Console.Error so they do not mix with normal output.

cards.prompt: After var b = a; where a is a class instance, what does changing b.Name do?
cards.answer: Changes the object that a also refers to Class assignment copies the reference, so both variables name the same object.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Value types and reference types'?
cards.answer: A classic bug is mutating a copy: list[0].X = 5 on a List<MutablePoint> struct is a compile error (CS1612) because the indexer returns a copy. Before mutating, check whether the expression gives you the original storage or a copy, and prefer immutable structs so the question rarely matters.

cards.prompt: What does the null-forgiving operator x! do at runtime?
cards.answer: Nothing; it only silences the compiler's nullable warning Nullable reference types are compile-time analysis. ! removes a warning but adds no check.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Nullable value types and nullable reference types'?
cards.answer: Public methods should still validate arguments at runtime, because callers may have nullable warnings disabled: ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(arg). When you see ?, check whether the code handles the null path; when you see !, check what proves the value is present.

cards.prompt: Why must an override of Equals be accompanied by GetHashCode?
cards.answer: Hash-based collections assume equal objects have equal hash codes Dictionary and HashSet look in the bucket chosen by GetHashCode before calling Equals; mismatched hashes hide equal keys.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Equality, identity and boxing'?
cards.answer: Boxing costs an allocation and the boxed copy does not track later changes to the original. Before comparing, check which equality a type defines and whether a value type is being boxed by an object or non-generic API; generics (stage 7) usually avoid boxing.

cards.prompt: What does primes[1..4] produce for an int[] in C#?
cards.answer: A new array with the elements at indices 1, 2 and 3 Range ends are exclusive, and slicing an array allocates a copy; use AsSpan() for a non-copying view.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Arrays, indices and ranges'?
cards.answer: A range on an array copies, while a range on a span (stage 10) is a view without copying. Before slicing, check whether you need an independent copy or a view of the same memory, and remember that an out-of-range index is a runtime failure, not a compile error.

cards.prompt: Is (Status)42 legal when Status has only members 0, 1 and 2?
cards.answer: Yes; enums accept any value of the underlying type Enums are named integers. Validate with Enum.IsDefined or TryParse and keep a default arm in switches.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Enums and flags'?
cards.answer: When adding a member later, check every switch over the enum; the compiler only warns about missing cases in switch expressions without a discard arm. Treat enums read from files or networks as untrusted numbers until validated.

cards.prompt: What happens to the compiler-supplied parameterless constructor once a class declares its own constructor?
cards.answer: It is no longer generated The implicit default constructor exists only when you declare none, so new Account() stops compiling once you add Account(string).

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Classes, constructors and static members'?
cards.answer: this refers to the current instance and disambiguates a field from a parameter of the same name. Before adding state, check whether it belongs to each object (instance) or to the type (static), and whether a constructor leaves every field in a valid state.

cards.prompt: Inside a C# 14 property accessor, what does field refer to?
cards.answer: The compiler-generated backing field of that property field lets you add logic to an auto-property without declaring the backing field yourself.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Properties, init, required and the field keyword'?
cards.answer: Property getters should be cheap and side-effect free; callers assume reading twice gives the same answer. Check that setters keep the object valid, that init/required express the construction contract, and that expensive work lives in a method whose name says so.

cards.prompt: A class exposes public List<string> Items { get; }. What can callers still do?
cards.answer: Add and remove items through the returned list get-only stops callers replacing the reference, not mutating the object it refers to.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Encapsulation, access modifiers and immutability'?
cards.answer: Immutability makes objects easier to share across threads and to reason about. Before adding a setter or a public field, check which invariant could be broken through it and whether a method with validation, init or a new object would serve better.

cards.prompt: Given Shape s = new Circle(); and a virtual Area overridden in Circle, which Area runs for s.Area()?
cards.answer: Circle.Area, chosen at runtime virtual/override dispatches on the runtime type; only hiding with new uses the static type.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Inheritance, virtual dispatch and abstract classes'?
cards.answer: Calling a virtual method from a base constructor runs the derived override before the derived constructor has initialized its fields. Before designing a hierarchy, check whether composition or an interface would be simpler, and mark classes sealed unless they are designed for inheritance.

cards.prompt: What does obj as Circle return when obj is a Rect?
cards.answer: null as never throws for reference conversions; a direct cast (Circle)obj would throw.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Interfaces and type tests'?
cards.answer: Before adding an interface, check that there are (or will be) multiple implementations or a testing seam; an interface for a single class adds indirection without benefit. Keep interfaces small and named for a capability.

cards.prompt: In C# 14, what can public void operator +=(int value) on a class achieve that operator + cannot?
cards.answer: Update the existing object in place instead of creating a new one User-defined compound assignment lets mutable types avoid allocating a new result for every +=.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Object members and operator overloading'?
cards.answer: Operators must not surprise readers: + should not have side effects, and an in-place += must leave the object consistent with what + would produce. Check that equality operators agree with Equals and that conversions say clearly whether they can lose data.

cards.prompt: Two separately constructed record Person(string Name) objects with the same Name compare with ==. What is the result?
cards.answer: true, because records compare property values Records generate value-based equality; ReferenceEquals would still be false.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Records: value equality and non-destructive mutation'?
cards.answer: Use a class when identity matters (two customers with the same name are still two customers) and a record when the data is the identity. Check collection-valued properties: either use an immutable collection or remember that equality and with copy only the reference.

cards.prompt: What does (a, b) = (b, a); do?
cards.answer: Swaps a and b The right-hand tuple is built first from the old values, then deconstructed into a and b.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Tuples and deconstruction'?
cards.answer: Tuple element names do not participate in type identity: (int A, int B) and (int X, int Y) convert to each other silently. Check that positional order, not just names, matches when passing tuples between methods.

cards.prompt: What happens at runtime when no arm of a switch expression matches?
cards.answer: A SwitchExpressionException is thrown The compiler warns about non-exhaustive switches (CS8509); add arms or a discard to handle every input.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Switch expressions and patterns'?
cards.answer: Order arms from most to least specific and avoid _ when you want the compiler to tell you about a new case. Check for null explicitly: a type pattern never matches null.

cards.prompt: In [var first, .. var rest] applied to an int[], what is rest?
cards.answer: A new array holding every element after the first Slices of arrays are copies; use spans if you need a non-allocating view.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'List patterns and slices'?
cards.answer: Check the empty case first and remember the compiler's exhaustiveness analysis for list patterns is limited; keep a discard arm for inputs you did not anticipate.

cards.prompt: When does a finally block run?
cards.answer: After the try (and any matching catch) whether it returned, threw or completed finally exists for cleanup that must happen on every exit path.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Throwing and catching exceptions'?
cards.answer: Common built-in types and their meaning: ArgumentException/ArgumentNullException/ArgumentOutOfRangeException (caller passed bad input), InvalidOperationException (object is in the wrong state), NotSupportedException, KeyNotFoundException, IOException. Check that the type you throw tells the caller what they did wrong.

cards.prompt: Why is throw; preferred over throw e; inside a catch block?
cards.answer: throw; keeps the original stack trace throw e; restarts the stack trace at the rethrow line, hiding where the failure began.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Exception filters, rethrow and custom exceptions'?
cards.answer: Never swallow exceptions silently with an empty catch. Check that each catch either recovers, translates with the inner exception attached, or logs and rethrows with throw;.

cards.prompt: When is the Try pattern a better fit than throwing an exception?
cards.answer: When failure is an expected, frequent outcome such as invalid user input Exceptions are for unexpected failures; Try methods make the common failure path cheap and explicit.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Guard clauses, the Try pattern and result values'?
cards.answer: Check that guards run before any state changes, so a rejected call leaves the object unchanged, and that the Try pattern never throws for ordinary bad input.

cards.prompt: What does dict[key] do when the key is absent and you are reading?
cards.answer: Throws KeyNotFoundException Reading through the indexer requires the key; use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault for optional keys.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'List<T> and Dictionary<TKey, TValue>'?
cards.answer: Before choosing, check the operations you perform most often: indexed access and appends suit List; lookups by key suit Dictionary. Check missing-key behaviour on every read.

cards.prompt: Which item does PriorityQueue<TElement, int> dequeue first?
cards.answer: The element with the smallest priority value It is a min-heap; ties are not ordered, so add a sequence number to the priority for stability.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Sets, queues, stacks and priority queues'?
cards.answer: Check empty-collection behaviour before every Dequeue, Pop or Peek, and check whether ties in a priority queue need a deterministic order.

cards.prompt: What does ImmutableList<T>.Add return?
cards.answer: A new list containing the extra element; the original is unchanged Immutable collections return new versions that share structure with the old one.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Collection expressions, immutable and frozen collections'?
cards.answer: Choose by the guarantee you need: a read-only view for encapsulation, an immutable collection for safe sharing with occasional updates, a frozen collection for build-once/read-many lookup. Check that 'immutable' items do not themselves contain mutable objects.

cards.prompt: What happens if you Add to a List<T> while a foreach over the same list is running?
cards.answer: The next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException List enumerators check a version counter; any structural change invalidates them.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'IEnumerable, enumerators and modification during iteration'?
cards.answer: Before mutating inside a loop, check whether you are enumerating the same collection. Prefer RemoveAll, building a new collection, or an index-based loop that accounts for shifting indices.

cards.prompt: Does List<int> box its integers?
cards.answer: No; .NET generates specialized code for value-type instantiations Reified generics keep List<int> storing raw ints, unlike the old non-generic ArrayList.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Generic types and methods'?
cards.answer: Prefer generics whenever the algorithm does not care about the element type. Check that default(T) is a meaningful value for your algorithm, especially when T may be a non-nullable value type.

cards.prompt: Why does a generic method need where T : IComparable<T> before calling a.CompareTo(b)?
cards.answer: Without the constraint the compiler only knows T has object's members Constraints are the compiler's evidence about what T can do; they cost nothing at runtime.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Constraints'?
cards.answer: Add the weakest constraints that let the code compile, and prefer interface constraints to base-class constraints. Check that a new() constraint really is needed; a factory delegate is often more flexible.

cards.prompt: Why can't List<Cat> be assigned to List<Animal>?
cards.answer: List<T> is invariant because it both reads and writes T If the assignment were allowed you could add a Dog through the List<Animal> view.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Covariance and contravariance'?
cards.answer: When an assignment between generic types fails to compile, check whether the type parameter is only read (could be out) or only written (could be in); if it is both, invariance is protecting you.

cards.prompt: What lets generic code write T.AdditiveIdentity or a + b for a type parameter T?
cards.answer: Constraining T to interfaces with static abstract members Static abstract interface members expose operators and static factories to generic code at compile time.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Static abstract members and generic math'?
cards.answer: Generic math code is compiled per value type, so it runs as fast as hand-written code. Check overflow behaviour: T.CreateChecked(x) throws when a value does not fit, CreateSaturating clamps and CreateTruncating wraps.

cards.prompt: What does a multicast Func<int> return when invoked?
cards.answer: The return value of the last method in its invocation list All methods run in order, but only the final result is returned; multicast suits Action and events.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Delegates, Func and Action'?
cards.answer: Delegates hold strong references to their targets. Before storing a delegate in a long-lived place (a static field, a cache, an event on a long-lived object), check what object it keeps alive.

cards.prompt: Three lambdas created in for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) each return i. What do they return when called after the loop?
cards.answer: 3, 3 and 3 A for loop has one i shared by every closure; foreach creates a fresh variable per iteration.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Lambdas, closures and captured variables'?
cards.answer: Check what each lambda captures, whether it captures a shared loop counter, and whether storing the delegate extends the lifetime of large objects.

cards.prompt: What can code outside the declaring class do with a public event?
cards.answer: Only subscribe with += and unsubscribe with -= The event keyword restricts outside access to add and remove; raising and resetting stay private.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Events and the event pattern'?
cards.answer: Check that every subscription has a matching unsubscription when the subscriber's lifetime is shorter than the publisher's, and that handlers do not assume they run in a particular order unless the publisher documents it.

cards.prompt: Why can a subscriber stay in memory after the rest of the program drops it?
cards.answer: The publisher's event delegate still references the subscriber Delegates hold their target strongly, so a longer-lived publisher keeps subscribers reachable until they unsubscribe.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Event subscriptions and object lifetime'?
cards.answer: When a subscriber lives shorter than its publisher, check where its subscription ends. Static events deserve special suspicion because their publisher lives for the whole process.

cards.prompt: When does the body of an iterator method start running?
cards.answer: On the first MoveNext call of an enumerator, not when the method is called Iterators are lazy state machines; that is why validation inside them is deferred too.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Iterators with yield'?
cards.answer: Check whether the caller may stop early (put cleanup in finally), whether validation should be eager, and whether enumerating twice re-runs side effects.

cards.prompt: A LINQ query is enumerated by Count() and then by foreach. How many times does its Where predicate run per element?
cards.answer: Twice: each enumeration re-runs the pipeline Queries are recipes, not results. Materialize with ToList when you need several passes.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'LINQ and deferred execution'?
cards.answer: Analyzers warn about possible multiple enumeration of an IEnumerable<T> parameter. Check where each query is enumerated and how many times, and decide deliberately between a lazy view and a materialized snapshot.

cards.prompt: Which .NET 10 operator keeps outer elements that have no match in the inner sequence?
cards.answer: LeftJoin Join is an inner join. LeftJoin passes null/default for the missing inner element, replacing the GroupJoin + DefaultIfEmpty idiom.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Filtering, projection, ordering, grouping and joins'?
cards.answer: Check sort keys for ties, choose ToLookup when keys repeat, and in outer joins check how the code handles the missing side.

cards.prompt: What does Average() do on an empty int[]?
cards.answer: Throws InvalidOperationException Non-nullable Min/Max/Average have no meaningful empty result; project to a nullable type or check Any() first.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Aggregation and the newer LINQ operators'?
cards.answer: Before calling an aggregate, check what happens on an empty input and whether duplicates should count. Prefer Any() to Count() > 0, which may enumerate everything.

cards.prompt: What does assigning a lambda to Expression<Func<int, bool>> produce?
cards.answer: A tree of objects describing the lambda's code Expression trees are data a provider can inspect and translate; Compile() turns them into a delegate.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'IQueryable and expression trees'?
cards.answer: Check the static type of a query variable: IQueryable<T> means the predicate becomes data for a provider, IEnumerable<T> means it runs as your code, possibly after fetching everything.

cards.prompt: Two objects reference only each other and nothing else references them. What does the .NET GC do?
cards.answer: Collects both, because neither is reachable from a root The GC traces reachability from roots; it does not use reference counts, so cycles are not leaks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'The managed heap and garbage collection'?
cards.answer: Do not call GC.Collect() in production code to fix memory issues; find what keeps objects reachable instead. Check long-lived roots first: statics, singletons, caches and events.

cards.prompt: In what order are using var a and then using var b disposed at the end of a method?
cards.answer: b first, then a using declarations unwind in reverse order, like nested using blocks, so dependents are released before what they depend on.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'IDisposable and using'?
cards.answer: Check every new of a disposable type: who owns it, where it is disposed, and what happens if an exception occurs between creation and the using. Analyzer CA2000 flags objects not disposed on all paths.

cards.prompt: Why should a finalizer not use other managed objects referenced by fields?
cards.answer: They may already have been finalized or collected in the same cycle Finalization order is undefined; only touch the unmanaged resource the object owns. Prefer SafeHandle.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Finalizers, SafeHandle and the dispose pattern'?
cards.answer: Check whether a type truly owns an unmanaged resource. If not, do not add a finalizer; if so, prefer SafeHandle, and make sure finalizer code touches only that resource.

cards.prompt: Why can't a Span<T> be stored in a field of a class?
cards.answer: It is a ref struct that must stay on the stack so it cannot outlive its memory The ref struct rules let the compiler prove a span never refers to memory that is gone; use Memory<T> for storage.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Span<T>, Memory<T> and ref structs'?
cards.answer: Use spans in parsing, formatting and buffer code where allocation matters. Check that a span never escapes the lifetime of its memory (the compiler enforces most of this) and that a stackalloc size is small and bounded, because a large stack allocation can overflow the stack.

cards.prompt: What must you track when renting from ArrayPool<T>.Shared?
cards.answer: The length you actually use, since the rented array may be longer Rent returns at least the requested size. Use your own length, return the array exactly once and never touch it afterwards.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Pooling and reducing allocations'?
cards.answer: Pools turn memory bugs into data bugs: a returned array still in use gets overwritten by the next renter. Check every Rent has exactly one Return on every path and that nothing keeps the array afterwards.

cards.prompt: Two async calls are awaited one after the other: var x = await A(); var y = await B();. When does B start?
cards.answer: Only after A has completed Start both tasks first and then await them (for example with Task.WhenAll) to overlap the waits.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Tasks, async and await'?
cards.answer: Name async methods with an Async suffix and return Task, not void. Check every task you create is awaited (or deliberately observed): an unawaited task's exception is silently lost and analyzers warn with CS4014.

cards.prompt: Why is calling .Result on a task from a UI thread risky?
cards.answer: The continuation may need the blocked UI thread, causing a deadlock Sync-over-async blocks the thread the async continuation is waiting to run on; go async all the way.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'How await works: continuations, contexts and pitfalls'?
cards.answer: Code before the first incomplete await runs synchronously on the caller's thread, including argument validation. Check that expensive synchronous work is not hiding before the first await, and that .Result/.Wait() never appear in code that could run on a context-bound thread.

cards.prompt: What does calling CancellationTokenSource.Cancel() do to running work?
cards.answer: It signals the token; the work must observe it and stop itself Cancellation is cooperative: code checks the token or passes it to APIs that do.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Cancellation tokens and timeouts'?
cards.answer: Accept a CancellationToken cancellationToken = default as the last parameter of public async methods and pass it to everything you call. Check that every registration is disposed, every CTS is disposed, and that cancellation leaves shared state consistent.

cards.prompt: What does await Task.WhenAll(a, b) throw when both a and b fail?
cards.answer: The first exception; the task's Exception property holds both await unwraps to the first inner exception. Inspect the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions for all failures.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'WhenAll, WhenAny, WhenEach and timeouts'?
cards.answer: Throttle large fan-outs: starting ten thousand HTTP requests at once can exhaust sockets. Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism or a SemaphoreSlim bounds concurrency. Check what happens to the tasks that lose a race or exceed a timeout.

cards.prompt: Which rule applies to a ValueTask<T> but not to a Task<T>?
cards.answer: It must be awaited at most once A ValueTask may wrap a pooled object reused after completion; await it once or convert with AsTask().

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Async streams, await using and ValueTask'?
cards.answer: Check that async streams honour cancellation, that resources acquired inside them are released in finally, and that every ValueTask is consumed exactly once.

cards.prompt: Why can count++ from several threads lose updates?
cards.answer: It is a separate read, add and write that other threads can interleave with Use Interlocked.Increment or a lock so the read-modify-write is atomic.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Threads, the thread pool and data races'?
cards.answer: The safest shared state is no shared state: give each thread its own data and combine results at the end, or communicate through channels. Before sharing a variable between threads, check every read and write path for atomicity and visibility.

cards.prompt: What is the standard way to prevent deadlocks when a method must take two locks?
cards.answer: Always acquire the locks in one global order If every thread acquires locks in the same order, no cycle of waiting can form.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Locks, System.Threading.Lock and deadlocks'?
cards.answer: ReaderWriterLockSlim allows many readers or one writer, worthwhile only for read-heavy, long critical sections. Check that each piece of shared state has exactly one guarding lock, that the lock is private, and that nested acquisitions follow one order.

cards.prompt: What does await writer.WriteAsync(item) do on a full bounded channel with FullMode.Wait?
cards.answer: Waits until a reader makes room Waiting writers are backpressure: the producer runs no faster than the consumer, keeping memory bounded.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Concurrent collections and channels'?
cards.answer: Check that every channel is completed exactly once (or consumers wait forever), that cancellation stops both sides, and that bounded capacity matches how much memory you can afford.

cards.prompt: By default, in what order does a PLINQ query produce results?
cards.answer: Unspecified; use AsOrdered or sort to impose an order PLINQ partitions the input across threads; ordering costs extra and must be requested.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Data parallelism with Parallel and PLINQ'?
cards.answer: Check iterations are independent, that shared results are combined safely, and that ordering requirements are explicit (AsOrdered, or sort afterwards).

cards.prompt: What does an extension(Temperature) { public static ... } block without a parameter name declare?
cards.answer: Static extension members called like Temperature.Member A receiver-type-only block extends the type itself; a named receiver declares instance-style members.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Extension methods and C# 14 extension members'?
cards.answer: Extensions are resolved statically from the variable's compile-time type and the imported namespaces. Check for ambiguity when two imported namespaces define the same extension, and prefer instance members when you own the type.

cards.prompt: In customer?.Order = Compute();, when is Compute() called?
cards.answer: Only when customer is not null Null-conditional assignment evaluates the right side only after the receiver passes the null check.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Null-conditional assignment, nameof and partial members'?
cards.answer: When adopting ?.=, check that skipping the right-hand side is intended: side effects there (logging, increments) no longer happen when the target is null.

cards.prompt: Why is heavy reflection a problem for Native AOT and trimmed apps?
cards.answer: The trimmer cannot see members used only via reflection and may remove them Annotate with DynamicallyAccessedMembers or replace reflection with source-generated code.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Attributes and reflection'?
cards.answer: Use reflection at boundaries (startup, configuration, tooling), cache what you discover, and check whether the app will be trimmed or AOT-compiled before depending on it.

cards.prompt: What does the fixed statement do in unsafe code?
cards.answer: Pins a managed object so the GC cannot move it while its address is used The GC compacts the heap; pinning keeps addresses valid for the duration of the fixed block only.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'ref locals, ref structs, scoped and unsafe code'?
cards.answer: C# 15 begins redefining unsafe so that only memory-accessing operations require unsafe (final stage). Today, check every unsafe block for bounds, pinning duration and aliasing, and keep it as small as possible.

cards.prompt: What does a source generator add to a compilation?
cards.answer: New C# source code that is compiled with your project Generators emit ordinary source during the build, so the result is type-checked and works with trimming and AOT.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Source generators and compile-time code'?
cards.answer: Prefer a built-in generator when one exists (regex, JSON, logging, interop). Check that the generated code is what you expect and that the generator is pinned to a version, like any other dependency.

cards.prompt: What does Central Package Management change about PackageReference items?
cards.answer: Versions move to Directory.Packages.props and references omit them One file owns every version, preventing projects in a repository from drifting apart.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Projects, solutions, packages and analyzers'?
cards.answer: dotnet publish -c Release produces a deployable app. Options include framework-dependent versus self-contained output, a single-file bundle, trimming (PublishTrimmed) and Native AOT (PublishAot), which compiles ahead of time for fast startup and small memory use but forbids unconstrained reflection and runtime code generation. Check those constraints before choosing AOT.

cards.prompt: Why does Searcher.Search validate its arguments before returning a local iterator function?
cards.answer: So invalid arguments throw at the call instead of on first enumeration Iterator bodies are deferred; splitting validation from iteration makes failures immediate while keeping lazy reading.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Project: a tested text-search CLI'?
cards.answer: Keep logic in a library that reads from a TextReader so tests need no files; validate arguments eagerly before a lazy iterator; send errors to stderr with distinct exit codes; and prove tests catch a deliberately injected bug.

cards.prompt: In the base pipeline, what can happen when one worker throws?
cards.answer: Other workers and the producer keep waiting, so the call can hang and work outlives it Nothing links the failure to the others. Owning a linked CancellationTokenSource lets the failure stop all work before the call returns.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Project: a bounded async pipeline with cancellation'?
cards.answer: This ownership rule (work started by a call finishes, or is cancelled, before the call returns) is what prevents leaked tasks, captured state and unobserved exceptions in long-running services.

cards.prompt: Why does Stats use two type parameters, T : INumber<T> and TResult : IFloatingPoint<TResult>?
cards.answer: So integer inputs can produce fractional results such as a mean of 2.5 Averaging ints in int arithmetic would truncate; converting into a floating-point TResult keeps precision while still accepting any numeric input.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Capstone: a generic statistics library and CLI'?
cards.answer: Constrain inputs to INumber<T> and results to IFloatingPoint<TResult> so integer data yields fractional statistics; accept ReadOnlySpan<T> without copying the caller's data; parse with invariant culture; and cover odd/even and empty cases with theory tests.

cards.prompt: What happens when a switch over a union omits one of its case types?
cards.answer: The compiler warns that the switch is not exhaustive (CS8509) The compiler knows every case of a union, so incomplete switches are reported; with warnings as errors they fail the build.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Union types'?
cards.answer: The runtime support types (UnionAttribute, IUnion) arrived in .NET 11 Preview 5, and Microsoft notes that some parts of the specification are still being implemented. Use unions for closed sets of alternatives such as results, messages and parse outcomes, and check new releases for additions to the feature.

cards.prompt: Why does a switch over a closed class need no discard arm when it handles every direct descendant?
cards.answer: Only the declaring assembly can add descendants, so the compiler knows them all closed fixes the set of direct descendants at compile time, enabling exhaustiveness checks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Closed class hierarchies'?
cards.answer: Choose between the two C# 15 tools by shape: a union when the alternatives are unrelated existing types, a closed hierarchy when the alternatives are your own types that share a base. Check that adding a new descendant is meant to break incomplete switches, because that is exactly what it will do.

cards.prompt: In HashSet<string> s = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "a", "A"];, what does with(...) do?
cards.answer: Passes the comparer to the HashSet constructor before the elements are added with(...) must come first and supplies constructor or factory arguments, so the set holds one element.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Collection expression arguments and extension indexers'?
cards.answer: Extension indexers are resolved statically like other extensions, and an instance indexer on the type always wins: an extension indexer on string is never chosen for text[1], because string already has one. Check the cost hidden behind the brackets: indexing an IEnumerable<T> by position is O(n), unlike an array or list.

cards.prompt: What does continue outer; do inside a nested loop in C# 15?
cards.answer: Starts the next iteration of the loop labelled outer A labeled continue targets the named enclosing loop; break outer would leave it instead.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'Labeled break and continue'?
cards.answer: Check that the label names the loop you mean; continue outer re-evaluates the outer loop's condition and increment, which is easy to forget when the outer loop also maintains state.

cards.prompt: Under the C# 15 preview rules, which operation still requires an unsafe context?
cards.answer: Dereferencing a pointer with *p The redesign keeps unsafe for operations that access memory; creating pointers and pinning are relaxed.

cards.prompt: What should you check when applying 'The memory-safety redesign (preview)'?
cards.answer: The goal is that reviewers can find every memory-accessing operation by searching for unsafe. Until the feature ships in a released language version, keep production code on stage 13's rules and check the C# 15/16 notes for the final design.

cards.prompt: What does fmt.Println put between its operands?
cards.answer: A single space, followed by a newline at the end Println always separates operands with spaces and appends a newline. That is why "Go:" and 42 appear as "Go: 42".

cards.prompt: What should you check when using your first go program and the go command?
cards.answer: Go compiles quickly and refuses to build code that imports a package it does not use or declares a local variable it never reads. These rules feel strict at first; they keep programs free of dead dependencies and half-finished edits. Treat a compiler error as precise feedback: it names the file, line and column.

cards.prompt: What does the go directive in go.mod control?
cards.answer: The Go language version and semantics the module is written for go 1.27 selects language features and defaults (such as per-iteration loop variables from 1.22). Dependencies are recorded on require lines, and the toolchain line or GOTOOLCHAIN selects a compiler.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using modules, go.mod, and building a binary?
cards.answer: Programs read their command-line arguments through os.Args, where os.Args[0] is the program name. Exit codes come from os.Exit; returning from main exits with status 0. Deferred functions do not run when os.Exit is called, so do cleanup before exiting.

cards.prompt: Which verb prints a value together with its Go type name?
cards.answer: %T prints the type; combine it with %v for the value %T formats the dynamic type of its operand. %#v prints a Go-syntax representation of the value, which often includes the type for composite literals but is not the type name alone.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using printing with fmt: print, printf and verbs?
cards.answer: Printf does not add a newline; put \n in the format. go vet checks that verbs match their arguments, so a %d given a string is reported before the program ever runs. Use %% for a literal percent sign.

cards.prompt: Why does putting a function's opening brace on the next line fail to compile?
cards.answer: Automatic semicolon insertion ends the declaration at the line break The lexer inserts a semicolon after the closing parenthesis, so the brace starts a separate statement. gofmt is a formatter, not part of the compiler.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using gofmt, comments, and the shape of go source?
cards.answer: Line comments start with //; block comments use /* */. A comment directly above a declaration is its doc comment and should begin with the declared name, for example // Area returns.... go doc and pkg.go.dev render those comments as documentation.

cards.prompt: What does strings.Cut return when the separator is missing?
cards.answer: The whole input, an empty string, and false Cut returns before=s, after="" and found=false, so code can test found instead of comparing indices against -1.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading the standard library with go doc?
cards.answer: strings.Cut(s, sep) splits around the first separator and reports whether it was found; Go 1.27 adds strings.CutLast for the last separator. Prefer Cut over Index plus slicing because the found flag makes the not-found case explicit.

cards.prompt: Why check scanner.Err() after the Scan loop?
cards.answer: Scan returns false for both end of input and failures such as a too-long line A false Scan is ambiguous. Err returns nil at a clean end of input and the error otherwise, for example bufio.ErrTooLong.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading standard input line by line?
cards.answer: Write results to os.Stdout and diagnostics to os.Stderr so pipelines can separate them. fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, ...) writes a diagnostic without mixing it into the data stream.

cards.prompt: What value does a newly declared var m map[string]int hold?
cards.answer: nil: reads work and return zero, but writes panic The zero value of a map is nil. Looking up a key in a nil map returns the zero value, but assigning to one panics, so maps are made with make or a literal before writing.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using variables, short declarations and zero values?
cards.answer: Declarations can be grouped in var ( ... ) blocks, and several variables can be declared at once: a, b := 1, 2. Swapping is a single statement, a, b = b, a, because all right-hand values are evaluated before any assignment happens.

cards.prompt: Why does const huge = 1 << 100 compile even though no integer type can hold it?
cards.answer: Untyped constants have arbitrary precision until converted to a type Untyped constant arithmetic is exact. It only fails if the value is used where it must fit a concrete type, such as assigning huge to an int.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using constants, untyped constants and iota?
cards.answer: Go has no enum keyword. The idiom is a named integer type with iota constants and a String method for printing. A named type stops values of one enumeration from being mixed with plain integers by accident.

cards.prompt: What happens when int and float64 values are added directly?
cards.answer: A compile error; one operand must be converted explicitly Go has no implicit numeric conversions between variables of different types. Untyped constants are flexible; typed variables are not.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using integers, floats, overflow and explicit conversion?
cards.answer: Integer arithmetic wraps on overflow with no error: an int8 holding 127 plus one becomes -128. Integer division truncates toward zero, and % keeps the sign of the dividend. Dividing an integer by a constant zero is a compile error; dividing by a variable that is zero panics at run time. Floating-point division by zero gives ±Inf or NaN.

cards.prompt: What does len("é") return?
cards.answer: 2, because len counts the UTF-8 bytes Strings are byte sequences. "é" (U+00E9) is encoded in UTF-8 as two bytes, 0xC3 0xA9.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using strings, bytes, runes and utf-8?
cards.answer: Converting a string to []byte or []rune copies it. Building strings by repeated + allocates a new string each time; use strings.Builder for loops. Raw string literals in backquotes keep backslashes and newlines literally, which suits regular expressions and multi-line text.

cards.prompt: How does a<<1 + 1 group in Go?
cards.answer: (a<<1) + 1, because shifts bind tighter than addition << shares the multiplication precedence level, which is above +. gofmt even removes the spaces around << to show the grouping.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using operators, precedence and bit manipulation?
cards.answer: Bitwise operators work on integers: & and, | or, ^ xor (and unary ^ for bitwise not), &^ and-not (bit clear), << and >> shifts. && and || short-circuit, which makes guards such as p != nil && p.ok safe.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between type A B and type A = B?
cards.answer: The first defines a distinct type; the second is an alias for the same type A type definition creates a new, distinct named type with no methods of its own yet. An alias is just another name, so values flow between A and B freely.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using defined types, aliases and underlying types?
cards.answer: Conversion between a defined type and its underlying type is always allowed, and so is conversion between two defined types that share an underlying type. Untyped constants convert implicitly, so var c Celsius = 100 compiles without a cast.

cards.prompt: Where is a variable declared in if v := f(); v > 0 { } visible?
cards.answer: In the condition, the if block and any else blocks The init statement opens an implicit scope covering the whole if/else chain and ending after it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using if with init statements and the single for loop?
cards.answer: Since Go 1.22 you can range over an integer: for i := range 5 runs i = 0..4. Use it when you only need a count; it removes off-by-one mistakes in the condition.

cards.prompt: What does break do inside a switch that is inside a for loop?
cards.answer: It leaves only the switch; use a labelled break to leave the loop break targets the innermost for, switch or select. A label names the outer statement explicitly.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using switch: no fallthrough by default, tagless switch?
cards.answer: break inside a switch leaves the switch, not an enclosing loop. To leave a loop from inside a switch, label the loop and use break Label.

cards.prompt: Which statement starts the next iteration of an enclosing loop labelled outer?
cards.answer: continue outer continue with a label applies to that labelled for statement. break outer would leave it, and goto outer would restart the loop from its initialisation.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using labels, break, continue and goto?
cards.answer: Unused labels are compile errors, like unused variables. A labelled continue is usually clearer than a flag variable checked after the inner loop.

cards.prompt: What does a bare return do in a function with named results?
cards.answer: Returns the current values of the named result variables Named results are ordinary local variables initialised to zero. A bare return returns whatever they hold at that moment, including changes made by deferred functions.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using functions, multiple results and named results?
cards.answer: Results can be named. Named results start as zero values and a bare return returns their current values. Use them for short functions or for documentation; in long functions bare returns hide what is being returned.

cards.prompt: What does a variadic function receive when called as f(s...)?
cards.answer: The caller's slice itself, sharing its backing array s... passes the slice header unchanged, so writes to elements are visible to the caller. Calling f(a, b) instead builds a new slice.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using variadic functions and functions as values?
cards.answer: Function values compare only to nil. Passing behaviour as a function is often simpler than defining a one-method interface, and the sort and slices packages accept comparison functions this way.

cards.prompt: With go 1.27 in go.mod, what do closures created in for i := range 3 capture?
cards.answer: A distinct i for each iteration, so they see 0, 1 and 2 Go 1.22 made loop variables per-iteration for modules declaring go 1.22 or later. The closures capture variables, but each iteration has its own.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using closures and per-iteration loop variables?
cards.answer: Closures make small strategies and callbacks easy, but capturing a variable that another goroutine also writes is a data race. Pass values as arguments when in doubt.

cards.prompt: When are the arguments of a deferred function call evaluated?
cards.answer: When the defer statement executes defer evaluates the function value and its arguments immediately and saves them; only the call is postponed.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using defer: cleanup that runs on every return path?
cards.answer: The common pattern is acquire, check the error, then defer the release: f, err := os.Open(p); if err != nil { return err }; defer f.Close(). A defer inside a loop does not run until the function returns, so a loop that opens many files should call a helper function per item.

cards.prompt: What happens when an array is passed to a function?
cards.answer: The whole array is copied Arrays are values. To share one, pass a pointer (*[3]int) or a slice of it (a[:]).

cards.prompt: What should you check when using arrays are values with a fixed length?
cards.answer: Arrays of comparable elements can be compared with ==. In practice most Go code uses slices, which are views onto arrays; arrays appear in hashes ([32]byte), coordinates and buffers sized at compile time.

cards.prompt: After t := s[:2]; t = append(t, 9), when is s[2] overwritten?
cards.answer: When cap(t) > 2, because append writes into the shared array With spare capacity, append places the new element in the backing array that s also uses. A full slice expression s[:2:2] prevents this.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using slices: length, capacity and shared backing arrays?
cards.answer: A nil slice has length and capacity zero, and works with len, append and range. make([]T, n, c) allocates a slice with length n and capacity c.

cards.prompt: Why use SortStableFunc rather than SortFunc?
cards.answer: It keeps equal elements in their original relative order SortFunc may reorder elements that compare equal. Stability matters when sorting by a secondary key after an earlier sort.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the slices package: sort, search, insert, compact?
cards.answer: Delete, Insert and Compact return the new slice and may reuse the old backing array. Since Go 1.22 the removed tail elements are zeroed, so pointers left behind do not keep objects alive. As with append, use the returned slice.

cards.prompt: How should you print a map's entries in a stable order?
cards.answer: Collect and sort the keys, then range over the sorted keys Map iteration order is unspecified and randomised. fmt prints maps with sorted keys, but range does not.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using maps: lookup, comma-ok, deletion and iteration order?
cards.answer: Maps are reference-like: assigning a map copies the header, so both names see the same entries. Writing to a nil map panics. Maps are not safe for concurrent writes; the runtime detects many such races and crashes with "concurrent map writes".

cards.prompt: When Dog embeds Animal and you call d.Hello(), what is the receiver?
cards.answer: The embedded Animal value inside d Promotion rewrites d.Hello() to d.Animal.Hello(). The method has no knowledge of the outer Dog, which is why embedding is not virtual dispatch.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using structs, field tags and embedding?
cards.answer: Field tags are string metadata read by reflection, for example `json:"name,omitempty"`. They do not change the language semantics; packages such as encoding/json interpret them. Anonymous structs are useful for one-off groupings and table-driven tests.

cards.prompt: Why is &m["k"] a compile error?
cards.answer: Map elements are not addressable because the map may relocate them Growing a map rehashes and moves entries, so a pointer to an element could dangle. Store pointers as values (map[string]*T) if you need shared mutable elements.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using pointers, new, new(expr) and addressability?
cards.answer: Composite literals are addressable through &: &Point{1, 2} is idiomatic. Map elements are not addressable (&m[k] is a compile error) because a map may move its entries as it grows. The field selector p.X automatically dereferences a pointer to a struct.

cards.prompt: What does Named{X: 3} mean under Go 1.27 when Named embeds Point?
cards.answer: It initialises the promoted field Named.Point.X The 1.27 rule allows any valid field selector as a key. X selects the promoted field inside the embedded Point.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go 1.27 struct literals with promoted field keys?
cards.answer: This only works when the selector is unambiguous and does not pass through an embedded pointer, which could be nil. Older modules with a go line below 1.27 reject the shorter form, so the go directive matters for which literals compile.

cards.prompt: What does clear(s) do to a slice s?
cards.answer: Zeroes every element; the length is unchanged clear on a slice zeroes elements up to len(s). For a map, clear removes all entries. Use s = s[:0] to reset a slice's length.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using built-ins: len, cap, copy, clear, min and max?
cards.answer: min and max (Go 1.21) are built-ins for any ordered type and take one or more arguments. For floats, if any argument is NaN the result is NaN. They work with constants at compile time too.

cards.prompt: Why did BrokenInc not change c?
cards.answer: A value receiver increments a copy of c The receiver is a parameter passed by value. Only a pointer receiver can change the caller's Counter.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using methods, value receivers and pointer receivers?
cards.answer: Calls are convenient in both directions. If v is addressable, v.Inc() on a pointer method is shorthand for (&v).Inc(). If p is a pointer, p.Value() on a value method is shorthand for (*p).Value(). The shorthand does not apply to values that are not addressable, such as map elements or return values.

cards.prompt: If Write has a pointer receiver on Buffer, which type satisfies io.Writer?
cards.answer: *Buffer only The method set of the value type Buffer excludes pointer-receiver methods, because a value stored in an interface is not addressable.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using interfaces are satisfied implicitly?
cards.answer: Method sets decide satisfaction. The method set of T contains its value-receiver methods; the method set of *T contains both value- and pointer-receiver methods. So if Write has a pointer receiver, *Buffer satisfies io.Writer but Buffer does not. A compile-time assertion var _ io.Writer = (*Buffer)(nil) documents and checks this.

cards.prompt: Why is bad() != nil even though e was nil?
cards.answer: The interface has a dynamic type (*MyError) even though its value is nil An interface compares equal to nil only if it has no dynamic type. Return untyped nil to signal "no error".

cards.prompt: What should you check when using nil interfaces versus interfaces holding nil pointers?
cards.answer: A method with a pointer receiver can be called on a nil pointer, and can even handle it deliberately. That is why the runtime cannot simply treat "interface holding nil" as nil.

cards.prompt: What does v, ok := x.(T) do when x does not hold a T?
cards.answer: Sets ok to false and v to T's zero value, without panicking The comma-ok form makes the assertion non-panicking. The single-result form panics on failure.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using type assertions and type switches?
cards.answer: Prefer methods and small interfaces to large type switches: a type switch must be edited for each new type, while an interface lets new types plug in. Type switches are right for closed sets of message or AST node types.

cards.prompt: Where should a Go interface usually be declared?
cards.answer: In the package that uses it, with only the methods it needs Implicit satisfaction lets consumers declare the minimal interface they depend on without the implementer importing it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using small interfaces, embedding and any?
cards.answer: Define interfaces in the package that consumes them, sized to what that code needs. Returning concrete types and accepting interfaces keeps APIs flexible: callers can pass anything with the needed methods.

cards.prompt: Why convert to int(d) inside Weekday.String before formatting?
cards.answer: Formatting d itself would call String again and recurse forever fmt checks for a String method on the operand. The underlying int has none, so the conversion breaks the recursion.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using stringer, error and custom formatting?
cards.answer: For full control implement fmt.Formatter, or fmt.GoStringer for %#v. Most code only needs String. go vet warns when a String method has the wrong signature, because fmt would silently ignore it.

cards.prompt: What happens when two any values holding slices are compared with ==?
cards.answer: It compiles but panics at run time Interface comparison is checked dynamically. The static type any is comparable, but the dynamic type []int is not, so the runtime panics.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using equality, comparability and interface comparison panics?
cards.answer: Pointers are equal when they point to the same variable. Two distinct zero-size variables may or may not have equal addresses, so do not rely on pointer identity for empty structs.

cards.prompt: What is the idiomatic way to handle an error you cannot resolve locally?
cards.answer: Return it with added context, without also logging it Each error should be handled once. Adding context while returning builds a readable chain for whoever finally handles it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using errors are values: return, check, add context?
cards.answer: Handle each error once: either deal with it (retry, use a default, report it) or return it with added context. Logging an error and also returning it produces duplicate reports further up the stack.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between wrapping with %w and formatting with %v?
cards.answer: %w keeps the original error inspectable through Is/As; %v keeps only its text %w records the operand as the wrapped error returned by Unwrap. %v formats it into a string, so callers can no longer match it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using wrapping with %w, errors.is, errors.as and errors.astype?
cards.answer: Never compare wrapped errors with ==; use errors.Is. go vet reports %w used with a non-error operand, and Go 1.27's vet also reports %w given a pointer to an error.

cards.prompt: When should an error be a struct type rather than a sentinel?
cards.answer: When callers need structured details such as the failing field Sentinels answer "which error?". Types answer "what are the details?" and are matched with errors.As or AsType.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using designing errors: sentinels, types and opaque errors?
cards.answer: An error type can customise matching by implementing Is(target error) bool or As(target any) bool, for example to say that every ValidationError counts as ErrInvalid. Expose as little as callers need; opaque errors that are only printed are the easiest to evolve.

cards.prompt: What does errors.Join(nil, nil) return?
cards.answer: nil Join discards nil errors and returns nil if none remain, so it is safe to accumulate optional failures.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using combining errors with errors.join and multiple %w?
cards.answer: Join suits validation that reports every problem, and cleanup where both the operation and Close failed: err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()).

cards.prompt: Why could the deferred function change err in safeIndex?
cards.answer: err is a named result, and deferred functions run before the caller receives the results Deferred closures can assign to named results after a panic or return. That is how recovery is converted into an ordinary error.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using panic, recover and when not to use them?
cards.answer: Use panic for programmer errors and impossible states, not for expected failures like a missing file. Since Go 1.21, panic(nil) becomes a *runtime.PanicNilError, so recover() == nil reliably means "no panic".

cards.prompt: Why can defer f.Close() be wrong for a file you are writing?
cards.answer: It discards the Close error, which may report data that failed to flush Write errors can surface at Close. Capture the error into a named result so the caller learns the write failed.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using cleanup errors, defer ordering and close?
cards.answer: Readers can usually ignore Close errors, but writers, network transactions and database commits should not. os.CreateTemp, then write, sync, close and rename is the safe way to replace a file: a failure at any step leaves the old file in place.

cards.prompt: In what order do package-level variables, init functions and main run?
cards.answer: Imported packages first; within a package, variables then init functions; main last Initialisation follows the import graph. Each package finishes initialising its variables and running its inits before packages that import it start.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using packages, exported names and initialisation order?
cards.answer: This lesson is a two-package module. Run it as shown, then do the practice by changing only the price package.

cards.prompt: What does go 1.27 in go.mod mean?
cards.answer: The module requires at least Go 1.27 language semantics and toolchain Since Go 1.21 the go line is a mandatory minimum. Newer toolchains build it with 1.27 semantics; older ones must switch or fail.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the go and toolchain lines, gotoolchain and versions?
cards.answer: runtime.Version reports the toolchain that built the binary, and runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo reports the module path, main version and dependency versions embedded at build time. go version -m binary prints the same information for an existing executable.

cards.prompt: Which version does minimal version selection choose when A needs lib v1.2.0 and B needs lib v1.3.0?
cards.answer: v1.3.0, the highest of the stated minimums Each requirement is a minimum. MVS selects the smallest version that satisfies all of them, which is the maximum of the minimums.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using requirements, go.sum, replace and minimal version selection?
cards.answer: Go 1.27 makes go mod tidy merge duplicate require blocks for modules with go 1.27 or later.

cards.prompt: What does GOWORK=off do?
cards.answer: Ignores go.work so each module builds from its own go.mod CI often sets GOWORK=off to make sure a module does not depend on unpublished local edits.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using multi-module workspaces with go.work?
cards.answer: Workspaces suit a service and a library changing in the same pull request, or trying a fix to a dependency before it is released.

cards.prompt: Who may import example.com/shop/billing/internal/tax?
cards.answer: Only packages under example.com/shop/billing The rule is rooted at the parent of the internal directory, here billing, not at the module root.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using internal packages and enforced boundaries?
cards.answer: vendor directories are a different mechanism: go mod vendor copies dependencies into vendor/ so builds need no network. Since Go 1.14 the go command uses vendor automatically when vendor/modules.txt matches go.mod.

cards.prompt: What does a tool line in go.mod give you over installing a tool globally?
cards.answer: A tool version pinned and verified with the module's other requirements go tool runs the version selected by the module graph, so every developer and CI job uses the same tool.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using tracking developer tools with tool directives?
cards.answer: This lesson uses a local replace so the tool builds offline. In real projects the tool comes from a published module.

cards.prompt: Why does a v2 module need a /v2 suffix in its path?
cards.answer: So incompatible major versions are distinct import paths that can coexist Semantic import versioning: an incompatible API gets a new import path, so existing importers of v1 are never broken by v2.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using semantic versions, major-version paths and retract?
cards.answer: A retract directive in a later release marks bad versions: go get and go list -m -u avoid them and explain why, but existing builds that require them still work. Retraction is how a maintainer withdraws a broken or accidentally published tag.

cards.prompt: Which files does GOOS=linux go build include from plat_linux.go, plat_darwin.go and plat_other.go (//go:build !darwin && !linux)?
cards.answer: Only plat_linux.go The _linux suffix selects plat_linux.go, the _darwin suffix excludes plat_darwin.go, and the expression excludes plat_other.go on Linux.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using build constraints, goos/goarch and file suffixes?
cards.answer: Set GOOS and GOARCH to cross-compile: GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build produces a Linux binary on macOS with no extra toolchain, as long as cgo is not needed. go vet and go list with those variables check the other platform's files too.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between t.Errorf and t.Fatalf?
cards.answer: Errorf marks the test failed and continues; Fatalf marks it failed and stops the test Fatalf calls FailNow, which ends the current test function via runtime.Goexit. Other tests still run.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go test and table-driven tests?
cards.answer: This project starts with a byte-based Reverse that breaks multi-byte characters. One check adds a failing case on purpose to show what a failure looks like; the answer fixes the function.

cards.prompt: What does t.Helper() change?
cards.answer: Failures inside the helper are reported at the caller's line Helper removes the function from the reported call site, so the message points to the test that called it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using subtests, helpers, cleanup, temp dirs and parallel tests?
cards.answer: t.Parallel() lets a test run alongside other parallel tests. Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration has its own variable, so parallel subtests in a loop no longer need the old tc := tc copy. t.Setenv and t.Chdir change process-wide state and therefore cannot be combined with Parallel.

cards.prompt: What does for b.Loop() do that the older for range b.N did not?
cards.answer: It times only the loop and keeps the body's results alive against dead-code elimination Loop resets and stops the timer itself and prevents the compiler from discarding results computed in the body, two classic benchmark mistakes.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using benchmarks with b.loop and allocation reports?
cards.answer: Benchmarks measure one machine at one moment. Compare variants on the same machine, look at allocations as well as time, and treat small differences as noise unless benchstat shows them as significant.

cards.prompt: What does plain go test do with a fuzz test?
cards.answer: Runs it on the seed corpus and saved failing inputs only Fuzzing proper needs -fuzz. Without it, seeds and testdata/fuzz entries run as ordinary regression cases.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using native fuzzing with seed corpora?
cards.answer: Fuzz targets should check properties rather than exact outputs: reversing twice gives the input back, the output is valid UTF-8, parsing what you formatted round-trips. Inputs that are invalid by design should be skipped with t.Skip or rejected with an error, not crash.

cards.prompt: When does go test run an Example function?
cards.answer: When it has an // Output: or // Unordered output: comment Without an output comment there is nothing to compare, so the example is compiled to keep it correct but not executed.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using testable examples as documentation?
cards.answer: Examples are best for typical use; edge cases still belong in table tests. Keep them short and deterministic, without map iteration order or timing in the output.

cards.prompt: What does 100% statement coverage prove?
cards.answer: Only that every statement ran during the tests Coverage measures execution. Correctness needs assertions on results, which coverage tools cannot see.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using coverage profiles and what they do not prove?
cards.answer: Coverage shows what was executed, not what was checked. A test that calls every function without asserting anything reaches 100%. Use coverage to find untested branches, especially error paths, then write tests that check the behaviour there.

cards.prompt: What does httptest.NewTestServer (Go 1.27) use by default?
cards.answer: An in-memory network, with the server closed automatically when the test ends NewTestServer takes testing.TB, registers cleanup, and serves over an in-memory network; srv.Client() is configured to reach it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using testing http handlers with httptest and newtestserver?
cards.answer: Check status codes, content types and bodies. Close response bodies; since Go 1.27 the HTTP/1 client also drains a closed body automatically so the connection can be reused.

cards.prompt: When does fake time advance inside a synctest bubble?
cards.answer: Only when every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked The clock jumps to the next timer only when nothing in the bubble can make progress, which makes timing-dependent tests deterministic.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using deterministic concurrent tests with testing/synctest?
cards.answer: Go 1.27 adds synctest.Sleep, which advances the fake clock and then waits for the bubble to settle. Durably blocked means blocked on something inside the bubble, such as a channel created there, a timer or a sync.WaitGroup; blocking on real I/O or an outside mutex is not durable.

cards.prompt: When is an interface parameter a better choice than a type parameter?
cards.answer: When the function only calls methods and does not need the concrete type back Interfaces give dynamic dispatch with simple signatures. Type parameters help when the type must be preserved in results or containers.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using type parameters and generic functions?
cards.answer: Generics remove duplicated code for containers and algorithms that are the same for every type. They do not replace interfaces: if a function only calls methods, an interface parameter is simpler. Reach for type parameters when you need to keep the concrete type, such as returning []T rather than []any.

cards.prompt: Which types satisfy interface{ ~int }?
cards.answer: int and every defined type whose underlying type is int ~ widens a type element to its underlying type. Without it the set contains int alone.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using constraints, type sets, ~ and cmp.ordered?
cards.answer: The standard library provides cmp.Ordered (types supporting < <= > >=) and comparable (types supporting == and !=). Interfaces containing type elements can only be used as constraints, never as ordinary variable types.

cards.prompt: Can any be used as a type argument for a comparable type parameter?
cards.answer: Yes since Go 1.20, though == may panic for non-comparable dynamic types Go 1.20 allowed interfaces to satisfy comparable. Strict comparability, which rules out run-time panics, holds only for non-interface comparable types.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using comparable, map keys and strict comparability?
cards.answer: Generic sets and deduplication are typical uses: type Set[T comparable] map[T]struct{}. The empty struct value takes no space, so the map stores only keys.

cards.prompt: Why does Scale take S ~[]E instead of a plain []E?
cards.answer: So it returns the caller's named slice type, keeping its methods With []E the result would be []float64 and lose Prices.Total. Constraint inference derives E from S.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using type inference, including go 1.27's assignment inference?
