cards.answer: Go 1.21 allowed inference when a generic function is assigned to a variable of a function type. Go 1.27 generalises this to every context where a generic function is assigned or converted to a matching function type, such as struct fields and return values. You no longer need to write Double[int] when the target type already says int.

cards.prompt: How do you return "no value" from a generic method returning T?
cards.answer: Declare var zero T and return it with a false flag or an error nil is not valid for every T, and T{} is not valid syntax for all types. var zero T is the zero value of whatever T is.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using generic types, methods on them and generic aliases?
cards.answer: Since Go 1.24 type aliases can be generic: type Set[T comparable] = map[T]struct{}. That helps move generic types between packages without breaking callers.

cards.prompt: Can a generic method be used to satisfy an interface?
cards.answer: No; generic methods are not part of any interface's method set An interface method has one fixed signature, while a generic method has a family of signatures chosen per call.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go 1.27 generic methods?
cards.answer: A generic method does not belong to any interface's method set, because an interface cannot list a method whose type depends on a parameter chosen per call. So generic methods are for convenience on concrete types, not for satisfying interfaces. Older modules need go 1.27 in go.mod to use them.

cards.prompt: How do you branch on the concrete type of a type parameter value v?
cards.answer: Convert it to an interface: switch any(v).(type) Type switches apply to interface values. Converting with any(v) gives an interface holding the concrete type argument.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using generics: limits, costs and design trade-offs?
cards.answer: Start with concrete code; introduce type parameters when a second or third type needs the same logic. Constraints should be as loose as possible: any, then comparable, then cmp.Ordered, then custom sets.

cards.prompt: What must an iterator do when yield returns false?
cards.answer: Stop immediately and never call yield again false means the loop body executed break or return. Calling yield after that panics at run time.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using range-over-func iterators: iter.seq and iter.seq2?
cards.answer: Iterators are lazy: nothing happens until a loop or a consumer such as slices.Collect pulls values. They let collections expose traversal without allocating a slice, and let infinite sequences, such as Fibonacci numbers, be consumed in bounded amounts.

cards.prompt: Why defer stop() after iter.Pull?
cards.answer: So the iterator ends and runs its cleanup even if you stop pulling early A pulled iterator is suspended mid-loop. stop resumes it with yield returning false so its deferred cleanup runs.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using pull iterators with iter.pull and cleanup?
cards.answer: Iterators may also need to release resources, such as files, when the consumer breaks early. Put the cleanup in a defer inside the iterator function: it runs whether the loop finishes, breaks, or the pull iterator is stopped.

cards.prompt: What does strings.Lines yield for "one\ntwo\n"?
cards.answer: "one\n" and "two\n", keeping each newline Lines yields each line including its terminating newline, so rejoining them reproduces the input exactly.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using iterator helpers in slices, maps and strings?
cards.answer: Chaining is explicit and still lazy: slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) collects only once. There is no built-in Map or Filter over iterators in the standard library; writing them is a few lines with iter.Seq.

cards.prompt: Why does walk return a bool?
cards.answer: To stop the whole recursive traversal once yield returns false After the consumer breaks, every level must stop. The && chain short-circuits as soon as any call reports false.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using designing collection apis with iterators?
cards.answer: Document whether an iterator can be used more than once and whether the collection may change during iteration. Single-use iterators, such as those reading a stream, should say so in their doc comment.

cards.prompt: A Read call returns n > 0 and io.EOF together. What should the caller do?
cards.answer: Use the n bytes first, then stop because of EOF The io.Reader contract allows data and EOF in the same call. Processing p[:n] before checking err is the safe pattern.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using io.reader and io.writer composition?
cards.answer: Accepting io.Reader instead of a filename makes code testable: tests pass strings.NewReader, production passes a file or network connection. io.ReadAll is fine for small inputs; for large or untrusted input, wrap with io.LimitReader first.

cards.prompt: Why did "buffered line" print after "unbuffered first"?
cards.answer: bufio.Writer held it in memory until Flush The buffered bytes reached os.Stdout only when Flush ran. Forgetting Flush loses output entirely.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using buffered i/o: bufio.reader, writer and scanner splitters?
cards.answer: bufio.Reader offers ReadString('\n'), ReadRune and Peek. ReadString returns the data read before an error, so the last line without a trailing newline comes back together with io.EOF.

cards.prompt: Why use os.Root instead of filepath.Join for user-supplied names?
cards.answer: Root rejects paths and symlinks that escape the directory Join only cleans the string; it does not stop ".." or symlinks pointing elsewhere. Root checks every resolved component.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using files, directories and traversal-safe os.root?
cards.answer: Use os.Root whenever paths come from users, archives or network requests. root.FS() adapts it to fs.FS. Close the root when done.

cards.prompt: Which separator do fs.FS paths use on Windows?
cards.answer: Always forward slashes fs.FS names are slash-separated and unrooted on every platform; filepath converts to OS form only at the edges.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using path/filepath, io/fs and embedded files?
cards.answer: //go:embed patterns before a variable of type string, []byte or embed.FS include files at build time. Embedded files ship inside the executable, so templates and static assets need no deployment step. fstest.MapFS is the in-memory fs.FS for tests.

cards.prompt: What does strconv.ParseInt("300", 10, 8) return?
cards.answer: 127 and a range error, because 300 does not fit in 8 bits bitSize limits the accepted range. Out-of-range input returns the nearest limit with ErrRange.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using strconv, strings, bytes and unicode?
cards.answer: unicode classifies runes: IsLetter, IsDigit, IsSpace, IsUpper. Go 1.27 updates the tables to Unicode 17. Case conversion is per rune and does not handle every language's rules; golang.org/x/text covers those.

cards.prompt: Why should elapsed time be measured with time.Since rather than subtracting wall-clock readings you saved as strings?
cards.answer: Since uses the monotonic clock, which is immune to wall-clock changes The monotonic reading inside time.Now values only moves forward. Serialised times keep only the wall clock.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using time: durations, monotonic clocks, layouts and zones?
cards.answer: Formatting uses a reference time, Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006, written in the desired layout: t.Format("2006-01-02 15:04"). time.RFC3339 and time.DateOnly are predefined layouts. time.LoadLocation reads zone data; time.Parse defaults to UTC.

cards.prompt: What does sort.Search(n, f) require of f?
cards.answer: f must be false for a prefix of indices and true for the rest Search is a binary search over a monotone predicate and returns the first index where it becomes true, or n if never.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sorting, searching and ordering with cmp?
cards.answer: Ordering functions must be consistent: if a < b and b < c then a < c. An inconsistent comparator, such as one that compares floats containing NaN with <, can produce unsorted output. cmp.Compare treats NaN as less than every other value, which gives a total order.

cards.prompt: Why did Tags marshal as null in the first line?
cards.answer: A nil slice encodes as null in encoding/json v1 v1 distinguishes nil slices (null) from empty slices ([]). json/v2 encodes nil slices as [] by default.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using encoding/json: struct tags, decoding and streaming?
cards.answer: json.NewDecoder(r) and json.NewEncoder(w) stream values from and to readers and writers, which avoids holding a whole document in memory. Encoder.SetIndent pretty-prints.

cards.prompt: How does json/v2 encode a nil []string by default?
cards.answer: As an empty array [] v2 treats nil and empty slices alike by default. The FormatNilSliceAsNull option restores v1-style null.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go 1.27 encoding/json/v2 and jsontext?
cards.answer: jsontext.Value is a raw JSON value with methods for formatting and canonicalising, and jsontext.Encoder and Decoder stream tokens. MarshalWrite and UnmarshalRead read and write io streams directly. Prefer v2 for new code that targets 1.27; migrate v1 code by checking the documented behaviour differences.

cards.prompt: How do you stop a secret type from appearing in logs?
cards.answer: Implement slog.LogValuer to return a redacted value Handlers resolve LogValuer before formatting, so the redacted value is all any handler sees.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using structured logging with log/slog?
cards.answer: slog.SetDefault installs a logger used by the top-level functions and by the older log package. Use typed attributes such as slog.Int and slog.Any in hot paths to avoid allocation, and implement slog.LogValuer to control how a type is logged, such as redacting secrets.

cards.prompt: Why parse flags with a FlagSet and an explicit argument slice?
cards.answer: So tests can pass arguments and receive errors instead of the process exiting With ContinueOnError, Parse returns an error. The global flag.Parse uses ExitOnError and os.Args.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using command-line flags with the flag package?
cards.answer: For testable programs use a flag.FlagSet created with flag.ContinueOnError and parse an explicit []string, instead of the global flag set and os.Args. FlagSet.Parse then returns an error instead of exiting.

cards.prompt: Why might you prefer uuid.NewV7 over uuid.New for database primary keys?
cards.answer: V7 values start with a timestamp, so new keys sort near each other Time-ordered keys keep B-tree inserts local. V4 values are uniformly random, which scatters inserts.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the go 1.27 uuid package?
cards.answer: Random UUIDs are unpredictable but not secret tokens; use crypto/rand for credentials. Nil() is the all-zero UUID and Max() the all-ones value.

cards.prompt: Why seed a rand.Rand with rand.NewPCG(1, 2) in a simulation?
cards.answer: The same seed reproduces the same sequence, which makes runs repeatable Deterministic sources let you replay a simulation or test. The top-level functions are randomly seeded.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using math, math/big and math/rand/v2?
cards.answer: math/rand/v2 (Go 1.22) has rand.IntN, rand.N for any integer type or duration, and seedable sources such as rand.NewPCG for reproducible simulations. Go 1.27 adds the generic Rand.N method. These are not suitable for secrets; use crypto/rand for keys and tokens.

cards.prompt: Why is writing results[i] from separate goroutines safe here?
cards.answer: Each goroutine writes a different element, and Wait orders those writes before the read Distinct elements are distinct memory locations, so there is no data race. wg.Wait synchronises with each Done, making the writes visible to main.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using goroutines and the go scheduler?
cards.answer: Goroutine execution order is not specified. Output from several goroutines interleaves differently between runs unless you synchronise. The scheduler is preemptive (since Go 1.14), so a tight loop cannot starve the others forever.

cards.prompt: When does a send on an unbuffered channel complete?
cards.answer: When another goroutine receives the value An unbuffered channel has no storage, so sender and receiver must meet. That rendezvous is also a synchronisation point.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using unbuffered and buffered channels?
cards.answer: Use unbuffered channels for hand-offs and synchronisation, small buffers to absorb bursts, and never a buffer size chosen to "avoid deadlock": if correctness depends on the buffer size, the design has a bug. Channel direction types, chan<- int (send-only) and <-chan int (receive-only), document intent in signatures.

cards.prompt: Who should close a channel with several senders?
cards.answer: A coordinator that closes it after every sender has finished Closing twice or sending after close panics. Waiting for all senders, then closing once, avoids both.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using closing channels, comma-ok receives and ownership?
cards.answer: Closing is a broadcast: every receiver sees it, which makes a closed chan struct{} a cheap "done" signal. You do not have to close a channel for garbage collection; close it to tell receivers to stop.

cards.prompt: Which case runs when several select cases are ready?
cards.answer: One chosen uniformly at random Random choice stops one busy channel from starving the others. Code must not rely on case order.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using select, timeouts and non-blocking operations?
cards.answer: A select with no cases, select {}, blocks forever. Each case expression is evaluated once on entry, including the right-hand side of sends.

cards.prompt: What does a select case on a nil channel do?
cards.answer: It is never ready, so the case is effectively disabled Operations on nil channels block forever, and select simply never chooses a case that cannot proceed.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using nil channels to disable select cases?
cards.answer: Closing a nil channel panics. A nil channel is the zero value of a channel type, so an uninitialised struct field of channel type blocks every operation; make channels in constructors.

cards.prompt: Why does every send in a stage select on done?
cards.answer: So the stage can exit instead of blocking forever if the consumer stops early A blocked send with no receiver never completes, leaking the goroutine. done gives it a way out.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using pipelines of stages connected by channels?
cards.answer: Return receive-only channels from stage constructors (func square(in <-chan int) <-chan int). The types then prevent callers from sending into or closing a stage's output.

cards.prompt: How do you keep results in input order after fanning out?
cards.answer: Send each result with its index and store it at that position Workers finish in arbitrary order. Carrying the index restores order deterministically without serialising the work.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using fan-out, fan-in and preserving order?
cards.answer: Fan-out helps CPU-bound work up to GOMAXPROCS goroutines and I/O-bound work further, until an external limit such as a connection pool is reached. Measure; more goroutines than useful parallelism only adds scheduling cost.

cards.prompt: How does a buffered channel of capacity n act as a semaphore?
cards.answer: Each worker sends to acquire and receives to release, so at most n hold a slot A send blocks when the buffer is full, which happens exactly when n slots are held.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using bounded concurrency: worker pools and semaphores?
cards.answer: Collect errors as well as results. Common patterns are a result struct carrying an error, or the first-error-cancels-the-rest pattern of errgroup (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup), which combines a WaitGroup, a context and an error.

cards.prompt: Why did two goroutines leak in the original firstOf?
cards.answer: They sent on an unbuffered channel after its only receiver had returned Only one receive happens. The two slower senders block forever on a channel nothing can reach, which is exactly what the leak profile detects.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using goroutine leaks and the go 1.27 goroutineleak profile?
cards.answer: Go 1.27 adds a goroutineleak profile to runtime/pprof (and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof). Collecting it runs a garbage collection that finds goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives no running goroutine can reach, and reports their stacks. It finds leaks that can be proven; a goroutine blocked on a reachable channel is not reported even if it will never be woken.

cards.prompt: Why must a struct containing a sync.Mutex have pointer receivers?
cards.answer: A value receiver copies the struct and its mutex, so methods lock different mutexes Each copy has its own lock state. go vet copylocks flags copies of values containing locks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sync.mutex and rwmutex: protecting shared state?
cards.answer: sync.RWMutex allows many concurrent readers or one writer. It helps only when reads dominate and the critical sections are long enough to matter; otherwise a plain Mutex is simpler and often faster. Go mutexes are not re-entrant: locking twice in the same goroutine deadlocks.

cards.prompt: Why must wg.Add(1) run before the go statement rather than inside the goroutine?
cards.answer: Otherwise Wait might run while the counter is still zero and return too early If the goroutine has not started yet, its Add has not happened and Wait sees zero. wg.Go performs Add before starting the goroutine.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sync.waitgroup and waitgroup.go?
cards.answer: The return of each function started by Go synchronises before Wait returns, so results written by the goroutines are visible after Wait. f must not panic; recover inside f if it can.

cards.prompt: What happens if the function passed to OnceValue panics?
cards.answer: Every call, including later ones, panics with the same value The Once helpers remember the panic and re-raise it, so a failed initialisation is never silently retried or ignored.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sync.once, oncefunc, oncevalue and lazy initialisation?
cards.answer: Prefer package-level variable initialisation when the value is always needed; use Once when initialisation is expensive or may not be needed at all.

cards.prompt: Why is Cond.Wait always called inside a for loop?
cards.answer: The condition may be false again by the time the waiter relocks Another goroutine can change the state between Signal and the waiter reacquiring the lock, so the condition must be rechecked.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sync.cond for waiting on state changes?
cards.answer: Channels usually express the same thing more simply. Cond is useful when many goroutines wait for a condition on data already protected by a mutex, such as a bounded queue with "not empty" and "not full" states.

cards.prompt: When is a mutex better than several atomics?
cards.answer: When several values must change together as one consistent update Each atomic operation is individually atomic, but other goroutines can observe states between them. A mutex makes the whole update indivisible.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using typed atomics: atomic.int64, bool and pointer?
cards.answer: Atomics suit counters, flags and publishing an immutable snapshot through atomic.Pointer. When an update touches several values together, use a mutex; combining several atomics does not make the group atomic.

cards.prompt: What must you assume about objects put into a sync.Pool?
cards.answer: They may be discarded at any garbage collection Pool contents are weakly held per-P caches cleared over GC cycles. New must be able to recreate any object.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sync.map and sync.pool: specialised tools?
cards.answer: Both are tools for measured hot spots. Benchmark first; a Pool adds complexity and can retain memory you expected to be freed.

cards.prompt: What does the race detector guarantee about a passing run?
cards.answer: No race occurred on the paths that run executed The detector is dynamic: it reports races it observes. Code paths not exercised by the run are not checked.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using finding data races with the race detector?
cards.answer: The detector costs roughly 5–10x CPU and memory, so use it in CI and staging rather than production. It needs cgo on most platforms; this project runs it on macOS.

cards.prompt: Why is reading message after <-done guaranteed to see the write?
cards.answer: The write precedes close in its goroutine, and close happens before the receive that observes it Program order plus the close/receive synchronisation edge give a happens-before chain from the write to the read.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the go memory model: happens-before?
cards.answer: Programs free of data races behave as if goroutines were interleaved in some sequential order (DRF-SC). Make that your rule: every shared variable is protected by a channel, a lock or an atomic, and then you can reason sequentially.

cards.prompt: Why is publishing a struct through atomic.Pointer safe for lock-free readers?
cards.answer: The Store happens before any Load that observes it, so the struct's fields are visible Atomic operations synchronise. Writes to the fields before Store are ordered before reads after the matching Load, provided the struct is not modified afterwards.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using what racy programs may do, and why atomics fix it?
cards.answer: A store to an atomic and a load observing it create a happens-before edge, just like a channel. That is why atomic.Pointer can safely publish an immutable configuration that readers then use without locks.

cards.prompt: Why call cancel even after a WithTimeout context has expired?
cards.answer: It releases resources such as the timer and the parent's reference to the child Cancel is idempotent and cheap. Not calling it keeps the child registered with its parent until the parent ends.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using context: cancellation and deadlines?
cards.answer: Code that blocks should select on <-ctx.Done() and return ctx.Err(), which is context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded. Standard library functions that take a context, such as http.NewRequestWithContext and net.Dialer.DialContext, stop their work when it is cancelled.

cards.prompt: What does context.WithoutCancel(ctx) keep and drop?
cards.answer: It keeps ctx's values and drops its cancellation and deadline The derived context is never cancelled and has no deadline, but Value lookups still reach the parent.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using causes, afterfunc, withoutcancel and values?
cards.answer: context.WithoutCancel(ctx) keeps values but drops cancellation, for work that must finish after a request ends, such as an audit write. context.WithValue carries request-scoped data like trace IDs. Use an unexported key type to avoid collisions, and never pass optional parameters through values.

cards.prompt: With go 1.23 or later in go.mod, what can you rely on after t.Stop() returns?
cards.answer: No stale value from before the Stop will be received from t.C Timer channels became synchronous in Go 1.23, which removed the need for the drain idiom for modules declaring 1.23+.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using timers, tickers and the go 1.23 timer semantics?
cards.answer: Use time.AfterFunc to run a function after a delay in its own goroutine. For deadlines on a whole operation, a context is usually better than hand-managed timers.

cards.prompt: Why does p escape in NewPoint?
cards.answer: Its address is returned, so it must outlive the function The stack frame disappears when NewPoint returns, so a pointer to p must point into the heap.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using stack, heap and escape analysis?
cards.answer: Escape is not wrong; it is how Go makes pointers safe. Look at it only for hot paths, after a profile shows allocation cost. Returning a value instead of a pointer, or letting callers pass a buffer, often removes allocations.

cards.prompt: What does GOGC=100 mean?
cards.answer: The heap may grow to about twice the live heap before the next collection GOGC is a growth percentage relative to the live heap after the last cycle. GOMEMLIMIT is the absolute limit.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the garbage collector, gogc, gomemlimit and green tea?
cards.answer: GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19) sets a soft memory limit for the whole runtime, such as GOMEMLIMIT=512MiB. The GC works harder as the limit approaches, which suits containers with fixed memory. runtime.ReadMemStats and runtime/metrics report heap size and GC counts.

cards.prompt: How does Go 1.25+ choose the default GOMAXPROCS inside a Linux container with a CPU limit?
cards.answer: It uses the cgroup CPU limit rather than the host's CPU count Container-aware GOMAXPROCS avoids running more parallel threads than the quota allows, which reduces throttling and tail latency.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using gomaxprocs and container-aware scheduling?
cards.answer: Setting the GOMAXPROCS environment variable, or calling runtime.GOMAXPROCS with a positive value, disables the automatic adjustment. runtime.SetDefaultGOMAXPROCS (1.25) restores it.

cards.prompt: Which pprof sample index shows total bytes allocated over the run, including freed memory?
cards.answer: alloc_space alloc_space accumulates every allocation; inuse_space shows only what was still live when the profile was written.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using profiling cpu and memory with pprof?
cards.answer: Profile first, then optimise the largest cost. Allocation profiles are often more revealing than CPU profiles, because allocation also costs GC time later. Setting -memprofilerate=1 records every allocation, which is exact but slow, so use it only in focused tests like this one.

cards.prompt: What problem does trace.FlightRecorder solve?
cards.answer: It keeps a cheap rolling window so you can save a trace of what just happened Full tracing of a long-running service is expensive and huge. A flight recorder captures the recent past on demand, when an anomaly is detected.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using execution traces, regions and the flight recorder?
cards.answer: Go 1.25 added trace.FlightRecorder: it keeps the last few seconds of trace data in a ring buffer with low overhead. When something unusual happens, such as a slow request, call WriteTo to save just that recent window. This makes tracing practical in production.

cards.prompt: Why are allocation counts better than nanoseconds for a CI regression test?
cards.answer: They are deterministic across machines, while timings vary with hardware and load Allocs per op depends on the code, not the machine. Timings need repeated runs and statistics to compare fairly.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using benchmarking method: variance, benchstat and fair comparisons?
cards.answer: testing.AllocsPerRun and the allocs/op column are stable across machines, which makes them good regression tests. Wall-clock numbers vary with CPU, frequency scaling and other processes, so they belong in reports rather than pass/fail tests.

cards.prompt: How does go build find a PGO profile without flags?
cards.answer: It uses default.pgo in the main package's directory -pgo=auto is the default and looks for default.pgo next to the main package. The setting is embedded in the binary's build info.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using profile-guided optimisation?
cards.answer: Profiles from production are best; profiles from benchmarks work if they exercise the same hot paths. Commit default.pgo and refresh it periodically. Builds stay reproducible because the profile is a normal input.

cards.prompt: Why does m[string(key)] not allocate even though key is a []byte?
cards.answer: The compiler recognises the lookup and uses the bytes without copying them into a new string The temporary string cannot escape a map index expression, so the compiler skips the copy. A conversion stored in a variable would allocate.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reducing allocations: preallocation, reuse and value types?
cards.answer: Reuse long-lived buffers with sync.Pool only after measuring. Clarity first: most code is not hot, and the allocator got about 30% faster for small objects in Go 1.27.

cards.prompt: Why should runtime.AddCleanup not be the only way to close a file?
cards.answer: Cleanups run at an unspecified time and may never run before the program exits Collection timing depends on the GC. Deterministic release needs an explicit Close; a cleanup is a backstop for forgotten calls.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using weak pointers, unique handles and runtime.addcleanup?
cards.answer: runtime.AddCleanup (Go 1.24) runs a function after an object becomes unreachable, replacing most uses of runtime.SetFinalizer. Cleanups receive a separate argument, not the object itself, so they cannot resurrect it; they run on a runtime goroutine at an unspecified time and are not guaranteed to run before exit. Use them as a safety net, never as the main way to release resources: call Close explicitly.

cards.prompt: Why does a line-based protocol need bufio.Scanner on a TCP connection?
cards.answer: TCP delivers a byte stream, so message boundaries must be reconstructed Reads return whatever bytes have arrived, which may be part of a line or several lines. Framing restores message boundaries.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using tcp servers and clients with package net?
cards.answer: Set deadlines with SetDeadline, SetReadDeadline and SetWriteDeadline; a blocked Read then fails with an error satisfying os.ErrDeadlineExceeded. Close the listener to stop Accept, and close each connection when its handler returns.

cards.prompt: What does ServeMux return for DELETE /items/42 when only GET /items/{id} is registered?
cards.answer: 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow header The path matches a registered pattern but the method does not, so the mux reports 405 and lists the allowed methods.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using http.servemux routing patterns: methods and wildcards?
cards.answer: Handlers implement ServeHTTP(w, r); http.HandlerFunc adapts a function. Write headers before the body: the first Write sends status 200 if WriteHeader was not called.

cards.prompt: Is a 404 response an error from client.Get?
cards.answer: No; err is nil and you must check resp.StatusCode The client returns an error only when it could not get a response at all. Status codes are application-level results.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using http clients: timeouts, contexts and closing bodies?
cards.answer: Reuse one Client (and its Transport) across requests; it pools connections and is safe for concurrent use. Since Go 1.27 the HTTP/1 client drains a closed body automatically so the connection can be reused.

cards.prompt: How does middleware observe the status code a handler writes?
cards.answer: By wrapping the ResponseWriter and recording WriteHeader calls The status goes to the ResponseWriter. A wrapper that embeds it and overrides WriteHeader sees the value as it passes through.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using middleware: wrapping handlers for logging, limits and recovery?
cards.answer: http.MaxBytesReader limits request bodies, protecting servers from huge uploads. http.TimeoutHandler bounds handler time. Go 1.25 added http.CrossOriginProtection, which rejects unsafe cross-origin browser requests using Fetch metadata headers, a modern defence against CSRF.

cards.prompt: What does srv.Serve return after a successful Shutdown?
cards.answer: http.ErrServerClosed, which signals a normal stop Serve always returns a non-nil error. ErrServerClosed distinguishes a requested shutdown from a real failure.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using server timeouts and graceful shutdown?
cards.answer: Typical main: start Serve in a goroutine, wait for SIGINT or SIGTERM with signal.NotifyContext, call Shutdown with a deadline, then exit. RegisterOnShutdown and BaseContext help close long-lived connections such as WebSockets.

cards.prompt: Why does http.Get fail against httptest.NewTLSServer?
cards.answer: The default client verifies certificates and does not trust the test server's self-signed one srv.Client() is configured with the test certificate. The default client uses the system roots, which correctly reject it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using tls clients and servers with crypto/tls?
cards.answer: Go 1.24 enabled the hybrid post-quantum key exchange X25519MLKEM768 by default. Go 1.27 adds ML-DSA signature support in crypto/tls and crypto/x509, an MLKEM1024 key exchange, and the crypto/mldsa package.

cards.prompt: Which status suits a well-formed JSON body whose title is empty?
cards.answer: 422 Unprocessable Entity 400 means the request could not be parsed. 422 means it parsed but failed validation, which helps clients fix the right thing.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using a json api handler: decode, validate, respond?
cards.answer: Keep handlers thin: parse and validate HTTP input, call ordinary functions that hold the logic, and map their errors to statuses. Those functions are then testable without HTTP.

cards.prompt: Why is exec.Command("rm", userPath) safer than exec.Command("sh", "-c", "rm "+userPath)?
cards.answer: Arguments go straight to the program, so no shell parses the untrusted text A shell interprets spaces, semicolons and $(…). Passing arguments directly keeps the path a single, literal argument.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using running processes with os/exec?
cards.answer: exec.LookPath finds programs on PATH and, since Go 1.19, refuses to run a program found in the current directory through a relative PATH entry, a common attack. Never build a command line by concatenating untrusted input into "sh -c".

cards.prompt: Why must the channel passed to signal.Notify be buffered?
cards.answer: The runtime does not block when sending, so signals arriving while you are busy would be dropped Signal delivery uses a non-blocking send. A buffer gives the receiver time to catch up.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using handling signals with os/signal?
cards.answer: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught. Signal handling is process-wide, so libraries should not install handlers; leave that to main.

cards.prompt: Why does reflect.ValueOf(u).Field(0).SetString("x") panic?
cards.answer: ValueOf(u) holds a copy, which is not addressable; use ValueOf(&u).Elem() Setting needs an addressable value that refers to the original variable. Passing a pointer and calling Elem provides one.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reflection with reflect: types, values and struct tags?
cards.answer: Reflection powers encoding/json, fmt and template packages, but it is slower, bypasses compile-time checking and panics on misuse. Prefer generics or interfaces in ordinary code; use reflection for generic infrastructure such as encoders and validators.

cards.prompt: Why is storing uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(p)) in a variable and converting it back later invalid?
cards.answer: The GC does not see a uintptr as a reference, so the object may be freed or moved Only unsafe.Pointer values keep objects alive. A stored integer address can dangle, so conversions must stay within one expression.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using unsafe.pointer and its valid conversion patterns?
cards.answer: unsafe code is not portable across architectures or Go versions, and go vet's unsafeptr check flags suspicious conversions. Use it only for interoperability (cgo, syscalls) or measured performance work, and isolate it behind a safe API.

cards.prompt: What must stay true after creating a string with unsafe.String over a []byte?
cards.answer: The bytes must never be modified while the string is in use Go assumes strings are immutable. Mutating the shared bytes silently changes a "constant" string and breaks that assumption.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using unsafe.slice, unsafe.string and zero-copy views?
cards.answer: Most programs never need this. The compiler already avoids copies for common cases (map lookups, comparisons, range over []byte(s)), and strings.Builder hands its buffer to a string without a copy. Reserve unsafe conversions for profiled hot paths.

cards.prompt: Why is struct{ a bool; b int64; c bool } 24 bytes on 64-bit platforms?
cards.answer: Padding aligns b to 8 bytes and rounds the total up to a multiple of 8 a takes 1 byte plus 7 padding, b 8, c 1 plus 7 trailing padding: 24 in total.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using struct layout, alignment and padding?
cards.answer: 64-bit atomic operations need 8-byte alignment; on 32-bit platforms a plain int64 field may not be aligned, which is one reason the typed atomic.Int64 exists: it guarantees alignment. A zero-size field at the end of a struct also gets padding so a pointer to it never points past the object.

cards.prompt: Who frees memory returned by C.CString?
cards.answer: You must, with C.free, because it is allocated by C malloc CString copies into C heap memory that Go's GC does not manage. Pair it with defer C.free.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using calling c with cgo?
cards.answer: cgo needs a C toolchain and disables simple cross-compilation; CGO_ENABLED=0 builds pure-Go binaries and makes import "C" files fail to build. Prefer pure-Go libraries unless you need an existing C library.

cards.prompt: What does the stdversion analyzer report?
cards.answer: Standard-library symbols newer than the go version declared for the file A go 1.22 module promises to build with Go 1.22, which lacks strings.CutLast. stdversion catches that broken promise early.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go vet, analyzers and the stdversion check?
cards.answer: Additional analyzers come from golang.org/x/tools and tools such as staticcheck. go vet -vettool=prog runs a custom analysis binary; analyzers are written with the golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis framework.

cards.prompt: What does go fix -diff do when modernisations are available?
cards.answer: Prints the patch without changing files and exits with a non-zero status -diff is a dry run suited to CI; plain go fix applies the changes.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go fix and modernizers?
cards.answer: Each fix respects the go version declared for the file, so it never introduces a feature the module cannot use. //go:fix inline directives let library authors mark functions whose calls go fix should inline, which helps migrate users off deprecated APIs.

cards.prompt: What does a token.FileSet provide to tools built on go/ast?
cards.answer: A mapping from compact positions to file, line and column AST nodes store token.Pos integers. The FileSet translates them into human-readable positions for diagnostics.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading go source with go/parser, go/ast and go/token?
cards.answer: go/format formats an AST or source the same way gofmt does, so generated code can be canonical.

cards.prompt: When does go generate run?
cards.answer: Only when you invoke go generate explicitly Generation is a deliberate developer step. Its output is committed so builds stay fast and need no generator tools.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using code generation with go generate?
cards.answer: A small generator can be a Go program in the same module run with go run, guarded by //go:build ignore so it is not part of the package build. Since Go 1.24, versioned generators can be declared as tool dependencies and run with go tool.

cards.prompt: What does -trimpath change?
cards.answer: It removes local directory paths from the compiled binary Without -trimpath, file paths of your machine appear in stack traces and build info, which hurts reproducibility.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using cross-compilation, -ldflags -x, -trimpath and build info?
cards.answer: Builds also embed version-control information (vcs.revision, vcs.modified) when built inside a repository, readable with go version -m or debug.ReadBuildInfo. Go 1.27's linker adds -macos and -macsdk options for the macOS load command.

cards.prompt: What does GOTRACEBACK=all add to a crash report?
cards.answer: Stacks of every goroutine, not just the one that panicked By default only the failing goroutine is shown. all reveals what other goroutines were doing, which is vital for deadlocks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using debugging: stack traces, gotraceback, delve and govulncheck?
cards.answer: govulncheck (golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck) checks dependencies against the Go vulnerability database and reports only vulnerabilities your code actually reaches. Run it in CI alongside go vet and the race detector.

cards.prompt: Why can Registry.Get be called before any Add?
cards.answer: Reading a nil map returns the zero value, so the empty registry is valid Only writes need the map to exist. Lazy creation in Add keeps the zero Registry fully usable.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using make the zero value useful?
cards.answer: When a zero value cannot be valid, for example a client that needs a URL, provide a New function and make the type's fields unexported so the invalid state cannot be built from outside the package.

cards.prompt: Why does the Config solution use *int for Retries?
cards.answer: To distinguish "not set" from an explicit 0 The zero value of int is 0, which might be a real choice. A nil pointer means "use the default"; new(0) (Go 1.26) sets an explicit zero.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using constructors, functional options and config structs?
cards.answer: Either way, validate in the constructor and return an error rather than building an invalid object. Keep defaults in one place.

cards.prompt: Why return *Store rather than a StoreInterface from NewStore?
cards.answer: Callers get the full concrete API, and adding methods later breaks nobody Consumers can define the small interface they need themselves. Returning an interface fixes a method set that is costly to change.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using accept interfaces, return concrete types?
cards.answer: Test doubles follow naturally: a fake that implements the consumer's small interface replaces a database or HTTP client in tests, with no mocking framework.

cards.prompt: Where should a module's private helper packages live?
cards.answer: Under internal/, so other modules cannot import them internal/ is enforced by the go command. pkg/ is only a convention with no special meaning.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using package and project layout?
cards.answer: Package names are short, lower-case and singular (http, json, user). Avoid stutter in exported names: user.New, not user.NewUser. Unit tests sit next to the code; larger test data goes in testdata/, which the go tool ignores.

cards.prompt: What must Close do for a type that starts its own goroutine?
cards.answer: Signal the goroutine to stop and wait until it has exited Returning before the goroutine exits leaves it running, possibly touching freed resources. Wait makes shutdown deterministic.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using designing concurrent apis?
cards.answer: Document whether a type is safe for concurrent use. Many standard types are not (maps, bytes.Buffer, strings.Builder); http.Client and *sql.DB are. Hide locks inside the type rather than asking callers to lock.

cards.prompt: Why does main only call os.Exit(run(os.Args[1:], os.Stdin, os.Stdout, os.Stderr))?
cards.answer: So the whole command can be tested with buffers and fake inputs, without exiting the test process os.Exit skips deferred calls and would end a test run. Keeping logic in run, with injected streams, makes every path testable.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a tested word-count command?
cards.answer: The practice adds a -w flag for words only. Make it mutually exclusive with -l: when both are given, print usage and exit 2.

cards.prompt: How does All keep results in input order without a mutex?
cards.answer: Each goroutine writes only its own index of a pre-sized slice, and Wait orders the writes before return Distinct slice elements are separate memory locations, so there is no race. WaitGroup.Wait synchronises with every goroutine's completion.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a bounded, cancellable concurrent fetcher?
cards.answer: The practice adds per-request timeouts: each URL gets its own deadline derived from the parent context, so one slow server cannot use up the whole budget.

cards.prompt: Why is JSON encoding done after s.mu.Unlock()?
cards.answer: To keep the critical section short; encoding and network writes do not need the lock Holding a lock during I/O makes every other request wait on a slow client. Copy what you need under the lock, then release it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: an in-memory json rest api?
cards.answer: The practice adds DELETE /tasks/{id} returning 204 No Content, then 404 for later reads.

cards.prompt: Why must Safe.Get take the full lock rather than a read lock?
cards.answer: Get moves the entry to the front of the list, which is a write An LRU read updates recency. Concurrent RLock holders would modify the list together, a data race.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a generic lru cache with iterators?
cards.answer: The cache is documented as not safe for concurrent use; the practice adds a concurrent wrapper with a mutex and a race-tested test, which is the usual way to add locking without slowing single-goroutine users.

cards.prompt: Why can the test assert exactly 400ms for five Wait calls?
cards.answer: synctest's fake clock advances only to the next timer when all goroutines block, so durations are exact Inside a bubble there is no real-time jitter: each timer fires at its exact fake instant, so the schedule is fully deterministic.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a token-bucket rate limiter tested with synctest?
cards.answer: The practice adds a Reserve-style method, Tokens() float64, reporting the current balance, and a test showing it rises fractionally over time.

cards.prompt: Why does bump look up a *int instead of writing m[string(key)]++?
cards.answer: Only the lookup form m[string(b)] avoids allocating; an increment or assignment converts the key every time The compiler can use the bytes in place for a read, because the key is not retained. A write may store the key, so it needs an allocated string. The validator measured 1004 allocations for 1000 lines with ++ and stays within 10 with bump.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a zero-allocation log summariser?
cards.answer: The practice adds a per-message count while preserving the budget. The obvious s.Msgs[string(m)]++ would cost one allocation per line and fail the budget test; reuse bump so repeated messages are lookups only.

cards.prompt: Is len a keyword in Go?
cards.answer: No; it is a predeclared identifier that can be shadowed Built-in functions, types and constants live in the universe block as predeclared identifiers. Only the 25 keywords are reserved.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading the spec: notation, source text, identifiers and keywords?
cards.answer: Go has exactly 25 keywords: break, case, chan, const, continue, default, defer, else, fallthrough, for, func, go, goto, if, import, interface, map, package, range, return, select, struct, switch, type, var. Names such as int, len, true, nil, any and error are predeclared identifiers, not keywords, so they can be shadowed, which is legal and usually a mistake.

cards.prompt: What value does the literal 0x1p-2 denote?
cards.answer: 0.25, because p gives a power-of-two exponent Hex floating-point literals scale the mantissa by 2 to the power after p: 1 × 2⁻² = 0.25.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using integer, floating-point, imaginary and rune literals in full?
cards.answer: The built-ins complex, real and imag build and take apart complex values; complex128 holds two float64s. math/cmplx provides Abs, Sqrt, Exp, Pow and friends. Rune literals can use escapes: '\n', '\x41', '\u00e9', '\U0001F600' and octal '\101'.

cards.prompt: Why can an IntSlice value be passed to func sum(xs []int)?
cards.answer: They share an underlying type and []int is not a named type Assignability allows identical underlying types when at least one side is unnamed. Two different named types, such as Celsius and Fahrenheit, need a conversion.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using types, type identity, assignability and representability?
cards.answer: Representable means the constant fits: 1.0 is representable as an int, while 1.5 or 300 as a byte is not. bool is its own type: there is no implicit conversion between booleans and integers, which removes a whole class of C bugs.

cards.prompt: Why can later() use early even though early is declared after it?
cards.answer: Package-level identifiers are scoped to the whole package block Order matters inside function bodies, but at package level every name is visible throughout; initialisation order is then computed from dependencies.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using blocks, scope, predeclared identifiers and uniqueness?
cards.answer: Two identifiers are different if they are spelled differently, or if they appear in different packages and are not exported: the unexported name count in package a is unrelated to count in package b. A qualified identifier, pkg.Name, reaches an exported name through an import.

cards.prompt: Why does get() still return 1 after two inc() calls?
cards.answer: The method value c.Get copied the value receiver when it was created inc was bound to &c, so it changes c. get was bound to a copy of c taken before the increments.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using operands, primary expressions, method values and method expressions?
cards.answer: A method expression T.M (or (*T).M) is an ordinary function whose first parameter is the receiver: Point.Dist has type func(Point, Point) float64. Method expressions turn methods into plain functions for tables and higher-order code.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between (*[4]byte)(s) and [4]byte(s)?
cards.answer: The pointer shares s's memory; the array value is a copy Array pointers alias the backing array, so writes are visible through s. Array values are independent copies.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using converting slices to arrays and array pointers?
cards.answer: These conversions are handy for fixed-size keys, hashes and headers: parsing a 16-byte UUID from a slice, or using the first bytes of a buffer as a map key.

cards.prompt: After i := 0; x := []int{0, 0}; i, x[i] = 1, 2, which element of x is 2?
cards.answer: x[0], because index expressions are evaluated before any assignment Phase one evaluates x[i] with i == 0; phase two assigns i = 1 and x[0] = 2.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using order of evaluation and statements?
cards.answer: Function calls, method calls and receive operations can appear as statements (expression statements); most other expressions cannot, so len(s) on its own line is an error. An empty statement does nothing; it appears, for example, as the missing post statement in for i := 0; i < n; {.

cards.prompt: Why does a switch without a default, whose cases all return, still cause "missing return"?
cards.answer: A switch is terminating only with a default case; the compiler does not prove exhaustiveness The rule is syntactic. Without default, control may fall out of the switch, so a return must follow.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using terminating statements and missing returns?
cards.answer: When the compiler reports "missing return", either add the return or restructure, for example by turning if/else chains into a final return or a panic("unreachable") for truly impossible states.

cards.prompt: Where does println write?
cards.answer: To standard error, in an implementation-defined format The bootstrapping built-ins are for runtime development; fmt.Println is the stable, documented way to print.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using bootstrapping built-ins, the spec's example package and system considerations?
cards.answer: System considerations covers package unsafe and the size and alignment guarantees: for example, a struct or array of size zero may share an address with another variable, and unsafe.Sizeof of a value of a given type is the same on every call. Program execution begins by initialising the main package and its imports, then calls main.main; when it returns, the program exits without waiting for other goroutines.

cards.prompt: Why does a go 1.20 module fail to compile min(3, 1, 2) with a 1.27 toolchain?
cards.answer: The go line fixes the language version, and min was added in Go 1.21 Newer toolchains honour the declared language version, rejecting features from later versions so the module keeps building with the toolchains it claims to support.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using the language-version appendix: features gated by the go line?
cards.answer: This project declares go 1.20 and uses min, which arrived in 1.21: the compiler refuses. Raising the go line to 1.21 fixes it.

cards.prompt: Why does regexp reject the backreference \1?
cards.answer: RE2 guarantees linear-time matching, which backreferences would break Backreferences make matching NP-hard in general. Go trades that feature for predictable performance on untrusted input.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using regular expressions with regexp and regexp/syntax?
cards.answer: regexp/syntax parses patterns into an abstract syntax tree and simplifies them. It is what regexp uses internally, and is useful for tools that analyse or rewrite patterns. Prefer strings functions for fixed substrings; regular expressions are for structure.

cards.prompt: Why must HTML output use html/template rather than text/template?
cards.answer: text/template performs no escaping, so user data could inject markup or script html/template understands HTML, CSS, JavaScript and URL contexts and escapes each correctly. text/template prints values verbatim.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using text/template and its parse tree?
cards.answer: text/template/parse exposes the parsed tree: tmpl.Tree.Root lists ActionNodes, TextNodes and others. Tools use it to inspect which fields a template reads. Never use text/template for HTML: it does no escaping.

cards.prompt: What does html/template do with a value "javascript:alert(1)" in an href?
cards.answer: Replaces it with #ZgotmplZ because the URL scheme is unsafe The URL context filter only allows safe schemes such as http, https and mailto. Anything else becomes an inert placeholder.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using contextual escaping with html/template and package html?
cards.answer: Package html provides the low-level EscapeString and UnescapeString for the five characters < > & ' ". Use them for plain text outside templates.

cards.prompt: How many UTF-16 code units encode "😀"?
cards.answer: Two, a surrogate pair, because it lies outside the Basic Multilingual Plane UTF-16 represents code points above U+FFFF with a high and a low surrogate.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using aligned columns, tokenising text and utf-16?
cards.answer: unicode/utf16 converts between runes and UTF-16 code units, which Windows APIs, JavaScript strings and some file formats use. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane become surrogate pairs: utf16.Encode([]rune("😀")) yields two units.

cards.prompt: Why use base64.URLEncoding for tokens placed in URLs?
cards.answer: It replaces + and / with - and _, which need no percent-escaping The standard alphabet uses characters with special meaning in URLs. The URL-safe alphabet avoids them.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using base64, base32, hex, ascii85, pem and the encoding interfaces?
cards.answer: Package encoding defines the interfaces that let types choose their own representation: TextMarshaler/TextUnmarshaler (used by JSON, XML and flag), BinaryMarshaler/BinaryUnmarshaler (used by gob), and since Go 1.24 TextAppender/BinaryAppender for allocation-free encoding.

cards.prompt: Can a CRC32 checksum protect data against deliberate tampering?
cards.answer: No; it detects accidental corruption, while tampering needs a MAC or signature An attacker can recompute or forge a CRC easily. Use crypto/hmac or digital signatures against adversaries.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using encoding/binary, checksums, maphash and math/bits?
cards.answer: math/bits gives portable bit tricks that compile to single instructions: OnesCount, LeadingZeros, TrailingZeros, RotateLeft, Reverse and overflow-detecting Add64 and Mul64.

cards.prompt: Why did the second input fail with a ParseError on line 2?
cards.answer: FieldsPerRecord defaults to the first record's width, and line 2 has one field instead of two A zero FieldsPerRecord means "match the first record". Set it to -1 to allow ragged rows.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading and writing csv with encoding/csv?
cards.answer: csv.NewWriter quotes fields only when needed. Call Flush and then check Error, because writes are buffered.

cards.prompt: What does the tag `xml:"authors>author"` mean?
cards.answer: Each slice element is an <author> nested inside an <authors> element a>b paths describe nesting, so the decoder walks into authors and collects every author child.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using xml with encoding/xml: struct tags and token streams?
cards.answer: The decoder does not resolve external entities or fetch DTDs, which avoids XXE attacks. Namespaces appear in Name.Space.

cards.prompt: How does gob match struct fields between sender and receiver?
cards.answer: By field name, so added or removed fields are tolerated Name matching lets V1 decode into V2: Name transfers, Age is dropped and Email stays zero.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go-native binary streams with encoding/gob?
cards.answer: Gob is not a cross-language format and is not hardened against hostile input of unbounded size; use JSON or protocol buffers for public APIs, and bound inputs from untrusted sources.

cards.prompt: What do the bytes 02 01 05 encode in DER?
cards.answer: An INTEGER (tag 02) of length 1 with value 5 DER is tag, length, value. Tag 0x02 is INTEGER, and the single content byte is 5.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using asn.1 der with encoding/asn1?
cards.answer: Most code reaches ASN.1 through crypto/x509 rather than directly. golang.org/x/crypto/cryptobyte is a safer, more flexible parser for new protocol code.

cards.prompt: What does mime/multipart need to find part boundaries?
cards.answer: The boundary string from the Content-Type header's parameters Multipart bodies separate parts with --boundary lines. ParseMediaType extracts the boundary parameter for the Reader.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using mime types, multipart bodies, quoted-printable and mail messages?
cards.answer: net/mail parses RFC 5322 messages and addresses: mail.ReadMessage splits headers from the body, and mail.ParseAddress handles display names. Together these are what an email client needs below the network layer.

cards.prompt: What must a type implement to be used with container/heap?
cards.answer: sort.Interface plus Push(any) and Pop() any heap.Interface embeds sort.Interface for ordering and adds Push and Pop to grow and shrink the underlying slice.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using index/suffixarray, container/heap and container/ring?
cards.answer: container/ring is a circular doubly linked list: Next, Prev, Move, Link and Do. It fits fixed-size round-robin buffers, though a slice with a moving index is often simpler.

cards.prompt: Why must MD5 not be used to sign documents?
cards.answer: Collisions can be crafted, so two different documents can share one digest A signature over an MD5 digest covers every document with that digest, and attackers can construct such pairs.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using cryptographic hashes: sha-2, sha-3 and the legacy md5/sha-1?
cards.answer: Package crypto names algorithms with crypto.Hash constants (crypto.SHA256, crypto.SHA3_256) and links them to implementations; Available reports whether an implementation is linked in. Signature APIs take these constants to say which hash was used.

cards.prompt: Why compare MAC tags with hmac.Equal instead of bytes.Equal?
cards.answer: hmac.Equal takes the same time regardless of where bytes differ, so timing reveals nothing bytes.Equal can return at the first mismatch. Measuring that lets an attacker guess a valid tag byte by byte.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using hmac, constant-time comparison, key derivation and secure randomness?
cards.answer: crypto/rand is the only correct source of randomness for keys, nonces and tokens. rand.Read never fails on supported platforms since Go 1.24, and rand.Text returns a secure random string suitable for tokens.

cards.prompt: What happens if a GCM nonce is reused with the same key?
cards.answer: Confidentiality and authenticity both break; an attacker can forge messages GCM is a stream construction. Reuse reveals the XOR of plaintexts and the authentication key, which enables forgeries.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using authenticated encryption: aes-gcm, and why des and rc4 are legacy?
cards.answer: crypto/des (including triple DES) and crypto/rc4 remain for interoperability with old systems only: DES keys are brute-forceable, 3DES has a 64-bit block that leaks over large data, and RC4 has statistical biases. Never choose them for new designs.

cards.prompt: Why should a signing function accept crypto.Signer instead of *ecdsa.PrivateKey?
cards.answer: Any key type, including keys held in hardware, can then be used Signer abstracts where and how the private key lives. TLS uses it so certificates can be backed by HSMs or cloud KMS.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using digital signatures: ed25519, ecdsa, rsa-pss and crypto.signer?
cards.answer: crypto/elliptic exposes the NIST curves' parameters; its low-level point arithmetic is deprecated in favour of crypto/ecdh and crypto/ecdsa. crypto/dsa is deprecated and insecure at its common sizes; it remains only to verify old signatures.

cards.prompt: Why does Go's TLS use the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 by default?
cards.answer: It stays secure if either the classical or the post-quantum component is broken Hybrids combine both secrets, defending against future quantum attacks without trusting the newer scheme alone.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using key exchange: x25519 with crypto/ecdh and ml-kem?
cards.answer: crypto/mlkem/mlkemtest exposes deterministic encapsulation from fixed randomness for known-answer tests; it must never be used in production. Always derive working keys from a shared secret with HKDF rather than using it directly.

cards.prompt: What does Options.Context do in ML-DSA?
cards.answer: Binds a signature to a purpose, so it does not verify under another context Domain separation prevents a signature produced for one protocol from being replayed in another.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using post-quantum signatures, hpke and fips 140-3 mode?
cards.answer: crypto/fips140 reports whether the program runs in FIPS 140-3 mode (GODEBUG=fips140=on), which restricts algorithms to approved ones. Version names the Go Cryptographic Module in use. Most programs never need it; regulated environments do.

cards.prompt: What does cert.Verify check besides the signature chain?
cards.answer: Validity period, key usage constraints and, if given, the DNS name Verify builds a chain to a trusted root and applies the standard constraints. Revocation checking is not included.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using certificates with crypto/x509 and pkix names?
cards.answer: crypto/x509/pkix holds the ASN.1 structures for names, extensions and revocation lists. Go 1.27 adds ML-DSA certificate support. For TLS, tls.Config consumes these certificates; for an internal CA, keep the root key offline.

cards.prompt: Why can SetGlobalRandom not be used in a parallel test?
cards.answer: It replaces the process-wide cryptographic randomness source Another test running concurrently would also draw from the deterministic source, breaking both tests' assumptions.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using deterministic cryptographic tests with testing/cryptotest?
cards.answer: This project tests a token-signing package: one test proves determinism under a fixed seed, another proves that different seeds give different keys, and the practice adds a tampering test.

cards.prompt: What happens if you forget to Close a gzip.Writer?
cards.answer: The final compressed block and the trailer are never written, so the output is truncated Compressors buffer data. Close flushes the last block and writes the CRC and size trailer readers check.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using compression: flate, gzip, zlib, lzw and bzip2?
cards.answer: compress/lzw implements the LZW codes used by GIF and TIFF. compress/bzip2 only decompresses: the standard library has no bzip2 writer. Always bound decompressed size from untrusted input with io.LimitReader, because a tiny archive can expand to gigabytes.

cards.prompt: Why check entry names before extracting an archive?
cards.answer: Names like ../../x can write outside the target directory (a "zip slip") Archives are untrusted input. filepath.IsLocal or an os.Root keeps writes inside the destination.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using archives: archive/tar and archive/zip?
cards.answer: zip.Writer.Create adds a deflated file; CreateHeader sets the method and timestamps. Both archive writers must be closed to write their trailers.

cards.prompt: Why use placeholders instead of formatting values into the SQL string?
cards.answer: The driver sends values separately from the SQL text, so they can never be parsed as SQL SQL injection happens when data is interpreted as code. Placeholders keep data and code apart by construction.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using database/sql and writing a driver with database/sql/driver?
cards.answer: Drivers implement the small interfaces in database/sql/driver: Driver.Open returns a Conn, which prepares Stmts that return Rows. This lesson implements a toy in-memory driver to show what a real one (for PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite) provides. Go 1.27 adds sql.ConvertAssign and driver.RowsColumnScanner for drivers that scan columns themselves.

cards.prompt: Why is static/.hidden missing from the embedded file system?
cards.answer: Directory patterns skip files starting with . or _ unless all: is used The default excludes dot and underscore files, such as editor backups. all:static includes them deliberately.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using embedding files in the binary with embed?
cards.answer: The package must import embed (a blank import is enough when only string or []byte variables are used). Embedded data is read-only and requires no deployment step, which makes single-binary tools and servers easy to ship.

cards.prompt: Why import _ "time/tzdata" in a binary for a minimal container?
cards.answer: It embeds the time-zone database so LoadLocation works without system zoneinfo files LoadLocation normally reads /usr/share/zoneinfo. Scratch or distroless images lack it; tzdata is the embedded fallback.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using classic packages: log, io/ioutil, math/rand v1, os/user, time/tzdata and structs?
cards.answer: os/user looks up the current user and groups. time/tzdata embeds the time-zone database into the binary (about 450 KB), so time.LoadLocation works on systems without zoneinfo, such as minimal containers; importing it for its side effect is enough. Package structs (Go 1.23) provides HostLayout, a marker field that requests the platform's C memory layout for a struct passed to foreign code.

cards.prompt: What does the <28> at the start of the syslog message encode?
cards.answer: The priority: facility daemon (3) × 8 plus severity warning (4) Syslog priority is facility*8 + severity. LOG_DAEMON is 3 and LOG_WARNING is 4, giving 28.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using exported metrics with expvar and logging to syslog?
cards.answer: For new services, structured logs to standard output collected by the platform, and metrics through a client library, are usual. expvar and syslog remain useful for small daemons and legacy integration.

cards.prompt: Why does a plain http.Client not send cookies back on the second request?
cards.answer: It has no Jar; cookies are only stored and resent when Client.Jar is set Cookie handling lives in the jar. Without one, Set-Cookie headers are ignored by the client.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using urls with net/url and client cookies with net/http/cookiejar?
cards.answer: An http.Client ignores cookies unless it has a Jar. cookiejar.New returns an in-memory jar that stores Set-Cookie responses and sends matching cookies back, following domain and path rules; pass publicsuffix.List from golang.org/x/net to stop sites setting cookies for whole top-level domains.

cards.prompt: What does GotConnInfo.Reused tell you?
cards.answer: Whether the request used an existing keep-alive connection instead of dialling Reuse avoids TCP and TLS setup. Seeing false on every request reveals bodies not being closed or drained.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using request tracing with httptrace and proxies with httputil?
cards.answer: A reverse proxy should set timeouts on its Transport and limit request sizes, like any server. Never dump requests containing credentials into logs.

cards.prompt: Why serve net/http/pprof on a separate localhost listener?
cards.answer: The endpoints expose internals and expensive operations, so they must not be public Anyone reaching /debug/pprof/profile can make the server spend 30 seconds profiling and can read stack traces.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using live profiling endpoints with net/http/pprof?
cards.answer: The handlers can also be mounted explicitly on any mux with pprof.Index, pprof.Profile, pprof.Symbol, pprof.Trace and pprof.Handler(name), which avoids relying on the default mux at all.

cards.prompt: Why does smtp.PlainAuth refuse to authenticate to most servers over plain TCP?
cards.answer: It would send the password unencrypted; it only allows TLS or localhost PLAIN authentication transmits credentials in base64, which is not encryption. The check protects against accidental leaks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using line protocols with net/textproto and email with net/smtp?
cards.answer: This lesson runs a tiny fake SMTP server on a loopback listener, built with textproto, and sends a message to it with net/smtp, so the whole protocol exchange happens without the internet.

cards.prompt: What signature must a method have to be exported by net/rpc?
cards.answer: func (t *T) Name(args A, reply *R) error with exported names and types rpc uses reflection to find methods with exactly one argument, one pointer reply and an error result.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using remote procedure calls with net/rpc and net/rpc/jsonrpc?
cards.answer: Errors returned by a method arrive at the client as rpc.ServerError strings; transport failures return rpc.ErrShutdown or the network error.

cards.prompt: What is the main cost CGI has that FastCGI avoids?
cards.answer: Starting a new process for every request FastCGI keeps one long-lived application process and sends many requests to it over a socket.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using cgi and fastcgi with net/http/cgi and net/http/fcgi?
cards.answer: Both exist mainly for integration with traditional hosting. A Go service normally serves HTTP directly behind a reverse proxy.

cards.prompt: What does go/types add that go/parser alone cannot provide?
cards.answer: The type of every expression and the object every identifier refers to The parser builds syntax. The checker resolves names across files and packages and computes types and constant values.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using type-checking source with go/types, go/importer, go/constant and go/printer?
cards.answer: go/printer prints an AST back as source, honouring comments and positions; go/format is the gofmt-styled wrapper. Together these packages let you build linters, code generators and refactoring tools that understand types, not just syntax.

cards.prompt: Why use go/version.Compare instead of comparing version strings with <?
cards.answer: String order is wrong for versions: "go1.9" sorts after "go1.10" lexically Version components are numbers with release-candidate suffixes. Compare parses them; < compares bytes.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using documentation, build contexts and versions: go/doc, go/doc/comment, go/build, constraints and go/version?
cards.answer: go/version (Go 1.22) compares Go version strings correctly, where simple string comparison fails: go1.9 < go1.10, and go1.27 < go1.27rc1 < go1.27.0 < go1.27.2, because a bare go1.27 names the language version, which precedes every release of it. Lang returns the language version of a toolchain version, so Lang("go1.27.2") is go1.27.

cards.prompt: Which package reads the Go version and module information embedded in an ELF, PE or Mach-O binary?
cards.answer: debug/buildinfo buildinfo understands ELF, PE, Mach-O, XCOFF and Wasm and finds the embedded build information in each; the project shows it reports none for Plan 9.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: inspecting elf, pe, mach-o and plan 9 binaries?
cards.answer: debug/gosym decodes Go's own symbol and line tables (.gopclntab), mapping program counters to functions and source lines. This project cross-builds one program for Linux, Windows, macOS and Plan 9, then a second command inspects every binary.

cards.prompt: When is runtime/coverage.WriteCountersDir useful?
cards.answer: For long-running programs built with -cover that must report coverage without exiting Normally coverage is written at exit. Servers in integration tests can write snapshots on demand instead.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: runtime/race, runtime/cgo and runtime/coverage?
cards.answer: This project builds a server-like program with -cover, has it write coverage for two phases into a directory, and reports the percentage with go tool covdata. A blank import of runtime/cgo is included to show the build still works with CGO_ENABLED=1 and fails with CGO_ENABLED=0.

cards.prompt: What must match between a plugin and the program that loads it?
cards.answer: The toolchain version, build flags and versions of shared dependencies The runtime checks that packages shared by host and plugin are identical builds; any mismatch makes plugin.Open fail.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: loading code at run time with plugin?
cards.answer: Because of those constraints, most Go programs prefer other extension mechanisms: separate processes speaking RPC (as HashiCorp's go-plugin does), WebAssembly, or simply compiling extensions in. Use plugin only when you control both builds.

cards.prompt: What does slogtest.TestHandler check?
cards.answer: That a handler's output follows the rules every slog.Handler must obey It logs records exercising groups, attributes and edge cases, then compares your parsed output with the expected structure.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: property tests with testing/quick and handler conformance with testing/slogtest?
cards.answer: This project tests an encoding function with properties, then writes a minimal key=value slog handler and proves it conforms with slogtest.Run.

cards.prompt: Why call image.DecodeConfig before decoding an untrusted image?
cards.answer: It reads only the header, so you can reject huge dimensions before allocating memory A few kilobytes can declare a gigapixel image. Checking width and height first prevents memory exhaustion.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using images: image, color, draw, palette and the png, gif and jpeg codecs?
cards.answer: image/png (lossless), image/gif (palettes and animation) and image/jpeg (lossy) encode and decode. Decoders register themselves when imported, so image.Decode and image.DecodeConfig detect the format from the data. Use DecodeConfig to check dimensions before decoding untrusted images, because a small file can describe an enormous image.

cards.prompt: What does go get example.com/greet@none do?
cards.answer: Removes the requirement, and downgrades or removes anything that depends on it @none is the version query for "not required". go get edits requirements; the cache is managed with go clean -modcache.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go mod and go get: init, edit, tidy, graph, why, verify, vendor?
cards.answer: go get changes requirements: go get mod@v1.4.0 upgrades or downgrades, go get mod@latest moves to the newest release, and go get mod@none removes the requirement along with anything that needs it. Since Go 1.17 go get only edits requirements; go install builds and installs commands.

cards.prompt: What does go work sync do?
cards.answer: Pushes the workspace's selected dependency versions back into each module's go.mod Modules in a workspace share one build list. sync records it in each module so they build consistently on their own.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go work: init, use, edit and sync?
cards.answer: Workspaces are for local development across modules. Before releasing, make sure each module builds alone with GOWORK=off and real requirements.

cards.prompt: Which wins when GOFLAGS is set both by go env -w and in the environment?
cards.answer: The environment variable go env -w only provides defaults in the GOENV file. A variable set in the process environment overrides it.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go env, go install and go clean?
cards.answer: go clean removes build products: plain go clean deletes binaries built in the package directory; -testcache expires cached test results; -cache, -modcache and -fuzzcache delete whole caches. This lesson points GOENV and GOBIN into the project, so the checks never change your real settings.
