cards.prompt: What does an empty output from go fmt ./... mean?
cards.answer: No file needed changes; the code was already gofmt-formatted go fmt prints the names of files it rewrote, so silence is the success case CI can check.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go fmt and go doc on your own packages?
cards.answer: Run both in CI: go fmt (or gofmt -l) to keep diffs clean, and go doc to check that exported names have doc comments that read well.

cards.prompt: Why does the validator never run go bug?
cards.answer: It opens a browser to file an issue on the user's behalf Automated checks must not take outward-facing actions. The command is documented with go help bug instead.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using go telemetry, go bug and go help?
cards.answer: go help lists every subcommand, and go help topic explains concepts such as go help modules, go help packages, go help testflag, go help buildconstraint and go help environment. With the 19 subcommands covered in this guide (bug, build, clean, doc, env, fix, fmt, generate, get, install, list, mod, run, telemetry, test, tool, version, vet, work) you have used the whole go command.

cards.prompt: Why is printf usually preferred over echo for exact output?
cards.answer: Its format controls every byte, including whether a newline is printed printf follows its format exactly and reuses it for extra arguments; echo option and backslash handling varies between shells and settings.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using shells, commands and arguments?
cards.answer: Every command finishes with an exit status: 0 means success and 1–255 mean some kind of failure. You will build control flow from these statuses later. For now, notice that a command which prints nothing can still succeed, and a command that prints an error message usually also returns a non-zero status. Output and success are separate channels of information.

cards.prompt: In what order does Bash search for a command name?
cards.answer: Aliases, keywords, functions, builtins, then PATH directories The first match wins, so a function can hide a builtin or program; type -t reveals which kind a name resolves to.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using builtins, keywords, functions and programs?
cards.answer: The command builtin runs a name while skipping functions, and builtin forces a builtin. These are the standard ways to write a wrapper function named like the thing it wraps without calling itself forever.

cards.prompt: Why does running ./script.sh that changes directory leave your shell where it was?
cards.answer: The script runs in a child process with its own working directory Executing a file starts a new process; its directory and variables vanish with it. source runs the file in the current shell instead.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using scripts, the shebang line and permissions?
cards.answer: Inside a script, $0 is the name used to invoke it and the script ends with the status of its last command unless you call exit N explicitly. A script runs in a new process, so variables it sets and directories it changes do not affect the shell that started it. Use `source file` (or `. file`) when you deliberately want a file to run in the current shell.

cards.prompt: What does an empty element in PATH, such as a trailing colon, mean?
cards.answer: The current directory is searched An empty PATH element means the current directory, an easy accidental security hole; write directories explicitly.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using path and how programs are found?
cards.answer: Scripts that run under cron, launchd, sudo or CI often receive a much shorter PATH than your interactive shell. Robust scripts either set PATH explicitly at the top or check for required tools with command -v and fail with a clear message.

cards.prompt: When does c run in `a && b || c`?
cards.answer: When a fails or when a succeeds and b fails && and || have equal precedence and are left-associative; the expression is (a && b) || c, so it is not a safe if/else.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using lines, comments and command lists?
cards.answer: Braces { list; } group commands in the current shell, so redirections or && can apply to the whole group; the spaces and the final ; or newline are required because { and } are keywords. Parentheses ( list ) run the group in a subshell, an isolated copy of the shell.

cards.prompt: What is the only character that cannot appear inside single quotes?
cards.answer: A single quote Single quotes have no escape mechanism; end the quotes, add \' and reopen them, or use $'...'.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using single quotes, double quotes and backslashes?
cards.answer: A useful rule: single-quote fixed text, double-quote anything containing an expansion, and leave a word unquoted only when you deliberately want splitting or globbing — which is rare and deserves a comment.

cards.prompt: What does $'\t' produce?
cards.answer: A literal tab character $'...' decodes backslash escapes and then behaves like single quotes; $"..." is unrelated locale translation.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using ansi-c quoting with $'…' and printf %q?
cards.answer: Do not try to build shell commands by concatenating strings and running eval; later lessons show safer array-based approaches. When you must produce shell-readable text, %q is the tool.

cards.prompt: Which three things can happen to an unquoted $var after expansion?
cards.answer: It can split into several words, glob into file names, or vanish when empty Unquoted expansions go through word splitting, pathname expansion and empty-word removal; double quotes prevent all three.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using word splitting and why to quote expansions?
cards.answer: Splitting is not useless: it is how `for word in $line` or `read -a` divide text. The point is to choose it deliberately, ideally with a locally set IFS, rather than receive it by accident.

cards.prompt: What does `IFS=, read -r a b <<< "$line"` change?
cards.answer: IFS only for that read command An assignment before a command applies only to that command, so IFS stays at its default afterwards.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using controlling ifs for deliberate splitting?
cards.answer: An IFS set to the empty string disables splitting completely. The idiom `while IFS= read -r line` uses that to keep leading and trailing whitespace on each line exactly as it was.

cards.prompt: Why does {1..$n} not produce a numeric range?
cards.answer: Brace expansion runs before parameter expansion Brace expansion is the first expansion, so it sees the literal $n; use a C-style for loop or seq instead.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using metacharacters, operators and the parse order?
cards.answer: When in doubt, print the words a command receives with printf '[%s]\n' followed by the same arguments. Seeing each argument in brackets is the fastest debugging tool for quoting problems.

cards.prompt: What does `count = 1` do in Bash?
cards.answer: Runs a command named count with arguments = and 1 Assignments must have no spaces around =; otherwise the first word is a command name.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using variables, assignment and attributes?
cards.answer: Attributes are convenient but invisible at the point of use: with declare -i n, the assignment n=2+3 stores 5, surprising anyone who did not see the declaration. Prefer explicit arithmetic $(( )) for clarity and reserve attributes for constants (readonly) and case normalization.

cards.prompt: Which commands can see a non-exported shell variable?
cards.answer: Subshells of the same shell, but not separately executed programs Subshells are copies of the shell and inherit all variables; external programs receive only the exported environment.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using shell variables, the environment and export?
cards.answer: export -n removes the export mark; env prints the environment; env -i runs a command with an empty environment, which is how this guide tests every script. declare -x is equivalent to export and also works inside functions together with local.

cards.prompt: How do ${v:-x} and ${v-x} differ?
cards.answer: The colon form also substitutes x when v is set but empty With the colon, both unset and empty trigger the default; without it, only unset does.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using defaults, required values and alternatives?
cards.answer: ${v:+word} is handy for optional flags: `cmd ${verbose:+--verbose}` adds the flag only when verbose is non-empty. Because the result must vanish when empty, this is one of the few places where an unquoted expansion is intentional; with arrays you can avoid even that.

cards.prompt: Why must a negative offset be written ${v: -3} with a space?
cards.answer: Without the space, :- is the use-default operator ${v:-3} means "v or 3 if unset or empty", so the space (or parentheses) distinguishes a substring offset.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using trimming, slicing, replacing and case?
cards.answer: These operations run inside the shell without starting a process, which matters in loops over thousands of lines. Patterns here are glob patterns, not regular expressions; use [[ =~ ]] when you need a regex.

cards.prompt: What does `local -n out=$1` give a function?
cards.answer: A reference through which it reads and writes the caller-named variable A nameref aliases another variable by name, letting functions return results into variables the caller chooses.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using indirection and name references?
cards.answer: Indirection is a power tool. Associative arrays (stage 6) are usually a clearer way to store key/value data than many variables with computed names.

cards.prompt: How should a wrapper forward all of its arguments unchanged?
cards.answer: "$@" Only quoted "$@" keeps each argument as its own word, including empty ones and ones with spaces.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using positional and special parameters?
cards.answer: Bash-specific arrays describe the call stack: FUNCNAME, BASH_SOURCE and BASH_LINENO. These are the basis for useful error messages and are covered in the debugging lessons.

cards.prompt: What happens to `*.log` in a command when no file matches, with default options?
cards.answer: The pattern is passed unchanged as a literal word Without nullglob or failglob, an unmatched glob stays literal, so loops run once with the pattern itself.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using glob patterns and pathname expansion?
cards.answer: The same pattern syntax appears in case statements, [[ $x == pattern ]], and the trimming expansions ${v#pattern}. In those places nothing is matched against the filesystem; the pattern is tested against a string. Quote any part you want to be literal: [[ $x == "*" ]] tests for a literal star.

cards.prompt: Which option makes an unmatched glob expand to nothing?
cards.answer: nullglob nullglob removes unmatched patterns; failglob turns them into errors; dotglob and extglob change what can match.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using nullglob, failglob, dotglob and globstar?
cards.answer: globstar walks the tree in the shell and follows no symbolic links to directories since Bash 4.3. For very large trees or when you need filtering by type, size or time, find is still the right tool; combine them by using find -print0 with read -d '' (stage 8).

cards.prompt: What does !(*.txt) match when extglob is enabled?
cards.answer: Every name that does not match *.txt !(pattern-list) matches anything except the listed patterns.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using extended globs?
cards.answer: Trimming with extended patterns is a neat trick: ${s##*( )} removes all leading spaces, where plain ${s##* } would remove everything up to the last space.

cards.prompt: Why does mkdir {1..$n} create a directory literally named {1..3} when n=3?
cards.answer: Brace expansion happens before the variable is expanded Brace expansion is first and textual; it sees $n literally and cannot form a range.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using brace expansion?
cards.answer: Brace expansion is a Bash (and ksh/zsh) feature, not POSIX sh. In a #!/bin/sh script it may be passed through literally, which is one reason to choose your shebang deliberately.

cards.prompt: How does GLOBSORT=numeric order the names 10, 2 and file1?
cards.answer: 2, 10, then file1 All-digit names sort by numeric value first; names with other characters come afterwards in name order.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using sorting glob results with globsort (bash 5.3)?
cards.answer: GLOBSORT is ignored by older shells: macOS /bin/bash 3.2 simply sorts by name. If a script relies on the order, require Bash 5.3 explicitly (check BASH_VERSINFO) or fall back to an external sort.

cards.prompt: What exit status does Bash report for a command killed by SIGINT (signal 2)?
cards.answer: 130 Death by signal N is reported as 128+N, so SIGINT gives 130.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using exit status: success, failure and conventions?
cards.answer: Scripts should end with a meaningful status: 0 when they did their job, non-zero with a message on stderr otherwise. Callers, CI systems and && chains rely on it.

cards.prompt: Why is [[ 10 < 9 ]] true?
cards.answer: < inside [[ ]] compares strings lexicographically Use -lt or (( )) for numbers; inside [[ ]], < and > compare strings.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using if, test, [ ] and [[ ]]?
cards.answer: The right side of == in [[ ]] is a pattern unless quoted. That is useful ([[ $f == *.txt ]]) but means [[ $a == $b ]] compares a against b as a pattern; write "$b" for an exact comparison.

cards.prompt: Why store a regex in a variable before using =~?
cards.answer: Quoted parts of the right side are matched literally, so an unquoted variable keeps regex meaning without escaping problems Quoting the right-hand side turns regex characters into literals; [[ $s =~ $re ]] keeps them as regex syntax.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using regular expressions with =~ and bash_rematch?
cards.answer: For extracting several fields from structured lines, =~ with groups is clean and avoids external processes. For processing whole files, awk or grep -E are usually faster than a Bash loop.

cards.prompt: What is $(( 7 / 2 )) in Bash?
cards.answer: 3 Bash arithmetic is integer-only; division truncates toward zero.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using integer arithmetic with $(( )) and (( ))?
cards.answer: Never put untrusted text into arithmetic. Arithmetic evaluation expands array subscripts, so input like a[$(cmd)] can execute commands. Validate that input is numeric with [[ $x =~ ^-?[0-9]+$ ]] first.

cards.prompt: What does the ;& terminator do in a case branch?
cards.answer: Runs the next branch's commands without testing its pattern ;; stops, ;& falls through unconditionally and ;;& keeps testing later patterns.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using case: matching words against patterns?
cards.answer: Keep each branch short. When a branch grows, call a function, so the dispatch table stays readable at a glance.

cards.prompt: Why are variables set inside `cmd | while read line; do ...; done` lost afterwards?
cards.answer: Each pipeline part runs in a subshell by default Pipeline elements are subshells; redirect from a file, use < <(cmd), or enable lastpipe.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using for, while, until, break and continue?
cards.answer: A loop fed by a pipe (cmd | while read ...) runs in a subshell, so variables set inside it are lost afterwards. Use redirection from a file, process substitution < <(cmd), or shopt -s lastpipe (stage 9) to keep them.

cards.prompt: What does $arr (without a subscript) expand to?
cards.answer: The element at index 0 A bare array name refers to element 0; use "${arr[@]}" for all elements.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using indexed arrays?
cards.answer: Arrays cannot be exported to child processes and cannot be nested. To pass a list to another program, pass it as arguments ("${a[@]}") or write it NUL-separated to a pipe or file.

cards.prompt: How do you test whether key k exists in associative array m?
cards.answer: [[ -v m[$k] ]] -v checks that the element is set, even when its value is empty.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using associative arrays (maps)?
cards.answer: Associative arrays need Bash 4 or later — the macOS /bin/bash 3.2 rejects declare -A. Requiring a modern Bash, or failing early with a clear message, is better than failing halfway through.

cards.prompt: Why use mapfile -t items < <(cmd) instead of cmd | mapfile -t items?
cards.answer: The pipeline version runs mapfile in a subshell, so the array is lost Pipeline parts run in subshells; process substitution keeps mapfile in the current shell.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading lines into arrays with mapfile?
cards.answer: mapfile keeps empty lines as empty elements, unlike splitting with read -a or an unquoted $(...).

cards.prompt: What is the safe way to run a command whose arguments are stored in a variable?
cards.answer: Store them in an array and run "${cmd[@]}" Array elements map one-to-one to arguments; strings lose word boundaries or invite injection.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using building command lines with arrays?
cards.answer: Functions can return arrays through a nameref (local -n) or by printing NUL-separated values that the caller reads with mapfile -d ''.

cards.prompt: What problem does shopt -s array_expand_once address?
cards.answer: Builtins expanding an array subscript a second time, which can run code hidden in a key With the option set, subscripts given to builtins like test -v, printf -v and unset are expanded only once.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using safe subscripts with array_expand_once (bash 5.3)?
cards.answer: The option is unknown to older Bash versions, so shopt -s array_expand_once fails there. That failure is a useful early signal that the script needs a newer shell.

cards.prompt: What does exit inside a function do?
cards.answer: Ends the entire script (or current shell) exit terminates the shell process; use return to leave just the function.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using defining and calling functions?
cards.answer: Keep functions small and named for what they do. A good test is whether you can describe a function in one sentence that does not use "and".

cards.prompt: Why should you write `local out; out=$(cmd)` instead of `local out=$(cmd)`?
cards.answer: The combined form returns local's status and hides cmd's failure $? after local out=$(cmd) is the status of local itself, almost always 0.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using local variables and dynamic scope?
cards.answer: A local array is declared with local -a and a local map with local -A. local - (a single dash) makes shell option changes made with set local to the function, restoring them on return.

cards.prompt: Why should error messages from a function go to stderr?
cards.answer: So $(...) captures only the real result Command substitution captures stdout only; mixing diagnostics into it corrupts the result.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using returning results from functions?
cards.answer: Bash 5.3 adds ${ command; } and ${| command; } command substitutions that run in the current shell without forking; stage 9 covers them. They make output capture cheap and let the function set variables too.

cards.prompt: What does a leading colon in the getopts option string do?
cards.answer: Enables silent error reporting so your code handles unknown options and missing arguments With a leading colon, getopts sets opt to ? or : and puts the offending letter in OPTARG instead of printing its own message.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using parsing options with getopts?
cards.answer: When parsing inside a function, set local OPTIND so repeated calls start fresh; OPTIND is global state otherwise.

cards.prompt: What does Bash 5.3's source -p PATH change?
cards.answer: The file is searched in the given directories instead of $PATH source -p takes an explicit colon-separated search path, avoiding dependence on the user's PATH.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using libraries, source -p and the main pattern?
cards.answer: Put the program's logic in a main function and finish the file with main "$@". To make a file usable both as a program and as a library, run main only when executed directly: if [[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == "$0" ]]; then main "$@"; fi. Use if rather than the shorter [[ ... ]] && main: when the file is sourced, the && form leaves status 1 as the file's last status, so `source tool.sh && next` would wrongly fail.

cards.prompt: Where does stderr go in `cmd 2>&1 > out`?
cards.answer: To the original stdout, because 2>&1 is applied before stdout is redirected Redirections are applied left to right; 2>&1 copies the destination of fd 1 at that moment.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using file descriptors and redirection?
cards.answer: Redirections can appear on compound commands: { ...; } > file, a while loop's done < file, or a function definition, so a whole block shares one redirection — and the file is opened once instead of on every line.

cards.prompt: What changes when a here-document delimiter is quoted, as in <<'EOF'?
cards.answer: The body is taken literally, with no expansions Quoting any part of the delimiter disables expansion inside the body.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using here-documents and here-strings?
cards.answer: Here-documents are a convenient way to write files from scripts: cat > config.ini <<'EOF'. For generated files containing user data, still prefer printf with explicit quoting so values cannot break the file's format.

cards.prompt: What does `exec {fd}> file` do?
cards.answer: Opens file for writing on a free descriptor number stored in fd The {varname} form asks Bash to allocate a descriptor of 10 or above and record its number.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using managing descriptors with exec?
cards.answer: exec with a command replaces the shell process with that command — nothing after it runs. Wrapper scripts end with exec real-program "$@" so that signals and exit statuses go directly to the real program.

cards.prompt: Why should read almost always be used with -r?
cards.answer: Without -r, backslashes in the input are interpreted and can alter the data -r keeps backslashes literal; IFS= is what preserves surrounding whitespace.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using reading input with read?
cards.answer: A final line without a trailing newline makes read return failure even though it filled the variable. Process it with while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]. Timeouts with -t 0 test whether input is available without reading anything.

cards.prompt: Which character can never appear in a Unix path and so is a safe separator?
cards.answer: The NUL byte Paths may contain every byte except NUL (and / separates components), so NUL-delimited lists are unambiguous.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using nul-safe file name handling?
cards.answer: find -exec cmd {} + passes many names directly to the command with no parsing at all, and is often the simplest safe choice.

cards.prompt: Why can `yes | head -n 1` fail under pipefail?
cards.answer: yes is killed by SIGPIPE when head exits, giving status 141 An early-exiting reader makes the writer die with SIGPIPE (128+13), which pipefail reports as failure.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using pipelines, pipestatus and pipefail?
cards.answer: Prefer one tool over long chains where you can: grep pattern file | wc -l is grep -c pattern file, and cat file | cmd is cmd < file. Fewer processes are faster and have fewer failure points.

cards.prompt: Why does `cmd || ( echo failed; exit 1 )` not stop the script?
cards.answer: exit only ends the subshell created by the parentheses Use { echo failed; exit 1; } so exit runs in the current shell.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using subshells versus the current shell?
cards.answer: Forking costs time: thousands of $(...) in a loop are measurably slow. The next lesson shows how to avoid forks for capturing output.

cards.prompt: What is the key difference between $(cmd) and ${ cmd; }?
cards.answer: ${ cmd; } runs in the current shell, so no fork happens and side effects persist Both capture stdout and strip trailing newlines; the 5.3 form avoids the subshell.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using command substitution, including ${ cmd; } (bash 5.3)?
cards.answer: These forms are unknown to older shells — macOS /bin/bash 3.2 reports "bad substitution" — so use them only in scripts that require Bash 5.3. Within such scripts they are the preferred way to capture output from shell functions.

cards.prompt: What does <(cmd) expand to?
cards.answer: A file name, such as /dev/fd/63, connected to cmd's output Process substitution turns a command's output into a readable path for programs expecting files.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using process substitution?
cards.answer: Process substitution is a Bash/ksh/zsh feature; it needs /dev/fd or named pipes and is not POSIX sh.

cards.prompt: What does `wait -n -p var` do?
cards.answer: Waits for the next background job to finish and stores its PID in var -n waits for any single job; -p records which PID finished, enabling concurrency-limited loops.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using background jobs, wait and wait -n?
cards.answer: Since Bash 5.3, wait -n can also report process substitutions and already-notified jobs, behaving more like plain wait. Write loops that track their own PIDs instead of assuming which job will finish first.

cards.prompt: Why can a request/response coprocess deadlock with an external program?
cards.answer: The program may buffer its output when writing to a pipe, so the reply never arrives Block-buffered output waits for a full buffer; the script waits for a reply; neither progresses.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using coprocesses?
cards.answer: Coprocesses are powerful but easy to deadlock. For one-shot work, a pipeline or process substitution is simpler; reach for coproc when the per-request cost of starting a process would otherwise dominate.

cards.prompt: Why does `if myfunc; then` disable set -e inside myfunc?
cards.answer: errexit is ignored for every command executed as part of an if condition, including function bodies Bash suppresses errexit throughout a condition context, so failures inside the function do not exit.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using set -e, set -u and their real limits?
cards.answer: Strict mode is a safety net, not error handling. Check the commands whose failure you can anticipate explicitly (if ! cmd; then ...), give a useful message, and let errexit catch the rest. Some teams avoid set -e entirely for this reason; whichever you choose, know these rules.

cards.prompt: Which trap runs on normal completion, explicit exit and errexit alike?
cards.answer: EXIT The EXIT pseudo-signal fires whenever the shell exits, making it the place for cleanup.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using trap: cleanup and signals?
cards.answer: Traps are reset in subshells (except that the EXIT trap of a subshell is its own), ignored signals stay ignored, and SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be trapped at all. A script cannot guarantee cleanup after kill -9; design so that leftover files are harmless.

cards.prompt: Why is /tmp/script.$$ a poor temporary file name?
cards.answer: It is predictable, so another process can pre-create or symlink it mktemp creates an unpredictable name atomically with safe permissions.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using temporary files and directories?
cards.answer: Guard destructive commands: rm -rf -- "${work:?}" fails safely if work is unexpectedly empty instead of operating on the wrong path, and the -- protects against names starting with a dash.

cards.prompt: Why combine an ERR trap with set -E (errtrace)?
cards.answer: Without it, the ERR trap does not fire for failures inside functions and subshells ERR traps are not inherited by functions, command substitutions and subshells unless errtrace is enabled.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using err traps, stack traces and die?
cards.answer: Report errors where the user can act on them: say what failed, with which input, and what to do next. Messages like "error" alone waste the reader's time.

cards.prompt: Why write to a temporary file and then mv it over the target?
cards.answer: A rename within one filesystem is atomic, so readers never see a half-written file Writing in place can be interrupted midway; rename replaces the file in a single step.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using idempotent, atomic and locked operations?
cards.answer: Return clear statuses and print what changed. "created X", "X already present" output tells the operator exactly what the rerun did.

cards.prompt: What is the safest way to assign to a variable whose name is computed?
cards.answer: Validate the name, then use printf -v "$name" '%s' "$value" printf -v assigns without re-parsing the value; validating the name prevents subscript code execution.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using eval, printf -v and generating shell code safely?
cards.answer: declare -p var produces a re-loadable definition of a variable, including arrays and attributes; sourcing that output recreates it. This is a clean way to save shell state to a file.

cards.prompt: What does BASH_XTRACEFD control?
cards.answer: The file descriptor that set -x trace output is written to By default trace output goes to stderr; BASH_XTRACEFD redirects it to another descriptor.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using debugging: xtrace, ps4, bash_xtracefd and debug traps?
cards.answer: Debug systematically: reproduce with the smallest input, trace only the suspect section, print values with declare -p or printf '[%s]\n' to see boundaries, and run ShellCheck before guessing.

cards.prompt: Why is ${path##*/} much faster than $(basename "$path") inside a loop?
cards.answer: It runs inside the shell without starting a process Every $(basename ...) forks and executes a program; parameter expansion costs no process.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using performance: builtins first, fewer forks?
cards.answer: Optimize only hot paths. Clear code that runs once is better than clever code that saves a millisecond; a loop over a large dataset is where these techniques matter.

cards.prompt: Why can a script using declare -A fail on a default macOS install?
cards.answer: /bin/bash on macOS is Bash 3.2, which has no associative arrays Use #!/usr/bin/env bash with a modern Bash installed, and check BASH_VERSINFO for required features.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using portability: posix sh, bash versions and macos?
cards.answer: Choose deliberately: for scripts run on machines you control, require Bash 5.x and use its features freely; for installers that must run anywhere, write POSIX sh and keep them small.

cards.prompt: How should you silence a ShellCheck warning that reflects a deliberate choice?
cards.answer: A narrow disable directive with a comment explaining why Narrow, explained directives keep the remaining checks useful and document intent.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using static analysis with shellcheck?
cards.answer: Make ShellCheck a gate in CI: every .sh file must pass. Every script in this guide does, except where a lesson deliberately shows a pitfall and declares the expected finding.

cards.prompt: How should user data be passed to `bash -c`?
cards.answer: As extra arguments that the inner script reads as "$1", "$2"… Arguments are never parsed as code; interpolating values into the string allows injection.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using security: injection, path, privileges and secrets?
cards.answer: Validate early with allow-lists — explicit patterns like ^[a-z0-9-]+$ — rather than trying to block dangerous characters. Run with least privilege, and prefer failing closed: refuse input you do not understand.

cards.prompt: Why does complete write to a mktemp file in the same directory and then mv it?
cards.answer: A same-filesystem rename replaces the list atomically, so an interruption cannot leave a partial file Writing a new file and renaming it means readers see either the old or the new list. The answer adds undo and count using the same write_lines helper and four new checks.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a tested command-line task manager?
cards.answer: Validation in this guide also runs a mutation check: the completion line is deliberately broken and the suite must fail. A test suite that still passes after a real bug is introduced is not testing that behaviour.

cards.prompt: Why does the report slice a mapfile array instead of piping sort into head?
cards.answer: head exiting early can kill sort with SIGPIPE, which pipefail and errexit turn into a failure Reading the complete sorted output avoids a spurious 141 status; the answer adds -e by scanning status keys after the report.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a streaming access-log analyzer?
cards.answer: A mutation check reverses the ranking order; the suite must fail, showing that the report test pins the ordering, not just the counts.

cards.prompt: Why copy the original with cp -p into the temporary file before writing new content?
cards.answer: So the file that replaces the original keeps its permissions mktemp files are private (600); overwriting a cp -p copy keeps the original mode. The answer adds render_delete and reuses the same atomic path.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: an atomic, locked configuration updater?
cards.answer: The mutation check removes the cp -p line; the permission test must fail, demonstrating that the test protects a real, easily broken property.

cards.prompt: How does prun.sh know which input a finished job belonged to?
cards.answer: wait -n -p stores the finished PID, which an associative array maps to the input index -p records the PID that wait -n reaped; index_of[PID] gives the input index for status and ordered output.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using project: a bounded parallel job runner?
cards.answer: The mutation check lets one extra job start; the concurrency tests must fail.

cards.prompt: Why is the archive first written to a mktemp file in the destination and then moved?
cards.answer: So a failed or interrupted run never leaves a truncated archive under a real name The rename publishes only a complete, verified archive. The answer adds checksums and a -V mode that fails cleanly on corruption.

cards.prompt: What should you check when using capstone: a verified, rotating backup tool?
cards.answer: The mutation check makes rotation keep one archive too many; the suite must fail. Going further: add compression choice, exclusion patterns via an array of --exclude arguments and remote copies with rsync, keeping each feature tested.

problems.prompt: Print a greeting on one line and the product 6 * 7 on the next.
hints: A C++ source file is text. Preprocessing resolves directives, compilation produces object code, and linking resolves definitions from other translation units and libraries. The executable is a separate artifact from the source.

Use the displayed command in a terminal with a C++ compiler. A missing compiler, a compile error, a linker error, and unexpected program output are different failures; diagnose the stage before changing code.

Initialize every object deliberately. A default constructor may establish a class invariant; zero-filled bytes are not a universal substitute for construction.

problems.prompt: Compare integer and floating division for -7 divided by 2.
hints: Integer and floating types represent different sets of values. A conversion is not proof that the mathematical value is preserved. An explicit cast documents an operation but does not make an out-of-range conversion safe.
Mixed signed/unsigned arithmetic follows the usual arithmetic conversions. Check representability before changing signedness or narrowing a value.
problems.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero, so -7/2 is -3. Casting the numerator before division preserves the fractional part in the floating calculation.

rubric: Integer division truncates toward zero, so -7/2 is -3. Casting the numerator before division preserves the fractional part in the floating calculation.

hints: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than the largest representable value. Signed overflow has undefined behavior; it is not a portable wrapping mechanism.
A test that happens to print a plausible number after signed overflow has not validated the program. Derive bounds and test values at the boundary.

hints: Binary floating-point approximates many decimal fractions. Rounding happens during intermediate operations, so changing the evaluation order can change a computed result.
Check special values with facilities such as isfinite. Do not use exact equality as a general numerical accuracy test or assume every platform has the same floating representation.

Avoid depending on unsequenced side effects or an unspecified argument evaluation order. Extra parentheses can clarify grouping without establishing sequencing.

problems.prompt: Transition to running and verify the new state.
hints: A scoped enumeration defines a distinct type whose enumerators remain qualified by the enum name. It avoids many accidental integer conversions and name collisions.
An exhaustive switch communicates the intended state handling. Keep error states visible rather than treating every unknown integer as a valid enum.

problems.title: Strings own characters
problems.prompt: Append s to the copy without changing the original.
hints: std::string owns a sequence of char values and manages its storage. Copying a string produces an independently modifiable value. Its size counts char elements, not user-perceived Unicode characters.
Check encoding and boundary assumptions when processing external text. A byte position is not automatically a Unicode character boundary.
problems.explanation: The two strings own independent values. Append may reallocate the copy; it does not change original.

problems.title: Vectors manage contiguous sequences
problems.prompt: Append a second value and report the last element.
hints: std::vector<T> owns a contiguous sequence of T objects. size is the number of constructed elements; capacity describes available storage before another reallocation is needed.
Growth can invalidate pointers, references, and iterators. Do not retain them across operations unless the precise invalidation rules permit it.
problems.explanation: push_back constructs an element and increases size. reserve alone would not make a second element accessible.
problems.quizExplanation: reserve allocates storage without constructing elements or changing size.

problems.prompt: Make observed a value snapshot instead of a reference.
hints: Scope controls where a name can be found. Lifetime controls when an object exists. Storage duration describes the storage policy; these concepts do not always coincide.
Avoid returning references to local automatic objects. The name may have gone out of scope because the object itself has already been destroyed.

problems.title: Inspect object bytes without breaking the aliasing rule
problems.prompt: Inspect the bits of -2.0f with the same well-defined copy.
